units.la: MErito equidem ille admirabilis patientiæ athleta S. Jobus questus est cap. vii. i. הלא צבא לאנוש Annon militia est vita hominis ? Militiam certè continuam Supremus Imperator tum singulis fidelibus, tum universæ Ecclesiæ, quam & multi, & sævi in mundo hostes circumsistunt, indixit; in qua, uti piè & scitè Tertullianus loquitur, Agonotheta est Deus Pater, Epistates Jesus Christus, Xystarches Spiritus Sanctus. Et ut de singulorum fidelium agonibus nihil dicam, in propatulo, si unquam alias, hodie sanè sunt certamina & παιγαλιεια Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ, quæ in mundo sustinet ab iis, qui soli Ecclesiæ
units.tr: Rightly, indeed, that wonderful athlete of patience, St Job, complained (ch. 7:1): Is not man's life a warfare? [הלא צבא לאנוש]. Certainly the Supreme Commander has declared a continual warfare, both for individual believers and for the whole Church, which many fierce enemies in the world surround. In it, as Tertullian speaks piously and wittily, God the Father is the judge of the games, Jesus Christ the trainer, and the Holy Spirit the leader of the contest. To say nothing of the struggles of individual believers, there are open struggles today, if ever at any other time, and mockery [παιγαλιεια] of the Evangelical Church, which it suffers from those who, claiming for themselves alone the name of the Catholic Church, and seizing its goods not so much by price as by force, proudly and without limit insult it, who belong only to the Church [of Rome].

units.la: The initial letter M is a woodcut initial; the Hebrew phrase הלא צבא לאנוש is Job 7:1 and the Greek word παιγαλιεια is printed as it stands. siæ Catholicæ axiomate, quod non tam pretio, quàm vi auferunt, superbientes, sine fine & modo ei insultant. Hoc illis negotium, hoc otium; hic labor, hæc quies; in his vigilia, in his somnus reponitur, ut eorum omnium, qui Romani Pontificis jugum excusserunt, seque in libertatem dignam iis, qui solum Christum Regem & Dominum agnoscunt, ejusque solius præceptis & oraculis obediunt, asseruerunt, Tros Rutulúsve suant, etiamsi, ita bullæ eorum loqui, seu potius paratragœdiare, imò bullare amant, Imperiali, Regali, Ducali, Principali authoritate, fastigio præfulgeant: nomen sub Cœlo aboleatur, funditus eradicetur; adeóque Cœlestia & terrena, spiritualia & temporalia omnia pedibus & libidini hominis unius subjiciantur, ut (sic enim Dictator Gregorius in Dictatibus suis præcipit) unum sit terris nomen, videlicet Papæ; reliqui volitent velut umbræ. Testis est tot jam Seculorum, novissimi inprimis, quod agitamus, experientia. Cui enim non dictus Hylas? Quis ignorat molimina, quis epinicia, lætósque triumphos, quos canunt illi, qui conclamatum ubique de Ecclesia Anti-Pontificia esse, insolenter etiam jactant? qui pleno gutture clamant: Ubi est Deus eorum, ubi Rupes, in qua sperârunt? Scilicet ob peccata & ingratitudinem, & quia, uti S. Cyprianus Sermone de Lapsis causam turbatæ olim à Decio Imperatore pacis Ecclesiæ aperuit, traditam nobis Divinitus disciplinam pax longa corruruperat, jacentem fidem, & pœne dixerim, dormientem cœlestis censura erigere conatur. Hinc procul absistente Domino, & faciem suam ad tempus occultante, in infolentia impii ardet afflictus. Impius in altitudine nasi sui nil pensi habet. Instituta ejus cruciatum adferunt, idque omni tempore. Alte sublata sunt e conspectu ejus judicia Domini, in omnes adversarios suos efflat. Dicit in corde suo: Non nutabo, per Secula ero absque incommodo. Os ejus perjurio, dolis & usura scatet: sub lingua ejus afflictio & vanitas. Sedet in atriis insidians, clam trucidat innocentem, oculi ejus ad inopum turbam intenti sunt. Insidiantur in occulto, quemadmodum leo in lustro insidias struit, ut corripiat afflictum, afflictum inquam corripiat, dum in rete suum pertraxerit. Conteritur, opprimitur, ac cadit viribus ejus miserorum turba: Dixit corde suo: Deus oblitus est, avertit faciem suam, ne unquam videat. Neque certè Papa Clerúsque Romanus vero zelo domus Dei, sed utilitatis solius, commodorúmque suorum ratione in perniciem nostram agitur,& à Ventre, qui ipsorum Deus est, suetam pristinarum deliciarum copiam efflagitante, stimulatur. Nimirum quia tot Civitatibus, provinciis, regnis, nihil amplius in istam voraginem conferentibus, metus est, ne quandoque res ad Saguntinam famem spectet: quia Papalis Regni provectior ætas tantummodò quæstui, non autem luxuriæ modum fecit: quia denique, uti ille in oratione funebri Periclis,apud Thucydidem libro II, narrata, dixit, λύπη ἐχ ὧν ἂν πις μὴ πυπεισθ ... ἀγαθῶν πλείονῶν· ἀλλ' ὃ ἂν ἐξ ἐθὰς γενόμενον ἀφαυ-ρεθέν, dolor non ex ablatione boni, sed ex consueti privatione existit; Hinc illæ lachrymæ: hinc dolor, ira, quæstus: hinc effrœnatus in Protestantes ille furor, omnia sursque deque verti malentium, quàm nidorem culinæ ex offertoriis Missarum, ignémque Purgatorii luculentissimum extingui: quàm Annatas, Indulgentias, Pallia, Regalias, & id genus alia ὤς ἀλφίζ, & ad cuticulam profusius curandam pertinentia, sibi suaeque culinæ decedere. Professus id olim est ἀπηρυθεὶς μένως famosus ille Pontificii furoris satelles, Caspar Scioppius, libello ad Clementem VIII. exarato, ubi, si minùs, inquit, charitas lex & officii ratio: ipsa certè UTILITAS, & CURIÆ ROMANÆ EMOLUMENTUM impellere Romanos ad suscipiendam majorem convertendæ (dicere volebat evertendæ) Germaniæ curam merito deberet. Laudavit idem authorem ἀνώνυμον, id ipsum haud obscurè significantem his verbis: Ut agonizantibus vires concrescunt: ita Catholici, tot amissis reditibus ecclesiasticis, interitum cognoscentes, pro aris & focis (plus tamen haud dubiè pro focis, quàm pro aris) evigilandum sibi esse ducunt. Quomodo naturæ quoque consultus Plinius Histor. Natur. lib. VIII. 16. aliíque tradidere, Pardum decrepitum & morti vicinum, mitiorem non fieri, sed in senecta magis etiam homines appetere: & serpentes mox morituri, acriùs periculosiusque mordere, ac obtrito capite, postremum cauda minari solent. Hæc in-titima, hæc verissima moliminum Pontificiorum causa est. Jam olim, Hieronymo teste, Prætextatus gentilis, non è fœce homo, sed Romano Prætorio Præfectus, designatúsque Consul, Episcopi Romani, Matronarum oblationibus, uti Ammianus Marcellinus loquitur, ditati, opulentia illectus, dicere solitus est: Facite me Romanæ urbis Episcopum, & ero protinus Christianus. Quæ non rabida orexis eum stimulâsset, si ætate Reformationi proxima Romanæ Curiæ splendorem & potentiam oculis usurpare ipsi integrum suisset? Sed imminutum per doctrinam Euangelii eum splendorem, infractam non parùm potentiam, & magis jam fama nonnulla residua, quàm vi stare res suas, reputans, omnibus collectis viribus in integrum se restituere, & pristinæ amplitudinis ornamenta recipere satagit. Hinc diræ illæ non uno in Regno, non una in Provincia machinationes, quas modis omnibus patres illi, qui in Domini sui commoda jurati, per publicam mundi calamitatem clarescunt, juvare & provehere non desinunt. Accedunt eorundem publica etiam scripta, non tam atramento, quàm sanguine exarata, quibus id unum insatiabiliter agunt, ut prodigiosis mendaciis, tetris calumniis, insidiosis, sinuosisque, & ad aucupandos efferandósque adversus opportunos quibusvis injuriis, Dominantium animos, ingeniosissimè confictis comparatísque narrationibus, non tantùm Sanstorum & præclarè deChristiana republica meritorum virorum manes pios, famámque nequiter proscissam, ludibrio mundi hujus objiciant: sed ipsam etiam doctrinam, Prophetarum & Apostolorum fundamento unicè superstructam, ceu impietatis & ἀγνωσίας τῆ θεῷ, turbarúmque & perduellionis omnigenæ fœtam matrem, capitaliter lacessitam, odio, invidiæ & execrationi omnium exponant. Quorum in censu haud sanè postremum locum obtinet novissima illa Lutheranismi & Calvinismi historia, non tam recentibus, quàm inveteratis odiis composita ab eo, qui ira studióque percitus, afflictis afflictionem addere, & Ægyptiaci exactoris instar populo Dei lateres duplicare, in votis flagrantissimis habuit. Ex eo enim ordine, eáque secta sacerimorum hominum oriundus est, qui Seculorum aliquot veternosos, turpissimos, perniciosissimos errores incrustare palliaréque: omnia Papæ (sit venia verbo) stercora, tum per se graviter olentia, tum vero hoc tempore, quo doctis ab hominibus crebrò commoventur, multò magis sœtentia, orationis amaricino condita, pro aromatibus orbi Christiano venditare ita sueverunt, ut nihil tam crassum, tam putidum, tam impurum, insulsum, impium in illa superstitionis Pontificiæ παταγεσμία deprehendatur, quod illi gravi serióque vultu, licet oblatrante intus conscientia, non asseverent. Et quamvis absurditatum suarum ὀφθαλμοδείκτως arguantur: citiùs tamen sua lusciniolæ cantio, quàm
units.tr: ...siæ Catholicæ axiomate: they take away by force rather than by purchase, and they insult without end or measure. Their business is this, their leisure is this; here is their labour, here their rest; in these their waking and their sleep are spent. Against all who have shaken off the yoke of the Roman Pontiff, and have asserted a liberty worthy of those who acknowledge Christ alone as King and Lord and obey his precepts and oracles alone, they fight as if Trojans and Rutulians were at war: they are at it, even though, as their bulls speak (or rather, as they love to strut and bluster), they shine forth with imperial, royal, ducal, and princely authority. Their aim is that the name of such people be wiped out under heaven and uprooted from the ground; and that all things heavenly and earthly, spiritual and temporal, be made subject to the feet and lust of one man, so that (as Pope Gregory commands in his Dictates) there be one name on earth, namely that of the Pope, while the rest flit about like shadows. The experience of so many centuries, and especially of the most recent, which we are discussing, bears witness to this. For who has not heard of Hylas? Who does not know the schemes, the victory songs and the joyful triumphs that those men sing, who insolently boast that the Anti-Papal Church is everywhere finished? They cry out with full throat: Where is their God, where is the Rock in which they trusted? Clearly this is on account of sins and ingratitude; and because, as St Cyprian explained in his sermon On the Lapsed, the cause of the peace of the Church, once disturbed under the Emperor Decius, was that long peace had broken the discipline handed down to us by God, and the heavenly censure tries to raise up faith that lies fallen, and I might almost say sleeping. Hence, with the Lord standing far off and hiding his face for a time, the afflicted man burns with the insolence of the wicked. The wicked man in the height of his nose takes no thought. His ways bring torment, and that at all times. The judgments of the Lord are taken far out of his sight; he puffs at all his adversaries. He says in his heart: I shall not totter; I shall be free of harm through all generations. His mouth is full of perjury, deceit and usury; under his tongue are trouble and vanity. He lies in wait in the courtyards, secretly slaying the innocent; his eyes are fixed on the crowd of the helpless. They lie in wait in secret, as a lion lays snares in its den, to seize the afflicted, yes, to seize the afflicted, while he draws him into his net. The throng of the wretched is crushed, oppressed, and falls by his strength. He says in his heart: God has forgotten; he turns away his face, so that he never sees. Certainly the Pope and the Roman clergy act to our ruin, not from true zeal for the house of God, but only from regard for their own advantage and profit; and they are goaded by the Belly, which is their god, demanding its accustomed abundance of former delights. Surely, since so many cities, provinces and kingdoms contribute nothing further to that abyss, they fear that the matter may one day come to Saguntine famine. Because the more advanced age of the Papal kingdom has made a limit only for profit, not for luxury. And finally, as that famous man said in the funeral oration of Pericles, related by Thucydides in Book II: λύπη ἐκ τῶν ἂν τις μὴ πυθηται ... ἀγαθῶν πλειόνων· ἀλλ' ὃ ἂν ἐξ ἐθὰς γενόμενον ἀφαιρεθῇ, that is, grief arises not from the loss of a good, but from the deprivation of what had become customary. Hence those tears: hence grief, anger and complaint; hence that unbridled fury against the Protestants, since they would rather see everything turned upside down than see the stench of the kitchen from the offerings of the Masses, and the most splendid fire of Purgatory, put out; or see their annates, indulgences, palls, royalties, and other things of that kind, which pertain to filling their purses and caring for the skin more abundantly, go away from themselves and their kitchen. This was once professed, shamelessly [ἀπηρυθεὶς μένως], by that notorious henchman of Papist fury, Caspar Scioppius, in a little book written to Clement VIII, where he says: If charity, the law and the duty of office do not move the Romans, the very profit, and the advantage of the Roman Curia, ought rightly to impel them to take up a greater care for converting (he meant overturning) Germany. The same man praised an anonymous author who clearly signified the same thing in these words: As strength gathers in the dying, so the Catholics, having lost so many ecclesiastical revenues and recognising their ruin, think they must keep watch for their altars and hearths (yet surely for their hearths more than for their altars). Just as Pliny, consulted on matters of nature, Natural History, Book VIII, ch. 16, and others have taught, a decrepit leopard near death does not become gentler, but seeks men even more in old age; and snakes about to die bite more fiercely and dangerously, and when their head is crushed, they are wont to threaten with their tail at the end. This is the innermost and truest cause of the Papist undertakings. Long ago, as Jerome bears witness, the heathen Praetextatus, a man not from the dregs but the Prefect of the Roman praetorium and Consul-designate, enriched by the offerings of matrons, as Ammianus Marcellinus puts it, and enticed by the wealth of the Roman bishopric, used to say: Make me Bishop of Rome, and I shall at once be a Christian. Would not such a raging appetite have stirred him, if in the age nearest to the Reformation it had been open to him to enjoy with his eyes the splendour and power of the Roman Curia? But reckoning that its splendour had been diminished by the doctrine of the Gospel, its power not a little broken, and that its affairs stood more on some remaining reputation than on strength, he strives with all his gathered forces to restore himself to his former state and recover the ornaments of its earlier greatness. Hence those dreadful plots, not in one kingdom or one province, which those fathers, sworn to serve their Lord's interests, and made famous by the public calamity of the world, never cease to help and advance by every means. To these are added their public writings too, drawn up not so much with ink as with blood, by which they do this one thing insatiably: that by monstrous lies, foul calumnies, and tales ingeniously invented and arranged, crafty, winding, and suited to catch and inflame the minds of rulers against any opportune injuries whatever, they may expose to the mockery of this world not only the pious memory and wrongly torn reputation of the saints and of men who have deserved well of the Christian commonwealth, but also the doctrine itself, built solely on the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, as if it were the mother of impiety and ignorance of God [ἀγνωσία τῆς θεοῦ], of disturbances and treason of every kind, attacked as a capital offence, and exposed to the hatred, envy and execration of all. Among these writings the most recent History of Lutheranism and Calvinism certainly holds no small place, composed not so much from recent hatreds as from long-standing ones by a man who, driven by anger and zeal, and like the Egyptian taskmaster wishing to double the bricks of God's people, has longed with the most ardent desires to add affliction to the afflicted. For he sprang from that order and that sect of sacred men who have been accustomed to plaster over and cover some old, foul and most pernicious errors of several centuries, and to hawk to the Christian world, as spices, all the dung of the Pope (pardon the word): dung that stinks heavily in itself, and that now, when it is stirred up often by learned men, stinks much more, seasoned with a bitter style of speech. So that nothing so gross, so foul, so impure, so insipid or impious is found in that clatter [παταγεσμία] of Papist superstition, which they do not assert with a grave and serious face, even though their conscience barks within. And although their absurdities are refuted by manifest evidence [ὀφθαλμοδείκτως], nevertheless their little nightingale's song is sung more quickly than

units.la: quàm iis contortulæ captiones & sophismata desuerint, quæ reponant: ita ut, etiam cùm iis maximè satisfit, nunquam tamen satisfiat: & quàm Δυσθήρατον ζῷον Sophista sit, in his maximè appareat. Nôrunt quippe callidissimi omnium, secundum decantatum celeberrimi Cardinalis apophtegma, Mendacii vim in pertendendo consistere. Quod genus hominum perfrictorum præfractorúmque scitè Julius Cæsar Scaliger triremibus ἐπρηρέτμοις, remos ab uno tantùm latere habentibus comparat, utpote quæ semper in seipsas in gyrum recurrunt. Et hac quidem versipelli Sophistica duo illi, Pontificio Regno aprimè utilia consequuntur, vel certè spectant. Primò enim homines suos, istis non vanitatibus, sed fatalibus stuporibus oppressos in Papæ obsequio retinent: tantóque id facilius, quò magis adversarios suos gravissimis mendaciis apud eos infamant, probè etiam probeque ut hæreant calumniæ,caventes, ne nostrorum scripta, soporis veternum excussura, in ipsorum manus veniant; gnari utique certíque, id si contingeret, fore, ut non tantùm curato superstitionis morbo ad se decepti redirent, & sese pudendis fraudibus, quibus irretiti tenentur, feliciter exsolverent: sed eorum etiam, qui fraudem ita faciunt, ærufcationes omnes intervertantur; adeóque ἀεγνομήνης illa Arx Babylonica, jam ante ad lapsum prona, penitus Subruta succensis mox corruat ima tigillis.
units.tr: Nor do they lack twisted quibbles and sophisms with which to answer, so that even when they seem fully answered, they are never answered at all. And how hard-to-track creature [Δυσθήρατον ζῷον] a Sophist is appears most clearly in these matters. The most cunning of all men know, according to the famous saying of the much-celebrated Cardinal, that the force of a lie lies in persisting. Julius Caesar Scaliger aptly compares this stubborn and obstinate kind of men to oar-fitted [ἐπρηρέτμοις] triremes, which have oars on one side only, since they always turn back upon themselves in a circle. By this turning, versatile sophistry, two results are achieved, or at least aimed at, which are most useful to the Papal Kingdom. First, they keep their own people, oppressed not by mere vanities but by fatal stupors, in obedience to the Pope. They do this all the more easily the more they defame their opponents with the gravest lies, and they take great and proper care that the slanders stick, lest the writings of our side, which would shake off the drowsy torpor of sleep, fall into their hands. They know well and surely that if this happened, not only would those who have been deceived be cured of the disease of superstition and come back to themselves, happily freeing themselves from the shameful frauds in which they are held entangled, but also all the schemes of those who practise such fraud would be overturned. And so that Babylonian citadel, ever-renewed [ἀεγνομήνης], already before prone to fall, is utterly undermined and will soon collapse, its lowest beams burned away.

units.la: Tum etiam apud hæreticos, quos ἀντιλογικῶτάτοις[?] sic vocare solent, hoc proficiunt, ut contentionum serram ifthanc riciprocando, in hanc eosdem curam conversos, minùs cautos attentósque ad improbas molitiones & technas, quibus libertatem & capita nostra interim licitantur, petúntque, efficiant; haud dissimiles vel calidis gladiatoribus, ictum alia parte qui minantur, alia inferunt: vel astutis πολυτρόποις[?], qui alibi speciem expugnationis faciunt, alibi ferìò expugnant. Has similésque verè Sinonias artes quemadmodum exercuerit famosus ille Historiæ Lutheranismi & Calvinismi faber (à Societate illa Ignatianorum ferìò jam, an per ludum exauthoratus sit, parùm nostra scire refert. jam pridem enim est, quòd histrioniam in mundo homines isti scitè exercent) in propatulo est. Etenim præcipuæ id curæ habuit, ut putidissima de Luthero, Zwinglio, Calvino, Beza mendacia, à Cochleis, Bolsecis, Suriis, Santesiis, Petrasanctis, similibúsque nugarum, fabularum, calumniarum hamaxariis prodita, totiésque à viris cordatis, quin ipsis etiam, quorum jugulum illi appetierunt, superstitibus adhuc solidè discussa, atque in aprico ita posita, ut pellucerent magis quàm solis radii, cùm sudum est; ex orco revocaret, & iis fidem si non faceret, at certè, quod ingenui hominis fuerat, non demeret etiam. Suâ enim, & malæ, quam tuetur, causæ interesse putavit, ut mendacia ista, sive probata, sive non improbata saltem, in medio cubarent, quæ
units.tr: Moreover, among the heretics, whom they are accustomed to call "most contentious" [ἀντιλογικωτάτοις], these men achieve this: by sawing back and forth at this quarrel, they turn their opponents' attention to it and make them less cautious and less watchful against the wicked contrivances and tricks by which our liberty and our heads are meanwhile threatened and sought. They are not unlike skilled gladiators, who threaten a blow from one side and deliver it from the other, or like the crafty "many-turned" [πολυτρόποις] men, who in one place feign an attack and in another strike outright. How the famous craftsman of the History of Lutheranism and Calvinism has practised these arts and similar true Sinonian tricks is plain to see. Whether he has been dismissed from that Society of the Ignatians in earnest or in jest matters little to us; these men have long since played their part skilfully in the world. For his chief concern was to call back from the dead the most foul lies about Luther, Zwingli, Calvin and Beza, put forward by Cochlaeus, Bolsec, Surius, Sanders, Petrasancta and other cart-men of trifles, fables and calumnies. These lies had been solidly refuted so many times by sensible men, and even by the survivors whose throats they had attacked, and had been set out in the open so that they shone more clearly than the rays of the sun on a cloudless day. If he did not make them believable, he at least did not take away from them what a fair-minded man would have granted. For he thought it was in the interest of his own cause, and of the bad cause he defends, that these lies, whether proved or at least not disproved, should lie about in the open, which

units.la: quæ ita subdolè propinata ab iis, quibus malivolentia & odio inde à prima face juventæ a dversus nos imbutis suffusisque, hominum talium dicta oraculorum vice funguntur, cupidissimè haustum iri non dubitavit. Ne dicam infamiam, qua aspergere viros illos conatur ille τ̄ ἁγίων καλλήγραφῶν[?], redundare in Papatum ipsum, cùm non Euangelium sed Papatum adhuc professi criminibus illis arcessantur. Neque magis Ecclesiis nostris, si tales pœnitentes gremio sinubúsque suis recepissent, verti vitio posset, quàm olim versum vitio fuit Ecclesiæ, cùm S. Cyprianum ante conversionem magicis artibus deditum; & S. Augustinum Manichæismi & illiciti concubitus impietate, priusquam in Christi castra transfivisset, alligatum, utrumque non tantùm in cœtum suum cooptavit, sed Episcopum etiam constituit. Scilicet hominis Dei facta non debent aliunde numerari, nisi ex quo Deo natus est, uti scitè Pontius in vita Cypriani dixit. Solentque quibus multum remissum est, vicissim amare multum. Tum doctrinam Ecclesiarum nostrarum ex Lutheri, Zwinglii, Calvini, aliorum (in quorum verba non ita juravimus, ut illi solent in Romani sui Pythagoræ αὐλῷ· ἔφα) verbis dictisque nonnullis, maligna interpretatione depravatis, & consequentiarum tortuosarum equuleo impositis, ejusmodi fingit, ut similis nequitiæ vel ipsum illum, qui ab initio mendax & latro fuit, pudere debuerit. Præterea, quantas turbas, tumultus, contentiones secum cùm nostræ doctrinæ prædicatio traxerit, ita invidiose commemorat, ut præstigiosis suis sophismatis perfidiæ, perduellionisque matrem non obscurè eam traducat. Quasi scilicet non hic sit Divini verbi quasi genius, ut nunquam emergat quieto ac dormiente Sathana; neque nisi illo ringente, turbante, Cœlum terræ miscente, fideles persequente, opprimente; & conscientiarum libertatem ubique terribiliter oppugnante, denique periclitante libertate omni, conscientia, fortunis & vita, ad acre telum, extremam necessitatem, quæ piam honestámque reddit quamlibet expediendæ salutis rationem, compellente, emergat: vel Christus etiam ipse non sit lapis offensionis & petra scandali, positus in ruinam & resurrectionem multorum, & in signum, cui contradiceretur. Scilicet illi regnorum inversionem, Regum oppressionem meditabantur, quorum nulla unquam vox factiosa audita est, & vita semper quieta simpléxque apparuit: qui imbelles, quieti, placido ingenio, opportuni injuriæ, metuentes magis quàm metuendi: qui non cœdibus aliorum, sed martyriis continuis fidei suæ ὁμολόγων confessorum adoleverunt creverúntque: qui, ceu oves mactationi destinatæ, tot horribiles Cyclopicásque lanienas subiverunt: qui legitimos Principes, & successionum jura, adversus impias insidiatorum machinationes toties strenuè defensitárunt: qui denique quandoque sontica necessita-
units.tr: These things, served up so craftily by those whose minds have been steeped and soaked in malice and hatred against us from the first flower of their youth, and who treat the sayings of such men as oracles, he had no doubt would be swallowed most eagerly. I say nothing of the infamy with which he tries to besmirch those men (τ̄ ἁγίων καλλήγραφῶν[?]), an infamy that spills over onto the Papacy itself, since the charges brought are against people who still profess not the Gospel but the Papacy. Nor could our Churches be blamed for receiving such penitents into their bosom and lap any more than the Church was once blamed for doing so. St Cyprian, given to magic arts before his conversion, and St Augustine, bound by the impiety of Manichaeism and illicit intercourse before he crossed over into Christ's camp, were both not only admitted into the Church's company but even made bishops. Surely the deeds of a man of God ought not to be counted from any other point than from the time he was born of God, as Pontius wisely said in the Life of Cyprian. And those to whom much has been forgiven are wont in turn to love much. Then he fabricates, from some words and sayings of Luther, Zwingli, Calvin and others (whose words we have not sworn to, as they are wont to do with their Roman Pythagoras' "ipse dixit" [αὐτὸς ἔφα]), a doctrine of our Churches, distorting these words by malicious interpretation and stretching them on the rack of twisted inferences, so that even the very one who was a liar and a murderer from the beginning ought to be ashamed of such wickedness. Moreover, he recounts so spitefully the great disturbances, tumults and contentions that the preaching of our doctrine has brought with it, that by his deceptive sophistries he plainly represents it as the mother of treachery and treason. As if, forsooth, this were not the very genius of the divine Word, that it never emerges while Satan sleeps quietly; and that it does not emerge unless he rages, troubles, throws heaven into confusion with earth, persecutes and oppresses the faithful, and everywhere fiercely assails liberty of conscience; and finally, when all liberty, conscience, property and life are in peril, that it emerges with the sharp weapon of extreme necessity, which makes any honest and godly way of securing salvation right. Or as if Christ himself were not a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, set for the fall and rising of many, and for a sign to be spoken against. Surely they were plotting the overthrow of kingdoms and the oppression of kings, when no seditious voice of theirs was ever heard, and their life always appeared quiet and simple: they who were unwarlike, peaceable, of a gentle disposition, ready to be wronged, more inclined to fear than to be feared; who grew and flourished not by the slaughter of others but by the continual martyrdoms of their faith, as confessors [ὁμολόγων]; who, like sheep destined for slaughter, underwent so many horrible, Cyclopean butcheries; who so often vigorously defended lawful princes and the rights of succession against the impious plots of conspirators; who, finally, at some point, from necessity of guilt...

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: tate adacti libertatem, jura, privilegia, fortunas omnes, conjuges, liberos, sanguinem non adversus Principes, sed adversus Principum seductores, hominesque nefarios, qui religionis praetextu & via ad dominationem iter gradumque struxerunt; vim injustam justa vi repulerunt! Illos vero criminum talium reos agere proclivius longe fuisset, qui pridem Secularibus negotiis, homines de templo vel Schola, se ingesserunt: qui Principum & Rerum publicarum arcana scrutati, prodiderunt exteris: qui ipsum humanae societatis vinculum, quod in data fide, & pactorum observantia consistit, pervertere toties conati sunt: qui Clementibus, qui Catisbeiis, qui Castellis, qui Ravaillacis, qui sicariis aliis ad parricidia muniverunt iter: qui Regnorum excidia machinati sunt: qui variis technis sanguinem ac vitam nostram, & vel ipsa vita chariorem libertatem, assiduis studiis, & vineis, quod ajunt, pluteisque admotis, impetierunt! Jam & Atheismi foedissima labe cum aspergere sanctissimam doctrinam nostram, quae ad Deum verum Israelis in uno Jesu Christo propitium, recto tramite, & procul facessere jussis humanarum inventionum & ratiocinationum aviis praecipitiisque, ducit; ausus est homo, furenti quam scribenti similior, quis non extremam intemperiem profligatissimae mentis palpat? Quis homini tam proterve crasseque mentienti in coeteris, si qua vere etiam prolocutus esset, fidem dem adhibere tutò potest? Viderit autem ἄθυρον illud φύμα, quò domestica de Vicariatu Romani Pontificis, qui plerunque & notitia rerum Divinarum, & solida virtute vacuus, Guicciardino διxείῳ teste, tum bonus censetur, cùm bonitas ejus aliorum hominum malitiam non super-rat, doctrina aurigetur. An induci quis poterit, ut bona fide credat, verum Deum esse, qui ejusmodi in rebus ad salutem animæ æternam pertinentibus, vicarium in mundo constituit? Annon potiùs vel sola ea doctrina,in qua totius Papatus cardo vertitur (de cæteris nihil dicam)decumanam ad quamvis impietatem portam aperire idonea est? Neque forte altiores uspiam radices Atheismus agit, quàm apud eos,qui persuasione tali dementati creduntur. Ne verò, ut tale quid asseram, partium studio me provehi accusator ille clamitet, audiat domesticos testes, qui ante Reformationis tempora scriptis publicis inclaruerunt. Alvarus Pelagius Johannis XXII. Pœnitentiarius, de Planctu Ecclesiæ, lib. II. art. 2. sol. 104. sic jam olim scripsit: Plangit Ecclesia peccata populi, maximè CLERICORUM quasi majora peccata Sodomorum. Videmus enim, quòd fides & justitia terram reliquerunt. Sacra pagina,sacrique Canones PRO FABULIS habentur. Francifcus Petrarcha Epistolarum sine titulo XVI. de Curia Papali, qualis tum Avinione erat, sic loquitur: In Regno avaritiæ nihil damno adscribitur, modò pecunia salva sit. Futuræ ibi vitæ spes, INANIS quæ-dam
units.tr: Driven by the necessity of the moment, they defended their liberty, rights, privileges, all their property, wives, children and blood, not against princes but against the seducers of princes and wicked men, who under the pretext of religion built a road and steps to domination, and they repelled unjust violence with just force! Yet it would have been far more fitting to accuse of such crimes those who long ago thrust themselves into secular affairs, men from the temple or the school. Those who pried into the secrets of princes and commonwealths and betrayed them to foreigners; those who have so often tried to subvert the very bond of human society, which consists in pledged faith and the keeping of covenants; those who paved the way to parricide for Clements, Catisbeis, Castels, Ravaillacs and other assassins; those who plotted the ruin of kingdoms; those who by various devices, with constant effort and, as they say, with sheds and mantlets brought up, have assailed our blood and our life, and our liberty, dearer even than life! Moreover, a man more like a madman than an author has dared to sprinkle our most holy doctrine with the foulest stain of atheism. This doctrine leads by a straight path to the true God of Israel, propitious in the one Jesus Christ, and away from the pathless wilds and precipices of human inventions and reasonings. Who would not recognise the extreme folly of a thoroughly depraved mind? Who could safely give credence to a man who lies so brazenly and crudely in other things, even if he had said something true? But let him see to that open sore [ἄθυρον φύμα] by which the domestic doctrine about the Vicariate of the Roman Pontiff is driven along, as it were, by the reins of doctrine. The Pontiff is a man who, as Guicciardini testifies, is for the most part empty both of knowledge of divine things and of solid virtue, and is judged good only when his goodness does not surpass the wickedness of other men. Can anyone be brought to believe in good faith that God is the true God who appoints such a man as his vicar on earth in matters pertaining to the eternal salvation of the soul? Is not that doctrine alone, on which the whole hinge of the Papacy turns (I say nothing of the rest), fit to throw open a broad gate to any impiety whatever? Nor perhaps does atheism take deeper root anywhere than among those who are believed to have been driven mad by such a persuasion. But lest that accuser cry out that I am carried away by partisan zeal in asserting such a thing, let him hear domestic witnesses, who became famous through public writings before the time of the Reformation. Alvarus Pelagius, penitentiary of John XXII, in his De planctu Ecclesiae, book II, art. 2, sol. 104, wrote thus long ago: The Church laments the sins of the people, especially those of the CLERGY, whose sins are as if greater than the sins of Sodom. For we see that faith and justice have left the earth. Holy Scripture and the sacred canons are held AS FABLES. Francis Petrarch, in Letter XVI of the Letters without title, concerning the Papal Curia, such as it then was at Avignon, speaks thus: In the kingdom of avarice nothing is counted a loss, provided the money is safe. The hope of a future life there is a certain EMPTY

units.la: Note: the final line "dam" is the catchword. dam FABULA, & quæ de inferis narrantur, FABULOSA omnia, & resurrectio carnis, & mundi finis, & Christus ad judicium venturus, inter nænias habentur. Ad compendium alia pono, quæ historia Papatus hinc inde propalat. Neque forte deerunt alii, qui periti linguæ, qua author sublestæ fidei historiam suam contexuit, premént propediem oppriméntque [illegible, ~6 letters] vestigia fraudis, & inglorium fœtum ifthunc penitus conterent. Mihi verò insignitè audax facinus visum est, hominis consumpto pudore omni Lutheranismi & Calvinismi probrosam narrationem molientis, & sordidissima ulcera, quibus totum Ecclesiæ, in qua versatur, corpus pridem correptum, lethalem morbum contraxit, stolidè supineque negligentis. Occurrit haud immeritò Horatianum illud:
units.tr: FABLE; and what is told of the underworld is all FABULOUS; and the resurrection of the flesh, and the end of the world, and Christ's coming to judgement, are held as old wives' tales. For brevity I set down other things which the history of the Papacy brings to light here and there. Nor will there perhaps be lacking others, skilled in the language in which the author has woven his history of a flimsy faith, who will soon press down and crush [illegible] the tracks of the fraud and utterly grind to dust this inglorious offspring. To me, however, it seemed a remarkably bold deed, on the part of a man who has lost all shame and is undertaking a shameful narrative of Lutheranism and Calvinism, and who foolishly and idly neglects the most foul ulcers by which the whole body of the Church in which he lives, long since seized, has contracted a deadly disease. That line of Horace rightly comes to mind:

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: Mevius absentem Nevium cùm roderet; Heus tu! Quidam ait, ignoras te? an ut ignotum dare nobis Verba putas?
units.tr: Mevius, while he was gnawing at the absent Nevius, said: "Hey you! Someone tells you that you don't know yourself. Or do you think you can pass off an unknown man on us?"

units.la: Jure ille Luthero-& Calvino-Mastix, cum Mævio sibi ac suis ignoscens, audiat, quæ in Mævium ibidem sic Poëta lusit:
units.tr: Rightly, let that scourge of Luther and Calvin, while he pardons himself and his own along with Mevius, hear what the poet there mocked Mevius with, in these words:

units.la: Stultus & improbus hic amor est, dignúsque notari, Cùm tua pervideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, Cur in amicorum vitiis tam cernis acutum, Quàm aut aquila, aut serpens Epidaurius?
units.tr: "This love is foolish and wicked, and deserves to be noted, when you, blear-eyed with ointment in your eyes, cannot see your own faults, yet you look so sharply into the faults of your friends, as keen as an eagle or an Epidaurian serpent?"

units.la: Sicut igitur ille Lutheranismum & Calvinismum improbo calamo perstrinxit: sic impedire non potest, quin & illi, quos Lutheranismi & Calvinismi nominibus & convitiis, velut stigmatibus quibusdam inurere, pipulóque differre conatus est, de censoris Mæviani sententia, in Papatus, quem per alieni nominis ruinam ædificare nequicquam ille sustinuit, vitia, non fictitia illa, sed verissima testatissimáque inquirant, adeóque Historiam Papatus velut ἀντιπαπικὸν eidem, nec sine commentariorum quadam mantissa, reponant. Sicut porro elinguis ille Croesi filius Atys, patris periculo perculsus, in vocem erupit: ita infacundus ego, Ecclesiæ; cujus salus imis æquè ac summis, doctis indoctisque curæ esse debet. Contigitque provido Numine, ut in conscribenda, & ex authoribus idoneis, qui copiosissimè argumentum isthoc prosecuti sunt, in usum meum privatum (non aliud planè institutum fuit) contrahenda Ecclesiæ Romanæ historia occuparer eo ipso tempore, quo adversarius ille gloriosi militis fœtus lucem aspexit. Jam enim ad sextam usque periodum historiam illam ex integris voluminibus à viris doctissimis, Platina, Onuphrio Panvinio, Baronio, Genebrardo, Mornæo inprimis Plessiaco, Bullingero, Ussherio Armachano, Salmasio, Blondello, Hottingero, Spanhemio, Hornio, Reisero, aliisque contextis, breviatam produxeram; in qua sic Authorum subinde verbis totidem (ultro enim id profiteri, non sine gratitudinis testificatione publica, haud erubesco, in-
units.tr: So, just as he lashed Lutheranism and Calvinism with a shameless pen, so he cannot prevent those whom he has tried to brand with the names and insults of Lutheranism and Calvinism, as with certain marks, and to drive away with a pipe-stick, from examining the faults of the Papacy, in the judgement of Mevius' censor. Those faults are not fictitious ones but the most true and well-attested, and he tried in vain to build up the Papacy by the ruin of another's name. So they may set against it the History of the Papacy as an antipapal [ἀντιπαπικὸν] work, and not without some appendix of commentaries. Again, as the tongue-tied Atys, son of Croesus, struck by his father's danger, burst into speech, so I, unskilled in eloquence, speak for the Church, whose safety ought to be the concern of the lowest as much as the highest, of the learned as much as the unlearned. And by the providence of God it happened that, while I was composing, and drawing from suitable authors who have treated this subject most copiously, I was engaged, for my own private use (no other purpose was ever intended), in abridging the history of the Roman Church, at the very time when that adversary of the glorious soldier's work saw the light. For by then I had already produced an abridgement of that history up to the sixth period, drawn from complete volumes by learned men: Platina, Onuphrius Panvinius, Baronius, Genebrardus, Mornaeus above all Plessiacus, Bullinger, Ussher of Armagh, Salmasius, Blondel, Hottinger, Spanheim, Horn, Reiser, and others compiled, in which I repeated, from time to time, the very words of the authors, so many times over (for I am not ashamed to admit this freely, and not without a public testimony of gratitude, in-

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: AD LECTOREM.

units.la: inprimis cùm destinatio mihi non alia primùm fuerit, quàm in privum usum collecta in scriniis meis recondere) inhæsi, & brevitati etiam studui, ut idonea tamen testimonia eorum, quorum authoritatem ipsimet adversarii jure defugere non queant, neutiquam omiserim; quædam scitu non indigna iis, quæ ab aliis edita sunt, hinc inde addiderim; & rebus gestis, quoad summam rei, pœne nihil subduxerim. Sexta periodus Reformationis historiam complexa, nisi ab aliis luculentissimè tradita jam esset, ampliorem tractationem merebatur utique. Nunc satis habui summa rerum capita, & Pontificum, à quibus omnis in Ecclesiam corruptio solis defluxit, tergiversantium haud secus, quàm ursus palo alligandus solet, contrarias artes & studia, comparatis subinde nuperi etiam Cardinalis Pallavicini vel prætextibus frivolis, vel tacitis etiam confessionibus, in medio statuere. Septimam verò ultimámque, à fine Concilii Tridentini ad nostra usque tempora excurrentem periodum, quæ præ cæteris ob Pontificum adversus Ecclesiam insignes technas & violenta molimina (vis enim, an dolus, quis in hoste requirat?) iisque oppositam benignissimi Numinis Ecclesiam tot insidiis appetitam clementissimè protegentis vigilantiam, aliáque cognitu dignissima est, quámque dedita opera, quod sciam, nemo hactenus tradidit, paulò fusiùs accuratiúsque edisserendam putavi. Ipsa periodorum Romanæ Eccle-
units.tr: especially since at first my intention was only to store away in my chests what I had gathered for private use. I adhered closely to the sources and also aimed at brevity, yet I would by no means have omitted suitable testimonies from those whose authority the opponents themselves cannot rightfully evade. I have added here and there some things worth knowing that others have published, and as to the sum of the matter I have left out almost nothing of the events recorded. The sixth period, which embraces the history of the Reformation, would certainly have deserved a fuller treatment, had it not already been set out most splendidly by others. For now I have been content to set forth the main heads of events and of the Popes, from whom all corruption of the Church flowed as from a source. These men, like a bear tied to a stake, shift about in every direction, setting against the facts contrary arts and pursuits, and from time to time placing before the reader either frivolous pretexts or even tacit confessions, as the recent Cardinal Pallavicini did. But the seventh and last period, running from the end of the Council of Trent down to our own times, I thought should be set out somewhat more fully and accurately. It is above all other periods marked by the Popes' notable schemes and violent contrivances against the Church (for who, when dealing with an enemy, asks whether force or fraud is used?), and by the most gracious vigilance of the most benign God, who clemently protects His Church, opposed to these schemes and assailed by so many snares. It also contains other things most worth knowing, and so far as I know, no one has yet treated it deliberately. The periods of the Roman Eccle-

units.la: PRÆFATIO
units.tr: PREFACE

units.la: siæ distinctio non tam affectata quàm nativa, utpote rebus gestis insita prorsùsque accommodata, lucem nonnullam historiæ, & instituto etiam nostro (nam historiam Papatus processu tractationis cum Prophetia de Babylone magna ita comparare constituimus, ut discussis falsis de Babylone interpretationibus, certissimis argumentis, & rerum ipsarum notionibus apertæ veritati daturi simus, Prophetia de Babylone magna non alium coetum, quàm Hierarchicum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Divinitus proclamatum esse) uti plane confido, fœnerabitur. Habebunt sic Epitomen succinctam, qui Ecclesiæ Romanæ historiam cœtera vastissimam compendiosa lectione cognoscere properant. in qua si quid liberius dixi, verè tamen, & postulante re ipsa, ac instituto suscepto, dixi, atque insuper ipsa nominis mei involutus obscuritate latitabo lubens; paratus de cætero rationem dictorum expetentibus, vel provocantibus etiam promptissimè reddere. Neque tamen is ego cuiquam videri velim,
units.tr: ...distinction, not so much contrived as native, since it is inherent in the events themselves and wholly fitted to them. It will, I confidently trust, shed some light on the history and also on our purpose. For in the course of this treatise we have resolved to compare the history of the Papacy with the prophecy concerning Great Babylon, so that, once the false interpretations of Babylon are set aside, we may give clear truth by the most certain arguments and by the plain meaning of the facts: that the prophecy concerning Great Babylon was divinely proclaimed to refer to no other body than the hierarchical Church of Rome. Those who hurry to learn the history of the Roman Church, which is otherwise very vast, will thus have a succinct epitome in a brief reading. If I have spoken somewhat freely in it, I have nonetheless spoken truly, as the matter itself and the task I undertook required. Moreover, I will gladly lie hidden, wrapped in the obscurity of my own name, and I am ready to give an account of what I have said most readily to any who seek it or even challenge me. Yet I would not wish to seem to anyone to be

units.la: Pellem rodere qui velit caninam;
units.tr: one who would gnaw a dog's hide,

units.la: & cum maledicis maledictis convitiisque certare. Nam Indignis si maledicitur, maledictum esse dico: Verùm si dignis dicitur, benedictum est, meo quidem animo.
units.tr: or to contend with slanderers in slanders and abuse. For if one is reviled unworthily, I say it is a curse; but if it is said to the worthy, it is a blessing, at least in my own mind.

units.la: Longèque de sententia Ciceronis, aliud est maledicere, aliud accusare. Maledictio nihil habet propositi præter contumeliam: Accusatio vero crimen desiderat, rem ut definiat, hominem ut notet, argumento probet, teste confirmet. Liquebit autem ex historia Papatus sic a me concinnata (summam enim ejus paucis constringere etiam heic juvabit) primos Ecclesiae Romanae Episcopos, viros sanctissimos, a quibus Papa magnitudinis suae primordia ac jura deducit, non modo potentia civili & mundana penitus nudatos; verum etiam ab eadem misere divexatos, diu obscuros, ac fere ignotos fuisse; neque alia re magis ipsorum nomen, quam cruciatibus & suppliciis perferendis, quae una cum iis, qui eos sequebantur, admirabili pietatis zelo sustinuerunt, innotuisse. Hac illi purpura, hoc ostro solo fulgebant. Unus illis sanguis suus, coccus; una crux, gloria fuit.
units.tr: And far from the opinion of Cicero, it is one thing to revile, another to accuse. Reviling has no aim beyond insult; accusation, however, requires a charge, so that it may define the matter, mark the man, prove by argument, and confirm by witness. It will become clear from the history of the Papacy, so put together by me (for it will also help to sum it up briefly here), that the first bishops of the Roman Church, men most holy, from whom the Pope derives the beginnings and rights of his greatness, were not only utterly stripped of civil and worldly power, but were also cruelly harassed by that same power, and were long obscure and almost unknown. Their name became known by nothing more than the torments and punishments they bore, which they endured together with their followers with admirable zeal for piety. Their purple and their scarlet shone with nothing else. Their only blood was their own, their only dye the scarlet of martyrdom; their only glory was the cross.

units.la: Cum deinde discussis praeteritorum malorum nebulis, post trium Seculorum decursum Constantini M. & sequentium Imperatorum benignitate, velut liquidiore Coelo, e latibulis, cryptis ac specubus, in quibus persecutionum tempore delituerunt, evocati, liberè cultum Divinum exercerent, & palam ritus Christianos profiterentur; factum est, ut partim vitae morumque admiratione; partim praeceptorum, quae Christiana religione continentur, sanctitate, nomen Christianum omnibus locis mirificè propagaretur: illa vero Ministrorum Christi beata paupertas imminueretur, religiosis Principibus, aliisque certatim omni genere beneficiorum eos promemereri conantibus, tum ut pietatem suam testatam facerent: tum etiam, ut glisceret dignatio Sacerdotum, atque ipsis promptior animus ad capessandas ceremonias foret. Bono id quidem animo, nec infelici successu, quoad intra fines hæc liberalitas stetit. Postquam vero magnorum Principum munera modum excesserunt, & humana aviditas dulcissimo terrenarum rerum gustu lacessita fuit, statim filia (divitiæ) matrem (pietatem) devoravit, & ritus sacrorum inter ambigua culti, per prospera paulatim obliterati sunt. Secundæ scilicet res sapientum sanctorumque virorum animos fatigant, & acrioribus, quàm adversæ stimulis explorant; quia miseriæ tolerantur, felicitate corrumpimur. Ubi divitiarum cupido invasit, neque disciplina, neque bonæ artes, neque religio satis pollent. Exemplo igitur Gallinæ Æsopicæ, dum est strigosa & male habita, singulis diebus singula parientis ova, saginatæ vero post, parere definentis, qui labores, pericula, dubias atque asperas res, ipsaque martyria quondam facile toleraverant, iis otium, divitiæ optandæ aliis, oneri miseriæque fuerunt. Quid enim miserius aut dolendum magis esse queat, quàm sacram disciplinam, sanámque religionem, quæ adhuc paupertate magistra steterat, opibus oppressam adeò fœdè labascere: Sacerdotum integritatem in nequitiam, humilitatem in fastum, cœlestem gloriam in mundi pompam converti? Atqui res ipsa loloquitur, & sacerdotalis dignitatis splendor, supra fasces etiam Imperiales Regiósque elatus; sensim id quidem, ac placidis mollibúsque principiis, ut non secus ac ille Europæ amator, orbem è littore in altissimum pelagus nihil sentientem homines callidissimi deducerent. Facilius enim dignitas crescit quàm incipit. Pecunia quoque circa paupertatem plurimam moram habet, dum ex illa ereptat: Ubi verò inconsulta illa Principum liberalitate ereptavit, tum, uti mos est hominum, parvula initia pertinaci studio persequentium, clericalem illam ambitionem magnis auctibus progressam cernere fuit, quæ contenta esse eo, quod obtulerat occasio, non potuit. quippe sordent prima, cùm majora quæque sperantur. Omnibus igitur expeditius videbatur augere regnum (verè regnum cum Bellarmino in Recognitionum libello, Pascere oves sit Regio more imperare) quàm fuisset accipere. Hinc non solùm in spiritualibus Universalis Episcopi titulum (etsi S. Petrum, cujus nomen dicis causa, per ludibrium tantùm obtenditur, συμπρεσβύτερον potiùs, quàm Αρχιποιμένα fuisse constet) post multas contentiones, non Deo, non Christo, non Principe pio, sed hoca patricida indulgente, tandem Bonifacius III. obtinuit, eodem fere tempore in Occidente cristas attollens, quo Muhammed in Oriente magnitudinem suam erigere cœpit: verùm etiam, spiritualis potestatis religionem universam paulatim corrumpentis abolentisque,
units.tr: Then, after the mists of past evils were dispelled and, after the passage of three centuries, by the kindness of Constantine the Great and the emperors who followed him, they were called forth as if into a clearer sky, from their hiding places, vaults and caves, where they had concealed themselves in times of persecution, and they practised divine worship freely and openly professed Christian rites. The result was that the Christian name was wonderfully spread in every place, partly through admiration for their life and manners, partly through the holiness of the precepts contained in the Christian religion. But that blessed poverty of the ministers of Christ was diminished, as religious princes and others vied with one another to deserve well of them by every kind of benefaction, both to show their piety and so that the esteem of the priests might grow and their minds might be more ready to take up ceremonies. This was done in good faith and with no unhappy outcome, so long as this generosity kept within bounds. But after the gifts of great princes exceeded their measure, and human greed was provoked by the sweetest taste of earthly things, at once the daughter (riches) devoured the mother (piety), and the rites of worship, amid uncertain fortunes, were gradually effaced through prosperity. Clearly, prosperity wearies the minds of wise and holy men, and tests them with sharper goads than adversity does; for hardships are endured, but we are corrupted by good fortune. Where the desire for riches has taken hold, neither discipline, nor good arts, nor religion is strong enough. So, like the hen of Aesop, which, while she was lean and ill-kept, laid an egg every day, but after she was fattened stopped laying, so those who had once easily endured labours, dangers, uncertain and harsh conditions, and even martyrdoms, found leisure and riches, which others desire, to be a burden and a misery. For what could be more wretched or more lamentable than that sacred discipline and sound religion, which had stood firm so far with poverty as its teacher, should be crushed by wealth and so shamefully totter; that the integrity of priests should be turned into wickedness, their humility into arrogance, and heavenly glory into worldly pomp? And indeed the thing itself speaks: the splendour of priestly dignity rose above even imperial and royal fasces, gradually, to be sure, and by gentle and soft beginnings, so that, just as that lover of Europe led the world from the shore into the deepest sea while it was unaware, the most cunning men led men along the same path. For dignity grows more easily than it begins. Money, too, has much difficulty near poverty, as long as it is snatched from it; but once it had been seized through the thoughtless generosity of princes, then, as is the custom of men, the clerical ambition, which had begun with small beginnings pursued with stubborn zeal, was seen to advance by great increases, and it could not be content with what opportunity had offered. Indeed, the first steps are despised when greater things are hoped for. Therefore it seemed to everyone easier to enlarge a kingdom (truly a kingdom, since, as Bellarmine says in his little book of Recognitions, to feed sheep is to rule in the manner of kings) than it had been to receive one. Hence, not only in spiritual matters, the title of Universal Bishop (although Saint Peter, whose name is put forward only for show and by way of mockery, is established to have been a fellow elder [συμπρεσβύτερον] rather than chief shepherd [Αρχιποιμένα]) was at length obtained, after many contests, by Boniface III, not by the grace of God, nor of Christ, nor of a pious prince, but by the indulgence of that parricide Phocas. At almost the same time he raised his crest in the West as Muhammad began to raise his greatness in the East. Indeed, the religion of spiritual power was gradually corrupted and abolished in its entirety,

units.la: Divina & humana polluentis, contra jus & fas omne ita usurpatæ beneficio, longius longiusque progrediens, miris artibus, anfractibus, cuniculis, Gregorio VII. Hildebrando, Furia illa humani generis, efficacissimè ambiente, ac demum Bonifacio VIII. plenissimè rerum potiente, factus est Rex Anius, Rex idem hominum, Phœbique sacerdos; in illud scilicet terrenæ quoque potentiæ, adeoque παραβασιλέας culmen evectus, ex quo postea non Clerum duntaxat plebemque universam, sed imperatores, Reges, Principes, longè infra se positos ὀφεῦς ἔχων χιλιοταλάντων, ἀναχυλισσομένας, supercilia habens mille talentorum pondere, sursum replicata, uti Alexis apud Athenæum Dipnos VI. 8. loquitur, intolerabili superbia despexit depressitque. Nam ille quondam sub soliorum ictu positus, quibuscunque Principibus obsequens, Servorum Servus, nunc suæ felicitatis authores dedignatus, triplicem illam gemmis auróque coronam, è fragmentis alienorum diadematum conflatam, quam è re ipsa REGNUM nuncupatam, (uti quidem Sigebertus, & Marcellus ipse lib. I. Sacr. Cerem. Sect. 2. cap. quod, testis est) quin & MYSTERII titulo, Brocardo memorante, olim inscriptam (ne dubium sit, quo referendus sit titulus Babylonis magnæ) suo aptavit capiti, ut Regum Regem, imò Monarchomachum agnoscere liquidò queas. Ad hæc summos quoque Principes, obsequio olim tyrannis assesectato, cernuos, fulguritos, adorabundos ad oscula pedum admovet: hos sibi lecticarios, hos ftratores admittit: requirit, ut fi fella gestari cupiat, abjectis suæ dignitatis insignibus, ipsi succollent: equum conscenfuro descensuróve strepam teneant: equo impositum, aliquot passus fræno ducant. Cæsarem designatum, imò creatum, coronam Imperii submisse à se petere jubet, auri massa, in signum tributi, ad pedes suos projecta. In omnibus actibus seu Ecclesiasticis, seu civilibus etiam, eminentiori gradu collocatur, & definita quidem altitudine, sic ut Imperatoris locus non altior sit, quàm ubi Pontifex tenet pedes: Cathedra etiam minus alta, & scabellum parvum. Præterea lavandis manibus aquam Papæ præbet Cæsar, primum ferculum apponit, in officio Missæ caudam ejus trahit, in collatione mantile ei offert: ac omnibus item aliis in rebus, ultra servilem modum, fasces suos Pontificiæ dignitati submittere cogitur. Indigniora etiam his Papæ ἀλαζονείαις produci possent, ex quo Cœlestia & terrena, spiritualia & temporalia omnia pedibus suis subjecta calcavit, & unicus ille mundi universi Dominus, unicus, ut ipsi appellant, Vice-Deus, unus Imperator, unus Rex, unus verè Princeps: quì res hominúmque Deúmque Æternis regit imperiis, & fulmine terret;
units.tr: polluting the divine and the human, and, advanced by the favour of a power usurped in defiance of all law and right, it went further and further, by wondrous arts, windings and tunnels, until, under Gregory VII, Hildebrand, that Fury of the human race, who most effectively canvassed, and finally under Boniface VIII, who took full possession of affairs, it became King Anius, king of men at once and priest of Phoebus. It was raised, of course, to the summit of earthly power too, and so to that of a quasi-king [παραβασιλέας]. From there, it looked down upon and oppressed with intolerable arrogance not only the clergy and the whole common people, but also emperors, kings and princes, who were placed far beneath it, having a brow of a thousand talents' weight, lifted up [ὀφεῦς ἔχων χιλιοταλάντων, ἀναχυλισσομένας], as Alexis says in Athenaeus, Deipnosophists VI. 8. For he who once stood under the blows of thrones, obsequious to whatever princes, the servant of servants, now disdained the authors of his good fortune. He fitted to his own head that triple crown of gems and gold, forged from the fragments of others' diadems, which is called, as Sigebert and Marcellus himself testify (Sacr. Cerem. lib. I, sect. 2, cap. quod), REGNUM, and which, as Brocardus records, was once inscribed with the title MYSTERY (so there is no doubt to which the title of Great Babylon should be referred), so that you may clearly recognise him as King of Kings, nay, as a rebel against monarchs. Besides, he brings to his feet, bowed, prostrate and adoring, for kisses, even the highest princes, who once in tyrannical fashion had paid obsequious service. He admits these as his litter-bearers, these as his stable-grooms. He requires that, if he wishes to be carried in a chair, the princes, having laid aside the insignia of their dignity, should bear him on their shoulders; that they hold the stirrup for him when he is about to mount or dismount; and, once he is mounted, that they lead his horse by the bridle for some paces. He commands the Caesar, designated, or indeed already created, to ask humbly of him the crown of the Empire, with a mass of gold thrown at his feet as a sign of tribute. In all acts, whether ecclesiastical or even civil, he is placed on a higher level, and at a fixed height, so that the place of the Emperor is no higher than where the Pontiff keeps his feet; the chair is also less high, and the footstool small. Moreover, Caesar gives water to the Pope for washing his hands, sets the first course before him, holds up his train during the Mass, and offers him a napkin at the meal; and in all other matters, beyond servile measure, he is compelled to submit his fasces to Pontifical dignity. Even more shameful boasts [ἀλαζονείαις] than these might be brought forward for the Pope, since he has trampled underfoot all things, heavenly and earthly, spiritual and temporal, under his feet; and that one lord of the whole world, the one, as they themselves call him, Vice-God, the one Emperor, the one King, the one true Prince, who rules the affairs of men and gods with eternal command and terrifies with the thunderbolt;

units.la: En in quantum superciliosæ potestatis fastigium ex humili adeò in mundo forte partim seipsum Pontifex extulerit: partim etiam cùm præpostera majorum nostrorum pietate, tanquam Lupereo Antonio, diadema omnium gentium ipsi tradente; tum etiam assentatorum suorum, quâ juris Canonici Interpretum, quâ Theologorum vocibus, ex more adulandi, nimiis & falsis, evectus fuerit! Tametsi verò invicto & planè Divino Heroum superioris Seculi zelo gravem admodum potentiæ hujus malis artibus quæsitæ, & pejoribus exercitæ, cladem passus est; utcunque tamen per Tridentini Conciliabuli anathematismos obfirmatus, vires animósque denuo sumpsit. & eo tempore adversus eos, qui Majestatem ejus dedignantur, continua fraude & aperta vi horribiliter decertat, nequicquam ad pristinæ potentiæ robur omnibus viribus suis contendens. Quippe limites ei fixit irrefragabiles Æterna Dei potentia & providentia, quæ non patietur iniquitatis isthoc sceptrum perpetuò Sorti Sanctorum dominari. Quin destruet definito tempore Deus eos, qui terram ipsi destruxerunt, horribilemque adeò confusionem & ἀταξίαν in mundum invexerunt. At qui fidunt Domino, ut mons Sion non movebuntur, sed permanebunt in æternum. Quemadmodum circa Jerusalem sunt montes: ita DOMINUS circa suum populum ab hoc tempore in æternum. Non enim permanebit impietatis sceptrum in sorte justorum, ne justi manus suas ad-mo-
units.tr: Consider how far the Pontiff has lifted himself from a humble beginning to the heights of arrogant power in the world. Partly he has raised himself up, and partly he has been raised, as with the Lupercal Antony, when our forebears, with misguided piety, handed him the diadem of all nations. He has also been exalted by his flatterers, with the usual excessive and false praise, through the voices of the interpreters of canon law and of the theologians. Yet although he suffered a grievous defeat of this power, gained by wicked arts and wielded more wickedly, at the hands of the unconquered and truly divine zeal of the heroes of the previous age, he was nonetheless strengthened by the anathemas of the Council of Trent and has again taken up strength and courage. In this period he fights terribly, by constant fraud and open force, against those who scorn his majesty, striving with all his might in vain to recover the strength of his former power. Indeed, the eternal power and providence of God has set him unbreakable limits, and it will not allow this sceptre of iniquity to rule forever over the lot of the saints. Rather, God will destroy at a set time those who have destroyed the earth and brought such dreadful confusion and disorder (ἀταξίαν) into the world. Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved but abides forever. As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the Lord surrounds his people from now on and forever. For the sceptre of wickedness will not remain over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands tomo-

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: moliantur iniquitati. Benefaciet Dominus bonis, & iis, qui sunt proba mente. Qui vero deflectunt ad suas pravitates, eos ducet DOMINUS damnatos cum facinorosis; Pax vero erit super Israele. Haec votorum meorum summa; haec prora puppisque est libri mei, qui Papatus demonstrando lethali & Epidemio morbo, retundendoque virulento & vere Lojolitici Genii ingeniique scripto hominis, qui aestu torrentis animi raptus, exercitui viventis Dei maledixit; agnituri deinceps, & nostra tela cuspidem habere acuminatam, atque si machaeram ipse habet, & nobis urbinam esse domi: destinatus, professione pietatis in Ecclesiam aut laudatus erit (quanquam hoc supra voti mei modestiam est) aut excusatus. Ita servet Te Deus, pie & benevole Lector: servet Ecclesiam suam in mundi hujus impetuoso pelago misere adeo jactatam, & ad exoptatum tranquillitatis portum feliciter denique perducat! Perscriptum בארץ הצבי prid. Kal. Augusti Anno Christiano M. D. C. LXXXII.
units.tr: ...may not stretch out their hands to iniquity. The Lord will do good to the good, and to those who are upright in heart. But those who turn aside to their own perversities, the LORD will lead away with the workers of iniquity; but peace will be upon Israel. This is the sum of my wishes, this is the prow and the stern of my book, which, by exposing the Papacy as a deadly and epidemic disease, and by refuting the venomous writing of a man with a truly Loyolite genius and mind, who, carried away by the heat of a fiery spirit, cursed the army of the living God. Let him come to recognise that our weapons have a sharp point, and that if he has a sword, we too have a whetstone at home. I have resolved that, by its profession of piety, the book will be praised by the Church (though that is beyond the modesty of my wish) or at least excused. So may God keep you, kind and gracious reader: may he keep his Church, so miserably tossed on the stormy sea of this world, and at last bring it happily into the desired harbour of tranquillity! Written in the land of the gazelle [בארץ הצבי], on the day before the Kalends of August, in the Christian year 1682.

units.tr: III. The same Church, gaining dominion over spiritual matters by the grant of Phocas and degenerating in doctrine and rites, from Boniface III, that is, the year of Christ 607, down to Gregory VII, that is, the year of Christ 1073.

units.tr: IV. The same Church, aspiring also to dominion in temporal matters and daily declining further in doctrine and rites, from Gregory VII, that is, the year of Christ 1073, down to Boniface VIII, that is, the year of Christ 1294.

units.la: V. Ejusdem dominationem in temporalibus etiam adeóque Cæsareo-Papatum adipiscentis, & eundem, profligata doctrina puriori omni, flagitiosè exercentis. A Bonifacio VIII. seu A. C. M. cc. xciv. ad Leonem X. seu A. C. M. D. xvii. usque.
units.tr: V. Of the same power, which also attained dominion over temporal affairs and so became the Caesaro-Papacy, and which it exercised shamefully after all purer doctrine had been destroyed. From Boniface VIII, or in the year of Christ 1294, to Leo X, or in the year of Christ 1517.
