units.la: I. Origo Ecclesiæ Romanæ varie disceptata est. II. Circa eam certa ac explorata ab incertis, dubüs, suspectis & falsis distinguuntur. III. Historia ejus septem periodis divisa. IV. Ejus ab Apostolis fundatæ celebritas. Elogia eidem à S. Patribus tributa. V. Primorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Antistitum gloria fuit humilitas. VI. Virgo Ecclesia paulatim degeneravit. VI. Apostolorum tempore nondum impune grassari hæreticis licuit. VII. Ecclesia Romana prima præ cæteris ab hæresi immunis fuit. VIII. Cypriani & Hieronymi elogia, quibus ejus sinceritatem commendant, ad ejus perpetuitatem perperam trahuntur. IX. Epistolæ Decretales primis Ecclesiæ Romanæ Episcopis nonnulla simplicitati eorum parum convenientia tribuunt. X. Earum γνησιότης oppugnata. XI. Ecclesiæ Romanæ regimen paulatim deflexit. XII. Episcopi & Presbyteri identitas ex Hieronymo asserta. Alexandrinæ Ecclesiæ, Presbyterorum præsidem eligentis mos ad alias Ecclesias, non malo primum consilio, transivit. XIII. Id successu temporis Romæ inprimis Episcoporum ambitionem aluit. Unde Ecclesiæ Romanæ typhus cæteris maturè displicuit. XIV. Victor Romanus Episcopus adversus Ecclesias Asiaticas sese effert. XV. Stephani jus appellationis ad Ecclesiam Romanam ambientis, & Africanas ac Orientales Ecclesias communione arcentis conatus à Cypriano & Orientalibus repressus.
units.tr: I. The origin of the Roman Church has been variously disputed. II. Among the matters concerning it, the certain and well-established are distinguished from the uncertain, doubtful, suspect and false. III. Its history is divided into seven periods. IV. The renown of the Church founded by the Apostles. The praises given to it by the holy Fathers. V. The glory of the first bishops of the Roman Church was their humility. VI. The Church, once a virgin, gradually degenerated. VI. In the time of the Apostles, heretics were not yet allowed to spread with impunity. VII. The first Roman Church was free from heresy beyond the others. VIII. The testimonies of Cyprian and Jerome, by which they commend its purity, are wrongly drawn to prove its perpetual purity. IX. The Decretal Epistles attribute to the earliest bishops of the Roman Church some things little in keeping with their simplicity. X. Their genuineness [γνησιότης] is attacked. XI. The government of the Roman Church gradually declined. XII. The identity of bishops and presbyters is asserted from Jerome. The custom of the Alexandrian Church, which chose a president of the presbyters, passed to other churches, not at first from a bad intention. XIII. In time this fed, especially at Rome, the ambition of the bishops. Hence the arrogance of the Roman Church displeased the others early on. XIV. Victor, the Roman bishop, asserts himself against the Asian churches. XV. The attempt of Stephen, who sought a right of appeal to the Roman Church and excluded the African and Eastern churches from communion, was repressed by Cyprian and the Easterners.

units.la: I. [Initial E ornamented] Cclesiæ Romanæ origo variis contendentium studiis disceptata hactenus est. A S. Petro Apostolo præsente, & annos viginti quinque ejus gubernacula tenente, fundatam esse, non desunt, qui mordicus pertendant. Adjungunt alii S. Petro Achatem fidum, S. Paulum, & ab utroque Ecclesiam fundatam, ab utroque, seu uno, seu duobus capitibus Pontificibusque, gubernatam asserunt. Quorum causam non ita pridem dedita opera doctis. Arnaudus Sorbonista, & plurium etiam S. Patrum testimoniis fretus Baptista Casalius libro de sacris veterum Christianorum ritibus Romæ impresso; denique formosus ille Græco-Romanus Leo Allatius libro de Consensu Orientalis & Occidentalis Ecclesiæ, egerunt. Extant etiam Bullæ ipsorummet Romanorum Pontificum, in quibus imagines Apostoli utriusque, & quidem S. Pauli dextram occupantis, expressas cernere est. Non desunt tamen Viri doctissimi, quorum nonnulli, velut Bapt. Mantuanus, Michaël Cæsenas, Marsilius Patavinus, Johan. Aventinus, Carolus Molinæus, in ipsius etiam Ecclesiæ Romanæ visceribus hæserunt, qui S. Petrum Romam vidisse unquam, nedum ejus Ecclesiæ fundatorem, & viginti quinque annos integros Pontificem egisse, vel ambigant multum, vel apertè, productis etiam in medium rationum haud contemnendarum castris, inficientur.
units.tr: I. [Initial E ornamented] The origin of the Roman Church has so far been disputed with various eager efforts. There are not lacking those who stubbornly maintain that it was founded by the Apostle Peter, who was present there and held its helm for twenty-five years. Others add to Peter the faithful Achates, and Paul, and assert that the Church was founded by both, and governed by both, whether under one head or two Pontiffs. Their cause has been taken up deliberately, not long ago, by learned men: Arnaud the Sorbonnist, and Baptista Casalius, relying also on the testimony of many holy Fathers, in his book de sacris veterum Christianorum ritibus, printed at Rome; and finally that handsome Greco-Roman, Leo Allatius, in his book de Consensu Orientalis & Occidentalis Ecclesiæ. There also exist Bulls of the Roman Pontiffs themselves, in which one may see images of both Apostles, and indeed of Paul occupying the right hand. Yet there are not lacking most learned men, some of whom, such as Baptista Mantuanus, Michael Caesenas, Marsilius of Padua, Johannes Aventinus and Carolus Molinaeus, stuck fast even in the very bowels of the Roman Church itself, and who either doubt greatly or openly deny, bringing forward arguments not to be scorned, that Peter ever saw Rome at all, let alone that he was its founder and held the Pontificate there for twenty-five full years.

units.la: II. Licet verò, ut ambiguæ litis hujus fata dirimamus, haud ferat instituti præsentis ratio, operæ tamen pretium facturi videmur, si paucis certa & explorata ab incertis, dubiis, suspectis & falsis distinxerimus. Illud igitur certum exploratumque est, S. Paulum, gentium Apostolum, non tantum de Romanorum conversione fuisse quàm maximè sollicitum atque id egisse, ut Romam videret, Act. XIX. 21. Rom. I. 9. 10. 11. &c. quin & secundum Evangelium suum, ab illis, quos Romam misit, ejus ceu ministri Christi nomine prædicatum, eos primum Christo lucrifecisse. Rom. XVI. 25. Deo odorem cognitionis suæ per ipsum spargente εν παντὶ τόπῳ in omni loco, 2 Cor. II. 14. Certum quoque exploratumque est maturè satis Romæ Evangelium prædicatum, plurresque ad illud conversos esse. Omitto equidem definire, an, quod Claudius jussit Judæos Roma facessere, Act. XVIII. 2. tumultuantes impulsore Chresto, uti in ejus vita Suetonius narrat, ad Christianam Religionem pertineat. Neque etiam certò liquere puto, Andronicum & Juniam, quos ante se in Christo fuisse Paulus Rom. XVI. 7. affirmat, persecutione, quam Saul movebat, dispersos statim Romam, uti nonnulli conjectant, abiisse, aut ibi prædicâsse. Illud verò extra dubitationis aleam positum est, sub Nerone ingentem multitudinem Christianorum Romæ fuisse. De quo sic Tacitus A. XV. 44. 4. &c. loquitur: Ergo abolendo rumori (incensæ à se urbis) Nero subdidit reos, & quæsitissimis pœnis affecit, quos vulgus Christianos appellabat. Auctor nominis ejus Christus, &c. Repressaque in præsens exitiabilis superstitio rursus erumpebat, non modo per Judæam, originem ejus mali, sed per urbem etiam, quò cuncta undique atrocia aut pudenda confluunt, celebranturque. Igitur primò correpti, qui fatebantur, deinde indicio eorum MVLTITVDO INGENS, haud perinde crimine incendii, quàm odio humani generis convicti sunt. Certum non minus est, ipsam Romam tandem eum vidisse, ibi in libera custodia Regnum Dei prædicâsse, & Dominum Jesum Christum concernentia cum omni libertate ἀκωλύτως procul impedimento omni docuisse, Act. xxviii. 30, 31. denique Romæ intrepidum pro Christo martyrium subiisse, 2 Tim. iv. 16. 17. 18. Tum & illud æquè certum est, S. Scripturarum testimoniis, quod Petrus vel Romæ fuerit unquam, vel Pontificem ibi erecta cathedra egerit, probari vel evinci neutiquam posse. Ejus enim historiæ ne apicem quidem uspiam reperire est. Ut rei tanti momenti, à qua Ecclesiæ militantis salutem nonnulli suspendunt, si vera omnino est, nullam vel à Luca historiæ Apostolorum scriptore divino, & solertissimo, qui alia minora longè accuratè pertexere non omisit: vel ab aliis etiam scriptoribus sacris, & iis quidem locis, quæ rei gravissimæ narrationem flagitâsse quodammodo videretur, mentionem factam esse, admiratio ingens incessere omnes debeat. An igitur Petrus unquam Romam viderit, inter ἀμφισβητήσιμα dubia merito reponimus. Tametsi enim, teste Eusebio Hist. Eccles. II. 15. primus Papias tradiderit, Petrum, Claudio imperante, Romam venisse, ibi Simonem Magum confecisse, Evangelium Marci confirmâsse, & Epistolam suam priorem scripsisse; atque traditioni illi procedente tempore fidem habuerint plures pii doctique Patres: tamen illud ἀσφαλῶς certaque fide cognosci nequit, tum quia S. Literarum monumenta altum hic silent: tum quia Papiam fuisse hominem σμικρὸν ἐν νῷ exiguo judicio praeditum, idem Eusebius testatur : tum quia eundem Papiam manifeste falsa Apostolicæ traditionis fuco illita venditâsse constat : tum quia Papia antiquior Clemens Romanus Epistola priore ad Corinthios, à Patricio Junio Oxonij edita, utriusque Apostoli, Petri & Pauli labores ac itinera memorans, Paulum quidem ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ τέρμα τῆς δύσεως ad fines Occidentis, adeoque Romam delatum, ibique sub Nerone Martyrio sublatum scribit : at de Petro paucissimis defungens, nec locum martyrii ejus designat, nec profectionem in Occidentem ullam, nec Romanum ejus Episcopatum, nec suam in ejus locum successionem commemorat : tum denique quia veterum de Petri Romanis laboribus aliisque narratio discors, historiæ incertitudinem planissimè prodit. Egisse autem S. Petrum, annos viginti quinque Romanum Pontificem, prudentibus suspectum merito est, quia cum historia sacra Apostolorum ἀναγραφὴν esse, sic satis solidè à viris doctissimis comprobatum videtur. Denique inter aperte falsa numeramus, quòd S. Petrum Romæ Pontificatu in Universalem Ecclesiam militantem defunctum, atque ejusdem Pontificatus œcumenici lampadem suis in eadem Romana sede successoribus tradidisse, novelli Romanæ sedis gnathones, sine tabulis divinis, instrumentisque idoneis, quæ ψηλαφοφοείαν generare valeant, ullis, imò contra difertissimam eorundem contestationem, asseverare non erubescunt.
units.tr: II. Indeed, although the scope of the present work does not allow us to settle the fate of this doubtful dispute, we shall think it worth the effort if we briefly distinguish what is certain and well established from what is uncertain, doubtful, suspect and false. That, then, is certain and well established: that Paul, the Apostle of the Gentiles, was not only most anxious for the conversion of the Romans, but also worked to see Rome, Acts 19:21; Rom. 1:9, 10, 11, &c.; indeed, that according to his Gospel, preached in his name as Christ's minister by those whom he sent to Rome, he first won them to Christ, Rom. 16:25, God spreading through him the odour of the knowledge of himself in every place [ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ], 2 Cor. 2:14. It is also certain and well established that the Gospel was preached at Rome early enough and that many were converted to it. I will indeed refrain from deciding whether the edict by which Claudius ordered the Jews to leave Rome, Acts 18:2, they being in tumult at the instigation of Chrestus, as Suetonius relates in his life of Claudius, pertains to the Christian religion. Nor do I think it is clearly settled that Andronicus and Junia, whom Paul, Rom. 16:7, affirms were in Christ before him, were scattered at once by the persecution which Saul was stirring up, and went to Rome, as some conjecture, or preached there. But this is placed beyond all doubt: that under Nero there was a huge multitude of Christians at Rome. Tacitus speaks of this thus, Annals 15.44 and following: Therefore, to lay the rumour (that the city had been set on fire by him) to rest, Nero put forward as culprits, and punished with the most exquisite torments, those whom the crowd called Christians. The author of that name was Christ, &c. And the deadly superstition, checked for the moment, broke out again, not only in Judaea, the origin of that evil, but also in the city, where all things horrible or shameful from everywhere flow together and are celebrated. Therefore, first those were seized who confessed, then on their information A VAST MULTITUDE, convicted not so much of the crime of arson as of hatred of the human race. It is no less certain that Paul himself at last saw Rome, and there, under free custody, preached the Kingdom of God, and taught the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all freedom, unhindered [ἀκωλύτως] without any obstacle, Acts 28:30, 31; and finally that at Rome he underwent martyrdom, undaunted, for Christ, 2 Tim. 4:16, 17, 18. Moreover, it is equally certain, by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, that it cannot be proved or demonstrated in any way that Peter was ever at Rome, or that he exercised a Pontificate there from a seat set up. For not even the tip of any such history can be found anywhere. That a matter of such great moment, on which some make the salvation of the militant Church depend, should, if it were true at all, have been mentioned nowhere, neither by Luke, the divine and most skilful writer of the history of the Apostles, who did not omit to set out other, far less important matters with the greatest accuracy, nor by other sacred writers, and indeed in those places which seemed in some way to demand the narration of so weighty a matter, ought to excite great wonder in everyone. Whether Peter ever saw Rome, therefore, we rightly place among doubtful [ἀμφισβητήσιμα] matters. For although, according to Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.15, Papias was the first to hand down that Peter came to Rome in the reign of Claudius, there confuted Simon Magus, confirmed the Gospel of Mark, and wrote his first Epistle; and although many pious and learned Fathers gave credit to that tradition as time went on, yet it cannot be known for certain [ἀσφαλῶς] and with sure faith: partly because the monuments of the sacred Scriptures are wholly silent here; partly because Eusebius himself testifies that Papias was a man of small mind [σμικρὸν ἐν νῷ], endowed with a slender judgement; partly because it is clear that the same Papias sold off things under the false cover of Apostolic tradition; partly because Clement of Rome, older than Papias, in his first Epistle to the Corinthians, edited at Oxford by Patricius Junius, recalling the labours and journeys of both Apostles, Peter and Paul, writes that Paul was brought as to the limit of the West [ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ τέρμα τῆς δύσεως], that is, to Rome, and there was taken off by martyrdom under Nero; but, dealing with Peter in very few words, he neither names the place of his martyrdom, nor any journey to the West, nor his Roman episcopate, nor his successor in that office; and finally, partly because the narrations of the ancients about Peter's labours at Rome and elsewhere disagree, which plainly reveals the uncertainty of the history. Moreover, that St. Peter was Roman Pontiff for twenty-five years is rightly suspect to prudent men, because the sacred history of the Apostles is a record [ἀναγραφὴν] of their deeds, as is seen to have been sufficiently solidly proved by most learned men. Finally, among things plainly false we count this: that the upstart flatterers of the Roman see are not ashamed to assert, without any divine tablets or suitable instruments that could generate groping [ψηλαφοφοείαν] reasoning, indeed against their own most explicit testimony, that Peter died at Rome as Pontiff of the Universal militant Church, and handed on the torch of that ecumenical Pontificate to his successors in the same Roman see.

units.la: III. De origine Ecclesiæ Romanæ pauca hæc præfati, ad institutum venimus.
units.tr: III. Having said these few things by way of preface about the origin of the Roman Church, we come to our subject.

units.la: Multùm autem juvabit cognoscere Ecclesiæ illius progressum, mutationes, in doctrina cœlesti & regimine ἀλλοίωσιν, sinceritatem omni laude majorem, & ab eadem discessionem conversionemque multiplicem per gradus provecta, tandem pudenda & erubescenda nomini Christiano evasit. Liquebit enim inde res, hrs ininprimis temporibus aprimè cognitu necessaria ; aliud scilicet esse florem, aliud Floram ; aliud Veterem, aliud novam Romam ; aliud fidelem civitatem, aliud adulteram ; & pro vero ante ducentos annos Theodoricum Uriam, Augustinianum Monachum affirmâsse, Ecclesiam Romanam ex aurea in argenteam ; ex argentea in ferream ; ex ferrea in terream ; ex terrea in stercoream abiisse ; adeóque, quod scitum Scaligeri filii apophtegma fuit, juxta ϖολυϑεύλλητων illud Hebræorum, חמר בן יין Acetum filius est vini ; generosissimi vini veteris pessimum hodie acetum esse. Id vero manifestius ut faceremus, visum est Ecclesiæ Romanæ historiam certis notoriisque periodis inclusam & arctatam distinguere. Atque in universum periodi distinctæ septem se nobis offerunt ; quarum Prima historiam ejus in doctrina & regimine purioris, ab ejus initio ad Constantinum M. usque. Secunda doctrinam puriorem in præcipuis retinentis, at in regimine dominationem affectantis, à Constantino M. ad Bonifacium III. usque. Tertia dominationem in spiritualibus indultu Phocæ adipiscentis, & in doctrina ac ritibus degenerantis, à Bonifacio III. ad Gregorium VII. usque. Quarta dominationem etiam in temporalibus affectantis & in doctrina ritibusque in pejus indies vergentis, à Gregorio VII. ad Bonifacium VIII. usque. Quinta dominationem etiam in temporalibus,adeoque Cæsareo-Papatum adipiscentis, & eundem profligata doctrina puriori omni flagitiose exercentis, à Bonifacio VIII. ad Leonem X. usque. Sexta per Reformationem & separationem fidelium potestatis utriusque cladem gravissimam patientis, à Leone X. ad Concilii Tridentini finem usque. Septima denique per novella decreta fidei, & anathematismos diros in errore obfirmatæ,& cum vera Christi Ecclesia fraude & vi continuè decertantis ; certis rerum testimoniis documentisque ϭωϭομως τε ϰ' ϭπʹ ϭομως repræsentabit.
units.tr: It will be very helpful to learn the progress of that Church: its changes in heavenly doctrine and in government, its alteration [ἀλλοίωσις], and its many-sided falling away from a sincerity that deserves all praise. Advancing by stages, it at last became something shameful and disgraceful to the Christian name. For from this it will become clear what is especially necessary to know in these times: that one thing is Flower and another Flora; one Old Rome and another New; one a faithful city and another an adulterous one. It is also clear that Theodoric Uria, an Augustinian monk, asserted about two hundred years ago, and truly, that the Roman Church passed from golden into silver; from silver into iron; from iron into earth; from earth into dung. So, as the saying of Scaliger's son went, following the Hebrew proverb חמר בן יין [vinegar is the son of wine], the most noble old wine has today become the worst vinegar. To make this more manifest, it seemed good to divide the history of the Roman Church into certain and well-known periods. In general seven distinct periods present themselves. The First covers its history while it was still purer in doctrine and government, from its beginning to Constantine the Great. The Second covers a Church that kept the purer doctrine in its chief points but aspired to domination in government, from Constantine the Great to Boniface III. The Third covers a Church that gained domination in spiritual matters by the grant of Phocas and degenerated in doctrine and rites, from Boniface III to Gregory VII. The Fourth covers a Church that also aspired to domination in temporal matters and daily sank further into error in doctrine and rites, from Gregory VII to Boniface VIII. The Fifth covers a Church that obtained domination in temporal matters as well, and so the Caesaro-Papacy, and shamefully exercised it after casting off all purer doctrine, from Boniface VIII to Leo X. The Sixth covers a Church that suffered the most grievous loss of both powers through the Reformation and the separation of the faithful, from Leo X to the end of the Council of Trent. The Seventh covers a Church that, by new decrees of faith and dreadful anathemas, persisted in error and continued to contend with fraud and force against the true Church of Christ; this period will be set out by certain testimonies and documents.

units.la: III. Tempore Apostolorum, ut à prima periodo, eáque laudatissima exordiar, Ecclesiam Romanam recens natam licet, sic S. Paulus Rom. I. 8. celebrat, ut Deo gratias agat per Jesum Christum, quòd fides Romanorum prædicetur ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ in toto mundo. Erat scilicet Roma ipsa οἰκουμένης ἐπιτομὴ totius mundi compendium, caput & vertex mundi, & confluxus hominum ex toto mundo, cui etiam totus ferè orbis habitabilis parebat. Nam teste Polybio lib. 1. Ῥῶμα ... ἐπὶ Ῥωμαίων. Propemodum totus orbis habitabilis intra annos non totos quinquaginta-tres victus unum imperium Romanorum. Non poterat igitur magis latere Romanorum fides, quam civitas in monte posita latere potest. Quamprimùm igitur Christo nomen Romani multi dederunt, mox fama per orbem volitavit: Ecce Roma, caput orbis, Evangelii fidem suscepit! Domina mundi, quæ Draconi, Diabolo servivit hactenus, Christo crucifixo servit! Jam ab Hierosolymis Romam usque metropolin vanitatis, impuritatis, idololatriæ arcem ac thronum Draconis, Evangelium penetravit! Sed & cap. xv. 14. sic eandem Ecclesiam exornat: Persuasum habeo & ipse ego de Vobis, fratres mei, quòd ipsi per vos pleni sitis bonitate, impleti omni cognitione. Denique cap. xvi. 19. ἡ γὰρ ὑμῶν ὑπακοὴ εἰς πάντας ἀφῖκται. Obedientia vestra (puta juxta τύπον διδαχῆς, typum doctrinæ, in quem eos traditos esse cap. vi. 17. dixerat) ad omnes pervenit. Neque etiam contemnenda sunt elogia, quibus Ecclesiam Romanam sui etiam temporis, S. Ignatius mactavit. Vocat enim illam epistolà ad eosdem datâ ἀξιόθεον, ἀξιοπρεπῆ, ἀξιομακάριστον, ἀξιέπαινον, ἀξιοπίτβυζον, ἀξίαγνον, ἡ τεθηκαθημένην τῆς ἀγάπης, ἀξιρόνυμον, πατρόνυμον, πνευματοφόρον Deo dignam, decentissimam, beatissimam, laudandam, dignam qua quis potiatur, castissimam, eximiam charitate, Christi
units.tr: III. Beginning with the time of the Apostles, the first and most praiseworthy period, I say that although the Roman Church was newly born, St Paul celebrates it in Romans 1:8, giving thanks to God through Jesus Christ that the faith of the Romans is proclaimed in the whole world [ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ]. Rome itself was clearly a compendium of the whole world [οἰκουμένης ἐπιτομή], the head and summit of the world, and a meeting place of people from everywhere, to which almost the whole inhabited earth was subject. For, as Polybius says in book 1, almost the whole inhabited world was conquered within not quite fifty-three years and made one empire of the Romans. The faith of the Romans could therefore no more remain hidden than a city set on a hill can remain hidden. So as soon as many at Rome had given their name to Christ, the report flew through the world: Behold, Rome, the head of the world, has received the faith of the Gospel! The mistress of the world, who had served the Dragon and the Devil until now, now serves the crucified Christ! Now from Jerusalem the Gospel has penetrated all the way to Rome, the metropolis of vanity and impurity, the stronghold of idolatry and the throne of the Dragon! Paul also praises this same Church in chapter 15, verse 14: I am persuaded, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge. Finally, in chapter 16, verse 19: For your obedience [to the pattern of teaching, to which he had said in chapter 6, verse 17, that they had been delivered] has reached everyone [ἡ γὰρ ὑμῶν ὑπακοὴ εἰς πάντας ἀφῖκται]. Nor are the praises which St Ignatius gave to the Roman Church in his own time to be despised. In a letter to the same people he calls it worthy of God, becoming, worthy of blessing, worthy of praise, worthy to obtain, most chaste, eminent in charity of Christ, bearing the name of the Father, full of the Spirit [ἀξιόθεον, ἀξιοπρεπῆ, ἀξιομακάριστον, ἀξιέπαινον, ἀξιοπίτβυζον, ἀξίαγνον, ἡ τεθηκαθημένην τῆς ἀγάπης, ἀξιρόνυμον, πατρόνυμον, πνευματοφόρον].

units.la: Elogia eidem à S. Patribus tributa. sti & Patris nomine fruentem, plenam spiritu. Meritoque Apostolorum proximorumque temporum Ecclesia cùm universa, tum Romana etiam cum virgine comparatur. Revera enim παρθένον καθαρὰ ἡ ἀδιάφθορον ἔμεινεν ἡ ἐκκλησία. Virgo integra atque incorrupta permansit Ecclesia; Uti vetustus Scriptor Hegesippus apud Eusebium lib. iv. 22.& Nicephorum lib. iv. 7. loquitur. Si qui enim erant, uti idem Hegesippus loquitur, qui sinceram salutaris prædicationis regulam depravare studebant, in obscuris tenebrarum latebris delituerunt.
units.tr: Praises given to the same Church by the Holy Fathers. Rightly, therefore, the Church of the Apostles and of the times immediately after them is compared to a virgin, both as a whole and in its Roman part. Indeed the Church remained a pure and incorrupt virgin [παρθένον καθαρὰ ἢ ἀδιάφθορον ἔμεινεν ἡ ἐκκλησία], as the ancient writer Hegesippus says in Eusebius, book 4, chapter 22, and in Nicephorus, book 4, chapter 7. For, as the same Hegesippus says, if there were any who tried to corrupt the sincere rule of the saving preaching, they lay hidden in the dark recesses of shadows.

units.la: V. Ipsos Ecclesiæ Romanæ Antistites, non statim ambitio, Ecclesiæ venenum, infecit. Sacerdotum quippe gloria fuit (ita in confutatione Primatus Papæ ante annos pene ducentos scripta Gregorius Heymburgensis J.U.D. & Norimbergensis Syndicus loquitur) non purpura, non divitiæ, non equus albus, non fastus, non dominatus; sed: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia, & secuti sumus Te, Domine. Tum igitur florente Ecclesia, & nondum malo laborante (ut Isidori Pelusiotæ lib. iii. Epist. verbis utar) τὰ θεῖα χαρίσματα τῆς ἁγίας πνεύματος διαμαγωγοῦντος, ἡ τῶν ἑκάστου χωροῦντος, ἡ γεγενὸν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ποιοῦντος. Divinæ gratiæ circa eam velut chorum agebant, Sancto Spiritu res administrante, Antistitum unumquemque incitante, ac Ecclesiam in Cælum convertente.
units.tr: V. Ambition, the poison of the Church, did not at once infect the leaders of the Roman Church. For, as Gregory of Heimburg, Doctor of Law and syndic of Nuremberg, says in his refutation of the Primacy of the Pope, written almost two hundred years ago, the glory of the priests was not purple, not riches, not a white horse, not pomp, not domination, but: Behold, we have left all things and followed you, Lord. Then, therefore, while the Church was flourishing and not yet labouring under evil (to use the words of Isidore of Pelusium, book 3, Epistles), the divine gifts of the Holy Spirit were dancing around it, the Spirit directing affairs, stirring up each of the leaders and turning the Church towards heaven.

units.la: VI. Cœterùm non absurdè in Possiacena responsione retulit Carolus Lotharingus Cardinalis: de quindecim (nos addimus de sedecim) à Christo seculis, primum verè esse aureum: reliqua, quò longiùs abscederent, eò esse nequiora atque deteriora. Testis ejus rei idem, qui, supra, Hegesippus est, qui præfatus, Ecclesiam Apostolorum tempore castam Virginem fuisse, sequentia subjungit: Postquam autem sacer Apostolorum chorus diverso mortis genere vitam finiit, præteriitque illorum ætas, quibus à Christo donatum erat, ut auribus bus divinam sapientiam coram acciperent, tum primum falsa & veteratoria impii erroris conspiratio per fraudem eorum, qui doctrinam à veritate prorsus alienam disseminare laborârunt, initium cepit. Qui deinde, nullo jam ex Apostolis reliquo, nudato, ut ajunt, capite, sincero veritatis sermoni, falsam & commentitiam doctrinam ex adverso opponere ausi sunt. Sensus est, tum post Apostolorum tempora mox hæreses nefarias caput suum protulisse, & impletum esse, quod prænunciaverat S. Paulus Act. xx. 30. futurum scilicet, ut post ἀφιξιν discessum, abitum suum & Apostolorum graves lupi, & viri perversa loquentes, ex ipsius Ecclesiæ visceribus surrecturi sint: tum etiam ipsam Ecclesiam paulatim degenerâsse, nævisque ejusmodi, qualibus Ecclesia Apostolica caruit, laborare incepisse.
units.tr: VI. Moreover, Cardinal Charles of Lorraine said, not absurdly, in his reply at Poissy, that of the sixteen centuries since Christ (we add 'sixteen') the first alone was truly golden; the rest were the worse and the more corrupt the further they went from it. The witness to this is the same Hegesippus, who, having said before that the Church was a chaste virgin in the time of the Apostles, adds the following: After the sacred band of the Apostles had ended their lives by various kinds of death, and the age passed of those to whom it had been granted by Christ to receive divine wisdom with their own ears, then for the first time the false and crafty conspiracy of impious error began, through the deceit of those who laboured to spread a doctrine utterly alien to the truth. Then, with none of the Apostles left, they dared, as they say, with head uncovered, to set a false and invented doctrine against the sincere word of truth. The meaning is that, soon after the times of the Apostles, nefarious heresies raised their heads, and what St Paul had foretold in Acts 20:30 was fulfilled: that after his departure, grievous wolves and men speaking perverse things would arise from within the Church itself. It also means that the Church itself gradually degenerated and began to suffer from blemishes of the kind the Apostolic Church had not had.

units.la: VI. Tametsi etiam Apostolorum etiam temporibus non defuerint, qui Evangelium prædicatum ab illis depravare conatagerent, cum Apostoli jam tum, cum Evangelium prædicârunt, obtestati sint, in quibusdam esse ἀγνωσίαν ignorantiam Dei, 1 Cor. xv. 35. &Spiritum Antichristi in mundo esse, 1 Joh. iv. 3. multosque jam Antichristos in mundo extitisse ib. cap. 11. 18. adeoque Diabolum gnarum utique, se mox ex regno suo, quod in gentes habebat, ejiciendum, id jam machinari omnibus viribus, ut haberet commeatum ad Antichristum aliquando in scenam producendum; nondum tamen γυμνῃ κεφαλῇ nudato capite, uti Hegesippus loquitur, adeoque impune & prostituto pudore omni hæretici grassari cœperunt, uti quidem post Apostolorum tempora, cum Apostolici Spiritus repagulum remotum esset, factum esse, hæreticorum catalogi à Veteribus consignati testantur.
units.tr: VI. Even in the times of the Apostles there were not lacking those who tried to corrupt the Gospel once it had been preached, since the Apostles, even when they first preached the Gospel, warned that the ignorance of God was among some (1 Cor. 15:35), that the spirit of Antichrist is in the world (1 John 4:3), and that many Antichrists had already appeared in the world (ibid., chapter 2, verse 18). The Devil, who certainly knew that he would soon be cast out of the kingdom he held over the nations, was therefore already plotting with all his might to have a way of access for bringing Antichrist on to the stage at some time. Nevertheless, heretics did not yet run wild with head uncovered, as Hegesippus puts it, nor with shame thrown off and without restraint. That this began to happen after the times of the Apostles, when the restraint of the Apostolic Spirit had been removed, is attested by the catalogues of heretics recorded by the Ancients.

units.la: VII. Ab immani tamen hæreticorum talium licentia Ecclesia Romana magis, quàm cæteræ, immunis satis diu fuit. Sicut enim verbum Dei ex Sione prodiit, Evangeliumque primum in Judæa & Asia reliquaAfricaque prædicatum est : ita in iisdem locis primùm hæresès obortæ à Judæis & Græcis Philosophis cumprimis defensæ Ecclesiam Dei infestare, & Evangelium prædicatum corrumpere coeperunt. Ex iis verò, quos S. Augustinus, Epiphanius, Philastrius hæreticorum catalogo inserunt, pauci primis temporibus Romani fuerunt ; Pauci Romanam Ecclesiam exercuerunt. Persecutiones creberrimæ, martyria gloriosa, fidei simplicitatem, & charitatis sinceritatem, ita sustinuerunt, ut Diabolus ostium apertum, per quod vel vi, vel fraude irrumperet, non invenerit.
units.tr: VII. Yet the Roman Church was, for quite a long time, more free than the others from the monstrous licence of such heretics. For just as the word of God went forth from Zion, and the Gospel was first preached in Judea, Asia, the rest of Africa, so heresies first arose in those same places, were chiefly defended by Jews and Greek philosophers, and began to infest the Church of God and corrupt the preached Gospel. Of those whom St. Augustine, Epiphanius and Philastrius list in their catalogues of heretics, few were Romans in the earliest times, and few troubled the Roman Church. Very frequent persecutions and glorious martyrdoms sustained the simplicity of faith and the sincerity of love, so that the Devil found no open door through which he might break in, either by force or by fraud.

units.la: VIII. Hanc Ecclesiæ Romanæ primævam felicitatem
units.tr: VIII. This primal happiness of the Roman Church

units.la: S. Patres prædicant & extollunt. Omnium instar S. Cyprianus & Hieronymus sunto. S. Cyprianus Epistola ad Cornelium inter alia eos esse Romanos ait ; ad quos perfidia non possit habere accessum. Suo tempore innuit, tales esse Romanos, ob compertam in fide constantiam & zelum veritatis, continuis ferè eorum martyriis obsignatæ, quem etiam damnatis & rejectis strenuè hæresibus, eorum cumprimis, qui Romæ etiam turbare connixi fuerunt (quales Cerdon Valentinus, Marcellus, Novatiani) demonstrârunt. Perpetuò tamen tales futuros esse, ut ad eos perfidia habere accessum non posset, non dixit ; neque, si dixisset, recipiendum ἀδιαφόρως esset. Pietas, zelus, prudentia, devotio, obstacula sunt perfidiæ, ne accessum habere posset. At iis successu temporis vel languescentibus, vel intereuntibus decumana perfidiæ janua aperiri potuit. Sed & S. Hieronymus lib. 3. Apol. contra Rufinum ; Scito, inquit, Romanam fidem Apostolica voce laudatam ejusmodi præstigias non recipere, etiamsi angelus aliter annuncict, quàm semel prædicatum est, Pauli authoritate munitum non posse mutari. Corrigit autem hanc Hieronymi paulò crudiorem gnomam ipse Rigaltius Not. ad Cypr. Epist. 55. asserens, non id velle Paulum, rectiorem firmioremque Romanorum fidem esse, quàm aliorum, sed hoc tantùm eum dicere, agere se gratias Deo, quod ubique fama sit, etiam Romanos rerum Dominos, fidem Christianam suscepisse: quod sane, inquit ille, ob dignitatem urbis, quæ totius orbis erat caput, & gentium Domina, valde ad Christianæ fidei propagationem faciebat.
units.tr: The Fathers proclaim and extol it. St. Cyprian and St. Jerome may stand for all. St. Cyprian, in his Epistle to Cornelius, says among other things that they are Romans, to whom perfidy cannot have access. By this he indicates that in his own time the Romans were such, on account of the constancy in faith and zeal for the truth that was found among them, sealed by an almost continual series of martyrdoms, and which they also showed by vigorously rejecting and condemning heresies, especially those who tried to disturb them even at Rome (such as Cerdo, Valentinus, Marcellus, and the Novatians). But that they would always be such that perfidy could have no access to them, he did not say; nor, if he had said it, should it be received without distinction. Piety, zeal, prudence and devotion are the obstacles that keep perfidy from gaining access. But when these grew weak or died out with the passing of time, the back gate of perfidy could be opened. St. Jerome too, in book 3 of the Apology against Rufinus: Know, he says, that the Roman faith, praised by the apostolic voice, does not receive such tricks, even if an angel announces otherwise than was once preached; fortified by the authority of Paul, it cannot be changed. Rigaltius himself, however, corrects this rather crude maxim of Jerome in his note on Cyprian's Epistle 55, asserting that Paul did not mean that the Roman faith was more upright and firmer than that of others, but only that he says he gives thanks to God, because it is everywhere reported that even the Romans, masters of the world, have received the Christian faith; which indeed, he says, because of the dignity of the city, which was the head of the whole world and mistress of the nations, greatly furthered the propagation of the Christian faith.

units.la: IX. Primis Ecclesiæ Romanæ Pastoribus & Episcopis, Clementi cumprimis, Anacleto, Evaristo, Alexandro, Sixto, Telesphoro, Hygino, Pio, Aniceto, Soteri, aliis tribuuntur epistolæ nonnullæ, vulgò Decretales insignitæ, & ab Isidoro Hispalensi, si Francisco Turriano Jesuitæ fides est, collectæ. Quæ quidem epistolæ, siquidem genuinæ essent, non parùm Ecclesiæ Romanæ primitivæ gloriam offuscarent. In iis enim laudati illi Episcopi Romani velut ex tripode dictantes nova quædam oracula circa ritus maximè & ceremonias Ecclesiæ, Apostolicæ simplicitati & puritati non parùm repugnantia, inducuntur. Clemens, verbi gratiâ, sancit, ut Sacerdotes paludamentis sacris, Episcopi infula & pastorali pedo, sandaliis & chirothecis, Archiepiscopi pallio; Pontifex, Cardinales & Legati crucis vexillo ad concionis & Missæ sacra veherentur. Anacletus, ne Præsul, neve Clerici barbam vel comam nutrirent; nec Episcopus à paucioribus, quàm à tribus Episcopis ordinaretur; utque Clerici publicè non privatim ad Sacros Ordines ascisccrentur, edicit. Alexander, aquam lustralem profugandis dæmonibus, hominibusque post finita sacra, aspergendis præscribit. Sixtus, Corporalis seu linteoli, super quo inter sacra corpus Christi ponitur, formam præcipit. Telesphorus, jejunium quadragesimale ante Pascha: Hyginus, dedicationes solennes Templorum, neve ea augerentur & diminuerentur sine Metropolitani & Episcopi consensu, nec non compatrum in Baptismo usum. Pius, Paschatis non nisi Dominicæ celebrandi necessitatem: Anicetus, ut vertex capitis sacerdotum sphærulæ instar raraderetur : Victor, ut Baptismus extra necessitatem solo Paschate administraretur : Calixtus, ut ordines sacri in quatuor jejunii temporibus conferrentur, qui hactenus solo Decembri conferri sueverint: Vrbanus, ut Ecclesia praedia ac fundos à fidelibus collatos reciperet : Fabianus, ut singulis annis die Coenæ Domini Chrisma, vetere combusto, renovaretur : Stephanus, tegumenta altarium & vestes sacerdotum : Felix, annua sacra pro Martyribus : Eutychianus, ut frugum primitiæ in altari à Sacerdotibus benedicerentur, utque per gradus ad Episcopatum ascenderetur, ordinarunt. Omittam prorsus, quæ hi simul omnes de Primatu Romani Pontificis, de forma judiciorum, & qualitate testium, de non accusandis clericis, maximè Episcopis à Laicis, de appellatione ad sedem Romanam, aliisque hujus generis decrevisse dicuntur. Quæ omnia si cum vero consentanea essent, de Ecclesiæ Romanæ veteris puritate & prærogativa fidei supra Ecclesias reliquas haud dubiè conclamatum foret. Quis enim talia Apostolicæ simplicitati congruere vel somniare ausit?
units.tr: IX. To the first pastors and bishops of the Roman Church, above all Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, Soter and others, are ascribed certain letters, commonly marked as the Decretals, and collected by Isidore of Seville, if one trusts the Jesuit Francis Turrianus. Indeed, if these letters were genuine, they would not a little obscure the glory of the primitive Roman Church. For in them those praised Roman bishops are introduced, as if dictating from a tripod, delivering new oracles about the rites and ceremonies of the Church, which are not a little at odds with apostolic simplicity and purity. Clement, for example, decrees that priests be carried to the sermon and the Mass with sacred mantles, a bishop with mitre and pastoral staff, sandals and gloves, an archbishop with the pallium, and the Pontiff, cardinals and legates with the banner of the cross. Anacletus orders that neither prelate nor clergy should let their beards or hair grow; that a bishop should not be ordained by fewer than three bishops; and that clergy should be admitted to the sacred orders publicly, not privately. Alexander prescribes lustral water to be sprinkled to drive away demons, and on people after the sacred rites are finished. Sixtus lays down the form of the corporal, or little linen cloth, on which the body of Christ is placed during the sacred rites. Telesphorus prescribes the Lenten fast before Easter. Hyginus prescribes solemn dedications of temples, that these not be increased or diminished without the consent of the metropolitan and the bishop, and also the use of godparents in baptism. Pius lays down that Easter must be celebrated only on a Sunday. Anicetus orders that the crown of the priests' heads be shaved like a little sphere. Victor orders that baptism, outside of necessity, be administered only at Easter. Calixtus orders that holy orders be conferred in the four seasons of fasting, whereas hitherto they had been conferred only in December. Urban orders that the Church receive the estates and lands contributed by the faithful. Fabian orders that the chrism be renewed every year on Maundy Thursday, the old being burned. Stephen orders the coverings of altars and the vestments of priests. Felix orders annual sacred rites for the martyrs. Eutychian orders that the first-fruits of the crops be blessed by the priests at the altar, and that one ascend to the episcopate by degrees. I will altogether omit what all of these together are said to have decreed about the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, the form of judgments and the qualities of witnesses, the rule that clergy, especially bishops, may not be accused by laymen, appeal to the Roman see, and other matters of this kind. For if all these things agreed with the truth, the old purity of the Roman Church and the prerogative of its faith above the other churches would undoubtedly have been proclaimed loudly. For who would dare to think that such things agree with apostolic simplicity, let alone dream them?

units.la: X. Sed salva res est. Alia longè pietas, mens alia, castiorque longè fuit primorum illorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Episcoporum, iis temporibus, quibus continuo fere persecutionum incendio flagrantibus, alia omnia, quàm inania, frivola & absurda ejusmodi, ad instruendum fastum ministrorum Ecclesiæ composita, meditanda fuerunt. Et detecta jam fraus est, clariusque meridiano sole ex iis, quæ primùm Magdeburgenses Centuriatores, post adversus Turrianum David Blondellus in Pseudo, Isidoro, & Turriano vapulantibus, (ne de Sirmondo, Petavio, aliis Pontificiis γνησιότητα earum oppugnantibus dicam) publicam in lucem protulerunt, constat, hunc Decretalium epistolarum lumbricum demum Caroli M. ætate, obstetricante nescio quo Isidoro, cognomento Mercatore, natum. tum, Isidori Hispalensis larvâ tectum, vilissimas fæces pretiosissimis antiquorum Urbis Romanæ Episcoporum titulis appositis venditâsse, atque ita plus quàm octo seculorum decurrentium ordini, nefariè impositae; quam in rem inferius Sect. lxiv. plura.
units.tr: X. But the matter is safe. Far different was the piety, far different the mind, and far purer was that of those first bishops of the Roman Church, in those times when the fire of persecution was blazing almost continually; they had to devote their thoughts to anything but such empty, frivolous and absurd inventions, composed to furnish the pomp of church ministers. And the fraud is now detected, and clearer than the noonday sun it is evident from what the Magdeburg Centuriators first, and afterwards David Blondel against Turrianus, brought publicly to light, while Pseudo-Isidore and Turrianus were thrashed (not to mention Sirmond, Petavius and other Papists who oppose their genuineness [γνησιότητα]): this worm of the Decretal letters was born in the age of Charlemagne, with some Isidore, surnamed Mercator, acting as midwife. Then, covered with the mask of Isidore of Seville, it sold the vilest dregs, with the most precious titles of the ancient bishops of the city of Rome attached, and was thus impudently foisted upon the order of more than eight centuries; on this matter, more below, in section 64.

units.la: XI. Tametsi verò de depravata primis illis temporibus Ecclesiæ Romanæ doctrina nihil constat: Ecclesiæ tamen regimen ab eo, quod Christus & Apostoli instituerunt, paulatim deflexit. Verissimè quidem Florimundus Ræmondus in fabula Joh. cap. 20. sic primorum Pontificum humilitatem depinxit: Prioribus illis seculis, & multorum annorum fluxu Pontifices martyrii sacri laureâ contentos fuisse, quam omni diademate & sceptro potiorem habebant, reliquisque ornamentis ducebant superiorem, nemo ignorat. Prima illa ætate, gloria eorum erat ignominia; Majestas, humilitas; felicitas, tyrannorum iræ; quies, supplicium; vita, mors ipsa. Nihilominus eum paulatim supra reliquos gradum affectârunt, qui, procedente tempore, præter intentionem & consilium eorum, malorum Iliadem post se traxit.
units.tr: XI. Although nothing certain is known of any corruption of doctrine in the Roman Church in those first times, nevertheless the government of the Church gradually drifted away from what Christ and the apostles had instituted. Florimundus Raemundus, in his tale on John chapter 20, has very truly depicted the humility of the first Pontiffs in this way: that in earlier centuries, and through the passing of many years, the Pontiffs were content with the laurel of sacred martyrdom, which they held more precious than any diadem or sceptre, and regarded as superior to other ornaments, is known to nobody. In that first age their glory was disgrace; their majesty, humility; their happiness, the anger of tyrants; their rest, punishment; their life, death itself. Nevertheless they gradually aspired to a step above the rest, and this, as time went on, beyond their intention and plan, dragged after it an Iliad of evils.

units.la: XII. In universum quidem S. Hieronymus Comment. cap. 1. ad Titum, fusè comprobat, eundem S. Paulo esse Presbyterum & Episcopum. Et antequam, inquit, Diaboli instinctu studia in religione fierent, & diceretur in populis: Ego sum Pauli, ego Apollo, ego autem Cephæ, communi Presbyterorum consilio Ecclesiæ gubernabantur. Postquam verò unusquisque eos, quos baptizaverat, suos putabat esse, non Christi; in toto orbe decretum est, ut unus de Presbyteris electus superponeretur cæteris, ad quem omnis Ecclesiæ cura pertineret, ut schismatum semina tollerentur. Subjicit: Noverint Episcopi, se magis consuetudine, quàm dispositionis Dominicæ veritate Presbyteris esse superiores. Annotatum etiam est, Alexandriæ usque ad Heraclam & Dionysium Episcopos, Presbyteros ex numero suo unum, quem digniorem reputârunt, selectum in celsiori gradu collocâsse, futurum scilicet Πρεσβυτέρων, Presbyterorum, seu Presbyterii Præsidem quem morem à Marco Evangelista initium sumpsisse, idem Hieronymus epistola ad Evagrium testatur. Et quod Alexandriæ ab initio factum est, id alibi post initia Ecclesiarum fieri etiam coepisse, idem asserit. Quod autem, inquit ille, POSTEA unus electus est, qui cæteris præponeretur, in Schismatis remedium factum est, ne unusquisque ad se trahens, Christi Ecclesiam rumperet. Proin quicquid hic præter institutionem Christi maturè in Ecclesia accidit, sicut non malo consilio accidisse largimur ultro, ita non tam propter ἐξουσίαν potestatem majorem, resignandam scilicet in manus Episcopi, vel propter πρωτοκαθεδρίαν quandam, quàm προεδρίαν præsidentiam, adeoque τιμήν ἐν τάξει majorem duntaxat honorem & ordinem accidisse pertendimus.
units.tr: XII. In general, St. Jerome, in his commentary on Titus chapter 1, shows at length that the same man was presbyter and bishop as St. Paul was. And before, he says, the factions in religion arose through the instigation of the Devil, and it was said among the peoples: I am of Paul, I of Apollos, and I of Cephas, the Church was governed by the common counsel of the presbyters. But after each one thought that those whom he had baptized were his own, and not Christ's, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters, chosen, should be set over the rest, to whom the whole care of the Church should pertain, so that the seeds of schism might be removed. He adds: Let bishops know that they are superior to presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord's arrangement. It is also noted that at Alexandria, down to the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters chose one from their own number, whom they judged worthier, and placed him in a higher rank, namely as president of the [Πρεσβυτέρων] presbyters, that is, of the presbytery. Jerome himself testifies in his letter to Evagrius that this custom took its beginning from the evangelist Mark. And he asserts that what was done at Alexandria from the beginning began elsewhere too, after the beginnings of the churches. But that afterwards one was chosen to be placed over the others, he says, was done as a remedy for schism, so that no one, drawing others to himself, might break the Church of Christ. Therefore, whatever happened in the Church here early on, beyond the institution of Christ, we freely grant did not happen by evil design; yet we maintain that it did not happen because of a greater power [ἐξουσίαν], to be surrendered into the hands of the bishop, nor from some first-seat primacy [πρωτοκαθεδρίαν], but rather from a presidency [προεδρίαν], and thus only a greater honour [τιμήν] and rank in order (ἐν τάξει).

units.la: XIII. Solent autem optima & saluberrima quæque hominum instituta successu temporis degenerare. Id hic etiam contigit. Honos enim ille collatus Episcopis subinde animos eorum ita mutavit, ut more humani ingenii, plusculum sibi arrogare, & se extollere supra alios inciperent. Quod Romæ inprimis, urbe scilicet Imperatoriâ & Orbis domina, evenisse constat. Sanè etiam Socrates Hist. Eccles. lib. VII. 11. Episcopos Romanos paulatim ita degenerâsse dixit, ut τέως τῆς ἱεροσύνης ὅτι δυναστείαν ultra sacerdotii limites ad externum dominatum progressi sint. Qua re gentilibus aliquando offendiculo fuerunt. Nam Ammianus Marcellinus homo gentilis lib. 27. de Pontificibus Romanis ita scribit: Processerunt vehiculis insidentes circumspectè vestiti, epulas curantes profusas, adeò ut eorum convivia Regales superaverint mensas. Addita hac animadversione, potuisse eos esse beatos revera, si magnitudine urbis despecta, quam vitiis opponunt, ad imitationem Antistitum quorundam Provincialium viverent: quos tenuitas edendi potandique parcissimè, vilitas etiam induindumentorum, & supercilia humum spectantia perpetuo Numini, verisque ejus cultoribus velut puros commendaret & verecundos. Sed & S. Basilius Epist. 10. non obscure Τὼ δυτικῶ ὀφρύων Occidentalem illum fastum pulsat. Si ira Dei permanserit, inquit, πόσα βοήθεια ἡμῖν ἀπὸ δυτικῆς ὀφρύος; quale nobis auxilium ab Occidentalium fastu & supercilio aderit? Vatem fuisse, tristis eventus docuit. Alibi quoque fatente, & nonnihil stomachante Baronio ad A. C. cccLxxii. §. 32. de Ecclesia Romana idem S. Basilius dixit: Odi fastum illius Ecclesiae.
units.tr: XIII. The best and most wholesome human institutions usually degenerate over time, and this happened here too. The honour conferred on the bishops gradually changed their minds, so that, as human nature tends to do, they began to claim a little more for themselves and to raise themselves above others. This is known to have happened especially at Rome, the imperial city and mistress of the world. Socrates, in Hist. Eccles. lib. VII. 11., also said that the Roman bishops had gradually degenerated, so that they advanced beyond the limits of the priesthood to external lordship [τέως τῆς ἱεροσύνης ὅτι δυναστείαν]. For this reason they at times became a stumbling block to the Gentiles. Ammianus Marcellinus, a Gentile, writes thus of the Roman Pontiffs in lib. 27.: "They went about in carriages, dressed with care, providing lavish banquets, so that their feasts surpassed royal tables. Yet one could remark that they might be truly blessed, if, despising the greatness of the city, which they set against their vices, they lived in imitation of certain provincial bishops, whose meagre eating and drinking, and whose plain clothing, and eyes fixed on the ground, commend them, as pure and modest, to the constant Deity and to its true worshippers." But St Basil also, in Epist. 10., plainly strikes at the Western pride: Τὼ δυτικῶ ὀφρύων [the Western brows]. "If the wrath of God remains," he says, "πόσα βοήθεια ἡμῖν ἀπὸ δυτικῆς ὀφρύος" [what help for us from the Western brow]; "what help will come to us from the pride and haughtiness of the Westerners?" The sad outcome showed that he was a prophet. Elsewhere too, Baronius, somewhat grumbling, reports at A. C. 372, §. 32, that the same St Basil said of the Roman Church: Odi fastum illius Ecclesiae. ("I hate the pride of that Church.")

units.la: XIV. Exempla ambitionis Episcopos Romanos maturè satis concipientis, Victor & Stephanus suppeditant.
units.tr: XIV. Victor and Stephen supply examples of the ambition that the Roman bishops conceived quite early.

units.la: Victor enim A. C. cxcv. Polycratem & Ecclesias Asiaticas ob levem circa tempus Paschatis celebrandi dissensum temerè condemnans, γναῖτεν ... ἀδελφὰς, datis literis universos, qui illic erant, fratres proscribit, & ab unitate Ecclesiae prorsus alienos esse pronuntiat, uti Eusebius Histor. Eccles. lib. V. 24. loquitur. Addit idem parum id placuisse Episcopis reliquis, puta etiam Occidentalibus, de caetero in re ipsa concordibus, qui scriptis ad eum literis acerbè satis illum perstrinxerint; & Irenaeum etiam Victori ad animum revocasse exempla Praedecessorum, Aniceti, Pii, Hygini, Telesphori, & Xysti, qui nunquam Orientalibus ob diversitatem rituum succensuerint, nedum eos ab Ecclesiae communione amputaverint.
units.tr: Victor, around A. C. 195, rashly condemned Polycrates and the Asian Churches over a slight disagreement about the time of celebrating Easter. He wrote letters and banished all the brethren who were there, [γναῖτεν ... ἀδελφὰς], and declared them utterly alien to the unity of the Church, as Eusebius says in Histor. Eccles. lib. V. 24. The same writer adds that this displeased the other bishops, namely the Western ones too, who otherwise agreed with him on the matter; they rebuked him sharply in letters written to him. Irenaeus also called to Victor's mind the examples of his predecessors, Anicetus, Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus and Xystus, who never were angry with the Easterners over a difference of rites, much less cut them off from the communion of the Church.

units.la: XV. Stephanus quoque Papa ejus rei documenta prae- buit.
units.tr: XV. Pope Stephen also provided evidence of this.

units.la: Is enim non tantum circa A. CCL. Basilidem Episcopum Asturiensem, & Martialem Melidensem, Hispanum utrumque immorigerum in fidem recipiens, Ecclesias Hispanicas sic satis graviter adoritur, & jus appellationis ad Ecclesiam Romanam ambit, multum reclamante licet S. Cypriano Epist. 18. nec non libro de unitate Ecclesiae, ubi illa occurrunt: Hoc utique erant & caeteri Apostoli, stoli, quod fuit Petrus, pari consortio præditi & honoris & potestatis; sed exordium ab unitate proficiscitur, ut una Christi Ecclesia, & Catholica una monstretur. (quæ verba accuratè Salmasius de Primatu Papæ pag. 74. 75. 76. expendit) verùm etiam non multò post, suborta, de baptismo eorum, qui ab hæreticis baptizati erant, quæstione, ipse quidem causæ meliori addictus, dissentientes tamen primò Africanas, mox etiam Orientales Ecclesias reliquas iis adhærentes, arroganter satis à communione sua amputat. Ad quem ita apud Cyprianum Orientales, epistola ad Cyprianum data, quæ Pamelianæ Cypriani Operum Editionis 75 est, ζηλιτευτικῶς satis scribit: Homo animosus parit lites, & vir iracundus exaggerat peccata. Lites enim & dissensiones quantas parasti per Ecclesias totius mundi? Peccatum verò quàm magnum tibi exaggerasti, quando te à tot gregibus scidisti? Excidisti enim te ipsum. Noli te fallere, siquidem est verè ille schismaticus, qui se à communione Ecclesiasticæ unitatis apostatam fecerit. Dum enim putas, à te omnes abstineri posse, solum te ab omnibus abstinuisti. Ambulate vocatione, quà vocati estis, digne cum omni humilitate sensus & lenitate, cum patientia sustinentes invicem in dilectione, satis agentes servare unitatem Spiritus in conjunctione pacis. Hæc Apostoli mandata & monita salutaria, quàm diligenter Stephanus implevit, humilitatem sensus & honestatem primo loco servans? Quid enim humilius aut lenius, quàm cum tot Episcopis per totum mundum dissensisse? Pacem cum singulis vario discordiæ genere rumpentem, modò cum Orientalibus, quod nec vos latere confidimus, modò vobiscum, qui in Meridie estis, à quibus legatos Episcopos patienter satis & leniter suscepit, ut eos nec ad sermonem saltem colloquii communis admitteret? Adhuc insuper præcepit, ne quis eos in domum suam reciperet, ut venientibus non solum pax & communio, sed & tectum & hospitium negaretur. Apud talem hominem potest esse unum corpus, & unus spiritus, apud quem fortassis anima una non est; sic lubrica, mobilis & in-cercerta ? Et tamen non pudet Stephanum talibus adversus Ecclesiam patrocinium præstare, & propter hæreticos afferendos fraternitatem scindere: insuper & Cyprianum Pseudo-Christum, Pseudapostolum, & dolosum operarium dicere ? Quæ omnia in se esse conscius prævenit, ut alter; ea per mendacium objiceret, quæ ipse ex merito audiret. Hactenus illi, quorum Epistolam libenter se, exemplo Manutii, omissurum fuisse Pamelius, nisi Morellius & Turnebus ipse, priores in lucem eam produxissent, fatetur.
units.tr: For about A. C. 250 he not only received Basilides, bishop of Astorga, and Martialis of Mérida, both Spaniards who were unyielding, but attacked the Spanish Churches rather severely and claimed a right of appeal to the Roman Church. St Cyprian objected strongly, in Epist. 18. and in his book de unitate Ecclesiae, where these words occur: "The other apostles were indeed what Peter was, endowed with equal partnership in honour and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the one Church of Christ and the one Catholic Church may be shown." (Salmasius weighs these words carefully at de Primatu Papae, pp. 74, 75, 76.) Yet not long after, when a question arose about the baptism of those who had been baptized by heretics, Stephen, though himself inclined to the better cause, arrogantly cut off from his communion first the dissenting African Churches and then the remaining Eastern Churches that adhered to them. The Easterners, in a letter to Cyprian (which is number 75 in Pamelius's edition of Cyprian's works), write to him rather jealously [ζηλιτευτικῶς]: "A bold man breeds quarrels, and a headstrong man magnifies sins. How many quarrels and dissensions have you stirred up throughout the Churches of the whole world? And how great a sin have you magnified for yourself, when you have torn yourself away from so many flocks? For you have cut off yourself. Do not deceive yourself: he is truly a schismatic who has made himself an apostate from the communion of the ecclesiastical unity. For while you think that all can abstain from you, you alone have abstained from all. Walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, with all humility and gentleness, bearing with one another in love, and endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. How diligently has Stephen fulfilled these apostolic commands and wholesome admonitions, keeping humility of mind and courtesy first of all? For what is more humble or gentle than to disagree with so many bishops throughout the whole world? Breaking the peace with each in a different kind of discord, now with the Easterners, which we trust does not escape you, and now with you who are in the South, from whom he patiently and gently received bishops as legates, yet would not admit them even to a word of common discourse? Moreover he has further commanded that no one receive them into his house, so that to those who come not only peace and communion but even roof and hospitality are denied. Can there be one body and one spirit with such a man, with whom perhaps there is not one soul? So slippery, changeable and uncertain! And yet Stephen is not ashamed to lend such men his protection against the Church, and to tear the brotherhood apart in order to bring in heretics; and besides, to call Cyprian a false Christ, a false apostle and a deceitful workman? He anticipates all these things, being conscious of them in himself, so that by a lie he may object to another what he himself deserves to hear." So far these writers, whose letter Pamelius admits he would gladly have omitted, after the example of Manutius, had Morellius and Turnebus not brought the earlier letters to light.

units.la: ECCLESIÆ ROMANÆ PERIODUS SECUNDA.
units.tr: THE SECOND PERIOD OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.

units.la: Seu
units.tr: Or:

units.la: Historia Ecclesiæ Romanæ Doctrinam puriorem, quoad præcipua, retinentis, at in regimine dominationem assectantis.
units.tr: A history of the Roman Church, retaining the purer doctrine in its principal points, but aspiring to domination in its government.

units.la: Inde à Constantino M. seu A. C. cccxiv. ad Phocam & Bonifacium III. seu A. C. DCVII. usque.
units.tr: From Constantine the Great, or A.D. 314, to Phocas and Boniface III, or A.D. 607.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: XVI. Constantini M. favor & liberalitas Episcoporum Ecclesiæ Rom. ambitionem auxit. Neque tamen Ecclesiæ ejus principatum is agnovit, quod ex historia Donati & Arii in Arelatensi & Nicæna Synodo damnatorum probatur.
units.tr: XVI. The favour and generosity of Constantine the Great increased the ambition of the bishops of the Roman Church. Yet the Church did not acknowledge his primacy, as is proved by the history of Donatus and Arius, who were condemned at the Synods of Arles and Nicaea.

units.la: XVII. Marcus Papa universalis Episcopi titulum sibi arrogat. Julius primus impetrat, ut Episcoporum in Oriente depositorum causam sibi cognoscere denuo liceat, protestantibus tamen Episcopis Orientalibus.
units.tr: XVII. Marcus, Pope, claims for himself the title of universal bishop. Julius I obtains that he may again examine the case of bishops deposed in the East, though the Eastern bishops protested.

units.la: XVIII. Liberius Papa in gratiam Constantii cum Arianis contra Athanasium facit.
units.tr: XVIII. Liberius, Pope, takes the side of the Arians against Athanasius, to win the favour of Constantius.

units.la: XX. Da-
units.tr: XIX. Da-

units.la: XIX. Damasi & Vrsicini pro obtinendo Papatu violenta molimina.
units.tr: XIX. The violent schemes of Damasus and Ursinus to obtain the papacy.

units.la: XX. Hieronymus Ecclesiæ Romanæ ambitione motus, eam cum Babylone comparat.
units.tr: XX. Jerome, moved by the ambition of the Roman Church, compares it with Babylon.

units.la: XXI. Imperatorum Valentiniani, Valentis & Gratiani edictum adversus Cleri Romani avaritiam, ab Hieronymo etiam laudatum, & à Theodosio, Arcadio confirmatum.
units.tr: XXI. The edict of the emperors Valentinian, Valens and Gratian against the greed of the Roman clergy, praised also by Jerome and confirmed by Theodosius and Arcadius.

units.la: XXII. In Concilio Constantinopolitano Episcopus Constantinopolitanus Romano exæquatur.
units.tr: XXII. At the Council of Constantinople, the bishop of Constantinople is made equal to the Roman bishop.

units.la: XXIII. Siricius Papa amplificat potestatem Papalem.
units.tr: XXIII. Siricius, Pope, enlarges papal power.

units.la: XXIV. Et doctrinam etiam inducta lege cœlibatus Sacerdotum contaminat.
units.tr: XXIV. He also defiles doctrine by introducing a law of celibacy for priests.

units.la: XXV. Innocentii I, Zosimi, Bonifacii I, Sixti III, Leonis I, pro stabiliendo Primatu molimina.
units.tr: XXV. The efforts of Innocent I, Zosimus, Boniface I, Sixtus III and Leo I to establish the primacy.

units.la: XXVI. Reclamante Ecclesia Orientali in Concilio cumprimis Chalcedonensi, quo prærogativa Romani non juri Divino, sed humano & politico accepta fertur. Inde æmulatio Romanos inter & Constantinopolitanos gliscere cœpit.
units.tr: XXVI. The Eastern Church objected, especially at the Council of Chalcedon, where the Roman prerogative is said to have been accepted not by divine right but by human and political right. From this, rivalry between the Romans and the Constantinopolitans began to grow.

units.la: XXVII. Felix III. Acacium Constantinopolitanum excommunicat: hic illius nomen è diptychis eradit. Gelasius I. primatum suum ex jure divino arcessere conatur.
units.tr: XXVII. Felix III excommunicates Acacius of Constantinople, and he erases Felix's name from the diptychs. Gelasius I tries to derive his primacy from divine right.

units.la: XXVIII. Romæ vastatio à populis septentrionalibus ambitionis affectum in Pontificibus non extinxit; teste historia Symmachi Papæ electi.
units.tr: XXVIII. The devastation of Rome by the northern peoples did not extinguish the love of ambition in the popes, as the history of Symmachus, elected pope, shows.

units.la: XXIX. Seculum sextum promovendo Pontificio Regno, ob absentiam Imperatorum, hæreticos Romam appellantes, & barbaros Pontificibus adulantes, præ cæteris opportunum fuit.
units.tr: XXIX. In the sixth century, the absence of the emperors, the heretics who appealed to Rome, and the barbarians who flattered the popes made the time especially favourable for advancing the papal kingdom.

units.la: XXX. Hormisdæ Papæ pro stabiliendo Papæ in Occidente & Oriente conatus; resistentibus Johanne Patriarcha Constantinopolitano, Anastasio & Justino Impp.
units.tr: XXX. The efforts of Pope Hormisdas to establish the papacy in West and East, opposed by John, patriarch of Constantinople, and by the emperors Anastasius and Justin.

units.la: XXXI. Johannes P. Constantinopoli legatione fungens cum Epiphanio Patr. de Primatu contendit. Redux à Theodorico in carcerem compingitur.
units.tr: XXXI. Pope John, acting as envoy at Constantinople, contended with Epiphanius the patriarch about the primacy. On his return, Theodoric threw him into prison.

units.la: XXXII. JuXXXI. Justiniani de sede Rom. sensus. XXXII. Concilii Constantinopolitani V. historia. Defectio Episcoporum Italorum ab Ecclesia Romana. XXXIII. Johannes jejunator Constantinopolitanus Patr. Oecumenici titulum sibi vendicat. XXXIV. Indignantibus multum Pelagio Papa & Gregorio I. Magno, qui apud Imper. Mauritium Antichristi præcursorem insignit, quisquis titulum eum affectat. XXXV. Vaticinium Gregorii M. de sequentibus temporibus.
units.tr: XXXI. Justinian's view of the Roman see. XXXII. History of the Fifth Council of Constantinople. The defection of the Italian bishops from the Roman Church. XXXIII. John the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople, claims for himself the title of Ecumenical Patriarch. XXXIV. Pope Pelagius and Gregory I the Great were greatly indignant; Gregory, at the court of the emperor Maurice, branded whoever aspired to that title as the forerunner of Antichrist. XXXV. Gregory the Great's prophecy about the following times.

units.la: XVI. Tque hi fuerunt Episcoporum Romanorum, sævientibus adhuc persecutionibus, pro obtinendo in reliquas Ecclesias primatu conatus, quorum in bona licet causa ambitione non segniter jam tum Satan abusus est. Qui etiam, ex quo Constantinus M. Ecclesiae Christianae pacem reddidit, eique favere coepit, ambitionis hujus igniculos, ejus liberalitate incalescentes, immane quantum flatu suo accendit. Nam profusis opibus Ecclesiae donatis, crescere Episcopis ipsis supercilium coepit, auditaque, uti Silvestri Legenda testatur, coelitus vox est: Hodie venenum effusum est in Ecclesiam. Nihilominus, cum de Donato ab Ecclesiis Africanis damnato ageretur, Constantinus causam non Miltiadi, Romano Episcopo, judicandam obtulit, sed judices pro sua authoritate dedit Episcopos, Maternum Coloniensem, Rheticium Augustodunensem, & Marinum Arelatensem, quibus post ejusdem diplomate adjunctus etiam Miltiades Episcopus Romanus est. Cumque eorum judicio Donatus non acquiesceret, Constantinus Arelatensem Synodum, cui ipsemet praesedit, judicem constituit, tandemque Mediolani sententiam tulit. In Arii quoquoque controversia nec solus Episcopus Romanus judicem egit, nec praecipuas etiam partes habuit, Constantino & convocante & moderante Nicaenam Synodum, in qua Alexandrini Episcopi ἐξουσία, exemplo Romani, confirmata est, cautumque insuper, ne Episcopus fieret praeter sententiam Metropolitani; allaboratum quoque, ne in civitate una plures uno Episcopi essent. Sic igitur Episcopalis dignitas & potestas incrementa cepit, ut Romani tamen Episcopi supra reliquos πρωτεροχὴ & praerogativa nulla hactenus emicuerit, quin ipse potius Conciliari decreto ad curiam parium relegatus, ejusque conatus sufflaminati fuerint. De quo cum alios, tum maxime doctissimas Beveregii in Concilium Nicaenum, Canonem inprimis ejus sextum, aliorumque etiam animadversiones videre est.
units.tr: XVI. And these were the attempts of the bishops of Rome, while persecutions still raged, to obtain primacy over the other churches. Satan, even then, was not slow to abuse for ambition a cause that was in itself good. From the time Constantine the Great restored peace to the Christian Church and began to favour it, Satan, by his breath, kindled to a vast degree the sparks of this ambition, which grew hot through Constantine's generosity. For once wealth was poured out and given to the Church, the bishops themselves began to grow proud. And, as the Legend of Silvester attests, a voice was heard from heaven: Today poison has been poured out into the Church. Nevertheless, when the case of Donatus, condemned by the African churches, was under discussion, Constantine did not refer the matter for judgement to Miltiades, the Roman bishop, but on his own authority appointed as judges the bishops Maternus of Cologne, Rheticius of Autun and Marinus of Arles, to whom Miltiades, the Roman bishop, was afterwards added by the same imperial edict. And when Donatus would not accept their judgement, Constantine appointed the Synod of Arles, over which he himself presided, as judge, and at last pronounced sentence at Milan. In the controversy with Arius too, the Roman bishop neither alone acted as judge nor held the chief part, since Constantine both summoned and presided over the Synod of Nicaea. At that synod the authority of the bishop of Alexandria was confirmed, on the model of the Roman bishop's; and it was further provided that no one should be made bishop against the judgement of the metropolitan, and care was also taken that there should not be more than one bishop in a single city. Thus the episcopal dignity and power grew, yet no primacy or prerogative of the Roman bishop above the rest has yet emerged; rather, by a decree of the Council, he was himself relegated to the rank of the equals, and his attempts were checked. On this subject one may consult Beveridge's most learned commentary on the Council of Nicaea, above all on its sixth canon, and also the observations of others.

units.la: XVII. Nihil tamen Episcopi Romani, ut rerum in Ecclesia potirentur, reliqui fecerunt.
units.tr: XVII. The bishops of Rome nevertheless left nothing undone in order to gain control of affairs in the Church.

units.la: Et Marcus quidem A. cccxxxv. Papa lectus, si genuina est, quae ei ad Anastasium & Aegypti Episcopos adscribitur Epistola sibi Vniversalis Episcopi titulum arrogans, sic Ecclesiae Romanae jura detonat: Ecclesia Romana immaculata semper mansit, & Domino providente & Beato Petro opem ferente in futurum manebit. Item: Dominus discipulorum suorum principi in suis fatus est Evangeliis: Petre, rogavi pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. Post eum Julius I. Episcopos in Oriente diversas ob causas loco motos, pro authoritate sua in integrum restituere conatus est. De quo ita Sozomenus Histor. Eccles. III. 8. Οἷα δὲ τῆς πάντων κινδυνούσης ... Quoniam propter sedis dignitatem omnium cura ad ipsum spectabat, suam cuique Ecclesiam restituit. Quin A. cccxlvii. suggerente Osio, in Synodo Sardicensi conditus est canon, quo Episcopi depositi, bonae causae sibi conscii, ad Julium
units.tr: Marcus, who was elected pope in A.D. 335, if the letter ascribed to him addressed to Anastasius and the bishops of Egypt is genuine, arrogating to himself the title of universal bishop, thunders thus on behalf of the rights of the Roman Church: The Roman Church has always remained immaculate, and with the Lord providing and blessed Peter bringing help, it will remain so in the future. Likewise: The Lord said in his Gospels to the prince of his disciples: Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. After him, Julius I tried, by his own authority, to restore to their places bishops who had been removed from office in the East for various reasons. Sozomen speaks of this in his Ecclesiastical History III.8: Οἷα δὲ τῆς πάντων κινδυνούσης [since, because of the dignity of the see, the care of all things belonged to him, he restored each to his own church]. Indeed, in A.D. 347, at the suggestion of Hosius, a canon was enacted at the Synod of Sardica, by which bishops who were deposed, conscious of a good cause, were to be sent back to Julius, the Roman bishop, who was to examine their case again.

units.la: Julius primus impetrat, ut Episcopo-lium lium Episcopum Romanum remittuntur, qui causam eorum denuo cognituros sit. Quodque Julio in particulari casu tributum, ad omnes generaliter extendere successores non dubitârunt. Sed protestati tamen adversus hæc molimina Orientales Episcopi sunt, diserte asseverantes, se χειροτονίζεσθαι παρ' αὐτῶ legem ab eo accipere nolle, uti Socrates Hist. Eccl. lib. II. 17. testatur.
units.tr: Julius I obtained that bishops deposed were to be sent back to the Roman bishop, who was to examine their case again. And what had been granted to Julius in a particular case, the successors did not hesitate to extend generally to all. But the Eastern bishops protested against these attempts, plainly asserting that they would not accept the law that they should be ordained παρ' αὐτῶ [by him], as Socrates testifies in his Ecclesiastical History II.17.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Julio surrogatus A. cccl i i. Liberius, Constantio Imperatore Ariano dominante, metu ejus subactus, & ne Papalis dominatus detrimenti quid pateretur, in gratiam Constantii Arianis adversus ὁμοούσιον & Athanasium subscribit, editam Sirmii confessionem approbat, lapsuque suo in errorem plurimos inducit. Cui merito sic Hilarius occlamavit: Hæc est perfidia Ariana! Anathema tibi à me dictum, Liberi, & sociis tuis! Iterum tibi anathema, & tertio, prævaricator Liberi! De quo quidem Liberii Arianismo eruditissimam Larroquani dissertationem nuper editam, cui lubet, consulat.
units.tr: Julius was succeeded by Liberius in the year 352. While Constantius, an Arian emperor, held power, Liberius was cowed by fear of him. To keep the Papal domination from suffering any harm, he sided with the Arians against the homoousion [ὁμοούσιον] and against Athanasius. He approved the confession published at Sirmium and, by his fall, led many into error. Hilarius rightly cried out against him: "This is Arian treachery! I pronounce anathema upon you, Liberius, and upon your associates! Again I pronounce anathema upon you, and a third time, traitor Liberius!" Whoever wishes may consult the very learned dissertation on Liberius's Arianism by Larroque, published recently.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: In eligendo A. cccLxv i. successore Liberij, Damasi & Ursicini ambientium & contendentium studiis immane quantum certatum est. Liber Pontificalis in sede collocatum Damasum dicit, quia fortior, & plurima cum eo multitudo erat. Ruffinus, author coævus lib. II. 10. sic ea de re scribit: Ex facto tanta seditio, imo vero tanta bella coorta sunt, alterutrum defendentibus populis, ut replerentur humano sanguine orationum loca. Ammiano Marcellino lib. 27. teste in Basilica Sicinini, ubi ritus Christiani conventiculum erat, uno die centum triginta septem reperta cadavera perem̃ptorum, efferataque diu plebs ægrè postea delinita est. Hieronymus quoque Epist. 61. testis est, Prætextatum Prætorio Præfectum Consulem designatum Episcopi Romani, Matronarum oblationibus, uti Ammianus Marcellinus loquitur, ditati opulentia illectum dicere solitum esse: Facite me Romanæ Vrbis Episcopum, & ero protinus Christianus. Ita Paparum splendor maximis jam Potestatibus esse invidendus coepit.
units.tr: In electing the successor to Liberius in the year 365, the rival efforts of Damasus and Ursinus, who were canvassing and contending for the see, caused an enormous struggle. The Liber Pontificalis says that Damasus was placed in the see because he was the stronger, and because he had the larger crowd with him. Rufinus, a contemporary author (Book 2, ch. 10), writes about the matter thus: "From this such strife, indeed such wars, arose, each side defended by its people, that the places of prayer were filled with human blood." Ammianus Marcellinus (Book 27) testifies that in the Basilica of Sicininus, which was the meeting place of the Christian religion, one hundred and thirty-seven corpses of the slain were found in a single day, and the enraged populace was afterwards calmed only with difficulty. Jerome also bears witness (Letter 61) that Praetextatus, the Praetorian Prefect and designated Consul, who was enriched by the offerings of matrons, as Ammianus Marcellinus puts it, used to say, having been drawn in by the wealth of the Bishop of Rome: "Make me Bishop of the city of Rome, and I shall at once become a Christian." Thus the splendour of the Popes began to be envied even by the greatest powers.

units.la: XX. Vixit tum Hieronymus, cui ambitio & fastus Papalis navseam ita movit, ut non obscure in Ecclesia Romana Babylonem commonstraverit. Inducit in Epist. ad Marcellam Paulum & Eustochium sic Marcellam compellantes: Lege Apocalypsin Johannis, & quid de muliere purpurata, & scripta in fronte ejus blasphemia, septem montibus, aquis multis & Babylonis cantetur exitu, contuere. Est quidem ibi Sancta Ecclesia: sunt trophea Apostolorum & Martyrum: Est Christi vera confessio; est ab Apostolis prædicata fides. Sed ipsa ambitio, ipsa potentia a bono avertunt. Ipse vero Præf. in libros Didymi de Spiritu S. sic liberè os suum resolvit: Cum, inquit, in Babylone versarer, & purpurata Meretricis essem colonus, & jure Quiritum viverem, volui garrire aliquid de Spiritu Sancto, & cæptum opusculum ejusdem Urbis Pontifici dedicare. Et ecce illa olla, quæ in Jeremia post baculum cernitur, à facie aquilonis cœpit ardere, & Pharisæorum occlamavit senatus, & nullus scriba vel fictus, sed omnis quasi indicto sibi prælio doctrinarum, adversus me imperitiæ factio conjuravit. Illica ego velut postliminio Hierosolymam sum reversus, & post Romuli casam, Lupercalia, diversorium Mariæ & Servatoris spelunca aspexi. Quid hic Hieronymo Babylon nisi Clerus Romanus, quem senatum Pharisaicum, factionem ignorantium, conjurationem vocat? Alibi ad Eustoch. epist. 22. ad Nepot. 2. Cleri Romani luxuriam & in emungendis hominibus, ambiendisque seniorum virorum & fœminarum legatis, artes turpiaque officia graviter exagitat. Huc etiam de fastu Ecclesiæ Romanæ querela S. Basilii supra memorata referenda est.
units.tr: XX. Jerome lived at that time, and papal ambition and pride so disgusted him that he openly pointed to Babylon in the Church of Rome.
