In his Letter to Marcella he introduces Paula and Eustochium addressing Marcella in these words: Read the Apocalypse of John, and look at what is said of the woman clothed in purple, with blasphemy written on her forehead, of the seven hills, the many waters, and the fall of Babylon. There indeed is the holy Church; there are the trophies of the Apostles and Martyrs; there is the true confession of Christ; there is the faith preached by the Apostles. But ambition itself, and power itself, turn people away from the good. In his own Preface to the books of Didymus on the Holy Spirit he speaks his mind even more freely: When, he says, I was living in Babylon, and was a dweller in the house of the purple harlot, and lived under the Roman law, I wished to say something about the Holy Spirit and to dedicate the little work I had begun to the Pontiff of that city. And behold, that pot which is seen in Jeremiah, which is after the staff, began to burn from the face of the north, and the Pharisees' senate cried out, and not one scribe, real or pretended, but the whole faction of ignorance, as though a battle of learning had been declared against me, conspired against me. There I returned, as by right of postliminy, to Jerusalem, and after Romulus's hut, the Lupercalia, the inn of Mary, and the Saviour's cave, I looked upon them. What is Babylon here for Jerome, if not the Roman clergy, whom he calls a Pharisaic senate, a faction of ignorant men, a conspiracy? Elsewhere (Letter 22 to Eustochium; Letter 2 to Nepotian) he sharply attacks the luxury of the Roman clergy, their skill in fleecing people, and their base practices of courting the legacies of elderly men and women. The complaint of St Basil, mentioned above, about the pride of the Church of Rome should also be referred to here.

units.la: XXI. Memorabilis est Imperatorum Valentiniani, Valentis & Gratiani lex Damaso inscripta, quam in C. Theod. lib. 16. de Episc. & Cler. videre est. Cum enim insatiabilis jam videretur Clericorum vorago, huic veluti carcinomati cauterium adhibituri prohibent: Ne Ecclesiastici, vel qui volunt continentium se nominibus nuncupari, viduarum ac pupillorum domos adeant. Ut nihil de ejus mulieris, cui se privatim sub praetextu religionis adjunxerunt liberalitate quacunque, vel extremo judicio possint adipisci, & omne in tantum efficax sit, quod alicui horum ab his fuerit derelictum, ut nec per subjectam personam valeant aliquid, vel donatione, vel testamento percipere. Quin, ajunt, si forte post admonitionem legis nostrae aliquid his de foeminis, vel donatione, vel extremo judicio putaverint relinquendum, id fiscus usurpet. Lecta in Ecclesiis Romae. Quam legem etiam Hieronymus Epist. cit. sic commendat, ut causam ejus magnopere vituperet. Pudet, inquit, dicere: Sacerdotes idolorum, mimi & aurigae, & scorta haereditates capiunt. Solis Clericis & Monachis hac lege prohibetur, non a persecutoribus, sed a Principibus Christianis. Nec de Lege conqueror, sed doleo, cur meruerimus hanc Legem. Cauterium bonum est: Sed quod mihi Vulnus, ut indigeam cauterio? Provida severaque Legis cautio: & tamen nec sic refrenatur avaritia. Per fidei commissa legi illudimus, & quasi majora sint Imperatorum scita quam Christi, leges timemus, Evangelia contemnimus. Cumque licentia cleri pergeret, Imperatores Valentinianus, Theodosius & Arcadius legem hanc L. 27. de Episc. & Cler. in C. Theod. sic ingeminant roborantque: Nihil de monilibus & supellectili caeterisque claris domus insignibus sub Religionis defensione consumant viduae: sed universa in liberos proximos transscribat, ac si quando diem obierit, nullam Ecclesiam, nullum clericum, nullum pauperem haeredem scribat. Tantae molis erat Cleri Romani avaritiam, ne perrumperet, coercere.
units.tr: XXI. The law of the Emperors Valentinian, Valens and Gratian, addressed to Damasus, is noteworthy and can be seen in the Theodosian Code, Book 16, On Bishops and Clergy. For since the clerical maw already seemed insatiable, they prescribed this, as if applying a cautery to a cancer: Let ecclesiastics, or those who wish to be called by the names of continent persons, not visit the houses of widows and orphans. Let them gain nothing from the generosity of any woman whom they have joined privately under the pretext of religion, either by a final judgment or in any other way. Let this be so effective that whatever has been left to any of them by such women cannot be received by them, either by gift or by will, even through a person put in their place. Indeed, they say, if perhaps after the admonition of our law they think anything from these women should be left to them, either by gift or by final judgment, let the treasury seize it. Read in the churches of Rome. Jerome too commends this law in the letter already cited, in such a way that he greatly censures the cause of it: I am ashamed to say it: the priests of idols, mimes, charioteers and prostitutes take inheritances. Only clerics and monks are forbidden this by the law, not by persecutors but by Christian princes. I do not complain about the law, but I grieve that we have deserved such a law. A cautery is good, but what good is it to me if I have a wound that needs a cautery? It is a wise and strict precaution of the law, and yet avarice is not restrained even so. We mock the law through trust arrangements, and as if the decrees of emperors were greater than those of Christ, we fear the laws and despise the Gospels. And when the clergy's licence continued, the Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius repeated and reinforced this law in Law 27, On Bishops and Clergy, in the Theodosian Code: Let widows not spend anything on necklaces, household furniture, or other notable ornaments of the house under the pretext of defending religion; but let them transfer everything to their nearest children, and if they should die, let them name no church, no cleric, no poor person as heir. So great a task was it to check the avarice of the Roman clergy and keep it from breaking through.

units.la: XXII. Damaso adhuc Pontifice A. cccLxxxi. indicente Theodosio, & moderante Nectario Episcopo Constantinopolitano, celebrata est Synodus Generalis Constantinopolitana, ne quidem interveniente Legato Damasi: Ibi Patres Synodi Nicaenae vestigia retegunt, Provincias disfidiis vitandis partiuntur, & Can. 3. sedis Constantinopolitanæ Episcopo ᾱρεσβεῖα τῆ τιμῆς μετὰ τὴ Ῥώμης ἐπισκοπον pri- vilegia honoris post Romanum Episcopum, eo scilicet argumento, quòd Constantinopolis sit νέα Ῥώμη nova Roma decernunt; quòd fusius Socrates, Hist. Eccles. V. 8. & Sozomenus lib. VII. 9. narrant. Quæ quidem πρεσβεία τιμῆς privilegia honoris non tam ad prærogativam potestatis (utpote quæ in Chalcedonensi demum Synodo ei accessit) quàm dignitatis referenda esse, Doctiff. Beveregius observat. ad Can. 3. ostendit.
units.tr: XXII. While Damasus was still Pope, in the year 381, at the instigation of Theodosius, and under the presidency of Nectarius, Bishop of Constantinople, a general Council was held at Constantinople, at which not even a legate of Damasus was present. There the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea were traced in their footsteps, the provinces were divided to avoid disputes, and in Canon 3 they decreed that the Bishop of the see of Constantinople should have "the privileges of honour after the Bishop of Rome" [πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς μετὰ τὸν Ῥώμης ἐπίσκοπον], on the ground that Constantinople is "New Rome" [νέα Ῥώμη]. Socrates (Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, ch. 8) and Sozomen (Book 7, ch. 9) relate this more fully. Doctor Beveridge, in his notes on Canon 3, shows that these "privileges of honour" [πρεσβεῖα τιμῆς] are to be referred not so much to a prerogative of power (which was granted to that see only later, at the Council of Chalcedon) as to dignity.

units.la: XXIII. Damasi successor Siricius & Papalem potesta- tem amplificare strenuè laboravit, & doctrinam polluere cœpit.
units.tr: XXIII. Siricius, the successor of Damasus, zealously laboured to enlarge papal power and began to corrupt doctrine.

units.la: Is enim sub A. cccLxxxvI. in prima ad Himerium Tarraconensem Epistola decretoria. Statuta, inquit, sedis Apostolicæ, vel canonum venerabilia definita, nulli Sacerdotum Domini ignorare fit liberum. Rogat proin, ut in omnium Coëpiscoporum perferri faciat notionem, & non solum eorum, qui in sua sunt diœcesi constituti, sed etiam ad universos Carthaginenses, atque Boëticos, Lusitanicos, Gallicos, &c. Per Himerii ambitionem ad suam ipsius per totam Hispaniam sibi viam sternit. In quarta etiam ad Africanos Episcopos epistola præfractè vetat, ne quis extra conscientiam sedis Apostolicæ, hoc est, Primatis, ausit ordinare Episcopum. Neque tamen Africani Episcopi herbam statim porrigunt. Illi enim in Synodo Carthaginensi secunda vetant quidem Episcopum ordinare inconsulto Primate, sed cujuslibet Provinciæ, non Romano: in tertia verò ulterius progressa primæ sedis Episcopum, Principem Sacerdotem; & Episcopum universalem, Romanum etiam Pontificem appellari prohibent.
units.tr: In his first decretal letter, to Himerius of Tarragona, under the year 386, he says: The statutes of the Apostolic See, or the venerable decisions of the canons, must not be unknown to any priest of the Lord. He therefore asks that they be made known to all fellow bishops, not only to those established in his own diocese but also to all the bishops of Carthage, Baetica, Lusitania, Gaul, and so on. Through the ambition of Himerius he thus paves his own way through the whole of Spain. In his fourth letter, too, to the African bishops, he peremptorily forbids anyone to presume to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the Apostolic See, that is, of the Primate. Yet the African bishops do not at once yield. In the Second Council of Carthage they do forbid ordaining a bishop without the Primate being consulted, but of any province, not specifically the Roman one. In the third council they went further and forbade that the bishop of the first see be called Prince of Priests, universal bishop, or even Roman Pontiff.

units.la: XXIV. In Doctrina idem Siricius innovavit, Cœliba- tus lege inter Ecclesiasticos sancita.
units.tr: XXIV. Siricius also introduced innovations in doctrine, by enacting the law of celibacy among the clergy.

units.la: Quam paulò ante Synodus Nicæna, Episcopis consentientibus explosit. Et primum quidem hanc legem Siricium tulisse, non tantùm Glossa Juris Canonici Dist. 84. c. 3 innuit; sed etiam Clichtovæus, Espensæus, Cassander, alii fatentur. Legem hanc in Epistola ad Himerium expressam videre est. Ubi insigni ignorantia ad eam S. Scripturæ testimonia torquet. Certè Hieronymus Epist. 65. Legis hujus insolentiam graviter detestatur. Et sero admodum in Occidente, in Oriente verò nunquam eam valuisse constat.
units.tr: The Council of Nicaea, with the agreement of the bishops, had rejected this a little earlier. That Siricius was the first to enact this law is suggested not only by the Gloss on the Canon Law, Dist. 84, c. 3, but also admitted by Clichtove, Espencaeus, Cassander and others. The law can be seen set out in the letter to Himerius. There he twists the testimonies of Holy Scripture to support it with remarkable ignorance. Jerome, in Epist. 65, certainly detests the outrageousness of this law with great severity. And it is well established that it took hold very late in the West, and in the East it never prevailed.

units.la: XXV. Nihil deinceps, ut cupitis modò potirentur, intentatum reliquerunt Pontifices, ædilitatem quod ajunt, sine suffragiis gerentes; Innocentius I. qui in Epistola ad Victricium Episcopum Rhotomagensem decrevit, ut majores causæ ad sedem Apostolicam devolvantur, per appellationem scilicet: Zosimus, qui ad Synodum Carthaginensem sextam Legatos misit, qui vicem ibi suam gererent, pertenderentque Episcoporum Africæ esse, concedere appellationem ad sedem Romanam: Bonifacius I. idem per legatos suos, Nicæni etiam Concilii authoritate prætensa, molitus: Sixtus III. de Primatu cum Polychronio Episcopo Hierosolymitano contendens: inprimis autem Leo I. ob excellentem cœtera eruditionem & vigilantissimum adversus Hæreticos, Manichæos cumprimis studium, dictus Magnus, qui Anno circiter cccc. suum illud: Tu es Petrus, strenuè inculcans, Petrus, inquit, petra dicitur, dum fundamentum pronunciatur, &c. In sua sede vivit potestas, excellit authoritas. Fratres omnium Episcoporum noverant esse primatem. Nunquam nisi per ipsum dedit, quicquid aliis non negavit Christus. Cumque ex decreto Concilii Constantinopolitani Episcopus Constantinopolitanus secundam sedem adeptus, in Oriente authoritatem magnam jam, Romanisque invidendam obtineret, idem Leo M. per Legatos suos in Synodo Chalcedonensi intercedere obtentu Nicænorum Canonum, quibus aliter cautum sit, conatur. XXVI. Variè equidem moliminibus & meditamentis hisce Romanorum Pontificum Ecclesia, Orientalis cumprimis se oppositu. In Synodo maximè Chalcedonensi A. ccccli. celebrata, in qua Eutyches à 630. Episcopis damnatus, Leonis M. machinatio repressa, & de thronis seu sedibus Patriarchalibus ejusmodi cusum decretum est. Τῶ ϑεόνῳ ϛ πρεσβυτέρας Ρώμης, ᾧ ἐξ τὸ βασιλεύειν τὴν πόλιν ἐκείνῳ, οἱ πατέρες εἰκότως ἀποδεδώκασι τὰ πρεσβεῖα. Καὶ ἵνα αὐτῷ σκοπῶ κινούμενοι οἱ ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα ϑεοφιλέστατοι ἐπίσκοποι, τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα ἀπένειμαν ἢ τὴ νέας Ρώμης ἀγνωτάτῳ ϑεόνῳ βούλόγως
units.tr: XXV. After this the popes left nothing untried, so that they might at last gain what they wanted, carrying on, as the saying goes, an aedileship without votes. Innocent I, in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, decreed that the greater cases should be referred to the Apostolic See, namely by appeal. Zosimus sent legates to the sixth Council of Carthage to act in his place, and insisted that the bishops of Africa must grant appeal to the Roman See. Boniface I pursued the same aim through his legates, under the pretended authority of the Council of Nicaea. Sixtus III contended over primacy with Polychronius, bishop of Jerusalem. Above all, Leo I, called "the Great" for his excellent learning in other respects and his most watchful zeal against heretics, especially the Manichaeans, around the year 400 vigorously pressed his familiar text, "You are Peter": Peter, he says, is called a rock, while the foundation is proclaimed, and so on. Power lives in his see, authority excels. The brothers of all bishops knew him to be the primate. He never gave to anyone anything that Christ did not deny to others. When, by decree of the Council of Constantinople, the bishop of Constantinople had obtained the second see and already held great authority in the East, and was an object of envy to the Romans, this same Leo the Great tried, through his legates at the Council of Chalcedon, to intervene on the pretext of the canons of Nicaea, in which some other arrangement was made. XXVI. The Eastern Church, especially, set itself against these schemes and contrivances of the Roman pontiffs. Indeed, at the Council of Chalcedon, celebrated in the year 451, where Eutyches was condemned by 630 bishops, the machinations of Leo the Great were checked, and a decree was passed concerning such matters as the jurisdiction of the patriarchal thrones or sees. "To the most holy see of Old Rome, because the city was the seat of empire, the Fathers rightly gave the privileges of seniority. And moved by the same consideration, the one hundred and fifty most God-loving bishops granted equal privileges to the most holy see of New Rome, judging rightly that the city which is honoured by empire and senate, and enjoys privileges equal to the older Rome, should in ecclesiastical matters also be extolled and magnified like it, being second after it" [Τῶ ϑεόνῳ ϛ πρεσβυτέρας Ρώμης, ᾧ ἐξ τὸ βασιλεύειν τὴν πόλιν ἐκείνῳ, οἱ πατέρες εἰκότως ἀποδεδώκασι τὰ πρεσβεῖα. Καὶ ἵνα αὐτῷ σκοπῶ κινούμενοι οἱ ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα ϑεοφιλέστατοι ἐπίσκοποι, τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα ἀπένειμαν ἢ τὴ νέας Ρώμης ἀγνωτάτῳ ϑεόνῳ βούλόγως].

units.la: Sedi senioris Romæ, quod Urbs illa imperaret, Patres jure privilegia tribuerunt. Et eadem consideratione moti centum quinquaginta Deo amantissimi Episcopi æqua privilegia tribuerunt sanctissimæ sedi novæ Romæ, rectè judicantes, urbem quæ & imperio & senatu honorata sit, & æqualibus privilegiis cum seniore Roma fruatur, etiam in rebus Ecclesiasticis non secus ac illam extolli ac magnifieri, secundam post illam existentem. Qui Canon Romanum Episcopum, ad altiora immodicè nitentem, manifestè in ordinem redigit. Primatum quippe Romani Episcopi non juri divino, & successioni Apostolicæ, sed constitutioni Patrum & causæ politicæ, prærogativæ scilicet Urbis adscribit: τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα jura æqualia, potestatis scilicet (nam dignitatis prærogativa jam ante, uti th. XXII. vidimus, Constantinopolitanæ Ecclesiæ concessa fuit) sine respectu ad Romanam Ecclesiam, Constantinopolitanis vindicat; Constantinopolitanum, qui Anatolius tum erat, Romano, Leoni scilicet, excepta primæ sessionis prærogativa (quæ ordinis, prioritatis, potestatis æqualitatem non tollit) æquans, Romani jurisdictionem coercet: denique sine consensu Romani de thronorum jurisdictione statuit. Quam ob causam ne quicquam acriter Leo I. se ei Canoni opposuit: & gliscere inde Romanos inter & Constantinopolitanos perpetuæ æmulationes visæ sunt ; faventibus Romano etiam Alexandriæ & Antiochiæ Episcopis, Constantinopolitani succrescentem authoritatem haud æquo animo ferentibus.
units.tr: To the see of the elder Rome, because that city ruled, the Fathers rightly granted privileges. And moved by the same consideration, the one hundred and fifty most God-loving bishops granted equal privileges to the most holy see of New Rome, judging rightly that the city which is honoured with empire and senate, and enjoys privileges equal to the elder Rome, should in ecclesiastical matters too be exalted and magnified just like it, coming second after it. This canon plainly brings the Roman bishop, who was immoderately striving towards higher things, back into line. For it attributes the primacy of the Roman bishop not to divine right and apostolic succession, but to the constitution of the Fathers and to a political cause, namely the prerogative of the city. By equal privileges (τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα), meaning equal rights of power (for the prerogative of dignity had already been granted to the Church of Constantinople earlier, as we saw in chapter XXII), it claims for the bishop of Constantinople, who was then Anatolius, equality with the Roman, that is, Leo, except for the prerogative of the first session. (This does not remove the equality of order, priority and power.) And it restrains the jurisdiction of Rome. Finally, it decided the jurisdiction over the thrones without the consent of the Roman bishop. For this reason Leo I did not oppose that canon at all sharply. And from this, perpetual rivalries between the Romans and the Constantinopolitans seem to have arisen, with the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch siding with Rome, while they bore the growing authority of Constantinople with no good grace.

units.la: XXVII. Et Anno quidem ccccLxxxiii. Felix III. Papa Romanus in Romano Concilio Acacium Constantinopolitanum, decretæ sibi potestatis vindicem, accusante Johanne Alexandrino, damnavit & excommunicavit. Vicissim Acacius nomen Felicis è diptychis erasit. Euphemius eo restituto tum à Felice, tum à Gelasio jussus eradere nomen Acacii, in animum induxit Papam in judicium vocare, & apud Anastasium eundem criminatus est. Unde etiam in Oriente subortum schisma est. Papæ vero cum iis, qui Acacii memoriam damnare detrectarent, ne quidem communicare amplius dignati sunt. Mox A. ccccxciv. Gelasius I. in Concilio Romæ habito primatum Papæ contra Constantinopolitanorum præsumptionem ex Divino jure asserere conatus est.
units.tr: XXVII. In the year 483, Felix III, Roman pope, in a Roman council condemned Acacius of Constantinople, a champion of the power decreed to him, on the accusation of John of Alexandria, and excommunicated him. In return Acacius erased the name of Felix from the diptychs. Euphemius, when Felix and afterwards Gelasius had ordered him to restore it, and to erase the name of Acacius, resolved to summon the pope to judgment and brought charges against him before Anastasius. From this a schism also arose in the East. The popes, however, did not even deign to communicate any longer with those who refused to condemn the memory of Acacius. Soon afterwards, in the year 494, Gelasius I, in a council held at Rome, tried to assert the primacy of the pope by divine right against the presumption of the Constantinopolitans.

units.la: XXVIII. Jam ante septentrionales populi universam Italiam devastabant, & in eam quasi perrupto aggere, exundabant. Eudoxia Maximi, à qua A. ccccLv. Valentinianus III. interfectus est, conjunx Genserici Vandalum in Italiam vocavit. Is Romam bis cepit, theatra incendit, ornamenta, thesauros abstulit. Avitus, Majoranus, Severus, Anthemius, Olybrius, Glycerius, Julius Nepos, Augustulus ad Ann. ccccLxxv. rerum potiti sunt. Inde Odoacer Herulus, Theodoricus, Athalaricus, Theodatus, Vitiges, Theobaldus, Totilas, Tejas, à Narsete A.DLV. victus, Ariani omnes, Italiam annos septuaginta octo rexerunt. Intra quod tempus bis Roma capta est. Neque tamen diuturnæ & concatenatæ hæ calamitates ambitionis affectum in Romanis Episcopis extinxerunt. Graffabatur illa perpetuo, obrepebat, imperitabat aliis. Eoque etiam deventum, ut Episcopatum Romanum nemo jam nisi per vim, sordes & ambitum consequeretur. In annos Pontificis inquirere, de ejus successione ante obitum pacisci, suffragia numerata pecunia redimere; verbo, jurejurando, sigillo pacta illa contra bonos mores firmare adeò religio non fuit, ut pœne vim legis obtinuerit. Testis ααξιας est historia Symmachi A. cccccxcviii. Papæ electi. De quo sic Sabellicus 8. Ennead. 2. Col. 455. scribit: Fuit Symmachi creatio tumultuosa, ordinumque discordia infamis, estque non inter cives solùm, sed inter ordines etiam opibus & authoritate certatum, quum Senatus in hunc propensior esset, ignobilis multitudo in illum. Testis etiam Romana Synodus, quæ sub ipso Symmacho nefarium ambitum refrænare nequicquam studuit. Testes barbari Reges, Odoacer, Theodoricus, alii, qui authoritate interposita identidem motos fluctus componere necessum habuerunt. Si solam ovium Christi curam animo pio volutâssent: Si aliud in eo munere lucrum non spectâssent Episcopi, tam acriter de Papatu dimicaturos, quis sanus existimet?
units.tr: XXVIII. Already before this the northern peoples were laying waste all of Italy, and, as though the dyke had burst, they overflowed into it. Eudoxia, daughter of Maximus, by whom Valentinian III was killed in the year 455, and wife of Gaiseric, summoned the Vandals into Italy. He took Rome twice, set fire to the theatres, and carried off its ornaments and treasures. Avitus, Majorian, Severus, Anthemius, Olybrius, Glycerius, Julius Nepos and Augustulus held power until the year 475. Then Odoacer the Herulian, Theodoric, Athalaric, Theodatus, Vitiges, Theobald, Totila and Teias, who was defeated by Narses in the year 555, all Arians, ruled Italy for seventy-eight years. Within that time Rome was taken twice. Yet these long and unbroken calamities did not extinguish the ambition of the Roman bishops. That ambition was constantly on the rise, creeping in and lording it over others. It came to such a point that no one could now obtain the Roman bishopric except by violence, filth and bribery. To enquire into the years of the pontiff, to bargain over his succession before his death, to buy votes with counted money, in short, to confirm such bargains against good morals by oath, seal or agreement, was so little regarded as a sin that it almost gained the force of law. The history of Symmachus, elected pope in the year 498, is a witness to this. Of him Sabellicus writes thus (Ennead 8, book 2, col. 455): The election of Symmachus was tumultuous, and the discord of the orders was notorious, and the contest was waged not only between citizens but also between the orders, by wealth and authority, since the Senate was more inclined to him, and the common crowd to the other. The Roman Synod also bears witness, which under Symmachus himself strove in vain to check the wicked ambition. The barbarian kings bear witness too, Odoacer, Theodoric and others, who, by interposing their authority again and again, had to calm the waves that were stirred up. If the bishops had pondered with a devout mind only the care of Christ's sheep, if they had not looked for any other gain in that office, who of sound mind would think they would have fought so fiercely over the papacy?

units.la: XXIX. Seculum imprimis à Christo nato Sextum pro- vehendæ machinationi Pontificum ταμβασιλείαν quandam in Ecclesia meditantium, opportunum supra modum fuit.
units.tr: XXIX. The sixth century after the birth of Christ was exceedingly favourable to the Popes, who were planning a kind of universal kingship [παμβασιλείαν] in the Church.

units.la: Nam & Imperatores peregre, Constantinopoli ut plurimum agebant: & iidem, ut in fide Romanos retinerent, demulcendis Pontificibus, à quorum fere nutu Christianus Romæ populus pendebat, nihil non indulgebant. Septentrionales quoque populi turmatim in Italiam influentes & in ea pedem figere, stabilemque dominationem obtinere parantes, Pontificum gratiam ad id futuram non parum proficuam, exquisitis adulationibus demerebantur. Hæretici, irriguæ herbæ instar succrescentes, modò in Africa, modò in Oriente damnati legitimè profligatique, ut juri se subducerent, seu appellationis specie, seu retractationis spe, Romam se conferebant, non ingrati Pontificibus, quod Primatum sic stabilire viderentur. Omnes denique toto orbe primæ sedis Episcopi gratiam exambiebant, eò quòd Roma Urbs princeps mundi, orbis epitome, & in gravioris momenti rebus consilii quondam fons & origo clueret. Solentque etiam aliâs consultationes frequentes pro supplicationibus haberi, consilium in merum imperium, arbitrium in judicium, seu rem judicatam successu temporis degenerare. Cumque doctrinæ labes disciplinæ corruptelam consequi soleat, mirum equidem non est, in religionem ipsam errores fonticos paulatim irrepere, Sanctorum & Martyrum invocationem & adorationem circa tempus idem radices agere; Ethnicorum pampinos Christi vineam, dum pauci admodum destringebant, & superstitioni grassanti obnitebantur, obumbrare coepisse.
units.tr: For the emperors mostly resided far away at Constantinople, and in order to keep the Romans in the faith they indulged the Popes in everything, since the Christian people at Rome depended almost entirely on their nod. The northern peoples also poured into Italy in droves, and while they were preparing to settle there and gain a stable dominion, they courted the favour of the Popes with elaborate flattery, since that favour would be of no small use to them in this. Heretics, springing up like weeds in watered ground, were condemned and lawfully crushed now in Africa, now in the East. To escape the reach of the law, whether under the pretext of an appeal or in the hope of a retrial, they betook themselves to Rome, which was not ungrateful to the Popes, since it seemed to establish their primacy. Finally, bishops of the first see throughout the whole world courted the favour of the Pope, because the city of Rome was famed as the chief city of the world, an epitome of the globe, and once the fountain and origin of counsel in matters of greater weight. Moreover, frequent consultations were often held for other purposes as well, and counsel gradually degenerated into command, opinion into judgment, or a matter already decided into a settled ruling over time. And since corruption of doctrine usually follows corruption of discipline, it is indeed no wonder that errors of a spreading kind slowly crept into religion itself: the invocation and worship of saints and martyrs took root at about the same time, and the shoots of the pagans began to overshadow the vine of Christ, while only a very few cut them back and resisted the spreading superstition.

units.la: XXX. Anno DXIV. Romanam sedem Cœlius Hormisda occupavit.
units.tr: XXX. In the year 514, Hormisdas, Cœlius, occupied the Roman see.

units.la: Is & in Occidente & Oriente primatum firmare haud segniter perrexit. In Occidente diversis Provinciis vicarios, Galliæ Narbonensi Avitum Viennensem, Hispaniæ cis Bœtim Johannem Tharasconensem, trans Bœtim Salluftium Hispalensem imposuit. Qui, ut supra fratres se extollerent, haud inviti munus illud acceptârunt. In Orientem ad Imperatorem Anastasium Legatos misit, qui religionis causa obortas discordias componerent, Synodique Chalcedonensis adversus Eutychianos decreta stabilirent. A decreto interim Synodi illius præcipuo, quo Patriarchales throni discernebantur, & nova Roma veteri coæquabatur, manifestè recedit, alia licet in causa, protestatus, se præter Synodum Nicænam nihil agnoscere. Excepti ab Anastasio honorificè eidem imponere potius, quàm suadere visi sunt. Cùmque in Patriarcham Johannem incidissent, is jurisdictionem alienam involantes sic allocutus est: Scio Augustorum esse, non Pontificis imperare. Aut si quid foret, in quo hunc, cui Divina curae sunt, jubere oporteat, me eum esse, à quo alii multò melius exspectent jussa, quàm sua exequenda proponant. Dimissi ab Anastasio, insolentia eorum offenso, minùs humaniter sunt. Ejus successor Justinus in eadem causa Constantinopoli Synodum coëgit in cujus Actis Constantinopolitanus Episcopus, in Romani contemptum, Oecumenicus Patriarcha perpetuò appellatur. Ad eam Synodum Hormisdas etiam legatos misit, instructos libello, quo quid subscribendum esset Episcopis Orientis, siquidem cum Romano in gratiam redire vellent, aliaque pro Romano magnifica continebantur. Quibus inter alia sic Justinus respondit: Pro una eademque habeo utrasque Ecclesias, tam senioris quàm novae Romae. Johannes verò Constantinopolitanus Hormisdam simpliciter Fratrem & Comministrum vocat, & suam Ecclesiam Romanae subordinari ubique vetat. In gratiam etiam Hormisdae Acacii & Euphemii nomina è Diptychis erasa sunt: non tamen coeterorum, qui cum iis communicassent quod malè Hormisdam habuit.
units.tr: He pressed on vigorously to strengthen the primacy both in the West and in the East. In the West he appointed vicars over various provinces: Avitus of Vienne for Narbonese Gaul, John of Tarragona for Hispania Citerior, and Sallustius of Seville for the lands beyond the Baetis. Being elevated above their brethren, they accepted that office not unwillingly. To the Emperor Anastasius in the East he sent legates, to settle the disputes that had arisen over religion and to uphold the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon against the Eutychians. Yet he plainly departed from the chief decree of that council, by which the patriarchal thrones were distinguished and New Rome was made equal to Old Rome, protesting, though in another matter, that he recognised nothing beyond the Council of Nicaea. Received with honour by Anastasius, they seemed rather to impose on him than to persuade him. When they came upon Patriarch John, he, intruding on a jurisdiction not his own, addressed them thus: I know it belongs to Emperors to command, not to a Pope. Or if there were anything in which it is fitting to give orders to him to whom divine matters are entrusted, I am the one from whom others would expect commands far better than they would propose to carry out their own. Dismissed by Anastasius, who was offended by their insolence, they were treated with less courtesy. His successor, Justin, in the same cause, convened a council at Constantinople, in whose Acts the bishop of Constantinople, to the scorn of the Roman, is continually styled Ecumenical Patriarch. Hormisdas also sent legates to that council, equipped with a little book stating what the bishops of the East were to subscribe, if they wished to be restored to favour with the Roman, and other grandiose claims for the Roman were contained in it. To these things Justin replied, among other things: I hold both Churches, that of old Rome and that of new Rome, to be one and the same. But John of Constantinople simply calls Hormisdas brother and fellow minister, and forbids his own Church to be made subordinate to the Roman anywhere. Even the names of Acacius and Euphemius were erased from the diptychs to please Hormisdas; not, however, those of the others who had communicated with them, who had done what displeased Hormisdas.

units.la: XXXI. Anno DXXV. Johannes Papa à Theodorico, Rege Ariano, Constantinopolin ad Justinum missus, pacem Arianis, à Justino loco motis, conciliaturus, non satis habuit, pari in loco cum Episcopo Constantinopolitano Epiphanio sedere, obtinuitque tandem, ut supra Epiphanium collocatus, altius subsellium, forte quòd Theodorici Regis nomine legatione fungeretur, occuparet. De honore eidem ab Imperatore Justino Constantinopoli amplissimè exhibito nescio quid ampullatur Liber Pontificalis, quem penes fides sit. Redux à Theodorico ambitionis illius impatiente, seu alias etiam ob causas Ravennae in carcerem detrusus est, in quo etiam supremum diem clausit.
units.tr: XXXI. In the year 525, Pope John was sent by Theodoric, the Arian king, to Justin at Constantinople, to reconcile the Arians, who had been dislodged by Justin. He was not content to sit in the same place as the bishop of Constantinople, Epiphanius, but obtained at last that he should sit above Epiphanius, occupying a higher seat, perhaps because he was acting as legate in the name of King Theodoric. The Liber Pontificalis, in which trust may be placed, babbles something about the honour lavishly shown to him by the Emperor Justin at Constantinople, I know not what. On his return from Theodoric, who was impatient of that ambition, or perhaps for other reasons, he was thrust into prison at Ravenna, and there he also closed his last day.

units.la: XXXI. Johanni secundo Papæ, cui cognomentum fuit Mercurius, ob insignem scilicet eloquentiam, sic Anno DXXXII. Justinianus in Codice lib. I. tit. I. de summa Trinitate (si modo germana est epistola, quod pluribus argumentis Celeberrimus J C. Jacobus Lectius in Præscriptionibus Theologicis negat) abblanditur: Semper nobis fuit magnum studium unitatem vestræ Apostolicæ sedis, & statum Sanctarum DEI Ecclesiarum custodire, qui hactenus obtinet & incommotè permanet, nulla intercedente contrarietate. Ideoque omnes sacerdotes universi Orientalis tractus & subjicere & unire sedi vestræ Sanctitatis properavimus. Justinianus scilicet, si ejus hæc verba sunt, ad se pertinere putavit, ut cui videretur, subjiceret Episcopos; & si videretur, Papam etiam subjiceret sibi. Quod parum sententiæ Pontificum congruit, primatum suum non arbitrio Imperatorum, sed verbis: Tu es Petrus; superstruentium. Sicut autem Pontificii moderni quiritari solent, Justinianum hactenus nimium sibi arrogâsse: ita boni quiritantur merito, Justinianum Pontificiis nimium dedisse. Idem tamen Novella 100. Constantinopolitanum Romano secundum facit. Proin ex mente Justiniani verba, Properavimus subjicere, eum habere sensum videntur, non esse, quòd conqueratur Papa, cùm ei Constantinopolitanus non prælatus, sed secundo post eum loco collocatus, adeoque, quoad ordinis prærogativam, subjectus sit. Caput, fateor, omnium Ecclesiarum Ecclesiam Romanam Justinianus in eadem Epistola, sed suspecta, uti diximus, vocavit. At cùm alia in Lege Ecclesiam Constantinopolitanam caput esse omnium Ecclesiarum aliarum, idem definivit, tum Zeno etiam repetiit, proclive judicatu est, ibi Occidentales, hic Orientales Ecclesias intelligi. Sanè etiam Novella 42. Mennam Constantinopolitanum Patriarcham Oecumenicum Patriarcham insignire Justinianus idem nullus dubitavit.
units.tr: XXXI. To John II, Pope, who was surnamed Mercurius, clearly on account of his remarkable eloquence, Justinian in the year 532 flatters him in the Code, book I, title I, on the most high Trinity (if indeed the letter is genuine, which the most celebrated jurist Jacobus Lectius in his Theological Prescriptions denies on many grounds): It has always been our great concern to guard the unity of your Apostolic see and the state of the holy Churches of God, which has held until now and remains unmoved, with no contrariety intervening. Therefore we have hastened to subject all the priests of the whole Eastern region and to unite them to the see of your Holiness. Justinian, clearly, if these are his words, thought it belonged to him to subject bishops to whom he pleased, and, if he pleased, would subject the Pope to himself as well. This agrees poorly with the view of the Popes, who build their primacy not on the will of emperors but on the words You are Peter. Just as the modern Papists are wont to complain that Justinian had hitherto arrogated too much to himself, so the good justly complain that Justinian gave the Papists too much. Yet in Novella 100 he likewise makes Constantinople second to Rome. Therefore, in Justinian's mind, the words we have hastened to subject seem to have this sense: the Pope has no cause for complaint, since the bishop of Constantinople was not set above him but placed second after him, and so, as far as precedence of rank goes, was subject to him. I admit that in the same letter, though a suspect one, as we have said, Justinian called the Roman Church head of all the Churches. But since in another law he defined that the Church of Constantinople is the head of all other Churches, and Zeno later repeated the same, it is easy to judge that there Western and here Eastern churches are meant. Indeed, in Novella 42, Justinian likewise did not hesitate to style Menas, the patriarch of Constantinople, Ecumenical Patriarch.

units.tr: XXXII. In the year-

units.la: XXXII. Anno DLIII. Constantinopoli Synodus quinta celebrata est, invito equidem Vigilio, Romano Pontifice, cujus authoritatem licet Baronius, & post ipsum Halloixius floccipenderint, afferere tamen adversus eosdem Henricus de Noris, Augustinianus Monachus, dedita operâ non dubitavit. Ipse quidem Vigilius, quòd Synodum illam rejiceret, à Justiniano in exilium actus est. Ex eo tamen, cùm Concilium illud, Epistola ad Eutychium Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum exarata, & non itapridem ex MS. Veteri, unà cum Petri de Marca ad eam animadversionibus, à Stephano Baluzio edita, approbare se profiteretur, revocatus, in Sicilia, cùm Romam proficisceretur, mortuus est. Inde Aquilejensis, Mediolanensis, Ravennensis, aliique tractuum eorum Episcopi sese authoritati Ecclesiæ Romanæ, cujus propemodum conclamatæ tum res erant, subtraxerunt, Synodum etiam Constantinopolitanam ejurantes. Quos Pelagius I. per Narsetem & Pelagius II. per Smaragdum Exarchum in ordinem redigere ne quicquam laborârunt. XXXIII. Neque Romæ tantum Veteris Pontifices, sed Novæ quoque eundem in modum rebus cessere secundis. Quinimo id Constantinopolitani Episcopi agebant, ut Romanos nova præsumptione atque superbia, uti Gregorius Regist. lib. IV. epist. 34. loquitur, superarent. Johannes enim, cui à Jejuniis νηστευτὴς seu Jejunatoris inditum cognomentum est, animadvertens scilicet, imperiale solium Constantinopoli, & Ravennæ Exarchatus sedem stabilitam, Romam à Longobardis obsessam, Romanum proin Episcopum magnas in angustias redactum; A. DLXXX. contra Deum, ita Gregorius idem, lib. VII. epist. 69. loquitur, contra pacem Ecclesiæ, in omnium despectum & injuriam Sacerdotum, modestiæ ac mensuræ suæ terminos excedens, & illicitè in Synodo superbum ac pestiferum Oecumenici Patriarchæ sive Universalis Episcopi, sibi vocabulum usurpavit.
units.tr: XXXII. In the year 553 a fifth synod was held at Constantinople, though Vigilius, the Roman Pontiff, was unwilling. Baronius, and Halloixius after him, held his authority in low esteem, but Henricus de Noris, an Augustinian monk, did not hesitate to assert it against them, and worked hard at it. Vigilius himself, because he rejected that synod, was driven into exile by Justinian. Afterwards, however, he professed that he approved that council, as set out in his letter to Eutychius, Patriarch of Constantinople. That letter was published by Stephen Baluze not long ago, from an old manuscript, together with Pierre de Marca's notes on it. Vigilius was recalled, but he died in Sicily on his way to Rome. Thereupon the bishops of Aquileia, Milan, Ravenna and other bishops of those regions withdrew from the authority of the Roman Church, which at that time was almost completely in ruin, and they also repudiated the Constantinopolitan synod. Pelagius I, through Narses, and Pelagius II, through Smaragdus the Exarch, took no little trouble to bring them back into line. XXXIII. Not only the old pontiffs at Rome but the new ones too, at New Rome, things went their way. Indeed the bishops of Constantinople aimed to outdo the Romans with a new presumption and pride, as Gregory puts it, Register, book IV, letter 34. John, who was given the surname Jejunator [νηστευτὴς] (the Faster), noticed, of course, that the imperial throne was established at Constantinople, and the seat of the Exarchate at Ravenna, while Rome was besieged by the Lombards and the Roman bishop was therefore reduced to great straits. In the year 580, as Gregory says again, book VII, letter 69, against God, against the peace of the Church, to the contempt and injury of all priests, exceeding the limits of his modesty and measure, he unlawfully usurped for himself in a synod the proud and pestilent title of Ecumenical Patriarch or Universal Bishop.

units.la: XXXIV. Ea res Romanorum Pontificum, uti mos est ingenii humani contra audentius ire, contentionem auxit, & rabidam stimulavit orexin.
units.tr: XXXIV. This matter, since it is the habit of the human mind to go more boldly against [authority], increased the contention of the Roman pontiffs and stirred up a raging appetite.

units.la: Et Pelagius quidem secundus, obsidione urbis Romæ soluta levatus, collecto animo Johannem districtissima, uti loc. cit. Gregorius loquitur, increpatione admonuit, ut se à novo & temerario superstitionis nomine cohiberet. In Epistola ejusdem Pelagii ad Constantinopolitanæ Synodi Episcopos scripta inter alia hæc verba habentur: Adversarius noster Diabolus, qui contra humiles sævicns, sicut Leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret, non jam, ut cernimus, cautos circuit; sed ita valide in quibusdam Ecclesiæ membris dentem figit, ut nulli sit dubium, quin, nisi unanimiter, favente Domino, cunctorum provida Pastorum turba concurrat, omne citius ovile dilaniet. Perpenditis, fratres charissimi, quid è vicino subsequatur, cùm & è Sacerdotibus erumpunt tam perversa primordia. Quia enim juxta est ille, de quo scriptum est: Ille est Rex super universos filios superbiæ, quod non sine gravi dolore dicere compellor, dum frater & Coepiscopus noster Johannes mandata Dominica, & Apostolica præcepta, regulasque Patrum despiciens, cùm per elationem præcurrere conatur in nomine; puta, Antichristum. Manifeste enim ad locum 2 Thess. II. 4. alludit. Subjungit secundam rationem: quòd ex ea, quam prætendebat, humilitate, universa sibi tentet adscribere, quæ soli uni capiti cohærent, nempe Christo. Alia eundem in sensum non minùs prægnantia subjicit. Neque minori ardore Johannem hunc Jejunatorem persequitur Pelagii successor Gregorius I. cognomento Magnus, qui primus se servum servorum appellavit. In Epistola ad Johannem illum, Universalem Episcopum dici, & Solum Episcopum dici, perinde esse asserit. Revera enim si unus est universalis Episcopus, reliquis non datur esse Episcopis, sed universalis illius Episcopi vicariis duntaxat & subdelegatis. Epistola ad Constantiam Augustam, quæ Epist. lib. IV. ep. 34. est:
units.tr: And Pelagius II, relieved when the siege of Rome was lifted, gathered his spirits and admonished John with the most severe rebuke, as loc. cit. Gregory says, that he should restrain himself from the new and rash name of superstition. In a letter of the same Pelagius to the bishops of the Constantinopolitan synod, these words are found among others: Our adversary the Devil, who rages against the humble, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. He no longer goes about cautiously, as we see; but he so firmly fixes his tooth in certain members of the Church that there is no doubt that, unless by the Lord's favour the whole provident company of ministers comes together unanimously, he will tear apart every sheepfold quickly. You weigh, most beloved brethren, what follows from nearby, since such perverse beginnings break out even from among priests. For because he is near, of whom it is written: "He is King over all the sons of pride," which I am compelled to say not without heavy grief, while our brother and fellow bishop John, despising the Lord's commands, the Apostolic precepts and the rules of the Fathers, tries to run ahead by elation in name, namely Antichrist. Clearly he alludes to 2 Thess. 2:4. He adds a second reason: that by the humility he pretends, he tries to claim for himself everything that belongs only to one Head, namely Christ. He adds other points of equal weight to the same effect. Pelagius's successor, Gregory I, surnamed the Great, who was the first to call himself servant of servants, pursues this John the Faster with no less ardour. In his letter to John he asserts that to be called Universal Bishop and to be called Sole Bishop amount to the same thing. For indeed, if there is one universal bishop, the others are not allowed to be bishops, but only vicars and sub-delegates of that universal bishop. The letter to Constantina Augusta, which is Epist. lib. IV. ep. 34, runs:

units.la: Per omnipotentem Dominum rogo, inquit, ne pietatis vestrae tempora permittatis unius hominis elatione maculari: alludens ut ibi, ita & alibi ad illum ὑψηλαυχούμενον sese efferentem seu elatum de quo S. Paulus 2 Thess. II. 4. vaticinatur. Subjicit: In hac ejus superbia quid aliud, nisi propinqua jam esse Antichristi tempora designatur. Quia videlicet illum imitatur (Luciferum) qui spretis in Sociali gaudio Angelorum legionibus ad culmen conatus est singularitatis erumpere, dicens: super astra cæli exaltabo solium, &c. Ero similis Altissimo. Epistola ad Mauritium Imp. quæ lib. IV. Epist. 32. est, eodem sensu: Cunctis, inquit, Evangelium scientibus hiquet, quod voce Dominica Sancto, & omnium Apostolorum Petro principi Apostolo, totius Ecclesiæ cura commissa est. Cura ei totius Ecclesiæ & principatus committitur; & tamen Universalis Apostolus non vocatur. Et Vir Sanctissimus, Consacerdos meus, Johannes vocari Universalis Episcopus conatur. Exclamare cogor ac dicere: O tempora, O mores! Ea cuncta in Europa barbarorum juri sunt tradita. Destructæ urbes, eversa castra, depopulatæ provinciæ, nullus terrarum cultor inhabitat. Et tamen Sacerdotes, qui in pavimento & cinere flentes jacere debuerunt, vanitatis nomina sibi expetunt, & novis ac prophanis vocabulis gloriantur. Cumque Mauritius Imperator præcepisset, ne frivoli vocabuli prætextu scandalum inter Episcopos digladiantes exoriatur, Epistola ad eundem data, quæ lib. VI. Epist. 30. est; Imperialis, inquit, pietas penset, quia alia sunt frivola, valde innoxia, atque alia vehementer noxia; Numquid non, cum Antichristus veniens se Deum dixerit, frivolum valde erit, sed tamen nimis perniciosum? Si quantitatem sermonis attendimus, duæ sunt syllabæ. Si vero pondus iniquitatis, universa pernicies. Ego autem fidenter dico, quia quisquis se universalem Sacerdotem vocat, vel vocari desiderat, in elatione sua Antichristum præcurrit: quia superbiendo se cæteris præponit. Nec dispari superbia ad errorem ducitur, quia sicut perversus ille Deus videri vult super omnes homines, ita quisquis est, qui solus Sacerdos appellari appetit, super cæteros Sacerdotes se extollit.
units.tr: "Through the almighty Lord I beg," he says, "that you do not allow the times of your piety to be stained by the arrogance of one man," alluding there, as elsewhere, to that man who exalts himself [ὑψηλαυχούμενον] or lifts himself up, of whom St Paul prophesies at 2 Thess. 2:4. He goes on: "In this man's pride what else is indicated than that the times of Antichrist are now near? For he imitates that one (Lucifer) who, scorning the legions of angels rejoicing in their fellowship, tried to break out to the summit of singularity, saying: 'I will raise my throne above the stars of heaven,' etc. 'I will be like the Most High.'" The letter to Emperor Maurice, which is book IV, letter 32, is to the same effect: "It is plain to all who know the Gospel," he says, "that by the Lord's voice the care of the whole Church was committed to the holy Peter, the chief of the Apostles. The care and leadership of the whole Church is committed to him, yet he is not called Universal Apostle. And my most holy colleague in the priesthood, John, tries to be called Universal Bishop. I am forced to cry out and say: O the times! O the manners! All those lands in Europe have been handed over to the law of barbarians. Cities are destroyed, camps overthrown, provinces laid waste, and no inhabitant of the land is left. And yet priests, who ought to lie weeping on the floor and in ashes, seek for themselves names of vanity and boast of new and profane titles." When Emperor Maurice had ordered that no scandal should arise among the bishops fighting over a frivolous title, Gregory wrote to the same emperor, in book VI, letter 30: "Let imperial piety weigh that some things are frivolous and quite harmless, and others very harmful. When Antichrist comes saying that he is God, will not that be quite frivolous, yet exceedingly pernicious? If we consider the length of the word, it has two syllables; but if we consider the weight of its wickedness, it is utter ruin. I confidently say that whoever calls himself, or desires to be called, Universal Priest, in his self-exaltation runs ahead of Antichrist, because by puffing himself up he puts himself before others. Nor is he led to error by a lesser pride; for just as that perverse god wishes to be seen above all men, so whoever seeks to be called the only priest raises himself above other priests."

units.la: XXXV. Sunt hæc Gregorii Pontificis verè Χαλεπα ῥήματα. Majus tamen illud est, quòd idem Gregorius proximè futuram tempestatem, tanquam ex specula quapiam ante prospiciens, de sequentibus temporibus ita lib. VIII. Ep. 36. vaticinatur: Qui post nos vixerint, deteriora tempora videbunt, ita ut in comparatione sui temporis felices nos æstiment dies habuisse. Alibi lib. IV. Epist. 38. expressius: Omnia quæ prædicta sunt, fiunt. Rex superbiæ prope est, & (quod dici nefas est) Sacerdotum est præparatus exercitus.
units.tr: XXXV. These are truly harsh words [Χαλεπα ῥήματα]. Yet it is more serious that the same Gregory, looking out beforehand from some lookout over the storm soon to come, prophesies about later times in book VIII, letter 36, thus: "Those who live after us will see worse times, so that in comparison with their own times they will count us happy to have had our days." Elsewhere, in book IV, letter 38, more plainly: "All things that have been foretold are coming to pass. The king of pride is near, and (what it is wrong even to say) an army is being prepared from among the priests."

units.la: ECCLESIÆ ROMANÆ PERIODUS TERTIA.
units.tr: THE THIRD PERIOD OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.

units.la: Seu
units.tr: Or

units.la: Historia Ecclesiæ Romanæ Dominatio- nem in Spiritualibus, indultu Phocæ, adipi- scentis, & in doctrina ac ritibus de- generantis.
units.tr: The History of the Roman Church: its dominion over spiritual matters, gained by the grant of Phocas, and its degeneration in doctrine and rites.

units.la: Inde à Bonifacio III. seu A. C. DCVII. ad Gregorium VII. seu A. C. MLXXIII. usque.
units.tr: From Boniface III, in the year of Christ 607, down to Gregory VII, in the year of Christ 1073.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: XXXVI. Phocæ Imperatoris decretum, quo Ecclesia Romana caput omnium Ecclesiarum declaratur à Bonifacio III. confirmatum. XXXVII. Syllogismo Pontificum verbis contexto Ecclesia Romana αὐτοκατάκριτος convincitur. XXXVIII. Exceptiones elisæ. Quo sensu Ecclesiæ Romanæ Episcopi Universales, Oecumenici à Patribus dicti? XXXIX. Ab eo tempore verus Papatus in Ecclesiam Occidentis; & simul etiam in Ecclesiam Orientis Muhammedismus introduci cœpit. XL. Honorii Bonifacio succedentis in hæresin Monothelitarum lapsus, à Gregorio prædictus. XLI. Pontificum sequentium studia quæ fuerint, exponitur. Agathonis Siculi superbissima effata. Theologiæ & bonarum literarum supinus iisdem temporibus neglectus. XLII. Concilium Constantinopolitanum VI. in Trullo habitum, à Constantino Pogonato solo & convocatum, & directum est. Romani in eo in ordinem redacti. XLIII. Leonis II. Benedicti II. Sergii I. ambitio. XLIV. Synodus Quini-sexta Romanæ Ecclesiæ minùs propitia, & ab eadem rejecta. XLV. Ecclesiæ Romanæ seculo octavo status, provehendæ Paparum dominationi idoneus fuit, Imperatore, Exarchis & Longobardis æmulis, Pontificum gratiam aucupantibus. Justinianus II. cum Ecclesia Romana conciliationem frustra quærit. Papæ Constantini pedes osculatur. XLVI. Historia certaminis de imaginibus Ecclesiam inter Romanam & Orientales, cui Philippicus Bardanes, & Johannes Patriarcha Const. imagines Patrum Concilii VI. è porticu Sophiæ removentes; Constantinus verò Papa easdem, aliasque etiam Romæ in porticu Petri collocantes, ansam dederunt. Ea occasione Ecclesia Romana ab Imperatore Orientali deficit, & mox Longobardis etiam à Pipino & Carolo M. domitis, Romanæ ditionis dominium feudali nexu adipiscitur. XLVII. Historia Synodi Generalis septimæ Constantinopoli habitæ, qua imaginum cultus damnatus: nec non Nicænæ II. qua idem stabilitus est. Carolus M. adversus Synodum Nicænam illam Francofurti Synodum celebrat, & imaginum cultum, libris etiam editis, damnat. XLVIII. Carolo tamen Imperatore liberius se Papatus movet, benevolentia & liberalitate tum Caroli, tum Inæ Saxonum Regis, in Britannia Denarium S. Petri Pontifici pensitandum instituentis adjutus, ceremoniis etiam in Franciam introductis, & Episcopis appellatione Romam concessa. XLIX. Re-
units.tr: XXXVI. The decree of the Emperor Phocas, by which the Roman Church was declared the head of all churches, confirmed by Boniface III. XXXVII. By a syllogism composed from the Popes' own words, the Roman Church is convicted of being self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτος]. XXXVIII. The exceptions refuted. In what sense were the bishops of the Roman Church called universal and ecumenical by the Fathers? XXXIX. From that time the true Papacy began to be introduced into the Western Church, and at the same time Muhammadanism into the Eastern Church. XL. The fall of Honorius, who succeeded Boniface, into the Monothelite heresy, foretold by Gregory. XLI. What were the pursuits of the following Popes is set out. The most arrogant sayings of Agatho the Sicilian. Theology and good letters were neglected at that time. XLII. The Sixth Council of Constantinople, called "in Trullo," was convened and directed by Constantine Pogonatus alone. The Romans were brought into line in it. XLIII. The ambition of Leo II, Benedict II and Sergius I. XLIV. The Quinisext Synod, not favourable to the Roman Church, and rejected by it. XLV. The state of the Roman Church in the eighth century was suitable for advancing the dominion of the Popes, the Emperor, the Exarchs and the Lombards being rivals, while the Popes courted favour. Justinian II seeks reconciliation with the Roman Church in vain. He kisses the feet of Pope Constantine. XLVI. The history of the controversy over images between the Roman Church and the Eastern Churches. Philippicus Bardanes and John, Patriarch of Constantinople, who removed the images of the Fathers of the Sixth Council from the portico of Sophia, gave the occasion; but Pope Constantine placed the same images, and others, in the portico of St Peter at Rome. On that occasion the Roman Church revolted from the Eastern Emperor, and soon, with the Lombards subdued by Pepin and Charlemagne, it acquired dominion over the Roman territory by feudal bond. XLVII. The history of the Seventh General Synod held at Constantinople, which condemned the veneration of images, and also of the Second Synod of Nicaea, which established the same. Charlemagne, against that Synod of Nicaea, holds a synod at Frankfurt and, with books published, condemns the veneration of images. XLVIII. Yet under the Emperor Charlemagne the Papacy moved more freely, aided by the goodwill and generosity both of Charlemagne and of Ina, King of the Saxons, who in Britain established the Denarius of St Peter to be paid to the Pope, ceremonies also having been introduced into France, and bishops being granted the right of appeal to Rome. XLIX. Re-

units.la: XLIX. Religionis prora & puppis quibus tum in rebus consiterit? Novelli ritus Caroli tempore in Ecclesiam invecti. Crassa ignorantia Cleri.
units.tr: XLIX. What were the prow and stern of religion at that time, in which matters did it consist? The new rites introduced into the Church in Charlemagne's time. The gross ignorance of the clergy.

units.la: L. Seculi IX. historia ex Pontificum ejusdem rebus liquet.
units.tr: L. The history of the ninth century is clear from the affairs of the Popes of that time.

units.la: LI. Electio Stephani V. & Paschalis I. anomala.
units.tr: LI. The election of Stephen V and Paschal I was irregular.

units.la: LII. Eugenius II. in schismate eligitur. Valentinus osculum pedum a senatu Romano primus admittit.
units.tr: LII. Eugenius II was elected during a schism. Valentine is the first to admit the kissing of the feet, by the Roman senate.

units.la: LIII. Synodi Parisiensis ad Ludovicum Imp. de Nicaena II. Synodo rescriptum. Eugenii II. in iconolatria tuenda obstinatio.
units.tr: LIII. The rescript of the Synod of Paris to Louis the Emperor concerning the Second Synod of Nicaea. The obstinacy of Eugenius II in defending image-worship.

units.la: LIV. Gregorius IV. Ludovici filios adversus Patrem fovet, & anathema comminatus, ab Episcopis Galliae spernitur. Sergius II. Os porci, electus Papa, primus nomen mutat. Idem, & post ipsum Leo IV. sedem, neglecto Imp. consensu occupant. Johannes VIII. foemina.
units.tr: LIV. Gregory IV favours the sons of Louis against their father, and, threatening anathema, is scorned by the bishops of Gaul. Sergius II, elected Pope, is the first to change his name, having been called "Pig's Snout." He and, after him, Leo IV occupy the see, neglecting the consent of the Emperor. Joan VIII, a woman.

units.la: LV. Nicolai I. judicari se a seculari potestate, eo quod Papa a Constantino Deus vocatus fuerit, vetantis: Lotharium excommunicantis: cum Michaele Imp. Constantinopolitano ob Photium Ignatio substitutum expostulantis, & anathema eidem intentantis: Ravennatensem Ecclesiam opprimentis: Sacerdotes conjugatos persequentis insolentia.
units.tr: LV. Nicholas I forbids himself to be judged by the secular power, because the Pope had been called God by Constantine. He excommunicates Lothair; he demands, with Michael the Emperor of Constantinople, an account concerning Photius, put in place of Ignatius, and threatens him with anathema; he oppresses the Church of Ravenna; he persecutes married priests with insolence.

units.la: LVI. Historia controversiae de Praedestinatione Godeschalcum inter & Rabanum Maurum ac Erigenam Scotum agitata, ex qua declinatio orthodoxae de gratia & praedestinatione doctrinae colligitur.
units.tr: LVI. The history of the controversy on predestination, debated between Godeschalc and Rabanus Maurus and Erigena the Scot, from which the decline of the orthodox doctrine of grace and predestination is gathered.

units.la: LVII. Hadriani II. molimina adversus Carolum Calvum, ab Hincmaro & ipso Rege fortiter repressa.
units.tr: LVII. The machinations of Hadrian II against Charles the Bald, bravely repressed by Hincmar and the King himself.

units.la: LVIII. Historia Synodi octavae Oecumenicae, in qua Photio ob reprehensum Basilium Imperat. parricidam depositio Ignatius substituitur, parricidae partes Hadriano fovente in cujus gratiam in eadem primatus Papae & imaginum cultus confirmatus est.
units.tr: LVIII. The history of the Eighth Ecumenical Synod, in which Photius was deposed, and Ignatius substituted, because he had rebuked the parricide Emperor Basil. The parricide was favoured by Hadrian, in whose favour the primacy of the Pope and the veneration of images were confirmed in the same synod.

units.la: LIX. Johannes IX. tres Augustos pronuntiat. Unde posthac titulus Imperatoris Papae beneficium esse coepit.
units.tr: LIX. John IX pronounces three Augusti. From then on the title of Emperor began to be a benefit conferred by the Pope.

units.la: LX. Hadriani III. decreta, ne in creando Pontifice Imperatoris authoritas exspectetur: utque post mortem Imper. Crassi Regnum Italicis Principibus cum titulo Imperii tribuatur.
units.tr: LX. The decrees of Hadrian III, that in creating a Pope the authority of the Emperor should not be awaited, and that after the death of the Emperor Charles the Fat the kingdom should be given to the Italian princes with the title of Empire.

units.la: LXI. Stephani VI. Sanctio, ut leges Ecclesiæ Rom. sint irrefragabiles. Stephani VII. adversus cadaver Formosi horrenda sævitia: vindicantibus mox Formosum successoribus.
units.tr: LXI. The sanction of Stephen VI, that the laws of the Roman Church should be irrefragable. The horrible savagery of Stephen VII against the corpse of Formosus; his successors soon avenged Formosus.

units.la: LXII. Baronii de infelicitate illorum temporum, & monstris sedi Rom. ab Adelbertis Thuscis impositis querela. Successionis Paparum turbatio.
units.tr: LXII. Baronius's complaint about the unhappiness of those times, and the monsters imposed on the Roman see by the Tuscan Adalberts. The disorder of the succession of Popes.

units.la: LXIII. Historia certaminis Sacramentarii inter Paschasium Ratbertum & Rabanum Maurum, ac Bertramum agitati.
units.tr: LXIII. The history of the Sacramentarian controversy, debated between Paschasius Radbertus and Rabanus Maurus, and Bertram.

units.la: LXIV. Potestatem Pontificis temporalem circa ea tempora multum fictæ donationes Constantini M. Ludovici Pii & Othonis M. promoverunt, quarum vopɛia panditur. Spiritualem eorundem potestatem firmårunt Epistolæ Decretales primis Pontificibus eodem tempore per fraudem suppositæ.
units.tr: LXIV. Around those times the temporal power of the Pontiff was greatly advanced by the fictitious donations of Constantine the Great, Louis the Pious and Otto the Great, whose fraud is exposed. Their spiritual power was confirmed by the Decretal Epistles, falsely ascribed to the earliest Pontiffs of the same time.

units.la: LXV. De Seculi decimi miseranda facie querela Bellarmini & Baronii.
units.tr: LXV. Bellarmine's and Baronius's lament over the pitiable face of the tenth century.

units.la: LXVI. Romæ tum sordidissimæ meretrices, Theodora & Marozia imperitârunt. Gerberti & Genebrardi de eodem seculo querimonia.
units.tr: LXVI. At Rome the most foul prostitutes, Theodora and Marozia, held power. The complaint of Gerbert and Genebrard about the same century.

units.la: LXVII. Infelicitatis illius causæ nunquid penes Imperatores Germanos hæserint?
units.tr: LXVII. Did the cause of that unhappiness perhaps lie with the German Emperors?

units.la: LXVIII. Seculi illius Pontifices à Gerberto
units.tr: LXVIII. The Popes of that century, as depicted by Gerbert

units.la: LXIX. nec non Platina, Stella, Baronio, Genebrardo graphicè depicti. Exempla nonnullorum producuntur.
units.tr: LXIX. and also vividly by Platina, Stella, Baronius and Genebrard. Some examples are produced.

units.la: LXX. Cleri totius corruptio immanis.
units.tr: LXX. The immense corruption of the whole clergy.

units.la: LXXI. Novas hæreses seculum isthoc nullas protulit, quia in Prælatos & Monachos hæretici fugerunt omnes.
units.tr: LXXI. This century produced no new heresies, because all the heretics fled to the prelates and monks.

units.la: LXXII. Ecclesiæ circa annum millesimum status ex Wernero, Glabro Radulpho repræsentatur.
units.tr: LXXII. The state of the Church around the year one thousand, as represented by Werner, Glaber and Radulf.

units.la: LXXIII. Seculum decimum ferreum à Dithmaro appellatum quo revelandum, vel revelatum jam esse Antichristum, passim percrebuit. LXXIII. Silvestri II. Necromantia. Discipuli & successores ejus eodem, aliisque etiam criminibus infames. LXXIV. Cardinalium nomen tempore Benedicti IX. in pretio esse incipiti. Cardinalis fixus Ecclesiæ minister. Eorum definitio verbis M. Anton. de Dominis texitur. LXXV. Potestas eorum unà cum Papæ potestate crevit; Seculo inprimis undecimo quo primæ in eligendo Papa partes iis sub Nicolao II. decretæ, donec exclusò ab ea electione Imperatore & Clero reliquo, solis iis jus hoc cessit. Ita sub appellatione ecclesiastica Principes seculares facti sunt. LXXVI. Ea ratione Papa Christi æmulus collegium Apostolicum, ex Cardinalibus constatum, constituit. LXXVII. Cardinalium ex eo tempore prærogativæ multiplices. LXXVII. Galerus ruber senatus hujus Edomitici tessera. Cujus auctoramento principes hujus seculi viri ad Pontificias partes trahuntur. LXXVIII. Certaminis Sacramentarii continuatio per Berengarium, ad horribilem palinodiam coactum. Libertati restitutus idem veritatem ad finem usque vitæ asseruit.
units.tr: LXXIII. The tenth century, called the iron age by Dithmar, when Antichrist was either to be revealed or was already revealed, spread everywhere. LXXIII. Silvester II. Necromancy. His disciples and successors were infamous for this and for other crimes. LXXIV. The name of cardinal began to be held in esteem in the time of Benedict IX. The cardinal is a fixed minister of the Church. Their definition is woven together in the words of M. Antonius de Dominis. LXXV. Their power grew together with the power of the Pope, especially in the eleventh century, when under Nicholas II. the first part in electing the Pope was assigned to them, until, with the Emperor and the rest of the clergy excluded from that election, this right passed to them alone. Thus, under the ecclesiastical title, secular princes were made. LXXVI. By this device the Pope, a rival of Christ, established an apostolic college made up of cardinals. LXXVII. From that time the prerogatives of the cardinals have been manifold. LXXVII. The red hat is the badge of this Edomite senate, and by its authority men of princely rank in this age are drawn to the Papal side. LXXVIII. The continuation of the Sacramentarian controversy through Berengar, who was forced into a dreadful recantation. Restored to freedom, the same man asserted the truth to the end of his life.

units.la: XXXVI. ANte verò Gregorium, quem supra vaticinantem induximus, ex semet ipso ea prolocutum esse, an prophetâsse potiùs, quòd esset Pontifex anni illius, putabimus? Quicquid sit, augurium non fefellit. Successores enim ejus, quod in Johanne Constantinopolitano gravissimè merito detestatus Gregorius est, ipsimet avidissimè rapuerunt, raptum defensitarunt quibus libet interdictis, & præfractè, si quid aliud. Phocas enim, alter Zimri, Domini sui, Mauritii sub ipso ferali ictu justa Dei judicia celebrantis, cujusque centurio fuit, occisor nefarius, Tyrannus Calydonius ci-
units.tr: XXXVI. But before Gregory, whom we introduced above as prophesying, shall we think that he spoke these things from himself, or rather prophesied them, because he was pope of that year? Whatever the case, the omen did not deceive. For his successors eagerly seized for themselves what Gregory had most gravely and deservedly condemned in John of Constantinople, and defended the usurped title with whatever prohibitions they pleased, and stubbornly, with anything else they could use. For Phocas, another Zimri, the impious murderer of his lord Maurice, under whose very deadly blow the just judgments of God were being carried out, and whose centurion he had been, a Calydonian tyrant, ci-

units.la: F [illegible, ~25 letters] ferro obtectus, homo semibarbarus, de Cyclopum genere, in modesta purpura centaurus petulantissimus, cui de ebrietatis Regno erat certamen (en notas, quibus Phocam Pontificii Regni architectum coætaneus ejus Theophylactus Simocatta insignivit:) rogante Papa Bonifacio (tertio, patria Romano, A. DCVII. electo Pontifice) statuit, sedem Romanæ Ecclesiæ caput esse omnium Ecclesiarum, quia Ecclesia Constantinopolitana primam se omnium Ecclesiarum scribebat, uti Beda de sex ætatibus mundi, Paulus Diaconus Rerum Romanarum lib. II. Anastasius Bibliothecarius in vita Bonifacii III. aliique commemorant; vel, uti Pomponius Lætus in Hist. Rom. compendio loquitur: Urbem Romam totius salutaris vitæ caput esse sanxit, cum antea propter sedem Principis Constantinopolis haberetur. Erat nempe Phocas Cyriaco Patriarchæ infensus, tantoque magis Romani Pontificis exquisitis adulationibus appetitus, ut Constantinopolitani odio, & in favorem Romani non tantum Ecclesiam Romanam Ecclesiarum omnium caput: Sed Romanum etiam Episcopum Universalem seu Oecumenicum Ecclesiarum scil. omnium Episcopum esse, dicique debere statuerit. Quod imperiale scilicet statutum Bonifacius mox in Synodo Episcoporum LXXII. sanciri jubens, simul definivit, electionem Episcopi à Clero pariter & populo fieri debere, eamque ita ratam fore, si à Principe civitatis approbata esset, & si summus Pontifex denique his verbis authoritatem suam interposuisset: Volumus & jubemus: uti in vita ejus Platina loquitur.
units.tr: F [illegible] armed with iron, a half-barbarian man, of the race of the Cyclopes, a most wanton centaur in modest purple, with whom there was a contest over the kingdom of drunkenness (behold the notes by which his contemporary Theophylact Simocatta marked Phocas, the architect of the Papal kingdom:) at the request of Pope Boniface (the third, a Roman by birth, elected pope in 607) he decreed that the see of the Roman Church is the head of all churches, because the Church of Constantinople wrote itself the first of all churches, as Bede in On the Six Ages of the World, Paul the Deacon in Roman History, book II, Anastasius the Librarian in the Life of Boniface III, and others record; or, as Pomponius Laetus says in his Roman History compendium: He decreed that the city of Rome is the head of all saving life, whereas before it had been regarded as such because of the seat of the Emperor at Constantinople. Phocas was indeed hostile to the Patriarch Cyriacus, and was all the more eagerly courted by the Roman Pontiff with exquisite flattery, so that out of hatred for the Constantinopolitan and in favour of the Roman, he decreed that not only the Roman Church should be the head of all churches, but also that the Roman bishop should be, and should be called, Universal or Ecumenical bishop, that is, bishop of all churches. Bonifacius soon ordered this imperial decree to be confirmed in a synod of seventy-two bishops, and at the same time defined that the election of a bishop must be made by the clergy and the people alike, and would be ratified if it were approved by the prince of the city, and if the supreme Pontiff had finally interposed his authority in these words: We will and command; as Platina speaks in his life.

units.la: XXXVII. Fingamus hic ad vivos redire Gregorium, quid dicturum putamus, si successorem suum titulo superbientem Universalis Episcopi, quem tantopere in Johanne Constantinopolitano damnaverat, vidisset? Saltem [illegible, ~12 letters] Sedes Romana efficitur Syllogismo ipsorum Pontificum verbis confuto: Qui Episcopus universalis appellari vult, Antichristi præcursor est. Bonifacius tertius Universalis Episcopus appellari & vult, & ut appelletur, poscit, obtinetque. Bonifacius igitur tertius, si non Antichristus ipse, at ejus certè præcursor est.
units.tr: XXXVII. Let us imagine Gregory returning to life. What do we think he would say if he saw his successor, puffed up with the title Universal Bishop, the very title he had so bitterly condemned in John of Constantinople? At least [illegible] the Roman See is shown to be wrong by the Popes' own words, in a syllogism: Whoever wishes to be called Universal Bishop is the forerunner of Antichrist. Boniface III wishes to be called Universal Bishop, and he asks for it and obtains it, so that the title is his. Therefore Boniface III, if he is not Antichrist himself, is certainly his forerunner.

units.la: XXXVIII. Neque hic tralatitia χρυσοφύγετα moramur, cujusmodi sunt, Phocam universalem Episcopatum Romani non instituisse, sed asseruisse: ante Phocam titulo capitis Ecclesiæ, universalis Episopi ab Imperatoribus aliisque Romanos exornatos esse. Aliter longè Scriptores vetusti. Paulus Diaconus scriptor coævus lib. IV. cap. 37. de gestis Longobard. sic: Phocas, rogante Papa Bonifacio, statuit, (en statutum novum, non veteris statuti assertionem!) Sedem Romanæ & Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ caput esse omnium Ecclesiarum, &c. Sic etiam posteriores, Freculphus, Regino, Anastasius, Hermannus Contractus, &c. qui omnes: Bonifacius rogavit, obtinuit, impetravit à Phoca, ut esset, vel haberetur caput omnium Ecclesiarum. Nonnulli etiam Phocæ authoritate factum esse caput Ecclesiarum. Sigonius de Regno Italiæ lib. II. scribit, Bonifacium ad Phocam legationem misisse, quo decretum obtinuerit, ut sedes B. Petri esset prima omnium Ecclesiarum. Sanè etiam Justinianus (siquidem γνώμη ejus Epistola est) ante Phocam Ecclesiam Rom. omnium Ecclesiarum caput insignivit, sed eodem utique sensu, quo etiam Constantinopolin caput omnium aliarum Ecclesiarum esse dixit. Mos fuit SS. Patribus, omnes Patriarchas Oecumenicos seu Universales, hoc est, universalis Ecclesiæ contutores, seu Catholicæ Ecclesiæ curam in sua portione, suoque districtu gerentes (quamquam ne is quidem sensus Gregorio placuit, aperte testato, à suis antecessoribus vocabulum id rejectum esse) nuncupare; quod abundè à nostris probatum. In ipsa Synodo Chalcedonensi Mennas Constantinopolitanus Episcopus passim Oecumenicus; in Nicæna Tharasius Patriarcha generalis ab ipso Adriano Episcopo Romano vocantur. Observatumque jam olim etiam Benedicto Renato, S. Euftachii apud Parisianos Parocho, in amica Disquisitione super Doctrina Hugenottorum, Patres aliquando universaliùs de Ecclesia Romana locutos esse, eò quòd per Romanam Ecclesiam Occidentalem seu Latinam, Orientali seu Græcæ, contradistinctam intellexerint, & à sede præcipua ac Metropoli utrumque Imperium atque Ecclesia denominata fuerit. Ut manifestum planè sit, Phocam capitis Ecclesiarum, & Universalis Episcopi titulum, qui communis antehac fuerat, Romano ita appropriâsse, ut ab ejus communione Constantinopolitanus, aliique excluderentur, & Romanus in posterum rerum in Ecclesia potiretur solus. Unde perpetuum Occidentalem inter & Orientalem Ecclesiam schisma posthac incessit, malumque paulatim factum immedicabile est.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Nor shall we linger here on the gilded evasions [χρυσοφύγετα] of the kind that claim Phocas did not institute the universal episcopate for the Roman bishop but only asserted it, and that before Phocas the Roman bishops had been adorned by emperors and others with the title of head of the Church, Universal Bishop. The early writers say something quite different. Paul the Deacon, a writer of the same period, book 4, chapter 37, on the deeds of the Lombards, says: Phocas, at the request of Pope Boniface, decreed (see, a new decree, not an affirmation of an old one!) that the See of the Roman and Apostolic Church should be the head of all the Churches, etc. Later writers say the same: Freculphus, Regino, Anastasius, Hermann Contractus, and the rest, all of whom write: Boniface asked, obtained and secured from Phocas that it should be, or be regarded as, the head of all the Churches. Some even say that the headship of the Churches was made by the authority of Phocas. Sigonius, in On the Kingdom of Italy, book 2, writes that Boniface sent an embassy to Phocas, by which he obtained a decree that the See of St Peter should be first of all the Churches. Indeed Justinian too (if the opinion is his letter) before Phocas gave the Roman Church the mark of head of all the Churches, but in the same sense in which he also called Constantinople head of all the other Churches. It was the custom of the holy Fathers to call all the patriarchs œcumenical or universal, that is, co-guardians of the universal Church, who bear the care of the Catholic Church within their own portion and district. (Even this sense did not please Gregory, who openly testified that his predecessors had rejected that term.) Our writers have amply shown this. In the Council of Chalcedon itself, Mennas, bishop of Constantinople, is repeatedly called œcumenical; in the Council of Nicaea, Tarasius is called general patriarch by Adrian, bishop of Rome himself. Benedict Renatus, parish priest of St Eustace among the Parisians, observed long ago in his friendly Disquisition on the Doctrine of the Huguenots that the Fathers sometimes spoke of the Roman Church in a more general way, because they understood by the Roman Church the Western or Latin Church, as distinct from the Eastern or Greek, and both empires and the Church were named from the principal see and metropolis. So it is quite clear that Phocas appropriated the title of head of the Churches and Universal Bishop, which had been common until then, so exclusively to Rome that the Constantinopolitan and others were excluded from its fellowship, and the Roman alone would henceforth hold power in the Church. From this came the lasting schism between the Western and Eastern Church, and the evil, step by step, became incurable.

units.la: XXXIX. Ex hoc tempore verus Papatus in Ecclesiam Romanam invehi, errores & superstitiones in ea incrementum capere, sacra omnia refigi & refingi, paulatim ex serpigine gangræna nasci. Plurimis tamen in Oriente & Occidente, Gallia cumprimis, Germania & Britannia in maximi momenti rebus, in quibus summa salutis vertitur, à Romani Pontificis sententia divortio facto discedentibus. Accedit, quòd circa id ipsum tempus in Oriente exortus est Pseudopropheta Muhammed, cujus sectatores Saraceni mirabiles adeò successus habuerunt, ut tertio post excessum illius anno, Omaro dynastiam capessente, intra sexennii spatium Ægyptum, Arabiam, Phœniciam, Palæstinam, Syriam, Mesopotamiam occupaverint. Sic duæ voragines, duo scopoli, duo carcinomata Ecclesiæ externæ corpus invaserunt corripueruntque subitò.
units.tr: XXXIX. From this time the true papacy began to creep into the Roman Church, errors and superstitions grew in it, and all sacred things were unmade and remade, the ulcer gradually becoming a gangrene. Yet very many in the East and West, especially in Gaul, Germany and Britain, departed from the judgment of the Roman Pontiff in matters of the greatest importance, in which the sum of salvation lies. In addition, about this same time there arose in the East the false prophet Muhammad, whose followers, the Saracens, had such marvellous success that in the third year after his death, when Omar had taken up the dynasty, they occupied Egypt, Arabia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Syria and Mesopotamia within six years. Thus two whirlpools, two rocks, two cancers suddenly invaded and seized the outward body of the Church.

units.la: XL. Jam ante Gregorius M. Si unus Episcopus vocaretur Universalis, corruituram Ecclesiam universam, si unus caderet, prædixerat. Augurio illi fidem statim fecit specimen notorium, Honorii, quarti post Bonifacium Papæ, qui A. DCXXVI. Bonifacio V. successit, lapsus, ex quo cernere fuit, quàm lubrica res sit, à fide unius hominis pendere.
