In Monotheletarum scilicet hæresin præceps lapsus, errorem suum literis ad Sergium Constantinopolitanum datis, & in Synodo Sexta Universali, actione duodecima & decima tertia prolatis, omniumque Patrum judicio igni damnatis, prodidit. Anathemati proin etiam in Synodo Nicænæ secunda, actione ultima: nec non in Octava ab Adriano Papa subjicitur. Egregium scilicet Papam, Episcopum Universalem, & caput omnium Ecclesiarum: quem Wicelius dicit fuisse bonum virum, sed malum Papam & Pastorem negligentem, reformatorem scilicet Cleri in rebus iudicris observandis, non in Verbo Dei propagando. Licet vero ab haeresis nota liberare eum Bellarminus conetur, à doctissimo tamen nuper Sorbonista Launoio, Epistolis ea de re editis, ejusdem reus aperte peragitur.
units.tr: XL. Long before, Gregory the Great had foretold: If one bishop were called Universal, the whole Church would fall, if that one fell. A notorious example soon made his prophecy credible: the fall of Honorius, the fourth Pope after Boniface, who succeeded Boniface V in 626, showed how slippery a thing it is to depend on the faith of one man. Honorius fell headlong into the Monothelite heresy, and he revealed his error in a letter to Sergius of Constantinople, and in the Sixth Ecumenical Council, in the twelfth and thirteenth sessions, where it was condemned to the fire by the judgment of all the Fathers. Accordingly he is also anathematized in the Second Council of Nicaea, in its last session, and in the Eighth Council under Pope Adrian. This was the excellent Pope, the Universal Bishop and head of all the Churches, whom Wicelius calls a good man but a bad Pope and a negligent pastor, a reformer, that is, of the clergy in observing judicial matters, not one who spread the Word of God. Although Bellarmine tries to free him from the mark of heresy, the very learned Sorbonne doctor Launoy, in letters published on this matter, openly proves him guilty of it.

units.la: XLI. Sequentium Pontificum, Honorii ipsius, Zephyrini, Theodori, Martini, Eugenii, Vitaliani &c. studium fuit, non tam Ecclesiam Dei vivae vocis praeconio aedificare, & lapides vivos undique congerere: quàm magnifica Templa, sacella, statuas exstruere, aliisque etiam ridiculis ꝏ operam omnem navare; ad exteras regiones quosdam à latere ablegare, non Evangelium promulgaturos, sed ceremonias ritusque Romanos, Cantum, Latinum officium, Horas, altaria, organa, cereos, & nugamenta similia; præ cæteris autem primatum Papæ, Phocæ suffragatione collatum obtrusuros. Agatho certè Siculus A. DCLXXVIII. Papale solium adeptus D. 19. C. sic omnes 2. Papaliter ita pronunciat: Sic omnes Sanctiones Apostolicae sedis accipiendae sunt, tanquam ipsius Divina voce Petri firmatae. Ad Constantinum etiam Pogonatum scribit idem, Ecclesiam Apostolicam (Romanam) numquam Pontificum sequentium studia quae fuerint, exponitur. Agathonis Siculi superbissima effata. quam à Via veritatis deflexisse, sed illibatam permansisse, nec errare potuisse, secundum ipsius Salvatoris Divinam pollicitationem, quam suorum discipulorum Principi in Sacris Evangeliis fatus est. Sub eodem tamen Papa tantam bonarum literarum sterilitatem, & Theologiæ universæ neglectum Ecclesiam pervagatum esse, ut ne unus quidem Romæ Theologus fuerit, & Theodorus Theologus nequicquam ex Britannia accitus fuerit; Papæ ipsius testimonio Baronius ad A. DCLXXX. confirmat. Scilicet omnia sapientiæ cœlestis mysteria in penetrale & adytum novi Apollinis, Universalis Episcopi immeârunt.
units.tr: XLI. The studies of the Popes who followed, of Honorius himself, of Zephyrinus, Theodore, Martin, Eugene, Vitalian and others, were not to build up the Church of the living God by the proclamation of the living voice and to gather living stones from every side, but to erect magnificent temples, chapels and statues, and to devote all their effort to other such trifles. They sent certain men abroad, not to publish the Gospel but to thrust upon foreign lands Roman ceremonies and rites: Latin chant, the Latin office, the hours, altars, organs, candles and similar trifles; and above all they meant to force on them the primacy of the Pope, conferred by the support of Phocas. Agatho of Sicily certainly, who obtained the papal throne in 678, speaks in papal fashion, as in D. 19. C. sic omnes 2: Thus all the decrees of the Apostolic See are to be received as if confirmed by the divine voice of Peter itself. The same man writes to Constantine Pogonatus: The Apostolic Church (Roman) has never strayed from the way of truth, but has remained unimpaired, and cannot err, according to the divine promise of the Saviour himself, which he uttered to the prince of his disciples in the holy Gospels. Such were the proud declarations of Agatho of Sicily. Yet under this same Pope, Baronius confirms, from the Pope's own testimony, for the year 680, that such barrenness of good letters and such neglect of all theology had spread through the Church that there was not even one theologian at Rome, and Theodore the theologian was summoned in vain from Britain. So all the mysteries of heavenly wisdom went into the inner shrine and sanctuary of the new Apollo, the Universal Bishop.

units.la: XLII. Anno DCLXXX. Constantinopoli in Trullo ad compescendos Monotheletas, Synodus VI. habita est, indicente non Agathone, sed Constantino Pogonato, uti Zonaras, Gratianus, Anastasius diserte testantur.
units.tr: XLII. In the year 680 the Sixth Synod was held at Constantinople in the Trullo to suppress the Monotheletes. It was convened not by Agatho but by Constantine Pogonatus, as Zonaras, Gratian and Anastasius clearly testify.

units.la: Agatho ipse Cæsari vocanti promptam obsequentiam se exhibere testatur. In literis ad Agathonem & Episcopos Romanos, nec non Gregorium Constantinopolitanum, illos Papas Universales, hunc Patriarcham Universalem vocat. Præses seu Præsidens non alius in omnibus Concilii actis, quàm Constantinus designatur. Neque Agatho ipse in Concilio ὑπέρτερον supra alias Ecclesias venditare ausus, se per Legatos suos in parium curia sedere perspexit. Quin Episcopum Romanum ejus Synodi Patres, juxta antiquum Synodi Constantinopolitanæ decretum ita in ordinem redigunt, ut ἴσων ἀπολαβεῖν πρεσβείων pari dignitate frui & Romanum & Constantinopolitanum scisicant. Adeò nondum in Orientem Universalis potestatis fimbrias, ut ut concupiverint, dilatare Romanis integrum fuit.
units.tr: Agatho himself testifies that he showed ready obedience to the summoning emperor. In his letters to Agatho and the Roman bishops, and also to Gregory of Constantinople, he calls the former Universal Popes and the latter Universal Patriarch. The president, or presiding officer, in all the acts of the Council is designated as none other than Constantine. Nor did Agatho himself dare to put on airs in the Council as higher than the other Churches; he saw that his legates sat in the court of equals. Indeed, the Fathers of that Synod, following the ancient decree of the Synod of Constantinople, so ranked the Roman bishop that they assigned both Rome and Constantinople to enjoy equal honour [ἴσων ἀπολαβεῖν πρεσβείων]. So the Romans, however much they coveted it, were not yet free to extend the fringes of universal power into the East.

units.la: XLIII. Agathonis Successor Leo II. à Constantino impetravit, ut qui Archiepiscopus Ravennæ impositerum eligetur, Romam ordinandus se conferat, ea tamen lege, ne quid pro Pallio ab eo exigatur. Amplius quid ab eodem Benedictus II. obtinet, ut scilicet quem Clerus, populus & exercitus Romanus Pontificem delegerit, is è vestigio, non exspectata vel Imperatoris, vel Exarchi licentia, confirmetur & consecretur. Quae libertas quàm noxia fuerit, mox in electione Cononis aliorumque emicuit. Cononis successor Sergius I. schismate populi suborto, aliis Theodorum Archipresbyterum, aliis Paschalem Archidiaconum obtrudere molientibus, ex media populi turba raptus Papa creatur, & ilico ab omnibus, ipsis etiam rivalibus, salutatur; vel, ut Sigonius, recentiori adulatione, ait, adoratur. Eo sedis hujus superbia, & invadendae ejusdem cupiditas, & ambitio jam processerat.
units.tr: XLIII. Agatho's successor, Leo II, obtained from Constantine that whoever was elected again as archbishop of Ravenna should go to Rome to be ordained, on the condition, however, that nothing was to be demanded from him for the pallium. Furthermore, Benedict II obtained from the same emperor that whoever the clergy, people and Roman army chose as Pope should be confirmed and consecrated at once, without waiting for the permission of either the emperor or the exarch. How harmful this freedom was soon became clear in the election of Conon and others. When Conon's successor, Sergius I, was chosen amid a schism among the people, some trying to thrust Theodore the archpriest upon them and others Paschal the archdeacon, he was seized from the midst of the crowd and created Pope, and at once greeted by everyone, even by his rivals; or, as Sigonius puts it with more recent flattery, he was adored. By then the pride of this see, its desire to seize power, and its ambition had already advanced so far.

units.la: XLIV. Eodem Sergio Pontifice Anno DCXCII. Constantinopoli in Trullo, authoritate Justiniani Rhinotmeti à Callinico Patriarcha convocata, celebrataque adeò est Synodus, cui vulgò πεντεκτης, quini-sexta nomen inditum est, eò quòd quintae & sextae Synodi generalis, in quibus Canones de Disciplina, regimine, ritibus, moribus Clericorum & Monachorum decreti nulli fuerant; quoddam supplementum esset. Varios ibi Canones Ecclesiae Romanae disciplinae, praxi, authoritati oppositos, seu, uti Anastasius in vita Johannis VII. loquitur, capitula Romanae Ecclesiae contraria videre est. Quamobrem etiam moderni Ecclesiae Romanae gnathones Synodum erraticam, & nonnulli etiam plane confictam appellare non verecundantur; licet ab ipso Sergio, ea parte, qua Ecclesiae Romanae authoritatem non laedit, subscripta, aliisque etiam Pontificibus approbata constet. Auxeruntque Canones hi schisma jam ante coeptum Orientales inter & Occidentales, fatente Baronio, eorum causa diu Graecos inter & Latinos disceptatum esse. XLV. Seculi octavi status Romanorum Pontificum domi- miminationi provehendæ idoneus fuit. In Oriente remoti adeò, sedebant Imperatores. Italiam barbari, Longobardi invaserunt. Subditi Romani ab obsequio paulatim Imperatoris Constantinopolitani se subduxerant, Exarchorum imperium exuere parati. Omnes hæ partes Romanorum Pontificum gratiam ambiverunt. Imperator & Exarchi, ut se adversus Longobardos & subditos infideles, favore eorum freti, munirent: Longobardi haud segniores, ut imperium malis artibus quæsitum stabilirent. Proin A. DCCV. Johanni VII. Aripertus Longobardorum Rex, immania scelera sua expiaturus, qui jam Seculi illius error & terror fuit, Alpes Cottias in patrimonium donavit, quas Taurino Genuam usque indeque in Gallias Blondus & Platina extendunt. Ex adverso Justinianus II. domesticis seditionibus conflictatus, imperio exutus, ac demum restitutus, & vindictam spirans, eundem Pontificem Johannem VII. demulcere conatur, missis ad eum Actis Synodi Sextæ, ut, verbis Anastasii utor, quæ ei visa essent, stabiliret, & quæ adversa, renuendo excluderet. Sic utriusque Ecclesiæ Orientalis & Occidentalis reconciliationem tentare voluit. Cœterum Papa schisma sibi futurum conducibilius ratus, Legatos re infecta remisit. Post Imperator idem Callinicum Patriarcham, oculorum usura privatum, Romam ad Constantinum Papam gratificaturus ei, misit: Papamque ad se Constantinopolin in vitavit, seu, uti Paulus Diaconus loquitur, ad se venire jussit, specie consilii de Republica cum ipso ineundi; revera, ut honoribus cumulatum sui eum beneficii faceret. Adventantis Papæ pedes Imperatorem Regium (diadema) in capite habentem exosculatum, Paulus Diaconus idem tradit, addens, Justinianum cuncta Ecclesiæ Romanæ privilegia innovâsse, & Papam Romam onustum muneribus dimisisse.
units.tr: XLIV. In the same pontificate of Sergius, in the year 692, a synod was convened and held at Constantinople in the Trullo, summoned by Callinicus the Patriarch on the authority of Justinian Rhinotmetus. It was commonly called the Pentekte [πεντεκτης], or Quini-sexta, because it was meant as a supplement to the fifth and sixth general synods, which had decreed no canons concerning discipline, government, rites, and the conduct of clergy and monks. Here one may see various canons opposed to the discipline, practice, and authority of the Roman Church, or, as Anastasius puts it in his life of John VII, capitula Romanae Ecclesiae contraria (chapters contrary to the Roman Church). For this reason the modern flatterers of the Roman Church do not hesitate to call this synod a wandering one, and some even call it plainly fabricated, although it is established that Sergius himself subscribed to it in the part that does not injure the authority of the Roman Church, and that other popes approved it. These canons increased the schism that had already begun between the Eastern and Western churches; Baronius admits that for their sake the Greeks and Latins disputed for a long time. XLV. The state of the Roman pontiffs in the eighth century was suited to advancing their dominion. The emperors sat far away in the East. The barbarian Lombards invaded Italy. The Roman subjects had gradually withdrawn their obedience from the emperor at Constantinople and were ready to cast off the rule of the exarchs. All these parties courted the favour of the Roman pontiffs: the emperor and the exarchs, so that they might fortify themselves against the Lombards and their unfaithful subjects by relying on the pontiffs' favour, and the Lombards, no less eager to establish by wicked arts the power they had gained. Accordingly, in the year 705, Aripert, King of the Lombards, wishing to atone for his monstrous crimes, who was already the error and terror of that age, gave the Cottian Alps to John VII as a patrimony. Taurinus, Blondus and Platina extend these from Turin as far as Genoa, and from there into Gaul. On the other side, Justinian II, harassed by domestic uprisings, stripped of his empire, then restored, and breathing vengeance, tried to win over the same pontiff John VII by sending him the acts of the Sixth Synod, so that, to use Anastasius' words, he might confirm what seemed favourable to him and reject by refusing what was adverse. In this way he wanted to attempt a reconciliation of the Eastern and Western churches. The pope, however, thinking the schism more advantageous for himself, sent the legates back with nothing accomplished. Afterwards the same emperor sent Callinicus the Patriarch, who had been deprived of his eyesight, to Rome to do a favour to Pope Constantine. He also invited the pope to come to him at Constantinople, or, as Paul the Deacon puts it, ordered him to come, under the pretext of consulting with him about affairs of state; in truth it was so that he could heap honours on him and make him a beneficiary of his kindness. Paul the Deacon also reports that the emperor, wearing the royal diadem on his head, kissed the feet of the arriving pope, adding that Justinian renewed all the privileges of the Roman Church and dismissed the pope back to Rome laden with gifts.

units.la: XLVI. Mox
units.tr: XLVI. Soon

units.la: XLVI. Mox certamen de Imaginibus, earumque cultu Romanam & Orientalem Ecclesiam admodum exercitam habuit. Certaminis occasio incidit in A. DCCXII. quo Philippicus Bardanes Imperator, & Johannes Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus Monotheleta uterque, Concilio Oecumenico sexto, quo Monotheletis Anathema dictum est, reprobato, Synodi ejus Patrum imagines è Porticu S. Sophiæ, ubi paulo ante à Justiniano collocatæ fuerant, sustulerunt. Mox Constantinus Papa in adversum nixus, Romæ celebrata Synodo, easdem imagines, additis etiam præcipuorum, qui præcedentibus Conciliis intererant, Patrum imaginibus, in porticu S. Petri collocavit: definiens insuper, etiam in Templa imagines inferendas esse. Hinc quæstio de imaginibus non accessoria amplius mansit, sed principalis evasit; Papa Constantino Philippicum in Iconomachiæ hærefin lapsum (ita Platina) imperio spoliare auso. Leo tertius Isaurus A. DCCXVII. Imperio admotus mox edictum adversus imagines A. DCCXXVI. promulgat, & Constantini successorem Gregorium II. cui Dialogi nomen erat, ab imaginum tutela dehortatur graviter. Ille adversus Imperatorem æstuans, Ravennates, Venetos populumque omnem adversus Imperatorem & Exarchum concitat. Quo facto effrenes populi in Paulum, Ravennæ Exarchum, impetu facto, universam Italiam seditione, rapina, cœdibus implent. Ac tandem tot tantisque sceleribus obligati Romani, si quidem vera est narratio authorum Græcorum, Zonaræ, Theophanis & Cedreni (quam nuper tamen Launojus Epist. lib. 7. suspectam reddere conatus est) ab obsequio & fide Leonis Orientalis Imperatoris, sublato mox etiam Exarchatu, ducentos annos in Italia obtinente, descisount, & solenni Sacramento se Pontificis Romani vitam statumque in perpetuum defensuros, & authoritati ejus obtemperaturos recipiunt. De quo ita Sigonius de Regno Italiæ lib. 2. scribit: Ita Roma Romanusque Ducatus à Græcis ad Romanum Pontificem propter infandam eorum hæresin (Iconomachiam) impietatémque pervenit: exactis à Romanis Episcopis Italia Orientis Imperatoribus deinceps oculos Romam versus cum suspiriis & gemitibus vix contorquentibus. Unus superat metus à Longobardis, in Italia tum latè dominantibus, quorum imperio Pipini, quem succollaturum sibi Zacharias Papa abdicato (si narrationi Trithemii & Sigonii, quam idem eodem libro Launojus in dubium etiam revocat; fides haberi potest) Childerico, ceu minùs ad destinata exequenda idoneo, Regem Francorum fecerat, & Caroli M. operâ excusso, adeoque vicina potentia remotioris auxilio subruta, Papa Romanæ ditionis dominium obligatum feudali vinculo adeptus est; quo jure, quave injuria, nihil ultra dicere attinet; rebus certè, ut Sigonius idem loc. cit. loquitur, pro Ecclesiæ salute, & sedis Apostolicæ authoritate, non tam piè, quàm prosperè gestis.
units.tr: XLVI. Soon a dispute about images and their veneration greatly occupied the Roman and Eastern Church. The occasion for the dispute arose in the year 712, when Philippicus Bardanes the Emperor and John the Patriarch of Constantinople, both Monothelites, rejected the Sixth Ecumenical Council, in which the Monothelites had been anathematized, and removed from the portico of St Sophia the images of the Fathers of that council, which Justinian had placed there shortly before. Soon afterwards Pope Constantine took the opposite stand: he held a synod at Rome, placed these same images in the portico of St Peter's, adding images of the chief Fathers who had attended the earlier councils, and further declared that images ought to be introduced into the churches as well. From this point the question of images ceased to be incidental and became principal. The pope dared to strip Philippicus of the empire, calling him fallen into the heresy of Iconoclasm (so Platina). Leo III the Isaurian, raised to the empire in 717, soon published an edict against images in 726 and sternly dissuaded Gregory II, Constantine's successor, who was called Dialogus, from protecting the images. He, raging against the emperor, stirred up the people of Ravenna, Venice and all the population against the emperor and the exarch. Thereupon the unbridled people made an assault on Paul, the exarch at Ravenna, and filled all Italy with sedition, plunder and slaughter. Finally, the Romans, bound by so many and such great crimes, if the account of the Greek writers Zonaras, Theophanes and Cedrenus is true (though Launoy has recently tried to make it suspect, Epist. lib. 7.), revolted from the obedience and loyalty of Leo the Eastern Emperor, after the exarchate, which had held Italy for two hundred years, was soon abolished. They received an oath, solemnly sworn, that they would defend the life and state of the Roman pontiff for ever, and would obey his authority. Sigonius writes of this in de Regno Italiae lib. 2. as follows: Thus Rome and the Roman Duchy passed from the Greeks to the Roman Pontiff on account of their unspeakable heresy (Iconoclasm) and impiety: after the Roman bishops had driven out the Eastern emperors from Italy, their eyes were turned towards Rome with sighs and groans, scarcely turning back. The only fear that remained was of the Lombards, who then ruled widely in Italy. Pope Zachary, by whose power Pepin (whom Zachary had made King of the Franks, having deposed Childeric as unfit to carry out what was intended, if the narrative of Trithemius and Sigonius, which Launoy also calls into doubt in the same book, can be trusted) was to support him, and by the work of Charlemagne the Lombards were thrown off, and so a neighbouring power, overthrown by the help of one farther away, the pope obtained dominion over the Roman territory, bound by a feudal tie. By what right or what wrong, there is no need to say more. Certainly the affairs, as Sigonius says in the same place, were carried out for the salvation of the Church and the authority of the Apostolic See, not so much piously as successfully.

units.la: XLVII. Ano DCCLIV. sub Constantino Copronymo Constantinopoli indicta & habita est Synodus Generalis Septima, ex Episcopis trecentis triginta octo conflata, qua, explosis aliis imaginibus unica definitur esse imago ab ipso Christo instituta, nimirum panis & vinum in Eucharistia, quæ repræsentant Christi corpus & sanguinem. Cui Synodo post triginta tres annos A. DCCLXXXVII. se oppositus Synodus Nicæna Secunda latrocinalis vulgò dicta, annitente Irene, Leonis IV. conjuge, & Constantini Septimi tum adhuc impuberis matre, quæ Adriano I. Rom. Pontifici & imaginibus simul addicta, cum eodem Papa conspirans eò denique rem perduxit, ut imagines honorandas, venerandas, salutandas, osculandas, incensis, cereis prosequendas, publico decreto sanciretur. Cui post decreto se oppositæ Constantinus ipse factus adultior, à matre Irene, verissima Erynnide, & oculis & vita propterea orbatus: Constantini successores, Nicephorus, alii, & Græci in universum: nec non Carolus M. ipse scriptis quatuor adversus cultum imaginum libris, & habita Francofurti {A} A. DCCXCIV. Synodo, ex Episcopis Francis, Germanis, Italis, Anglis pluribus conflata, qua, uti Walafridus Strabo, Author Annalium Fuldensium, loquitur, Pseudo-Synodus Græcorum pro adorandis imaginibus habita, & falsò Septima vocata ab Episcopis damnata est. De eadem Synodo sic Hincmarus Rhemensis Archiepiscopus libro contra Hincmarum Laudunensem edito: Tempore Caroli Magni Imperatoris, jussione Apostolicæ sedis, Generalis Synodus in Francia, convocante præfato Imperatore, celebrata, & secundùm Scripturarum tramitem, traditionémque majorum, ipsa Græcorum Pseudo-Synodus destructa, & penitus abdicata est. De cujus destructione non modicum volumen, quod in Palatio adolescentulus legi, ab eodem Imperatore Romam est per quosdam Episcopos missum. Paulò post: Authoritate itaque hujus Synodi nonnihil repressa est imaginum veneratio. Sed tamen Hadrianus & alii Pontifices in sua opinione perseverarunt, & mortuo Carolo suarum partium cultum vehementius promoverunt; adeò ut Ludovicus Caroli filius, libro longè acriori insectatus sit imaginum cultum, quàm Carolus. Cùm igitur Græci, Occidentales Franci, Alamanni, Itali, Angli, à Concilii Nicæno, à Pnntificiis Legatis directo, pro & universali se venditantis, & à Pontifice ipso Hadriano confirmati definitione libere recesserint, neque minùs tamen pro Christianis & orthodoxis habiti fuerint, (quis enim Divum Carolum, quis tot Episcopos hæreticos dixerit?) citra orthodoxiæ periculum à definitionibus Conciliorum Pontificiorum, Tridentini nominatim, cùm ab iis violatam esse legem Dei credi potest, recedi, fusè eruditéque Celeberrimus Allixius, dissertatione peculiari confecit.
units.tr: XLVII. In the year 754, under Constantine Copronymus, a General Seventh Synod was announced and held at Constantinople, made up of 338 bishops, which, after the other images were rejected, defined that the only image is the image instituted by Christ himself, namely the bread and wine in the Eucharist, which represent the body and blood of Christ. Thirty-three years later, in 787, the Second Synod of Nicaea, commonly called the robber synod, was set against this synod. It was promoted by Irene, the wife of Leo IV and mother of the still underage Constantine VII. She was devoted to Hadrian I, the Roman pontiff, and to images, and conspiring with that pope, she finally brought the matter to the point where it was enacted by public decree that images should be honoured, venerated, greeted, kissed, and followed with incense and candles. After this decree was opposed, Constantine himself, when he had grown older, was blinded in both eyes and deprived of life by his mother Irene, a true Erinys. Constantine's successors, Nicephorus and others, and the Greeks in general, opposed it, and so did Charlemagne himself, who wrote four books against the veneration of images. He also held a synod at Frankfurt {A} in 794, made up of many bishops of the Franks, Germans, Italians and English. As Walafrid Strabo, author of the Annals of Fulda, says, the synod judged the pseudo-synod of the Greeks, which was held in favour of adoring images and falsely called the Seventh, and condemned it. Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, writes of this same synod as follows, in a book published against Hincmar of Laon: In the time of the Emperor Charlemagne, by the order of the Apostolic See, a general synod was held in France, convened by the aforesaid emperor, and according to the path of Scripture and the tradition of the elders, the Greek pseudo-synod itself was destroyed and utterly rejected. He mentions a sizeable volume about its destruction, which he read as a young man in the palace, sent to Rome by the same emperor through certain bishops. A little later he adds: By the authority of this synod the veneration of images was somewhat restrained. But Hadrian and the other pontiffs persisted in their opinion, and after Charles died they promoted the worship of their party more vehemently, so that Louis, son of Charles, attacked the worship of images in a book far more fiercely than Charles had. Since, therefore, the Greeks, the Western Franks, Alemanni, Italians and English freely departed from the definition of the Council of Nicaea, which the papal legates had presented as universal and which Pope Hadrian himself had confirmed, and yet were regarded as Christians and orthodox (for who would call the divine Charles, or so many bishops, heretics?), the renowned Allix has shown at length and learnedly, in a special dissertation, that one may depart from the definitions of the papal councils, especially that of Trent, without danger to orthodoxy, when it can be believed that the law of God has been violated by them. {A} Charlemagne, against that Nicene Synod, held the Synod at Frankfurt and condemned the veneration of images, also by publishing books.

units.la: {A} Carolus M. adversus Synodum Nicænam illam Francofurti Synodum celebrat, & Imaginum cultum, libris etiam editis, damnat.
units.tr: {A} Charles the Great held a synod at Frankfurt against that Nicene Synod, and condemned the veneration of images, also publishing books to that effect.

units.la: XLVIII. Liberius nihilominus Papatus Romanus,
units.tr: XLVIII. Nonetheless the Roman Papacy,

units.la: Carolo Imperatore, lacertos movit, Pontificum obsequiis claritudinem & protegens, & provehens. Stephanus Papa jam ante Pipino retaliaturus Francorum Regibus Imperiales dignitates & titulos decreverat, eúmque populi Romani nomine Patritium dixerat. Carolus Filius post aliquot in Italiam expeditiones prosperè suscEPTAS, Franciæ jam, Italiæ & Germaniæ Dominus, meruit, ut primùm Patritius Romanus, mox etiam à Leone tertio, authoritate non propria, sed populi Romani, uti diserte Sigebertus Gemblacensis, Marianus Scotus, aliique testantur (quicquid etiam hic Baronius aliique sedis Romanæ gnathones pertendant, immane dogma inde eruentes, Episcopi Romani jus esse, Imperia & Regna mutare & transferre) Imperator Romanus proclamaretur, coronaretúrque. Ubi Leonem suo populíque nomine non imperium Carolo, seu rem (nam Franciæ, Italiæ, Germaniæ jam tum dominio potitus erat) sed rei & imperii titulum duntaxat contulisse, nuper Joh. de Buffieres Jesuita Hist. Franc lib. 4. fatetur. Transfegeratque jam Carolus cum Imperatoribus Orientis, ea lege, ut Imperator diceretur uterque; Carolus & posteri Occidentis: Orientis caeteri. Sicut autem gratia gratiam parere, & manus manum lavare solet: ita Carolus benefactis Paparum hostimentum retulit, Pipini donatione non confirmata duntaxat, sed immodicè etiam aucta: universis feré opibus, quas Hunnis eripuit, in Ecclesiæ ærarium illatis: Episcopis vicissim pro modo liberalitatis, (uti quidem ipse Petrus de Marca de Concordia Sacerd. & Imp. lib. VIII. 19:2. fatetur) de rigore antiquæ pœnitentiæ remittentibus: Ecclesiæ Romanæ ceremoniis plerisque in Franciæ Regnum introductis; &, quod Pontificiæ dominationis Palladium est, Episcopis Metropolitanorum vel Comprovincialium judicio non acquiescentibus appellatione ad Papæ judicium concessa. Neque Francos duntaxat Reges propitios adeò Pontifices experti sunt; sed Inam etiam, Regem Occidentalium Saxonum,cui tum Britannia parebat.Ejus enim indultu Britanniam universam Gregorio III. ita factam tributariam esse, ut ex singulis domibus quotannis singuli denarii ( Denarium S. Petri insignire moris erat ) S. Petro, seu Romanæ sedi pensitari debuerint, Polydorus Vergilius testatur.
units.tr: under the Emperor Charles, flexed its muscles, protecting and advancing its prestige by serving the Popes. Pope Stephen, even before Pepin, had decreed imperial dignities and titles to the Frankish kings in return, and had called him patrician in the name of the Roman people. Charles, his son, after several successful expeditions into Italy, already lord of France, Italy and Germany, earned first the title of Roman patrician, and then also, from Leo III, was proclaimed and crowned Roman Emperor, not by his own authority but by that of the Roman people, as Sigebert of Gembloux, Marianus Scotus and others expressly testify. (Whatever Baronius and other flatterers of the Roman See here may contend, deducing from it the monstrous dogma that it is the right of the Roman Bishop to change and transfer empires and kingdoms.) Joh. de Buffieres the Jesuit recently admitted in Hist. Franc. lib. 4. that Leo, in his own name and that of the Roman people, conferred on Charles not the empire itself (for he already held dominion over France, Italy and Germany) but only the title of the thing and of the empire. Charles had already come to terms with the Emperors of the East, on the condition that each should be called Emperor: Charles and his successors in the West, the others in the East. Yet just as favour is wont to beget favour, and hand to wash hand, so Charles repaid the Popes' services in kind, not merely confirming Pepin's donation but immoderately enlarging it, with almost all the wealth he had snatched from the Huns brought into the treasury of the Church. In turn he relaxed the rigour of ancient repentance for bishops in proportion to their generosity (as Peter de Marca himself admits in de Concordia Sacerd. & Imp. lib. VIII. 19:2). Many ceremonies of the Roman Church were introduced into the kingdom of France, and, which is the palladium of papal domination, appeal to the Pope's judgment was granted to bishops who did not acquiesce in the judgment of their metropolitans or provincial colleagues. Nor did the Popes find only the Frankish kings so favourable; they also found Ine, King of the West Saxons, to whom Britain was then subject. For by his indulgence all Britain was made tributary to Gregory III in such a way that each year a single penny from every household (it was customary to mark this as Peter's Penny) had to be paid to St Peter, that is to the Roman See, as Polydore Vergil testifies.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: Quibus tum gradibus mediisque Romanorum Pontificum, qui legitimi Domini, Orientalis Imperatoris & Exarchorum jugum iniquis prætextibus excutere religioni non duxerunt, Francorum Reges deposuerunt, Longobardos Francorum operâ Italia exegerunt, Francorum Regum indulgentia abusi turpiter sunt; authoritas & potestas in majus processerunt, Catalogus Testium veritatis lib. VIII. pag. 732. &c. Aphorismis plus quàm quinquaginta κατὰ λέπτὸν ediderit. Præterea religionis circa ea tempora prora & puppis in propagando Papæ suprematu,imaginum & sanctorum veneratione, cantionibus, Missarum solennibus, consecrationibus, oblationibus, orationibus apud statuas, imagines, reliquias, Festorum observantia, Templorum ornatu, cœlibatu Sacerdotum, votis Monachorum, aliisque oculiferiis meris constituta est. Sigillatim autem circa id tempus Missæ solitariæ seu privatæ, lex abstinendi à certis cibis, puta graculis, leporibus, fibris aliisque injuncta pœnitentibus, uti ex Gregorio II. Epistolis & Zacharia ad Bonifacium liquet: novæ peregrinationes institutæ ad Ecclesias noviter constructas, qualis in Galliciam ad Jacobum Majorem, hoc potissimum tempore repertum Compostellæ, Carolo M. Ecclesiam illam privilegiis dotante; juramentum Episcoporum, quo se erga Romanam sedem obstrinxerunt, præeunte eunte Bonifacio in formula Tomis Conciliorum inserta; apices dignitatum in Ecclesia, quales sunt Abbatum, Episcoporum, Archiepiscoporum, diribitore Papa; ritus ἀποθεώσεως à Leone III. Divinos honores Guiberto, Verdensi Episcopo decernente; (quam primam Canonizationem se legisse Bellarminus lib. I. de Sanct. Beat. fatetur) originem sumpserunt. Et hæc omnia Ecclesia Romana Ecclesiis aliis, Gallicis, Britannicis, Germanicis, Hispanicis, cumprimis iis, quæ ad Christum recens conversæ sunt, obtrudere primas inter curas, nihil non in hisce indulgente Carolo, habuit. Denique ignorantiæ tenebris ita immerso clero, ut in ordinando Episcopo non doctrina quæpiam exquisitior, & in Sacris Literis subactum judicium, sed peritia modò cantandi orationem Dominicam, Symbolum & Psalterium, Computum recitandi requisita fuerit, nihil mirum (ita Mezeræus Pontificius Hist. Gallic. Tomo I. in Carolo M. arguit) crassam ignorantiam occupâsse plebes. Religio tota conversa erat in superstitiones.
units.tr: By these steps, and through the mediation of the Roman Pontiffs, who did not scruple to shake off, on unjust pretexts, the yoke of their lawful lord, the Eastern Emperor, and of the exarchs, the Frankish kings deposed the Lombards and drove them out of Italy with Frankish help. Having shamefully abused the indulgence of the Frankish kings, authority and power grew greater. The Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth, lib. VIII. pag. 732. etc., has set out more than fifty aphorisms with exact care. Besides, at about this time the prow and stern of religion, in spreading papal supremacy, were established in the veneration of images and saints, in chants, solemn Masses, consecrations, oblations, prayers before statues, images and relics, the observance of feasts, the adornment of temples, the celibacy of priests, the vows of monks, and other eye-catching trifles. In particular, around this time, private or solitary Masses were introduced, and a law of abstinence from certain foods, such as jackdaws, hares and entrails, was imposed on penitents, as is clear from the Letters of Gregory II and from Zachary to Boniface. New pilgrimages were established to churches recently built, such as the one to Compostela in Galicia to St James the Greater, a shrine discovered at that time and endowed with privileges by Charlemagne. The oath of bishops, by which they bound themselves to the Roman See, was inserted in the formula in the Tomes of the Councils, with Boniface leading the way. The badges of dignity in the Church, such as those of abbots, bishops and archbishops, were distributed by the Pope. The rite of deification, by which Leo III decreed divine honours to Guibert, bishop of Verden (which Bellarmine, lib. I. de Sanct. Beat., admits he read as the first canonization), took its origin. The Roman Church, granting everything to Charles, regarded all this as a primary concern: to impose it on other churches, Gallic, British, German and Spanish, and especially on those recently converted to Christ. Finally, the clergy was so immersed in the darkness of ignorance that for ordaining a bishop no more exact learning and no judgment trained in Holy Letters was required, but only skill in chanting the Lord's Prayer, the Creed and the Psalter, and in reciting the calendar. No wonder (so the Papist Mézeray argues in Hist. Gallic. Tomo I. in Carolo M.) crass ignorance seized the common people. All religion was turned into superstitions.

units.la: L. Cujusmodi seculo nono Ecclesiæ Romanæ facies fuerit, Pontificum illius seculi historia, & res iis sedentibus gestæ propalant. Fuerunt autem Pontifices ordine Stephanus V. Paschalis I. Eugenius II. Valentinus, Gregorius IV. Sergius II. Leo IV. Johannes VIII. Fœmina, Benedictus III. Nicolaus I. Hadrianus II. Stephanus VI. Formosus, Bonifacius VI. Stephanus VII. Ἀξιομνημόνευτα[?] nonnulla commemorare haud pigebit.
units.tr: L. What the face of the Roman Church was like in the ninth century, the history of the Popes of that century and the deeds done under their rule make plain. The Popes, in order, were Stephen V, Paschal I, Eugene II, Valentine, Gregory IV, Sergius II, Leo IV, John VIII (the woman), Benedict III, Nicholas I, Hadrian II, Stephen VI, Formosus, Boniface VI and Stephen VII. I shall not be ashamed to recall some matters [ἀξιομνημόνευτα] worthy of record.

units.la: LI. Stephanus V. contra legem, ita Aimonius lib. IV. p. 103. loquitur: electus & ordinatus, non exspectato scilicet Imperatoris jussu; errorem mox emendaturus, omnem populum Romanum fidelitatem cum juramento promittere Ludovico iussit. Ejus etiam sanctio D. 69. C. quia sancta 28. extat, ut Pontifex convenientibus Episcopis & universo Clero eligatur, præsente Senatu & Populo; utque sic electus ab omnibus præsentibus Legatis gatis Imperialibus consecretur. Neque tamen ei sanctioni pondus fuit in electione successoris Paschalis I. qui inscio Imperatore Ludovico Pio Papa creatus, Cleri & populi impetum apud Cæsarem causatus est, monente Romanos Cæsare, ne deinceps Majestatem laederent, & Majorum ut statuta in Pontifice creando servarent.
units.tr: LI. Stephen V, as Aimoin says in lib. IV. p. 103., was elected and ordained against the law, that is, without waiting for the Emperor's command. Soon, to correct the error, he ordered all the Roman people to promise fidelity to Louis with an oath. His decree also survives in D. 69. C. quia sancta 28.: that the Pope be chosen by the bishops and the whole clergy assembled, in the presence of the Senate and the People, and that he thus elected be consecrated by all the imperial legates present. Yet this decree had no weight in the election of Paschal I's successor. Paschal was created Pope without the knowledge of the Emperor Louis the Pious, and he excused himself before Caesar for the assault of the clergy and people, while Caesar warned the Romans not to injure his majesty from now on, and to keep the ancestral statutes in creating a Pope.

units.la: LII. Eugenius II. A. DCCCXXIV. Papa electus est in schismate, cujus componendi gratia missus à Ludovico Lotharius filius, qui, Aventini lib. IV. Annal. verba sunt, statum Reipub. quem superiorum Pontificum ambitio immodica, insatiabilis avaritia, versutiaque improba conturbarat, componit, intercepta direptaque fraude a aminibus Flantiquis possessionibus reddit. Superbiae quinetiam Pontificum specimen praebuit Successor Eugenii Valentinus, cujus electi & ad Lateranense Patriarchium deducti pedes omnis Romanorum Senatus (ita Anastasius loquitur) osculatus est.
units.tr: LII. Eugene II was elected in A.D. 824 in a schism. Lothair, the son of Louis, was sent to settle it, and, in the words of Aventinus, Annal. lib. IV., he settled the state of the commonwealth, which the immoderate ambition, insatiable avarice and wicked craftiness of the earlier Popes had thrown into confusion, and he restored the intercepted and plundered possessions to the churches by a just decision. The successor of Eugene, Valentine, also gave an example of pride: when he was elected and led to the Lateran Patriarchate, the whole Senate of the Romans (so Anastasius says) kissed his feet.

units.la: LIII. Anno DCCCXXIV. Michael & Theophilus Orientis Imperatores ad Ludovicum & Lotharium Occidentis Imperatores Legatos miserunt, de imaginum controversia & Nicæna Synodo consilium expetituros, rogaturósque, ut interventu suo Legationem ad Papam ejusdem negotii causâ destinatam favorabiliorem redderent. Sequenti igitur anno Ludovici jussu Parisiis Synodum celebrant Gallicani Præsules, unanimíque sententia sic ad Ludovicum inde rescribunt. Nicænam Synodum cum Sanctæ memoriæ genitor vester coram se suisque perlegi fecisset, & multis in locis, ut dignum erat, reprehendisset, & quædam capitula, quæ reprehensioni patebant, prænotasset, atque per Angilbertum Abbatem Adriano Papæ direxisset, ut ab illius judicio & authoritate corrigerentur. Ipse rursus favendo illis, qui ejus instinctu tam superstitiosa, tamque incongrua testimonia memorato operi inseruerant, per singula capitula in illorum excusationem respondere, quæ voluit, non tamen, quæ decuit, conatus est. Talia quippe quædam sunt, quæ in ilillorum objectionem opposuit, quæ, remota in Pontificali authoritate, & veritati & authoritati refragantur. Imperatores collecta à Theologis contra cultum imaginum testimonia veterum Patrum ad Romanum Pontificem Eugenium II. per Hieremiam Senonensem, & Jonem Aurelianensem Episcopum transmiserunt, addito mandato, ut patienter ac modeste cum eo de hac causa disputarent, ne nimis resistendo eum in aliquam irrevocabilem pertinaciam incidere compellerent. Papa ea de re parum folicitus, rogantibus Imperatoribus testimonium sibi ex Divina Scriptura, quo imaginum adoratio constaret, ut proferretur, Legatos uno verbo ablegat; arrogantes esse, qui talia sciscitarentur. Adeò pertinaciter εἰκονοδουλεία Pontifices propugnarunt, & rectiora sentientibus præfractè se opposuerunt.
units.tr: LIII. In A.D. 824 the Eastern Emperors Michael and Theophilus sent legates to the Western Emperors Louis and Lothair, to seek advice about the controversy over images and the Nicene Synod, and to ask that, by their intervention, they make more favourable the embassy sent to the Pope on the same business. Therefore, in the following year, by Louis's command, the Gallican prelates held a synod at Paris and, by unanimous judgment, replied to Louis as follows. When your father of holy memory had the Nicene Synod read before himself and his men, and had rebuked it in many places, as was fitting, and had marked certain chapters open to censure, and had sent them through Abbot Angilbert to Pope Hadrian, so that they might be corrected by his judgment and authority, he, in turn, favouring those who at his prompting had inserted such superstitious and incongruous testimonies into that work, tried to answer on behalf of their excuse, point by point, as he wished, but not as he ought. Indeed, there are some things he set against their objections which, apart from the papal authority, are opposed to both truth and authority. The Emperors sent the testimonies of the ancient Fathers against the veneration of images, gathered by theologians, to the Roman Pontiff Eugene II through Jeremiah of Sens and Jonas, bishop of Orléans, with the added command that they should dispute with him about this matter patiently and modestly, lest by resisting too much they drove him into some irrevocable obstinacy. The Pope, little troubled about this, when the Emperors asked that he produce some testimony from Divine Scripture establishing the adoration of images, dismissed the legates with one word: that those who asked such things were arrogant. So obstinately did the Popes defend image-worship [εἰκονοδουλεία] and so stubbornly did they oppose those who thought more rightly.

units.la: LIV. Gregorium IV. A. DCCCXXVII. lectum Papam Ludovici Imp. Pii filiorum adversus Patrem pessima machinantium partes fovisse, ut Lotharium sibi devinciat, historiæ tradunt. Cúmque in Galliam venire eum, ut Ludovicum Patrem excommunicaret, fama tulisset, qui à partibus Ludovici stabant Episcopi, ausi sunt afferere, nullo modo se ejus voluntati velle succumbere, sed si excommunicaturus veniret, excommunicatus abiret, cum aliter se habeat antiquorum canonum authoritas. Ejus Successor Sergius II. Os porci dictus, Papa factus, fœdum nomen mutavit; ejusque exemplo deinceps alii. Idem neglecto Imperatoris Lotharii consensu, sedem occupavit; & post ipsum etiam Leo IV. quo defuncto Johannes, seu potius Johanna Octava, Fœmina virilem sexum mentita A. DCCCLIV. Papalem thronum conscendit. Quod fabulis licet hodie gnathones Pontificum, aliíque deputent: Anastasius tamen Bibliothecarius coætaneus in Codice MS. Lutetiæ conservato, nec non iis Codicibus, qui ex Heidelbergensi Bibliotheca Moguntiam transmissi sunt Jesuitis, Anastasii edi-
units.tr: LIV. Historians report that Pope Gregory IV, elected in 827, favoured the sons of Emperor Louis the Pious in their wicked schemes against their father, in order to bind Lothair to himself. When word spread that he was coming into Gaul to excommunicate Louis the Father, the bishops who sided with Louis dared to assert that they would in no way submit to his will: "if he came to excommunicate, he would leave excommunicated, since the authority of the ancient canons stands otherwise." His successor, Sergius II, who was called Os porci, "Pig's mouth," on becoming pope changed his ugly name, and others followed his example afterwards. Likewise, disregarding the consent of Emperor Lothair, he took possession of the see; and after him Leo IV did the same. When Leo died, John, or rather Joan the Eighth, a woman who pretended to be a man, mounted the papal throne in 854. Although the flatterers of the Pontiffs and others today count this as a fable, Anastasius the Librarian, a contemporary, in a manuscript kept at Paris, and also in those codices which were sent from the Heidelberg library to Mainz for the Jesuits, the Anastasius' edi-

units.la: Eugenii II. in Iconolatria tuenda obstinatio.
units.tr: The obstinacy of Eugene II in defending image-worship.

units.la: Gregorius IV. Ludovici filios adversus Patrem fovet, & anathema commina-tus, ab Episcopis Galliæ spernitur.
units.tr: Gregory IV favours the sons of Louis against their father, and, having threatened anathema, is spurned by the bishops of Gaul.

units.la: Sergius II. Os porci, electus Papa, primus nomen mutat. Idem & post ipsum Leo IV. sedem, neglecto Imp. consensu, occupant.
units.tr: Sergius II, "Pig's mouth," elected pope, is the first to change his name. The same, and after him Leo IV, occupy the see, disregarding the Emperor's consent.

units.la: Johannes VIII. fœmina. editoribus, crimen falsi, à Doctissimo Marquardo Frehero publicè iis impactum admittentibus (uti ex historia huius seculi à Celeb. Böklero edita liquet) disertè affirmat. Affirmat etiam Radulphus Flaviacensis in Polychronico, & post eum innumeri Pontificii Reformationis temporibus antiquiores, ut, si fabulis accensere pro lubitu illi voluerint, saltem mendacium ex Papatu, in quo ante Reformationem plurimi testes rem liquidò affirmârunt, originem trahere ne ignorent.
units.tr: John VIII, a woman. The editors, admitting the charge of forgery brought against them by the most learned Marquard Freher (as is clear from the history of this century edited by the celebrated Böckler), state this plainly. Radulphus of Flavigny also affirms it in his Polychronicon, and after him countless Papists who lived before the Reformation, so that, if they wish to count these as fables at their pleasure, at least they should not fail to know that the lie comes from the Papacy, since before the Reformation very many witnesses clearly affirmed the matter.

units.la: LV. Anno DCCCLVIII. Nicolaus I. Paparum fuperbiffimus, ad potentiam augendam per fas & nefas incitatus, Papatum iniit. Extat Dist. 96. Satis evidenter, ejus vox decretoria: Satis evidenter ostenditur, à seculari potestate, nec solvi prorsus, nec ligari Pontificem, quem constat à pio Principe Constantino Deum appellatum, cùm nec posse Deum ab hominibus judicari, manifestum sit. Ubi si utrobique Dei nomen idem significat, verum & æternum Deum blasphemè Papam profitetur: si diversum, manifestus paralogismus committitur. In Lotharium Galliæ Regem anathema vibravit primus omnium id ausus in Reges Galliæ. Epistola ad Michaelem Imperatorem Constantinopolitanum, Majestatis Papalis plena, ab Episcopatu remotum Ignatium, eíque substitutum Photium, se inconsulto graviter conqueritur. Eidem excommunicationem, ni Calabritanum Siculúmque patrimonium Ecclesiæ suæ debitum restituerit, comminatus. Magnanimo pectore Regibus & Tyrannis eum imperasse, eisque, ac si orbis terrarum dominus esset, authoritate sua præfuisse, Regino scribit. Sed & Ravennatensem Ecclesiam, quæ diu se primatui suo oppositi, unà cum Johanne Archiepiscopo, qui se Majestatis Pontificiæ læsæ reum fateri debuit, sibi Sedíque suæ subjicit. Quin & diris multis Sacerdotes conjugatos incessit, ob quas eum Huldricus Augustanus Episcopus graviter reprehendit.
units.tr: LV. In 858 Nicholas I, the proudest of popes, driven by a lust for power by right and by wrong, entered upon the papacy. His decisive saying stands in Dist. 96, Satis evidenter: "It is sufficiently evident that the Pontiff, whom it is agreed was called God by the pious prince Constantine, is neither absolved nor bound at all by secular power, since it is plain that God cannot be judged by men." Here, if on both sides the name God means the same thing, he blasphemously declares the true and eternal God to be the Pope; if it means something different, a manifest paralogism is committed. He was the first of all to dare to hurl anathema against Lothair, King of Gaul, and against the kings of Gaul. In a letter to Michael, Emperor of Constantinople, full of papal majesty, he complains bitterly that Ignatius had been removed from the episcopate and Photius put in his place without his being consulted. He threatened him with excommunication unless he restored the Calabrian and Sicilian patrimony owed to his Church. Regino writes that with a magnanimous spirit he commanded kings and tyrants, and presided over them with his authority as if he were lord of the world. He also subjected to himself and to his see the Church of Ravenna, which had long opposed his primacy, together with Archbishop John, who had to confess himself guilty of injuring papal majesty. Moreover he assailed married priests with many curses, for which Huldrich, Bishop of Augsburg, sharply rebuked him.

units.la: Nicolai I. judicari se à seculari potestate; eò quòd Papa à Constantino Deus vocatus fuerit, vetantis, Lotharium excommunicantis; cum Michaele Imp. Constant. ob Photium Ignatio substitutum expostulantis & anathema eidem intentantis: Ravennatensem Ecclesiam opprimentis: Sacerdotes conjugatos persequentis insolentia. prehendit. Denique extant ejusdem Epistolæ Decretales à Gratiano collectæ, quibus Majestatem Pontificiam mirè is statuminatum ivit.
units.tr: Of Nicholas I: that he forbade being judged by secular power, because the Pope had been called God by Constantine; that he excommunicated Lothair; that he demanded an explanation from Michael, Emperor of Constantinople, about Photius being put in place of Ignatius, and threatened him with anathema; that he oppressed the Church of Ravenna; and the insolence with which he persecuted married priests. Finally, his decretal letters, collected by Gratian, are extant, by which he wonderfully raised high the papal majesty.

units.la: LVI. Nicolai ejusdem ætate in Gallia de Prædestinatione & Libero arbitrio vehementer agitata controversia est. Godescalcus in Ecclesiæ Rhemensis Monasterio Monachus; non omnes ad vitam æternam, sed quosdam ad exitium prædestinatos, neque Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse, palàm docuerat. De sententia sua scriptum etiam libellum Synodo Moguntinæ jussu Ludovici Imper. A. DCCCXLVIII. exhibuit. Qua occasione sententia ea, quam antehac ipse S. Augustinus adversus Pelagianos propugnavit, à Rabano Mauro Archiepiscopo Moguntino, & Haimone Halberstadiensi, cæterisque Germaniæ Episcopis condemnari coepit. Insuper iidem cum literis Synodalibus Godescalcum ad Hincmarum Rhemensem Archiepiscopum miserunt. Eò cùm venit, sententiam suam constanter asseruit: proin à Rhemensis Ecclesiæ & Galliæ Belgicæ Episcopis denuo damnatus, & cùm se iis irreverentiùs opposuisset, virgis cæsus, cœnobiiqnc carceri mancipatus est. Interea adversus eundem præter alios Johannes Erigena Scotus librum novendecim capitulorum scripsit; refutatus mox à Remigio Lugdunensi Archiepiscopo, Godeschalci causam adversum Erigenam, aliósque suscipiente: Lugdunensis etiam, ut & Arelatensis ac Viennensis Ecclesiæ Episcopis in Synodo Valentina A. DCCCLV. Canones aliquot sancientibus, quibus, quid in Godeschalco, quid item in adversariis ejus desiderent, probéntve, exponunt, simulque quatuor capitula ab Hincmaro Godescalco opposita, & librum ab Erigena Scoto scriptum condemnant. Demum Hincmarus A. DCCCLIX. libro integro hac de materia scripto Valentinam Synodum oppugnat: Scriptúmque suum Regi Carolo Calvo exhibet. qui litem sopiviße videtur. Eam historiam doctissimus Usserius singulari libro de Godeschalco edito ediderit, & paucis etiam Forbesius Instruct. lib. VIII. 3. 4. nec non G. J. Vossius de Histor. Pelag. lib. VII. pag. 4. constringunt. Ex eo declinatio doctrinæ orthodoxæ de Gratia, Prædestinatione & morte Christi constare potest.
units.tr: LVI. In the same age as Nicholas, a violent controversy about predestination and free will arose in Gaul. Godescalc, a monk in the monastery of the Church of Reims, had openly taught that not all are predestined to eternal life, but some to destruction, and that Christ did not die for all. By order of Emperor Louis, in 848 he presented to the Synod of Mainz a written pamphlet setting out his opinion. On this occasion that opinion, which St Augustine himself had defended against the Pelagians, began to be condemned by Rabanus Maurus, Archbishop of Mainz, Haimo of Halberstadt, and the other bishops of Germany. Moreover, they sent Godescalc to Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, with synodal letters. When he came there, he steadfastly maintained his opinion; therefore he was condemned again by the bishops of the Church of Reims and of Belgic Gaul, and when he opposed them too disrespectfully, he was beaten with rods and shut up in a monastery prison. Meanwhile, among others, John Erigena the Scot wrote against him a book in nineteen chapters, which was soon refuted by Remigius, Archbishop of Lyons, who took up Godescalc's cause against Erigena. The bishops of the Churches of Lyons, Arles and Vienne, in the Synod of Valence in 855, enacted several canons in which they set out what they desire or approve in Godescalc and likewise in his opponents, and at the same time condemned the four chapters that Hincmar had set against Godescalc, and the book written by the Scot Erigena. Finally, in 859 Hincmar attacked the Synod of Valence in a whole book written on this subject, and presented his writing to King Charles the Bald, who seems to have ended the quarrel. The most learned Ussher has treated that history in his separate book de Godeschalco, and Forbes, Instruct. lib. VIII, 3, 4, and G. J. Vossius, de Histor. Pelag. lib. VII, p. 4, touch on it briefly. From this one can establish the departure from orthodox doctrine concerning grace, predestination and the death of Christ.

units.la: LVII. Nicolai successor Hadrianus II. Hincmaro Rhemensi Archiepiscopo in mandatis dedit, ut Regem suum Carolum Calvum communione privaret, nī in Regno fratris sui Lotharii, filio ejus Ludovico cederet. Cui Conventus Rhemensis nomine acriter admodum Hincmarus respondet, inter alia objiciens: Regna seculi hujus bellis quaeri, victoriis propagari, non Apostolicè, vel Episcoporum excommunicationibus obtineri: & Scripturam dicere, quia Domini est Regnum, per quem Reges regnant, & cui voluerit dare illud, ministerio Angelorum & hominum, &c. Antecessores ejus ordinem Ecclesiasticum, non Rempublicam, quæ Regum cura sit, disposuisse: jugum Pontificis Francos portare non posse, & quæ ςηλιτϑυλικά plura in Epistola, à Bochello Decretis Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ lib. 2. pag. 3. 7. inserta occurrunt. In literis vero ad ipsum Regem ejusdem Hadriani ἐπιγραφὴ hæc legere est: Volumus & authoritate Apostolica jubemus Hincmarum Laudunensem Episcopum, vestra fretum potentia, ad limina Sanctorum, nostramque venire clementiam. Non parum insolentia hæc Regem offendit, questus, Seculi umbrosum typhum in Ecclesiam sic induci; & inter alia sic Pontifici scribens: Nobis scribere non piget, sed exigente causa necessarium est; quia Reges Francorum, ex Regio genere nati, non Episcoporum ViceDomini, sed terræ Domini hactenus fuimus computati. Et, ut Leo ac Romana Synodus scripsit: Reges & Imperatores, quos terris Divina potentia præcipit præesse, jus distinguendorum negotiorum Episcopis sanctis, juxta Divalia constituta permiserunt, non autem Episcoporum villici extiterunt. Quis igitur hanc inversam legem infernus evomuit? Quis tartarus de suis abditis & tenebricosis cuniculis eructavit?
units.tr: LVII. Nicholas's successor, Hadrian II, instructed Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, to deprive his king, Charles the Bald, of communion unless he yielded the kingdom of his brother Lothair to Lothair's son Louis. To this, Hincmar answered sharply in the name of the Council of Reims, objecting among other things: "The kingdoms of this age are got by wars and extended by victories; they are not obtained apostolically or by the excommunications of bishops. Scripture says that the kingdom is the Lord's, through whom kings reign, and he gives it to whom he will, by the ministry of angels and men, etc. His predecessors arranged the ecclesiastical order, not the commonwealth, which is the care of kings. The Franks cannot bear the yoke of a pontiff," and many other jealous [ζηλοτυπικά] things found in the letter, more in the Epistle, cited by Bochellus, Decreta Ecclesiae Gallicanae, lib. 2, pp. 3, 7. In the letters to the king himself, the address of this Hadrian reads: "We wish, and by apostolic authority command, Hincmar, Bishop of Laon, relying on your power, to come to the thresholds of the saints and to our clemency." This insolence offended the king not a little; he complained that "the shadowy pride of the world is thus introduced into the Church", and, writing to the Pontiff among other things, said: "It does not irk us to write to you, but the cause makes it necessary, because the kings of the Franks, born of royal stock, have hitherto been reckoned not as vicars of the bishops but as lords of the land. And, as Leo and the Roman Synod wrote: kings and emperors, whom divine power commands to rule the lands, have permitted holy bishops the right to distinguish business according to divine constitutions, but they were not stewards of bishops. Who, then, did hell vomit up this inverted law? What Tartarus belched it out of its hidden and dark tunnels?"

units.la: LVIII. Sedem Hadriano Pontifice Basilius Orientis Imperator, qui Michaele Imperii consorte nefariè cæso summam rei ad se contraxit,à Photio Patriarcha ob id facinus à sacræ Synaxeos communione repulsus, ulturus ignominiam istam, Synodum Generalem convocaturus, facile assensum Papæ, discordiam illam in potestatis suæ incrementum versuri, & non obscurè Bonifacii III. Phocam parricidam laudantis exemplo, Basilio parricidæ supparasitantis, impetrat. Impetrat ab eodem Imperatore τὰ ἀμοιβαῖα Hadrianus, ut videlicet sibi in Synodo tali ληρικῇ A. DCCCLXIX habita præsidere per Legatos, quos inter Anastasius Bibliothecarius principem locum obtinuit, integrum esset quod in nulla Synodo Oecumenica antehac factum. In ea Synodo Photio ob reprehensum Basilium parricidam depositò, restitutus est Ignatius. Libellum legatis suis tradiderat Hadrianus, à Nicolao I. ante confectum, quo quid de Primatu Papæ & adoratione imaginum tenendum in primis sit, continebatur, lege etiam præscripta, ne quisquam in Synodum eam cooptaretur, nî priùs signaculo suo ad eam fidem se devinxisset, quod religiosè adeò observatum, ut quotquot dicto audientes non essent, à Synodo excluderentur. Unde dominari & pervincere, adeóque omnia pro nutu gerere, & in Oriente etiam res suas strenuè promovere, lenocinante insigni parricida, facilè licuit. Sed Synodum eam, quòd aperta vi omnia illic gesta, & per eam Ecclesia Constantinopolitana in Romanam potestatem redacta, & Symbolo etiam Nicæno-Constantinopolitano addita sit vox Filióque; vel pro legitima, vel pro Oecumenica Octava neutiquam Græci recipiunt: & contra eam Marcus Ephesinus in Concilio Florentino disertè protestatus est. de quo doctissidoctissimus Beveregius, Annot. in Synod. Constant. primam & secundam, p. 170. pluscul& dixit.
units.tr: LVIII. Hadrian being pope, Basil, Emperor of the East, who had gained the sole power by the wicked murder of Michael, his co-emperor, and had been repelled from communion in the holy Synaxis by Photius the Patriarch on account of that crime, wished to avenge this disgrace and to call an Ecumenical Council. He easily obtained the Pope's assent, since the Pope would turn the discord to the increase of his own power, and, following openly the example of Boniface III, who praised the parricide Phocas, he fawned on Basil the parricide. From the same Emperor Hadrian obtained τὰ ἀμοιβαῖα [a quid pro quo], namely that he might preside through legates in such a ληρικῇ ["robber"] synod held in 869, among whom Anastasius the Librarian held the first place, something that had not happened before in any Ecumenical Council. At that Synod Photius, who had been deposed for rebuking the parricide Basil, was removed, and Ignatius was restored. Hadrian had handed his legates a little book, composed earlier by Nicholas I, which contained what must above all be held about the primacy of the Pope and the adoration of images. A rule was also laid down that no one should be admitted to that Synod unless he had first bound himself to that faith by his seal; this was so religiously observed that all who would not obey were excluded from the Synod. Hence it was easy for them to dominate and prevail, and to manage everything at their nod, and to push their own affairs vigorously even in the East, with the notorious parricide as their go-between. But the Greeks by no means accept that Synod as either lawful or Ecumenical, the Eighth, because everything done there was by open force, and through it the Church of Constantinople was reduced under Roman power, and the word Filioque was added to the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed. Against it Mark of Ephesus protested expressly at the Council of Florence, on which the most learned Beveridge, Annot. in Synod. Constant. primam & secundam, p. 170, said somewhat more.

units.la: LIX. Hadriani II. Successor Johannes IX. intra decennium tres Imperatores, Carolum Calvum, (Ludovico Ludovici Pii filio & natu majore, & moratiore politicas ob rationes posthabito) Ludovicum Balbum, & Carolum Crassum ad se Romam invitatos Augustos pronunciat, consecrátque. Hinc, inquit Sigonius, titulus Imperatoris Augusti posthac sincerum Pontificis beneficium esse, annique Imperii à consecratione Pontificia repeti coepti. Non exiguum etiam inde ad Pontificem lucrum rediit. Carolus enim Calvus ei Ducatum Spoletanum, Aricium & Clusium civitates Beneventi; Samnium, Calabriam, aliaque donavit. Sed & Ludovicum, qui ab Adalgiso Beneventi captus, juramento multa ei, prius quàm liberatetur, promisit, juramenti religione, authoritate Dei & Sancti Petri exsolvit. Quod ante eum nemo, post eum plures tentárunt.
units.tr: LIX. Hadrian II's successor, John IX, within a decade proclaimed and consecrated as Augustus three emperors whom he had invited to Rome: Charles the Bald (a son of Louis the Pious, the elder, though passed over for political reasons), Louis the Stammerer, and Charles the Fat. From this, says Sigonius, the title of Emperor Augustus became thereafter a pure gift of the Pope, and the years of the Empire began to be counted from the Papal consecration. No small profit also came to the Pope from this. Charles the Bald gave him the Duchy of Spoleto, the cities of Arezzo and Chiusi, the lands of Benevento, Samnium, Calabria, and others. And Louis, who had been captured by Adalgis of Benevento and had promised him many things under oath before he was set free, was released from his oath by the authority of God and St. Peter, by the sanctity of the oath. Before him no one had attempted this, and many attempted it after him.

units.la: LX. Mortuo Johanni, & post hunc etiam Martino II. malis artibus ad fastigium hoc enixo, à cujus tempore, ita Sigonius de Regno Italiæ lib. V. pag. 137. loquitur, Romana Ecclesia gravissime laboravit; & paulatim vetus Ecclesiæ disciplina est lapsa; successit A. DCCCLXXXIV. Hadrianus III. Is decreta duo Sedi Romanæ perquam favorabilia, uti sperabat, sutura cudit. Prius, ne in creando Pontifice Imperatoris exspectaretur authoritas. Ita ausos esse Pontifices suos contemnere merito Cranzius 5 Metrop. n. 4. p. 1. queritur. Posterius, ut moriente Rege Crasso sine filiis, Regnum Italiæ Principibus unà cum titulo Imperii traderetur. Utrumque Sigonius loc. cit. memorat, & prius quidem infra lib. VI. pag. 144. à Johanne IX. (x) statuente, ne Pontifices designatos nisi in conspectu Legatorum Regiorum, jus esset consecrari, abrogatum; testatur idem, ad vitanda, inquit, quæ in Comitiis oriebantur, cum maxima Ecclesiæ offensione, dissidia. Posterius verò secutos Italicos Reges intestinis populorum discordiis perturbâsse, ac se ipsos prorsus unà cum Ecclesia perdidisse, ea tempora in Rempublicam inferentes, quibus nulla alia tetriora fuisse, vel principum nequitia, vel populorum insania in tota antiquitate reperiuntur: idem initio libri quinti commemorat.
units.tr: LX. After John died, and after Martin II, who had climbed to this height by evil arts, from whose time, as Sigonius speaks in De Regno Italiae, book 5, p. 137, the Roman Church suffered very grievously, and little by little the old discipline of the Church fell away, Hadrian III succeeded in 884. He issued two decrees, very favourable to the Roman See, as he hoped they would be. The first: that the authority of the Emperor should not be awaited in creating a Pope. Cranzius, in book 5 of his Metropolis, no. 4, p. 1, rightly complains that they had dared to despise their Popes in this way. The second: that when King Charles died without sons, the kingdom of Italy should be handed over to the princes together with the title of Emperor. Sigonius, loc. cit., records both. The first he records as abrogated later, in book 6, p. 144, by John IX, who decreed that it should not be lawful to consecrate Popes designate except in the presence of the royal legates; the same author attests that this was done to avoid the disputes that arose in the assemblies, with the greatest offence to the Church. But the second he records as follows: that the Italian kings who followed disturbed the kingdom with the internal discords of the peoples, and utterly destroyed themselves together with the Church, bringing into the commonwealth those times, than which none more hideous can be found in all antiquity, whether through the wickedness of the princes or the madness of the peoples; the same author mentions this at the beginning of book 5.

units.la: LXI. Quò Sanctitatis, doctrinæ, Virtutis in Pontificibus horum temporum minus, hoc audaciæ plus in iis extitit. Nihil iis prius, antiquius nihil, quàm stabilire Hierarchiam. Stephanus VI. Hadriani III. successor ejusmodi decretum eò pertinens, quod apud Gratianum D. 19. C. enim vero extat, sanxit: Quicquid Ecclesia Romana statuit, quicquid ordinat, perpetuò quidem & irrefragabiliter observandum est. Eum qui excepit Formosus, qui ante Episcopatum Romanum nunquam se affectaturum juraverat, cùm à rivalis Sergii factione exagitaretur nimiùm, Arnulphum, Carlomanni filium in Italiam evocatum, Romamque armata manu ingressum, Imperatorem pronuntiavit, unxit, coronavit. Cumque post ejus & Bonifacii VI. mortem Sergiana factio caput exereret, eò deventum, ut Stephanus VII. A. DCCCXCVII. Papa creatus, furore nefario percitus, Formosi Pontificis cadaver ex Sepulchro refossum, præsente Synodo, in sede Pontificatus Romani, Sacerdotalibus indumentis exornatum, collocari, atque sic Formosum tanquam impium, doctrinarumque Sanctarum inscium (ita miserum cadaver compellabat) ejusque Acta condemnari, móxque exutum vestimentis, digitisque tribus, quibus benedicere moris erat, abscissis, in Tiberim jactari curaverit. Historiam horrendam Luitprandus, Ticinensis, Ecclesiæ Diaconus, qui tum vixerat, lib. I. cap. 8. Sigonius lib. VI. alii, in primis Auxilius in Dialogo contra intestinam Ecclesiæ Romanæ discordiam, cujus Sigebertus lib. de Eccl. Scriptoribus, à Miræo edito, narrant. Baronius nefas id extenuans ad A. DCCCXCVII. art. 2. ait, non fuisse errorem in fide, sed violentam tyrannidem in facto. Neque tamen vel horribile illud factum ex fide processisse: vel veritatis infallibilis Spiritum in ejusmodi raptoribus & latronibus habitasse, persuaderi sanus quispiam poterit. Proin etiam Stephani hujus tyrannidem detestatos Successores ejus, Romanum, Theodorum, Johannem X. Ravennatem, alios, constat; utpote qui Formoso Papalis dignitatis formam restituerunt, ordinatos ab approbarunt, quin & Acta Stephani combusserunt. Ita gravissimo totius Christianismi scandalo Romanos Pontifices, velut ebrios, furiosos jactatos esse, Cranzius Saxon. lib. 2. queritur. Et Stephanus ipse dignam piaculari scelere poenam luens, e throno dejectus, in carcere laqueo gulam fregit.
units.tr: LXI. The fewer holiness, learning, and virtue among the Popes of these times, the more audacity appeared in them. Nothing was more important or more pressing to them than to establish the hierarchy. Stephen VI, successor of Hadrian III, enacted a decree to this effect, which is found in Gratian, D. 19, C. enim vero: Whatever the Roman Church decides, whatever it ordains, must be observed always and without exception. His successor was Formosus, who had sworn that he would never aspire to the Roman bishopric; when he was too greatly harassed by the faction of his rival Sergius, he summoned Arnulf, son of Carloman, into Italy, and when Arnulf entered Rome with an armed hand, Formosus declared him Emperor, anointed him and crowned him. And when, after the death of Formosus and of Boniface VI, the Sergian faction raised its head, things came to such a pass that Stephen VII, created Pope in 897, stirred by nefarious fury, had the corpse of Pope Formosus dug out of its tomb, and, in the presence of a synod, had it set in the seat of the Roman Pontificate, dressed in priestly vestments, and then, calling the wretched corpse impious and ignorant of holy doctrines (so he addressed the miserable body), condemned Formosus and his acts. He then had the corpse stripped of its vestments, the three fingers with which it was customary to bless cut off, and thrown into the Tiber. Luitprand of Pavia, deacon of the Church, who lived at that time, recounts this horrible story in book 1, chapter 8; so do Sigonius, book 6, and others, above all Auxilius in his dialogue against the internal discord of the Roman Church, which Sigebert mentions in his book on ecclesiastical writers, published by Miraeus. Baronius, minimising this crime, says at 897, art. 2, that it was not an error in faith but a violent tyranny in action. Yet no sane person can be persuaded that this horrible deed proceeded from faith, or that the infallible Spirit of truth dwelt in such plunderers and robbers. Indeed it is well known that the successors of this Stephen, Romanus, Theodore, John X of Ravenna, and others, detested his tyranny; they restored to Formosus the form of papal dignity, approved his ordinations, and even burned the acts of Stephen. Thus Cranzius, in book 2 of his Saxony, complains that the Roman Popes were thrown about like drunkards and madmen, to the most grievous scandal of all Christendom. Stephen himself, paying a penalty worthy of his crime, was cast down from the throne and, in prison, broke his throat with a noose.

units.la: LXII. Baronius tamen de his temporibus loquens, inhorrescit totus. Ad A. DCCCXCVIII. n. 4. infelicissima & luctuosissima Romanae Ecclesiae tempora fuisse, quibus ipsam contigit domestico bello exagitari, atque persecutione vexari, ita ut nullam unquam sive a Gentilibus, sive ab Haereticis, sive a Schismaticis diuturniorem atque molestiorem persecutionem passa sit illa, quam pertulit ab Adelbertis Thusciae Marchionibus, queritur. Imputat nempe mala isthaec Adelbertis Thuscis Principibus, per quos sive pecuniis, sive armis populo Cleroque Romano dominantes, intrusi in cathedram Petri, solium Christi, sint homines monstrosi, vita turpissimi, usquequaque foedissimi. Tum, inquit, Domina gentium (Ecclesia Romana) vestimentis exuta gloriae atque laetitiae maerens, dolens & lugens sedit in tristitia. Sed nec alii omnes sanctiores Pontifices dederunt, & per ambitum malasque artes plures alii solium isthoc jam pridem invaserunt. Et labat mire jactata illa Successio Pontificum, cum familias a monstris profeminari, nemo unquam viderit.
units.tr: LXII. Baronius, however, when speaking of these times, shudders all over. At 898, no. 4, he complains that these were the most unhappy and mournful times of the Roman Church, in which it was afflicted by civil war and harassed by persecution, so that it never suffered a longer or more troublesome persecution, either from the Gentiles, or from heretics, or from schismatics, than that which it endured from the Adalberts, Marquises of Tuscany. He attributes these evils, namely, to the Tuscan princes Adalbert, through whom, dominating the people and the clergy of Rome either by money or by arms, intruders into the chair of Peter and the throne of Christ were monstrous men, most vile in life, foul in every way. Then, he says, the Mistress of the nations (the Roman Church), stripped of her garments, sat in sorrow, grieving, mourning and lamenting, deprived of glory and joy. But not all the other Popes were holier, and many others, through ambition and evil arts, had long since invaded this throne. And that much-vaunted succession of Popes was wonderfully shaken, since no one ever saw families of monsters arise from it.
