units.la: Incidit in Seculum isthoc nonum certamen Sacramentarium, quod originem erroris de Cœna Domini, & corporali in ea præsentia propalat. Definiverat jam ante Synodus Generalis septima, unicam esse imaginem à Christo institutam, panem & vinum in Eucharistia. Exortus verò hoc seculo Paschasius Ratbertus, Corbejensis in Dioecesi Ambianensi Monachus, libellum de Sacramento Eucharistiæ, seu de Corpore & sanguine Domini edidit, eóque corporalem præsentiam primus omnium asseruit. Novello errori statim se opposuerunt viri doctissimi, Rabanus Maurus, Bertramus, Corbejensis quoque Monachus, vulgò Ratramnus dictus, Scotus Erigena, alii. Et Rabani quidem Mauri, cui nec Italiam similem, nec Germaniam peperisse æqualem Trithemius affirmat; de instit. Cleric. lib. 1. cap. 31. luculenta de Cœna Domini confessio ejusmodi fuit: Maluit Dominus Corporis & sanguinis sui Sacramenta fidelium ore percipi, & in partem (alii pastum) eorum redigi, ut per visibile opus invisibilis ostenderetur effectus. Sicut enim cibus materialis forinsecus nutrit corpus, & vegetat; ita etiam Verbum Dei intus animam nutrit & roborat. Quam ob causam ab authoribus Pontificiis, Guilhelmo Malmesburiensi quarto, & Thoma Waldensi sexto post Seculo in Stellarum erraticarum relatus numerum est. Ratramnus verò, seu Bertramus libello de Corpore & sanguine Domini scripto, & Carolo Calvo inscripto, eidem Carolo quærenti, an ipsum corpus, quod de Maria natum, passum, mortuum & sepultum est, quodque ad dextram Patris consideat, sit, quod ore fidelium per Sacramentorum mysterium quotidie in Ecclesia percipitur? respondit: discrimen esse tantum, quantum est inter pignus & eam rem, pro qua pignus traditur: quantum inter imaginem, & rem, cujus est imago; & quantum inter speciem & veritatem. Deniqué eandem adversus subnascentem corporalis præsentiæ errorem tutatus est Johannes Scotus Erigena tractatu de Eucharistia edito, & Anno demum ML. in Synodo Vercellensi, sub Leone IX.damnato. Taceo Scriptores hujus Seculi haud minùs celebres, Walafridum Strabonem, Christianum Druthmarum, Heribaldum Altisfiodorensem, alios, quibus ob impugnatum corporalis præsentiæ errorem à Pafchafii asseclis per insignem Contumeliam Stercoranistarum nomen fœdum impositum est, eò scilicet, quòd asserarent, ea quæ ore corporis assumuntur, Symbola secessui obnoxia esse.
units.tr: In this ninth century arose the Sacramentarian controversy, which brought to light the origin of the error concerning the Lord's Supper and a bodily presence in it. The seventh General Synod had already defined that the only images instituted by Christ are the bread and wine in the Eucharist. Then in this century Paschasius Radbert, a monk of Corbie in the diocese of Amiens, published a little book On the Sacrament of the Eucharist, or On the Body and Blood of the Lord, and was the first of all to assert a bodily presence. The most learned men at once opposed this new error: Rabanus Maurus, Bertram, also a monk of Corbie, commonly called Ratramnus, John Scotus Erigena, and others. Rabanus Maurus, whom Trithemius says neither Italy nor Germany produced an equal to, gave a clear confession about the Lord's Supper of this kind: The Lord preferred that the sacraments of his body and blood be received by the mouths of the faithful and turned into their food, so that through a visible work an invisible effect might be shown. For just as material food nourishes and gives life to the body from outside, so too the Word of God nourishes and strengthens the soul from within. For this reason the Papist writers, William of Malmesbury in the fourth place and Thomas Waldensis in the sixth after him, have listed him among the wandering stars. Ratramnus, or Bertram, in his book On the Body and Blood of the Lord, written and addressed to Charles the Bald, answered Charles when he asked whether the very body which was born of Mary, suffered, died and was buried, and which sits at the right hand of the Father, is the same that is received every day in the Church by the mouths of the faithful through the mystery of the sacraments? He replied that there is only as much difference as there is between a pledge and the thing for which the pledge is given; as between an image and the thing of which it is the image; and as between the appearance and the truth. Finally, John Scotus Erigena defended the same view against the error of bodily presence then springing up, in a treatise on the Eucharist which was published, and in the year 1050 it was condemned at the Synod of Vercelli under Leo IX. I pass over the writers of this century, no less famous: Walafrid Strabo, Christian Druthmar, Heribald of Auxerre, and others. Because they opposed the error of bodily presence, Paschasius's followers gave them the foul name Stercoranists as a notorious insult, namely because they asserted that the elements taken into the body by the mouth are subject to excretion.

units.la: LXIV. Potestatem verò Pontificis tum temporalem, tum Spiritualem dici nequit, quantum commenta callidissima circa hæc potissimum tempora miseræ hominum credulitati propinata promoverint firmaverintque. Et ad temporale quidem imperium statuendum plurimum contulerunt, ex quæstuosissima falsorum chirographorum ossicina petitæ Donationes, Constantini puta Magni, Ludovici Pii, & Ottonis M. Donationis Constantinianæ, quam pro idoneo documento allegârunt Pontifices Leo IX. Nicolaus III. aliique & in Jus Canonicum Gratianus, Yvo, Anshelmus, Deusdedit, ipséque etiam Gregorius XIII. retulerunt; putidissimum commentum per Johannem quemdam Diaconum, cognomento Digitorum, uti quidem ipsum Diploma Ottonis tertii, quod etiam num Assisii inter cimelia & Archiva Paparum asservatur, & à Marquardo Frehero editum ac notis illustratum est, testatur, nefariè suppositum, orbi persuadere sustinuit, Constantinum M. Imperatorem non solùm Romanam urbem, sed etiam omnes Italiæ, seu Occidentalium Regionum Provincias, loca & civitates, Romano Pontifici Silvestro ac ejus Successoribus perpetuo dono tradidisse. Ludovici quoque Pii prodigiosa donatio Paschali, & Sedi Romanæ A. DCCCXVII. facta, ferebatur, qua scilicet, Volaterrano, Sigonio, Baronio aliisque narrantibus, Romanus Ducatus, Ravennæ Exarchatus, & pleraque omnis Italia in Sedis illius potestatem concesserit: Simulque Ludovicus Pontificum electioni, quam Leonis III. & Stephani V. Canones Imperatori vindicaverunt, absolutè renuntiaverit. Accessit sequente Seculo non minùs ampla Donatio, quam ad A. DCCCCLXII. Baronius affert Ottonis M. nomine, qua ille Johanni XII. & Romanæ Sedi donat civitatem Romanam cum Ducatu suo, suburbanis suis, atque viculis omnibus & territoriis ejus montanis & maritimis, littoribus & portubus, seu cunctis civitatibus, castellis, oppidis ac viculis, Thusciæ partibus, id est, Portum, Centum cellas, Cerem, Bledam, Maturianum, Sutrium, Nepem, Castellum, Gallisem, Ortem, Polimartium, Ameriam, Tudam, Perusiam cum tribus insulis suis &c. nec non Exarchatum Ravennatem, Pentapolim, territorium Sabinense, Almum cum Insula Corsica, Ducatum Spoletinum; Patrimonium Neapolitanum, &c. Quando nempe verecundiæ fines semel transire statutum erat, bene & naviter impudentes esse oportebat. Multum certè grani paleæ illæ Ecclesiæ attulerunt uti vetus de Constantini Palea illa proverbium sonat. Omnésque curiosos Canoniστas magnum semper de hoc (Constantini) diplomate fecisse festum, Paulus Langius in Chronico ad A. MCCCCIV. ait. Sed critico Donationes illæ virorum Doctorum Freheri, Goldasti, Mornæi, Voetii, Usserii, Conringii, aliorum veru confossæ, pridem νοθείας suæ notas & fraudis simplicioribus à Papæ ciniflonibus enormiter nimis factæ, indicia plurima prodiderunt. Ad Spiritualem verò Principatum confirmandum, veterum Romanorum Episcoporum nomine prodierunt ore & calamo plus quàm ferreo confictæ Decretales Epistolæ supra §. IX. X. memoratæ, quas ex Hispania tempore Caroli M. Riculfum, Archipiescopum Moguntinum in Gallias primùm attulisse, Hincmarus Rhemensis in libro contra Hincmarum Laudunensem scripto, testatur. Quas quidem Epistolas unà cum Pseudo-Constantini Donatione ne, atque aliis etiam Decretis Ecclesiasticis in unum volumen compactas Isidorus non Hispalensis ille, sed cognomento Mercator, planus post homines natos nequissimus & improbissimus, qui posteris tamen Ignaris scelerum tantorum, artisque Pelasgæ,
units.tr: LXIV. It cannot be said how much the most cunning inventions, put before the wretched credulity of mankind chiefly at this period, have advanced and strengthened the power of the Pope, both temporal and spiritual. For establishing the temporal rule, the Donations contributed very much. They were drawn from the most profitable workshop of false charters: those of Constantine the Great, Louis the Pious and Otto the Great. Popes Leo IX and Nicholas III and others cited the Donation of Constantine as a suitable proof, and Gratian, Ivo, Anselm, Deusdedit and even Gregory XIII repeated it in the canon law. That most foolish fiction, which the diploma of Otto III itself testifies (it is still kept at Assisi among the treasures and archives of the Popes, and has been published and annotated by Marquard Freher), was wickedly forged by a certain John the Deacon, nicknamed Digitorum, who dared to persuade the world that the Emperor Constantine the Great had given the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places and cities of Italy or of the western regions, in perpetual gift to the Roman Pontiff Sylvester and his successors. There was also said to be a prodigious donation by Louis the Pious made to Paschal and the Roman See in 817, by which, as Volaterranus, Sigonius, Baronius and others relate, the Roman duchy, the exarchate of Ravenna and most of Italy were conceded to that See's power; and at the same time Louis absolutely renounced to the Emperor the right to elect Popes, which the canons of Leo III and Stephen V had claimed for the Emperor. In the following century came a donation no less ample, which Baronius brings forward under the name of Otto the Great, for the year 962, by which he gave to John XII and the Roman See: the city of Rome with its duchy, its suburbs, all its villages, and its mountain and maritime territories, shores and harbours, or all its cities, castles, towns and villages, in the parts of Tuscany, that is, Porto, Centumcellae, Cere, Bleda, Maturanum, Sutrium, Nepi, Castellum, Gallese, Orte, Polimartium, Amelia, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, etc., and also the exarchate of Ravenna, the Pentapolis, the territory of Sabina, Alma with the island of Corsica, the duchy of Spoleto, the Neapolitan patrimony, etc. Once it had been decided to pass the limits of shame, it was necessary to be thoroughly and boldly shameless. Certainly those chaffs brought much grain to the Church, as the old proverb about that chaff of Constantine runs. And Paul Lange, in his Chronicle for the year 1404, says that all the curious canonists have always made a great feast over this diploma (of Constantine). But the critical scholars Freher, Goldast, Mornay, Voetius, Ussher, Conring and others have thoroughly pierced those Donations, and many indications have revealed their spuriousness and the fraud that was carried out far too outrageously upon the simpler folk by the Pope's flatterers. The Decretal Epistles mentioned above in §§ IX and X, fabricated in the names of the early Roman bishops, and produced by mouth and pen more than iron-hard, were put forward to confirm the Spiritual primacy. Hincmar of Reims, in his book written against Hincmar of Laon, testifies that Riculf, Archbishop of Mainz, first brought them into Gaul from Spain in the time of Charlemagne. Isidore, not the Isidore of Seville but the one nicknamed Mercator, a priest most wicked and dishonest of all men since they were born, collected these Epistles into one volume together with the Pseudo-Donation of Constantine and other ecclesiastical decrees. He did not hesitate to offer them for sale, having thus happily imposed them on posterity, ignorant of so great crimes and of Pelasgian craft.

units.la: feliciter sic impositit, venditare non dubitavit. Quo in genere an quidquam unquam prodierit simile, quod plus ad causæ Pontificiæ firmamentum momenti attulerit, haud scire se Doctiff. Usserius profitetur merito.
units.tr: as the saying goes. As to whether anything similar was ever produced which contributed more weight to the support of the Papist cause, the learned Ussher rightly confesses that he does not know.

units.la: LXV. Decimum Seculum ejusmodi fuit, ut eo nullum indoctius aut infelicius extitisse Bellarminus de Pontif. Rom. lib. IV. 12. fateatur. Baronius etiam ad A. DCCCC. §. 1. ejus explicationem sic orditur: En incipit annus Redemptionis nongentesimus, Indictione tertia notatus, quo & novum incipit Seculum, quod sui asperitate, & boni sterilitate ferreum, malique exundantis deformitate plumbeum, atque inopia Scriptorum appellari consuevit obscurum. In cujus limine constituti, antequam progrediamur ulterius, hic Lectorem monendo, præfari aliquid necessarium duximus, ne quid scandali pusillus animo patiatur, si quando videre contigerit abominationem desolationis in Templo, sed magis miretur, & cognoscat in ejus custodia Divinam invigilare potentiam, cum non, ut olim, tantam abominationem secuta mox fuerit desolatio Templi, intelligatque, solidioribus illo niti hoc fundamentis, promissionibus Christi, &c. Sed forte non parum opinio Baronium fefellit, cum abominationem illam spiritualis Templi desolatio & ἅλωσις, captivitas Babylonica magis magisque insecuta fuerit, & nondum sera vespera venerit.
units.tr: LXV. The tenth century was of such a kind that Bellarmine, in On the Roman Pontiff, book IV, chapter 12, admits no century was more unlearned or more unhappy. Baronius, too, in the year 900, § 1, begins his account of it thus: Behold, the year of Redemption nine hundred begins, marked with the third indiction, in which there also begins a new century, which is commonly called iron because of its harshness and its lack of good, leaden because of the deformity of the overflowing evil, and dark because of the poverty of writers. Standing at its threshold, before we advance further, we have thought it necessary to say something beforehand, warning the reader, so that the little one may not suffer any scandal in his mind if he happens to see the abomination of desolation in the Temple; rather let him marvel and recognize that the divine power keeps watch over its guardianship, since, unlike of old, no desolation of the Temple followed at once upon so great an abomination; and let him understand that this foundation rests on firmer supports, the promises of Christ, etc. But perhaps the opinion deceived Baronius not a little, since that abomination of a spiritual temple was followed more and more by desolation and capture [ἅλωσις], the Babylonian captivity, and the evening has not yet come late.

units.la: LXVI. Sic porro luridam Ecclesiæ Romanæ hoc Seculo faciem idem ad A. DCCCCXII. §. 8. Baronius depingit: Quæ tum facies sanctæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ? Quàm fœdissima, cùm Romæ dominarentur potentissimæ æquè ac fœdissimæ meretrices. (Theodora, Marozia) quarum arbitrio mutarentur Sedes, darentur Episcopi, & quod horrendum auditu & infandum est intruderentur in Sedem Petri earum amasii, Pseudo-Pontifices &c. Sic vendicaverat omnia sibi libido, seculari potentia freta, insaniens, astro percita dominandi. Dormiebat tunc planè alto sopore Christus in navi, cùm hisce flantibus validis ventis navis ipsa fluctibus operiretur. &c. Et quod deterius erat, deerant, qui Dominum sic dormientem clamoribus excitarent, discipuli, stertentibus omnibus. Quales-nam reris delectos ab his monstris Presbyteros & Diaconos Cardinales putandum: cùm nihil tam natura sit insitum, quàm unumquemque sibi similem generare? &c. Platinæ, Sabellici, aliorum querelis ad compendium positis, paucis multa, sub finem hujus seculi, Epistola ad Stephanum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Diaconum scripta, Gerbertus dixit: Romanorum mores mundus perhorrescit. Et Genebrardus Chronogr. lib IV. his coloribus seculum isthoc depingit: Infelix dicitur hoc Seculum, exhaustum hominibus ingenio & doctrina claris, sive etiam claris Principibus & Pontificibus, in quo nihil feré dignum memoria posteritatis gestum sit. Unde ferunt, tunc repertum fuisse quoddam monstrum capite Leonino, & cæteris membris humanis, quod statum illius temporis mirificè referret. Hoc verò uno infelix, quod per annos 150. Pontifices circiter 50 à virtute majorum prorsus defecerunt, Apostatici, Apostaticive potiùs, quàm Apostolici.
units.tr: LXVI. Again, Baronius paints the grimy face of the Roman Church in this century, in the year 912, § 8: What then was the face of the holy Roman Church? How most foul, when the most powerful and equally most foul harlots, Theodora and Marozia, ruled at Rome! By their decision sees were changed, bishops were given, and, what is horrible to hear and unspeakable, their lovers, pseudo-popes, were thrust into the See of Peter. Thus lust, relying on secular power, raging and driven by the star of domination, claimed everything for itself. Christ was then fast asleep in the ship, while the ship itself was covered by waves with these strong winds blowing. And what was worse, there were none of the disciples, all of them snoring, to rouse the sleeping Lord with their cries. What sort of men, do you suppose, were the presbyters and deacons, the cardinals chosen by these monsters, since nothing is so inborn in nature as for each thing to beget its like? When the complaints of Platina, Sabellicus and others are reduced to a summary, Gerbert, in an epistle written to Stephen, deacon of the Roman Church, near the end of this century, said in few words what could be said at length: The world shudders at the morals of the Romans. And Genebrard, in Chronography, book IV, paints this century in these colours: This century is called unhappy, drained of men distinguished in talent and learning, or even of distinguished princes and Popes, in which almost nothing worth remembering by posterity was done. Hence they say that at that time there was found a certain monster with a lion's head and other human limbs, which marvellously represented the condition of that time. But this one thing made it unhappy: that for about 150 years about fifty Popes fell utterly away from the virtue of their ancestors, apostates, or rather apostates rather than apostles.

units.la: LXVII. Infelicitatis tantæ illius Seculi causam idem Genebrardus nequissimè fingit hæsisse penes Imperatores Germanicos, sub quibus, inquit ille, captiva & gemens fuit Ecclesia usque ad Henricum IV. in ordinem redactum.
units.tr: LXVII. Genebrard wrongly claims that the cause of so great an unhappiness in that age lay with the German emperors, under whom, he says, the Church was captive and groaning until Henry IV was brought into order.

units.la: Dolet scilicet Papæ gnathonibus nimiùm, quòd eo seculo Otto I. alias Magnus, remoto Johanne XIII (aliis XII) scelerum plurium, incestûs cumprimis & necromantiæ convicto, surrogavit Leonem VIII. sub quo restitutum Imperatoribus est jus eligendi Pontifices, & investiendi Episcopos, Clerumque omnem: quódque Otto III. nepos depositó, & de monte Tarpejo præcipitato Johanne Placentino, Gregorium V. ante à se electum & factione Crescentii deturbatum restituit, & si quae alia illi Pontificiae potestati minus propitia gesserunt. De caetero Sanctitatem Papam dimisisse & ad Imperatores hoc tempore accessisse, Wernerus, Monachus Carthusianus Fascic. Temp. stat. 6 art. 744. diserte queritur.
units.tr: Clearly the Pope's flatterers are much displeased that in that century Otto I, called the Great, after removing John XIII (others say XII), who was convicted of many crimes, especially incest and necromancy, put in Leo VIII in his place. Under Leo the right to elect popes and to invest bishops and all the clergy was restored to the emperors. Likewise Otto III, his grandson, deposed John of Piacenza, threw him from the Tarpeian rock, and restored Gregory V, whom he had earlier elected and who had been driven out by the faction of Crescentius; and they did other things unfavourable to papal power. Otherwise, Werner the Carthusian monk plainly complains in his Fascic. Temp., stat. 6, art. 744, that at this time the Holy Father let go and came over to the emperors.

units.la: LXVIII. Et Pontifices quidem cauteriatum isthoc se- culum triginta passum est.
units.tr: LXVIII. And indeed the popes suffered this branded century for thirty years.

units.la: de quibus vetus illud adagium: Sardi venales, alius alio nequior; usurpaveris merito. Gerbertus Archiepiscopus Rhemensis, qui post ad Papale culmen evectus Silvester II. cognominatus est, coram Synodo Rhemensi adversus seculi sui Pontifices multa inclementer satis dixit; quae ad A. CMXC. Baronius ipse non dissimulat. Inter alia Antichristi nota sic illos aspergit: Quid hunc, Reverendi Patres, in sublimi solio residentem, veste purpurea & auro radiantem, quid hunc, inquam, esse censetis? Nimirum si charitate destituitur, solaque scientia inflatur, & extollitur, Antichristus est in Templo Dei sedens, & se ostendens tanquam sit Deus. Si autem nec charitate fundatur, nec scientia erigitur, in Templo Dei tanquam statua, tanquam idolum est, a quo responsa petere, marmora consulere est. In eadem Oratione sic φιλιππός. O Lugenda Roma! quae nostris majoribus clara Patrum lumina praebuisti, nostris temporibus monstruosas tenebras, futuro seculo famosas offudisti! &c. Quid sub haec tempora non vidimus? Vidimus Johannem, cognomento Octavianum, in volutabro libidinum etiam contra eum Ottonem, quem Augustum creaverat, conjurasse. Quo fugato, Leo Neophytus in Pontificem creatur. Sed Ottone Caesare Roma discedente, Octavianus Romam redit, Leonem fugat, Johannem Diaconum naso dextrisque digitis ac lingua mutilat, multaque caede primorum in urbe debacchatus brevi moritur. Cui Benedictum Grammaticum, cognomento Diaconum Romani substituunt. Eum quoque Leo Neophytus cum suo Caesare non longe post aggreditur, obsidet, capit, deponit, perpetuoque exilio in Germaniam dirigit, succedit Ottoni Caesari Caesar Otto. Succedit Romæ in Pontificatu horrendum monstrum, Malefacius (Bonifacium sic appellat) cunctos mortales nequitia superans, etiam prioris Pontificis sanguine cruentus. Sed hic etiam fugatus & in magna Synodo damnatus est. Talibus monstris hominum ignominia plenis scientia humanarum & Divinarum rerum vacuis innumeros Sacerdotes Dei per Orbem terrarum scientiæ & vitæ merito conspicuos subjici decretum est?
units.tr: Of them the old saying may rightly be used: the Sardinians are for sale, one worse than another. Gerbert, Archbishop of Reims, who was later raised to the papal summit and named Sylvester II, spoke quite harshly against the popes of his age before the Synod of Reims. Baronius himself does not conceal this, under the year 990. Among other marks of Antichrist he lashes them thus: What do you think this man is, Reverend Fathers, sitting on the high throne, clothed in purple and shining with gold? Surely if he is destitute of charity and puffed up and exalted by knowledge alone, he is Antichrist sitting in the temple of God and showing himself as if he were God. But if he is founded neither on charity nor raised up by knowledge, he is in the temple of God like a statue, like an idol, from which to seek answers is to consult marble. In the same oration he goes on: O Rome, worthy of lamentation! You who gave clear lights of the Fathers to our forebears, in our times you have spread monstrous darkness, notorious for the future age! etc. What have we not seen in these times? We have seen John, surnamed Octavian, plotting in a sty of lusts, even against that Otto whom he had made Augustus. When he was put to flight, Leo the Neophyte was created pope. But when Caesar Otto left Rome, Octavian returned to Rome, put Leo to flight, mutilated John the Deacon by cutting off his nose, right hand fingers and tongue, and after raging in the city with great slaughter of the leading men, he soon died. In his place they put up Benedict the Grammarian, surnamed the Deacon of Rome. Leo the Neophyte with his Caesar also attacked him not long after, besieged him, captured him, deposed him, and sent him into perpetual exile in Germany; Caesar Otto succeeded Otto Caesar. In Rome there succeeded to the pontificate a dreadful monster, Malefacius (so he calls Boniface), surpassing all mortals in wickedness, bloodied even with the blood of the previous pope. But this one too was put to flight and condemned in a great synod. Has it been decreed that countless priests of God, conspicuous across the world for knowledge and life, should be made subject to such monsters, full of human shame and empty of knowledge of human and divine things?

units.la: LXIX. Quid vero multis? Platinam, Baronium, Genebrardum, Johannem Stellam consulentibus occurrent ea ætate frequentes fures, invasores, Magi, prodigiosi, Simoniaci, tyranni, facinorosissimi, monstra & portenta, perjuri, grassatores, ἀσπονδοι, sacrilegi in manes defunctorum, Divini humanique juxta juris violatores, scelestissimi. Romanus, Theodorus II. Johannes IX. Christophorus, Sergius III. Formosis actis vel rescindendis, vel vindicandis insudant. Sergius etiam Maroziæ adulteræ suæ, ex qua Johannem XI. suffulit, artibus Papatum invadit. Johannes X. alterius Glycerii Theodoræ Marozia matris artibus Papa creatur, & hara quàm ara dignior, ab altero scorto Marozia cervicali in os conjecto, necatur. Johannes XI. Patre Sergio & matre Marozia natus ille est, de cujus tempore Baronius exclamavit: Quæ tum facies Ecclesiæ Romana? Johannes XII. puer annorum duodecim Papa eligitur, sceleratissimus omnium, in adulterio deprehensus ab adulteræ marito confossus, & à Diabolo, Luitprando teste, verberibus percussus interiit. Leo VIII. Laicus adhuc Papatum invadit. Bonifacius XII. Benedicto VI. vi prius deturbato, & in carcere strangulato, Papatum rapit, bestia verius, quàm homo, Malifacius à Gerberto dictus. Johannes XV. Divina & humana omnia cognatis & assinibus suis erogavit, Nepotismi studiis præludens posteris. Silvester II. seu Mathematicus, seu Necromanta (quod posterius plerique affirmant) statuæ caput ex certo to siderum cursu conflatum, sibi Oraculum, ex quo fata expiscaretur, constituit. Johannes XVII. fur, latro & proditor Stellæ cluet. En Romæ ea ætate Archiflamines & Antistites!
units.tr: LXIX. What more need be said? Those who consult Platina, Baronius, Genebrard and John Stella will find that in that age the following were common: thieves, invaders, magicians, prodigies, simoniacs, tyrants, most criminal men, monsters and portents, perjurers, brigands, men without truce, sacrilegious toward the spirits of the dead, violators of divine and human law, most wicked. Romanus, Theodore II, John IX, Christopher, Sergius III laboured either to annul or to vindicate the acts of Formosus. Sergius also seized the papacy by the arts of Marozia, his adulterous mistress, by whom he fathered John XI. John X was made pope through the arts of Theodora, mother of Marozia, another prostitute, and, more fit for a sty than an altar, he was killed by Marozia's other lover, who threw a pillow into his face. John XI, born of father Sergius and mother Marozia, is the one of whose time Baronius cried out: What then was the face of the Roman Church? John XII was elected pope as a boy of twelve, most wicked of all, caught in adultery and stabbed by the husband of his adulteress, and, according to Liutprand, struck by blows from the Devil, he died. Leo VIII, still a layman, seized the papacy. Boniface XII, after first driving out Benedict VI by force and having him strangled in prison, seized the papacy, more a beast than a man, called Malefacius by Gerbert. John XV gave away everything divine and human to his relatives and in-laws, anticipating the practice of nepotism for posterity. Sylvester II, whether mathematician or necromancer (most say the latter), set up for himself an oracle, a head of statue cast under a certain course of the stars, from which he might fish out the fates. John XVII, whom Stella calls thief, robber and traitor. Behold the archflamens and bishops of Rome in that age!

units.la: LXX. Cleri igitur totius, quæ tum conditio etiam fuerit, monstris ejusmodi clavum tenentibus, divinare licet. Edgarus Rex Angliæ ad Episcopos Anglicanos habita Oratione difertissima, quæ ab Alredo Abbate Rhievallense literis consignata extat, sic ejus mores depingit: Dicam, dicam, quod boni lugent, mali ridènt. Dicam dolens, si tamen dici potest, quomodo diffluant in comessationibus & ebrietatibus, in cubilibus & impudicitiis, ut jam domus Clericorum putentur prostibula meretricum, conciliabulum histrionum. Ibi aleæ, ibi saltus & cantus; ibi usque ad medium noctis protractæ cum clamore & horrore vigiliæ. Sic, sic patrimonia Regum, eleemosynas Principum, imò quod magis est, illius pretiosi sanguinis pretium profligatis. Ab eadem etiam Pontificum inertia factum est, ut passim Monachi in Sacerdotum collegia venerint, & mox velut jure suo ubique gentium opes immodicas sibi parere inciperent. uti Polydorus Virgilius lib. VI. Histor. Angl. notat. Et quid multis? Accidit illi ætati, inquit, in vita Benedicti IV. Johannes Stella, quod omnis virtus, tam in capite, quam in membris ex hominum ignavia consumpta fuerit.
units.tr: LXX. From such monsters holding the helm, one may guess what the condition of the whole clergy was at that time. Edgar, King of England, in a most eloquent address to the English bishops, which Ailred, Abbot of Rievaulx, has preserved in writing, depicts their morals thus: I will say, I will say what the good lament and the wicked laugh at. I will say, grieving, if it can be said, how they dissolve in drinking bouts and drunkenness, in beds and immodesty, so that now the houses of clerics are thought to be brothels of harlots and assemblies of actors. There are dice, there are dances and songs; there the vigils are prolonged until midnight with shouting and uproar. Thus, thus the patrimonies of kings and the alms of princes, or rather, what is more, the price of that precious blood, are squandered. Through the same inertia of the popes it also came about that everywhere monks came into colleges of priests, and soon, as if by their own right, began to acquire for themselves immense wealth among all peoples, as Polydore Vergil notes in book VI of his English History. And what more? It happened in that age, he says, in the life of Benedict IV, that John Stella said, that all virtue, both in head and in members, was consumed through men's idleness.

units.la: LXXI. Sed forte hoc uno nomine haud planè infelix hoc seculum dixeris, quod novas hæreses protrusit nullas. Equidem Gabriel Prateolus in suo successionis hæreticorum catalogo notat, seculo nono & decimo Hæreticorum interregnum factum esse. Scilicet fugerunt Hæretici, atque in Prælatos & Monachos Pontificios sese abdiderunt. Par enim erat, ut magnus Usserius de Eccl. Success. cap. 2. loquitur, ut hæretici, qui tanquam devoti milites Antichristi copias sunt antegressi, summo Imperatore cum stativis castris proximè accedente, retrahere sese, omnesque minutiores atque angustiores hæreses Apostasiæ, cui hactenus viam parārant omnia longè latèque jam occupaturæ concederent.
units.tr: LXXI. But perhaps you would not say that this century was entirely unhappy for this one reason, that it put forth no new heresies. Indeed Gabriel Prateolus, in his catalogue of the succession of heretics, notes that in the ninth and tenth centuries there was an interregnum of heretics. Clearly the heretics fled and hid themselves among the Papist prelates and monks. For it was fitting, as the great Ussher says in De Eccl. Success., chapter 2, that the heretics, who went ahead like devoted soldiers of Antichrist, should withdraw when the supreme Emperor approached with his standing camp, and should yield all the smaller and narrower heresies of apostasy, which had hitherto prepared the way for it, to be about to occupy everything far and wide.

units.la: LXXI. De Ecclesiæ circa annum millesimum statu sic
units.tr: LXXI. On the state of the Church around the year 1000, as follows

units.la: Wernerus in fasciculo Temporum: Tempus effœminatum incipit circa annum Domini 1000, in quo fides Christiana valde cœpit deficere & declinare à pristina virilitate; uti patet in prophetia Sanctæ Hildegardis, & in multis regionibus Christianitatis. Nec sacramenta, nec Ecclesiastici ritus servabantur: Erántque auguriis & maleficiis intendentes. Et erat Sacerdos sicut populus. Neque aliter Glaber Radulphus, ejus temporis scriptor, qui lib. II. 6. queritur, circa annum millesimum plus solito friguisse charitatem, ac superabundasse iniquitatem, ut ille antiquum Leviathan fiduciam conceperit, quod inundatio Jordanis fluvios illaberetur illius; ut videlicet baptizatorum multitudo per avaritiæ appetitum viam veritatis deserens demergeretur in interitum.
units.tr: Werner, in the Fasciculus Temporum: A effeminate age begins about the year of the Lord 1000, in which the Christian faith began greatly to fail and to decline from its earlier manliness, as is evident from the prophecy of Saint Hildegard and from many regions of Christendom. Neither the sacraments nor the ecclesiastical rites were observed. People were given to omens and sorcery. And the priest was just like the people. Glaber Radulphus, a writer of that time, says much the same. In book 2, chapter 6, he complains that around the year 1000 charity had grown colder than usual and iniquity had overflowed, so that the ancient Leviathan conceived the hope that the flood of the Jordan would pour into his mouth, that is, that a multitude of the baptized, through greed, would abandon the way of truth and be plunged into destruction.

units.la: LXXII. Sequens vero seculum undecimum ob malorum excrescentiam ferreum à Dithmaro appellari solitum, Baronius ad A. MI. narrat; praefatus etiam, asseruisse tum nonnullos, adesse tempus, quo revelandus esset ille homo peccati, filius perditionis dictus cognomine Antichristus. Quæ in Galliis promulgata, & Parisis primùm praedicata, ac per orbem vulgata, creditàque à plurimis, addit. Aventinus quoque lib. V. p. 59. fatetur, plerosque omnes bonos, apertos, justos, ingenuos, simplices, tum imperium Antichristi cœpisse, quod ea, quæ Christus Servator noster tot annos ante nobis cantavit, eo tempore evenisse cernebant, memoriæ literarum prodidisse. Genebrardus ad A. MLXXIX. Quàm tum deploratus fuerit status Ecclesiæ, cernere licet apud Sigebertum, Vincentium & Antoninum. Magnæ simultates inter Imperatorem & Pontificem. Sacerdotes erant moribus depravatissimis. Berengarius lib. de Corpore & sang. Dom. Veritatem ait expertam esse non Sanctam Ecclesiam, sed Ecclesiam malignantium, tium", concilium vanitatis, non Apostolicam, sed Sedem Sathanæ.
units.tr: LXXII. The following eleventh century, which was customarily called iron by Dithmar because of the increase of evils, is described by Baronius at the year 1011. He also notes that some then asserted that the time had come when that man of sin, the son of perdition, called by the name Antichrist, was to be revealed. These claims were published in Gaul, first preached at Paris, spread throughout the world, and were believed by many, he adds. Aventinus, too, in book 5, page 59, admits that most of the good, open, just, noble, and simple men then began to speak of the rule of Antichrist, because they saw that the things which our Saviour Christ had foretold so many years before were coming to pass in that time, and they handed this down in writing. Genebrardus, at the year 1079: How deplorable the state of the Church then was can be seen from Sigebert, Vincent, and Antoninus. There were great quarrels between the Emperor and the Pope. The priests were of most depraved morals. Berengarius, in his book On the Body and Blood of the Lord, says that he has found the truth to be not the Holy Church but the Church of the wicked, the council of vanity, not the Apostolic but the seat of Satan.

units.la: LXXIII. Initio seculi sacerrimam illam sedem tenuit Silvester II. de cujus necromantia testes Pontificii plures, Benno, Wernerus, Rollfink, Martinus Polonus, Nauclerus, Platina, Matthæus Westmonasterienfis, alii dubitare non sinunt. Ei dæmon consultus, quamdiu regnaturus esset, respondit, non prius moriturum, quàm in Hierusalem missam celebrâsset. Quod oraculum ἐπαμφοτεῖζον dæmon de Ecclesia S. Crucis Romana, cui Hierosolymæ nomen, Silvester de civitate Hierosolyma intellexit. Sed posterior deceptus à Cacodæmone suo, cùm in Ecclesia S. Crucis sacra fecisset, Orci victima piacularis subitò factus est quam tragœdiam pluribus Malmesburiensis ediderit. Discipulos eum habuisse, Theophylactum (postea factum Papam, Benedictum IX.) & Laurentium, qui dæmonibus litaverint, Benno Cardinalis affirmat. Eum exceperunt Johannes XIX. XX. Sergius IV. Benedictus VIII. IX. Johannes XXI. Silvester III. Gregorius VI. nulla re insignes, nisi quòd plerique illi factione Comitum Thusculanorum, adeoque vitio creati, & magiæ crimine, si quæ fides suis authoribus constat, infames fuerunt. Certè Benedictum IX. (quem Sacris dæmoniorum fuisse deditum & in silvis ac montibus mulieres post se currere fecisse, quas magicis artibus ad sui amorem coëgerit, ex libellis domi ejus inventis, Benno probat.) Silvestrum III. & Gregorium VI. Henricus Imperator convocata Synodo, ceu Simoniacos, sanguinarios, monstra damnavit; Ingemuisse tum orbem, ob intrusos Papas, Papatum intercedente thesauro pecuniarum emptum, & PræIatos auro potiùs quàm merito exaltatos, Glaber Radulphus lib. IV. 5. & V. 5. & Leo Cardinalis Ostiensis scribunt.
units.tr: LXXIII. At the beginning of the century, Silvester II held that most sacred see. Many Papists, including Benno, Werner, Rollfink, Martin of Poland, Naucler, Platina, and Matthew of Westminster, are witnesses about his necromancy, and others do not allow anyone to doubt it. When he consulted a demon about how long he would reign, the demon answered that he would not die before he had celebrated Mass in Jerusalem. The demon's oracle was ambiguous: he meant the Roman church of the Holy Cross, which bore the name Jerusalem, while Silvester understood the city of Jerusalem. But Silvester, deceived by his own demon, celebrated Mass in the church of the Holy Cross, and he suddenly became a sacrificial victim for Orcus. Malmesbury has told this tragedy at length. Cardinal Benno affirms that he had disciples, Theophylact (later made Pope Benedict IX) and Lawrence, who sacrificed to demons. Silvester was succeeded by John XIX and XX, Sergius IV, Benedict VIII and IX, John XXI, Silvester III, and Gregory VI. None of them was notable for anything, except that most of them, raised to office by the faction of the Counts of Tusculum, and so by corruption, and (if any trust is to be placed in their authors) guilty of magic, were infamous. Certainly Benedict IX, whom Benno proves, from little books found in his house, to have been given to demonic rites and to have made women run after him in the woods and on the mountains, whom he forced by magic arts to love him, and Silvester III and Gregory VI were condemned by Emperor Henry, who convened a synod, as simoniacal, bloody monsters. Glaber Radulphus (book 4, chapter 5, and book 5, chapter 5) and Leo, Cardinal of Ostia, write that the world then groaned over the intruded popes, who had bought the papacy with money, and prelates who had been promoted for gold rather than merit.

units.la: LXXIV. Benedicti IX. quem insuper ut ignavum, & nullius pretii Platina & Stella; probrosum & infamem Volaterranus; hominem nefarium Baronius perstringunt; tempore Cardinalium nomen esse in pretio, Genebrardo Chronogr. lib. IV. fatente, occœpit. Et Cardinales quidem dicti à cardine, παραγωνύμως fixos & proprios Ecclesiæ suæ ministros significant. Unde vocabula incardinandus, incardinatus, annexus cardini. Eorum tamen appellatio neque in S. Literis, neque in antiquis Patribus, ne historicis quidem, sive Christianis, sive etiam gentilibus, qualis est Marcellinus, occurit. Scribunt quidam à Marcello I. Cardinales constitutos esse propter Baptismum. Sed in actis ejus Cardinalium nomen non comparet. Viginti quinque titulos in urbe, quasi diœcesès, propter baptismum & pœnitentiam multorum, qui convertebantur ex Paganis & propter sepulturas Martyrum eum constituisse Baronius ad A. cccix. 4. memorat, sine Cardinalium mentione ulla. Demum circa A. DLX. prima Cardinalium mentio extat, quando Johannes III. dilectis filiis Cardinalibus Clericis scribens, significat, se Ecclesiam illam Titulum Cardinalem constituere. Id verò certum, Cardinalium nomen ab initio nihil aliud significâsse, quàm ordinarios atque fixos in certa Ecclesia Clericos; neque Romanæ duntaxat Ecclesiæ fuisse Cardinales suos, sed etiam Ecclesiis aliis titulatis. Unde Cardinales Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ, Mediolanensis, Compostellanæ, aliarum legere est. Testimonia eam in rem plura Marcus Antonius de Dominis de Rep. Eccl. IV. 5.8.19.20.21. allegat, ubi etiam qui proprie Cardinales olim fuerint, definit, asserens fuisse Clerum proprium cujuscunque Ecclesiæ in ea fixum, & titulatum, & ordinarium. Et quæcunque, inquit, Ecclesiæ esset collegiata, illa plures etiam in se continebat Cardinales, sive etiam subdiaconos.
units.tr: LXXIV. Benedict IX, whom Platina and Stella also censure as lazy and of no worth, Volaterranus as disgraceful and infamous, and Baronius as a wicked man, was the pope in whose time, as Genebrardus admits in his Chronography, book 4, the name of Cardinals began to be prized. Cardinals are so called from cardo, a hinge, and by paronymy [παραγωνύμως] signify ministers fixed and belonging to their own Church. Hence the words incardinated, to be incardinated, and attached to the hinge. Yet the name does not occur in Holy Scripture, nor in the ancient Fathers, nor even in the historians, whether Christian or pagan, such as Marcellinus. Some write that Cardinals were established by Marcellus I because of baptism. But the name of Cardinals does not appear in his acts. Baronius, at the year 309, section 4, records that he set up twenty-five titles in the city, as it were dioceses, for the baptism and repentance of the many who were converted from paganism and for the burial of the martyrs, with no mention of Cardinals at all. Finally, around the year 560 the first mention of Cardinals appears, when John III, writing to his beloved sons the Cardinal clergy, indicates that he had established that church as a Cardinal title. It is certain, however, that the name of Cardinals at first meant nothing other than the ordinary clergy fixed in a particular church. Nor were there Cardinals only in the Roman church; other churches with titles also had theirs. Hence one may read of the Cardinals of the church of Constantinople, of Milan, of Compostela, and of others. Marcus Antonius de Dominis, in On the Commonwealth of the Church, book 4, sections 5, 8, 19, 20, and 21, cites many testimonies to this effect, and there he also defines who were properly Cardinals in former times, asserting that they were the proper clergy of any church, fixed in it, titled, and ordinary. And whatever church was collegiate, he says, it also contained within itself several Cardinals, or even subdeacons.

units.la: LXXV. Tales scilicet Cardinales Episcopis etiam subjecti fuerunt ad tempora usque Caroli M. quibus Papatus imperio multarum Provinciarum auctus est. Incrementa enim potestas eorum una cum Pontificiæ potestatis incrementis nacta est. Acciditque sic Romæ, quod in eadem Roma aliquando accidisse apud Tacitum A. II. 33. 3. Gallus Asinius his verbis asleruit: Auctu Imperii adolevisse etiam privatas opes idque non novum, sed vetustissimis moribus; aliam apud Fabricios, aliam apud Scipiones pecuniam, & cuncta ad Rempub. referri; qua tenui angustas civium domos; postquam eò magnificentiæ venerit, gliscere singulas, &c. Non potuerunt ergo hi non attolli magnificè, cùm plerumque Papæ curam gererent, eumque ope & consilio juvarent. Certè A. DCCIXIX. Stephano IV. Pontifice in Synodo Romana decretum est, ne Papa nisi ex Cardinalibus legeretur. Neque tamen ea ætate tanta est facta mutatio, ut non adhuc vetus institutum, licet varie jam labefactatum, agnosceretur. Undecimo demum seculo, quo Pontificum in Imperatores odia in primis flagrare, adeóque Pontificia potestas majoribus auctibus increscere cœpere, eorum etiam authoritas & potestas altiores radices egit. Nam & Legationibus magnificis fungi cœperunt, in quibus, quod de Cardinalibus à Johanne XVII. in Galliam missis testatur Glaber, Pontificis Romani authoritatem assumpserunt: & Anno MXXVI. Pontifice Nicolao II. in Concilio Lateranense de Pontificis Romani electione edita est constitutio, qua, teste Gratiano Dist. 23. cap. 1. In nomine. Cardinalibus Episcopis in eligendo Pontifice primæ partes delatæ sunt. Tandem etiam excluso à Pontificis electione tum Imperatore, tum populo Romano, ad solos Cardinales tum Episcopos, tum Presbyteros, tum Diaconos, eligendi Papæ jus devolutum est, atque sic novo quodam eorum principatu paulatim exorto, Cardinales sub appellatione Ecclesiastica seculares Principes facti sunt. Creatos enim à se sic Papa alloqui suevit: Estote fratres nostri & principes mundi. Pius vero secundus sunt.
units.tr: LXXV. Such Cardinals, of course, were subject even to bishops until the time of Charlemagne, when the papacy was enlarged by the rule of many provinces. For their power grew along with the growth of papal power. And it happened at Rome as Tacitus, Annals 2.33, records of the same city. Gallus Asinius stated it in these words: With the growth of the Empire, private wealth also grew, and this was not new but of most ancient custom: the money of the Fabricii was one thing, that of the Scipios another, and everything was referred to the commonwealth; but when, with this modest wealth, their narrow houses had become a matter of magnificence, each individual's fortune swelled, etc. These men, therefore, could not fail to rise to great magnificence, since for the most part they took care of the popes and helped them with aid and counsel. Certainly in the year 769, under Pope Stephen IV, it was decreed in a Roman synod that no one should be chosen pope except from among the Cardinals. Yet at that age the change was not so great that the old institution, though already variously weakened, was not still recognized. Finally, in the eleventh century, when the hatred of the popes against the emperors flared up most of all and papal power began to grow by greater increments, the authority and power of the Cardinals also struck deeper roots. For they began to discharge splendid legations, in which, as Glaber testifies concerning the Cardinals sent into Gaul by John XVII, they assumed the authority of the Roman pontiff. And in the year 1026, under Pope Nicholas II, a constitution on the election of the Roman pontiff was issued at the Lateran Council, by which, according to Gratian, Dist. 23, cap. 1, In nomine, the first place in electing the pope was given to the Cardinal bishops. At last, with both the emperor and the Roman people excluded from the election of the pope, the right to elect the pope fell to the Cardinals alone, both bishops, priests, and deacons. Thus, with a new sort of princely power gradually arising for them, the Cardinals were made secular princes under an ecclesiastical name. For the pope was accustomed to address those he had created thus: Be our brothers and princes of the world.

units.la: hoc cessit. cundus primos Cardinales à se creatos sic, uti Sacr. Ceremon. Eccl. lib. 1. sect. 8. cap. 3. legere est, compellavit: Maxima, dilectissimi filii, & excellentissima dignitate donati estis: ad Collegium Apostolicum vocati, consiliarii nostri & conjudices orbis terrarum eritis: inter causam & causam; inter sanguinem & sanguinem, inter lepram & lepram discernere vos oportebit. Successores Apostolorum circa thronum sedebitis. Vos Senatores urbis & Regum similes eritis veri mundi cardines, super quos militantis ostium Ecclesiæ volvendum ac regendum est.
units.tr: This came to pass. Pius the Second, addressing the first Cardinals created by him, spoke in this way, as can be read in the Sacred Ceremonies, book 1, section 8, chapter 3: Most beloved sons, you have been endowed with the greatest and most excellent dignity. Called to the Apostolic college, you will be our counsellors and co-judges of the world. You will have to distinguish between cause and cause, between blood and blood, between leprosy and leprosy. You will sit about the throne as successors of the Apostles. You will be like the senators of the city and like kings, the true hinges of the world, upon which the door of the militant Church is to turn and be governed.

units.la: LXXVI.
units.tr: LXXVI.

units.la: Parum scilicet erat Romano Pontifici, quòd ab hominibus pro Apostolico vel Apostolo etiam haberetur, nisi æmulum etiam se ostenderet Apostoli & Pontificis confessionis nostræ, Christi. Sicut igitur Apostolos instituit Christus, iisque thronos, in quibus sessuri duodecim tribus Israëlis judicent, promisit: ita institutii hujus æmulus Papa ὁ ἀντὶ τῶ Χριστῶ, Apostolicum etiam Collegium constituit, Apostolorum loco tradito Cardinalibus, quos Manfredus Tractat. de Card. cap. 6. vocat Apostolorum Antecessores, quique circa thronum ejus sedentes Orbis terrarum cum eo conjudices forent. Neque certè desunt, qui ipsos Apostolos Cardinalatus munere functos pertendant, atque ea mirabili ratione institutionem eam Divino jure niti asserant, quòd Cardinales Papæ vicarii Christi, tanquam Principi assistentes, Apostolorum Christo assistentium personas repræsentent. Quam in rem sic Cardinalis Petrus de Aliaco Tract. de Eccl. & Card. authoritate, p. 1. col. 899. loquitur: Apostoli Petro tanquam Papale officium gerenti assistebant, tanquam Cardinalatus ministerium exercentes, de quorum Cardinalatu spiritualiter intelligi possit illud Propheticum: (1 Sam. II. 8.) Domini sunt cardines terræ, & posuit super eos Orbem.
units.tr: It was apparently not enough for the Roman Pontiff to be regarded by men as an Apostolic man or even an Apostle. He also had to show himself a rival to the Apostles and to the Pontiff of our confession, Christ. Just as Christ instituted the Apostles and promised them thrones on which they would sit and judge the twelve tribes of Israel, so this rival of the institution, the Pope, the one in place of Christ [ὁ ἀντὶ τῶ Χριστῶ], set up an Apostolic College as well. He handed over the place of the Apostles to the Cardinals, whom Manfredus, in Tractat. de Card. cap. 6., calls Apostorum Antecessores (the predecessors of the Apostles), and who, sitting around his throne, were to be co-judges of the world with him. Nor are there lacking those who claim that the Apostles themselves held the office of Cardinal, and who assert, by a remarkable line of reasoning, that this institution rests on divine right, since the Cardinals, as assistants to the Pope, the Vicar of Christ, represent the persons of the Apostles who assisted Christ. On this point Cardinal Pierre d'Ailly speaks thus in Tract. de Eccl. & Card. authoritate, p. 1. col. 899.: The Apostles assisted Peter, as one exercising the papal office, as men exercising the ministry of the Cardinalate; and of their Cardinalate that prophetic saying may be understood in a spiritual sense: (1 Sam. II. 8.) The pillars of the earth are the Lord's, and he has set the world upon them.

units.la: LXXII.
units.tr: LXXII.

units.la: Certè Cardinalium ex eo tempore mirum in modum prærogativæ multiplicatæ sunt hodiernum usque in diem, quo his feré ϖλεoνεκͅτημαʹσι gaudent, quòd scilicet, præter vestem eximiam, soli creant & coronant Pontifices, soli creantur: quòd post Papam anteponuntur omnibus; Papæ consiliarii & Senatores, totius Ecclesiæ procuratores & Commissarii sunt: quòd conjunctim cum Papa nominantur; & sine iis Papa legem generalem condere non potest; quòd veniunt in partem Majestatis Pontificiæ & cognati Regum dicuntur: Regibus æquiparantur, & Electoribus atque Regibus cedere gravantur: quòd purpurati sunt; purpura Imperatoribus olim eximiè donati à Papa: quòd Regum in aula Pontificia protectores sunt: quòd Papa invito convenire & Concilium cogere possunt, monendíque Papam jus habent: quòd denique Patriarchis præferuntur. Quas aliásque eorum Prærogativas ex variis authoribus collectas Celeberr. Freinshemius libro de S. R. I. Electorum & Rom. Eccles. Cardinalium. Præcedentia edito; Diatriba 4. copiosius retulit.
units.tr: Certainly, from that time onward the prerogatives of the Cardinals have multiplied in a remarkable way, down to the present day, when they enjoy these almost most excessive advantages [πλεονεκτήμασι]. Namely, besides their distinguished dress, they alone create and crown the Popes, and they alone can be created Pope. After the Pope they take precedence over everyone. They are the Pope's counsellors and senators, and the procurators and commissaries of the whole Church. They are named together with the Pope, and without them the Pope cannot enact a general law. They share in the majesty of the papacy and are called kinsmen of kings. They are placed on a level with kings, and they are considered too great to yield even to electors and kings. They are clothed in purple, a colour once generously granted by the Pope to emperors. They are protectors of kings in the papal court. They may convene a council and summon one even against the Pope's will, and they have the right to admonish the Pope. Finally, they are preferred to patriarchs. The celebrated Freinsheim has set out these and their other prerogatives, collected from various authors, at greater length in Diatriba 4, in his book on the Electors of the Holy Roman Empire and the Cardinals of the Roman Church, published as Praecedentia.

units.la: LXXVII. Galerum rubrum Cardinalibus Innocentius IV. A. MCCXLII. donavit, tesseram scilicet conjurationis Pontificiæ cum Cardinalibus, ceu Senatu quodam Edomitico Romanæ Ecclesiæ adversus Cæsares, Potestates humanas, omnes denique Papalem Majestatem dedignatos.
units.tr: LXXVII. In 1242 Innocent IV gave the red hat to the Cardinals. This was, of course, a sign of the Papal conspiracy with the Cardinals, as with a kind of Edomite senate of the Roman Church, against the Caesars, the human powers, and in short against everyone who scorned papal majesty.

units.la: De quo sic Onuphrius Panvinius in Epitome Romanorum Pontificum: Papa Innocentius IV. Pileum rubrum Cardinalibus dedit. Quo significare voluit, illos qui in illum ordinem legerentur, paratos esse debere pro libertate Ecclesiastica, (Papali puta licentia & libidine) si opus erit, propriam vitam morti exponere. Hinc deinceps Cardinales Ecclesiæ Rom. rubro pileo uti consuevere, qui tantæ pietatis insigne factus est, ut tiara Pontificatus & Episcopatus. Non sine Numine sanè rubro vestitu amiciri cœperunt, ne ambiguum esset sanguinariis eos consiliis adversus heri sui Pontificis adversarios quoscunque innecti. Opportunúmque ita Pontifici fuit quoscunque in Orbe terrarum viros doctos, peritos, spirituali Monarchiæ suæ vel profuturos, vel obfuturos, rubri galeri auctoramento suas in partes pertrahere. Neque ex una, sed variis ex gentibus familiisque nobilioribus senatum hunc conflare placuit, ut unà cum Cardinalibus ipsas quoque diversas gentes illustrésque familias sui beneficii faceret, arcana populorum per clientes hosce expiscaretur, & per instrumenta hæc dominationis latissimè regnaret. Non aliam certè instituti hujus rationem fuisse, seculorum sequentium experientia docuit.
units.tr: On this matter Onuphrius Panvinius writes thus in his Epitome Romanorum Pontificum: Pope Innocent IV gave the red hat to the Cardinals. By this he wished to signify that those who were chosen into that order ought to be prepared, for the sake of ecclesiastical liberty (that is, papal licence and lust), to expose their own lives to death if need be. Hence the Cardinals of the Roman Church afterwards customarily used the red hat, which became a token of such great devotion that it was made a mark of the papal tiara and of the episcopate. Certainly they began to be clothed in red not without divine providence, so that it would be unmistakable that they were bound by bloody counsels against whatever adversaries of their Pontiff lord. And it was thus expedient for the Pope to draw into his party, by the grant of the red hat, whatever learned and skilled men throughout the world would either help or hinder his spiritual monarchy. It pleased him to form this senate not from one nation but from various nations and more noble families, so that, together with the Cardinals, he might also bring the diverse nations and illustrious families under his favour, fish out the secrets of the peoples through these clients, and reign most widely by these instruments of domination. The experience of the following centuries has taught that there was certainly no other purpose in establishing this institution.

units.la: LXXVIII. E diverticulo hoc in viam ut redeamus, in seculum idem undecimum incidit continuatio controversiæ sacramentariæ.
units.tr: LXXVIII. To return from this digression to our path: in the same eleventh century there occurred a continuation of the sacramentarian controversy.

units.la: Floruerant ea ætate Berengarius Turonensis, Andegavensis Ecclesiæ Diaconus, Bertrami & Scoti Erigenæ partibus addictus. Is animadvertens serpere & in animis hominum radices agere errorem de corporali præsentia Christi in Cœna Domini, locutiones quinetiam S. Scripturæ & veterum improprias & sacramentales ad incrustandum errorem novum detorqueri, veram sententiam ex orthodoxo sensu repetitam corruptelis invalescentibus, libris etiam de eo editis, oppositum. Thesis ab eo asserta, uti constanter historiæ tradunt, fuit, in Cœna non ipsum corpus & sanguinem Christi, sed ejus figuram & sacramentum præstò esse. Quæ Thesis pro erronea & hæretica primum in Synodo Vercellensi, Pontifice Leone IX. damnata est. Neque tamen cessit errori Berengarius, sed contra audentior ivit, donec Pontifice Nicolao II. Synodo Romæ habita, strenuè licet confligens cum Alberico Diacono Cassinensi, nullo volente abjicere, ut Leo Ostiensis lib. III. 33. loquitur; & post etiam A. MLXXIX. Pontifice Gregorio VII. palinodiam canere subactus est. Palinodiæ formulam Capernaitæ Romani sub Nicolao II. Papa
units.tr: In that age Berengar of Tours, deacon of the Church of Angers, flourished, attached to the party of Bertram and of Scotus Erigena. Noticing that the error concerning the bodily presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper was creeping along and taking root in men's minds, and that even the improper and sacramental expressions of Holy Scripture and of the ancients were being twisted to plaster over the new error, he opposed it, drawing the true view from the orthodox sense, while the corruptions gained strength, and he also published books on the subject. The thesis he maintained, as the histories constantly relate, was that in the Supper the body and blood of Christ themselves are not present, but only their figure and sacrament. This thesis was first condemned as erroneous and heretical in the Synod of Vercelli, under Pope Leo IX. Yet Berengar did not yield to the error but went on more boldly, until under Pope Nicholas II, at a synod held in Rome, although he fought vigorously with Alberic, deacon of Monte Cassino, no one willing to cast him off, as Leo of Ostia says in lib. III, chapter 33. Afterwards, too, in 1079, under Pope Gregory VII, he was compelled to sing a palinode. The formula of the palinode was... [the Roman Capernaites under Pope Nicholas II].

units.la: Certaminis sacramentarii continuatio per Berengarium, ad horribilem palinodiam coactum. Papa ejusmodi ipsi praeiverunt: Ego Berengarius indignus Diaconus Ecclesiae S. Mauritii Andegavensis, cognoscens veram & Apostolicam fidem, anathematizo omnem haeresin praecipuè eam, de qua informatus sum, quae astruere conatur, panem & vinum, quae in altari ponuntur, post consecrationem solummodo sacramentum, & non verum corpus & sanguinem Domini nostri Jesu Christi esse, nec posse sensualiter, nisi in solo sacramento, manibus sacerdotum tractari, vel frangi, vel fidelium manibus atteri. Consentio autem sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae, & Apostolicae sedi, & ore & corde profiteor, de sacramento Dominicae mensae eam me fidem tenere, quam Dominus & venerabilis Papa Nicolaus, & haec sancta Synodus authoritate Evangelica & Apostolica tenendum tradidit, mihique formavit: scilicet panum & vinum, quae in altari ponuntur, post consecrationem non solum sacramentum, sed etiam verum corpus & sanguinem Domini nostri Jesu Christi esse: & sensualiter non solum in sacramento, sed in veritate manibus sacerdotum tractari, frangi & fidelium dentibus atteri, jurans per sanctam & homousion Trinitatem, & per haec sacro-sancta Christi Evangelia. Crassius etiam est juramentum posterius A. MLXXIX. Hildebrando Pontifice in haec ipsi verba praeitum: Ego Berengarius corde credo, & ore confiteor, panem & vinum, quae ponuntur in altari per mysterium sanctae orationis, & verbo nostri Redemptoris, substantialiter converti in veram & propriam ac vivisicam carnem & sanguinem Jesu Christi Domini nostri, & post consecrationem esse verum Christi corpus, quod naturale est de Virgine, & quod pro salute mundi oblatum in cruce pependit, & quod sedet ad dextram Patris; & verum sanguinem Christi, qui de latere ejus effusus est, non tantum per signum & virtutem sacramenti, sed in proprietate naturae & veritate substantiae, sicut in hoc Brevi continetur, & ego legi, & vos intelligitis. Sic credo, nec contra hanc fidem ulterius docebo. Sic me Deus adjuvet, & haec sancta Dei Evangelia. Haec quidem ille temerè jurata, praestanda tamen resipiscens neutiquam duxit. Libertati enim restitutus & voce & scripto errorem novitium superstitionémque Papæ damnavit, discipulos, quos in Gallia & Germania habuit permultos, in veritate confirmavit, & in eadem, uti etiam Baronius conjicit, ad finem usque vitæ perseveravit.
units.tr: The continuation of the sacramentarian contest through Berengar, who was forced into a horrible palinode. Popes of this kind went before him: I, Berengar, unworthy deacon of the Church of St Maurice at Angers, recognising the true and Apostolic faith, anathematise every heresy, especially that which I have been informed attempts to maintain that the bread and wine placed on the altar, after consecration, are only a sacrament and not the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they cannot be handled or broken by the hands of priests, or ground by the teeth of the faithful, in a sensual way, except in the sacrament alone. I consent, however, to the holy Roman Church and the Apostolic See, and I profess with mouth and heart, concerning the sacrament of the Lord's table, that I hold the faith which the Lord and the venerable Pope Nicholas, and this holy Synod, by evangelical and Apostolic authority, have delivered to be held and have instructed me in: namely, that the bread and wine placed on the altar, after consecration, are not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they are handled by the hands of priests and broken and ground by the teeth of the faithful sensually, not only in the sacrament but in truth, swearing by the holy and consubstantial Trinity and by these most sacred Gospels of Christ. Cruder still was the later oath, sworn in 1079 under Pope Hildebrand, in these very words: I, Berengar, believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that the bread and wine which are placed on the altar, through the mystery of the holy prayer and the word of our Redeemer, are substantially converted into the true and proper and life-giving flesh and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord, and that after consecration there is the true body of Christ, which is natural, born of the Virgin, which hung on the cross offered for the salvation of the world, and which sits at the right hand of the Father; and the true blood of Christ, which flowed from his side, not only by sign and power of the sacrament, but in the property of nature and the truth of substance, as is contained in this Brief, which I have read and which you understand. So I believe, and I shall not teach anything further against this faith. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels of God. Indeed, although he had rashly sworn these things, Berengar, coming to his senses, by no means thought he ought to keep them. For, restored to freedom, he condemned with voice and pen the novel error and the superstition of the Pope, confirmed in the truth the very many disciples he had in France and Germany, and, as Baronius also conjectures, persevered in the same view to the end of his life.

units.la: ECCLESIÆ ROMANÆ PERIODUS QUARTA.
units.tr: THE FOURTH PERIOD OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.

units.la: Seu
units.tr: That is,

units.la: Historia Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Dominatio- nem etiam in temporalibus affectantis, & in doc- trina ritibusque in pejus in dies vergentis.
units.tr: History of the Roman Church, aspiring to dominion even in temporal affairs, and sliding for the worse day by day in doctrine and rites.

units.la: Inde à Gregorio VII. seu A. C. MLXXIII. ad Bonifacium VIII. seu A. C. MCCXCIV. usque.
units.tr: From Gregory VII, that is, A.D. 1073, to Boniface VIII, that is, A.D. 1294.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: LXXIX. Gregorius VII. sede Pontificia rapta strenuè Papatum provehit. Sub quatuor Pontificibus Dominus Papæ cluebat. Daemoniacis artibus imbutum fuisse testes sunt Episcopi 30. Brixinæ coacti, aliúque.
units.tr: LXXIX. Gregory VII, seizing the papal see, vigorously advances the Papacy. Under four popes he was known as the Lord of the Pope. That he was steeped in demonic arts is attested by thirty bishops gathered at Brixen, and others.

units.la: LXXX. Henrico Imp. se opponit, potentia Mathildis & Normannorum fretus. Senatus consultum Imp. & Ordinum adversus eum Wormatiæ factum, quo Papatu exuitur. Vicissim is in concilio R. Imperatorem excommunicat, S. Petro vindice compellato. Henricus Romam pergens, supplex Gregorio, & iniquas leges accipiens, anathemate solvitur. Nihilominus à Confæderatis Germanis à Gregorio inflammatis Porcemii Regno idem, Rodolpho Suevia & Burgundiæ Duce surrogato, exuitur; & injuriam vindicans, denuo à Gregorio excommunicatur. Vicissim
units.tr: LXXX. He sets himself against the Emperor Henry, relying on the power of Matilda and the Normans. A decree of the Emperor and the estates was made against him at Worms, by which he was stripped of the Papacy. In turn, in a council, he excommunicated the king, calling on St Peter as avenger. Henry, going to Rome, came as a suppliant to Gregory and accepted unjust conditions, and was released from the anathema. Nevertheless, at the instigation of Gregory, the German confederates set aside his kingdom, and Rodolf, Duke of Swabia and Burgundy, was put in his place; Henry, avenging the injury, was again excommunicated by Gregory. In turn

units.la: L sim Brixinæ Gregorius ab Henricianis denuo scelerum multorum reus peractus deponitur: & mox Rodolphus prælio victus perit; atque Roma occupata Gregorius pulsus Salerni exul moritur. LXXXI. Dictatus Gregoriani, Papatus Hildebrandini fundamenta, recensiti. LXXXII. Ejusdem Gregorii de abstinentia à cibis certis, & sacerdotum cœlibatu decreta dæmoniaca. LXXXIII. Hæresis Simoniacorum & Nicolaitarum fictitia. LXXXIIII. Vrbani II. Hildebrandini, & Clementis III. Cæsarei Papæ contraria statuta Aventini verbis memorata. LXXXV. Bellum sacrum ab eodem Vrbano decretum, exitu infelix. LXXXVI. Ejus belli prætextus, LXXXVII. nec non causæ suasoriæ, Pontificum avaritia, dominandi libido, & Christianorum Principum oppressio, distinctæ. LXXXVIII. Concilii Claromontani Canones, Potestatem & superstitionem Papalem amplificantes. LXXXIX. Seculi XII. historia. Ejus etiam initio fama fuit, Antichristum mox revelatum iri. Bernhardi & Platinæ eam in rem testimonia. XC. De calamitosa circa id temporis Ecclesiæ Romanæ facie testimonia Malmesburiensis, Hildeberti, Bernhardi, Martinensis, Honorii Augustodunensis (qui Babylonem R. describit graphicè) Arnoldi de Brixia. XCI. Bernhardi Claraevallensis de corruptione Hierarchiæ R. querelæ acerbæ. XCII. De eadem Joh. Sarisburiensis ad Hadrianum IV. Epistola. XCIII. Cleri Leodiensis ad Paschalem II. responsio, qua R. Ecclesiam Babylonem esse pertendit. XCIV. Tot querelarum causa hærebat in Pontificibus. Paschalis II. Henricum IV. ad mortem usque persequitur. Callistus II.
units.tr: Vicissim at Brixen Gregory, having been declared by Henry's party guilty of many crimes, was deposed; and soon Rodolf, defeated in battle, perished; and Rome being occupied, Gregory was driven out and died in exile at Salerno. LXXXI. The Dictates of Gregory, the foundations of Hildebrandine Papacy, are recounted. LXXXII. The diabolical decrees of the same Gregory concerning abstinence from certain foods and the celibacy of priests. LXXXIII. The fictitious heresy of the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans. LXXXIV. The statutes of Urban II, Hildebrandine, and of Clement III, the Caesarean pope, opposed to each other, recorded in the words of Aventinus. LXXXV. The holy war decreed by the same Urban, unhappy in outcome. LXXXVI. The pretext of that war, LXXXVII. and likewise the motives urging it, distinguished as the greed of the popes, the lust for domination, and the oppression of Christian princes. LXXXVIII. The canons of the Council of Clermont, magnifying papal power and superstition. LXXXIX. History of the twelfth century. At its beginning there was also a rumour that Antichrist would soon be revealed; the testimonies of Bernard and Platina on this point. XC. Testimonies on the calamitous face of the Roman Church at that time: of Malmesbury, Hildebert, Bernard, Martin of Troppau, Honorius of Autun (who describes Rome graphically as Babylon), and Arnold of Brescia. XCI. The bitter complaints of Bernard of Clairvaux on the corruption of the Roman hierarchy. XCII. On the same subject, the letter of John of Salisbury to Hadrian IV. XCIII. The reply of the clergy of Liège to Paschal II, in which they maintain that the Roman Church is Babylon. XCIV. The cause of so many complaints lay in the popes. Paschal II persecuted Henry IV to his death. Callistus II, from Henry V, wrung from him the right of investiture. So the pope prevailed. The king was absolved, and the schism expired. units.la: LXXIX. Umprimis verò Papatus Gregorii VII. Hildebrandi vulgò dicti, Pontificium Regnum, depressa Majestate Imperatoria, ad ἀρχὴν strenuè perduxit. Erat Hildebrandus ille natione Hetrufcus, Sena oriundus, professione Cluniacensis Monachus. Papatum A. MLXXIII. spreta authoritate Imperatoris, contemptóque Cleri & populi suffragio, vi remotis, qui obstare improbis conatibus viderentur, rapiens, abusus eam in rem pupillari ætate Henrici III. juxta quosdam IV. Imperatoris, qui quinquennis tum sub tutela matris Agnetis educabatur. Jam ante sub quatuor Pontificibus, Pontificiis artibus assuetus, earúmque callentissimus, plus quàm Papam se gessit, adeò ut eum Petrus Damiani Dominum Papæ appellaverit, eíque dicere non erubuerit: Papam rite colo, sed te prostratus adoro, Tu facis hunc dominum, te facit ipse Deum.
units.tr: LXXIX. Above all, the Papacy of Gregory VII, commonly called Hildebrand, with the imperial majesty humbled, strenuously carried the pontifical kingdom to its height [ἀρχήν]. This Hildebrand was by nation a Tuscan, born at Siena, and by profession a monk of Cluny. In 1073, having disregarded the authority of the Emperor and scorned the suffrage of clergy and people, he seized the Papacy by force, removing those who seemed likely to obstruct his wicked attempts. He abused for this purpose the minority of Henry III, according to some the IV, Emperor, who was then five years old and being brought up under the guardianship of his mother Agnes. Already earlier, under four Popes, having been trained in papal arts and being most skilled in them, he had conducted himself as more than a pope, so that Peter Damian called him Lord of the Pope, and was not ashamed to say to him: I duly honour the Pope, but prostrate I adore you. You make him lord, and he himself makes you God.

units.la: Ejus adventum fuisse ex operatione Sathanæ, insignis nis & prodigiis mendacibus, non unus Cardinalis Benno prodidit, asserens scilicet eum Diabolicarum artium studiis ab antecessoribus Benedicto IX. & Gregorio VI. pessimis magistris pejorem discipulum imbutum esse, ex mantica ignem, quoties vellet excutere edoctum: sed affirmarunt etiam Episcopi triginta, qui A. MLXXX. ex Italia, Gallia, Germania Brixinæ Noricæ convenerunt. In eo conventu Hildebrandum accusatum, quòd per artem magicam, necromanticam, & Dæmonum suffragio sedem Apostolicam invaserit; condemnatúmque, ceu falsum Monachum, magnum divinaculum, somniorum prodigiorúmque conjectorem, & Cæsareanarum & Pontificiarum partium scriptores, Marianus Scotus, Aventinus, Sigonius, Trithemius, alii testantur.
units.tr: That his coming was from the working of Satan, with signs and lying wonders, was declared by more than one cardinal, Benno, who asserted that he had been steeped in the study of diabolical arts by his predecessors Benedict IX and Gregory VI, "worse masters making a worse pupil", and had been taught to strike fire from his wallet whenever he wished. But thirty bishops also affirmed it, who in 1080 gathered at Brixen in Noricum from Italy, Gaul and Germany. In that assembly Hildebrand was accused of having invaded the Apostolic See by magic arts, necromancy and the aid of demons, and was condemned as a false monk, a great diviner, and an interpreter of dreams and portents. Writers on the imperial and papal sides, Marianus Scotus, Aventinus, Sigonius, Trithemius and others, bear witness to this.

units.la: LXXX. Sperni proculcarique à Monacho tali Majestatem Imperatoris, iniquè merito Henricus Imp. tulit, certus collectis copiis jus Imperii, Majestatémqne adversus eum tueri. Successerátque propositum, si præeuntem bona fide subsecuti essent ii, quos id facere plane decuerat.
units.tr: LXXX. Henry the Emperor took it badly, and rightly so, that the majesty of the Emperor was spurned and trampled by such a monk. Being certain that he could defend the right of the Empire and its majesty against him, he gathered his forces. His purpose would have succeeded, had those who should plainly have followed the lead of this man done so in good faith.

units.la: Gregorius haud segniter Imperatori obsistens, se Mathildis opulentissimæ fœminæ (quam non sine suspicione incesti amoris eum deperiisse, ex Lamberti Schafnaburgensis narratione prudentibus pridem suboluit.) & Normannorum potentia muniit. Atque insuper Saxones duce Ottone, antehac Bavariæ Regulo, adversus Imperatorem, Dominum suum concitavit. Cúmque A. MLXXV. Saxones ingentem stragem passi essent, alia via adversus Dominum suum grassandum rati, eum apud Gregorium, ceu sceleꝛum grauium compertum accusant; qui Legatos Imperatoris causam acturos in vincula rapit, frigore, fame, siti excruciat, per urbem circumductos Romå pellit. Quo comperto, Imperator Wormatiæ Concilium cogit, cui Episcopi omnes Galliæ & Germaniæ, præter Saxones (quorum nomina Polyhistor Stumpfius Chron. lib. IV. 40. ex Abbatissano Tigurinorum Cœnobio eruta repræsentat.) interfuere, lectis ibi literis flaminum primorum Populi Romani, quas Hugo Bloncus Cardinalis Roma attulerat, factum senatusconsultum, quod ejusmodi verbis Aventinus Annal. Boj. lib. 5. recitat: Hildebrandus, qui se Gregorium nuncupat, primus sine consensu nostro adversus Imperatoris Romani, rerum domini à Deo constituti, voluntatem, contra auspicia Pontificatum maximum, quem pridem ambivit, & judicio convictus perpetuò abjuravit, invasit, Monachus desertor est, novis dogmatibus sacro-sanctam philosophiam adulterat, Divinas literas falsò interpretando suæ causæ servire cogit, concordiam Collegii scindit, sacra, profana, Divina, humana commiscet, utrumque juxta polluit. Diabolicis, hoc est, arcerbissimorum hostium spurcissimis criminationibus, iniquorum maledictis aurem commodat & credit. Testis, judex, accusator, inimicus idem est. Maritos ab uxoribus separat, scorta pudicis conjugibus, stupra, incestus, adulteria casto præfert connubio, populares adversus Sacerdotes, vulgus adversumEpiscopos concitat. Neminem ritè initiatum esse docet, nisi qui ab eo sacerdotium emendicaverit, atque ab ejus aurisugis mercatus fuerit. Vili plebeculæ gratificari studet, vulgi imperiti auram captat, simulata religione decipit, defraudat, circumvenit, in senatulo muliercularum de sacratissimis mysteriis religionis pertractat, Supremi Numinis legem, qua se idem quoque ligavit, solvit, utrumque & Imperium & Pontificatum, sicut Decii & falsorum Deorum cultores facilitare consueverunt, usurpat, &c. Divinæ Majestati refragatur. Christianissimo Principi Divinitus constituto, & à Deo inaugurato resistit, versutus, fallax, obscurus, callidus imperium orbis, titulo Christi, sub ovina pelle ambit. Inde exauthorandi ejus sententiam his verbis ferunt. Hasce ob causas Sanctissimus Imperator, Pontifices, Senatus Populúsque Christianus illum Hildebrandum abdicandum, sibi eundem non placere, nec oves lupo committendas censent. Cui decreto non solùm Germaniæ, Galliæque, sed Italiæ quoque Episcopos, conventu Ticini acto, subscripsisse juràsseque, se nunquam Pontificem Maximum isthoc nomine recepturos, Aventinus, qui & superiora refert, Annal. lib. V. testis est. Ad ipsum quoque Gregorium Synodus ea literas misit, quas apud Goldastum Constit. Imper. lib. I. adversus Baronium defensas videre est; ubi inter alia hæc habentur: Quia & introitus tuus tantis periculis est initiatus, & Ecclesia Dei tam gravi tempestate per abusionem novitatum tuarum periclitatur, & vitam per conversationem tuam tam multiplici infamia de honestâsti, obedientiam, quam nullam promisimus, nec de cætero ullam servaturos esse, renuntiamus. Et quia nemo nostrûm, ut tu publicè declamabas, tibi hactenus fuit Episcopus, tu quoque nulli nostrûm à modo eris Apostolicus. Neque tamen Gregorius animum abjecit, quin eò potiùs audaciæ processit, ut A. MLXXVI. in concilio Romano promulgatis priùs Dictatibus, de quibus paulò post dicemus, Imperatorem ipsum excommunicare, Regno Germaniæ & Italiæ spoliare, Principes & populos juramento fidelitatis ei præstito liberare non erubuerit. Eo decreto Petrum vindicem sic compellat: Audi me, Apostolorum Princeps Petre, Tu mihi, beatúsque Paulus frater tuus, optimi præter crebros testes esse potestis, me invitum ad sanctæ tuæ Ecclesiæ gubernationem esse protractum; Ob eam rem mihi persuadeo, tibi placere, ut ego populo Christiano, Tibi præcipuè à Deo commissò, præsim. Hac igitur fiducia nixus, pro Ecclesiæ tuæ honore ex parte omnipotentis Dei Patris, & Filii & Spiritus S. jure authoritatis tuæ, Henrico Regi, Henrici Imperatoris filio, qui adversus Ecclesiam tuam inaudita superbia insurrexit, toto Regno Germaniæ atque Italiæ interdico, &c. ut gentes sentiant, quòd tu es Petrus, & super tuam Petram filius Dei ædificaverit Ecclesiam suam. Contradicentibus nonnullis, ea ratione, quòd Reges anathemate feriri nequeant, respondit: An verò cum -cùm Deus Ecclesiam suam ter beato Petro commisit, dicens: Pasce oves meas, ipsos Reges excepit? Atque ita Henricus Hildebrandum exauthoravit. Hildebrandus exauthoratus Henricum potestate omni abdicavit, quod novissimum facinus detestantes Sigebertum Gemblacensem, Gothofredum Viterbiensem, aliosque videre elt.
