Certè etiam Gallicanam Ecclesiam Hildebrandinis moliminibus adversus seculares Potestates nunquam consensisse, nuper Doctiss. Petrus de Marca de Concord. Sacerd. & Imp. lib. VI. 33. VIII. 21. &c. demonstravit. Hildebrandi partibus sese addixerunt Hugo, Alsatiæ Dux, ære alieno oppressus, Rodolphus Sueviæ Dux, Imperatoris Sororius, imperii spe lactatus, Bertholdus Zeringiæ Dux, ejus gener, Welpho Dux Bavariæ, Moguntinus, Metensis & Wormatiensis Episcopi; nec non Abbates aliquot, sive anathematis terrore perculsi, sive Principibus illis obnoxii, qui rebellibus pridem Saxonibus auxiliares manus porrigentes Germaniam universam ferro flammáque peragrarunt; donec Henricus, remoto exercitu, pœnitentia acta, reconciliationem cum Gregorio attentaturus, Romam proficisceretur, ubi intra secundum murorum ambitum receptus, abjecto cultu Regio omni; sine calceis, sæviente hieme, jejunus usque ad vesperam, forfices & scopas (uti Malmesburiensis loquitur) in manu habens, ut se attonderi & flagellari paratum ostenderet, responsum Gregorii nequicquam operitur; & quarta demum vice redux, inaudita patientia præfractum Pontificis animum hactenus expugnat, ut Henricum in conspectum suum admitteret, atque ita cum eo pacisceretur, ut die & loco, quem ipse constitueret, in communi Germanorum conventu, in judicio se sisteret, & criminibus objectis, quæstionem exercente Gregorio, responderet, atque extremo ejus judicio staret: interea omnia Regiæ dignitatis ornamenta deponeret, ac de re-bus bus publicis nihil pro suo jure statueret: eos, quorum hactenus usus erat consilio, Bambergensem Episcopum, coeterosque à sua familiaritate in perpetuum depelleret, & qui sacramento ei dixissent, ejus religione exolveret omnes. Quæ cum se facturum per omnia sacra jurâsset, anathemate à Gregorio solvitur, magno adhuc in lucro, id, quod consecutus erat, reputans. Sed fluxam fidem gerens Pontifex, missis ad confoederatos Germanos, Saxones cumprimis, Legatis, ne pacta cum Henrico attendant, monet. Nam licet reconciliatus sit Curiæ Cælesti, non tamen Regno, quo auspicato Romæ privatus sit, restitutum esse. Ita cum Legatis illis juncti Foederati Porcemii mense Martio Anni MLXXVII. convenientes, communi consilio Rodolphum Sueviæ & Burgundiæ Ducem, Henrici Sororium, Imperatorem eligunt, ea scilicet lege, ut omnia Pontificalia abjuret, clientelas Episcoporum abdicet, nêve velut hæreditario jure filios suos successores declaret. Cui mox etiam Imperialem coronam Papa misit, his verbis inscriptam.
units.tr: Gregory, not slow to resist the Emperor, fortified himself with the support of Matilda, a very wealthy woman (whom, as the prudent had long since learned from Lambert of Schaffnaburg's account, he loved with a suspicion of incestuous passion), and with the power of the Normans. Moreover, he stirred up the Saxons against the Emperor, their lord, under Duke Otto, formerly king of Bavaria. When the Saxons suffered a huge slaughter in 1075, they judged that another way must be taken against their lord, and they accused him before Gregory of grave crimes, which they had discovered. Gregory seized the Emperor's envoys, who were to plead the case, and put them in chains; he tortured them with cold, hunger and thirst, led them about the city, and drove them out of Rome. When this became known, the Emperor called a council at Worms, which all the bishops of Gaul and Germany attended, except the Saxons (whose names Stumpf the polymath gives, drawn from the Abbatissa convent of the Tigurini, Chron. lib. IV. 40.). There the letters of the chief priests of the Roman people, which Hugo Blonc, cardinal, had brought from Rome, were read, and a decree of the senate was passed, which Aventinus recites in these words, Annal. Boj. lib. 5.: Hildebrand, who calls himself Gregory, has, without our consent and against the auspices, seized the highest pontificate, which he had earlier sought and, convicted by judgement, had forever renounced. He is a deserter monk. He corrupts the sacred philosophy with new dogmas, forces the divine letters, by false interpretation, to serve his cause, splits the harmony of the college, mixes sacred with profane, divine with human, and defiles each. He lends his ear to diabolical accusations, that is, to the foulest slanders of the most bitter enemies, and believes them. He is witness, judge, accuser and enemy all at once. He separates husbands from wives, prefers prostitutes to chaste spouses, and fornication, incest and adultery to chaste marriage. He stirs up the common people against the priests and the crowd against the bishops. He teaches that no one is rightly initiated unless he has bought the priesthood from him and from his ear-whisperers. He strives to please the cheap rabble, catches the breath of the ignorant crowd, deceives with feigned religion, defrauds, circumvents, and in the little senate of women treats of the most sacred mysteries of religion. He dissolves the law of the Supreme Divinity, by which he himself was also bound, and usurps both empire and pontificate, as the Decii and the worshippers of false gods were accustomed to do, etc. He resists the Divine Majesty. He resists the most Christian prince, divinely established and inaugurated by God, crafty, deceitful, obscure, cunning, and under the title of Christ, under a sheep's skin, he seeks dominion over the world. From this they report the sentence of his deposition in these words: For these reasons the most holy Emperor, the bishops, the senate and the Christian people judge that this Hildebrand is to be deposed; that he is not pleasing to them, and that sheep are not to be entrusted to a wolf. Aventinus, who also reports the earlier matters, Annal. lib. V., bears witness that bishops not only of Germany and Gaul but also of Italy, at a meeting held at Pavia, subscribed to this decree and swore that they would never receive him as Supreme Pontiff under that name. The synod also sent letters to Gregory himself, which may be seen defended against Baronius in Goldast, Constit. Imper. lib. I.; among other things these stand there: Because your entry was begun amid such great dangers, and the Church of God is endangered by such a grave storm through the abuse of your novelties, and because you have dishonoured your life by your conduct with such manifold infamy, we renounce the obedience which we promised to no one and will keep none in future. And because none of us, as you proclaimed publicly, has hitherto been a bishop to you, you too will be apostolic to none of us from now on. Yet Gregory did not lose heart; rather, he advanced to greater audacity, so that in 1076, at a Roman council, after first promulgating the Dictates, of which we shall speak shortly, he was not ashamed to excommunicate the Emperor himself, to strip him of the kingdoms of Germany and Italy, and to release the princes and peoples from the oath of fidelity sworn to him. By that decree he addresses Peter as avenger: Hear me, Peter, prince of the apostles. You and your brother Paul, the blessed one, may be the best witnesses besides many others that I was drawn unwillingly to the government of your holy Church. For this reason I am persuaded that it pleases you that I should preside over the Christian people, which was committed above all to you by God. Relying therefore on this confidence, for the honour of your Church, on behalf of almighty God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, by the right of your authority, I forbid King Henry, son of the Emperor Henry, who with unheard-of pride has risen against your Church, throughout the whole kingdom of Germany and Italy, etc., so that the nations may feel that you are Peter, and that on your rock the Son of God has built his Church. When some objected that kings cannot be struck with anathema, he replied: Did not God, when he committed his Church to the blessed Peter three times, saying, Feed my sheep, except kings themselves? Thus Henry deposed Hildebrand. Hildebrand, deposed, deprived Henry of all power; the authors who detest this last deed may be seen in Sigebert of Gembloux, Gottfried of Viterbo and others. Certainly the Gallican Church never agreed to the Hildebrandine efforts against secular powers, as the very learned Peter de Marca recently demonstrated, de Concord. Sacerd. & Imp. lib. VI. 33, VIII. 21, etc. On the side of Hildebrand there joined Hugh, Duke of Alsace, weighed down by debt; Rudolf, Duke of Swabia, the Emperor's brother-in-law, elated by hope of the empire; Berthold, Duke of Zähringen, his son-in-law; Welf, Duke of Bavaria; and the bishops of Mainz, Metz and Worms; also several abbots, either struck with terror of the anathema or bound to those princes who had long before given auxiliary forces to the rebel Saxons and had roamed all Germany with sword and fire. Until at last Henry, having withdrawn his army and performed penance, set out for Rome intending to seek reconciliation with Gregory. Received within the second circuit of the walls, he laid aside all royal dress, went without shoes in the raging winter, fasting until evening, holding scissors and brooms (as the Malmesbury writer says) in his hand, to show that he was ready to be shorn and flogged. He waited in vain for Gregory's reply; and at last, returning a fourth time, by unheard-of patience he overcame the Pontiff's hitherto obstinate mind, so that he admitted Henry into his presence, and agreed with him on these terms: that on a day and at a place which Gregory himself should appoint, at a common assembly of the Germans, he would present himself for judgement, and when the charges were laid against him, with Gregory examining, he would answer and abide by the final verdict of that court; meanwhile he would lay aside all the ornaments of royal dignity, and would decide nothing in public affairs by his own right; he would remove forever from his company those whose counsel he had used until then, namely the bishop of Bamberg and the others; and he would release from their oaths all who had sworn allegiance to him. When Henry had sworn by every sacred thing that he would do all this, he was released from the anathema by Gregory, who still counted as a great gain what he had obtained. But the Pontiff, keeping faith loosely, sent envoys to the allied Germans, especially the Saxons, warning them not to keep the agreement with Henry: For although he has been reconciled to the heavenly Court, he has not been restored to the kingdom, from which he was deprived at Rome by an ill-omened decision. So the allied princes, joining with those envoys and meeting at Forchheim in March 1077, by common counsel chose as Emperor Rudolf, Duke of Swabia and Burgundy, Henry's brother-in-law, on this condition: that he should abjure all pontifical claims, renounce the clientages of the bishops, and not declare his sons his successors by hereditary right. Soon the Pope also sent him the imperial crown, inscribed with these words:

units.la: Petra dedit Petro, Petrus diadema Rodolpho.
units.tr: The rock gave to Peter; Peter gave the diadem to Rudolf.

units.la: Qua quidem insigni injuria ignominiáque accensus Henricus, Italia profugus, & pœnitudine ductus servilis patientiæ, animum & amicos colligit, ac instructo exercitu Rodolphum justo prœlio fusum fugatúmque insigni clade afficit. Gregorius ejus rei nuncio sauciatus non parum, denuo Henricum anathemate ferit, Rodolphum confirmat. Ex altera parte Italiæ, Galliæ, Germaniæ Episcopi A. MLXXX. Brixinæ, quæ Bojorum urbs est, habito Concilio, Gregorium iterum ambitionis, hæresèos, impietatis, Sacrilegii reum peragunt, & ceu falsum Monachum, magum divinaculum, somniorum prodigiorúmque conjectorem, male de religione sentientem; conjuratum hostem Reipub. atque sacro-sancti Imperii, Sacrilegia, perjuria, mendacia, homicidia, incendia velut bene facta, indulgentem & collaudantem, & ad ea perpetranda classicum canentem ; sacerdotes conjugatos ab altari removentem, scortatores vero, adulteros, incestuosos eidem admoventem ; authore Deo O. M. Pontificatu maximo amovendum decernunt. Gregorius susque deque habito decreto, denuo animos Rodolpho & Saxonibus facturus, ex revelatione scire se, inquit Sigebertus, asseverat, falsum Regem, Henricum scilicet eodem anno moriturum; vetans se haberi pro Papa, si falleret augurium. Fretus eo Oraculo Rodolphus, secunda, tertia quartaque vice instaurato proelio non solum, falsus scilicet Rex superatur, sed amputata dextra, qua fidem Henrico dederat, interit. Mox etiam Henricus cum exercitu Romam perrexit, eam obsedit, occupavit, in locum Gregorii Clemente constituto Pontifice. Fugit Apostolicus, (Gregorius) & qui omnes in periculum impulerat omnes in periculo deseruit, inquit Benno. Demum reverso in Germaniam Henrico, Hildebrandus Salerni VIII. Kal. Junii A. MLXXXV. exul moritur, postquam, Gemblacense narrante; confessus est, se Diabolo suadente odium & iram contra humanum genus concitasse. Hæc Hildebrandinæ tragœdiæ catastrophe fuit.
units.tr: Henry, inflamed by this remarkable injury and disgrace, fled from Italy, and, moved by regret for his servile patience, gathered his spirit and friends, and with his army drew up in battle, defeated Rudolf in a just battle, and inflicted on him a notable defeat and flight. Gregory, sorely wounded by news of this, again struck Henry with anathema and confirmed Rudolf. On the other side, the bishops of Italy, Gaul and Germany, having held a council at Brixen, which is a city of the Boii, in 1080, charged Gregory again with ambition, heresy, impiety and sacrilege, and declared that he should be removed from the supreme pontificate by God the Almighty; they called him a false monk, a magician, a diviner, an interpreter of dreams and prodigies, one who thinks ill of religion, a conspirator and enemy of the commonwealth and of the most holy empire, one who indulges in and praises sacrileges, perjuries, lies, murders and arson as if they were good deeds, and who sounds the trumpet for committing them, and who removes married priests from the altar while bringing to it fornicators, adulterers and incestuous men. Gregory, treating the decree as nothing, intending to rouse Rudolf and the Saxons again, asserted, as Sigebert says, that he knew by revelation that the false king, namely Henry, would die in that same year, forbidding himself to be regarded as Pope if the augury should fail. Trusting in that oracle, Rudolf was not only defeated in the second, third and fourth renewed battles, the false king as he was, but, having his right hand cut off, the hand with which he had pledged faith to Henry, he perished. Soon afterwards Henry marched with his army to Rome, besieged it, took it, and set Clement in place of Gregory as Pontiff. The Apostolic one fled, (Gregory), and he who had driven everyone into danger abandoned everyone in danger, says Benno. At last, when Henry had returned to Germany, Hildebrand died in exile at Salerno on the 8th day before the Kalends of June, 1085, after, as the Gembloux writer relates, he confessed that at the Devil's urging he had stirred up hatred and wrath against the human race. This was the catastrophe of the Hildebrandine tragedy.

units.la: LXXXI. In Concilio Romano A. MLXXVI. habito, in quo Henricum Gregorius exauthoravit, & sacrorum etiam communione privavit, idem Gregorius Canones edidit, quibus Hildebrandini Papatus fundamenta continentur.
units.tr: LXXXI. At the Roman Council held in 1076, in which Gregory deposed Henry and also deprived him of communion in the sacred rites, the same Gregory issued canons that contain the foundations of Hildebrandine Papacy.

units.la: Eos Dictatus Papæ novus Dictator appellavit, quorum major pars, uti in ejus vita Onuphrius loquitur, antea parum in usu fuerat, & à nemine prædecessorum ejus unquam attentata. Sunt autem decreta ejusmodi: Quòd Romana Ecclesia à solo Domino sit fundata; quòd solus Pontifex Romanus jure dicatur universalis; quod ille solus possit deponere Episcopos, vel reconciliare: quòd Legatus ejus omnibus Episcopis præsit in Concilio, etiam inferioris gradus, & adversus eos sententiam depositionis possit dare: quòd absentes Papa possit deponere; quòd cum cum excommunicatis ab illo, inter caetera nec in eadem domo debemus manere: quod illi soli licet pro temporis necessitate novas leges condere, novas plebes congregare; de Canonica Abbatiam facere, & e contra divitem Episcopatum dividere, inopes unire: quod solus possit uti imperialibus insignijs: quod solius Papae pedes omnes Principes deosculentur: quod illius solius nomen in Ecclesijs retinetur: quod unicum est nomen in mundo: quod illi liceat Imperatores deponere; quod illi liceat de sede ad sedem, necessitate cogente, Episcopos transmutare: quod de omni Ecclesia, quacunque voluerit clerum valeat ordinare: quod ab illo ordinatus alii Ecclesiae praesse potest, sed non militare: & quod ab aliquo Episcopo non debet superiorem gradum accipere: quod nulla Synodus absque praecepto ejus debeat generalis vocari: quod nullum capitulum, nullúsque liber Canonicus habeatur absque illius authoritate: quod sententia illius a nullo debeat retractari, & ipse omnium solus retractare possit: quod a nemine ipse judicari debeat: quod nullus audeat condemnare Apostolicam sedem appellantem: quod majores causae cujuscunque Ecclesiae ad eum referri debeant: quod Romana Ecclesia nunquam erravit: nec in perpetuum, Scriptura testante, errabit: quodRom. Pontifex, si canonice fuerit ordinatus, meritis B. Petri indubitanter efficitur Sanctus, testante Sancto Ennodio, Papiensi Episcopo, ei multis Sanctis Patribus faventibus, sicut in decretis beati Symmachi Papae continetur: quod illius praecepto & licentia subjectis liceat accusare: quod absque Synodali conventu ei liceat Episcopos deponere & reconciliare: quod Catholicus non habeatur, qui non concordat Romanae Ecclesiae: quod a fidelitate iniquorum subjectos potest absolvere. Non aliud scilicet supererat, quàm ut pauca superadderet; quod Papa sit Christus, proin & Antichristus ipse.
units.tr: The new Dictator called these the Dictatus Papae, of which the major part, as Onuphrius says in his life of Gregory, had been little used before and had never been attempted by any of his predecessors. The decrees are of this kind: That the Roman Church was founded by the Lord alone; that the Roman Pontiff alone is rightly called universal; that he alone may depose or reconcile bishops; that his legate presides over all bishops in a council, even those of lower rank, and may pronounce sentence of deposition against them; that the Pope may depose the absent; that we ought not to remain in the same house as those excommunicated by him; that he alone may, as the needs of the time require, enact new laws, gather new peoples, make an abbey out of a canonry, divide a rich bishopric and unite poor ones; that he alone may use the imperial insignia; that all princes shall kiss the feet of the Pope alone; that his name alone is spoken in the churches; that his is the only name in the world; that he may depose emperors; that he may transfer bishops from see to see as necessity requires; that he may ordain clergy from any church he wishes; that a man ordained by him may preside over another church but not serve in it, and that he must not receive a higher rank from any bishop; that no synod may be called a general one without his command; that no chapter and no canonical book is held authoritative without his authority; that his sentence may be retracted by no one, and that he alone may retract the sentences of all; that he is to be judged by no one; that no one may dare condemn the Apostolic See when it is appealed to; that the greater causes of every church ought to be referred to him; that the Roman Church has never erred and, as Scripture testifies, never will err in perpetuity; that the Roman Pontiff, if he has been canonically ordained, becomes undoubtedly holy through the merits of St. Peter, as Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, testifies, with many holy Fathers favouring him, as is contained in the decrees of blessed Pope Symmachus; that he may, by his command and permission, allow his subjects to make accusations; that without a synodal assembly he may depose and reconcile bishops; that he who does not agree with the Roman Church is not to be regarded as Catholic; that he can absolve subjects from their fidelity to wicked men. Clearly nothing remained except to add a few more, namely that the Pope is Christ, and therefore he is himself the Antichrist.

units.la: LXXXII. Illud quoque non praetereundum, fuisse Gregorium, sicut daemoniacarum artium studio infamem, ita daemoniorum etiam doctrinae, quae abstinere à cibis, quos Deus condidit ad participationem cum gratiarum actione fidelibus, jubet, & matrimonium contrahere
units.tr: LXXXII. It must not be passed over either that Gregory was, just as he was infamous for his devotion to demonic arts, so also a most fierce propagator of the doctrine of demons, which forbids abstaining from foods that God created to be received by the faithful with thanksgiving, and forbids marriage to be contracted

units.la: {*} here prohibet, propagatorem acerrimum. Liquet id ex duabus Synodis Romæ sexto Pontificatûs ejus anno habitis, in quarum altera editus est hic Canon: Quia dies Sabbathi apud sanctos Patres nostros in abstinentia celebris est habitus, nos eorundem authoritatem sequentes salubriter admonemus, ut quicunque se Christianæ religionis participem esse desiderat, ab esu carnium eadem die, nisi majore festivitate interveniente, vel infirmitate impediente, abstinceat. In altera verò damnavit scriptum sancti Udalrici ad Papam Nicolaum, de nuptiis Presbyterorum, & Paphnutii de eadem re capitulum. De eo sic Sigebertus Gemblacensis in historia A. mlxxiv. Gregorius Papa, celebrata Synodo, Simoniacos anathematizavit, & uxoratos sacerdotes à Divino officio removit, & laicis Missam eorum audire interdixit, novo exemplo, & (ut multis visum est) inconsiderato præjudicio, contra sanctorum Patrum sententiam &c. Ex qua re tam grave oritur scandalum, ut nullius hæresis tempore sancta Ecclesia graviori schismate discissa sit; his pro justitia, illis contra justitiam agentibus; continentiam paucis tenentibus, aliquibus eam modò quæstus ac jactantiæ causâ simulantibus; multis incontinentiam perjurio aut multipliciori adulterio cumulantibus, adhæc hac opportunitate laicis insurgentibus contra sanctos Ordines, & se ab omni Ecclesiastica subjectione excutientibus. Laici sacra mysteria temerant, & de his disputant, infantes baptizant, sordido humore aurium pro sacro oleo & chrismate utentes: in extremo vitæ viaticum Dominicum, & usitatum Ecclesiæ obsequium sepulturæ à Presbyteris conjugatis, parvipendunt, decimas Presbyteris deputatas igne cremant, & (ut in uno cætera perpendas) laici corpus Domini à Presbyteris conjugatis consecratum sæpe pedibus conculcaverunt, & sanguinem Domini voluntariè effuderunt; & multa alia contra jus & fas gesta sunt in Ecclesia. Et hac occasione multi Pseudomagistri exsurgentes in Ecclesia profanis novitatibus plebem ab Ecclesiastica disciplina avertunt. Lambertus Schafnaburgensis addit, adversus decretum hoc protinus vehementer infremuisse totam factionem Clericorum, hominem plane hæreticum & væfani dogmatis esse clamitantem, utpote qui oblitus Sermonis Domini, qui ait: Non omnes capiunt hunc sermonem: qui capere potest, capiat; & Apostoli: Qui se non continet, nubat. Melius est enim nubere, quam uri, violentâ exactione homines cogat vivere more Angelorum; & dum consuetum cursum naturæ negaret, fornicationi & immunditiæ fræna laxaret. Quas porro turbas ferale isthoc Gregorii decretum passim inter contendentes renitentésque excitaverit, scribere heic nihil attinet.
units.tr: {*} here prohibits. The evidence for this is two synods held at Rome in the sixth year of his pontificate, in the second of which this canon was issued: Because the Sabbath day has been observed among our holy Fathers as a day of abstinence, we, following their authority, wholesomely admonish that whoever desires to share in the Christian religion abstain from eating meat on that same day, unless a greater festival intervenes or infirmity prevents it. In the other, however, he condemned the writing of St. Ulrich to Pope Nicholas on the marriage of priests, and the chapter of Paphnutius on the same matter. Concerning this, Sigebert of Gembloux says thus in his history, under the year 1074: Pope Gregory, having held a synod, anathematized the Simoniacs, removed married priests from the divine office, and forbade laymen to hear their Mass, in a new example and, as it seemed to many, an inconsiderate prejudgment, against the opinion of the holy Fathers, etc. From this matter there arose so grave a scandal that the holy Church was never torn by a more serious schism at any time of any heresy: some acting for justice, others against justice; a few keeping continence, some only feigning it for gain and display; many piling incontinence upon perjury or manifold adultery; and besides, on this occasion laymen rose up against the holy orders and shook off all ecclesiastical subjection. Laymen profane the sacred mysteries and dispute about them; they baptize infants, using filthy moisture from the ears in place of holy oil and chrism; at the end of life they hold the Lord's viaticum and the customary service of the Church for burial of little account when administered by married priests; they burn with fire the tithes assigned to priests; and (to weigh the rest by one instance) laymen have often trampled underfoot the body of the Lord consecrated by married priests, and have wilfully poured out the blood of the Lord; and many other things contrary to law and right have been done in the Church. And on this occasion many false teachers rising up in the Church turn the people away from ecclesiastical discipline by profane novelties. Lambert of Hersfeld adds that the whole faction of the clergy immediately raged vehemently against this decree, crying out that the man was plainly a heretic and of a frenzied doctrine, since he had forgotten the word of the Lord, who says: Not all receive this saying; let him who can receive it receive it, and the Apostle: Let him who cannot contain himself marry; for it is better to marry than to burn; that he compelled men by violent exaction to live after the manner of angels, and while denying the customary course of nature, he loosened the reins to fornication and uncleanness. What troubles this deadly decree of Gregory stirred up everywhere among those who contended and resisted, it is not worth writing about here.

units.la: LXXXIII. Controversia gemina, quæ Hildebrando huic partim cum Henrico Imperatore, secularique adeò potestate, partim cum sacerdotibus conjugatis intercessit, ansam eidem præbuit fingendi duas novitias hæreses, earumque improperio imparentes dicto suo deprimendi. Henricianos enim Simoniacorum & hæreticorum Henricianorum: Sacerdotes verò conjugatos Nicolaitarum probrosis, Simoniacorum & Nicolaitarum pessimus ipse, titulis aspersit, exosòsque reddidit. Hæretici nempe Papæ jam dici meruerunt, non qui doctrinam verbo Dei repugnantem, & æternæ saluti perniciosam propugnarent pertinaciter, sed qui Papæ libidini suæ lenocinantis imperio audientes non essent.
units.tr: LXXXIII. The double controversy that Hildebrand had, partly with the Emperor Henry and secular power, and partly with married priests, gave him the occasion of inventing two new heresies, and of crushing those who disobeyed his word by reproach against them. For he branded the Henricians as Simoniacs and heretical Henricians, and the married priests with the disgraceful titles of Nicolaitans, being himself the worst of Simoniacs and Nicolaitans, and made them odious. Indeed, the name of heretics was now deserved for the Pope's sake not by those who stubbornly defended a doctrine opposed to the Word of God and destructive to eternal salvation, but by those who were not obedient to the rule of his lust, which acted as a pander.

units.la: LXXXIV. Mortuo Gregorio factione Pontificia annitente, Victor III. Beneventani Principis filius successit. Is Clementem III. Gregorio ab Imperatore Henrico surrogatum, anathematis vinculo constrictum deposuit, & post biennium moribundus Ottonem de Castellione, Cardinalem Ostiensem, successorem designavit, qui post mortem ejus electus Urbani II. (Turbanum vocant alii, ob excitatas turbas multifarias) nomen sumpsit. Quibus studiis Urbanus ille, qui Gregorii VII. causam egit acerrimè, cum Clemente III. Cæsareo Papa collisus fuerit, fusè Aventinus commemorat, cujus verbis continuatam tragoediam narrare juvabit. Sic ille lib. V. Annal. scribit:
units.tr: LXXXIV. After Gregory's death, with the Pontifical faction striving, Victor III, son of the Prince of Benevento, succeeded. He deposed Clement III, who had been substituted for Gregory by the Emperor Henry, and bound him with the chain of anathema; and after two years, dying, he designated as successor Otto of Châtillon, Cardinal of Ostia, who after his death was elected and took the name of Urban II (some call him Turbanus, because of the many tumults he stirred up). With these pursuits, Urban, who pleaded the cause of Gregory VII most fiercely, clashed with the imperial Pope Clement III. Aventinus relates this at length, and it will be helpful to narrate the continued tragedy in his words. Thus he writes in book V of his Annals:

units.la: Clemens III. urbe à Conrado pellitur, Vrbanus restituitur. Mox invicem diras inferiásque dicunt. Vrbanus acta Hildebrandi tueri: Clemens rescindere pergit. Imperator quoque summa ope contra Vrbanum nititur. Moveri rursus civitas Christiana, & dissensio civilis, quasi permissio terræ erumpere cœpit; scinditurque populus Christianus; pauci reperti, qui veram pietatem injustæ potentiæ anteponerent; partium studia, quæ extincta erant, glisciunt, &c. Dum alteri alteros quovis modo vincere volunt; Vrbanus criminando Imperatorem, plebem Christianam exagitat occultè largiendo, indulgendo, pollicitando magis incendit, ita ipse clarus, potens factus ex libidine suæ victoriæ utitur, plúsque sibi ac successoribus spinarum ac potentiæ, quàm pietatis atque amoris comparavit; sub titulo Christi pro sua magnitudine amplitudineque laboravit. Namque, ut paucis verum absolvam, post illa tempora, quicunque concionem divinam agitavere, honestis nominibus, quasi jura Ecclesiæ libertatémque Religionis defenderent, & quò Romani Episcopi authoritas maxima foret, bonum publicum simulantes pro sua quisque potentia certaverunt. Imperator quidem contra hæc summa ope connisus fuit: utraque pars miraculis se tutata est. Deinceps fictitia quædam miracula visionésque recenset.
units.tr: Clement III is driven from the city by Conrad; Urban is restored. Soon they pronounce curses and funeral rites upon each other. Urban undertakes to defend the acts of Hildebrand; Clement goes on to rescind them. The Emperor also strives with all his might against Urban. The Christian state and civil dissension, as if permitted by the land, began again to break out; and the Christian people is split; few were found who would prefer true piety to unjust power; the zeal of the factions, which had been extinguished, flares up, etc. While each wishes to overcome the other by any means, Urban, by accusing the Emperor, stirs up the Christian people, inflaming them more by secret largesse, indulgence and promises; thus he, made famous and powerful, uses the license of his victory and procured for himself and his successors more of thorns and power than of piety and love; under the title of Christ he laboured for his own greatness and extent. For, to speak the truth briefly, after those times, whoever stirred up a divine assembly, under honourable names, as if they were defending the rights of the Church and the liberty of religion, and so that the authority of the Roman bishop might be greatest, pretending to the public good, each struggled according to his own power. The Emperor indeed strove against these things with all his might: each side protected itself by miracles. Thereafter he recounts certain fictitious miracles and visions.

units.la: LXXXV. Inter τὰ νύεια seu supremæ potestatis civilis jura politici belli decernendi potestatem numerare solent. Hanc quoque ad se rapere Pontifices coeperunt. Urbanus quippe Bellum, quod Sacrum, eò quòd ad expugnationem terræ Sanctæ, & à personis Sacris, Episcopis, Monachis &c. suscipiendum esset, appellari placuit; Monachi cujusdam Petri Eremitæ, seu Franci, seu, ut alii scribunt, Hispani, Divinam visionem jactantis, suasu, in Concilio Claromontano (quod cum Synodo illa, quæ I. Reg. XXII. describitur, celebrata sub Josaphato & Achabo, de Ramoth Gilead ex manibus Syrorum recuperanda, da, scitè Bullingerus in Apoc. cap. 20. comparat, eò quòd in utroque fuerint spiritus seductor, Achabi, Josaphati, aliáque similia) decrevit. Sic A. MXCV. Ducibus Gothofredo Bullionensi, sive de Bullo, Lotharingiæ Principe, Eustathio & Balduino ejus fratribus, Hugone Magno, fratre Regis Francorum, Anicien-sis in Auvernia Episcopo, aliisque cum exercitu ex millies sexcenties millenis militibus cruce ex lana rubra facta signatis omnibus, (unde militiæ cruciatæ nomen, non quòd crucem Christi prædicare, sed quòd infideles crucifigere destinâssent) conflato, in terram sanctam adversus Saracenos properatum, & post fœlicia satis prœlia A. MXCIX. ipsa urbs Hierosolyma obsessa & occupata, sed A. MCCXLIV. imperante Friderico Barbarossa iterum amissa est, rebus Christianorum Orientalium in deterius longè inde vergentibus.
units.tr: LXXXV. Among the rights of supreme civil power, writers usually count the power to decide on a war of policy. The Pontiffs too began to seize this for themselves. Urban decreed that the war should be called holy, because it was to be undertaken to conquer the Holy Land and by sacred persons, bishops, monks and so on. At the Council of Clermont, on the urging of a monk named Peter the Hermit, a Frenchman or, as others write, a Spaniard, who boasted of a divine vision, he decreed this war. The council may fittingly be compared by Bullinger in Apoc. cap. 20. with that synod described in 1 Kings 22, held under Jehoshaphat and Ahab to recover Ramoth Gilead from the hands of the Syrians, since in both there were a lying spirit, Ahab, Jehoshaphat, and other similar things. So in the year 1095, under the leadership of Godfrey of Bouillon (or Godfrey de Bullo), prince of Lorraine, with his brothers Eustace and Baldwin, Hugh the Great, brother of the King of the Franks, the bishop of Le Puy in Auvergne, and others, an army was gathered of six hundred million soldiers, all marked with a cross made of red wool. This is why the soldiers were called crusaders: not because they meant to preach the cross of Christ, but because they had determined to crucify the infidels. They hastened into the Holy Land against the Saracens, and after fairly successful battles, in 1099 the city of Jerusalem itself was besieged and taken. But in 1244, under the emperor Frederick Barbarossa, it was lost again, and from then on the condition of the Eastern Christians went steadily downhill.

units.la: LXXXVI. Belli hujus sacri θεομαχία à causis ejusdem suasoriis distinguere haud ἄξιον fuerit. πρόφασις fuere damna, contumeliæ, supplicia gravissima, quæ Christiani sepulchrum Domini visitantes quotidie à Saracenis patiebantur, uti Sigonius ad A. MLXXIV. loquitur: addo, injuriæ etiam & contumeliæ, quas fideles Hierosolymis commorantes ab infidelibus perpetiebantur, quas fusè Wilhelmus Tyrius, Regni Hierosolymitani Concellarius, belli sacri scriptor, Historiæ belli sacri lib. 1. cap. 4. &c. Robertus Monachus de Christ. Principum bello contra Saracenos suscepto lib. 1. aliique ediderunt. Urbani Papæ exhortatio ad populum in Concilio Claromontano facta, & ab eodem Tyrio lib. 1. cap. 15. recitata prætextus eosdem propalat. Inter alia sic ille: Hæc salutis nostræ cunabula, Domini patriam, religionis matrem, populus absque Deo, ancillæ filius Ægyptiæ possidet violenter: & captivitatis liberæ filiis extremas imponit conditiones, quibus versa vice merito servire tenebatur. Sed quid scriptum est? Ejice ancillam & filium ejus. Saracenorum enim gens impia & immundarum secta- Ejus belli praetextus sectatrix traditionum, loca sancta in quibus steterunt pedes Domini, jam à multis retrò temporibus violenta premit tyrannide, subactis fidelibus, & in servitutem damnatis. Ingressi sunt canes in sancta, profanatum est sanctuarium, humiliatus est cultor Dei populus, angarias patitur indignas: genus electum servit in luto & latere: regale Sacerdotium, Principes Provinciarum, factum est sub tributo, civitas Dei. Cujus non liquefiat anima? Cujus non labescant præcordia, iis ad animum recurrentibus? Quis hæc siccis oculis audire potest, fratres charissimi? Hæc certè ut vera fuerint (de quo nulli ambigimus) justam tamen bello inferendo causam præbuerunt minimè. Neque enim vel terra sancta Christiani populi peculium & proprietas ἀναφαίρετον fuit: vel injuriæ illatæ Christianis sive indigenis, siveadvenis tanti fuerunt, ut propterea possessione terræ illius exui infideles debuerint. Inprimis cum post Christi ascensionem in Cœlum Palæstina terra aliis locis sanctior amplius non fuerit, & affectatio ejus superstitionem potius, quàm veram religionem aluerit. Considerandum fuit illud, quod à Pindaro dictum est; ἐα πόλεμον, ἐα μάχαι χωρὶς Θεῦ Mitte bellum, mitte pugnam sine Deo. Equidem ex Verbo Dei satis constat, sic Deum irasci terræ sanctæ, ut benedictionem in maledictionem converterit, & templum urbemque Hierosolymam ita everti funditus voluerit, ut reparari nunquam possit. Et quid est Ecclesia per omnes gentes dispersa, si vetus Templum, unde nova Ecclesia prodiit, requiris?
units.tr: LXXXVI. It would not be worthwhile to separate the impiety of this holy war from the causes that urged it. The pretext was the losses, insults and most severe punishments which Christians suffered daily from the Saracens when they visited the Lord's sepulchre, as Sigonius says under the year 1074. I add the injuries and insults which the faithful endured from the infidels while living in Jerusalem, which Wilhelm of Tyre, chancellor of the kingdom of Jerusalem and writer of the holy war, sets out at length in Historiae belli sacri lib. 1 cap. 4, and which Robert the Monk published in de Christianorum Principum bello contra Saracenos suscepto lib. 1, and others. The exhortation of Pope Urban to the people, delivered at the Council of Clermont and recited by the same Tyre in lib. 1 cap. 15, reveals the same pretexts. Among other things he says: "This cradle of our salvation, the homeland of the Lord, the mother of religion, is violently held by a people without God, the son of the Egyptian slave woman; and it imposes on the sons of free captivity the most extreme conditions, to which they were rightly bound to be slaves in turn. But what is written? Cast out the bondwoman and her son. For the impious race of the Saracens, the follower of traditions and of unclean sects, has long been oppressing with tyranny the holy places in which the feet of the Lord stood, subduing the faithful and condemning them to slavery. Dogs have entered the holy places, the sanctuary has been profaned, the people who worship God has been humbled, and suffers unworthy forced labour. The chosen race serves in mud and brick; the royal priesthood and the princes of the provinces have been put under tribute; the city of God... Whose soul does not melt? Whose heart does not grow faint when these things come to mind? Who can hear this with dry eyes, dearest brothers?" Even if these things were true (and no one doubts it), they provided hardly any just cause for making war. For the Holy Land was not the peculiar property and inalienable possession of the Christian people; nor were the injuries done to Christians, whether natives or foreigners, so great that the infidels ought for that reason to be stripped of possession of that land. This is especially so since, after Christ's ascension into heaven, the land of Palestine was no holier than other places, and the desire for it nourished superstition rather than true religion. That saying of Pindar should have been considered: Mitte bellum, mitte pugnam sine Deo ["Let go of war, let go of fighting without God" ἐα πόλεμον, ἐα μάχαι χωρὶς Θεῦ]. Indeed, it is clear enough from the Word of God that God was so angry with the Holy Land that he turned blessing into cursing, and willed the temple and the city of Jerusalem to be so utterly overthrown that they could never be rebuilt. And what is the Church, scattered through all nations, if you are looking for the old Temple from which the new Church came forth?

units.la: LXXXVII. Diversæ longè fuerunt belli illius suasoriæ causæ, avaritia Pontificum, dominandi libido, perfidia & oppressio Christianorum Principum. Ablegatis in Orientem per speciem pietatis Principibus proclive Papæ fuit vacua in aula dominari; cùm ambitioni avaritiæque Pontificum totus se Occidens aperiret, & ad frænandam domandámque eam exhaustis ejusmodi expeditionibus Principum subjectorumque opibus, impares posthac essent. Immensam etiam pecuniarum vim cruciata haec militia Pontificibus conciliavit. Certè Innocentius Papa, ita Matthæus Paris, Monachus Albanensis, Anglus, Histor. Major. pag. 200. loquitur, ad expeditionem terræ sanctæ, ut dixit, ad occultandam suam avaritiam, infinitam pecuniam ab ordine Cisterciensi extorquere proposuit. Addit, à B. Virgine correptum ab exactione cessasse, timore percussum. Pag. 707. narrat idem, cruce signatos voti poenitentes non modica pecuniæ summa votum redimere coactos fuisse. Non omnibus licebat ire in expeditionem. Neque tamen manentes domi carere debuerunt hac persuasione suæ salutis. Ut igitur indulgentiarum & illi participes fierent, pecuniam erogabant, exigentibus insatiabiliter Ecclesiasticis. Cognoscere id licet ex eodem Matthæo Paris; cujus inter alia pag. 388. Hæc verba sunt: Hæc (à Gregorio Papa de negotio crucis perscripta) cùm per Christianorum climata, præcipuè per Angliam Christi fidelibus innotescerent, & Prædicatio per Prælatos, maximè per fratres Prædicatores, & Minores fieret, quibus data fuit potestas cruce signandi, & votum data pecunia (confer pag. 346.) relaxandi, sese multi, quorum non erat numerus, cruce signaverunt. Sed citò in tantam nobilitatem, ne dicam, arrogantiam elevabantur Prædicatores, Minoresque, qui spontaneam paupertatem cum humilitate elegerunt, ut recipi curarent in cœnobiis & civitatibus in processione solenni, in vexillis, cereis accensis, & in dispositione vestimenti festivis indutorum, & concessum est eis veniam multorum dierum suis conferre auditoribus, signatosque hodie, cras data pecunia à crucis voto absolverunt. Parvòque tempore succedente, facta est tanta commutatio, tam multiformis pecuniæ exactio, nec sciri poterat, in quam abyssum tanta pecunia, quæ per Papales Procuratores colligebatur, est demersa, quòd fidelium circa negotium crucis tepuit, imò potius charitas refrixit generalis. Vnde negotium terræ sanctæ nunquam felix super hoc suscepit incrementum. Sed & pag. 864. exemplum prodit summæ Pontificis perfidiæ, qui crucem prædicari voluit, non ut periclitantes Christianos in Oriente juvaret, sed ut Siciliam & Apuliam invadere posset. Eodem cruce signatorum exercitu etiam contra Albigenses, teste eodem Paris pag. 336. nec non Imperatorem ipsum Fridericum Barbarossam, Fridericum II. ejusque filium Conradum, Imperatores, aliosque etiam Christianos Principes invisos sibi, Pontifices usi sunt.
units.tr: LXXXVII. The causes that urged that war were quite different: the greed of the Pontiffs, the lust to dominate, and the treachery and oppression of Christian princes. With the princes sent off to the East under the pretext of piety, it was easy for the Pope to rule in an emptied court, while the whole West lay open to the ambition and avarice of the Pontiffs; and, with the resources of princes and subjects exhausted by such expeditions, they were afterwards unable to restrain and subdue that ambition. This crusading army also brought the Pontiffs an immense sum of money. Certainly Pope Innocent, as Matthew Paris, an English monk of St Albans, speaks in Histor. Major. p. 200: "For the expedition to the Holy Land, as he said, but to conceal his own avarice, he proposed to extort an infinite amount of money from the Cistercian order." He adds that he was struck with fear by the Blessed Virgin and ceased from the exaction. On p. 707 the same author relates that those marked with the cross, penitents under a vow, were forced to buy off their vow for no small sum of money. Not everyone was allowed to go on the expedition. Yet those who stayed at home ought not to be deprived of this assurance of their salvation. So, in order to share in the indulgences too, they paid out money, as the clergy demanded it insatiably. This can be known from the same Matthew Paris, of whose words on p. 388 are these: "When these things (written by Pope Gregory about the business of the cross) became known to the faithful of Christ throughout the climes of Christendom, especially in England, and preaching was done by the prelates, especially by the Preaching and Minor friars, to whom the power was given of signing with the cross and of releasing the vow for money given (compare p. 346), many, who could not be counted, signed themselves with the cross. But soon the preachers and the Minorites, who had chosen voluntary poverty with humility, were lifted up into such great nobility, not to say arrogance, that they took care to be received in monasteries and cities in solemn procession, with banners, lit candles, and garments dressed up for festivity; and it was granted to them to confer the pardon of many days on their hearers; and those signed today and tomorrow they absolved from the vow of the cross for money paid." After a short time there came such a change and such a many-shaped exaction of money that no one could tell into what abyss all that money was sunk which was collected by the papal procurators; and the zeal of the faithful for the business of the cross grew lukewarm, or rather general charity cooled. "So the business of the Holy Land never received an increase that was happy in this respect." But on p. 864 he also reports an example of the Pope's treachery, who wanted the cross preached not to help Christians in danger in the East, but so that he could invade Sicily and Apulia. By the same army of crusaders, as the same Paris testifies on p. 336, the Pontiffs also used the forces against the Albigenses, and against the emperors Frederick Barbarossa, Frederick II and his son Conrad, and other Christian princes who were hateful to them.

units.la: LXXXVIII. In Concilio Claromontano, quo bellum illud minime sacrum decretum fuit, conditi, eodem Urbano annitente, sunt varii Canones, quibus Pontificia potestas & superstitio amplificata non parum fuit. Inter alia capitula hæc etiam à Paris pag. 20. commemorantur: Quod Ecclesia Catholica (Romana) sit in fide casta, & ab omni seculari servitute libera; ut Episcopi vel Abbates, vel aliquis de Clero aliquam Ecclesiasticam dignitatem de manu Principum, vel quorumlibet laicorum non recipiat: Quod nullus cujuslibet sacri ordinis carnali commercio utatur: Quod nemo laicorum a capite jejunii, nemo Clericorum a quinquagesima usque in Pascha, carnes comedat: Quod omni tempore primum jejunium quatuor temporum, prima hebdomada quadragesimæ fiat. Quod qui apprehenderit Episcopum, omnino exlex fiat: Quod qui sacri ordinis viros, vel eorum famulos apprehenderit, anathema sit: Quod una quaque Ecclesia decimas suas habeat, nec ad aliam transferantur: Quod laicus decimas non emat, nec vendat: aliáque id genus plura.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. At the Council of Clermont, at which that war was decreed, which was far from holy, various canons were drawn up, with Urban's support, by which Papal power and superstition were not a little increased. Among other chapters, Paris (p. 20) also records these: that the Catholic (Roman) Church should be chaste in faith and free from all secular servitude; that bishops, abbots or any of the clergy should not receive any ecclesiastical dignity from the hand of princes or any laymen; that no one in any holy order should have carnal intercourse; that no layman should eat meat from the beginning of Lent, and no cleric from Quinquagesima until Easter; that the first fast of the four seasons should always be kept in the first week of Lent; that whoever lays hands on a bishop should be utterly outlawed; that whoever lays hands on men of holy orders or their servants should be anathema; that each church should have its own tithes, and they should not be transferred to another; that a layman should not buy or sell tithes; and many other things of this kind.

units.la: LXXXIX. Seculo duodecimo ad majorem etiam gradum corruptionis Ecclesia Romana processit. Vulgarem famam fuisse, Antichristum eo tempore revelatum iri, Baronius ad A. C. MCVI. non diffitetur. Bernhardus certè, qui in ea tempora incidit, Epist. 56. ad Gaufridum eam in rem sic scribit. Cum ante hos paucos dies Norberti faciem videre, & de cælesti fistula, ore videlicet ipsius plurima haurire meruerim, rim, de Antichristo cum inquirerem, quid sentiret, durante adhuc ea, quæ nunc est generatione, revelandum illum certissimè sa scire, protestatus est. At cum eandem certitudinem unde haberet, sciscitanti mihi exponere vellet, audito quod respondit, non me illud pro certo credere debere putavi. Ad summam tamen hoc asseruit, non visurum se mortem, nisi prius videat generalem in Ecclesia persecutionem. De Paschali etiam Papa, qui initio hujus seculi Romanam Ecclesiam moderatus est, commemorat idem, quòd dum in itinere positus Florentiam pervenisset, de Antichristi adventu proximè futuro, fama fuerit sparsa. In ejusdem vita scribit Platina: Florentinum Episcopum affirmare solitum, Antichristum natum esse; sed ab ipso Papa silentium ei impositum esse.
units.tr: LXXXIX. In the twelfth century the Roman Church advanced to an even greater degree of corruption. Baronius, at the year of Christ 1106, does not deny that a popular rumour then circulated that Antichrist would be revealed at that time. Bernard, who lived in those days, certainly writes on this matter in Epistle 56 to Godfrey: A few days ago I was privileged to see the face of Norbert and to drink in very much from the heavenly pipe, that is, from his very mouth. When I asked him what he thought about Antichrist, he declared with certainty that Antichrist would be revealed while this present generation was still living. But when I asked him where he had this certainty and he wanted to explain it, I thought, on hearing his answer, that I ought not to believe that for certain. Nevertheless, he asserted this in sum: that he would not see death before he saw a general persecution in the Church. The same Bernard also records of Paschal, the Pope who governed the Roman Church at the beginning of this century, that when he was travelling and had reached Florence, a report was spread about the imminent coming of Antichrist. In the life of the same Paschal, Platina writes: It is said that the Bishop of Florence used to affirm that Antichrist had been born, but that the Pope himself imposed silence on him.

units.la: XC. Neque certè desunt plura scriptorum, qui eo ipso seculo scripserunt, testimonia, ex quibus, quæ circa id temporis facies Ecclesiæ Romanæ fuerit liquidò cognoscitur. De Romanis igitur, uti Guilhelmus Malmesburiensis de gestis Reg. Angl. lib. 4. loquitur, olim rerum Dominis, gentéque togata, qui nunc dicuntur hominum inertissimi, auro trutinantes justitiam, pretio venditantes communem regulam; carmen edidit Hildebertus Cenomanensis Episcopus, atque hoc disticho (quod in Lilii Giraldi quinto de Poëtis Dialogo Hispani Censores ferre non potuerunt) conclusit: Urbs felix, si vel Dominis urbs illa careret, Vel Dominis esset turpe, carere fide.
units.tr: XC. Indeed there is no lack of writers who, in that very century, left testimonies from which the state of the Roman Church at that time is clearly known. Concerning the Romans, then, William of Malmesbury, in On the Deeds of the Kings of England, book 4, speaks of them as once the masters of the world and a people in togas, who now are said to be the most spiritless of men, weighing justice in gold and selling the common rule for a price. Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, published a poem on this and concluded it with this couplet (which the Spanish censors could not bear to let stand in Lilius Giraldus's fifth dialogue on the poets): Happy would that city be, if it were either without masters or if it were a disgrace to its masters to lack faith.

units.la: eos scilicet Dominos innuens, quos simili disticho perstrinxit alius: Servierant tibi, Roma, diu Domini Dominorum; Servorum Servi nunc tibi sunt Domini.
units.tr: He clearly means those masters, whom another poet lashed in a similar couplet: Rome, the Lords of lords served you for a long time; now the servants of servants are your lords.

units.la: De eadem sic Bernhardus Morlinensis, ex Cluniacensi Ordine Monachus lib. 3. de contemptu mundi canit: Aurea tempora, castáque pectora præterierunt, Tempora pessima, scilicet ultima jam subierunt. Stant modo stantia lucra, superbia, pax sine pace, Fraus, Venus, otia, furtáque conscia noctis opacæ, Schismata, præliá, vis, homicidia, traditiones, Ira, protervia, livor, inertia, seditiones. Stat simulatio, corruit actio religionis Heu! sua propria deputat omnia Rex Babylonis.
units.tr: Of the same city Bernard of Morlaix, a monk of the Cluniac Order, sings thus in book 3 On the Contempt of the World: The golden times and chaste hearts have passed away; the worst times, that is the last, have now come. Now standing are gains, pride, peace without peace, fraud, lust, idleness, and thefts conscious of the dark night; schisms, battles, violence, murders, traditions, anger, obstinacy, envy, sloth, and seditions. Pretence stands; the action of religion falls. Alas! The King of Babylon reckons everything as his own.

units.la: Neque aliter Honorius Augustodunensis Ecclesiæ Presbyter Dial. de Prædest. & lib. Arb. sui temporis Babyloniam depingit: In tuere, inquit, Principes & Judices: Ecce posita in eis est Bestiæ sedes. Omni tempore ad malum sunt intenti, semper negotiis iniquitatis inexplebiliter occupati, flagitia non solum faciunt, sed & alios facere instruunt: Sancta vendunt, scelera emunt: totis viribus laborant, ne soli ad tartara veniant. Verte te ad Clerum, & videbis in eis Bestiæ tentorium. Dei servitium negligunt, terrenis lucris inserviunt; sacerdotium per immunditiam polluunt, populum per simulationem seducunt, Deum per mala opera abnegant, omnes scripturas ad salutem pertinentes abdicant, omnibus modis se laqueos & ruinam populo substernunt, quem cœlum ipsi cœci ad interitum præeunt. Contempcare & Monachorum conciliabula, & videbis in eis Bestiæ tabernacula. Per fictam professionem Deum irridentes, iram ejus provocant, normam regularum moribus & vita calcant, per habitum seculum fallunt, multos deceptos ipsi decepti decipiunt. Secularibus negotiis implicati sunt, in Dei servitio desides existunt, plerique illorum gulæ illecebris dediti sunt, quidam immunditiæ sordibus computrescunt. Aspice etiam habitacula Monialium, & cernes in eis Bestiæ præparatum thalamum. &c. Verte te ad plebem reliquam, & videbis in ea Bestiæ effigiem &c. Vulgus quoque indoctum Bestiæ habet idolum &c. Taceo Arnoldum de Brixia, à quo Arnoldistis nomen, qui quòd tyrannidem, luxum, superbiam, corruptionem Cleri & Pontificis palam argueret, A. MCLV. Romæ ultricibus flammis παῤῥησίαν suam expiavit: ipso etiam Platina ejus innocentiæ testimonium perhibente, & pietatem extollente. Quem etiam Tigurinis, apud quos aliquandiu prædicavit, sanioris doctrinæ gustum præbuisse, Guntherus Ligurinus, facto isthoc versu: Servat adhuc uvæ gustum gens ista paterna; prodidit.
units.tr: Honorius of Autun, a presbyter of the Church, in his Dialogue on Predestination and Free Will, portrays the Babylon of his own time in much the same way: Look, he says, at the princes and judges: behold the seat of the Beast is set among them. At all times they are intent on evil, always busy without end in the business of iniquity; they not only commit crimes but also teach others to commit them. They sell holy things and buy wickedness; they labour with all their strength lest they alone should go down to hell. Turn to the clergy, and you will see in them the tent of the Beast. They neglect the service of God and serve earthly gains; they pollute the priesthood with uncleanness, seduce the people by pretence, deny God by evil works, reject all the Scriptures that pertain to salvation, and in every way lay snares and ruin for the people, whom they themselves, being blind, lead to destruction. Consider also the assemblies of the monks, and you will see in them the tabernacles of the Beast. Mocking God by a feigned profession, they provoke his anger, they trample the rule of the monastic life under their habits, they deceive the world by their dress, and, deceived themselves, they deceive many. They are entangled in worldly business, they are idle in the service of God, most of them are given over to the allurements of the belly, and some rot in the filth of uncleanness. Look also at the dwellings of the nuns, and you will see in them the prepared bedchamber of the Beast, etc. Turn to the rest of the common people, and you will see in them the image of the Beast, etc. The uneducated crowd too has the idol of the Beast, etc. I pass over Arnold of Brescia, from whom the Arnoldists take their name. Because he openly denounced the tyranny, luxury, pride and corruption of the clergy and of the Pope, he atoned for his frankness [παῤῥησίαν] with avenging flames at Rome in the year 1155. Platina himself bears witness to his innocence and extols his piety. Günther of Liguria also records that he gave the Zurich people, among whom he preached for some time, a taste of sounder doctrine, in the line: That people still keeps the taste of its ancestral grape.

units.la: XCI. Incidit in seculum isthoc infelix Bernhardus Claræuallensis Abbas, nobili familia Burgundiæ satus. Addictus is Pontifici licet, calamitate seculi illius optimis quibusque fascinum quodammodo inducente, subinde tamen Hierarchiam Romanam graphicè depingit. Libro ad Eugenium Papam & ejus satellites Episcopos & spirituales Antichristi ministros diserte nominat, & Apostolica authoritate ambitiosos, avaros, Simoniacos, concubinarios, incestuosos, & quæque ejusmodi monstra honores Ecclesiasticos obtinere: Denique Dæmonum magis quàm ovium pascua Romæ esse queritur. Et serm. 33. super Cantica querimoniam isthanc gravissimam inspergit: Væ generationi huic à fermento Pharisæorum, quod est hypocrisis, si tamen hypocrisis dici debet, quæ jam latere præ abundantia non valet, & præ impudentia non quærit. Serpit hodiè putida tabes per omne corpus Ecclesiæ & quo latius eò desperatius, eóque periculosius, quò intestinius. Nam si insurgeret apertus hæreticus, mitteretur foras & exaresceret; si violentus inimicus, abscónderet se quis forsitan ab eo, nunc verò quem ejiciet, aut à quo abscondet se? Omnes amici, & omnes inimici: Omnes necessarii, & omnes adversarii: omnes domestici, & nulli pacifici: omnes proximi, & omnes quæ sua sunt, quærunt. Ministri Christi sunt, & serviunt Antichristo. Honorati incedunt de bonis Domini, qui Domino honorem non deferunt. Inde is quem quotidie vides, meretricius nitor, histrionicus habitus, Regius apparatus; inde aurum in frenis, in sellis & calcaribus. Et plus calcaria, quàm altaria fulgent, &c. Intestina & insanabilis est plaga Ecclesiæ, & ideo in pace amaritudo ejus amarissima. Et Serm. 6 in Psal. 90. superest, inquit, ut reveletur homo peccati, filius perditionis, dæmonium non modò dturnum, sed & meridianum: quod non solùm transfiguratur in Angelum lucis, sed extollitur supra omne, quod dicitur Deus: Nimirum insidiatur crudelis, calcaneo matris Ecclesiæ, à qua dolet caput suum esse contritum, &c. Creditur idem Bernhardus author Sermonis in Rhemensi Concilio coram Innocentio II. & ejus Clero A. MCXXXI. habiti, in quo sic παρρησιαζόμενον Episcopos compellat: Fratres, aliam Synodum pronuntio vobis, ubi Dominus Deus sedebit in judiciis, & ibi omnes nos oportet repræsentari, & ibi Deus juste judicabit orbem terrarum. Hic includitur injustitia in marsupio: sed juste judicabit Deus in illo judicio, & ibi omnes, nos oportet repræsentari, sive sit Papa sive Cardinalis, sive Archiepiscopus, sive Episcopus, sive divesive pauper, sive doctus, sive indoctus, ut referat unusquisque rationem de his quæ gessit in corpore, sive bonum, sive malum. Et si reddenda est ratio de his, quæ quisque gessit in corpore suo, heu quid fiet de his, quæ quisque gessit in corpore Christi, quod est Ecclesia? Ecclesia Dei vobis commissa est, & dicimini Pastores, cum sitis raptores. Et paucos habemus, heu, Pastores, multos autem excommunicatores. Et utinam vobis sufficeret lac, sititis enim sanguinem. Idem Serm. 1. in conversionem S. Pauli hujusmodi ad Deum querelam ingeminat: Amici tui, Deus & proximi, ad versus te appropinquaverunt & fleverunt, Conjurasse videtur contra Te universitas populi Christiani à minimo usque ad maximum: à planta pedis usque ad verticem non est sanitas ulla. Egressa est iniquitas à senioribus judicibus, vicariis tuis, qui videntur regere populum tuum. Non est jam dicere: Sicut populus, sic sacerdos: quia nec sic populus ut sacerdos. Heu, heu, Domine Deus, quia ipsi sunt in persecutione tua primi, qui videntur in Ecclesia tua primatum diligere, gerere principatum. Arcem Sion occupaverunt, apprehenderunt munitiones, & universam deinceps liberè & potestativè tradunt incendio civitatem.
units.tr: XCI. Into this century came the unfortunate Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, born of a noble family of Burgundy. Although he was devoted to the Pontiff, the calamity of that age bewitched, as it were, even the best men, yet from time to time he depicts the Roman hierarchy vividly. In a book addressed to Pope Eugenius and his satellites, he names the bishops and spiritual ministers of Antichrist outright, and complains that the ambitious, greedy, simoniacal, concubinous and incestuous men, and all such monsters, hold ecclesiastical honours by apostolic authority. Finally, he laments that at Rome there are pastures for demons rather than for sheep. And in Sermon 33 on the Song of Songs he scatters this most grave complaint: Woe to this generation, from the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, if indeed it ought to be called hypocrisy, which by reason of its abundance can no longer lie hidden and by reason of its impudence does not seek to. Today a foul rot creeps through the whole body of the Church, and the wider it spreads the more hopeless and the more dangerous it becomes, the more inward it is. For if an open heretic rose up, he would be sent out and wither; if a violent enemy, one might perhaps hide from him; but now whom will one cast out, or from whom will one hide? All are friends, and all are enemies; all are kinsmen, and none are peaceable; all are neighbours, and all seek their own things. They are ministers of Christ, and they serve Antichrist. They go about honoured with the goods of the Lord, who do not render honour to the Lord. Hence come that meretricious finery, that theatrical dress, that royal display, which you see every day; hence gold on the bridles, on the saddles and on the spurs. And the spurs shine more than the altars, etc. The wound of the Church is internal and incurable, and therefore in peace its bitterness is most bitter. And in Sermon 6 on Psalm 90 he says: It remains that the man of sin, the son of perdition, be revealed, a demon not only of night but also of noonday, who not only transforms himself into an angel of light but is exalted above everything that is called God. Surely the cruel one lies in wait at the heel of mother Church, by whom he grieves that his head has been crushed, etc. The same Bernard is believed to be the author of a sermon delivered at the Council of Reims before Innocent II and his clergy in 1131, in which he addresses the bishops thus, speaking frankly [παρρησιαζόμενον]: Brethren, I announce to you another Synod, where the Lord God will sit in judgment, and where all of us must be presented, and where God will justly judge the world. Here injustice is hidden in the purse; but God will judge justly in that judgment, and there all of us must be presented, whether he be Pope or Cardinal, Archbishop or Bishop, rich or poor, learned or unlearned, so that each may give account of what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. And if an account must be rendered of what each has done in his own body, alas, what will happen to what each has done in the body of Christ, which is the Church? The Church of God has been committed to you, and you are called shepherds, though you are plunderers. We have few shepherds, alas, and many excommunicators. Would that milk were enough for you, for you thirst after blood. The same Bernard, in Sermon 1 on the Conversion of St Paul, repeats such a complaint to God: Your friends, O God, and your neighbours have drawn near against you and wept. The whole body of the Christian people, from the least to the greatest, seems to have conspired against you; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness. Iniquity has gone out from the elder judges, your vicars, who seem to rule your people. It can no longer be said: As the people, so the priest; for the people are not so bad as the priest. Alas, alas, Lord God, for they are first in your persecution, who seem to love the first place in your Church and to hold its leadership. They have occupied the citadel of Sion, they have seized the fortifications, and they hand over the whole city at once, freely and with full power, to the fire.

units.la: XCII. De corruptione hujus seculi vocem populi ad Hadrianum IV. Pontificem Johannes Sarisburiensis, quem
units.tr: XCII. Concerning the corruption of this age, the voice of the people addressed to Hadrian IV, the Pope: John of Salisbury, whom

units.la: Joh. Sarisburiensis. nuperus Cardinalis Bona in Notitia Scriptorum, ceu virum gravem, etiam cum de nugis scribit, commendat; Policrat. seu de Nugis Curialium lib VI. 24. perscripsit: Scisncitanti enim Hadriano, quid de se & Ecclesia Romana sentirent homines, respondet in haec verba: Romana Ecclesia, quae mater omnium Ecclesiarum est, se non tam matrem exhibet aliis, quam novercam. Sedent in ea scribae & Pharisaei, ponentes onera importabilia in humeris hominum, quae digito non contingunt. Dominantur in Clero, nec forma fiunt gregi, qui recto calle pergit ad vitam: pretiosam supellectilem congerunt: auro & argento onerant mensas, siti etiam ab avaritia nimis parci. Nam pauper aut nullus, aut rarus admittitur, quem interdum non tam Christus, quam vana gloria introducit. Concutiunt Ecclesias; lites excitant, collidunt Clerum & populum, laboribus & miseriis afflictorum nequaquam compatiuntur, Ecclesiarum latantur spoliis, & quaestum omnem reputant pietatem. Justitiam non tam veritati, quam pretio reddunt. Omnia namque cum pretio hodie, sed nec cras aliquid sine pretio obtinebis. Nocent saepius, & in eo daemones imitantur, quod tunc prodesse putantur, cum nocere desistunt, exceptis paucis, qui nomen & officium pastoris implent. Sed & ipse Romanus Pontifex omnibus gravis, & fere intolerabilis est, &c.
units.tr: John of Salisbury. The late Cardinal Bona, in his Notitia Scriptorum, commends him as a grave man, even when he writes about trifles. In his Policraticus, or On the Trifles of Courtiers, book VI, chapter 24, he wrote at length. When Hadrian asked what people thought of him and of the Roman Church, he replied in these words: The Roman Church, which is the mother of all churches, shows itself to others not so much as a mother as a stepmother. Scribes and Pharisees sit in it, laying on men's shoulders burdens too heavy to bear, which they will not touch with a finger. They lord it over the clergy and are no pattern to the flock, which walks the straight path to life. They pile up costly furnishings, load their tables with gold and silver, and are too sparing when it comes to thirst for gain. For a poor man is admitted rarely or not at all, and when one is admitted it is often less Christ who brings him in than empty vainglory. They shake the churches, stir up quarrels, and set clergy and people against one another. They have no pity for the labours and miseries of the afflicted, they rejoice in the spoils of the churches, and they count every profit as piety. They render justice not so much for the sake of truth as for a price. For everything today has its price, and you will obtain nothing tomorrow without a price. They do harm more often, and in this they imitate demons: they are thought to be helpful only when they stop doing harm, except for the few who fill the name and office of pastor. But the Roman Pontiff himself is a burden to all and nearly intolerable, etc.

units.la: XCIII. Aperto vero ore Episcopi, Canonici & Cle- rus universus Dioecesis Leodiensis Romanam Ecclesiam Babylonem eodem jam tempore insigniunt.
units.tr: XCIII. The bishops, canons and whole clergy of the diocese of Liège, speaking out openly at the same time, also brand the Roman Church as Babylon.

units.la: Extat enim in secundo Volumine Conciliorum, eorum ad Paschalem II. ejusmodi responsio: Quae major olim fuit confusio in Babylonia, quam hodie est in Ecclesia? In Babylonia confusio fuit linguae gentium; in Ecclesia dividuntur linguae & mentes credentium. Ait Petrus in Epistola sua: Salutat vos Ecclesia quae est in Babylone collecta. Hactenus interpretabar; ideo voluisse Petrum per Babylonem signare Romam, quia tum temporis Roma confusa fuit idololatria & omni spurcitia. At nunc dolor meus mihi interpretatur, quod Petrus Prophetico spiritu dicens Ecclesiam in Babylone collectam, lectam, prævidit confusionem dissensionis, qua hodie scinditur Ecclesia &c. Qui sint turbines ab Africo, discimus patiendo magis, quam legendo, de terra horribili, à Romana scilicet Ecclesia, visio dura nuntiata est mihi; inde turbo ut tempestas venit ab Africo. &c.Sed & Petrus Blesensis in Epistola ad Officialem apertè Romam Babylonem vocat, monétque Officialem, ut ex ea discedat.
units.tr: In the second volume of the Councils there is a reply of theirs to Paschal II of this kind: What greater confusion was there once in Babylon than there is today in the Church? In Babylon there was the confusion of the tongues of the nations; in the Church the tongues and minds of believers are divided. Peter says in his epistle: The church that is gathered in Babylon greets you. Hitherto I used to interpret this as meaning that Peter wished Rome to be signified by Babylon, because at that time Rome was filled with idolatry and every kind of filth. But now my grief explains it to me: Peter, speaking by the prophetic Spirit of the Church gathered in Babylon, foresaw the confusion of the division by which the Church is now torn apart, etc. What the whirlwinds from the south-west are, we learn more by suffering than by reading. A harsh vision has been announced to me from a dreadful land, namely from the Roman Church; from there the storm comes like a whirlwind from the south-west. etc. Peter of Blois too, in his letter to the official, plainly calls Rome Babylon and advises the official to depart from her.

units.la: XCIV. Miraris causam acerbarum adeò querelarum? Hæret illa in Pontificum maximè Romanorum tyrannide, dominandi libidine, rerum Divinarum contemptu, persecutione Imperatorum & verè fidelium, aliisque profligatæ eorundem mentis natis. Paschalis II. Hildebrandinis partibus addictus Henricum Imperatorem Romæ in Synodo denuo excommunicat, hæresin Henricianam docentem contemnere bruta adversus Imperatores fulmina, damnat; Episcopos obedientiam sedi Romanæ jurare subigit. Henricum filium seducit; ut Patrem ad deprimenda Imperii insignia compelleret, adeóque serpentinam parenti gratiam referret. Henricum Romam venientem, de investituris omittendis interpellat; ab eodem cùm Episcoporum Regalia, ut prius promiserat, Imperatori relaxare detrectaret, captus, ut liberationem obtineret, juramenti fide denuo promittit, se Imperatorem nec de investituris interpellaturum amplius, nec excommunicaturum: at mox in Concilio Lateranensi fallens fidem privilegium hoc, seu, uti vocabant alii, pravilegium, damnat, & laicos investituras, seu jus prodendi Flamines Episcopulósque, & sacerdotia per virgam & baculum confirmandi; sub anathemate dantis & accipientis laici prohibet; (quam in rem plura doctissimus Petrus de Marca Concord. Sac. & Imp. lib. VIII. 20. narrans consuli poteft) in mortuum Imperatorem ita sævit, ut cadaver Leodii jam sepultum ex sepulchro extrahi jusserit, staréque que in secreto quinquennium totum coegerit. Gelasius II. Henricum V. diris devovet & excommunicat. Calliftus II. A. MCXXII. Henrico extorquet, ut juri investiturae renunciaret. Ita Papa absolutus Rex factus est, & dirum Schisma diuque agitatum exspiravit. Quanquam alia etiam Schismata horrenda idem seculum exercuerunt; frequentissimis scilicet Antipapis, cum sederent Paschalis II. Gelasius II. Calixtus II. Honorius II. Innocentius II. Alexander III. Taceo Innocentium II. a Lothario Imperatore juramentum fidelitatis exigentem, & eundem ante pedes suos prostratum, coronamque Imperii expetentem, Antichristiano fastu, in tabula pingi curantem, cum superba inscriptione; Rex venit ante fores &c. denique Ludovicum VII. eo quod Gallicanae Ecclesiae libertates defensitaret, anathemate obstringentem. Eugenium III.quem bellum cum Romanis gerentem sic Bernhardus pulsavit: Habent haec infirma & terrena Reges, Judices, Principes terrae. Quid vos alienos fines invaditis? Tibi Sarculo opus est, non sceptro, ut opus facias prophetae, &c. Hadrianum IV. cum Hildebrandi nequitia paria facientem, utpote qui tum Imperium Romanum contendit esse Papale feudum, coronam & dignitatem Imperialem Papale beneficium; eóque nomine Friderico Barbarossae impotenter insultavit, compellens ei de equo descendenti strepam sinistram tenere, uti Helmoldus Histor. Slav. lib. I. scribit, eundemque Majestatem tueri conatum excommunicans; tum Hiberniam & omnes insulas ad jus B. Petri pertinere pertendit; tum denique Guilhelmum Siciliae Regem ad pedes suos prostratum, Siciliam omnem patrimonio Petri consecrare subegit. Alexandrum III. qui pulso Victore, palam asserente, Alexandrum Antichristi tempora praefigurare, in Templo Dei sedere, ostendentem se, tanquam sit Deus, abominationem desolationis, stantem in loco sancto esse; & Papae in Concilio Alexandro prælato, aliisque etiam Antipapis superatis Papatum rapuit; Henricum II. Anglorum Regem, insimulatum quòd conscius esset necis Thomæ Bequeti (qui protestatus licet, Romam factam esse meretricem, ab Alexandro inter Martyres relatus est) nudum virgis cædi à Religiosis jussit, dicente uno Legatorum ejus: Domine noli minari. Nos enim nullas minas timemus, qui de tali curia sumus, quæ consuevit imperare Regibus & Imperatoribus; in Waldenses persecutionem immanem excitavit; Cardinales in Concilio Laterani habito ad supremæ potestatis apicem evexit; Fridericum Barbarossam, cujus filius Otto à Sebastiano Venetorum Duce maritimo prœlio victus, & Venetias ad Papam captivus abductus ibidem inter Patrem & Papam pacem conciliavit; Venetiis, quò postero die ipse Imperator se contulit, indignissimè habuit, collo ejus ad pedes suos provoluti compresso, additisque ex Psalte vocibus: super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis & conculcabis leonem ac draconem; Cúmque honorem huncce χαμδνίας se Petro, non Alexandro habere Imperator protestaretur, denuo deprimens collum Cæsaris, respondit: Et mihi & Petro, teste Historia Veneta, antiquissimo in primis Codice Chronico Venetiis asservato, aliisque etiam pluribus à Viris doctissimis, Gerhardo Præfat. in part. 2. Confess. Cath. Wagenseilio de Impp. XI. & XII. Seculi, & Reiscero Romæ Non-Gloriosæ pag. 467–481. copiosissimè allegatis: Vrbanum III. Anathematis fulmen in Fridericum eundem intorquentem, & majora etiam moliturum, nisi fatis præpeditus esset; Clementem III. & Danos, qui sacerdotes conjugatos retinebant, excommunicantem, & Philippum Gallorum Regem (cui Messinæ Abbas Curatii Joachimus, explicans Apocalypsin, dixit, Antichristum jam Romæ natum esse, & in sede Apostolica sublimandum) jussa ejus detrectantem, ejusdem fulminis metu nequicquam perpercellentem : Cœlestinum III. Coronam inter pedes sultentatam, prostrato ad pedes Pontificis Henrico VI. offerentem, & mox capiti ejus impositam denuo proturbantem, & pede percutientem, ac in terram dejicientem, documentum scilicet imminentis ipsi fortunæ, siquidem exemplo Parentis Friderici Ænobarbi Pontificis frœnum admordere præsumeret; Baronio ad A. MCXCI. n. 10. Francisco Carriere Chronol. Pontif. ex Rogerio aliisque horribile scelus neutiquam dissimulantibus; sacris toti Franciæ ob divortium Philippi Regis ab Ingeberga, interdicentem, & adversus Henricum Imperatorem excommunicationis sententiam machinantem: denique Innocentium III. fabrum Capituli Venerabilem, lib 1. Decret. 6. in quo jus sibi vendicavit electum Cæsarem examinandi approbandique, si sit idoneus, rejiciendi contra, si sit indignus; imò etiam eligendi, si Electores eligere nolint; ac, si Electorum suffragia paria sint, gratificandi utri parti velit. De cujus impietate plura inferius dicenda se offerent.
units.tr: XCIV. Are you surprised at the cause of such bitter complaints? It lies chiefly in the tyranny of the Roman Pontiffs, their lust for domination, their contempt for divine things, their persecution of the emperors and of true believers, and other offspring of a corrupt mind of the same kind. Paschal II, devoted to the party of Hildebrand, excommunicated the Emperor Henry again at Rome in a synod, and condemned as heresy the Henrician doctrine that despised the impotent thunderbolts against emperors; he forced the bishops to swear obedience to the Roman see. He led astray Henry's son, so that he might compel his father to give up the insignia of the Empire, and so repay the father with a serpent's favour. When Henry came to Rome, Paschal pressed him to give up the investitures; when Henry refused to relinquish the regalia of the bishops, as Paschal had earlier promised, Paschal had him seized, and to obtain his release Henry again promised under oath that he would no longer press the Pontiff about investitures nor excommunicate him. But soon, at the Lateran Council, Paschal broke his word, condemned this privilege, which others called pravilegium, and forbade under anathema any layman to give or receive investitures, that is, the right to appoint archbishops and bishops and to confirm priesthoods by the staff and the rod. (On this matter the most learned Petrus de Marca, Concord. Sac. & Imp. book VIII, chapter 20, may be consulted.) He raged so fiercely against the dead Emperor that he ordered the corpse, already buried at Liège, to be dug out of its tomb, and forced it to remain for five years in a secret place. Gelasius II cursed and excommunicated Henry V with dreadful curses. In 1122 Calixtus II extorted from Henry that he renounce the right of investiture. So the Pope was absolved and the king was made, and the dreadful schism, long disputed, expired. Yet this same age also suffered other horrible schisms, namely through the very frequent antipopes, while Paschal II, Gelasius II, Calixtus II, Honorius II, Innocent II and Alexander III held the see.
