I pass over how Innocent II, when Lothair the Emperor demanded an oath of fealty, saw him prostrate at his feet and seeking the crown of the Empire, and in an Antichristian display of pride had a picture made of it, with the proud inscription: The king comes before the doors, etc.; and finally how he bound Louis VII under anathema because he defended the liberties of the Gallican Church. Eugene III, when he waged war against the Romans, was struck by Bernard with these words: Kings, judges and princes of the earth have these weak and earthly things. Why do you invade the territories of others? You need a mattock, not a sceptre, to do the work of a prophet, etc. Hadrian IV, matching the wickedness of Hildebrand, because he then claimed that the Roman Empire was a papal fief and the imperial crown and dignity a papal benefice, insulted Frederick Barbarossa without restraint, compelling him, as he dismounted from his horse, to hold the left stirrup, as Helmold writes in his Historia Slavorum, book I; and he excommunicated the man who tried to defend his majesty. Then he claimed that Ireland and all the islands belonged to the right of St Peter; and finally he compelled William, King of Sicily, to lie prostrate at his feet and to dedicate all Sicily to the patrimony of Peter. Alexander III, having driven out Victor, who openly asserted that Alexander prefigured the times of Antichrist, sitting in the Temple of God, showing himself as if he were God, the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, and having seized the papacy when Alexander was presented at a council and the other antipopes were also overcome, forced Henry II, King of the English, who was accused of being privy to the murder of Thomas Becket (who, though he protested that Rome had become a harlot, was counted among the martyrs by Alexander), to be stripped naked and beaten with rods by monks. One of his legates said: Lord, do not threaten us. For we, who belong to such a court, fear no threats; it is accustomed to command kings and emperors. He stirred up a monstrous persecution against the Waldenses. At the Lateran Council he raised the cardinals to the summit of supreme power. He treated Frederick Barbarossa, whose son Otto had been defeated in a naval battle by Sebastiano, Doge of the Venetians, and brought captive to the Pope at Venice, where he arranged a peace between father and Pope; but when the Emperor himself came to Venice the next day, the Pope treated him most disgracefully: he pressed his neck while he lay prostrate at his feet, adding words from the Psalm: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon. When the Emperor protested that he owed this honour [χαμδνίας] to Peter, not to Alexander, the Pope again pressed down Caesar's neck and replied: And to me and to Peter. This is attested by the Venetian history, preserved above all in a very ancient chronicle codex at Venice, and by many other most learned men who are copiously cited: Gerhard in the Praefatio in partem 2 Confessionis Catholicae, Wagenseil in De Imperatoribus XI et XII Saeculi, and Reiser in Roma Non-Gloriosa, pp. 467–481. Urban III hurled the thunderbolt of anathema against this same Frederick and would have undertaken greater things had fate not hindered him. Clement III excommunicated the Danes who kept married priests, and Philip, King of the French, who disregarded his orders (to whom Joachim, abbot of Curazzo near Messina, explaining the Apocalypse, said: Antichrist has already been born at Rome and is to be raised to the apostolic see), and who in vain spared himself for fear of that same thunderbolt. Celestine III, holding the crown between his feet, offered it to Henry VI, who was prostrate at the Pontiff's feet, and then soon afterwards, having placed it on his head, drove him away again and struck him with his foot and threw him to the ground, a warning to him of the fortune that threatened, since he had presumed to bite the bridle, following the example of his father Frederick Barbarossa. Baronius, ad A. 1191, n. 10; Francesco Carriere, Chronologia Pontificum, drawn from Roger and others, who by no means hide this dreadful crime; Celestine placed the whole of France under interdict on account of King Philip's divorce from Ingeborg, and plotted to pronounce sentence of excommunication against Henry the Emperor. Finally there was Innocent III, the craftsman of the chapter Venerabilem, book 1 of the Decretals, title 6, in which he claimed for himself the right to examine and approve an elected emperor, to reject him if he was unworthy, and indeed even to elect one if the electors refused to elect, and, if the votes of the electors were equal, to favour whichever side he wished. More will appear below about his impiety.

units.la: XCV. In primis autem hoc seculo ad stabilimentum sacræ Monarchiæ Pontificibus grassari duobus modis placuit. Obstare suis moliminibus Verbi Divini Majestatem, & legum humanarum authoritatem animadverterunt facilè. Ad convellendum igitur & labefactandum utrumque hoc præsidium hanc sibi viam muniverunt, ut refractis juris divini & humani claustris, ad suum arbitrium libidinémque omnia miscerent temperarentque: juríque adeò Cæsareo jus Pontificium, Divino vero Theologiam Scholasticam opponerent.
units.tr: XCV. In this century the Pontiffs chose to push forward the establishment of their sacred monarchy in two ways. They readily saw that the majesty of the Word of God and the authority of human laws stood in the way of their schemes. To overthrow and weaken both of these defences, they built this path for themselves: once the barriers of divine and human law were broken down, they could mix and manage everything at their own will and pleasure. They would set Pontifical law against the Caesarean law, and Scholastic Theology against the Divine law.

units.la: XCVI. Erat ea ætate recens juris Romani seu Cæsarei reparatio, & in forum quasi postliminii jure reductio, Irnerii opera, Lotharii vero authoritate suscepta. Id vero tanquam frœnum suis cupiditatibus injectum, ut eluderet Pontifex, callidè jus novum ex Pontificum decretis seu statutis compilatum protulit, quo scilicet ad firmandum Regnum suum commodè uteretur. Cui rei operam strenuam navavit Gratianus Monachus Bononiensis, qui ad imitationem Juris Civilis Pandectarum, ex veterum Conciliorum decretis, Patrumque scriptis compositum decretorum opus, quod Juris Canonici fundamenta, Regnique Pontificii nervos continet. Factum id est circa Annum Christi mcli. auspiciis Pontificis summi Eugenii III. qui opus ad umbilicum perductum authoritatis suæ robore firmavit, prælegique etiam in Academiis curavit. Gratianum Ducem secuti sunt alii; Gregorius quidem IX. ad imitationem Codicis Justinianei, operâ Raymundi Barcinonensis, Decretalium libros ex Pseudepigraphis Romanorum Pontificum Epistolis, A. mccxxvii. conflavit & publicavit, quibus Eugenii decretis quasi alas circumdare voluit. Bonifacius verò A. mccxciv. circiter opera usus Richardi Senensis, Berengarii Widerensis Episcopi, & Wilhelmi Eberodunensis Archiepiscopi, sextum Decretalium librum, in quo suas & antecessorum proximorum constitutiones novas ex novellis constitutionibus expressit, adjecit. Qui tamen, quòd maximam partem, flagrante adversus Philippum Galliarum Regem odio cuius esset, in Gallia, teste Duareno, Præfat. lib. de Sacr. Eccl. minist. pag. 2. receptus non fuit. Tandem A. mcccxvii. Johannes XXII. inchoato pridem operi fastigium impositurus, Clementinas Institutiones, Extravagantesque edidit, mandans severè, ut in judiciis & scholis usurparentur. Utque adeò à pluribus & majori cum applausu jus hoc sacrum acciperetur & excoleretur, Doctores etiam Juris Canonici creati sunt Bononiæ, additis constitutionibus de promotione & ritibus in ea adhibendis. Canonistarum nomine tales posthac venerunt, quos Papalis Monarchiæ Janizaros nonnemo rectius insignivit.
units.tr: XCVI. At that time the Roman or Caesarean law had recently been restored and brought back into the courts, as if by right of return, through the work of Irnerius and with the authority of Lothar. The Pontiff, however, cunningly put forward a new body of law, compiled from the decrees and statutes of the Popes, as a bridle thrown on to his own desires, so that he could evade the old law. He would use it conveniently to strengthen his own kingdom. Gratian, a monk of Bologna, zealously devoted himself to this task. In imitation of the Pandects of the Civil Law, he compiled from the decrees of the ancient councils and the writings of the Fathers a work of decrees, which contains the foundations of Canon Law and the sinews of the Papal kingdom. This was done around the year of Christ 1151, under the auspices of the supreme Pontiff Eugenius III, who confirmed the work by the strength of his authority, brought it to completion, and also saw to it that it was read publicly in the universities. Other men followed Gratian as their leader. Gregory IX, in imitation of the Justinianic Code and by the labour of Raymond of Barcelona, drew up and published the books of Decretals, made from the spurious Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs, in 1227; he wanted to put these decrees of Eugenius around himself, as it were, like wings. Boniface, around the year 1294, with the help of Richard of Siena, Berengar, Bishop of Vedera, and William, Archbishop of Embrun, added a sixth book of Decretals, in which he set out his own constitutions and those of his immediate predecessors, new ones drawn from recent constitutions. Yet this book was not received for the most part in France, since, with hatred blazing against Philip, King of the French, it was whose it was, as Duaren testifies in his Preface to the book on the Sacred Ministry of the Church, p. 2. At last, in 1317, John XXII, about to crown the work begun long before, published the Clementine Institutes and the Extravagants, and strictly ordered that they be used in the courts and schools. And so that this sacred law might be received and cultivated by more people and with greater applause, Doctors of Canon Law were also created at Bologna, with added constitutions on their promotion and the rites to be observed in it. From then on, men of this kind came to be called canonists, whom someone rightly branded Janizaries of the Papal Monarchy.

units.la: XCVII. Ita jure, tanquam septo quodam, dominationem suam Pontifices muniverunt. Quo vero jure? Validissimo utique omnium; utpote quod Papam tum supra omnes creaturas efferet, Imperatores, Reges, Principes & mortales quosque ei subjicit: tum legibus etiam solvit, & ἀνυπεύθυνον, hoc est, nullis rationibus reddendis obnoxium pronuntiat. Alibi omnia jura in scrinio pectoris ejus recondit, alibi omnis creaturæ Dominum constituit; alibi auro Pontificem summum, Imperatorem vero plumbo, alibi eundem soli, Imperatorem vero Lunæcomparat. Alibi Imperatorem facit serram, quæ, nisi à Pontifice trahatur, navare & efficere nihil queat. Alibi nullius judicio subesse Papam, alibi à potestate seculari nulla vel ligari, vel solvi posse scisscit. Vin' textus eam in rem? Paucos prodere lubet. Dist. 19. cap. 2. Sic omnes. Leges Romanæ servandæ sunt, tanquam ipsius Petri voce pronuntiatæ. Ib. cap. 3. in memoriam. Quod Ecclesia Romana jugum imponit, etiamsi tolerabile non sit, perferendum est. Dist. 40. C. Si Papa. Si Papa innumerabiles populos catervatim secum ducat in gehennam, culpam redarguere nemo Mortalium præsumat. Quia cunctos ipse judicaturus, à nemine judicandus est. Dist. 22. cap. omnes. Christus beato Petro æternæ vitæ clavigero terreni simul & cælestis imperii jura commisit. Dist. 96. cap. 10. Si Imperator Item cap. 12. Imperator debet subesse Papæ, non præesse. Extravag. comm. lib. 1. tit. 8. Utrque ergo in potestate Ecclesiæ, spiritualis scil. gladius & materialis. Ille sacerdotis, is manu Regum & militum, sed ad sacerdotis (Papæ) nutum & patientiam. Oportet autem gladium esse sub gladio, & temporalem authoritatem spirituali subjici potestati. C. 6. Solicitæ. X. de major. & obed. Duo præsunt mundo luminaria magna, Sol atque Luna. Solis loco Papa est, Cæsar vero Lunæ. cap. unam sanctam. De major. & Obed. Extravagant. Com. Ad salutem necessarium est, omnes homines Pontifici Romano subsint. Extat denique tit. 9. de de jure jur. lib. 2. Clem. expressa jurisjurandi formula, qua ad fivini Verbi vis atque Majestas obstitit. Hanc ut retundedem & obedientiam Papæ Imperatores diserte obligantur.
units.tr: XCVII. Thus the Pontiffs fortified their dominion with law, as with a kind of hedge. But what law? Assuredly the most powerful of all: for it raises the Pope above all creatures, and subjects emperors, kings, princes and all mortals to him; it also releases him from the laws, and declares him irresponsible [ἀνυπεύθυνον], that is, not liable to render any account. In one place it stores all rights in the chest of his breast; in another it makes him Lord of every creature; in another it compares the supreme Pontiff to gold and the Emperor to lead, and in another compares the one to the sun and the Emperor to the moon. In another it makes the Emperor a saw, which can do nothing and accomplish nothing unless it is drawn by the Pope. In another it decrees that the Pope is subject to no one's judgement, and in another that he cannot be bound or loosed by any secular power. Do you want texts to this effect? I am pleased to produce a few. Dist. 19, cap. 2: "Thus all." The Roman laws are to be observed, as if pronounced by the very voice of Peter. Ibid., cap. 3, "In memory": What the Roman Church imposes as a yoke, even if it is not bearable, must be endured. Dist. 40, C. "If the Pope": If the Pope drags countless peoples in crowds with him into hell, let no mortal presume to rebuke his fault. For he who is to judge all is to be judged by no one. Dist. 22, cap. "All": Christ entrusted to blessed Peter, the keeper of eternal life, the rights of both earthly and heavenly empire. Dist. 96, cap. 10: "If the Emperor"; likewise cap. 12: The Emperor ought to be subject to the Pope, not to preside over him. Extravagants Common, book 1, title 8: Both swords, then, are in the power of the Church, the spiritual sword and the material. The one is wielded by the priest, the other by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the nod and permission of the priest (the Pope). For the sword must be under the sword, and temporal authority must be subjected to spiritual power. C. 6, "Solicitae", X. de maioritate et obedientia: Two great lights rule the world, the Sun and the Moon. In the place of the sun is the Pope, and Caesar is in the place of the moon. Chapter "Unam sanctam", De maioritate et obedientia; Extravagants Common: For salvation it is necessary that all men be subject to the Roman Pontiff. Lastly, there is in title 9, "De jure iurando", book 2 of the Clementines, an express formula of oath, by which the Emperors are expressly bound to resist the power and majesty of the divine Word, and to render obedience to the Pope.

units.la: XCVIII. Ex altera vero parte Pontificiis conatibus Dirent, inducta est eadem ætate Theologia Scholastica, qua ex humanis traditionibus & commixtione Philosophiæ religio Divina posthac comprobari cœpit; curiositate inutili veram Theologiam fœdante, uti jam olim Trithemius questus est. Parens hujus Theologiæ fuit Lanfrancus, qui A. MLXXI. Archiepiscopum Cantuariæ egit, quem in eodem munere & professione A. MXCIV. Anshelmus, mox Hugo de S. Victore, & circa A. MCXXVII. Petrus Lombardus, Magister sententiarum, exceperunt. Theologiæ hujus historiam & crisin alibi fusius prosecuti sumus. Desitum sic est legere libros Propheticos & Apostolicos, qui fontes Ecclesiæ limpidissimi & saluberrimi sunt, & id totum habitum ratum fuit, quod vel Magister sententiarum docuisset, vel Romana Ecclesia approbasset, aut decrevisset. Ita Ecclesia Christi alligari cœpit Ecclesiæ Papæ, & Ecclesia universalis Catholica restricta est ad Ecclesiam particularem Romanam, quæ non amplius verbum Dei, sed decreta Papæ & figmenta hominum professa est. Nec libertati Euangelicæ aliquid relictum, sed paulatim subjecta omnia sunt servituti Pontificiæ, ut à Scriptura, quàm à Decretis Papæ recedere tutius longè fuerit. Et quod rei caput est, turpissimo mercatu venalia facta sunt, quæ Christus credentibus in se gratis offert: detrectantésque imperata Papæ ilico supplicii metum, vel periculum capitis subire coacti sunt.
units.tr: XCVIII. On the other hand, against the Pontifical attempts there was introduced in the same age Scholastic Theology, by which from then on the divine religion began to be established on human traditions and a mixture of philosophy; by useless curiosity it defiled true theology, as Trithemius complained long ago. The father of this theology was Lanfranc, who was Archbishop of Canterbury in 1071. In the same office and professorship, in 1094, Anselm succeeded him, soon followed by Hugh of St Victor, and about 1127 Peter Lombard, the Master of the Sentences. We have discussed the history and critique of this theology more fully elsewhere. It came to be the custom no longer to read the Prophetic and Apostolic books, which are the purest and most wholesome fountains of the Church, and everything was held as settled that either the Master of the Sentences had taught or the Roman Church had approved or decreed. Thus the Church of Christ began to be bound to the Church of the Pope, and the universal Catholic Church was restricted to the particular Roman Church, which no longer professed the Word of God but the decrees of the Pope and the inventions of men. Nothing was left to evangelical liberty; gradually all things were subjected to Papal servitude, so that it was by far safer to withdraw from Scripture than from the Decrees of the Pope. And, what is the heart of the matter, things which Christ offers freely to believers in himself were put up for sale in the most shameful trade, and those who refused the Pope's commands were forced to undergo the fear of punishment or the danger of death at once.

units.la: XCIX. Neque tamen sic Ecclesia Christi extingui, vel portæ inferorum ei prævalere potuerunt. Præterquam enim quòd in medio Papatu Deus electos suos servavit atque ex ignorantia, qua Pontifices vulgus detinendum censuerunt, id boni consecuti sunt, ut τὰ βάθη τῆς Σατανᾶ profunditates Sathanæ, hoc est, præcipuas & maximè perniciosas Papatus corruptelas ignoraverint, Divina providentia ita disponente, ut sub Antichristi sacerdotibus (ita cum Hilario contra Antin. loquimur) Christi populus non occideret: quòdque præcipua religionis Tridentinæ capita nondum pro fidei articulis, ne inter ipsos quidem Doctores Pontificios constanter recepta, sed inter doctos controversa, variéque disputata sunt; longéque etiam plurimi sub Pontificia tyrannide ingemuerunt propter abominationes, quas in medio Babylonis grassari viderunt. Non defuerunt etiam in omnibusferè terris numerosi piorum coetus, qui Antichristo procedente tempore bellum indixerunt. Cujusmodi erant, quos Papistæ à quodam Petro Waldo Lugdunensi, Waldensium, Pauperum Lugdunensium, & Leonistarum nominibus insigniverunt. Quam in rem Doctoris Pontificii, qui in rerum Bohemicarum Scriptoribus à Frehero editis extat, quémque esse Reinerum Inquisitorem Pontificium, XII. vel XIII. seculo inclarescentem, ex opere Ingolstadii integriùs edito constat; grave firmúmque testimonium habemus. Secta (ita ille pag. 222, 223.) hæreticorum ab olim fuerunt multæ. Inter quas omnes sectas, quæ sunt, vel fuerunt, non est perniciosior Ecclesiæ Dei, quàm pauperum de Lugduno, tribus de causis. Prima, quia DIVTVRNIOR. Quidam dicunt, quòd duraverit à tempore Silvestri: alii dicunt; quòd à tempore Apostolorum. Secunda est, quia GENERALIOR. Fere enim nulla terra est, in qua hæc secta non serpat. Tertia, quòd omnes aliæ cum immanitate blasphemiarum in Deum horrorem inducant, hæc Leonistarum magnam habet speciem pietatis, eò quòd coram hominibus juste vivant, & bene omnia de Deo credant, & omnes articulos, qui in Symbolo continentur; solam Romanam Ecclesiam blasphemant & oderunt; cui multitudo facilis est ad credendum.
units.tr: XCIX. Yet the Church of Christ could not thus be extinguished, nor could the gates of hell prevail against it. For apart from the fact that God preserved his elect in the midst of the Papacy, and from the ignorance by which the Pontiffs thought the common people should be kept, they gained this advantage: that, with divine providence so arranging, they were ignorant of the depths of Satan [τὰ βάθη τῆς Σατανᾶ], that is, the principal and most destructive corruptions of the Papacy. (So we speak with Hilary, against Antinus): that under the priests of Antichrist the people of Christ did not perish. Also, the principal heads of Tridentine religion were not yet accepted as articles of faith, nor consistently received even among the Papist teachers themselves; they were debated among the learned and disputed in various ways. Far more people groaned under Papal tyranny on account of the abominations which they saw rampant in the midst of Babylon. Nor were there lacking, in almost every land, numerous assemblies of the pious, who declared war on Antichrist as time went on. Such were those whom the Papists marked with the names of a certain Peter Waldo of Lyons: Waldenses, Poor Men of Lyons, and Leonists. On this matter we have a grave and firm testimony from a Papist doctor, who appears among the Bohemian writers edited by Freher, and who, as is clear from the work published more fully at Ingolstadt, was Reiner the Papal Inquisitor, who flourished in the twelfth or thirteenth century. There have been many sects of heretics from of old (so he writes, p. 222, 223). Among all the sects that are, or have been, none is more pernicious to the Church of God than that of the Poor Men of Lyons, for three reasons. The first is that it is the most long-lasting: some say that it has endured from the time of Sylvester, others that it has lasted from the time of the Apostles. The second is that it is the most widespread: there is almost no land in which this sect does not creep. The third is that, while all the others inspire horror of God by the enormity of their blasphemies, this sect of the Leonists has a great appearance of piety, because its members live justly before men, believe all things rightly about God and all the articles contained in the Creed, and blaspheme and hate only the Roman Church; and the multitude is easily led to believe this.

units.la: C.
units.tr: C.

units.la: C. De origine Waldensium seu Albigensium varias opiniones Cl. Usserius de Christ. Eccl. Success. cap. 8. p. 257. &c. Forbesius, Legerus, aliique referunt. Ad seculi XII. annum MCLX. vel MCLXX. adeoque tempora Hadriani IV.vel successoris Alexandri III. plerique revocant. Alii etiam altiorem originem pandunt. De eo quicquid sit, hoc, quod tractamus, seculo XII. nomen eorum innotuisse, & Pontifici Cleróque ejus exosum supra modum fuisse, satis constat. Crimini illis datum, quòd à praxi & doctrina recepta Ecclesiæ Romanæ recederent: quòd Ecclesiam Romanam Babylonem, & confusionis omnis Matrem appellarent; ejus tyrannidem ac superstitionem, ex Scripturis coarguerent: S. Literas in sermonem vernaculum transfunderent, familiaritérque declararent. Impacta iisdem ab adversariis multa sunt, Manichæismi inprimis impietas, non tam ex vero, quàm ad invidiam, uti fieri solet, conflandam seu quòd revera talia afferentes se iis immiscerent, hoc unum cum iis commune habentes, quòd Pontificis Romani communionem aversati sunt. Excitati mox plurimi Proceres, Episcopi, Viri, Fœminæ, literati, illiterati, qui luce hac capti, & S. Scripturæ deliciis inescati, segreges conventus primò Lugduni, mox Tolofæ & in Gallia Narbonensi, unde in omnem fere Europam, factis velut agminibus, dispersi sunt, instituerunt. Sed oppugnari hoc jam seculo iidem varie coeperunt, à Pontificibus cumprimis, puta Alexandro III. habitis Romæ & in Gallia Synodis missóque Cardinale qui Castrum Vauri obsedit; Lucio III. in Generali, quam vocant, Synodo; Clemente III. ac post in primis Innocentio III. sub quo bellum contra eos crudelissimum exarsit. Plurima eam in rem ex monumentis indubiis apud Usserium loco cit. legere est.
units.tr: C. Various opinions about the origin of the Waldenses or Albigenses are reported by the learned Ussher, de Christ. Eccl. Success. cap. 8. p. 257. &c., and by Forbes, Léger and others. Most people refer it to the years 1160 or 1170 of the twelfth century, that is, to the times of Hadrian IV or his successor Alexander III. Others trace a still earlier origin. Whatever the truth of that, it is well established that their name became known in the twelfth century and that they were intensely hated by the Pope and his clergy. They were charged with departing from the practice and accepted doctrine of the Roman Church; with calling the Roman Church Babylon and the mother of all confusion; with refuting its tyranny and superstition from the Scriptures; and with translating the holy letters into the vernacular and making them familiar to all. Their opponents brought many charges against them, above all the impiety of Manichaeism. This was stirred up to provoke hatred rather than from the truth, as usually happens; or because those who really taught such things mixed in with them, having only this in common with them, that they shunned communion with the Roman Pontiff. Soon many nobles, bishops, men and women, learned and unlearned, were roused. Captivated by this light and enticed by the delights of holy Scripture, they set up separate assemblies, first at Lyons, then at Toulouse and in Narbonese Gaul, from which they spread out across almost all of Europe as if in armies. In this century, however, they began to be attacked in various ways, especially by the Popes: Alexander III, who held synods at Rome and in Gaul and sent a cardinal who besieged the castle of Vaux; Lucius III, in what they call a general council; Clement III; and afterwards above all Innocent III, under whom a most cruel war against them broke out. Much on this matter can be read from reliable records in Ussher, loco cit.

units.la: CI. Ad seculum Decimum tertium pergimus. Predixerat autem jam ante Joachimus Abbas Comment. in Jerem. periculosum fore tempus inde ab anno Domini MCC. usque ad ultimos dies. In quibus, inquit, apparebit lex libertatis. Euangelium enim Christi tunc prædicabitur & Ecclesia purgabitur, ut à palea & zizanio triticum. Quæ verò seculi hujus facies fuerit, verbis Matthæi Paris Histor. pag. 421. Ecclesiæ suæ Anglicanæ miseriam explanantis pandere lubet. Sic autem ille: Temporibus illis igniculus fidei cæpit nimis refrigescere, ut pene in cinerem redactus vix videretur scintillare. Jam enim Simonia sine rubore perpetrata, usurarii manifestè diversis argumentis à popularibus & minoribus pecuniam impudenter extorquebant. Exspiravit charitas, libertas Ecclesiastica emarcuit, religio villuit suppeditata, & est facta filia Sion quasi meretrix effrons, non habens ruborem. Quotidie vilissimæ personæ & illiteratæ bullis Romanis armatæ, in minas statim erumpentes, reditus à piis Patribus in victus religiosorum & sustentationem pauperum, & hospitalitatem peregrinorum collatos spretis privilegiis à sanctis nostris antecessoribus indultis, diripere non formidaverunt. Fulgurantibus enim sententiis sine dilatione raptim postulata receperunt. Quod si ad refugium appellationis vel privilegii recurrerent injuriam petentes & spoliati, statim suspendentes per aliquem Prælatum, authentico Papæ compellente, fecerunt excommunicare. Et sic non prece, non Canonicè, sed imperiosa exactione, simplices spoliârunt, juxta illud Poëticum: Armato supplicat ense potens. Unde factum est, quòd ubi solebant Nobiles & dapsiles Clerici, Ecclesiarum custodes & patroni, circumjacentis patriæ latitudinem sua opulentia nobilitare, transeuntes suscipere, pauperes recreare: ibidem abjectæ personæ moribus vacui, versutia pleni, Procuratores & firmarii Romanorum, quicquid pretiosum in terra fuit & utile, abradentes, dominis suis in remotas terras deliciosè ex patrimonio Crucifixi viventibus, & ex alieno superbientibus transmiserunt. Erat igitur videre dolorem præcordialem, genas sanctorum irrigare, querelas crumpere, suspiria multiplicare: dicentibus multis cum singultu cruentato: Melius esset nobis mori, quàm videre mala gentis nostræ & sanctorum. Et pag. 878. sic exclamat: O Romanæ curiæ sterilis solicitudo, cæca ambitio! Ecce in tuis jacturis omnes punimur. Omnes enim compatimur; universalis Ecclesia, quæ à Romana tenetur curia defendi, in multis se queritur prægravari. In eadem Anglia Waltherus Mapez, Archidiaconus Oxoniensis, libro, cui titulus: Diversa Poëmata de corrupto Ecclesiæ statu, quem his versibus exorsus est:
units.tr: CI. We come now to the thirteenth century. Joachim the Abbot had already predicted in his Comment. in Jerem. that the time from the year of the Lord 1200 until the last days would be dangerous. In them, he says, the law of liberty will appear. For then the gospel of Christ will be preached and the Church will be purged, so that the wheat is separated from the chaff and the tares. I should like to set out in the words of Matthew Paris, Histor. pag. 421, what kind of face this century had, when he describes the misery of his English Church. He speaks thus: In those times the little spark of faith began to grow too cold, so that, reduced almost to ash, it scarcely seemed to glimmer. For simony was now committed without blushing, and usurers, by various devices, openly and shamelessly extorted money from the common people and the lesser folk. Charity expired, ecclesiastical liberty withered, religion lay low, deprived of support, and the daughter of Zion has become like a brazen harlot, with no blush at all. Every day the vilest and most unlearned persons, armed with Roman bulls, burst out at once into threats, and did not fear to plunder the revenues which pious Fathers had bestowed for the sustenance of religious men, the relief of the poor and the hospitality of pilgrims, scorning the privileges granted by our holy predecessors. For they received swift sentences, flashing forth without delay, demanded in haste. And if the injured and despoiled took refuge in an appeal or a privilege, then at once, with the authority of the Pope compelling some prelate, they had them excommunicated. And so they despoiled the simple not by prayer nor canonically, but by imperious exaction, according to that poetic saying: The powerful man begs with an armed sword. Hence it came about that where nobles and generous clergy, guardians and patrons of the churches, used to ennoble the surrounding countryside with their wealth, receive travellers and refresh the poor, there abject persons, empty of morals and full of cunning, agents and farmers of the Romans, scraped off whatever was precious and useful in the land and sent it to their lords, who lived luxuriously in distant lands on the patrimony of the Crucified and swelled with what belonged to others. So one could see heartfelt grief, wetting the cheeks of the saints, breaking out in complaints, multiplying sighs, many saying with bloody sobs: It would be better for us to die than to see the evils of our nation and of the saints. And at p. 878 he cries out thus: O barren solicitude of the Roman court, blind ambition! Behold, we are all punished by your losses. For we all suffer; the universal Church, which is supposed to be defended by the Roman court, complains that it is heavily burdened in many things. In the same England, Walter Map, Archdeacon of Oxford, in a book entitled Diverse Poems on the Corrupt State of the Church, which he began with these verses:

units.la: Roma mundi caput, sed nihil caput mundum,
units.tr: Rome is the head of the world, but a head that is not itself clean,

units.la: Quod pendet à capite, totum est immundum;
units.tr: So whatever hangs from the head is all unclean;

units.la: nec non altero libro, qui inscribitur, Apocalypsis Pontificis Goliath; aliisque etiam adversus Romanam curiam vulgatis Libris Ecclesiæ Romanæ ulcera masculè tetigit.
units.tr: and in another book, entitled The Apocalypse of the Pontiff Goliath, and in others published against the Roman court, he touched the sores of the Roman Church manfully.

units.la: CII. Initium seculi hujus Romæ occupaverat Innocentius III. furialis fax multarum turbarum; alterque velut Hildebrandus; qui Abbate Urspergensi συγγεγόνῳ narrante, multúmque quiritante, de Imperio certantibus Philippo Henrici defuncti fratre, & Othone Saxoniæ Duce oleum addens, Principibus Germaniæ, ut Othoni obsequantur, mandat, sacramenti erga Philippum nexu Archiepiscopos solvit; & nî pareant, diras interminatur. At Philippo usque quaque victore, ita Othonem ei conciliat, ut hic illius filia ducta Othoni, paulò post trucidato, ex pacto succedat; filia verò Philippi altera nepoti suo nubat, ea spe, ut Hetruria, Spoletum, Marcha Anconitana per hoc conjugium in manum ejus venirent. Anglorum quoque Regis Johannis, quòd Cardinalem Langetonum Cantuariensi Archiepiscopatui obtrudi non pateretur, Regnum interdicto subjicit, primi occupantis arbitrio exponit, Regem exauthorat, subditos sacramento solvit, Philippum Francorum Regem executorem sententiæ facit, ei & Regnum Angliæ & remissionem peccatorum ceu laboris præmium, donat; denique cruciatam contra Anglos undiquaque concitat; donec periculis circumventus Rex Angliæ & Hiberniæ Regna in manus Papæ resignaret, & ejus se vasallum profiteretur, magnamque ei pecuniarum vim, salvo Petri denario promitteret, quam etiam, ceu subjectionis arrham Pontificius Legatus pedibus prius calcatam accepit. Cùmque Rex Papæ sic reconciliatus vindictam adversus Langetonum, aliosque qui adversus se pro Papa steterant, meditaretur, Papa ampliori pecuniæ summa à Rege accepta, suppetias eidem fert, & anathemate ferit eos, qui paulò ante sua adversus Regem imperata fecerant. Quæ fusiùs à Matthæo Paris narrata pium lectorem in stuporem facilè abripiunt. Toti mundo, inquiebant Angliæ Episcopi, propter excommunicationes suas volunt dominari ignobiles usurarii & Simoniales!
units.tr: CII. At the beginning of this century Innocent III occupied Rome, a furious torch of many disturbances, and another like a second Hildebrand. The Abbot of Ursperg, relating events as a contemporary [συγγεγόνῳ], says much about this and complains greatly. Adding oil to the fire between Philip, brother of the dead Henry, and Otto, Duke of Saxony, who were contending for the empire, he ordered the princes of Germany to obey Otto, and he released the archbishops from the bond of their oath to Philip; and if they did not obey, he threatened them with curses. But since Philip was victorious everywhere, he so reconciled Otto to him that Otto, having married Philip's daughter, should succeed him after his own murder; and Philip's other daughter should marry his grandson, in the hope that Tuscany, Spoleto and the March of Ancona would come into his hands through this marriage. Also, because King John of England would not allow Cardinal Langton to be forced on the see of Canterbury, he placed the kingdom under interdict, exposed it to whoever should first seize it, deposed the king, released the subjects from their oath, made Philip, King of the Franks, the executor of the sentence, and granted him both the kingdom of England and the remission of sins as the reward of his labour. Finally he stirred up a crusade against the English on every side, until the king, surrounded by dangers, resigned the kingdoms of England and Ireland into the hands of the Pope, professed himself his vassal, and promised him a large sum of money, saving the Peter's penny; and the Papal Legate received this sum, as a pledge of subjection, after first trampling it under foot. When the king, thus reconciled to the Pope, was planning revenge against Langton and others who had stood against him on behalf of the Pope, the Pope, having received a larger sum from the king, came to his aid and struck with anathema those who had shortly before carried out his orders against the king. Matthew Paris relates these things at greater length, and they easily plunge the pious reader into amazement. The English bishops said: Because of their excommunications, base usurers and simoniacs want to rule over the whole world!

units.la: CIII. Celebratum est Pontifice eodem A. MCCXV. Romæ in Laterano Concilium, cui plus quàm mille Prælati interfuisse feruntur. In actis ejus Concilii cap. 1. asseritur, Corpus & Sanguinem Jesu Christi, in sacramento altaris, sub speciebus panis & vini veraciter contineri transsubstantiatis pane in corpus, & vino in sanguinem, potestate Divina. Quod transsubstantiationis vocabulum in nullo prius Concilio usurpatum, primus quidam Stephanus Eduensis Episcopus Tract. de Sacr. Alt. cap. 13. adhibuit. Concinnati quoque Canones sunt de Confessione peccatorum auriculari quotannis semel edenda, de cura tegendi ea, quæ in confessione aperiuntur. De Chrismate & Hostia includendis & asservandis; de Divorum reliquiis ex capsa non monstrandis, de fidelitate laicis à clericis non promittenda; de immunitate Ecclesiæ à tributis; de electione civilis Magistratus in sacris beneficiis irrita; de damnatis ab Ecclesia Romana morte plectendis, &c. quibus rebus Regni Pontificii nervus continetur. Scripsit idem Papa sex libros de sacramento Altaris, in quibus præ aliis omnibus Deum Maozim exaltavit. Sacerdotes conjugatos idem
units.tr: CIII. In the same year, A.D. 1215, under the same Pontiff, a Council was held at the Lateran in Rome, which more than a thousand prelates are said to have attended. In the acts of that Council, chapter 1, it is asserted that the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ are truly contained in the sacrament of the altar under the species of bread and wine, the bread being transubstantiated into the body and the wine into the blood, by divine power. The word transubstantiation, which had not been used in any earlier council, was first employed by a certain Stephen, Bishop of Autun, in Tract. de Sacr. Alt. cap. 13. Canons were also drawn up: on the annual auricular confession of sins, to be made once a year; on the care to keep secret what is disclosed in confession; on the chrism and the host, to be enclosed and kept; on the relics of the saints, not to be shown outside their case; on the fidelity of laymen, not to be promised by clergy; on the immunity of the Church from taxes; on the election of civil magistrates to sacred benefices, being void; on those condemned by the Roman Church, to be punished by death, etc. On these matters rests the sinew of the Papal kingdom. The same Pope wrote six books on the sacrament of the altar, in which above all others he exalted the god Maozim.

units.la: igni mancipavit. Denique ordines Monachorum Mendicantium, puta Prædicatorum, Franciscanorum, Augustinianorum & Carmelitarum, totidem videlicet fulcra & sustentacula Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ, quique, uti Azorius Institut. Moral. XIII. 1. loquitur, multa præter Monachorum commune jus, institutum, morem ac disciplinam solitam introduxerunt; idem instituit. Et Prædicatorum quidem, seu potius Ismaëlitarum, utpote quorum manus contra omnes, & omnium vicissim contra ipsos glisçebant; princeps Dominicus, seu mavis Dæmonicus: Franciscanorum vero Franciscus extiterat: Pseudo-prophetarum, qui ea ætate floruerunt, par ignobile; ille Hispanus, hic Italus: hic ab Innocentio, ille à Successore Honorio comprobatus; à clientibus vero & sectatoribus Christo coæquatus, imo supra Christum evectus uterque; uti detestabiles libri Conformitatum, Bartholomæo Pisano authore editi, & à Gregorio IX. sub pœna hæreseos obtrusi, nec non Antonini Archiepiscopi de Dominico, aliorumque de utroque, Bonaventuræ cumprimis, qui in vita Francisci à Christo sibi revelatum scripsit, quòd Franciscus sit Angelus ascendens ab ortu solis, de quo Apoc. VII. 2. (confer. Cl. Usserium de Succeff. Eccles. p. 323. &c.) scelesta scripta testantur.
units.tr: He also consigned them to the fire. Finally, he established the orders of the Mendicant friars, namely the Preachers, Franciscans, Augustinians and Carmelites, as so many props and supports of the Papal Church. As Azorius says in Institut. Moral. XIII. 1., they introduced many things beyond the common law, rule, custom and accustomed discipline of the monks. Among the Preachers, or rather the Ishmaelites, whose hands were raised against everyone and everyone's hands against them in turn, the leader was Dominic, or rather I would say Demonic; the Franciscans had Francis as their founder. The pseudo-prophets who flourished in that age were an unremarkable pair: the one a Spaniard, the other an Italian. The one was approved by Innocent, the other by his successor Honorius. Each was raised to equality with Christ by his clients and followers, indeed above Christ, as the detestable books of the Conformities, published under the name of Bartholomew of Pisa and imposed by Gregory IX under penalty of heresy, attest, together with the writings of Archbishop Antoninus about Dominic and of others about both, especially Bonaventure, who in the life of Francis wrote that it had been revealed to him by Christ that Francis is the angel ascending from the rising of the sun, of whom we read in Rev. 7:2 (compare the learned Ussher, de Succeff. Eccles. p. 323, etc.).

units.la: CIV. Propagabantur interim in Gallia Waldenses seu Albigenses, qui doctrinam Pontificiæ oppositam strenuè propugnârunt, indè ab Alpibus ad Pyrenæos usque montes diffusi. Eis adhæserant etiam Proceres plerique, Raimundus Comes Tolosæ, & S. Ægidii, Regis Franciæ consobrinus, Raimundus Rogerius Biterrarum & Carcassonæ Comes, Petrus Rogerius Gabareti Regulus, Raimundus Foxensis, Regis Aragoniæ propinquus, Guasto Bearnii Princeps, Comes Bigerronum, Comes Carmanii, Raimundus de Thermis, Americus de Monstrolio, Guliel-mus mus de Minerbio, & innumeri alii nobilitate insignes. Quos non alio nomine, quàm quòd Ecclesiæ Romanæ corruptelas reprehenderint, vexatos Gulielmus Paradinus in Annalibus Burgundiæ testatur. Innocentius igitur A. MCCVIII. duos primùm Legatos mittit, Episcopum Oxoniensem & Dominicum, qui Colloquium Carmanii cum iis ineant; addito mox Abbate Cisterciense, cum aliis duodecim ejusdem Ordinis. Ex parte Albigensium Theodorus, Canonicus ante Nivernensis, Balduinus & Bernhardus de Simorra congrediuntur. Cùmque primoribus illis colloquia non satisfacerent, neque etiam Dominici, quem Innocentius in somniis, uti dicebat, admonitus, ædem Lateranensem alias ruinam minitantem suffulturum, delegerat; cuique post Reinerium & Guidonem Inquisitionis officium mandaverat; concionibus non moverentur quicquam; ad asperiora consilia Papa deflectens, Raimundum Comitem, cujus præcipua erat authoritas, Sacrorum Communione, aqua & igne interdicit; & in ejus sociorumque, perinde ut in Saracenorum capita sæviendi potestatem, iisdem etiam promissis indulgentiis, concedit; denique crucem in infideles olim, prætextu saltem, assumptam, crucifigendo verè in membris suis Christo adhibet. Ubi strenuam Papæ operam Monachi Prædicatores navârunt, qui sumpto hujusmodi themate: Quis consurget mihi adversus malignantes, aut quis stabit mecum adversus operantes iniquitatem (Psal. xciv. 16.) conciones ad populum habitas tali Epilogo claudere consueverunt: Ecce videtis, charissimi, quanta est malitia hæreticorum! Videtis etiam, quantum nocent in mundo! Videtis, quàm piè laborat Ecclesia eos revocare. Sed apud tales nihil ista poterunt proficere. Et ideo sancta mater Ecclesia contra eos convocat exercitum Christianorum. Quicunque igitur habet zelum fidei &c. veniat & accipiat signum crucis, adjungat se militiæ crucifixi, &c. Fregitque primus cruciatorum certatim concurrentium impetus Raimundum, ut obsequium Pontifici sponderet. quem mox Almaricus, Pontificis Legatus, exercitús & ipse Dux, stola collo injecta, flagris Templum intrare compellit, ditionibus ejus omnibus Simoni Montfortio Comiti in Lateranensi Concilio resignatis. qui tamen paulò post Raimundo & Albigensibus animos virésque recolligentibus, Tholosam obsidens ictu lapidis miserè periit, & Albigensibus victoriam cessit. Sed dispersi magis Albigenses variam fortunam experti sunt. Author enim Trithemius, & ante ac post eum alii, Argentinæ octoginta combustos fuisse, inque vicino agro trucidatos centum uno die. In Italia Nauclerus doctrinam hanc mirificè tum in equestri,tum in plebejo ordine crevisse narrat. Bruschius Moguntiæ triginta novem ustulatos scribit. Nec quicquam deinceps frequentius: cineribus quippe his, tanquam diffiante Dei Spiritu, in omnes Europæ fines disseminatis. Horribilis cum primis Inquisitor Generalis, Frater Conradus de Marpurg, eodem Trithemio teste, miseros judicio ferri candentis, si negâssent hæresin, probare consuevit. Quos enim, inquit ille, exuffissset ferrum, velut hæreticos judicio seculari comburendos tradidit. Unde paucis exceptis omnes, qui semel fuissent accusati, & ad ejus Examen perducti, per eum ad incendium condemnabantur. &c. Eodem die, quo quis accusatus, sive juste, sive injuste, nullius appellationis, nullius defensionis sibi refugio proficiente damnatus, & crudelibus flammis injectus est. Non idem tamen eorum fatum fuit in Lombardia, Provincia aliisque regnis, in quibus (ita hostis illorum infensissimus Rainerius scribit) plures auditores habebant, & in publico disputabant, & populum vocabant ad stationes solennes in foro, & in campo, & in lectis prædicabant. Non erat qui eos impedire auderet, propter potentiam & multitudinem fautorum suorum. Inquisitioni & examinaminationi frequenter interfui, & computatæ sunt 40 Ecclesiæ, quæ hæresi infectæ fuerunt. Ac in sola Parochia Cammach fuerunt decem scholæ hæreticorum. Eam porrò Albigensium historiam Celeb. Ussherius de Succeff. Eccl. cap. 9. & 10. ex monumentis certissimis eruit.
units.tr: CIV. Meanwhile the Waldenses, or Albigenses, spread in Gaul; they vigorously defended a doctrine opposed to the Papists' and were scattered from the Alps to the Pyrenees. Many nobles had also joined them: Raymond, Count of Toulouse and Saint-Gilles, cousin of the King of France; Raymond Roger, Count of Béziers and Carcassonne; Peter Roger, lord of Gaillac; Raymond of Foix, a relative of the King of Aragon; Gaston, Prince of Béarn; the Count of Bigorre; the Count of Comminges; Raymond de Thermes; Amaury de Montfort; William de Minerve; and countless others distinguished by their nobility. William Paradin, in his Annals of Burgundy, testifies that they were harassed for no other reason than that they had rebuked the corruptions of the Roman Church. Therefore in 1208 Innocent first sent two legates, the Bishop of Oxford and Dominic, to hold a colloquy with them at Carmain; soon the Abbot of Cîteaux was added, with twelve others of the same order. On the side of the Albigenses, Theodore, formerly a canon of Nevers, and Baldwin and Bernard de Simorre came to the meeting. When these leaders were not satisfied with the colloquies, and neither were they moved by the sermons of Dominic, whom Innocent (as he said) had been warned in dreams to choose to prop up the Lateran church, which otherwise threatened to collapse, and to whom after Reinerius and Guido he had entrusted the office of the Inquisition, the Pope turned to harsher counsels. He placed Count Raymond, whose authority was chief among them, under interdict from the sacred communion, from water and from fire; and he granted to the Count and his associates the power to rage against them as against the heads of the Saracens, with the same promised indulgences. Finally, he employed against Christ's own members, in effect, the cross once taken up against unbelievers, at least in pretence. The Preaching Monks lent energetic service to the Pope; taking as their theme the words, Who will rise up for me against the evildoers, or who will stand with me against the workers of iniquity? (Ps. 94:16), they were accustomed to end their sermons to the people with this epilogue: Behold, dearly beloved, how great is the malice of heretics! You see also how much harm they do in the world! You see how devoutly the Church labours to recall them. But these things can achieve nothing with such men. Therefore holy mother Church summons an army of Christians against them. Whoever therefore has zeal for the faith, let him come and receive the sign of the cross, and join himself to the soldiery of the Crucified, etc. The first onrush of the crusaders, who rushed to take part, broke Raymond, so that he promised obedience to the Pontiff. Almaric, the Pope's legate and also leader of the army, soon compelled him, with a stole thrown about his neck, to enter the temple under the lash, after all his lands had been surrendered at the Lateran Council to Simon de Montfort, Count. Yet soon afterwards, when Raymond and the Albigenses gathered their spirits and strength again, Simon, besieging Toulouse, was miserably killed by a stone, and victory passed to the Albigenses. But the Albigenses, dispersed, experienced varied fortunes. The author Trithemius, and others before and after him, say that eighty were burned at Strasbourg, and a hundred were slaughtered in the neighbouring field in one day. In Italy, Nauclerus relates that this doctrine grew wonderfully among both the knightly and the common orders. Brusch writes that thirty-nine were burned at Mainz. Nothing happened more often after this, for these ashes, as if scattered by the breath of God, were disseminated to all the borders of Europe. Trithemius again testifies that Brother Conrad of Marburg, a most terrible Inquisitor General, was accustomed to prove the wretched by the ordeal of red-hot iron, if they denied heresy. For those whom the iron had burned, he says, he handed over to the secular court to be burned as heretics. Hence, with a few exceptions, all who had once been accused and brought before his examination were condemned by him to the fire, etc. On the same day on which anyone was accused, whether justly or unjustly, he was condemned, with no refuge of appeal or defence available to him, and was cast into the cruel flames. Their fate was not the same, however, in Lombardy, in Provence and in other kingdoms, where (as their most hostile enemy Rainerius writes) they had many hearers, and disputed in public, and called the people to solemn assemblies in the forum and in the field, and preached in the houses. No one dared to hinder them, on account of the power and number of their supporters. I was often present at the inquisitions and examinations, and forty churches were counted which were infected with heresy. And in the parish of Cammach alone there were ten schools of heretics. The learned Ussher, in de Succeff. Eccl. chapters 9 and 10, draws out this history of the Albigenses from the most certain records.

units.la: CV. Innocentii successores Honorius puta III. Gregorius IX. & Innocentius IV. adversus Fridericum II. Imperatorem Sapientissimum fortissimúmque, virtutum plurium concentu pœne incomparabilem, πολυγλώτταν (nam Græcæ Latinæ, Saracenicæ Linguæ callentissimus fuit) conceptum odium inexpiabile atrocibus cum eo certaminibus prodiderunt. Longæ sunt ambages, injuriæ verò acerbissimæ. Fuit is Innocentii III. post excommunicatum Othonem pupillus. Anno verò MCCXX. Imperium capessens, & in Italiam iter molitus, Conradum Episcopum Spirensem Cancellarium cum amplissimo mandato præmittit. Eum Honorius diplomatum, in quibus se Regem Romanorum & Siciliæ ferebat, tenore, & quod à Principibus Italiæ juramentum fidelitatis, aliáque jura, ita ut ab eo nulla appellatio fieret, postularet, offensus, fecialem interpretatur, ipsique Friderico Italiam ingressuro nullum non negotium facessit. Mediolanenses, eo instigante, Legato portas occludunt; aliæ urbes idem parant. Cæsar illos nihil moratus, Romam pergit, & Urbium Legatos eodem sequi jubet. Ibi à Papa coronari petit, oblato juramento solito. Annuit Papa, sed ea lege, ut in certum tempus expeditionem sacram suscipiat. Nihil enim Papæ antiquius erat, quàm ut sudem hunc in oculis procul ab Italiæ finibus & rebus amandaret. Fridericus Sicilia lustrata, & statu Regni ejus composito, nec non Conrado in Italia relicto, in Germaniam revertitur, ibíque biennium, non sine Papæ tædio consumit. Inter has moras A. MCCXXIII. Johannes Brennensis, seu de Bregna, Rex Hierofolymitanus Romam appellit, cui Papa suadet, filiam Jolandam Friderico desponder at, & Regnum Hierosolymitanum eidem destinet, ea tamen lege, ut infidelibus illud eripiat. Accipit conditionem Fridericus, excipiens tamen biennium componendis rebus Lombardiæ. Honorio A. MCCXXVII. Gregorius IX. succedit, quo urgente Fridericus expeditioni sacræ se accingit, sed vix tridui spatio sulcato mari, morbo pressus littus repetit. Hic Papa in eum debacchari, anathema denique vibrare. Fridericus vero rebus Siculis compositis (eorum enim gratia morbum simulasse putabatur, gnarus Papam Siciliæ inhiare) cum classe Palæstinam adit; excandescente Papa, quòd id nondum sibi reconciliatus tentaret. Proin Apuliam invadit, sociias Lombardiæ urbes in Fridericum accendit, denique totam Italiam factionibus Guelforum (qui à Guelfone Bavariæ Duce ita dicti, à partibus Pontificiis stabant) & Gibellinorum (qui à villa Giblingen, in qua Fridericus Dux Suevia à nutrice lactatus fuerat, ita dicti, Imperatoriarum partium erant) factione jam ante Innocentio II. Pontifice coepta, miscet. Fridericus coeptis insistens Hierosolymam capit, diadema ibi recipit, & res Christianas constituit. Gregorius & una cum eo Templarii ac Hospitalarii cum Sultano adversus Fridericum conspirant, eúmque ut ad Jordanem eum opprimat, rogant. Sultanus horrens Papæ perfidiam, ejus literas Friderico mittit, qui inducias cum eo pactus Italiam repetit, cum quo Papa, metuens poenam perfidiæ, pacem exambit, dissoluto anathemate. Pax certis legibus facta est. Fridericus pedes Papæ osculari jussus, vix summa genua amplectitur & osculatur, indignante denuo Papa, & glisceatibus odiis Fridericum in die S. Coenæ ante Pascha iterum excommunicante; denique filium Henricum adversus Patrem nefariè instigante. Hic vero se defendere certus, Papæ hos versus misit:
units.tr: CV. The successors of Innocent, namely Honorius III, Gregory IX and Innocent IV, displayed an inexpiable hatred, with the bitterest conflicts, against the most wise and most brave Emperor Frederick II, almost incomparable in the harmony of his many virtues, a man of many tongues (for he was most skilled in Greek, Latin and Saracen languages) [πολυγλώτταν]. The story is long, and the injuries most bitter. He was the ward of Innocent III after Otto had been excommunicated. In 1220, taking up the Empire and preparing the journey into Italy, he sent ahead Conrad, Bishop of Speyer and Chancellor, with very full powers. Honorius, offended by the wording of the diplomas in which Frederick styled himself King of the Romans and of Sicily, and by his demand that the princes of Italy swear fidelity and other rights, so that no appeal could be made from him, interpreted this as an act of war, and caused every kind of trouble for Frederick himself as he was about to enter Italy. At his instigation the Milanese closed their gates against the legate, and other cities prepared to do the same. Caesar, without delay, went on to Rome, and ordered the envoys of the cities to follow him. There he asked the Pope to crown him, offering the customary oath. The Pope agreed, but on the condition that he undertake a holy expedition within a set time. For nothing was more important to the Pope than to send this stake away from the eyes of Italy and its affairs. Frederick, having visited Sicily and settled the state of his kingdom, and having left Conrad in Italy, returned to Germany and spent two years there, not without the Pope's weariness. During these delays, in 1223, John of Brienne, or of Brienne, King of Jerusalem, landed at Rome. The Pope persuaded him to betroth his daughter Yolanda to Frederick and to assign to him the Kingdom of Jerusalem, on the condition that he should wrest it from the unbelievers. Frederick accepted the terms, but asked for two years to settle affairs in Lombardy. Gregory IX succeeded Honorius in 1227. Under his urging, Frederick prepared himself for the holy expedition, but after sailing for barely three days he was seized by illness and returned to shore. The Pope raged against him and at last hurled anathema. Frederick, however, having settled affairs in Sicily (for it was thought that he had feigned illness for their sake, knowing the Pope was eager for Sicily), went to Palestine with a fleet; the Pope was enraged that he attempted this without first being reconciled to him. Therefore the Pope invaded Apulia, stirred up the allied cities of Lombardy against Frederick, and finally mixed all Italy in the factions of the Guelfs (so called from Welf, Duke of Bavaria, and who stood on the papal side) and the Ghibellines (so called from the village of Waiblingen, where Frederick, Duke of Swabia, had been suckled by his nurse; they were of the imperial party), a faction already begun earlier under Pope Innocent II. Frederick, persisting in his undertaking, took Jerusalem, received the crown there, and set the Christian affairs in order. Gregory, together with the Templars and Hospitallers, conspired with the Sultan against Frederick, and asked him to crush him near the Jordan. The Sultan, shocked at the Pope's treachery, sent his letters to Frederick, who made a truce with him and returned to Italy. The Pope, fearing punishment for his treachery, sought peace with him, and the anathema was dissolved. Peace was made on certain terms. Frederick was ordered to kiss the Pope's feet; he scarcely embraced and kissed his knees, and the Pope, again indignant, and with hatreds growing, excommunicated Frederick once more on the Thursday before Easter; and finally he wickedly stirred up Frederick's son Henry against his father. But Henry, confident of defending himself, sent these verses to the Pope:

units.la: Roma diu titubans, longis erroribus acta, Corruet, & mundi desinet esse caput.
units.tr: Rome, long wavering and driven about by long errors, will fall, and will cease to be the head of the world.

units.la: Post Romam cum exercitu petit, & Papam cum Cruciatorum, & Venetorum, quos sibi foedere univit, exercitu se ei opponentem vincit, sacratúmque hunc exercitum orco mactat; mox etiam Romam petens, Papae, qui nudis pedibus capita Petri & Pauli circumgestaverat, exercitum turpiter fundit. Induciae ita pactae ad Concilium usque, quas iterum Papa, pecuniis in Gallia sacrae expeditionis pretextu corrogatis, abrumpere tentaverat. Qua re cognita Rex Galliae pecuniam in Regno suo collectam Pontificio Legato extorquet, sibíque servat. Pergit Papa Friderici subditos fidelitatis sacramento solutos, aliósque etiam adversus Fridericum bullis per Albertum Beham clam emissis, & tentatis etiam ejus consilariis, concitare; Conciliúmque Romae habendum, ad quod Episcopos sibi devotos vocavit, indicit. Erumpit haec conjuratio, in Italia tum haerente Friderico. Cujus partes in Germania gnaviter suscipit ejus filius Conradus, quo monitore nec Episcopi, nec Abbates Germaniae bullis parent, protestati, nullum jus esse Papae in Germania, Episcopis non conscíis & consentientibus. Ipse suos Italos pascat, inquiunt; Nos a Deo constituti canes a nostris ovilibus lupos ovilla pelle tectos arcebimus. Fridericum excommunicatum Eberhardus Episcopus Salisburgensis absolvit. Mox una cum Othone Bavariae Duce Ratisbonae Episcopi conveniunt, ubi Salisburgensis gravi & φιλιβλικῇ Oratione Pontificem cum suis Pharisaeos, flamines Babylonis, ipsum denique Antichristum esse non perfunctorie, sed prolatis ex Apocalypsi & S. Paulo testimoniis ostendit; simúlque ut maturè ei obviam eatur, & Albertus ejus emissarius, ac incendiarius, proscribatur, monet. Episcopis contra Pontificiarum partium Romam ad Concilium properantibus, Imperator salvum conductum promisit, si terrestri, non maritimo itinere eò tenderent. Sed Episcopi hi parant Classem viginti sex navium, quibus Imperatoris filius Conradus viginti & unius navium apparatu instructus ita occurrit, ut captis viginti navibus, & tribus submersis Prælatos hosce vicerit, & Pontificis ipsius urbes invaserit. Unde Papa mœrore animi confectus, cùm adversa omnia ei acciderent, mox die xxi. Aug. A. MCCXLIV. oppetiit. Ei Celestinus IV. & huic post septemdecim dies mortuo, & anni unius & octo mensium inter-Pontificio finito, Innocentius IV. succedit. qui præter quam quòd in Anglia & in Gallia turbas gravissimas à Matthæo Paris graphicè depictas, excitavit; etiam Friderici, cui ante Papatum amicus fuerat, acerrimum sese hostem gessit. Concilio enim Lugduni indicto, & die xxvi. Jun. A. MCCXLV. inchoato Cæsarem eò evocat, non venientem gravissimè accusat, horrendis devotionibus imperio indignum pronuntiat, abdicat & sacrorum etiam communione privat. Cujus quidem Conciliabuli iniquum decretum cùm ab aliis, tum nuper à Sorbonista Launojo Epist. lib. 7. solidè consutatum est. Sic tamen devotus Imperator eodem anno Italiam invadit, Mediolanenses graviter affligit, Papam ipsum eas in angustias redigit, ut excommunicationis eum pœnituerit. Nihilominus ille pecuniis undique corrasis Henricum Thuringiæ Landgravium, per juratos Friderici hostes Moguntinum & Colonien-sem, Imperatorem eligi curat, & Friderico Sicarios immittit, qui deprehensi capitis supplicio nefas luerunt. Henricus quoque vulnere ad Ulmam accepto d. vii. Feb. A. MCCXLVIII. defungitur. Ejus in locum, annitente Papa, Wilhelmus Hollandiæ Comes substituitur; sed premente Conrado, Friderici filio, cedit. Papæ Romæ iterum duos sicarios, & inter eos Petrum de Vineis, quem ante hac fidum Imperatorem... peratori auro corrupit, subornat, qui ab Imperatore in suum caput emissi fingebantur, velamen patrandi sceleris. Detecta fraude, alter medicus suspenditur. Petrus de Vineis oculis privatus circumducitur per urbes Italiæ, ut crimen ubique profiteatur, tandémque metu gravioris supplicii capite columnæ, cui alligatus erat in carcere, alliso, se ipsum enecat. Prædictum autem Friderico fuerat, eum in castro quodam Florentino moriturum. Florentia igitur semper vitata, die xiii. Dec. A. mcci. in arcem quandam Apuliæ, quæ Florentina dicebatur, veniens morbo corripitur & xxvi. ejusdem mensis, cum annos xxxviii. imperâsset, fato defungitur. Ægrotum à filio notho Manfredo, instinctu Papæ, pulvillo in os conjecto, extinctum nonnulli memorant, contradicentibus tamen aliis, Collenutio inprimis in ejus Vita. Ab ejus morte per annos fere viginti duos interregnum fuit, cum subinde alii & alii eligerentur, qui tamen in ea temporum perturbatione à Pontificibus invecta, summam rei non tenebant. Perpetuis etiam simultatibus & inimicitiis defatigati Cæsares paulatim remissiores facti, Italiam deseruerunt, & tantum non Pontificibus, tantis scilicet turbarum Æolis, succubuerunt.
units.tr: Afterwards he marched on Rome with his army. He defeated the Pope, who opposed him with an army of Crusaders and Venetians whom the Pope had bound to himself by treaty. He slaughtered this consecrated army and sent it to Hades. Soon afterwards he also marched on Rome, and he routed shamefully the Pope, who had carried the heads of Peter and Paul about barefoot. A truce was then agreed until the Council, which the Pope had tried to break again, after raising money in France under the pretext of a holy expedition. When the King of France learned of this, he extorted the money collected in his kingdom from the papal legate and kept it for himself. The Pope went on to stir up Frederick's subjects, whom he declared released from their oath of allegiance, and others too against Frederick, by means of bulls secretly issued through his agent Albert Beham, and by attempting to win over Frederick's counsellors. He also called and appointed a Council to be held at Rome, to which he summoned bishops devoted to himself. This conspiracy broke out while Frederick was still tied down in Italy. In Germany his cause was vigorously taken up by his son Conrad, under whose guidance neither the bishops nor the abbots of Germany obeyed the bulls. They protested that the Pope had no right in Germany without the knowledge and consent of the bishops. Let him feed his own Italians, they say; we, the dogs appointed by God, will keep off from our sheepfolds the wolves that are covered in sheepskin. Eberhard, Bishop of Salzburg, absolved Frederick, who had been excommunicated. Soon afterwards he met with Otto, Duke of Bavaria, at Regensburg, where the Bishop of Salzburg, in a grave and Philippic [φιλιππικῇ] oration, showed not superficially but by testimonies drawn from the Apocalypse and St Paul that the Pope with his followers were Pharisees, priests of Babylon, and indeed that he himself was Antichrist. At the same time he advised that Albert, the Pope's emissary and firebrand, should be outlawed, so that they might act promptly against him. The bishops of the papal party were hastening to Rome for the Council. The Emperor promised them safe conduct if they made their way there by land rather than by sea. But these bishops prepared a fleet of twenty-six ships, against which the Emperor's son Conrad came up with a fleet of twenty-one ships. He captured twenty of the ships, sank three, and defeated these prelates and invaded the cities of the Pope himself. Then the Pope, worn down in mind with grief, since all things were going against him, died soon afterwards, on 21 August 1244. He was succeeded by Celestine IV, who died seventeen days later, after a papacy of one year and eight months, and then by Innocent IV. Besides stirring up the gravest disturbances in England and France, vividly described by Matthew Paris, Innocent also showed himself the most bitter enemy of Frederick, who had been his friend before he became Pope. For when he had called a Council at Lyons, which began on 26 June 1245, he summoned the Emperor there. When Frederick did not come, Innocent accused him most severely, pronounced him unworthy of the empire with dreadful curses, deposed him, and deprived him even of communion in the sacraments. The unjust decree of this conciliabulum has been solidly refuted, both by others and recently by the Sorbonnist Launoy, Epist. lib. 7. Nevertheless, the Emperor, devoted as he was, invaded Italy that same year, afflicted the Milanese severely, and reduced the Pope himself to such straits that he repented of the excommunication. Still, Innocent, having raised money from every side, arranged for Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia, to be elected Emperor through the Archbishops of Mainz and Cologne, who had sworn against Frederick. He also sent assassins against Frederick, who were caught and paid the penalty of death for their crime. Henry too died of a wound received at Ulm on 7 February 1248. In his place, with the Pope's support, William, Count of Holland, was put forward, but under pressure from Conrad, Frederick's son, he gave way. At Rome the Pope again bribed with gold two assassins, among them Peter de Vinea, who had earlier been a faithful servant of the Emperor, and suborned them. They were pretended to have been sent out by the Emperor against his own life, as a cover for the deed. When the fraud was discovered, the other was hanged as a doctor. Peter de Vinea was blinded and led about through the cities of Italy so that he might confess the crime everywhere. Finally, out of fear of a more severe punishment, he dashed his head against the column to which he had been chained in prison, and killed himself. It had been foretold to Frederick that he would die in a certain castle at Florence. So he always avoided Florence, and on 13 December 1250 he came to a certain fortress in Apulia, which was called Florentina, and was seized by illness. On 26 December of the same month, after reigning thirty-eight years, he died. Some report that the sick man was smothered by his bastard son Manfred, at the instigation of the Pope, who pushed a cushion into his mouth. Others contradict this, especially Collenuccio in his Life of him. From his death there was an interregnum of nearly twenty-two years, during which one and another were elected in turn, yet in that time of upheaval, which the Popes had brought in, they did not hold the substance of power. Worn out also by constant quarrels and hostilities, the Emperors gradually became more lax and deserted Italy, and they all but yielded to the Popes, those Aeolus-like winds of such great disturbances.

units.la: CVI. Implacabilis verò adversus Fridericum Impera- torem odii à Pontificibus Romanis concepti causas his fere verbis Aventinus, Annal. Boj. lib. VII. p. 411. pandit.
units.tr: CVI. The causes of the implacable hatred that the Roman Pontiffs conceived against the Emperor Frederick, Aventinus sets out in roughly these words, Annals of Bavaria, book VII, p. 411.

units.la: Ejus (Fridorici) potentia, vires, prudentia, magnitudo animi, rerum bellicarum peritia, vicinitas (nam in Italia contra morem veterum Imperatorum habitabat, Germaniam per filium administrabat bis duntaxat ex Italia in Germaniam egressus) formidolosa atque suspecta fuere Romano sacerdotum senatui. Quod Gregorius IX. Pont. Max. non it inficias, sed ingenuè fatetur. Visum est flaminibus Romanensibus Imperium Romanum magis florere, quàm ipsis utile foret. Placuit id contundere, atque discordia non solum debilitare, sed in cineres quoque atque favillas redigere, & Fridericum huncce à fastigio rerum humanarum deturbare.
units.tr: Frederick's power, his forces, his prudence, his greatness of spirit, his skill in warfare, and his proximity (for he lived in Italy, contrary to the custom of the older emperors, and governed Germany through his son, having come out of Italy into Germany only twice) were frightening and suspect to the Roman senate of priests. Pope Gregory IX, the Supreme Pontiff, does not deny this but openly admits it. It seemed to the Roman flamens that the Roman Empire was flourishing more than was useful to themselves. They resolved to crush it, to weaken it not only by discord but to reduce it to ashes and embers, and to hurl this Frederick down from the height of human affairs.

units.la: CVII. Operæ etiam pretium non nullum hic facturus videor, si tum ipsius Friderici II. tum Eberhardi etiam Salisburgensis Archiepiscopi adversus Romanam curiam orationes gravissimas, ab eodem Aventino descriptas, lectori repræsentavero, cùm institutum nostrum propius attingant. Fridericus igitur Imperator ad Othonem Bavariæ Ducem, reliquôsque Germaniæ Principes literas mittit, quarum, teste Aventino Annal. Bojor. lib. VII. p. 416417. hæc sententia fuit: Pontifices Romanos auctos divitiis & dignitate à se atque cæteris Imperatoribus, æmulos esse pertinacissimos omnium Regum atque Principum, neque parem ultra ferre posse. Manibus pedibúsque, noctes diésque id eos conari, ut non tam se, quàm sacrosancto Romano Imperio tanquam capite oppresso, facile cæteris membris omnibus servitutem imponant: affectare eos dominationem atque Divinitatem, nempe ut ab omnibus haud aliter, imò magis quàm Deus timeantur. Nam multos Antichristos inesse Romanensibus illis, nec ullos alios, quemadmodum opera ostendunt, exitio Christianæ religioni esse. Se quidem optimè sentire de Christo atque ejus religione prædicat, nihilque magis cupere, quàm ut suo tempore Respub. Christiana pristinam Majestatem, simplicitatem & pacem recuperet. Quod fieri nequaquam potest, nisi spinæ eradicentur, hoc est, ambitio, superbia, fastus, luxus, sacerdotum Romanorum, subtractis opibus atque divitiis extirpentur radicitus. Copia rerum sapientissimos quosque corrumpere solet. In rebus Divinis non solum Episcopum Romanum, sed unumquemque sacerdotem sibi Patrem fore, modo rebus prophanis sibi commissis abstineat, proponit. Imperium Christianum, cujus ipse caput constitutus sit à Deo, non armis, non vi opprimi posse; sed luxuria, cupiditate, quæ radix omnium malorum est, enervari, adulterari, corrumpi. Quod ne fiat, se obviam iturum, se summopere pro commisso sibi à Deo negotio, potestate ensêque Divinitus tradito contra enisurum, ut ovili Pastorem, populo Pontificem, mundo parentem, detracta persona lupi, tyranni atque Domini restituat: ut eundem abdicata regnorum, humanarum litium cura, prophanorum negotiorum administratione, quibus illi interdictum sit, ad æmulanda pauperis Christi, cujus se vicarium jactitat, vestigia cogat; se amplius non passurum, ut Christianæ plebi lupus ovina pelle tectus diutius imponat. Opus vel maximum pietatis esse atque charitatis, gratissimum immortali Deo, opes & aurum, irritamenta malorum sacerdotibus auferre. Nam hæc, inquit, perniciem esse religionis, adeo ut homo ille, qui dicitur Papa, divitiis nimium auctus, maximo pietatis Christianæ detrimento, omnia sibi licere more tyrannorum pessimorum putet, rationem actuum nemini, quasi sit Deus, reddere velit: Id quod soli Deo convenit, usurpet; se errare ullave mendacii religione adstringi non posse, credi sibi impudentissime simulque imperiose postulet. Fraudes, dolos, commenta, fucum taceri; sibi ut vicino eum intus & in cute notum esse. Proinde quicunque rem Christianam salvam esse velint, faveant, adsint, & causam Christi servatoris nostri, omnium denique Christianorum agenti, bene precentur. Post missis ad Wenceslaum Regem Bojemiæ legatis inter alia nunciat; jam pridem eos, qui Babyloniæ, hoc est, Romæ Templo Dei incubent, Divinitatem affectare, & astute id dissimulare, solàsque Germanicas vires ab his timeri. Similes Augusti hujus sermones graphicos etiam Matthæus Paris Hist. Major. pag. 483. ad Comi tem Cornubiæ Richardum, & pag. 502. 503. ad Angliæ Regem, nec non pag. 680. 681. &c. ad Proceres Angliæ describit.
units.tr: CVII. I think it will be worth doing something here if I set before the reader the very weighty speeches, described by the same Aventinus, both of Frederick II himself and of Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, against the Roman curia, since they touch our purpose fairly closely. Emperor Frederick therefore sent letters to Otto, Duke of Bavaria, and to the other princes of Germany, whose substance, according to Aventinus, Annals of Bavaria, book VII, pp. 416–417, was this: The Roman Pontiffs, enlarged in riches and dignity by himself and the other emperors, are the most stubborn rivals of all kings and princes, and cannot bear anyone's equal. With hands and feet, night and day, they strive to reduce not so much him as the most holy Roman Empire, as a head crushed, and so to impose slavery on all the other members with ease. They aim at lordship and divinity, so that they may be feared by all no differently, indeed more, than God. For, as their works show, there are many Antichrists in those Romans and none others, and they are a ruin to the Christian religion. He declares that he himself thinks most rightly about Christ and his religion, and desires nothing more than that in due time the Christian commonwealth recover its ancient majesty, simplicity and peace. This cannot be done in any way unless the thorns are uprooted, that is, ambition, pride, haughtiness and luxury of the Roman priests are eradicated to the root by removing their wealth and riches. An abundance of things usually corrupts even the wisest. He proposes that in divine matters not only the Roman bishop but every priest should be a father to him, provided he abstains from the secular affairs committed to him. The Christian empire, of which he himself has been appointed head by God, cannot be oppressed by arms or force, but is weakened, adulterated and corrupted by luxury and greed, which is the root of all evils. Lest this happen, he will go to meet it, and will strive with all his might, with the power and sword divinely handed to him by God for the business committed to him, so that he may restore to the fold a Shepherd, to the people a Pontiff, to the world a father, the mask of the wolf, tyrant and lord having been stripped off; so that, with the care of kingdoms and human disputes laid aside and the administration of secular business, from which they are forbidden, given up, he may compel the same man to imitate the footsteps of the poor Christ, whose vicar he boasts himself to be. He will no longer allow a wolf covered in sheep's skin to lie upon the Christian people for long. It is the greatest work of piety and charity, and most pleasing to the immortal God, to take away wealth and gold, the incitements of evils, from the wicked priests. For these, he says, are the ruin of religion, to such an extent that that man who is called the Pope, swollen beyond measure with riches, to the greatest detriment of Christian piety, thinks that everything is permitted to him in the manner of the worst tyrants, wishes to render an account of his acts to no one, as if he were God; he claims for himself what belongs to God alone, and demands most shamelessly and imperiously that he be believed when he says he cannot err or be bound by any obligation of lying. Frauds, tricks, inventions and disguises are kept silent; to me, as a neighbour, he is known inside and out. Therefore, whoever wishes the Christian cause to be safe, let them favour it, support it, and pray well for the cause of Christ our Saviour and of all Christians. Afterwards, having sent envoys to Wenceslaus, King of Bohemia, he announces among other things that those who sit in Babylon, that is, in the temple of God at Rome, have long been aiming at divinity and craftily concealing it, and that only German forces are feared by them. Matthew Paris, Chronica Majora, p. 483, describes similar graphic speeches of this Augustus to Richard, Earl of Cornwall, and at p. 502–503 to the King of England, and also at p. 680–681, etc., to the nobles of England.

units.la: CVIII. Eberhardus vero Salisburgensis Archiepiscopus, quem Archimystam Juuaniæ Aventinus insignit, orationem ejusmodi, eodem Aventino lib. VII. p. 420, 421. narrante in Reginoburgensibus Comitiis A. MCCXLI. habuit: Christus Servator, Dominus & Deus noster relicto æthereo solio, atque, ut ita loquar, immortalitate, mortalis pauperque effectus est,
units.tr: CVIII. Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, whom Aventinus styles the Archmystic of Bavaria, delivered a speech of this kind at the Diet of Regensburg in the year 1241, as Aventinus relates in book VII, pp. 420–421: Christ our Saviour, Lord and God, leaving the heavenly throne and, so to speak, immortality, was made mortal and poor,

units.la: Eberhardi Salisburgensis Archiepiscopi Oratio adversus Hierarchiam R. Babylonios flammes pathetica. est, ut nos immortales atque divites efficeret. Cúmque devictis inferis, triumphabundus rursus in Cœlum rediturus esset, pacem suam nobis dedit, pacem suam nobis reliquit, concordiam atque mutuum amorem, tanquam notam atque tesseram, qua cives sui à militibus inferi Jovis discernerentur, assignavit. Summo opere quoque admonuit, ut falsos Christos, falsos prophetas vitaremus, qui tecti pelle ovina, nimirum Christiano nomine atque Pontificio titulo, nobis dominari atque illudere cuperent. Quos ex spinis atque operibus, nempe avaritia, luxu, contentione, odio, invidia, bellis, discordia malis, libidine dominandi, ambitione cognosci debere docuit. Quid nam apertius hisce verbis, quàm Babylonis Pharisaeos atque Scribas, Cœlestis Imperator indicavit? Sub Pontificis Max. titulo, pastoris pelle, lupum saevissimum, nisi caeci sumus, sentimus. Romani flamines arma in omnes habent Christianos, audendo, fallendo, & bella ex bellis serendo magni facti, oves trucidant, occidunt, pacem concordiam terris depellunt, intestina bella, domesticas seditiones ab inferis eliciunt, &c.
