Non Pontificis more gregi consulunt, sed potius immanitate tyranni, licenter debacchantur. Justitia rarescit, impietas, avaritia, cupiditas honorum, pecuniæ studium crebrescit, &c. Flamines illi Babyloniæ soli regnare cupiunt, ferre parem non possunt, non desistent, donec omnia pedibus suis conculcaverint, atque in templo Dei sedeant, extollantúrque supra omne id quod colitur. Fames opum, sitis honorum inexplebilis est. Qui servus servorum est, dominus dominorum, perinde ac si foret Deus, esse cupit. Sacros cœtus atque concilia fratrum, imò dominorum suorum aspernatur. Timet ne eorum, quæ adversus auspicia, leges, intercessiones indies magis atque magis gerit, rationem reddere cogatur. Ingentia loquitur, quasi verò Deus esset. Nova consilia sub pectore volutat, ut proprium sibi constituat imperium: leges commutat, suas sancit, contaminat, diripit, spoliat, fraudat, occidit perditus homo ille, quem Antichristum vocare solent, in cujus fronte nomen contumeliæ scriptum est: Deus sum, errare non possum. In Templo Dei sedet, longè latéque dominatur. Sed sicut in arcanis S. literarum, qui legit, intelligat: docti intelligent, omnes impii impie agent, neque intelligent. Imperator vana appellatio & sola umbra est: Reges decem pariter existunt, qui orbem terrae, Romanum quondam imperium, non ad regendum, sed ad consumendum partiti sunt. Decem cornua, id quod D. Aurelio Augustino incredibile visum est, Turcae, Graeci, Ægyptii, Afri, Hispani, Galli, Angli, Germani, Siculi, Itali Romanas Provincias possident, Romanosque in his excidere colonos. Cornúque parvulum sub his succrevit, quod oculos habet, & os loquens grandia, tria potissimum, Italiae, Siciliae, Germaniae regna in ordinem redegit, sibíque servire cogit insustentabili dominatione populum Christi sanctosque Dei vexat, divina humana miscet, infanda, execrabilia molitur. Quid hac prophetia apertius? &c. Liceat verò Everhardo huic jungere alterum in Anglia σύγχρονον nisi fallor, virum pietate & doctrina maximum, Robertum Lincolnien-sem Episcopum, qui postquam illa ipsa, qua obiit, nocte, & praecedente longam querimoniam apud circumstantes Presbyteros & Monachos de infelicissimo Ecclesiae statu effudisset, Papam omnium malorum causam esse confirmans, eúmque propterea haereticum & Antichristum appellans, tandem in his verbis fatidicis beatam animam Deo reddidit: Non liberabitur Ecclesia ab Ægyptiaca servitute, nisi in ore gladii cruentandi.
units.tr: Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, his fiery and passionate Oration against the Hierarchy of the Roman Babylonians. so that he might make us immortal and rich. And when, the powers of hell having been defeated, he was about to return triumphantly to heaven, he gave us his peace, left us his peace, and assigned concord and mutual love, as a mark and token by which his citizens might be distinguished from the soldiers of the infernal Jove. He also warned most earnestly that we should avoid false Christs and false prophets, who, covered with sheep's skin, that is, under the Christian name and the Pontifical title, wish to rule over us and mock us. He taught that they must be recognised from their thorns and works, namely avarice, luxury, strife, hatred, envy, wars, discord, and lust for domination and ambition. What could be plainer than these words, in which the heavenly Emperor pointed out the Pharisees and Scribes of Babylon? Under the title of Supreme Pontiff, in the skin of a shepherd, we perceive a most savage wolf, unless we are blind. The Roman flamens have arms against all Christians; by daring, deceiving, and sowing wars out of wars they have grown great, they slaughter and kill the sheep, they drive peace and concord from the earth, they stir up internal wars and domestic seditions from the depths of hell, etc. They do not look after the flock in the manner of a Pontiff, but rather, with the savagery of a tyrant, they rage without restraint. Justice grows scarce; impiety, avarice, desire for honours, and the pursuit of money increase, etc. Those flamens of Babylon alone wish to reign, cannot bear an equal, and will not cease until they have trampled everything under their feet and sit in the temple of God, exalted above everything that is worshipped. The hunger for wealth and the thirst for honours are insatiable. He who is the servant of servants wishes to be lord of lords, as if he were God. He spurns the sacred gatherings and councils of his brothers, indeed of his lords. He fears lest he be compelled to render an account of those things which he does daily more and more against the auspices, the laws and the protests. He speaks grand things, as if he were God. He turns new plans over in his breast so that he may establish a dominion of his own; he changes laws, enacts his own, defiles, plunders, despoils, defrauds, and kills. That lost man, whom they are accustomed to call the Antichrist, on whose forehead the name of insult is written: "I am God, I cannot err", sits in the temple of God and rules far and wide. But, as in the mysteries of the holy Scriptures, let him who reads understand: the learned will understand, while all the impious will act impiously and will not understand. The Emperor is an empty name and a mere shadow; ten kings likewise exist, who have divided the world, formerly the Roman empire, not to rule it but to consume it. Ten horns, which seemed incredible to the blessed Augustine: the Turks, Greeks, Egyptians, Africans, Spaniards, Gauls, English, Germans, Sicilians, and Italians possess the Roman provinces, and the Romans have perished in them as colonists. And from among these a little horn has grown up, which has eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and has brought three kingdoms in particular, of Italy, Sicily and Germany, into order, and forces them to serve it; it harasses the people of Christ and the holy ones of God with an unbearable domination, mixes divine things with human, and undertakes unspeakable and execrable deeds. What is plainer than this prophecy? etc. Moreover, I may here join to Eberhard another, if I am not mistaken, a contemporary in England, a man greatest in piety and learning, Robert, Bishop of Lincoln, who, after pouring out in the very night on which he died, and the night before, a long lament before the surrounding elders and monks on the most unhappy state of the Church, affirming that the Pope was the cause of all evils and therefore calling him a heretic and Antichrist, at last in these prophetic words rendered his blessed soul to God: The Church will not be freed from Egyptian servitude unless it is to be stained by the mouth of the sword.

units.la: CIX. Invalescebant in Ecclesia Romana magis magisque ordines Mendicantium, Franciscanorum cumprimis & Dominicanorum, quos rebus suis augendis prae coeteris conducibiles esse, facile Pontifices animadvertebant. Omnis eorum conatus huc jam tendebat, ut & superstitiones Paparum tyrannide obtrusas, & Monarchiam ejus tot jam fulminibus, arte & Marte stabilitam, masculè defenderent. Sicut igitur manus manum lavat, & gratia gratiam parit; ita nihil non Monachis indulsere Pontifices. Lutetiae orta inter Universitatis Professores Dominicanos controversia, Romæ pro his contra illos decisa est, & Dominicanis Domino Papæ devotis & propter eorum multimoda obsequia, in hoc certamine meliorem calculum reportantibus, facultas legendi licenter in Theologia data est, ut Matthæus Paris pag. 880. loquitur. Sed & Alexander IV. Papa eos, qui statum Ordinum Dominici & Francisci acribus libellis impetebant anathemate perculit. Inde flammis mancipatum est Opus Guilhelmi de S. Amore, & Magistrorum Parisiensium reliquorum, cui titulum secerant: Tractatus de periculis novissimorum temporum, quo Prædicatorum & Minorum ordines perstringentes, statum salutis eorum in dubium vocabant, simulque eos, ob adulationem, hypocrisin, otium sumptuosum, & justitiæ propriæ, posthabita justitia Christi, jactantiam, graviter pulsabant. Exemplar libri in Sorbona Parisiensi custodiri, Carolus Molinæus Orat. de Theol. dignitate pag. 184. testatur. Ediditque etiam Wolphgangus Wissenburgius Basileæ A. MDLV. Guilielmi illius sermones duos, una cum aliis melioris commatis scriptoribus veteribus, qui de corrupto Ecclesiæ statu publicas querelas consignarunt.
units.tr: 109. The Mendicant orders, especially the Franciscans and the Dominicans, grew ever stronger in the Roman Church, since the Popes readily saw that they were more useful than others for advancing their interests. All their efforts now aimed at manfully defending both the superstitions imposed by the Popes' tyranny and their monarchy, which had already been established by so many thunderbolts, by craft and by arms. So, as one hand washes another, and favour begets favour, the Popes granted the monks everything. A controversy that arose at Paris among the Dominican professors of the University was decided at Rome in their favour against the others. The Dominicans, devoted to the Lord Pope and, on account of their manifold services, carrying off the better vote in this contest, were given the right to lecture freely in theology, as Matthew Paris speaks p. 880. But Pope Alexander IV also struck with anathema those who attacked the state of the Orders of Dominic and Francis with bitter pamphlets. Hence the work of William of St Amour and of the other Parisian Masters was consigned to the flames. They had entitled it Treatise on the Dangers of the Last Times. In it, while censuring the Orders of the Preachers and the Minors, they called their state of salvation into doubt, and at the same time severely struck at them for flattery, hypocrisy, expensive idleness, and boasting of their own righteousness, with the righteousness of Christ set aside. Carolus Molinaeus testifies, in his oration on the dignity of theology, p. 184, that a copy of this book is kept in the Sorbonne at Paris. Wolfgang Wissenburg also published at Basel in 1555 two sermons of that William, together with other older writers of better style, who set down in writing public complaints about the corrupt state of the Church.

units.la: CX. Perquam vero notatu dignum est, quòd Magistri illi Parisienses in Tractatu illo memorato, de horrendis Monachorum Æternum Euangelium meditantium machinationibus, narrant hæc in verba: Jam sunt anni 55. quòd aliqui laborant ad mutandum Euangelium Christi in aliud Euangelium, quod dicunt fore perfectius, melius & dignius, quod appellant Euangelium Spiritus S. quo adveniente evacuabitur, ut dicunt, Euangelium Christi; ut parati sumus offendere in Euangelio illo maledicto. Dixerant autem paulò ante, ab adventu Domini transfactos jam esse annos MCCLV. & paulò post subjiciunt, Euangelium æternum Parisiis, ubi viget S. Scripturæ studium positum fuisse publicè ad exemplandum anno Domini MCCLIV. Addunt tria illa verba, quorum Daniel cap. 5. fit mentio, tio, Mane, Tekel, Phares, jam visa esse in Ecclesia. Scripta enim sunt, inquiunt, in maledicto illo libro, quem appellant Euangelium æternum, quod in Ecclesia iam propalatum est, propter quod timendum est de subversione Ecclesiæ. Primum verbum est, Mane, id est, Numeravit Deus Regnum tuum, & complevit illud, vel conclusit, ut exponit Daniel 5 Capitulo. Ibi enim numeratur Regnum Ecclesiæ scilicet Euangelium Christi & concluditur in 1260. annis ab incarnatione. Item ibi invenitur Tekel, quod est appensum in statera, & inventum est minus habens, ut exponit Daniel 5. Capitulo. Nam ibi comparatur Euangelium Christi ad Euangelium æternum, quanto minus lucet Luna quam Sol, quanto minus valet testa, quam nucleus. Et multæ tales ibi sunt scriptæ comparationes quibus probatur minus valere Euangelium Christi, quam Euangelium æternum. Item in Scriptura illa, scilicet in Euangelio æterno invenitur Phares, id est, divisum est Regnum tuum à Te, ut exponit Daniel cap. 5. Nam ibi invenitur, quod Regnum Ecclesiæ dividetur post prædictum tempus ab illis, qui tenent Euangelium æternum. Mysteriorum Euangelii hujus catalogum ampliorem ex Henrico Erphordiensi Chronicorum cap. 93. nec non Nicolao Eymerico Direct. Inquis. par. 2. q. 9. §. 4. Cl. Usserius de Christ. Eccl. succeff. cap. 9. p. 240. &c. fusius repræsentat. Verbo, dogmata hujus Euangelii, seu potius Alcorani Monastici, hæc fuere: Deum Patrem sub lege regnâsse, filium sub gratia, sed jam exortis quatuor mendicantium ordinibus Spiritum S. suo Regno inaugurari, ad finem usque mundi duraturo, atque eos solos salvatum iri, qui novo huic Euangelio credituri essent. Christi enim Euangelium non esse verum, persectum & salutare, proin abolendum & rejiciendum. Parvi etiam æstimanda esse ejus Sacramenta. Aliud etiam sacerdotium sacerdotio Christi sub eo Euangelio successurum. Solos Nudipedales idoneos fore ad instruendum homines de spiritualibus & æternis. Religionem Christi, quæ jam multos peperit vocatos ad fidem Christi, non esse veram Ecclesiam. Euangelio Christi neminem perfectum reddi. Spiritum S. sub hoc Euangelio accepturum aliquid ab Ecclesia, sicut Christus in quantum homo, accepit à Spiritu S. Christum & Apostolos non fuisse perfectos in vita contemplantium: contemplativam vero vitam sub hoc demum Euangelio fructificaturum per ordinem Monachorum: & per eosdem Spiritum sanctum Ecclesiam recturum, sicut in V. T. eam conjugati, in Novo sub Euangelio Christi Clerici rexerint. Quis non hic cum Campiano Rat. 8. exclamet: Tempora, Tempora, cujusmodi monstrum aluistis!
units.tr: 110. It is indeed worth noting that those Parisian Masters, in the Treatise mentioned above, concerning the dreadful machinations of the monks who were devising an Eternal Gospel, relate these words: For it is now fifty-five years since some have laboured to change the Gospel of Christ into another gospel, which they say will be more perfect, better and more worthy, and which they call the Gospel of the Holy Spirit. When it comes, the Gospel of Christ will, as they say, be emptied out; and we are ready to take offence at that accursed Gospel. They had said a little earlier that 1255 years had passed since the coming of the Lord, and shortly afterwards they add: The Eternal Gospel was publicly set forth at Paris, where the study of Holy Scripture flourishes, for copying, in the year of the Lord 1254. They add that those three words mentioned in Daniel chapter 5, Mane, Tekel, Phares, have now already been seen in the Church. For they are written, they say, in that accursed book which they call the Eternal Gospel, which has now been spread abroad in the Church, on account of which the overthrow of the Church is to be feared. The first word is Mane, that is, God has numbered your kingdom and completed it, or concluded it, as Daniel explains in chapter 5. For there the kingdom of the Church, namely the Gospel of Christ, is numbered and concluded in 1260 years from the incarnation. Likewise there is found Tekel, which is weighed in the balance and found wanting, as Daniel explains in chapter 5. For there the Gospel of Christ is compared with the Eternal Gospel: as the moon gives less light than the sun, and as the potsherd is worth less than the kernel. And many such comparisons are written there, by which it is proved that the Gospel of Christ is worth less than the Eternal Gospel. Likewise in that Scripture, namely in the Eternal Gospel, is found Phares, that is, your kingdom is divided from you, as Daniel explains in chapter 5. For there it is found that the kingdom of the Church will be divided, after the said time, by those who hold the Eternal Gospel. Cl. Usher sets out a fuller catalogue of the mysteries of this Gospel, drawing on Henry of Erfurt, Chronicles, chapter 93, and also on Nicolas Eymeric, Directorium Inquisitorum, part 2, question 9, §4; see De Christianarum Ecclesiarum successionibus, chapter 9, p. 240, etc. In short, the doctrines of this Gospel, or rather of this Monastic Alcoran, were these: That God the Father reigned under the law, and the Son under grace; but that now, with the four Mendicant orders having arisen, the Holy Spirit is to be inaugurated in his kingdom, to last until the end of the world, and that those alone will be saved who are going to believe this new Gospel. For the Gospel of Christ is not true, perfect and saving, and therefore must be abolished and rejected. Its sacraments are also to be held in little esteem. Another priesthood will also succeed the priesthood of Christ under that Gospel. Only the Barefoot friars will be fit to instruct men about spiritual and eternal things. The religion of Christ, which has already brought forth many called to the faith of Christ, is not the true Church. No one is made perfect by the Gospel of Christ. The Holy Spirit under this Gospel will receive something from the Church, just as Christ as man received from the Holy Spirit. Christ and the Apostles were not perfect in the contemplative life; only under this Gospel will the contemplative life at last bear fruit, through the order of monks; and through the same Holy Spirit the Church will be ruled, just as in the Old Testament married men ruled it, and in the New Testament, under the Gospel of Christ, the clergy have ruled it. Who here would not, with Campian in his eighth Ration, cry out: Times, times, what a monster you have nurtured!

units.la: CXI.
units.tr: CXI.

units.la: Ecquid vero Monachis Euangelio Christi stragem ita inferentibus à Pontifice Romano factum putamus? Scilicet visum illis, homines sibi quàm maximè necessarios tractare quàm lenissimè, omnique ratione providere, ne illi quoquo modo odium offensámque populi incurrerent. Lubet eam in rem Matthæum Paris in historia anni MCCLVI. pag. 909. 910. audire ubi sic ille: Crebrescentibus scandalis & odiis inter Magistros Parisienses & Fratres Prædicatores, electi sunt cum magna deliberatione celeberrimi magistri Lectores, videlicet Magister Guilhelmus de sancto Amore, & Magister Odo de Duaco (qui nobiliter rexerant in artibus, in Decretis & tunc in Theologia) Magister Christianus Canonicus Beluacensis (qui maximus quasi Philosophus emeritus, postquam in artibus rexerat, in Theologia lecturivit) Magister Nicolaus de Baro super Albam (qui rexerat in artibus, Legibus & Decretis, ad Legendum in Theologia præparatus.) Magister Johannes de Sicca villa Anglicus, Rhetor Universitatis, & Magister Belin Gallicus (nominatissimi Philosophi, regentes in artibus) omnes isti de nobilissimis viris procreati, præelecti sunt per magnum (quia fides patiebatur detrimentum) consilium & deliberationem, ut Romam adeant, & Dominum Papam pro tranquillitate Universitatis Parisiensis, & fidei redintegratione (maximè cùm hoc malum majus generare comminetur) collectáque sunt eis ex Universitate viatica. Fratres námque quædam nova prædicabant, legebant & docebant (ut dicebatur) deliramenta, quæ de libro Joachim Abbatis (cujus scripta
units.tr: Did we think, then, that the Roman Pontiff did nothing about the monks who were inflicting such ruin on the Gospel of Christ? Evidently it seemed good to him to handle the men he most needed as gently as possible, and to take every care that they should not in any way incur the hatred and offence of the people. On this matter let us hear Matthew Paris in his history of the year 1256, pp. 909, 910, where he speaks as follows: As scandals and hatreds grew between the Parisian masters and the Preaching Friars, the most famous master readers were chosen after careful deliberation: namely Master William of Saint-Amour and Master Odo of Douai (who had taught nobly in the arts, in the Decretals, and then in theology), Master Christian, canon of Beauvais (a very great philosopher, long since retired, who after teaching in the arts had lectured in theology), Master Nicholas of Bar-sur-Aube (who had taught in the arts, in law and in the Decretals, and was prepared to lecture in theology), Master John of Sicca Villa, an Englishman, rhetor of the University, and Master Belin, a Frenchman (most renowned philosophers, teaching in the arts). All these men, born of the noblest families, were chosen by great deliberation (since the faith was suffering harm) to go to Rome and ask the lord Pope for the peace of the University of Paris and the restoration of the faith (especially since this evil threatened to breed a greater one). Travelling money was collected for them from the University. For the friars were preaching, reading and teaching certain new things, (as it was said) mad notions, which they had drawn from the book of Joachim the Abbot (whose writings

units.la: Et à Pontificibus segniter repressus. pta Gregorius Papa damnaverat) extraxerunt. Et quendam librum composuerunt, quem sic eis intitulare complacuit: Incipit Euangelium æternum: & quædam alia, quæ non expedit recitari. Prædicatores autem contra Vniversitatem suos expeditos nuntios ilico mittebant, ut Magistris in faciem contradicerent. Subsannavit populus eleemosynas consuetas substrahendo, vocans eos hypocritas, Antichristi successores, Regum & Principum adulatores & falsos consiliatores, ordinariorum contemptores, & eorundem supplantatores, thalamorum Regalium subintratores, confessionum prævaricatores, qui peragrantes ignotas Provincias, peccandi audaciam subministrabant. Auditis igitur hinc inde querelis, præcepit Papa, ut novus ille liber, quem Euangelium æternum nominant, secretò, & si fieri posset, sine fratrum scandalo, combureretur: & alia, quæ de Joachim corruptela dicuntur emanâsse. Vigilanter igitur procurante diligentia Domini Hugonis Cardinalis,& Johannis de Columna Archiepiscopi Messanensis, qui de ordine Prædicatorum erant, cautè ac tacitè procuratum est, ut tumultus ad horam conquiesceret. Utque minori cum Monachorum invidia nefarius liber supprimeretur, visum est Pontifici, ut etiam Magistrorum Parisiensium liber ille, quo horribile arcanum detectum est, damnatus combureretur tum in Curia, quæ tunc Anagniæ residebat, tum Parisiis coram multitudine copiosa, non propter hæresin (ait Guilhelmus Nongiacus in gestis Regis Philippi pag. 537.) sed quia contra præfatos Religiosos seditionem & scandalum movebat.
units.tr: And was sluggishly repressed by the Pontiffs. Pope Gregory had condemned them. They also composed a book, which they were pleased to entitle as follows: Here begins the Eternal Gospel, along with certain other things that it is not expedient to recite. The Preachers, meanwhile, at once sent their ready messengers against the University, to contradict the masters to their faces. The people mocked them by withholding the customary alms, calling them hypocrites, successors of Antichrist, flatterers of kings and princes, false advisers, despisers of the ordinary clergy and their supplanters, sneaking into royal bedchambers, betrayers of confessions, who, roaming through unknown provinces, supplied boldness in sinning. Having heard the complaints on both sides, the Pope ordered that the new book, which they call the Eternal Gospel, be burned secretly and, if possible, without scandal to the friars, along with the other things said to have come out of Joachim's corruption. Then, through the careful diligence of Lord Hugh the Cardinal and John of Columna, Archbishop of Messina, who were of the Order of Preachers, it was quietly and cautiously arranged that the tumult should subside for the time being. And so that the wicked book might be suppressed with less ill-will towards the monks, the Pope judged that the book of the Parisian masters, in which the dreadful secret had been revealed, should also be condemned and burned, both at the Curia, which then resided at Anagni, and at Paris before a large crowd. This was not on account of heresy (says William of Nangis in the deeds of King Philip, p. 537), but because it stirred up sedition and scandal against the said religious.

units.la: CXII.
units.tr: CXII.

units.la: Neque tamen sic Euangelium illud æternum exspirâsse censendum est. Revera enim Papatus horum sequentiúmque temporum, ad ejus amussim factus, Euangelium diversum longè ab Euangelio Christi complectitur. Ut non sine omine & Numine externa quædam prosessio Euangelii æterni, Euangelio Christi abolendo surrogandi, innotescere circa hæc tempora debuerit. Numquid enim non Monachi ad aliud, & quidem Æternum illud (apud inferos scilicet æternum flagraturum) Euangelium transtulerunt, sacramenta Christi genuina vel confpurcarunt, vel aboleverunt, & spuria introduxerunt; sacerdotio Christo sublato sacerdotium aliud, cujus victima est Deus panaceus Maozim stabiliverunt; perfectione Euangelii Christi, quæ in mandato fidei & resipiscentiæ, promissisque cœlestis gloriæ consistit, abnegata, perfectionem Euangelii illius novi Monastici, quæ in supererogatione operum nec à Mose, nec à Christo præceptorum, promissionibúsque præmiorum singularium, quæ aureolas vocant, consistit, substituerunt; Christi spiritu exacerbato novum spiritum Papæ seu Ecclesiæ, rerum Divinarum judicem arbitrúmque unicum obtruserunt; denique vita activa, fide, pœnitentia & charitate pensi non amplius habita, religionis Christianæ apicem in Monachorum contemplationibus infrugiferis collocârunt; quæ ipsissima sunt Euangelii illius æterni mysteria? Deleto igitur licet Euangelio illo Diabolico literali, mansit tamen eadem in Deum blasphemia ac summa, à recta fide in Christum, unicum humani generis servatorem, defectio, in Monachorum scilicet meritis de congruo & condigno, in sanctorum suffragiis, Papæ largitionibus & indulgentiis, in novis bonis operibus, scilicet oblationibus, donis, votis, solutionibus, cœnobiorum erectionibus, jejuniis, vigiliis, somniis, silentiis, horis, organis, sequentiis, hymnis, cantilenis, campanis, altaribus, simulachris, purgatoriis, missis, murmurationibus, mitris, delubris, Templis, Synagogis, Sacrificiis, breviariis, bullis, lustralibus aquis, rosariis, unctionibus, cœmiteriis, cineribus, palmis, calculis precatoriis, candelis, calicibus, crucibus, cathedris, cappis, cereis, turibulis, pompis, ritibus Babylonicis, Ægyptiacis cultibus, spectaculis, reliquiis, regulis, Monachis, mendicabulis, chorchordis, sententiis, summis, picturis, & rebus mille id genus aliis, quas in Euangelio Christi non magis, quàm veterum Babyloniorum, Ægyptiorum, Græcorum, Romanorum profanas religiones reperias.
units.tr: Yet we must not suppose that the Eternal Gospel was thereby extinguished. For indeed the Papacy of these and later times, shaped entirely to its rule, embraces a Gospel far different from the Gospel of Christ. So it is no accident, and not without some sign from heaven, that an open profession of an "Eternal Gospel", to be put in place of the Gospel of Christ and abolish it, should have come to light about this time. For have not the monks transferred the Gospel to another thing, indeed to that "eternal" one (namely, the Gospel which is to burn eternally in hell)? Have they not either defiled or abolished the genuine sacraments of Christ and introduced spurious ones? With the priesthood of Christ taken away, have they not set up another priesthood, whose victim is the god Panaceus Maozim? Having denied the perfection of the Gospel of Christ, which consists in the command of faith and repentance and in the promises of heavenly glory, have they not substituted the perfection of that new monastic gospel, which consists in works of supererogation, commanded neither by Moses nor by Christ, and in the promises of special rewards, which they call aureoles? Having embittered the Spirit of Christ, have they not thrust forward a new spirit of the Pope or the Church, the sole judge and arbiter of divine things? Finally, with the active life no longer valued at the weight of faith, repentance and charity, have they not placed the summit of the Christian religion in the unfruitful contemplations of the monks? Are these not the very mysteries of that "eternal Gospel"? So although that diabolical, literal Gospel has been erased, the same blasphemy against God remains, and the same great apostasy from the right faith in Christ, the sole Saviour of mankind: namely in the merits of the monks, de congruo and de condigno, in the intercessions of the saints, in the Pope's largesses and indulgences, in new good works (that is, oblations, gifts, vows, payments, the erection of monasteries, fastings, vigils, dreams, silences, hours, organs, sequences, hymns, songs, bells, altars, images, purgatories, masses, mumblings, mitres, shrines, temples, synagogues, sacrifices, breviaries, bulls, lustral waters, rosaries, anointings, cemeteries, ashes, palms, prayer beads, candles, chalices, crosses, chairs, copes, wax tapers, censers, processions, Babylonian rites, Egyptian cults, spectacles, relics, rules, monks, begging-friars, chorus-dances, sentences, summae, pictures, and a thousand other things of that kind), which you will find in the Gospel of Christ no more than in the profane religions of the ancient Babylonians, Egyptians, Greeks and Romans.

units.la: CXIII. Mortuo, uti supra memoravimus Friderico II. qui eum exceperunt Imperatores Conradus IV. Wilhelmus Comes Hollandiæ, Richardus, Alphonsus, ferè Pontificum, qui infirmis illis suarum rerum satagere strenuè perrexerunt, libidini succubuerunt, licet subinde adversis partibus confligeretur, & factiones contrariæ Welphorum & Gibellinorum pro suis quæque partibus acriter contenderent. Nihilque Pontificibus prius & antiquius fuit, quàm Imperatores, Reges & Regna infestare, modis omnibus emungere & expilare, & in Albigenses vim crebrò parare & exercere. Qui Innocentio IV. A. MCCLIV. successit Alexander IV. cum Manfredo, Friderici notho bella gerit, in ejus locum Edmundum Regis Angliæ filium Regem Apuliæ & Siciliæ per annulum investit, in Gallia Simoniam exercet, cui Ludovicus Rex sanctionem pragmaticam, qua cautum erat, ne quid nummorum Rege & Regno inscio & dissentiente ex Regno eo in Romanam curiam inferatur, opponit: Flagellantium sectam confirmat. Vrbanus IV. A. MCCLXII. Papa factus, suasu Thomæ Aquinatis festum corporis Christi instituit, idololatria multiplici contaminatum. Clemens IV. inclementissimus omnium Conradi IV. Imperatoris filium unicum Conradinum, Carolo Andegavensium Duci, Regis Galliæ fratri prodidit, eíque etiam de captivo Conradino consulenti, cædem ejus, ut & Friderici Austriaci, inauditi utriusque, suasit hisce verbis: Vita Conradini mors est Caroli: & mors Conradini vita Caroli. Ita par juvenum Principum lectissimum, nemine opinante & ex improviso, carnificis manu, cum insanabili dolore totius orbis melioris, occubuit, simulque Friderici Barbarossæ progenies, universaque adeò stirps Suevica periit, & vacuo Siciliæ, Apuliæ, Calabriæ Regno, unà cum Austriaco Ducatu aliisque etiam ditionibus, pro arbitrio Pontificis dominos mutárunt. Et Sicilia quidem in Gallorum potestatem, ea scilicet lege, ut Pontifici quadraginta quotannis auri marcas Carolus pensitet, concedens, mox vesperis Siculis dignam sævitia Caroli mercedem retulit. Dignissima lectu apud Goldastum in Constit. Imp. occurrit Conradini ad ordines Germaniæ ante fatalem casum Epistola, qua Pontifices infortunii sui fabros flebili sermone apud Ecclesiam accusat. Inclementis hujus successor Gregorius X. A. MCCLXX. Papatum sortitus, Rodolphum Habspurgicum recens electum Imperatorem Romam invitavit, ut corona ex manibus ejus accepta ratum imperium haberet. quod sapientissimus Imperator constanter detrectavit, causatus, Italiam multos Alemannorum Reges consumpsisse, & recitans identidem illud Horatii lib. I. Epist. I.
units.tr: CXIII. After Frederick II died, as we recorded above, he was succeeded by the emperors Conrad IV, William, Count of Holland, Richard, and Alfonso, and nearly all the Pontiffs, who, while these weak men pursued their own affairs vigorously, gave way to lust. Meanwhile there was frequent fighting on opposing sides, and the rival factions of the Guelphs and the Ghibellines contended fiercely each for its own cause. Nor was anything more important or more ancient to the Pontiffs than to harass emperors, kings and kingdoms, to drain and plunder them by every means, and often to prepare and exercise violence against the Albigenses. Innocent IV was succeeded in the year 1254 by Alexander IV, who waged war with Manfred, the bastard son of Frederick. In his place he invested Edmund, son of the King of England, with the kingdom of Apulia and Sicily by a ring. In Gaul he practised simony, and King Louis opposed him with the Pragmatic Sanction, by which it was provided that no money should be carried from that kingdom to the Roman Curia without the king's knowledge and against his will. He also confirmed the sect of the Flagellants. Urban IV, made Pope in the year 1262, at the urging of Thomas Aquinas instituted the feast of Corpus Christi, a thing polluted by manifold idolatry. Clement IV, the most merciless of all, betrayed Conradin, the only son of the Emperor Conrad IV, to Charles, Duke of Anjou, brother of the King of France. When Charles consulted him about the captive Conradin, Clement urged the killing of him, as also of Frederick of Austria, both unheard of, in these words: The life of Conradin is the death of Charles, and the death of Conradin is the life of Charles. Thus that most choice pair of young princes, unexpectedly and without anyone suspecting it, perished by the hand of the executioner, to the unending grief of the whole better part of the world. At the same time the line of Frederick Barbarossa and the whole Swabian stock perished, and the kingdoms of Sicily, Apulia and Calabria, now empty, together with the Duchy of Austria and other domains, changed masters at the Pope's pleasure. Sicily indeed passed into the power of the French, on the condition that Charles should pay the Pope forty marks of gold every year. Soon after, the Sicilian Vespers brought Charles a punishment worthy of his cruelty. A letter of Conradin to the orders of Germany, written before his fatal fall, is most worth reading; it is found in Goldast's Imperial Constitutions. In it he accuses the Pontiffs, in tearful language before the Church, as the architects of his misfortune. The successor of this merciless man, Gregory X, obtained the Papacy in the year 1270 and invited Rudolf of Habsburg, lately elected emperor, to Rome, so that he might hold the empire ratified by receiving the crown from his hands. The most wise Emperor steadfastly declined this, pleading that many kings of the Germans had perished in Italy, and repeatedly quoting that line of Horace, Epistles I.1.

units.la: Me vestigia terrent, Omnia te adversum spectantia, nulla retrorsum.
units.tr: Footprints terrify me, all of them turned toward you, none turned back.

units.la: Ingeminánsque sæpius: Non ibo Romam. Rex sum, Imperator sum. Nec minus pro utilitate Reipub. me facturum confido, quàm si Romæ coronatus fuissem. Ex quo tempore Italiam prorsus Imperatores dereliquerunt, nullis quidem ingratiis Pontificum. Cessit tamen idem Rodolphus Papæ, solitum fulmen minitanti, Romandiolam, quæ septuagies mille auri drachmas annuas pendebat. Bolum hùnce minimè contemnendum bonus & pacificus ille Princeps in os cerberi illius conjecit, quò placatus electionem ejus ratam haberet. Impletum scilicet in Pontificibus quod de Pseudoprophetis olim Micheas pronuntiavit cap. III. 5. Si quis non dederit aliquid in ore eorum עליון מלחמה sanctificant contra eum bellum. Sed & Michaëlem Palæologum promittentem, novam Romam se veteri subjecturum, si Carolo Andegavensi adversario suo resisteret, admittere voluit his legibus, ut in Officio Græcorum primus inter Patriarchas Papa nominetur: Ut Romam è Græcia appellare fas sit: denique ut in omnibus rebus principem ipse locum obtineat. Sed mortuo mox Michaele, & contra-nitentibus Episcopis Græciæ, negotiatio evanuit. Constuxit idem Papa conclave Cardinalium, lege in Concilio Lugdunensi lata, qua conclavis ratio in electione novi Pontificis continetur. Nicolaus III. A. MCCLXXVII. ex Ursinorum familia Pontifex creatus, Platina teste, munus senatorium, quod ante hoc Principibus & Regibus demandari consueverat, solus obivit; Caroloque Andegavensi, Siciliæ Regi, quòd electioni ejus minùs faveret, & major etiam potentiorque, quàm Romanæ Curiæ expediret, videretur, infensus, Hetruriæ vicariatum abstulit, & Siciliam Gallis erepturus, Petrúmque Aragonum Regem adversus eum concitans, conjurationem, quæ in Siculas tandem noctes, erupit, horribilem fovit. Contra Martinus IV. Gallus sordido genere natus, A. MCCLXXXI. Papatus fasces rapiens, Carolum restituere parat, Siculis rebus suis conclamatis itaque eum ter innvocantibus: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, dona nobis pacem. Imperatorem Constantinopoleos, quòd Aragoniæ Regi faveret, anathemate percussit. Germaniæ adeò infensus, ut in stagnum eam conversam videre sæpe optaverit. Qui hunc excepit, Honorius IV. Petrum Arragoniæ Regem, quòd Siciliæ Regnum sibi à Nicolao III. collatum Gallis restituere abnueret, anathemate ferit. Ejus Legatus Thusculanus Cardinalis in Germaniam ablegatus, ut per quinquennium ab omni Clero proventuum quadrantem poscat, Wurzburgi in Conventu Episcoporum repulsam passus, Antichristi Satrapa ab iisdem per os Tullen-sis fis Episcopi Probi, cujus gravissimam contra vultures Romulæos apud Aventinum lib. VII. legere est orationem; vocatur merito. Malè tamen sub successore hujus Nicolao IV. similis παρρησία[?] cessit Johanni Bitterensi Franciscano, & Petro Cassiodoro Italis, qui quòd Papam Antichristum insignivissent, è monumentis extracti & combusti sunt. Excommunicatus ab eodem est Mænardus Tiroli Comes, quòd ambitioni Episcopi Tridentini resistens, ejus arces invasisset. qui publica in apologia Episcoporum scelera exagitans, effœminatos Antichristos & prodigiosos Eunuchos eos vocat, pejores Turcis, Saracenis, Tartaris, & Judæis; proin à sævo sibíque iniquo Pontifice ad æquum Pastorem, pientissimúmque Patrem provocat.
units.tr: Repeating it often: I will not go to Rome. I am King, I am Emperor. Nor do I doubt that I shall serve the public good no less than if I had been crowned at Rome. From that time the emperors utterly abandoned Italy, though not without the goodwill of the Popes. Yet the same Rudolph gave way to the Pope, who was threatening his customary thunderbolt, and surrendered Romagna, which paid seventy thousand gold drachmas a year. That bribe, by no means to be despised, the good and peaceable prince threw into the jaws of that Cerberus, so that the Pope, placated, would ratify his election. Thus what Micah long ago pronounced concerning the false prophets (ch. 3:5) was fulfilled in the Popes: If anyone does not put something into their mouths, [קדשו עליו מלחמה] they sanctify war against him. Michael Palaeologus, too, who promised to subject New Rome to Old Rome if the Pope would oppose his rival Charles of Anjou, the Pope was willing to admit on these conditions: that in the Office of the Greeks the Pope be named first among the Patriarchs; that it be lawful to appeal to Rome from Greece; and finally that he himself hold the chief place in all matters. But Michael soon died, and the bishops of Greece resisted, and the negotiation came to nothing. The same Pope built a conclave of cardinals, under a law passed at the Council of Lyons, which sets out the procedure for electing a new Pontiff. Nicholas III, created Pope in 1277 from the family of the Orsini, according to Platina, alone discharged the senatorial office, which before this had customarily been entrusted to princes and kings. Being hostile to Charles of Anjou, King of Sicily, because he seemed less favourable to Nicholas's election and too great and powerful for the interests of the Roman Curia, he took away the vicariate of Tuscany. Intending to snatch Sicily from the French, he stirred up Peter, King of Aragon, against Charles and fostered a dreadful conspiracy, which at last broke out in the Sicilian Vespers. Then Martin IV, a Frenchman of lowly birth, who seized the fasces of the papacy in 1281, prepared to restore Charles, his own affairs in Sicily having been given up, the Sicilians thrice invoking him with the words: Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant us peace. He struck the Emperor of Constantinople with anathema because he favoured the King of Aragon. He was so hostile to Germany that he often wished to see it turned into a pond. His successor, Honorius IV, anathematized Peter, King of Aragon, because he refused to surrender to the French the Kingdom of Sicily, which Nicholas III had granted to him. His legate, the Cardinal of Tusculum, was sent into Germany to demand for five years a quarter of the revenues of all the clergy; he met with rejection at an assembly of bishops at Würzburg, where, through the mouth of Probus, bishop of Tullensis, he was called "Satrap of Antichrist". The name is rightly given to him, and Aventinus, book VII, records Probus's most weighty oration against the Roman vultures. Under the successor of this man, Nicholas IV, a similar boldness of speech (παρρησία) came badly off for John of Bitterre, a Franciscan, and Peter Cassiodorus, Italians, who, because they had branded the Pope as Antichrist, were dragged from their tombs and burned. Excommunicated by the same Pope was Meinhard, Count of Tyrol, because, resisting the ambition of the Bishop of Trent, he had invaded the bishop's strongholds. In a public apology, denouncing the crimes of the bishops, he calls them effeminate Antichrists and prodigious eunuchs, worse than Turks, Saracens, Tartars and Jews; and so from a savage and unjust Pontiff he appeals to a just minister and most devout Father.

units.la: CXIV. Mænardi illius Comitis Gente & mente generosi, cujus filia Elisabetha Alberto Imperatori post nupta est; Orationem lectu dignissimam, Avent. Annal. Bojor. lib. VII. p. 444. his verbis recitat: Equidem (ita me Deus amet) bellum non infero, sed propulso. Nihil unquam magis mihi cordi fuit, quàm pacem cum quovis hominum, maximè cum Episcopis conservare, nisi boni Patres, ut cæteri Mortalium, copia rerum corrupti, nobis immeritissimis ultro arma prava libidine dominandi intulissent, nósque terris avitis spoliare conati fuissent. Arma sumpsi, castella hostibus patriæ ademi, quo mihi ac popularibus otio frui absque armis liceat. Quòd si quispiam vas atque præs fuerit, ne metuere perfidiam & lupos habeam, nève de cætero hujusmodi nobis à fastuosis illis Archisynagogis (nam Pastoribus dicere religio est) contingant, actutum omnia reddam: aliter nunquam committam, ut tam stultus videar, ut è manu manubrium mihi eripi patiar, atque memet ultrò atque meos ludibrio effœminatis Antichristis atque prodigiosis Eunuchis esse sinam. Nemo magis concordiam Christianam labefactat, non sacris literis interpretandis aut edisendis, sed liberis dant operam, Liberum amant, divitias colligunt, Regna, gloriam, dominationem avidissimè appetunt. tunt. Pro hisce nobiscum sanguine ovium decertant, Christi paupertatem, comitum ejus simplicitatem non solum non æmulantur, sed irrid" ent quoque atque antiquare conantur. Si Antichristi non sunt, quid aliud obsecro sunt? Est ne illud pascere oves? amare gregem? Regna, opes, aliena appetere, pro gloria, dignitate digladiari, oviculas opprimere, occidere, belligerare; Christi præceptum invertunt, donanti tunicam & pallium vi auferunt. Quis tam ferreus, ut verius dicam, tam stolidum pecus fuerit, ut superbiam, fastum, perfidiam, fraudem, flagitia, scelera, luxum, avaritiam nebulonum æquo animo ferat? Pejores Turcis, Saracenis, Tartaris, Judæis sunt, plus his omnibus Christianæ simplicitati officiunt, libertatem Christi sanguine partem exscindere conantur, dominationem arripiunt. Cum nostri servi sint, ipsi dominari contra jus gentium, adversus leges, auspicia & oracula Divina, dominos sibi servire volunt. Scitum est vulgi Proverbium, sacerdotes superstitionum præstigiis caliginem oculis offundere Mortalium, & ceremoniis carminibúsque cassis veluti mandragoræ soporiferæ poculo mentem mutare, & humanis animis atque sensibus stuporem propinare. Num quid pastor aut oves tondet, aut mulget; nonne nuntius rem domini atque eorum, ob quorum utilitatem mittitur, agere debet? Proinde à sævo, & nobis iniquo Pontifice, ad æquum Pastorem, pientissimúmque Patrem provoco.
units.tr: CXIV. The oration of that Count Meinhard, noble in birth and in mind, whose daughter Elizabeth was afterwards married to the Emperor Albert, is worth reading in full. Aventinus, Annal. Bojor. lib. VII. p. 444., recites it in these words: Indeed (so may God love me) I do not wage war, but repel it. Nothing has ever been dearer to me than to keep peace with everyone, most of all with the bishops; but if the good fathers, like other mortals corrupted by an abundance of goods, had of their own accord, against us who have deserved nothing, taken up arms out of a depraved lust for domination, and tried to strip us of our ancestral lands, I took up arms and took from the enemies of my country their strongholds, so that I and my people may enjoy peace without arms. And if anyone should be found who is a vassal and a surety, I will not fear treachery or wolves; and lest in future such things befall us from those haughty archsynagogues (for it is a matter of conscience to call them ministers), I shall at once restore everything. Otherwise I shall never allow myself to appear so foolish as to suffer the handle to be snatched from my hand, and to let myself and mine be made a plaything of effeminate Antichrists and prodigious eunuchs. No one undermines Christian concord more, not by interpreting or publishing the sacred letters, but by giving their attention to liberty. They love liberty, they gather riches, they most eagerly seek kingdoms, glory and domination. For these things they struggle with the blood of sheep; they not only do not emulate the poverty of Christ or the simplicity of his companions, but mock them and try to abolish them. If they are not Antichrists, what else, I ask, are they? Is it to feed sheep? To love the flock? To seek kingdoms, wealth, and what belongs to others, to fight for glory and dignity, to oppress, kill and wage war on the little sheep? They invert Christ's precept: they forcibly take the tunic and cloak from one who would give them. Who would be so hard, or rather so stupid a herd, as to bear with equanimity the pride, arrogance, treachery, fraud, crimes, wickedness, luxury and avarice of these scoundrels? They are worse than Turks, Saracens, Tartars and Jews; they do more harm to Christian simplicity than all of these together; they try to cut away a part of Christ's liberty with his blood, and they seize dominion. Though they are our servants, they want to rule over us, against the law of nations, against the laws, the auspices and the divine oracles, and want their lords to serve them. It is a common saying that priests cover men's eyes with the deceptions of superstitions, and by ceremonies and empty songs, like a sleep-inducing draught of mandrake, change the mind and pour stupor into human souls and senses. Does a minister shear or milk the sheep? Ought he not rather to be a messenger, to carry out the affairs of the master and of those for whose benefit he is sent? Therefore I appeal from a savage and unjust Pontiff to a just minister and most devout Father.

units.la: ECCLESIÆ ROMANÆ PERIODUS QUINTA.
units.tr: THE FIFTH PERIOD OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.

units.la: Seu
units.tr: Or

units.la: Historia Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Dominatio- nem in temporalibus etiam, adeóque Cæsa- reo-Papatum adipiscentis, & eandem, profligata doctrina puriori omni, fla- gitiosè exercentis.
units.tr: The Church of Rome: how it obtained dominion even over temporal affairs, and so the Caesaro-Papacy, and how it practised that dominion shamefully once all purer doctrine had been destroyed.

units.la: Inde à Bonifacio VIII. seu A. C. MCCXCIV. ad Leonem X. seu A. C. MDXVII. usque.
units.tr: From Boniface VIII, or the year of Christ 1294, down to Leo X, or the year of Christ 1517.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: CXV. Bonifacius VIII. Papalis fastigii consummator, fraude sedem rapuit. Gibellinis, seu fidis Imperii civibus gravem se gerit.
units.tr: CXV. Boniface VIII, the consummator of the papal summit, seized the see by fraud. He behaves harshly toward the Ghibellines, that is, toward the citizens faithful to the Empire.

units.la: CXVI. Obsolescente Jubilæo Christiano, utroque habitu, Pontificali & Imperiali indutus, duósque gladios ostentans, Pontificium instituit. quod solennis quædam inauguratio fuit, qua se Dominum in orbe Christiano supremum, Pontificem & Cæsarem esse, declaravit.
units.tr: CXVI. With the Christian Jubilee falling into disuse, he was clothed in both garments, Pontifical and Imperial, and displaying two swords, he instituted the Papacy. This was a certain solemn inauguration by which he declared himself the supreme lord in the Christian world, Pontiff and Caesar.

units.la: CXVII. Quid Jubilæo illo spectârit, ex vita & moribus ejus colligitur.
units.tr: CXVII. What that Jubilee aimed at is gathered from his life and morals.

units.la: CXVIII. Causa continuati à successoribus, & subinde ad brevius tempus restricti Jubilæi.
units.tr: CXVIII. The reason why the Jubilee was continued by his successors, and at times restricted to a shorter period.

units.la: CXIX. Potestatem supremam Bonifacius exercet adversus Imper. Albertum, quem à se non conscio electum imperare non posse pertendit.
units.tr: CXIX. Boniface exercises supreme power against the Emperor Albert, whom he claimed could not rule, having been elected without his knowledge.

units.la: CXX. Nec non Philippum pulchrum Galliæ Regem, quem Regno, utpote ad sedem Petri pertinente, arcere conatur, subditis fidelitatis sacramento exsolutis. Captus à Philippo & ludibrio habitus ex phrenesi moritur.
units.tr: CXX. He also tries to keep out Philip the Fair, King of France, from the kingdom, which he said belonged to the see of Peter, and he releases the subjects from the oath of fidelity. Captured by Philip and mocked, he dies of madness.

units.la: CXXI. Roberti Galli liber editus una cum vaticiniis Hildegardes adversus Papam. ubi Ecclesiæ Rom. facies in visionibus graphicè depingitur.
units.tr: CXXI. The book of Robert the Gaul, published together with the prophecies of Hildegard, against the Pope, where the face of the Roman Church is vividly portrayed in visions.

units.la: CXXII. Fratricellos Papam Antichristum, Romam Babylonem appellantes, Papa persequitur.
units.tr: CXXII. The Pope persecutes the Fraticelli, who call the Pope Antichrist and Rome Babylon.

units.la: CXXIII. Clemens V. Roma Avenionem migrat. Durandi Mimatensis de Concilio celebrando liber Clerum Romanum describit, ejusque reformandi formam præit. at reformari posse desperat.
units.tr: CXXIII. Clement V migrates from Rome to Avignon. The book of Durandus of Mende on holding a Council describes the Roman clergy and sets out a plan for reforming them, but he despairs that they can be reformed.

units.la: CXXIV. Spem reformationis vanam fuisse, Concilii Viennensis, quo Decretalis de Potestate Papæ supra Cæsares edita, fratrum Minorum religio confirmata est, eventus docuit. Templariorum horribile excidium. quibus innocentiæ nonnulli testimonium perhibent.
units.tr: CXXIV. The outcome showed that hope of reformation was vain: at the Council of Vienne, where the decretal on the power of the Pope above Caesars was issued, and the order of the Friars Minor was confirmed. The horrible destruction of the Templars, to whose innocence some bear witness.

units.la: CXXV. Henricus VII. Romæ Cardinalibus sacramento dicere renuens à Bernhardo Politiano venenatæ hostiæ subsidio necatur.
units.tr: CXXV. Henry VII, refusing to take an oath to the Cardinals at Rome, is killed by poisoned consecrated bread, with the help of Bernardo Poliziano.

units.la: CXXVI. Dantis Aligerii de Ecclesia R. querelæ. Fridericus III. Siciliæ Rex Ecclesiæ R. statu offensus, de Euangelii ipsius veritate dubitat, & ab Alphonso Villanovano in ea confirmatur.
units.tr: CXXVI. The complaints of Dante Alighieri concerning the Roman Church. Frederick III, King of Sicily, offended by the state of the Roman Church, doubts the truth of the Gospel itself, and is confirmed in it by Alphonso Villanovanus.

units.la: CXXVII. Johannes XXII. se ipsum eligens, animas ante finem mundi Deo frui negat; & Papam Imperatori, ut Solem Lunæ præstare, aliáque superbissimè decernit.
units.tr: CXXVII. John XXII, electing himself, denies that souls enjoy God before the end of the world; and he most arrogantly decrees that the Pope should be superior to the Emperor as the sun is to the moon, and other such things.

units.la: CXXVIII. Cæsareo-Papatum suum tuetur adversus Ludovicum Bavarum, quem anathemati subjicit. Ludovicus verò Romam occupans, ibidem coronatur, & deposito Johanne Nicolaum V. Antipapam creat.
units.tr: CXXVIII. He defends his Caesaro-Papacy against Louis of Bavaria, whom he puts under anathema. Louis, however, occupying Rome, is crowned there, and, with John deposed, creates Nicholas V as antipope.

units.la: CXXIX. Johannes paupertatem palam irridet, & Franciscanos repugnantes, ceu hæreticos damnat. Certamen Franciscanos inter & Dominicanos de Christo in cruce pendente nudóne, an corona Regia & toga purpurea vestito, acerrimum. Alvarus Pelagius Johannis impietatem damnat.
units.tr: CXXIX. John openly mocks poverty and condemns the resisting Franciscans as heretics. The very bitter contest between the Franciscans and the Dominicans over whether Christ hanging on the cross was naked or clothed with a royal crown and a purple robe. Alvarus Pelagius condemns the impiety of John.

units.la: CXXX. Johannis ejusdem Bulla fere Babylonica adversus Ludovicum Bavarum.
units.tr: CXXX. The almost Babylonian bull of the same John against Louis of Bavaria.

units.la: CXXXI. Et Ludovici adversus Johannem Edictum ex Aventino repræsentantur.
units.tr: CXXXI. And the edict of Louis against John is presented from the Aventine.

units.la: CXXXII. Ejudem Ludovici adversus Benedictum XII. absolutionem à diris Johannis negantem heroicum diploma. Clemens VI. absolutionem promittit, sed diris conditionibus, quibus repudiatis Papa Cæsarem alium eligi jubet. Electus Carolus Spiræ in Comitiis repudiatur, & ad arma dum concurritur, Ludovicus veneno propinato moritur.
units.tr: CXXXII. The heroic decree of the same Louis against Benedict XII, who refused absolution from the curses of John. Clement VI promises absolution, but on dreadful conditions, which being rejected, the Pope orders another Emperor to be chosen. Charles, elected at Speyer in the Diet, is rejected, and while they rush to arms, Louis dies after being given poison.

units.la: CXXXIII. Clementi sese opposuerunt viri celebres plures, Occamus & Leopoldus Bambergensis Episcopus cumprimis.
units.tr: CXXXIII. Several famous men opposed Clement, Ockham and Leopold, Bishop of Bamberg, above all.

units.la: CXXXIV. Carolus IV. coronam ab Innocentio VI. magno cum dedecore obtinet, promittens se nunquam Italiam repetiturum. Ita Carolus Majestatem Imperii R. prodidit, & aquilam deplumavit.
units.tr: CXXXIV. Charles IV obtains the crown from Innocent VI with great disgrace, promising that he would never return to Italy. Thus Charles betrayed the majesty of the Roman Empire and plucked the eagle.

units.la: CXXXV. Petracha id Carolo exprobrat, & curiam Romanam nomine Babylonis Occidentalis graviter exagitat.
units.tr: CXXXV. Petrarch reproaches Charles for this, and severely harasses the Roman curia under the name of Western Babylon.

units.la: CXXXVI. Plures etiam cordati ejusdem curiæ impietatem liberè notant. Veluti Joh. à Rupescissa, M. Nicolaus Oremus. S. Brigida & Catharina Senensis in Revelationibus.
units.tr: CXXXVI. Several discerning men of the same curia also freely note its impiety, such as John of Rupescissa, Master Nicholas Oresme, and Saint Bridget and Catherine of Siena in their Revelations.

units.la: CXXXVII. Wiclefus Anglus imprimis, cujus in detegendo Antichristo, oppugnanda falsa, Magnatibus ipsis veritatis succo imbuendis, Zelus & patientia incomparabilis laudantur.
units.tr: CXXXVII. Wycliffe of England above all, in whom is praised his zeal and incomparable patience in unmasking Antichrist, in assailing false doctrines, and in imbuing even the great men with the juice of truth.

units.la: CXXXVIII. Schismatis pertinacissimi à tempore Urbani VI. ad Concilium Constantiense usque historia. Contraria Urbani VI. & Clementis VII. studia.
units.tr: CXXXVIII. The history of the most stubborn schism from the time of Urban VI to the Council of Constance. The opposing aims of Urban VI and Clement VII.

units.la: CXXXIX. Antipapárum Benedicti XIII. & Gregorii XII. in eo schismate malignitas, ex Thcodorico de Nyem adumbrata. Deposito utroque in Concilio Pisano Alexander V. eligitur: renitente utroque. Alexandro Balthasar Cossa, seu Johannes XXIV. succedit, qui Sigismundum coronaturus, & Ecclesiam tranquillaturus Concilium Romanum, cui bubo præfuit, coëgit.
units.tr: CXXXIX. The malice of the antipopes Benedict XIII and Gregory XII in that schism, sketched out from Theodoric of Niem. With both deposed at the Council of Pisa, Alexander V is elected, though both resist. Alexander is succeeded by Balthasar Cossa, or John XXIV, who, about to crown Sigismund and to calm the Church, forced a Roman council over which an owl presided.

units.la: CXL. Sigismundus Imp. ingentibus studiis Ecclesiæ pacem restituere conatus, Constantiæ Concilium à Johanne convocari curat. In eo depositis tribus Antipapis eligitur Martinus V. qui reformationem Ecclesiæ à Sigismundo tentatam eludit.
units.tr: CXL. The Emperor Sigismund, striving with immense zeal to restore peace to the Church, arranges for a council at Constance to be convoked by John. There, with three antipopes deposed, Martin V is elected, who mocks the reformation of the Church attempted by Sigismund.

units.la: CXLI. Eugenius IV. Basileense Concilium cogit, mox verò à Patribus ejus sibi metuens illud Ferrariam, atque inde Florentiam transfert, & à Basileensibus deponitur, Amadeo Sabaudo seu Felice V. surrogato. Florentinorum cum Græcis negotiatio lubrica, à Græcis post rejecta. Eugenii & Felicis contraria studia. Carolus Galliæ Delphinus Basileense Concilium turbare conatus cladem ingentem ab Helvetiis victis licet patitur.
units.tr: CXLI. Eugenius IV convenes the Council of Basel, but soon, fearing its Fathers, transfers it to Ferrara and thence to Florence, and he is deposed by the Baselites, Amadeus of Savoy, or Felix V, being substituted. The dealings of the Florentines with the Greeks were slippery, and afterwards the Greeks rejected them. The opposing aims of Eugenius and Felix. Charles, the Dauphin of France, trying to disturb the Council of Basel, suffers a huge defeat at the hands of the Swiss, though defeated.

units.la: CXLII. Constantinopolis à Papa ob negatum primatum turpiter deserta, à Turcis occupatur, & unà Oriens Christianus fere totus eorum jugum subit.
units.tr: CXLII. Constantinople, shamefully abandoned by the Pope because the primacy was refused, is occupied by the Turks, and with it almost the whole Christian East submits to their yoke.

units.la: CXLIII. Nicolai V. erga literas & literatos amor insignis prædicatur. Ita in ipsa Antichristi aula nutriuntur literæ, quarum post auxilio Antichristus revelatus fuit.
units.tr: CXLIII. The outstanding love of Nicholas V for letters and men of letters is praised. Thus letters are nurtured in the very court of Antichrist, by whose help Antichrist was afterwards revealed.

units.la: CXLIV. Ad revelationem Antichristi etiam Typographia eadem ætate inventa contulit multum.
units.tr: CXLIV. Printing, invented in the same age, also contributed much to the revelation of Antichrist.

units.la: CXLV. Pius II. promissam reformationem neutiquam præstat, sed Majestati Pontificiæ augendæ unicè intentus est. Ingloria ejus adversus diversos Principes facinora.
units.tr: CXLV. Pius II by no means carries out the reformation he promised, but is intent solely on enlarging the papal majesty. His inglorious deeds against various princes.

units.la: CXLVI. Sixti IV. impuritas variè testata. Lupanaria instituit primus: & bella iniqua gerens cum Helvetiis fœdus init, iisdémque pudendâ bullâ vexillum donat. Alexandri VI. impietas.
units.tr: CXLVI. The impurity of Sixtus IV, attested in various ways. He was the first to establish brothels; waging unjust wars, he made an alliance with the Swiss and presented them with a banner through a shameful bull. The impiety of Alexander VI.

units.la: CXLVII. Nubes testium, quæ ea ætate adversus Ecclesiam R. ceu Antichristianam & Babylonicam emersit, indigetata.
units.tr: CXLVII. The cloud of witnesses who in that age arose against the Roman Church, as Antichristian and Babylonian, not yet named.

units.la: CXLVIII Pontificiæ adversus eosdem tyrannidis specimina in Hussi, Hussi, Hieronimi aliorum suppliciis & Bohemorum persecutione producuntur.
units.tr: CXLVIII. Examples of papal tyranny against them are presented in the sufferings of Hus, Jerome and others, and in the persecution of the Bohemians.

units.la: CXLIX. Julii II. tyrannis & saevitia. Bella ejus adversus Venetos, Maximilianum & foederatos Gallos improbè gesta. Helvetios fraudulento foederi innexos bullatis indulgentiis mactat. Pisano Concilio instituto ad reddendam rationem villicationis suae citatus, anathemate adversarios ferit, & Concilium Lateran i indictum iisdem opponit. De utroque Concilio illo judicia Scriptorum. Sforziae Pallavicini de Julio judicium, & ejusdem frivola excusatio.
units.tr: CXLIX. The tyranny and savagery of Julius II. His wars against the Venetians, Maximilian and the allied French, waged wickedly. He slaughters the Swiss, bound by a fraudulent alliance, with indulgences issued in bulls. Summoned to give an account of his stewardship after the Council of Pisa was convened, he strikes his opponents with anathema, and opposes to them the Lateran Council which he had announced. Judgments of writers on both councils. Sforza Pallavicino's judgment on Julius, and Julius's own frivolous excuse.

units.la: CL. Testes veritatis ea aetate, Waldenses, Faber Stapulensis, Budaeus, Picus Mirandulanus, Ludovicus XII, Ecclesiae Bohemicae, Moravicae &c.
units.tr: CL. Witnesses of the truth in that age: the Waldenses, Faber Stapulensis, Budé, Pico della Mirandola, Louis XII, the Churches of Bohemia, Moravia, etc.

units.la: CXV.
units.tr: CXV.

units.la: QUI hactenus ad fastigium magnis passibus contendebat Papatus, Seculo Decimo quarto ineunte ad eum pervenisse videtur, Bonifacio VIII. Romanae Ecclesiae habenas moderante. Is Platina, Stella, Nauclero, Wernero in fasciculo Temporum, aliis referentibus, Praedecessori suo Coelestino, homini simplici & bono (qui reformaturus Ecclesiam, non equo vel mulo, sed asino vehi voluit, & Cardinales idem facere jussit) ut Papatum resignaret, persuasit, insigni fraude usus, canali scilicet in ejus cubiculum immisso, pluribus noctibus, quasi Angelica voce, insonans: Coelestine, Coelestine, cede, negotium enim supra vires est. Cessit Coelestinus Papatum Sceleftino huic, viribus ad provehendum mysterium iniquitatis pollenti magis. De eo sic Langius Citicensis Monachus ad A. MCCXCV. loquitur: Leonina mente tyrannizans magis, quam papissans, universo orbi metum sui & terrorem incutere moliebatur. Et Joachimus Abbas, quem Spiritus Prophetíphetici virum nuperus Cardinalis Bona appellavit, sic eum in vaticiniis suis compellavit: Fraudulenter intrâsti, potenter regnâsti, gemens morieris! Vulgatúmque de eo mortuo proverbium ferebatur: Intravit ut vulpes, regnavit ut Leo, mortuus est ut canis. Gibellinis, id est, bonis Imperii civibus, præ cœteris infensum se gessit. Cujus rei testem habemus Porchetum Spinolam, in locum Jacobi Voragine electum Genuensem Archiepiscopum, Imperatori addictum. Confirmandus is in munere suo Romam venit, quo die frontes cinere signantur. Provolvitur ad Bonifacii pedes Porchetus post alios complures, frontem cineris cruce signandus. Tum Bonifacius carmine mutato: Memento, inquit, quòd Gibellinus es, & cum Gibellinis in cinerem reverteris. Cineribúsque in oculos ejus sparsis, Archiepiscopatum eodem die ei abrogavit. Unde quo in pretio suas ipse ceremonias habuerit, judicari potest.
units.tr: The Papacy, which had been advancing to its summit with great strides, seems to have reached it at the beginning of the fourteenth century, when Boniface VIII governed the Roman Church. Platina, Stella, Naucler, and Werner in his Fasciculus Temporum report, as do others, that he persuaded his predecessor Celestine, a simple and good man who had wished to reform the Church and to be carried on an ass rather than on a horse or mule, and who had ordered the cardinals to do the same, to resign the Papacy. Boniface did this by a notable trick: he had a speaking tube put into Celestine's bedchamber and, on several nights, it boomed in what seemed an angelic voice: "Celestine, Celestine, give way, for the business is beyond your strength." Celestine yielded the Papacy to this scoundrel, who was more able to advance the mystery of iniquity. Concerning him, the monk Langius of Citicum speaks thus under the year 1295: "Tyrannizing with a lion's mind rather than acting as a pope, he was striving to strike fear and terror into the whole world." And Joachim the Abbot, whom the late Cardinal Bona called "a man of the prophetic Spirit," addressed him thus in his prophecies: "You entered by fraud, you reigned by power, you will die groaning!" There was also a proverb about him once he was dead: "He entered like a fox, reigned like a lion, died like a dog." He showed himself more hostile than others to the Ghibellines, that is, to the good citizens of the Empire. We have a witness to this in Porchetto Spinola, elected archbishop of Genoa in place of Jacobus de Voragine, who was devoted to the Emperor. He came to Rome to be confirmed in his office, on the day when foreheads are marked with ashes. Porchetto, along with many others, threw himself at Boniface's feet to have his forehead signed with the cross of ashes. Then Boniface, changing his formula, said: "Remember that you are a Ghibelline, and that with the Ghibellines you will return to ashes." Ashes were then thrown into his eyes, and on the same day Boniface stripped him of the archbishopric. From this one may judge how highly he valued his own ceremonies.

units.la: CXVI. Obsolescere jam fatali hominum superstitione coepit Jubilæum verè Christianum, quod unico Christi merito afflictos conscientias confidere docet. Anno igitur seculari millesimo trecentesimo, adeóque sub initium sequli hujus Decimi quarti, Bonifacius ille tempus idoneum nactus, aliud Jubilæum, Pontificium scilicet, seu potius novum mercatum indulgentiarum, centesimo quoque anno aperta Romæ aurea porta celebrandum, in ejus locum substituit. Usque ad illum Bonifacium (ita Kranzius Saxon. lib. VIII. 36. scribit) Pontificibus non venerat in mentem tam festo negotio commovere Christianismum. Quod ipso apparatu in eo, qui tum agebatur in urbe, Jubilæo solenniter fertur ostentâsse: Prima quidem solenni die in Pontificalibus apparens populo, Apostolicam illis benedictionem impartitur. Postera autem die imperiali habitu (idque præsentibus legatis Imperatoris) infula nihilominus Cæsarea insignis, gladium ante se nudatum jussit deferri & sedens alta voce testatur: Ecce duo gladii hic. Kranzii hæc ἐπιχείρησις est: Vides ô Petre, successorem tuum, & tu salutifer Christe tuum cerne vicarium! (Quæ tamen verba nonnulli ipsi Papæ ascribunt) Vide quo ascendit superbia servi servorum! Nempe calcata potestate humana, civili, quæ post mortem Friderici II. fere succubuit, & Ecclesiastica omni, jam Papa regnare ubique sine pari, & αὐτοκρατορικῶς[?] cœpit. Quod ipsum etiam testatur superbissima ejus Bulla, quæ, ceu novissimum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Symbolum, in Extravagantibus Tit. de Major. & obed. c unam S. Ecclesiam legitur, in qua diserte: Unam sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam, & ipsam Apostolicam urgente fide credere cogimur & tenere. Et ilico nos ad Romanam, uni Pontifici parituros revocat, cui in Petri persona dictum sit, Pasce oves meas, ita ut, seu Græci, seu alii in Christi ovibus non censeantur, nisi ei obsequantur. In hoc, inquit, ejusque potestate, duos esse gladios, spiritualem videlicet & temporalem, Euangelicis dictis instruimur. Nam dicentibus Apostolis: Ecce gladii duo hic, in Ecclesia scilicet, cum Apostoli loquerentur, non respondit Dominus nimis esse, sed satis. Certè qui in potestate Petri temporalem gladium esse negat, male verbum attendit Domini proferentis: Converte gladium tuum in vaginam. Ex his verbis contra quàm omnes Patres & Interpretes, apertè ratiocinatus: Uterque ergo est in potestate Ecclesiæ, spiritualis scilicet gladius & materialis, sed is quidem pro Ecclesia; ille verò ab Ecclesia exercendus, ille sacerdotis, is manu Regum & militum, sed ad nutum & patientiam sacerdotis, id est, Papæ. Oportet autem gladium esse sub gladio, & temporalem authoritatem spirituali subjici. Nam cum dicat Apostolus: Non est potestas nisi à Deo: quæ autem sunt, à Deo ordinatæ sunt: non autem ordinatæ essent, nisi gladius esset sub gladio, & tanquam inferior reduceretur per alium ad suprema &c. Sic de Ecclesia & Ecclesiastica potestate verificatur vaticinium Ieremiæ: Ecce constitui te hodie super gentes & Regna, & cætera, quæ sequuntur. Ergo si deviat terrena potestas, judicabitur à potestate spirituali; sed si deviat spiritualis minor, à suo superiori: Si verò suprema deviat, à solo Deo, non ab homine poterit judicari, testante Apostolo: Spiritualis homo judicat omnia, ipse verò à nemine judicatur. Postquam sic Scripturam Papa, non secus ad Pasquillus aliquis Romanus ludibrio habuit, ex ridiculis antecedentibus impudenter ita concludit: Porrò subesse Romano Pontifici omni humanæ creaturæ declaramus, dicimus, definimus, & pronuntiamus omnino esse de necessitate salutis. Clarissimè hinc liquet, Jubilæum isthoc Bonifacii solennem quandam inaugurationem fuisse, qua se Dominum in Orbe Christiano supremum, Cæsarem & Pontificem esse, veterum Augustorum Romanorum imitatione, qui Imperatores simul & Pontifices erant; magnificè Papa declaravit, eadem opera pecunias, supremi imperii nervum, undequaque in rete suum piscatorium attrahens. Dignúmque memoratu est, quòd eodem die Jubilæo, quo Papa-Cæsareatum suum Bonifacius ostentavit, Monarchiam etiam Turcicam Ottomannus auspicatus fuerit: planè sicut antehac eodem tempore Bonifacius III. Universalis Episcopi axioma sibi vendicavit, quo etiam Muhammed ex orco caput intulit, & nefariæ sectæ fundamenta jecit.
units.tr: CXVI. The truly Christian Jubilee, which teaches that troubled consciences should trust in the single merit of Christ, had already begun to fall into disuse through the fatal superstition of men. So in the year 1300, that is, at the beginning of this fourteenth century, that same Boniface, seizing a fitting time, put in its place another Jubilee, a Papal one, or rather a new trade in indulgences, to be celebrated every hundredth year with the Golden Door opened at Rome. Before that Boniface, Kranz writes (Saxony, book VIII, 36), it had not occurred to the Popes to stir up Christendom with so festive a business. By the very display that was made at that Jubilee in the city, it is said, he showed himself: on the first solemn day, appearing before the people in pontifical vestments, he gave them the apostolic blessing. But on the next day, dressed in imperial robes (with the Emperor's envoys present), and likewise adorned with the Caesarean crown, he ordered a sword to be carried before him unsheathed, and, seated, declared in a loud voice: Behold, here are two swords. Kranz's argument [ἐπιχείρησις] is this: See, O Peter, your successor, and you, O saving Christ, behold your vicar! (though some attribute these words to the Pope himself) See to what height the pride of the servant of servants has risen! Indeed, with human power, civil power, which had nearly succumbed after the death of Frederick II, trampled down, and with all ecclesiastical power, the Pope now began to reign everywhere without equal and autocratically [αὐτοκρατορικῶς]. His very arrogant Bull also bears witness to this; it is read, as the last creed of the Roman Church, among the Extravagants, Tit. de Major. & obed. c unam S. Ecclesiam, where it says plainly: We are compelled by the urgency of faith to believe and hold one holy Catholic Church, and indeed apostolic. And at once it calls us back to the Roman one, to be subject to one Pontiff, to whom, in the person of Peter, it was said, Feed my sheep, so that whether Greeks or others are not counted among Christ's sheep unless they obey him. In this, it says, and in his power, we are instructed by the Gospel sayings that there are two swords, the spiritual and the temporal. For when the Apostles said, Behold, here are two swords, in the Church, that is, when the Apostles were speaking, the Lord did not reply that they were too many, but that they were enough. Certainly he who denies that the temporal sword is in Peter's power has badly attended to the Lord's word when he says: Put your sword back into its sheath. Reasoning openly from these words, against what all the Fathers and Interpreters hold, he goes on: Both swords, then, are in the power of the Church, the spiritual and the material, but the one is to be wielded for the Church, the other by the Church; the one by the hand of the priest, the other by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the nod and the permission of the priest, that is, of the Pope. For the sword must be under the sword, and temporal authority must be subjected to the spiritual. For since the Apostle says: There is no power but of God, and the powers that exist are ordained of God; they would not be ordained unless the sword were under the sword, and as the lesser were led back by another to the highest, and so on. Thus of the Church and ecclesiastical power is fulfilled the prophecy of Jeremiah: Behold, I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, and the rest that follows. Therefore, if earthly power goes astray, it will be judged by spiritual power; but if the lesser spiritual power goes astray, by its superior. But if the highest goes astray, it can be judged by God alone, not by man, the Apostle testifying: the spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one. After the Pope had thus made sport of Scripture, no differently from some Roman lampooner, he impudently concludes from these absurd premises: Furthermore, we declare, state, define, and pronounce that it is altogether necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff. It is quite clear from this that this Jubilee of Boniface was a kind of solemn inauguration, in which the Pope proclaimed with great pomp that he was the supreme Lord in the Christian world, Caesar and Pontiff, in imitation of the ancient Roman Augusti, who were at once Emperors and Pontiffs; and by the same means he drew money, the sinew of supreme power, from every side into his fishing net. And it is worth recording that on the same Jubilee day on which Boniface displayed his Papal-Caesarean power, the Ottoman also began the Turkish monarchy. Just so, at about the same time, Boniface III had claimed for himself the axiom of universal bishop, by which Muhammad also brought his head up out of hell and laid the foundations of his impious sect.

units.la: CXVII. Quid potissimum spectârit Bonifacius iste Ju- bilæo instituto, si quis ambigat, ex vita & moribus ejus æstimabit facilè.
units.tr: CXVII. If anyone doubts what this Boniface chiefly aimed at in instituting the Jubilee, he will easily judge from his life and morals.

units.la: Præclarè enim M. Tullius, Omnibus in rebus, inquit, quæ graviores majoresque sunt, quid quisque voluerit, cogitaverit, admiserit, non ex crimine, sed ex moribus ejus, qui arguitur, est ponderandum. Anne ergo hic Papa, ut nomine ita re quoque fuit Bonifacius? Imò omnium hominum, quos sol vidit, pessimus fuit, & flagitiosissimus, procella Ecclesiæ, turbo & tempestas Reipub. Christianæ, Dei juxta atque hominum contemptor, idemque gurges profundissimus & insatiabilis, aurum undiquaque conquisitum infernaliter sitiens. Hoc enim testimonium Sabellicus, Nauclerus & Platina ei perhibent. Ex mera igitur dominandi libidine, & auri sacerrima fame, quam Apostolus radicem omnium malorum vocat, ingeniosus in rem suam Bonifacius, indulgentiarum plenissimarum prætextu, novum aucupium excogitavit, promulgavit, & Purgatorium, quod Papæ conflatorium est, terriculamentis dementatis hominibus obtrusit. Ausus tamen impostor hic est venerandæ antiquitatis authoritatem prætendere. Sic enim bullam indictionis suæ inchoat: Antiquorum habet fida relatio, quod accedentibus ad honorabilem Basilicam Principis Apostolorum concessæ sint magnæ remissiones & indulgentiæ peccatorum. Sic audet ille verum antiquæ Ecclesiæ Jubilæum, nimirum gratuitam remissionem peccatorum per Christum profligare, & venerandæ nihilominus antiquitatis nomine nugas & superstitionem suam venditare. Enimverò, si per antiquos intelligit vetulos Bulliftas, & Datarios, concedo, hoc relationem illorum tulisse. Sed quòd antiqui Patres, vel alii antiqui scriptores de Jubilæo Pontificio, quod Papæ auriferum Pactolum scite non nemo insignivit; quicquam retulerint, mendacium est παταζπηγ imo centum cubitos longum.
units.tr: Admirably, Marcus Tullius says: In all matters that are weightier and more important, what each man wished, thought, or permitted must be weighed not by the accusation but by the character of the one who is accused. Was this Pope, then, a Boniface in fact as well as in name? Indeed he was the worst and most depraved of all men whom the sun has seen: a storm to the Church, a whirlwind and tempest to the Christian commonwealth, a despiser of God no less than of men, and at the same time a most profound and insatiable whirlpool, thirsting after gold gathered from every quarter in a hellish way. Sabellicus, Naucler and Platina bear this witness concerning him. Out of sheer lust for domination and the most accursed hunger for gold, which the Apostle calls the root of all evils, Boniface, clever at serving his own interest, under the pretext of the most complete indulgences devised and published a new fowling-net, and foisted upon frightened and deluded men a Purgatory, which is the Pope's crucible. Yet this impostor dared to claim the authority of venerable antiquity. For he begins his bull of announcement thus: A faithful report of the ancients holds that great remissions and indulgences of sins have been granted to those who come to the honourable basilica of the Prince of the Apostles. So he dares to pass off the true Jubilee of the ancient Church, namely the free remission of sins through Christ, and at the same time to peddle his trifles and superstition under the name of venerable antiquity. Indeed, if by the ancients he means the old bullists and datary officials, I grant that their report says this. But that the ancient Fathers, or other ancient writers, reported anything about the Papal Jubilee, which someone aptly called the golden Pactolus of the Pope, is a lie, indeed a lie a hundred cubits long.

units.la: CXVIII. Cœterum quæ Bonifacio Jubilæi, centesimo quoque anno primitus instituendi, eadem sequentibus Papis ejusdem ad brevius temporis spatium contrahendi causa sine dubio extitit.
units.tr: CXVIII. Moreover, the reason why Boniface first instituted the Jubilee to be celebrated every hundredth year was without doubt the same reason why the Popes who followed him shortened it to a briefer span of time.

units.la: Quid enim impulit Clementem VI. ut hanc festivitatem centesimo quoque anno secundum Bonifacium celebrandam, ad quinquagesimum reduceret?
