Auri sacra fames, & offertoriorum ex indulgentiis amplissimorum magna spes, qua sic elatus & dementatus fuit, ut in Bulla sua Angelis Paradisi mandaret, ut animas morientium in itinere à Purgatorio penitus absolutas in Paradisi gloriam introducant. Quid Bonifacium IX. impulit, ut ipse non exspectato anno quinquagesimo ad trigesimum tertium, ætate Christi sacratum, festivitatem suam contraheret? Auri sacra fames & ἀισχροκερδία. Fuit enim etiam hic Papa, authore Theodorico à Niem, vorago insatiabilis. Quid porrò movit Sixtum IV. illum non solùm bipedum, sed etiam quadrupedum impurissimum, ut cùm triginta tres anni nimis longi viderentur, ipse quinto & vicesimo quoque anno Jubilæum celebrandum institueret? Auri sacra fames & πλεονεξία. Fuit enim tam avarus & impurus, ut ædificato lupanari publico, ex meretricio etiam quæstu plurimùm ærario suo emolumenti accumulaverit. Ita Vespasianis his argenti odor bonus est ex re qualibet. Neque impostèrum Malifacio cuipiam Jubilæum ad septimum quemque annum contrahendi prætextus speciosus deerit, eò quòd sub lege etiam septimus quisque annus שנה שמטה annus remissionis fuerit. Implentque adeò facerimi hic caupones S. Petri 2. Epist. II. 3. vaticinium, fore scilicet falsos Doctores, qui ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ πλάνοις λόγοις per avaritiam fictis sermonibus, fideles sint negotiaturi.
units.tr: For what drove Clement VI to reduce this festival, which Boniface had ordered to be celebrated every hundredth year, to every fiftieth year? The sacred hunger for gold, and a great hope of offerings from indulgences, by which he was so elated and deluded that in his bull he commanded the angels of Paradise to lead into the glory of Paradise the souls of the dying who, on the way, have been wholly absolved from Purgatory. What moved Boniface IX to shorten his festival, without waiting for the fiftieth year, to the thirty-third, the age of Christ? The sacred hunger for gold and shameful gain. For this Pope too, according to Dietrich of Niem, was an insatiable whirlpool. What further moved Sixtus IV, that most impure creature not only of two feet but also of four, when thirty-three years seemed far too long, to institute the Jubilee to be celebrated in the twenty-fifth year? The sacred hunger for gold and greed. For he was so avaricious and impure that, having built a public brothel, he greatly increased the income of his treasury even from the profit of prostitution. So for these Vespasians the smell of silver is good from any source whatever. Nor will some future Malefactor lack a specious pretext for shortening the Jubilee to every seventh year, since under the law also every seventh year was a year of release [שנה שמטה, shenat shemittah]. Thus these most sacred innkeepers of St Peter fulfil the prophecy of 2 Peter 2:3, namely that there would be false teachers who, through covetousness with feigned words [ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ πλάνοις λόγοις], would trade upon the faithful.

units.la: CXIX. Sed ad Bonifacium redimus. Potestate utrumque Spirituali & civili suprema se pollere, jam publicè promulgaverat. Exercere eandem necessum duxit, ut pondus haberet Jubilæa isthæc promulgatio. Exercuit adversus duo inprimis summa Orbis Christiani capita, Albertum Imperatorem, & Philippum pulchrum, Galliæ Regem. Defuncto igitur Rodolpho Imperatore, vacante Pontificia sede, & in partes scisso Imperio, pars Principum, Ecclesiastici cumprimis, Adolphum Comitem Nassovium eligit, pars Albertum, Rodolphi filium. Bonifacius ubi ad Papatum pervenit, repudiat utrumque, eò quòd se inconsulto de electione Principes deliberare non potuerint. Inde bellum civile in Germania, tandémque prœlium, in quo Adolphus occubuit. Post cujus mortem Albertus ab omnibus Electoribus confirmatus fuit. Jubilæo peracto Romam Albertus mittit, electionem suam Pontifici probaturus. Quid verò hic Bonifacius? Respondet animosus (inquit Kranzius Saxon. lib. VIII. cap. 36.) quòd sine sua authoritate electio facta robur non haberet. Nam utriusque penes se gladii potestatem manere affirmabat. Vitoduranus in Annalibus MS. narrat, objecisse Papam Alberto, quòd Regem Adolphum trucidaverit, indignúsque adeò sit Imperio. Albertum verò ex sententia Principum suorum Bonifacio respondisse: quòd Papam patrem habere contemnat, nec coronam, aut Imperium ab eo accipere ambiat, quippe quod sibi dare nequeat, contradicente malitia sua, quia non per ostium, sed aliunde tanquam fur & latro ingressus, in sedem ascenderit, insuper & Cœlestinum Papam prædecessorem suum, ficto cœlesti oraculo, deceperit.
units.tr: CXIX. But let us return to Boniface. He had already publicly proclaimed that he possessed supreme power in both spiritual and civil matters. He judged that he must exercise this power so that the proclamation of the Jubilee might carry weight. He exercised it chiefly against two of the highest heads of the Christian world, the Emperor Albert and Philip the Fair, King of France. So when Emperor Rudolf had died, the Papal see was vacant and the Empire was split into factions: one part of the princes, especially the ecclesiastical ones, elected Adolf, Count of Nassau; another part elected Albert, son of Rudolf. When Boniface came to the papacy, he rejected both, because the princes had not been able to deliberate about the election without consulting him. Hence civil war in Germany, and at last a battle in which Adolf fell. After his death Albert was confirmed by all the electors. When the Jubilee was over, Albert sent to Rome to have his election approved by the Pope. What did Boniface do? He answered boldly, says Kranzius (Saxony, book 8, chapter 36), that an election made without his authority would have no force. For he asserted that the power of both swords remained in his hands. Vitoduranus, in his unpublished Annals, relates that the Pope charged Albert with having slain King Adolf and therefore being unworthy of the Empire. Albert, acting on the advice of his princes, answered Boniface: that he despised having the Pope as a father, and did not seek to receive the crown or the Empire from him, since he could not give it to him, his own malice standing in the way; because he had entered the seat not by the door, but from elsewhere like a thief and robber; moreover, he had deceived his predecessor Celestine the Pope by a feigned heavenly oracle.

units.la: CXX.
units.tr: CXX.

units.la: Majore etiam fastu Philippum Pulchrum Galliæ Regem, calcare conatur. Tragœdiam nuper etiam Petrus de Marca de Concordia Sacerdotii & Imperii lib. IV. 16. ex Spondano fusiùs, nec non Joh. de Buslieres Hist. Franc. lib. 9. narrârunt. Sic autem res habet. Ad Philippum A. MCCCI. Bonifacius Episcopum Apameensem mittit, qui ad Sacrum bellum eum excitaret, anathema minatus, nisi imperata faceret. Legatus jussa denuntians, pro sua protervia, persuasionibus duriora verba interserebat. Indignatus Rex Legatum comprehensum Narbonensi Archiepiscopo custodiendum tradit, usque dum de eo certi quid statuerit. Æstuans hic Bonifacius Archidiaconum Narbonensem, gente Romanum, ad Philippum delegat, cujus verbis Regi præcipit, sine mora Legatum liberet, die etiam dicta Episcopis & Patriciis Franciæ, qua Romæ coram Concilio se sistant. Cunctante Philippo protestatur, Regnum Franciæ ad Ecclesiam Romanam pertinere; proinde Rex abstineat ejus administratione, illúdque Pontifici & Ecclesiæ regendum relinquat. Mox etiam subditos fidelitatis sacramento exsolvit, & obsequium detrectantibus indulgentias, concessiones, gratias omnes Pontificias negat; caussatus etiam, in Archivis Romanis instrumentum certum reperiri, unde Franciam Pontificii juris esse constet. Philippus hisce exulceratus merito Episcopos Regno exire vetat. Pontifex anathemata sua acrius in Regem vibrat, eò quòd in Episcopum manum injecerit, de vacantium sedium bonis statuere, & Episcopos investire ausus fuerit. Tum verò Philippus Episcopum quidem ex carcere liberat, at Bullam Archidiaconi in Palatii Parisiensis atrio comburi jubet. Juvat hic audire literas Papæ ad Regem; quæ sic sonant: Deum time & mandata ejus observa. Scire te volumus, quòd in spiritualibus & temporalibus nobis subes. Beneficiorum & præbendarum ad te collatio nulla spectat; & si aliquarum vacantium custodiam habeas, fructus earum successoribus reserves. Et si quæ contulisti, collationes tales irritas decernimus, & quantum de facto processerunt, revocamus. Aliud credentes Hæreticos reputamus. Cui cordatè sic Philippus respondit: Sciat tua maxima fatuitas, in temporalibus nos alicui non subesse, aliquarum Ecclesiarum & præbendarum vacantem collationem ad nos pertinere jure Regio, & fructus earum vacatione durante nostros facere: Collationes à nobis hactenus factas, & imposterum faciendas fore validas, & illarum vigore possessores contra omnes viriliter nos tueri. Secus autem credentes fatuos & dementes reputamus. Conveniunt mox Lutetiæ ordines Regni cum Clero & Theologis, & multorum scelerum Papam reum agunt, inter alia etiam, quòd non adhibeat fidem Eucharistiam conficientibus: quòd animas mortales putaret: quòd esset Simoniacus, usurarius; quòd concubinas haberet duas neptes, & ex utráque filios progenuerit &c. Bonifacius Romæ Concilio habito, Regem Franciæ interdicto subjicit, Regem cum posteris ad quartam usque generationem Ecclesia excludit. Res eum exitum pudendum habuit, ut Bonifacius Philippo procurante captus à Nogareto, Narbonensi Archiepiscopo, Anagniæ per insidias, & impositus effreni equo, ad caudam versa facie, phrenesi correptus in carcere mortuus fuerit, dans exemplum cunctis Prælatis, quæ verba Langii & Rolevinccii sunt, ne alta saperent, sed formia facti gregis magis studerent amari à subditis, quàm timeri.
units.tr: With even greater arrogance he tries to trample Philip the Fair, King of France. Peter de Marca, in de Concordia Sacerdotii & Imperii lib. IV. 16., recently recounted this tragedy at greater length, following Spondanus, and so did Johannes de Buslidius in Hist. Franc. lib. 9. The matter stood as follows. In 1301 Boniface sent to Philip the bishop of Pamiers, to rouse him to a holy war, threatening anathema unless he did what was commanded. The legate delivered his orders and, out of his own insolence, added harsher words than persuasion called for. The king, angered, had the legate seized and handed over to the archbishop of Narbonne to be held until the king decided what to do with him. Boniface, fuming, sent to Philip the archdeacon of Narbonne, a Roman by birth, and through him ordered the king to release the legate at once, and he summoned the bishops and nobles of France to appear before a council at Rome on a set day. When Philip hesitated, Boniface protested that the kingdom of France belonged to the Roman Church; therefore the king should keep his hands off its administration and leave it to the Pope and the Church to govern. Soon he also released the subjects from their oath of fealty and denied indulgences, grants, and all the Papal favours to those who refused obedience; he added that a certain document had been found in the Roman archives showing that France was under papal jurisdiction. Philip, justly exasperated by this, forbade the bishops to leave the kingdom. The Pope hurled his anathemas more fiercely at the king, because he had laid hands on a bishop, had dared to decide on the goods of vacant sees, and had invested bishops. Then Philip did release the bishop from prison, but he ordered the archdeacon's bull to be burned in the courtyard of the Parisian palace. It is worth hearing the Pope's letter to the king here, which reads as follows: Fear God and keep his commandments. We want you to know that you are subject to us in spiritual and temporal matters. The conferral of benefices and prebends does not belong to you; and if you hold the custody of any vacant ones, you are to reserve their revenues for the successors. And whatever you have conferred, we decree such conferrals void, and we revoke them insofar as they have taken effect. Whoever believes otherwise we regard as heretics. To this Philip replied with spirit: Let your great foolishness know that we are subject to no one in temporal matters; that the conferral of certain churches and prebends belongs to us by royal right, and that during a vacancy we take their revenues for ourselves. The conferrals made by us hitherto, and those to be made in future, shall be valid, and by their force the holders shall be defended by us manfully against all. Whoever believes otherwise we regard as fools and madmen. Soon afterwards the estates of the kingdom met at Paris together with the clergy and theologians, and they indicted the Pope on many crimes, among them that he did not trust those who consecrate the Eucharist; that he thought souls are mortal; that he was a simoniac and a usurer; that he kept two concubines, nieces, and had children by both, and so on. Boniface, having held a council at Rome, placed the king of France under interdict and excluded the king, with his descendants to the fourth generation, from the Church. The affair ended so shamefully for him that Boniface, through the scheming of Nogaret, was seized at Anagni by Philip's agents, and placed on a wild horse with his face to the tail; he was seized with madness and died in prison, giving an example to all prelates. These words are those of Lang and Rolevinck, that they should not think high thoughts, but should rather strive to be loved by their subjects, as the flock of their deeds, than to be feared.

units.la: CXXI. Florebat ea ætate in Gallia Robertus Gallus, quem Possevinus in Appar. Tom. 2. Excellentem verbi Divini concionatorem vocat. Ejus extat libellus Lutetiæ cum Hildegardæ Vaticiniis editus, Visiones etiam quasdam ejus complexus. Cap. 5. Papam Idolum diserte vocat, his verbis Deum loquentem inducens: Quis posuit Idolum hoc in sede mea, ut imperaret gregi meo? Sed & cap. I. ac 12. sub serpentis nomine Papam ceu Antichristum describit, qui se supra modum extollit, pios quosque opprimat, multis Pseudoprohetis circumseptus, qui in contemptum Dei & Christi eum solum prædicent & extollant, Jesu contrà nomen obscurent. Demum Ecclesiam Romanam depingens inquit: Orabam flexis genubus, erecta facie ad Cœlum, juxta altare S. Jacobi Parisiis à dextris, & vidi in aere ante me corpus unius summi Pontificis albis sericis indutum, tenebatque dorsum ad Orientem, elevatis manibus ad Occidentem, sicut sacerdotes solent stare, dum agunt Missarum decreta. Non videbatur caput ejus, diligentiùsque intuens, an esset omnino sine capite, vidi caput ejus aridum, macilentum, ac si esset ligneum; dixitque spiritus Domini: Statum Ecclesiæ Romanæ significat, in qua scilicet nihil sanguinis, succi vitalis nihil superest. Mox etiam cujusmodi panem Ecclesia Romana filiis suis famelicis tribuat, sic explicat: Iterum alio die idem operis me agente, fui fui videns in spiritu. Et ecce vir ejusdem habitus circuibat, panem delicatum portans in humeris, cum vino optimo, dependebántque panis & vinum per latera ejus, ipse vero tenebat manibus lapidem oblongum durissimum dentibus rodens illum, ut famescens circa panem agere solet, nihil autem agebat. Et de lapide egrediebantur duo capita serpentum, & instruebat me Domini spiritus dicens: Lapis hic quaestiones inutiles & curiosæ sunt, in quibus famescentes laborant, animarum substantialia relinquentes; & dixi, quid ergo capita illa dicunt. Et dixit nomen uni, vana gloria; alteri, dissipatio religionis. Aptioribus verbis temporum illorum sophistica exprimi non potuit, quæ rejecto, quod ad manum erat, Dei verbo, tota futilibus, & ad salutem hominum nihil proficientibus, sed ei officientibus magis quæstionibus immorabatur & immoriebatur. Tandem etiam futuram Reformationem Ecclesiæ Deus in visione ipsi aperuit, futuræ scilicet quandoque lucidæ per munditiem vitæ, sonoræ per claram vocem prædicationis veræ veritatis.
units.tr: CXXI. At that time in France flourished Robert the Gaul, whom Possevinus, in Appar. Tom. 2., calls an excellent preacher of the Divine Word. A little book of his was published at Paris together with the prophecies of Hildegard, and it also contains certain visions of his. In chapter 5 he plainly calls the Pope an Idol, introducing God speaking in these words: Who set this idol in my seat, to rule over my flock? But also in chapters 1 and 12, under the name of the serpent, he describes the Pope as Antichrist, who exalts himself beyond measure, oppresses all the godly, and is surrounded by many false prophets, who proclaim him alone and exalt him in contempt of God and Christ, while they obscure the name of Jesus. Finally, describing the Church of Rome, he says: I was praying on my knees, with my face raised to heaven, beside the altar of St. James at Paris on the right, and I saw in the air before me the body of one supreme Pontiff clothed in white silk; he stood with his back to the East and his hands raised to the West, as priests are wont to stand when they perform the decrees of the Masses. His head was not visible, but looking more carefully, whether he was altogether without a head, I saw his head dry and emaciated, as if it were wooden; and the Spirit of the Lord said: It signifies the state of the Church of Rome, in which indeed there is nothing of blood or of vital juice left. Then he explains what kind of bread the Roman Church gives to her starving children: Again on another day, while I was at the same work, I fell into a trance and saw a man of the same appearance going round, carrying delicate bread on his shoulders, together with the best wine; the bread and the wine hung down by his sides; he himself held in his hands a long, very hard stone, gnawing it with his teeth, as hungry people are wont to do with bread, yet he got nothing done. And from the stone two serpents' heads came forth, and the Spirit of the Lord instructed me, saying: This stone is useless and curious questions, over which the hungry labour, leaving aside the substance of souls; and I said, what then do those heads say? And he named one, vainglory; the other, the dissolution of religion. The sophistries of those times could not be expressed in more fitting words, for, rejecting the Word of God which lay at hand, they lingered over, and wore themselves out upon, questions that were wholly futile and profited nothing for men's salvation, but rather stood in its way. At last God also revealed to him in a vision the future Reformation of the Church, which would at some time be bright through the purity of its life, and resounding through the clear voice of the preaching of the true truth.

units.la: CXXII. Erant tum in Italia quoque Doctores, Fratricellorum nomine insignes, quos inter Gerhardus Sagarelli Parmensis, & Dulcinus Novariensis, Hermanni cujusdam discipuli, eminebant. In hos severissimè Bonifacius animadvertit, insimulatos nescio quarum turpitudinum. Cœterùm satis constat, non ullius sceleris compertos, sed hanc ferè ob causam ferro flammáque infestatos esse, quòd Papam Romanum Antichristum; Ecclesiam Romanam Babylonem Apocalypticam, & spirituales, qui maximè videri volebant, à Deo rejectos esse, contenderent. Fatentibus iis ipsis, qui nescio quarum hæreseon dicam iis scribere conati sunt.
units.tr: CXXII. There were then also in Italy teachers distinguished by the name of Fraticelli, among whom Gerard Segarelli of Parma and Dolcino of Novara, a disciple of a certain Hermann, stood out. Boniface punished these severely, charging them with I know not what shameful deeds. Yet it is quite clear that they were not convicted of any crime, but were assailed with fire and sword mainly for this reason: that they maintained the Roman Pope to be Antichrist, the Roman Church the Apocalyptic Babylon, and that the spirituals, who most wished to appear such, were rejected by God. Those very men who have tried to write about them, I know not on what heresies, admit this.

units.la: CXXIII. Clemens V. Gallus A. MCCCV. Pontifex dissentientibus mirè Cardinalibus, Philippi Pulchri Gallorum Regis favore, postquam splendidis eum promissis lactalaftavit, electus, Roma sedem Pontificiam Avenionem in Galliam transtulerat. Ubi Romam per Cardinales tres Senatoria potestate, tanquam per Consules & Senatores gubernans, septuaginta integros annos (unde captivitatis Babylonicæ septuaginta annorum tempus illud commorantium Avenione Pontificum à scriptoribus venire solet) ipse & quinque ejus successores commorati sunt, nemine excipiente, Romam Petri sedem esse, illuc proin remeandum. Reformandæ Ecclesiæ; quam ipse tamen vita turpi, cujus specimina nonnulla Paulus Langius profert, graviter offendit; spem faciens, Durando Rotæ Auditori & Episcopo Mimatensi Gallo, cui Speculatori vulgò nomen, ut quædam capita eò pertinentia, in Concilio proponenda, consignaret, in mandatis dederat. Extat adhuc Tractatus ille, cui Titulus, de Concilio celebrando, A. MDXLV. Lutetiæ impressus ἀξιομνημόνευτος, si quisquam alius. Initio à Cleri Romani reprehensione ducto sic loquitur: Secuti sunt viam Balaam ex Bosor, qui mercedem iniquitatis amavit, correctionem verò habuit suæ vesaniæ. Nam subjugale mutum, quod hominis voce locutum est, Prophetæ insipientiam probavit. Quod etiam hodie accidit, cùm tam stulta & dissoluta in Ecclesia Dei à dictis personis Ecclesiasticis, quæ deberent esse lumen aliorum, & lucernæ super candelabrum positæ; juxta id quod Dominus ait: sensus hebetant Iudæorum & etiam Paganorum: Et etiam illi, qui ratione Divinæ agnitionis omni modo carent, istorum detestantur insaniam, & istorum distorta & Deo contraria itinera saniùs sapiendo redarguunt. Inde quæ via in Reformatione tenenda sit, explicans, pertendit, in Concilio tali ad Legem Dei, ad Euangelium, ad Concilia instinctu Spiritus S. approbata, ad bonas etiam leges humanas recurrendum, & abusus omnes, consuetudines, dispensationes, privilegia, libertates, exemptiones illis adversantes abolendas esse. Papam ipsum se & sua facta Divinis nis & humanis legibus conformare debere: Ecclesiam Romanam in multis à sacra primitivæ Ecclesiæ institutione, sanctorum Patrum & Conciliorum & Decretorum sententia deviantem, & primæ institutionis oblitam scripturæ subjiciendam esse: Papæ interdicendum, ne causæ ex Provinciis in Curiam transferantur: Simoniam, quæ in Romana Curia perinde regnet, ac si nullum peccatum esset, pluralitatem beneficiorum, Cardinalium pensiones, titulum universalis Episcopi à Gregorio M. repudiatum, abolenda esse, renovandumque Milevitani Concilii Canonem, ut una quaeque causa in sua Provincia terminetur: Matrimonium in Concilio eo sacerdotibus concedendum: cogendos esse Monachos ad laborem manuum: reprimendum abusum imaginum, indulgentiarum & poenitentiarum, Monachorum licentiam humana inventa praedicantium. Identidem vero exclamat, tanquam in morbo desperato, spem omnem abjiciens: Proh dolor (ita par. 3. Tit. 28. & sequ. exclamat) quia videtur in ipsa Ecclesia verisicari dictum Esai. 34. in figuram Babylonicæ civitatis, gloriosæ in Regnis & inclytæ in superbia Chaldæorum, de qua dicitur: Erit cubile Draconum & pascua struthionum, occurrent daemonia, Onocentaurus & pilosus clamabit alter ad alterum: ibi cubabit lumia, & invenit sibi requiem ibi habuit foveam ericius, & enutrivit catulos illic congregati sunt milvi alter & alterum. Utinam non verificetur verbum in Clero Esajæ dicentis: Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longè est à me.
units.tr: CXXIII. Clement V, a Frenchman, was elected Pope in 1305, to the striking disagreement of the cardinals, through the favour of Philip the Fair, King of the French, after Philip had lulled him with splendid promises. He transferred the Papal see from Rome to Avignon in France. There, governing Rome through three cardinals with senatorial power, as though through consuls and senators, he and his five successors remained for seventy full years (whence that period of Popes dwelling at Avignon is usually called by writers the Babylonian captivity of seventy years), while no one denied that Rome was the see of Peter and that they must therefore return there. He had indeed promised reform of the Church, but by his own shameful life, of which Paul Lang gives some examples, he gravely offended it. He had instructed Durandus, Auditor of the Rota and a French bishop of Mende, who was commonly called the Speculator, to set down certain heads pertaining to this, to be proposed in a council. That treatise still exists, entitled On Calling a Council, printed at Paris in 1545, worthy of being remembered [ἀξιομνημόνευτος], if any other is. Beginning from a rebuke of the Roman clergy, he speaks thus: They have followed the way of Balaam, son of Bosor, who loved the wages of iniquity, but received rebuke for his madness. For the dumb beast, speaking with a human voice, checked the prophet's folly. This happens today too, when such foolishness and dissolution in the Church of God is found in the said ecclesiastical persons, who ought to be the light of others and lamps set on a candlestick; according to what the Lord says: they dull the senses even of the Jews and also of the pagans. And even those who lack in every way the reason of the divine knowledge detest their madness, and by wiser reasoning refute their crooked paths, which are contrary to God. Then, explaining what course should be held in the Reformation, he argues that in such a council one must have recourse to the Law of God, to the Gospel, to the councils approved under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and also to good human laws; and that all abuses, customs, dispensations, privileges, liberties, and exemptions opposed to these must be abolished. The Pope himself must conform himself and his acts to divine and human laws; the Roman Church, which in many respects deviates from the sacred institution of the primitive Church, from the judgement of the holy Fathers, councils and decrees, and has forgotten its first institution, must be made subject to Scripture; the Pope must be forbidden to transfer cases from the provinces to the Curia; simony, which reigns in the Roman Curia as though it were no sin at all, the plurality of benefices, the pensions of cardinals, and the title of universal bishop, rejected by Gregory the Great, must be abolished, and the canon of the Council of Milevis must be renewed, so that each cause be settled in its own province. Marriage should be granted to priests in that council; monks should be compelled to manual labour; the abuse of images, indulgences and penances, and the licence of monks who preach human inventions, must be curbed. Again and again he cries out, as in a desperate illness, casting off all hope (so he cries out in part 3, title 28, and following): Alas (for so he cries out in part 3, title 28, and following), because it seems that what is said in Isaiah 34 is verified in the Church itself, concerning the figure of Babylon, the city glorious among kingdoms and famous for the pride of the Chaldeans, of which it is said: It shall be a den of dragons and a pasture of ostriches; demons shall meet there, the onocentaur and the hairy one shall cry to one another; there the night-monster shall lie down and find rest for herself; the hedgehog made her nest there and nursed her young, and the kites gathered there, each with its mate. Would that the word of Isaiah, spoken of the clergy, were not fulfilled: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.

units.la: CXXIV. Fuisse vero spem illam de reformatione Ec- clesiæ conceptam vanam, eventus docuit.
units.tr: CXXIV. That the hope of reforming the Church which had been conceived was vain, the outcome showed.

units.la: Neque enim in Concilio mox Viennæ praesente Rege Philippo, celebrato, commonefactionum ejusmodi fructus ullus fuit. Quinimo in eo edita est Decretalis illa, cui initium Pastoralis, in qua Clemens sese supra Imperatores longè extollit, vicarium se Regis Regum profitus. Tum etiam fratrum
units.tr: Indeed, no fruit at all came from such admonitions at the Council of Vienne, which was held soon afterwards in the presence of King Philip. On the contrary, that Decretal was issued there which begins Pastoralis, in which Clement raised himself far above the emperors, professing himself the vicar of the King of kings. Then too the order of the Minor Friars was sanctioned, by that absurd law whose opening words in the Clementines are: Exivi de Paradiso, "I went out from Paradise"; "I will water the garden of plantings," says that heavenly farmer, who truly is the door of wisdom, the Word of God, remaining from the Father in the Father...

units.la: par. 3. Tit. 28. & sequ. trum Minorum religio auctorata est, ridicula illa lege, cujus in Clementinis initium: Exivi de Paradiso, dixi: Rigabo hortum plantationum, ait ille Cœlestis agricola, qui vere fores sapientiæ, verbum Dei à Patre in Patre manens, genitum ab æterno &c. Talia præfatus pergit: Hic hortus siquidem est fratrum Minorum sancta religio, quæ muris regularis Observantiæ firmiter undique circumclusa, intra se solo contenta Deo, adornatur abundè novellis plantationibus filiorum. Denique in eo Concilio dam-mnantur hæreseos & aliorum criminum Templarii, exinde pluribus locis crudelissimè combusti, totaque Ecclesia proscripti, bonis spoliati. Innocentiæ testimonium iis perhibent Bocatius, Villanus, Antoninus, Nauclerus, Aventinus, alii. Neque desunt, qui incanduisse in eos Pontificem afferant, eò quòd curiam Romanam, cui excidium Palæstinæ tribuebant merito, detestati essent. Certè plerique tormentis nullis, ut crimina sibi impacta confiterentur, adduci potuerunt. Quin potiùs nonnulli ad supplicia rapti Clementem & Pulchrum, uti etiam Haraldus in Epitome Annalium Ordinis Minorum ex octo Tomis Lucæ Waddingi excerpta, testatur, ad Dei tribunal animosè citârunt, quos inter Jacobus Burgundio Ordinis princeps, quæ in quæstione dirissima confessus erat, ad ignis supplicium productus, cùm spes veniæ ipsi, dummodo quæ in custodia fassus erat, palam confiteretur, facta essent, palinodiam cecinit, & sævissimè ac lentè ustulatus licet, Ordinis innocentiam ad finem usque vitæ constanter professus est. Quid quòd suppliciis sublatos Templarios pro Martyribus cultos Nauclerus Generat. 44. p. 244. testatur: & nuper Drexelius lib. 2. Trib. Christi cap. 3. §. 2. pro iis apologiam texuit?
units.tr: par. 3. Tit. 28. & sequ. The Order of the Friars Minor was given authority by that ridiculous law, whose opening words in the Clementines are: I have gone forth from Paradise, I said: I will water the garden of plantations, says that heavenly farmer, "who truly is the door of wisdom, the Word of God, remaining in the Father, begotten from the Father from eternity, etc." He goes on with such introductory words: For this garden is indeed the holy religion of the Friars Minor, which, firmly enclosed on every side by the walls of the regular Observance, content within itself with God alone, is abundantly adorned with new plantings of sons. Finally, in that Council the Templars were condemned for heresy and other crimes, and afterwards were most cruelly burned in many places, and were proscribed by the whole Church and stripped of their goods. Bocatius, Villanus, Antoninus, Nauclerus, Aventinus and others bear witness to their innocence. Nor are there lacking those who claim that the Pontiff was inflamed against them because they had detested the Roman curia, to which they rightly attributed the ruin of Palestine. Certainly most of them could not be brought by any torments to confess the crimes laid upon them. Rather, several who were dragged to execution boldly summoned Clement and Philip the Fair to the tribunal of God, as Haraldus testifies in his Epitome of the Annals of the Order of Minors, excerpted from the eight volumes of Luke Wadding. Among them was Jacob of Burgundy, prince of the Order, who had confessed under the most dreadful questioning. When he was brought out to the punishment of fire, hopes of pardon were held out to him if he would publicly confess what he had admitted in custody; but he recanted, and although he was burned most cruelly and slowly, he constantly professed the innocence of the Order until the end of his life. What of the fact that Nauclerus Generat. 44. p. 244. reports that the Templars who had been removed by execution were honoured as martyrs, and that Drexelius recently wove an apology for them in lib. 2. Trib. Christi cap. 3. §. 2.?

units.la: CXXV. Eodem Pontifice A. MCCCVIII. Cæsar à Prin- cipibus Germaniæ Henricus VII. Lucelburgensis creatus est.
units.tr: CXXV. In the same pontificate, in the year 1308, Henry VII of Luxembourg was elected Caesar by the princes of Germany.

units.la: Mox Romam contendit, coronam à Pontifice indepturus. Cùm verò Cardinalibus (quos cum Senatoria potestate Romæ Pontifex reliquerat) sacramentum præstandum denegàsset, dictitans, contra morem majorum, libertatémque Religionis Christianæ militare, ut Princeps Principum, Orbisque terrarum dominus, servo servorum sacramento dicat, Papæ odium internecinum incurrit. Per Robertum igitur Regem Neapolitanum insidias ei struxit, quibus brevi succubuit, venenata hostia à Bernhardo Politiano Dominicano confessore suo, ad id subornato, cum Florentiam obsideret, sublatus. Deus scilicet Panaceus Imperatori optimo cor percussit atque deturbavit. Papa quidem edita Bulla ab ordine Prædicatorum infamiam abstergere conatus est. Nefarium tamen facinus unanimi consensu historici omnes affirmant. Et Vitoduranus noster Henrici σύγγεον fusè in primis & ἐπιχαλικῶς apud Celeb. Hottingerum Hist. Eccles. Sec. XIV. p. 752. &c. historiam edidit.
units.tr: Soon he hastened to Rome to receive the crown from the Pope. But when the Cardinals, whom the Pope had left at Rome with senatorial authority, refused to let him take the oath, he protested that it was contrary to the custom of our forefathers and to the liberty of the Christian religion that the Prince of princes and lord of the world should swear an oath to the servant of the servants of God. He thereby incurred the deadly hatred of the Pope. Through King Robert of Naples, therefore, the Pope laid snares for him, and he soon succumbed, being removed by a poisoned host administered by his confessor, the Dominican Bernhardus Politianus, who had been suborned for this purpose while the emperor was besieging Florence. God, the All-Healer, had evidently struck and overthrown the excellent Emperor's heart. The Pope, indeed, by issuing a bull, tried to wipe away the infamy of the Dominican Order. Yet all the historians affirm with one voice that the deed was wicked. Our Vitoduranus also published a full and detailed account of Henry's death [σύγγραμμα], especially in the work of the renowned Hottinger, Hist. Eccles. Sec. XIV, p. 752 and following.

units.la: CXXVI. Non defuerunt sanè perditis illis temporibus, qui propalam Romanæ Ecclesiæ corruptionem detestarentur merito; Dantes Aligerius, Florentinus, edito tractatu, cui titulus Monarchia, Donationem Constantini refutavit, & usurpationes Pontificias graviter reprehendit. In Poëmate de Paradiso Italica lingua conscripto, acerbè quiritatus est; Papam in lupum evasisse, oves Christi à vera via divertisse, propterea Euangelium deseri, Patrum scripta negligi, solis Decretalibus incumbi; de Nazaretho, ubi Gabriel alas suas expandit, neminem cogitare, Vaticanum tantum & alia selectiora Romæ loca à Papa & Cardinalibus attendi. Et hæc, inquit, militiæ Christi, cui nomen dederat Petrus, cœmiterium fuerunt, cùm interim doctrinam Romæ verè sepeliverunt. Olim illatum Ecclesiæ gladio bellum: inferri jam fame, sublato pane illo, quem Deus ei alenda dederat, nempe Verbi Divini Prædicatione &c. Scripturam Divinam aut omnino à tergo relinqui, aut violenter torqueri: Vnumquemque in suis commentis sibi plaudere: Euangelium vero taceri. In cathedra toto anno vanas quæstiones, meras fabulas personare; oviculas interim hoc vento pastas tabescere. Memorabile cumprimis, quòd eodem tempore Fridericus III. Siciliæ Rex, Princeps cætera religiosus, Ecclesiæ Romanæ scandaloso regimine ita commotus fuerit, ut de Veritate Euangelij subdubitare jam cœperit, anxius scilicet: Euangelii ne doctrina, an Ecclesiæ traditio humanum inventum esset. Confirmatus autem in vera fide est ab Arnoldo Villanovano, ostendente ei scandala illa in ipso Dei Verbo jam pridem prædicta; & bis jam Sedi Apostolicæ Apostasiam Diabolicam, sub Bonifacio VIII. & Benedicto XI. denuntiatam, & tertia vice mox denuntiandam iterum esse. Et dubitationes Regis, & Villanovani discussionem dubitationum lectu dignissimam Cl. Mornæus Myst. Iniq. pag. m. 973. &c. fusè admodum repræsentat.
units.tr: CXXVII. When Clement V had died, and there was an interregnum of two years, with the cardinals wonderfully divided, and the choice of the Pontiff was at last left to one cardinal, James of Ossa of Cahors, a Frenchman, he mounted the throne, contrary to everyone's expectation, and cried out: "I am the Pope." And so, judging like Jove himself, he elected himself, called John XXII by some and XXIII by others. This was the man who openly taught and preached that the souls of the faithful departed are not admitted to the blessed vision of God before the time of the resurrection. The Sorbonne condemned this error, Gerson bearing witness in his Easter Sermon, and others too everywhere refuted it as a heresy, above all Thomas Wallis, an English Dominican, whom the Pope for that reason thrust into prison. (On this matter Launoy has lately disputed learnedly in many places, Epist. lib. I, 5, and lib. III, last epistle.) This same man also published the Extravagantes, in which the Pope is vindicated as preferred to the emperor as the Sun to the Moon, and the power of transferring empires, of excommunicating angels, of making the round from the square, of making right out of wrong, of dispensing against natural, international, and civil law, decrees, canons, councils, the Old Testament, and the Gospels.

units.la: CXXVII. Clemente V. mortuo cum Cardinalibus mirè dissidentibus duorum annorum Inter-pontificium esset, & eligendi tandem Pontificis arbitrium uni Cardinali de Ossa Cadurcensi Gallo deferretur, præter omnium exspectationem conscenso throno, Ego sum Papa, clamavit; atque sic Jove scilicet æquo judicans, se ipsum elegit, dictus Johannes, ab aliis XXII. ab aliis XXIII. ille scilicet, qui aperte docuit & prædicavit animas defunctorum fidelium ad beatam Visionem Dei ante tempus resurrectionis non admitti, quem ejus errorem Sorbona, Gersone in Sermone Paschali teste, damnavit, aliíque etiam passim, in primis Thomas Wallis Anglus Dominicanus, quem Papa propterea in carcerem compegit, ceu hæresin graviter refutârunt: (quam in rem multa nuper Launojus Epist. lib. I. 5. & lib. III. Epist. ult. erudite disseruit) quíque etiam Extravagantes edidit, quibus Papa Imperatori, ut Sol Lunæ præfertur: eíque facultas transferendi impe- Fridericus III. Siciliæ Rex Ecclesiæ Rom. statu offensus de Euangelii ipsius Veritate dubitat, & ab Alphonso Villanovo in ea confirmatur. Johannes XXII. seipsum eligens, animas ante finem mundi Deo frui negat. Et Papam Imperatori, ut Solem Lunae praestare aliaque superbissimè decernt. imperia, excommunicandi Angelos, ex quadrato rotundum, ex injuria jus faciendi, contra jus naturale, gentium, civile, decreta, Canones, Concilia, Testamentum Vetus, Euangelia, dispensandi vindicatur.
units.tr: 127. When Clement V died, the Cardinals were badly divided and there was an interregnum of two years. At last the choice of a Pontiff was left to the judgment of one Cardinal, de Ossa of Cahors, a Frenchman. Contrary to everyone's expectation, he mounted the throne and cried, I am Pope. Judging himself as impartial as Jove, he thus chose himself. He was called John, by some XXII and by others XXIII. This was the man who openly taught and preached that the souls of the faithful departed are not admitted to the blessed vision of God before the time of the resurrection. The Sorbonne condemned this error, as Gerson attests in his Easter Sermon, and others everywhere also refuted it strongly as heresy, above all Thomas Wallis, an English Dominican, whom the Pope on that account threw into prison. (Launoy has lately discussed this matter learnedly in Epist. lib. I. 5. and lib. III. Epist. ult..) He also issued the Extravagantes, in which the Pope is preferred to the Emperor as the Sun is to the Moon, and the power of transferring empires... Frederick III, King of Sicily, offended by the state of the Roman Church, doubts the truth of the Gospel itself, and is confirmed in this doubt by Alphonso of Villanova. John XXII, choosing himself, denies that souls enjoy God before the end of the world. And he decrees most arrogantly that the Pope is to be preferred to the Emperor as the Sun is to the Moon, and claims for himself the power of excommunicating angels, of making the square round, of making right out of wrong, and of dispensing against natural law, the law of nations, civil law, decrees, canons, councils, the Old Testament, and the Gospels.

units.la: CXXVIII. Talis verò cùm fuerit, non potuit non Cæsareo-Papatum suum proferre, & inimicitiis adversus Cæsarem, supremum in terris Dominum gestis exerere. Mortuo scilicet Henrico VII. scindebantur Germanorum studia, aliis Ludovicum Bavarum, Fridericum Austriacum aliis eligentibus. Uterque confirmari à Papa cùm petiisset, rejectus uterque ab eodem est, Fridericus, quòd sapientis Salomonis stolidus filius esset: Ludovicus, quòd ea jam ausus esset, quæ nondum confirmatum Cæsarem dedeceant. Postea tamen cum Friderico, fatuo scilicet illo, adversus Ludovicum Papa conspiravit. Ludovicus contra, victo Friderico, in Italia Gibellinos contra Welphos corroboraverat. Id verò contineri tacitis discordiis non potuit, sed in fortunas Cæsaris & Imperii erupit. Nam & publico scripto Papa Cæsarem citavit, ut intra trimestre se Avenione sisteret, factíque sui rationem redderet; & ut interea Imperium deponeret, praecepit. Imperator verò adhibitis in consilium omnibus Academiis Guilhelmo cumprimis Occam, Bona Gratia Bergamensé & Michaele Cæsenate Franciscanorum Antistite, Marsilio Patavino, aliisque, Cæsareis adversus Papam partibus sese applicantibus; ad Generale Concilium provocavit. Quod indignè cùm ferret Papa, eum excommunicavit. Non multò post Romani à Pontifice postulârunt, ut Avenione relicta Romam rediret. Quod cùm facere detrectaret, Ludovicum Imperatorem accersunt, qui A. MCCCXXVII. Italiam cum exercitu intrans, mox Romæ per Stephanum Columnam Cardinalem, invito Pontifice, in Laterano una cum Conjuge coronatus & Augustus proclamatus est. Mox de consilio Cardinalium, Cleri & Populi Romani Pontificem Johannem Romam citavit, & coram sententiam dicere jussit; non Imperatorem ab Ecclesia, sed Ecclesiam ab Imperatore pendere afferens, uti Onuphrius scribit. Cùm autem comparere nollet, Pontificatu eum privat, & imagine ejus coram combusta Nicolaum V. cui ante Petro Corbario, Minoritæ, nomen erat; Antipapam constituit, quo proditione Pisanorum Johanni tradito, ac in carcere mortuo, tandem Johannes etiam A. MCCCXXXV. moritur, relicta in thesauris tanta auri vi, quantam nullus ante eum Pontisex reliquerat. Nauclerus millies viginti quinque millia aureorum reliquisse scribit.
units.tr: CXXVIII. Being such a man, he could not fail to put forward his Caesaro-Papacy and to display his enmity against the Emperor, who was supreme lord on earth. When Henry VII died, the Germans were divided: some chose Louis of Bavaria, others Frederick of Austria. When each asked the Pope to confirm him, the Pope rejected both: Frederick, because he was the foolish son of the wise Solomon; Louis, because he had dared to do things that did not befit an emperor not yet confirmed. Afterwards, however, the Pope conspired against Louis together with Frederick, that foolish man. Louis, on the other hand, after defeating Frederick, had strengthened the Ghibellines against the Guelphs in Italy. This could not remain hidden under silent discord, but broke out against the fortunes of the Emperor and the Empire. For the Pope cited the Emperor by public writ to appear at Avignon within three months and render an account of his conduct, and he ordered him meanwhile to lay down the Empire. The Emperor, however, took counsel from all the universities, especially William of Occam, Bonagratia of Bergamo and Michael of Cesena, head of the Franciscans, and Marsilius of Padua, and others who joined the Imperial side against the Pope; and he appealed to a General Council. The Pope took this badly and excommunicated him. Not long afterwards the Romans asked the Pontiff to leave Avignon and return to Rome. When he refused, they summoned Louis the Emperor, who, entering Italy with an army in 1327, was soon crowned and proclaimed Augustus in the Lateran, along with his wife, by Stephen Colonna the Cardinal, against the will of the Pontiff. Then, by the counsel of the Cardinals, the clergy and the people of Rome, he summoned Pope John to Rome and ordered him to appear and hear the sentence, asserting, as Onuphrius writes, that the Church depends on the Emperor and not the Emperor on the Church. When John would not appear, he deprived him of the Pontificate, and after burning his image in his presence, he set up as antipope Nicholas V, who formerly had been called Peter Corbario, a Minorite. Then, by the treachery of the Pisans, John was handed over and died in prison; at last John himself died in 1335, leaving in his treasury such a vast quantity of gold as no Pontiff before him had left. Naucler writes that he left twenty-five million gold pieces.

units.la: CXXIX. Erat scilicet Johannes adeò divitiarum appetens, ut paupertatem non solum à Christo ejúsque Apostolis, sed à Philosophis etiam, Poëtis & Oratoribus gentilibus collaudatam, palam irriserit, & Franciscanos opinioni suæ adversantes, ceu hæreticos excommunicaverit, Fraterculos appellaverit, plurésque etiam combufferit. Glisccbátque adeò vehementer hæc de paupertate Christi contentio Franciscanos inter & Dominicanos Johannis aßeclas; affirmantibus illis, Christum nudum pependisse in cruce, neque habuisse, ubi reclinaret caput suum, spinea corona obseptum; his verò pertendentibus, Christum in cruce pependisse non nudum, nec spinea corona caput redimitum, sed ornatum in capite corona Regia & aurea, indutum vero prætexta, id est, toga purpurea, usque ad talos demissa, & limbis aureis prætextata, insuper & cinctum zona aureis bullis insigni, pedésque calceis deauratis seu bracteatis circumdatum; Talem scilicet Christum crucifixum Johannes & cum eo Dominicani etiam pingi & in Templis suspendi curárunt, testante Bullingero in M. S. historia Joh. XXII. sua etiam ætate te multis in locis visas esse imagines tales Domini crucifixi, vetustate propemodum erosas. In nonnullis locis, teste Johanne Barvota Vitodurano Minorita, qui his ipsis temporibus vixit, visæ sunt imagines crucifixi, altera quidem manu ad crucem affixa, altera verò immissa in crumenam ex zona dependentem, veluti inde pecuniam in usus necessarios & pauperum prolaturā. Quo figmento, Christum tantùm non in Judam transformante, rudi populo significare voluerunt, Christum non ita, sicut à Franciscanis prædicabatur, pauperem fuisse. Et quò væsana hæc Papæ, cui opulentissimo omnium, in divitiis tantùm non beatitudinis apicem reponenti, adeóque argentum Euangelio, aurum Christi inopiæ præferenti (uti quidem etiam Ludovicus Imp. ipsi in Edicto objecit) Christi, cujus vicariam dignitatem sibi arrogavit, pauperras, sudes in oculis fuit; consilia flexerint, facile piis omnibus suboluit. Certè Alvarus Pelagius, Papæ illius Pœnitentiarius, Hispaniæ suæ decus, & edito de Planctu Ecclesiæ, magno & insigni, uti Trithemius vocat, opere, quo Ecclesiasticorum inprimis, hypocrisin graviter perstrinxit, celebris, in hanc Papæ & supparasitantium ei Dominicanorum, seu potiùs Dæmoniacorum impietatem acriter invectus est. Et nuper etiam Haraldus in Epitome Annalium Waddingi, Johanni huic adversus decreta præcedentium Pontificum, Nicolai III. & Clementis V. sub anathemate pro Franciscanis, quòd Cristus pauper fuerit, definientium, ejusdem opulentiam propugnanti, temeritatis notam haud obscurè impegit.
units.tr: CXXIX. John was so eager for riches that he openly mocked the poverty praised not only by Christ and his Apostles but also by the pagan philosophers, poets and orators. He excommunicated the Franciscans who opposed his opinion, calling them heretics, named them "little brothers," and had several of them burnt. The dispute over Christ's poverty between the Franciscans and the Dominicans, who were followers of John, grew so fierce that the Franciscans maintained that Christ hung naked on the cross and had no place to rest his head, crowned with thorns. The Dominicans, on the other hand, insisted that Christ did not hang naked on the cross, nor with his head wreathed in thorns, but with a royal golden crown on his head, clothed in a purple robe reaching down to his ankles and edged with golden borders, girded with a belt adorned with golden studs, and with his feet encased in gilded or foil-covered shoes. John and the Dominicans with him had such a crucified Christ painted and hung in the churches, as Bullinger attests in his manuscript history of John XXII, and he says that in his own day many such images of the crucified Lord, nearly worn away by age, could be seen in many places. In some places, according to John Barvota of Winterthur, a Franciscan who lived in those very times, images of the crucified were seen with one hand fixed to the cross and the other thrust into a purse hanging from the belt, as if money were being drawn from it for necessary uses and for the poor. By this fiction, which almost turned Christ into Judas, they wished to signal to the unlearned people that Christ was not poor in the way the Franciscans preached. That these mad designs of the Pope, who, the richest of all men, set the summit of blessedness in riches, and who preferred silver to the Gospel and gold to the poverty of Christ (as Emperor Louis also objected to him in his Edict), whose vicarious dignity he claimed for himself, were an offence in the eyes of Christ, was easily grasped by all the godly. Certainly Alvarus Pelagius, that Pope's Penitentiary and the glory of his Spain, famous for his great and notable work, as Trithemius calls it, On the Lament of the Church, which sharply censured above all the hypocrisy of churchmen, vehemently attacked this impiety of the Pope and of the Dominicans, or rather demoniacs, who fawned on him. And recently Haraldus too, in his Epitome of the Annals of Waddingus, has plainly branded with the mark of rashness John, who defended his own opulence against the decrees of his predecessors, Nicholas III and Clement V, who under anathema had defined for the Franciscans that Christ was poor.

units.la: CXXX. Haud præter rem fuerit, tum Bullam Johannis, qua is Cæsarem Ludovicum afflavit, tum ex Ludovici etiam adversus Johannem Edicto nonnulla, præeunte Aventino, repræsentare. Sic autem Bulla illa, quam vento plenam Aventinus, Bestialem Bullingerus non immeritò
units.tr: CXXX. It will not be out of place to set forth both the Bull by which John assailed Emperor Louis, and some passages from Louis's Edict against John, following Aventinus. That Bull, which Aventinus calls full of wind and Bullinger not unjustly calls bestial,

units.la: Johannis ejusdem Bulla vere Babylonica adversus Ludovicum Bavarum. ritò appellant, nos Babylonicam insignire haud verecundamur; apud Aventinum lib. VII. p. m. 468. discribitur: Postquam à decessoribus nostris res Romana, à Græcis ad Germanos transflata, Carolo M. in fidem atque tutelam commissa est, summus ille honor, beneficium Pontificis Maximi esse solet. Decretum siquidem est, ut cùm Germani Principes Regem jussissent, id demum ratum esset si Romanus Pontifex, Orbis Christiani Pater atque Princeps author fieret, nec ante cuiquam Comitiis Cæsareis, suffragiis Principum designato Regi, neque administrandi, neque Regij tituli usurpandi jus est, quàm primarius sacerdos, Dei O. M. Legatus, suo numine faveat, & aspiret. Præterea summa potestas, maximum imperium, ubi orbum capite fuerit, penes Max. Pontificem, cujus beneficium illud est, existit. Itidem ubi septem suffragatores Comitiis Cæsareis discordes fuerint, neuter Rex est. Episcopus Romanus, sicut communis omnium Mortalium parens, fasces Romanos ob dissensionem destitutos, Rempub. derelictam, suo arbitrio temperat. Quemadmodum animus imperare, corpus illi, cujus beneficio vivit, servire debet: ita optimè consultum esse rebus Christianis, nemo ambigit, ubi fragilia æternis, prophana sacris, corporalia spiritualibus subdita sunt, atque obtemperant. Quod tum fiet, quando Pontifex Max. dignitatem utramque suo arbitratu moderatur. Ecclesia dominatur, ejus lege atque imperio omnis potestas redigitur. Et Imperator religione sacramenti ei, qui terris præsidendo, vicem Cælestis Imperatoris perfungitur, addictus est. Hæce ob causas cùm post fata Imperatoris Henrici septimi, duo, Fridericus atque Ludovicus Reges consalutati fuerint, ambo utpote contra auspicia creati, indigni sunt summo rerum humanarum fastigio. Respublica in medio derelicta atque dilacerata à nobis jure nostro administratur. Proinde Ludovicus maximo malo suo, non minore Ecclesiæ Romanæ detrimento, nec dum à nobis dignus, qui imperet, judicatus, sua sponte Regium nomen, rerum habenas temerè usurpavit, atque vi in Italia atque Germania occupat. &c. Nos igitur juxta munus cœlitus nobis datum, Ludovico præcipimus, ut intra menses tres sese abdicet ab ReRegio nomine, gubernatione, functionibus publicis, rebus gerendis penitus abstineat, à se hactenus acta rescindat, nec posthac nisi jussu & mandato nostro dignitatem resumat. Quòd si obtemperare detrectaverit, Patriarchis, Episcopis cunctis, sacerdotibus, principibus, civitatibus imperamus, ut eundem deserant, ac nobis parere cogant. Data atque publicata Avinione. A.C. 1321.
units.tr: Babylonian Bull of John himself against Louis of Bavaria, which they rightly name. We are not ashamed to label it Babylonian. In Aventinus, book VII, page 468, it is described thus: Since the Roman government was transferred from the Greeks to the Germans by our predecessors and entrusted to Charlemagne for its protection and defence, that highest honour has customarily been the gift of the Supreme Pontiff. For it has been decreed that when the German princes have chosen a king, that choice shall be ratified only if the Roman Pontiff, Father and Prince of the Christian world, approves and favours it. Nor may anyone designated king by the votes of the princes at the imperial diet have the right either to administer or to use the royal title until the chief priest, legate of God Almighty, favours and supports him. Moreover, when supreme power and the greatest empire are left without a head, it rests with the Supreme Pontiff, by whose favour it exists. Likewise, when the seven electors at the imperial diet are divided, neither is king. The Roman Bishop, as the common parent of all mortals, regulates at his own discretion the Roman fasces, left derelict and the state abandoned because of disagreement. Just as the mind should rule and the body serve him by whose benefit it lives, so no one doubts that the affairs of Christians are best arranged when the temporal are subject to the eternal, the profane to the sacred, and the bodily to the spiritual, and obey them. This will happen when the Supreme Pontiff governs both dignities at his own pleasure. He rules the Church, and by his law and command all power is brought back to him. And the Emperor is bound by the sanctity of his oath to him who, presiding over the earth, performs the office of the heavenly Emperor. For these reasons, since after the death of Emperor Henry VII two kings, Frederick and Louis, were acclaimed, both, being created contrary to the auspices, are unworthy of the highest pinnacle of human affairs. The commonwealth, left in the middle and torn apart, is administered by us by our right. Therefore Louis, to his own great harm and no small detriment to the Roman Church, not yet judged worthy by us to rule, has rashly and of his own accord usurped the royal name and the reins of government, and occupies by force Italy and Germany. And so on. Therefore we, according to the office given us from heaven, command Louis that within three months he renounce the royal name and government, abstain entirely from public functions and from carrying on affairs, rescind what he has done hitherto, and not resume the dignity hereafter except by our order and mandate. But if he refuses to obey, we command the patriarchs, all bishops, priests, princes and cities to desert him and compel him to submit to us. Given and published at Avignon, in the year of Christ 1321.

units.la: CXXXI. Neque vero Johanni Ludovicus parcit. In Edicto enim Comitiorum Reginoburgensium consensu vulgato, quod idem mox Aventinus fusissimè describit, inter alia isthæc legere est: Johannes ille, qui se Papam XXII. nuncupat, qualis sit, oviculis Christi nostro beneficio operæ pretium est agnoscere, ne decepta ovilla pelle à sævissimo lupo devorentur.
units.tr: CXXXI. Nor indeed does Louis spare John. For in the Edict of the Diet of Regensburg, which was made public with the consent of the princes, and which Aventinus soon describes at great length, among other things the following may be read: That John who calls himself Pope XXII, what sort of man he is, it is worth our while to recognise, lest the flock, deceived by a sheep's skin, be devoured by the most savage wolf.

units.la: Nempe sanguinem Christi annum sitit, discordiæ seditionumque mala ubique gentium inter Christianos serit. In Germania & Italia pollicitationibus auroque Principes, Sacerdotes, & cives corrumpere nititur. Non licet per hunc ANTICHRISTVM Christianis pacem à Deo datam servare. Tanta est hominis, vel potiùs SATHANÆ illius væcordiæ. Publicè pro concione scelera sua quasi beneficta prædicat. Cum Christiani, inquit, Principes inter se discordant, tum verè Romanus Papa est. Pontifex Maximus, demum regnat, demum dominatur. Seditio atque discordia Germanorum salus est Pontificum Romanorum. Ideo etiam discordiam nostram aluit, modò mihi, modò Austriaco favebat, imo se favere simulabat. Ad consecrationem ultrò invitabat, sed per sallaciam utrisque verba dedit, & ad pacem pronos rursus arma sumere persuasit. Astu hæc omnia egit, ut interea dum domesticis cognatisque bellis atterimur, ille sic imperium labefactet, & adversus Sanctos Dei pugnet. Præterea nihil videt, nihil facit nisi quod lubet. SATHANÆ Spiritum sibi sumit, se similem Altissimo facit, se ADORARI, quod tamen Angelus sibi à Johanne fieri prohibuit, pedes sibi osculari, more Diocletiani atque Alexandri, crudelissimorum tyrannorum, permittit. Ludibrium naturæ abominabile, ira Dei, socordia atque ignavia nostra est, Principem Principum servo servire servorum. Si servus servorum Dei est, cur non servit ministrando atque docendo? Cur mentitur, fallit & dominatur? Pascat bonus Pastor oviculas Christi & amet, non armis oppugnet & vi opprimat. Illius Conversatio sit in Cœlis, spiritualibus deditus, corporalibus se non contaminet. Nos nostro jure, Majorum instituto, sicut jus gentium est, & sacra docent Oracula, res nostras, nimirum terrenas agere sinat, & verbum inter nos non commutabimus. Et tandem desinat tam impudenter mentiri, nisi forsan omnes Germanos (ut Romanenses autumant) stultos, caudices, asinos, stipites & plumbeos existimat. Me haereticorum, ut ejus verbis utar, fautorem falsò vocat. Christianus sum, & IPSE HÆRESIARCHA est. Non enim discipulus est Christi, qui vitam ejus irridet, paupertatem contemnit, religionem polluit, sacra prophanat, & dogmata vilipendit, &c. Ab ipso ad totius Orbis Christiani Senatum provocamus. Et reliqua.
units.tr: Indeed he thirsts yearly for the blood of Christ, and everywhere among the Christian nations he sows the evils of discord and sedition. In Germany and Italy he strives to corrupt princes, priests and citizens with promises and gold. Through this ANTICHRIST Christians are not permitted to keep the peace given by God. Such is the madness of this man, or rather of that SATAN. Publicly, from the pulpit, he proclaims his crimes as if they were benefits. When Christian princes disagree among themselves, he says, then truly the Roman Pope is. The Supreme Pontiff at last reigns, at last rules. The sedition and discord of the Germans is the salvation of the Roman Pontiffs. Therefore he has also fed our discord, at one time favouring me, at another the Austrian, or rather pretending to favour both. He invited each to the consecration of his own accord, but by deceit he gave his word to both, and persuaded those inclined to peace to take up arms again. He did all this cunningly, so that while we are worn down by domestic and kinsmen's wars, he may thus undermine the empire and fight against the saints of God. Moreover, he sees nothing and does nothing except what pleases him. He takes to himself the spirit of SATAN, makes himself like the Most High, wishes himself to be ADORED, which yet an angel forbade John to do, allows his feet to be kissed after the manner of Diocletian and Alexander, the most cruel tyrants. The mockery of nature is abominable: the wrath of God and our sloth and cowardice have made the Prince of princes serve as the servant of servants. If he is the servant of the servants of God, why does he not serve by ministering and teaching? Why does he lie, deceive and domineer? Let the good Shepherd feed the little sheep of Christ and love them; let him not assail them with arms and oppress them by force. Let his conversation be in heaven, let him be devoted to spiritual things and not defile himself with bodily ones. We, by our right, according to the institution of our ancestors, as is the law of nations and the sacred oracles teach, will let him manage our affairs, that is, earthly ones, and we will not exchange the word among ourselves. And at last let him cease to lie so shamelessly, unless perhaps he thinks all the Germans (as the Romans suppose) foolish, blockheads, asses, stumps and leaden-headed. He falsely calls me, to use his words, a supporter of heretics. I am a Christian, and HE is the HERESIARCH. For he is not a disciple of Christ who mocks his life, despises his poverty, pollutes religion, profanes sacred things and vilifies doctrines, and so on. We appeal from him to the Senate of the whole Christian world. And the rest.

units.la: CXXXII. Qui Johanni successit Benedictus XII. simultates cum Ludovico Imperatore hostiliter admodum continuat & absolutionem à diris Johannis cujus spem nonnullam Legatis ejus fecerat, pertinaciter negat tamen. Qua injuria incitatus Imperator A.M CCCXXXVIII. Francofurti ad Moenum, præsente etiam Eduardo III. Angliæ Rege, Pontificiæ tyrannidis oppugnator acris, de communi Imperii & Episcoporum etiam plurium consilio heroicum diploma edit, in quo Papam cum suis Pharisæos, perditissimos Antichristos, in Templo Dei instar Dei sedentes, nuncupat. Acta Johannis XXII contra Cæsarem abrogat, aperte demonstrans, Romanum Imperium non à Pontifice, sed à solo Deo, per legitimam Ordinum Imperii electionem, potestatem suam accipere, coronationem vero Pontificis neque addere, neque adimere quicquam potestati Imperatoriæ: neque etiam convenire Pontifici ullam jurisdictionem aut potestatem politicam, denique Generale Concilium anteferendum esse judicio Papæ. pæ. Diploma Aventinus lib. VII. & Nauclerus sol. 886. &c. recitant. Post Clemens VI. absolutionem quidem Cæsa- ri, intercedente Philippo Galliarum Rege, promisit, sed durissimis conditionibus; si Occamum Pontifici dederet, acta contra Pontificem rescinderet, edicto sanciret, Imperium esse beneficium Papæ, omnes errores & hæreses objectas confiteretur: Imperium deponeret, nec nisi volente Papa resumeret, & se ipsum, liberos, omnesque ditiones in manus Pontificis traderet. Hæc ubi Imperatori expösita sunt, convocatis Francofurtum Imperii Proceribus, formulam reconciliationis recitari jubet: Displicet ea omnibus. Fit decretum, postulata iniqua esse, ac pertinere ad Imperii oppressionem, & Pontificiam tyrannidem confirmandam: proin repudiandam eam esse. Neque tamen Reges Francorum & Bohemorum reconciliationis negotium deponunt, sed strenuè urgent; operam nihilominus ludentes apud superbissimum, pertinacissimum & inclementissimum Monachum Clementem. Consulti ab iisdem Theologi Parisienses & Bononienses. Qui rescripserunt, postulata Clementis non iniqua solùm & superba, sed æquitati etiam Christianæ prorsus contraria esse. Rursus igitur Legatio ad Pontificem ab Imperatore, omnibúsque Imperii statibus mittitur, monetúrque Pontifex, à frivolis & in eversionem Imperii excogitatis conditionibus desisteret. Ille verò, elusæ instar tigridis, efferatus A. MCCCXLVI. in Cœna Domini, atroci oratione in Ludovicum habita, omnes Johannis XXII. processus innovavit, Ludovicum schismaticum & hæreticum declaravit, & Electoribus alium brevi Regem eligerent, nisi malint ab ipso Pontifice Regem sibi dari, præcipit. Electores dicto audientes Rhenfii alium Romanorum Regem, Carolum Moraviæ Marchionem, & Johannis Regis Bohemiæ filium eligunt. Repudiatur ille Spiræ in Comitiis à Ludovico indictis, & utrinque ad arma concurritur. Inter turbas has, incendia, devastationes & strages Ludovicus veneno à vidua Alberti Austriaci, uti suspicio erat, propinato, quod agitatione corporis inter venandum cum excutere laborasset, ex equo, in quo ursum ingentem impetierat, præcipitatus v Id. Octob. A. MCCCXLVII. beatam animam Deo reddidit; Clarissimus Heros merito summis Imperatoribus annumerandus; cum in summis discriminibus & periculis, cum Pontificum trium tyrannide assiduè colluctatus annos triginta tres Princeps omni laude major, qui bellum nunquam cuiquam intulit, sed ab aliis illatum masculè depulit, regnasset; cui ad omnium virtutum magno Principe dignarum cumulum unum defuisse videtur, quòd leniùs Pontifices tractavit, nimiaque submissione eorum in se superbiam magis exasperavit, ignarus scilicet, non esse cantanda carmina cordi pessimo, uti Solomon Proverb. xxv. 20. monuit. Sed tyrannide quadam temporum abreptus Princeps optimus præstare, quod forte voluit, non potuit. Meretúrque inprimis lectionem liber Doctissimi Georgii Herwarti Bavari, quo is adversus impudentissimum Bzovium pro Ludovico apologiam gravissimam texuit.
units.tr: CXXXII. Benedict XII, who succeeded John, kept up a bitter quarrel with Emperor Louis. Although he had given some hope of absolution from John's curses to the emperor's envoys, he stubbornly refused it in the end. Provoked by this injustice, the emperor, in the year 1338, at Frankfurt am Main, with Edward III, King of England, present, and with the common counsel of the Empire and of several bishops, issued a bold decree against the Papal tyranny. In it he called the Pope and his followers Pharisees, most destructive Antichrists, sitting in the Temple of God as if they were God. He annulled the acts of John XXII against the emperor, plainly showing that the Roman Empire receives its power not from the Pope but from God alone, through the lawful election of the princes of the Empire. He also showed that the Pope's coronation neither adds to nor takes away anything from the imperial power, that the Pope has no jurisdiction or political authority, and that a general council is to be preferred to the judgment of the Pope. Aventinus, book VII, and Nauclerus, p. 886, etc., recite this decree. Afterwards Clement VI, through the mediation of Philip, King of France, did promise the emperor absolution, but on the harshest conditions: if he handed Occam over to the Pope, rescinded the acts against the Pope, sanctioned by edict that the Empire is a benefice of the Pope, confessed all the errors and heresies charged against him, laid down the Empire, took it up again only if the Pope willed it, and surrendered himself, his children and all his dominions into the Pope's hands. When these terms were set out to the emperor, he summoned the princes of the Empire to Frankfurt and ordered the formula of reconciliation to be read. It displeased everyone. A decree was passed that the demands were unjust and tended to the oppression of the Empire and the confirmation of Papal tyranny, and so they were to be rejected. Nevertheless the kings of the French and of the Bohemians did not drop the business of reconciliation but pressed it vigorously, though their efforts were wasted on the most proud, most obstinate and most merciless monk, Clement. The Parisian and Bolognese theologians were consulted by them, and they replied that Clement's demands were not only unjust and arrogant but utterly contrary to Christian equity. Therefore an embassy was sent again to the Pope by the emperor and by all the estates of the Empire, and the Pope was warned to desist from frivolous conditions devised for the ruin of the Empire. But he, like a tigress thwarted, in a fury in the year 1346, on Maundy Thursday, delivered a savage speech against Louis, renewed all the proceedings of John XXII, declared Louis a schismatic and a heretic, and ordered the electors to choose another king within a short time, unless they preferred that a king be given them by the Pope himself. The Rhenish electors, obeying his command, chose as King of the Romans Charles, Margrave of Moravia, son of John, King of Bohemia. He was rejected at the diet of Speyer, which Louis had called, and both sides took up arms. Amid these disturbances, fires, devastations and slaughters, Louis, as was suspected, was poisoned by the widow of Albert of Austria, and while he was struggling to shake off the poison by exercise during the hunt, he was thrown from the horse on which he had attacked a huge bear. He gave up his blessed soul to God on 5 days before the Ides of October, in the year 1347. He is rightly to be numbered among the greatest emperors, a most famous hero; for he had reigned thirty-three years as a prince above all praise, in the greatest dangers and perils, constantly struggling against the tyranny of three popes. He never made war on anyone, but manfully repelled the wars others waged on him. He seems to have lacked only one thing to crown all the virtues worthy of a great prince: he treated the Popes too mildly, and by his excessive submission he rather exasperated their pride toward himself, being unaware, of course, that songs are not to be sung to a heart that is wicked, as Solomon warned in Proverbs 25:20. But the best of princes, carried away by a certain tyranny of the times, could not accomplish what perhaps he wished. The book of the most learned Georg Herwart of Bavaria deserves to be read above all, in which he wove a most weighty defence of Louis against the most shameless Bzovius.

units.la: CXXXIII. Sed Ludovici causam adversus Clementis inprimis rabiem fortissimè omnium scripto egit Guilhelmus Occam, natione Anglus, Ordinis fratrum Minorum, Johannis Scoti discipulus, Ludovici συγχορ, Vir, ita de eo Trithemius, in Divinis Scripturis eruditus, & in Philosophia Aristotelica nobiliter doctus, ingenio subtilis & clarus eloquio.
units.tr: CXXXIII. But the cause of Louis, especially against the raging of Clement, was defended most vigorously of all in writing by William Occam, an Englishman by birth, of the Order of Friars Minor, a disciple of John Scotus, a companion [συγχορ] of Louis. Trithemius says of him: a man learned in the Divine Scriptures and nobly trained in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence.

units.la: Is enim libro adversus Clementem emisso, Clementem hæreseos nota inurit, ipsum Antichristum, paupertatis Christianæ oforem, hostem Reipub. conjuratum, Germanorum, gentis Christianissimæ inimicum, sectatorem falsorum Pontificum & saevissimorum luporum, appellat. Leopoldus quoque Bambergensis Episcopus, & Occami Collega, in tractatu, cui titulus, Vindex pacis Christiana, publicè asseveravit: Pontificem, nisi Antichristi factum, quàm Christi & ejus comitum paupertatem æmulari malit, infimi cujusque Christiani, nedum supremæ potestatis servum esse, tantum abesse, ut cum maxima Reipublicæ Christianæ jactura dominari, quicquid libitum fuerit, facilitare, Deus non solum dici, sed credi postulet. Hæc aliáque Aventinus lib. VII. Annal. memorat. Cœteri Theologi, & juris utriusque periti, eandem in sententiam pleraque disputárunt, & in libellos redegerunt. Quorum opera in Bibliothecis cum blattis & tineis diu collucta perierunt. Author etiam Nauclerus est, Papæ imperanti, ut Ludovicum mortuum pro hæretico omnes censerent, cùm alibi, tum Basileæ cum primis cordatos viros se opposuisse, negantes primùm, se Ludovicum pro hæretico habere velle; deinde protestantes aperte, se eum semper agnituros & habituros Imperatorem, quem Imperii Principes elegerint, sive approbatus & consecratus, sive improbatus à Pontifice fuerit.
units.tr: For in a book he issued against Clement, Occam branded Clement with the mark of heresy, calling him Antichrist, an assailant of Christian poverty, an enemy of the commonwealth, a conspirator against the Germans, a nation most Christian and his enemy, a follower of false popes and of the most savage wolves. Leopold also, Bishop of Bamberg and colleague of Occam, openly affirmed in a treatise entitled Vindex pacis Christiana: unless the Pope prefers to imitate the deeds of Antichrist rather than the poverty of Christ and his companions, he is so far from being the servant of even the lowest Christian, let alone of supreme power, and so far from ruling as he pleases to the great loss of the Christian commonwealth, that God demands he not only be called but be believed to be such. Aventinus, book VII of the Annals, records these and other things. The other theologians, and experts in both laws, argued much to the same effect and put their views into little books. Their works, after struggling for a long time with moths and worms in the libraries, perished. Nauclerus also records that when the Pope ordered everyone to pronounce the dead Louis a heretic, wise men, both elsewhere and especially at Basel, opposed him, first denying that they wished to hold Louis a heretic, and then openly protesting that they would always acknowledge and hold as emperor the one whom the princes of the Empire had chosen, whether he was approved and consecrated or disapproved by the Pope.

units.la: CXXXIV. Ludovico Imperatori, post varios discor- dibus consiliis electos, tandem successit ille, qui Ludo- vico vivo oppositus erat, Carolus, quartus postea dictus.
units.tr: CXXXIV. After Emperor Louis, and after the electors had chosen various candidates whose counsels disagreed, the one who had been set against Louis while he lived finally succeeded, Charles, later called the Fourth.

units.la: Is primo vere A. MCCCLV. ingressus Italiam cum exercitu Germanorum & Bohemorum, à Pontifice Innocentio VI. sibi per Cardinales ejus Romæ subsistentes coronam dari petivit; ac eam quidem obtinuit, sed majore dedecore, quàm superiorum Imperatorum quisquam. Imperator ex equo ad portam Romanæ urbis descendens, pedes urbem ingreditur. Id quod falsè exagitavit Senator non nemo Romanus, qui in Capitolio Orationem habens; Ecce Rex tuus, inquiebat, venit tibi mansuetus, &c. Si venisset, ut digni erant nebulones isti Romani, venisset armatus stricto gladio, quem in ipsorum viscera ac capita strinxisset. Hostiensis verò Cardinalis Avinione Romam missus hac demum conditione coronam ei promisit, si promitteret, Italiam se mox deserturum, in Germaniam vel Bohemiam suam rediturum, & Italiam nunquam deinceps repetiturum, nisi vocatum ab ipso Italiæ domino Pontifice. Quam etiam conditionem iniquissimam Cæsar ille, sacrificulorum cliens (unde Presbyterorum Cæsar der Pfaffenkeyser vulgò nuncupari suevit) turpiter admisit, adeóque quæ verba Aventini lib. VII. Annal. sunt, Libertatem Germanam, Majestatem Imperii Romani, populi victoris gentium fortunam, Christianam simplicitatem hostibus Reipub. Christianæ prodidit. Alia etiam enormia satis Carolus admisit, Abbatibus parem Principibus in Imperio locum tribuens, Delphinatum Regi Galliæ vendens; Silesiam, Lufatiam, aliáque Bohemiæ suæ addens; & Electoribus, ut filio Wenceslao faverent, Rheni vectigalia oppignerans. Atque ita Aquila deplumata est, ut cæteris avibus posthac contemptui esset. Talémque Imperatorem Romæ, omnium fere malorum architecta, & verè ἀπολλύοντα dedit.
units.tr: In the spring of 1355 he entered Italy with an army of Germans and Bohemians. He sought the crown from Pope Innocent VI, through the cardinals who remained at Rome for him, and he obtained it, but with greater disgrace than any of the earlier emperors. The emperor dismounted from his horse at the gate of the city of Rome and entered the city on foot. A certain Roman senator wrongly mocked this, when he made a speech on the Capitol: Behold, your king comes to you gentle, and so on. If he had come as those Roman scoundrels deserved, he would have come armed, with drawn sword, and he would have plunged it into their vitals and heads. But the cardinal of Ostia, sent from Avignon to Rome, at last promised him the crown on this condition: that he would promise to leave Italy soon, return to his Germany or Bohemia, and never again come back to Italy unless summoned by the lord of Italy, the Pope himself. This most unjust condition that emperor, the client of the priests (whence he was commonly called the Priests' Emperor, der Pfaffenkeyser), shamefully accepted. So the words of Aventinus in book VII of his Annals apply: He betrayed German liberty, the majesty of the Roman Empire, the fortune of the people who conquered the nations, and the Christian simplicity, to the enemies of the Christian commonwealth. Charles also committed many other outrages. He gave abbots a place in the Empire equal to that of princes, sold the Dauphiné to the King of France, added Silesia, Lusatia and other territories to his Bohemia, and pledged the tolls of the Rhine to the electors so that they would favour his son Wenceslas. And so the eagle was stripped of its feathers, so that it became despised by the other birds from then on. At Rome he produced such an emperor, the architect of almost every evil, and truly a destroyer.

units.la: CXXXV. Vixit ea ætate Franciscus Petrarcha, natione Florentinus, Parmensis Archidiaconus, Seculi sui lumen.
units.tr: CXXXV. At that time lived Francis Petrarch, a Florentine by birth, archdeacon of Parma, the light of his age.

units.la: Is ignominiosa hæc Caroli coronatione motus, sic ad eum scripsit. Nescio quid Romano Pontifici pollicitus, jurejurando interposito, quasi manu valida, seu monte invio, Romanæ urbis aditu prohiberis. Quænam ista superbia est, Principem Romanum, publicæ libertatis authorem, libertate privare, ut cujus esse debent omnia, ipse non sit suus? In alia Epistola idem sic scribit: Omnis potestas impatiens consortis erit. Cujus rei si qua antiqua non sufficerent, vereor ne recens nobis exemplum casus attulerit, neu jam Pontifex Romanus Principem Romæ esse vetuerit: quod fama loquitur. Quem nunc Diademate contentum, ac Imperii titulo Roma non solum patitur, sed jubet; & quem
units.tr: Moved by this shameful coronation of Charles, he wrote to him as follows: I know not what you promised the Roman Pontiff, confirmed with an oath, but you are kept from entry into the city of Rome as if by a strong hand or an untrodden mountain. What pride is this, that the Roman prince, the author of public liberty, should deprive liberty itself, so that he who ought to own everything is not his own master? In another letter he writes thus: Every power will be impatient of a partner.
