If older examples were not enough for this matter, I fear that a recent case may have furnished us with one, lest the Roman Pontiff should already have forbidden there to be a prince at Rome, as report has it. Rome not only tolerates, but commands, that he who is now content with the diadem and the title of Empire ...

units.la: Ita Carolus Majestatem Imperii Rom. prodidit, & Aquilam deplumavit.
units.tr: Thus Charles betrayed the majesty of the Roman Empire and stripped the eagle of its feathers.

units.la: Petrarcha id Carolo exprobrat, & Curiam Romanam nomine Babylonis Occidentalis graviter exagitat. quem dici Imperatorem finit, imperare nullo modo permittit. Idem Petrarcha tum in Poëmatis suis Romam Babylonicam meretricem, erroris scholam, hæreseos Templum passim vocat; tum in Epistolis suis disertissimis gravissimisque Curiam Romanam sub nomine Babylonis Occidentalis graphicè depingit. Inter multa alia Epist. xiv. sic scribit: Quis, oro, non fugiat Babylonem (Curiam Romanam Avinione tum residentem innuit) & Vitiorum simul omnium, & laboris ac totius miseriæ domum. De qua quidem aliquid nosse debes. Visa loquor, non audita. Ibi nulla pietas, nulla charitas, nulla fides, nulla Dei reverentia, nullus timor, nihil sancti, nihil justi, nihil æqui, nihil pensi, nihil denique humani. Amor, pudor, decor, candor inde exulant. De Veritate quidem silco. Nam quis unquam vero locus, ubi omnia mendaciis plena sunt, aër, terra, domus, turres, vici, atria, plateæ, porticus, vestibula, aulæ, thalami, tectorum laquearia, murorum rimulæ, diversoria ædium, penetralia Templorum, Judicum subsellia, Pontificum sedes? Epistola superiore nona Romanam Curiam Labyrinthi & Babylonis tertiæ nomine infamaverat: ubi non carcer horrendus (sic enim loquitur) non tenebrosæ domus error, non fatalis urna humani generis fata permiscens, denique non imperiosus Minos, non Minotaurus vorax, non damnatæ Veneris monumenta defuerint, sed remedia, sed amor, sed charitas, sed promissorum fides, sed amica consilia, sed fila perplexum iter tacita ope signantia, sed Ariadna, sed Dædalus; una spes salutis in auro esset, auro placaretur Rex ferus, auro immane monstrum vinceretur, auro tristis janitor emolliretur, auro Cælum panderetur, auro Christus venderetur. Epistola decima sexta ore liberimo de universa Pontificis aula sic pronuntiat: In Babylone Regno avaritiæ, futuræ vitæ spes inanis quædam fabula: & quæ de inferis narrantur, fabulosa omnia: & resurrectio carnis, & mundi finis, & Christus ad judicium venturus, inter nænias habentur. Similia plura ex eodem Petrarcha Bzovius excerpsit, & nos in loco repræsentabimus.
units.tr: Petrarch reproaches Charles for this, and sharply assails the Roman Curia under the name of the Western Babylon: he allows him to be called emperor, but in no way permits him to rule. The same Petrarch, in his poems, repeatedly calls Rome the Babylonian harlot, the school of error, the temple of heresy; and in his most eloquent and weighty letters he vividly depicts the Roman Curia under the name of the Western Babylon. Among many other things, in letter 14 he writes: Who, I ask, would not flee Babylon (he means the Roman Curia, then residing at Avignon), the home of all vices, of toil, and of all misery? Of this you ought to know something. I speak of what I have seen, not what I have heard. There is no piety there, no charity, no faith, no reverence for God, no fear, nothing holy, nothing just, nothing fair, nothing weighed, nothing human at last. Love, modesty, grace and candour are banished from there. I say nothing of truth. For what place is there where truth dwells, where all things are full of lies: the air, the earth, the houses, the towers, the villages, the courts, the squares, the porticoes, the vestibules, the halls, the bedchambers, the ceilings of the roofs, the cracks in the walls, the lodgings of the houses, the inner shrines of the temples, the benches of the judges, the seats of the Pontiffs? In his ninth letter, earlier, he had infamously called the Roman Curia by the name of the Labyrinth and third Babylon: where there is no lack of a dreadful prison (for so he speaks), nor of the error of a dark house, nor of the fatal urn mixing the fates of the human race, nor of the imperious Minos, nor of the devouring Minotaur, nor of the monuments of accursed Venus; but there are remedies, there is love, there is charity, there is the faith of promises, there are friendly counsels, there are threads marking out a tangled path by secret help, there is Ariadne, there is Daedalus. The only hope of salvation lies in gold; with gold the savage King is appeased, with gold the monstrous beast is conquered, with gold the gloomy doorkeeper is softened, with gold heaven is opened, with gold Christ is sold. In his sixteenth letter he pronounces with the most unrestrained freedom on the whole papal court: In Babylon, the kingdom of greed, the hope of a future life is a certain empty fable; all that is told of the underworld is fabulous; and the resurrection of the flesh, the end of the world, and Christ coming to judgment, are regarded as idle tales. Bzovius excerpted many similar passages from the same Petrarch, and we shall present them in their place.

units.la: CXXXVI. Neque verò ea ætate viri cordati ταπεινοφρονοῦντες ζόμενοι defuére plures. Innocentius VI. Pontifex Johannem à Rupe-scissa, Monachum Franciscanum Avinione captivum attinebat, propter res miras, ita Froissardus vol. 3. cap. 24. scribit, quas eventuras ille dicebat, præsertim super Prælatos & Præsidentes in Ecclesia, scilicet ob immensum luxum & ambitionem, quibus dediti erant, &c. Probaturum autem se dicebat omnia dicta sua per Apocalypsin, & veteres libros S. Prophetarum, qui ipsi per gratiam Spiritus S. essent retecti, &c. Retulit is aliquando eodem teste, Cardinali Hostiensi, contigisse Ecclesiæ, quod olim pulcherrimæ aviculæ, quæ implumis nata, cum volare non posset, de vita periclitabatur: Aves alias ejus misertas, plumis eam operuisse, hoc est, Reges & Principes Ecclesiam effusis in eam suis patrimoniis ditasse, & supra modum exaltasse. Avem verò, ut se auctam viderit, superbire & ferocire, aliáque rostro & unguibus petere coepisse, hoc est, Ecclesiam cum Imperatoribus inimicitias graves suscepisse. At aves plumas suas inde repetiisse. Ita Principes beneficia & dona sua repetituros. (confer hic Apoc. xv ii. 13. 16.) Addit Froissardus, prædictiones ejus multas evenisse, omnia eum per Apocalypsin confirmasse, & comprobationes veras, quibus se armabat, sæpius ipsum, quo minus combureretur, servasse. Scripsit idem Franciscanus in carcere Tractatum Propheticum, cui titulus; Vade mecum in tribulationem in quo Antichristum in Papatu regnare asseveravit, & Ecclesiæ reformationem præsagiebat. Sed & Magister Nicolaus Oremus, Theol. D. ille scilicet, qui urgente Carolo V. Galliarum Rege Biblia sacra in linguam Gallicam transtulit; coram Urbano V. concionem habuit in verba Esaiæ cap. lvi. 1. Juxta est salus mea, ut veniat, & justitia mea ut reveletur, in qua Antichristum venisse his scilicet argumentis comprobat: quia jam tum Imperium Romanum desolatum sit; quia Ecclesia sit pejor moribus, quàm fuerit olim Synagoga: quia Sacerdotes sint majores, quàm Principes seculi: quia fastus Prælatorum ad fastigium enixus sit; quia tyrannis Præsidentium summa sit; quia in Ecclesia non promoveantur nisi indigni, & vilipendantur meliores; quia Politia sæcularium tribuletur, & populi passim commoveantur; quia Ecclesiæ Principes incorrigibiles sint. Et deinceps etiam objectiones diluit. Inprimis autem iis temporibus S. Brigidæ & Catharinæ Senensis revelationes celebrabantur. Et Brigida quidem, gente Scota, in Revelationibus suis A. MDCXXVIII. Coloniæ una cum Turrecremata, Recognitione & Consalvi Duranti observationibus editis, maturo Theologorum judicio (ita Cardinalis Bona ipse in Notitia Scriptorum nuper scripsit) approbatis; Christum sibi visum lib. I. cap. 41. inducit, qui Pontificem Clementem VI. vocat animarum interfectorem, Ovium Jesu Christi dispersorem & laceratorem, abominabiliorem Judaeis, inimiciorem Juda, injustiorem Pilato, pejorem Lucifero, sedem ejus demergendam esse, sicut lapidem ponderosum: Assessores suos arsuros in igne sulphureo & inextinguibili. Sacerdotes etiam reprehendit, quòd eorum culpa doctrina Christi neglecta, & ferme abolita, & Divina sapientia in pravam & vanam conversa sit. Alicubi etiam vidisse se ait Virginem, dicentem ad filium, Romam esse feracem agrum. Respondisse Christum: Est, sed zizania. lib. V. cap. 41. Christus ita de Gregorio XI. Papa judicat: Gregorius Papa est similis Paralytico, qui non movet manus ad operandum, nec pedes ad ambulandum. Tenet eum quasi impeditum immoderatus amor sanguinis sui, & frigus tepiditatis ad me. Catharina quoque Senensis , cujus Legendam Raimundus conscripsit, audita Perusinorum adversus Pontificem rebellione: Non incipiatis, inquit,
units.tr: CXXXVI. Nor, at that time, were there lacking several men of sound judgment who were humble-minded [ταπεινοφρονοῦντες]. Pope Innocent VI held captive at Avignon John of Rupescissa, a Franciscan monk, on account of his marvellous claims, as Froissart writes in volume 3, chapter 24: which he said would come to pass, above all concerning the prelates and presidents in the Church, namely on account of their immense luxury and ambition, to which they had given themselves, and so on. He said that he would prove all his statements by the Apocalypse and the old books of the holy prophets, which had been revealed to him by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and so on. On one occasion, according to the same witness, he related to Cardinal of Ostia that something had happened to the Church, as with a most beautiful little bird which, born unfledged and unable to fly, was in danger of its life. Other birds, taking pity on it, covered it with their feathers; that is, kings and princes enriched the Church by pouring their patrimonies upon it and raised it beyond measure. But when the bird saw itself increased, it began to grow proud and fierce, and to attack others with beak and talons; that is, the Church took up serious enmities with the emperors. But the birds took back their feathers. So princes will take back their benefits and gifts (compare here Apoc. xvii. 13, 16). Froissart adds that many of his predictions came true; that he confirmed everything by the Apocalypse, and that the true proofs with which he armed himself often saved him from being burned. The same Franciscan wrote in prison a prophetic treatise entitled Vade mecum in tribulationem, in which he asserted that Antichrist reigned in the papacy, and foretold a reformation of the Church. But also Master Nicolaus Oremus, doctor of theology, that is the man who, at the urging of Charles V, King of the French, translated the holy Bible into French, delivered a sermon before Urban V on the words of Isaiah 56:1: My salvation is near, that it may come, and my righteousness, that it may be revealed. In it he proved that Antichrist had already come, by these arguments: because the Roman Empire was already laid waste; because the Church was worse in morals than the Synagogue had once been; because the priests were greater than the princes of the world; because the pride of the prelates had risen to the height; because the tyranny of the presidents was supreme; because in the Church none but the unworthy were promoted and the better sort were despised; because the polity of the laity was troubled and the people everywhere stirred up; because the princes of the Church were incorrigible. And afterwards he also answered objections. Above all, in those times the revelations of St Bridget and of Catherine of Siena were celebrated. Bridget, a Scot by birth, in her Revelations, published at Cologne in 1628 together with the Recognition of Turrecremata and the observations of Consalvus Durandus, was approved after mature judgment of theologians (so Cardinal Bona himself recently wrote in his Notitia Scriptorum). In book I, chapter 41, she introduces Christ appearing to her, who calls Pope Clement VI a destroyer of souls, a scatterer and mangler of the sheep of Jesus Christ, more abominable than the Jews, more hostile than Judas, more unjust than Pilate, worse than Lucifer; his seat is to be sunk like a heavy stone, and his assessors will burn in sulphurous and inextinguishable fire. She also rebukes the priests, because through their fault the doctrine of Christ has been neglected and almost abolished, and divine wisdom turned into a perverse and vain thing. Somewhere, she says, she also saw the Virgin saying to her Son, Rome is a fertile field. Christ replied: It is, but full of tares (book V, chapter 41). Christ judges Pope Gregory XI thus: Gregory the Pope is like a paralytic, who moves neither his hands to work nor his feet to walk. An immoderate love of his own blood holds him back as if hindered, and the coldness of lukewarmness towards me. Catherine of Siena also, whose Legend Raymond wrote, when she heard of the rebellion of the Perugians against the Pontiff, said: Do not begin, she said,

units.la: S. Brig. quit, fletum vestrum tam citò, quia nimis habebitis flere. Istud enim quod modò videtis, est lac & mel respectu subsequentium, &c. Hoc modò faciunt laici, & citò videbitis, quòd deteriora facient Clerici. Facient enim scandalum universale toti Ecclesiæ Dei, quod tanquam pestis hæretica ipsam scindet & conturbabit. Non enim proprie hæresis, sed quasi hæresis, & quædam divisio Ecclesiæ, totiúsque Christianitatis. Id Raimundus interpretabatur de Schismate quod Gregorii abitum consecutum est. Addit idem Raimundus: Ego curiosus factus ad investigandum de suturis post illam conquassationem, interrogavi eam (Catharinam) ex quo manifestè innotuerat, futura sibi Divinitus revelari, &c. His tribulationibus & angustiis modo imperceptibili hominibus, purgabit Deus Ecclesiam suam sanctam, & suscitabit Spiritum electorum suorum. Sequetúrque post hæc tanta Reformatio Ecclesiæ Dei, & renovatio Sanctorum Fastorum, quòd ex solo cogitatu exultat spiritus meus in Domino. Et sicut alias pluries dixi, Sponsa, quæ nunc est, tota deformis & pannosa, erit pulcherima monilibus pretiosis ornata, cunctíque fideles gaudebunt, tam sanctis Pastoribus decorati.Quæ Prædictio ad Ecclesiæ reformationem referenda omnino est.
units.tr: St. Bridget says: "Do not begin your weeping so soon, for you will have too much reason to weep. What you now see is milk and honey compared with what follows, etc. The laity are doing this now, and soon you will see that the clergy will do worse. For they will cause a universal scandal to the whole Church of God, which, like a heretical plague, will tear it apart and throw it into confusion. It will not be a heresy properly speaking, but as it were a heresy, and a certain division of the Church and of all Christendom." Raimundus understood this as referring to the Schism that followed Gregory's departure. The same Raimundus adds: "Being eager to inquire about what would come after that upheaval, I asked her (Catherine), since it had become plain that the future was revealed to her by God, etc. Through these tribulations and distresses, which men cannot yet perceive, God will purge his holy Church and will stir up the Spirit of his elect. After these things there will follow such a great reformation of the Church of God and renewal of the holy observances that my spirit exults in the Lord at the mere thought of it. And, as I have said several times before, the Bride, who is now wholly deformed and ragged, will be most beautiful, adorned with precious jewels, and all the faithful will rejoice, adorned with such holy ministers." This prophecy must certainly be referred to the reformation of the Church.

units.la: CXXXVII. Circa eadem tempora, Anno nimirum MCCCLX. caput extulit Johannes Wiclefus, Oxonii natus, Philosophus & Theologus insignis, qui præ cœteris Ecclesiæ Romanæ ulcera mascule detexit.
units.tr: CXXXVII. About the same time, namely in 1360, John Wycliffe, born at Oxford, a distinguished philosopher and theologian, rose to prominence. Above all others, he boldly laid bare the sores of the Church of Rome.

units.la: Non satis habuit ille, ex Scripturis, historiarum serie, validis rationibus, propriisque actibus luci manifestæ dare, Papam esse Hæresiarcham, Antichristum in Scripturis designatum, abominationem desolationis in abstracto, astu Sathanæ introductam, apostema Ecclesiæ; sed ipsius etiam doctrinæ penetralia ingressus, vanitatem, superstitionem, idololatriam coarguit; cultum à Creatore ad creaturas, ad Mortales, Sanctos, reliquias, imagines derivatum reprehendit; Redemptoris Sacrificium in ineptum Missæ spectaculum conversum; mortis & Passionis Christi beneficium in dispensationes, peregrinationes, indulgentias, puri, vel potius impurissimi hominis beneficia, an veneficia commutatum; populum à Christi merito ad propria merita; à solido crucis Christi præsidio ad cassam operum arundinem; à Deo universi Creatore ad hostiolam panis revocatum gravissimè questus est. Testantur id multifaria ejus scripta, à Johanne Barlæo Cent. 6. memorata plusquàm ducenta, inter quæ ejus Commentationes de veritate Scripturæ, de Christo & Antichristo & ejus membris, de Papa Romano, de nequitiis ejusdem, de Officio Pastorali, de Ministrorum Conjugio, de non saginandis sacerdotibus, de seductione simplicium, de impedimentis Euangelizantium, de amplexando Euangelio, de falsatoribus Divinæ Legis, de otio in mendicitate, de ultima ætate Ecclesiæ; in Danielem & Apocalypsin, de fide Eucharistiæ, &c. demonstrationibus ejusmodi plenæ sunt. Et compendium doctrinæ ejus tum Thomas Walsinghamus Pontificius apud Bzovium ad A. MCCCLXXXVII. tum Catalogus testium veritatis, aliiqué etiam texuêre. Ut verò susceптum Dei opus promoveret felicius, etiam S. Biblia in linguam vernaculam transtulit. In Prælectionibus & Concionibus ordinariis Oxonii habitis frontem æneam contra effrontem meretricem, & pectus adamantinum contra totius Cleri impetum indutus, in ipsum Regis Eduardi aurem intonat, magnorumque etiam virorum, qui sive literis, sive armis florebant, animos commovet & percellit, atque id denique labore & zelo suo efficit, ut veritas à Magnatibus etiam, ipsóque Rege in Parlamento decernente, ne Episcopi Romam ampliùs adirent; de quo videndus Paulus Waldensis Epist. ad Mart. V. avidè ex ore ejus audiatur, suscipiatur, multósque annos feliciter personet; adeò quidem ut lumen Euangelii ejus opera revivíscens, nullus exinde ventus, turbo nullus extinguere potuerit. Et temporibus quidem illis tenebricosissimis turbulentissimisque, inter tot fulmina Româ in maximorum etiam Principum capita vibrata, doctrinam Romæ usque quaque repugnantem Wiclefus proferre & eò usque propagare non potuisset, nisi ejus Spiritus coelitus lucem, robur, fiduciam accepisset, Deúsque per eum imbecillem & abjectissimum, si mundum spectes, homuncionem egisset, imperiíque Sathanæ ac Antichristi ruinam moliri jam jam incepisset. Nihilominus eandem, quam Sancti omnes assolent, fortem expertus etiam est, stantibus contra eum ursis, prædonica gente, Monachorum imprimis mendicantium, cum tota congregatione Chore, in perniciem ejus jurata. Ejectus enim in exilium sub Richardo II. & aliquandiu in Bohemia oberravit, ubi magnam Waldensium doctrinæ fœneratus est lucem, & Johanni etiam Husso juveni adhuc veritatis femina instillavit. Ab exilio revocatus, & Eduardo Rege ei ob pietatem favente, A. MCCCLXXXVII. ultimo Decembris in patria piè obdormivit, honestéque sepultus; sed post A. MCDXXIV. Martini V. væsana rabie correpti, jussu, à Prælatis Angliæ exhumatus & combustus est.
units.tr: He was not content to make it clear, from the Scriptures, from the sequence of history, by strong arguments and by plain facts, that the Pope is the chief of heretics, the Antichrist designated in the Scriptures, the abomination of desolation set up in the abstract by the cunning of Satan, an abscess of the Church; but, entering also into the inner parts of her doctrine, he exposed her vanity, superstition and idolatry. He condemned worship transferred from the Creator to creatures, to mortals, to saints, to relics and images. He lamented that the Redeemer's sacrifice had been turned into a useless spectacle of the Mass; that the benefit of Christ's death and passion had been changed into indulgences, pilgrimages and dispensations, the benefits, or rather the poisons, of a most impure man; that the people had been called away from the merit of Christ to their own merits, from the solid protection of Christ's cross to the brittle reed of works, and from God, the Creator of all things, to the little wafer of bread. Many of his writings bear witness to this, more than two hundred of them, as John Bale records in Century 6. Among them are his treatises on the truth of Scripture, on Christ and Antichrist and his members, on the Pope of Rome, on his wickedness, on the pastoral office, on the marriage of ministers, on not fattening priests, on the seduction of simple people, on the hindrances to evangelists, on embracing the Gospel, on the falsifiers of the divine law, on idleness in begging, on the last age of the Church; on Daniel and the Apocalypse, on faith in the Eucharist, and so on, full of arguments of this kind. A summary of his teaching has been woven together both by the Papist Thomas Walsingham, in Bzovius at the year 1387, and by the Catalogue of the Witnesses of Truth, and by others too. In order to promote the work of God he had undertaken more successfully, he also translated the Holy Bible into the vernacular tongue. In his lectures and regular sermons given at Oxford, armed with a brow of brass against the shameless harlot and a breast of adamant against the assault of the entire clergy, he thundered into the very ear of King Edward, and he stirred and struck the minds of great men too, those who flourished in letters or in arms. Finally, by his labour and zeal he brought it about that the truth was decreed in Parliament, with the Magnates and the King himself agreeing, that bishops should no longer go to Rome. On this, see Paulus Waldensis, Letter to Martin V; let it be eagerly heard from his mouth, received, and let it resound happily for many years, so that, the light of the Gospel reviving through his work, no wind or whirlwind could ever extinguish it afterwards. Indeed, in those most gloomy and turbulent times, amid so many thunderbolts hurled from Rome at the heads of even the greatest princes, Wycliffe could not have brought forward, and spread so widely, a doctrine everywhere opposed at Rome, unless his spirit had received light, strength and confidence from heaven, and unless God had acted through him, a feeble and most abject man (if you look at the world), and had already begun to undermine the rule of Satan and of Antichrist. Nevertheless, he experienced the same strength that all the saints are accustomed to experience, with the bears standing against him, a predatory tribe, especially the begging Monks, with the whole company of the choir sworn to his destruction. For under Richard II he was driven into exile and wandered for a while in Bohemia, where he sowed the light of the Waldensian doctrine, and he also instilled the seeds of truth into the young John Hus. Recalled from exile, and favoured by King Edward because of his piety, he peacefully fell asleep in his homeland on the last day of December 1387, and was honourably buried. But after 1424, in the time of Martin V, when he had been seized by a mad rage, he was exhumed and burned by order of the prelates of England.

units.la: CXXXVIII. Inde ab Urbano V. ad Concilium usque Constantiense, adeoque annos plus quadraginta in Ecclesia Romana Schisma maximum & pertinacissimum omnium, seu, uti Author Fasciculi temporum describit, omnium schismatum, quæ antea fuerant, pessimum ac subtilissimum, adeóque perplexum, ut etiam doctissimi & conscientiosi viri non valerent discutere, cui esset adhærendum; & continuatum cum gravi scandalo totius cleri, & grandi jactura animarum propter hæreses & alia devia, quæ tunc pullulárunt; grassatum est. Mortuo scilicet Gregorio XI. in diversa studia Itali & Galli abrepti sunt. Quòd illi Papam qui Romam, hi, qui Avinionem insideret, optârunt. Illi Bartholomæum Archie- Schismatis pertinacissimi à tempore Urbani VI. ad Concilium Constantiense usque historia. chiepiscopum Barrensem Neapolitanum, qui Urbani VI. nomen induit, eligunt. Hi quiritantes, in suffragiis vim sibi illatam, Cardinalem Genuensem, qui nomen Clementis VII. sibi imposuit, Pontificem creant; Urbanus Romæ, Clemens Avinione sedit. Urbano Italia, Germania, Pannonia: Clementi vero Gallia, Hispania, Britannia, Polonia, Suecia, Dania, Borussia, Bohemia, Frisia, Lombardia adhæserunt. Afferebant Obedientiales (sic enim se nuncupabant) Clementis, suum esse verum Papam; Urbanum Apostaticum & Antipapam. Neque minori fervore Urbaniani in Clementis sequaces invehebantur, asserentes, eos damnatos esse. Nauclerus affirmat multas tum hac de re disputationes esse exortas, quis inter illos verus Christi vicarius sit? Nihil tamen certi definitum fuisse. Definiri vero poterat, NEUTRUM. Bullas etiam Pontifices hi duo terrificas ad diversas mundi partes transmiserunt, & libellos famosos sparserunt, quibus se mutuo damnabant, excommunicabant, & se invicem, scapham scilicet scapham appellantes, Antichristos, Schismaticos, Hæreticos, Fures, Proditores, Latrones, Tyrannos, Iniquos, Filios Belial, Zizaniæ satores, & si quid aliud fœdum dictu, insigniebant. Cœdes & contumelias utrinque illatas expositit accurate libris de Schismate editis Theodoricus à Niem, author auritus & oculatus testis, utpote qui in Curia & apud Urbanum annos circiter triginta vixit. Memoratu digniora, & fœditatem Schismatis inprimis arguentia post alios Doctiss. Mornæus Myster Iniq. p. 1085. &c. excerpsit.
units.tr: CXXXVIII. From Urban V until the Council of Constance, that is, for more than forty years, the greatest and most obstinate of all schisms raged in the Roman Church, or, as the author of the Fasciculus temporum describes it, "the worst and most subtle of all the schisms that had occurred before, and so perplexing that even the most learned and conscientious men could not judge to which side they should adhere; and it continued with grave scandal to the whole clergy and great loss of souls, because of heresies and other errors that then sprouted up." When Gregory XI died, the Italians and the French were pulled in different directions. The former wanted a Pope who would reside at Rome, the latter one who would sit at Avignon. The former elected Bartholomew, archbishop of Bari, a Neapolitan, who took the name Urban VI. The latter, complaining that they had been forced in the voting, created as Pope the Cardinal of Genoa, who took the name Clement VII. Urban sat at Rome, Clement at Avignon. Italy, Germany and Hungary adhered to Urban; France, Spain, Britain, Poland, Sweden, Denmark, Prussia, Bohemia, Friesland and Lombardy adhered to Clement. The Obedientiales (for so they called themselves) of Clement claimed that theirs was the true Pope and that Urban was an apostate and an antipope. Urban's followers attacked Clement's supporters with no less fervour, asserting that they were damned. Naucler affirms that many disputations arose at that time on this question: which of the two is the true vicar of Christ? Nothing certain, however, was defined. It could have been defined, however, that neither was. These two Popes also sent terrifying bulls to distant parts of the world and scattered infamous libels, in which they mutually condemned and excommunicated each other, and branded one another with "Antichrists, schismatics, heretics, thieves, traitors, robbers, tyrants, wicked men, sons of Belial, sowers of tares," and whatever other foul names could be uttered. Theodoric of Niem, an attentive author and eyewitness, who had lived about thirty years at the Curia and with Urban, set out accurately, in his books on the Schism, the slaughter and insults inflicted on both sides. Among others, the most learned Mornay has excerpted the more memorable passages, especially those exposing the foulness of the Schism, in Mystery of Iniquity, p. 1085 etc.

units.la: CXXXIX. Omisso Bonifacio IX. qui Paulo Langio in Chronico suo teste, erat pecuniæ avidus, ad quam colligendam plures Legatos per diversas mundi partes ad negotiandum cum indulgentiis misit: fuit maximus Simoniacus, & Simoniæ cultores multis dignitatibus sublimavit: tanti animi consiliúque, ut primus mus Romani Populi vim omnem transtulerit in Pontificem, suo nutu in urbe disponens, & ordinans sigula; & Annatas quoque, Genebrardo commemorante, Sacerdotiis imposuit, (de quo fusè Petrus de Marca de Concord. Sacerdot. & Imp. lib. VI. 10. 11. &c. agit) seculi Decimi quinti τὰ κοεμόπιες perstringenda veniunt. Post ejus initium A. MCCCCVI. Schisma pridem coeptum altiores jam radices egit, Ecclesiámque Romanam mirum in modum exercitam habuit. Innocentio VII. Romæ defuncto, & Petro de Luna, seu Benedicto XIII. Avinione pro Papa se gerente, Romæ successit Gregorius XII. Angelus Corrarius, Venetus Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus. De hoc Schismate librum integrum idem, qui supra, Theodoricus de Nyem scripsit. Ubi non Gregorium, sed Errorium vocat. Quàm maligni in hoc Schismate Pontifices illi fuerint, sic ille inter alia lib. 3. describit: Si quis, inquit, fraudes, machinationes, Erroríi & Petri per singula describere vellet, vix chartæ & atramentum huic sufficerent. Veruntamen clarum est, quòd cauteriatas habent suas conscientias, dicentes, se esse simplices, cùm sint astutia Diabolica repleti. Et pro opere pietatis dixerunt & dicunt, se utique voluisse & velle unionem facere, quod tamen in eorum cordibus non habebant, nec habent. Quid igitur erit in tam lamentabili Schismate finaliter? De his duobus Senioribus Babylonis, Petro & Errorio, major progressa est iniquitas & passim progreditur in universam terram, quàm unquam ante nostra tempora ab aliquibus de Papatu contendentibus emanavit. Et proh dolor! hæc adeò manifesta sunt & notoria, quòd nulla possunt tergiversatione celari. Unde ipsa fides Catholica obnubilatur. Omnis religio naufragium patitur, bella & aliæ calamitates multæ pullulant, Dei timor & hominum verecundia & virtutes à plerisque regnantibus & præsidentibus populis atque aliis inferioribus omnis status propterea in longum abierunt, in eorum loca successerunt vitia, justitia corruit in plateis, & in effectu. In universali Ecclesia, & in ejus membris bris à capite usque ad plantam pedis non est sanitas. Et Cardinales quidem Dei & Spiritus S. nutu tacti, ut Gerson loquitur, A. MCCCCIX. Concilio Pisis indicto, funestum adeò Schisma, depositis Benedicto & Gregorio, ceu criminis haeresefos, schismatis, perjurii scelerumque plurimorum reis; uti quidem Coriolanus & Bailius ex Blondo & Antonino referunt; electoque Petro Philargo Cretensi, qui nomen Alexandri V. assumpsit, abolere nequicquam conati sunt. Benedictus enim eorum conatus suaviter irrisit: Gregorius vero vocatus ad Concilium, respondit, non Cardinalium, sed suum esse Concilium convocare. Quin propter pervicacem utriusque ambitionem, qui ante mutuo infensi, jam simul conspirabant ad tuendam, quam possidebant dignitatem, atque ut in communi causa colludebant, uti Cabassutius in Notitia Conciliorum loquitur. Alexandro electo Gregorius Ariminum, Benedictus in Cataloniam aufugit. Uterque novos Cardinales creat, & verus Pontifex uterque haberi contendit.Factaque sic Ecclesia Romana Triceps est.Mortuo quin etiam sequente anno Alexandro V. veneno uti putatur, à Balthassare Cossa ei propinato, ipse Balthasar Cossa Neapolitanus, Johannes XXIV. post dictus, subrogatus est. Is statim Legatos ad Principes Germaniae misit, rogavitque, ut Sigismundum Hungariae Regem Imperatori Ruperto defuncto sufficerent. Quod cum ex voto successisset, Romae Imperatorem coronaturus, & Ecclesiam tranquillaturus Concilium indicit, in cujus prima sessione teste, apud Bailium, Nicolao Clemangis, Bajecensi Archidiacono, post missam de Spiritu S. celebratam, bubo, ferale omen, apparuit, supra Templi trabem sedens, horrifica voce, oculis in Papam conjectis, ipsum monstrifico ore salutavit, nec nisi fustibus interemptus abigi potuit. Unde false admodum Concilio huic Romano ab Antipapis objectum, Spiritum S. in specie bubonis ei præsedisse. Certè illud Concilium nulla fruge dimissum est.
units.tr: CXXXIX. I pass over Boniface IX, who, as Paulus Langius reports in his Chronicle, was greedy for money. To collect it he sent many legates through various parts of the world to peddle indulgences. He was a great simoniac, and he raised simoniacs to many dignities. He was of such a spirit and such counsel that he was the first to transfer all the power of the Roman people to the Pontiff, disposing and ordering every single matter in the city at his nod. Genebrardus also records that he imposed annates on benefices (on which Peter de Marca treats at length in de Concordia Sacerdotii et Imperii, book 6, chapters 10, 11, etc.). The abuses of the fifteenth century must be censured here. After the beginning of his reign, in 1406, the Schism, begun some time earlier, had already struck deeper roots and had troubled the Roman Church in a remarkable way. When Innocent VII died at Rome, Gregory XII, Angelo Corrario, a Venetian and Patriarch of Constantinople, succeeded at Rome, while Peter de Luna, or Benedict XIII, claimed to be pope at Avignon. Theodoric of Niem, mentioned above, wrote an entire book on this Schism, in which he calls Gregory not Gregorius but Errorius. He describes in book 3, among other things, how malicious those pontiffs were in this Schism: If anyone wished to describe the frauds, machinations and errors of Errorius and Peter one by one, scarcely paper and ink would suffice. Yet it is clear that their consciences are cauterized. They say that they are simple, when they are full of diabolical cunning. And as a work of piety they have said, and say, that they have wished, and wish, to bring about union, which nevertheless they did not and do not have in their hearts. What, then, will finally become of such a lamentable Schism? From these two elders of Babylon, Peter and Errorius, a greater iniquity has proceeded, and proceeds everywhere throughout the whole earth, than ever before in our times emanated from any who contended for the papacy. And alas! These things are so manifest and notorious that they cannot be concealed by any evasion. Hence the Catholic faith itself is obscured. All religion suffers shipwreck; wars and other many calamities spring up; the fear of God, the shame of men and virtues have for that reason long departed from most ruling and governing peoples and from all other conditions of the inferior orders, and vices have succeeded in their places; justice has fallen in the streets, and in effect, in the universal Church and in its members, from head to sole of the foot, there is no soundness. And the Cardinals, indeed, moved by the will of God and the Holy Spirit, as Gerson puts it, in 1409 convened a Council at Pisa. They deposed Benedict and Gregory, as guilty of heresy, schism, perjury and many crimes, which is what Coriolanus and Bailius report from Blondus and Antoninus. Having elected Peter Philargus of Crete, who took the name Alexander V, they tried in vain to abolish the Schism. For Benedict mildly ridiculed their attempt, and Gregory, when summoned to the Council, replied that it was for him, not the Cardinals, to convoke a Council. Indeed, on account of the stubborn ambition of both, who before were hostile to each other, they now conspired together to defend the dignity they held, and colluded in a common cause, as Cabassutius says in his Notitia Conciliorum. After Alexander was elected, Gregory fled to Rimini and Benedict to Catalonia. Each created new Cardinals, and each insisted that he alone was the true Pontiff, and so the Roman Church became three-headed. Indeed, in the following year Alexander V died, supposedly by poison given him by Balthasar Cossa, and Balthasar Cossa himself, a Neapolitan, afterwards John XXIII, was put in his place. He at once sent legates to the princes of Germany and asked that they appoint Sigismund, King of Hungary, in place of the deceased Emperor Rupert. When this succeeded as he wished, intending to be crowned emperor at Rome and to calm the Church, he called a Council. At its first session, as Bailius reports on the testimony of Nicolas Clemanges, archdeacon of Bayeux, after a Mass of the Holy Spirit had been celebrated, an owl, an ominous omen, appeared, sitting on a beam of the temple, and with a horrible voice, eyes fixed on the Pope, it greeted him with a monstrous mouth, nor could it be driven off except by being killed with clubs. Hence it was quite falsely objected by the Antipopes to this Roman Council that the Holy Spirit had presided over it in the form of an owl. Certainly that Council was dismissed without any fruit.

units.la: CXL. Cœterùm rebus ita deploratis Imperator Sigismundus, ut Ecclesiam miserè laceratam & inexhausta quadam vitiorum ac morborum colluvie inundatam sanaret & recolligeret, tantos pro Romana Ecclesia suscepit pertulitque labores, quantos ante ipsum pro Ecclesiæ salute paucissimi Regum vel Imperatorum subiisse leguntur. Etenim quò cœteri Reges in publicum Concilium (qua unica ratione Schisma tolli, & deploratis ferè Ecclesiæ malis medicina adhiberi posse videbatur) coirent, non sine gravissimis laboribus, sumptibus & periculis, Regna fere omnia totius Orbis Christiani peragravit, Galliam & Hispaniam adivit, in Angliam navigavit, Regibus nationum illarum persuasit, ut & ipsi in Concilium universale consenserint. Sed & in Italiam profectus Johanni Papæ Mantuæ persuasit, ut Constantiam ad Concilium veniret. Ita cœptum mense Octobre A. MCCCCXIV. Concilium Constantiense, seu potius, ut festivè Lutherus insignivit, Obstantiense (eò quòd in eo inter alia definitum est, licet Christus post cœnam instituerit, & suis discipulis administraverit sub utraque specie Panis & Vini venerabile Sacramentum, hoc tamen non obstante, postea à conficientibus sub utraque & à laicis sub una specie panis accipiatur) ad quod sexaginta millia hominum confluxerunt. Gerebatur ibi res quinque nationum, Italicæ, Gallicæ, Germanicæ, Hispanicæ & Anglicæ suffragiis. Sigismundus Imperator in ejus prima Missa, ut Diaconus, Euangelium cantavit. Conventu aperto, & data liberè loquendi potestate, plus quam quadraginta crimina, eáque gravissima Johanni objecta & probata sunt, inter quæ etiam illud, quòd Alexandrum decessorem conducto Marsilio Parmensi Medico, veneni ope sustulisset. Egit tamen cum
units.tr: CXL. Meanwhile, with affairs thus desperate, the Emperor Sigismund undertook and endured such great labours for the Roman Church, in order to heal and gather together the Church, miserably torn and flooded by a certain inexhaustible flood of vices and diseases, as we read that very few kings or emperors had undergone for the salvation of the Church before him. For while the other kings were gathering at a general Council (the only means by which the Schism could seem to be removed and a remedy applied to the almost desperate evils of the Church), not without the most serious labours, expenses and dangers, he travelled through almost all the kingdoms of the whole Christian world, visited France and Spain, sailed to England, and persuaded the kings of those nations that they too should consent to a universal Council. And when he went on to Italy, he persuaded John at Mantua to come to the Council at Constance. Thus the Council of Constance was begun in October 1414, or rather, as Luther wittily named it, the Obstantiense (because among other things it was defined there that, although Christ after supper instituted and gave to his disciples the venerable Sacrament under both kinds of bread and wine, nevertheless, notwithstanding this, it is afterwards to be received under one kind of bread by laymen and under both by those who consecrate). About sixty thousand people flocked to it. The business was conducted there by the votes of five nations: Italian, French, German, Spanish and English. At the first Mass of the Council, the Emperor Sigismund, acting as deacon, sang the Gospel. When the assembly was opened and freedom of speech was granted, more than forty crimes, and very grave ones, were brought against John and proved, among them that he had removed his predecessor Alexander by poison, employing Marsilius of Parma, a physician. Nevertheless he dealt with

units.la: Sigismundus Imperator ingentibus studiis Ecclesiæ pacem restituere conatus, Constantiæ Concilium à Johanne convocari curat. Friderico Auftriaco, ut se ex Concilio subducere velit. Quod cum fecisset ille, Papa abducto, Helvetii, inprimis Tigurini, suasu Concilii, Papam & Fridericum persequuntur & opimis ob id feudis ab Imperatore donantur. Retractus ex fuga Papa, & Manhemii in carcerem compactus, coactus est, Concilio dictante, Papatu se abdicare, ceu haereticus, negata animarum immortalitatis reus, atheus, Simoniacus, mendax hypocrita, homicida, veneficus, aleator, adulter, Sodomita, incarnatus denique Diabolus, quae & similia Johannis scelera ex Cosmodromico Gobelini Personae nuper etiam Odoricus Rainaldus in Annalium Baronii continuatione, aliisque repetiit. Mox Synodi Praesides decretum edunt, quo declarant, Concilium Generale Legitime congregatum habere potestatem immediate a Christo, atque eidem Papam subjectum esse. Supererant duo Papae, Gregorius & Benedictus, qui & ipsi citati, cum comparere detrectarent, Pontificia dignitate exuti sunt. Ita Gregorius animi moerore confectus mox obiit: Benedictus cum se praefractius gereret, etiam Ecclesiae communione motus est. Inde perventum in Concilio ad negotium Reformationis, cujus capita a P. de Aliaco digesta Sigismundus proponi mandat, sigillatim de causis, propter quas Pontifex corripi & deponi posset; quas ante novi Pontificis electionem definiri petit. Urgentibus nonnullis, a Minoritis Reformationis initium sumendum, Sigismundus idem merito respondit: Imo vero a Majoritis. Perculsis ea voce Majoritis, ne, Pontifice nullo Imperator id exsequeretur, annitentibus iisdem, die Martini A. MCCCCXVII. eligitur nationum omnium & Cardinalium consensu Otho Columna Romanus, Cardinalis Divi Gregorii, qui quod in festo Martini Papa creatus esset, Martinus V. dici voluit. Cujus electi pedes magna laetitia primus Sigismundus osculatus est. Primum atque is consecutus est imperium, nulla amplius reformationis facta mentio est. Imperatore vero eam strenuè urgente, Papa respondit, in aliud tempus opportunius remedium isthoc differendum esse. Rem enim esse magni momenti, periculosæ aleæ plenam, maturi consilii indigam, ne, vi pace composita, novæ in Clero turbæ exoriantur. Ex Hieronymi quippe sententia, unamquamque provinciam suos habere mores, suosque sensus, qui è medio tolli sine gravi rerum perturbatione nequeant. Et quia decreta sint Concilia consequentibus temporibus celebranda, iccirco reformationem temporibus illis reservandam, finemque Constantiensi Concilio per quatuor jam annos extracto imponendum esse. Ita scilicet egregius Veterator Imperatori & reliquis Principibus illusit, relictaque die XXII April. MCCCCXVIII. Constantiâ, & impositio Concilio fine in Italiam ad Voluptates se contulit & Romæ Jubilæum celebravit.
units.tr: Sigismund the Emperor, with great zeal, tried to restore peace to the Church, and he took care that a Council should be convoked at Constance by John. Frederick of Austria, however, wished to withdraw from the Council. When he had done so, the Pope was carried off, and the Swiss, especially those of Zurich, at the urging of the Council, pursued the Pope and Frederick, and for this they were given rich fiefs by the Emperor. The Pope, dragged back from his flight and thrown into prison at Mannheim, was compelled, at the Council's dictation, to abdicate the papacy as a heretic, guilty of denying the immortality of souls, an atheist, simoniac, lying hypocrite, murderer, poisoner, gambler, adulterer, sodomite, and finally an incarnate devil. These and similar crimes of John were repeated from the Cosmodromium of the Gobelinus Persona, and more recently by Odoricus Raynaldus in his continuation of Baronius's Annals, and by others. Soon the presidents of the Synod issued a decree in which they declared that a General Council lawfully assembled has power immediately from Christ, and that the Pope is subject to it. Two popes remained, Gregory and Benedict, who were also cited, and when they refused to appear, they were stripped of the papal dignity. Gregory, worn out by grief, soon died; Benedict, because he behaved more obstinately, was also cut off from communion with the Church. Then the Council came to the business of reformation, the heads of which Sigismund ordered to be proposed, drawn up by P. de Ailly, one by one, concerning the causes for which a Pontiff could be rebuked and deposed; he asked that these be defined before the election of a new Pontiff. When some urged that reformation should begin with the Minorites, Sigismund rightly replied: Nay rather, with the Majorites. Struck by this word "Majorites", and lest the Emperor should carry out the reform without a Pope, the same men struggled on, and on St. Martin's day, 1417, Otto Colonna, a Roman, Cardinal of St. Gregory's, was elected with the consent of all the nations and the Cardinals. Because he had been made pope on the feast of St. Martin, he wished to be called Martin V. Sigismund, first of all, joyfully kissed the feet of the newly elected man. As soon as he obtained the empire, no further mention was made of reformation. When the Emperor urgently pressed it, the Pope replied that this remedy must be deferred to another, more opportune time. For the matter was of great moment, full of perilous hazard, and in need of mature counsel, lest, once peace was restored by force, new disturbances should arise in the clergy. Indeed, according to Jerome's opinion, each province has its own customs and its own feelings, which cannot be removed from the midst without serious disruption of affairs. And since it was decreed that Councils should be held at later times, the reformation must therefore be reserved for those times, and an end must be put to the Council of Constance, which had now dragged on for four years. So that outstanding old fox mocked the Emperor and the other princes, and, leaving Constance on 22 April 1418, and the Council having been brought to an end, he betook himself to pleasures in Italy and celebrated a Jubilee at Rome.

units.la: CXLI. Qui Martino successit Eugenius IV. initio
units.tr: CXLI. Eugenius IV, who succeeded Martin, at the start

units.la: statim Pontificatus sui ratam habuit sententiam Martini defuncti, cujus in eo concilia steterant, ut novum Concilium Basileæ coiret. Coactum illud reformandæ Ecclesiæ gratia, indicente Eugenio A. MCCCCXXXI. usque ad A. MCCCCXLVI. duravit. Cæterùm cùm audiret Eugenius, disputari palam, Papam subesse Concilio debere, & potiorem esse Concilii quàm Papæ authoritatem, abrumpendi Concilii & Ferrariam transferendi consilium, eo prætextu, quòd Græci locum eum sibi delegissent; cepit, Sigismundo Imperatore & Præsidibus Concilii multum refragantibus. Cúmque coeptis suis Papa ἀντιπθύτως insisteret, & Ferrariæ Concilium suum Papale, Johanne Palæologo Imperatore Constantinopolitano eò invitato, & irreverenter excepto, inchoaret, & mox etiam lue Epidemia ibi serpente Florentiam illud transferret; Concilium Basileense bullam A. MCCCCXXXVII. edit, qua ab Officio Pastorali Eugenius suspenditur ob lupinam tyrannidem, simúlque sancitur, Ecclesiam in capite & membris reformandam esse, & Papam ipsum Concilio subjacere. Quod nisi est, inquit, quis unquam Romano Pontifici quanquam improbissimo contradiceret? Cujus Concilii authoritatem Stanislaus Felix in Notis ad Pallavicini Historiam Concilii Tridentini, strenuè tuetur; licet Basileam Basilicum peperisse Antoninus Florentinus dicitaverit. Sed & Concilium Florentinum ab Eugenio ἐξ ἐναγίας celebratum, ceu illegitimum, adeóque Conciliabulum damnat, denique Eugenio, eò quòd, ut Sess. 26. loquuntur Patres, nulla exhortatione ad emendationem morum, & abusuum correctionem trahi potuerit, electioni Pastorum proborum non præbuerit assensum, Beneficia Simoniacè contulerit, Concilio non adfuerit, bonos expulerit, pro gravi pecunia dignitates contulerit, Synodalia piorum Pontificum decreta revocârit &c. mox Sess. 34. ceu contumace exauthorato novum Pontificem, Amadeum Ducem Sabaudiæ, Felicis V. nomine insignem creant. Documenta ejus rei multifaria ἀξιομνημόνευτα à Goldasto in Constitutiones Imperiales relata legere est. Interim Florentiæ cum Palæologo reliquisque Græcis, auxilia adversus Turcas, unione & communione fidei promissa, paciscentibus, transfigitur, convenitúrque sequentes in Articulos: Purgatorium esse, Papam Ecclesiæ caput esse, Spiritum S. à Patre & Filio procedere, S. Eucharistiam in azymo & fermento indifferenter confici. Hæc omnia Imperator Græcus à suis comprobari curat; repugnante acriter Michaele Episcopo Ephefino, & articulos de Papa inprimis & Purgatorio strenuè oppugnante. Domum reversi Græci συνυπογεγραμμένοι odium incurrerunt omnium, articulos, quibus illi consenserant, aperte damnantium. Extat Epistola Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ ad Bohemos, die 18 Jan. A. MCCCCLI. missa, & Catalogo Testium Veritatis Græco-Latinè inserta; in qua inter alia sic scribunt: Hortamur vos nobiscum ad concordiam; non autem secundum illam Florentinam unionem simulatam, à certo veróque consilio abalienatam, quæ diremptio à veritate jure appellanda est. Quam ob causam illam quoque minimè admisimus, imo prorsus repudiavimus: sed secundum immutabile Veritatis decretum, in quo solo verè ac tutò uniri possumus. Isidorus tamen Ruthenorum, & Bessarion Niceæ Episcopi, Pontificias partes amplexi, Cardinalium Romanorum in chorum cooptati sunt. Decretum mox Eugenius edit, tantum abesse, ut Concilio ulli ipse subjaceat, ut tunc maximè mereatur, cùm Concilii decreta contemnit. Quin & thesin hanc, Concilium esse supra Papam, ceu hæreticam damnat; dimissoque Florentiæ Conciliabulo Romam A. MCCCCXXXIX. revertitur. Inde in Felicem tonat, & hic Basilea non minore ardore in Eugenium; convitia statuæ Nabuchodonosoris, idoli, Beelzebubis, Luciferi adversus se invicem jactante strenuè. Concilium verò Basileense comparentibus Bohemis, post quinquaginta dierum disputationem, communionem sub utraque specie, ceu liberam, scilicet jure Divino, non necessariam, permittit: Annatas & alias rapinas abolet; Hussitis negantibus, se ullam doctrinam Scripturis sacris non comprehensam admissuros, per Cardinalem Cusanum respondet: Scripturas non ad esse, sed ad bene esse Ecclesiæ facere. Tanto dignius Verbum Dei tradi, quanto ab omni Scriptura remotius. Explicandam Scripturam esse juxta currentem Ecclesiæ ritum, qua sententiam mutante Dei etiam judicium mutetur. Tandem Eugenius ad dissipandum Basileense Concilium Carolum Franciæ Delphinum armavit. Qui cum gentium quadam perditissima colluvie, Alsatiæ vicos & civitates nonnullas dolo, proditione & blandimentis ingressus, Alsatiam omnem, vini atque frumenti feracissimam miserè vastavit, ac ædes civium, casas pauperum orphanorum & vidua-
units.tr: At the very beginning of his pontificate, Eugenius upheld the decision of the late Martin, under whose term the councils had remained in force, that a new council should assemble at Basel. That council, gathered for the reform of the Church at Eugenius's summons, met in 1431 and lasted until 1446. But when Eugenius heard it openly argued that the Pope ought to be subject to the council, and that the authority of the council is greater than that of the Pope, he resolved to break up the council and transfer it to Ferrara, on the pretext that the Greeks had chosen that place for themselves. He carried out this plan although Emperor Sigismund and the presidents of the council strongly objected. When the Pope stubbornly [ἀντιπθύτως] persisted in his undertakings, and began his own papal council at Ferrara, to which John Palaeologus, Emperor of Constantinople, had been invited and was received without due reverence, and soon moved it to Florence when plague spread there, the Council of Basel issued a bull in 1437. By this bull Eugenius was suspended from the pastoral office on account of his wolfish tyranny, and it was at the same time decreed that the Church must be reformed in head and members, and that the Pope himself is subject to the council. Unless this is so, he says, who would ever have opposed the Roman Pontiff, however wicked he was? Stanislaus Felix vigorously defends the authority of this council in his Notes to Pallavicini's Historiam Concilii Tridentini, although Antoninus of Florence has claimed that Basel gave birth to a basilisk. But the Council of Florence, which Eugenius celebrated ἐξ ἐναγίας [under a curse], he condemns as illegitimate, and therefore a conciliabulum. Finally, because, as the Fathers say in Sess. 26., no exhortation to amend morals and correct abuses could be drawn from him, he would not assent to the election of upright ministers; he conferred benefices by simony, did not attend the council, drove out good men, conferred dignities for heavy sums of money, revoked the synodal decrees of pious Popes, and so on. Then, in Sess. 34., they deposed him as contumacious and created a new Pope, Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, known by the name Felix V. Many notable documents on this matter, recorded by Goldast in the Imperial Constitutions, can be read. Meanwhile at Florence, with Palaeologus and the other Greeks, a pact was struck: aid against the Turks was promised in exchange for union and communion of faith, and they agreed to the following articles: Purgatory exists; the Pope is head of the Church; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; the Holy Eucharist is consecrated indifferently in unleavened and leavened bread. The Greek Emperor took care to have these all approved by his people, though Michael, Bishop of Ephesus, opposed them strongly and attacked especially the articles on the Pope and Purgatory. On returning home, the Greeks who had co-signed incurred the hatred of all, who openly condemned the articles to which they had agreed. There exists a letter of the Church of Constantinople, sent to the Bohemians on 18 January 1451 and included in the Catalogue of the Testimonies of Truth in Greek and Latin. In it, among other things, they write: We exhort you to unity with us; but not according to that Florentine union, which was feigned and estranged from a certain and true counsel, and which is rightly to be called a separation from the truth. For this reason we did not admit it at all, indeed we utterly rejected it; but we unite according to the unchangeable decree of truth, in which alone we can be united truly and safely. Nevertheless Isidore of Ruthenia and Bessarion, Bishop of Nicaea, who embraced the Papal side, were co-opted into the college of Roman cardinals. Eugenius soon issued a decree that he was so far from being subject to any council that he deserved this most when he despised the decrees of a council. Indeed, he condemns the thesis Council is above the Pope as heretical. Dismissing the conciliabulum at Florence, he returned to Rome in 1439. From there he thundered against Felix, and Felix from Basel with no less ardour against Eugenius, the two hurling insults at each other vigorously: statue of Nebuchadnezzar, idol, Beelzebub, Lucifer. When the Bohemians appeared, the Council of Basel, after fifty days of disputation, allowed communion under both kinds as free, but not necessary, by divine right. It abolished annates and other plunder. When the Hussites denied that they would admit any doctrine not contained in holy Scripture, it replied through Cardinal Cusanus: Scriptures are made not for the being but for the well-being of the Church. The Word of God is handed on all the more worthily the further it is from all Scripture. Scripture must be explained according to the current rite of the Church, since if that changes, the judgment of God itself changes too. At last Eugenius armed Charles, the Dauphin of France, to scatter the Council of Basel. With a most depraved rabble of mixed peoples, he entered some villages and several towns of Alsace by trickery, treachery and flattery, and miserably laid waste all of Alsace, so fertile in wine and grain. He wickedly set fire to the houses of citizens, the huts of poor orphans and widows, and even the most sacred temples of God.

units.la: Carolus Gallia Delphinus Basileense Concilium turbare conatus cladem ingentem ab Helvetiis visus licet, patitur. viduarum, ipsáque sacratissima Dei Templa igni nefarie succendit. Cumque crudelitate extrema in Alsatia perpetrata, tandem cum armatis triginta millibus Basileam adortus esset, à quatuor millibus Helvetiorum ita exceptus est, ut victor licet vix tertiam exercitus sui partem, eámque mutilam & fractam, amisso etiam belli Duce Arminiaco, in Galliam reduxerit; Concilio Basileensi interim perseverante. Retulitque hic Princeps dignam planè militia Pontificia mercedem. Perierunt enim in ea pugna, incentore Papa, ultra quatuordecim millia virorum fortium. Hæ scilicet Papales virtutes, hæ indulgentiæ fuerunt! Concilii ipsius Basileensis infelicem exitum his verbis Rollfinxius in fasciculo deplorat: Concilium Basileense, in quo multa bona fuerunt instituta pro reformatione in capite & membris, habuit principium gloriosum, sed finem humilem ac tribulatione plenum propter Schisma. Mirabilis rerum eventus. Prævaluit Concilium Constantiense contra tres Papas, eos dejiciendo, & quartum instituendo, cum tot haberet adversitates, & à nullo confirmatum fuisset. Illud autem tanta authoritate collectum & firmatum, nec unum potuit vel in modico reducere ad normam propositi sui, imò è contra processus ejus fuit impeditus ab uno. Ibi debile principium & finis gloriosus. Hic è contra præcisè fuit. Et Matthias Ugolinus in Synodico suo: Quid, inquit, tenendum tunc fuerit, cùm eodem tempore Concilia duo congregata, & ad invicem discrepantia reperirentur, videlicet Basileense & Florentinum, solvat Christus Jesus, Magister & Doctor infallibilis Veritatis, pro sinceritate fidei Ecclesiæ inviolabilis & sponsa suæ.
units.tr: Charles, Dauphin of France, who tried to disturb the Council of Basel, suffered a great defeat at the hands of the Swiss. He wickedly set fire to the houses of citizens, the huts of poor orphans and widows, and even the most sacred temples of God. When, after the extreme cruelty committed in Alsace, he at last attacked Basel with thirty thousand armed men, he was met by four thousand Swiss. The victor, though he brought back to France scarcely a third of his army, and that maimed and broken, and having also lost his commander Armagnac, was thus received, while the Council of Basel went on. This prince thus brought back the reward truly worthy of papal soldiery. For in that battle, with the Pope as instigator, more than fourteen thousand brave men perished. These, then, were the papal virtues, these the indulgences! Rollfinck laments the unhappy end of the Council of Basel itself in these words, in his little bundle: The Council of Basel, in which many good things were established for the reform in head and members, had a glorious beginning, but a humble end, full of tribulation because of the Schism. A remarkable turn of events. The Council of Constance prevailed against three Popes, deposing them and installing a fourth, although it had so many adversities and had been confirmed by no one. But that council, gathered and confirmed with such authority, could not bring a single thing, even a small one, back to the rule of its own purpose; on the contrary, its progress was hindered by one man. There a weak beginning and a glorious end. Here, on the contrary, it was exactly the reverse. And Matthias Ugolinus in his Synodicon: What, he says, was to be held at that time, when two councils, Basel and Florence, were gathered at the same time and were found to be at odds with each other? Let Christ Jesus, the infallible Master and Teacher of truth, decide, for the sincerity of the faith of the Church, which is inviolable and his bride.

units.la: CXLII. Tandem Eugenius, postquam Divina & humana omnia perturbavit, A. MCCCCXLVI. satis concessit, ... nactus Nicolaum V. (alii VI. vocant) qui Thomas Sarzanus antea dictus est. Friderici III. Imperatoris intercessione cessit ei Felix V. dignitate Cardinalis contentus, abolendi Schismatis perniciosi gratia. Obsessa à Turcis Constantinopoli, Constantinus Palæologus apud Nicolaum Papam suppetias nequicquam implorat eò quòd Græci Papæ primatum constanter abnuerent. Græci, inquit Nauclerus, ad Latinorum opes frustra confugiunt, à Pontifice Nicolao V. lacrymis ac fletibus auxilia petentes. Sic deserto malignè Imperatore, urbs Constantinopolis die xxix Maji A. MCCCCLIII. à Muhammede capta, Turcicum jugum, unà cum Imperio Orientali universo subiit: Constantino ipso in fuga graviter vulnerato, cujus mox caput resectum, Muhammedi suave spectaculum offertur. Tanta Romanensium perfidia fuit, qui Imperium universum Orientale Christianum Turcis horrendum in modum subjugatum, quàm Pontificia dominatione solutum maluerunt. Pereuntes tot Christianos, qui servare cum potuissent, & ob Christi Salvatoris amorem debuissent, non servârunt tamen, eos perdidisse censentur merito. Ita malorum & calamitatum omnium fundus & architecta Roma fuit.
units.tr: CXLII. At last Eugenius, after he had thrown all things divine and human into confusion, at length gave way in 1446. He was succeeded by Nicholas V (others call him VI), who was formerly named Thomas Sarzanus. At the intercession of Emperor Frederick III, Felix V yielded to him, content with the dignity of cardinal, for the sake of abolishing the pernicious schism. When Constantinople was besieged by the Turks, Constantine Palaeologus implored help from Pope Nicholas in vain, because the Greeks steadfastly denied the Pope's primacy. The Greeks, says Naucler, fled in vain to the resources of the Latins, begging for help from Pope Nicholas V with tears and wailing. So with the Emperor maliciously abandoned, the city of Constantinople was taken by Muhammad on 29 May 1453, and it underwent the Turkish yoke along with the whole Eastern Empire. Constantine himself was gravely wounded in flight, and his head was then cut off and offered to Muhammad as a pleasing spectacle. Such was the treachery of the Romans, who preferred that the whole Eastern Christian empire be horribly subjugated to the Turks rather than be freed from papal domination. Those many Christians who perished, whom they could have saved, and ought to have saved out of love for Christ the Saviour, they nonetheless did not save; they are rightly judged to have destroyed them. Thus Rome was the source and architect of all evils and calamities.

units.la: CXLIII. Cœterum Nicolai liberalitatem, & erga literas literatósque benevolentiam incomparabilem, vehementer Scriptores prædicant. Omnium instar Nauclerus, Generat. 49. Sic illum commendat: Laudatur Nicolai liberalitas, qua erga omnes usus est, maximè verò literatos. Quos & beneficiis, & officiis mirificè juvit, eos præmiis ad componendum, & ad vertendos Græcos authores in Latinum ita perpulit, ut literæ Græcæ & Latinæ, quæ sexcentis jam annis in situ & tenebris jacuerant, denuò splendorem aliquem adeptæ sint. Certè negari nequit, Pontificis hujus opera literas & Musas in Europa quodammodò reformatas & renatas esse, proximaque adeò etiam Religionis ipsius reformationi quodammodo præluxisse. Ex Oriente inprimis Turcarum, qui Constantinopoli diu imminentes eam tandem ceperunt, & bonis etiam literis exilium indixerunt, metu Romam se contulerunt Viri undiquaque doctissimi, Emanuel Chrysoloras, Byzantinus seu Constantinopolitanus, qui Græcæ Grammaticæ Erotemata scripsit; Theodorus Gaza Thessalonicensis, Græcè & Latinè doctissimus; Georgius Trapezuntius, Chalcondylas Atheniensis; Joh. Lascaris, Demetrius, aliique, qui immenso Dei beneficio artium igniculos in Græcia per Turcarum barbariem tantùm non extinctos, in Latium aliásque regiones transduxerunt. Nicolao certè Georgius ille Trapezuntius, Demetrius, & ex Europæis, Georgius Valla, Nicolaus Perottus aliíque viri celebres in deliciis unicè fuerunt. Meritóque Pontifici huic acceptum referimus quicquid splendoris Latinæ & Græcæ literæ in Italia primùm; postea etiam in Germania acceperunt. Sicut autem olim Moses in aula Ægyptiaca educatus est, qui postea filios Israelis ex Ægypto eduxit: ita in ipsa quoque Antichristi aula bonas literas promotas, earumque deinceps auxilio Antichristum Orbi revelatum, & in multorum cordibus confossum esse, mirum certè non est.
units.tr: CXLIII. Writers loudly praise Nicholas's generosity and his incomparable goodwill toward letters and learned men. Naucler, Generation 49, is the foremost of them all, and commends him thus: Nicholas's liberality is praised, by which he treated all men, and especially men of letters. He helped these with benefits and services wonderfully, and moved them with rewards to compose and to turn Greek authors into Latin, so that Greek and Latin letters, which had lain in neglect and darkness for six hundred years, have regained some splendour. Certainly it cannot be denied that through this Pontiff's work literature and the Muses were in some measure reformed and reborn in Europe, and that this in some measure foreshadowed the very reformation of religion that was soon to come. Above all, from the East, when the Turks, who had long threatened Constantinople, finally took it and also banished good letters, learned men from every quarter went to Rome in fear: Emanuel Chrysoloras, the Byzantine or Constantinopolitan, who wrote the Greek grammar Erotemata; Theodore Gaza of Thessalonica, most learned in Greek and Latin; George of Trebizond; Chalcondyles of Athens; John Lascaris; Demetrius; and others, who by the immense benefit of God carried the sparks of the arts, which the barbarism of the Turks had all but extinguished in Greece, into Latium and other regions. Certainly that George of Trebizond, Demetrius, and among Europeans George Valla and Nicholas Perotti and other famous men were the particular delights of Nicholas. And rightly we credit to this Pontiff whatever splendour Latin and Greek letters first received in Italy, and afterwards in Germany too. But just as Moses was once brought up at the Egyptian court and afterwards led the sons of Israel out of Egypt, so it is certainly no wonder that good letters were advanced in the very court of Antichrist, and that by their aid Antichrist was revealed to the world and pierced in the hearts of many.

units.la: CXLIV. Neque parum ad bonarum literarum increnmenta, & consequentem verae etiam religionis, & oppositae eidem Antichristianae tyrannidis, quam Romana hactenus Hierarchia in Ecclesia exercuit, cognitionem divinum chalcotypiae aut typographiae, quam impressuram fere appellant, inventum ac beneficium nunquam satis laudatum contulit.
units.tr: In no small measure, the divine invention of copper-printing, or typography as it is usually called, has also contributed to the growth of good letters, and to the knowledge of true religion that followed from it, and of the Antichristian tyranny opposed to it, which the Roman hierarchy has hitherto exercised in the Church. This invention and benefit can never be praised enough.

units.la: Anno scilicet MCCCCCXL. Johannes Gutenbergius Argentinensis aurifex, Moguntii primùm magnis artem eam sumptibus protulit. Eandem postea Johannes Mentel ibidem auxit, & Sixtus Reofingerus Argentinensis Neapolin in Italiam transduxit. De inventore tamen artis controversiam Moguntinis alii movent, quos inter Hadrianus Junius Batavia suæ cap. 17. ejus inventionem nem civi cuipiam Harlemensi acceptum retulit. Quam controversiam pluribus Doctiss. Mollincrodius discussit. Sed de inventore quicquid sit (nam etiam cum Pomponius Lætus utrisque laudem præreptam voluit, scribens ad Augustinum Maphæum, imprimendi facultatem multis seculis intermissam, paulo ante revocatam esse: tum Jovius histor. lib. 14. in regione Sinarum libros ante multos annos impressos extare ait; tum denique Alphonsus Mendoza lib. III. 16. in Regno Chinæ artem typographicam quingentis annis ante, quam ad Germanos veniret, in usu fuisse scribit) nobilissimum isthoc inventum libros, quibus Romanæ Ecclesiæ pudenda detecta sunt, aperuit, & longè latéque invitis adversariis omnibus dispersit, & adhuc dum per omnes Orbis angulos spargit. Sibylla etiam Erythræa de Antichristo vaticinans, prædixit, fore ut per linum tandem perdatur. Sic enim carmen habet. Ἀίλιῳ ἐκ ζῶντε ἡλιρὸς, ὅτι λίνῳ ἀυτῷ ὀλεῖται. Miserum inde tempus, quia linum illud perdet. Charta scilicet, in qua libri excuduntur, ex lineo panno conficitur.
units.tr: In the year 1440, John Gutenberg, a goldsmith of Strasbourg, first brought this art to Mainz at great expense. John Mentelin afterwards improved it in the same place, and Sixtus Reinfinger of Strasbourg carried it over to Naples in Italy. Some of the people of Mainz, however, raise a controversy about the inventor of the art. Among them Hadrianus Junius, in chapter 17 of his Batavia, ascribed the invention to a certain citizen of Haarlem. The very learned Mollinkroth has discussed this controversy at length. But whoever the inventor was (for Pomponius Laetus, writing to Augustinus Maphaeus, wanted the praise taken from both parties, saying that the power of printing, lost for many centuries, had been recovered only a little before; then Jovius, in history, book 14, says that books printed many years earlier are extant in the region of the Sinae; and finally Alphonsus Mendoza, in book III, 16, writes that in the kingdom of China the art of typography had been in use five hundred years before it came to the Germans), this most noble invention has opened up books in which the shameful things of the Roman Church have been exposed, has spread them far and wide to the dismay of all its adversaries, and still spreads them through every corner of the world. The Erythraean Sibyl too, prophesying about Antichrist, foretold that he would at last be destroyed by flax. Her verse runs: "Woe then to the time, because flax will destroy him" [Ἀίλιῳ ἐκ ζῶντε ἡλιρὸς, ὅτι λίνῳ ἀυτῷ ὀλεῖται]. Miserable then will be the time, because it will destroy that flax. Of course, the paper on which books are printed is made from linen cloth.

units.la: CXLV. Nicolao V. in sede Pontificia Calliastus III.
units.tr: CXLV. Callixtus III succeeds Nicholas V in the Papal See.

units.la: huic vero Æneas Sylvius Piccolominæus Genuensis, Vir cætera doctissimus, & in Concilio Basileensi paulo ante celeberrimus, qui Pii II. nomen sibi impositum, successit. Exspectárunt ab ejus eruditione, aureisque promissis Viri boni Ecclesiæ pacem & tranquillitatem: sed fefellit eos spes concepta plurimum, documentumque impietas Pii dedit, quam deplorata sit Ecclesiæ salus. Papa enim creatus Augustini Exemplum præferens Bullam retractationis scripsit, qua ea, quæ in Basileensi Concilio adversus Eugenium gessit, revocavit; rectius facturus, si ejusdem S. Augustini exemplo Confessionum libro edito peccatum juventutis, quod Epistola ad Patrem data (quæ decima quinta est,) confessus Patri est, magis etiam ipsi Deo confessus esset deinceps. Majestatem Pontificiam neutiquam minuere, sed augere in immensum conatus nihil intentatum inausumque reliquit, palam prae se ferens, se neque Reges, neque Duces, neque populos ullos formidare; quin adversari sibi ausos aperta vi ad Obedientiam Apostolicam reducturum; Bulla insuper de non appellando a Papa ad Concilium edita. Palam igitur se Regi Galliae Pontificiam tyrannidem & rapinam in Regno suo coercere non nihil paranti; Regi Apuliae, Sigismundo Archiduci Austriae; quod Nicolaum Cusanum a Pio designatum, ut ditionis suae homines excoriaret, rejecisset, oppositi; Germaniam horribilibus bellis intestinis intricavit; Dietherum Comitem ab Ifenburg, electum Archiepiscopum Moguntinum, pallium Episcopale viginti millibus sexcentis quinquaginta aureis Rhenensibus redimere tardantem, eo quod authoritate Concilii Basileensis Annatae damnatae abolitaeque essent; ita cum Adolpho Nassoviensi aemulo ejus commisit, ut praecipuis Germaniae Principibus in partes concedentibus, horribilibus bellorum civilium incendiis universa fere Germania conflagraverit.
units.tr: To him succeeded Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini of Genoa, a man otherwise most learned, and much celebrated shortly before at the Council of Basel, who took the name Pius II. Good men expected peace and tranquillity for the Church from his learning and golden promises, but the hope they had conceived was largely disappointed, and Pius's impiety gave proof of how desperate the Church's salvation was. For once he had been made pope, imitating Augustine, he wrote a Bull of retraction, by which he revoked what he had done against Eugenius at the Council of Basel. He would have acted more rightly if, following the example of the same St. Augustine, he had confessed to God himself, in a book of Confessions, the sin of his youth, which he had confessed to his father in the letter he sent him (the fifteenth). He made no attempt to diminish papal majesty, but to increase it immensely, leaving nothing untried or unattempted, openly declaring that he feared neither kings, nor dukes, nor any peoples; indeed, that he would bring back by open force to apostolic obedience those who dared to oppose him. In addition, he issued a Bull forbidding appeal from the Pope to a council. Openly he set himself against the King of France, who was somewhat preparing to restrain papal tyranny and plunder in his kingdom; against the King of Apulia and Sigismund, Archduke of Austria, because they had rejected Nicholas of Cusa, whom Pius had designated to flay the men of his dominion. He entangled Germany in dreadful civil wars. He dealt harshly with Diether, Count of Isenburg, elected Archbishop of Mainz, who was slow to buy the episcopal pallium for 20,600 Rhenish gold coins, because by the authority of the Council of Basel the annates had been condemned and abolished. So he set himself against his rival Adolf of Nassau, and with the chief princes of Germany taking sides, almost all of Germany was set ablaze by the dreadful fires of civil war.

units.la: CXLVI. Jam visi Pontifices erant ad eum tyrannidis & impietatis gradum pervenisse, cui nihil amplius addi posset.
units.tr: CXLVI. The Popes had by now been seen to reach such a degree of tyranny and impiety that nothing more could be added to it.

units.la: Et tamen sequentes Pontifices rationem invenerunt, qua & fastigium & pinnulas ipsas huic aedificio imponerent. Inter eos post Paulum II. Montium pietatis, seu potius impietatis (de quibus Dorothei Asciani liber singularis extat) authorem Sixtus IV. A. MCCCCLXXXI. Papa creatus, cujus quidem subactum in omni genere literarum judicium laudatur, excusso pudore omni, iis libidinibus impurissimum se mancipavit, ut eas prodere pudor Scriptores prohibuerit. Aliquid tamen dicere Wesselus Groningensis, vulgo Lux Mundi dictus in Tractatu de Indulgentiis Papalibus; nec non Cornelius Agrippa in dedeclamatione ad Lovanienses, sustinuerunt. Idem Agrippa de Incertitud. & Vanitate scient. cap. 64. Lenoniam à Sixto institutam sic describit: Recentioribus temporibus Sixtus Pontifex Max. nobile lupanar instituit, &c. Romæ scorta in singulas septimanas Julium pendunt Pontifici. Qui census annuus nonnunquam viginti mille ducatos excedit (sunt qui quadraginta mille post numeraverint) Adeoque Ecclesiæ Procerum id munus est, ut una cum Ecclesiarum proventibus etiam lenociniorum mercedem numerent. Sic enim illos supputantes aliquando audivi. Habet (inquientes) ille duo beneficia, unum Curatum aureorum viginti, alterum, prioratum ducatorum quadraginta, & tres putanas in bordello. Quis verò ad nefandam fœditatem hanc non obstupescat? Impurissimum tamen & obscoenissimum Antichristi Regnum hoc in facinore aperte cernitur. Taceo iniqua bella ab ipso adversus Nicolaum, Vitellium, Florentinos, Regem Siciliæ Venetos gesta. Bello quidem adversus Venetos suscepto Helvetios fœdere sibi junxit, quibus dono misit vexillum rubrum, Bulla singulari ad eos destinata commendatum, sub cujus finem ita scribit. Nos vexillum ipsum benediximus, ut sub eo militantes benedictionem Omnipotentis Dei semper vobiscum habeatis. Eapropter (quod huic Sedi sanctæ ac vobis faustum ac felix sit) læto & magno animo vexillum hoc, quod præfata sedes vobis donat, accipientes, contra ejusdem Sedis inimicos, Virtutem vestram ostendite. Ite animis lætis contra hostes Ecclesiæ, & illam ab oppressoribus LIBERTATIS ECCLESIASTICÆ, ac facientibus contra illam, solita illa vestra magnanimitate, defendite. Inferat præpotens exercitus vester vexillum, Altissimi nomine invocato contra dictæ Sedis inimicos. Et quemadmodum columna nubis in deserto populum Dei præcedebat & dirigebat in viam salutis & victoriæ, ita quicunque sub ea pro ipsa Ecclesia Romana pugnaverint, à Domino nostro Jesu Christo benedicti sint, & plenariam habeant peccatorum suorum omnium remissionem & indulgentiam, quam ex tunc, & per praesentes concedimus. Maledictus sit quicunque contra vos pro Ecclesia Romana praedicta pugnantes, pugnabit, aut facere contra praesumpserit. Vobiscum autem sit benedictio Domini perpetua, cum laude & gloria Omnipotentis Dei, ejusque Beatae Mariae Virginis, in saecula saeculorum. Ex qua Bulla cernere est Antichristi artes nefarias, & dolos, quibus gentibus fortissimis & simplicissimis imposuit. Neque major religio vel pietas fuit Alexandri VI. A. MCCCCXCII. ex intervallo succedentis. Cui, ita Guicciardinus loquitur, non sinceritas, non verecundia, non veritas, non fides, non religio ulla aderat. Quóque Pontifice Romam, gentium illud asylum, carnificinam factam esse, venalibus in ea cunctis sacris, Paulus Langius Monachus in Citizensi Chronico ex Volaterrano commemorat. Mores ejus turpissimos, avaritiam insatiabilem, ambitionem sine modo, crudelitatem plusquam ferinam, spurios, quos plures habebat, per fas & nefas ad summa provehendi cupidinem foedam, passim Scriptores memorant. Ditiones temporales ad ipsum nullo jure pertinentes, in utraque scilicet India noviter detectas, Bullâ inter Reges Hispaniae & Lusitaniae distribuit, haud equidem exemplo Christi, qui legitimam haereditatem partiri gravatus est, sed potius Sathanae, qui Christo se adoraturo in celso monte mundi Regna ostentavit & promisit, licet eorum vola vel vestigium ad eum jure nullo pertinuerit. Cum Lucretia filia notha, quam primum Ludovico Sforciae, mox Aloisio Aragoni, Alphonsi Regis filio, & denique hoc interfecto Alphonso Estensi, Ferrariae Duci elocavit, furtivam incestamque consuetudinem & ipse & filius Caesar Borgias habuisse creduntur. Certe Jacobus Sannazarius Poeta celebris & eximius, Lucretiae huic Epitaphium ejusmodi cecinit: Hic jacet in tumulo Lucretia nomine, sed re Thais, Alexandri filia, sponsa, nurus. Habuitque exitum impietate sua dignum. Testibus enim Panvinio, Guicciardino, Bembo, Jovio, ex quibus etiam Staroulscius & Carriere repetunt, poculo venenato, quo Cardinales nonnullos letho dare paraverat, per errorem ipsi propinato, perfidia in caput detestabile authoris recidente, periit.
units.tr: And yet the following Popes found a way to place both the pinnacle and the little pinnacles on this edifice. Among them, after Paul II, the author of the Mounts of Piety, or rather of impiety (there is a separate book about them by Dorotheus Ascianus), was Sixtus IV, created in 1481, whose judgment in every kind of learning is praised.
