Having cast off all shame, he gave himself over to such impure lusts that writers have refrained from disclosing them. Yet Wessel of Groningen, commonly called the Light of the World, in his treatise on papal indulgences, and Cornelius Agrippa, in his declamation to the men of Louvain, ventured to say something about them. Agrippa himself, in On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences, chapter 64, describes the brothel set up by Sixtus in these words: In more recent times Pope Sixtus, the Supreme Pontiff, established a noble brothel, etc. At Rome prostitutes pay the Pope a tax every week. This yearly revenue sometimes exceeds twenty thousand ducats (some have counted forty thousand since). So it is the office of the leaders of the Church to count the wages of brothels together with the revenues of the churches. For I once heard them reckoning in this way. He (they say) has two benefices, one a parish worth twenty gold pieces, the other a priory worth forty ducats, and three whores in a brothel. Who would not be astonished at such unspeakable filthiness? Yet the most impure and obscene kingdom of Antichrist is plainly seen in this crime. I pass over the unjust wars waged by him against Nicholas, Vitellius, the Florentines and the King of Sicily, and against the Venetians. In the war he undertook against the Venetians, he joined the Swiss to himself by a treaty, and sent them as a gift a red banner, commended by a special Bull addressed to them, at the end of which he writes: We have blessed this banner itself, so that those who fight under it may always have with you the blessing of Almighty God. Therefore (may it be happy and fortunate for this holy See and for you) receive this banner, which the said See gives you, with a glad and great spirit, and show your valour against the enemies of the same See. Go with cheerful minds against the enemies of the Church, and defend her with your accustomed greatness of spirit from those who oppress ECCLESIASTICAL LIBERTY and act against her. Let your mighty army bear the banner, invoking the name of the Most High against the enemies of the said See. And just as a pillar of cloud went before the people of God in the desert and guided them on the way of salvation and victory, so whoever fights under it for the Roman Church itself may be blessed by our Lord Jesus Christ, and have full remission and indulgence of all their sins, which we grant from now on and by these presents. Cursed be whoever shall presume to fight, or to act, against you who fight for the aforesaid Roman Church. And may the blessing of the Lord be upon you forever, to the praise and glory of Almighty God and of his Blessed Virgin Mary, for ever and ever. From this Bull one can see the nefarious arts and deceits by which he deceived the most valiant and most simple peoples. Nor was there greater piety or religion in Alexander VI, who succeeded at an interval in 1492. To him, as Guicciardini says, there was no sincerity, no shame, no truth, no faith, no religion whatever. Paul Langius, the Monk, in the Citizen Chronicle, following Volaterranus, records that under this Pope Rome, that refuge of the nations, was made into a slaughterhouse, with every sacred office up for sale. Writers commonly report his most shameful morals, his insatiable greed, his immoderate ambition, his more than savage cruelty, and his foul desire to advance his many bastard children to the highest offices by right and wrong alike. He distributed by Bull, between the Kings of Spain and Portugal, the temporal dominions which in no way belonged to him by right, namely in both Indies, newly discovered; certainly not after the example of Christ, who refused to divide a lawful inheritance, but rather after that of Satan, who showed Christ, when he was about to worship him, all the kingdoms of the world on a high mountain and promised them, though no right to them, nor even a trace of their soil, had belonged to him. With his illegitimate daughter Lucretia, whom he first married to Lodovico Sforza, then to Alfonso of Aragon, son of King Alfonso, and finally, when that Alfonso had been killed, to Alfonso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, both he and his son Cesare Borgia are believed to have had a secret and incestuous relationship. Certainly the famous and distinguished poet Jacopo Sannazaro composed this epitaph for Lucretia: Here lies in the tomb Lucretia, by name, but in fact a Thais, daughter, bride and daughter-in-law of Alexander. And she met an end worthy of his impiety. For according to Panvinio, Guicciardini, Bembo and Giovio, whom Starovolscius and Carrière also follow, she perished by a poisoned cup which he had prepared to give to some cardinals, but which was by mistake offered to himself, so that his treachery recoiled upon the detestable head of its author.

units.la: CXLVII. Ecclesia Romana hoc in primis Seculo in capite & membris, doctrina & moribus corruptissima, non defuit νέφος μαρτύρων nubes testium veritatis, qui & Veritati coelesti locuples testimonium perhiberent, & corruptionem Ecclesiae extremam propalam insectarentur.
units.tr: CXLVII. In this century the Roman Church, in head and members most corrupt in doctrine and morals, did not lack a cloud of witnesses [νέφος μαρτύρων] to the truth, who both bore full testimony to the heavenly Truth and openly attacked the utter corruption of the Church.

units.la: Urbani & Clementis Antipapae temporibus Universitates Parisiensis, Oxoniensis & Pragensis Papam cum suis tyrannidem in Ecclesia exercere, & Papam errare posse saepiusque errasse aperte contendebant. Joh. Andreas Romam a latronibus fundatam, in pristinum statum rediisse asseruit. Dialogus editus Petri & Pauli totam curiam Romanam erroneam, & in statu damnationis esse docuit. Vincentius Ecclesiastes Venetus, Matthæus Parisiensis in Bohemia, Joh. Purvæcis in Anglia, Waldenses & Lollardi passim Papam Antichristum esse affirmarunt. Theodoricus a Nyem Gregorium & Benedictum Pontifices Seniores Babylonis insignivit. Johannis XXIV. cumprimis tempore Nicolaus Clemangis Archidiaconus Bajocensis, Papam Antichristum, Ecclesiam Romanam Babylonem, meretricem magnam esse, a qua non affectu duntaxat, sed pedibus etiam exeundum sit: Petrus de Aliaco, Zabarella Cardinalis, & cum iis utrumque concilium Constantiense & Basileense, Papam Concilio subesse: Johannes Gerson, Concellarius Parisiensis, Papam errare deponi, ab Ecclesia auferri posse: Indulgentias & traditiones Ecclesiae inutiles esse: ruinam Ecclesiae imminere: Theodoricus Urias, Monachus Germanus, Ecclesiam Romanam ex aurea argenteam, ex argentea ferream, ex ferrea terream factam esse, neque aliud superesse, quàm ut in stercus abiret: Theodoricus, Episcopus Croatiæ, Ecclesiam Romanam ruituram, ac tum Ecclesiam florem pristinum recuperaturam: Johannes Huffus, & Hieronymus Pragensis, & cum iis Bohemi ac Wiclefiftæ innumeri ipsáque Husfitis consentiens Regina Bohemiæ Sophia, nec non militiæ Husliticæ dux fortissimus Zisca, Ecclesiam Romanam Antichristianam, Babylonicam meretricem esse, tyrannide, Idololatria, magia scatere, &c. ássa voce clamârunt. Eugenio IV. Pontifice in Concilio Basileensi, Pet. de Aliaco Cardinalis Cameracensis, Joh. Segoviensis Theologus Hispanus. Ludovicus Cardinalis Arelatensis, Cardinalis Julianus Æneas Sylvius, aliíque innumeri, Papæ Potestatem & Ͳαφοχλω strenuè oppugnârunt, & Ecclesiæ Romanæ reformationem gravissimè urserunt; quam in rem etiam Pet. de Aliaco libellus aureolus extat.
units.tr: In the times of Urban and of the anti-Pope Clement, the universities of Paris, Oxford and Prague contended openly that the Pope with his followers exercised tyranny over the Church, and that the Pope could err and had often erred. John Andreas asserted that Rome, founded by robbers, had returned to its former state. A published dialogue of Peter and Paul taught that the whole Roman Curia was erroneous and in a state of damnation. Vincent the Venetian preacher, Matthew of Paris in Bohemia, John Purvey in England, and the Waldenses and Lollards everywhere affirmed that the Pope was Antichrist. Dietrich of Niem marked Gregory and Benedict as the "Elders of Babylon." Especially in the time of John XXIII, Nicolas Clamanges, archdeacon of Bayeux, declared that the Pope was Antichrist and the Roman Church Babylon, the great harlot, from whom one must depart not only in affection but on foot. Peter d'Ailly and Zabarella the cardinal, and with them both the Council of Constance and the Council of Basel, taught that the Pope is subject to the Council. John Gerson, chancellor of Paris, taught that a Pope who errs can be deposed and removed by the Church; that indulgences and the traditions of the Church are useless; and that the ruin of the Church is at hand. Dietrich Urias, a German monk, said that the Roman Church had been made from gold into silver, from silver into iron, and from iron into earth, and that nothing remained but that it should pass into dung. Dietrich, bishop of Croatia, said that the Roman Church would fall and that the Church would then recover its former flourishing. John Huss and Jerome of Prague, and with them countless Bohemians and Wycliffites, and also Queen Sophia of Bohemia, who agreed with the Hussites, and the most valiant leader of the Hussite army, Zizka, cried out in one voice that the Roman Church was Antichristian, the Babylonian harlot, that it abounded in tyranny, idolatry, magic, and so on. Under Pope Eugene IV in the Council of Basel, Peter d'Ailly the cardinal of Cambrai, John of Segovia the Spanish theologian, Louis the cardinal of Arles, the cardinal Julian Aeneas Sylvius, and countless others vigorously attacked the power of the Pope and the (garbled Greek term) and urgently pressed for reform of the Roman Church. There is also a little golden book by Peter d'Ailly on this matter.

units.la: Extra Concilium Alanus Carterius, Carolo VII. Regi Galliæ à Secretis adversus Romanam Ecclesiam librum composuit: ipse Carolus VII. Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Concilium celebravit Biturigibus, ubi sub titulo Pragmaticæ Sanctionis Concilii Basileensis acta confirmavit, adeóque beneficiorum Regni collationes, & ad Romanam Curiam appellationes severè prohibuit: aliíque etiam, inprimis Thomas Rhedonensis Carmelita, Manfredus Vercellensis, Guilhelmus Taylour, Wilhelmus Withe Veritati adversus Romanam Ecclesiam luculentum testimonium perhibuerunt, Pio II. Pontifice Sigismundus Dux Austriæ, auctore Gregorio Heimburgense J. V. D. à Papa ad Concilium, & à Concilio ad Christum ipsum provocans, impiis Pii, dicentis; provocationem ad Concilium novam hæresin, & inspirationem Diabolicam esse, diris devotus est: Heimburgensis ipse, Noribergensis Syndicus celebris, scripto adversus Primatum Papæ libro, Synagogam Romanam Babylonem & meretricem vocavit, Pontificis Potestatem meram tyrannidem & usurpationem esse pertendit: denique Babylone ea exire omnes pios jussit: Bohemi publicâ adversus Papam apologia Veritatem asseruerunt. Universitates pleraeque Germaniæ, Galliæ, Angliæ, Bohemiæ Constantiensis & Basileensis Concilii decretis adversus Papam cusis adhæserunt: denique Antonius Rozellus Juris Professor Patavii, vulgato de Monarchia libro, omnem Papæ potestatem temporalem oppugnavit. Paulo II. Pontifice Rodericus Zanches Zamarensis Episcopus, Papæ Referendarius, Romanæ Ecclesiæ extremam superstitionem deploravit: Stephanus Brulifer Sorbonista Franciscanus libris editis, Papæ & Concilio competere potestatem novos fidei articulos cudendi negavit, & operum etiam merita refutavit. Sixto IV. Pontifice Ludovicus XI. Galliarum Rex pro Pragmatica sanctione tres constitutiones edidit: Johannes de Wesalia Wormatiensis Concionator Papæ tyrannidem notavit palam: Wesselus Groningensis libris editis Papatus abusibus contradixit. Gochius Pupperus Mechliniensis Presbyter articulum de justificatione orthodoxè veréque tradidit. Denique Alexandro VI. Pontifice impurissimo, Mancinellus pro concione Papæ scelera exagitavit: Guicciardinus Ecclesiæ Romanæ Vexillarius Pontificum scelera detexit: Baptista Mantuanus Carmelita, & cum eo Jacobus Jannazarius poëmatis suis in abominationes Romanas invecti sunt. Hieronymus Savanarola, à Pico Mirandulano, Marsilio Ficino, Guicciardino, Flaminio, aliisque publicis scriptis defensus, Ecclesiæ Romanæ traditiones evertit, doctrinam sanam de Justificatione egregiè illustravit, indulgentias rejecit, denique Antichristum Romanum digito veluti commonstravit. Horum omnium testimonia consignatissima Catalogus Testium Veritatis, Wolphii Lectiones Memorabiles, Plessæus, Martyrologia, Bohemicum inprimis, aliíque exhibent. Tantis verò doctoribus & testibus veritatis cum abundaverit circa ea tempora Ecclesia Dei, non potuit non titubare Roma, & Christi Regnum paulatim emergere, tenebrásque Antichristi depellere.
units.tr: Outside the council, Alain Chartier, secretary to Charles VII, King of France, wrote a book against the Roman Church. Charles VII himself held a council of the French Church at Bourges, where under the title of the Pragmatic Sanction he confirmed the acts of the Council of Basel, and strictly forbade both the granting of benefices of the kingdom and appeals to the Roman Curia. Others also, especially Thomas of Rennes the Carmelite, Manfred of Vercelli, William Taylour, and William Withe, bore a clear testimony to the truth against the Roman Church. Under Pope Pius II, Sigismund, Duke of Austria, appealing from the Pope to the Council and from the Council to Christ himself, on the advice of Gregory Heimburg, Doctor of both Laws, was cursed with the impious words of Pius, who said that "appeal to a council is a new heresy and a diabolical inspiration." Heimburg himself, the famous syndic of Nuremberg, in a book written against the primacy of the Pope, called the Roman synagogue Babylon and the harlot, maintained that the power of the Pope was pure tyranny and usurpation, and finally commanded all the pious to depart from that Babylon. The Bohemians asserted the truth against the Pope in a public apology. Most of the universities of Germany, France, England and Bohemia adhered to the decrees of the Councils of Constance and Basel, which were directed against the Pope. Finally, Antonio Rozzelli, professor of law at Padua, in a published book on monarchy, attacked the whole temporal power of the Pope. Under Pope Paul II, Rodrigo Sánchez, bishop of Zamora and referendary of the Pope, lamented the extreme superstition of the Roman Church. Étienne Brulefer, a Franciscan of the Sorbonne, in books he published, denied that the Pope and the Council had power to coin new articles of faith, and also refuted the merit of good works. Under Pope Sixtus IV, Louis XI, King of France, issued three edicts in favour of the Pragmatic Sanction. John of Wesel, preacher of Worms, openly denounced the tyranny of the Pope. Wessel of Groningen, in books he published, opposed the abuses of the papacy. Gochius Pupperus, a presbyter of Mechelen, taught the article of justification soundly and truly. Finally, under Alexander VI, the most impure Pope, Mancinelli in a sermon to the Pope denounced his crimes; Guicciardini, standard-bearer of the Roman Church, exposed the crimes of the Popes; Baptista Mantuanus the Carmelite, and with him Jacopo Sannazaro, attacked the Roman abominations in their poems. Girolamo Savonarola, defended by Pico della Mirandola, Marsilio Ficino, Guicciardini, Flaminio and others in public writings, overturned the traditions of the Roman Church, set out the sound doctrine of justification with great clarity, rejected indulgences, and finally, as it were, pointed out the Roman Antichrist with his finger. The testimonies of all these are set down in the Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth, in Wolf's Memorable Lectures, in Plessis, in the Martyrologies, especially the Bohemian one, and in others. Since the Church of God abounded with such great teachers and witnesses of the truth around that time, Rome could not but totter, and the Kingdom of Christ gradually emerged and drove back the darkness of Antichrist.

units.la: CXLVIII. Densissimam illam testium Veritatis nubem Romanenfis Factio equidem discutere magno nisu, ferro flammaque adversus eos sæviendo, sustinuit. Quid enim fortissimis heroïbus & Callinicis Christi Johanni Huffo & Hieronymo Pragensi, contra fas obstrictæ multis modis fidei, abituros scilicet fide qua venissent, adeóque dato commeatu ejusmodi, qualem ægrotus Leo promittebat bestiis ad fe visendum accedentibus; Constantiæ contigerit, lippis certè & tonsoribus notum est. Neque contenti ea strage Pontificii, consilia de tota Bohemia abolenda mox agitárunt. Cùm enim Proceres ejus præcipui scriptis Constantiam literis graves ob iniquissima de Huffo & Hieronymo sumpta supplicia querelas movisfent; Martinus V. A. M CCCCXXX. excommunicatione adversus eos Florentiæ publicata classicum insuper canens, Cæsarem, Reges, Principes, Marchiones, Comites &c. ad arma contra eos invitat, & per vulnera Christi, ejúsque salutem orat, ut junctis viribus eos penitus extirpent; sceleftiffimo cuique, dum unum Bohemum occiderit, plenaria peccatorum omnium remissione promissa. Quo incentivo inflammatus Sigifmundus, totius Germaniæ, vicinorúmque Regnorum viribus succinctus, Antichriftiani furoris satellitem se gerit, valido cum exercitu Bohemiam ingressus, eámque bellis decimum tertium in annum continuatis fatigans. Quæ bella Huffitica plus admirationis, quàm fidei apud posteros habitura Æneas Sylvius dixit; eò quòd semper Huffitarum, quàm Pontificiorum arma prosperiora fuerunt. Non paucos tamen intrepidum pro Veritate martyrium passos Martyrologium Bohemicum Capp. 10. 11. &c. inducit. Taceo Oldocastelum, plurésque alios in Anglia, Thomam Rhedunensem Carmelitam, Manfredum Vercellensem, Guilhelmum Taylour, Witthe, Hieronymum Savanarolam Florentinum, aliósque strenuos pro Veritate cœlesti athletas, Pontificum furore horribiliter cruciatos extinctósque. Adeò Romanenses.
units.tr: CXLVIII. The Roman faction, indeed, strove with great effort to scatter that dense cloud of witnesses to the truth, raging against them with sword and fire. What happened at Constance to the most valiant heroes and victors of Christ, John Huss and Jerome of Prague, who were bound by faith in many ways, namely that they were to depart with the faith with which they had come, and yet were given a safe-conduct of the sort the sick lion promised to beasts that came to visit him, is known even to the bleary-eyed and the barbers. Not content with that slaughter, the Papists soon began to plan the abolition of the whole of Bohemia. For when the leading nobles of that kingdom had sent serious complaints by letter to Constance about the most unjust punishments inflicted on Huss and Jerome, Martin V in the year 1430, having published an excommunication against them at Florence and moreover sounding the trumpet, invited the Emperor, kings, princes, marquises, counts and others to take up arms against them, and begged them by the wounds of Christ and by his salvation to join forces and utterly exterminate them, promising full remission of all sins to any most wicked man who should kill a single Bohemian. Sigismund, inflamed by this incitement, girded with the strength of all Germany and the neighbouring kingdoms, became a henchman of this Antichristian fury; entering Bohemia with a strong army, he wore that land down with wars continued for thirteen years. Aeneas Sylvius said that these Hussite wars would attract more admiration than faith from posterity, because the arms of the Hussites were always more successful than those of the Papists. Yet the Bohemian Martyrology, in chapters 10, 11 and so on, names not a few who fearlessly suffered martyrdom for the truth. I say nothing of Oldcastle and several others in England, of Thomas of Rennes the Carmelite, Manfred of Vercelli, William Taylour, Withe, Girolamo Savonarola of Florence, and other vigorous athletes of the heavenly truth, who were horribly tormented and put to death by the fury of the Popes. So far the Romanists.

units.la: Jam pridem verum non didicere pati.
units.tr: Long ago they did not learn to bear the truth.

units.la: CXLIX. Seculi Decimi Sexti, quod renascentis in eo Euangelii & concussi non leviter Regni Pontificii gloria inclytum fuit; initio Ecclesiæ Romanæ habenas moderatus est Julius II. quem ante Papatum omnes, Guiciardino teste, morosissimum, intolerabilem, truculentum & quietis impatientem, quique in eximios quosque viros immanes jam inimicitias exercuisset, noverant. Tyrannidis, quam statim Papa factus exercuit, specimina Onuphrius, Guiciardinus idem, alii narrant. Statum certè utrumque Politicum & Ecclesiasticum miserè perturbavit: neque quisquam antehac Pontificum ita turpiter ulli Imperatori illusit, sicut hic Maximilianum nefariis suis artibus circumscripsit. Cùm enim ad bellum Venetum gravissimum eum impulisset, ac is Venetos, Pontificiæ Sedi rebelles, captis eorum uribus præstantissimis, & effuso immenso cruore, ingentes ad angustias redegisset: Julius abstersó omni pudore, contra fidem datam, coram Imperii Ordinibus Augustæ congregatis non tantùm Venetos pacem petentes in gratiam recepit, sed & percusso cum ipsis fœdere, exercitum suum adversus Imperatoris confœderatos, Ferrariensem & Ludovicum XII. Regem Francorum, iniquissimus & perfidissimus bellator eduxit, cum ea voce, quæ ipsum non S. Petri, sed perditissimi & sceleratissimi latro- Julii II. tyrannis & saevitia. Bella adversus Venetos, Maximilianum & fœderatos Gallos improbè gesta. latronis successorem esse commonstravit. Cum exercitu enim Roma egressus, Petri clavem furibundus in Tiberim jactavit, adeoque, ubi ingeniose Bibliander conclusit, omne, quod à S. Petro se habere finxit jus, Tiberino flumini resignavit; additis hisce verbis: Quia clavis S. Petri amplius nil juvat, (evaginato gladio) valeat gladius S. Pauli. Sed Deus justus scelerum vindex nequitiam multam non sivit. Commisso enim apud Ravennam ipso die Paschatis cruento proelio, ingentem stragem à Gallis passus, victoriam quamvis cruentam iisdem concessit. Ita ἀλλοπρόσαλλ@ denuo opera Matthaei Langi, Episcopi Salisburgensis, Imperatoris Maximiliani amicitiam ambiens impetránsque, & Helvetios Matthaei Schyneri, Episcopi Valesiani, & post ἀνλμιαδίας ἔνεκα Cardinalis creati, hominis versutissimi, icto cum iis foedere, sibi adjungens. Venetisque auxiliantibus, mox Mediolanum obsidet, &, pulsis inde Gallis occupat. Helvetiis ob rem praeclare scilicet gestam, bullatas indulgentias, titulos amplos, pileum, gladium, aliáque privilegia contulit, quin & signis militaribus eosdem exornavit; atque sic exemplo patrui sui Sixti IV. egregie illis illusit. Bellum hoc, auspice Julio, contra Regem Francorum inceptum, per multa post proelia cruentissima & calamitates gravissimas extractum, vix tandem compositum & finitum est. Retulitque Orbis Christianus Patri suo Beatissimo acceptum, quod sub ejus, ceu verissimi τῆς ἀπωλείας filii perditionis auspiciis, gladio, inedia, aliisque belli incommodis plus quam ducentena hominum millia interierunt. Visum tandem Patribus nonnullis sincerioribus Papam ad rationem reddendam villicationis suae adigere, instituto Pisis, Imperatore & Rege Francorum consentientibus Concilio. Sed effecit Julius artibus suis, ut non sine tumultu & vulneribus, & re infecta, Concilium dissolveretur. Concilii illius Pisani posterioris acta una cum actis Pisani prioris, apologia Philippi Decii Jurisconsulti Itali munita, ex Bibliotheca Regia Lutetiæ ante annos plus sexaginta publicam in lucem prodierunt. Alterius etiam Concilii ejusdem apologiæ Bailius in summa Conciliorum meminit; cujus cap. 6. Cardinales protestantur, se nunquam dignitatem Pontificiam affectâsse, sed Aristocraticam moderationem voluisse restituere, qua Christus primatum Sedis Apostolicæ temperaverit. Cumque Concilium illud alio translatum esset, Julius ad solitas Pontificibus artes conversus, Regem Francorum unà cum Patribus illis diris devovit, & dignitatibus exuere conatus est. Et ne causæ suæ diffidere videretur, ipsemet Romæ Concilium indixit, in Lateranno, eo videlicet loco, in quo nihil metuendum ipsi erat, & in quo vota omnia in potestate sua habuit. Julio (ita ipsemet Onuphrius scribit) mens non fuit quicquam boni in illo Concilio agere, sed tantum Concilio, & Cardinalibus sibi adversantibus adversari. Neque vero Lateranense isthoc Concilium Generalis Concilii nomen mereri, etiam Stanislaus Felix adversus Pallavicinum solidè comprobat. Et Cætum quendam non in Spiritu Dei congregatum illud fuisse, Gallia, teste Launojo, affirmavit. Fertur porro sæpe Imperator Maximilianus ingeminâsse verba hæc: Deus æterne, nisi vigilares, quàm male esset mundo? Quem regimus nos, ego miser venator, & ebriosus ille ac sceleratus Julius! Quin & ipse novissimus Concilii Tridentini scriptor & Cardinalis Pallavicinus non diffitetur, fuisse Julium feroci animo atque iracundo: indulsisse illum militiæ studiis, supra quàm opus fuit, & supra quàm tanti capitis sanctitatem deceret. Stolidè tamen sic illum excusat. Ne, si tam ferox non fuisset, nunquam Ecclesiæ recuperâsset majorem potiorémque suæ ditionis partem. Ferocem ergo temporalium & mundi gratia esse Christi huncce Vicarium oportet!
units.tr: In the sixteenth century, which was famous for the revival of the Gospel and for the no slight shaking of the papal kingdom, Julius II took the reins of the Roman Church at its beginning. Before he became Pope, as Guicciardini attests, everyone knew him as "very difficult, intolerable, savage, and impatient of quiet," who had already carried on fierce enmities against all the most distinguished men. Onuphrius, Guicciardini again, and others describe examples of the tyranny he practised as soon as he became Pope. At any rate, he miserably disturbed the state, both political and ecclesiastical. No Pontiff before him had so shamefully deceived any Emperor as he did Maximilian, whom he got around by his wicked tricks. When he had driven Maximilian into the very grievous war with Venice, and when the Venetians, who were rebels against the Papal See, had been stripped of their most outstanding strongholds, and much blood had been poured out, and he had reduced them to great straits, Julius, shedding all shame and breaking his given word, not only received the Venetians, who were seeking peace, back into favour in the presence of the Orders of the Empire gathered at Augsburg, but also, having struck a treaty with them, led his army against the Emperor's allies, the Duke of Ferrara and Louis XII, King of the Franks, as the most unjust and treacherous warrior. With that cry he showed that he was not the successor of St Peter but of the most abandoned and wicked robber. Setting out from Rome with his army, he furiously threw Peter's key into the Tiber, and so, as Bibliander cleverly concluded, he gave back to the Tiber river all the right which he pretended to have from St Peter, adding these words: "Since the key of St Peter helps no longer" (with his sword drawn) "let the sword of St Paul prevail." But God, the just avenger of crimes, did not allow such great wickedness to go unpunished. For when a bloody battle was fought at Ravenna on Easter Day, he suffered a huge slaughter at the hands of the French and yielded victory to them, though a bloody one. So, once again, the changeable man [ἀλλοπρόσαλλος], through the efforts of Matthew Lang, Bishop of Salzburg, courting and obtaining the friendship of Emperor Maximilian, and through Matthew Schiner, Bishop of Sion, a most crafty man, later made Cardinal for his sly dealings [ἀνλμιαδίας ἔνεκα], he joined the Swiss to himself by a treaty. With the Venetians helping him, he soon besieged Milan and, having driven the French out of it, seized it. To the Swiss, for the deed they had so splendidly done, he granted sealed indulgences, grand titles, the cap, the sword and other privileges, and indeed decorated them with military standards; and so, after the example of his uncle Sixtus IV, he mocked them splendidly. This war, begun under Julius's auspices against the King of the Franks, dragged on through many very bloody battles and most grievous calamities, and was at last with difficulty settled and ended. The Christian world reported to its Most Blessed Father that under his auspices, as of the true son of perdition [τῆς ἀπωλείας], more than two hundred thousand men perished by sword, starvation and other miseries of war. At length some more sincere Fathers thought fit to compel the Pope to give an account of his stewardship, and with the Emperor and the King of the Franks agreeing, a Council was called at Pisa. But Julius by his tricks brought it about that the Council was dissolved, not without tumult and wounds, and with nothing accomplished. The acts of that later Council of Pisa, together with the acts of the earlier Council of Pisa, supported by the apology of Philip Decius, an Italian jurist, came into public light from the Royal Library at Paris more than sixty years ago. Bailly also mentions an apology of the same Council in his Summa of Councils, where in chapter 6 the Cardinals protest that "they never aspired to the papal dignity, but wished to restore the aristocratic moderation by which Christ tempered the primacy of the Apostolic See." When that Council had been transferred elsewhere, Julius, turning to the usual arts of the Popes, cursed the King of the Franks together with those Fathers and tried to strip them of their dignities. And lest he seem to distrust his own cause, he himself called a Council at Rome, in the Lateran, that is, in the very place where he had nothing to fear and where he held all the votes in his power. "Julius (so Onuphrius himself writes) had no intention of doing anything good at that Council, but only of opposing the Council and the Cardinals who were against him." Nor does Stanislaus Felix, against Pallavicini, fail to prove solidly that this Lateran Council does not deserve the name of a General Council. And France, as Launoy attests, affirmed that it was "a gathering not assembled in the Spirit of God." Moreover, it is often reported that Emperor Maximilian repeated these words: "Eternal God, if you were not watching, how bad would the world be! Whom do we rule? I, a wretched hunter, and that drunken and wicked Julius!" Indeed, even the most recent writer on the Council of Trent, the Cardinal Pallavicini, does not deny "that Julius had a fierce and angry spirit, that he indulged in military pursuits beyond what was needful and beyond what the holiness of so great a head ought to allow." Yet he foolishly excuses him thus: "Had he not been so fierce, he would never have recovered for the Church the greater and better part of its dominion." So this Vicar of Christ must be fierce for the sake of temporal and worldly things!

units.la: C L. Non defuerunt etiam Julii hujus ætate Veritatis propromachi plures, qui Romanæ Ecclęsiæ ulcera tangerent. Et in Gallia quidem non tantùm Waldenses, Romanæ Curiæ adversarii, qui à trecentis jam annis in montibus Narbonensis Galliæ, Provinciæ & Allobrogum sub Alpinis Vallibus aliisque locis in eadem fide, puritate & simplicitate pergebant: Regi Ludovico suam à Romana Ecclesia discessionem & innocentiam comprobavere, eíque fidem & vitam eorum edocto memorabilem hancce vocem: Illi me cæterisque subditis meis meliores sunt; extorsere. Sed Faber quoque Stapulensis Theologiam ad limpidos fontes revocavit, nequicquam à Sorbona eo nomine vexatus. Guilhelmus etiam Budæus, Vir doctissimus, pragmaticam Sanctionem strenuè laudavit, & Ecclesiam factam esse meretricem, provinciatim merentem asseruit; quin & tota Ecclesia Gallicana plenitudinem potestatis Pontificiæ plenitudinem tempestatis appellare non dubitavit. Ne dicam Ludovicum XII. Regem monetæ jussu suo cusæ hæc verba inscribi curasse: Perdam Babylonis nomen, cui proin magno Authori Roma Babylon fuit. Sed & Johannes Picus Mirandulanus aperte contra Transsubstantiationem & cultum imaginum disputavit. Erfordiæ verò Sebastianus Brand Pontificias merces vehementer explosit, & Reformationem Ecclesiæ instare prædixit. Denique Ecclesiæ Bohemicæ, Moravicæ & Silesiæ, Confessionem in præcipuis nostræ conformem, & Apologiam Uladislao Hungariæ Regi obtulerunt.
units.tr: 150. In the age of this Julius there were not lacking several champions of the truth who touched the sores of the Roman Church. In France, indeed, the Waldenses, adversaries of the Roman Curia, who for more than three hundred years had persisted in the same faith, purity and simplicity in the mountains of Narbonne in Gaul, in Provence and in the Alpine valleys of the Allobroges and other places, not only proved to King Louis their separation from the Roman Church and their innocence, but also extorted from him, when he had been taught their faith and life, this memorable saying: "They are better than I and my other subjects." Faber Stapulensis also restored theology to its clear springs, though he was harassed for this by the Sorbonne in vain. William Budé, a most learned man, warmly praised the Pragmatic Sanction and asserted that the Church had become a harlot, selling herself province by province; indeed the whole Gallican Church did not hesitate to call the "fullness of power" of the Pope the "fullness of tempest." Not to mention that Louis XII, King of France, had these words inscribed on coins struck by his order: "I will destroy the name of Babylon," since for this great author Rome was therefore Babylon. But also John Pico of Mirandola openly disputed against Transubstantiation and the worship of images. At Erfurt, Sebastian Brant vehemently exploded the Papist wares and foretold that a Reformation of the Church was at hand. Finally, the Churches of Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia offered to King Ladislaus of Hungary a Confession agreeing with ours in the chief points, and an Apology.

units.la: Waldenses, Faber Stapulensis, Budæus, Picus Mirandulanus, Ludovicus XII. Ecclesiæ Bohemicæ, Moravicæ, &c.
units.tr: Waldenses, Faber Stapulensis, Budé, Pico Mirandola, Louis XII, the Churches of Bohemia, Moravia, etc.

units.la: ECCLESIÆ ROMANÆ PERIODUS SEXTA.
units.tr: THE SIXTH PERIOD OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.

units.la: Seu
units.tr: Or

units.la: Historia Ecclesiæ Romanæ per Reforma- tionem, seu separationem fidelium, suæ in Spi- ritualibus & temporalibus potestatis cladem gravissimam patientis.
units.tr: History of the Roman Church through the Reformation, that is, the separation of the faithful, which suffered the gravest collapse of its power in spiritual and temporal affairs.

units.la: Inde à Leone X. seu A. C. M. D. XVII. ad Concilii Tridentini finem, seu A. C. M. D. LXIII.
units.tr: From Leo X, or 1517 A.D., to the end of the Council of Trent, or 1563 A.D.

units.la: BREVIARIUM.
units.tr: SUMMARY.

units.la: CLI. Leonis X. Papatus. De eo vaticinium Abbatis Johannis Lateranense Concilium sub eo continuatum Pisanum extinguit. Honores Divini in eodem Concilio ipsi tributi. Principum dissidia fovet, & primò Cæsarearum, mox conversa fortuna, Gallicanarum partium fit. Caroli V. electioni obsistit; & denuo mutata fortuna Cæsareis partibus se adjungit. Opera Sedunensis Cardinalis Helvetios nefariè dividit.
units.tr: CLI. The papacy of Leo X. A prophecy about him by Abbot John of the Lateran. The Council of Pisa, which was continued under him, he brings to an end. Divine honours paid to him at the same council. He fosters the quarrels of princes: first he favours the Imperial party, then, as fortune turns, he becomes a partisan of the French. He opposes the election of Charles V; and when fortune changes again, he joins the Imperial side. By the work of the Cardinal of Sion he wickedly divides the Swiss.

units.la: CLII. Mercator & Cananæus ingens fuit. Ejus avaritia ex Paulo Langio describitur. Falsis pratextibus indulgentiarum commercium exercet.
units.tr: CLII. He was a great merchant and Canaanite. His greed is described from Paul Lang. He carries on the trade in indulgences under false pretexts.

units.la: CLIII. Omen ruituri mox Papatus, Zwinglii & Lutheri heroicis ausibus impletur.
units.tr: CLIII. The omen of the Papacy, which was soon to fall, is fulfilled by the heroic daring of Zwingli and Luther.

units.la: CLIV. Leonis Atheismus & impietas probata ex disputatione de immortalitate animæ ab eo decisa ; Pico Mirandulano.
units.tr: CLIV. Leo's atheism and impiety are proved from the disputation on the immortality of the soul which he settled, against Pico Mirandola.

units.la: CLV. Cardinale Pallavicino ;
units.tr: CLV. Cardinal Pallavicini.

units.la: CLVI. Ecclesiæ Romanæ Reformationis indigæ corruptio ; asserta ex Paulo Langio.
units.tr: CLVI. The corruption of the Roman Church, in need of reformation; asserted from Paul Lang.

units.la: CLVII. Authore libri, cui nomen Onus Ecclesiæ ; nec non Authore libelli de decimis non præstandis, & Appellatione Vniversitatis Parisiensis.
units.tr: CLVII. The author of the book entitled The Burden of the Church; and also the author of the pamphlet on not paying tithes, and the Appeal of the University of Paris.

units.la: CLVIII. Adriano imprimis VI. Pontifice, ejusque instructione per Cheregatum Ordinibus Germaniæ exhibita.
units.tr: CLVIII. Especially Pope Adrian VI, and his instruction, delivered to the Orders of Germany through Chieregati.

units.la: CLIX. Adrianus idem à Pallavicini & Masenii cavillationibus à Launojo vindicatus.
units.tr: CLIX. The same Adrian, defended by Launoy against the cavils of Pallavicini and Maimbourg.

units.la: CLIX. Responsum Ordinum ad Cheregati propositionem : eorúmque gravamina centum : Novem Cantonum Helvetiæ tentata reformatio.
units.tr: CLIX. The reply of the Orders to Chieregati's proposal, and their hundred grievances. The reformation attempted by the nine Cantons of Switzerland.

units.la: CLX. Reformatio Adriani & Romanensium tentata qualis fuerit ?
units.tr: CLX. What was the nature of the reformation attempted by Adrian and the Romans?

units.la: CLXI. Qualis etiam Ordinum Imperii & Cantonum Helvetiæ?
units.tr: CLXI. And what was that of the Orders of the Empire and of the Swiss Cantons?

units.la: CLXII. Zwinglii & Lutheri Reformatio primitus tentata manca fuit, at contranitentium studio evasit perfectior : & Pontificis dominationem passim coercuit.
units.tr: CLXII. The reformation first attempted by Zwingli and Luther was incomplete, but through the zeal of their opponents it became more thorough, and it everywhere curbed the dominion of the Pope.

units.la: CLXIII. Clementis VII. Papatus. Schisma ipsum inter & Vrbanum VI. Ejus ingenium ex Jovio depictum. Centum gravamina Ordinum expendit, & Campegium ad Comitia Norimbergensia mittit. Eo rejecto Ordines ad Concilium liberum provocant : Pontificii tamen in Comitiis peculiaribus, & post etiam Carolus ipse executionem decreti Wormatiensis urgent. Clementis perfima erga Cæsarem fides.
units.tr: CLXIII. The papacy of Clement VII. The schism between him and Urban VI itself. His character, drawn from Jovius. He weighs the hundred grievances of the Estates and sends Campeggio to the Diet of Nuremberg. When that was rejected, the Estates appeal to a free Council. The Papists, however, press for execution of the Edict of Worms at special Diets, and afterwards Charles himself does so too. Clement's most treacherous loyalty to the Emperor.

units.la: CLXIV. Vnde bello in Italia flagrante Roma capta, direpta, & ipse Clemens in Castro Angeli captivus retentus : Carolo improbante factum sui militis. Liberatus Papa, fœdere cum Cæsare inito, eum Bononiæ coronat. Principes Pontificii fœdere inito adversus Euangelicos conjurant. De Concilio contentio Cæsarem inter inter & Papam. Vi decernere Cæsar instituit: at mox Augusta cum Protestantibus de pace ad tempus usque Concilii transfigit. Papæ defectio à Cæsare ad Gallum (cujus filio Henrico II. neptim Catharinam Medicæam, quartam Francorum Furiam post dictam, despondet:) & mors subsecuta. De eo Suavis, Pallavicini, & Jovii testimonia.
units.tr: CLXIV. Hence, with war blazing in Italy, Rome is taken and plundered, and Clement himself is held captive in the Castel Sant'Angelo, Charles disapproving of what his soldiers did. The Pope, freed, makes a treaty with the Emperor and crowns him at Bologna. The Papist princes conspire against the Evangelicals by a treaty. Contention between the Emperor and the Pope over the Council. The Emperor sets out to decide the matter by force, but soon at Augsburg he concludes a peace with the Protestants for the time until the Council. The Pope's defection from the Emperor to the French king (to whose son Henry II he betroths his niece Catherine de' Medici, the fourth Fury of the French, as she is called), and the death that followed. The testimonies of Soave, Pallavicini and Jovius on this.

units.la: CLXV. Pauli III. Papatus. De eo testimonia libri Italici, Onuphrii. Simonia ejus à Pallavicino nequiter defensa.
units.tr: CLXV. The papacy of Paul III. Testimonies on him from the Italian book and from Onuphrius. His simony wickedly defended by Pallavicini.

units.la: CLXVI. Qualemse erga Cæsarem Paulus hic gesserit?
units.tr: CLXVI. What was Paul's conduct toward the Emperor?

units.la: CLXVII. Concilii celebrandi studium testatur. Consilium ejus jussu à Cardinalibus & Episcopis conscriptum de reformanda Curia Romana.
units.tr: CLXVII. He attests his zeal for holding a Council. A plan for reforming the Roman Curia, drawn up by the Cardinals and Bishops at his command.

units.la: CLXVIII. Ejus præcipua capita. In nervum tamen, dissidentibus in ejus examine Cardinalibus, non erumpit.
units.tr: CLXVIII. Its principal heads. Yet it does not break into the sinews, the Cardinals disagreeing when it was examined.

units.la: CLIX. Iesuitæ exorti & à Paulo confirmati labantem causam Ecclesiæ Romanæ sustinent. De novello Ordine eo judicium Sorbonæ.
units.tr: CLXIX. The Jesuits, who arose and were confirmed by Paul, sustain the tottering cause of the Roman Church. The judgement of the Sorbonne on that new Order.

units.la: CLXX. Successu temporis ordo ille degenerat, teste in peculiari scripto Iulio Clemente Scoto.
units.tr: CLXX. In course of time that order degenerates, as Julius Clement the Scot attests in a separate writing.

units.la: CLXXI. Capucinorum ordo ab eodem Paulo confirmatus. Iesuitæ & Capucini iunctis viribus Romanam Ecclesiam ruentem sustinent.
units.tr: CLXXI. The Capuchin order, likewise confirmed by Paul. The Jesuits and Capuchins, with united forces, sustain the Roman Church as it falls.

units.la: CLXXII. Concilium Tridentum indicitur.
units.tr: CLXXII. The Council of Trent is convened.

units.la: CLXXIII. Reformatio in eo Concilio suscepta qualis fuerit?
units.tr: CLXXIII. What was the reform undertaken at that Council like?

units.la: CLXXIV. A Reformatione seria abhorruisse Pontifices, ex Pallavicino probatur.
units.tr: CLXXIV. That the Popes shrank from serious reform is proved from Pallavicini.

units.la: CLXXV. Cornelii Mussi Bitontini, & Caranzæ orationes in Concilio habitæ, ex quibus Ecclesiæ R. corruptio asseritur.
units.tr: CLXXV. The orations delivered at the Council by Cornelio Musso of Bitonto and by Caranza, from which the corruption of the Roman Church is asserted.

units.la: CLXXVI. Iulii III. Papatus. Ejus spurci mores, & prima purpura Innocentio, non sine gravi suspicione donata; aliáque impietatis ejus argumenta.
units.tr: CLXXVI. The papacy of Julius III. His filthy morals, and the first purple given to Innocent, not without grave suspicion; and other proofs of his impiety.

units.la: CLXXVII. Sardanapalus talis Concilium Tridenti restaurat, protestante contra illud Gallo. Prorogatio ejus ad biennium usque decreta, decennium integrum durat. CLXXVIII. Conversis in Germania rerum vicibus, Passavii & mox Augustæ libertas religionis sancitur, frustra ringente Pontifice, aliisque vi extortam caussantibus. CLXXIX. Anglia ad Papatum relapsa ingens gaudium Papæ, sed non diuturnum affert. CLXXX. Marcelli II. Papatus. Salutem Pontificum is pro conclamata habet. CLXXXI. Ei Paulus IV. succedit. Deeo Oraculum male prætsagiens impletur. Draconicus ejus adversus Cæsares Carolum & Ferdinandum animus. CLXXXII. Studium reformandæ Curiæ Romanæ simulans, palam Concilium detestatur. CLXXXIII. Iuxta oraculum Draconem & Leonem se gerit, edita Bulla de puniendis Hæreticis, etiam Regia & Imperiali dignitate fulgentibus: instituto tribunali Inquisitionis: & conscripto Indice librorum prohibitorum; adeóque more Turcico Papatum promovens. CLXXXIV. Pii IV. Papatus. CLXXXV. Concilium Tridentinum postliminio revocans, ad finem perducit. CLXXXVI. Ferdinandi Imperatoris de Concilio querelæ; & Gallorum adversus illud protestatio. CLXXXVII. Anathematismi Concilii quales? CLXXXVIII. Recipitur Concilium & promulgatur à Pontificiis non omnibus. CLXXXIX. A protestantibus verò omnibus, ceu Conciliabulum profanorum hominum, damnatur.
units.tr: CLXXVII. A Sardanapalus of this kind restores the Council of Trent, with the Frenchman protesting against it. Its prorogation is decreed for two years, but it lasts a full ten years. CLXXVIII. With the course of affairs turned in Germany, freedom of religion is sanctioned at Passau and soon afterwards at Augsburg, the Pope struggling in vain, while others allege it was extorted by force. CLXXIX. England, relapsed into the Papacy, brings the Pope great joy, but not a lasting one. CLXXX. The papacy of Marcellus II. He regards the salvation of the Popes as given up for lost. CLXXXI. Paul IV succeeds him. Concerning him an ill-omened oracle is fulfilled. His draconian spirit against the Emperors Charles and Ferdinand. CLXXXII. Pretending a zeal for reforming the Roman Curia, he openly detests the Council. CLXXXIII. Following the oracle, he behaves like a dragon and a lion: he issues the Bull on punishing heretics, even those shining with royal and imperial dignity; he establishes the tribunal of the Inquisition and compiles the Index of prohibited books, and so, in the Turkish manner, promotes the Papacy. CLXXXIV. The papacy of Pius IV. CLXXXV. Recalling the Council of Trent from its suspension, he brings it to an end. CLXXXVI. The complaints of Emperor Ferdinand about the Council, and the protest of the French against it. CLXXXVII. What were the anathemas of the Council? CLXXXVIII. The Council is received and promulgated by not all the Papists. CLXXXIX. By all Protestants, however, it is condemned as a conciliabulum of profane men.

units.la: CLI. Ulio Johannes Medices, patria Florentinus, dictus Leo X. opera ju- niorum Cardinalium, uti Augusti- nus Oldoinus Notis ad Pontificium Necrologium, memorat, successit.
units.tr: CLI. Giovanni de' Medici, a Florentine by birth, called Leo X, succeeded to the papacy, as Augustinus Oldoinus records in his notes to the Pontifical Necrology, through the efforts of the junior cardinals.

units.la: Qui eruditorum amans, de cœtero voluptarius carnem nutrivit, & genialiter vixit. Vaticinium de eo venturo Abbas quidam Johannes ejusmodi prodidit: Veniet Leo sub pelle Agni, & devorabit oves. Continuatum sub eo Concilium Lateranense à Julio institutum, facile Pisanum extinxit. In Concilio eo Anthonius Puccius Sessione nona Orationem habens, verba illa Psal. LXXII. II. Omnes Reges terra adorabunt eum, & servient ei, Pontifici tribuere non dubitavit, subjiciens: Omnes Reges terra sciunt, quænam potestas Tibi data sit in Cœlo & in terra. Alludens aperte ad ea, quæ de se Christus dixerat. Eadem vena Archiepiscopus Stephanus Sessione X. Omnis, inquit ad Papam, potestas tibi data est. Qui omne dicit, nihil excipit. Sessione VI. Papa Leo venit nomine Leonis de tribu Iuda, radicis Davidis, Salvatoris & Liberatoris Israelis. Eodem pertinent de Pontifice phrases Concilio huic familiares, cujusmodi sunt Sess.I. Respectus vestræ Divinæ Majestatis. Sess.III. Princeps totius Mundi. Sess.IV. Princeps est & Rex. Sess.IX. Papa Princeps est Apostolorum &c. Passim etiam Sponsi Ecclesiæ nomine venit. Per initia quidem Papatus sui simulavit Leo, se laboraturum, ut dissidentes Principes componeret, & bella atrocissima sopiret. Sed Julii insistens vestigiis, sublæstæ fidei homo, illa nefarie potius fovit. Cæsaris enim primum, Venetorum & Sforciadum partibus favens, opera Sedunensis Cardinalis, furiæ infernalis, Helvetios contra Gallos Mediolano imminentes in Italiam induxit. Ita, præsidente Leone die v I. Junii A. M.D.XIII. pugnatum est ab Helvetiis ad Novariam, cœsáque sunt Gallorum multa millia. Biennio post iterum memorabili pugna ad Marignanum in agro Mediolanensi, cum Gallis Helvetii conflixere, ubi Gallorum supra duodecim, Helvetiorum supra sex millia letho data sunt. Captus est autem Dux Sforcia, & Mediolanum ipsum in potestatem Francisci I. pervenit. Leo versipellis & fortunam partium speculatus, ubi fortunam Gallis favere animadvertit, foedere Cæsareo violato, cum Francisco Gallorum Rege amicitiam connectit, eíque Imperii Constantinopolitani coronam, quam nunquam habuit, confert. Comperta ea re Maximilianus dixisse fertur, jam vere se affirmare posse, quod Paparum nullus sibi fidem servaverit. Maximiliano defuncto magis etiam ad Galli partes adversus fortunas Caroli V. deflexit. Scriptis enim ad Electores literis pertendit, Carolo ad honorem Imperii aspirare non licere, eò quòd Reges Neapolitani Pontificis Romani clientes sint, & fide data jam olim cum Pontificibus pepigerint, se Romanum Imperium nunquam appetituros. Cúmque Cæsar crearetur nihilominus Carolus, multa adversus illum machinari, utriusque Siciliæ Regno eum exuere, & Italico Regno subverso, protectionem Civitatum Italiæ inter Sedem Pontificiam, Gallúmque dividere conatus est. Cùm verò machinatio parùm succederet, iterum Protheus insignis, astutam vapido servans sub pectore vulpem, probéque doctus oblitquare sinus in ventum; à Gallo ad Cæsarem deficit, fœdúsque cum eo pangit has feré in leges, ut Parma & Placentia, Sedi Romanæ restituerentur, Franciscus Sforcia in Ducatum Mediolanensem reduceretur, Galli ex Italia pelleren-tur, Sedésque adeò Romana, omni Gallorum metu liberata, in tuto collocaretur. Hic conversus denuo ad Helvetios, opera Cardinalis Sedunensis, veri Sinonis, tandem per insignem fraudem à Tigurinis suppetias sex millium impe-
units.tr: Though a lover of learned men, he was otherwise given to pleasure, indulged the flesh, and lived a worldly life. A certain Abbot John foretold of him that he would come: "Leo will come under the skin of a lamb, and will devour the sheep." The Council of the Lateran, which Julius had instituted and which was continued under Leo, easily extinguished the Council of Pisa. In that council Anthony Puccio, speaking in the ninth session, did not hesitate to apply to the Pope the words of Psalm 72:11, "All kings of the earth shall worship him, and serve him," adding, "All kings of the earth know what power has been given to you in heaven and on earth," openly alluding to what Christ had said of himself. In the same vein Archbishop Stephen, in the tenth session, said to the Pope: "All power has been given to you. He who says all excepts nothing." In the sixth session Pope Leo came in the name of "Leo of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, Saviour and Deliverer of Israel." To the same purpose belong the phrases about the Pope that were familiar to this council: in the first session, "the respect of your divine Majesty"; in the third, "prince of the whole world"; in the fourth, "he is prince and king"; in the ninth, "the Pope is prince of the apostles," and so on. Everywhere too he is called "Bridegroom of the Church." At the beginning of his pontificate Leo pretended that he would labour to reconcile quarrelling princes and to quell the most savage wars. But, following in the footsteps of Julius, a man of feeble faith, he rather nefariously fostered them. For first, favouring the side of the Emperor, the Venetians and the Sforzas, through the work of the Cardinal of Sion, a fury from hell, he brought the Swiss into Italy against the French who threatened Milan. Thus, with Leo presiding, on 6 June 1513 the Swiss fought at Novara, and many thousands of the French were slain. Two years later the Swiss clashed again in a memorable battle at Marignano in the territory of Milan, where more than twelve thousand French and more than six thousand Swiss were given over to death. Duke Sforza was taken, and Milan itself came into the power of Francis I. Leo, a turncoat who watched the fortunes of the parties, when he saw that fortune favoured the French, violated the treaty with the Emperor, joined friendship with Francis, King of the French, and conferred on him the crown of the Empire of Constantinople, which he himself never possessed. When this became known, Maximilian is reported to have said that he could now truly affirm that no Pope had kept faith with him. After Maximilian's death Leo leaned even more towards the French side against the fortunes of Charles V. For by letters written to the Electors he contended that Charles might not lawfully aspire to the honour of the Empire, because the Kings of Naples are clients of the Roman Pontiff and had long ago pledged by oath to the Popes that they would never seek the Roman Empire. Although Charles was nevertheless created Emperor, Leo schemed much against him, tried to strip him of the Kingdom of both Sicilies, and, with the Kingdom of Italy overthrown, sought to divide the protection of the cities of Italy between the Papal See and France. But when this scheme did not succeed, the notable Proteus again, "keeping a cunning fox under his sultry breast," and well trained "to turn his sails to the wind," deserted from the French to Charles and made a treaty with him on roughly these terms: that Parma and Piacenza be restored to the Roman See, that Francis Sforza be brought back into the Duchy of Milan, that the French be driven out of Italy, and that the Roman See, freed from all fear of the French, be placed in safety. Turning again to the Swiss, through the work of the Cardinal of Sion, a true Sinon, he at last obtained by a notable fraud from the men of Zurich six thousand auxiliaries,

units.la: Cc impetravit, in speciem ad defendendam ditionem Pontificiam, revera autem ad pellendos ex Italia Gallos. Quibus sese oppositerunt ii Helvetii, qui signa Gallicana secuti tandem Mediolanum perdiderunt; & Cæsari Pontificique cesserunt. Certè artibus hisce perfidis totam Helvetiam Leo conturbavit, & concordiam antehac sartam maximam in discordiam permutavit, quam boni omnes uni Pontifici Leoni, ejusque proxenetæ Cardinali Sedunensi, patriæ proditori, acceptam merito referunt.
units.tr: obtained them, in appearance to defend the Papal dominion, but in truth to drive the French out of Italy. Against the French were set those Swiss who, having followed the French standards, had at last lost Milan, and had yielded to the Emperor and the Pope. Certainly by these perfidious arts Leo threw all of Switzerland into confusion, and exchanged the concord hitherto firmly kept for the greatest discord, which all good men rightly credit to Pope Leo alone and to his go-between, the Cardinal of Sion, a traitor to his country.

units.la: CLII. Fuit porro Leo hic ‎כנעני Cananæus (Zach. XIV. v. ult.) seu Mercator grandis ac nefandus, & profusus supra modum in distribuendis per orbem Christianum indulgentiis, hoc est, instruendis rationibus, quibus ex hominum stultitia immensam sibi pecuniam, voluptatibus bellisque sustinendis, & charitatibus suis locupletandis, compararet. Patrio more (ita Langius συγχρον Monachus Chron. Citiz. A. M. D. XIII. scribit) Leo auri sitientissimus est, nimirum cùm Romanorum avaritiæ Florentinorum accesserit cupiditas, auríque sacra fames creverit in immensum, crescitque usque modò amor nummi, quantum ipsa pecunia crescit; saeviorque ignibus Ætnæ ardet amor habendi, quemadmodum & Naso inquit: Creverunt & opes & opum furiosa libido; quò magis sunt potæ, plus sitiuntur aquæ. Numerant certè historiæ immensum auri & argenti pondus, quod indulgentiarum propolæ undique corraserunt. Sed & octo Cardinalium ordinationibus Cardinales duos & quadraginta creavit, ex quibus, insignem per Simoniam thesaurum pretiosissimum collegit. Quinta ordinatione Cardinales triginta & unum creavit, atque inter eos opulentissimos & principes Viros, quibus Papatum non tantum ditavit mirum in modum, sed etiam ceu columnis quibusdam suffultum roboravit. Memorat idem, qui supra Langius, ex quinta illa triginta Cardinalium ordinatione Leonem quingenta millia Ducatorum in patrimonium Divi Petri intulisse ; facta tamen iisdem spe restitutionis. Cúmque aliunde Cardinalibus ita emunctis satisfacere non potuisset , indulgentiarum turpissimam illam fraudem ausum , huc illuc œrusca-tores misisse, qui belli Turcici & structurae Vaticanae prætextu pecunias , ex quibus Cardinalibus satisfaceret, corraderent. Neque vero ex thesauris , insignem per imposituram ita comportatis, vel Vaticanam structuram, vel Turcicum bellum , uti ignathones ejus, & ipse quoque prætenderant; promovit ; (nam & satis pecuniarum ad structuram ejusmodi perficiendam Julius reliquerat ; & lapides interdiu Romae ad Vaticanum construendum cæsos, noctu Florentiam ad palatium Mediceum fabricandum asportatos esse, historiae produnt : & ad bellum Turcicum aprime quidem necessarium contulit omnino nihil ; ) sed Valerio Anshelmo, Paulo, Langio, Guicciardino , aliisque οἰκείοις testibus,tum Cardinalibus illis retribuit : tum Sororem Magdalenam , agnatos & Amicos ditavit , & alios simul ad utriusque ordinis principatum , aliorum cum injuria, evexit. Julianum enim ex Sorore Nepotem , Mutinensem ; & Laurentianum Urbini Duces creavit ; isti Sorore Caroli Sabaudi , huic Boloniae Ducissa, uxoribus conciliatis.
units.tr: CLII. Moreover, this Leo was a Canaanite [כנעני] (Zech. 14, last verse), or a great and wicked merchant, and extravagant beyond measure in distributing indulgences throughout the Christian world; that is, in devising schemes by which he might acquire for himself immense sums from men's folly, to sustain his pleasures and wars and to enrich his charities. "After the native fashion" (so the contemporary monk Lange writes in the Chronicle of Citizens, 1513), "Leo is most thirsty for gold; for since the greed of the Romans has been joined by the lust of the Florentines, the sacred hunger for gold has grown immensely, and the love of money grows as money itself grows; and the love of having burns more fiercely than the fires of Etna, as Naso also says: 'Wealth and the furious lust of riches have grown; the more they are drunk, the more they thirst for water.'" Histories certainly record the immense weight of gold and silver which the hawkers of indulgences scraped together from everywhere. But also, by eight ordinations he created forty-two cardinals, from whom he gathered by simony a notable and most precious treasure. In a fifth ordination he created thirty-one cardinals, among them very wealthy and princely men, whom he not only enriched wonderfully for the Papacy, but also strengthened as if supported by columns. The same Lange, mentioned above, records that from that fifth ordination of thirty cardinals Leo brought five hundred thousand ducats into the patrimony of St Peter, yet with the promise of restitution made to those same men. And since he could not otherwise satisfy the cardinals so fleeced, he dared that most shameful fraud of indulgences, sending hither and thither hawkers who would scrape together money with which to satisfy the cardinals, under the pretext of the Turkish war and the building of the Vatican. But the treasure thus gathered by notable imposture he did not advance either to the Vatican building or to the Turkish war, as his hawkers and he himself had pretended. (For Julius had left enough money to complete such a building; and histories report that stones cut by day in Rome for the building of the Vatican were carried off by night to Florence to build the Medici palace; and he contributed absolutely nothing to the Turkish war, which was indeed most necessary.) Instead, as Valerio Anshelmo, Paulus, Lange, Guicciardini and other intimate witnesses attest, he paid it out to those cardinals; he also enriched his sister Magdalena, his kinsmen and friends, and at the same time raised others to princely rank in either order, to the injury of others. For he created Giuliano, his nephew by his sister, Duke of Modena, and Lorenzo Duke of Urbino; to these he joined in marriage, respectively, the sister of Charles of Savoy and the Duchess of Bologna.

units.la: CLIII. Pessimum vero omen interpretati multi sunt , quod Leone Cardinales quintum ordinante, fulmen Templum ipsum, in quo ordinatio fiebat, feriit, non sine pavore omnium & trepidatione maxima, stupentium etiam, cum fulminis ictu pueruli Jesu imaginem ex gremio matris excussam, & claves ex manibus Petri dejectas cernerent. Indicium scilicet, fore, ut propediem Papatus convellatur, Sedésque illa ad ruinam gravem impellatur. Neque falsum isthoc omen fuit. Mox enim Quirinalis illius prædonis emissarii Tezelius Monachus in Germania, & Samson Franciscanus Mediolanensis in Helvetia Sacerima illa impletur. indulgentiarum, seu tesserarum non modò venialium, sed etiam venalium, impunitatem scelerum, & solutionem Sacrarum legum (veluti si quis sanctissimæ etiam Christi Matri vitium obtulisset) impia & sordida benignitate largientium, nundinatione effecerunt, ut patientia nimiùm jam læsa, ducibus magnanimis & χειροτονημένοις ·Ἰωάν· ἑῆς, in Germania quidem Marthino Luthero; in Helvetia verò Huldrico Zwinglio, ipsius Capitolini Jovis jugulum strenuè invaderetur; sana ac verè Divina de vera peccatorum remissione & justificatione peccatoris per Christi solius obedientiam & fidem in eum, doctrina Papalibus indulgentiis quæstuosissimis opposita restitueretur, & Pontifici ipsi coronæ, Monachisque ventres auferrentur. Quæ duo fecisse Lutheri peccata, Principi cuidam de eo sciscitanti, festivè Erasmus respondit. Frustràque hic Leo ad solitas Pontificibus artes conversus, Lutherum, omnésque ei adhærentes anathemate percussit. Non tantùm enim anathema ceu brutum quoddam fulmen, non tam in homines, quàm in Christum ipsum, utpote cujus honori vindicando & amplificando merito unicè piorum studia velificabantur, jactatum sperni; sed etiam Sedes Romana, ceu γνώσιμ Babylon & Sodoma, ac super ea sedens, ceu Antichristus verissimus certissimis indiciis demonstrari, totis viribus oppugnari, & vicissim damnari; Romana denique superstitio, idololatria & impietas in apertam ubique Scenam produci, convinci, & pro eo atque merebatur, exagitari cœpit. Durabitque sacrum illud bellum, quo per Spiritum oris Christi perditus ille & perdens terram paulatim aboletur & consumitur, donec Christus τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τ' παρουσίας eum penitus abolebit, conficiet, & orco, unde caput suum extulit, totum adjudicabit.
units.tr: Many have interpreted it as a very bad omen that, while Leo was creating cardinals, lightning struck the temple itself in which the ordination was taking place, not without terror and the greatest trembling of all who were present, who were astonished too when, by the stroke of the lightning, an image of the infant Jesus was shaken from his mother's lap, and the keys were cast from Peter's hands. It was clearly an indication that, before long, the papacy would be shaken and that the See would be driven to a grievous fall. Nor was this omen false. For soon afterwards the sacred trade in indulgences, or tickets not only of venial but also of saleable sins, the impunity of crimes, and the dissolution of sacred laws (as if someone had offered an insult even to the most holy Mother of Christ), granted by an impious and base kindness and sold at market, had so wearied patience that, under magnanimous leaders and [χειροτονημένοις ·Ἰωάν· ἑῆς], in Germany Martin Luther, and in Switzerland Ulrich Zwingli, boldly attacked the very throat of the Capitoline Jupiter; and the sound and truly divine doctrine of the true remission of sins, and of the justification of the sinner through the obedience of Christ alone and faith in him, was restored, set against the most profitable Papal indulgences, and the crown was taken from the Pope himself and the bellies from the monks. When a certain prince asked him about the two sins committed by Luther, Erasmus wittily answered that they were these. But Leo, turning in vain to the arts usual to the Popes, smote Luther and all who adhered to him with an anathema. For the anathema was thrown out like some dumb thunderbolt, not so much against men as against Christ himself, since for the vindication and enlargement of his honour the zeal of the pious had rightly set sail; and it was not only despised, but the Roman See, like spiritual Babylon ([γνώσιμ]) and Sodom, and the one sitting upon it as the true Antichrist, began to be demonstrated by the most certain signs, to be assailed with all strength, and in turn to be condemned; and finally Roman superstition, idolatry and impiety began to be brought onto the open stage everywhere, to be convicted, and to be pursued as they deserved. And that sacred war will last, in which that lost man, who destroys the earth, is gradually abolished and consumed by the Spirit of the mouth of Christ, until Christ by the appearing of his coming ([τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τ' παρουσίας]) will utterly abolish and destroy him, and will hand over the whole of him to the abyss, whence he raised his head.

units.la: CLIV. Qualis fuerit Leo ille, sub quo, & quo occa- sionem præbente, Ecclesiæ diu Babylone captivæ Divina libe-
units.tr: CLIV. What sort of man Leo was, under whom, and with whose occasion, the divine liberation of the Church, long held captive at Babylon,

units.la: liberatio & παλιγγενεσία feliciter processit, abundè ex iis, quæ diximus, constat. Constabit tamen luculentius etiam, si de ejus summi scilicet Pontificis & Vicarii Christi impietate & Atheismo, nonnihil attexuerimus. Ille scilicet ὁμολογῶν Johannis XXIV. animam in corporis domicilio sic insinuatam statuentis, ut extra illum carcerem non duret; juslit aliquando (uti Recusat. Synod. Trid. par. 2. cauf. 8. pag. 266. comprobatum videre est) personatos Philosophos duos, ceu moriones ex adverso ad mensam assistere; quos animi gratia de immortalitate animæ disputantes audiret; alterum qui affirmaret, & qui impugnaret, alterum. Cumque finita disputatione judicium in arbitrium Pontificis hi rejicerent: ille sic definita sententia controversiam diremit: Etsi tu, inquit ad affirmantem, pulchras & bonas rationes habeas; tamen ego sententiam hujus, negantis, probo, ceu firmiorem, & quæ faciat bonum vultum. Eidem Leoni cùm aliquando Bembus, vir excellenter doctus, & post Cardinalis delectus, locum quendam è sacris Bibliis in sermone privato retulisset, molestius id ferens Papa, quid, inquit, mihi narras istam de Christo fabulam? Et ne ab hæreticis hæc conficta clamitent οἱ ἐξ εὐαγγελίας, ejus rei ἀνθρωπῶ & αὐτήκοον testem damus, qui & scire debebat: & causam, cur mentiretur, non habebat; Johannis Pici, Mirandulani Comitis nepotem ex fratre minimè degenerem, qui in illo Pisani & Lateranensis Concilii conflictu, quæstionem tractans, utrùm Concilia vel Pontifices errare possint, inter alia de Leone hoc loquens: Meminimus, inquit, Pontificem creditum & adoratum, qui nullum Deum credens, omne infidelitatis (ἀθεότης) culmen excederet: pessimáque ejus opera in coëmendo Pontificatu, in omnigenis sceleribus exercendis, id ipsum testabatur: sed & pessima quoque dicta confirmabant. Námque fassum eum affirmabatur domesticis quibusdam, nullum se Deum aliquando, etiam dum Pontificiam Sedem teneret, credidisse quæ ejus verba libro de fide & ordine credendi, theorem. 4. pag. 259. 260. legere est.
units.tr: liberation and palingenesis happily came about, is clear enough from what we have said. It will be clearer still if we add something about the impiety and atheism of that Pope, the highest Pontiff and Vicar of Christ. That man, holding with John XXIV that the soul is so inserted into the body's dwelling that it cannot survive outside that prison, once ordered two masked philosophers, like buffoons, to stand at a table opposite him. (This is confirmed in Recusat. Synod. Trid. par. 2. cauf. 8. pag. 266.) He listened to them for amusement as they disputed the immortality of the soul, one arguing for it and the other against. When the disputants handed the decision over to the Pope's judgment, he settled the controversy by pronouncing sentence: "Although you, he said to the affirmer, have fine and good arguments, nevertheless I approve the opinion of this negator as firmer, and as the one that gives a better face to things." Once, when Bembus, a man of outstanding learning who was afterwards chosen Cardinal, had recounted some passage from the sacred Bible in private conversation, the Pope took it badly and said: "What is this tale about Christ you are telling me?" Lest the men of the Gospel cry out that these things are invented by heretics, we offer as witness of this matter a man who ought to know, who had no reason to lie, and who was an earwitness: the nephew of John Pico, Count of Mirandola, who was by no means degenerate from his uncle's stock. In the conflict between the Councils of Pisa and the Lateran, while treating the question whether Councils or Popes can err, he said among other things about this Leo: "We remember that a Pope was believed and adored who, believing in no God, exceeded every summit of unbelief (atheism). His worst deeds in buying the papacy and in committing every kind of crime bore witness to this, and his worst sayings confirmed it as well. For it was reported that he confessed to certain intimates that he had never believed in any God, even while he held the Papal See." These are his words, which may be read in the book On Faith and the Order of Believing, theorem 4, pag. 259, 260.

units.la: C L V. Quid vero multis ? Ipse Sforcia Pallavicinus Histor. Concil. Trid. lib. I. cap. 2. modernos parasitos, atque inter illos Lojolitam Ottonem, qui sicut alios, ita Leonem etiam hunc nitrum & lomentum facere non erubuit, suo testimonio confundit. Opponit, ita ille num. 2. scribit, Suavis, magis Leonem in literis profanis versatum, quam in sacris & ad religionem pertinentibus. Haud quidem illi repugno ? Leo ingenio capacissimo, ac singulariter studiis addictus a Deo, vix pueritiam egressus, cum se in supremo Senatu Ecclesiæ collocatum cerneret, suo plane officio defuit, neglecta in literarum studio parte non solum nobiliore, sed suæ magis congrua dignitati. Gravior apparuit deformitas, quando trigesimo septimo ætatis anno Præses ac Magister religionis constitutus, non continenti solum studio prosanarum literarum curiositati se totum impendit, sed in Regiam ipsius Religionis majori cura eos accersivit, quibus essent perspectæ Graecorum fabulæ, Poëtarumque delicię, quam Ecclesiæ historia, ac Patrum doctrina, &c. Non æque Theologorum ac Poëtarum consuetudine est delectatus, nec juxta sacram eruditionem promovit ac profanam. Mox num. 4. & 5. Suavi objectanti, Leoni haud magnæ curæ pietatem fuisse, largitur; in Leone, cum Pontifex electus est, tantam curam pietatis non eluxisse, quantam celsitudo illa pene Divina postulabat. Nam, inquit, ut ea praeteream, quæ sub famæ suspicione magis, quam affirmatione delitescunt; constat, venationes, facetias, pompas adeo frequentes, fuisse in Leone vitia partim Seculi, partim potentiæ, partim etiam ingenii : non tamen exiguo in eo inter mortales fastigio, cui nil par esse potest, nisi summa perfectio. Post num. 6. ait, Leonem in Sede Romana collocatum passum esse se dementari ab ea specie, quæ magnificum cum bono confundit, plausumque multitudinis cum Reipublicæ emolumento.
units.tr: C L V. But why say more? Sforza Pallavicino himself, in his Histor. Concil. Trid. lib. I. cap. 2, refutes by his own testimony the modern flatterers, and among them the Jesuit Otto, who did not blush to make a lye and a whitewash of this Leo as of the others. "Opponit", he writes at no. 2, "Suavis, that Leo was more versed in profane letters than in sacred ones and those pertaining to religion." Do I contradict him? Leo, of most capacious intellect and singularly given by God to study, scarcely out of boyhood, when he found himself placed in the supreme Senate of the Church, plainly failed in his duty, neglecting in his study of letters the part not only more noble but more fitting to his dignity. The deformity appeared graver when, in his thirty-seventh year of life, he was made President and Master of religion, and he devoted himself wholly not merely to the restrained pursuit of profane letters but, with greater care for the Royal Court of religion, summoned men who were well versed in the Greek fables and the delights of the poets, rather than in the history of the Church and the teaching of the Fathers, etc. He delighted not equally in the company of theologians and of poets, and he promoted those versed in profane learning no less than those versed in sacred learning." Soon after, at nos. 4 and 5, he concedes to Suavis, who objected that "Leo had little concern for piety": "In Leo, when he was elected Pope, there did not shine forth as much care for piety as that almost divine loftiness demanded. For," he says, "to pass over those things which lie hidden more under suspicion of fame than under affirmation, it is established that hunting, jesting and pomp were so frequent in Leo that they were vices partly of the age, partly of power, and partly of his talent; yet he stood on no small height among mortals, to which nothing can be equal except supreme perfection." After no. 6 he says that "Leo, placed in the Roman See, allowed himself to be dazzled by that appearance which confuses the magnificent with the good, and the applause of the multitude with the advantage of the commonwealth."

units.la: C L V I. Fuisse ea tempestate Ecclesiam Romanam corruptam supra modum, adeóque Reformationis indigam, pariter οἰκεῖοι seu domestici testes diffitentur nulli. Idem, qui supra, Monachus Paulus Langius in Chronico Citizensi, quod A. M. D. XX. se scripsisse profitetur; ad A. M. D. XIIII. de Ecclesiæ Romanæ statu ejusmodi querelam texit:
units.tr: C L V I. That the Roman Church was at that time corrupted beyond measure, and therefore in need of reformation, none of the domestic witnesses deny either. The same Paul Lang, the monk mentioned above, in his Citizen Chronicle, which he professes to have written in 1520, weaves into his account for the year 1514 this complaint about the state of the Roman Church:

units.la: Amore equidem auri & nunc Romæ cuncta venalia sunt; auro mediante Simonia toleratur; præbendarum pluralitas in infinitum conceditur; beneficia dignitatesve cujusvis qualitatis & Cardinalibus & Protonotariis, atque amicis Papæ reservantur; expectativæ gratiæ sine numero conceduntur; annatæ sive medii fructus absque ulla dilatione temporis exiguntur. Quin imo ipsæ Annatæ, in quas tempore Callisti Papæ tertii, ad quatuor Principes consenserunt annos, non modo adhuc durant, sed & in dies magis crescunt, duriúsque premunt & opprimunt. Et nisi iidem Principes remedium adhibere procurent; omne æs & aurum pedetentim hoc malo è Germania corrasum & haustum Romam velut in Sacculum pertusum, & inexplebilem voraginem portabitur. Dimembrationes Monasteriorum, & Ecclesiarum permutationes injustissimè admittuntur; Ecclesiarum quoque regimina non magis merenti, sed magis asserenti committuntur; electiones Prælatorum passim rejiciuntur, & Romanis tribuuntur; pro palliorum Archiepiscopalium redemptione ingens pecunia in damnum Ecclesiarum contra Sanctionem Leonis Papæ, ejus nominis Secundi, imo contra Sacri Basileensis Concilii decretum, pro usu pallii, aliorumque officiorum confirmatione & impetratione, nihil persolvendum statuentis, exigitur & extorquetur. Quam quidem exactionem præter Simoniam alia complura incommoda sequuntur. Nam nostra ætate Archiprasules pecuniam, quam pro pallio seu etiam confirmatione obtinenda Romam mittere coguntur immediatè, quatenus ipsi indemnes maneant, & thesauros suos non minuant; æquivalentem, imo multò ampliorem sub nomine subsidii extorquent pecuniam; quemadmodum nuper in Archiepiscopatu Magdeburgensi contigisse haud absque querela pauperum (proh dolor) audivimus. Per prædicta igitur & similia, qua ex ex Romana Curia manant gravamina, per orbem Christianum ruinæ, destructiones & ærumnæ oriuntur. Nec mirum, cum ipsa Germania suprema & principalis, quondámque potentissima, Moguntinensis Archiepiscopalis Ecclesia, ob eas res causasque maximis & permultis onerata sit debitis, & vehementer exhausta. Proinde non immeritò cum supra memorata gravamina sub Leone X. in Gallia plus solito grassari inciperent; Universitas Parisiensis pro conservatione & bono Ecclesiarum totius Regni contra eundem Papam ad Concilium appellavit Generale, &c. Post indulgentiarum historiam pertexens, ita quidem laudat Lutheri Simoniam illam aggressi Zelum, ut tamen subjiciat: Quæ de Martini Lutheri doctrina disserui, non sicut discipulus illius assertive, sed potius admirative posui, utpote nullius adhuc juratus in verba Magistri. Sed cum sim & ego more suspensus multorum, quousque per Oecumenicum, Universale & Generale Concilium, quid in tam ardua re tenendum sit, decretum fuerit. Clauditque suam narrationem his verbis: Quæ utinam vera non essent, utinam mendaces in hac parte essemus omnes, ut vitiis eliminatis Romæ Sanctitas ipsa & morum integritas, justitia & veritas, ad salutem totius orbis & fidei robur inveniretur, destrueturque ceu falsum & injuriosum illud vulgatissimum etiam laicorum dictenium, quo dicunt, Romæ propiores Christianos esse deteriores, & Curiam Romanam non quærere ovem sine lana.
units.tr: "Indeed, through love of gold, everything at Rome is now for sale; through gold, simony is tolerated; plurality of prebends is granted without limit; benefices and dignities of any kind are reserved for Cardinals, Protonotaries and friends of the Pope; expectative graces are granted without number; annates, or half-year revenues, are exacted without any delay of time. Moreover, the annates themselves, to which four princes consented in the time of Pope Callistus III for four years, not only still continue but grow day by day and press down and oppress more harshly. Unless these same princes take care to apply a remedy, all the money and gold scraped and drained from Germany by this evil will be carried to Rome as into a leaking sack and an insatiable whirlpool. The dismemberment of monasteries and churches and the exchanges of benefices are admitted most unjustly; the government of churches is entrusted not to the more deserving but to the more insistent; elections of prelates are rejected everywhere and given to Romans; for the redemption of archiepiscopal palls an enormous sum is extorted, to the loss of the churches, against the sanction of Pope Leo II, contrary even to the decree of the Sacred Council of Basel, which decrees that nothing be paid for the use of the pall, or for the confirmation and obtaining of other offices. Besides this exaction, many other evils follow from it. For in our own age the archbishops, in order to remain unharmed and not diminish their treasuries, extort under the name of subsidy an equivalent, or rather a much larger sum, from the money which they are forced to send immediately to Rome to obtain the pall or even confirmation; as we have heard, not without the complaint (alas!) of the poor, happened lately in the archbishopric of Magdeburg. Through these and similar burdens, which flow from the Roman Curia, ruins, destructions and miseries arise throughout the Christian world.
