Nor is it surprising, since Germany itself, the supreme and principal church, the once most powerful Church of the Archbishop of Mainz, has been burdened with very great and very many debts on account of these matters and causes, and is violently drained. Therefore, not undeservedly, when the aforesaid burdens under Leo X began to rage in France more than usual, the University of Paris appealed against the same Pope to a General Council, for the preservation and good of the churches of the whole kingdom, etc." Going through the history of indulgences, he indeed praises the zeal of Luther in attacking that simony so far, yet he adds: "What I have discussed about the teaching of Martin Luther I have set forth not as his disciple asserting it, but rather marvelling at it, since I am not yet sworn to the words of the master. But since I too, like many, am for the time being suspended until it has been decreed by the Ecumenical, Universal and General Council what must be held in so arduous a matter." He closes his narrative with these words: "Would that these things were not true! Would that we were all liars in this respect, so that, with vices removed, holiness itself and integrity of morals, justice and truth might be found at Rome for the salvation of the whole world and the strength of the faith; and that the very common saying of the laity, by which they say that Christians nearer Rome are worse and that the Roman Curia seeks no sheep without wool, might be destroyed as false and injurious."

units.la: CLVII. Author libri decantati, cui nomen Onus Ecclesiæ, circa initium Reformationis scripti, & Coloniæ denuò A. M. D. C. XXXI. impressi, qui Episcopus Suffraganeus Salisburgensis putatur; Pontificius certè, utpote qui adversus Lutherum contendit passim; Ecclesiæ Romanæ circa eadem tempora statum graphicè depingit. Sectione V. sic scribit: Ecclesiastica modo sublimitas multifariam est lacerata. Hoc in Apocalypsi ostenditur in Sigilli Sexti apertione, id est, moderni temporis nostri, quando Sol, qui est spiritualis Potentatus, factus est niger, quia non Serenum Cœlum, sed sed tetrum infernum aperit. Propterea perversus Pontifex nuncupatur Angelus Abyssi. Sect. VIII. Heu, inquit, sicut olim in imperio Romano, sic hodie in Curia Romana est vorago divitiarum turpissima. Crevit avaritia, periit Lex à Sacerdote, ac visio de Propheta, & consilium à Senioribus. Claves Ecclesiae sunt in abusu, & servitute ambitionis & Simoniae. Vitia enim ferme Curialium celari negarique vix possunt. Roma quasi gurges flagitiorum. Sect. XV. Ecce Roma nunc est vorago & Mammona inferni, ubi Diabolus totius avaritiae Capitaneus residet, vendens patrimonium Christi, quod sua passione promeruit, qui nobis praecipit, ut gratis demus, quod gratis accepimus. Id modo versum est in proverbium: Curia Romana non petit ovem sine lana: Dantes exaudit, non dantibus ostia claudit. Mox etiam Sigismundi Imperatoris contradispensationum exorbitantiam in Constantiensi Concilio dictum repetit: Legere scilicet nos, Christum Petro potestatem duntaxat relaxandi peccata, non admittendi dedisse. Addit autem ipse: Quot & quantae exorbitantiae cum concessione & publicatione Apostolicarum indulgentiarum committantur, explicare poteit nemo. Ipse vero impudentissimum illum indulgentiarum mercatum Sect. XXIX. XXX. XXXIX. XLI. XLV. feriis vocibus exagitat, & ad extremum sic concludit: Adparet, nostram matrem Ecclesiam unâ cum filiis suis Christianis circa normam & modum Poenitentiarum & veniarum non mediocriter esse perplexam atque dilaceratam, & absque Divina ope semetipsam ex illis arumnis resolvere impotentem, vehementérque lamentantem de indulgentiarum quaestoribus &c. Addi potest duplex documentum, Germanicum unum, alterum Gallicum. Germanicum prompsit Vir insignis, qui à Principibus, quos Leo ad decimas in usum belli sacri erogandas solicitavit, consultus, librum scripsit de decimis non praestandis; in quo Ecclesiae Romanae miseram faciem ad vivum depingit. Copia ejus apud Wolphium Lect. Mem. Cent. 16. p. 230. 231. extat. Gallicum vero est appellatio folennis Universitatis Parifienfis die XVII. Marti A. M. D. XVII. congregatæ, in qua Reformatio Conftantienfis & Bafileenfis urgetur strenuè, & remedia adversus Simoniam Romanæ Curiæ proponuntur. Ejus Doctiff. Mornæus Myft. Iniq. p. 1391. &c. meminit.
units.tr: CLVII. The author of the much-praised book entitled Onus Ecclesiæ, written near the beginning of the Reformation and printed again at Cologne in 1631, who is thought to have been a suffragan bishop of Salzburg, and who was certainly a Papist since he argues vigorously against Luther, depicts the state of the Roman Church of those same times in vivid colours. In section V he writes: Ecclesiastical sublimity has now been torn in many ways. This is shown in the Apocalypse at the opening of the sixth seal, that is, in our own modern times, when the Sun, which is the spiritual power, has become black, because it opens not a serene heaven but a foul hell. For this reason the wicked Pope is called the Angel of the Abyss. Section VIII: Alas, he says, just as once in the Roman empire, so today in the Roman Curia there is a most shameful whirlpool of riches. Avarice has grown, the law has perished from the priest, the vision from the prophet, and counsel from the elders. The keys of the Church are in abuse, and in the bondage of ambition and simony. For the vices of the courtiers can scarcely be hidden or denied. Rome is like a whirlpool of crimes. Section XV: Behold, Rome is now a whirlpool and the Mammon of hell, where the Devil, the captain of all avarice, sits, selling the patrimony of Christ, which he earned by his passion, he who commands us to give freely what we have freely received. This has now become a proverb: The Roman Curia does not seek a sheep without its wool. It hears those who give, and shuts its doors on those who do not give. Soon afterwards he also repeats the phrase, spoken at the Council of Constance, about the excessive abuse of dispensations of Emperor Sigismund: We read, namely, that Christ gave Peter only the power of loosing sins, not of admitting them. He adds himself: No one can explain how many and how great excesses are committed under the granting and publication of apostolic indulgences. He himself lashes that most shameless trade in indulgences in sections XXIX, XXX, XXXIX, XLI and XLV with harsh words, and at last concludes thus: It appears that our mother the Church, together with her Christian children, is not a little perplexed and torn concerning the rule and manner of repentance and pardons, and is unable to free herself from those troubles without divine help, and she laments loudly about the indulgence-sellers, etc. Two further documents may be added, one German and one French. The German was produced by a distinguished man who, when consulted by the princes whom Leo had urged to devote the tithes to the holy war, wrote a book on not paying tithes, in which he depicts to the life the wretched face of the Roman Church. A copy of it is found in Wolf, Lect. Mem. Cent. 16, pp. 230–231. The French document is the solemn appeal of the University of Paris, gathered on 17 March 1517, in which the reform of Constance and Basel is strenuously urged and remedies against the simony of the Roman Curia are proposed. Its most learned author is mentioned by Mornay, Myst. Iniq. p. 1391 and following.

units.la: CLVIII.
units.tr: CLVIII.

units.la: CLVIII. Quid vero multis? Ipsemet, qui Leoni A. M. D. XXI. ex profusa ob exactos Mediolano totáque Italia Gallos lætitia defuncto, successit, Hadrianus VI. Ultrajectinus, formator olim principalis juventæ Caroli V. misso A. M. D. XXII. ad Comitia Norimbergenfia Francifco Cheregato, Episcopo Aprutino, in mandatis dedit, palàm Germaniæ Principibus hæc in verba profiteretur: Dices: Nos ingenuè fateri, quòd Deus hanc persecutionem Ecclesiæ suæ (persecutionem scilicet Ecclesiæ ejusdem tentatam ex Dei verbo renovationem interpretatur) inferre permittit propter peccata hominum, maximè Sacerdotum & Ecclesiæ Prælatorum. Certum enim est, non esse abbreviatam manum Domini, ut salvare nequeat: sed peccata dividere inter nos & ipsum, & abscondere faciem suam à nobis, ut non exaudiat. Clamant Scripturæ, peccata populi derivari à peccatis Sacerdotum: propterea que, ait Chryfoftomus, Salvator noster curaturus infirmam Civitatem Hierusalem, ingressus est prius Templum, ut peccata Sacerdotum primò castigaret, instar boni medici, qui morbum à radice curat. Scimus, in hac sancta Sede aliquot jam ab annis multa abominanda fuisse, abusus in Spiritualibus, excessus in mandatis, & omnia denique in perversum mutata. Nec mirum fi ægritudo à capite in membra, à Summis Pontificibus in alios inferiores Prælatos defcenderit. Omnes nos (Prælati Ecclesiastici) declinavimus unusquisque in vias suas: nec fuit jam diu qui faceret bonum: non fuit usque ad unum. Quamobrem neceffum est, ut omnes demus gloriam Deo, & humiliemus animas nostras ei: videatque unusquisque nostrûm, unde ceciderit: & fe potius quilibet judicet, quàm in Deo virga furofuroris sui judicari velit. Qua in re, quod ad nos attinet, polliceberis, nos omnem operam adhibituros, ut primum Curia hæc (unde forte omne hoc malum processit) reformetur: ut sicut inde corruptio in omnes inferiores emanavit, ita etiam ab eadem sanitas reformatio omnium emanet: ad quod procurandum nos tanto arctius obligatos reputemus, quanto universum mundum hujusmodi reformationem avidius desiderare videmus &c. Nemo tamen mirari debet, si non statim omnia errata & abusus omnes per nos emendatos viderit. Inveteratus nimirum morbus est, nec simplex, sed varius & multiplex: pedetentim in ejus cura procedendum est, & prius gravioribus magisque periculosis occurrendum: ne omnia pariter reformare volentes, omnia perturbemus. Omnes subitæ mutationes, inquit Aristoteles in Rep. perniciosæ sunt. Qui nimis emungit, elicit sanguinem. Hactenus ille in Instructione, cujus exemplar non tantum Wolphius in Lectionibus Memorabilibus Cent. 16. pag. m. 195. Sed etiam Ottuinus Gratius in Fasciculo rerum expetendarum Coloniæ A. M. D. XXXV. impresso; & post ipsum etiam Pallavicinus Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. II. 7. (ne instructionis illius γνησιότητα quicquam dubitetur) vulgarunt. Acclamamus merito: Bene, Pater sancte; bene vidisti, quod res est; ut in corporibus (quod Plinius lib. IV. Epist. 23. scite observavit) Sic in Hierarchia, & alio quovis imperio, gravissimum esse morbum, qui a capite diffunditur.
units.tr: CLVIII. But why say more? Adrian VI of Utrecht, who succeeded Leo in 1521 after Leo died amid the excessive joy over the expulsion of the French from Milan and all Italy, and who had once been the principal tutor of the youth of Charles V, in 1522, when he sent Francesco Chieregati, bishop of Aprutium, to the Diet of Nuremberg, gave him instructions to declare openly to the princes of Germany these words: You will say: We frankly confess that God permits this persecution of his Church (namely, the persecution attempted against the Church, which he interprets as the renewal brought about by the word of God) to be inflicted on account of the sins of men, and especially of the priests and prelates of the Church. For it is certain that the hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that it cannot save; but sins divide between us and him, and hide his face from us, so that he does not hear. The Scriptures cry out that the sins of the people are derived from the sins of the priests. Therefore, says Chrysostom, our Saviour, about to heal the sick city of Jerusalem, first entered the Temple, so that he might first punish the sins of the priests, like a good physician who cures a disease at its root. We know that for some years now many detestable things have been in this holy See: abuses in spiritual matters, excesses in commands, and in short everything turned into perversity. Nor is it surprising that the sickness has descended from the head to the limbs, from the supreme Pontiffs to the other lower prelates. We all (ecclesiastical prelates) have turned aside, each to his own way; nor for a long time has there been anyone who did good, no, not even one. Therefore it is necessary that we all give glory to God and humble our souls before him; and let each of us see from where he has fallen, and let each judge himself rather than wish to be judged by God in the rod of his fury. In this matter, as far as concerns us, you may promise that we will apply all effort so that first this Curia (from which perhaps all this evil has proceeded) may be reformed; so that as corruption has flowed from it into all the lower ranks, so also from the same place health and reformation may flow to all; and we shall consider ourselves bound to procure this the more closely, the more we see the whole world desiring such a reformation more eagerly, etc. Yet no one ought to wonder if he does not at once see all the errors and all the abuses corrected by us. The disease is indeed inveterate, and not simple but varied and manifold; the cure must proceed gradually, and the more grave and dangerous matters must be met first, lest, wishing to reform everything at once, we throw everything into confusion. All sudden changes, says Aristotle in the Republic, are harmful. He who blows his nose too hard draws blood. So far he spoke in the Instruction, a copy of which was published not only by Wolf in the Lectiones Memorabiles, Cent. 16, p. 195, but also by Ottuin Gratius in the Fasciculus rerum expetendarum, printed at Cologne in 1535; and afterwards Pallavicini too, Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. II, 7, published it (so that no doubt may be cast on the genuineness of that instruction). We rightly cry out: Well said, holy Father; you have rightly seen how things stand; for as in bodies (as Pliny wisely observed, Book IV, Letter 23), so in the hierarchy and in any other government, the most serious disease is the one that spreads from the head.

units.la: CLIX. Displicuit quidem Batava illa Simplicitas, (nam Ultrajectinus Adrianus erat) non parum cum aliis, tum nuper etiam Pallavicino, emunctiorum scilicet narium homini, & novissimæ Politices Hierarchicæ architecto vaferrimo. Etiamsi Pontifex, (inquit inter alia ib. num. 11.) ea in animo haberet sensa, liberioris tamen, quam par erat, sinceritatis fuisse visum est, ea conventui patefacere, & vel ab ipso, vel ab ejus Nuntio proponi scripto. Satis noverat, in eo cœtu complures adesse fidei Romanæ adversarios, qui libenter accepturi essent
units.tr: CLIX. That Dutch simplicity (for Adrian was a Utrechter) displeased not a little others, and recently also Pallavicini, a man of sharper nose and the most cunning architect of the modern hierarchical policy. Even if the Pontiff, (he says among other things, ib. n. 11) had such feelings in his mind, it nevertheless seemed that he was too free and sincere, more than was fitting, in disclosing them to the assembly, and in having them put forward in writing, either by himself or by his nuncio. He knew well that many enemies of the Roman faith were present in that gathering, who would gladly accept

units.la: Adrianus idem à Pallavicini Confessionem eam dimidiatam, qua Romanos Pontifices accusabat &c. Paulò post: Aberravit nonnihil Adrianus ab officio Prudentiæ perfectæ in exquirendo à singulis, ad quos scripserat, consilio. Satis erat, si Nuntius per se audita singulorum consilia Pontifici significaret, nulla illi injecta palam necessitate, ea per se ipsum excipiendi. Displicuit etiam valide alteri Jesuitæ Germano Masenio, qui in Anima historiarum hujus temporis inter alia sic de Adriano scribit: Hac simplicitate, qua Germanis se aperiebat, & diffidentia, qua minus se credebat Italis, reconditi magis animi sensusque hominibus displicuit. Vindicavit tamen Adrianum à Jesuitarum horum perversa Politica Sorbonista Launojus, qui Epist. IV. 7. cujus inscriptio ita habet: Adrianus defenditur adversus Pallavicinum & alios Aulæ Sectatores, qui Adrianum ad regendam Sedem Apostolicam minus idoneum fuisse, calumniantur; inter alia sic loquitur: In Episcopalis officii non bene gesti suspicionem venit apud eos, qui seculari potius, quàm religiosa prudentia regendam esse Ecclesiam, præ se ferunt. Cur verò Magistri illi Curiales, qui tempori serviendum esse putant, sic Adriano detrahant, in causa fuisse tria, idem asserit: Primùm, inquit, Adrianus vivere instituit, ut docuerat. Lovaniensis Theologus docuerat, Clerico de bonis Ecclesiæ nihil præter victum & vestitum sumendum esse. Romanus verò Pontisex de bonis Ecclesiæ nihil præter victum & vestitum sibi sumpsit, ut cæteris exemplum præberet, forma gregis factus. Deinde secutus est eam de Apostolicis dispensationibus doctrinam, quam Theologus Lovaniensis tradiderat in Scholis, ut quæstionem hanc solveret: Utrum omnis Apostolica dispensatio super pluralitate beneficiorum hominem faciat tutum & securum in foro conscientiæ? Tertium, idque omnium maximum & gravissimum fuit, quòd sanctissimus Pontifex Romanæ Curiæ vitia & abusus emendare statuit. Addit verò, vix posse excusari Cardinalem Pallavicinum, qui probitatis antiquæ & moris prisci Pontificem contumeliosè prosecutus sit, ut Curiæ blandiretur.
units.tr: Adrian himself was (according to Pallavicini) a confession that was half-hearted, by which he accused the Roman Pontiffs, etc. A little later: Adrian strayed somewhat from the duty of perfect prudence in seeking advice from individuals to whom he had written. It would have been enough if the nuncio, having heard the opinions of individuals on his own, had reported them to the Pontiff, without any open necessity being laid upon him to receive them himself. The German Jesuit Masenius, who also took strong offence, writes in Anima historiarum hujus temporis among other things thus about Adrian: By that simplicity with which he opened himself to the Germans, and by that distrust with which he trusted the Italians less, he displeased men of more hidden minds and feelings. Yet Launoy, the Sorbonne doctor, vindicated Adrian from the perverse politics of these Jesuits, in Epist. IV. 7, whose title reads: Adrian is defended against Pallavicini and the other followers of the court, who slander Adrian as less fit to rule the Apostolic See; among other things he says thus: He came under suspicion of having not well performed his episcopal office among those who profess that the Church ought to be governed by secular rather than religious prudence. Why those courtly masters, who think one must serve the times, so disparage Adrian, the same author states was due to three causes: First, he says, Adrian resolved to live as he had taught. The Louvain theologian had taught that a cleric should take from the goods of the Church nothing beyond food and clothing. The Roman Pontiff therefore took for himself from the goods of the Church nothing beyond food and clothing, so as to give an example to the others, having become the model of the flock. Next, he followed that doctrine concerning apostolic dispensations which the Louvain theologian had taught in the schools, in order to resolve this question: Whether every apostolic dispensation on the plurality of benefices makes a man safe and secure in the court of conscience? Third, and this was the greatest and most serious of all, the most holy Pontiff decided to correct the vices and abuses of the Roman Curia. He adds that Cardinal Pallavicini can scarcely be excused, since he abused with insults a Pontiff of ancient probity and old-fashioned manners, in order to flatter the Curia.

units.la: CLIX. Re-
units.tr: CLIX. Re-

units.la: CLIX. Responsum Pontificio Legato à Cæsare & Ordinibus Imperii perhibitum idem Wolfius mox etiam recitat. In eo inter alia promittunt, se abusus & gravamina, specialesque articulos reformandos scripto Pontifici exhibituros esse. Absque qua Reformatione, veram pacem & concordiam inter Seculares & Ecclesiasticos Ordines farciri posse pernegant. Mox igitur A. M. D. XXIIII. ab omnibus tum Euangelicis tum Pontificiis Imperii Ordinibus in Norimbergensibus Comitiis Centum Nationis Germanicæ Gravamina, quæ omnia tamen tribus capitibus comprehendebantur, nempe quod Romana Curia gravissima servitute populum premat: Germaniam facultatibus expoliet: & Magistratus Secularis jurisdictionem sibi vindicet, Legato eidem Adriani exhibita sunt, cum obtestatione gravissima, det operam Pontifex, ut quantocijùs serióque illa emendentur. Sed mox ac rediit Romam Legatus, Adrianus mortalitatem explevit, simúlque tentatæ Reformationis conatus evanuerunt. Paulò post etiam Anno scilicet M. D. XXV. uti domestici Annales produnt, novem Cantonum Helvetiæ & Valesiorum Legati Lucernæ ausi Reformationis condere articulos, temporum suorum calamitatem Sacerdotum iniquitati diserte imputant, nundinationes fœdas prohibent, & Curtisanis, quos Romanos nebulones vocant, pessulum obdunt. CLX. Neque tamen Reformatio, quam Adrianus, & cæteri etiam Curiæ Romanæ antesignani moliebantur, perfecta fuit. Neglecta enim, imò repudiata doctrinæ & Sacramentorum correctione, crassissimos tantùm morum defectus, & damnatam ubique Simoniam notoriam emendare statuerunt. Nimirum ut Medea capiti consulendum putavit jactura discerptorum sparsorúmque fratris membrorum: sic istis consultum videbatur, jactum facere ludicrorum aliquot, aut inanium impedimentorum, ut salsalvo capite Capitolióque naufragii discrimen ultimum evitarent. Nam, uti Sallustius ad Cæs. orat. 2. loquitur, in navigationibus etiam si quid adversi coortum est, de illis potissimum jactura fit, quæ pretii minimi sunt.
units.tr: CLIX. The reply that the Emperor and the Estates of the Empire gave to the papal legate, which Wolf also immediately recites, contains, among other things, a promise that they will present to the Pope in writing the abuses, grievances and particular articles to be reformed. They deny that true peace and concord between the secular and ecclesiastical orders can be secured without this reformation. Then at once, in 1524, at the Diet of Nuremberg, all the Estates of the Empire, both Evangelical and Papist, presented to Adrian's legate the grievances of the German nation, a hundred in number, though all of them were grouped under three heads: that the Roman Curia oppresses the people with a most grievous servitude: strips Germany of its resources: and claims for itself the jurisdiction of the secular magistrate. They urged him, with the most solemn entreaty, to see to it that the Pope have these corrected as quickly and earnestly as possible. But as soon as the legate returned to Rome, Adrian died, and at the same time the attempts at reformation evaporated. Shortly afterwards, in 1525 as the domestic annals report, the legates of the nine cantons of Helvetia and of the Valais, meeting at Lucerne, dared to draw up articles of reformation. They plainly blame the calamity of their times on the wickedness of the priests, forbid disgraceful trading, and bar the door against the courtiers whom they call Roman scoundrels. CLX. Yet the reformation which Adrian and the other leaders of the Roman Curia were undertaking was not carried through. For, neglecting, or rather rejecting, the correction of doctrine and of the sacraments, they resolved to amend only the grossest moral failings and the simony that was condemned everywhere and openly practised. Just as Medea thought it wise to save her head at the cost of throwing away the pieces of her scattered brother's body, so these men thought it right to throw overboard some trifling or useless baggage, so that, with head and Capitol saved, they might escape the final peril of shipwreck. For, as Sallust says in his Speech to Caesar 2, in voyages too, if anything adverse arises, the loss falls chiefly on those things which are of least value.

units.la: CLXI. Sed & Ordines Imperii, ac Cantones Helvetiæ novem ea cum primis sub ferulam vocabant, quibus ipsi se gravari senserant; adeóque de verbi Dei honore & Christi gloria parùm soliciti, temporalibus duntaxat commodis suis velificabantur. Quo quidem indicio demonstrárunt, se à semetipsis loqui, & Dei Spiritu instructos nondum esse. Hunc enim indagandæ & cognoscendæ veritatis canonem Christus ipse ostendit Joh. VII. 18. Qui à se ipso loquitur, gloriam propriam quærit. Qui autem quærit gloriam ejus, qui misit me, is verax est, & injustitia in eo non est.
units.tr: CLXI. But the Estates of the Empire and the nine cantons of Helvetia summoned to the rod above all those things by which they had felt themselves burdened; and so, little concerned for the honour of God's Word and the glory of Christ, they set their sails only for their own temporal advantage. This indeed showed that they spoke from themselves and were not yet taught by the Spirit of God. For Christ himself gives this rule for searching out and knowing the truth, John 7:18: He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory. But he who seeks the glory of him who sent me, he is true, and there is no injustice in him.

units.la: CLXII. Ipsi quin etiam Reformatores Ecclesiæ, Zwinglius in Helvetia, & Lutherus in Germania, initio qualicunque nundinationum & libidinum inhibitione fuissent contenti, nisi eos ad majora audenda singularis adversariorum intemperies & obstinatio, providente Ecclesiæ saluti quasi per contraria Numine, irritâsset. Zwinglius equidem in causa indulgentiarum faventem Hugonem Episcopum Constantiensem habebat. Sed is ad alia æquè necessaria procedere noluit. Lutherum quoque, Cajetano minùs consentientem Leo Papa anathemate ferire, quàm postulatis ejus primis concedere quicquam maluit. Dissensio illa & exacerbatio nostrorum studia exacuit, ut de reformatione in dies perfectiore cogitarent, quod Vergerio Pauli III. Legato palam Lutherus, apud Suavem Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. I. ad A. M. D. XXXV. confessus est. Atque ita adversariis usu venit, quod pertinacibus solet, & propugnatoribus suorum vitiorum, juxta fabulam non illepidam de claudo, qui uno nummo redimere se potuisset, postea renitens, pluribus in eo vitiis conspectis, plures nummos persolvere coactus fuit. Ita Pontifices Romani uno & altero nummo forsan expedire se potuissent, cùm postea totam fere crumenam amiserint. Universo enim Ecclesiæ corpore diligenter inspecto & considerato, nihil sani in illo deprehensum fuit. Doctrina Ecclesiæ multis hæresibus infecta, Sacramenta magicis ritibus profanata, disciplina in Paganismum vel gentilem licentiam conversa erat. Universalis ergo corruptio panaceam seu medicinam universalem requirebat. Quæ Dei gratiâ stupendâ passim ita feliciter processit, ut in Helvetia, Germania, Gallia, Anglia, Bohemia, Suecia, Dania; Belgio, Polonia innumera hominum multitudo puro, sincero & ardente Euangelii præconio, solius Spiritus Divini potentiâ compuncta, Romani Pontificis communionem ejuraverit, & veritati Cœlesti Sacramento promptissimè dixerit.
units.tr: CLXII. Indeed, the Reformers of the Church themselves, Zwingli in Helvetia and Luther in Germany, at first would have been content with some kind of restraint on trading and lust, had not the singular violence and obstinacy of their adversaries, God providing for the Church's safety as it were through contraries, provoked them to dare greater things. Zwingli, to be sure, had in the matter of indulgences Bishop Hugo of Constance on his side, but he was unwilling to proceed to other matters that were equally necessary. Pope Leo also preferred to strike Luther with an anathema, since he did not agree with Cajetan, rather than concede anything at all to his first demands. That dissent and exasperation sharpened our men's zeal, so that they began to think about a more thorough reformation day by day; Luther openly confessed this to Vergerio, legate of Paul III, as Sarpi (Suave) relates in his History of the Council of Trent, book I, under the year 1535. And so it befell the adversaries, as it usually does with the stubborn and the defenders of their own vices, that, in accordance with the not unpleasant fable of the lame man who could have bought himself off for one coin, but afterwards, resisting, when more of his faults had been seen, was forced to pay more coins. So the Roman Pontiffs might perhaps have got away with one or two coins, whereas afterwards they lost almost their whole purse. For when the whole body of the Church was carefully examined and considered, nothing sound was found in it. Its doctrine was infected with many heresies, its sacraments profaned by magical rites, and its discipline turned into pagan or heathen licence. Universal corruption therefore called for a panacea or universal remedy. By the wonderful grace of God this was everywhere so happily carried out that, in Helvetia, Germany, France, England, Bohemia, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium and Poland, countless multitudes, pricked in heart by the pure, sincere and fervent proclamation of the Gospel, and by the power of the Divine Spirit alone, renounced communion with the Roman Pontiff and most readily assented to the heavenly truth.

units.la: CLXIII. Adriano non sine veneni propinati suspicione extincto, Julius Medices, Papæ Leonis cognatus, dictus Clemens VII. successit. De ejus natalibus & Simonia Suavis nonnulla recenset, quæ Pallavicinus segniter refellit. Schisma certè ipsum inter & creatum Antipapam Urbanum VI. glisccebat. Quem posteriorem unicum & verum Ecclesiæ caput Richardus VI. Angliæ Rex agnovit. Clementem verò nullis prope literis tinctum, sacræque doctrinæ ignarum, artibus mechanicis delectatum, ingenio fuisse adeò dimisso hærentique, ut opificum arcana, subtilitatesque operum nimia & prope turpi solertia scrutaretur; Histor. lib. XXXII. testis est. Reformatione Adriani, quam tacitè damnaverat, dissimulata; distinctisque centum Germanorum Gravaminibus, quorum alia Curiam Romanam; plura verò Episcopos, Officiales, Curatos & alios Germaniæ Sacerdotes spectabant; prioribus eò quòd authoritati Pontificis derogent, & hæresin sapiant; neglectis, posterioribus utcunque satisfacturus, Cardinalem Campegium gium ad Comitia Norimbergensia ablegat, cum Ordinibus de Reformatione cleri per Germaniam deliberaturum. Cùm verò Reformationem oblatam non veram, sed personatam esse, utpote quæ non alios, quàm minutos & tenues è Clero tangeret, & crederetur cum magno Secularis potestatis præjudicio, Curiæ Romanæ & magnorum Præsulum dominio vires potiùs subministratura, atque ad majores rapinas majorémque tyrannidem aditum patefactura; Ordines intelligerent, ea rejecta, Concilium liberum in Germaniæ loco idoneo celebrari expetunt. Qui tamen Pontificiarum partium erant, Ferdinandus, Archiepiscopus Salisburgensis, Duces Bavariæ, Tridentinus & Ratisbonensis Episcopi, novémque etiam Episcoporum Legati, die sexto Julii A. M. D. XXIV. Norinbergæ unà cum Campegio convenientes Wormatiense edictum, quo Lutherus damnatus erat, urgent, Missæ abrogationem, aliáque severè prohibent, & post etiam canones Ecclesiasticos à Campegio reformandæ Ecclesiæ confectos, sanciunt. Carolus quoque Cæsar audito Comitiorum Norimbergensium, se absente, celebratorum edicto, Ordinibus indignatus, perinde ac si ad imminutionem potestatis suæ tenderet, in Comitiis Spirensibus sub finem Junii A. M. D. XXVI. habitis, Wormatiensis decreti executionem, quo ad scilicet cum Pontifice de Concilio egerit; literis plus satis imperiosis injungit. Cui tamen se parere posse Ordines reliqui negant. Interea Cæsarem inter & Gallos suborta sunt bella, in quibus Clemens suspectam habens Cæsaris Gallum captivum attinentis potentiam, tam non fidus in Carolum fuit memoria beneficiorum ante Pontificatum ab eodem acceptorum, ut fœdera fœderibus adversus ipsum accumulaverit, & perfidiam perfidiæ subinde junxerit. Quæ omnia sigillatim hoc loco commemorare nimis longum, & quia apud Authores, Johannem Ferranum in vitata Francisci I. Jovium, Tilium, alios passim obvia, supervacaneum fuerit. Id quidem constat, Clementem, quoties in foederis societatem à Carolo receptus fuit, toties ex socio hostem evasisse.Extant duae Epistolae A. M. D. XXVII. Oeniponte editae, Clementis una ad Carolum; altera Caroli ad Clementem, quâ is acriter Papae adversus Caesarem & Imperium iniquitatem, gladii politici usurpationem temerariam, collusionem cum Gallo, perfidiam, fraudulentam & callidam machinationem, perjuria perstringit.
units.tr: CLXIII. After Adrian died, not without suspicion of poison, Julius Medici, a kinsman of Pope Leo, called Clement VII, succeeded. Suave recounts several things about his birth and simony, which Pallavicini feebly refutes. Certainly the schism itself between him and the antipope Urban VI, whom he had created, was growing. Richard II, King of England, acknowledged the latter as the sole and true head of the Church. That Clement was almost entirely unlearned in letters and ignorant of sacred doctrine, delighted in mechanical arts, and of such a slack and lazy temperament that he investigated the secrets of craftsmen and the subtleties of their works with excessive and almost shameful cleverness, is attested by History, book XXXII. Adrian's reformation, which he had tacitly condemned, he passed over in silence; and, setting aside the hundred grievances of the Germans, of which some concerned the Roman Curia, but more the bishops, officials, parish priests and other clergy of Germany, he dealt with the former, because they detract from the authority of the Pope and smack of heresy, and neglected the latter, promising to satisfy them somehow. He sent Cardinal Campeggio to the Diet of Nuremberg, to deliberate with the Estates about a reformation of the clergy throughout Germany. But since the reformation offered was not genuine but a mask, as it touched only the petty and minor members of the clergy, and was believed to be going to strengthen the power of the Roman Curia and of the great prelates with great prejudice to the secular authority, and to open the way to greater plunder and greater tyranny, the Estates, understanding this, rejected it and demanded a free council in a suitable place in Germany. Yet Ferdinand, Archbishop of Salzburg, the Dukes of Bavaria, the bishops of Trent and Regensburg, and also the legates of nine bishops, who were on the papal side, met at Nuremberg on 6 July 1524 together with Campeggio, and pressed the Edict of Worms, by which Luther had been condemned, insisted strictly on the abrogation of the Mass and other matters, and afterwards sanctioned the ecclesiastical canons drawn up by Campeggio for the reform of the Church. Charles the Emperor also, having heard of the edict issued by the Diet of Nuremberg in his absence, was indignant with the Estates, as if they aimed at diminishing his power; and at the Diet of Speyer, held towards the end of June 1526, he enjoined by letters, far too imperiously, the execution of the Edict of Worms, by which, namely, he had dealt with the Pope about a council. The remaining Estates, however, refused to obey him. Meanwhile wars broke out between Charles and the French, in which Clement, regarding the power of Charles, who had taken the French king captive, with suspicion, was so untrue to Charles, forgetting the benefits he had received from him before his pontificate, that he kept piling treaties upon treaties against him, and repeatedly added perfidy to perfidy. To recount all these things one by one in this place would be too long, and superfluous, since they are found everywhere in authors such as John Ferrand in his life of Francis I, Jovius, Tillius and others. This much is certain: as often as Clement was received by Charles into alliance, so often did he turn from an ally into an enemy. Two letters were published at Innsbruck in 1527: one from Clement to Charles, the other from Charles to Clement, in which the latter sharply censures the Pope for his injustice against the Emperor and the Empire, his rash usurpation of the political sword, his collusion with the Frenchman, his perfidy, and his fraudulent and crafty machinations and perjuries.

units.la: CLXIV. Ob perfidiam illam Clementis in Italia etiam bellum gravissimum exarsit, in quo Ducibus Bor-
units.tr: CLXIV. Because of Clement's treachery, a most grievous war also broke out in Italy, in which, under the dukes Bor-

units.la: bonio & Freundspergio Roma capta, magnaque atrocitate in Romanos saevitum, & Clemens ipse nec quicquam adversus Hispanos & Germanos, ceu haereticos, Lutheranos & Marrhanos fulminans, in Adriani mole obsessus, atque inde in castrum Angeli captivus abductus, ibidemque propemodum fame dira confectus, ac vix tandem, ut contumeliosae servituti se eriperet, ad aequas conditiones foederis adactus est. Excusavit quidem se Pontifici Caesar, contestatus, injussu suo illud omne à feroci & indomito milite attentatum. Neque tamen minus justo Dei injurias sibi illatas ulciscentis judicio id omne acceptum tulit; rectius etiam & pro dignitate Imperatoris, quod cordati ejus consiliarii suaserant, facturus, si Romam ipse, dejecto Pseudo-Caesare Pontifice, occupâsset, & se non nomine solo, sed reapse Romanum Imperatorem esse patefecisset. Sed haesit altè nimis in latere ejus lethalis, nullóque dictamno sanabilis superstitio, quae ceu θεὸς ἀλλὰ πάθῳ illum, quò minùs sacerrimam impostura m Papae animo compleceretur, occaecavit. Neque aliud etiam in fatis erat, & Scripturas impleri oportuit. Ita novo foedere Caesar & Papa coaluere, cujus praecipua lex erat, ut sociatis auxiliis Lutherani omnes excidantur. Et Bononiam progressus
units.tr: Bononia, Freundsberg, having taken Rome, raged against the Romans with great savagery. Clement himself, who fulminated against the Spaniards and Germans as heretics, Lutherans and Marranos, was besieged in the mole of Hadrian and from there led away captive to the castle of Sant'Angelo, where he was nearly worn down by dreadful hunger. At last, to free himself from a humiliating servitude, he was forced to accept equal terms of treaty. Indeed, the Emperor excused himself to the Pope, declaring that all those outrages had been committed by his fierce and unruly soldiers without his command. Yet he took all this no less as a judgment of God punishing the injuries done to himself. He would have acted more rightly, and in a manner worthy of an Emperor, as his wise counsellors had advised, if he had himself occupied Rome, deposed the pseudo-Caesar, the Pope, and shown that he was Roman Emperor not in name only but in fact. But a deadly superstition, for which no dittany could cure, had stuck too deeply in his side; as though a god yet [θεὸς ἀλλὰ πάθῳ] by passion, it blinded him so that he did not embrace the most sacred imposture of the Pope in his heart. Nor was anything else in the fates, and the Scriptures had to be fulfilled. Thus Emperor and Pope were joined in a new covenant, the chief term of which was that, with aid pooled together, all the Lutherans should be destroyed. And advancing to Bologna...

units.la: E e Cæsar, ibi die, xxiv. Febr. A. M. D. xxx. à Pontifice, tanto apparatu luxúque, quanto ante eum Cæsarum nemo, coronam accepit. Paulò ante etiam quàm coronatio hæc contingeret, die nimirum xxiii. Decembr. A. M. D. xxix. Papa, Cæsar, Rex Ferdinandus, Gallus, Anglus, Principes Itali, Mediolanensis, Montferratensis, Mantuanus, urbes quoque Genua, Sena, Luca, aliæque arctissimum fœdus percusserunt, cujus palmaria conditio erat, συμφεξήν ἀξεῖν tueri Majestatem Pontificiam, & ad Sedis Romanæ obedientiam hæreticos & inobedientes quosvis modis quibuslibet compellere. Bononiæ etiam Cæsarem inter & Clementem de Concilio generali indicendo disceptatum; illo Concilium suadente & probante, hoc improbante & aversante vehementissimè. Conflictum rationum Suavis Polanus Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. I. ad A. M. D. xxix. prodidit. Cessitque tandem Carolus Papæ desideriis, certus posthac cum inobedientibus non tam rationum ponderibus, & suasionis illecebra, quàm authoritatis imperiique sui viribus decernere. Eo certè animo A. M. D. xxx. Augustam ad Comitia venit, ubi Confessione à Protestantibus exhibita, & partium conciliatione frustra tentata, sententiam nihil ominus mutat, & decreto de religione cusfo, etiam Concilium, invito & ringente post Pontifice, intra annum auspicandum promittit; móxque etiam de Pace cum Protestantibus ad Concilii tempus usque ineunda consilia agitat. Licet verò Papa sinuatis hic velis non alienum se à Concilio, dummodo in Italia illud celebretur, simulaverit; ejus tamen Cardinales Concilii necessitatem refutant palam, & executionem diplomatis Leonis urgent. Cæsar Concilium in Germania habendum pertendit, simulque Confessionis Augustanæ sectatoribus ad Concilium illud usque libertatem religionis indulget. Qua indulgentia, aliisque etiam causis irritatus Papa deserto iterum Cæsare, fœdus cum Galliæ Rege Francisco pangit Massiliæ, ubi Rex ad pedes Papæ prostratus eum adoravit; atque illud matrimonio proneptis suæ Catharinæ Medicæ cum filio Regis Henrico (cui Papa numeratis centum millibus aureorum, tres etiam gemmas nobilissimas, Genuam, Mediolanum, & Neapolin, pixidem scilicet Pandaræ in manu habens, dotis vicem promisit) firmat. Catharina illa est, quæ quarta Francorum furia dicta, trium Regum, Francisci II. Caroli IX. & Henrici III. mater, mirè post Galliam artibus & furore in filiis regnans turbavit. Celebratæ sunt nuptiæ tanto cum splendore & luxu dies triginta tres integros, ut hominum memoria nuptiæ Regum majori agitatæ nullæ sint. Rediitque ex nuptiis illis Franciscus à Pontifice in tyrannum & Maxentium quendam ita efferatus, ut fideles Regni sui dirissimis suppliciis afficere cœperit. Tandem Clemens, ceu Epiphanes & Herodes alter viscerum, quæsitissimis doloribus diu excruciatus, die xxv. Sept. A. M. D. XXXIV. miserè expiravit; non sine gaudio communi aulicorum etiam. Etsi enim, verba Suavis ad A. M. D. XXXIV. refero, quibusdam dotibus, naturali gravitate, parsimonia exemplari ac dissimulatione insigni multorum in se admirationem concitârat: ob avaritiam tamen, austeritatem & crudelitatem, quas semper exercuit, sed in morbo plus solito manifestavit, multo pluribus erat odiosus. Certè mortem ejus tanto exceptam esse gaudio, quanto erat electio. Pallavicinus etiam Hist. Concil. Trid. III. 16.8. fatetur; addens, caruisse ipsum dotibus, quæ animos conciliant; beneficentia & humanitate eum caruisse, creditumque caput Pontificatus, cujus revera solum dextera extiterit. Neminem plane oderat, ita de eo etiam Jovius Hist. lib. 32. scribit, quum neminem adamaret, præterquam ab occultiore causa conciliatos. His certè unis adeò favit intemperanter, ut ad summos honores, aut ad summum authoritatis locum, stabilesque divitias nullo proveheret pudore; multorum vero constanter oblivi​sceretur, qui ab optimis literarum studiis, veteríque obsequio commendationem & præmia meruissent. Hos quidem blandè appellabat, ut imagine gratiæ detineret, sed occultè oderat tanquam creditores.
units.tr: was there, on 24 February 1530, crowned by the Pontiff with a display and luxury greater than any of the Emperors before him had enjoyed. Shortly before this coronation, namely on 23 December 1529, the Pope, the Emperor, King Ferdinand, the French, the English, the Italian princes of Milan, Montferrat and Mantua, and the cities of Genoa, Siena, Lucca and others struck a most close alliance. Its chief term was to maintain [συμφωνὴν ἄγειν] the Pontifical Majesty and to compel heretics and all disobedient persons, by whatever means, to obey the Roman See. At Bologna too, the Emperor and Clement disputed about calling a general Council: the Emperor urged and approved it, while the Pope opposed it and vehemently resisted. Suavis Polanus has recorded the clash of opinions in his Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. I. under 1529. In the end Charles yielded to the Pope's wishes, being convinced that henceforth he must deal with the disobedient not so much by the weight of arguments and the allurement of persuasion as by the strength of his authority and power. With that intention, certainly, he came to the Diet at Augsburg in 1530. There, after the Confession had been presented by the Protestants and an attempt at reconciling the parties had failed, he nonetheless changed his mind. By a decree concerning religion he promised that a Council would be opened within a year, even though the Pope was unwilling and grumbling. Soon afterwards he also began to devise plans for making peace with the Protestants until the time of the Council. Although the Pope, with sails trimmed, pretended here that he was not opposed to a Council, provided it were held in Italy, his Cardinals openly denied that a Council was necessary and insisted on carrying out the decree of Leo. The Emperor insisted that the Council be held in Germany, and at the same time granted the followers of the Augsburg Confession freedom of religion until that Council. Irritated by this indulgence and by other causes, the Pope deserted the Emperor again and struck an alliance with the French King Francis at Marseilles. There the King, prostrate at the Pope's feet, adored him. And he confirmed the alliance by the marriage of his grand-niece Catherine de' Medici to the King's son Henry. The Pope promised as her dowry a hundred thousand gold crowns and three most noble gems, Genoa, Milan and Naples, holding, as it were, Pandora's box in his hand. This Catherine is the one called the fourth Fury of the French, mother of three kings, Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III, who, after France, reigned and troubled it wonderfully through her arts and her fury towards her sons. The wedding was celebrated with such splendour and luxury for thirty-three full days that no wedding of kings in human memory has been compared with it. From that marriage, Francis returned so inflamed by the Pope, and by a certain Maxentius, into a tyrant that he began to subject the faithful of his realm to the most dreadful punishments. At last Clement, like another Epiphanes and Herod of the bowels, long tortured by most exquisite pains, died miserably on 25 September 1534, not without the general joy of the courtiers too. For, as Suavis says under 1534, "although he had won the admiration of many by certain gifts, by natural dignity, exemplary frugality and notable dissimulation, yet on account of his avarice, harshness and cruelty, which he always practised but showed more plainly in his illness than usual, he was far more hated by very many." Certainly his death was received with as much joy as his election had been. Pallavicini, in Hist. Concil. Trid. III. 16.8., also admits this, adding that he lacked the gifts that win souls; that he lacked beneficence and humanity; and that he was thought the head of the Pontificate, whose right hand alone he really was. "He hated no one outright," so Jovius also writes of him in Hist. lib. 32., "since he loved no one, except those whom he had attached by some hidden cause. To these alone he showed such unrestrained favour that he advanced them to the highest honours, or to the highest place of authority, and to lasting wealth, without any shame. But he constantly forgot the many who had earned commendation and rewards by the best literary studies and by long loyalty. These he indeed addressed kindly, to keep them held by the image of grace, but secretly he hated them as creditors."

units.la: C L X V. Clemente fati clementia humanis rebus exempto P. Petrus Lossius Romanus, ex Furnesiorum familia, qui Pauli III. nomen sibi vendicavit, successit. De vita & moribus, parricidiis inprimis, proditionibus, sacrilegiis, veneficiis, incestibus & stupris ejus nefandis, peculiaris liber Italicè scriptus, qui Ochini nomen præfert, sed ab alio, cui Paulus ille propiùs innotuit, scriptus putatur, à Thuano, Sleidano aliisque allegatus, talia prodidit, ut insanire eum, qui alium Antichristum tum expectavit, oportuerit. Alibi recitata, & ab Adversario cætera protervo satis in C. T. veritate inextincta, ipsoque etiam præcentore ejus Pallavicino Lib. III. 17:5. leviter, nullisque rationibus solidis discussa, repetere heic non libet. Id quidem certum & à Panvinio etiam memoratum, illum quatuordecim Cardinalium electionibus septuaginta & unum in Purpuratorum Senatum adoptâsse, atque ea ratione immensam auri vim corrogâsse. Pecunias plerasque tum ad luxum & voluptates, quibus deditum eum supra modum fuisse facinora ejus loquuntur: tum ad Petrum Aloysium Parmæ & Placentiæ Ducem à se creatum, nothum suum, Sodomæ spurcissimo crimine infamem; & ex eodem notho, nec non Constantia itidem filia notha, progenitos nepotes Alexandrum Farnesium, & Guidonem Ascanium Sforziam, (quorum illum quatuordecim, hunc sedecim annos natum Cardinales creavit;) exornandos impendit. Quam Pauli Simoniam ita Pallavicinus loco citato extenuat, ut asserat, eum, qui ob hanc humanæ conditionis labem Pontifices vituperat, inesse Divinum quidpiam in Pontificatu fateri. Belle scilicet, ceu ἄτοπον & absurdum, in Pontificatu Divinum quidpiam non inesse, inferens; & Simoniam labem esse ne quidem vituperandam in Pontifice, statuens.
units.tr: CLXV. When Clement had been removed from human affairs by the mercy of fate, P. Petrus Lossius of Rome, of the Farnese family, who claimed for himself the name of Paul III, succeeded him. A special book written in Italian, which bears the name of Ochino but is thought to have been written by someone else, to whom that Paul became better known, describes his life and morals, above all his parricides, treacheries, sacrileges, poisonings, incests and his unspeakable debaucheries. It was cited by Thuanus, Sleidan and others, and it reported such things that anyone who then expected another Antichrist would have had to be mad. I do not wish to repeat here what has been recited elsewhere, and what the stubborn Adversary has in C. T. veritate inextincta and what his own precentor Pallavicini has passed over lightly, in Lib. III. 17:5., without any solid arguments. This much is certain, and Panvinio also records it: that he adopted seventy-one men into the Senate of Cardinals through fourteen elections of Cardinals, and by this means gathered an immense heap of gold. He spent much of this money on luxury and pleasures, to which, as his deeds show, he was given beyond measure. Some he spent on Peter Aloysius, whom he created Duke of Parma and Piacenza, his bastard son, infamous for the most filthy crime of Sodom; and on the grandsons born of that same bastard and of Constance, also a bastard daughter, Alexander Farnese and Guido Ascanius Sforza, whom he created Cardinals, the first at fourteen years of age, the second at sixteen, to adorn them. Pallavicini, in the place cited, so softens this Simony of Paul that he asserts that "whoever blames Popes for this stain of human condition must admit that something divine dwells in the Pontificate." Nicely indeed, as if inferring, absurdly, that nothing divine dwells in the Pontificate; and, judging that Simony is a stain not even to be blamed in a Pope.

units.la: CLXVI. Dissidia in religione mota latiùs serpere cùm cerneret Paulus, antecessore suo astutior, studium amicitiæ Cæsareæ singulare præ se tulit, quò facilius ipsum cum aliis Principibus ad arma in Protestantes capienda, sanguinis Germanici sitientissimus concitare posset; Et importuna quidem flagitatione ita concitavit denique, ut bellum dirissimum in Germania exarserit, in quo duo Principes præpotentes Euangelici acie inferiores in Cæsaris potestatem captivi concesserunt. Veruntamen ea rerum conversio facta est, ut dimissis Principibus captivis, ac religionis libertate Germanis concessa, Papalis amicitiæ fructus spe multò minores Cæsar senserit, malueritque se, post impensa Papæ servitia, Germanorum Principum amicitiam Pontificio fœderi præposuisse. Nam etsi minores in ipsum Pauli tardiorésque quàm aliorum Pontificum machinationes fuerunt: tamen factus tandem à Cæsare alienior, quòd is Parmam atque Placentiam post filium Aloysium conjuratione sublatum reposcenti, negâsset, eas se civitates in ditionis ac dignitatis Imperialis præjudicium alienare posse; vindictam agitans de transitu ad Gallicas partes consilia suscepit; perfecturus etiam, nisi præveritente morte ad plures abiisset.
units.tr: CLXVI. Seeing that the disputes about religion were creeping more widely, Paul, shrewder than his predecessor, displayed a singular zeal for friendship with the Emperor, so that he could more easily stir up the Emperor, who thirsted for German blood, together with other Princes, to take up arms against the Protestants. And by importunate urging he at last stirred him up so that a most dreadful war blazed up in Germany, in which two very powerful Evangelical Princes, inferior in the field, surrendered captive into the Emperor's power. Yet the situation turned out so that, after the captive Princes were released and freedom of religion was granted to the Germans, the Emperor perceived far smaller fruits from the Papal friendship than he had hoped. He preferred, after lavishing services on the Pope, to have placed the friendship of the German Princes above the Pontifical alliance. For although Paul's machinations against him were milder and slower than those of other Popes, nonetheless he at last became more estranged from the Emperor, because when the Emperor refused to give back Parma and Piacenza, which had been taken from his son Aloysius after a conspiracy, claiming that he could not alienate those cities to the prejudice of the Imperial jurisdiction and dignity, Paul, planning vengeance, undertook plans for going over to the French side. He would have carried them out, had not death, coming first, taken him away to the many others.

units.la: CLXVII. Concilii Generalis convocandi, & reformandæ Ecclesiæ statim atque electus Papa est, studium einixum præ se tulit. Delectis igitur sive tribus, uti Suavis habet, sive pluribus, uti Pallavicinus narrat Purpuratis, de reformanda Ecclesia consultationem injungit: diplomate etiam exhibito, quo rerum capita tractanda exponebantur. Decretum tamen mox, ne vulgaretur diploma illud, quippe quod (verba Pallavicini lib. III. 17:3. refero( dum reformari mores jubebat, fatebatur in iis deformationem inesse, adeóque obtrectationes hæreticorum apud vulgus confirmasset. Missis dein huc illuc Legatis, Petro Paulo Vergerio cum primis in Germaniam, consilium suum de Concilio celebrando aperit. Quod, à Protestantibus graves ob causas rejectum licet, ille prosequitur, diplomate edito, quo Mantuam Concilii locum designavit. Cùm vero id Ducis Mantuæ, uti quidem Papa tricabatur, culpa non succederet, suspicionis, quasi minùs vel Concilio vel Reformationi faveret, amoliendæ causa, diploma aliud de emendanda Curia Romana vulgavit, consiliique de ea maturè capiendi negotium quatuor Cardinalibus, puta Contareno, Theatino, Sadoleto & Reginaldo, nec non quinque Præsulibus dedit. Extat adhuc delegatorum illorum Cardinalium & Præsulum Consilium, sub hoc titulo: Consilium delectorum Cardinalium & Præsulum aliorum de emendanda Ecclesia jussu Papæ Pauli III. conscriptum & exhibitum A. M. D. XXXVIII. In consilio eo Romanæ Curiæ morbi & ulcera olidissima ingenuè deteguntur.
units.tr: CLXVII. As soon as he was elected Pope, he openly showed his eager zeal for convoking a General Council and reforming the Church. He therefore charged a group of chosen cardinals, three as Suavis reports or more as Pallavicini relates, with consulting on the reform of the Church, and he also presented a document setting out the main points to be treated. Soon afterwards, however, he ordered that this document not be made public, since (I quote Pallavicini's words, lib. III. 17:3) while he ordered morals to be reformed, he admitted that deformity was present in them, and so he had confirmed the slanders of the heretics among the common people. Then he sent legates here and there, above all Pietro Paolo Vergerio into Germany, and revealed his plan for holding a Council. Although the Protestants rejected it for serious reasons, he pursued it, issuing a document that designated Mantua as the place of the Council. But since this did not succeed through the fault of the Duke of Mantua, as the Pope was persuaded, he issued another document concerning the amendment of the Roman Curia, to remove the suspicion that he favoured the Council or reform less. He gave the task of deliberating on it with due care to four cardinals, namely Contarini, the Theatine, Sadoleto and Reginald, and also to five prelates. The Consultation of those delegated cardinals and prelates still survives, under this title: Consultation of the chosen cardinals and other prelates on the amendment of the Church, drawn up and presented by order of Pope Paul III, A.M.D. XXXVIII. In that consultation the foul diseases and festering ulcers of the Roman Curia are candidly laid bare.

units.la: CLXVIII. Et initio quidem Cardinales laudato Paulo, ejúsque instituto, ab eodem sibi in mandatis datum narrant, ut nullius aut commodi Papæ, aut cujuscunque alterius habita ratione ipsi significarent abusus illos, gravissimos videlicet morbos, quibus jam pridem Ecclesia Dei laboret, ac præsertim hæc Romana Curia, quibus effectum prope sit, ut paulatim ac sensim ingravescentibus pestiferis his morbis magnam hanc, quam vident, ruinam traxerit, Addunt, ἀξιομνημόνευτα hæc: Et quoniam Sanctitas tua, Spiritu Dei erudita, qui, ut inquit Augustinus, loquitur in cordibus nullo verborum strepitu, probè noverat, principium horum malorum inde fuisse, quòd nonnulli Pontifices tui Prædecessores prurientes auribus, ut inquit Apostolus Paulus, coacervaverunt sibi Magistros ad desideria sua, non ut ab eis discerent, quod
units.tr: CLXVIII. At the beginning the cardinals praise Paul and his plan, and report that he had instructed them to point out to him, without regard to the advantage of the Pope or of anyone else, those abuses, namely the most grievous diseases from which the Church of God has long been suffering, and especially this Roman Curia, diseases which have brought about, as they gradually and steadily grew worse, the great ruin that they now see. They add these remarks, [ἀξιομνημόνευτα]: And since Your Holiness, taught by the Spirit of God, who, as Augustine says, speaks in hearts without any noise of words, knew well that the origin of these evils lay in the fact that some of your predecessors, itching in their ears, as the Apostle Paul says, heaped up for themselves teachers to suit their desires, not to learn from them what they ought to do, but so that by their zeal and cunning a method might be found by which what pleased them would be allowed. From this it followed, apart from the fact that flattery follows every principate like a shadow follows a body, that access of truth to the ears of princes has always been most difficult, because…

units.la: Concilium ejus jussu à Cardinalibus & Episcopis conscriptum de reformanda Curia Romana.
units.tr: The Council, drawn up by order of the Pope by the Cardinals and Bishops, on the reform of the Roman Curia.

units.la: Ejus præcipua capita. quod facere deberent, sed ut eorum studio & calliditate inveniretur ratio, qua liceret id quod liberet: inde effectum est, praeterquam quòd Principatum omnem sequitur adulatio, ut umbra corpus: difficilimúsque semper fuit aditus veritatis ad aures Principum, quòd confestim prodirent Doctores, qui docerent, Pontificem esse Dominum beneficiorum omnium; ac ideò cum Dominus jure vendat id quod suum est, necessariò sequi, in Pontificem non posse sadere Simoniam, ita quòd voluntas Pontificis, qualiscunque ea fuerit, sit regula qua ejus operationes & actiones dirigantur: ex quo procul dubio effici, ut quicquid libeat, liceat. Ex hoc fonte, Sancte Pater, tanquam ex equo Trojano irrupere in Ecclesiam Dei tot abusus, & tam gravissimi morbi, quibus nunc conspicimus eam ad desperationem ferè salutis laborare, vel manâsse harum rerum famam ad infideles usque; credat Sanctitas vestra scientibus, qui ob hanc praecipuè causam Christianam religionem derident adeò, ut per nos, per nos, inquimus, blasphemetur nomen Christi inter gentes. Tu verò Sanctissime Pater, vidisti, inde incipiendam esse medicationem, unde primùm ortus est morbus. Antea verò quàm abusus perstringerent, monent Pontificem, ne putet sibi dispensare licere in legibus, nisi urgenti de causa & necessaria: neque licere Pontifici & Vicario Christi in usu potestatis clavium lucrum aliquod sibi comparare. Post abusus plures, eósque gravissimos, in primis circa ordinationem Clericorum, collationem beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum, maximè Curatorum, expectativas, reservationes beneficiorum, absentiam Clericorum ab Ecclesiis suis, exemptiones à jurisdictione Ordinarii, multitudinem Ordinum Religiosorum, institutionem publicam in Gymnasiis, Gratias & dispensationes, aliosque similes ad incudem revocant. Demum ad ipsum Romanum Episcopum & Romanam Ecclesiam in specie accedentes, inter alia scribunt: In hac urbe meretrices ut matronae incedunt per urbem, seu mula vehuntur, quas assectantur de media die nobiles familiares Cardinalium, Clericíque. Nulla in urbe vidimus hanc corruptionem, praeterquam in hac omnium exemplari. Habitant etiam insignes ædes. Consilium isthoc scriptum ad Cardinalium Senatum Pontifex retulit, ubi de eo dimicatio gravis inter Cardinalem Scombergium, Capuanum Archiepiscopum, & Johannem Petrum Caraffam, Cardinalem Theatinum suborta est; illo pertendente, temporum conditionem nullam ejus generis emendationem pati, & Lutheranos inde jactantiæ occasionem sumpturos, habituros scilicet Pontificios reos confitentes: hoc vero necessitatem reformationis ejusmodi irrefragabilem demonstrante. Cùm ita sententiis Cardinales variarent, Papa in aliud tempus consilium rejecit, & de toto negotio illo sacrum silentium suis injunxit. Emanavit nihilominus scriptum per Cardinalem Capuanum, qui ejus exemplar in Germaniam misit, conscio, uti rebantur multi, Pontifice, ut colligerent inde Germani reformationem Ecclesiæ sibi curæ cordíque esse.
units.tr: Its main heads. It was what they ought to do, but a method was found, through their zeal and cunning, by which it was lawful to do whatever pleased. From this it has come about that, as shadow follows body, flattery follows every princely rule; and access of truth to the ears of princes has always been most difficult, because teachers at once came forward who taught that the Pope is lord of all benefices, and therefore, since a lord may lawfully sell what is his own, it necessarily follows that simony cannot be committed by the Pope; so that the will of the Pope, whatever it may be, is the rule by which his operations and actions are directed; from which, without doubt, it follows that whatever he pleases is lawful. From this source, Holy Father, as from the Trojan horse, so many abuses and such grievous diseases, by which we now see her suffering almost to the point of despair of salvation, have burst into the Church of God, or the report of these things has spread even to the unbelievers. Let Your Holiness believe those who know, who for this reason above all deride the Christian religion, so that, through us, through us I say, the name of Christ is blasphemed among the nations. But you, most holy Father, have seen that healing must begin where the disease first arose. Before they touch on the abuses, they warn the Pope that he should not think he may dispense from the laws except for an urgent and necessary cause, and that it is not lawful for the Pope and Vicar of Christ to gain any profit for himself in using the power of the keys. After many abuses, and very grievous ones, they recall to the anvil in particular the ordination of clergy, the conferring of ecclesiastical benefices, above all parish benefices, expectancies, reservations of benefices, the absence of clergy from their churches, exemptions from the jurisdiction of the ordinary, the multitude of religious orders, public teaching in the schools, graces and dispensations, and other similar matters. Finally, coming to the Roman bishop himself and the Roman Church in particular, they write among other things: In this city prostitutes walk through the city like matrons, or are carried on mules, and they are attended in broad daylight by noble household servants of Cardinals and clerics. We have seen this corruption in no other city, except in this exemplar of all. They also keep splendid houses. The Pope referred this written counsel to the senate of Cardinals, and there a serious dispute about it arose between Cardinal Scomberg, the Archbishop of Capua, and Giovanni Pietro Carafa, the Theatine Cardinal. The former maintained that the condition of the times allowed no reform of this kind, and that the Lutherans would take from it an occasion for boasting, since they would have the Papists as confessed culprits; the latter declared that the necessity of such a reform was undeniable. Since the Cardinals thus differed in their opinions, the Pope put off the counsel to another time and enjoined on his men a sacred silence about the whole business. Nevertheless a writing was circulated by Cardinal Capua, who sent a copy of it into Germany, with the Pope's knowledge, as many thought, so that the Germans might gather from it that the reform of the Church was a matter of care and concern to him.

units.la: CLXIX. Liquet autem ex his Pauli III. & superiùs etiam memoratis Adriani consiliis, aliorùmque etiam, Rivii cumprimis; qui circa hæc tempora de abusibus Ecclesiasticis scripsit; confessione, Papistas magis ingenuos se ante Concilium Tridentinum præstitisse, neque vel morbos Ecclesiæ Romanæ plane dissimulâsse, vel Pontificis impeccantiam, detur venia Tertulliani verbo, mordicus propugnâsse. Sicut autem accidere crebrò videmus ut aciem inclinatam jam & labantem supervenientes integri restituant, & vi majore in hostem obvertantur: ita sub eodem Paulo Jesuitæ natales suos inauspicatos nacti, tempore scilicet novus & collectitius miles, paulatim verò factus usu veteranus, & ferè triarius, aliíque etiam, nihil fracti pugnarum priorum eventu, cunctatione conditionibúsque omnibus animosè excussis, & quæ molliores illi dederant, receptis, pugnam fortiter redintegrárunt, perfrictè negantes, Papam in fide, imò etiam, quod nuper addiderunt, runt, in facto unquam errasse, vel errare potuisse. Sicut igitur ante annos circiter quadringentos, cum Pontificia Sedes a Waldensibus impeti graviter coepisset, Papatum ruentem a Monachis Dominicanis recens exortis suffultum esse, supra observavimus: ita hoc tempore a Jesuitis ceu Catholicae fidei Principibus (ita eos, appellat in Philippica Sylvanus Jesuita, mulos mulus) caput infelix orco proferentibus, Papatus idem gravissimè concussus, sustineri potissimum coepit. Eorum institutum primus Paulus III. edita V. Cal. Octob. A. M. D. XL. Bulla, quam Polyhistor Hospinianus Historiae Jesuitarum pag. 250. 251. inseruit, & laudavit & approbavit, commemorans, dilectos filios, Ignatium de Loyola, Petrum Fabrum, Jacobum Laynez, Franciscum Xavier &c. Spiritu S. ut pie credatur, afflatos, jamdudum e diversis mundi regionibus discedentes in unum convenisse, & Socios effectos, abdicatis hujus Seculi illecebris, vitam suam perpetuo Domini nostri Jesu Christi, atque suo & aliorum Successorum suorum Romanorum Pontificum servitio dedicasse, &c. Subjecta formula Regulae Societatis, cujus initium est: Quicunque in Societate nostra, quam Jesu (Loyolae scribere debuerant) nomine insigniri cupimus, vult sub crucis vexillo (egregium scilicet crucis vexillum, sub quo militantes mundi hujus potentia suffulti, carnis desideriis toti indulgent!) Deo militare, & soli Domino atque Romano Pontifici ejus in terris Vicario servire &c. declarat Paulus, se praemissa omnia Apostolica authoritate ex certa scientia approbare, confirmare & benedicere: ac perpetuae firmitatis munimine roborare; non obstantibus Generalis Concilii (Lateranensis scilicet, quo novorum Ordinum institutio prohibita est) & felicis recordationis Gregorii Papae X. Praedecessoris sui, ac quibusvis aliis constitutionibus & ordinationibus Apostolicis, caeterisque contrariis quibuscunque. Ubi non sine Numine Papae exciderunt verba, se non obstantibus quibusvis constitutionibus & ordinationibus Apostolicis Jesuitarum tarum Ordinem laudare & approbare. Obstabant sanè Ordinationes Apostolicæ impiis moliminibus. Sed non obstantibus iis, adeóque neglectis, posthabitis, rejectis nefas Papa tentavit, dum nova munimenta ad manum succederent, quibus Sedes Pontificia insisteret. Nam peculiare esse huic Societati tueri Apostolicam Sedem, Romanque Pontificis authoritatem, ex Bulla Canonizationis Ignatii, Mutius Vitellesius comprobat. Talis omnino cum fuerit novella illa & Atlantica Societas, non immeritò paulò post A. M. D. LIV. Sorbona à suprema Galliæ Curia de ea judicium suum promere jussa, illud satis φηλίβλυκον promsit, & sub finem omnia in pauca contrahens sic declaravit: His omnibus atque aliis diligenter exploratis & examinatis & perpensis, hæc Societas videtur in negotio fidei periculosa, pacis Ecclesiasticæ perturbativa, Monasticæ religionis eversiva, & magis ad destructionem quàm ædificationem.
units.tr: CLXIX. It is clear from these counsels of Paul III and of Adrian mentioned above, and of others as well, especially Rivius, who wrote about ecclesiastical abuses around this time, that before the Council of Trent the Papists showed themselves more candid, and neither entirely dissembled the diseases of the Roman Church nor defended, to use Tertullian's word with pardon, the impeccability of the Pope with tooth and nail. But just as we often see that the wavering and tottering battle line is restored by fresh troops arriving, and is turned against the enemy with greater force, so under the same Paul the Jesuits, whose birth was unlucky, and others also, not broken by the outcome of the earlier battles, shaking off with spirit all delay and all conditions, and accepting what those softer men had given, renewed the fight vigorously, flatly denying that the Pope had ever erred, or could err, in faith, or indeed, as they have recently added, in fact. So, as we observed above, about four hundred years ago, when the Pontifical See had begun to be grievously attacked by the Waldensians, the falling Papacy was propped up by the newly arisen Dominican monks; so at this time, the same Papacy, sorely shaken, has begun to be sustained chiefly by the Jesuits, who, as Princes of the Catholic faith (so Sylvanus the Jesuit calls them in his Philippic, mule the mule), are sending an unlucky head down to Orcus. The first to approve their institute was Paul III, by the bull issued on the 5th day before the Kalends of October in the year 1540, which the learned Hospinian included in his History of the Jesuits, pp. 250, 251, and in which he both praised and approved it, recalling our beloved sons Ignatius of Loyola, Peter Faber, James Laynez, Francis Xavier, etc., inspired, as we piously believe, by the Holy Spirit, who, having left various regions of the world, came together into one and became companions, having renounced the allurements of this age, and dedicated their lives to the perpetual service of our Lord Jesus Christ and of their successors the Roman Pontiffs, etc. The formula of the Rule of the Society is attached, beginning: Whoever wishes to serve God under the banner of the cross in our Society, which we desire to be distinguished by the name of Jesus (they ought to have written Loyola) and to serve the Lord alone and the Roman Pontiff, his Vicar on earth, etc. (the splendid banner of the cross, under which soldiers, supported by the power of this world, give themselves wholly to the desires of the flesh!). Paul declares that he approves, confirms and blesses all the foregoing by Apostolic authority, from certain knowledge, and strengthens them with the safeguard of perpetual firmness; notwithstanding the General Council (namely the Lateran, by which the institution of new orders was forbidden), and of Pope Gregory X of happy memory, his predecessor, and any other Apostolic constitutions and ordinances, and all other things to the contrary. Here words slipped out, not without the will of the Pope, that he praises and approves the Order of the Jesuits notwithstanding any Apostolic constitutions and ordinances. Certainly the Apostolic ordinances stood in the way of their impious undertakings. But the Pope attempted an outrage by setting these aside, neglecting, postponing and rejecting them, while new defences came to hand on which the Pontifical See could stand. For Mutius Vitellesius shows from the bull of canonization of Ignatius that it is peculiar to this Society to defend the Apostolic See and the authority of the Roman Pontiff. Since that new and Atlantean Society was of such a kind from the beginning, not without reason, shortly after the year 1554, the Sorbonne was ordered by the supreme court of France to give its judgment on it; it pronounced with rather smooth-tongued words [φηλίβλυκον: smooth-tongued, flattering], and at the end, summing everything up briefly, declared: After all these things and others have been diligently explored, examined and weighed, this Society seems dangerous in matters of faith, disruptive of ecclesiastical peace, subversive of monastic religion, and more for destruction than for building up.

units.la: CLXX. Atque talis cum fuerit in prima sui origine, authoritatem sacerimæ professionis præferens licet Societas; multò magis etiam successu temporis, uti solent mali εἰς πλεῖον προκόπτειν ἀσεβείας ad majorem in dies impietatem proficere (2 Tim. II. 16.) in pejus ita degeneravit, ut malorum omnium sentina quædam hodie dici mereatur. Cujus rei testes domestici complures cordatíque in medium afferri possent, quorum non paucos recentiores Celeb. Hottingerus Histor. Eccles. Tom. v. pag. 495. &c. indigitat. Omnium instar esse potest Scriptor nuperus, paucis licet inter nostros notus, ex media Italia, gravissimus, Julius Clemens Placentinus, ex illustri Scotorum familia, qui scripto, & opera Francisci Solanguis Nobilis Cremensis Parisiis (ita frons libri habet, cum Venetiis potius impressus sit) vulgato de Potestate Pontificia in Societatem Jesu libro, Societatis hujus morbos procedente tempore contractos fusè & eruditissimè detexit. Et parte quidem libri ejus lectu dignissimi
units.tr: CLXX. Although the Society was of this character in its first origin, while professing the authority of a most sacred calling, it degenerated much more as time went on, as bad men usually do, who "advance further in impiety" from day to day (2 Tim. 2:16) [εἰς πλεῖον προκόπτειν ἀσεβείας]. It became so corrupt that it may now rightly be called a sink of every vice. Many trustworthy witnesses from among its own members could be produced on this point, and the distinguished Hottinger, Histor. Eccles. vol. 5, p. 495, etc., names not a few of the more recent ones. Among them all, the most serious writer may stand as an example. He is a recent author from the middle of Italy, little known among us, Julius Clemens of Piacenza, of the distinguished Scottish family. In his work, published in Paris (so the title page says, though it was printed rather in Venice), On the Papal Power over the Society of Jesus, written with the help of Francisco Solanguis, a noble of Cremona, he laid bare in full and in a most learned way the diseases that the Society contracted as time went on. Some parts of his book are very well worth reading.

units.la: Su cessu temporis ordo ille degenerat,
units.tr: As time went on, that order degenerated.

units.la: teste in peculiari scripto Julio Clemente Scoto. gnissimi tertia pag. 108-149. proponit multa, in quibus Religiosi Societatis Jesu derogarint Constitutionibus ab Ignatio conscriptis, aliisque Legibus in Congregationibus Generalibus editis. Parte quarta pag. 149-195. exponit illa, in quibus Societatis Jesu Religiosi a primævo Majorum suorum Spiritu, a Constitutionum Regularumque observantia, & a religiosa perfectione defecerint. Parte quinta pag. 195-235. ex ipsis Jesuitarum libris recenset causas, propter quas deficere potuerit primigenius Spiritus in Societatis Jesu Religiosis. Parte sexta pag. 235-364. declarat illa, in quibus Religio Societatis Jesu praesenti Reformatione indigere possit. Parte septima pag. 364-382. damna ab hac Societate a primævo Spiritu deficiente imminentia prosequitur.
units.tr: as witnessed in a separate writing by Julius Clemens the Scot, a very serious writer, in the third part, pp. 108-149, he sets out many points in which the religious of the Society of Jesus departed from the Constitutions written by Ignatius and from the other laws issued in the General Congregations. In the fourth part, pp. 149-195, he sets out those points in which the religious of the Society of Jesus fell away from the spirit of their founders, from observance of the Constitutions and Rules, and from religious perfection. In the fifth part, pp. 195-235, he lists from the Jesuits' own books the causes on account of which the original spirit could have failed among the religious of the Society of Jesus. In the sixth part, pp. 235-364, he explains those points in which the religion of the Society of Jesus might need reform at the present time. In the seventh part, pp. 364-382, he follows up the harms threatening this Society now that the original spirit has failed.

units.la: CLXXI.
units.tr: CLXXI.

units.la: Eodem Paulo Pontifice, uti etiam Masenio in Anima historiarum observatum; Capucinorum quoque Secta caput infelix extulit; incerto licet authore, quem alii Bernhardinum Ochinum: alii Gotfridum Varaglium Buscanum, Pedemontanum, qui etiam Ordinis Generalis electus, at post Euangelicam veritatem amplexus Taurini penult. Dec. A. M. D. LVII. ob constantem ejus profesionem vivus combustus est; alii Matthæum Bascium Umbrum suisse conjectant. Uti Jesuitæ doctrinæ profunditatem & prudentiam singularem: ita Capucini innocuam simplicitatem præ se tulerunt. Temperata igitur Jesuitarum serpentina prudentia, & Capucinorum simplicitate columbina egregiè suffulciri Papatum, & simpliciorum credulitati imponi posse, Paulus forte credidit. Sed detracta utrisque larva pridem est, & illorum perfidia, doli, sævitia; horum hypocrisis apertam in lucem prolata est.
units.tr: In the same pontificate of Paul, as also observed by Masenius in Anima historiarum, the sect of the Capuchins also put forth its unhappy head. The author is uncertain. Some name Bernardino Ochino; others suppose Gottfried Varaglio of Buscano in Piedmont, who was also elected General of the Order but afterward embraced the Evangelical truth, and was burned alive at Turin on the last but one day of December 1557 because of his steadfast profession. Others conjecture that Matthew Bascio was an Umbrian. As the Jesuits showed a singular depth of doctrine and prudence, so the Capuchins displayed an harmless simplicity. Paul perhaps believed that the Papacy could be well supported by the serpentine prudence of the Jesuits and the dove-like simplicity of the Capuchins, and imposed on the credulity of the simpler sort. But the mask has long since been stripped from both, and the treachery, deceit and cruelty of the one, and the hypocrisy of the other, have been brought into the open light.

units.la: CLXXII.
units.tr: CLXXII.

units.la: Cùm non procederet Concilium Mantuæ indictum, Pontifex Novembri A. M. D. XXXVII. novo diplomate illud Vincentiam indicit, & propinquam hiemem causatus, ad Calendas usque Majas A. M. D. XXXVIII. tempus ejus extrahit. Cúmque ne sic quidem negotium procederet, tandem Tridentum, vicinum Germaniæ oppidum deligitur. Eò cùm vocasset Paulus Bulla indictionis ad Idus Augusti A. M. D. XLII. Pontificii consilium probárunt: at improbárunt Protestantes, qui liberum Concilium, nec à Papa convocatum, nec in Urbe Papæ obnoxia celebrandum constanter flagitárunt. Neque tamen, intercedentibus variis, ejus initium ante diem XIII. Dec. A. M. D. XLV. quo prima Sessio successit, factum est.
