Et decem quidem primis Sessionibus sub Paulo III. habitis decreta fidei est Reformationis, variáque contra Euangelicos anathemata cusa, alibi ad partes vocata, historiamque Sessionum, Pontificis & Curiæ Romanæ παυσρ-γίαν propalantem discussam, heic repetere nihil attinet.
units.tr: Since the Council announced at Mantua did not proceed, the Pontiff, in November of the year 1537, by a new decree summoned it to Vicenza, and on the plea of the approaching winter, he prolonged the time for it until the first of May 1538. When even so the business did not go forward, at last Trent, a town near Germany, was chosen. When Paul had summoned the Council there by the bull of indiction for 13 August 1542, the Papists approved the plan, but the Protestants disapproved. They steadily demanded a free council, not convoked by the Pope, and not to be held in the city subject to the Pope. Nevertheless, through various interventions, it was not begun before 13 December 1545, when the first session took place. As for the decrees of faith and reformation issued in the first ten sessions under Paul III, and the various anathemas struck out against the Evangelicals, which have been called to account elsewhere, it is pointless to repeat here the history of the sessions, which reveals the idleness of the Pope and the Roman Curia, and has been discussed.

units.la: CLXXIII. Reformatio certè in capite & membris Ecclesiæ ab universo orbe Christiano desiderata, & ab Adriano Pontifice etiam promissa fuerat. Fidei verò reformatio sincera tantùm abest ut successerit ulla, ut deformatio ejus major, & errorum deterimorum solennis confirmatio Ecclesiam Pontificiam incestaverit magis. Morum verò Reformatio vel nulla omnino, vel ludicra tota fuit. Omnium pæne malorum radicem in Papa & Curia Romana, & utriusque tyrannide, ambitione, avaritia, luxu fixam non attingere, nedum tollere ausi Patres sunt. Et si qua salutaria decreta Pontificem & Curiam obliquè ferientia cudi visa sunt, iis nervos succidit omnes tum secutum Sess. XXV. 21. decretum, ut in omnibus de morum Reformatione & Ecclesiastica disciplina decretis salva semper Sedis Apostolicæ authoritas & sit & esse intelligatur: tum jus interpretandi & declarandi singula Concilii decreta. quod Synodo indulgente sibi Papa reservavit. quæ duo efficere posse, ut omnia Papæ & Curiæ noxia decreta in nihilum recidant, & sensim sine sensu in antiquum cuncta statum redigantur; Pontifici Concilium confirmare, eò quòd Sedi Pontificiæ nonnullâ ejus decreta præjudicare viderentur, cunctanti, Cardinalis Amulius, & Episcopus Vestanus suggesserunt.
units.tr: CLXXIII. Reformation of the Church in head and members had certainly been desired by the whole Christian world, and Pope Adrian had even promised it. Yet a sincere reformation of faith has been so far from happening at all that its deformation was greater, and the solemn confirmation of worse errors defiled the Papist Church all the more. Reformation of morals was either wholly absent or entirely a sham. The Fathers did not dare even to touch, much less to uproot, the root of almost all evils, which is fixed in the Pope and the Roman Curia and in the tyranny, ambition, avarice and luxury of both. And if any wholesome decrees that struck indirectly at the Pope and the Curia seemed to have been framed, the decree that followed them, Sess. XXV. 21., cut all their sinews: that in all decrees on the reformation of morals and ecclesiastical discipline the authority of the Apostolic See always remains, and is to be understood to remain, safe. Then there was the right of interpreting and declaring the individual decrees of the Council, which the Pope, with the Synod's indulgence, reserved to himself. These two things could bring it about that all the Pope's and the Curia's harmful decrees come to nothing, and that gradually, without anyone noticing, everything is brought back to its former state. When the Pope hesitated, Cardinal Amulio and the Bishop of Vestanum advised him to have the Council confirm these decrees, since some of them seemed to prejudice the Pontifical See.

units.la: CLXXIV. Unum addo, in Congregatione die XVIII. & XXII. Jan. A. M. D. XLVI. habita quæsitum anxiéque disceptatum esse, à decisione dogmatum fidei, an à reformatione morum & abusuum capiendum sit initium? Prius Pontificii, Cæsarei posterius pertenderant. Et Pontificiorum quidem rationes Pallavicinus Hist. C. T. lib. VI. 7 : 2. 3. fusè edidferit. Operæ autem pretium puto, nonnulla ejusdem Pallavicini verbis attexere, ex quibus liquere possit, quis circa reformationem abusuum & morum Pontifici [illegible, ~5 letters] fuerit, quámque vehementer illi animus à seria reformatione abhorruerit. Haud ipsis deerant, inquit num. 2. validissimæ duplicis generis rationes: aliæ ad populi captum, aliæ minus in speciem apertæ &c. Accedebat, hanc adeò efflagitatam emendationem tendere potissimum in ritus ac Romanæ Curiæ tribunalia: nec prudentis esse consilii, à Principe Regiam suam subdi correctioni subditorum. Cunctorum quidem sententiam explorandam; paucorum consilium petendum. Cæterum illius esse familiæ suæ leges ferre, ne gens sibi subjecta illius gesta accusare consuesceat, quem venerari debet; ac longè minus eum dirigere, à quo est regenda. Esse homines plerunque acerbos chirurgos in alienis membris; parùm ab his intelligi, minúsque ipsis dolere vulneris acerbitatem. Episcopos, alios rerum imperitia, alios imprudenti religionis studio, alios etiam privatæ rei commodo, desiderio gratificandi Principi, in cujus ditione nati sunt, ira atque invidia in supremum Principem, meditari severissimas Aulæ Romanæ leges, quæ non tam corruptelas purgarent, quàm imminuerent ejusdem potentiam, Majestatem, ad eum confluentium frequentiam, & quicquid habet præstantissimi succi, quæ quasi vitis mystica in Christianarum Ecclesiarum palmitibus vim & unitatem sustentat.
units.tr: CLXXIV. I add one point: in the congregations held on 18 and 22 January 1546 it was asked and anxiously debated whether the beginning should be made with the decision on the articles of faith or with the reformation of morals and abuses. The Papists maintained the former, the Emperor's side the latter. Pallavicini (Hist. C. T. lib. VI. 7 : 2. 3.) has set out the Papists' reasons at length. But I think it worth adding some words of Pallavicini himself, from which it may be clear who was [illegible] in regard to the reformation of abuses and morals, and how vehemently his mind shrank from serious reform. There were not lacking to them, he says, n. 2. very strong reasons of two kinds: some suited to the understanding of the people, others less openly stated, etc. It was added that this much-demanded correction aimed chiefly at the rites and the tribunals of the Roman Curia; and that it was not prudent for a prince to submit his own royal person to the correction of his subjects. The opinion of all should indeed be sounded, but the advice of a few should be sought. Moreover, it was for him to make laws for his own household, lest a people subject to him should become accustomed to accuse the deeds of the one whom they ought to venerate; and much less was he to take direction from the one by whom he is to be governed. Men are generally harsh surgeons on other people's limbs; they understand little of them, and feel the bitterness of the wound much less themselves. Bishops, some through ignorance of affairs, some through an imprudent zeal for religion, some even for private advantage, out of a wish to please the Prince in whose dominion they were born, plotted in anger and envy against the Supreme Prince the most severe laws for the Roman Court, which would not so much purge abuses as diminish his power and majesty, the crowds that flock to him, and whatever is most excellent in its sap, which, like a mystical vine, sustains life and unity in the branches of the Christian Churches.

units.la: Cæterum illius esse familiæ suæ leges ferre stentat ac fovet. Quid porro agendum, ubi Tridenti ea statuerentur? Num ignavè cedendum, ac plus detrimenti inferendum Petri solio, per Concilium à se adversus hæresin coactum, quàm ipsamet hæresis intulisset? An repugnandum, abrogandaque fides illi conventui, cujus in hæresin arma, nonnisi publica veneratio futura erant? Nonne Duci cum suo exercitu decertandum, ubi cum hoste congrediendum erat? turbæque Basileenses iterum excitandæ, eò certè in præsentia periculosiores, quò materia promptior erat ad incendium concipiendum hujusmodi favillarum injectu? Nec hic discrimen hæsurum. Etenim veritos forsitan Episcopos, ne decreta de Romana Curia in irritum caderent, tentaturos priùs judiciariam sibi potestatem stabilire, Basileensem plane cœtum imitantes, conaturósque statuere Concilii supra Pontificem excellentiam: quibus haud liceret Pontifici consentiri, dignitate & conscientia reluctantibus; quippe doctrinis perquam perniciosis, quæ non modò Pontificalem Sedem dejicerent sed universum Hierarchiæ ordinem perverterent, ac sub specioso libertatis colore, pacifici Regis Ecclesiam in perennis discordiæ campum converterent &c. Ad tam gravia arcenda pericula par esse, ut primo loco Synodus in doctrinis examinandis distineretur; interim verò ab ipso Pontifice pro dignitate ac prudentia leges esse sanciendas Aulæ Romanæ opportunas. Paulò inferiùs num. 8. fatetur idem, invaluisse ad eam usque diem (apud Patres ipsos Concilii) persuasionem, ab hominibus Romanæ Aulæ addictis nihil æquè formidari ac leges, quibus ipsi reformarentur. Fidem & dogmata speciosa quædam esse vocabula, & fucum simulati studii religionis tuendæ. Sequenti capite 8. num. 4. Pallavicinus ipse animi sui notionem implicatam hactenus his verbis explicat: Existimo, cuicunque hominum, cui livoris tabes rationem non infecerit, satis esse, si repetat animo, ambitionis artem non esse, sedulo tueri supremam potestatem in Romano Pontifice divinitus constitutam, & Ecclesiæ incolumitati necessariam. Quòd si liceat hujusmodi solertiam vituperare, quoniam ea est dominanti jucunda; vituperandus etiam erit, quicunque cibo vitam sustentat, quia cibaria gustatui voluptatem afferant. Hæc scilicet mysteria Pontificiæ iniquitatis, Pontificem, ceu alterum in terris Numen ἀνυπεύθυνον omni justissimæ etiam censuræ hominum subducentis, & reformationem in capite, quam necessariam ipsemet Adrianus confessus fuerat, tanto ardore oppugnantis; adeóque verbo dicam, Romam ἀληφθαρτον infanabilem manifestè propalant. Si potestas suprema Divinitus in Pontifice omnino constituta esset, regulis tamen verbi Divini subjectus ejus usus & abusus Concilii examen neutiquam effugisset.
units.tr: Moreover, he tries and encourages it to make laws for his own household. What, then, was to be done, when such things were decreed at Trent? Was one to yield feebly and inflict more harm on the throne of Peter, through a Council that he himself had gathered against heresy, than heresy itself would have inflicted? Or was one to resist, and abrogate the authority of that assembly, whose arms against heresy would be received only with public veneration? Ought one not to fight with one's army, when one had to engage the enemy? And should the Basel tumults be stirred up again, which at this moment would certainly be more dangerous, since the material was more ready to catch fire from the casting of such sparks? Nor would the difficulty stop here. For the bishops, perhaps fearing that the decrees about the Roman Curia would come to nothing, would perhaps first try to establish a judicial power for themselves, imitating exactly the Basel gathering, and would strive to set up the excellence of the Council above the Pope; and the Pope could not be made to agree to this, since he would resist from dignity and conscience, as these doctrines are most pernicious, which would not only overthrow the Pontifical See but would pervert the whole order of the Hierarchy, and under the specious colour of liberty would turn the Church of the peaceful King into a field of perpetual discord, and so on. To ward off such grave dangers, it is necessary that, first of all, the Synod be kept busy examining doctrines; meanwhile, the Pope himself, according to his dignity and prudence, should enact laws suited to the Roman Court. A little further on, in n. 8., the same man admits that up to that day the conviction had taken hold (even among the Fathers of the Council themselves) that men devoted to the Roman Court feared nothing so much as laws by which they themselves would be reformed. Faith and doctrines are certain specious words and a cloak of a pretended zeal for defending religion. In the following chapter 8, n. 4, Pallavicini himself explains in these words the notion of his mind that has so far been involved: I think that to anyone whom the canker of envy has not infected, it is enough to reflect that it is not the art of ambition to watch carefully over the supreme power in the Roman Pontiff, established by God and necessary for the safety of the Church. But if such skill may be blamed, because it is pleasing to those who rule, then whoever sustains life with food will also have to be blamed, because food gives pleasure to the taste. Surely these are the mysteries of Papist iniquity: the Pope, as another divine power on earth, unaccountable and withdrawn from every most just censure of men, and the one who attacks so ardently the reformation at the head that Adrian himself had confessed to be necessary. In a word, they openly reveal Rome as incurable. If the supreme power had been established by God entirely in the Pope, even so his use and abuse, being subject to the rules of the Divine Word, would by no means escape the examination of the Council.

units.la: CLXXXV. Non defuerunt equidem in Concilio etiam Theologi nonnulli παῤῥησιάζοντες, qui Romanæ Ecclesiæ ulcera & intestinos morbos masculè detegerent.
units.tr: CLXXXV. There were, to be sure, some outspoken theologians in the Council as well (παῤῥησιάζοντες [parrhēsiazontes]), who manfully exposed the ulcers and inward diseases of the Roman Church.

units.la: Inter alios, Paulo Pontifice Cornelius Mussus, Episcopus Bitontinus, initio Concilii fassus est: nulla esse turpitudinum monstra, sordidium colluviem & pestem, quibus non fœdati essent populus & Sacerdos &c. Vtinam, inquit, non à religione ad superstitionem, à fide ad infidelitatem, à Christo ad Antichristum, quin à Deo ad Epicurum vel Pythagoram, velut prorsus inanimes declinâssent dicentes in corde impio & ore impudico, Non est Deus. Nec jam diu fuit pastor, qui requireret, quia omnes quæ sua sunt, quærebant, quæ Jesu Christi, ne unus quidem. Bartholomæus quoque Caranza Oratione eodem in Concilio habita, sic Patres conscriptos allocutus: Peregre abeunte Rege, juxta Parabolam Euangelicam, eos reliquit Vicarios suos; Episcopos domus suæ, Speculatores, Vigiles, Doctores, Custodes Civitatis suæ, Duces militiæ, Gubernatores Regni, Pastores gregis, Patronos familiæ, Sponsos Ecclesiæ. Vestri muneris erat vigilâsse super custodia hujus Civitatis. Vestrum erat juxta præscriptas à Christo leges Regnum hoc gubernâsse. Vestrum erat facere, ut juxta illas irreprehensibiliter viveret fidelis populus. Ad vos pertinebat Servâsse hanc Christi Sponsam Sanctam, impollutam, eisdemque ornatam ornamentis, quibus reliquit illam Christus. Fingite nunc, redire Christum, (redibit autem
units.tr: Among others, under Pope Paul, Cornelius Mussus, Bishop of Bitonto, declared at the beginning of the Council: that there were no monstrous forms of wickedness, no filth and pestilence, by which the people and the priesthood were not defiled, etc. Would that, he said, they had not turned away from religion to superstition, from faith to unbelief, from Christ to Antichrist, and even from God to Epicurus or Pythagoras, becoming utterly lifeless, saying in an impious heart and with a shameless mouth, "There is no God." Nor for a long time has there been a minister who sought what belongs to Jesus Christ, not even one, while all sought what was their own. Bartholomew Carranza too, in an oration delivered in the same Council, addressed the Fathers in this way: When the King went abroad, according to the Gospel parable, he left his vicars behind: the bishops of his household, watchmen, guards, teachers, guardians of his city, commanders of his army, governors of his kingdom, shepherds of his flock, patrons of his family, the bridegrooms of the Church. It was your duty to keep watch over the guarding of this city. It was your task to govern this kingdom according to the laws prescribed by Christ. It was yours to make the faithful people live blamelessly according to them. It was your charge to preserve this holy, unspotted bride of Christ, adorned with the same ornaments with which Christ left her. Now imagine that Christ returns (and he will return quickly)

units.la: Cornelii Mussi Bitontini, & Caranza Orationes in Concilio habita, ex quibus Ecclesiæ Romanæ corruptio asseritur. autem citò) & requirere Sponsam suam, qualem reliquit vobis; quam, obsecro, illi restituetis? Num hanc ad hunc angulum orbis (Tridentum) contractam? Num hanc profana pompa, & adparatu Seculari superbientem? Num hanc, quæ Palatiorum magnificentia cum Principibus etiam decertat? Num omnium deliciarum corporalium copia affluentem? Hæccine est illa Civitas Sancta, mundi spiritu sejuncta? Hæccine est illa Dei Civitas Divinis gubernata legibus? Ipsissima. Heu quantum ab illa mutata? Hæccine est illa Civitas nova? Nunc universa in ea cum Ethnicis & barbaricis civitatibus video communia & antiqua. Antiqua in ea regnat avaritia, vetus dominatur ambitio, ad delicias & divitias adspirant & suspirant in ea cives universi. Heu, heu, quis hæc cogitare audeat? Hæccine est civitas illa perfecti decoris, & gaudium orbis universi? Hæccine est illa tota pulchra & decora? Num quid est, quò minus illam possimus dicere totam deformem? Vbi sunt ornamenta tua, quibus parabaris Sponso tuo tradenda? Vbi sunt monilia tua, quibus ornabaris Christi Sponsa? Vbi fides illa, quæ etiam mortuos suscitat? Vbi charitas, ubi contemptus vitæ & rerum præsentium? Vbi ardor ille mortis & rerum cœlestium? Vbi sitis illa videndi Regnum Dei? Vbi amor paupertatis? Nunc omnes, ut olim dixit Jeremias, student avaritiæ, à minimo usque ad maximum, à Propheta usque ad Sacerdotem, cuncti faciunt dolum. Vbi olim regnabat castitas & innocentia, nunc regnat ambitio, luxuria, dominandi cupiditas & vanitas. Heu, heu, quis eam siccis contemplabitur oculis, quis hæc consideret sine lachrymis? O cives Jerusalem, ó cives hujus Regiæ & Sanctæ civitatis, quis hæc intelligens non commoveatur; quis, si Christianus est, hæc audiens non perhorrescat? Quis non miserebitur matris suæ? Ego cum Jeremia precabor: ó utinam caput meum aqua, & oculus meus fons lachrymæ, & plorabo interfectos filiæ populi mei. Plura ejusdem argumenti subjicit verbis planè patheticis, claudítque hunc in modum: Aperuit Dominus os asinæ, ut moneret Prophetam Bileamum. Potuit Dominus os aperire hujus peccatoris, ut commoneret vos. vos. Mementote eorum, quæ dixi vobis. Testis eorum ero, quæ vobis hodie significavi, cum pariter veniemus ante Dominum, quando inutilis erit conatus, & sera omnis pœnitentia. Extant hæc inter Orationes Concilii Tridentini à Janfenio primum editas, & nuper etiam à Labbeo recognitas: Tacentibus hominibus, & hiscere non ausis, quis non asinæ Bileami à Deo apertum os intelligit?
units.tr: Orations of Cornelius Mussus of Bitonto and of Carranza, delivered in the Council, from which the corruption of the Roman Church is asserted. and asks for his bride, such as he left her to you. What, I beg you, will you restore to him? Will it be this one, shrunk into this corner of the world (Trent)? Will it be this one, puffed up with worldly pomp and secular display? Will it be this one, who vies even with princes in the magnificence of her palaces? Will it be this one, abounding in every abundance of bodily delights? Is this that holy city, separated from the spirit of the world? Is this that city of God, governed by divine laws? It is indeed. Alas, how far changed from what she was! Is this that new city? Now I see in her everything in common and old with the heathen and barbarian cities. Ancient avarice reigns in her, old ambition holds sway; all her citizens aspire and sigh after pleasures and riches. Alas, alas, who dares to think of these things? Is this that city of perfect beauty, the joy of the whole world? Is this the one wholly fair and comely? Is there anything to prevent us from calling her wholly deformed? Where are your ornaments, with which you were prepared to be delivered to your Bridegroom? Where are your jewels, with which you were adorned as the bride of Christ? Where is that faith which even raises the dead? Where is charity, where is contempt of life and of present things? Where is that burning desire for death and for heavenly things? Where is that thirst to see the kingdom of God? Where is the love of poverty? Now all, as Jeremiah said of old, study greed, from the least to the greatest, from the prophet to the priest, all practise deceit. Where once chastity and innocence reigned, now ambition, luxury, the lust for domination and vanity reign. Alas, alas, who can look upon her with dry eyes, who can consider these things without tears? O citizens of Jerusalem, O citizens of this royal and holy city, who that understands these things would not be moved; who, if he is a Christian, would not shudder to hear them? Who will not pity his own mother? With Jeremiah I will pray: O that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people. He adds more on the same subject in plainly emotional words, and closes in this manner: The Lord opened the mouth of the ass to warn the prophet Balaam. The Lord could open the mouth of this sinner to warn you, you. Remember the things I have said to you. I will be a witness of the things I have declared to you today, when we together come before the Lord, when every attempt will be useless and all repentance too late. These words are found among the orations of the Council of Trent, first published by Jansenius and lately also edited by Labbe. While men are silent and dare not open their mouths, who would not recognise in them the ass of Balaam whose mouth God opened?

units.la: CLXVI. Paulo IV. Idus Nov. A. M. D. XLIX. defuncto successit Julius III. Aretinus, antea Joh. Maria de Monte dictus, Cardinalis, & Pauli III. in Concilio Legatus princeps. Post longam Cardinalium in Conclavi disceptationem, cum, teste in Musæo Historico Johanne Imperiali, ὁμωνύμως Papa jam electus esset Reginaldus Polus, eámque electionem promulgare nocte appetente inauspicatum duxissent iidem; nocte transacta & mutatis rationibus aureis Julius Papa subito emersit. Vaticinium de eo futuro Papa, teste Rota Ægidii Minoritæ, ejusmodi circumferebatur: Tertius Mons Sion vertetur in opprobrium, caro prævalebit, non erit quies. Nempe Cardinalis de Monte Julius ante dictus est, qui Papa etiam per licita & illicita fœdatus, luxui & saginæ mancipatus, in Venerem ac libidinem projectus omnem est. Novem montes (ita declaratio vaticinii habet) ac terni faciunt insigne domus de Monte, & multorum fuit sententia, Julium non omnia sua facta cum dignitate consensisse, retulisseque ad prudentiam & experientiam, quæ plenissime in Cardinalatu primum apud ipsum obtinuerunt locum. Impura se vita contaminasse, veneri ac ventri dedisse, quasque Cardinalis nonnisi furtim voluptates sequebatur, Pontificem, etsi sexagesimum quintum annum implesset, ultro complexum esse; abdicata rerum maximarum cura hilaritati & genio, conviviisque assiduis, etiam in villa agitatis, indulsisse; levibus & inanibus verbis suam aliquando Majestatem minuisse, in vita ejus Onuphrius Papirius Massonus, & post utrumque Thuanus Annal. lib. XV. memorant. Soluti ad omnem licentiam animi hominem fuisse, hoc etiam argumento Thuanus lib. VI. p. m. 181. probat, quòd statim adepta dignitate galerum suum juveni cuidam, cui Innocentio nomen, (quem seu Bononiæ, uti Suavis, seu Placentiæ, uti Pallavicinus memorat, in deliciis habuit, at nefario amore inflammatus depériit. de quo videnda Epistola Erasti apud Celeberrimum Hottingerum Histor. Eccl. Tom. V. pag. 571. &c. sub qua etiam impurissimi Johannis Casæ Archiepiscopi Beneventani de laude Φαυδλεγασ liber impune lucem salutavit) quíque, quòd in familia Simiæ curam gereret, Simia etiam post adeptam dignitatem nomen retinuit, cognomine etiam suo (nam il Cardinal de Monte dictus est) atque insignibus attributis donavit; & querentibus Cardinalibus, quòd indignum hominem ad tantum fastigium evexisset, respondit: Et vos quid tandem in me meritorum comperistis, quem christianæ Reip. principem constitueretis? Addit Sleidanus, Romæ famam fuisse, & libellis quoque perscriptum, à Jove Ganymedem foveri, licet deformem. Sed nec ipsum Pontificem hoc ad reliquos Cardinales dissimulare, & per jocum ferri aliquando commemorare, quàm sit lascivus. Talia cùm de eo etiam Suavis narraverit, adeò in dubium non revocavit Pallavicinus, ut lib. XI. 7:4. historiam Innocentii hujus seu primam Purpuram, ceu principia Pontificatus decolorantem pluribus cum circumstantiis, ad favorem licet Julii detortis, tradiderit: & lib. XIII. 10:8. palam confessus fit, pronum eum fuisse ad laxamenta: suum sanguinem deamavisse, variis purpuris inter consanguineos distributis: præ cæteris unum extra consanguinitatem amavisse evexisseque, nec antea, nec postea dignum, qui fuerit Innocentius de Monte: æstimatione tenui, nec majore benevolentia mortuum esse: quandam ipsius libertatem ac familiaritatem, quæ ipsi privatam gerenti personam amorem inter æquales conciliaverant.
units.tr: CLXVI. Paul IV died on the Ides of November, 1549, and was succeeded by Julius III of Arezzo, formerly called Giovanni Maria del Monte, a cardinal and chief legate of Paul III at the Council. After a long dispute among the cardinals in the conclave, when, according to Johann Imperiali in his Musaeum Historicum, Reginald Pole had already been elected pope by acclamation (ὁμωνύμως), and the same men thought it an ill omen to announce that election as night was approaching, Julius suddenly emerged as pope once the night had passed and the plans had been changed by gold. A prophecy about this future pope circulated, according to the Rota of Giles the Minorite, in this form: The third Mount Sion will be turned to reproach, the flesh will prevail, there will be no rest. He was indeed the cardinal called Julius del Monte beforehand, who, as pope, defiled himself with lawful and unlawful things alike, was given over to luxury and gluttony, and was thrown into lust and sensuality. Nine mountains (so the explanation of the prophecy has it) and three make up the coat of arms of the house of del Monte, and many were of the opinion that Julius had not agreed to all his acts with dignity, but had referred them to prudence and experience, which had held first place with him above all while he was a cardinal. That he had defiled himself with an impure life, given himself to lust and gluttony, and that he had embraced pleasures which as cardinal he had pursued only in secret; that, though he had reached his sixty-fifth year, he had given himself up to mirth and pleasure and to constant banquets, even held in his villa; that at times he diminished his majesty by light and empty words, Onuphrius Panvinius and Massonus in his life, and afterwards Thuanus in Annals Annal. lib. XV. record. That his mind was given over to every licence, Thuanus proves by this argument as well, lib. VI. p. m. 181: that as soon as he had obtained the dignity he gave his cardinal's hat to a young man named Innocent (whom he kept as a favourite, either at Bologna, as Soave records, or at Piacenza, as Pallavicino mentions, but was consumed by unnatural love for him; on this see the letter of Erastus in the work of the most distinguished Hottinger, Histor. Eccl. Tom. V. pag. 571, etc., under which also the book of the most impure Giovanni della Casa, Archbishop of Benevento, On the Praise of Phaudlegas Φαυδλεγασ, greeted the light with impunity), and because he had charge of the monkey in his household, he kept the name Simia (monkey) even after obtaining the dignity, and gave him his own surname as well (for he was called il Cardinal de Monte) together with the insignia attached to it; and when the cardinals complained that he had raised an unworthy man to so high a rank, he replied: And what merits did you ever find in me, that you should make me prince of the Christian commonwealth? Sleidanus adds that at Rome there was a rumour, and it was also written up in lampoons, that Ganymede, though ugly, was cherished by Jove. But the pope himself did not conceal this from the other cardinals, and sometimes mentioned it in jest, how wanton he was. When Soave had also related such things about him, Pallavicino did not so far call them into doubt that in lib. XI. 7:4. he recounted the story of this Innocent, who discoloured his first purple, as the beginning of his pontificate, with many circumstances, though twisted to favour Julius; and in lib. XIII. 10:8. he openly confessed that he was inclined to indulgence: he loved his own blood, distributing various purples among his relatives; above all he loved and promoted one outside his kinship, and neither before nor after was there anyone worthy of it, who was Innocent del Monte: he died with a slight esteem and no greater goodwill; a certain freedom and familiarity of his, which he showed toward him as a private person, had won him love among his equals.

units.la: {&} prima purpura Innocentio, nem sine gravi suspicione donata verant, in excelso postea Principis gradu venerationem minuisse: ipsius vitia majora quidem quoad speciem fuisse quàm virtutes, sed non fortasse quoad pondus. Hæc de Julio mollissimè dicta quid sibi velint, perspicaciores intelligunt facilè. Neque hic præterire possum levitatis (libertatem vocat Pallavicinus) ejus specimen, quod in vita ejus MS. Bullingerus de ipso scriptum circumferri, his verbis prodidit: Cum aliquando exutis vestibus, diploide & caligis tantùm indutus, in aula, quòd ferveret tempestas, obambularet, venerunt Cardinales duo, colloquuturi cum ipso. Quos ipse ad exuendas vestes suas, & deambulandum secum urgebat, mox autem nudos interrogabat: Quid si in Campo Florae, aut per plateas nudi sic deambularemus, quid oro populum existimatis de nobis judicaturum? Responderunt: Judicarent, nos esse nebulones, & conjicerent in nos rudera atque lapides. Excepit Pontifex: Ergo quòd non habemur pro nebulonibus, id acceptum ferre debemus nostris vestibus. Quantum igitur, ó fratres, debemus illis nostris vestibus?
units.tr: And the first purple, given to Innocent not without grave suspicion, had, in his later elevation to the rank of prince, diminished reverence for him: his vices were indeed greater than his virtues in appearance, but perhaps not in weight. What these very gentle words about Julius are meant to convey, the more discerning will easily understand. Nor can I pass over a specimen of his levity (Pallavicini calls it "freedom"), which Bullinger reported in these words, saying that a manuscript life of Julius written by him is in circulation: "Once, when a storm was raging, he was walking about in the hall, having taken off his clothes and wearing only his undershirt and breeches. Two cardinals came to speak with him. He urged them to take off their clothes and walk with him, and then asked them, naked, 'What do you think the people would judge of us if we walked about like this, naked, in the Campo di Fiore or through the streets?' They replied, 'They would judge us to be scoundrels and would throw rubbish and stones at us.' The Pontiff answered, 'So, since we are not taken for scoundrels, we must credit our clothes with that. How much, then, brothers, do we owe to our clothes?'"

units.la: CLXXVII. Talis Sardanapalus reformationem Ecclesiae se meditari, restaurato, Cæsare urgente, & juramento, quod Cardinalibus recens electus fecerat, ita potulante; Tridentino Concilio, quod eo Cardinale adhuc Bononiæ elanguerat, ipsomet validissimè repugnante, ne unquam Tridentum revocaretur; simulavit.
units.tr: CLXXVII. Such a Sardanapalus pretended to be meditating a reform of the Church, although Caesar, with the Empire restored, was pressing for it, and although the oath he had sworn as a newly elected cardinal required it. He himself most strongly opposed that the Council of Trent, which had languished at Bologna while he was a cardinal, should ever be recalled to Trent.

units.la: Extat Bulla indictionis, in qua inter alia se Concilium, Calendis Maji A. M. D. LI. resumendum, moderaturum profitetur, authoritatémque suam supra modum effert. Cúmque Cæsar, cui talia displicuerunt, metuenti scilicet, ne Protestantes conditionibus ejusmodi offensi, ad Concilium venire gravarentur, Bullam mitigari expetiisset, Oratórque Cæsaris verborum comitatem & blanditias, quibus Protestantes ad Concilium pellici, pellecti demum facilius instrui possint; suasisset: respondit Papa; Nolle se dimicare cum hoste, tanquam cum fele cavea inclusó. Quod Christus docuit, semper
units.tr: The bull of indiction survives, in which, among other things, he declares that the Council, to be resumed on the Calends of May 1551, he will moderate, and he greatly magnifies his own authority beyond measure. When Caesar, who disliked such things, fearing that the Protestants, offended by conditions of this kind, would be reluctant to come to the Council, asked that the bull be softened, and Caesar's orator advised a courteous manner of speech and flattering words, by which the Protestants might be enticed to the Council and, once enticed, could more easily be instructed, the Pope replied: "He was unwilling to fight with an enemy as with a cat shut in a cage. What Christ taught must always be preached and impressed, namely that the Divine Majesty has appointed his vicar as head of the Church and lamp of the world; this truth must be taught in season and out of season."

units.la: Sardanapalus Concilium Tridenti restaurat. semper prædicandum & inculcandum esse, nempe Majestatem Divinam vicarium suum caput Ecclesiæ, & lucernam mundi constituisse ; æque eam veritatem doceri oportere tempestivè & intempestivè. Ita Sessio XI. Concilii, quæ sub Julio prima fuit, Calendis Maji A. M. D. LI. successit. Interea bello Parmensi Gallum inter & Pontificem æstuante, Galliæ Episcopis, ne Concilium frequentarent, à Rege Henrico II. injunctum fuerat. Rege ipso contra Concilium protestante. Processere nihilominus sub Julio Sessiones aliquot, & decreta de Sacramento Eucharistiæ & extremæ unctionis cusa sunt, talia, qualia à cœtu illo expectari poterant. Sed & Electoris Saxoniæ Mauritii Legati in Concilio appulerunt, postulantes à Cæsare, ut sibi æquè ac Theologis Saxonicis, aliisque Protestantibus, ad Concilium venire paratis, eadem fide, qua in Concilio Basileensi Bohemis factum, caveatur idonee, anteacta retractentur, Papa Concilio se submittat, Episcopis iuramentum remittatur, & suffragari ipsis quoque Protestantibus liceat. Conditiones haud iniquas cum detestarentur Pontificii, aliáque intercederent, Concilium prorogari ad biennium usque placuit. Sed prorogatum mansit integros annos decem, ad XVIII. Jan. A. M. D. LXII. usque.
units.tr: Sardanapalus restores the Council of Trent. In this way the eleventh session of the Council, the first under Julius, followed on the Calends of May 1551. Meanwhile, with the war of Parma blazing between France and the Pontiff, the bishops of France had been ordered by King Henry II not to attend the Council, the king himself protesting against it. Nevertheless, under Julius several sessions proceeded, and decrees concerning the Sacrament of the Eucharist and extreme unction were drafted, of the kind that could be expected from that assembly. But also legates of the Elector of Saxony Maurice arrived at the Council, asking Caesar that, for them as for the Saxon theologians and other Protestants prepared to come to the Council, safe conduct be given with the same good faith that had been granted to the Bohemians at the Council of Basel; that past decisions be reconsidered; that the Pope submit himself to the Council; that the bishops' oath be remitted; and that the Protestants too be allowed to vote. When the Papists protested against these conditions, which were not unfair, and others interceded, it was decided to adjourn the Council for two years. But it remained adjourned for a full ten years, until 18 January 1562.

units.la: CLXXVIII. In Germania interim, in qua Carolus extinguendæ veritati intentus, hactenus victricia arma circumtulit, mirè conversa rerum facies est. Fatigata enim nimium Principum Protestantium patientia, Mauritius Saxoniæ Elector, cui etiam Albertus Brandenburgicus & Duces Megalopolitani suppetias tulere. A. M. D. LII. in Cæsarem, cui etiam Gallus graviter imminebat, movens, Augustam capit, & superatis Alpium Rhæticarum jugis, captáque Ehrenberga arce, tantum Carolo metum incutit, ut noctu, accensis funalibus, unà cum fratre Ferdinando Oenipontem relinqueret, & se Villacum versus in Carniolam reciperet. In diplomate, quo causæ illati Cæsari belli exponebantur, religio adversariorum artibus, & contra fidem datam, convulsa in dies: per dissidium religionis extractum strata ad dominationem iniquam via: Hassiæ Landgravii captivitas violenta: Germanicæ libertatis oppressio tyrannica: Monarchiæ universalis machinatio, allegabantur. Rebus Protestantium sic satis prospere fluentibus die x x. Jul. A. M. D. L I I. Passavii, Ferdinandi Regis cui sapienter visum præcipitem publicæ calamitatis, obvia cuncta obtriturae rotam, salutari Pacificationis edicto quasi sufflaminandam esse; interventu, Pax Religiosa toti orbi Christiano saluberrima sancita, & A. M. D. L V. etiam Augustæ, frequentissimis & augustissimis Comitiis, firmata est. Quæ quidem Pax Religiosa non iccirco rata minus & valida censeri debet, quòd, uti ofores Pacis Jesuitæ, aliíque vociferari solent, vi & metu extorta sit, atque insuper Pontificis consensu destituta, imò à Paulo IV. aperte rejecta, & damnata sit. Etsi enim, cùm pax primùm Passavii sanciretur, conflictus aliqui & velitationes, & occupatio castri Ehrenbergæ, Augustæ & Oeniponti antecesserint; nondum tamen totis viribus aut castris pugnatum erat, ut altera pars vicisse, altera victa esse dici potuerit. Atque adeo rebus utrinque integris in Pacificationem illam consensum ultro; eademque sequentium item Imperatorum consensu firmata est. Imò si vel maximè pars alterutra succubuisset, & ad indignas durásque conditiones adacta fuisset, indignitas tamen rerum sponsionis vinculum non levat. Neque etiam consensus Pontificis requirebatur, cùm Imperator nec ita puer fuerit, ut promiserit, quæ promittere sibi non licere nôsse debuerit: vel ita servus, ut mitræ mancipato diademate, necesse habuerit à Dictatoris illius Ecclesiastici nutu superciliòque per omnia pendere. Resolvitur enim vis Principatus, cuncta vocando ad Papam: nec quisquam Princeps est alio imperante.
units.tr: CLXXVIII. Meanwhile in Germany, where Charles, intent on extinguishing the truth, had hitherto carried his victorious arms, the face of affairs was strangely reversed. For the patience of the Protestant princes was worn out. Maurice, Elector of Saxony, to whom Albert of Brandenburg and the dukes of Mecklenburg also brought help, moved against the Emperor in 1552, against whom the King of France was also pressing hard. He took Augsburg, and, crossing the ridges of the Rhaetian Alps and capturing the fortress of Ehrenberg, struck such fear into Charles that at night, with torches lit, he left Innsbruck together with his brother Ferdinand and withdrew toward Villach in Carniola. In the manifesto in which the causes of the war against the Emperor were set out, it was alleged that religion, day by day, was being torn apart by the tricks of the adversaries and against the faith given; that through the division of religion a path had been opened to unjust domination; that the Landgrave of Hesse had been violently imprisoned; that German liberty had been tyrannically oppressed; and that a plot for universal monarchy was afoot. With the affairs of the Protestants thus flowing quite prosperously, on 26 July 1552 at Passau, through the mediation of King Ferdinand, who wisely judged that the headlong rush of public calamity, which would crush everything in its path, had to be checked, as it were, by the healing edict of pacification, the Religious Peace was sanctioned, most beneficial to the whole Christian world; and in 1555 it was also confirmed at Augsburg, in a very well attended and most august Diet. This Religious Peace ought not to be considered any less valid and binding because, as the Jesuits and others, the enemies of peace, are wont to clamour, it was extorted by force and fear, and moreover lacked the Pope's consent, indeed was openly rejected and condemned by Paul IV. For although, when the peace was first sanctioned at Passau, some skirmishes and light engagements had preceded it, and the seizure of the fortress of Ehrenberg, of Augsburg and of Innsbruck, nevertheless no battle had yet been fought with full forces or camps, so that one side could be said to have conquered and the other to have been conquered. And so, with both sides' forces intact, they consented freely to that pacification, and it was confirmed by the consent of the emperors who followed. Indeed, even if one side had been overcome and driven to unworthy and harsh conditions, the unworthiness of the terms of an agreement does not lighten the bond. Nor was the consent of the Pope required, since the Emperor was neither so much a boy that he could promise what he ought to have known he was not permitted to promise, nor so much a slave that, with the diadem handed over to the mitre, he had to depend in all things on the nod and frown of that ecclesiastical dictator. For the power of a prince is dissolved when everything is referred to the Pope; and no prince rules when another rules.

units.la: Passavii & mox etiam Augustæ libertas religionis sanctitur. Frustra ringente Pontifice, aliisque vi extortam caussam tibus.
units.tr: At Passau, and soon also at Augsburg, freedom of religion was sanctioned. The Pope and others struggled in vain against it, claiming that the cause had been extorted by force.

units.la: CLXXXIX. Majorem Julius voluptatem ex turbis Anglicanis, quæ Eduardi VI. Religiosissimi & indubitatæ ac summæ spei Principis mortem, quam is præmaturam A. M. D. LIIII. Julii die VI. oppetiit, consecutæ sunt, cepit.
units.tr: CLXXXIX. Julius took greater pleasure in the disturbances in England that followed the death of Edward VI, the most religious prince of undoubted and highest promise, which he met prematurely on 6 July 1553.

units.la: Nam & Johannam Suffolciam declaratam hæredem Regni, virtutis & eruditionis incomparabile speculum, ac orthodoxiæ etiam addictissimam, capite plexam : & Mariam sævire igni & ferro in eos, qui Euangelium amplexi fuerant, ac matrimonio insuper cum Philippo Hispanorum Rege coaluisse, lætus, si quid aliud, inaudiit. Miserat autem in Angliam Cardinalem Reginaldum Polum, qui Rege Philippo atque Maria præsente Anglos ad obedientiam Papæ hortatus, morigeris absolutionem promisit. Ordines Angliæ conditiones ejus impias amplexi mox Euangelium ejurârunt. Ingens inde Romæ lætitia, accensi ignes, institutæ ad Templa supplicationes, indulgentiæ largissimæ tributæ sunt. Eóque insaniæ Julius pervenit, ut in perpetuam rei memoriam excudi curaverit monetam, cujus altera pars ejus imaginem tricorniferam ostentavit, altera inscriptionem ejusmodi habuit: Gens & Regnum, quod non servierit tibi, peribit. Sibi stolidè vendicans, quod Christo Esaias. Sed diuturnum & stabile gaudium neutiquam fuit. Nam & sterile fuit Mariæ matrimonium cum Philippo: & Maria à spe bona omni deserta, & ex mœrore die XVII. Nov. M. D. LVIII. mortua (comitante eam Cardinale Polo post sedecim horas) locum cessit sorori Elisabethæ, quæ Pontifici servire dedignata, Christóque soli sacramento dicens, blasphemam Julii inscriptionem damnavit.
units.tr: For he heard with joy, as if of something else, that Lady Jane Suffolk, declared heir to the kingdom, an incomparable mirror of virtue and learning and also most devoted to orthodoxy, had been beheaded; and that Mary was raging with fire and sword against those who had embraced the Gospel, and had moreover united herself in marriage with Philip, King of the Spaniards. He had sent Cardinal Reginald Pole into England, who, with King Philip and Mary present, urged the English to obedience to the Pope and promised absolution to those who complied. The English orders, embracing his impious conditions, soon abjured the Gospel. Thereupon there was immense rejoicing at Rome: fires were lit, supplications were ordered in the churches, and the most lavish indulgences were granted. Julius reached such madness that, to commemorate the event forever, he had a coin struck, one side of which showed his image wearing the triple crown, and the other bore the inscription: "The nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish." Foolishly claiming for himself what Isaiah said of Christ. But the joy was neither lasting nor secure. For Mary's marriage to Philip was barren; Mary, deserted by all good hope and dying of grief on 17 November 1558 (Cardinal Pole following her sixteen hours later), gave place to her sister Elizabeth, who disdained to serve the Pontiff, swore allegiance to Christ alone, and condemned Julius's blasphemous inscription.

units.la: CLXXX. Julio A. M. D. LV. X. Cal. Martii defuncto Marcellus Cervinus Thuscus, antehac in Concilio Tridentino Legatus Pontificius, successit, nomenque suum retinens, Marcellus II. dictus est.
units.tr: CLXXX. When Julius died on 10 days before the Kalends of March 1555, Marcellus Cervinus of Tuscany succeeded him. He had previously served as papal legate at the Council of Trent, kept his own name, and was called Marcellus II.

units.la: Scenicus licet diecularum aliquot Papa (dies enim x x i. duntaxat & aliquot horas vixit) putatur tamen reformationem quampiam Romanæ Curiæ molitus. Quam non processuram fuisse, utpote viribus ejus superiorem, merito Pallavicinus augurratur. Et forte hæc ipsa causa est, quòd difficilem esse salutem Pontificum Romanorum, Marcellus ingeminavit. Testis quippe in ejus vita est Onuphrius, Marcellum jam Pontificem pro mensa subitò conticescentem, sibi recitari jussisse verba Pontificis Adriani sequentia: Romano Pontifice nemo est miserabilior; conditione ejus nulla miserior. Totius enim vitæ ejus lætitia & felicitas est amaritudo. Cathedra Romani Pontificis est spinosa, iter undique confertum aculeis, pondus tantæ molis, ut robustissimos premat & confringat humeros. Quibus verbis recitatis, manu mensam percutientem eum dixisse: Non video, quomodo qui locum hunc altissimum tenent, possint salvari. Tales scilicet, quorum conclamata æterna salus est, Christus suos in Ecclesia adversus Sathanam & mundum militante vicarios esse voluit, jussit:
units.tr: Although he was a stage pope for a few days (he lived only 21 days and some hours), he is thought to have planned some reform of the Roman Curia. Pallavicini rightly suspects that this would not have come to anything, since it was beyond his strength. Perhaps this is also the reason why Marcellus repeatedly said that the salvation of Roman Pontiffs is difficult. Onuphrius, in his life of Marcellus, is a witness: once, when Marcellus was already pope, he suddenly fell silent at table and ordered the following words of Pope Adrian to be read to him: "No one is more wretched than the Roman Pontiff; no condition is more miserable than his. For the joy and happiness of his whole life is bitterness. The chair of the Roman Pontiff is thorny, the road on every side is crowded with thorns, and the weight of so great a burden crushes and breaks the strongest shoulders." When these words had been read, he struck the table with his hand and said: "I do not see how those who hold this highest place can be saved." Clearly, those whose eternal salvation is despaired of are the ones whom Christ willed and commanded to be his vicars, fighting in the Church against Satan and the world.

units.la: CLXXXI. De Paulo IV. Mediolanensi, ante dicto Johanne Petro Caraffa, Marcelli successore, sic Johannis Abbatis oraculum præsagiverat: Intrabit velut Draco, sedebit velut alter Leo, immitis in populo.
units.tr: CLXXXI. Concerning Paul IV of Milan, formerly called Giovanni Pietro Carafa, the successor of Marcellus: the oracle of the Abbot John had foretold him in this way: "He will enter like a dragon, he will sit like another lion, savage towards the people."

units.la: Qualem is se gessit adversus supremos mundi Principes, Pontificios etiam, historiæ commemorant. Cardinalis adhuc, malevolentia suffusus in Carolum V. Cæsarem, Paulo III. occupandi Regni Neapolitani suasor extiterat. Papa verò creatus, nactus majorem nocendi occasionem, conditum adversus Cæsarem odium promere, ejusque partibus addictos, incredibili rabie persequi cœpit. Vix enim consceñsa sede, magnos etiam ordinis Ecclesiastici viros, quos Cæsari favere suspicabatur, in carceres conjicit: quorundam bona publicat: ministros ac nuntios Cæsareos, quotquot potest, intercipit: proscriptos è Regno Neapolitano, in odium Caroli receptos, officiis publicis præficit: inducias inter Cæsarem & Gallum in Belgio pactas nefariè turbat: denique ne quid ad malevolentiam reliqui faciat, Philippo filio, cui Pater, Imperio abdicato, Regnorum omnium administrationem commiserat, Siciliæ Neapolisque Regna beneficiario titulo Ecclesiæ Romanæ obnoxia, conferre renuit. Unde tam horrida támque funesta bella exorta fuere, ut potentissimorum Regum viribus inter se hostiliter commissis, Italia Galliaque bello Pontificio implicita, sanguine suorum maduerit. Imperio ad fratrem Caroli Ferdinandum translato, cùm hic pro sua erga Sedem Pontificiam observantia Paulum Pontificem de Imperii administratione suscepta certiorem reddere statuisset, cum significatione voluntatis, de diademate Imperiali prima quaque occasione, petendo recipiendóque: Paulus idem tam improba malevolentia, elatáque protervia, observantiæ Cæsareæ respondit, ut se Petri, magistratum tanquam ordinationem Divinam, debito honore cultúque prosecuti, suffragatorem; vel hominem ad mutua benevolentiæ ac humanitatis officia propensum, hac quidem in re minimè demonstrárit. Ut enim Neronis potiùs quàm Petri se successorem ostenderet, quemadmodum olim Tiridatem Parthorum Regem, (ut Taciti verbis Annal. XV. 29. id exprimam) oportuit apud effigiem Cæsaris, insigne Regium ponere, nec nisi manu Neronis resumere: sic à Ferdinando novus iste Nero impudentissimè postulare ausus fuit, mitteret, (verba Thuani Histor. lib. XXI. refero) procuratorem, per quem, prius acta pœnitentia, cessioni fratris, ab Electoribus approbatæ renuntiaret: rem omnem Pontificis arbitrio permitteret, qui inaugurationem, quamvis rite non factam plena potestate confirmet. Carolum enim apud nullum, nisi se Pontificem, Cæsaream dignitatem ejerare; nec Ferdinandum eam citra suum Vicarii Christi consensum, cui claves cœlestis ac terreni (grandia loquitur Sullaturiens ille. Nam ut de cœlesti imperio nihil dicam, ubi terreni imperii claves Christus Pontifici tribuit?) imperii credita sint, accipere potuisse. Cúmque tres menses Romæ Legatum Cæsareum Husmannum detinuisset,ne quidem in conspectum ipsum admittere dignatus, ineptissimis interim de Papæ potestate, Ferdinandique persona (quem, teste etiam nuper Masenio, inconsulta Sede Romana in Comitiis colloquiisque multa de Religione tractâsse, Pacem Papæ iniquissimam Germanis Passavii indulsisse, utriusque speciei usum Austriis permittere, Filium Maximilianum pæne in consortio & familiaritate hæreticorum educâsse, inexpiabili crimini dabat) per Cardinales examinatis: postquam etiam Philippi Hispaniarum Regis, causam Ferdinandi patrui per Oratores obnixè commendantis preces esset aspernatus; tandem ipsum re infecta dimisit, quòd diceret, amplius ea de re deliberandum esse. Quæ deliberatio non aliud quàm deliberata elusio fuit, qua confirmationem Imperatoris splendidissimis ejus titulis efficere conatus, eousque protelavit, donec ipse è vita excederet.
units.tr: Church histories record what kind of man he proved to be towards the greatest princes of the world, even Catholic ones. While still a cardinal, filled with ill will towards Emperor Charles V, he had urged Paul III to seize the kingdom of Naples. Once he himself became pope, having found a greater opportunity to harm, he began to vent the hatred he had long harboured against the Emperor and to persecute with incredible fury those attached to his side. Scarcely had he taken the papal seat when he threw into prison the great men of the ecclesiastical order whom he suspected of favouring the Emperor; he confiscated the property of some; he intercepted, as far as he could, the ministers and messengers of the Emperor; he appointed to public offices those who had been outlawed from the Kingdom of Naples and taken in by Charles out of hatred; he wickedly disturbed the truce agreed between the Emperor and the French in Flanders; and finally, so that he might leave nothing undone in his ill will, he refused to grant the kingdoms of Sicily and Naples, which were held as fiefs owed to the Roman Church, to Philip, son of the Emperor, to whom his father, having abdicated the empire, had entrusted the administration of all his kingdoms. From this there arose such horrible and deadly wars that, while the forces of the most powerful kings fought each other with hostility, Italy and France, entangled in the papal war, were drenched with the blood of their own people. When the empire had passed to Charles's brother Ferdinand, and he, out of his respect for the Apostolic See, had resolved to inform Pope Paul of his taking up the administration of the empire, and to say that he would ask for and accept the imperial crown at the first opportunity, Paul answered the Emperor's respectful message with such wicked ill will and such arrogant obstinacy that in this matter he showed himself neither a successor of Peter, who would have honoured and worshipped the magistracy as a divine ordinance with due respect, nor a man inclined to the mutual duties of goodwill and humanity. For, to show himself the successor of Nero rather than of Peter, just as once Tiridates, King of the Parthians, had to (to express it in the words of Tacitus, Annals XV. 29) "lay the royal insignia before the statue of Caesar, and take them up again only from Nero's hand", so this new Nero dared to demand shamelessly from Ferdinand that he should "send" (I quote the words of Thuanus, History, book XXI) "a proxy, through whom, after first performing penance, he would renounce in favour of his brother the cession approved by the Electors; that he would leave the whole matter to the Pontiff's judgment, who would confirm the inauguration, even though it had not been properly done, with full power. For Charles could receive the imperial dignity from no one but the Pontiff; nor could Ferdinand receive it without the consent of his own Vicar of Christ, to whom the keys of heaven and earth" (that madman speaks grandly; for, to say nothing of the heavenly empire, where did Christ give the keys of earthly empire to the Pontiff?) "of the empire have been entrusted." When he had kept the Imperial ambassador Hussmann detained in Rome for three months, not even deigning to admit him to his presence, meanwhile he had the most absurd questions about the power of the Pope and the person of Ferdinand examined by cardinals (Ferdinand, as Masenius recently testified, was charged with an inexpiable crime: that, without the consent of the Roman See, he had discussed religion at many Diets and conferences, had granted the Germans at Passau a most unjust peace of the Pope, had allowed the use of both kinds of the sacrament in Austria, and had brought up his son Maximilian almost in the company and familiarity of heretics). Finally, after he had also rejected the prayers of Philip, King of Spain, who urgently commended the cause of his uncle Ferdinand through ambassadors, he dismissed him with nothing achieved, saying that the matter had to be considered further. This "consideration" was nothing but a deliberate evasion, by which he delayed the confirmation of the Emperor, trying to make it depend on his most splendid titles, until he himself departed this life.

units.la: CLXXXII. Talem se Paulus erga Principes summos gessit. ut Draconis & Leonis fidem vaticinio abundè fecerit. Neque Ecclesiæ mitius consuluit. Cardinalis quidem adhuc nomine Joh. Petri Cardinalis Theatini, inter alios etiam faber fuit illius de reformanda Ecclesia Concilii, quod Paulo III. perhibitum suprà memoravimus.
units.tr: CLXXXII. Paul behaved in this way towards the highest princes, so that he fully justified the faith of the prophecy of the "dragon and lion". Nor did he deal more gently with the Church. While still a cardinal, under the name of Giovanni Pietro, Cardinal Theatine, he was among others a maker of that Council for the reform of the Church which, as we mentioned above, was said to have been held under Paul III.

units.la: Tum equidem libero ore profitebatur Papas ad sua desideria coacervare sibi Magistros auribus prurientes, per Cardinales & Episcopos Christi nomen inter gentes blasphemari, clavium potestate emungi pecunias, improbos ordinari, Simoniacas nundinationes exerceri, ambitione & avaritia æstuare Prælatos, in Monasteriis horrenda flagitia committi & si quid aliud. An verò Pontifici creato Romanæ Curiæ & Ecclesiæ universæ emendatio curæ seriò fuit? Non liquebat equidem. Etsi enim curam ejus rei nonnullam simulâsset, instituta mense Ianuario A. M. D. LVI. Congregatione ex viginti quatuor Cardinalibus & quadraginta quinque Præsulibus constante; atque in ea argumentum de Simonia ventilari curâsset; non tamen tantùm res in nervum erupit nunquam, sed etiam negotium referri ad Concilium generale, cujus solius mentio bilem ei in nares concivit, prohibuit. Profitebatur palam, nunquam se probâsse, quòd Concilium indictum sit Tridentum, apud Cardinalem Bellajum affirmans, utiSuavis lib. V. ad A. M. D. LVI. loquitur;magna fuisse væcordia, sexaginta Episcopos, neque eos maximi nominis, & quadraginta doctores, non omnes de meliore nota, ad montes ablegâsse, sicuti jam bis factum esset: simul credere, Ecclesiæ doctrinam & disciplinam ab his rectiùs ad rationis normam designari posse, quàm ab ipso Christi Vicario, cui adminiculantur tum Collegium omnium Cardinalium, tum Præsules ac Doctores, quotquot sunt Romæ, eruditione cæteris per Europam superiores, & numero plures, quàm qui omni opera & studio Tridentum adduci poterant. Quæ à Suavi ita dicta, à Pallavicino revocata in dubium non reperio. Et vera eum scripsisse, res ipsa loquitur, cùm superstite Paulo Concilium Generale restauratum nunquam fuerit.
units.tr: Then indeed he openly declared that "Popes heap up for themselves teachers with itching ears to suit their desires; through cardinals and bishops the name of Christ is blasphemed among the nations; money is wrung out by the power of the keys; wicked men are ordained; simoniacal trading is carried on; prelates seethe with ambition and greed; horrible crimes are committed in monasteries; and whatever else." But was the reform of the Roman Curia and of the whole Church really a serious concern for the Pontiff once he was created? It was not clear. For although he had feigned some concern for this matter, when in January 1556 a congregation was set up, consisting of twenty-four cardinals and forty-five prelates, and he had arranged for the question of simony to be discussed in it, nevertheless the matter never came to the heart of the problem, and he also forbade it to be referred to a general council, the mere mention of which stirred his bile. He openly professed that he had never approved of the Council being summoned to Trent, stating this to Cardinal Bellay, as Sabinus, book V, on the year 1556, relates: "It was great madness to send sixty bishops, and not those of the greatest name, and forty doctors, not all of the best reputation, to the mountains, as had already been done twice before; at the same time he believed that the doctrine and discipline of the Church could be more rightly determined by reason from them than from Christ's own Vicar, who is supported both by the College of all the Cardinals and by the prelates and doctors, as many as there are in Rome, superior in learning to all the others throughout Europe and more numerous than those who could be brought to Trent with every effort and zeal." I do not find that what Sabinus said in this way, which Pallavicini called back into doubt, is questionable. The matter itself shows that he wrote the truth, since while Paul was alive the General Council was never restored.

units.la: CLXXXIII. Maluit nimirum Paulus, ceu Draco & Leo in oraculo designatus, cum iis, qui Romanæ Sedi mo- rem gerere dedignarentur, vi quàm jure decernere.
units.tr: CLXXXIII. Paul, as the Dragon and Lion designated in the oracle, preferred to deal by force rather than by right with those who scorned to obey the Roman See.

units.la: Testis est ejus Bulla de hæreticorum, schismaticorum & fautorum eorundem pœnis, Romæ x. Cal. Martii A. M. D. LVIII. edita, & Septimi Decretalium lib. V. tit. III. cap. 9. inserta. In ea præfatus, posse etiam Romanum Pontificem, qui Dei & Domini nostri Jesu Christi vices gerit in terris, & super gentes & Regna plenitudinem obtinet potestatis, omnesque judicat, à nemine in hoc Seculo judicandus, si deprehendatur à fide devius, redargui, mox omnes & singulas excommunicationis, suspensionis & interdicti ac privationis, & quasvis alias sententias, censuras & pœnas, à quibusvis busvis Romanis Pontificibus Prædecessoribus suis, aut pro tali habitis, etiam per eorum literas extravagantes, seu sacris Concilis ab Ecclesia Dei receptis, vel Sanctorum Patrum decretis & statutis, aut sacris canonibus & constitutionibus Apostolicis contra hæreticos aut Schismaticos quomodolibet latas aut promulgatas, Apostolica authoritate se approbare & innovare, ac perpetuò observari velle scribit, adversus omnes scilicet hæreseos convictos, cujufcunque, inquit, status, gradus, ordinis, conditionis & præ-eminentia existant, etiamsi Episcopali, Patriarchali, Primatiali, aut majori dignitate Ecclesiastica, seu Cardinalatus honore, & Apostolicæ Sedis ubivis locorum, tam perpetuæ, quàm temporalis Legationis munere; vel mundana, etiam Comitati, Baronali, Marchionali, Ducali, Regali & Imperiali authoritate seu excellentia præfulgeant. Eorum quemlibet sententias, censuras & pœnas prædictas incurrere volumus atque decernimus. Omnes illos porro, adeoque etiam Reges & Imperatores hæreticos vel schismaticos, ultra censuras & pœnas prædictas, declarat dignitatibus omnibus, etiam Regnis & Imperiis, in totum & perpetuum privatos, & ad illa de cætero inhabiles & incapaces. Quinimò, addit, Seculares (puta etiam Reges & Imperatores) relinquantur arbitrio potestatis animadversione debita puniendi, nisi apparentibus in eis veræ pœnitentiæ indiciis, & pœnitentiæ condignæ fructibus, ex ipsius Sedis benignitate & clementia, in aliquo Monasterio, aut alio Regulari loco, ad peragendam perpetuam in pane doloris & aqua mæstitiæ pœnitentiam retrudendi, omni humanitatis solatio destituti. Regna, Ducatus, feuda, dominia & bona hujusmodi publicentur, & publicata sint efficiantúrque juris & proprietatis eorum, qui illa primo occupaverint, si in sinceritate fidei & unitate Sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ, ac sub nostra & Successorum Pontificum Romanorum canonicè intrantium obedientia fuerint. Quid quæso Draconica & Leonina hac Bulla horrendum magis: quid ad convellenda inani quovis prætextu læsi Pontificis, imperia, & ima summis miscenda idoneum mamagis? Testis insuper violentiæ Papalis est bos ille Phalaridis, Tribunal Inquisitionis, verè Draconicum, ab eodem Romæ erectum cujus etiam erigendi pridem Cardinalis adhuc author Paulo III. extiterat. Moribundus etiam Sanctæ Inquisitionis officium, quod sanctissimum appellabat, & quo uno niti affirmabat Apostolicæ Sedis authoritatem, Cardinalibus commendavit, inquit in vita ejus Onuphrius. Æterna laude dignum isthoc Pauli opus, cui Italia servatam fidei integritatem acceptam referre debeat, etiam Pallavicinus Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. XIV. 9: 5. scribit. Idem turbas ob eam rem mortem Pauli comitatas & consecutas, incensum à populo furente Inquisitionis carcerem, destructa Caraffarum insignia, aliáque ejusmodi, quæ parcius Suavis Polanus & Thuanus recensent, copiosissimè perstringit. ut satis vel ex iis colliquescat, quàm impatiente rigidóque cervice homines Romani immane isthoc jugum, & sanguinariam quandam per Syllogismos ex aquæ, ignis & laquei terminis confectos, disputandi rationem, tortoribúsque carnificibúsque magis, quàm Doctoribus Pontificibúsque convenientem, tulerint. Testis quoque est Index librorum Prohibitorum, jussu ejus Romæ ab Inquisitoribus compositus, & A. M. D. LIX. typis impressus, de quo pluscula alibi dicta hic non repetimus. Saltem inde constat, Paulo id unum curæ cordíque fuisse, ut omne veritatis lumen animis hominum excuteret, eósque ad brutam & sedentariam assentiendi oraculis suis, Papali Majestati amplificandæ unicè intentis, (nam amplitudinem omnem sacrosanctæ suæ potestatis habuisse eum pro mensura sapienter eam exercendi, etiam Pallavicinus loc. cit. fatetur) necessitatem compelleret. Ne eadem ratione Pontifices Papatum stabilivisse, qua Turcæ Muhammedismum stabiliverunt, dubitari ullatenus possit.
units.tr: The witness to this is his Bull On the punishments of heretics, schismatics and their supporters, issued at Rome on the tenth day before the Kalends of March 1558 and inserted in the Seventh Book of the Decretals, Book V, title III, chapter 9. In it he states, after a preamble, that the Roman Pontific, who holds the place of God and our Lord Jesus Christ on earth, and possesses the fullness of power over nations and kingdoms, and judges all men while being judged by no one in this age, may, if he is found to have strayed from the faith, be rebuked; and he declares that he himself by apostolic authority approves and renews, and wills to be observed forever, all and each of the excommunications, suspensions, interdicts, deprivations and any other sentences, censures and penalties, issued or promulgated in any way against heretics or schismatics by any of the Roman Pontiffs his predecessors, or by those regarded as such, even through their extravagant letters, or by the sacred councils received by the Church of God, or by the decrees and statutes of the holy Fathers, or by the sacred canons and apostolic constitutions. He writes this against all those convicted of heresy, of whatever state, rank, order, condition or pre-eminence they may be, even if they shine with episcopal, patriarchal, primatial or greater ecclesiastical dignity, or the honour of the cardinalate, or the office of the Apostolic See's legation, whether perpetual or temporary, in any place; or with worldly authority or excellence, even of count, baron, marquis, duke, king or emperor. We will and decree that each of them incur the aforesaid sentences, censures and penalties. Moreover, beyond the aforesaid censures and penalties, he declares that all such persons, and therefore even heretical or schismatic kings and emperors, are deprived wholly and for ever of all dignities, even of kingdoms and empires, and rendered henceforth unfit and incapable of them. Indeed, he adds, secular rulers (that is, even kings and emperors) are to be left to the discretion of the power to punish them with due severity, unless, by the kindness and clemency of this See, signs of true repentance and fruits worthy of repentance appear in them, so that they may be confined in some monastery or other religious place, to perform perpetual penance on bread of sorrow and water of mourning, deprived of every comfort of humanity. Their kingdoms, duchies, fiefs, dominions and goods of this kind are to be confiscated, and, once confiscated, they shall become the property and possession of those who first occupy them, provided they remain in sincere faith and in the unity of the Holy Roman Church, and in obedience to us and to our successor Roman Pontiffs canonically entering office. What, I ask, is more horrible than this Draconian and Leonine Bull? What is more suited to overthrowing the empires of any ruler harmed on some empty pretext, and to mixing the lowest with the highest? Further witness to Papal violence is that bull of Phalaris, the Tribunal of the Inquisition, truly Draconian, set up at Rome by the same pope, whose establishment a cardinal had long before been the author of under Paul III. Onuphrius, in his life of Paul, records that on his deathbed he also committed to the Cardinals the Office of the Holy Inquisition, which he called most holy, and on which he affirmed the authority of the Apostolic See alone rests. Pallavicinus too, in his History of the Council of Trent, Book XIV, 9:5, writes that this work of Paul is worthy of eternal praise, to which Italy should credit the preservation of the integrity of the faith. The same Pallavicinus, loc. cit., copiously describes the disturbances that accompanied and followed Paul's death: the Inquisition's prison set on fire by the raging people, the insignia of the Carafa family destroyed, and other such things that Suavis Polanus and Thuanus recount more sparingly. From these accounts alone it is clear how impatiently and stiff-necked the Romans bore this monstrous yoke, and that bloody manner of disputing through syllogisms formed from the limits of water, fire and the noose, a method more fitting to torturers and executioners than to teachers and pontiffs. The Index of Prohibited Books, compiled at Rome by the Inquisitors at his command and printed in 1559, is also a witness; we do not repeat here what has been said more fully elsewhere about it. At least from this it is evident that Paul had one care and one aim: to beat out every light of truth from men's minds, and to compel them to a dull and sedentary assent to his oracles, intent solely on enlarging Papal majesty. (For Pallavicinus, loc. cit., admits that Paul held all the amplitude of his most sacred power, and wisely exercised it according to its measure.) Let no one doubt in the least that the Popes established the Papacy by the same means by which the Turks established Muhammadanism.

units.la: CLXXXIV. Paulo publica lætitia omnium defun-
units.tr: CLXXXIV. At the death of Paul, public rejoicing among all

units.la: instituto tribunali Inquisitionis.
units.tr: having established the tribunal of the Inquisition,

units.la: & conscripto Indice librorum prohibitorum:
units.tr: and having drawn up the Index of prohibited books,

units.la: adeoque more Turcico Papatum promovens.
units.tr: and so, promoting the papacy in the Turkish manner.

units.la: Pii IV. Papatus. ʃto, Johannes Angelus de Medicis, Mediolanensis, Pii IV. nomen sibi arrogans, successit. Fuisse cum ingenio vivacem, mente sagacem, verbis & scommatibus acutum, cibi viniqve avidum, in voluptates pronum, occulte invidum, ad audiendum impatientem & difficilem, dominandi cupidum, vafrum, timidum, cujuslibet rei simulatorem & dissimulatorem, pecuniæ cupidum, amicitias non ex re, sed ex commodo æstimantem, Onuphrius Panvinius non dissimulavit. Confirmationem electionis Ferdinando Imperatori à prædecessore Paulo IV. superbissimè, uti supra diximus, negatam, ipse quidem ultro obtulit. Sed eam Cæsar animo excelso respuit, non modò, quia, uti Seneca de Benefic. lib. II. 1. loquitur; ingratum est beneficium, quod diu inter manus dantis hæsit: quod quis ægre dimittere visus est, & sic tanquam sibi præriperet: verum etiam, quòd eo facilè se carere posse putaret, exemplo Henrici Aucupis & Rodolphi Habspurgici, imo inde ab Augusto Augustorum omnium usque ad Carolum M. quos solus ille, per quem Reges regnant, & potentes justa decernunt, consecravit. Conatus tamen idem Pius est Florentinorum Principem creare Regem: creassetque nisi intercessisset Maximilianus, his non incongruè verbis usus: Non habet Italia Regem nisi Cæsarem.
units.tr: Pius IV's papacy. John Angelus de Medici of Milan, who styled himself Pius IV, succeeded. Onuphrius Panvinius did not hide that he was lively in intellect, shrewd in mind, sharp in words and jests, greedy for food and wine, prone to pleasures, secretly envious, impatient and difficult in listening, eager to dominate, crafty, timid, a pretender and dissembler of every matter, greedy for money, and valuing friendships not for their worth but for their advantage. The confirmation of his election, which his predecessor Paul IV had haughtily refused to Emperor Ferdinand, as we said above, Pius himself offered unasked. But the Emperor rejected it with a lofty spirit, not only because, as Seneca says in de Benefic. lib. II. 1., a benefit is ungracious when it has long stuck in the hands of the giver, and when he seems reluctant to let it go, as if he were snatching it back from himself, but also because he thought he could do without it, following the example of Henry the Fowler and Rudolf of Habsburg, and indeed from Augustus, the Augustus of all, down to Charlemagne, whom alone he who rules kings through whom kings reign, and who decrees justice to the powerful, consecrated. Yet this same Pius tried to make the Prince of Florence king, and would have done so had Maximilian not intervened, using these not inappropriate words: Italy has no king except the Emperor.

units.la: CLXXXV. Concilium Tridentinum denuo Pius aperuit, non quòd veræ Reformationis studio & amore flagraret, sed tum quia metuebat, ne in Gallia Nationale Concilium coiret: tum quia querelam publicam percrebescere audivit, quòd ob Concilium interruptum religio passim mutetur, & Scoti libertatem religionis, sancito cum Anglis adversus Reginam suam fœdere, sibi vindicaverint: tum denique quia suspectam habuit Maximiliani Regis Bohemiæ cum Protestantibus amicitiam, eousque progressam, ut Papa quiritaretur, habere se filium hæreticorum fautorem. Novo autem exemplo quinque Legatos Concilio præfecit, & Italis ut magna frequentia Concilium viserent, quamvis haud alii quàm Hispani adfuturi crederentur, mandavit. Muniturus se ea ratione, ne Pontificia potestas, cui ab omnibus Transalpinis insidias struì, ipsemet fassus est, ullum in periculum adduci posset. Sed & dicis gratia Euangelicos invitavit. Quorum plerique ejus literas aperire dignati non sunt, invitationem utpote ab illegitima potestate profectam respuerunt omnes. Sessiones eo Pontifice habitæ sunt novem, & in iis decreta de sacrificio Missæ, Ordine, matrimonio, aliaque etiam reformationem morum concernentia edita sunt. De quibus in loco dicto plura non repetimus.
units.tr: CLXXXV. Pius reopened the Council of Trent again, not from any zeal and love for true Reform, but because he feared that a national Council might gather in France; because he heard of a widespread public complaint that, with the Council interrupted, religion was being changed everywhere, and that the Scots had claimed for themselves liberty of religion, sanctioned by a treaty with the English against their own Queen; and finally because he regarded as suspect the friendship of King Maximilian of Bohemia with the Protestants, which had gone so far that the Pope complained that he had a son who was a supporter of heretics. By an unprecedented step, he placed five Legates over the Council, and he ordered the Italians to attend the Council in large numbers, although it was believed that none but Spaniards would be present. He did this so that the papal power, against which, as he himself admitted, plots were being laid by all the transalpine nations, might not be brought into any danger. But he also invited the Evangelicals, for the sake of appearances. Most of them did not deign to open his letters, and all rejected the invitation, as it came from an illegitimate authority. Nine sessions were held under this Pope, and in them decrees were issued concerning the sacrifice of the Mass, Orders, marriage, and other matters also concerning the reformation of morals. We do not repeat more about these in the place already mentioned.

units.la: CLXXXVI. Durante adhuc Concilio Ferdinandus
units.tr: CLXXXVI. While the Council was still in progress, Ferdinand

units.la: ad Pium Papam literas dedit, quibus graviter questus est, quòd Concilium non eo modo ac ordine procedat, quo pii vellent, & afflictus rei Christianæ status exposceret: quòd segniter negotia tractentur: quòd Patres contentionibus & dissidiis distrahantur: quòd Concilio salva & integra non sit libertas. aliáque ejusmodi. Misit etiam ad Concilium volumen postulatorum, cujusmodi erant, ut Pontifex seipsum & Curiam Romanam reformari benignè patiatur; ut numerus Cardinalium reducatur: ut provideatur, ne fiant amplius dispensationes scandalosæ: ut revocentur exemptiones passim contra communia jura concessæ: ut tollatur prorsus beneficiorum pluralitas: ut Episcopi omnino ad residentiam cogantur: ut communio sub utraque specie decernatur, in usu carnis & jejuniis de pristino rigore aliquid remittatur, conjugium Sacerdotum Nationibus quibusdam indulgeatur. Estant tum literæ, tum Articuli apud Goldastum, secunda Constitutionum Imperialium parte. At Legatos Tridenti scripto co Ferdinandi vehementer esse commotos, eò quòd prosectum sit ab eorum arte, qui omnem impendebant operam ad elevandam Synodi ac Præsidum dignitatem, splendorémque Pontificatus minuendum, ac proinde ne quidem Conventui tradendum, sed tantisper suspendendum, dum ipsi per officia Nuntii Ferdinandum ab eo officio dimoverent, judicasse; Pallavicinus Hist. Concil. Trid. lib. XVII. 1: 6. commemorat. Similes articulos à Galliæ Rege ad Concilium missos idem Goldastus parte tertia narrat, addita ejusdem adversus Concilium Protestatione solenni, in qua inter alia sic Galli loquuntur: Eramus nos Galli esurientes & famelici, petentes à Beatissimo Papa, veluti Patre communi, Panem, non equidem naturalem, cujus non indiget Gallia, Regio feracissima, sed illum Divinum Angelorum Supersubstantialem, cujus in toto fere orbe Christiano tanta primum fuit caritas, deinde nunc etiam inopia, ut vix unquam post Christum natum major. Ille vero non quidem Panem, quem petebamus, dedit, sed scorpium, cujus cauda unico ictu simul duos potentissimos Reges, Ecclesiam Gallicanam, & Theologorum Parisiensium doctrinam feriret. Post alia adversus Papam Pium Ϙιλιßοτιχως dicta, sic iidem Patres etiam Concilii alloquuntur: Quid vobis judicandum proponitur, aut à vobis judicatum publicatur, quod non prius Roma missum, & Pio quarto placuerit? Concludunt: Pii quarti imperium detrectamus, quaecunque sint ejus judicia & sententiae, rejicimus, respuimus & contemnimus. Rursumque sic Patres Concilii alloquuntur: Cum nihil à vobis, sed omnia magis Romae quam Tridenti agantur, & quae hic publicantur, magis Pii quarti placita, quam Concilii Tridentini decreta jure existimentur; denuntiamus & protestamur, quaecunque in hoc conventu, hoc est, solius Pii quarti nutu & voluntate decernuntur & publicantur, ea neque Regem Christianissimum probaturum, neque Ecclesiam Gallicam pro decreto Concilii Oecumenici habituram. Bruta porro haec fulmina non fuisse, rebus ipsis & experiundo innotuit, quando Gallia, obnitente Clero licet, & cum exceptione quadam in publicis etiam Comitiis Concilii confirmationem urgente, ad agnoscendam ejus authoritatem adduci hactenus non potuit.
