Gnarus enim ille, dejerare & pejerare suetus, neminem celerius opprimi, quàm qui nihil timet; & frequentissimum initium calamitatis esse securitatem; nimis credulos & bonæ fidei Protestantes, qui ab omni fraude & insidiis securi potiùs quàm tuti, in Regia fide, recenti fide cum Regibus Principibúsque vicinis inita, ad servandam pacem adstricta acquiescebant, nuptiarum Regiarum Henrici scilicet Navarri & Margarethæ Valesiæ, Caroli Regis Galliæ Sororis, evocatos illico, perfidiæ suæ crudelissimæ cassibus implicuit.
units.tr: CXCV. In the early days of the papacy of Gregory XIII of Bologna, who was previously called Hugo Boncompagni, a man most learned in human law but most ignorant of divine law, those dreadful Parisian Eastern scenes, known by the name of St Bartholomew, disgraced his reign. For on St Bartholomew's day in the year 1572 (in the year of which, on 13 May, Gregory came to the papacy), and in a few days following, Catherine de' Medici, the king's mother, a second Jezebel, and the Duke of Guise, the instigators, with the king himself not unaware, so much of Christian and Evangelical blood was poured out by those who wish to be called most Christian, that its streams flooded the channels of the streets everywhere. Moreover, such fury was unleashed against the bravest men, the nobles of the kingdom, the flower of both sexes, the most innocent and most beautiful, and the common crowd, by the agents of Orcus, that the public and most famous rivers were filled with corpses and seen black with blood; so that for a time even residents at a great distance found the water unusable for drinking and other necessary purposes, and fish fattened on human flesh were loathed, with great execration of an unheard-of butchery. The total of those slain in those few days, which the king himself admitted in his reply to the papal legate, as Cicarella reports in the life of Gregory XIII, amounted to about seventy thousand, or, as others reckoned, to more than a hundred thousand Christians. The infamy of the deed was increased because the king heaped the stain of perjury upon the mark of cruelty, which not even Thetis could wash away with all her waters. For he, being accustomed to swear and to forswear, knew that no one is crushed more quickly than one who fears nothing, and that the most frequent beginning of disaster is security. Trusting too readily, and being men of good faith, the Protestants, who were secure rather than safe, relied on the royal word, given in a recent pledge made with the neighbouring kings and princes and bound to keep the peace; and so he, with the royal marriage of Henry of Navarre and Margaret of Valois, the sister of King Charles of France, drew them at once to the snares of his most cruel treachery.

units.la: CVCVI. Hanc furoris inauditi lanienam, cùm ad æternam Gallici nominis & Pontificiæ religionis infamiam pertinere judicarent merito viri dignitate & doctrina præstantes, Scombergius, Morvillerius, Thuanus pater, Monlucius, Bibracius, Cujacius, alii, passim in Polonia, Germania, Gallia, alibíque, ut Regni Regísque bono, famæ & honori consulerent, officiosis mendaciis, scelus patratum aut simulatè laudare, aut astutè imminuere, vel exquisitissimis ex falsa narratione detortis ratiunculis ingeniosè diluere necesse habuerunt: quod intra se tamen omnibus diris & imprecationibus flagellabant.
units.tr: CVI. Men distinguished in rank and learning, Scombergius, Morvillier, the elder Thou, Montluc, Bibrac, Cujas, and others, rightly judged that this unheard-of slaughter of madness brought eternal infamy upon the French name and the Papist religion. So they found it necessary, here and there in Poland, Germany, France and elsewhere, for the good of the kingdom and the king, to look after his fame and honour: either to praise the crime committed, or to lessen it cunningly, with dutiful lies, or to wittily explain it away with petty arguments twisted from a false account. Yet within themselves they tormented themselves with every curse and imprecation.

units.la: Thuanus certè Parlamenti Parisiensis Præses, illos Statii Papinii, ex Theb. lib. II. versus, in causa impare licet, huc accommodavit:
units.tr: Certainly Thou, president of the Parliament of Paris, applied to this case, though the cause is unequal, those verses of Statius from the Thebaid, lib. II.:

units.la: Excidat illa dies ævo, nec postera credant Secula : nos certè taceamus & obruta multa Nocte tegi propria patiamur crimina gentis.
units.tr: Let that day fall out of the age, and let later generations not believe it; let us, at least, keep silent, and allow the crimes of our nation to be hidden under thick night.

units.la: Sed & optimum Imperatorem Maximilianum piaculare hoc facinus improbâsse non parum, ex literis ejus die XXII. Febr. A. M. D. LXXIV. Vienná ad Lazarum Schwendium exaratis, liquet. Ipsum Turcarum Imperatorem, & natura & instituto crudelissimum, in stuporem acroasi isthac raptum, non desunt qui scribant. Denique Rex Carolus IX. qui corruptus exoticis consiliis, initiò lanienam illam & probârat & imperârat, & se imperâsse etiam, prætextu fictitiæ conjurationis Amirallii Chastilonii adversus adolescentem Guisium, aliósque, apud exteros professus est (quid enim etiam Legatus ejus in Helvetiorum Concilio eam in rem affirmaverit, ex Prisbachii Responsione ad orationem ejusdem A. M. D. LXXIII. Rupellæ typis impressa liquet) perfecto demum scelere magnitudinem ejus intelligens, sauciatæ conscientiæ suriis agitatus, tempore noctis, haud secus quàm Nero interfecta matre (verbis Taciti Annal. XIV. 10. uti liceat) modò per silentium defixus, sæpius pavore exurgens & mentis inops, lucem operiens tanquam exitium allaturam; somni etiam & conscientiæ damna qualitercunque reparaturus, Symphoniacos pueros adhibens, &, paulò ante mortem, etiam Orlandum Lassum Musicum celebrem Norico evocans; detestatus est crudelis consilii auctores, ac pœnitentiæ suæ certis testimoniis editis, à cœdibus perpetuo deinceps abhorrens, Christianorum sanguini parcere decrevit, studuítque, uti de eo fusè Thuanus sub finem lib. LVII. commemorat.
units.tr: But that the excellent Emperor Maximilian greatly disapproved of this monstrous deed is clear from his letter written at Vienna to Lazarus Schwendi on 22 February 1574. Some write that the Emperor of the Turks himself, most cruel by nature and by custom, was struck dumb on hearing of it. Finally King Charles IX, who had been corrupted by foreign counsels, had at first both approved and ordered that butchery, and he declared to foreigners that he had also ordered it, under the pretext of a fictitious conspiracy of Admiral Coligny against the young Guise and others. (What his envoy also affirmed on this matter in the council of the Swiss is clear from Prisbach's reply to his speech, printed at La Rochelle in 1573.) But at last, when the deed was completed, he understood its enormity, and, driven by the furies of a wounded conscience, at night, much as Nero did after his mother was killed (to use the words of Tacitus, Annals XIV. 10), fixed in silence, often rising in terror and helpless in mind, awaiting the light as if it were to bring his destruction. Wishing somehow to repair the losses of sleep and conscience, he kept boys for singing and playing, and shortly before his death he summoned the famous musician Orlando Lasso from Nuremberg. He execrated the authors of the cruel plan, and, having published certain testimonies of his repentance, he thereafter kept utterly away from slaughter and resolved to spare Christian blood. He strove to do so, as Thou recounts at length near the end of book LVII.

units.la: CXCVII. Quid verò hic Sanctissimus ille Gregorius Papa?
units.tr: CXCVII. But what of that most holy Pope Gregory?

units.la: Is scilicet, eodem Thuano lib. LIII. narrante, & Strada etiam Dec. I. lib. 7. pag. 441. confirmante; tragœdiæ feliciter peractæ factus à Rege certior, statim cum Cardinalibus ad B. Marci concessit. DEO O. M. pro tanto beneficio Sedi Romanæ collato gratias solenni ritu egit: Jubilæum toti orbi Christiano lætam adeò ob causam publicavit: in Hadriani mole, publicæ lœtitiæ signum festa tormentorum displosione dedit: totam rei bene gestæ historiam artifici penicillo parietibus illevit: Cardinali quoque Lotharingo, tam optatum afferenti Euangelium, mille aureorum euangelia numeravit; denique Roma in Galliam misit Gabium Ursinum Cardinalem, laudaturum Regem ob egregium facinus, aurésque ei vellicaturum, ut Concilii Tridentini promulgatione illud obsignaret. Atque ille quidem recens tum flagitium, affectuum vehementia præpeditus, veris pretiis æstimari non potuit. Tantoque mirandum magis est, hodiéque reperiri Theologiam, & quod plus est, Jesu Societatem professos, qui non verentur immanitatis tantæ faninus & lanienam plus quàm Diocletianam non excusare duntaxat, uti Stradam fecisse constat: sed summis etiam laudibus efferre. uti quidem Andræas Eudæmon Johannes, verè Cretensis Jesuita, in Anticat. Confut. cap. 3. facere non erubuit. Alius quin etiam Jesuita sub fictitio Johannis Baptistæ Galli nomine latitans, Not. in histor. Thuani cap. 6. detestabilem illam Vitellii à Suetonio in ejus vita cap. 10. memoratam vocem, graveolentiam scilicet hostilium cadaverum quibusvis odoribus & pigmentis esse sibi fragrantiorem, exultabundus huc trahere non erubuit. Qua re abundè testantur, semel factam lanienam sibi satis non esse: ac dirissimum quodque scelus se probaturos facilè, dum specie pietatis admissum fuerit.
units.tr: He, as Thuanus relates in lib. LIII., and Strada confirms in Dec. I. lib. 7. pag. 441., was informed by the King, once the tragedy had been successfully carried out, and at once went with the Cardinals to St Mark's. He gave solemn thanks to God, the best and greatest, for so great a benefit conferred on the Roman See. He proclaimed a Jubilee for the whole Christian world on this joyful occasion. On the Mole of Hadrian he marked the public rejoicing with a festive discharge of artillery. He had the whole history of the deed painted on the walls by an artist's brush. He also counted out a thousand gold crowns to the Cardinal of Lorraine, who had brought such a desired gospel. Finally, he sent Cardinal Gabius Ursinus from Rome into France, to praise the King for his outstanding deed and to tickle his ears, so that he might seal it with the promulgation of the Council of Trent. Indeed, that man, hampered by the violence of his feelings, could not at the time estimate so recent a crime at its true worth. And it is all the more astonishing that even today there are to be found theologians, and, what is more, members of the Society of Jesus, who do not hesitate not merely to excuse so monstrous a crime and a slaughter worse than Diocletian's, as Strada is known to have done, but even to extol it with the highest praise. Andreas Eudaemon Johannes, a true Cretan Jesuit, did not blush to do this in Anticat. Confut. cap. 3. Another Jesuit, hiding under the feigned name of John the Baptist of Gaul, Not. in histor. Thuani cap. 6., exultantly dragged in that detestable saying of Vitellius, recorded by Suetonius in his life cap. 10., that the stench of enemy corpses was sweeter to him than any perfumes or spices, and did not blush to do so. By this they abundantly show that one slaughter was not enough for them, and that they would readily approve any most dreadful crime, provided it was committed under the appearance of piety.

units.la: CXCVIII. Idem etiam Gregorius mutandorum temporum potestatem sibi, novámque adeò jurisdictionem arrogans; Calendarium novum opera Liliorum confecit, atque ea ratione non tantùm Imperatori & Principibus Calendarii emendationem indignè præripuit, cùm tamen olim, Suetonio in Julio cap. 40. referente, nonnisi Cæsar conversus ad ordinandum Reip. statum, fastos correxit, jam pridem vitio Pontificum per intercalandi licentiam turbatos: sed etiam callido isthoc consilio Protestantes, Germanos inprimis, quos ejus jussa pridem aspectare desuevisse non ignoverat, irretire, civilemque eorum cum Pontificiis Societatem & commercia turbare conatus est. quod passim etiam ex voto ejus successisse, historiæ testantur. Neque minus subdolum ejus consilium fuit, passim Collegia seu feminaria instituentis, in quibus scilicet educarentur formarenturque novi ex Germania, Anglia, Græcia, &c. conducitii non tam haruspices, quorum apud Romanos olim famosa Collegia seu seminaria celebrata sunt, quam Cyclopes, Euangelicorum carnem mox laceraturi devoraturique, seu mavis, gigantei Atlantes, Cœlum Pontificium humeris suis passim, ne penitus corrueret, sustentaturi pacemque publicam turbaturi. Quo etiam animo Jesuitas propensissimè fovit, pro quibus Romæ Collegium splendidissimum erexit dotavitque. Eodem quinetiam animo Hiberniam Elisabethæ subtrahere; Belgas, oppugnantibus eos omnium peccatorum remissione promissa, debellare nequicquam molitus est. Denique ita se gessit; ut fidem impleverit oraculi, quod famosus ille Ægidius Franciscanus his in illum verbis enuntiavit: Ex cavernis Draco vel ex exibit, citò abibit, duræ cervicis gustabit pessima. Cujus vaticinii ejusmodi statim declaratio adjungitur: Quare Draconis nomen Gregorio XIII. convenire dicatur, explicatione non eget. Citò eum prænuntiat discessurum, non quòd in adfecta ætate non discesserit, sed quia inopinanter. In vitus gravia sustinuit, cum multifariam & ubivis gentium Ecclesia ipso Pontifice vexationes habuerit. Citò exiit, quia unanimiter primo die Conclavis eligitur. CXCIX. Paria etiam cum Gregorio Successor ejus Sixtus Sixti V. crudelitas. Sixtus V. fecit. Licet enim is Cardinalis adhuc ob injuriarum patientiam Asini Anconitani nomine venerit; Papa tamen factus, deposito mitra, lachrymas cruentas fundere, & sanguinem pro sudore toto corpore emittere aliquando, Thuano lib. XXXII. teste, visus; (natura ipsa crudelem ejus animum quodamodo prodente; nam & saevitiae ejus exempla plura apud Cicarellam & Thuanum reperire est) summos Reges Principesque vel dissentientes à Romana Sede, vel ejus commodis non strenuè satis velificatos, anathemate diro ferire, & ab obedientia juramento iis obstricta obnoxios absolvere, neutiquam reveritus est. Extat ejus Bulla seu Declaratio contra Henricum Borbonium assertum Regem Navarrae, & Henricum item Borbonium, praetensum Principem Condensem, Haereticos, eorumque Posteros & Successores: ac liberatio Subditorum, ab omni fidelitatis & obsequii debito. Romae & Coloniae A. M. D. LXXXV. edita. In ea feralem adversus eos sententiam multa de authoritate sua, cunctas terrenorum Regum potestates supereminente, & in firma petra consistente, praefatus, his verbis stringit: Itaque in praecelso hoc Solio, & in plenitudine potestatis, quam ipse Rex Regum & Dominus dominantium, licet nobis indignis tribuit, constituti, auctoritate Dei Omnipotentis, ac beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum ejus, & nostro (en suam potestatem a potestate Divina & Apostolica blasphemè distinguentem!) ac de Venerabilium fratrum nostrorum Sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ Cardinalium consilio, pronuntiamus & declaramus, Henricum quondam Regem, & Henricum Condensem supra dictos fuisse, & esse haereticos, in haereses relapsos, & impaenitentes, haereticorum quoque Duces, fautores & defensores manifestos, publicos & notorios, sicque laesae Majestatis Divinae reos, & Orthodoxae fidei Christianae hostes; ac proinde eos damnabiliter incurrisse in sententias, censuras & poenas sacris canonibus & constitutionibus Apostolicis, legibus generalibus & particularibus contentas, ac haereticis relapsis & impaeimpœnitentibus debitas, & specialiter eos fuisse, & esse ipso jure privatos, Henricum quondam Regem videlicet prætenso Navarræ Regno, illiúsque parte, quam adhuc obtinuit, nec non Bearni: alterum verò Henricum, Condensi, & utrumque, eorúmque posteros omnibus, & quibuscunque aliis Principatibus, Ducatibus, Dominiis, Civitatibus & locis; feudísque & bonis etiam amphyteuticis, & successionibus, nec non dignitatibus, honoribus, muneribus & officiis, etiam Regiis, ac jurisdictionibus & juribus, quæ de facto detinent, & ad quæ jus quomodolibet habuerunt, seu pretendunt, eosdemque propterea se illis reddidisse indignos, ac fuisse & esse inhabiles & incapaces ad illa retinenda, & alia hujusmodi in posterum obtinenda. Ac pariter eos ipse jure privatos & incapaces ac inhabiles ad succedendum in quibuscunque Ducatibus, Principatibus, Dominiis & Regnis, ac specialiter in Regno Franciæ, ac Regno ipsi annexis dominiis, jurisdictionibus & locis, &c. Pronuntiata pluribus sententia Henricum Regem Francorum Christianissimum per viscera misericordiæ Jesu Christi hortatur, rogat, ac etiam monet, ut memor præstantissimæ fidei, & Religionis Regum Majorum suorum, memor etiam juramenti, quod in ejus coronatione de exterminandis hæreticis, solenniter præstitit, authoritate, potestate, atque animi magnitudine verè Regia, ad executionem tam iustæ sententiæ suæ incumbat &c. Ab Henrico tamen utroque Navarro & Condensi, validè id omne spretum est, seu fulgur è pelvi. Quinimò Navarrus Programmate ad Marforii ac Pasquilli statuas, & aliis celebrioribus Romæ locis affixo de injusta damnatione questus, & ad Concilium liberum provocans, se Papam pro mendaci, hæretico, sectario & Antichristo habere declarat, donec, quæ sibi impegerat, probâsset. Addens etiam: Si Decessores mei Reges, hujusmodi nebulones, qualis hic Sixtus, coercere poterant, idem se factypum. Accessit Programmati illi Declaratio, authore, uti putatur, Francisco Perroto, qua Sixtum mentitum esse confirmatur, collectis etiam ex Petrarcha, Aligerio, Bocatio, locis, quibus Curiæ Romanæ mores ac libidines amarulentè carpuntur. Postea in eandem Bullam scripserunt tum Franciscus Hottomannus joculari stilo, libro Brutum fulmen titulum faciens; tum Theophilus Banosius: tum grandi libro Petrus Bellojus, ob id molesto carcere diu vexatus.
units.tr: CXCVIII. Gregory also, arrogating to himself the power to change the times and a new jurisdiction of that kind, produced a new Calendar through the work of the Lilies. By this means he not only unworthily snatched from the Emperor and the Princes the amendment of the Calendar, although once, as Suetonius relates in Julius cap. 40., Caesar, turning to the ordering of the state, corrected the calendar, long since thrown into confusion by the fault of the Pontiffs through their licence to intercalate; he also strove, by this crafty plan, to ensnare the Protestants, especially the Germans, whom he knew had long since grown unused to looking to his orders, and to disturb their civil fellowship and commerce with the Papists. History bears witness that this also succeeded everywhere according to his wish. No less deceitful was his plan of founding colleges or seminaries everywhere, in which there would be educated and trained new men from Germany, England, Greece and so on, hired not so much as soothsayers, whose famous colleges or seminaries were celebrated among the Romans of old, as Cyclopes who would soon tear and devour the flesh of the Evangelicals; or, if you prefer, giant Atlases, who would support the Papal heaven on their shoulders everywhere, lest it collapse altogether, and who would disturb the public peace. With this same purpose he warmly cherished the Jesuits, for whom he built and endowed a most splendid college at Rome. With the same purpose he also strove, in vain, to withdraw Ireland from Elizabeth and to subdue the Netherlands, promising forgiveness of all sins to those who fought against them. In sum, he so conducted himself that he fulfilled the oracle which that famous Giles the Franciscan uttered against him in these words: A dragon shall come out of the caverns; he shall quickly depart, and taste the worst things of a stiff neck. A declaration of this prophecy is added in this manner: That the name of the Dragon is said to fit Gregory XIII needs no explanation. He foretells that he will quickly depart, not because he did not depart at an advanced age, but because it was unexpected. He endured grave troubles, since the Church, with the Pope himself, suffered vexations in many ways and in every part of the world. He quickly departed, because he was elected unanimously on the first day of the Conclave. CXCIX. Sixtus V, the successor of Gregory, was equally cruel. For although that man came to the Cardinalate under the name of the Ass of Ancona, on account of his patience under injuries, nevertheless, once made Pope, he was seen, having laid aside his mitre, to shed bloody tears and to send forth blood instead of sweat from his whole body, as Thuanus lib. XXXII. testifies. Nature itself, as it were, revealed his cruel spirit; for many examples of his savagery are to be found in Cicarella and Thuanus. He did not in the least hesitate to strike with a dreadful anathema the greatest Kings and Princes who either dissented from the Roman See or did not sail sufficiently briskly to its advantage, and to absolve from the oath of obedience by which they were bound. His Bull, or Declaration against Henry of Bourbon, asserted King of Navarre, and Henry, likewise of Bourbon, the so-called Prince of Condé, heretics, and their posterity and successors; and the release of subjects from every debt of fidelity and obedience. Printed at Rome and Cologne, A.D. 1585. In it, after prefacing the deadly sentence against them with much about his own authority, which surpasses all the powers of earthly kings and stands on a firm rock, he expresses it in these words: Therefore, seated in this high Throne and in the fullness of power which the King of Kings and Lord of lords himself grants to us, though unworthy, by the authority of Almighty God and of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and by our own (behold, he blasphemously distinguishes his power from the Divine and Apostolic power!), and with the counsel of our venerable brothers the Cardinals of the holy Roman Church, we pronounce and declare that Henry, formerly King, and Henry of Condé, were and are the heretics named above, relapsed into heresy and unrepentant, manifest, public and notorious leaders, supporters and defenders of heretics, and so guilty of injured divine majesty and enemies of the orthodox Christian faith; and that therefore they have incurred damnably the sentences, censures and penalties contained in the sacred canons and apostolic constitutions, in general and particular laws, and due to relapsed and unrepentant heretics; and that in particular they have been, and are, by the law itself deprived of the so-called Kingdom of Navarre and of that part of it which he still holds, as well as Béarn; the other Henry of Condé, and both of them and their posterity of all and any other principalities, duchies, lordships, cities and places, and of fiefs and goods, even those held in emphyteusis, and successions, as well as dignities, honours, offices and duties, even royal ones, and jurisdictions and rights, which they hold de facto, and to which they have or pretend to have any right whatever; and that by this they have made themselves unworthy of them, and have been and are unfit and incapable of retaining them, and of obtaining such things in future. And likewise that they are by the law itself deprived, incapable and unfit to succeed to any duchies, principalities, lordships and kingdoms, and especially to the Kingdom of France and the lordships, jurisdictions and places annexed to that kingdom, etc. Having pronounced this sentence, he urges, begs and also admonishes Henry, the most Christian King of the French, by the bowels of mercy of Jesus Christ, that, mindful of the most excellent faith and religion of his greatest ancestors, and mindful also of the oath which at his coronation he solemnly took concerning the extermination of heretics, he should with authority, power and the truly royal greatness of spirit apply himself to the execution of so just a sentence, etc. Yet both Henrys, of Navarre and of Condé, scorned all this utterly, as a thunderbolt out of a basin. Indeed, the King of Navarre, through a Programme posted on the statues of Marforio and Pasquino and in other more famous places in Rome, complained of the unjust condemnation, appealed to a free Council, and declared that he held the Pope to be a liar, heretic, sectarian and Antichrist, until he should prove the charges he had brought against him. He added: If my predecessor Kings could restrain such scoundrels as this Sixtus, I too shall do the same. To that Programme was added a Declaration, the author of which is thought to be Francis Perrot, confirming that Sixtus had lied; it also gathered passages from Petrarch, Alighieri and Boccaccio, in which the morals and lusts of the Roman Curia are bitterly censured. Afterwards, writing against the same Bull, there came Francis Hotman in a jocular style, making the title Brutum fulmen; then Theophilus Banos; and then Pierre Bellojus in a large book, for which he was long harassed by an unpleasant imprisonment.

units.la: CC. Neque tamen sic satis Sixtus bullavit. Nam & Henrico III. Galliarum Regi infensus, quòd Ducem & Cardinalem Guisios, occupans scilicet facinus, quod ipsos adversus Regem meditari constabat, interfici jussisset, Cardinalem Borbonium & Episcopum Lugdunensem captivos attineret, monitorio diplomate ei diras intentavit. Ni fecerit jussa sua, declarat Sixtus, eum ab Ecclesiæ communione exclusum, anathematis fulmine feriendum, in omnes censuras Ecclesiasticas, ac præsertim in eas, quæ in Bulla Cœnæ Dominicæ leguntur, incurrisse. Præterea Regem ipsum citat, ut intra L X. dies vel ipse, vel per procuratores, cum idoneo mandato Romam veniat, ac se judicio sistat, rationem redditurus, cur Cardinalem Guisianum interfecerit, & nunc Cardinalem Borbonium, & Archiepiscopum Lugdunensem detineat. Horum autem L X. dierum viginti pro prima, totidem pro secunda, reliqui pro tertia admonitione Canonica sint assignati. His additum, ut numero illorum nec Rex ipse à quoquam, nisi à summo Pontifice, ne quidem in casu conscientiæ, hora seu periculo mortis excepto; & ne tunc quidem, nisi præstita cautione se pariturum Ecclesiæ in iis, quæ essent illi injuncta, absque hoc esset, non posset absolvi, nec in pleno jubileo, nec in sacra crucis militia. Decretum illud IX. Kal. Junii A. M. D. LXXXIX. publicatum, & ad valvas Basilicæ B. Petri & Johannis Lateranensis affixum, & in Gallia etiam in civitate Meldorum, & Autrici Carnutum solenniter promulgatum fuit. Adversus Edictum isthoc Senatus Venetus, magnus Etruriæ Dux, & Dux Mantuæ, Henrico Regi animosum consilium suppeditant, rati, cum Sixto agendum asperè, quia ita agreste sit ejus ingenium, ut nullo cultu & obsequio ad amicitiam inflecti, tantum vi ac convitiis ad officium cogi possit. Refert hæc similiáque Bucanus Histor. lib. XCV. Rex igitur respondit Pontifici, flocci se facere excommunicationem ejus, neque eum se excommunicandi in Francia jus ullum habere, ob causam præsertim politicam, non ecclesiasticam. Porro in Mœnium ac Legistas arma Rex sumit, fœdere cum Navarro inito, eóque legato copiis suis cum summa potestate præfecto. Ac hic demum in eum Papa fulminat, ac subditos obsequii sacramento solvit. quem & Sorboniste Regno excidisse, à Parisiensibus rebellibus consulti respondent, eisque in eum arma ferre permittunt. Tandem Lutetiam obsidentem Regem ad Clodovæi fanum, crudeli sicarius cucullo tectus Jacobus Clemens venenato cultro ancipite, imum in ventrem intra ilia adacto, interemit. Ita Henricus, ultimus Valesiorum sanguis, qui Monachorum ordines præcipua semper veneratione coluit, postremò à Monacho interfectus est, justo utique Dei judicio, ulcisicentis hac etiam ratione Parisiensem Lanienam, cujus Henricus Protestantes irreconciliabili odio ad ultimum usque vitæ spiritum prosecutus, eosdemque subdolè pace potiùs quàm bello labefactaturus deinceps, cùm parùm procedere vim animadverteret; præcipuus, in gratiam Lotharingorum, author suasorque extiterat.
units.tr: CC. Yet Sixtus did not stop at bulls. Angry also with Henry III, King of France, because he had ordered the murder of Duke Henry and Cardinal Guise, seizing the deed as an act he had learned they were plotting against the King, and because he kept Cardinal Bourbon and the Archbishop of Lyon in custody, Sixtus hurled dire threats at him in a monitory decree. Sixtus declared that unless the King obeyed his orders, he was excluded from communion with the Church, was to be struck with the thunderbolt of anathema, and had incurred all ecclesiastical censures, especially those read in the Bull In Coena Domini. He further summoned the King to appear in Rome, in person or through proctors with a proper mandate, within sixty days, to submit to judgment and give an account of why he had killed Cardinal Guise and was now detaining Cardinal Bourbon and the Archbishop of Lyon. Of these sixty days, twenty were assigned for the first canonical warning, as many for the second, and the rest for the third. It was added that the King himself could not be absolved by anyone except the supreme Pontiff, not even in a case of conscience, at the hour or danger of death; and even then not unless he first gave a pledge that he would obey the Church in whatever was enjoined on him, failing which he could not be absolved, either in a full jubilee or in the military order of the Cross. This decree, published on the ninth day before the Kalends of June 1589, was posted on the doors of the basilicas of St Peter and St John Lateran, and was also solemnly promulgated in France, in the town of Meaux and at Chartres. Against this edict the Venetian Senate, the Grand Duke of Tuscany and the Duke of Mantua offered King Henry a spirited plan, judging that Sixtus must be dealt with sharply, since his disposition was so rough that he could not be brought to friendship by any courtesy or deference, but could be forced to duty only by violence and abuse. Buchanan reports these and similar things in his History, book 95. The King therefore answered the Pontiff that he cared nothing for his excommunication, and that he had no right to excommunicate anyone in France, especially for a political rather than an ecclesiastical cause. Then the King took up arms against the Guisians and the lawyers, having made an alliance with the Navarrese and placed him, as his legate, in command of his troops with full power. At this the Pope at last thundered against him and released his subjects from the oath of obedience. The Sorbonnists, consulted by the rebellious Parisians, answered that he had fallen from the kingdom, and allowed them to take up arms against him. At last, while the King was besieging Paris, at the shrine of Clodoveus, Jacques Clément, hidden under a monk's cowl and wielding a poisoned double-edged knife, stabbed him deep into the belly between the bowels and killed him. Thus Henry, the last of the Valois blood, who had always shown the greatest reverence to the monastic orders, was at last killed by a monk, surely by the just judgment of God, who avenged in this way the Parisian slaughter. Henry had pursued the Protestants with implacable hatred to his last breath, and had been their chief author and adviser in the hope of Lorraine's favour, having seen that force was making little progress, and intending thereafter to shake them more cunningly by peace rather than by war.

units.la: CCI. Quid verò etiam hic Sixtus ille, cruentas alias lachrymas fundere, & sanguinem sudare compertus? In Pontifice, Thuani ejusdem Histor. lib. XCVI. verba referam, summè insolens, & pastorali moderatione indignum visum, quod de Clemente & Rege præconium ejus paulò post à fœderatis Lutetiæ publicatum est. Siquidem postquam de Regis morte Romæ allatum latum est, ille in Consistorio III. Eid. Sept. habito præmeditatam orationem habuit, qua factum Clementis operi assumptæ à Domino carnis, & resurrectionis ejusdem mysterio ab Habacuco vate prædicato, propter magnitudinem & rei admirationem, comparat, tum virtutem hominis, animi robur & ferventem erga Deum amorem supra Eleazarum & Judithan multis verbis extollit, ex eóque colligit, hoc nisi certa Divinæ providentiæ ordinatione ac auxilio confici non potuisse; neque verò ipsum crediturum fuisse, nisi fidem ad obsequium Christi flexisset, qui ratione omnem fidem superante Parisiensem civitatem liberâsset, & gravissima Regis peccata punivisset, eúmque tam infausta morte è medio sustulisset. Se verò id antea animo providisse, ac Joúsæ, Lenuncurio, Gandio Cardinalibus, & Pisanio Marchioni ipsius oratoris sæpius prædixisse, fore, ut quemadmodum esset familiæ suæ ultimus, ita aliquem insuetum & dedecorosum vitæ exitum habiturus esset. Itaque indignum iis officiis, quæ Imperatoribus ac Regibus exhiberi solent, quippe S. Scripturæ authoritate prohiberi, ne quis pro eo, qui in peccato ad mortem, hoc est, in Spiritum S. commisso, quale Regis peccatum fuit, moritur, preces faciat. En peccatum Henrici, Guisios scilicet perduelles suos punientis, armis cum Navarro junctis pacem Galliæ parantis, at de cœtero Ecclesiæ Romanæ addictissimi; Protestantibus infensissimi, à Pontifice peccati ad mortem & in Spiritum Sanctum stigmate inustum! In Spiritum S. scilicet peccat, quisquis Papæ imperata, qualiacunque non promptissimè exequitur, & amicos ejus qualescunque illos loedit. Et dicta hæc etiam scripto comprehensa & publicata sunt. Cui scripto infami oppositus est liber, Anti-Sixti titulo, Latine; nec non Gallica Declamatio, Fulminantis nomine, acerbior illa quidem, ita prosequitur Thuanus, sed tali oratione prorsus digna; quibus & Regis causa multis rationibus defenditur, & multa impia & absurda in illa Sixti oratione notantur; ad extremum superbo seni petulantia sua exprobratur, qui censuræ iniquissimæ fulmine in imme-
units.tr: CCI. But what of this same Sixtus, who was known to shed other tears and sweat blood? I will quote Thuanus' own words from his History, book 96: it seemed very insolent and unworthy of pastoral moderation, the eulogy of Clement and the King that was published at Paris by the allies a little later. For when news of the King's death had come to Rome, he delivered a prepared oration in consistory on 11 September, in which he compared Clement's deed to the mystery of the Lord's assumption of flesh and resurrection, foretold by the prophet Habakkuk, on account of its greatness and wonder. He then extolled the man's courage, strength of spirit and burning love of God in many words, above Eleazar and Judith, and concluded from this that it could not have been accomplished without the certain ordering and help of divine providence. He said he would not have believed it had he not bent his faith to the obedience of Christ, who by a means surpassing all faith had freed the city of Paris, punished the King's most grievous sins, and removed him from the midst by so unhappy a death. He said he had foreseen this in his mind beforehand, and had often predicted to Cardinals Joyeuse, Lenoncourt and Gondi, and to the Marquis Pisani, the ambassador's, that, just as the King would be the last of his family, so he would have some unusual and shameful end of life. Therefore, he said, it was unworthy to offer the honours customarily paid to emperors and kings, since Holy Scripture forbids anyone to pray for one who dies in sin unto death, that is, in the sin against the Holy Spirit, which was the King's sin. Behold the sin of Henry, who punished his own rebels the Guises, who joined arms with the Navarrese to bring peace to France, yet was most devoted to the Roman Church from then on and most hostile to the Protestants: he was branded by the Pope with the sin unto death and against the Holy Spirit! Clearly whoever does not most promptly carry out whatever the Pope commands, of whatever kind, and injures his friends, of whatever sort, sins against the Holy Spirit. These words were also set down in writing and published. Against this infamous writing was set a book entitled Anti-Sixtus in Latin, and also a French declamation named The Thunderer, rather harsher, as Thuanus goes on, but altogether worthy of such a discourse; in which the King's cause is defended on many grounds, and many impious and absurd things in that oration of Sixtus are noted; and at last the old man is rebuked for his arrogance, who, hurling the thunderbolt of most unjust censure against one undeserving, had stirred up a most deadly tragedy in France, and now insulted the fallen with the greatest impiety, like a hare plucking the beard of a dead lion.

units.la: Scripta eidem Anti-Sixti, & Fulminantis titulo ö posita. immerentem vibrato, funestissimam tragœdiam in Gallia excitâsset; & nunc jacenti summa impietate insultaret, & ipse lepus mortuo leoni barbam velleret.
units.tr: Writings against the same Sixtus, published under the titles Anti-Sixtus and The Thunderer. He had stirred up a most deadly tragedy in France against one undeserving, and now insulted the fallen with the greatest impiety, like a hare plucking the beard of a dead lion.

units.la: CCII. Recognoverat idem Sixtus vel ejus potiùs jussu, alii, ad Typographiam Vaticanam deputati, S. Bibliorum versionem Latinam vulgatam. Ita enim in Tridentino Concilio decretum fuerat, sanciente etiam, Seff. I V. ut ita recognita in publicis lectionibus, disputationibus prædicationibus & expositionibus pro authentica habeatur, ita ut nemo illam rejicere quovis prætextu audeat. Ita fœtum in utero Tridentinis baptizare placuit. Neglexerunt tamen hactenus Pontifices decreto Tridentino facere satis. Primo Sixto huic res curæ fuit. Is recognitam Versionem edita, eíque præfixa Bulla declaravit, Vulgatam sacræ tam Novi quàm Veteris Testamenti paginæ Latinam editionem, quæ pro authentica à Concilio Tridentino recepta est, sine ulla dubitatione ac controversia recipiendam, esse hanc ipsam, quam nunc, prout optimè fieri potuit, emendatam, & in Vaticana Typographia impressam, in universa Rep. Christiana, atque in omnibus orbis Christiani Ecclesiis legendam, evulget. Eam priùs quidem universali sanctæ Ecclesiæ ac S. Patrum consensione; deinde verò Generalis Concilii Decreto; nunc demum Apostolica sibi à Domino tradita authoritate comprobatam, pro vera, legitima, authentica & indubitata in omnibus publicis privatisque disputationibus, lectionibus, prædicationibus, & explanationibus recipiendam & tenendam esse. Eandem tamen editionem Sixtinam mox Clemens VIII. interpolavit, expunctis sententiis & vocibus, nec non restitutis passim lectionibus, à Sixtina discrepantibus, contrariis, contradicentibus, uti ad oculum Thomas Jamesius in bello Papali demonstravit. Neque etiam Bailius in Summa Conciliorum dissimulat, Clementem Bibliorum Sixti vulgatam editionem in multis emendatam, in pluribus emendatiorem edi curasse, mutatis, additis aut detractis aliquot verbis, aliis transpositis, nonnullis etiam apertam contrarietatem aut contradictionem habentibus. Quod nutantis infallibilitatis Pontificiae spiritusque vertiginis, quo Pontifices illi se correptos prodiderunt, notorium specimen praetereundum non fuit.
units.tr: CCII. The same Sixtus, or rather others at his command, appointed to the Vatican Printing House, had revised the Latin Vulgate version of the Holy Bible. For the Council of Trent had decreed, and sanctioned in Session IV, that the text so revised should be held authentic in public lectures, disputations, sermons and expositions, so that no one should dare to reject it on any pretext. Thus the Tridentine fathers chose to baptise the child while still in the womb. Yet hitherto the Popes had neglected to do enough to satisfy the Tridentine decree. The first to take the matter up was Sixtus. Having published the revised version, he prefaced it with a bull declaring that the Vulgate, the Latin edition of the sacred Scriptures of both the New and Old Testament, which the Council of Trent received as authentic, was to be received without any doubt or controversy; that it was this very edition, now emended as well as could be done and printed in the Vatican Press, which he was publishing for reading throughout the whole Christian commonwealth and in all the churches of the Christian world. He declared that it had been approved first by the universal consensus of the holy Church and the Fathers, then by the decree of a general council, and now at last by the apostolic authority given him by the Lord, and that it was to be received and held as true, legitimate, authentic and indubitable in all public and private disputations, lectures, sermons and explanations. Yet Clement VIII soon afterwards altered this Sixtine edition, deleting sentences and words and restoring readings here and there that differed from, contradicted and opposed the Sixtine text, as Thomas James clearly showed in his Bellum Papale. Nor does Bailius in his Summa Conciliorum conceal that Clement had caused the Sixtine edition of the Bible to be published, emended in many places and more emended in many more, with some words changed, added or removed, others transposed, and some even having a plain contrariety or contradiction. Since this is a notorious example of the wavering infallibility of the Papacy and of the spirit of giddiness by which those Popes showed themselves seized, it ought not to be passed over.

units.la: CCIII. Aliquid monstri idem Sixtus alebat adversus Hispanos, ut eos Italia, Regno inprimis Neapolitano, ubi crescens eorum potentia suspicionem nonnullam ipsi moverat, si qua pote, pelleret. Atque ambivisse ipsum eum in finem favorem tum Henrici IV. Regis Galliae, tum Elisabethae Angliae Reginae, utriusque excommunicati licet, non desunt idonei testes, qui affirment. Narrat id ipsum fusius Eduinus Santis de statu Relig. in Occidente cap. 29. Quodque utriusque & Henrici & Elisabethae virtutem ψυχμονικῶ se mirari & suspicere praecipue testaretur passim, Hispanicae factionis, ac Jesuitarum inprimis acerimum odium incurrit, a quibus etiam Navarristae nomen ipsi impositum est. Proin etiam decretas adversus Henricum fulminationes non solum revocare, sed etiam contra hostes ejus torsurum fuisse, ni mors praevenisset, Henricus ipse in Declaratione A. M. D. XCI. publicata, apud Thuanum Hist. lib. CI. testatus est. Quinimo Hispanorum odio acceleratam ipsi mortem, his verbis Bartholomaeus Morisotus Divionensis IC. vitae Henrici M. cap. 17. testatur. Cum Hispani, inquit ille, sensissent ejus (Sixti) consilia desertionem factionis molientis: ne hosti accederet, collum ejus tenui mantili implicitum per Monachum Franciscanum, aut nefarium Monachali veste de nocte compressum fuisse, continuato in mortem somno. Postero die Sixtum domesticos daemone strangulatum tota Roma vulgavisse. Et ut fidem rumori facerent, librum de ejus vita scriptum fuisse, typisque mandatum, ubi scelera omnia, quibus Alexander VI. asperaspersus est, author & invenit & exaggeravit. Justa scilicet ἀντιμισθία fuit, ut qui Clementem Francisca-rum Henrici III. parricidam ad tertium usque Cœlum extulerat, à Franciscano altero die VII. Aug. M. D. XC. coësus idem, ad genus Cereris descenderet. Reliquerat autem in thesauris, Onuphrio teste, decem milliones, quos ad Regnum quodpiam ad Romanæ Sedis obedientiam reducendum erogari jussit, Successoribus juramento ad id adactis. Neque tamen venales adeo Regni totius animas Mercatores illi reperire potuerunt.
units.tr: CCIII. Sixtus also nursed some monstrous scheme against the Spaniards: he wanted to drive them out of Italy, above all out of the Kingdom of Naples, where their growing power had caused him considerable suspicion. That he sought the favour of Henry IV, King of France, and of Elizabeth, Queen of England, to this end, though both were excommunicated, is affirmed by no lack of reliable witnesses. Eduin Sandys recounts the same thing at greater length, On the State of Religion in the West, ch. 29. Because he repeatedly declared that he admired and esteemed the virtue of both Henry and Elizabeth in a [ψυχομονικῷ] manner, he incurred the bitter hatred of the Spanish faction, and especially of the Jesuits, who even gave him the name "Navarrist." Henry himself, in his Declaration published in 1591, testifies (as reported by Thuanus, History, book CI.) that Sixtus had decided not only to revoke the decrees issued against him, but also to take up arms against his enemies, had death not intervened. Indeed, Bartholomaeus Morisotus of Dijon, Life of Henry the Great, ch. 17., states in these words that his death was hastened by the hatred of the Spaniards: When the Spaniards, he says, had perceived the plans of Sixtus to be a desertion of their faction, they had his neck wrapped in a thin towel by a Franciscan friar, or, by a wicked deed, he was smothered by a man in monastic dress during the night, so that he slid into a sleep that ended in death. The next day, Sixtus was said throughout all Rome to have been strangled by a demon of his household. And to lend credibility to the rumour, a book about his life was written and sent to the press, in which the author both invented and magnified all the crimes with which Alexander VI was charged. It was, of course, a just [ἀντιμισθία] recompense that he who had raised Clement, the murderer of Henry III of France, to the heavens, should himself be struck down by a Franciscan on the seventh day of August 1590 and go down to the realm of Ceres. Onuphrius reports that he left in his treasury ten million, which he ordered to be spent on bringing some kingdom back to obedience to the Roman See, having bound his successors by oath to do so. Yet those merchants could not find the souls of the whole kingdom so readily purchasable.

units.la: CCIV. Galliæ Regno Euangelii luce orbando insudatum tum inprimis est, cum Henricus Navarrus, legitimus hæres, Regni illius habenas capessens veritatis suscepturus patrocinium visus est. Tum enim Gregorius XIV. non tantum Pontificiorum in Gallia partes misso exercitu, cui Nepotem suum Herculem Sfondratum Ecclesiæ Generalis titulo præfecit; consumptis, quas Sixtus in ærario reliquerat, propriisque etiam, uti Carriere Chronol. Pap. pag. 83. testatur; pecuniis, bello adjuvit: sed etiam cum armis nihil se proficere posse, victore semper Rege, expertus esset, solemnia insaniens ad diras se convertit: monitoriisque Romā missis denuò Henricum maledictis onerat, & adversus ipsum subditos, obsequii religione solutos, instigat; misso etiam in Galliam Marcellino Landriano, cum mandatis acerbitatis plenis, qui cum Ecclesiasticis, qui à Regis partibus stabant, nisi eum protinus relinquerent, horrendi carminis lege ageret, Nobilesque, ut eum quamprimum desererent, & se cum Catholicis Unioni foederatis conjungerent, moneret. In Gallia contra Senatus consultum factum est, audito & postulante cognitore Regio, & pro eo perorante Antonio Seguierio, quo Monitoria Romæ facta declarantur nulla, abusiva, seditiosa, damnanda, impietatum & impostturarum plena, sanctis decretis, juribus, Monitoria ejus in Galliā ipreta; juribus, immunitatibus, libertatibus Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ contraria; decernitúrque simul, ut exempla eorum sigillo Marsillii Landriani firmata, & à Sextilio Lampineto subsignata à carnifice publicè lacerentur, & ante Palatii, in quo jus dicitur, portam igni consumantur: interdicitur sub perduellionis poena, ne quis Episcopus, curio, vicarius, aliúsve è sacro ordine ea publicet, aliis item, cujuscunque conditionis sint, ne iis pareant, aut habeant, ac penes se retineant. Prohibitúmque sub iisdem poenis, ne quis deinceps aurum argentúmve Romam mittat, aut per mensarios numerari curet ad obtinenda mandata; & si quæ impetrata fuerint, ne judices eorum rationem habeant. Edictum quin etiam, ut Landrianus se pro oratore Pontificis gerens, mandatorum illorum lator comprehendatur, & in jure sistatur, ex vinculis causam dicturus. Eodemque Senatus consulto Georgius Pontifex ipse, publicæ pacis, Vnionis Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, Apostolicæ, Romanæ, Regis, Regnique hostis, conjurationis Hispanæ particeps, rebellium fautor, immanis, detestandi & inhumani parricidii per proditionem contra Henricum III. Christianissimum & verè Catholicum Regem patrati reus, declaratur. Sed & Præsules ipsi Galli, qui in Regis comitatu erant, nominatim etiam Carolus Borbonius & Philippus Lenuncurius Cardinales, Reginaldus Belnensis Archiepiscopus Bituricensis, &c. ad omnes Regni Ordines Pontificios decretum miserunt, in quo inter alia queruntur, Gregorium Papam male de Regni statu instructum, mandata quædam monitoria, suspensiones, interdictiones, excommunicationes misisse non solùm contra Præsules, sed etiam Principes, Nobiles & Franciæ populos, qui rebellium partes sequi noluerunt. Adjúntque, post maturam consultationem, ex authoritate S. Scripturæ, sanctorum decretorum, Conciliorum generalium, Canonicarum constitutionum, perpensis Sanctorum Patrum exemplis, juribus & libertatibus Ecclesiæ GalliGallicanæ, interdictones tam in forma quàm in materia nullas, injustas, & hostium Franciæ suggestione factas declarant. Fusius hæc apud Thuanum Hist. lib. c i. legere est.
units.tr: CCIV. The attempt to deprive the Kingdom of France of the light of the Gospel was pressed especially hard when Henry of Navarre, the lawful heir, took up the reins of that kingdom and seemed about to undertake the defence of the truth. For then Gregory XIV not only aided the Papists' cause in France with money (spent, as Carrière testifies in his Chronology of the Popes, p. 83., from what Sixtus had left in the treasury and also from his own funds), sending an army under the command of his nephew Hercules Sfondrati with the title of General of the Church; but when he had found by experience that he could accomplish nothing with arms, the King always winning, he turned in a frenzy to dire measures. By sending monitory letters from Rome he again loaded Henry with curses, and stirred up his subjects against him, releasing them from the bond of obedience. He also sent Marcellinus Landrianus into France with mandates full of bitterness, who was to act under the terrible law of the curse against the churchmen who stood on the King's side unless they abandoned him at once, and to warn the nobles to desert him as quickly as possible and join the Catholic Union. In France, a decree of the Senate was passed, after hearing and at the request of the royal attorney, Antoine Séguier pleading on his behalf, by which the monitory letters issued at Rome were declared null, abusive, seditious, damnable, full of impieties and impostures, contrary to sacred decrees and rights, and to the rights, immunities and liberties of the Gallican Church; and at the same time it was decreed that copies of them, sealed by Marsilius Landrianus and countersigned by Sextilius Lampinetus, should be publicly torn up by the executioner and burned at the gate of the Palace where justice is administered. It was forbidden, under penalty of treason, for any bishop, parish priest, vicar, or anyone else of the sacred order to publish them, and likewise for anyone of whatever rank to obey them, or to have them and keep them in his possession. It was also forbidden, under the same penalties, for anyone henceforth to send gold or silver to Rome, or to have it counted out through the bankers, to obtain mandates; and if any had been obtained, judges were not to take them into account. Moreover, an edict was issued that Landrianus, who was acting as the Pontiff's envoy, and the bearer of those mandates, be arrested, brought before the court, and made to answer the charge from prison. By the same decree of the Senate, the Pontiff Gregory himself was declared a disturber of public peace, a enemy of the union of the Catholic, Apostolic, Roman Church, and of the King and kingdom, a participant in the Spanish conspiracy, a supporter of rebels, and guilty of the monstrous, detestable and inhuman parricide committed by treachery against Henry III, the most Christian and truly Catholic King. The French prelates themselves who were in the King's company, namely Cardinals Charles of Bourbon and Philip of Lenoncourt, and Reginald of Belin, Archbishop of Bourges, and others, also sent to all the orders of the realm a decree against the Pontifical party, in which, among other things, they complain that Pope Gregory, badly informed about the state of the kingdom, had sent certain monitory letters, suspensions, interdicts and excommunications not only against the prelates but also against princes, nobles and the people of France who had refused to follow the rebels' side. They add that, after mature deliberation, on the authority of Holy Scripture, the decrees of the saints, the general councils, and the canonical constitutions, and having weighed the examples of the holy Fathers, they declare the interdicts, both in form and in substance, null, unjust, and made at the instigation of the enemies of France, in accordance with the rights and liberties of the Gallican Church. These matters may be read more fully in Thuanus, History, book CI.

units.la: CCV. Neque curam eam pervertendi universum Galliæ Regnum, sequentes etiam Pontifices deposuerunt; Clemens VIII. in primis, cujus consilia in eo maximè steterunt, ut exauthorato Henrico Rege Pontificiis bona fide addictus aliquis Galliæ imponeretur. Igitur conjuratos Galliæ pecuniis juvit, Regemque ipsum tertium excommunicat, publicata per Galliam Bulla. à qua Parlamentum provocans Majestatis reos, quotquot ei obsequerentur, declarat. Tandem Rex tutius regnandi cupidine victus, simulque Pontificis & Hispanorum molimina elusurus, à Nobilitate persuasus abnegata religione vera Pontificiam amplexus, die xv. Jul. A. M. D. XCIII. nudis pedibus cum candela S. Dionysii Templum ingressus, ab Archiepiscopo Biturien si absolutionem impetrat. Neque tamen vel sic acquievit Clemens indignatus non parum, quòd conatus suos in irritum cadere animadvertisset, & se inconsulto absolutionem Rex impetrasset. Nihilominus die xvii. Febr. A. M. D. XCIV. Henricus Carnuti Rex coronatur, & à Parlamentis talis agnoscitur proclamaturque, etiamsi Pontifex in Ecclesiam eum recipere gravaretur. Quòd tamen à Pontifice nondum absolutus esset, Johannes Castellus, in Schola Jesuitica literis imbutus, vitiis monstrosis supra ætatem, (nam novendecim tantùm annos egerat malitiâ Senex recoctus,) obrutus, conscientiæ terroribus in salutis desperationem incidens, audito non semel à Sodalibus Jesu ita dictis, non impune duntaxat Regem interfici posse, sed plurimum etiam id ad religionis causam conducere, interficiendi Regis consilium cepit. Sed aberrante, qui in gulam dirigebatur ,ictu, culter in maxillam inferiorem incubuit, & dente tantùm rupto, neque ultra penetrans, obtorpuit. In nervum raptus sicarius, scelus confessus, in Jesuitarum Scola ejus patrandi licentiam, spe etiam facta poenæ æternæ damnationis, quam ob alia horribilia delicta commeruerit, aliquatenus levandæ; se didicisse affirmavit. Ita simul de reo sumptum supplicium; simul cùm juxta illud Thucydidis lib. 3. οἱ ἀρχόντες παρανομῶσι μᾶλλον τ᾿ ἐπομένων, authores plus peccant quàm actores; adversus Jesuitas Senatus consultum factum est, ut Scholæ Claromontatæ Sacerdotes ac discipuli, & alii omnes, qui Societati illi nomen dedissent, tanquam juventutis corruptores, publicæ tranquillitatis perturbatores, Regis Regnique hostes, intra triduum à die denuntiationis Lutetia, aliisque urbibus, in quibus ludos aperuerunt, facessant, & quindecim diebus post Regno prorsus excedant; nî paruerint, in eos tanquam Majestatis lœsæ reos animadvertatur; bona eorum tam mobilia, quàm soli ad opera pia destinentur, eáque arbitrio curiæ distribuantur. Ad extremum interdictum cunctis Regni subditis, ne ad scholas societatis illius extra Regnum pueros literarum discendarum causa mittant, poena perduellionis in eos, qui contra fecerint, sancita. Atque Senatus consultum isthoc aureis literis pyramidi ruinis paternæ Castelli domus superstructæ, futuro infamiæ illorum monumento perenni, inscriptum est. Ex Gallia profugi in Polonia & Borussia plebem Evangelicis Proceribus subditam in Dominorum perniciem, promissa impunitate, concitant. Tandem exacto decennio intercedente pro iis Clemente Papa, importuneque etiam instante Laurentio Majo, ejusdem Societatis primipilo, per jocum subinde Regi exprobrante, segniorem eum esse mulieribus, quæ per novem menses uterum gestant; (cui facetè Rex respondit, Reges diutius quàm fœminas parturire) in Mariæ Medicæ Henrici Conjugis gratiam, restituti in Regnum, multum resistente Parlamento licet (cujus contra restitutionem illam orationem apud Cel. Hospinianum Histor. Jes. p. 96. 97. &c. legere est) postliminio redierunt; pertexturi scilicet, quam nefarie coeperant, parricidii telam. Interim Clemens Papa, poenitentia retenti diutius Regis doctus, & gravioris mali metu concitus, Regem, cujus procuratores missi genubus Papae advoluti, errores ejus vice ejurârunt, obedientiamque promiserunt; cantato Psalmo LI. ad cujus singulos versiculos Papa virgula quasi vindicta, qua ut olim servi apud Romanos manumittebantur, sic hodie peccatis nexi absolvuntur; leviter supplices cernuósque procuratores Regios feriit; ex solio surgens, apertóque capite solennibus orationibus recitatis, & denuo in solio, recepta tiara confidens, & judicis ritu sententiam alta voce pronuntians, authoritate omnipotentis Dei B. B. Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, suáque à vinculo excommunicationis, haereseósque culpa absolvit. Neque sic tamen in tuto collocata est Regia salus; machinantibus ejus interitum continuè hostibus ejus, donec magno cum exercitu stans in procinctu, ut Germanos foederatos juvaret, Die IV. Maii, A. M. D. C.X. à Ravaillaco Engolismensi horribili parricida, ictu gemino sub quintam costam illato, in curru sedens interfectus nefariè est. A supremae authoritatis judicibus, de causa suscepti parricidii interrogatus sicarius, cùm in reorum sellula sederet, non per ambages & aenigmata, sed liquidò & diserte respondit: ideo se, quod fecisset, fecisse, quia Rex Protestantibus Germaniae Principibus in causa Clivensi opem ferre paratus, Pontifici maximo rem faceret ingratam; ac proinde dignus esset, qui periret. Deum enim se in terris Romanum Pontificem agnoscere; cujus voluntati qui sese quovis pacto opponeret, eum se habere ἀνλοκατάκγιλον & exitio devotum. Ipsissima feralis illius prodigii verba sunt: Papa est Deus, & Deus est Papa. Quod ilillum, cætera rerum omnium maximè ignarum in Jesuitarum Schola, ceu Catilinarum seminario, didicisse, dubitatum à nemine est. Tametsi enim obstirmatus animo ad dirissimæ mortis patientiam, & perfecti sceleris recordatione lætissimus, criminis commissi complices nullos prodidit: suasoribus tamen conscisque Jesuitis patratum esse nefas, manifestis indiciis Anti-Cottonus, seu Author refutationis literarum Cottoni Jesuitæ ad Reginam viduam, demonstravit. Saltem per Jesuitarum hypotheses ad committendum parricidium inductum fuisse, neutiquam ambiget, qui Marianæ de Institutione Regis librum, quo asserta voce pronuntiat, licere Regem suum tyrannum (tyrannus autem ei est, quisquis clitellarium Papæ mancipium non est) occidere: vel Apologiam Francisci de Verona pro Johanne Castello, aliósque volverit.
units.tr: CCV. Nor did the Popes who followed give up the aim of overturning the whole kingdom of France. Clement VIII above all, whose plans chiefly rested on setting some man devoted in good faith to the Papists over France once Henry the King had been deprived of his authority. So he aided the conspirators with money and excommunicated the King himself a third time, the Bull having been published throughout France. The Parlement, appealing against it, declared those who obeyed the Bull guilty of treason. At last the King, overcome by the desire to reign more safely, and also intending to thwart the schemes of the Pope and the Spaniards, was persuaded by the nobility to renounce the true religion and embrace the Papist one. On 15 July 1593 he entered the church of St Denis barefoot, carrying a candle, and obtained absolution from the Archbishop of Bourges. Yet Clement was not appeased even so, being not a little indignant that his efforts had come to nothing and that the King had obtained absolution without consulting him. Nevertheless, on 17 February 1594 Henry was crowned king at Chartres, and was recognised and proclaimed by the Parlements, even though the Pope was reluctant to receive him into the Church. Because he had not yet been absolved by the Pope, John Castel, steeped in letters in a Jesuit school and vicious beyond his years (for he was only nineteen, an old man ripened in malice), overwhelmed by terrors of conscience and falling into despair of salvation, having heard more than once from those called members of Jesus that the King could not only be killed with impunity, but that this would also greatly contribute to the cause of religion, took up the plan of killing the King. But the blow, aimed at the throat, went astray; the knife struck the lower jaw, broke only a tooth, did not penetrate further, and was blunted. The assassin was seized and dragged to the rack, confessed the crime, and affirmed that he had learned in the Jesuits' school that he had licence to commit it, with the hope also held out that the eternal damnation he had deserved for other horrible crimes might be somewhat lightened. Thus the punishment was taken from the guilty man, and at the same time, in accordance with that saying of Thucydides in book 3, "the rulers sin more than those who follow" [οἱ ἀρχόντες παρανομῶσι μᾶλλον τ᾿ ἐπομένων], the authors sin more than the actors, a decree of the Senate was passed against the Jesuits. It ordered that the priests and pupils of the Clermont school, and all others who had given their name to that Society, as corruptors of youth, disturbers of public tranquillity, enemies of the King and kingdom, should leave Paris and the other cities in which they had opened schools within three days of the announcement, and should leave the kingdom altogether within fifteen days; if they did not obey, they would be proceeded against as guilty of treason. Their goods, both movable and immovable, were to be devoted to pious works and distributed at the discretion of the court. Finally, all subjects of the kingdom were forbidden to send boys to the schools of that Society outside the kingdom to learn letters, on pain of treason for those who acted contrary. This decree of the Senate was inscribed in golden letters on a pyramid built on the ruins of Castel's paternal house, as a lasting monument of their infamy. Having fled from France, the Jesuits stirred up in Poland and Prussia the common people subject to the Evangelical nobles, to the ruin of their lords, with promises of impunity. At last, after a decade had passed, Pope Clement interceded for them, and Lorenzo Maggio, chief of the same Society, urged the matter importunately, reproaching the King now and then in jest that he was more sluggish than women who carry a child for nine months (to which the King wittily replied, Kings take longer to give birth than women). They returned, restored to the kingdom by the right of postliminy, for the sake of Mary de' Medici, Henry's wife, although the Parlement strongly resisted that restoration. (The speech against that restoration may be read in the learned Hospinianus, Histor. Jes. pp. 96, 97, etc.) They returned, of course, to weave further the web of parricide they had so wickedly begun. Meanwhile Pope Clement, taught by the King's being kept too long in penance and moved by fear of a graver evil, received the King, whose proxies, having thrown themselves at the Pope's knees, renounced his errors on his behalf and promised obedience. While Psalm 51 was sung, at each of its verses the Pope lightly struck the kneeling and prostrate royal proxies with a little rod, like the rod of manumission with which slaves were once freed among the Romans, just as today those bound by sins are absolved. Rising from the throne with head uncovered, after solemn prayers had been recited, and seating himself again on the throne, having resumed the tiara, he pronounced sentence in a loud voice in the manner of a judge: by the authority of Almighty God, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and his own, he absolved him from the bond of excommunication and the guilt of heresy. Yet even so the King's safety was not placed in security, for his enemies continually plotted his death, until, standing ready with a great army to march to help the allied Germans, on 4 May 1610 he was murdered in his carriage by Ravaillac of Angoulême, a horrible parricide, who struck him twice beneath the fifth rib. Questioned by the judges of the highest authority about the cause of the parricide he had undertaken, the assassin, sitting in the prisoner's seat, answered not in riddles and ambiguities but plainly and clearly: he had done what he did because the King, being ready to bring help to the Protestant princes of Germany in the Cleves affair, would have acted unpleasingly to the Supreme Pontiff; and therefore he deserved to perish. For he acknowledged the Roman Pontiff as God on earth, and whoever opposed his will in any way was to him [ἀνλοκατάκγιλον] and devoted to destruction. These are the very words of that deadly monstrosity: Papa est Deus, & Deus est Papa. That he learned this in the Jesuits' school, as in a nursery of Catilines, though otherwise utterly ignorant of everything, no one doubts. For although he was hardened of mind to endure the most dreadful death, and most joyful in remembering the crime committed, he betrayed no accomplices. Yet the Anti-Cotton, or author of the refutation of the letter of the Jesuit Cotton to the widowed Queen, showed by manifest indications that the crime was committed at the urging and with the advice of the Jesuits. At least that he was led to commit parricide by the Jesuits' hypotheses no one will doubt who has read Mariana's book on the institution of a king, in which he openly declares that it is lawful for one to kill his king if he is a tyrant (and a tyrant is whoever is not the servile tool of the Pope's packsaddle), or who has read the Apology of Francis of Verona for John Castel, and others.

units.la: CCVI. Clemente & Pontifice & coryphæo, connitentibus Jesuitis, Fœdus Sanctum inter Monarchas & Principes Pontificios ad extirpandos Evangelicos, callidóque consilio coaluisse, Author speculi Consiliorum Hispanicorum prodidit. Nomen fœderi dederant Principes Pontificii omnes, excepto M. Duce Hertruriæ, & Henrico Galliæ Rege, de quo Clemens crebrò dictitavit, artificiosum eum nimis esse, neutrique parti addictum. Constitutum præterea Romæ fuit, annuente etiam Cæsare, ut in omnibus civitatibus Imperii alerentur Jesuitæ, arma adversus Evangelicos occultè fabricata, juventuti dispertituri, & Hildebrandinam Bonifacianamque doctrinam, fatalem Ecclesiæ, funestam Principibus, etiam senibus instillaturi. Sed & geminus Senatus erectus, quorum alteri Congregationi de propaganda fide; alteri Congregationi sacri fœderis impositum nomen est. Singulis novem Cardinales, totidemque Consiliarii, frequente cœtu coituri, & consilia opprimendorum Protestantium, bellíque auspicandi sacri
units.tr: CCVI. With Clement as Pope and leader, and the Jesuits striving together, Author of the Mirror of Spanish Counsels revealed that a Holy League between the Papist monarchs and princes for the extirpation of the Evangelicals had been formed by a crafty plan. All the Papist princes had given their name to the league, except the Grand Duke of Tuscany and Henry, King of France, of whom Clement often said that he was too artful and addicted to neither party. It was further resolved at Rome, with the Emperor also consenting, that Jesuits should be maintained in all the cities of the Empire, secretly preparing arms against the Evangelicals to distribute among the young, and to instil the Hildebrandine and Boniface doctrine, fatal to the Church and baneful to princes, even into old men. A twofold senate was also set up, one named Congregation for Propagating the Faith and the other Congregation of the Holy League. Nine cardinals and as many counsellors were assigned to each, to meet in full assembly, and to take counsel for suppressing the Protestants and for beginning the sacred war.

units.la: Congregatio gemina de propaganda fide, & sacri fœderis erigitur. cri eri inituri, præfecti sunt. Decretum simul, ut eodem tempore Geneva & Argentoratum infestis armis impetantur, ad faciendum de consilio & viribus Protestantium periculum. Et anno quidem seculi hujus primo Cæsar Cardinale Dietrichsteinio Romam misso, fœderis illius executionem promisit, simulque in Styria jam initium factum renuntiavit. Extat liber, authore Johanne Regio A.M.D.C.IV. Francofurti ad Moenum impressus, quo sævissimæ & immanis persecutionis à Carolo & Ferdinando Archiducibus Austriæ, Jesuitis obstetricantibus, in Styria, Carinthia & Carniola, excitatæ, oppressæque in iis locis per vim injustam Ecclesiæ, historia tragice pertexitur. Paucis eandem historiam Thuanus Histor. lib. cxxiv. retulit. Viennæ in Austria libri etiam Euangelicorum exusti sunt. In Ducatum quoque Bergensem eadem vis penetravit.
units.tr: The twin Congregation, for propagating the faith and of the Holy League, is erected, and its members were placed in charge of beginning the sacred war. At the same time it was decreed that Geneva and Strasbourg should be attacked with hostile arms at the same time, in order to test the counsel and strength of the Protestants. In the first year of this century the Emperor, having sent Cardinal Dietrichstein to Rome, promised the execution of that league, and at the same time announced that a beginning had already been made in Styria. There is a book, by John Regius, printed at Frankfurt am Main in 1604, in which the history of the most savage and monstrous persecution, stirred up in Styria, Carinthia and Carniola by the Archdukes Charles and Ferdinand of Austria, with the Jesuits assisting, and in which the Church was suppressed in those places by unjust force, is tragically related. Thuanus related the same history briefly in Hist. lib. cxxiv. In Vienna in Austria the books of the Evangelicals were also burned. The same violence penetrated also into the Duchy of Berg.

units.la: CCVII. Sed & intestina dissidia eodem tempore Ro- manam Ecclesiam exercitam habuerunt.
units.tr: CCVII. But internal dissensions also troubled the Roman Church at the same time.

units.la: Jesuitici enim sodales fiducia seu doctrinæ, seu, qua plurimum ubique pollebant, authoritatis, quæstiones aliquot propositerunt, quæ magnæ animorum commotioni non solum Romæ, sed quacunque Romanæ religionis patebat ditio, præbuerunt. Inter alia ab iis assertum, Clementem VIII. tunc Romæ sedentem, credere legitimum B. Petri successorem, non esse ex articulis fidei. Id vero, nisi Philippicus Orator intervenisset, periculum non mediocre toti societati importaverat. Addebant, Confessionem, quæ inter Sacramenta Ecclesiæ habetur, per epistolam & præcursores peragi posse. Sed duæ illæ quæstiones jugulum Pontificis petere, & culinæ nidorem pertentare visæ, statim in herba magno consensu suffocatæ sunt. Tertia vero, de gratia Dei cum libero arbitrio in nobis ad salutem cooperante, pertinaciùs doctorum ingenia exercuit. In partes autem venerunt Jesuitæ & Prædicatores, primò Salmanticæ & Vallisoleti, tum Romæ, de-
units.tr: For the Jesuit brethren, relying on their learning or, as they chiefly did everywhere, on their authority, proposed several questions which caused great agitation of minds, not only at Rome but throughout every region subject to the Roman religion. Among other things they asserted that Clement VIII, then sitting at Rome, did not believe that he was the lawful successor of St. Peter, and this is not among the articles of faith. Had the Philippic orator not intervened, this would have brought no small danger upon the whole society. They added that confession, which is held among the sacraments of the Church, can be carried out by letter and by messengers. But these two questions, which seemed to attack the Pontiff's throat and to tempt the smell of the kitchen, were at once smothered in the bud by general agreement. The third question, concerning the grace of God together with free will co-operating in us for salvation, exercised the minds of the teachers more stubbornly. The Jesuits and the Dominicans took sides in this, first at Salamanca and Valladolid, then at Rome, and finally in Belgium and other provinces of Europe.

units.la: demum in Belgio, aliisque Europæ Provinciis. Et Jesuitæ quidem in publicis disputationibus Salmanticæ habitis gratiæ Divinæ prædeterminationem, ceu inimicam prorsus libero hominis arbitrio, hostiliter exagitaverant. Doctrinæ eorum ceu nova & prius inaudita, Dominicus Bannes, primarius tum Salmanticæ professor, generosè se opposuit, ita prædeterminationem gratiæ vindicans, ut simul modum ostenderet, quo illa cum hominis libero arbitrio in gratiam reduci valeat. Jacto hac ratione in medium contentionis pomo, non acquiescere Patres societatis, sed contra audentius ire. Et Ludovicus Molina quidem Lojolæ sodalis libro edito Bannes doctrinam maximo studio oppugnavit. Molinæ paulò post succollavit Anthonius de Padiglia, Vallisoleti Theologiæ Professor, publicis conclusionibus Molinæ doctrinam, ceu probabilem defendens. At Bannes ejusque assectæ rem primò ad Senatum Regium, mox evocato ex Hispania Romam Francisco Suarezio, Dominicanorum sententiæ fibulam imposituro; ad Clementem VIII. deferunt, cujus jussu primò in Comitio Cardinalium, deinde coram ipsomet hac de re ab utriusque familiæ Theologis disputatum est. Vix tandem post plura hinc inde publicata scripta, ex Concilii Tridentini verbis; in quo tamen quæstio minimè agitata fuerat, interpretatione adjecta, à Pontifice controversia ita composita est, ut eam non motam ab initio optâsse ostenderet, & in ea decidenda nihil existimationi eorum, qui eam moverant, detractum vellet. Clemente è vivis sublato, controversia sub Paulo V. recruduit, qui tandem decrevit, ut utriusque sententiæ authores suam sententiam, citra ullam tamen adversæ partis censuram, defenderent, donec aliquid ea de re ab ipso vel ejus successoribus statueretur. Cæterum nec ipse, nec Successorum ejus quisquam ausus est decretoriam sententiam ferre,
units.tr: The Jesuits, in public disputations held at Salamanca, attacked with hostility the predetermination of divine grace as wholly hostile to human free will. Dominicus Bannes, then the chief professor at Salamanca, opposed their teaching, which he called new and hitherto unheard of, with spirit, defending the predetermination of grace in such a way that he also showed how it could be reconciled with human free will. The apple of contention having been thrown into the middle in this way, the Fathers of the Society did not give way but advanced more boldly. Ludovicus Molina, a fellow of Loyola, published a book and attacked Bannes's doctrine with the greatest zeal. Shortly afterwards Anthonius de Padiglia, professor of theology at Valladolid, supported Molina, defending Molina's doctrine as probable in public conclusions. But Bannes and his followers brought the matter first before the royal Senate, and then to Clement VIII, who was to put a clasp upon the Dominican opinion, after Francisco Suarez had been summoned from Spain to Rome. By the Pope's order the matter was first debated in the college of Cardinals, and then before the Pope himself by theologians of both orders. At last, after many writings had been published on both sides, the controversy was settled by the Pope, who added an interpretation of the words of the Council of Trent, though the question had not been touched on in that council at all. The settlement showed that he had wished the dispute had not been raised at the start, and that he wanted nothing taken from the reputation of those who had raised it. After Clement's death the controversy broke out again under Paul V, who at last decreed that the authors of each opinion should defend their view, without any censure of the opposing party, until something was decided about the matter by himself or his successors. Yet neither he nor any of his successors dared to pronounce a decisive judgement,

units.la: Dominicanos diu agitata historia textitur. re, metu prævalidarum partium, quarum alterutra, Jesuitarum inprimis factio, Pontificiam authoritatem lœdere posset. Creverunt sic in immensum dissidia, & animorum efferbuit exulceratio; manifesto schismate, in re gravissimi momenti, in qua gratiæ & gloriæ Divinæ cardo vertitur, quando etiam factiosis nominibus (Jesuitæ enim Præscientistarum, Dominicani Prædeterminantium nomine venerunt) discreti sunt, & hodieque discernuntur. Salmanticensis Academia omnes jurisdictioni suæ subjectos, in Augustini & Thomæ verba, ringentibus Jesuitis licet, conceptis verbis adigere solet. Utramque sententiam nequaquam conciliare conatus est Franciscus de Arriba, in opere conciliatorio Gratiæ & liberi arbitrii. Verum ejus conciliatio, teste Camerario Scotista, tam improbabilis fuit, ut præter ipsum, patronum nullum, hostes omnes invenerit.
units.tr: for fear of the very powerful parties, one of which, chiefly the Jesuit faction, could injure papal authority. Thus the dissensions grew to an immense size, and the exasperation of minds boiled up, in an open schism over a matter of the gravest importance, on which the hinge of God's grace and glory turns; and they were distinguished even by factional names (for the Jesuits came to be called Præscientists, the Dominicans Prædeterminists), and are distinguished so even today. The University of Salamanca is accustomed to bind all who are subject to its jurisdiction to the words of Augustine and Thomas in express terms, even though the Jesuits protest. Francisco de Arriba tried in no way to reconcile the two opinions, in his conciliatory work on grace and free will. But his attempt at reconciliation, as the Scotist Camerarius testifies, was so unconvincing that, apart from himself, it found no patron and all as enemies.

units.la: CCVIII. Ex seminario Anglorum, quod Guilhelmi Alani Angli suasu, à Gregorio XIII. Romæ constitutum supra diximus, Jesuitarum cura sensim in Anglia novi Sacerdotes Angli, in eo seminario ad artes omnes explicandas ficti factique ac cum iis etiam Jesuitæ prorepserunt, qui non solum in confirmandis Pontificiorum in Anglia reliquiis sedulitatem maximam adhibuerunt, sed etiam, quod Archiepiscoporum & Episcoporum nomina, dignitates & bona in eo Regno Elisabethæ auspiciis penes Protestantes esse dolerent, secretam Hierarchiam ordine subsidiario constituerunt, in eoque Principatum tanquam à Pontifice delegati, sibi sumpserunt. Hierarchiam illam Alanus, ob zelum reducendi in Angliam Papatus, in Collegium Cardinalium à Sixto V. cooptatus; eoque mortuo Franciscus Toletus ex eodem sodalitio in Cardinalium Collegium allectus, rexerunt. Occulta tamen dissidia & æmulationes Jesuitas inter & seminarii alumnos, Sacerdotes, tes, quorum utrique imperium in Hierarchia illa affectârant, gliscebant, quæ post mortem Toleti in nervum etiam eruperunt, Sacerdotibus Anglicanis à Veftono, Roberto Parfono, Blacwello, apud Pontificem ceu schismaticis accusatis, gravibusque probris oneratis. Acerbissima hæc Sacerdotum Jesuitarum & Anglorum digladiatio cùm quadriennio integro duraffet, editis acribus adversus invicem, Jesuiticæ cum primis societatis institutum, libellis, ægre tandem à Clemente VIII. composita est, diplomate ad Georgium Blacwellum Archipresbyterum, qui turbis his inprimis occasionem dederat III. Non. Oct. A. M. D. C. I. misso, quo inter alia ei injunctum est, ut nulla negotia ad administrationem suam pertinentia cum Provinciali Societatis Jesuiticæ, aut cum viris religiosis ejusdem sodalitii per literas, aut coram communicet, sed de iis omnibus ad Pontificem & Sedem Romanam, aut Protectorem referat.
