Agnovisse Clementem infructuosos in eo Regno conatus, nimiámque pertinaciam ad rei Pontificiæ perniciem vergentem Thuanus Histor. lib. CXXVI. ubi dissidii illius narratio prolixa extat, testatur.
units.tr: CCVIII. From the English seminary, which we said above was founded at Rome by Gregory XIII at the suggestion of William Allen, the Englishman, new English priests, shaped and trained in that seminary for every kind of artifice, gradually crept into England under the care of the Jesuits, and with them the Jesuits themselves crept in. These men not only showed the greatest zeal in strengthening the remnants of the Papists in England, but also, grieving that the names, dignities and goods of archbishops and bishops in that kingdom were in the hands of Protestants under the auspices of Elizabeth, they set up a secret hierarchy in a subordinate order and claimed for themselves the primacy in it, as if delegated by the Pope. Alanus, out of zeal for restoring the Papacy in England, was co-opted into the college of Cardinals by Sixtus V; and after his death Francisco Toledo, also from the same fraternity, was admitted into the college of Cardinals, and they governed that hierarchy. Yet hidden dissensions and rivalries between the Jesuits and the seminary's students, the priests, each side having aimed at command in that hierarchy, kept growing; after Toledo's death these broke out into open conflict, the English priests being accused before the Pope, as schismatics, by Veston, Robert Persons and Blackwell, and loaded with serious reproaches. When this most bitter wrangling between the Jesuit and English priests had lasted a full four years, with sharp pamphlets published against each other, especially against the Jesuit institute itself, it was at last, with difficulty, settled by Clement VIII in a brief sent on 3 October 1601 to George Blackwell, the archpriest, who had especially given occasion to these disturbances. Among other things it was enjoined on him that he should not communicate any business belonging to his administration with the Provincial of the Jesuit Society, or with religious men of that fraternity, either by letter or in person, but should refer all such matters to the Pope and the Roman See, or to the Protector. Thuanus, in his History, book CXXVI, where a full account of that dissension is given, testifies that Clement recognised the fruitless efforts in that kingdom and the excessive obstinacy tending to the ruin of the Papal cause.

units.la: CCIX. Contra Regnum idem Angliæ, cujus ceu hortí deliciarum pro Papis, & putei inexhausti (uti quondam venustè Angliam Innocentius IV. nominavit) jactura, insanabilem Pontificibus dolorem attulit; Elisabetham cum primis Heroinam, sacrum illud superis caput, concatenatæ ferè conjurationes, architectis ut plurimùm Jesuitis, tentatæ, sed præsentissimo Numine discussæ sunt. Prostant Acta publica Garnetti Jesuitæ, in quibus manifestæ veritati datur, à primo Jesuitarum in Angliam ingressu quadriennium integrum nunquam effluxisse, quin conjurationes, turbas, seditiones, parricidia in perniciem Regni Jesuitæ machinati sint. Ita enim A. M. D. LXXXVIII. supplicium sumptum est de Guilhelmo Parrio, qui conscīis & & suasoribus Jesuitis Lugdunenfibus, aliisque Reginam Elifabetham è medio tollere pluribus vicibus tentans, Mariæ Scotorum Reginæ ad Regnum Angliæ viam sternere conatus est. A. M. D. LXXXVIII. ingens Hispanorum classis centum quinquaginta octo navibus bellicis constans, quamque benedictione sua Sixtus V. dignatus est, & invicta insuper classis nomine insignivit; in Angliam transfretatura, sed Ϲπο μηχανῆς horribiliter dissipata & perdita, prænuntios præviosque Jesuitas habuit. A. M. D. XCII. Patanius Cullen, instigante Jesuita Holte, peccatorum remissionem & Eucharistiam impertiente, facinorisque dignitatem & meritum extollente, furiali face armatus ejusdem Reginæ vitæ insidias struxit. Eodem Holte aliisque Jesuitis suasoribus A. M. D. XCIV. William & Jarke in Reginæ caput conspirârunt. A. M. D. XCVII. Richardus Walpot Jesuita Hispanus Eduardum Squirre subornavit, qui Reginæ sella Regia veneno inuncta, eandem interimeret. A. M. D. C. I. Henricus Garnettus, Jesuitarum in Anglia Provincialis, Robertus item Tesmondus, Catesby, aliique Thomam Winterum in Hispaniam ablegârunt, cum literis ad Grenwellum Jesuitam, mandatisque, ut Regi Hispaniæ author sit exercitum transmittendi in Angliam, conjuncturum se cum reliquiis in Anglia Pontificiis, & Reginam Protestantésque omnes παντραλιχ oppugnaturum. Clementer auditus Winterus, & promissis lactatus, plenus bonæ spei ad Cleones suos in Angliam rediit. Juvitque conjurationem Clemens Papa, missis duobus in Angliam Brevibus, quibus jubebantur omnes Pontificii operam dare, quantum in ipsis esset, ut post Elisabethæ obitum Rex eligeretur, omni sanguinis propinquitate spreta, ad Religionem Catholicam bene affectus. Duo in eandem sententiam Brevia lutea ab eodem Clemente, sub extrema vitæ Elisabethæ tempora, Garnetto transmissa sunt, quorum rum alterum Archipresbytero & reliquo Clero Anglicano erat inscriptum: alterum Principibus & Nobilibus Angliæ Catholicis, ut communi omnium opera negotium procurarent, si qua forte perduci ad exitum posset. Post obitum Reginæ statim atque Successor ejus Jacobus VI. Scotiæ Rex Regnum intravit, quæsitissimis insidiis appeti coepit. Nondum coronatum Watsonus & Clercus, Sacerdotes seculares A. M. D. C. III. machinatione clandestina tollere de vivis aggressi sunt. Qui capti & tortura interrogati constanter affirmârunt, se, cum sua consilia Jesuitis communicâssent, petiisséntque dignarentur venire in partes præclari adeò facinoris, hoc responsum tulisse: Non posse Jesuitas sese illis adjungere, ut qui suam ipsi parilem telam orsi, memorabilem in omne ævum technam parārent, tempore opportuno exitum habituram; pergerent modò illi in hoc suo instituto, & rem agerent strenuè. ad pulverariam, de qua mox dicturi sumus, conspirationem, digitum intendentes. Paulò ante ἐxλεvεῖs Zelotarum Anglorum petitiones per Christophorum Wrigthum ad Regem Hispaniarum delatæ sunt, obsecrantes, ut copias suas in Angliam ad Milfordum portum submitteret, ubi Angli Pontificii eas præstolaturi, & è Belgio Spinola cohortes suas conjuncturus sit. Quibus tamen precibus Hispaniæ Rex vacivas aures amplius non substrinxit, eò quòd in Angliam Legatum cum novo Rege de pace tractaturum jam misisset.
units.tr: CCIX. On the other hand, the loss of England itself, which was for the Popes like a garden of delights and an inexhaustible well (as Innocent IV once wittily called England), brought the Popes incurable grief. Elizabeth above all, that holy head of heroines under heaven, was attacked by a series of linked conspiracies, most of them architected by the Jesuits, but they were dispelled by the most present Deity. The public records of the Jesuit Garnet survive, in which it is shown to the manifest truth that during the whole four years from the Jesuits' first entry into England there was never a lapse in which the Jesuits did not plot conspiracies, riots, seditions and murders for the destruction of the kingdom. Thus in 1588 punishment was inflicted on William Parry, who, with the Jesuits of Lyon and others as accomplices and advisers, tried several times to remove Queen Elizabeth from the middle, and attempted to pave the way for Mary, Queen of the Scots, to the kingdom of England. In 1588 a great fleet of Spain, consisting of one hundred and fifty-eight warships, which Sixtus V had honoured with his blessing and further marked with the name Invincible Fleet, was about to cross to England, but it was horribly scattered and lost by a deus ex machina [ἀπὸ μηχανῆς], and it had Jesuits as its heralds and forerunners. In 1592 Patrick Cullen, at the urging of the Jesuit Holt, who granted remission of sins and Eucharist and extolled the dignity and merit of the deed, armed with a frenzied torch, plotted against the life of the same Queen. With the same Holt and other Jesuits as advisers, in 1594 William and Jarke conspired against the Queen's head. In 1597 Richard Walpole, a Spanish Jesuit, suborned Edward Squire, who was to kill the Queen by smearing poison on the royal seat. In 1601 Henry Garnet, Provincial of the Jesuits in England, and likewise Robert Tesmond, Catesby and others sent Thomas Winter to Spain, with letters to the Jesuit Greenwell and instructions that he should advise the King of Spain to send an army to England, which would join with the remaining Papists in England and attack the Queen and all Protestants on every side. Winter was heard kindly, and, being cheered by promises, returned to England full of good hope to his accomplices. Pope Clement also aided the conspiracy by sending two briefs into England, in which all Papists were ordered to do what lay in them, that after Elizabeth's death a king should be chosen, with all blood relationship set aside, who was well disposed to the Catholic religion. Two yellow briefs to the same effect were sent by Clement to Garnet near the very end of Elizabeth's life, one of which was addressed to the archpriest and the rest of the English clergy, the other to the Catholic princes and nobles of England, so that by the common effort of all they might promote the business, if by any chance it could be brought to a conclusion. After the Queen's death, as soon as her successor James VI, King of Scotland, entered the kingdom, he began to be attacked by the most carefully planned plots. Watson and Clark, secular priests, had not yet crowned him when in 1603 they set about removing him from the living by a secret device. When they were captured and questioned under torture, they constantly affirmed that they had communicated their plans to the Jesuits, and had asked them to deign to join in so illustrious a deed, and had received this answer: that the Jesuits could not join them, since they themselves, having begun a similar web, were preparing a memorable artifice for all time, which would have its issue at the opportune moment; let them only persist in their undertaking and act vigorously. pointing their finger at the gunpowder conspiracy, of which we shall speak shortly. A little earlier, the petitions of the zealous English were conveyed through Christopher Wright to the King of Spain, begging him to send his forces to Milford port in England, where the English Papists would await them, and where Spinola would join his cohorts from Belgium. Yet the King of Spain did not any longer lend his empty ears to these prayers, because he had already sent an envoy to England to treat of peace with the new King.

units.la: CCX. Ante verò quàm conjurationum hanc feriem prosequar ulterius, omittere non possum Clementis adversus Elisabetham molimina, quæ perfidiâ homine quolibet, nedum Pontifice Christi vices professo indignissimâ, cumulavit. Scribit enim non nostratum quispiam, sed Cardinalis Ossatus ad D. de Ville Roy Epist.87. Pontificem hunc ursisse Regem Galliæ Henricum IV. ut in Angliæ occupatione se Hispano jungeret, regerentíque inter alia Car-
units.tr: CCX. Before I go on with this series of conspiracies, I cannot pass over Clement's schemes against Elizabeth, in which he piled up a perfidy most unworthy of any man, let alone of a Pontiff who professes to act in Christ's place. For it is written, not by one of our countrymen, but by Cardinal Ossat, to M. de Villeroy, Epist. 87, that this Pontiff urged Henry IV, King of France, to join the Spaniard in occupying England. When the King answered, among other things, that

units.la: ¶ Jacobum VI. praesente Numine dijussa, Cardinali, Regem Anglorum Reginæ juramento teneri, respondisse, iuramentum fuisse præstitum hæretica, sed alio juramento illum Deo & Papæ teneri. Addidisse dein, Reges & alios Principes supremos sibi omnia permittere, quæ ad emolumentum suum redundarent: & eo usque rem processisse, ut id eis non imputaretur aut vitio verteretur; allegato insuper dicto Francisci Mariæ, Ducis Urbini, ab unoquoque quidem nobilem virum, vel etiam magnatem, qui supremus non esset, culpari, & infamem haberi, qui fidem non servaret: sed posse Principes supremos fœdera sancire, & ab iisdem resilire sine famæ periculo, mentiri, prodere, & alia similia perpetrare. Cui non hic in mentem veniat illud Poëtæ:
units.tr: James VI, by the will of God, ... replied to the Cardinal that the King of the English was bound to the Queen by oath. The oath had been sworn to a heretic, but he was bound to God and the Pope by another oath. He added then that kings and other supreme princes may permit themselves everything that serves their advantage, and the matter had gone so far that it was not imputed to them or counted as a fault; and he cited besides the saying of Francis Maria, Duke of Urbino: every noble man, or even great lord, who is not supreme, is blamed and held infamous if he does not keep his faith; but supreme princes can ratify covenants and withdraw from them without danger to their reputation, lie, betray, and commit other such things. Here one may well recall the poet's words:

units.la: Accipe nunc Danaum insidias, & crimine ab uno
units.tr: Now take the treachery of the Danaans, and from the crime of one man

units.la: Disce omnes.
units.tr: learn them all.

units.la: CCXI. Anni demum M. D. C. V. mense Novembri pate- facta est conjuratio cum immanitate & furore cerbereo conjunctissima, quam è re pulverariam vocant.
units.tr: CCXI. At last, in November of the year 1605, there came to light a conspiracy most closely joined with savagery and Cerberean fury, which they call the Gunpowder plot.

units.la: Scelus humanam fidem omnem supergressum, utpote cujusmodi post homines natos nemo unquam vel fando audivit; vel animo agitavit, vel quisquam cacodæmon hactenus molitus est. Cum enim furiæ nonnulli, zeli infernalis fervore siderati, deprehenderent, spem illam de igne cœlitus deducendo decollasse: nec ipsos præteriret, ejusmodi petitionem jam olim, dum Christus in terris agitaret, repulsam tulisse; statuerunt alium ignem, ab archipyrobola Sathana subdolè impetrare, &
units.tr: It was a crime that surpassed all human faith, since no one born of man has ever heard of its like, even in speech, nor has anyone conceived it in mind, nor has any cacodemon devised such a thing until now. For when some madmen, struck by the fervour of infernal zeal, perceived that the hope of bringing down fire from heaven had collapsed, and did not overlook the fact that such a request had long ago been refused, while Christ was walking on earth, they resolved to obtain another fire craftily from the arch-firebrand Satan, and

units.la: Flectere cum nequeant Superos, Archeronta movere.
units.tr: If they cannot bend the gods above, they will stir up Acheron.

units.la: Planè ex indubitatæ fidei actis publicè editis intelligitur, Catisbejum, dramatis hujus primum auctorem, statim ut de Rege Jacobo armis pellendo, & auxiliis Hispanicis spes est amissa (altero autem tertióve mense ab ejus adventu ea spes decollavit) nulla interjecta mora à vi aperta ad dolos & Sinonias artes sese contulisse. Non igitur hunc vel illum aut singulos carpendos, sed universos simul & eodem tempore conspiratione amplectendos censuit. Sic enim rationes subduxit, Regem solum multis modis tolli posse, sed nihil agi superstite Principe & Eboraci Duce. Rursus iis sublatis parum profici stante Senatu tam vigili, tam ad omneis casus intento. Et ut Senatus aut præcipui ex eo tolli possent, superare Magnates Regni, tot prudentes viros, tot præpotentes Comites, eidem religioni addictos, quibus obsisti vix posset, & qui authoritate sua, opibus & clientelis pares essent, si casus ferat, ipsi per se rebus suis instaurandis. Non igitur per spiramenta, sed uno ictu cunctos absorbendos, & simul ac semel tam laudabili conatu, ut ad exitum perduci possit, defungi oportere. Diu recoctum consilium ita se exequi posse Catisbejus speravit, si intra Parlamentariæ domus, in qua coactis Comitiis Rex, unà cum familia mascula, secretioris consilii Episcopis, Proceribus, nobilitate Anglicana, primariis Magistratibus, & inferiore loco ex Provinciis, civitatibus, oppidis, municipiis, pagis denique delegati, sapientissimi consultissimique viri, conventuri erant; parietes, cuniculo acto, equus Trojanus, non bellicosis Græcis, ut olim, refertus, sed infernali pulvere nitrato tormentario, cadis unà cum ferramentis & ingentibus saxis, incluso, oppletus introduceretur, eóque succenso ille totius Angliæ flos illibatus ejusdem ruinæ ruderibus involutus, uno impetu, difflaretur, & in aera impulsus membratim frustillatimque (ô crudelitatem!) discerperetur. Consilium ferinæ crudelitatis mox ille Thomæ Percio Comitatus Northumbriæ gentili verbis ad persuadendum efficacibus, aperuit, ejusdemque exequendi rationes pari artificio proposuit. Nec abnuit Percius, qui statim ædes loco vicinas & ad cuniculum agendum peropportunas conduxit. Indicta anno superiori Co-
units.tr: It is plain from the publicly issued records, whose authority no one doubts, that Catesby, the first author of this drama, turned at once from open force to tricks and Sinonian arts, without any delay, as soon as hope was lost of driving King James out by arms and with Spanish help. That hope collapsed one or two months after the King's arrival. He therefore judged that they should not pick off this man or that one by one, but embrace all of them together, in a single conspiracy at one time. For he reckoned thus: the King alone could be removed in many ways, but nothing would be achieved while the Prince and the Duke of York survived. And again, with those two removed, little would be gained while the Senate stood, so vigilant and so alert to every chance. So that the Senate, or its leading men, could be removed, they must overcome the magnates of the kingdom: so many prudent men, so many very powerful earls, all devoted to the same religion, whom it would scarcely be possible to resist, and who, if circumstances allowed, would be equal in authority, wealth and clients to restoring their own affairs by themselves. Therefore all must be swallowed up not piecemeal but with one blow, and once and for all they must carry through so praiseworthy an undertaking to its end. Catesby hoped that this long-simmering plan could be carried out in this way: if, within the Parliament House, where the King was to meet with his male family, the bishops of the privy council, the nobles, the English peerage, the chief magistrates, and, from a lower rank, men chosen from the provinces, cities, towns, municipalities and villages, the wisest and most learned men, were to assemble when the sitting was called; if, a tunnel having been dug, the walls were to be penetrated by a Trojan horse, not filled, as of old, with warlike Greeks, but stuffed with infernal nitrated gunpowder, casks together with iron tools and huge stones; and if, when this was fired, that unblemished flower of all England, wrapped in the rubble of the same ruin, were to be blown away in a single blast, flung into the air, and torn apart limb from limb and piece by piece (O cruelty!). Soon he disclosed this plan of savage cruelty to Thomas Percy, a kinsman of the Earl of Northumberland, in words persuasive enough, and set out the means of carrying it out with equal skill. Percy did not refuse, and at once he hired a house nearby, very convenient for digging the tunnel. The sitting of Parliament, summoned for the previous year,

units.la: Parliament Comitia in Februarium sequentem A. M. D. C. V. rejecta fuerant. Medio tempore Thomas Bates, Catisbeii famulus, homo manu promptus, & cui multum herus tribuebat, ex suspicione in facti conscientiam ascitus, cum initio rei atrocitate permoveri videretur, ad Jesuitam Tesmundum, qui & Grenwellus vocabatur, remissus, & ab eodem persuasus, ac rei merito demonstrato ad executionem mirum in modum confirmatus est. Postea Robertus Keies, & post eum Ambrosius Rookwodus, & Johannes Grauntius consilii participes facti sunt. Decembre A. M. D. C. I V. opus subterraneum inchoatum est, Christophoro Wrigthio, & paulo post Roberto Wintero, Thomae fratre, in societatem assumpto. Saepe intermisso, saepe repetito opere, tandem cuniculus ad Curiae murum perductus fuerat; ubi nova se difficultas, ob muri duritiem, & trium ulnarum crassitiem, se offerebat, paucis diebus ad Comitia restantibus. Jam pertinacia operariorum medium murum pene pertuderat, & non deficientibus animis solum tempus defuturum videbatur, cum Comitia in Octobrem mensem dilata sunt. Tum desperatio in gaudium vertit, cum certa rei exequendae fiducia. Dum vero murum alacriter pertundere pergunt, observatum, strepitum ex altera muri parte audiri eo missus Guido Fauxius, ut causam inquireret, renuntiat, cellam ibi subterraneam esse, inde removeri carbones, defuncto eo, qui cellam in eos usus conduxerat. Igitur conjurati hanc cellam commodiorem rati, opera Percii, ut alteras aedes locant, & in illam omnes opes, omnes spes suas conjiciunt. ob loci opportunitatem inprimis, utpote qui throno Regali fere subjectus erat. Pulvis nitratus per otium in cellam eam ex aedibus Catisbeii, è regione Curiae, ubi summo studio antea congestus fuerat, doliis triginta sex magna lapidum & lignorum strue contectis, convectus est. Denique jam parata erant omnia, & scena ultimum actum expectabat, cum justo Dei judicio, quidam ex iis, dum alteri salutem adferri cupit, sibi ac sociis suis exitium accersivit. Decem ad Comitia dies supererant, dum Saturni die sub vesperam literæ incerto auctore, incognito latore, ad Montaquilium regulum tanquam ab amico deferuntur, quibus monitus is est, ut primo Comitiorum die à conventu biduum se abstineret; magnum enim & inopinum malum congregationi imminere, terribilem ictum sensuræ, nec percutientem visuræ. Quid faceret Montaquilius, diu incertus; pensitato Regis periculo, nihil contemnendum, & quicquid erat, secretos Regis consiliarios minimè celandum judicavit. Factum igitur ab eo indicium Roberto Cœcilio, Sarisburii Comiti, & ab hoc Carolo Howardo, maris præsecto, Worcestriensi & Northomptoniensi Comitibus, atque demum Regi ipsi (cujus in obscuré dictis animadvertendis perspicax ingenium, & in ambiguis extricandis felicem conjecturam sæpius se expertos consiliarii ajebant) ex venatione reduci, qui lectis literis ad Montaquilium exaratis, & expensis verbis illis: Terriblem conventus ipse ictum sentiet, neque videbit percutientem, subodoratus primus est, subitum à pulveris tormentarii ictu exitium his verbis designari. Perlustratis die Lunæ, quæ proximè Comitia antecedebat, sub vesperam à magno Camerario & Montaquilio Curia & vicinis locis, in cella subterranea lignorum, fascium, carbonum strues deprehensa est. Rogatóque Wineardo, Regiarum ædium custode, in quem usum illa essent comportata, à Percio conductas ædes cum cella, & acervum illuc congestum didicere. Præterea astantem in cellæ angulo Fauxium cum efferato desperati ac perditi nebulonis vultu conspicati, Percii domesticum, & illarum ædium per Percii absentiam custodem esse, ex ipsomet intelligunt. Quibus perceptis indiciis iterum con-cucubia noête pervestigatione facta, denuo Fauxius vestitus & occreatus ante ædes offensus captúsque & amotis in cella lignis ac carbonibus triginta sex diversæ magnitudinis dolia pulvere nitrato repleta ; denique vestibus Fauxii excussis fomenta & tres funes canabei, quibus lenta flamma alitur, inventa sunt. Interrogatus Fauxius, in flagitio deprehensus, re desperata, quam negare non poterat, crimen ultrò confessus est, & interrita facie insuper addidit, bene quæsitoribus evenisse, quòd se ante ædes, jam cella egressum, in qua erant parata omnia, offendissent. Nam si intus eum nacti essent, non commissurum, quin se cum illis immisso igne contumulâsset. Patefactis insidiis, conjurati huc illuc diversi abeuntes, Holbechi ad Stephani Littetonii ædes in Stafordiæ finibus conveniunt: quò etiam aliunde complices, detectæ rei ignari, veniunt. Cúmque magnum in loco ibi condicto exercitum se aggregaturum factionis Duces considerent, re ex animi sententia perfecta, novam prorsus Angliæ faciem inducturum, & semel rectè placita sacra aboliturum, non nisi centum in armis comparuerunt, qui à Regiis cum valida manu superveniente, cincti cùm evadere non possent, & pulvere sulphureo, qui ad siccandum prope ignem positus erat, scintilla eò delapsa inflammato, obsessorum facies, latera, brachia, manus tam subito amburente, ut tractandis armis plerique inhabiles redditi, animos cum viribus amiserint: Catisbejus & Percius glande plumbea transfossi, utrique Wrigthii interfecti, Thomas Winterus, Grauntius, Digbejus, Rookwodus, Bates; & alio profugi latitantesque Treshamus, Robertus Winterus & Littetonius capti, & rei feriem, sicuti eam ex actis à viris doctissimis, Aug. Thuano Histor. lib. c x x x v. & Isaaco Casaubono, cujus Londini in aula apud Regem agentis Epistola ad Jesuitam Frontonem Ducæum exarata (ad quam non Fronto ipse, sed Eudæmon seu mavis Cacodæmon Johannes, novum è Creta prodigium, præter copiosa convitia regerere nihil potuit) inter Epistolas à Celeb. & amicissimo Grævio auctius editas pag. 704---798. extat, repetita paulo accuratius & præter instituti rationem prolixius, quia id res tanti momenti postulare visa est, narravimus, confessi, meritis supplicis horribile scelus expiârunt.
units.tr: was put off until the following February, 1605. Meanwhile Thomas Bates, Catesby's servant, a man ready with his hands, in whom his master placed much trust, was taken into the secret out of suspicion. At first he seemed moved by the atrocity of the deed, but he was sent to the Jesuit Tesmond, who was also called Greenway, was persuaded by him, and, once the matter had been shown to him as deserving, was wonderfully strengthened for carrying it out. Afterwards Robert Keyes, and after him Ambrose Rookwood and John Grant, became partners in the plot. In December 1604 the underground work was begun, with Christopher Wright, and shortly afterwards Robert Winter, brother of Thomas, taken into the partnership. The work was often interrupted and often resumed, and at last the tunnel had been carried to the wall of the Parliament House. There a new difficulty presented itself, because of the hardness of the wall and its thickness of three ells, with only a few days left before the sitting. The stubbornness of the workmen had now nearly pierced the middle of the wall, and while their spirits did not fail, only time seemed likely to fail them, when the sitting was postponed to October. Then despair turned to joy, with confident hope of carrying out the deed. But while they went on eagerly piercing the wall, Guy Fawkes, who had been sent to find out the cause of a noise heard from the other side of the wall, reported that there was an underground cellar there, from which coal was being removed, since the man who had rented the cellar for that purpose was dead. The conspirators, judging this cellar more suitable, therefore rented it through Percy's work, as if it were another house, and cast all their resources and all their hopes into it, chiefly for the sake of its position, since it lay almost directly beneath the royal throne. Nitrated powder was carried at leisure into that cellar from Catesby's house, opposite the Parliament House, where it had earlier been stored with the greatest care, and was covered with thirty-six casks, under a great pile of stones and wood. Finally everything was ready, and the stage awaited its last act, when, by the just judgment of God, one of them, wishing safety for another, brought ruin on himself and his fellow conspirators. Ten days remained before the sitting, when on Saturday towards evening a letter, by an unknown author and carried by an unknown messenger, was delivered to Lord Monteagle as if from a friend. In it he was warned to keep away from the assembly for two days before the first day of the sitting, for a great and unexpected disaster hung over the gathering: they would feel a terrible blow, and would not see who struck it. Monteagle, long uncertain what to do, weighed the danger to the King, judged that nothing was to be disregarded, and that whatever it was must not be concealed from the King's private counsellors. He therefore made the information known to Robert Cecil, Earl of Salisbury, and from him to Charles Howard, Lord Admiral, and the Earls of Worcester and Northampton, and at last to the King himself, who was returning from hunting. The counsellors said that the King's sharp wit in noticing obscure sayings, and his happy conjecture in unravelling ambiguities, had often been proven to them. He read the letter written to Monteagle, and when he had weighed the words, The assembly itself will feel a terrible blow, and will not see who strikes it, he was the first to suspect that the sudden destruction by a blow of gunpowder was indicated by these words. On Monday, the day before the sitting, in the evening, the Lord Chamberlain and Monteagle searched the House and the places nearby, and in the underground cellar they found heaps of wood, bundles and coal. Having questioned Whynniard, keeper of the royal buildings, as to what purpose these had been brought together, they learned that the house with the cellar had been rented by Percy, and that a heap had been piled there. Moreover, seeing Fawkes standing in a corner of the cellar with the wild look of a desperate and abandoned rogue, they learned from himself that he was Percy's servant and, in Percy's absence, the keeper of that house. With these clues, a second search was made by night; Fawkes was found dressed and booted in front of the house, seized, and when the wood and coal were removed from the cellar, thirty-six casks of various sizes full of nitrated gunpowder were found. Finally, when Fawkes's clothes were shaken out, slow-match and three hempen fuses, by which a slow flame is fed, were found. Fawkes, caught in the crime, questioned, and with his cause desperate, freely confessed the crime, which he could not deny; and with an undaunted face he added that it was well for the investigators that they had come upon him in front of the house, since he had already left the cellar, where everything was ready. For had they found him inside, he would not have failed to bury himself with them in the fire he had set. With the plots now exposed, the conspirators went off in different directions, and gathered at Holbeach's house, at Stephen Littleton's, in the county of Staffordshire; other accomplices also came there from elsewhere, ignorant that the affair was discovered. The leaders of the faction supposed that they would gather a great army at the appointed place, and when the deed was done they would bring about an entirely new face for England and abolish at a stroke the sacred rites rightly established; but only one hundred men came together under arms. The royal forces came up with a strong band and surrounded them; since they could not escape, and a spark fell into the sulphurous powder which had been placed to dry near the fire, the faces, sides, arms and hands of the besieged were so suddenly burned that most of them, rendered unfit to handle their arms, lost both courage and strength. Catesby and Percy were pierced by a leaden ball; both Wrights were killed; Thomas Winter, Grant, Digby, Rookwood and Bates were taken; Tresham, Robert Winter and Littleton, who had fled elsewhere and were hiding, were captured. I have narrated the course of the affair, repeating it a little more carefully and at greater length than the plan of this work allows, because so great a matter seemed to require it, as it is set out in the records by the most learned men, Thuanus, Hist. lib. CXXXV, and Isaac Casaubon, whose letter, written at London at court while he was acting for the King, addressed to the Jesuit Fronto Ducaeus (to which Fronto himself could return nothing but abundant insults, and a new prodigy from Crete, the Eudaemon, or rather Cacodaemon John), exists among the letters published with additions by the celebrated and most friendly Graevius, pp. 704–798. The condemned, having confessed, expiated with deserved punishments a horrible crime.

units.la: CCXII. Dubitari certè nequit, fuisse conjurationem
units.tr: CCXII. There can be no doubt that this conspiracy was

units.la: isthanc omnium, quæ nostri & prisci ævi temporibus memorantur, consilio, audacia & immanitate maximè admirandam. Nam fando ubique acceptum, & fama ad posteros transmissum est, multos Principes fraude cæsos, & Respublicas insidiis petitas fuisse. At nulla ætas, nulla tellus tale conspirationis monstrum unquam aluit, in qua Rex cum Regina, parentes cum omni sobole, Regni totius Ordines, totum denique Regnum, & in eo innocentes innumeri uni exitio uno momento destinabantur. Ut populus Romanus unam cervicem haberet, Caligulæ votum fuisse, narrant historiæ: sed votum duntaxat præterea-que nihil. Hi verò Zelotæ non voverunt illi quidem fortasse, ut universa Britania cervicem unam haberet, uno ictu præcidendam: sed, quod longè majus est, subtilissimam rationem, novi Sisyphi, novi Autolyci repererunt, quâ id ipsum ferè in Anglia effectum darent, quod Romæ Caligula volvit, nec potuit. Si enim istarum insidiarum magna moles, sed improspera ad votum succeßisseт, quid futurum erat aliud, nisi magnæ Britanniæ caput una veluti cervice nixum amputâsse, & reliqui corporis trunco vitam eripuisse? Et Caligulæ quidem votum, ut erat temeritate subitanea conceptum: ita fortasse, si ejus exequendi potestas ipsi esset ex inopinato facta, pœnitentia fuisset emendatum, pro eo ac animum revocata magnitudo facinoris metum, prolationes, diversa interdum consilia solet afferre: & omnia inconsulti impetus coepta, initiis valida, spatio languescere consueverunt. Isti vero non repente, neque temere, sed destinato consilio parricidium hoc suscepérunt: semel susceptum jugi meditatione concoxerunt, & ad consummationem illius cupiditate summa anhelantes, integrum ferme triennium in tanta immanitate obfirmati, duraverunt. Tum autem quae comparatio Imperatoris Pagani & mente capti, cum optimi Regis subditis: cum hominibus, qui se Christianos, qui Catholicos dici haberíque vellent: denique cum salutaris doctrinae Christi praeconibus, quales Jesuitae haberi volunt?
units.tr: the most remarkable of all those recorded in our own age and in earlier times for its planning, its audacity and its savagery. For it is reported everywhere by word of mouth, and handed down to posterity by fame, that many princes have been struck down by treachery and commonwealths attacked by ambush. But no age and no land has ever nurtured such a monstrous conspiracy, in which a king with his queen, parents with all their offspring, the orders of the whole kingdom, and finally the whole realm, together with innumerable innocent people, were marked for destruction in a single moment. Histories tell that Caligula wished the Roman people had one neck, but that was only a wish and nothing more. These zealots, however, perhaps did not wish that all Britain had one neck to be cut off with one blow; but, what is far greater, they devised a most subtle scheme, a new Sisyphus and a new Autolycus, by which they nearly brought about in England what Caligula wished for at Rome and could not achieve. For if the great mass of this plot had succeeded as they hoped, what else would follow but that the head of Great Britain, resting as it were on one neck, would be cut off, and life would be torn from the trunk of the rest of the body? And Caligula's wish, since it was conceived by a sudden rashness, might perhaps, had the power to carry it out been unexpectedly granted to him, have been corrected by repentance, as the greatness of the deed, returning to his mind, usually brings fear, delays, and sometimes different plans; and the undertakings of ill-considered impulse, strong at the start, usually grow weak with time. But these men undertook this parricide not suddenly or rashly, but with a settled plan; once undertaken, they nursed it through constant meditation, and, panting with the greatest desire for its completion, they persisted, hardened in such savagery, for almost three whole years. And what comparison, then, is there between a pagan emperor or a madman and the subjects of the best of kings? Between men who wished to be called and held Christians, Catholics, and finally the heralds of the saving doctrine of Christ, as the Jesuits wish to be regarded?

units.la: CCXIII. Nam quòd haec nihil ad Papatus, nihil ad Ecclesiae Romanae historiam attinere, regerent forsitan illi, qui tanti criminis infamiam ab ea abstersam cuperent; hoc uno efficacissimè refelluntur, quòd teterimae huic conjurationi immixtos fuisse professos Sodalitii Jesu Patres, Pontificiae dominationis instrumenta & satellites, Pontificumque ipsorum mancipia ὑδρόσπορα, nunquam eo nomine à Paulo V. qui eo tempore rerum potiebatur, vel reprehensos, vel admonitos, nedum damnatos, certo certius est. Quamvis enim hoc hominum genus, potentibus infidum, solita, sed non solida fide, ferreáque adeò fronte, quenquam è suae Societatis Patribus conspirationi huic interveniisse, negat: si tamen, prout prosperum ac felix scelus virtus vocatur, res bene cessisset, Ignatiana haec veréque ignea Societas, igneum isthoc ac nefarium scelus, quod ipsa praecipuè machinata est, non sibi modò vendicaret, sed summoperè insuper deprædicaret. Nunc vero vulpeculam istam imitatur, quae ad sublimem uvam, quam de vite dependentem conspicata erat, subsiliit iterum atque iterum, omnes vires corporis adhibens,
units.tr: CCXIII. For although those who wished to wipe away the infamy of so great a crime from the Papacy might perhaps reply that these matters have nothing to do with the Papacy or the history of the Roman Church, this is refuted most effectively by one fact, which is quite certain: that the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, who openly professed to have been involved in this foul conspiracy, the instruments and satellites of Papal domination and the hydra-born [ὑδρόσπορα] creatures of the Popes themselves, were never on that account rebuked or admonished, let alone condemned, by Paul V, who was then in power. For although this class of men, faithless to the powerful and holding to their faith in the usual way but not firmly, and with brazen foreheads, denies that any of the Fathers of their Society took part in this conspiracy, nevertheless, if the affair had turned out well and happily (for a successful crime is called virtue), this Ignatian, truly fiery society would not only have claimed for itself this fiery and nefarious crime, which it itself especially plotted, but would have proclaimed it loudly besides. As it is, it imitates that little fox which, having caught sight of a high grape hanging from the vine, leaped again and again, using all the strength of its body, to reach it, and at last, forced to withdraw, exhausted by its fruitless labour, consoled itself, as it were: "But indeed these grapes are still sour, and especially bitter; nor, even if one were found on the way, would it seem that they ought to be picked." Plainly they wish to seem not to have wanted what they could not attain.

units.la: Ecclesiam Romanam per Jesuitas conspirationis ejus participem jussie, probatur. si forte attingere posset: & tandem cùm defatigata inani labore discedere cogeretur, ipsa sese quasi consolata: At enim acerba nunc etiam, inquit, uva sunt, & ista cumprimis austera; nec si in via reperiatur, videretur tollenda esse. Scilicet homines noluisse videri voluit, quod assequi nequiverunt. Enimverò conjurationis pulverariæ negotio Jesuitas minimùm quatuor, Henricum Garnetum Provincialem, Hollum, qui & Oldcorni nomine venerat; Oswaldum Tesmondum sive Greenwellium, & Johannem Gerhardum implicitos fuisse, è publicatis actis, inconcussæ fidei monimento, Epistolisque Garneti propria manu exaratis, ex quibus τὰ κυφιώταλα tum Episcopus Elien-sis in Tortura Torti, tum Casaubonus in Epistola laudata, descripserunt vulgaruntque, planissimè constat. Qui etiam partim debitas meditati & aliquo usque producti parricidii, cujus flagitium Sathanicæ æquivocationis novo artificio non ita occultare potuerunt, quin judicum sagacium industria apertam denique in lucem prodiret; pœnas luerunt, à sociis postea perridiculè vanissiméque Cœlis inserti: partim matura sibi fuga consuluerunt, Romam & alio ad suos delati, minimè recipiendi, si quid Papæ & Jesuitis reliquis pudoris inesset. Neque etiam intra quatuor illos proditionis consilia stetisse, verisimile est, cùm pauci celandæ rei quàm agendæ aptiores esse solent. Constatque præterea prius quàm rebus, post acceptam ab Hispano repulsam, deploratis, in novi Angliæ Regis caput conspirari coepissent, adeóque devoluti in extrema consilia essent, ita conscientiam eorum à Jesuitis instructam: Regem deponere, Regna concedere, penes supremum Ecclesiæ judicem esse. Atqui hæreticos omnes ipso jure extra communionem positos diris fidelium proscriptionibus separari, & quotannis à Pontifice in Cœna Domini excommunicari. idque locum habere non solum in hæreticis professis, sed etiam occultis, quippe qui cùm ipso jure jure excommunicati censeantur, in poenas a professis ipso facto promeritas incidant. Ex eo sequi, Reges aut alios Principes Christianos, si in haeresin incidant, deponi posse, & subditos eorum dominio protinus liberari. nec jus illud recuperari posse, etiamsi Ecclesia reconcilientur. Nec solum ad Principes hac labe infectos poenam extendi, sed etiam ad eorum filios, qui a Regni successione ob vitium paternum pelluntur. Haeresin quippe lepram & morbum haereditarium esse. Atque ut distertius res exprimatur, Regnum amittere, qui religionem Romanam deserit, diris illum devoveri, abdicari, proscribi, nec unquam ipsum aut illius posteros in Regnum restitui, quoad animam a solo Pontifice posse absolvi. quibus verbis conscientiae instructionem a Theologis impertitam Thuanus Histor. lib. cxxxv. describit. Ac his rationibus cum se tutos conjurati existimassent, demum conjurationis munimenta quaesiverunt, atque inprimis secretum, quod confessionis fide & Sacramenti sumptione obsignarunt. conceptumque inter eos juramentum; quo per S. Trinitatem & Sacramentum mox sumendum fidem obligarunt, se nunquam consilium directe vel indirecte, verbo aut circumstantiis sibi communicandum declaraturos, nec ab illius executione destituros, nisi a sociis facta potestate. Neque ante Catisbejus doli totius architectus, quam ita a Theologis ad facinus, utpote non licitum duntaxat & laudabile, verum meritorium etiam, auctoratus esset, consilium pulverariae conspirationis vel animo agitavit ipse, vel sociis aperuit, vel Garneto, ad quem in rebus dubiis ceu oraculum se contulit, consiliis suis, uti propter longum rerum tractandarum usum, prudentiae & solertiae laude inter Anglos Pontificios erat clarissimus, etiam extra confessionis sigillum, universum negotium moderaturo, institutum suum prodidit.
units.tr: That the Roman Church was made a partner in this conspiracy through the Jesuits is proved, if it could perhaps reach it. Indeed, from the published records, a firm monument of faith, and from the letters of Garnet written in his own hand, it is quite clear that at least four Jesuits, Henry Garnet, the Provincial, Hall, who also came under the name of Oldcorne, Oswald Tesmond or Greenwell, and John Gerard, were involved in the gunpowder conspiracy. From these sources both the Bishop of Ely in the Tortura Torti and Casaubon in the letter cited above copied out and published the secret letters [τὰ κυφιώταλα]. Some of these men, having paid the due penalty for the parricide they had planned and carried some way towards execution (a crime which they could not hide well enough by the new artifice of Satanic equivocation to prevent its open disclosure at last through the diligence of shrewd judges), were afterwards, to the great ridicule and vanity of their fellows, enrolled among the saints in heaven; others looked to their own safety by timely flight, carried off to Rome and elsewhere to their own people, not to be received at all, if the Pope and the rest of the Jesuits had any shame. Nor is it likely that these four confined their plans of betrayal to themselves, since few are usually more suited to concealing a matter than to carrying it out. It is also established that, before the affairs were given up as lost after the rejection by the Spaniard, they had begun to conspire against the head of the new King of England; and when they had sunk into their final plans, their conscience was thus instructed by the Jesuits: "To depose a king, to yield kingdoms, to hold that the supreme judge of the Church is in authority. But all heretics are by law placed outside communion, to be separated by the dire proscriptions of the faithful, and excommunicated by the Pope every year at the Lord's Supper. And this holds good not only for heretics who openly profess their heresy, but also for secret ones, since, being considered excommunicated by law itself, they fall into the penalties that they have deserved by the very fact of professing. From this it follows that kings or other Christian princes, if they fall into heresy, can be deposed, and their subjects immediately freed from their rule; nor can that right be recovered even if they are reconciled to the Church. Nor is the penalty extended only to princes stained by this blemish, but also to their sons, who are excluded from the succession to the kingdom because of their father's fault. For heresy is indeed a leprosy and a hereditary disease. And, to express the matter more plainly, whoever deserts the Roman religion loses his kingdom, is cursed with dire curses, is disowned and proscribed, and neither he nor his posterity can ever be restored to the kingdom until his soul can be absolved by the Pope alone." Thuanus in his Histor. book cxxxv describes the instruction of conscience imparted by the theologians in these words. And when the conspirators, on these grounds, thought themselves safe, at last they sought the fortifications of the conspiracy, and above all secrecy, which they sealed with the faith of confession and the taking of the sacrament. They also made a mutual oath, by which, through the Holy Trinity and the sacrament about to be received, they bound their faith that they would never declare the plan directly or indirectly, by word or by circumstance, to be communicated to anyone, nor would they abandon its execution unless the power were granted by their fellows. Nor did Catesby, the architect of the whole deceit, either entertain in his mind the plan of this gunpowder conspiracy, or disclose it to his fellows, or reveal his designs to Garnet, to whom in doubtful matters he went as to an oracle, before he had been enlisted by the theologians for the deed, as one not merely permitted and praiseworthy but even meritorious. Garnet, who, on account of his long experience in managing affairs, was the most distinguished of the English Papists for his praise of prudence and skill, was to direct the whole business, even outside the seal of confession.

units.la: CCXIV. Lubet hoc loco Jesuitarum seu potius Igna- tianorum, quos ab igne jaciendo seu ciendo ita dictos non inepte
units.tr: CCXIV. It is fitting here to say a little about the Jesuits, or rather the Ignatians, who, as one writer has not unfittingly judged, are so named from throwing fire or stirring up.

units.la: nonnemo censuit; desperatam hæresin novissimam duplicem, qua veterem Hildebrandinam & Bonifacianam adversus sceptra Regum & Principum doctrinam, ceu novis fulcris, sustentare firmius conati sunt; cujusque etiam Ecclesia Romana, Pontifices inprimis, qui nunquam alterutram aperte improbasse, nedum damnasse vel proscripsisse comperti sunt; reos se fecerunt, paucis perstringere. Prior est, Regem vel Principem quemvis in hæresin prolapsum, etiam ante exploratam voluntatem & authoritatem Romani Pontificis, dummodo subditi Comitia habere prohibiti, Jesuitarum vel Theologorum similium consilio ad id usi fuerint; occidere, non fas duntaxat, sed pium etiam, laudabile & meritorium esse. Hanc hæresin gravissimam Regum & Principum jugulum nefarie appetentem; Divinæ Providentiæ, per quam Reges regnant, inimicam, verbo Divino, quod potestatibus, legitime scilicet electis, vel jus exercendæ potestatis honesto titulo obtinentibus, etiam iniquis obsecundare, & Unctos Domini non attingere jubet, contrariam; Ecclesiæ, cujus interest plurimum Nutritios amari, eorumque authoritatem sacrosanctam & ἀσυλον inviolabilem haberi, fatalem; denique religioni Christianæ apud infideles, si qua alia est, probrosissimam, non in sinu duntaxat Sinones illi fovent, sed publicis etiam scriptis, ne latere eos, quos libido incessit Unctos Domini attrectare, ullo modo queat, propalare non erubuerunt. Ex multis pauca de Draconica illa, non atramento sed sanguine, scripta Jesuitarum lege, testimonia proferam. Johannes Mariana, Jesuita Toletanus tractatum de Institutione Principum (occidendorum scilicet) scripsit, cujus imprimendi facultas à Stephano Hojeda, visitatore Societatis data est. Libro ejus primo hanc quæstionem certo consilio tractat: An liceat Regem legitimum, puta Henricum III. Regem Galliarum Christianissimum, postquam à paucis seditiosis, sed doctis (nam his his arbitrium ille, ut de capite Principis sui statuant, permittit) cœperit tyrannus appellari, occidere? Concludit ad extremum, licere: & intandam illam Sathanæ progeniem, Jacobum Clementem, ob patratum parricidium magnificis verbis in Cœlum extollit. Ejus libri cap. 6. hæc inter alia extant: A populis sive subditis volentibus Rex principatu spoliari potest. Et ab omni memoria in magna laude fuerunt, quicunque tyrannos opprimere aggressi sunt. Abdicandi vero Principis rationem ejusmodi ille ostendit: Expedita, inquit, & maximè tuta via est, si publici conventus facultas detur, ut communi consensu statuatur, quid fixum ratumque esse debeat. Et si monitis Princeps non obediat, consilia explicanda, arma expedienda, pecuniæ in belli sumptus subditis imperandæ, Princeps etiam privata authoritate ferro perimendus. Si verò publici Conventus facultas sublata erit, tum etiam, qui votis publicis favens Regem sive Principem perimere tentârit, haudquaquam eum iniquè fecisse existimabo. Ac nisi publica vox adsit, quæ Regem pro tyranno habeat, adhibendi sunt in consilium viri eruditi & graves. Subjicit: Præclarè, præclarè cum rebus humanis ageretur, si multi homines forti pectore invenirentur, pro libertate Patriæ vitæ contemptores & salutis. Et dolet, quod plerosque incolumitatis cupiditas retineat, magnis sæpè conatibus adversa. Mox cap. 7. temperamentum quoddam suadet: In Regibus, inquit, ferro aut veneno, nihil interest enim, interficiendis, hoc utendum temperamento, si non ipse, qui perimitur, venenum haurire cogitur, quo concepto pereat: Sed exterius ab alio adhibeatur, nihil adjuvante eo, qui perimendus est: nimirum cum veneni tanta vis est, ut eo sella aut veste delibuta, vim interficiendi habeat. Concluditque parricidiorum ille doctor: In vitam Regis aut Principis (quem viri eruditi & graves, hoc est, Jesuitæ, non-Regem, nonPrincipem judicaverint) grassari quacunque arte concessum, tantùm ne cogatur sciens aut imprudens sibi ipsi mortem conscire. Hæc igitur erga Reges & Principes Clementiæ Jesuiticæ ara est, quòd necessitas iis non imponitur, sed carnificis munus aliis delegatur: benignior scilicet ara illa Meroensium Sacerdotum, qui Diodoro Siculo Biblioth. hist. memorante, tanta polluerunt authoritate, ut quandocunque ipsis in mentem venit, missō ad Æthiopum Regem nuntio, vita seipsum abdicare juberent. Oraculis enim Deûm id edici, nec fas esse ulli mortalium eorum jussa contemnere. quomodo etiam nostri illi Pontifices Manlianis suis in Principes imperiis, veteri Ecclesiæ prorsus ignotis, jussum Divinum obtendunt. Libri etiam parricidales, eadem Marianæ decreta complexi, post tentatam à Castello cædem Henrici IV. à Jesuita Johanne Guignardo propria manu scripti, Lutetiæ in Collegio Claromontano reperti sunt, ex quibus nonnulla Thuanus Histor. plura verò Acta Parlamenti Parisiensis in Memor. Ligæ Tom. v excerpserunt. Doluit nebuloni illi inprimis, quòd Sanbartholomæano tumultu vena basilica sanguis non fit missus. quod si factum esset, inquiebat ille, ex febri in phrenesin res minimè recidisset. Nominavit etiam Academia Parisiensis in auribus Illustrissimi Senatus Petrum Barrerium, à Jesuitis ad parricidia auctoratum: Guilhelmum Parrium à Benedicto Palmio Jesuita persuasum, licere impunè Reges occidere à Pontifice diris devotos: Hannibalem Cadretum Jesuitam, qui factum Cælum mereri Parrio dixerit. Extat praeterea liber Jesuitarum, de abdicatione Henrici III. Regis Galliæ, Lugduni apud Johannem Pillehot, Ligæ Gallicanæ Bibliopolam A. M. D. XCI. editus, in quo Henricus III. ceu impius & impurus tyrannus accusatur, additurque præclarè actum iri, si is cum suis similibus Regibus & Principibus, ab uno vel pluribus vasallis aut subditis, non expectata speciali excommunicatione Papæ, interficeretur. idque opus & gloriosum & meritorium omnino futurum. Non desinemus etiam, inquiunt, auxilia & media quærere, quibus Rex iste, cum omnibus ei adhærentibus opprimi & interfici posset. Eadem Apologia pro Castello & Jesuitis edita, qua Castelli propositum ceu heroicum planè & justum in tertium usque Cœlum extollitur, ipséque Castellus inter Martyres numeratur: Martæ Neapolitani libri quibus ille χυρίας δόξας supra narratas rigidè tuetur: Ribadeneira, Henrici III. dirissimam cœdem probans, & parricidam tartareum sic memorans, ut propiùs multò absit à laudante quàm à detestante: denique Harnetus & complices cerbereo furore διςπολαλήμφοι, eorumque ex eodem Sodalitio hyperaspistæ strenui, Eudæmon Johannes Cretensis, in Garneti Apologia; Bellarminus in suo diri ominis Torto, alii, qui novos Cœlites, Garnetum & Oldcornum non secus ac διογενεῖς Heroas laudárunt defenderuntque mordicus, pædagogicis suis Syllogismis sceptra Regum ac Principum impunè lacessentes; aurigantur. Demum etiam Jesuitarum pro tempore, quo scilicet adhuc salem illorum lingere ei datum fuit; pullus, vix nominandus Alastor Scioppius in Classico belli sacri Fr. Jacobi Martenisii, Vicarii Generalis Inquisitionis Papiæ, jussu vulgato, cap. 3. p. 22. quod mussitant plures, aperte professus ipse, rationibus etiam comprobare instituit, hæreticos Principes jure à subditis contrucidari; producto etiam exemplo Zambri, Regis Israelitici, qui ab Amri obsessus seipsum cum domo Regia succenderat, ad oram libri hæc allinere non dubitavit: Quid ad hoc exemplum pulveraria illa Anglorum conjuratio? Quam probationem non minùs ἀπροσδιόνυσον, quàm canis in balneo est, tantum abesse à ratione, quantum distat Roma Londino, ab Idolatra Christianus, factum à jure, tyrannus à Rege, denique Scioppius à viro bono; Optimus & doctissimus Berneggerus in Aureola Tuba Pacis pag. 115. 116. &c. verè demonstrat. Neque verò obstat, quòd Claudius Aquaviva, Societatis Generalis, edita sanctione prohibuit, ne quis deinceps publicè vel privatim doceat, licitum esse cuicunque personæ, quocunque prætextu tyrannidis Reges aut Principes occidere. Ad minuendam scilicet invidiam prohibuit docere, non sentire vel facere; & cuilibet personæ, scilicet à Jesuitis non submissæ, vel à Papa non approbatæ. uti in Jesuita vapulante cap. 12. Cl. Rivetus solidè demonstrat.
units.tr: They have made themselves guilty of defending two recent and desperate heresies, by which they have tried to prop up more firmly, as with new supports, the old doctrine of Hildebrand and Boniface against the sceptres of kings and princes. The Roman Church, and especially the Popes, who have never been found to have openly disapproved of either, much less condemned or proscribed them, are implicated as well. I will briefly set out the first. It is: that any king or prince whatever who has fallen into heresy may be killed, even before the known will and authority of the Roman Pontiff, provided his subjects have been forbidden to hold assemblies, and have acted for this purpose on the advice of Jesuits or similar theologians; that such killing is not merely lawful but also pious, praiseworthy and meritorious. This most grave heresy, which wickedly aims at the throat of kings and princes, is hostile to the Divine providence by which kings reign, and contrary to the Word of God, which bids us obey powers, that is, those lawfully chosen or holding the right to exercise power under an honourable title, even wicked ones, and not to touch the anointed of the Lord. It is fatal to the Church, whose great interest it is that its nursing fathers be loved and that their sacred authority be held inviolable and sanctuary-proof. Finally, it is most disgraceful to the Christian religion, such as it is, among unbelievers. Those Sinons do not merely cherish it in their bosom, but in published writings they have not been ashamed to declare that nothing can keep hidden those whom lust has moved to lay hands on the anointed of the Lord. I will cite a few testimonies from the many writings of the Jesuits on this Draconian doctrine, written not in ink but in blood. Johannes Mariana, a Jesuit of Toledo, wrote a treatise on the Education of Princes (namely, on how to kill them), whose printing was licensed by Stephen Hojeda, the Visitor of the Society. In the first book he deliberately treats this question: Is it lawful to kill a lawful king, say Henry III, the most Christian King of France, once he has begun to be called a tyrant by a few seditious but learned men (for he leaves the decision on his prince's life to these men)? He concludes at last that it is lawful, and with high-flown words he exalts to heaven that monstrous offspring of Satan, Jacques Clément, for the parricide he committed. Among other things, the following stands in chapter 6 of this book: A king can be stripped of his principality by the peoples or subjects if they are willing. And from all memory, those who have undertaken to crush tyrants have been held in great praise. He shows the method of deposing a prince as follows: The way is easy, says he, and by far the safest, if the opportunity of a public assembly is granted, so that by common consent it may be decided what ought to be fixed and settled. And if the prince does not obey the admonitions, the plans are to be laid out, the arms made ready, money demanded from the subjects for the expenses of war, and the prince himself, even on private authority, is to be destroyed by the sword. But if the opportunity of a public assembly is taken away, then I shall think that whoever, favouring the public wishes, has tried to destroy the king or prince has by no means acted unjustly. And unless there is a public voice that holds the king to be a tyrant, wise and grave men are to be taken into counsel. He adds: How splendidly would human affairs go, if many men were found with brave hearts, despisers of life and safety for the liberty of their country! And it is a pity that the desire for safety holds back most men, which is often an obstacle to great endeavours. Soon after, in chapter 7, he recommends a certain moderation: In killing kings, says he, whether with the sword or with poison (for there is no difference), this moderation must be used: that the one who is to be killed should not be forced to drink the poison himself, so that he dies by it once it is taken. Rather, let it be applied from outside by another, the one to be killed contributing nothing; namely, when the poison is of such strength that a seat or garment smeared with it has the power to kill. And that doctor of parricides concludes: It is allowed to attack the life of a king or prince (whom learned and grave men, that is, the Jesuits, shall have judged not to be a king or prince) by whatever art, provided only that one is not compelled to bring about his own death knowingly or unknowingly. This, then, is the Jesuitical clemency towards kings and princes: they are not themselves under any obligation, but the office of the executioner is handed over to others. That altar is indeed milder than the altar of the priests of Meroë, who, as Diodorus Siculus relates in his Historical Library, held such authority that whenever it came into their minds, they sent a messenger to the king of the Ethiopians and ordered him to end his own life. For it was declared by the oracles of the gods, and it was not lawful for any mortal to despise their commands. In the same way those Pontiffs of ours put forward a divine command as a pretext for their Manlian edicts against princes, which are wholly unknown to the ancient Church. Also, the parricidal books which embodied the same decrees of Mariana, written out by the hand of the Jesuit Johannes Guignard after the attempted murder of Henry IV by Castel, were found in the Clermont College at Paris. Some passages from them Thuanus has excerpted in his History, and more from the Acts of the Parliament of Paris in the Memoirs of the League, vol. 5. That scoundrel was especially grieved that the basilica vein had not been opened at the St Bartholomew tumult; for, he said, had this been done, the affair would not have gone from fever into frenzy. The Academy of Paris also named in the ears of the most illustrious Senate Pierre Barrière, engaged for parricide by the Jesuits; Guillaume Parry, persuaded by the Jesuit Benedetto Palmio that it was lawful to kill kings with impunity when they had been cursed by the Pope; and Hannibal Cadret, the Jesuit, who said that Parry deserved heaven for the deed. There is moreover a Jesuit book on the deposition of Henry III, King of France, published at Lyon by Johannes Pillehotte, bookseller of the Gallican League, in the year 1591. In it Henry III is accused as an impious and impure tyrant, and it is added that it would be splendid if he, with his like among kings and princes, were killed by one or more vassals or subjects, without waiting for a special excommunication by the Pope; and that such a work would be altogether glorious and meritorious. We will not cease, they say, to seek aids and means by which that king, together with all who adhere to him, could be crushed and killed. The same Apology, published for Castel and the Jesuits, extols Castel's purpose as altogether heroic and just up to the third heaven, and Castel himself is numbered among the martyrs. Then there are the books of Marta of Naples, by which he rigidly defends the aforesaid glories; Ribadeneira, who approves the most dreadful murder of Henry III and recalls the parricide as a Tartarean figure in such a way that he is far closer to praise than to condemnation; and finally Harnett and his accomplices, raging with Cerberean fury, and the vigorous hyperaspists of the same fellowship: Eudaemon-Johannes of Crete in the Apology for Garnet, Bellarmine in his Tortus of ill omen, and others, who praised and stubbornly defended the new heavenly inhabitants Garnet and Oldcorne no less than the god-born heroes, and who, with their schoolroom syllogisms, drive on the sceptres of kings and princes with impunity. Last of all, the Jesuits' own pupil of the time (I mean, the one who was allowed to lick their salt), the scarcely nameable little cock Alastor Scioppius, in the Trumpet of Holy War of Fr. James Martenisius, General Vicar of the Inquisition at Pavia, by public command, chapter 3, page 22, openly professed what many mutter, and set himself to prove it by arguments as well: that heretical princes may rightly be cut down by their subjects. He also cited the example of Zimri, king of Israel, who, besieged by Omri, set fire to himself together with the royal house, and did not hesitate to write in the margin of the book: What of that gunpowder conspiracy of the English, in view of this example? That proof is no less out of place than a dog in the bath-house, as far from reason as Rome is from London, a Christian from an idolater, a deed done by right from a tyrant's act from a king, and, finally, Scioppius from a good man. The excellent and most learned Berneggerus, in his Golden Trumpet of Peace, pages 115, 116, etc., has truly demonstrated this. Nor does it stand in the way that Claudius Aquaviva, General of the Society, by a published decree forbade anyone henceforth to teach, publicly or privately, that it is lawful for any person whatever, under whatever pretext of tyranny, to kill kings or princes. Clearly he forbade the teaching, not the thinking or doing, of this, in order to lessen the odium; and forbade it for any person whatever, that is, one not subject to the Jesuits or not approved by the Pope. As the learned Rivetus solidly demonstrates in the chapter 12 where he flogs the Jesuit.

units.la: CCXV. Posterior Ignatianorum novella, nisi mavis, recoëta & ab inferis revocata hæresis est:
units.tr: CCXV. The later novelty of the Ignatians, unless you prefer, is a heresy reheated and called back from the dead:

units.la: Fas esse sive in judicio, sive in casu confessionis, etiam in juramento ipso, ejusmodi uti æquivocationibus & mentalibus reservationibus, quibus ad veritatem occultandam aliud pectore clausum teneatur, aliud ore verbisque promatur. Eum scilicet in finem induci hæresin placuit, ut parricidia aliáve etiam scelera sua coram judice pernegare, saltem involvere, & ne ad liquidum perducantur unquam, efficere possint. Tametsi verò hæresin illam in publicum parùm ingenuè & pœne inviti proferunt, atque adeò inter Societatis suæ arcana abscondere; tamen in scriptis non plané dissimularunt, & factis aperté probárunt. Scripta & Scriptores è pluribus nomino; Toletum lib. I V. Instructionis Sacerdotalis cap. 21. Gregorium de Valentia Tomo III. Disput. 5. quæst. 13. pag. 1350. &c. ubi prudentem defensionem vocat; Edmundum Campianum in Epistolis ad Generalem Societatis; Navarrum in Enchiridio; Andream Eudæmon. Johannem in Anticotoni refutatione, & Apologia Garneti, ad actionem proditoriam Eduardi Coqui, à Claudio Aquaviva, Societatis Præposito, comprobata, qua æquivocationis doctrinam ex Scripturis, Patribus, Scholasticis, Thomistis, defendere & explicare conatur; Personium Anglum, qui Romæ vixit & mortuus est, in disputationibus ejus argumenti à Mortono confutatis; Thomam Sanchez Oper. Moral. lib. III. 6. 15. Authorem Theologologiæ Moralis Jesuitarum Tract. 1. Exam. 3. cap. 4. & cap. 7. ubi ex Sanchez & Leslio exempla practica profert; Becanum Manualis libro V. alibique. Toletus addit limitationem: Si judex contra justitiam petat responsum aut juramentum. Est autem contra justitiam, cum de religione aut sociis interrogantur: tum quia haereticus non est judex competens, tum quia est in praejudicium religionis. Sed Becanus longius crimen removet, injuriam sibi, sociisque fieri, questus. Docere quippe ipsos, sincere, candide & seclusa omni aequivocatione respondendum esse. Unum tantum, de quo disputetur, casum esse: Anne reus, quando in iudicio interrogatur de crimine perpetrato, possit negare, vel aequivoce respondere? Sic autem ille distinguit, teneri respondere & fateri veritatem, si judex juridice, seu servato ordine juris interroget; secus autem non. Ratio, inquit, prioris est, quia quisque tenetur obedire superiori legitima praecipienti; quod fit, cum secundum ordinem juris reos interrogat. Ratio posterioris, quia judex non habet jus interrogandi nisi secundum ordinem juris. Juris autem ordo non servatur, cum interrogat de occulto crimine, de quo neque fama est contra reum, neque judicii competentia, neque plena probatio. Et in tali casu non mentitur, si neget a se patratum crimen; si videlicet crimen adhuc sit occultum. Caeterum Becanus hic more suo partim tergiversatur, partim etiam aequivocatione, ubi a Societate sua ejus crimen amoliri tentat, ludit. Distinguunt enim Jesuitae inter causas seculi sive forenses, & religiosas. In illis si quis juridice interrogetur, cum aequivocatione distinguendum esse negant. In his autem iis uti fas esse. Ipse vero respondet de causa Seculi & crimine perpetrato; quo nomine non censet sua illa clandestina sacra. Illud etiam juridice, sive Ordo juris ab aliis ad forensia speciatim applicatur. Sed & in altero illo genere reus perfidiae perjuriique tenetur. Neque enim vel judex haereticus ipsi est judex: vel judicium ejus judicium competens. Juris quoque ordo suspenditur ipsi ex æstimatione accusati seu rei, sit ne crimen publicum an privatum, judicium competens vel non competens, probatio plena, vel non plena. Sed & facta Jesuitarum, doctrinæ eorum interpres locupletior, ex historiis Anglorum & Belgarum, inprimis ex Negotiatione Jesuitica in Belgio edita, manifestiora sunt, quàm imber cùm pluit. Vel unius Garneti historia in Actis ejus vulgata, & à Doctiss. Casaubono in Epistola supra laudata, nec non Thuano Histor. lib. cxxxv. luculentius repetita, ejus rei fidem plenissimam faciet. Hujusmodi verò æquivocationum notitiam & usum prioribus Ecclesiæ Doctoribus atque Magistris non contigisse, adeóque suæ ætatis novissimum <>, &, & veluti munus quoddam esse, Societatis ejusdem Theologus percelebris, Gabriel Vasquez Tom. IV. quæst. 93. art. 5. dub. 13. apertissimè fatetur, & gloriatur. Negari, inquit, non potest, hujus (per æquivocationes) respondendi modi non meminisse antiquos Doctores, & ita credidisse, si negaretur factum tam coram judice quàm coram alio, esse mendacium. Et revera ita esset, si mens respondentis non esset cum illa, quam diximus, restrictione ad interrogationem respondere. Id colligitur ex Thoma, qui etiam in Reo, cum injustè interrogatur, alium modum non invenit, quàm non respondere. Colligitur etiam ex Augustino, qui loquens etiam de judice iniquè interrogante, non meminit hujus restrictionis & modi loquendi, ut excusaret responsum, sed tamen nec negavit. Scilicet S. Augustino, Thomæ aliisque vetustioribus Doctoribus mirabile isthoc donum linguarum non contigit; nec tam felicibus esse iis licuit, ut novæ ac serpentinæ istius linguæ usus iis innotesceret; agnoscerentque adeò duplici lingua, more serpentum, loqui fas piumque esse.
units.tr: It is lawful, whether in judgment, or in a case of confession, or even in an oath itself, to use such equivocations and mental reservations, by which, in order to conceal the truth, one holds one thing shut in the breast and utters another with the mouth and in words. Clearly they chose to introduce this heresy for the purpose that they might be able to deny outright their parricides and other crimes before a judge, or at least cloud them over, and never allow them to be brought into the open. Although they put forward this heresy in public rather ungenerously and almost reluctantly, and so keep it hidden among the secrets of their Society, nevertheless they have not entirely concealed it in writing, and they have clearly proved it by their deeds. I name some of the writings and writers: Toledo, book IV of the Instruction for Priests, chapter 21; Gregory of Valentia, Volume III, Disputation 5, question 13, page 1350, etc., where he calls it a prudent defence; Edmund Campion, in his Letters to the General of the Society; Navarre, in the Enchiridion; Andreas Eudaemon-Joannes, in the Refutation of the Anticotonus, and the Apology of Garnet, concerning the treacherous action of Edward Coke, approved by Claudius Aquaviva, Prefect of the Society, which tries to defend and explain the doctrine of equivocation from Scripture, the Fathers, the Scholastics and the Thomists; Persons, the Englishman, who lived and died at Rome, in his disputations on this subject, refuted by Morton; Thomas Sanchez, Moral Works, book III, 6, 15; the author of the Moral Theology of the Jesuits, Tract 1, Examination 3, chapters 4 and 7, where he brings forward practical examples from Sanchez and Leslie; Becanus, in the Manual, book V, and elsewhere. Toledo adds a limitation: if the judge asks for an answer or an oath contrary to justice. Now it is contrary to justice when they are questioned about religion or about companions: both because a heretic is not a competent judge, and because it is to the prejudice of religion. But Becanus removes the offence further, complaining that an injury is done to himself and his companions. For he teaches that they must reply sincerely, candidly and with every equivocation excluded. He says there is only one case open to debate: Can the accused, when in court he is asked about a crime committed, deny it or answer equivocally? He distinguishes thus: he is bound to answer and confess the truth if the judge questions him judicially, or in accordance with the order of law; otherwise not. The reason for the former, he says, is that everyone is bound to obey a superior who commands lawfully; which happens when he questions the accused according to the order of law. The reason for the latter is that a judge has no right to question except according to the order of law. But the order of law is not observed when he asks about a secret crime, about which there is neither general report against the accused, nor competence of the court, nor full proof. And in such a case he does not lie if he denies having committed the crime; namely if the crime is still secret. Moreover Becanus here, in his usual way, partly evades and partly, where he tries to remove that crime from his Society, plays with equivocation. For the Jesuits distinguish between secular or forensic causes and religious ones. In the former they deny that one ought to distinguish with equivocation if someone is questioned judicially. In the latter, however, they hold that it is lawful to use them. Yet he himself answers concerning a secular cause and a crime committed, under which heading he does not count those secret rites of theirs. Likewise the term judicially, or order of law, is applied by others specifically to forensic matters. But even in that other kind the accused is bound to his perfidy and perjury. For neither is a heretical judge truly a judge for him, nor is his court a competent court. The order of law is also suspended for him according to the estimation of the accused or defendant: whether the crime is public or private, whether the court is competent or not, whether proof is full or not. But the deeds of the Jesuits, a richer interpreter of their doctrine, are more manifest, from the histories of the English and the Belgians, above all from the Jesuit Negotiation published in Belgium, than rain when it rains. The history of Garnet alone, made public in his Acts, and more fully repeated by the most learned Casaubon in the letter cited above, and also by Thuanus in his History, book 135, will render complete proof of this matter. That the knowledge and use of such equivocations did not come to the earlier teachers and masters of the Church, and that this is therefore the latest <>, and as it were a certain office of that same Society, the very celebrated theologian of the Society, Gabriel Vasquez, openly confesses and boasts: It cannot be denied, he says, that the ancient Doctors did not remember this manner of answering (by equivocations), and so believed that if it were denied that the thing was done, whether before a judge or before another, it would be a lie. And indeed it would be so, if the mind of the respondent were not with that restriction which we have mentioned, to answer the question. This is gathered from Thomas, who even in the case of an accused person questioned unjustly found no other way than not to answer. It is also gathered from Augustine, who, speaking even of a judge who questions unjustly, does not mention this restriction and manner of speaking as an excuse for the reply, yet nor did he deny it. Clearly this wonderful gift of tongues did not come to Saint Augustine, Thomas and the other more ancient Doctors; nor were they so fortunate as to have the use of this new and serpentine language made known to them; and so they did not recognise that it is lawful and pious to speak with a double tongue, after the manner of serpents.
