units.la: Dan. XI. 39. Jesuitam & Cardinalem eruditionis & industriæ laude cœtera non defraudandum utrumque, Cæsarem Baronium, Sora, Campania Urbe oriundum; & Robertum Bellarminum, patria Politianum, Marcelli II. Papæ Sororis, Cynthiæ Cervinæ, filium; quorum ille seculi hujus septimo, hic vicesimo primo anno defunctus est. Scriptis illi in vulgus editis pluribus, giganteisque voluminibus ad scopum eundem, stabiliendam quæ inde à Reformatione nimium labefactata & pluribus in locis penitus collapsa est; Romani Pontificis potentiam, supra Mortalium omnium, imò ipsius Dei Omnipotentis potentiam sese efferentem, atque inde manantem religionem Pontificiam universam, diversa omnino via grassati sunt. Illi Annales Ecclesiæ condere, huic controversias Pontificias tractare, curæ cordique fuit. Ac ut de Baronio, qui sub auspiciis & ductu Philippi Nerii, Congregationis Oratorii fundatoris, Annalium illum partum suum plusquam elephantinum (nam cùm elephanti spacio decem annorum partus suos edant, ille ter decem annorum spacio suum edidit) enixus est, priore loco dicam; res ipsa manifeste arguit, quando ad scribendum Annales seu historiam Ecclesiæ animum appulit; non eum id negotii sibi credidisse dari, ut faciem veteris Ecclesiæ, qualem inveniebat quâ in Scripturis, quâ in Patrum & historiarum antiquissimis monumentis, penicillo suo bona fide exprimeret: sed potius ut talem ei σοφίᾳ quadam χαχοσυνθέτῳ faciem fingeret, qualem Ecclesiæ Romanæ suscepturn semel patrocinium postulabat. Cùm enim omnes hodiernæ de religione controversiæ ad duo capita, doctrinam scilicet de dogmatibus ritibusque, & Pontificis Romani potestate & Monarchia revocentur commodè, in utroque eam rationem Baronius tenuit, ut omissa quæstione de voluntate Domini, & vera antiquitate, omnia sine exceptione defenderet, quæ Romæ probari sciebat. In quo etsi subtilem artem seu χεύδος quandam vaferrimam adhibet, plerunque tamen implicatam animi sui notionem ita prodit, ut quisquis rudis & cæcus non est, consilium ejus subodoretur facile. De Scripturæ usu populo erepto, lingua ignota, traditionum etiam recentiorum authoritate, Transsubstantiatione, Missa, concomitantia, Sanctorum imaginum invocatione, cultu reliquiarum, purgatorio, indulgentiis, similibusque sequiorum Seculorum inventis, Protestantes inter & Pontificios controversis, asserendis Gibeonitica fraude ita ubique laborat, ut canæ & venerandæ antiquitatis colore ea invita licet imbuere annitatur unicè. Romani Pontificis verò Monarchiam, & illud infinitum imperium, ita assidue omnibus viribus εὐκαίρως ἀκαίρως propugnat, ut merito Doctifs. Pithoeus, prioribus inspectis tomis judicaverit, non titulo Annalium Ecclesiasticorum, sed potius de potestate Papæ insigniri debuisse. Hinc scilicet est, quod omnia ac singula, quæ in Ecclesia acciderunt, Pontificis authoritate gesta esse contendit: probatissimos quosque authores, sicubi Sedi Romanæ adversum quidpiam scripserunt, non sine stomacho rejicit: Pontificum Romanorum facta quantumvis enormia, truculenta, tyrannica excusat, tuetur, laudat: Hildebrandum, illum generis humani furiam, Regum & Principum potestati, libertati, cervici denique insidias quæsitissimas struentem, & Sathanicæ illius de ἐξουσίᾳ ὑπερδυνάμει Pontificis, doctrinæ elementa brevibus quasi aphorismis, qui Dictatuum nomine veniunt, complexum, amplis mirisque elogiis exornat, & perfectissimi Papæ ideam absolvere pronuntiat: Bennonem, aliosque contradicentes, auritos licet & oculatos testes, obelo suo confixos exagitat damnatque: Concilia non indicta authoritate Pontificum Pseudo-Synodos; Imperatores, Reges, Principes, Papæ sputa lingere dedignatos, hæreticos, schismaticos, tyrannos appellat; novissima quæque exempla promeritos, clamat: eosdem res Ecclesiasticas attingentes maledictis incessit; ausus etiam (ad A. DCCCLV.) Reges veteres Francorum eam ob causam cum latronibus in Sylvis comparare: fideles eorundem consiliarios, jura Regia adversus Romanam Curiam defensitantes teterrimæ hæreseos Politicorum crimine arcessit: denique non aliud fere omnibus sine discrimine, quàm cœcam obedientiam, & humile servitium Vicario Christi in hisce terris exhibendum suadet, commendat; & exhibere abnuentes, Campano supercilio suo, (Campanus quippe fuit) ubique detestatur damnatque. Scilicet venalitium erat Romani Pontificis mancipium, purpuræ mercede conductitium, ad Papatum aspirans & remis atque quadrigis contendens ipse. de quo sic merito Grotius cecinit:
units.tr: Dan. XI. 39. Both were Jesuits and Cardinals, and neither should be denied praise for learning and industry: Caesar Baronius, born at Sora in Campania, and Robert Bellarmine, born at Montepulciano, son of Cynthia Cervini, sister of Pope Marcellus II. The former died in the seventh year of this century, the latter in the twenty-first. Through many widely published writings and giant volumes, both set about the same goal: to shore up the papal power, which had been badly shaken since the Reformation and had collapsed entirely in many places. That power lifts itself above all mortals, indeed above the power of Almighty God himself, and from it flows the whole Papist religion. Baronius devoted himself to the Annals of the Church, Bellarmine to the Papist controversies. As for Baronius, who under the auspices and guidance of Philip Neri, founder of the Congregation of the Oratory, brought forth that Annals of his, more than elephantine (for elephants bear their young in ten years, while he produced his in thirty), I shall speak of him first. The thing itself clearly shows that when he turned his mind to writing the Annals, or history of the Church, he did not think he had been given the task of faithfully painting with his brush the face of the early Church, as he found it in Scripture and in the oldest monuments of the Fathers and of history. Rather, he was to fashion for it, with a certain subtle wisdom [σοφία] of ill-composed falsehood, the face that the Roman Church, once it had taken up its patronage, demanded. For since all the present controversies about religion can conveniently be traced to two heads, namely the doctrine of dogmas and rites, and the authority and monarchy of the Roman Pontiff, Baronius took this line on both: setting aside the question of the Lord's will and of true antiquity, he defended without exception everything he knew would be approved at Rome. In doing this he uses a subtle art, or a certain most cunning falsehood [ψεῦδος], yet for the most part his tangled purpose so betrays itself that anyone who is not crude and blind will easily smell out his design. On the withholding of Scripture from the people, on the unknown tongue, on the authority of more recent traditions, on transubstantiation, the Mass, concomitance, the invocation of the images of saints, the veneration of relics, purgatory, indulgences, and similar inventions of later ages, which are disputed between Protestants and Papists, he labours everywhere, with Gibeonite fraud, to assert them, aiming solely to dye them with the colour of a hoary and venerable antiquity, however unwillingly. As for the monarchy of the Roman Pontiff and that boundless empire, he defends them so constantly and with all his strength, in season and out of season [εὐκαίρως ἀκαίρως], that the learned Pithoeus, having looked through the earlier volumes, rightly judged that they should have been marked not with the title Ecclesiastical Annals, but rather On the power of the Pope. Hence, of course, he contends that everything and every event that has occurred in the Church was carried out by the authority of the Pontiff. Wherever the most approved authors have written anything against the Roman See, he rejects them not without bile. The deeds of the Roman Pontiffs, however enormous, savage and tyrannical, he excuses, defends and praises. Hildebrand, that fury of the human race, who laid the most cunning snares against the power, liberty and, finally, the necks of kings and princes, and who summed up in brief aphorisms, called the Dictates, the elements of that Satanic doctrine of the Pontiff's power beyond power [ἐξουσίᾳ ὑπερδυνάμει], he adorns with ample and wondrous praises, and pronounces him the perfect ideal of a Pope. Bennon and others who contradicted him, though they were ear- and eyewitnesses, he harries and condemns, pinning them to his obelus. Councils not convened by papal authority he calls pseudo-synods. Emperors, kings and princes who disdained to lick the spittle of the Pope he calls heretics, schismatics and tyrants, and he cries out that they deserve the latest examples. Those who touched church affairs he assailed with insults. He even dared (at the year 855) to compare the old kings of the Franks, for this reason, to brigands in the woods. The faithful counsellors of those kings, who vigorously defended royal rights against the Roman Curia, he charges with the crime of the most foul heresy of the Politicians. Finally, he urges and commends to almost everyone, without distinction, nothing but blind obedience and humble service to be shown to the Vicar of Christ on earth, and he denounces and condemns with his Campanian haughtiness (for he was indeed a Campanian) everywhere those who refuse to show it. Clearly he was a venal servant of the Roman Pontiff, hired for the reward of the purple, aspiring to the Papacy and himself striving for it with oars and chariots. Of him Grotius rightly sang:

units.la: Accedit ad hanc Ἀναθεσιν τῆς ξυγγραφῆς seu dispositionem scriptoris, quam in Scriptoribus inprimis spectandam Dionysius Halicarnasseus monet; modus etiam, quo singula hæc Baronius, Ἀναλύων τὴν ἐπιθεσι, prosecutus est; præposterus passim & perversus. Quò pertinent visiones, miracula, & putidissimæ fabulæ, quas ex recentioribus scriptoribus, Zonara, Vincentio, Nicephoro, Metaphraste, Antonino, Cypomanno, Surio, similibúsque fabularum anilium hamaxariis, eorúmque adeò fide itá collegit, ut ipsum inter & illos, aliósque etiam aurearum Legendarum consarcinatores, veluti Jacobum de Voragine, Petrum de Natalibus &c. non aliud discrimen appareat, quàm quòd illi sine arte, rusticè & pingui Minerva fabulati sunt; ipse verò majorem colorum apparatum, quippe nec ingenio, nec arte rudis, adhibuit: horrenda convitia, quæ passim vibravit in Protestantes, quos etiam ad A. D C C C. unâ cum Sergio Manichæo, hæreseon horrendarum patre, Diabolum Catechistam habere criminatur; & ad A. M. C. X V I I I. unâ cum Basilio Bongomiliorum auctore, Alexii Imp. jussu cremato, vivicomburio destinat: judiciorum temeritas. Veluti cùm sive adversa sive læta, quæ Principibus, populis, privatis contigerunt, vel observantiæ insigni erga Papam, Ecclesiamve Romanam: vel contumeliæ injuriæve, quam illi fecisse visi sunt; accepta refert: parachronismi manifesti, crassique ex ignorantia Linguarum Græcæ & Hebraicæ (quarum ignarissimus tantùm non ἀνιπλοις χεροι & impransus paratus ad opus isthoc accessit) admisli passim errores: corruptum erroneumque & inconstans de authoribus veris falsisque judicium: consignatissimæ notæ contemptus nefarii Regum & Principum, odiique adversus plures concepti inexpiabilis. quorum omnium exempla irrefragabilia Viri doctissimi, Casaubonus in Prolegumenis Exercitationibus præmissis, & Exercitationibus ipsis, Mornæus in Mysterio Iniquitatis, Otto in Examine Annalium; Blondellus, Pavius, Carolus, aliique deprompserunt. Ne dicam, segniter, Opus tot malæ fidei compunctum notis, probari etiam Pontificiis emunctiorum narium, Gallis inprimis. Certè Cardinalis & ipse Perronius in Posth. in Baronius; sic eum perstringit: Bonus homo (Baronius) multis in locis historia sua deceptus fuit, magni in eo parachronismi, in infinitis locis fallitur, minimè est exactus, ne in ipso quidem stylo. Nonnisi laboriosum est opus, &c. In voce Roma sic de eodem censet: Nimis magna temporalis potestas Papam exosum reddit Principibus Chri-
units.tr: To this is added the arrangement of the writing [Ἀνάθεσιν τῆς συγγραφῆς], which Dionysius of Halicarnassus advises should above all be observed in writers. The manner, too, in which Baronius pursued each of these things, resolving the composition [Ἀναλύων τὴν ἐπίθεσιν], is everywhere topsy-turvy and perverse. To this belong the visions, miracles and most stinking fables, which he gathered from more recent writers, Zonaras, Vincent, Nicephorus, Metaphrastes, Antoninus, Cyponanus, Surius, and similar hacks of old wives' tales, and gave them such credit, that between himself and those others, and also the compilers of the Golden Legend, such as Jacobus de Voragine and Petrus de Natalibus, there appears no other difference than that they told their fables artlessly, rustically and with a fat Minerva, while he, neither crude in wit nor in art, used a greater display of colours. There are the horrible insults that he hurled everywhere against Protestants, whom he even accuses, at the year 800, of having the Devil as their catechist, together with Sergius the Manichaean, father of dreadful heresies; and at the year 1018 he condemns them to be burned alive together with Basil, author of the Bogomils, who was burned by order of the Emperor Alexius. There is the rashness of his judgments: when he reports adverse or happy events that befell princes, peoples or private persons, as due either to a notable reverence towards the Pope or the Roman Church, or to an insult or injury they seemed to have done to it; the manifest and gross anachronisms; and everywhere the errors admitted through ignorance of Greek and Hebrew (of which he was so ignorant that he came to this work with unwashed hands [ἀνίπλοις χερσίν] and unfed, as it were). There is his corrupt, erroneous and inconstant judgment about true and false authors; the stamped mark of his unspeakable contempt for kings and princes; and his inexpiable hatred conceived against many. Of all these things the unanswerable examples have been drawn out by the most learned men: Casaubon in his Prolegomena prefixed to the Exercitations and in the Exercitations themselves; Mornay in the Mystery of Iniquity; Otto in the Examination of the Annals; Blondel, Pavius, Carolus and others. Not to mention that, lukewarmly, this work, pricked with so many marks of bad faith, is approved even by the Papists of keener nose, the French above all. Indeed the Cardinal Perron himself, in his Posthumous works under Baronius, so censures him: The good man (Baronius) was deceived by his own history in many places; there are great anachronisms, he is wrong in infinite places, he is not at all exact, not even in his style. It is a laborious work only, &c. Under the word Rome he judges the same man thus: Too great a temporal power makes the Pope hateful to the Christian princes

units.la: Pontificiorum de iisdem judicium minus favorabile. Christianis. Neque prudenter fecit Baronius, quando tantopere illam defendere conatus est. Doctissimus Launojus Sorbonicus de eodem cujusmodi in Epistolis fert judicium: Nemo nescit, tum sedis Romanae opportunitatum assertorem esse cupidissimum, & ubicunque & quomodocunque erogare, quae illius amplitudini, commodis, honori inserviunt. Alibi: Baronius nullam praetermittit occasionem amplificandae dignitatis Romani Pontificis. Neque etiam propitium de eo judicium Godavii Episcopi in Praefatione historiae Ecclesiasticae extat. Denique edito undecimo tomo Annalium, quo Hispanorum in Siciliam juribus derogare visus est, tantam eorundem offensam invidiamque incurrit, ut non tantum vacante post Clementis VIII. mortem Sede, quam conscensurum se Baronius, & cum eo alii sperabant; infestis Hispanorum Avilae inprimis & Ascanii Columnae Cardinalium artibus studiisque a Papatu exclusus fuerit: sed etiam eo res processerit, ut Antverpiae, ubi Annales eodem fere tempore recudebantur, undecimi tomi editio, Philippi jussu, prohibita, & Romae excusa exemplaria in terris Hispanorum distrahi vetita; duoque insuper librarii, quod contra edictum ea habuissent, ad triremes damnati fuerint. pluribus rem gestam narrante Thuano Histor. lib. CXXXIV. ubi etiam Baronii iracundum & thrasonicum ad literas ProRegis Siciliae responsum ejusmodi narratur: Melius est, mihi mori, quam ut evacuetur gloria mea. Deus meam laudem ne tacueris, quoniam os peccatoris, & os dolosi apertum est super me, quippe cum haec accusatio, non tam in me & meos Annaleis directa sit, quam adversus ipsum Pontificem, & Sanctae Sedis Majestatem, qui eos vidit, & cunctis Cardinalibus examinandos praebuit. Petrus vidit, Petrus approbavit: Huic petrae, atque adeo rupi infixus minime vereor, ne loco moveri aut concuti possim. CCXVII. Non minus famosus in Ecclesia Romana est alter, Robertus Bellarminus, Cardinalis & Archiepiscopus Bellarminus a Pontificiis quo in pretio habitus? scopus Capuanus, magnus scilicet Apollo, & gregis Pontificii vitula, qua disputaturi cum Protestantibus arare solent, usitatissima. quem apud Alegambium in Bibliotheca scriptorum Societatis Jesu, Cardinalis de Sourdis Sydus, malleum hæreticorum, verticem Theologorum hujus Seculi vocat; & apud eundem alter Cardinalis Visinus quoad castitatem etiam in florenti ævo cum Josepho; quoad pauperta-tem inter divitias cum Davide, quoad liberalitatem in egestate cum Tobia; quoad solitudinem interiorem inter occupationes aulæ, cum Gregorio; quoad humilem de se opinionem in conferta multitudine virtutum excellentissimarum cum Paulo; quoad liberam vocem erga dominantes cum Johanne Baptista liberaliter satis comparat. In quatuor, quos edidit, controversiarum tomis, mole sine nervis, sic procedit, ut primò Ecclesiæ Romanæ doctrinam, probationibus ex Scriptura S. Conciliis, Decretis Pontificum, Patribus & ratione, petitis, afferere conetur; deinde objectiones hæreticorum, quos vocat, solvere aggrediatur. Præfatione tomi primi ad lectorem ait, se omnes fidei controversias complecti, ut unum doctrinæ corpus integrum & perfectum, suisque numeris absolutum existat. Quomodo sperat, se hæreticos homines, ut eodem tomo perorat, ad lumen fidei revocare, vel saltem impetum eorum & furorem frangere posse.
units.tr: The judgment of the Papists on the same matters is less favourable. Christianis. It was not prudent of Baronius to try so hard to defend it. The most learned Launoy of the Sorbonne gives such a judgment of him in his letters: No one is unaware that he is most eager to assert the advantages of the Roman See, and to put forward everywhere and in every way whatever serves its greatness, its interests and its honour. Elsewhere: Baronius never lets slip an occasion to amplify the dignity of the Roman Pontiff. Nor is there any favourable judgment of him by Godeau, Bishop, in the preface to his Ecclesiastical History. Finally, when the eleventh volume of the Annals was published, in which he seemed to derogate from the rights of the Spaniards in Sicily, he incurred such offence and hatred of them that, the See being vacant after the death of Clement VIII, when Baronius and others hoped he would ascend it, he was excluded from the Papacy by the hostile machinations and efforts of the Spanish cardinals Avila in particular and Ascanio Colonna. Indeed the matter went so far that at Antwerp, where the Annals were being reprinted at about the same time, the edition of the eleventh volume was prohibited by order of Philip, and copies printed at Rome were forbidden to be sold in Spanish lands; and two booksellers, because they had them contrary to the edict, were condemned to the galleys. Thuanus, who narrates the affair at length in his History, book CXXXIV, also relates Baronius's angry and boastful reply to the letter of the Viceroy of Sicily, which ran thus: It is better for me to die than for my glory to be emptied. God, do not be silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful are opened against me, since this accusation is aimed not so much at me and my Annals as against the Pontiff himself and the majesty of the Holy See, who saw them and submitted them to all the Cardinals to be examined. Peter saw, Peter approved. Fixed to this rock, and indeed to this cliff, I have no fear of being moved from my place or shaken. CCXVII. Not less notorious in the Roman Church is the other, Robert Bellarmine, Cardinal and Archbishop of Capua, held in such esteem by the Papists: a great Apollo, a calf of the Papist herd, with which those about to dispute with Protestants are wont to plough, a very common one. Of him, in the Bibliotheca of the writers of the Society of Jesus of Alegambe, the Cardinal de Sourdis calls him a star, a hammer of heretics, the summit of the theologians of this age; and in the same work another Cardinal, Visconti, compares him fairly enough with Joseph in chastity even in his flowering age, with David in poverty amid riches, with Tobias in liberality in want, with Gregory in inner solitude amid the business of the court, with Paul in his humble opinion of himself amid a crowd of the most excellent virtues, and with John the Baptist in his free voice towards the powerful. In the four volumes of controversies that he published, massive but without sinews, he proceeds so that first he tries to assert the doctrine of the Roman Church, with proofs drawn from Scripture, the holy Councils, the decrees of the Pontiffs, the Fathers and reason; then he sets about answering the objections of those he calls heretics. In the preface to the first volume he says to the reader that he embraces all the controversies of faith, so that there may exist one whole and perfect body of doctrine, complete in all its parts. How he hopes that he can call heretical men, as he concludes in the same volume, back to the light of faith, or at least break their assault and fury.

units.la: Quòd igitur ex Scripturis, principio nobiscum communi, disputare instituit: quòd non perinde malignus atque Jesuitæ alii, Valentia inprimis, Vasquez, Becanus, Maldonatus &c. meliore ut plurimum fide adversariorum suorum argumenta allegavit, & amantior, quàm illi, veritatis, sicubi erravit, prudens sciensque errare non videtur: quòd, secus ac novi Methodistæ aperto Marte, non per cuniculos, & tergiversando nobiscum egit: quòd adversus falsa errantium & verorum hæreticorum dogmata rectè & ex veritate nonnulla dixit: quòd infamem illum Mo-
units.tr: Since he has undertaken to dispute from the Scriptures, the principle we hold in common; since he has not, like other Jesuits, above all Valentia, Vasquez, Becanus, Maldonatus and the rest, been so malicious, but has for the most part cited his opponents' arguments with better faith, and since, where he has erred, he does not seem to have erred knowingly and wisely, being more fond of truth than they are; since, unlike the new Methodists, he has not fought in the open field but dealt with us through mines and by evasion; since he has rightly and truthfully said some things against the false doctrines of erring men and the true heretics; and since he has attacked that infamous Mo-

units.la: Molinismo-Pelagianismum perosus, de praedestinatione orthodoxè satis disseruit: quòd in iis, quae praeter veritatem, constabiliendis Ecclesiae Romanae dogmatis, attulit, capita illa doctrinae, in quibus à vero aberrant, dissident aut instabiles sunt Pontificii, in unum compegit atque concinnavit, multasque multorum sententias summa Pontificum, Academiarúmque Pontificiarum approbatione munitas comportavit, & sententia sua conclusit, ut ad liquidum perduci possit, qua in re partes contendentes conveniant discrepentque; amplam certè laudem ille meretur: Sicut autem naucleris tria solent esse periculosa; si in scopulum alliserint, si in dorsum arenarium inciderint, si velificentur male: sic Bellarminus etiam vastissimam illam navigationem suam tribus incommodis illis obnoxiam reddidit. Etenim scopulus, seu rupes & petra firmissima est S. Scriptura, ad quam quicunque allidunt, ut cum Poëta loquar, infringunt dentem solido. Unus idemque scopulus nobis est pharus ad salutem: iis verò, qui veritatem in mendacio detinent, certissimus ad mortem Caphareus. Ad hunc verò scopulum quàm saepe, quàm graviter, crassè, oscitanterque Bellarminus alliserit, adeoque Romanam illam naviculam Petri, uti appellare solent, tabulato disjecto, corruptóque, non scapham ulla ex parte integram esse, ostenderit, tum res ipsa loquitur, tum viri doctissimi liquidò demonstrárunt. Dorsum verò arenarium, in quod ejus navis incidit; innumera sunt testimonia à disputatore eo adducta; puta Patrum testimonia falsò, mutilè, perversè citata: nostrorum dicta & scripta subinde iniquiore fide, quàm unquam scriptum, dictum, cogitatùmve fuerit, proposita: hominum mente desipientium, animo in nos causamque nostram infensissimorum prolata non secus testimonia, quàm si folia Sibyllina, & Divina quaedam vi ἀναπνοῇ essent; quorum tamen pleraque forte non tam judicio certo, quàm aliena fide, Collegarum scilicet & alumnorum, quorum alii hoc, alii aliud testimonium ex varia lectione, quasi hastas amentatas commilitoni (uti in Collegiis Papatus solent) subministrârunt, posuit. Denique & velificatio ipsa minùs prospera fuit. Navigii enim Christi pes, velum & signum non aliud, quàm Sacra Scriptura est. At ille opus suum scientiam prope infinitam non modò variarum disciplinarum & linguarum, sed etiam totius antiquitatis, omnium historiarum & temporum requirere praefatus, de fide, de scientia illa revelata & infusa Spiritus S. & Scripturæ sacræ, verbum nullum facit. malo utique augurio sese prodens, quod Scripturas passim in subsidium adhibens licet, sensum tamen earum γνῶσιν à Deo Spiritu S. & Scriptura ipsa demonstrare pensi non habiturus sit. Plenis Scripturæ solius velis ad Cœlum, thronum gloriæ usque rectà provehimur, si Deum audimus. sin alia & alios, circumducamur necesse est per sinuosas ambages, donec ad Scripturas recurramus, aut in ambagibus illis subsidentes miserimè pereamus. Alicubi etiam inconstantiæ suæ, non ingrata licet nobis documenta dedit. veluti cùm pro erroribus Papatus acerrimè contendens, alibi pia, sana, orthodoxa, & priorbus è diametro repugnantia protulit. Huc pertinent ejus effata, quæ utroque pollice probamus: (lib. 6. de gratia) voluntatem hominis esse liberam, ut velit quicquam salutare, absque auxilio Dei (lib. 5. de justif. cap. 17. 51--3.) Propter incertitudinem propriæ justitiæ, & periculum inanis gloriæ tutissimum esse, nostram fiduciam collocare in merito & fiducia Dei: Non absurdum esse, si quis dicat nobis imputari Christi justitiam & merita cùm nobis donentur & applicentur, perinde ac si nos ipsi satisfecissemus: (lib. 3. de Pœn. cap. 4.) A Spiritu S. esse lumen fidei, quo is intus & in domicilio cordis nobis dicit; Ita est, nihil hæsites; quibus verbis Spiritus S. testimonium internum, quod alibi impiè exagitat, asseasserit: (lib. 1. de verbo Dei cap. 11.) Scripturis sacris nihil esse notius, nihil certius, ut stultissimus sit, qui fidem illis habendam negat. quas etiam esse notissimas, certissimas, verissimas, iisdem, quibus & nos uti solemus, argumentis statim comprobat, conclusionem cedro dignam ejusmodi inferens: Quare S. Scriptura regula est credendi certissima & tutissima: (lib. 4. de Pontif. R. cap. 2. ss--ad Secundum; & lib. 2. cap. 3.) Papam posse in haeresin incidere, deficere a fide, judicari ab Ecclesia; ejus Sedem alio transferri posse sine violatione juris Divini: (lib. 2. de R. Pont. cap. 2.) Forte non esse de jure Divino, Romanum Pontificem Petro succedere, quia de ea successione ne γε quidem in S. Scriptura extet; mox contendens tamen, in successione illa totam religionem & summam rei Christianae verti, licet ea non sit de fide, nec in Scripturis testimonium consignatum habeat: (lib. 1. de R. Pont. cap. 12. ss. 5. & 48.) Claves non soli Petro datas esse; potestatem Petri cum caeteris Apostolis communicatam esse; aequalem fuisse Petrum & Paulum; aequum huius & illius jus in Episcopatu R. fuisse; Pauli majora fuisse quam Petri merita. Ex quibus similibusque gnomis Bellarminum Confessorem fidei Reformatae, & sibi ipsi discordem facere in proclivi foret. Inprimis autem erga Reges & Principes potestatesque summas ceu alter Mariana, animum infensissimum prodidit, astruens passim imperium Papae rectum, directum & absolutum in vitas, negotia & dominia Imperatorum & Regum, quos clientes facit Papae, obstrictos ad praestandum illi homagium, & ab ejus voluntate nutuque ita suspensos, ut exui imperio possint, quoties illi libet. In libro piacolari, quem titulo Matthaei Torti adversus M. Britanniae Regis Jacobi Apologiam pro juramento fidelitatis, cui titulum ille secerat, Triplici nodo triplex cuneus; edidit, sic Clementem Henrici III. parricidam laudat: Vltus est Deus Christum suum, dum per alium sacratum virum, alioqui militiae imperitum & inermem, mem', Regem eundem non sine manifesto Divinæ providentiæ miraculo interfecit. Ausus etiam poitea est cum Jacobo Rege palam & aperta fronte congredi, & tum triplicem ejus cuneum, tum præfationem Monitoriam, quæ interim à Rege prodierat, multa argumentorum mole oppugnare. non veritus eum Juliano similem appellare; ipse torquendis Scripturis, quò ambitioni serviret, tam Juliano apud B. Cyrillum similis, quàm Rex Jacobus erat dissimilis. De potestate etiam Pontificis in temporalibus, pro insidiatoribus Principum, adversus Barclajum librum scripsit, quem non solum hujus filius nænia soricina confosiorem reddidit; sed Suprema etiam Lutetiæ Curia, ceu seditiosum scriptum, severo interdicto subjecit. Ut non sine omine Cardinalis hic Bellarmini nomen indeptus videatur, cùm ferali illa doctrina nonnisi Bella, arma, minas spiraverit. Denique ita Papatum ruentem Bellarminus sustinere conatus est, ita quiescentibus ejus tantisper fatis, sustinuit, ut scriptis tamen suis Sedi Romanæ & Pontifici justissimam etiam invidiam conflaverit, & comperto, Romam esse ἀδιεόρπθλευ incurabilem, quippe in errore obstinatam, adagio Calliftrati apud Ariftophanem, quòd πεῳ- κτὸς λούτρῶ πειγίνη, podex lotionem vincat, fidem fecerit.
units.tr: linism-Pelagianism with considerable orthodoxy in his discussion of predestination. Among the things he has brought forward, apart from the truth, to establish the dogmas of the Roman Church, he has gathered and arranged in one place those heads of doctrine on which the Papists depart from the truth, disagree among themselves, or waver. He has assembled many opinions of many men, fortified by the approval of the supreme Pontiffs and the Papal universities, and has concluded with his own judgement, so that it may be made clear where the contending parties agree and where they differ. For this he certainly deserves ample praise. But as with sailors three things are usually dangerous, if they strike a reef, if they run onto a sandbank, or if they sail badly, so Bellarmine has made his very vast voyage liable to these three misfortunes. For the reef, or rock and most solid crag, is Holy Scripture; whoever strikes against it, to use the poet's words, breaks his teeth on something solid. One and the same reef is a beacon to salvation for us, but for those who hold the truth in falsehood it is most certainly a Caiaphas to death. How often, how gravely, how crassly and carelessly Bellarmine has struck against this reef, and so shown that the little ship of Peter, as they call it, with its planking broken and rotten, is sound in no part, the thing itself speaks, and very learned men have clearly demonstrated it. As for the sandbank onto which his ship ran, there are countless testimonies adduced by that disputant: the testimonies of the Fathers, falsely, partially and perversely cited; the sayings and writings of our side set forth with worse faith than anything ever written, said or thought; and testimonies drawn from men of deranged mind, most hostile in spirit to us and our cause, which are treated no differently than Sibylline leaves or some divine power of breath [ἀναπνοῇ]. Yet most of these he set down perhaps not so much from sound judgement as from the borrowed faith of his colleagues and pupils, who, as in the Papist colleges, supplied one fellow soldier with this testimony and another with that, like javelins fitted with thongs, from their varied reading. Finally, the sailing itself was none too prosperous. For the foot, sail and sign of Christ's ship is nothing other than Holy Scripture. Yet he, prefacing his work as requiring a nearly infinite knowledge not only of various disciplines and languages, but also of all antiquity, of all histories and times, says not a word about faith, or about that revealed and infused knowledge of the Holy Spirit and of Holy Scripture. This is a bad omen, for although he uses the Scriptures here and there as an aid, he will not think it his business to demonstrate the sense of them, the knowledge [γνῶσιν] of it, from God, the Holy Spirit, and Scripture itself. With full sails of Scripture alone we are carried straight to heaven, the throne of glory, if we listen to God. But if we listen to other things and other men, we must necessarily be led round by winding detours, until we return to the Scriptures, or else, sinking in those detours, we perish most wretchedly. Somewhere, too, he has given us, not unwelcome, proofs of his inconsistency: as when, while contending most fiercely for the errors of Papacy, he elsewhere puts forward pious, sound and orthodox doctrines that are diametrically opposed to his earlier ones. To this belong his sayings, which we approve with both thumbs: (book 6 On Grace) the will of man is free to will anything salutary without the help of God; (book 5 On Justification, ch. 17, 51–3) because of the uncertainty of one's own righteousness, and the danger of empty glory, it is safest to place our confidence in the merit and the trust of God; it is not absurd to say that Christ's righteousness and merits are imputed to us, since they are bestowed and applied to us, just as if we ourselves had made satisfaction; (book 3 On Penance, ch. 4) the light of faith comes from the Holy Spirit, who speaks to us inwardly and in the dwelling-place of the heart: Yes, it is so, do not hesitate. By these words he has asserted the inner testimony of the Holy Spirit, which elsewhere he impiously assails. (book 1 On the Word of God, ch. 11) Nothing is better known than the holy Scriptures, nothing more certain, so that whoever denies that they are to be believed is most foolish; he also at once proves that they are most known, most certain and most true, by the same arguments we are accustomed to use, drawing the conclusion, worthy of cedar: Therefore Holy Scripture is the most certain and safest rule of believing. (book 4 On the Roman Pontiff, ch. 2, ss., and book 2, ch. 3) The Pope can fall into heresy, fall away from the faith, be judged by the Church; his See can be transferred elsewhere without violating divine law; (book 2 On the Roman Pontiff, ch. 2) Perhaps it is not by divine right that the Roman Pontiff succeeds Peter, since there is not even a particle [γε] about that succession in Holy Scripture; soon, however, he contends that the whole of religion and the sum of the Christian cause turns on that succession, although it is not a matter of faith and has no testimony recorded in the Scriptures. (book 1 On the Roman Pontiff, ch. 12, ss. 5 and 48) The keys were not given to Peter alone; Peter's power was communicated with the other Apostles; Peter and Paul were equal; the right of this one and of that one in the Roman bishopric was equal; Paul's merits were greater than Peter's. From these and similar maxims it would be easy to make Bellarmine a confessor of the Reformed faith and at odds with himself. He showed a most hostile spirit, especially towards kings, princes and sovereign powers, like another Mariana, asserting everywhere that the Pope's power over the lives, affairs and dominions of emperors and kings is right, direct and absolute. He makes them clients of the Pope, bound to render him homage, and so dependent on his will and nod that they can be stripped of their rule whenever he pleases. In a little book, which he titled Matthaei Torti against the Apology of James, King of Britain, for the oath of allegiance, a work the King had titled Triplici nodo triplex cuneus, he published, praising Clement, the murderer of Henry III, in these words: God avenged his Christ, while by another consecrated man, otherwise unskilled in war and unarmed, he killed the same King not without a manifest miracle of divine providence. He later dared to meet King James face to face and openly, and attacked with a great mass of arguments both the triple wedge and the admonitory preface which the King had meanwhile published. He did not shrink from calling him a Julian; he himself, twisting the Scriptures to serve his ambition, was as like Julian in Cyril's account as King James was unlike him. On the power of the Pontiff in temporal matters, on behalf of the plotters against princes, he wrote a book against Barclay, which not only made its author more thoroughly stabbed, as it were, by the son of that man with a mouse's dirge, but was also placed under severe prohibition by the Supreme Court of Paris as a seditious writing. So this Cardinal seems to have gained the name Bellarmine not without omen, since with that deadly doctrine he breathed nothing but wars, arms, threats. Finally, Bellarmine tried to prop up the tottering Papacy, and sustained it so well, while its fates were for the moment quiet, that by his writings he nonetheless kindled the most just odium against the Roman See and the Pontiff. Having discovered that Rome is incurable [ἀδιόρθωτον], indeed obstinate in error, he bore out the adage of Callistratus in Aristophanes: the backside outdoes the bath [πυγὴ λουτροῦ κρείττων].

units.la: CCXVIII. Neque tamen Bellarmini isthæc Methodus, qua ille causam cum causa, rationes cum rationibus (infelici successu licet) contendit, ita astutioribus in Papatu ipso, qui nasum Rhinocerotis habent, satisfecit, quin nova & compendiaria magis via nobiscum transigendum, intráque arctiores gyros constringendos nos judicaverint. Exorti hinc sunt in Ecclesia Romana ad nostra usque tempora Methodistæ novi, vafríque non parum, nova scilicet dogmata sua novæ methodi fuco incrustaturi; qui deserta candidiore Bellarmini Methodo, expeditiorem suo judicio, artificiosiorem, saltem ad faciendam simpli-ciocioribus fraudem opportuniorem se struere posse sperârunt. Alii scilicet, præsultoribus Gonterio, Perronio, Francisco Veronio, (quanquam etiam his Renatum Benedictum Andegavum, Theologum Parisiensem, editis A. M. D. LXV. in universum organum Biblicum stromatis, prælusisse, Doctiss. Calixtus de Arte nova pag. 125. 126. &c. comprobat) placuit Protestantes eò adigere, ut omnia dogmata sua, tum affirmativa, uti vocant, tum negativa, puris putis Scripturæ verbis, nullo consequentiarum usu vel auxilio concesso, comprobent; non ignaris licet, sua, quæ adversus nos tuentur, dogmata nec puris putis Scripturæ verbis, nec consequentiarum fidiculis ullis, nedum nexu stringente & necessario probari unquam potuisse, vel etiam posse. Hanc Methodum etiam Fratres Walenburgii, & Missionarii deinceps plures suam fecerunt. Sed aliam tamen etiam breviorem, Bartholdus Nihusius, insignis Vertumnus, ab eodem Calixto graphicè depictus; Arte Nova confista; & iidem qui supra Walenburgii in Methodo Augustiniana seu Defensiva chorago artis, uti putatur, Anthonio Fabro J. C. Sebusiano, Fabriani Codicis sui initio; protulerunt, comprehensam via iuris & lege præscriptionis. Ecclesiam Romanam sciscunt illi in possessione esse veritatis, utpote cui longa temporis serie ita præscripserit, ut probandi onus ei non incumbat amplius, sed devolvi merito possit in humeros Protestantium, qui possessores antiquiores veritatis, in possessione sua turbare laborent; Ecclesiæ Romanæ non relicto alio, quàm excipiendi onere. Exceptionem autem efficacem esse, quòd ita majores crididerint, atque plurium Seculorum flexu fluxúque ita docuerint; quòd si qui negare animum induxerint, iis probandi onus similiter incumbere pertendunt. Sic nempe novi illi homines calculum subducunt, facilius esse placita semel defendere, quàm ritè probare: affirmantesque rem possessam imperare posse, negantes serviliter instrui, doceri cupere debere: illos judicis partibus susceptis hos hæreseos, schismatis, sacrilegii promptius accusare iis insidiosas quæstiones nectere posse: denique ad apologiam & demonstrationem doctrinæ suæ, utpote defendi, demonstrari nescias, adigi hac ratione se nunquam posse. Iidem Walenburgii post Cornelium Jansenium aliam etiam novam rationem adhibuerunt convincendi, seu potius seducendi nostros, controversia iis de vocatione, seu missione Ministrorum suorum mota; obtendentes scilicet, ex missione, vocatione de ipsa prædicatione & doctrina judicium ferendum esse. Sed & Armandus Richelius Cardinalis novam hic singularemque viam præivit, jubens in Richeliana Methodo posthuma, misso examine doctrinæ, utpote arduo & molesto nimis, de Ecclesia disputationem omnem suscipere, eamque inquirere non ex S. Scripturis, sed potius ex notis magis obviis, & fere sensus simpliciorum ferientibus. cujusmodi inprimis sint haud interrupta Pontificum successio, Ecclesiæ splendor, magnificentia, duratio. Tum præcipiebat ille controversiarum momenta librare, solicitéque astruere, quòd capita, de quibus disceptatum hactenus est, fundamentum fidei non contingant, adeóque salvo in iis dissensu Romana & Evangelica Ecclesia conciliari facili negotio queant. Inde non Pontificiorum duntaxat, quibus ipsemet Petrus de Marca, Archiepiscopus Parisiensis, exaratis de Sacramento Eucharistiæ diatribis, patrocinari visus est, sed nostratum, etiam, Milleterii inprimis & Grotii, Cardinalis hujus consiliis callidis obstetricantium, aliorumque scripta ἀλγμαxλxὰ exorta sunt. Neque alio Walenburgiorum, in omnes partes se convertentium, & unum ex alio dolum consuentium, libri de Unitate & Schismate Ecclesiæ, & nuper etiam Augustini Gibbonis de Burgo, Hiberni, de Luthero-Calvinismo, Schismatico quidem, sed reconciliabili, libelli, quibus momentum controversiarum minuere & elevare insigni fraude, à Viris Celeberrimis, Crocio & Coccejo in aprico collocata, conati sunt, spectant. Subit famosissimus ille Capucinorum, Valerianus Magnus, Mediolanensis, qui edito de Catholicorum & Acatholicorum Regula credendi judicio, ad unam cæteras omnes & plurimas & gravissimas quæstionem revocavit: Quae scilicet sit certior credendi regula, quis verus & infallibilis judex, Spiritus S. ne ex S. Scriptura singulos fideles eum invocantes seorsim instruens; an neglectis Scripturis Romana Ecclesia, à Spiritu S. in Conciliis Oecumenicis infallibiliter edocta, extra periculum erroris posita, totque regeneratis fulgens? Illud affirmantes Biblistarum nomine, quasi probrosò, insignis scilicet non Karræus sed Pharisæus, traducit. In æstu disputationis eò se abripi passus homo est, ut sua vineta graviter cœdens, quod res est, scriberet, Primatum & infallibilitatem Romani Pontificis ex Scripturis probari non posse, sed sola traditione constare. quod Majestati Pontificiæ violatæ nefas interpretati Jesuitæ λεγόμενοι, effecerunt, ut Valerianus in vincula raptus, ex iisdem causam dicere coactus fuerit. Ne verò novos hosce Methodistas recentissimis artibus suis Scripturæ Sacræ forum declinare, quod strenuè tamen faciunt, viderentur, diversam etiam Methodum ex eadem Ignatianorum Societate Jacobus Masenius secutus, scriptum, quod tum Alexandro VII. tum Protestantibus totius Europæ Principibus dedicavit, cuíque titulum ejusmodi fecit: Meditata Concordia Protestantium cum Catholicis in una Fide, & ex S. Scriptura desumpta; edidit; in quo Confessionem fidei Pontificiæ, ex Tridentinorum sententia claris & explicatis, uti ipse loquitur, sed revera à sensu germano in peregrinum & perversissimum detortis, & obtorto collo raptis, Scripturæ verbis contexere conatus est; parùm animo suo re-puputans, Scripturam non tam in literis, quàm in sensu genuino, ex Scripturarum ipsarum penetralibus depromepto, consistere; neque hic ullius vel hominis, vel coetus humani, hunc vel illum sensum ad conscientiam cujuslibet hominis cum certa Φηλώσι πνεύματι, non manifestantis, authoritatem in censum numerumque pervenire. Proin virilis animi fidem nemini bono fecit. Demum Henricus Marcellius, Sylvæ-Ducensis, Lojolæ itidem Sodalis Considerationes Pacificas, & Canones Benignæ Reconciliationis protulit, in quibus suppositis iis, quæ neutiquam ἀνεξαγώνια sunt, Veronii, Nihusii & Walenburgiorum artibus junctis ea reconciliationis media etiam Sapientissimis Germaniæ Principibus obtrudere ausus est, quæ acceptantes stultissimos reddere apta nata sunt. Denique non ita pridem Illustris in Gallia Præsul, Jacobus Benignus Bossuet, Condomiensis in Aquitanica secunda Episcopus, in nupera Expositione Doctrinæ Catholicæ, Richelianæ Methodo insistens, tum ex propriis Confessionibus palam facere instituit, nos in fundamento fidei, & singularibus etiam doctrinæ capitibus ad Romanæ Ecclesiæ sensum propiùs accedere; tum labem multiplicem ab Ecclesia sua abstergere conatus, ejusmodi Ecclesiæ Romanæ faciem pinxit, ut in amorem ejus credulos facilè abreptum iri, planè consideret. Scilicet ibi est
units.tr: CCXVIII. Yet Bellarmine's method, by which he contended cause with cause and argument with argument (though with unhappy success), did not satisfy the cleverer men within Papacy itself, who have a rhinoceros's nose. They judged that we must be dealt with by a new and shorter route and driven into narrower circles. From this arose in the Roman Church, down to our own times, new Methodists, and no small number of them crafty, who wanted to smear their novel dogmas with the varnish of a new method. Abandoning Bellarmine's more candid method, they hoped to devise one that was, in their judgment, quicker and more artful, or at least better suited to deceiving simpler folk. Some, led by Gonterius, Perronius and Francis Veron (though Renatus Benedictus of Angers, a Parisian theologian, had preluded these men with his Stromata on the whole biblical organon, published in 1665, as the learned Calixtus confirms in de Arte nova, pp. 125, 126, etc.), resolved to force the Protestants to prove all their dogmas, both the affirmative, as they call them, and the negative, by bare words of Scripture alone, with no use or aid of consequences allowed. They knew well that our dogmas, which they attack, could never be proved, or even could be proved, by the bare words of Scripture or by any cords of consequence, let alone by a binding and necessary connection. The brothers Walenburg and many missionaries after them adopted this method as their own. But another, shorter method was also set up by Bartholdus Nihusius, a notable Vertumnus, vividly depicted by the same Calixtus in his Arte Nova. And those same men who, as above, were the Walenburgs in their Methodo Augustiniana or Defensiva, the choragus of the art (as is thought) being Antonius Faber, the Savoyard jurist, at the beginning of his Fabrian Code, brought forward a method contained in the via iuris and lege praescriptionis. They maintain that the Roman Church is in possession of the truth, since a long series of time has so prescribed for her that the burden of proof no longer rests on her but may rightly be shifted onto the shoulders of the Protestants, who, as the older possessors of the truth, labour to disturb her in her possession, and nothing is left to the Roman Church but the burden of making an exception. Moreover, they claim that the exception is effective, because their elders judged so and taught so through the ebb and flow of many centuries; and if anyone has resolved to deny it, they contend that the burden of proof likewise rests on him. In this way those new men reckon up their account: it is easier to defend opinions once held than to prove them properly; those who affirm may command because the thing is possessed, while those who deny must be servilely instructed and ought to desire to be taught; by taking up the role of judge, the former can more readily accuse the latter of heresy, schism and sacrilege, and can weave snares for them with insidious questions; finally, when it comes to the apology and demonstration of their doctrine, since it is held to be defended but not demonstrated, they can never be compelled by this method. The same Walenburgs, after Cornelius Jansenius, employed yet another new method of convincing, or rather of seducing, our people, a controversy about the vocation, or mission, of their ministers having been raised; they insisted, namely, that a judgment about the preaching and doctrine itself must be made from the mission and vocation. But Cardinal Armand Richelieu also led the way into this new and singular path, bidding in his posthumous Richeliana Methodo, the examination of doctrine being dropped as too arduous and troublesome, to undertake the whole dispute about the Church, and to investigate it not from the Holy Scriptures but rather from more obvious marks, which strike the senses of simple folk almost at once; of which kind chiefly are the uninterrupted succession of the Popes, the splendour, magnificence and duration of the Church. Then he instructed them to weigh the weight of the controversies and to assert earnestly that the articles disputed hitherto do not touch the foundation of faith, and so, with dissent on these points preserved, the Roman and Evangelical Churches could be reconciled with ease. From this came not only the writings of the Papists, in whose defence Peter de Marca, Archbishop of Paris, seemed to appear with his learned treatises on the sacrament of the Eucharist, but also the monstrous writings of our own side, especially those of Milletius and Grotius, who acted as midwives to the crafty counsels of this Cardinal, and of others. Nor do the books de Unitate et Schismate Ecclesiae by the Walenburgs, who turn themselves to every side and stitch one trick from another, nor the recent little books of Augustine Gibbon of Burgh, an Irishman, de Luthero-Calvinismo, Schismatico quidem, sed reconciliabili, which attempt with notable deceit to lessen and raise the weight of the controversies, which the most celebrated men, Crocius and Coccejus, have placed in the open, belong to any other category. There comes the notorious Capuchin, Valerian Magni of Milan, who, having published his judgment de Catholicorum et Acatholicorum Regula credendi, reduced all the other, very numerous and very grave questions to one: What is the surer rule of belief, who is the true and infallible judge: the Holy Spirit instructing individual faithful who invoke him, apart, from Holy Scripture; or, with the Scriptures neglected, the Roman Church, infallibly taught by the Holy Spirit in the Ecumenical Councils, placed beyond the danger of error and shining with so many regenerated souls? Affirming the former, he disparages those who favour Scripture with the name of Biblicists, as if it were a reproach, being, of course, not a Karaite but a Pharisee. In the heat of the dispute the man allowed himself to be carried so far that, while severely cutting down his own vines, he wrote what was the case: The primacy and infallibility of the Roman Pontiff cannot be proved from the Scriptures, but rest on tradition alone. The Jesuits, the so-called λεγόμενοι, interpreted this as a crime against the violated majesty of the Pontiff, and they brought it about that Valerian was dragged into chains and compelled to plead his cause before the same men. Lest these new Methodists should seem, by their most recent arts, to shun the court of Holy Scripture, which nevertheless they do most vigorously, Jacob Masenius, following from the same Society of Ignatius a different method, published a writing dedicated both to Alexander VII and to the Princes of all Europe who are Protestants, which he entitled Meditata Concordia Protestantium cum Catholicis in una Fide, et ex S. Scriptura desumpta. In it he tried to weave the Papist Confession of faith, according to the opinion of the Tridentines, clear and explained, as he himself puts it, but in truth twisted from its genuine sense into a foreign and most perverted one and dragged by the neck, out of the words of Scripture; little considering in his own mind that Scripture consists not so much in the letters as in the genuine sense drawn from the very inner shrine of the Scriptures, and that here no authority of any man or human body can bring this or that sense into the judgment and reckoning of any person's conscience, where a certain deceitful spirit [φηλώσι πνεύματι] is not making itself known. Hence he won the trust of no good man with a manly spirit. At last Henry Marcellius of Sylvae-Ducensis, likewise a companion of Loyola, put forward his Pacific Considerations and Canons of Gentle Reconciliation, in which, on the assumption of things that are by no means unassailable [ἀνεξαγώνιστα], he dared, by joining the arts of Veron, Nihusius and the Walenburgs, to press upon the most wise Princes of Germany those means of reconciliation which are fit to make those who accept them utterly foolish. Finally, not long ago the illustrious prelate of Gaul, Jacques Benigne Bossuet, Bishop of Condom in Second Aquitaine, in his recent Exposition of the Catholic Doctrine, insisting on Richelieu's method, undertook to show openly, from our own confessions, that on the foundation of faith and even on the particular articles of doctrine we come closer to the sense of the Roman Church; and then, trying to wipe away the many stains from his Church, he painted the face of the Roman Church in such a way that he plainly expects credulous readers to be easily carried away into loving it. Of course, there it is.

units.la: Pergula pictorum, veri nil, omnia ficta.
units.tr: A painter's workshop: nothing true, everything made up.

units.la: Et pudere eum similésque pristini erroris eò magis liquet, quò plus lenocinii ad eum tegendum adhibent, victósque se ratione eò certiùs produnt, quò artificiosiùs pugnam hanc declinantes, ad infirmitatem carnis versi, uti graviter S. Cyprianus lib. ad Demetrium id in paganis reprehendit, cum terrenæ carnis imbecillitate contendunt. Ecquid verò novi illi Methodistæ, Cadmæi fratres; fraudum architecti, qui fidei salvificæ luminibus orbati, angulos ubique quæquærunt, in quibus se aliósque lucifugas ne doctrina & opera eorum ad lucem cœlestis veritatis penetrans argui possint ; abscondant, nostris illam consiliorum & laborum, moliminúmque desperationem perplexitatémque cernentibus, & plus satis intelligentibus, animi esse putant? An non identidem animo nostro obversari credunt Christi Salvatoris nostri cedro dignam sententiam, Methodistas illos ζητηταὶ τῆς αἰῶνος τούτου inquisitores hujus seculi tenebrarumque filios, fortissimè ferientem: Hoc illud Dei judicium est, quòd lux venit in mundum, & homines magis tenebras, quàm lucem amarunt. Mala enim fuerunt illorum opera. Omnis enim qui mala facit, lucem odit, & non venit ad lucem, ne arguantur opera ejus. Qui autem veritatem facit, venit ad lucem, ut manifesta fiant opera ejus, quod in Deo facta sint. Joh. III. 19.20.21.
units.tr: That they are ashamed of this, and of their like, of their former error, is all the clearer the more flattery they use to cover it. They betray that they have been beaten in argument all the more surely the more cunningly they avoid this battle, turning to the weakness of the flesh, as St Cyprian rebukes the pagans for doing in his book to Demetrius, when they contend with the frailty of earthly flesh. What, then, do those new Methodists, brothers of Cadmus, architects of fraud, think? Deprived of the lights of saving faith, they seek corners everywhere in which they and other shunners of the light may hide their doctrine and works, so that these cannot be exposed by the light of heavenly truth. They think their despair, and their perplexity over their plans and labours, is hidden from us, though we see it clearly and understand it well enough. Do they not believe that the sentence of Christ our Saviour, worthy of cedar oil, strikes them with great force, calling those Methodists zētētai tēs aiōnos toutou [ζητηταὶ τῆς αἰῶνος τούτου], inquirers of this age, sons of darkness? This is the judgment, that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light. For their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, lest his works be exposed. But he who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God. John 3.19–21.

units.la: CCXIX. E diverticulo isthoc, in quod nova illa molimina Methodistarum, Papæ mangonum, à Bellarmini & aliorum integriori fide de religione decernentium, vestigiis deviorum, nos induxerunt, in tramitem rectum historiæ ut redeamus, post Clementem VIII. & Leonem XI. ex Medicea Florentinorum domo oriundum, scenicum etiam viginti sex dierum Papam, (qui arcui suo triumphali à Florentinis suis inscribi passus est isthæc verba: Dignus est Leo in virtute Agni accipere librum, & solvere septem signacula ejus) Cardinalium Collegio per factiones mirè scissò, cùm Dominicus Thuscus Regiensis Cardinalis Hispanorum studiis & quadraginta quatuor suffragiis è cella sua in S. Sixti Sacellum ad adorationem jam elevatus & à pluribus adoratus, Baronii verò clamoribus & studiis obturbatus deturbatúsque esset, & Baronium denuo plures confuso clamore frustra depoposcissent; Camillus Borgesius, qui Pauli V. nomen assumpsit, à Gallica factione, cui Aldobrandini & Montaltani arbitrium detulerant, Papa electus est. Non sine justo Dei judicio evenit, ut arcana utriusque Conclavis, tum in quo Leo XI. tum in quo Paulus V. electus est, per Cardinalem inprimis Perronum, qui ejus historiam Die x. Mart. & xxvii. April. A. M. D. C. V. & VIII. ac XIX. Maii A. M. D. C. VI. literis consignavit; (quas ejus ut & Cardinalis Jousae literas sub finem primæ partis Legationum & negotiationum ejus videre est) in vulgus etiam emanârint. Inde enim penitus liquere omnibus coepit, non Sancti Spiritus, sed carnis consilia in electione Pontificum dominari. de quo inferius plura. Paulo jam Pontifice Conspiratio Anglicana pulveraria, & Henrici IV. parricidium, quæ supra fusius, connexa scilicet serie rerum, expositimus, acciderunt. Passus vero idem est in librorum Romæ, Bononiæ & Neapoli impressorum inscriptionibus, se salutari Vice-Deum, Christianæ Reip. Monarcham invictissimum, & Pontificiæ Omnipotentiæ Conservatorem acerimum; quin etiam sibi applicari dicta Scripturæ, veluti Jerem. xxvii. 8. Gens & Regnum, quod non servierit illi, in gladio, & in fame, & in peste visitabo super gentem illam, dicit Dominus: & Dan. vii. 14. Dedit ei Dominus potestatem & Regnum, & omnes populi ei servient. Potestas ejus potestas æterna, & Regnum ejus quod non corrumpetur: (quorum ille locus Regem Babyloniæ spectans non malè forte quadravit; at hoc de Christo sonans nonnisi blasphemè detorqueri potuit) denique Esaj. xlix. 23. Et erunt Reges nutritii tui, & Reginæ nutrices tuæ. Pront in terram incurvabunt se tibi, & pulverem tuum lingent.
units.tr: CCXIX. Let us now leave this byway, into which the new contrivances of the Methodists, the Pope-mongers, and the footsteps of those who decide about religion with the more complete faith of Bellarmine and others have led us astray, and return to the straight path of history. After Clement VIII and Leo XI, of the Medici house of Florence, came the theatrical Pope of twenty-six days (who allowed his Florentines to inscribe on his triumphal arch these words: Leo is worthy, in the power of the Lamb, to take the book and loose its seven seals). The College of Cardinals was wondrously split by factions. Dominic Tuscus of Reggio, a Cardinal, was already lifted from his cell into the chapel of St Sixtus, by the efforts of the Spaniards and forty-four votes, and was adored by many; but he was disturbed and thrown down by the outcries and efforts of Baronius. Many, demanding Baronius again with confused clamour, had demanded him in vain. Then Camillus Borghese, who took the name Paul V, was elected Pope by the French faction, to which Aldobrandini and Montalto had committed the decision. It did not happen without the just judgment of God that the secrets of both conclaves, in which Leo XI and in which Paul V were elected, were made public, chiefly by Cardinal Perron. He recorded their history in letters dated 10 March and 27 April 1605, and 8 and 19 May 1606 (these, as well as the letters of Cardinal Joyeuse, may be seen at the end of the first part of his Legations and Negotiations). For from that time it began to be clear to everyone that not the counsels of the Holy Spirit but those of the flesh rule the election of Popes, about which more below. Soon after this Pope's accession came the Anglican gunpowder conspiracy and the murder of Henry IV, which we have set out above at greater length, in their proper connection of events. The same thing happened in the title-pages of books printed at Rome, Bologna and Naples, where he is hailed as Vice-God, most invincible Monarch of the Christian Commonwealth, and fierce Preserver of Papal Omnipotence. Moreover, passages of Scripture are applied to him, such as Jer. 27.8: The nation and kingdom which will not serve him, I will punish with sword, famine and pestilence, says the Lord, upon that nation; and Dan. 7.14: The Lord gave him power and kingdom, and all peoples shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, and his kingdom shall not be corrupted. (Of these, the first passage, which refers to the King of Babylon, perhaps fitted not badly, but the second, which speaks of Christ, could only be twisted blasphemously.) Finally there is Isa. 49.23: Kings shall be your nursing fathers, and queens your nursing mothers. They shall bow down to you with their faces to the earth, and lick up your dust.

units.la: CCXX. Statim initio Papatus sui Paulus Venetiis litem gravissimam intentavit, eò quòd Respublica, dum Sedes vacaret, legem scivisset, qua Ecclesiasticis interdicebatur, ne quid soli & immobilium bonorum possent acquirere. Legem eam, utpote Concilio & Canonibus libertatique adeò Ecclesiasticæ adversantem abrogari Papa petiit. Rénuerunt Veneti, ostendentes per Oratorem multis tis verbis, nihil lege sua contra libertatem Ecclesiasticam decretum esse. nam legem ad subditos solutæ conditionis directam esse, de quorum bonis sibi, neminem in temporalibus præter Deum superiorem agnoscentibus, secundùm jura ac leges statuere liceat. Nihil Ecclesiasticis illa lege imperari aut injungi; non illis auferri rei donatæ, aut in favorem eorum quomodocunque alienatæ pretium, sed possessionem rerum soli, ne tractu temporis subditi, qui onera ordinaria & extraordinaria imperii sustinent, bonis illis omnino spolientur, & impares tandem ad ea sustinenda, imperium infirmum & omni ope destitutum deserant. Id ipsum alios Reges Principesque in suis ditionibus semper statuisse; nominatim Cæsares Valentinianum, Valentem & Gratianum edita,& ab Hieronymo laudata Constitutione; Carolum M. in Saxonia, Francorum Reges, Eduardum III. in Anglia, Carolum V. in Belgio, &c. Præcesserat Clemente VIII. Pontifice, jurisdictio ab iisdem exercita in Ecclesiasticos, Brixianum Monachum Augustinianum, qui undecennem virginem stuprasse & occidisse convictus fuerat: Scipionem Saracenum hominem impudica vita infamem, & Brandolinum Valdemarinum, scelerum plurium compertum: nec non interdictum, ne quis sive religioni sive sacris addictus, sive Scholas, sive Collegium, Sacras ædes, Xenodochia; cœnobia in suæ jurisdictionis territorio, inconsulto & non consentiente Senatu, ædificaret. Quæ dissimulata à Clemente, Paulus cum concoquere non posset, ad tria tandem capita suas adversus Venetos querimonias contraxit, videlicet de lege, quæ novas Templorum & ædium structuras spectabat: de lege altera, qua bonorum immobilium acquisitio vetebatur: denique de jurisdictione in Ecclesiasticos. Pro legibus igitur patriis, juribus, libertate publica pugnabant Veneti. Contra Pontifex jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam convelli, & suam authoritatem infringi clamitabat. Cúmque pro juribus suis Veneti strenuè contenderent, Pontisex ad diras conversus, diploma ad Præsules Venetæ ditionis misit, quo memoratas leges abrogavit, & nisi intra viginti quatuor dies à Republica abrogarentur, & captivi traderentur, jam nunc Principem & Senatum, qui nunc est, & deinceps erit, & totam Venetam ditionem interdicto seu anathemate subjiciebat. Veneti Duce novo Leonhardo Donato (qui excommunicationem Papæ brutum fulmen aëra feriens vocavit) contra audentius ire, Patriarchæ Aquilejensi diploma in ditione sua promulgare volenti, exilium præsens interminari; contraria ad suos Præsules mandata mittere, & ubique sacrum solenne templis apertis peragi, coetúsque Ecclesiasticos celebrari more solito jubere. Ita pauci Episcopi diplomati detulerunt, & sacra more solito peracta sunt. Jesuitæ & novorum Ordinum ferè cuncti devoti Venetias reliquerunt; Donato Duce Jesuitis valedicente his verbis: Ite, nihil auferte, nunquam redite. Jámque à verborum & dirarum jactatione res ad bellum inclinare visa est, Venetis triremes instruentibus, & novas copias conscribentibus. Pontificis interim diploma & censuram ad continendos in officio subditos censuræ subjicere placuit. Ubi Johannis Gersonis Cancellarii Parisiensis de clavium Ecclesiæ usu & abusu sententiâ pro fundamento substratâ, multa ad causam suam tuendam Veneti superstruxerunt. Ante omnia Antonius Quirinus Senator populare scriptum à Supremo Decem virorum Consilio, postquam à sex Theologis, totidemque Jurisconsultis approbatum fuit, subscriptum, plenum cæterra vehementis affectus, evulgavit, quo & legum controversarum promulgationem novam defendit, & nihil nisi ex necessitate, & honestè justéque à Senatu ea in re factum contendit. Aliud eodem tempore contra Pauli interdictum, scriptum evulgatum est, testimoniis Petri Antonii Ribetti, Archidiaconi Vicarii Generalis, F. Pauli Veneti, Reipublicæ Theologi, ex Servitarum Ordine, F. Bernhardi Jordoni, Michaëlis Angeli Bonicelli, F. M. Antonii Capelli Franciscanorum, F. Camilli Augustiniani, F. Fulgentii itidem Servitæ firmatum, quod novendecim propositionibus absolvitur, quo & exemplis & rationibus ac testibus recentibus ex jure Canonico petitis convincitur, Ecclesiasticos in ditione Veneta non teneri observare interdictum, & Principem posse ac debere citra peccatum ejus observationem prohibere.Sed inprimis punctum omne tulit F. Paulus Servita, in hac causa nominatissimus, & Reip. Theologus. qui judicium suum summa moderatione & prudentia, Considerationum nomine seorsim subjecit, quo originem primam & seriem rei repetiit, & quid utrinque aut præcipitanter, aut officiosè actum gestúmque fit, explicavit; leges, quæ impugnabantur à Pontifice, tanquam æquissimas, à legitima potestate latas defendit, jurisdictionem Principum in subditos, atque adeò sacrum ordinem ex Dei verbo per Beatissimos Petrum & Paulum sancitam asseruit, Patrúmque testimoniis confirmavit; exemptiones clericorum beneficio Principum concessas probavit; libertatem Ecclesiasticam amplius discussit, ac demum totam disputationem Leonis Papæ hac sententia, manere Petri privilegium, ubicunque ex ipsius fertur æquitate judicium, nec nimiam esse severitatem vel remissionem, ubi nihil erit ligatum vel solutum, nisi quod B. Petrus solverit vel ligaverit; conclusit. Sed & alio Authore anonymo, credito tamen eodem F. Paulo, prodiit liber, qui octo capitibus eandem causam masculè egit. Duo quinetiam Gersonis opuscula, cum præfatione ejusdem, uti putabatur, Pauli publicæ luci data sunt. Tum igitur Bellarminus, omissis Considerationibus, quibus F. Paulus nomen suum præscripserat, in authorem ânonymum & opuscula stylum stringere cœpit, graviter ante omnia cum Venetis expostulans, quòd contra Synodi Tridentinæ abiis receptæ decretum, in ditionibus suis libros de rebus sacris sine authoris nomine typis mandari patiantur. Neque alio potentiore, quàm Concilii Tridentini, telo pugnatum, quippe quo cunctæ constitutiones & decreta Pontificia, quibus suprema illa potestas asseritur, rata & firma habeantur. Bellarminus autem non contentus octo propositiones anonymi refutâsse, horrendis etiam ad servanda Pontificum interdicta exemplis cunctos hortatus est; veluti Boleslai Poloniæ Regis, qui à Gregorio VII. devotus suorum contemptum, rebelliones & dissensiones in Regno passus, & ad extremum extra se positus, vecors per silvas ferino more cum canibus errans, cùm repentino casu expirâsset, ab ipsis devoratus sit; deinde Ludovici Bavari Cæsaris, qui Johannis XXII. & Benedicti XII. spretis censuris, tandem, lapsante equo, subita morte, non facta pœnitentia, nec à peccatis per confessionem expiatus, correptus fuerit. Bellarmino respondit Johannes Marsilius Neapolitanus, ex Ordine Seraphico, & eidem errores innumeros ob oculos posuit, exempla quoque elevavit, ostendens scilicet, Boleslaum non ob Pontificias censuras, sed ob sceleratam vitam miserè periisse; & Ludovicum Cæsarem non morte subita, verùm veneno ab inimicis propinato vitam finivisse; aliis etiam duobus exemplis in contrarium adductis, Johannis XII. & Bonifacii VIII. quorum anathemata spreta nihil noxæ attulerint; ad extremum summum Pontificem nudum à donariis & privilegiis Principum, jure Pontificatus nullam habere laicam potestatem, neque supremam, neque mediam, neque infimam, neque actu, neque habitu, idque ex Navarri etiam sententia à Bernhardo descripta, conclusit. Scripserat idem Bellarminus adversus Opuscula Gersonis, cujus ceu hominis pii licet & docti, per tempora tamen scissurae in Scholis Galliae, ubi Pontificia dignitas in arctum cogebatur, educati, & erroneas in aestu illo opiniones imbibentis, authoritatem elevare inprimis conatus est. Neque tamen sic factus finis scribendi est. Nam mox F. Paulus, author praefationis, Gersonis Opusculis praemissae, creditus, jam renudato animo, nomen suum professus, tum praefationis illius, tum Gersonis etiam defensionem, prolixa & accurata apologia suscepit, & Concilii cum primis supra Papam eminentiam, ex mente Gersonis, solide demonstravit. Sed & ejusdem F. Pauli considerationes, quas intactas Bellarminus siverat, peculiari libro ad partes vocavit Joh. Antonius Bovius Novariensis Carmelitanus, contra quem longo & aeque accurato scripto F. Fulgentius Brixianus Servita, disputavit. Exceperunt deinceps duorum Cardinalium, Ascanii Columnae & Caesaris Baronii vota, quibus Censuras Pontificis non solum illi laudabant, sed etiam Pontificem, ut earum executioni strenuè insisteret, pleno affectu cohortabantur. Et Baronius quidem nulla praemissa salutatione, utpote agens cum devotis, ita differebat, Petri ministerium duplex fuisse, pascere & occidere, juxta illud: Pasce oves meas. Macta & manduca. Hoc ultimum jam Papae incumbere, excommunicare videlicet & mactare. Neque dissimulabat, se superabundaturum gaudio, si videre id sibi contigerit.
units.tr: CCXX. At the very start of his pontificate, Paul brought a most serious lawsuit against Venice, because the Republic, while the See was vacant, had passed a law forbidding churchmen to acquire land or immovable property. The Pope demanded that this law be repealed, as it was wholly opposed to the Council, the canons and the liberty of the Church. The Venetians refused. Through their ambassador they showed at length that nothing in their law had been decreed against ecclesiastical liberty. The law was addressed to subjects of an unexempt condition, whose goods the state may regulate by its rights and laws, since those subjects acknowledge no superior in temporal matters except God. That law imposed nothing on churchmen and took nothing from them: it did not strip them of property already given, nor demand the price of anything alienated in their favour in any way. It concerned only the possession of land, so that, over time, subjects who bear the ordinary and extraordinary burdens of the state should not be wholly stripped of their goods, and, no longer able to bear those burdens, leave the state weak and destitute of every resource. Other kings and princes had always made the same provision in their own domains. The Venetians named the Caesars Valentinian, Valens and Gratian, whose constitution was issued and praised by Jerome; Charlemagne in Saxony; the kings of the Franks; Edward III in England; Charles V in Belgium; and others. Under Pope Clement VIII, the same rulers had already exercised jurisdiction over churchmen: over an Augustinian monk of Brescia, who had been convicted of raping and killing an eleven-year-old girl; over Scipio Saracenus, a man infamous for his shameless life; and over Brandolinus Valdemarinus, found guilty of many crimes. They had also forbidden anyone, whether dedicated to religion or to the sacred ministry, to build schools, colleges, churches, hospices or monasteries within their territory without the consent and approval of the Senate. Clement had overlooked these things, but Paul could not stomach them, and at last he drew up his complaints against the Venetians under three heads: first, the law concerning the building of new churches and houses; second, the other law, which forbade the acquisition of immovable property; and finally, the jurisdiction over churchmen. The Venetians therefore fought for their ancestral laws, their rights and public liberty. The Pontiff cried out that ecclesiastical jurisdiction was being overthrown and his own authority broken. When the Venetians pressed their rights vigorously, the Pontiff turned to threats. He sent to the prelates of the Venetian territory a decree repealing the said laws, and declared that unless the Republic repealed them within twenty-four days and handed over the prisoners, he would then and there place under interdict, or anathema, the Prince and the Senate then in office and whoever should succeed them, together with the whole Venetian domain. The Venetians, under their new Doge, Leonardo Donato, who called the Pope's excommunication "a dull thunderbolt striking the air," dared to go further against him. When the Patriarch of Aquileia wished to promulgate the decree in his territory, Donato threatened him with immediate exile. He sent contrary orders to their own prelates, and commanded that everywhere the sacred rites be celebrated in the usual way, with the churches open and ecclesiastical assemblies held as before. So few bishops delivered the decree, and the sacred rites were performed as usual. The Jesuits and nearly all the members of the newer orders left Venice, Donato bidding farewell to the Jesuits with these words: "Go, take nothing, never return." Soon the matter, which had been carried on by words and curses, seemed to be turning toward war, as the Venetians fitted out triremes and enlisted new troops. Meanwhile it was thought fit to subject the Pontiff's decree and censure to examination, in order to keep the subjects in their duty. Here, taking as their foundation the opinion of John Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, on the use and abuse of the keys of the Church, the Venetians built up many arguments in defence of their cause. Above all, Antonio Quirino, a senator, published a popular writing, full of vehement feeling, which had been signed by the Supreme Council of Ten after its approval by six theologians and as many jurists. In it he defended the new promulgation of the disputed laws and maintained that the Senate had acted in this matter only from necessity, honourably and justly. At the same time another writing was published against Paul's interdict. It was confirmed by the testimonies of Pietro Antonio Ribetti, archdeacon and vicar general; Fra Paolo of Venice, theologian of the Republic, of the Order of the Servites; Fra Bernardo Giordano; Michelangelo Bonicelli; Fra Antonio Cappello of the Franciscans; Fra Camillo of the Augustinians; and Fra Fulgenzio, likewise a Servite. It is set out in nineteen propositions and proves by examples, arguments and recent witnesses drawn from canon law that churchmen in the Venetian territory are not bound to observe the interdict, and that the Prince can and ought, without sin, to forbid its observance. But the chief contribution came from Fra Paolo the Servite, the most famous man in this affair and theologian of the Republic. With the greatest moderation and prudence, under the title of Considerations, he published separately his judgement. In it he traced the first origin and sequence of the matter and explained what had been done or attempted on each side, sometimes hastily and sometimes dutifully. He defended the laws attacked by the Pontiff as most just and enacted by lawful authority; he asserted the jurisdiction of princes over their subjects, and so also the sacred order, established by the word of God through the most blessed Peter and Paul, and confirmed it with the testimonies of the Fathers; he proved that exemptions granted to clerics by the favour of princes were valid; he discussed ecclesiastical liberty at greater length; and finally he concluded the whole disputation with this sentence of Pope Leo: "Peter's privilege remains wherever judgement is pronounced in accordance with his fairness, and there is no excessive severity or remission where nothing is bound or loosed except what Blessed Peter has bound or loosed." But another anonymous author, though it was believed to be Fra Paolo, also issued a book which argued the same case manfully in eight chapters. Moreover, two little works of Gerson, with a preface which was thought to be by Paul himself, were given to the public. Then Bellarmine, passing over the Considerations, under which Fra Paolo had written his name, began to direct his pen against the anonymous author and the little works. Above all he sharply complained that the Venetians allowed books on sacred matters to be printed without the author's name in their territories, contrary to the decree of the Council of Trent, which they had received. Nor did he fight with any weapon more powerful than the Council of Trent, by which all the constitutions and decrees of the Popes, in which that supreme power is asserted, are held valid and firm. Bellarmine, however, was not content to refute the eight propositions of the anonymous author. He also urged everyone to observe the Pontiffs' interdicts by horrible examples: for instance, King Boleslaus of Poland, who, having been devoted to Gregory VII, suffered the contempt of his subjects, rebellions and dissensions in his kingdom, and at last, beside himself, wandered mad through the woods with the dogs like a wild beast, and when he suddenly died by chance, was devoured by them; and then the Emperor Louis of Bavaria, who, having scorned the censures of John XXII and Benedict XII, was at last seized when his horse stumbled and died suddenly, without repentance and without being cleansed of his sins by confession. John Marsilius of Naples, of the Seraphic Order, answered Bellarmine and set before his eyes countless errors. He also brought forward examples, showing that Boleslaus perished wretchedly not because of papal censures but because of his wicked life, and that Louis the Emperor ended his life not by sudden death but by poison given him by his enemies. He also adduced two other examples to the contrary, of John XII and Boniface VIII, whose anathemas, though despised, did them no harm. Finally, he concluded that the supreme Pontiff, stripped of the gifts and privileges of princes, has by the right of the Pontificate no lay power at all, neither supreme, nor middle, nor lowest, neither in act nor in habit; and he did this also according to the opinion of Navarrus, as set down by Bernard. Bellarmine had written against the little works of Gerson, a man who, though pious and learned, had been brought up at the time of the schism in the schools of France, where papal dignity was being constrained, and had imbibed erroneous opinions in that heat.
