Bellarmine above all tried to lower his authority. Yet the writing did not stop there. Soon Fra Paolo, believed to be the author of the preface prefixed to Gerson's little works, now stripped of disguise and professing his name, took up with a long and careful apology the defence both of that preface and of Gerson, and solidly demonstrated the pre-eminence of a Council above the Pope, according to Gerson's mind. Moreover, Giovanni Antonio Bovio of Novara, a Carmelite, called Fra Paolo's Considerations, which Bellarmine had let pass untouched, into the field with a separate book; and against him Fra Fulgenzio of Brescia, a Servite, disputed in a long and equally careful writing. Then followed the votes of two cardinals, Ascanio Colonna and Cesare Baronio. These not only praised the Pontiff's censures but also urged the Pope, with full feeling, to press their execution vigorously. Baronius, without any preliminary greeting, since he was addressing devoted followers, argued that the ministry of Peter was twofold, to feed and to kill, according to the words: "Feed my sheep" and "Kill and eat." He said that this last duty now rested upon the Pope, namely to excommunicate and to kill. Nor did he hide that he would overflow with joy if it should be his lot to see this done.

units.la: Utrique voto illi Joh. Marsilius respondit. Post obstinatum in amplissimo orbis theatro super re maxime seria certamen, plerique promiscua caede gregatim & catervatim concurrere coeperunt. Citatus interim ad Inquisitionis tribunal Johannes Marsilius cum se defenderet, non solum Ecclesiae communione, sed omni etiam bonorum tam mobilium quam immobilium possessione, & sacerdotiorum fructibus privatus est. Sententiam ut legit, pro nulla & invalida se habere declaravit. Citatus etiam F. Paulus, per literas ad Cardinales Inquisitores datas comparuit,caufamque dixit. Demum Fulgentius longo scripto non ad Inquisitores, sed ad Archiepiscopos, Episcopos & Ordines Religiosos directo, protestatus, præcipuè fiscales minas de privatione bonorum, quæ nulla possideat, risit. Rebus exacerbatis nimium Pontifex pecuniis tum aliundè, tum ex creatione novorum Cardinalium collectis exercitum instrui jussit, imperatore dicto Ranutio Parmensium Duce, eique etiam Philippus Hispaniæ Rex, literis artificiosè scriptis, suppetias obtulit. A Rege contra Galliæ Henrico IV. missus Venetias Cardinalis Jousa componere flagrans dissidium mira solertia tentavit. Intercessit tamen reconciliationi nonnihil severa Jesuitarum ex universa Venetorum ditione proscriptio, ob facinora, quæ susè Thuanus Histor. lib. cxxxvii. commemorat, inter quæ propius Venetos tangebant isthæc; quòd arcana imperii & familiarum per confessiones eos rimari, persuasum haberent: quodque pueros in Scholis, adolescentes in Rep. sensim ab obsequio Superiorum alienarent. Decretum igitur in Decem virorum consessu, ut si re ad concordiam inclinante aliquid pro tranquillitate publica remittere cogerentur, in Jesuitarum proscriptione constantiam servarent, & illorum restitutionem omnino à pacis negotio separarent. Probationes de aliis criminibus contra eos confectæ, ut haberet Senatus, quo se de negata restitutione Pontifici excusaret, si eos, quos belli jam accensi auctores, & porro novarum dissensionum incentores semper futuros timebat, intra viscera habere cogerentur. Visis actis & probationibus mense Junio A. M. D. C. VII. decretum tandem conditum, quo Jesuitæ exilio perpetuo multantur; addito, ne posthac possint restitui, nisi ex universi Collegii sententia, & acta primùm ac probationes in Decemvirorum consessu coram Ducentis triginta recitentur, exclusis iis, qui Pontificiis partibus favere in occulto putantur.Interdictum simul est omne cum iis commercium, & poenæ graves statutæ in quoscunque, qui à quoquam ex illo sodalitio literas accepisse comperti fuerint. Tametsi vero tum pacis proxeneta Cardinalis Joufa extremis viribus annixus fuerit, ut legem hanc refigeret Senatus: & Pontifex ipse non refixa hac lege à consiliis pacis se alienissimum ostenderit, perstitit tamen Venetis adamante fixa semel lata adversus Jesuitas sententia: & Pontifici tandem Cardinalis Perronus efficacissimis rationibus persuasit, ut Jesuitarum posthabita restitutione oblatas cæteras pacis conditiones amplecteretur. Ita Jesuitis exulare & plorare jussis, pax Venetos & Pontificem inter, parario Regis Galliarum nomine Cardinale Joufa, coaluit his feré conditionibus; ut Venetis libertas integra constaret circa ea, quæ in controversiam Papa vocavit: traderentur sine protestatione captivi: XI. Kal. Maii Venetiis coram Principe & XXV. primariis Senatoribus Joufa, adducto secum Fraxineo, clausis valvis, voce præconis interdictum Papæ revocaret, & Senatum universosque subditos & ordines, qui in censuram incurrerant, absolveret. Ita Pontifex litem gravem adeò contestatus Venetis, cum pupillæ oculorum suorum, Jesuitarum ignominia & damno præsentissimo, foro cessit, causáque cecidit, & documentum insuper posteris suis reliquit, bruta jam haberi ab ipsis etiam Pontificiis Potestatibus supremis Pontificum fulmina, neque magis quàm inanis fundæ sonum eos, in quos vibrantur, territare. Dissidio jam composito à conjuratis, Rodolpho Pomo, Michäele Vito Sacerdote, & Alexandro Parrasio, Jesuitis, Possevino inprimis, colludentibus; in caput F. Pauli Servitæ, cujus potissimum consiliis cordatis & prudentissimis, Venetorum res, difficilimis hisce temporibus
units.tr: Johannes Marsilius answered both of these wishes. After a stubborn contest on the greatest stage of the world over a most serious matter, many began to rush together in throngs and crowds to a general slaughter. Meanwhile Johannes Marsilius was summoned before the tribunal of the Inquisition, and when he defended himself, he was deprived not only of communion with the Church but also of all possession of goods, both movable and immovable, and of the revenues of his benefices. When he read the sentence, he declared that he regarded it as null and void. Fra Paolo was also summoned; by a letter addressed to the Cardinal Inquisitors he appeared and pleaded his cause. Finally Fulgentius, by a long written protest addressed not to the Inquisitors but to the archbishops, bishops and religious orders, mocked the threats of fiscal penalties, the deprivation of goods which he did not possess. With matters excessively inflamed, the Pope, having raised money from various sources and from the creation of new Cardinals, ordered an army to be raised, with Ranuccio, Duke of Parma, named as commander; and Philip, King of Spain, offered him aid in skilfully written letters. Sent to Venice by Henry IV, King of France, against them, Cardinal Joyeuse tried with remarkable skill to settle the blazing dispute. Yet the severe banishment of the Jesuits from the whole Venetian dominion stood not a little in the way of reconciliation, on account of the crimes which Thuanus recounts at length in his Histor. lib. cxxxvii; among these, those touching the Venetians more closely were these: that they pried into the secrets of state and of families through confessions, and were persuaded that they gradually alienated boys in the schools and young men in the commonwealth from obedience to their superiors. It was therefore decreed in the assembly of the Council of Ten that, if they were forced, as the matter moved towards agreement, to concede something for public tranquillity, they should keep firm in the banishment of the Jesuits and wholly separate their restitution from the business of peace. Proofs of other crimes were compiled against them, so that the Senate would have something with which to excuse itself to the Pope for refusing restitution, should it be forced to keep within its own borders those whom it feared would always be the authors of the war already kindled and the fomenters of new dissensions. The acts and proofs having been examined, in June 1607 a decree was at last drawn up by which the Jesuits were punished with perpetual exile; with the addition that they could not afterwards be restored unless by the judgement of the whole College, and the acts and proofs were first read out in the assembly of the Ten before two hundred and thirty members, excluding those thought secretly to favour the Papal side. At the same time all dealings with them were forbidden, and severe penalties were laid down for anyone found to have received letters from any member of that fellowship. Although Cardinal Joyeuse, then the broker of peace, strained every nerve to have the Senate revoke this law, and the Pope himself showed that he was utterly estranged from the counsels of peace while the law stood unrevoked, nevertheless the sentence once passed against the Jesuits remained fixed for the Venetians like adamant; and at last Cardinal Perron persuaded the Pope by most effective arguments that, setting aside the restitution of the Jesuits, he should accept the other terms of peace offered. So, with the Jesuits ordered into exile and to weep, peace was struck between the Venetians and the Pope, through Cardinal Joyeuse acting in the name of the King of France, on roughly these terms: that the Venetians should keep full liberty in regard to those matters which the Pope had called into dispute; that prisoners should be handed over without protest; on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May (21 April) at Venice, before the Prince and twenty-five leading Senators, Joyeuse, having brought Fraxineus with him, with the doors closed, should revoke the Pope's interdict by the voice of a herald, and absolve the Senate and all subjects and orders who had incurred the censure. Thus the Pope, having contested the suit with the Venetians so seriously, yielded the field, with the apple of his eye, the Jesuits, disgraced and most manifestly harmed, and lost his case; and he left his successors a further lesson: that the thunderbolts of the Popes, even when wielded by the highest Papal powers themselves, are now to be regarded as brute things, and frighten those at whom they are hurled no more than the sound of an empty sling. With the quarrel now settled, the conspirators, Rodolfo Pomo, Michele Vito the priest and Alessandro Parrasio, Jesuits, with Possevino above all colluding, turned against Fra Paolo the Servite, by whose especially wise and prudent counsels the affairs of Venice had stood firm in these most difficult times

units.la: Tt steterant triumpharántque; sicarii subornati sunt Johannes Paulli Florentinus & Paschalis Bitontius, qui eum ad Monasterium suum pergentem invadentes, tribus gravisfimis ictibus in facie & collo ferierunt, acinace uno in vulnere relicto. Neque tamen vulnera lethalia fuerunt; & patrocinium Servitæ Senatus non conjuratis duntaxat & percussoribus, qui effugerant, exilio perpetuo multatis, & proemio quater mille ducatorum ei, qui illos, ubicunque nactus fuerit, occiderit, promisso; sed vitæ etiam ejus securitate in posterum asserta, strenuè suscepit. Paulo prolixius dissidii illius historiam ex Thuano, aliisque etiam repetendam duxi, ut authoritatis & potestatis Pontificiæ decrementum, & apud ipsos etiam Pontificios status præsentissima imminutio magis inde colliquescceret. Nam ex eo quidem tempore Pontifices, serò sapientes licet, diris adversus Reges & Principes abstinuerunt, audientésque adeò fuerunt dicto Nicolai Pontani, Venetorum Ducis, Donati prædecessoris, uti scilicet Pontifices censuris seu anathematibus debere instar gladii vaginæ inclusi, non temerè distringendi, ne diceerent homines ejusmodi telum contemnere. qui etiam Gregorio XIII. obnuntiare non dubitavit, verendum esse, ne Veneti, qui Græci olim fuissent, à Papa irritati, è Latio in Græciam migrarent.
units.tr: and triumphed. Hired assassins were suborned: Giovanni Paolo of Florence and Pasquale Bitonto, who attacked him as he was making his way to his monastery and struck him with three very heavy blows to the face and neck, leaving a dagger in one wound. Yet the wounds were not lethal; and the Senate strenuously took up the protection of the Servite, not only by punishing with perpetual exile the conspirators and the assassins who had escaped, and by promising four thousand ducats to whoever killed them wherever he found them, but also by securing his safety for the future. I thought it worth recounting the history of that quarrel somewhat more fully, from Thuanus and others, so that the decline of papal authority and power, and its most manifest diminution even among the Papist states themselves, might become clearer. For from that time the Popes, though late to grow wise, abstained from dire measures against kings and princes, and they heeded so well the saying of Nicolò Ponte, Doge of Venice, Donato's predecessor, that Popes ought, so to speak, to keep their censures or anathemas like a sword sheathed in its scabbard, not to be drawn rashly, lest men should say that such a weapon is held in contempt. He did not hesitate even to declare to Gregory XIII: that it was to be feared lest the Venetians, who had once been Greeks, being provoked by the Pope, would migrate from Latium into Greece.

units.la: CCXXXI. Familiarem maximéque charum Paulo fuisse Claudium Espencæum, Theologum Parisiensem, non desunt, qui commemorent.
units.tr: CCXXXI. That Claudius Espencaeus, the Parisian theologian, was a close friend of Paul and especially dear to him, is recorded by not a few writers.

units.la: Et tamen ille jam A. M. D. LXXI. in vivis esse desiit. Sive igitur Paulus juvenis adhuc cum Espencæo amicitiam coluit, sive cum defuncti scriptis minimè equidem contemnendis familiaritatem contraxit, eáque in deliciis habuit, non parùm ejus judicio Espencæi scripta exornari commendarique liquet. Juvabit igitur ex doctissimo ejus in Epistolæ ad Titum caput primum commentario nonnulla huc sevocare, ex quibus, quæ facies Ecclesiae Romanae ejus temporibus fuerit, perspici facilius queat. Ubi de ἀὐτοχθονεῖς Ecclesiasticorum (Oper. pag. m. 478. &c.) agit, sic ille turpem cleri Romani quaestum traducit: Annon αὐτοχθονεῖς est clarissima, quod tam multa positivo tantum jure praecepta vel prohibita, eosque ligant homines, donec pecunia sibi harum constitutionum gratiam impetrent? Ita ut Regina rerum pecunia divitibus licitum faciat, quod pauperibus illicitum est, quia divitias, hoc est, spinas non habent. Haec enim ita demum procedunt, si gratis ea quis facere intendat. Quod si dolosi spes refulserit nummi, jam quod prius erat interdictum, libere fit ac impune. Tam diversa est in his relaxandis divitis atque pauperis conditio. Vix enim quicquam prohibetur, quam ut ne quis gratis contra veniat, & quod vetatur, numerata statim pecunia dispensatur, quasi nullum sit peccatum majus, quam nummis carere, &c. Turpius, quod Patrum canonibus impositam manifestis & scandalosis peccatis disciplinam, in pecuniariam redemptionem dispensationis titulo toties iidem commutant, & quasi contra quam illi, ovium hi lanam & pecuniam, quam poenitentiam & salutem malint, Ecclesiastici rigoris in inferendis poenitentiis & satisfactionibus immunitatem pecunia venditant. Quid quod liberos vulgo conceptos & ex damnato coitu, incestisque hymenaeis, contra Dei, Ecclesiae, legumque statuta editos, ejusdem pecuniae vi legitimant, ad omnium statuum & dignitatum capacitatem idoneos reddunt, illegitimos ad parem cum legitimis successionem habiles interim reddunt & admittunt? Et ut, quod quidam ajunt,
units.tr: And yet he had ceased to be among the living already in 1571. Whether Paul, while still a young man, cultivated friendship with Espencaeus, or formed his intimacy with the writings of the deceased man, which are by no means to be despised, and held them in high esteem, it is clear that Espencaeus's works were much adorned and recommended by his judgment. It will therefore be helpful to draw out from Espencaeus's very learned commentary on the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus a few points, from which it can more easily be seen what the face of the Roman Church was in his time. Where he treats of the autochthones [ἀὐτοχθονεῖς] of the churchmen (Oper. pag. m. 478. &c.), he thus criticises the shameful money-making of the Roman clergy: Is it not most evident that so many things are forbidden or commanded by positive law alone, and that they bind men until they obtain the favour of these regulations for money? So that the Queen of things, money, makes lawful for the rich what is unlawful for the poor, because the rich have no thorns, that is, difficulties. For these rules hold only if someone intends to do them for nothing. But if the hope of a purse shines forth, then what was previously forbidden is done freely and with impunity. So different is the condition of the rich and the poor in the relaxing of these rules. For scarcely anything is forbidden except that no one should act against them for nothing, and what is forbidden is at once dispensed for counted-out money, as if there were no greater sin than lacking coin, etc. More shameful still, that the discipline imposed by the canons of the Fathers on manifest and scandalous sins is so often commuted by the same men into pecuniary redemption under the title of dispensation, and, as though they wanted the wool and money of the sheep rather than their penance and salvation, they sell for money exemption from the strictness of the Church in imposing penances and satisfactions. What of the fact that children commonly conceived and born from condemned intercourse and incestuous marriages, contrary to the statutes of God, the Church and the laws, they legitimise by the power of the same money, make fit for the capacity of all ranks and dignities, and meanwhile make illegitimate children capable of succession on a par with the legitimate and admit them? And, as some say,

units.la: A bove majori discit arare minor.
units.tr: The lesser learns to plough from the greater ox.

units.la: Minores non tantum Episcopi, sed etiam Archidiaconi, eorumque male officiosi, officiales & Vicarii, plerunque dum dioeceses & paroecias obequitant, non tam facinorosos & criminum reos poenis & correctionibus a vitiis deterrent, quam pecunia praesenti & numerata, titulo procurationis, ne dicam, fictitiae jurisdictionis emungunt, & exugunt tam clericos quam laicos. Turpissimum, quod & hos cum concubinis, pellicibus & meretriculis cohabitare, liberosque que procreare sinunt, accepto ab eis certo censu. habeat, (ajunt) si velit. Allegat deinceps Taxam Cameræ seu Cancellariæ Apostolicæ, librum palam & publicè Lutetiæ impressum & venalem; à quo, inquit, plus scelerum discas licet, quàm in omnibus omnium vitiorum Summistis & Summariis; & plurimis quidem licentia, omnibus autem absolutio emptu rientibus proposita. Mirum, addit, hoc tempore, hoc schismate non suppressum tot tamque fœdorum, tamque horrendorum scelerum velut indicem adeò infamem, ut non putem in Germania, Helvetia, & ubicunque à Romana Sede defectum est, opus prostare majore scandalo. Et adeò tamen non supprimitur ab Ecclesiæ Romanæ favitoribus, ut tantorum facinorum licentia ac immunitates in facultatibus Legatorum illinc huc venientium, bona ex parte innoventur atque confirmentur, adversus (si Deo placet) quæcunque fatalia restituendi, ac etiam quoscunque spurios, Mamseres, Bastardos, ex illicito quocunque coitu, &c. cum his, qui se per adulterium polluerint, ut connubere possint, perjuros, simoniacos, falsarios item, raptores, usurarios, schismaticos, hæreticos, sed ad cor reversos, non absolvendi tantùm, sed & ad ordines, honores, dignitates & beneficia quæcunque, quotcunque, qualiacunque, dispensandi, homicidas quoque, sed casuales, seu involuntarios. nam nec voluntarios excepit Taxa, presbytericidas, parricidas, matricidas, fratricidas, sororicidas, uxoricidas, infanticidas, veneficos, incantatrices, concubinarios, adulteros, incestuosos, cum affinibus aut consanguineis, denique contra naturam, cum brutis &c. Habeat jam Roma pudorem, & tam nullius frontis criminum omne genus catalogum prostituere desinat. Deinceps acri sermone perstringit Annatos, expectativos gratiæ, reservationes in pectore, & infinita id genus, primùm quidem Ecclesiæ tam diu inaudita, nec à redivivis Petro & Paulo intelligenda, &c. Narrato insuper Adriani VI. propositio, Pauli III. de reformanda Ecclesia consilio, quod maculas, inquit, ostendens tantùm, non auferens, quemadmodum elusum sit, patefacit; Concilii ter Tridentum indicti narrata historia, queritur, adeo Papam Patribus curiae reformandae potestatem non fecisse, ut etiam quaecunque de reformatione morum & disciplina ecclesiastica inferioribus praescripsit, in his semper salvam S. A. authoritatem & esse & intelligi Sess. ult. can. 21. declararit. ut non minus grate quam pie Pius idem magnam gratiam Patribus Tridentinis publica oratione Romae in frequentissimo Cardinalium Consessu habuerit, quod in ecclesiastica emendatione tantam authoritatis illius rationem habuerint, tantaque in eum moderatione sint usi, ut si is se ipse suaque reformare voluisset, longe in se severior suturus fuisset. Monet autem graviter Pontificem, saltem deinceps reformandae ecclesiae serium studium suscipiat.
units.tr: The lesser men, not only the bishops but also the archdeacons, and their ill-dutiful officials and vicars, for the most part, while they ride about the dioceses and parishes, do not so much deter the criminals and the guilty of crimes from their vices by penalties and corrections, as they squeeze and drain both clergy and laity of ready-counted money under the title of procuration, not to say of fictitious jurisdiction. Most shameful is that they also allow these men to cohabit with concubines, mistresses and harlots, and to beget children, for a fixed fee received from them: let him have her, they say, if he wishes. He next cites the Taxa of the Camera or the Chancery of the Apostolic See, a book printed and sold openly and publicly at Paris: from which, he says, you may learn more wickedness than from all the summaries and digests of all vices; and licence is offered to many, and absolution to all who buy it. It is strange, he adds, that in this age, in this schism, so infamous an index of so many and so foul and horrible crimes has not been suppressed, so that I do not think any work more scandalous is on sale in Germany, Switzerland, or wherever there has been a revolt from the Roman See. And yet it is not suppressed by the favourers of the Roman Church, so that the licences and immunities for such great crimes, in the faculties of the legates coming hence and thither, are for the most part renewed and confirmed, namely for restoring whatever fated things (God willing) against whatever persons; and even for all spurious persons, mamzers, bastards, from any unlawful intercourse, etc., so that those who have defiled themselves by adultery may marry; for perjurers, simoniacs, likewise forgers, robbers, usurers, schismatics, heretics, but those who have come back to their senses, to absolve not only, but also to dispense them for orders, honours, dignities and benefices of any kind, however many, of whatever sort; likewise for murderers, but accidental or involuntary ones. For the Taxa has not even excepted voluntary ones: priest-killers, parricides, matricides, fratricides, sororicides, uxoricides, infanticides, poisoners, sorceresses, whoremongers, adulterers, incestuous persons with relatives by marriage or by blood, and finally those against nature, with beasts, etc. Let Rome now have shame, and let it cease to set forth a catalogue of crimes of every kind with such shameless brows. Then with a sharp tongue he assails the annates, expectative graces, reservations in petto, and countless things of this kind, never heard of in the Church until now, and not to be understood even by Peter and Paul risen again, etc. He further recounts the proposal of Adrian VI and the counsel of Paul III on reforming the Church, which, by showing the spots only and not removing them, reveals how it has been mocked. Having recounted the history of the Council of Trent, which was thrice convened, he complains that the Pope had so little given the Fathers power to reform the Curia that he declared, in the last session, canon 21, that whatever he had prescribed to inferiors concerning the reform of morals and ecclesiastical discipline, the authority of the Holy See always remained and was to be understood as saved in these matters. So also Pius himself, no less graciously than piously, gave great thanks to the Tridentine Fathers in a public oration at Rome before a very full assembly of Cardinals, because they had shown such regard for that authority in ecclesiastical reform, and had used such moderation towards him, that if he had wished to reform himself and his own, he would have been far more severe with himself. He, however, earnestly warns the Pontiff that at least from now on he should take up a serious study of reforming the Church.

units.la: Certe videt, inquit, propter aliquot ejus praecessorum sua, non quae Jesu Christi sunt, quaerentium αὐξοχειρίαν & avaritiam (ut ex scriptoribus ei licet Sedi addictissimis, probare possumus) in quem statum adducta sit S. S. A. & tota Christi Ecclesia, quam multa non multis abhinc annis area facta sit discessio, metuendum, ne major fiat, ni aliquando tandem remedium adhibeat, si tantis, quibus obruitur Ecclesia, malis medendis allata mora fuerit, hoc futura damnosior, quo longior. Et tam diuturnorum motuum non alia causa, quam quod tot annis nihil immutatur, nihil emendatur, & omnis reformandi spes inde abrupta, species ablata, quod reliquum Ecclesiae corpus reformatum velint, qui tam multis annorum centenariis urbem, in qua merum atque mixtum habent imperium, deformatissimam adhuc reliquerunt. Quid enim vel excusare vel excogitare verum aut verisimile possunt, quibus non vel Rex vel Caesar, non populus, non clerus, non generalis Synodus, non tota denique Ecclesia dicere potest, Cur ita facis? quid, inquam, praetexere possunt, quod eis sibi suisque reformandis moram vel remoram tandiu fecerit? Et tamen sub sole major malorum omnium licentia, clamor, impunitas, ne dicam infamia & impudentia? Talis sane ac tanta, ut nemo credat, nisi qui viderit, neget nemo, nisi qui non viderit. Subjungit, posse se inde ab Hieronymo querimoniam & quidem perpetuam, texere. Satis tamen habet produxisse testimonia ætatis proximæ, S. Bernhardi scilicet, Baptistæ Montuani, Volaterrani, Adriani VI. Cardinalium Pauli III. & eorum ipsorum, qui Concilium Tridentinum inchoarunt. Negatque, Pontificem Pium V. Galliam etiam deformem nimis reformare, nutantem continere posse, nisi juxta nomen suum sua primum piet ac repurget, juxta cognomen & generosissimum genus suum, suis primum, quod est in proverbio, medeatur, & taxas illas ἀιοχρονεξῆας nomine multis merito maledictis multorum taxatas, reliquámque Cameræ Cancellariæque Apostolicæ nihil minus quàm Apostolicam, quàm Paulinam aut Petreiam negotiationem nundinationémque, quasi quoddam Augiæ stabulum tandem vel repurget. Idem præfatione gravissima ad Cardinalem Carolum Lotharingum, Operibus, quæ superstes adhuc edidit, præfixa, non tam orat, quàm tonat in Pontifices, Cardinales, Episcopos, missó prædicandi ex Dei verbo munere proprio, alia omnia agentes. Quales quaeso, inquit, in istis, quibuscum mihi negotium est, Christi vices, quàm imaginaria discipulorum ejus hæreditas aut successio, in eas modo res quas illi non possidebant, ne somniabant quidem, involare, in latifundia, aulas, castra, satrapias, palatia: quas verò res sic iidem curárunt, ut prope solas curâsse videantur, doctrinam, orationem, sacra mysteria, in ea istos non succedere, aut quasi non successerint, eas nunquam ne per somnium quidem procurare? Talis scilicet successio est, à Pontificibus tantopere jactata! Claudit verò: Eant ergo, & Christi vicarios & Apostolicos se jactent, qui suas nunquam diœceses invisunt, neque Cathedras ascendunt, ac nec ascendere quidem possunt, immanissimi Ecclesiarum hodie magis incubatores, quàm ovilium excubitores. Hæc ex Espencæo Doctore Pontificio percelebri, quem Bellarminus Tom. I. Indic. I. in Auctoribus Romanæ Ecclesiæ refert, quique in Epitaphio Parisiis in marmore, in æde sacra Cosmæ ac Domiani, insculpto, vocatur Theologorum hujus Seculi princeps, & à Rege Christianissimo Francisco I. Melodunum, Henrico II. Bononiam, Francisco II. Aureliam, Carolo IX. Possiacum Religionis componendæ ordinandæque nomine, inter primos augustissimi Galliæ Regni Proceres, partim Legatus, partim orator de re Christiana sanctissime doctissimeque disceptâsse dicitur; quinque etiam Paulo V. familiaris & charissimus suisse fertur, occasione isthac, extra locum repræsentanda potius, quàm omnino negligenda duxi.
units.tr: Surely, he says, it is evident, on account of some of his predecessors seeking their own things and not the things of Jesus Christ, and seeking aggrandisement [αὐξοχειρίαν] and avarice (as we can prove from writers even most devoted to that See), into what a state the Holy See and the whole Church of Christ has been brought; and how many discords have been made, not many years ago, which we must fear will become greater, unless at last he applies a remedy; if delay is made in curing such great evils by which the Church is overwhelmed, it will be the more harmful the longer it lasts. And the cause of such long-standing disturbances is nothing other than that for so many years nothing is changed, nothing is amended, and all hope of reform is cut off and its appearance taken away, while those who want the rest of the Church's body reformed have left the city, in which they hold mere and mixed power, still most deformed after so many centuries. For what can they either excuse or devise that is true or probable, to whom neither king, nor emperor, nor people, nor clergy, nor a general council, nor finally the whole Church can say, Why do you act thus? What, I ask, can they put forward as a pretext for having so long delayed or hindered the reform of themselves and their own? And yet under the sun there is greater licence, clamour and impunity for all evils, not to mention infamy and impudence? So great and so plain that no one will believe it unless he has seen it, and no one will deny it except one who has not seen it. He adds that he could weave a complaint from Jerome, and indeed a perpetual one. Yet he is content to have produced the testimonies of the recent age, namely of St Bernard, Baptista Mantuanus, Volaterranus, Adrian VI, the Cardinals of Paul III, and of those very men who began the Council of Trent. And he says that Pope Pius V could not restrain France, which is too deformed, and is wavering, unless first he cleanses and purifies it in accordance with his own name, and first heals his own house, as the proverb goes, in accordance with his surname and his most noble family; and finally cleanses those Augean-stable taxes, rightly cursed by many, which were taxed by many, and the rest of the business and trading of the Camera and the Apostolic Chancery, which is nothing less than apostolic, nothing less than Pauline or Petrine. The same man, in a most weighty preface addressed to Cardinal Charles of Lorraine, prefixed to the works he published while still living, does not so much pray as thunder against the Popes, Cardinals and Bishops, who, having dropped the proper office of preaching from the Word of God, are busy with everything else. What sort of vicars of Christ, I ask, are those with whom I have business in these matters, who fly to the imaginary inheritance or succession of his disciples, to the things that they did not possess, did not even dream of: estates, courts, camps, satrapies, palaces; while the things which they themselves so attended to that they seem almost to have cared for these alone, doctrine, prayer, the holy mysteries, they never, not even in a dream, take care of, as though they did not succeed to these, or had never succeeded? Such, of course, is the succession so much boasted of by the Pontiffs! He concludes: Let them go, then, and boast themselves as the vicars of Christ and apostolic men, they who never visit their dioceses, nor ascend their cathedrals, and indeed cannot ascend them, today the most savage brooders over the Churches rather than the watchmen of the sheepfolds. These words are from Espencaeus, a very famous Papist doctor, whom Bellarmine mentions in Tom. I. Indic. I. among the Authors of the Roman Church, and who, in an epitaph carved in marble in the sacred church of Cosmas and Damian at Paris, is called the prince of the theologians of this age, who was sent by the most Christian King Francis I to Melun, by Henry II to Bologna, by Francis II to Orléans, and by Charles IX to Poissy, for the sake of settling and ordering religion, and who, as legate and orator, among the first nobles of the most august kingdom of France, disputed most holily and learnedly about Christian affairs. He is also said to have been very familiar and dearest to Paul V; I judged that this occasion should be mentioned here, outside its proper place, rather than omitted altogether.

units.la: CCXXII. An vero Espencæi hujus piis salutaribus- que consiliis morem gessisse Paulum constat? Nihil certè minùs.
units.tr: CCXXII. But is it certain that Paul complied with the pious and wholesome counsels of this Espencaeus? Certainly not in the least.

units.la: Ecclesiam enim adeò non reformavit, ut deformare etiam perrexerit. Inter altiores scilicet ejus curas erat, Parricidas Regum defendere: potestatis suæ malis artibus hactenus quæsitæ periștromata dilatare: dies festos jubilæos agitare: Cardinalem Carolum Borromæum, Archiepiscopum Mediolanensem, de quo magna Carolus Torniellus Italus, crepabat; in Sanctulorum; & Ignatium Lojolam, famosum Solipsorum regulum non in Sanctorum quidem, at Beatorum tamen (ut noverint ita Ignatiani, suum Ignatium licet minimè Sanctum, Beatum tamen, in terra scilicet, at non in Cœlo, in quod nemo non sanctus intrare potest, habendum fuisse) numerum referre: in Exquilini montis area Pacis columnam magnis sumptibus erigere: & si quæ alia ejusmodi sunt, oculiferia proferre.
units.tr: Indeed, he did not reform the Church at all; rather, he went on to deform it. His higher concerns, it seems, were to defend the murderers of kings, to extend the cushions of a power he had hitherto gained by wicked arts, to celebrate jubilee festivals, to enter in the list of the Saints Cardinal Charles Borromeo, Archbishop of Milan, of whom the Italian Carlo Torniello made such loud boasts, and Ignatius Loyola, the notorious little king of the Solipsists, not among the Saints indeed, but among the Blessed (so the Ignatians may understand that their Ignatius, though by no means a Saint, was to be held Blessed, that is, on earth, but not in heaven, into which no one who is not holy can enter). He also set up a column of Peace at great expense in the square of the Quirinal hill, and whatever other such things he produced to dazzle the eyes.

units.la: CCXXIII. Quàm se in componenda de gratiæ auxiliis & libero arbitrio controversia, Jesuitas inter & Dominicanos acerbissimè agitata, Palæmonem segnem idem Paulus gesserit, supra diximus. Neque viriliorem animum gessit in componenda vel decidenda de Conceptione B. Virginis Mariæ, maculatáne peccato, an immaculata fuerit, controversia, quæ antehac graviter Sathanicis etiam Bernæ A. M. D. IX. Wigando Wirtio Dominicano secundas post Diabolum partes in scena tractante, artibus intervenientibus; at Paulo Pontifice, inde ab A. m. d. c. xiv. ad A.m. d. c. xxi. usque gravissimè Ecclesiam Romanam exercitam habuit, quando motus impetuosissimi à conflictantibus Dominicanis & Franciscanis denuo suscitati, universam inprimis Hispaniam non concusserunt duntaxat, sed in anceps etiam, discrimen conjecerunt. Historiam fusè descripsit Lucas Waddingus, Hibernas Minorita, Antonii à Trejo, Episcopi Carthaginensis & Minoritarum Generalis, hac ipsa in causa Romam missi Theologus. Res eò processit, ut tota feré, verba ejus refero, arserit in dissidii incendium Hispania. An verò medicam malo huic manum Paulus adhibuit? Miseratus scilicet fortem Hispaniæ Die vi. Julii A. m. d. c. xvi. Apostolicum edictum strinxit, & emissa die xii. Septembr. A. m. d. c. xvii. Bulla Sixti iv. Concilii Tridentini, & Pii V. sanctiones, constitutionesque innovavit, omissáque sententia decisiva quæstionis dubiæ, id unum prohibuit, ne in coetibus publicis asseratur, B. Mariam virginem in peccato originali fuisse conceptam. Post multas deinceps Legationes à Rege Philippo Romam expeditas, definitionem quæstionis instantissimè flagitantes, nihil effici potuit; mansitque Paulus admortem usque ita in negotio eo suspensus, ut quamvis Waddingo teste, interior ejus sensus in Dominicanorum partes flexerit, certi tamen quidpiam, alterutrius partis metu, pronuntiare non sustinuerit. Cúmque eo mortuo non quievissent, sed magis etiam in Hispania æstuâssent turbæ, Gregorius XV. die xxiv. Maii A. m. d. c. xxii. edita bulla decretum Pauli ampliavit hactenus, ne quisquam etiam in scriptis & sermonibus privatis audeat asserere, quòd B. Virgo in peccato concepta sit, exceptis, quibus à Sede Apostolica fuerit hoc specialiter indultum. Ita tamen, ne novo hoc decreto opinioni illorum, qui maculatam conceptionem asserunt, præjudicium infe-raratur. Literis simul ad Philippum IV. exaratis, rationem nondum decisæ quæstionis hanc Papa reddidit: quòd nondum æterna Sapientia Ecclesiæ tanti mysterii penetralia patefecerit. Sic igitur conceptionis maculatæ assertores, hactenus loquaciores cicadis, ad ἐχεμυθίαν redacti, & in ranas Seriphias commutati sunt. Mox tamen xxii. Julii Gregorius etiam Dominicanis os subliturus, nova constitutione per formam indulti, non aliis quàm Dominicanis permisit, ut inter se duntaxat, & non inter alios & cum aliis, & in privatis colloquiis possint differere, & tractare de materia conceptionis B. Virginis. quod in priore decreto omnibus affirmativæ sententiæ tutoribus erat interdictum. Imitatus hic plane est Gregorius ingenium illius meretricis, quæ dum amasiorum suorum uni arrisit oculis, alterius manum apprehendit pressitque utrique ut satisfaceret. Demum Alexander VII. Cardinalis Pallavicini studiis, uti putatur, concitus, veteres Pontificum ea de re constitutiones innovatas, gravioribus poenis constitutis arctius adstrinxit. Extat ejus Bulla D. viii. Dec. A. M. D. C. lxi. vulgata, in qua ita asserit, B. Virginem præveniente Spiritus S. gratia à peccato originali præservatam; ut simul in gratiam Dominicanorum vetet, ne quisquam tenenti opinionem, quòd B. Virgo cum peccato originali concepta sit, hæreseos crimen impingat, cùm, inquit Bulla, ab Ecclesia Romana & ab Apostolica Sede nondum fuerit hoc decisum, prout nos nunc minimè decidere volumus aut intendimus. Ita controversiam per quinque ferè Seculorum decursum acriter adeò, multâsque per tristes tragœdias agitatam, nondum Alexander decidere voluit vel intendit. Cúmque Sixti, Pii, Pauli, Gregorii, Alexandri hi supremos se fidei in Ecclesia militante judices haberi voluerint: vel lumine Spiritús S. caruerunt; vel Spiritu soporis percussi; vel, quod verius est, gravi metu devincti fuerunt, ne scilicet sive Dominicani, quorum in Hispania maximè ob demandatum iis officium inquisitionis potentia ingens est; sive Franciscani, iisque hac quidem in causa conjunctissimi, Jesuitæ, Regibus & Principibus universis, Pontificíque etiam ipsi non tam venerabiles quàm formidabiles, decisione qualicunque offensi Pontificiæ posthac asserendæ & suffulciendæ Monarchiæ deessent, partésque, quas strenui adeò hactenus egerunt, desererent. Hanc scilicet ob causam Ausonius Præsul hic Ecclesiæ suæ tamdiu dormivit, & Gregorii seu Vigilantii ipsi Dormitantios; Alexandri Therfitas egerunt. Effecerúntque, hac sive socordia, sive astutia, ut immaculatæ conceptionis assertores Jesuitæ longius progressi, sequenti quarto post Bullam Alexandri VII. editam die, puta d. XI I. Dec. A.M.D.C.LXI. Parisiis in Collegio Claromontano hanc thesin pro assertione Catholica venditaverint: Quid non potuit Dei mater electa? Non tantum plures circumstantias incarnationis probabiliter meruit, verùm etiam maternitatis executionem. Quam novitiam hæresin merito alii statim traduxerunt.
units.tr: CCXXIII. I have said above how Pope Paul showed himself a sluggish Palaemon in settling the controversy over the auxiliary graces and free will, which was fiercely fought between the Jesuits and the Dominicans. Nor did he show a more manly spirit in settling or deciding the controversy concerning the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, whether she was conceived stained with sin or immaculate. This controversy had, through the arts of its intermediaries, long vexed the Roman Church with grave trouble, even with Satanic influence, when at Berne in 1509 the Dominican Wigand Wirt played the second part after the Devil on the stage. Under Pope Paul, from 1614 to 1621, it troubled the Roman Church most seriously, when the most violent movements, renewed by the Dominicans and Franciscans fighting each other, shook not only all of Spain but cast it into peril. Lucas Waddingus, an Irish Minorite and theologian sent to Rome in this very cause by Antonio de Trejo, Bishop of Cartagena and General of the Minorites, has described the history at length. Matters went so far that, to give almost his very words, Spain had blazed into a fire of discord. Did Paul apply a remedy to this evil? Evidently he pitied the unhappy state of Spain, and on 6 July 1616 he issued an Apostolic edict restricting matters; and on 12 September 1617 he renewed the Bull of Sixtus IV, the decrees of the Council of Trent, and the sanctions and constitutions of Pius V. But by omitting a decisive sentence on the doubtful question, he forbade only this, that it should not be asserted in public assemblies that the Blessed Virgin Mary had been conceived in original sin. After many embassies were sent to King Philip from Rome, most urgently demanding a definition of the question, nothing could be achieved. Paul remained so suspended in this business until his death that, although by Waddingus's testimony his inner feeling had inclined toward the Dominicans, he did not venture to pronounce anything certain, for fear of one party or the other. And when, after his death, the disturbances did not subside but seethed even more in Spain, Gregory XV, by a Bull issued on 24 May 1622, extended Paul's decree so far that no one may dare to assert, even in writings or private sermons, that the Blessed Virgin was conceived in sin, except those to whom this has been specially granted by the Apostolic See. Yet in such a way that by this new decree no prejudice be done to the opinion of those who assert the spotted conception. At the same time, in a letter written to Philip IV, the Pope gave this reason for the question not yet being decided: because the eternal Wisdom has not yet unveiled the secrets of so great a mystery. So the defenders of the spotted conception, who had hitherto been more talkative than cicadas, were reduced to silence [ἐχεμυθίαν] and turned into Seriphian frogs. Soon, however, on 22 July, Gregory, wishing also to stop the mouths of the Dominicans, by a new constitution in the form of an indult permitted only the Dominicans, and no others, to dispute and treat about the matter of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin among themselves only, and not among others or with others, and in private conversations. In the earlier decree this had been forbidden to all the defenders of the affirmative opinion. Gregory here plainly imitated the character of that harlot who, while she smiled at one of her lovers, took the hand of another and pressed both so as to satisfy them. At last Alexander VII, roused, as is thought, by the studies of Cardinal Pallavicini, renewed the ancient constitutions of the Popes on this matter and bound them more tightly with heavier penalties. His Bull, issued on 8 December 1661, survives, in which he asserts that the Blessed Virgin was preserved from original sin by the grace of the Holy Spirit going before; yet, to favour the Dominicans, he forbids anyone holding the opinion that the Blessed Virgin was conceived with original sin to incur the charge of heresy, since, says the Bull, it has not yet been decided by the Roman Church and by the Apostolic See, as we do not wish or intend to decide it now. Thus Alexander did not wish or intend to settle a controversy that had been fought so bitterly through almost five centuries and had been conducted through many sad tragedies. And since these men, Sixtus, Pius, Paul, Gregory, and Alexander, wished to be regarded as the supreme judges of the faith in the militant Church, either they lacked the light of the Holy Spirit, or they were struck by a spirit of sleep, or, what is more likely, they were bound by a great fear: namely, lest either the Dominicans, whose power in Spain is very great, especially because of the office of the Inquisition entrusted to them, or the Franciscans, who in this cause are most closely allied with them, or the Jesuits, offended by any decision whatever, should fail the Papal monarchy, which was to be asserted and supported henceforth, and should abandon the roles they had so zealously played until now, along with all the kings and princes and even the Popes themselves, who were less venerable than formidable. For this reason, that Ausonian prelate slept so long in his Church, and Gregory and Vigilantius, the sleepers, acted as Alexander's Thersites. And by this either laziness or cunning they brought it about that the Jesuits, defenders of the immaculate conception, went further. On the fourth day after the publication of Alexander VII's Bull, that is on 12 December 1661, at the Clermont College in Paris, they put forward this thesis as a Catholic assertion: What could not the chosen Mother of God have merited? She merited not only several circumstances of the Incarnation, probably, but also the carrying out of her maternity. This new heresy was rightly denounced at once by others.

units.la: CCXXIV. Eodem Paulo Pontifice, consiliis de propaganda fide novis Romæ cusis, turbarum Æolis Jesuitis, Germaniam universam gravissima tempestas corripuit, & pertinaci bello triginta annorum tantùm non consumpsit. Jesuitæ scilicet, in generis humani perniciem nati, in gratiam heri sui Pontificis, iterum post Carolum V. contra Ecclesias Reformatas bello experiri decreverunt, tentaturi alia via, an pridem cupitis potiri queant. Nacti autem furori suo idoneum instrumentum sunt Ferdinandum, Austriacæ Archiducem, inde Regem Bohemiæ, & post Imperatorem etiam, quem solitis artibus suis, & religionis calumnia consiliis suis innectere voluerunt. Initium facere à Bohemia placuit. In ea regnante & imperante Rodolpho II. A.M.D.C.IX. Euangelici seu Ordines sub Utraque, reclamantibus licet Papa, factione Hispanica, & Consiliariis nonnullis, Jesuitismo infectis, ob fidem, quam Hungaris & Austriacis ad Matthiam fratrem descisccentibus, eidem Rodolpho illibatam servaverant, plenam religionis libertatem, Majestaticis ab Imperatore eodem literis confirmatam, & ad easdem observandas successoribus etiam in Regno obstrictis; adepti sunt. Creati quoque, eodem Rodolpho consentiente, sunt Libertatis Religiosæ tutores & conservatores, composita rite sacra, denique inter Ordines sub Utraque & sub Una specie, hoc est, Evangelicos longè plures, & Pontificios paucos, de mutua pace amicè solenniterque transactum fuit. nequicquam resistentibus tribus Jesuitarum pullis, Popel de Lobkowitz, Regni Cancellario, Guilhelmo Slawata de Chlum, & Jaroslao de Matinitz Smeczansky, adversus quos si turbare quandoque animum inducerent, protestatio Ordinum sub Utraque edita, tabulis Regni, Rodolpho concedente, illata, inter privilegia asservata fuit, ea lege, ut unà cum cæteris Regni privilegiis à Rodolphi successoribus juramento solenni confirmentur. Atque tanta mox Evangelicæ religionis amor & confessio incrementa habuerunt, ut vix centesimus diversarum partium inveniretur amplius. Meditabatur idem Imperator & Rex Bohemiæ Rodolphus superstes adhuc Ordinem pacis, pro conscientiarum libertate aureæ torquis insigni condecorandum; ad cujus societatem Reges & Principes Evangelicos & Pontificios etiam invitare constituerat. Cùmque improles fratris Matthiæ similiter improlis, nec non Ferdinandi Archiducis cleri Pontificii à nutu pendentis utriusque, adeòque libertatem eam post mortem suam concussuri, ingenium suspectû haberet; Ferdinandi fratrem Leopoldum, Episcopum licet Passavii, at civilis animi fidem facientem, bonisque consiliis obtemperaturum, adoptare simul jam destinaverat.
units.tr: CCXXIV. Under the same Pope Paul, when new plans for propagating the faith had been forged at Rome, and the Jesuits, the Aeolus of these disturbances, had stirred up the storm, a most grievous tempest seized all Germany and, through a stubborn war, all but consumed it for thirty years. The Jesuits, born for the ruin of the human race, decided, for the sake of their new master the Pope, to try war once more against the Reformed Churches, after Charles V, intending to attempt by another way whether they could gain what they had long desired. They found a fit instrument for their rage in Ferdinand, Archduke of Austria, afterwards King of Bohemia and then also Emperor, whom by their usual arts and the pretext of religion they wished to bind to their plans. They chose to begin with Bohemia. There, under the reign and rule of Rudolf II, in 1609, the Evangelicals, or the Orders under both kinds, obtained full religious liberty, confirmed by the Emperor himself in a Royal Letter of Majesty, and binding even on successors in the kingdom to observe it. This was granted although the Pope protested, and the Spanish faction and some counsellors infected with Jesuitism objected, on account of the good faith which they had kept toward Rudolf himself, when the Hungarians and Austrians had revolted to his brother Matthias. With Rudolf's consent, they were also appointed guardians and conservators of religious liberty; and sacred matters being duly settled, a mutual peace was amicably and solemnly concluded between the Orders under both kinds, that is, the far more numerous Evangelicals, and the few Papists. Three Jesuit chicks, Popel of Lobkowitz, Chancellor of the Kingdom, William Slawata of Chlum, and Jaroslav of Martinitz Smeczansky, resisted in vain. If they ever intended to disturb this against them, a protest of the Orders under both kinds was issued and entered on the registers of the Kingdom with Rudolf's concession, and kept among the privileges, on the condition that together with the other privileges of the Kingdom it be confirmed by a solemn oath from Rudolf's successors. Soon the love and confession of the Evangelical religion grew so greatly that scarcely one in a hundred of the different parties could be found. The same Emperor and King of Bohemia, Rudolf, while still surviving, was planning an Order of Peace, to be adorned with the badge of the golden collar for the freedom of consciences, to whose fellowship he had resolved to invite Evangelical and Papist kings and princes alike. But since the childless brother Matthias was likewise childless, and Archduke Ferdinand and the Papist clergy, both dependent on his nod, were suspected of intending to shake that freedom after his death, he had already resolved to adopt Ferdinand's brother Leopold, who, though Bishop of Passau, gave good assurance of a civil temper and would follow sound counsel.

units.la: CCXXV.
units.tr: CCXXV.

units.la: Cæterùm ipsa hæc halcyonia sequentium motuum quin & horrendæ deinceps tempestatis præsaga fuerunt. Concurrentibus enim A. M. D. C. XI. infestis Rodolphi & Matthiæ signis, hujus exercitus acie superior tantum Rodolpho mœrorem attulit, ut è vivis statim excesserit. Ita Matthias fasces capessens, de successore solicitus & ipse A. M. D. C. XVII. patruelem suum Ferdinandum Ordinibus paucis tempore messis collectis, & tantùm non invitis obtrusit. cui in Moraviam secedenti Jesuitæ Olomutii arcum triumphalem erexerunt, illique inter alia ornamenta Insignia Austriaca unâ cum alligato catenæ hinc Bohemico Leone, inde Moravica Aquila, appinxerunt. Sequente etiam anno Molzheimii Alsatiæ prodiit ex recens fundata Jesuitarum Academia libellus, in cujus dedicatione Sodales Leopoldum, Academiæ fundatorem, ad igneum adversus Euangelicos Zelum concitârunt exemplo Fratris Ferdinandi, qui, inquiunt, utut hæreticis in Bohemia sub coronationis horam pro more juramentum præstiterit, priùs tamen in Sacrario Ecclesiæ deposituerit, nihil se unquam hæreticis in Ecclesiæ fraudem concessurum. Rebúsque & experiundo constitit, Ferdinandum Euangelicis ore, Papæ verò corde jurâsse. Statim enim initio Regni ejus homines nefarii, consultores pessimi, id unum operam dederunt, ut literas Majestatis convellerent, libertatisque adeò in religione concessiones illas, si non data fide sanctas, certè ingenti subditorum pretio redemptas, cuniculis subruerent, denique injurias injuriis cumulando patientiam Ordinum fatigarent. qui tandem inconsulto impetu abrepti, vi tamen protestationis jam A. M. D. c. IX. adversus turbatores pacis editæ, Smeczanium & Slawatam supra dictos, unâ cum Philippo Fabricio, technarum omnium conscio, è fenestris arcis præcipites dederunt; & mox d. XXIII. Maii, A. M. D. C. XVIII. Jesuitas, ceu malorum omnium Architectos ētos, Regno proscripserunt. Id verò, vigore licet literarum Majestatis attentatum, Cæsar Ferdinandi & Henoticorum, seu Ligistarum instinctu, injuriam læsæ Majestatis interpretatus armis vindicare statim statuit. Neque segniores Ordines defensionem parant, Moravis statim & Silesiis, quòd religionem communem peti cernerent, in Bohemorum partes concedentibus. Interim Matthias fato {ꝰ}functus, & spreto Ferdinando, in ejus locum Fridericus Elector Palatinus Rex Bohemiæ electus est. Atque tum demum
units.tr: Yet this calm was itself a forewarning of the storms that followed, and of the terrible tempest that came after them. In the year 1611 the hostile standards of Rudolf and Matthias met, and the army of Matthias, the victor, brought Rudolf such grief that he at once departed this life. Matthias then took up the reins of power, and in 1617, anxious about his own successor, he forced his cousin Ferdinand upon the Estates, who had been gathered at harvest time in small numbers and were almost unwilling. When Ferdinand withdrew into Moravia, the Jesuits at Olomouc erected a triumphal arch for him and painted on it, among other decorations, the Austrian arms, with the Bohemian lion chained on one side and the Moravian eagle on the other. In the following year a booklet was published at Molsheim in Alsace from the newly founded Jesuit academy. In its dedication the members of the Society urged Leopold, the founder of the academy, to a fiery zeal against the Evangelicals, citing the example of his brother Ferdinand, who, they said, although he had sworn an oath to the heretics in Bohemia at the hour of his coronation, as is customary, nevertheless deposited it first in the sacristy of the church, resolving never to concede anything to the heretics to the church's harm. And by experience it became clear that Ferdinand had sworn with his mouth to the Evangelicals, but with his heart to the Pope. For at the very beginning of his reign, wicked men and the worst counsellors devoted all their efforts to this one end: to overthrow the Letters of Majesty, and to undermine, with secret mines, those concessions of liberty in religion which, if not sanctified by a pledged faith, had at least been bought at a huge price by the subjects. Finally, by piling injury upon injury, they wore out the patience of the Estates. These, at last carried away by a rash impulse, yet relying on the protest issued in 1619 against the disturbers of the peace, threw the aforementioned Smeczanský and Slavata, together with Philip Fabricius, the author of all these schemes, headlong from the windows of the castle. Soon afterwards, on 23 May 1618, the Jesuits, as the architects of all these evils, were banished from the kingdom. But Caesar Ferdinand, at the instigation of the Henotici, that is the Leaguers, judged this act, although carried out under the authority of the Letters of Majesty, to be an injury to his majesty, and at once resolved to avenge it by arms. Nor were the Estates less prompt to prepare their defence; the Moravians and Silesians, seeing that the common religion was under attack, at once joined the cause of the Bohemians. Meanwhile Matthias died, and Ferdinand was set aside; in his place Frederick, Elector Palatine, was elected King of Bohemia. And only then

units.la: mansit alta mente repostum Judicium Paridis, spretaque injuria formæ.
units.tr: The judgment of Paris stayed lodged deep in her mind, and the wrong done to her scorned beauty.

units.la: Mox enim Bohemi à Ferdinando & Henoticis, Duce Maximiliano Bavaro, victi, Praga Metropolis capta, Rex novus pulsus, denique panico terrore perculsi omnes sunt. Fidem victor continuandæ libertatis Bohemis, Moravis & Silesiis, ut facilius universos subjugum mitteret, sanctè promisit, sed mox penitus idem destituit. Statim enim atrocissima insecuta persecutio Euangelicæ religioni panolethriam attulit.
units.tr: For soon the Bohemians were defeated by Ferdinand and the Henotici under Duke Maximilian of Bavaria; Prague, the capital, was taken, the new king was driven out, and at last all were struck with panic terror. The victor solemnly promised the Bohemians, Moravians and Silesians the continuance of their liberty, so that he might more easily subject them all; but he soon abandoned this altogether. For at once a most savage persecution followed, which brought universal ruin upon the Evangelical religion.

units.la: CCXXVI. Juvabit autem novæ & horrendæ Bohemorum persecutionis μηθοδείας novam cognoscere. Neque enim eodem, quo in Anglia, Gallia, Belgio, modo rem aggredi placuit, experientia scilicet edoctis, fortiores illas purgationes, sanguinis innocentis effusiones Cainiticas, vicomburia Hussitica & Hieronymiana, præcipitationes in fodinas Cutenbergenses; ad hæreseon morbos pellendos hactenus adhibitas, parum profuisse. Tentandum esse jam, utrum commoda diæta (sic loquebantur contemptim, cùm Ecclesiis pastores, uxoribus maritos, parentes liberis, bona singulis eriperent, & miseram vitam postea superpondii loco, nullo juris processu, sed per impios cruentósque milites spoliatis, longóque & tetro carcere maceratis vel adimerent, vel in exilium, quod Diætam vocabant, expellerent) curari possint. Hæreticos itaque non mortibus afficiendos (quibus illi tanquam martyriis exultarent) sed aliis viis fatigandos, & ad obedientiam reducendos esse. Proinde & odiosum illud ac durum nomen inquisitionis, in mollius Reformationis commutandum esse. Hoc decretum in secreto sacróque Consilio Romæ A. M. D. C. XVII. inter medios belli apparatus, initum conclusumque esse, certis indiciis post innotuit, & eventu ipso comprobatum est. Hispanus certè nonnemo, clarum per flagitia nomen adeptus, Martinus de Huerda, palam gloriari auditus est, cùm nuntium de victis Bohemis Viennam advolâsset, authorem se Cæsari fuisse, ut promiscuis adversus hæreticos coëdibus sæviret, & internecione universos deleret; at respondisse Cæsarem: Datam jam esse per Bavariæ Ducem Bohemis fidem: neque tamen defuturos modos, quibus hæresis & rebellandi libido gentis efferæ retundatur. Primò igitur omnium imbelles Anabaptistas, nullis in mundo præsidiis innixos proscripserunt: inde Euangelicos variis artibus aggressi, sensim eos tum nimiis exactionibus, tum oppressionibus, promissis, minis, etiam tormentis, carcere, partim ad apostasiam, partim ad fugam & exilia compulerunt: taliique, si Diis placet, diæta, universam Bohemiam, Moraviam & Austriam postliminio Romano Pontifici subjecerunt. non tam Diocletiani, Maxentii, Philippi Hispani, Caroli IX. leoninas meras, quàm Juliani apostatæ vulpinas cum leoninis mixtas artes imitati. Historiam vir doctissimus & integerimus, testis αὐτόπτης, historiæ persecutionum Bohemicarum author, cap. 45. 46. &c. narravit: qui merito cap. 107. his verbis hostibus, dicæta sua Bohemiam reformantibus, insultavit: Egregiam verò laudem & spolia ampla retulistis, ô animarum lenones! Gregem Epicuræorum effecistis, qui ollas sectantes, ob cucumeres & pepones, & porrum, & cæpas, Ægypti mancipia fieri sustinuerunt. Quin atheismi femine consevistis corda hominum, plerisque jam nihil credentibus; & ne quid conscientiam opio vestro sopitam remorderet, omnem Dei cultum sublatum, cupientibus. Si mitius loquamur: ecquid lucri, ut homines vos mentiri adigatis? An enim omnes illos, quos novum vestrum Catholicifmum profiteri coegistis, veftrates esse confiditis? Removete, quaeso, ab altera parte aurum & illecebras, ab altera gladios, eculeos & alia crudelitatis instrumenta, conscientiarumque libertatem restituite: quam ferio vestra sint amplexi, mox videbitis. Si igitur pfeudoamicus est, qui alterius fortunam sequitur, non animum; Vos cur tam stolidi estis, ut vobis tantopere de iis, qui assentandi solum gratia, aut coacti veftrae victoriae fortunam sequuntur gratulamini. Fastus Babylonicus stimulat vos, ut quacunque ratione allecti vel adacti, ad adorandam aueam vestram statuam populi, & nationes, & linguae veftrum sonum tibiae, citharae, sambucae, nablii, & omnium instrumentorum Musicorum audiant; Vos autem vino fcortationis inebriati, fecurius, & in majori spectantium ac plaudentium numero, jucundius consuetas choreas ducere possetis. Sed bene est, quod adventare scimus tempus, quo vocem Citharoedorum & Musicorum, in te, o Babylon, cessare faciet Dominus.
units.tr: CCXXVI. It will be worth while to learn the new and dreadful methods of the persecution of the Bohemians. For it was not their wish to proceed in the same manner as in England, France and Belgium, since they had learned by experience that those harsher purgings, the shedding of innocent blood worthy of Cain, the burnings of Hus and Jerome, and the casting of men into the mines of Kuttenberg, had done little good in driving out the diseases of heresy, which had been applied until now. It must be tried now whether they could be cured by a mild diet (so they spoke contemptuously, when they were taking away from the churches their ministers, from wives their husbands, from parents their children, and from individuals their goods, and when, without any legal process, they were stripping the wretched people by impious and bloody soldiers and wearing them down in long and foul prisons, or expelling them into exile, which they called the Diet). Heretics, therefore, were not to be put to death, which would have made them exult as in martyrdom, but were to be worn down by other means and brought back to obedience. Accordingly, that hateful and harsh name of Inquisition was to be changed into the gentler name of Reformation. This decree was drawn up in the secret and sacred council at Rome in 1617, amid the preparations for war; this was learned afterwards from certain signs, and was confirmed by the outcome itself. At any rate, a certain Spaniard, Martin de Huerta, famous for his crimes, was heard openly boasting that when the news of the defeated Bohemians had flown to Vienna he had been the author of the proposal to Caesar that he should rage against the heretics with indiscriminate slaughter and destroy them all to the last man; but Caesar replied: The Duke of Bavaria has already given the Bohemians a pledge of faith; yet there will not be lacking ways by which the heresy and the rebellious lust of a savage people may be curbed. First, therefore, they proscribed the unarmed Anabaptists, who rested on no defences in the world. Then they attacked the Evangelicals by various arts, and gradually, partly by excessive exactions, partly by oppressions, promises, threats, even torments and prison, they drove them, some to apostasy and some to flight and exile. And by such a diet, if it pleases the gods, they subjected all Bohemia, Moravia and Austria again to the Roman Pontiff. In this they imitated not so much the lion-like arts of Diocletian, Maxentius, Philip of Spain and Charles IX, as the fox-like arts of Julian the Apostate, mixed with lion-like ones. A most learned and upright man, an eyewitness and author of the history of the Bohemian persecutions, has recounted this history in chapters 45, 46 and following; and he rightly, in chapter 107, insulted those enemies who were reforming Bohemia by their diet, in these words: Truly you have brought back a splendid praise and ample spoils, O panders of souls! You have made a herd of Epicureans, who, pursuing the pots, endured to become slaves of Egypt for the sake of cucumbers and melons, leeks and onions. Indeed, you have sown the seed of atheism in men's hearts, so that most now believe nothing; and, lest anything should trouble the conscience lulled by your opium, you desire all worship of God to be abolished. To speak more mildly: what profit is there in forcing men to lie? Do you trust that all those whom you have compelled to profess your new Catholicism are yours? Remove, I beg you, gold and allurements from one side, and from the other side the swords, racks and other instruments of cruelty, and restore liberty of conscience; then you will soon see how sincerely they embrace your faith. If, therefore, he is a false friend who follows another's fortune and not his mind, why are you so foolish as to rejoice so greatly over those who follow your victorious fortune merely for the sake of flattery, or under compulsion? Babylonian pride urges you, that by whatever means men are enticed or driven to adore your golden statue, and that nations and tongues may hear at the sound of your pipe, harp, sackbut, psaltery and all musical instruments; while you, drunk with the wine of fornication, might lead your customary dances more securely and more gladly before a greater number of spectators and applauders. But it is well, for we know that the time is coming when the Lord will make the voice of harpers and musicians cease in you, O Babylon.

units.la: CCXXVII. Nunquam majori in discrimine positae erant res Euangelicorum, quam post illam cladem Bohem- orum.
units.tr: CCXXVII. The affairs of the Evangelicals were never in greater danger than after that defeat of the Bohemians.

units.la: Jesuitae enim jam quasi parta de universa Germania, imo omnibus Euangelicis, victoria insolenter triumpharunt, ac nil nisi coedes Protestantium, haereticorum excidia spirarunt. Ausuisque est eorum alimonia, servitio, cultu, omnibus externis infectus & conductus flagitiosissimus Grammaticus, Gaspar Schoppius, (sive ut se Italice appellari maluit, Scioppius) vibex & macula suae gentis, ex Palatinatu quippe Superiore Neogora oriundus, ob scelera Altorfi patrata ad apostasiam prolapsus, furiosus Alastor, & vivorum cerberus merito a Theodosio Berenico, (quod sibi nomen integerimum pectus, Mathias Berneggerus, qui Classicum belli edita tuba pacis doctissimè dicuisset ; induerat) dictus, sacri belli classicum canere, Protestantium omnium ferale excidium promittere, ipsisque adeo Regibus & Principibus Euangelicis (Classis pag. 4. & 56.) restim patibulúmque minari, ipse furcifer potius à restione collare, & si quid pejus, promeritus, quamcunque etiam sibi ex sanguinarii dogmatis diritate asserta, & portentosis mendaciis, vel opimam Episcopen, vel purpureum etiam galerum receperit. qua spe adeo miser defraudatus est, ut extrema senecta scriptis Patavio, ubi præ Jesuitarum, proditorem post irritam proditionem flagrantissimo & internecino odio profequentium, metu delitescebat, Leidam exaratis literis, ad Euangelicos reditum obtulerit, rejectus apostata contemptúsque ob vanitatem meritò. Sed & Pontifex ipse Paulus, invalescente Ferdinandum inter & Fredericum bello, universo per Italiam clero bis sex decimas, unas in monasteria, collegia, Ecclesias, &c. alteras in personarum ecclesiasticarum reditus ; in belli imminentis sumptus imperavit ; atque eodem Italiæ exemplo reliquum etiam clerum in aliis regionibus ad largiendum impulit, ad sacerimúmque ita bellum, classico veluti cantato, conclamavit.
units.tr: For the Jesuits, now as if they had already won all of Germany, and indeed all the Evangelicals, triumphed insolently and breathed nothing but the slaughter of Protestants and the destruction of heretics. Then there emerged that most infamous grammarian, Gaspar Schoppius (or Scioppius, as he preferred to be called in Italian), the disgrace and blot of his own nation. Born in Neumarkt in the Upper Palatinate, he fell into apostasy after crimes committed at Altdorf. Kept, hired and steeped in every kind of foreign service and cult, he became a raging Alastor and a cerberus of the living. He was rightly called Theodosius Berenicus (the name Matthias Berneggerus had assumed, a man of upright heart who had most learnedly sounded the trumpet of peace before sounding the signal of war). Schoppius sounded the signal of holy war, promised the utter destruction of all Protestants, and threatened the Evangelical kings and princes themselves with the rope and the gallows (Classis pp. 4 and 56). He deserved to be hanged from the gibbet rather than a collar, and anything worse. For his bloodthirsty doctrine and monstrous lies, he hoped to receive either a rich bishopric or even a red hat. He was so miserably cheated of this hope that in his extreme old age, from Padua, where he hid in fear of the Jesuits, who pursued the traitor after his failed treason with burning and deadly hatred, he sent letters to Leiden offering to return to the Evangelicals. He was rejected, and as an apostate he was deservedly despised for his vanity. Pope Paul himself, too, when the war between Ferdinand and Frederick was flaring up, ordered the whole clergy throughout Italy to pay twelve tenths: one part for monasteries, colleges and churches, and the other from the revenues of ecclesiastical persons, to meet the costs of the impending war. Following this Italian example, he also urged the rest of the clergy in other regions to give generously, and so he proclaimed this most holy war, as though sounding the trumpet.

units.la: CCXXVIII. Ex Bohemia translatum bellum est in Palatinatum, qui brevi totus, deserto ignavia, an fide mala dicam, amicorum communem causam destituentium in felice exitu ; Friderico, in Cæsaris potestatem redactus, colla jugo Pontificis subdere jussus est. Excepit passiva gentium populorúmque defectio, & pauci exilium pati, quàm veritatem semel agnitam abnegare maluerunt. Reformatis in ordinem redactis persecutio ad Lutheranos etiam, seu otiosos calamitatum præteritarum spectatores, seu Cæsareanorum etiam moliminum incautos, & seductos à cerebrosis & implacabilibus, in Schola crucis non edoctis, publicíque commodi moratoribus Theologis nonnullis, satellites, penetravit. In eo scilicet Cæsareanorum consilia steterant, ut Germania universa ad domus Austriacæ, Pontificis verò inprimis Romani obsequium reduceretur. Hinc ingens illud & pertinax tricennale bellum intestinum Germanicum, in quo plus sanguinis fusum, quàm aquas Danubius, Rhenus & Albis volvit: hinc miserima florentissimarum Provinciarum vastitas. Intra unum certè Magdeburgum Tillius triginta hominum millia & amplius obtruncata in Albim conjecit, ipsámque urbem vetustissimam & amplissimam funditus evertit. Hoc primum trophæum fuit, quo reliquæ civitates, præsertim Norimberga, Augusta, Ulma, Ratisbona, aliæque admonerentur, quid in secreto de propaganda fide consilio conclusum sit. Accessit ad depopulationes promiscuas, in quibus pari sorte amici & inimici premebantur, edictum Cæsareum, die VI. Martii A.M.D.C.XXIV. promulgatum, altioris planè indaginis, quo Protestantibus, ut bona Ecclesiastica dignitatésque inde à Pacificatione Passaviensi, annorum septuaginta quinque intervallo medio occupatas, clero Pontificio restituant, severè injunctum. Denique ita fortuna Pontificiis lenocinante, sic omnia gerebantur, ut Protestantium omnium jugulum peti nemini ampliùs ambiguum esset. Rebus ita inclinatis conclamatísque, suscitavit Deus ab Aquilone felicissimum fortissimúmque libertatis Germanicæ Vindicem, Gustavum Adolphum, Suecorum Regem, qui, ceu fulmen quoddam ab ultimo Septentrione, admirabili celeritate universam victoriis suis Germaniam peragravit, ac omnia Jesuitarum & homicidarum Papalium consilia, tot annorum conatus machinationésque repente disjecit & irrita redditit. Duabus victoriis, ad Lipsiam una, altera ad Lutzenam, ita Henoticorum ferocia domita est, ut non modò Protestantium partes superiores evaderent, sed ipsi etiam Papistæ de summa rerum periclitarentur. Immensi operis utique esset, omnes recensere victorias, quas invictum Dei robur ex eo tempore Euangelicis indulsit. Quem vero funestissimum isthoc bellum exitum habuerit, in loco, quantum instituti ratio exiget, exponere haud superseedebimus.
units.tr: CCXXVIII. The war was carried from Bohemia into the Palatinate, which, within a short time, was wholly subdued, its friends deserting it through cowardice (or, shall I say, through bad faith) and abandoning the common cause. With a fortunate outcome for the Emperor, Frederick was reduced to his power and ordered to bend his neck to the yoke of the Pope. A passive defection of peoples and nations followed, and few chose exile rather than deny the truth once acknowledged. When the Reformed had been brought back into line, the persecution also reached the Lutherans. Some were idle spectators of past calamities, others were careless and seduced by the Emperor's schemes, and some were led on by madmen and implacable men who had not been taught in the school of the cross, and by a few theologians who were guardians of public advantage. Their satellites penetrated everywhere. The plan of the Emperor's advisers was that all Germany should be brought back to obedience to the house of Austria and, above all, to the Roman Pope. Hence arose that huge and stubborn Thirty Years' War, the internal German war, in which more blood was poured out than the Danube, Rhine and Elbe carry in their waters. Hence came the most wretched devastation of the most flourishing provinces. In Magdeburg alone, Tilly cut down and threw into the Elbe more than thirty thousand men, and utterly overthrew that most ancient and most extensive city. This was the first trophy, by which the remaining cities, especially Nuremberg, Augsburg, Ulm, Regensburg and others, were warned of what had been decided in secret about the propagation of the faith. To the indiscriminate plundering, in which friends and enemies alike were oppressed by the same fate, was added the Imperial edict, promulgated on 6 March 1624. It was a plan of much deeper design, and it strictly enjoined the Protestants to restore to the Papist clergy the ecclesiastical goods and dignities they had occupied since the Peace of Passau, an interval of seventy-five years. Finally, with fortune flattering the Papists, everything went in such a way that no one could any longer doubt that the throat of every Protestant was being sought. When affairs had thus tilted and been given up for lost, God raised up from the North the most fortunate and most courageous defender of German liberty, Gustavus Adolphus, King of the Swedes. Like a thunderbolt from the farthest North, he traversed all Germany with his victories at astonishing speed, and suddenly scattered and made void all the plans of the Jesuits and the Papal murderers, and the efforts and machinations of so many years. By two victories, one at Leipzig and the other at Lützen, the ferocity of the Henotici was so subdued that not only did the Protestant side prevail, but the Papists themselves were in danger for the whole outcome. It would indeed be an immense task to recount all the victories that the unconquered strength of God granted to the Evangelicals from that time on. What the outcome of this most deadly war was, we shall not hesitate to set out in its proper place, as far as the plan of this work requires.

units.la: CCXXIX. Non dissimulanda hic videtur terribilis laniena Volturenensis, in valle Telina, Canis seu Grisonibus obnoxia, à Pontificiis adversus Euangelicos d. ix. x. &c. Julii A. M. D. C. XX. infandum in modum patrata. Litigaverat diu Provincia, quos penes Vallis jus & dominium stet. Lite ad Rhætos delata, dederunt illi Recuperatores, quos causa & religio Euangelicis æquiores fecit. In Recuperatorio judicio Pontificii, cœdis ac turbarum convicti, carcere, exilio, tormentis, securi pro merito multati sunt. Ancipiti motu, plures mortis metu in proxima Mediolanensis ditionis oppida profugerunt; ibique cum exulibus sæpe congressi, odio religionis, desperatione, inopiaque ad audaciam accensi, in partes traxerunt Papanos, Vallis incolas, tandemque vi atque armis agendum, & sacrorum novitatem inusitato etiam modo abolendam statuerunt. Suasor authorque consilii erat Jacobus Robustellus, equestris nobilitatis homo; complices præcipui Antonius Paravicinus, Sondrienits Archipresbyter, Johannes Guizardus, Johannes & Franciscus Venostæ, qui sicarios plerosque veneficiis, homicidiis, furtis, perjuriis infames, ex ditione Mediolanensi, Veneta, Tridentina conduxerunt. Cum tali manu Robustellus, qui super insitam naturæ ferociam, damnationis memoria, & instauratæ religionis odio abripi se passus est, Vallem Telinam subitus irrupit, & cuncta ferro, sanguine, igni miscuit. Pufcianum Castellum opportunè situm, simul transitus Alpium milite insedit, atque inde expedita manu Tiranum processit, ibique Euangelicos plerosque inermes oppressit; caeteros ad mutandam religionem pavore coëgit; Urbis Præfectum, Rhæticæ gentis & Provinciæ procuratorem inclementer ad laqueum damnavit. Post Carolus & Azo Bestæ seu bestiæ centuriones, diversos Provinciæ aditus invadunt. Carolus Tilio oppido improviso impetu occupato in Templo Euangelicos interceptos inopinanter horribiliter trucidavit. Quidam in campanile profugi fumo flammáque suffocati sunt. Sanctitas Templi inviolatos non servavit; nec misericordiæ locus ullus, quamvis supplices palmas tenderent. Inde Antonius Paravicinus Morbergum, Bertennum, Caspanum, Mantellum, Tropanum, & proxima quæque loca partibus adjunxit. Lætus his cladibus Robustellus, tota Valle potitus, ad Sondrium, urbem primariam, vi vel terrore subigendam ducit. Advenientem Pontificii prompti excipiunt: Euangelici ceu alterum Busiridem pertimescunt merito. Statim igitur iis promiscuè mortem diram acerbámque inflixit; implacabili ferocia eorum bona diripuit, ædes diruit aut incendit, parentes occidit, liberos conjuges seu ejecit, seu cladi implicuit, matres ab extremo complexu liberorum avulsas immaniter trucidavit. Sub adventum ejus nonnulli, ut barbaram crudelitatem effugerent, in montes sese abdiderant. Obscuritas latebrarum paucos texit: caeteri flebiles inopésque cœsi sunt. Ita Robustellus in exigua adeò Provincia quingentorum (inter quos ne Pontificiis quidem, qui à dirae immanitatis scelere abhorrentes in ejus societatem non venerunt, pepercit) strage edita, Vallis Telinæ præfectus receptus, advocatis tandem Mediolano Iberi cohortibus patriam insuper turpissimè prodidit, & vindicum justissimorum hac quidem in terra manus effugit. Si rabiem sævitiámque latronum spectes, præteritorum temporum omnium cru-dedelitatem laniena hæc plusquam tartarea longo post se intervallo reliquit. Multi pulvere tormentario ori intruso accensoque perierunt miserè: infantes ex matrum uberibus pendentes transfixi: corpora defunctorum ex sepulchris extracta, canibus & feris lanianda exposita sunt. denique nullum crudelitatis efferatæ genus Cyclopes hi, Hispanicis & Jesuiticis follibus inflati, intentatum infectúmque reliquerunt. In cæsorum censu fuerunt Bartholomæus Marlianus, Joh.
