Baptista Mallerii, Antuerpianus, Belga, (cujus caput amputatum, venter apertus & viscera extracta sunt) Petrus Danzius, Fracifcus Carolinus, Antonius Bassus, verbi Divini præcones; Bartholomæus ac Nicolaus Paravicini, juris utriusque Doctores; Andreas Enderlinus, Rhetorum omnium nomine Tilii, & Johannes à Capaulis Tirani Præfecti. taceo plures præcipuæ nobilitatis & dignitatis viros, qui per Christi & Evangelii causam parricidarum immanissimorum piaculares victimæ facti sunt. Celebratáque inprimis est fœminarum, quas ad necem latrones depoposcerunt, mira constantia ac inter eas Annæ de Liba, quæ Antonelli Crotti de Schio, Vicentini, ob religionem apud Volturenos exulis, uxor, in monte comprehensa, filiolam bimestrem in ulnis gestans, religionem mutare jussa, intrepidè id abnuit, & filiolæ lactandæ gremium aperiens, pectoréque denudato sic latrones allocuta est: Agite, corpus vobis sisto, quod occidere potestis; animam occidere non potestis. hanc in manus tuas, Christe Sospitator, commendo. Nec mora: Filiam in sinu affixam habens, sclopeto occisa, & quatuor in partes dissecta fuit.
units.tr: CCXXIX. The terrible butchery of the Valtelline, in the valley of Telina, subject to the Grisons, carried out in an unspeakable manner by the Papists against the Evangelicals on 9, 10 and following days of July 1620, should not be passed over here. The province had long disputed to whom the right and dominion of the valley belonged. When the case was referred to the Rhaetians, their arbiters, whom the cause and religion made more favourable to the Evangelicals, gave judgment. In the arbitral judgment the Papists, convicted of murder and disorder, were punished with prison, exile, torture and the axe, as they deserved. In a wavering move, many fled in fear of death to the nearby towns of the Milanese dominion, and there, often meeting with the exiles and inflamed to audacity by hatred of religion, despair and poverty, they drew the Papists of the valley into their party. At last they resolved to act by force and arms, and to abolish the newness of the sacred rites in an unusual way. The adviser and author of the plan was Jacob Robustelli, a man of knightly nobility. The chief accomplices were Antonio Paravicini, archpriest of Sondrio, Giovanni Guizardi, and Giovanni and Francesco Venosta. They hired many hitmen, infamous for poisonings, murders, thefts and perjuries, from the Milanese, Venetian and Trentine territories. With such a band Robustelli, who allowed himself to be carried away by the ferocity of his nature, the memory of his condemnation, and hatred of the restored religion, suddenly broke into the valley of Telina and mixed everything with sword, blood and fire. He garrisoned the well-placed castle of Pusciano, which controlled the passes of the Alps, and from there advanced to Tirano with a light force. There he oppressed many unarmed Evangelicals, and forced the others by terror to change their religion. He condemned the prefect of the city, the procurator of the Rhaetian people and province, to the noose without mercy. Afterwards Charles and Azo Besta, or Beast, centurions, invaded the various approaches to the province. Charles seized the town of Tirano by a sudden attack, and in the church he unexpectedly and horribly butchered the Evangelicals he had trapped there. Some who had fled into the bell tower were suffocated by smoke and flames. The sanctity of the church did not save the unhurt, nor was there any room for mercy, though they stretched out suppliant hands. Then Antonio Paravicini added to his side Morbegno, Berbenno, Caspano, Mantello, Tirano and every neighbouring place. Robustelli, delighted by these slaughters and having seized the whole valley, led his army to Sondrio, the chief city, to subdue it by force or terror. The Papists readily received him as he came, while the Evangelicals, rightly fearing him as another Busiris, [trembled]. So he at once inflicted a dreadful and bitter death on them indiscriminately. With implacable ferocity he plundered their goods, demolished or burned their houses, killed the parents, and either drove out the children and wives or involved them in the disaster, and he savagely slaughtered the mothers torn from the last embrace of their children. At his approach some, to escape his barbarous cruelty, had hidden themselves in the mountains. The darkness of the hiding places covered a few, and the rest were struck down, weeping and helpless. Thus Robustelli, in so small a province, after a slaughter of five hundred people (and he spared not even those Papists who, abhorring the crime of such dreadful savagery, had not joined his company), was received as prefect of the Valtelline valley. Finally, when Spanish troops had been summoned from Milan, he most shamefully betrayed his country as well, and escaped the hand of the most just avengers on this earth. If you look at the rage and savagery of these brigands, this butchery, more than hellish, has left behind it, at a long interval, the cruelty of all past times. Many perished wretchedly when gunpowder was forced into their mouths and set alight. Infants hanging from their mothers' breasts were pierced through. The bodies of the dead were dug out of their graves and exposed to be torn by dogs and wild beasts. In short, these Cyclopes, inflated by Spanish and Jesuit bellows, left no kind of cruelty untried or unperformed. Among the slain were Bartolomeo Marliano, Giovanni Battista Mallerii of Antwerp, a Fleming (whose head was cut off, whose belly was opened and whose entrails were drawn out), Pietro Danzio, Francesco Carolino, Antonio Basso, heralds of the divine Word; Bartolomeo and Niccolò Paravicini, doctors of both laws; Andreas Enderlin, on behalf of all the Rhaetians in Tirano; and Giovanni da Capaul, prefect of Tirano. I pass over the several men of chief nobility and dignity who became the atoning victims of the most savage murderers for the cause of Christ and the Gospel. Especially celebrated is the remarkable constancy of the women whom the brigands demanded for slaughter. Among them was Anna de Liba, wife of Antonello Crotti of Schio in Vicenza, an exile at Valtellina on account of religion. Seized on the mountain, carrying her two-month-old daughter in her arms, she was ordered to change her religion, and she fearlessly refused. Opening her bosom to feed her little daughter, and baring her breast, she addressed the brigands thus: Come on, I offer you my body, which you can kill; you cannot kill my soul. Christ, my Saviour, I commend this into your hands. Without delay, she was shot with a musket while holding her daughter fixed to her breast, and was cut into four pieces.

units.la: Peracto inauditæ atrocitatis scelere non tantùm literis ad Episcopum Curiensem exaratis de læto successu magnopere gloriati, illud una sancta resolutione, & una honorata intrapresa, hoc est, sanctam resolutionem & honorificum facinus insignire non erubuerunt: sed etiam Rationes & motiva con-
units.tr: When the deed of unheard-of atrocity was done, they not only boasted greatly of its happy outcome in letters written to the Bishop of Chur, but did not blush to describe it as a holy resolution and an honourable undertaking, that is, to mark a holy resolve and an honourable crime; they also set out the reasons and motives con-

units.la: A clero et Pontifice illa defenditur & probatur. filii sui contra haereticos initi vulgare ausi, putidissimis mendaciis & calumniis turpitudinem detestabilis maleficii obvelare conati sunt. Quin & Romam missus Pater Ignatius Capucinus, tum laetum Pontifici Paulo ob excisos ferro flammaque haereticos nuntium laturus, tum Curiensi Episcopo Volturenam Pontificia authoritate & opera conciliaturus. Non probari sibi violentiam, tum Paulus simulasse dicitur. Sed paulo post Jacobo-Paribello, Paravicino, Archiepiscopo Sondriensi, Sacrificulo Casponensi non tam violentiam exprobravit, quam violentiam se inscio & inconsulto susceptam. minime eam dissuasurus, dum in conscientiam sceleris admissus esset. Responderunt Cyclopes, non tam se conscientiam Pontificis reformidasse, quam metu anxios, ne per Cardinales Gallis & Venetis addictos secretum vulgaretur, seorsim negotium agitasse. Sed & Horatius Taurellus, Volturenus, Jesuita, ad Leopoldum Archiducem Austriae missus, sacram istam carnificinam utilitatis publicae, religionisque velo tegere conatus est. Ne non Circaeis Romae veneficiis excantatos, non tam sub ferarum figura humanam mentem, quam sub humana specie tetras pestiferasque belluas tegentes, ad audendum inexpiabile scelus prorupisse, Ecclesiae Romanae hyperaspistae caussari possint.
units.tr: The clergy and the Pontiff defended and approved these things. They dared to publish the undertakings of their sons against the heretics, and tried to veil the foulness of the detestable crime with the most putrid lies and calumnies. Indeed, Father Ignatius the Capuchin was sent to Rome, to bring the Pope Paul the joyful news that heretics had been cut down by sword and flame, and to win over the Bishop of Chur to Volturenus by papal authority and effort. Paul is said to have pretended that he did not approve of the violence. But shortly afterwards, to Jacob Paribellus, Paravicinus, the Archbishop of Sondrio, and the priest of Casponum, he reproached not so much the violence as the fact that it had been undertaken without his knowledge and counsel. He was by no means going to dissuade it, since he had been admitted to knowledge of the crime. The Cyclopes replied that they had not so much feared the Pope's knowledge as, anxious lest the secret be divulged through cardinals devoted to the French and the Venetians, they had handled the business separately. Horatio Taurellus, Volturenus, a Jesuit, sent to Leopold, Archduke of Austria, also tried to cover that sacred butchery with the veil of public utility and religion. Nor can the defenders of the Roman Church plead that men bewitched by Circean spells at Rome, who hid foul and deadly beasts under a human appearance rather than hiding a human mind under the form of beasts, broke out to dare the inexpiable crime.

units.la: CCXXXX. Paulo V. die x. Octobr. A. M. D. C. XXI. mortuo, & anno ejus emortuali ejusmodi eteosticho: Mortuus est VICe DeVs, signato; Alexander Lodovisius, Cardinalis & Archiepiscopus Bononiensis, qui Gregorii XV. nomen sumpsit, per viam adorationis, uti loquuntur, Papa electus est.
units.tr: CCXXXX. When Paul V died on 10 October 1621, and his death year was marked by the chronogram Mortuus est VICe DeVs (He is dead, the Vice-God, the capitals giving the date), Alexander Lodovisius, Cardinal and Archbishop of Bologna, who took the name Gregory XV, was elected Pope by way of adoration, as they say.

units.la: Adhaesit ei foemina quinquagenaria, versipellis, & negotiorum peritissima, cujus consiliis viribus universum fere Papatum, effoeminatus ipse administravit. Statim atque electus est, constitutionem de forma eligendi Papam edidit, qua, ut tacitis deinceps suffragiis Pa-
units.tr: A fifty-year-old woman, wily and most skilled in affairs, attached herself to him; by her counsels and powers he, being effeminate himself, administered almost the whole Papacy. As soon as he was elected, he issued a constitution on the form of electing a Pope, by which he decreed that from then on the Pope should be chosen by silent votes,

units.la: Papa eligatur, ne innotescere Principibus, cui electores suffragium præbuerint, posset, sanxit. Arte tum Chrysopoëtica, tum Theopoëtica usus, ad quæstuosissimum τὸ ἐξθεάζειν (liceat Herodiani voce uti) Deificandi artificium se convertens, per auream ἀποθεώσεως seu canonizationis (voce nova & barbara rem novam barbaram & impiam designare libuit) scalam in Cœlum Pontificium intulit non unum, sed plures æternitatis candidatos, hactenus quidem Beatos, sed non Sanctos; at nunc demum Gregorii opera seu factos seu declaratos Sanctos, puta Jesuitas quatuor, Ignatium Loyolam, societatis patrem, Franciscum Xaverium (Indorum Apostolum illum, cujus mendacia & nugas Indis venditatas ex historia Christi Perficè edita primus Ludovicus de Dieu produxit, ejusque post indicio fœdos lapsus Brochmannus Antopol. p. 2432. &c. deduxit) Aloisium Gonzagam, & Stanislaum Coskam; nec non Theresiam Hispanicam, Carmelitarum discalceatorum matrem; Philippum Nerium, Congregationis Oratorii authorem; Isidorum Agricolam, Hispanum itidem; Ambrosium Sonsedonium, Senensem, & Jacobum Saloniomum, Venetum. Prodiit mox è prœlo Ribadeneirae Jesuitæ Flos Sanctorum, ex Hispanica in Latinam Linguam traductus, in quo non tantùm Sancti fixi, sed etiam Extravagantes, ac inter eos etiam novitia isthæc Numina novis Legendis honorantur. Parùm etiam abfuit, quin Garnettus etiam straminea quadam impostura si non ad Sanctitatem, at certè ad Beatitudinem ascenderet. eam scilicet commeritus, quòd in gratiam Romani Molochi non tantùm filios & filias, sed Regem & Patriam per ignem sulphureum transmittere conatus est. Et Thasii quidem olim Deum Agesilaum cùm facerent, non insipidè homo nasutus retulit, si Deos faciendi potestatem habeant Thasii, priùs seipsos Deos facerent, quàm alios Deificarent. Idem Gregorio, idem aliis
units.tr: so that it could not become known to princes to whom the electors had given their votes. Using both the alchemical and the theological arts, and turning to the most profitable art of deifying (I may use the word of Herodian), to exthe­azein [τὸ ἐξθεάζειν] deifying, he brought into the Papist heaven, by a golden ladder of apotheosis [ἀποθεώσεως] or canonization (I chose to designate a new, barbarous thing by a new and barbarous word), not one but several candidates for eternity: hitherto Blessed, but not Saints; now at last made or declared Saints by Gregory's work. These were four Jesuits: Ignatius Loyola, father of the society; Francis Xavier (the apostle of the Indians, whose lies and trifles, sold to the Indians, were first brought to light from a fully published history of Christ by Ludovicus de Dieu, and whose later foul slips were pointed out by Brochmann, Antopol. p. 2432 &c.); Aloysius Gonzaga; and Stanislaus Kostka. Also Teresa of Spain, mother of the Discalced Carmelites; Philip Neri, author of the Congregation of the Oratory; Isidore the Labourer, likewise Spanish; Ambrose Sansedonius of Siena; and James Salonius of Venice. Soon the press of the Jesuit Ribadeneira produced the Flower of the Saints, translated from Spanish into Latin, in which not only the fixed saints but also the Extravagant ones are honoured, and among them these new deities are honoured with new Legends. Garnet also came close, by a certain straw imposture, if not to sanctity, at least to beatitude, which he deserved, namely because for the sake of the Roman Moloch he tried to send through sulphurous fire not only sons and daughters but also the King and the Country. A shrewd man rightly remarked, when the Thasians once made Agesilaus a god, that if the Thasians had the power of making gods, they should first make themselves gods before deifying others. The same was done for Gregory, the same for others,

units.la: & Jesuitas quatuor
units.tr: and four Jesuits

units.la: aliàsque in Divorum numerum refert. Numinum novorum architectis, qui nobis Ethnicæ & Judaicæ Apotheoseos editionem, auctiorem fortasse aliquo modo, sed neutiquam emaculatiorem vel emendatiorem, dederunt, merito regesseris.
units.tr: and others into the number of the Divine. You would rightly enrol these men among the architects of the new divinities, who have given us an edition of Ethnic and Jewish apotheosis, perhaps enlarged in some way, but by no means more purified or emended.

units.la: CCXXXI. Sed forte non plane apotheosi omni caruit Gregorius, belligeri in Mavortis, siderati Numinis locum suffectus. Nam bella certè ciendi & alendi haud plane indoctum fuisse, historia prodit. Testis est Carolus Carafa Comment. de Germ. restaur. pag. 95. 96. Gregorium hunc non tantum Ferdinando Cæsari ob exactum Regno Bohæmiæ Fridericum Optimum impensè gratulatum esse; sed eidem etiam in subsidium exercitus, & pecunias, & legiones duas, unam equitum, peditum alteram, Petro Aldobrandino Duce, summisisse, & Bibliothecæ etiam Heidelbergensis nobilissimæ, à Bavaris spoliatæ, splendidissimum munus ceu sacri illius belli manubias à Bavaro oblatas, & in Vaticani delubro paulo post ab Urbano VIII. magno sumptu ornatúque suspensas, dono accepisse. Galliæ etiam Regem Ludovicum XIII. ad bellum Protestantibus inferendum accendere conatus est tum epistola privata ad eum scripta, qua hortatus eum est ad imitationem decessorum suorum, qui Pontificum cohortationes non secus ac Dei jussa venerati sint: quámque his verbis clausit: Sequere, carissime fili, orbis decus, cælestia jussa, effunde iram tuam in gentes, quæ Dominum non noverunt, ut æternæ misericordiæ thesauros compares Majestati tuæ; (Epistolam integram Gramondus Histor. Gall. lib. ix. narrat) tum vulgata per totam Galliam adversus Euangelicos bulla, qua ad excidium eorum fideles suos impulit: tum denique misso Monacho Hispano Franciscanæ sectæ, Dominico JesuMaria, quem Imperator cum spoliis ac manubiis proelii Pragensis Romam miserat, cujusque precibus victoriam illam acceptam tulerat. qui ceu Δυοπετής, Divus quidam CoœCœlo delapsus à Rege & populo exceptus, non destitit conscientiam ejus onerare mandato extremæ fidelium internecionis. Hinc ardens in Gallia persecutio, & partim vi, partim deditione recuperatæ urbes nonnullæ, quas securitatis gratia Euangelicis Henricus IV. concesserat. Adversus Genevenses idem Gregorius hostilia agitabat, misso ad Regem Galliæ nuntio, veniam impetraturo, ut Sabaudo eos armata manu invadere integrum esset. Sed repulsam à Rege tulit. Indignatus idem Papa est Venetis, quòd conductis à se militibus Græcis Templum, & in eo religionis exercitium permisissent: eo nomine per Cardinales Molnium & Ludoisium graviter cum Veneto Legato expostulans. Cúmque Legatus respondisset, necessitate adactos esse Venetos ad conducendum è Græcia militem, quem è sua ditione conscribi Papa vetuerit; Cardinales subjecerunt, si adversus infideles milite Romano uti vellent, integrum id fore. Quibus falsè idem Legatus regessit, omnes infideles esse, qui Reipublicæ Venetæ ob injustas causas adversarentur. Permitti Romæ, ut fœno & avena templa opleantur. præstare utique, ut ea Christianis ad cultum aperiantur.
units.tr: CCXXXI. But perhaps Gregory was not entirely without apotheosis, having succeeded to the place of the warlike, starry deity Mars. For history shows he was certainly not unskilled at stirring up and feeding wars. Witness Carlo Carafa, Carafa Comment. de Germ. restaur. pag. 95, 96: this Gregory not only heartily congratulated Emperor Ferdinand on Frederick the Best's expulsion from the kingdom of Bohemia, but also sent him, to support his army, money and two legions, one of cavalry and the other of infantry, under the leadership of Pietro Aldobrandini. He also received as a gift from the Bavarian, as spoils of that holy war, the splendid gift of the most noble Heidelberg Library, despoiled by the Bavarians, which Urban VIII soon afterwards hung in the Vatican shrine at great expense and decoration. He also tried to stir King Louis XIII of France to wage war on the Protestants, both by a private letter in which he urged him to imitate his predecessors, who revered the exhortations of the Popes no less than the commands of God, and closed with these words: Follow, dearest son, glory of the world, heavenly commands; pour out your wrath on the nations that do not know the Lord, that you may win for your Majesty the treasures of eternal mercy. (Gramondus, Histor. Gall. lib. ix., relates the whole letter.) He also did so by a bull published throughout France against the Evangelicals, by which he impelled his faithful to their destruction; and finally by sending the Spanish monk of the Franciscan sect, Dominic Jesu Maria, whom the Emperor had sent to Rome with the spoils and booty of the battle of Prague, and by whose prayers he had credited that victory. Like a Diopetes [Δυοπετής], a certain divinity fallen from heaven, received by king and people, Dominic did not cease to burden his conscience with the command for the utter destruction of the faithful. Hence a fierce persecution in France, and some cities, which Henry IV had granted to the Evangelicals for their security, were recovered partly by force and partly by surrender. Against the Genevans the same Gregory was plotting hostile action, sending a nuncio to the King of France to obtain permission for the Savoyard to attack them with armed hand. But he met with a rebuff from the King. The same Pope was indignant with the Venetians because they had allowed the Greek soldiers they had hired a temple and the practice of their religion in it; on this account he complained sharply, through the cardinals Molinus and Ludovisius, to the Venetian legate. When the legate replied that the Venetians had been forced by necessity to hire soldiers from Greece, whom the Pope had forbidden to be enrolled from his dominion, the cardinals added that if they wished to use Roman soldiers against infidels, that would be allowed. To this the same legate falsely retorted, that all are infidels who oppose the Venetian Republic for unjust causes. It is allowed at Rome that temples be stuffed with hay and oats. It is at least preferable that they be opened to Christians for worship.

units.la: CCXXXII. Eodem Gregorio Pontifice, circa A. M. D. C. XXIII. Seviliæ in Hispania ingens hominum mul- titudo à Papatu defecit. Et Deficientes sibi nomen Illumi- natorum impostuerunt.
units.tr: CCXXXII. Under the same Pope Gregory, around the year 1623, a huge crowd of people at Seville in Spain fell away from Papacy. The defectors gave themselves the name Illuminati.

units.la: Incertum erat, an Euangelicorum in castra transfiverint, an erronea & fanatica dogmata sectati fuerint. Prius tamen multis creditum est. Constatque non tum demum Illuminatos coepisse, sed superiore jam seculo, in Hispania inprimis, caput protulisse. Nam & Innichum, seu Ignatium Lojolam jam ante A. M. D. X L. ex Hispania profugisse, ne ab Inquisitione, tanquam de Illuminatorum hæresi suspectus comprehenderetur, Melchior Canus peculiari de Societate Jesu scripto, testatus est. Sed hoc inprimis tempore plurimi non ex vulgi duntaxat foe-
units.tr: It was uncertain whether they had gone over to the camp of the evangelicals or had embraced erroneous and fanatical doctrines. Still, many believed the former. It is established that the Illuminati did not begin only then, but had already raised their head in the previous century, especially in Spain. Melchior Canus, in a special writing on the Society of Jesus, testifies that Innichus, or Ignatius Loyola, had already fled from Spain before 1540, lest he be seized by the Inquisition as suspected of the Illuminati heresy. But at this time very many, not only from the dregs of the common people,

units.la: etiam Genevenses accendit,
units.tr: It also inflamed the Genevans,

units.la: & Venetis ob concessum Græcis Templum, irascitur.
units.tr: and he is angered at the Venetians for granting the Greeks a temple.

units.la: In Hispania sectæ Illuminatorum emergens, fœce homines, sed illustribus etiam & splendidis prosapiis oriundi sese partibus illorum adjunxerant. Jamque numerus illorum ad decem millia hominum excreverat. Et quo graviori ab Inquisitoribus crudelitate in eos sævitum est, hoc magis crebrescere illi & radices agere cœperunt. Quamobrem persecutione superseder̄e, & spe veniæ ad gremium ecclesiæ aberrantes invitare, propositio tamen graviorum etiam supplicium metu, si qui animum adversus oblatam gratiam obstinaturi essent, coacti sunt. Blanda isthac vi, & graviore metu seducti, paulatim alii Pontificia postliminio sacra amplexi sunt: alii vero extera in loca concesserunt.
units.tr: In Spain the sect of the Illuminati emerged. Men from the dregs had joined their party, but so had men of illustrious and distinguished birth. Their number had already grown to ten thousand. The more cruelly the Inquisitors raged against them, the more they spread and took root. For this reason they were forced to give up persecution and to invite the wanderers back into the bosom of the Church with the hope of pardon, yet with the threat of heavier punishment, if any should stubbornly resist the offered grace. Led astray by this flattering pressure and the greater fear, some gradually embraced Papist worship again by right of return, while others withdrew to foreign places.

units.la: CCXXXIII. Sede Pontificia obitu Gregorii vacante, & ingressis jam conclave Cardinalibus, ingentes Ro- mæ turbæ subortæ sunt.
units.tr: CCXXXIII. With the papal see vacant on Gregory's death, and the cardinals now shut into the conclave, huge disturbances arose at Rome.

units.la: Plures per plateas trucidati, suffocati aquis, strangulati, naribus auribusque truncati. Raptus, spolia, stupra grassabantur impune. Pars Cardinalium in Mesinum, pars in Borrhomæum inclinabat; æquis utrinque suffragiis. Relicto utroque Galli, Veneti, Sabaudi Maphæum Barbarinum, Florentinum, quòd Hispanorum partibus minùs addictus videretur, præferunt. Fervente negotio & Barbarinus ipse, & cum eo viginti quatuor Cardinales, plurésque etiam Episcopi, Abbates, Equites, Secretiori Conclavi inclusi, lethaliter decumbere cœperunt. Et decem jam Cardinales, aliíque morte subita abrepti, Conclavis veneno infecti suspicionem præbuerunt. Tandem Barbarinus, prævio omine examinis apum, Musæum ejus involantium, Papa proclamatur, qui nomen Urbani VIII. assumpsit; celebris tum ob functiones varias, quas hactenus obivit, tum ob florens ingenium, artificium poëticum, & eruditionem multiplicem, quam in Scholis Jesuiticis sub Horatio Thurselino & Francisco Bonæo plurimum auxit. Certè linguæ GræGræcæ, sine pari Pontifice ullo, adeò peritus fuit, ut Apis Attica nuncupatus fuerit. Statim electus Papa tres fratres ad altiora evehens, natu maximum Carolum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Generalem; secundum Thaddæum arcis S. Angeli præfectum; tertium Antonium Satellitum seu apparitorum suorum ducem creavit. Neque id satis ei fuit. Etiam Franciscum Barbarinum è Fratre Nepotem, adolescentem adhuc in Cardinalium numerum cooptavit, cui pædagogum Ascanium Filomarinum præficere necessum habuit. Adeò animus privatis studiis corruptus diu latere non potuit.
units.tr: Many were butchered in the streets, suffocated in water, strangled, and had their noses and ears cut off. Plunder, robbery, and rape ran riot with impunity. Part of the cardinals leaned toward Mesinus, part toward Borromeo, and the votes were evenly divided. Both being set aside, the French, Venetians and Savoyards favoured Maffeo Barberini, the Florentine, because he seemed less devoted to the Spanish side. While the business was heated, Barberini himself, together with twenty-four cardinals, several bishops, abbots and knights, shut up in the inner conclave, began to fall gravely ill. Ten cardinals, and others carried off by sudden death, aroused suspicion that the conclave had been poisoned. At last Barberini, by the omen of a swarm of bees flying into his museum, was proclaimed Pope and took the name Urban VIII. He was famous both for the various offices he had held until then and for his lively talent, poetic skill and wide learning, which he had greatly improved in the Jesuit schools under Horace Tursellinus and Francis Bonaeus. Indeed he was so skilled in Greek, beyond any other pope, that he was called the Attic Bee. Immediately after his election the Pope raised three brothers to higher office: the eldest, Carlo, as General of the Roman Church; the second, Taddeo, as prefect of the Castel Sant'Angelo; and the third, Antonio, as commander of his guards or attendants. Nor was that enough for him. He also enrolled his brother's nephew, Francesco Barberini, still a young man, among the cardinals, and felt obliged to set Ascanio Filomarino over him as tutor. So a mind corrupted by private concerns could not stay hidden for long.

units.la: CCXXXIV. In Divorum numerum Gregorius, uti supra diximus, Ignatium Lojolam, Xaverium, aliósque retulerat. Cæterùm quas sive morte præventus, sive alias ob causas canonizationis tabulas non confecerat, Urbanus conficere primas inter curas habuit. Extat apud Cherubinum Bullar. Rom. tom. 4. pag. 11. Urbani hujus Canonizatio S. Ignatii Lojolæ, nec non pag. 15. Francisci Xaverii. In Bulla Canonizationis Ignatii præfatur Urbanus, cùm veterem religionem, omnémque perfectioris vitæ professionem Lutherus, monstrum teterrimum, aliaque detestabiles pestes blasphemis eorum linguis in Septentrionis partibus corrumpere, ac Sedis Apostolicæ authoritati detrahere conarentur, excitâsse Deum Spiritum Ignatii Lojolæ, qui ex medio honorum cursu, & à seculari ac terrena militia admirabili quadam ratione vocatus, ita se Divino imperio regendum & formandum tradiderit, ut demum nova Societas Jesu, quæ inter alia pietatis & charitatis opera gentilibus convertendis, hæreticis ad fidei veritatem revocandis, & Romani Pontificis potestati tuendæ ex instituto se totum impenderit, religione fundata, vitam admirabili sanctitate traductam sanctissimo pariter conclusęrit exitu, ac plurimis sit miraculis illustratus. Post Clementis VIII. & Pauli V. laudatis studiis, decretum prædecessoris, ut inter Sanctos omnino transcribatur, Ecclesiæ & altaria in ejus honorem ædificentur, & festum ejusdem die xxxi. Julii celebretur; commemorans, ex processibus & actibus Cardinalium pluscula de Lojolæ ortu, vita, sanctitate & miraculis repetit. Simili feré methodo Xaverii, cujus inprimis miracula fusè prædicantur, canonizatio concepta est. Merito tamen in dubium alii, Pontifi-cii etiam, miracula utriusque tantopere ab Urbano celebrata vocârunt. Quin & Petrus Deza in oratione sua de Ignatii Beatificatione pag. 52. hoc solum iis miraculum tribuit, quòd secus quàm cæteri Ordines religiosi, non tantum mendicent, orent, blandiantur, palpentur, sed etiam felicissimè emendicent, exorent, eblandiantur & expalpentur. Cùm Patres Jesuitæ, verba Dezæ, à Sciopio etiam apostata in Infamia Famiani pag. 159. &c. citata, referam, commoda sua quærunt, idem sibi proponunt consilium cum eo, quod Pharaoni Joseph suggessit, ut copiam frumenti in suis horreis coacervaret. Hoc MIRABILE est, & digitus Dei est hic, quòd hoc tempore adeò perverso & avaro, sicut alii Religiosi experiuntur pauca emendicando, Jesuitæ nôrint & possint abundè, quicquid illis necessarium est, extorquere. Non enim fit sine miraculo, quòd cùm homines sint adeò parci & tenaces, non tamen possunt in animum inducere, ut Jesuitis aliquid denegent, aut aliquam petitionem eorum rejiciant. Quod MIRACVLVM (Jesuiticum) conferri potest cum eo, quod Deus operatus est cum Ægyptiis in favorem populi sui, cùm Judæis mutuò dederunt, quicquid petierunt, quod TOTVM Deus voluit ipsos auferre. Idem omnino fit Jesuitarum respectu, ut totum auferant, quicquid petunt. quod argumento est, eos Deo curæ esse, & ab eo tenerimo affectu cos diligi: quando, qui adeò sunt avari, tamen libenter & cum animi lætitia Patribus istis subministrant, quicquid ipsis necessarium est. Addam verba Sciopii, utpote Jesuitarum quandoque alumni, inter Jesuitarum miracula novum linguarum donum, & vindicatum sibi Patrum nomen, referentis; subjuncta statim: Hoc scilicet est, quod Ignatio & Sociis ejus Christus fuerat pollicitus: Romæ vobis ero propitius. Tanti enim miraculi gratiam Apostolis ut impertiretur, animum inducere non potuit. Signa eos, inquit, sequentur; In nomine meo dæmonia ejicient, linguis loquentur novis, serpentes tollent, & si mortiferum quid biberint, non eis nocebit. Super ægros manus imponent, & bene habebunt. Horum quidem signorum nullum à propitio Jesu Ignatio & sociis ejus contigisse, vel ex vita Ignatii à filio ac discipulo ejus Ribadeneira diligenter conscripta apparet lib. 5. cap. 13. ubi Ignatium ejusmodi miraculis minime illustratum suisse agnoscit. Sed nec Franciscum Xaverium Indiæ, si superis placet, Apostolum, linguis novis loquendi gratia donatum fuisse, ex ipsa ejus confessione, vel dicam, querela constat. quæ talis legitur lib. 3. Indic. Epist. 5. Si nos lingua m calleremus Japonicam, non dubito, quin plurimi fierent Christiani. Faxit Deus, ut eam brevi addiscamus, tum demum aliquam rei Christianæ navabimus operam. Nam nunc quidem inter eos tanquam mutæ statuæ versamur. Tantum abfuit, ut se idoneum à Christo propitio Novi Testamenti ministrum factum, & dono linguarum ea causa affectum Pauli exemplo gloriari posset: Gratias ago Deo, qui omnium verborum lingua loquor 1 Cor. XIV. 18, Jesuitæ nihilominus doni linguarum sibi non omnino expertes videntur, cum lingua duplici more serpentum loqui soleant, quando suis amphiboliis sive æquivocationibus & mentalibus reservationibus utuntur, &c. Et paulò inferius: Apostoli Patres eorum censebantur, quos per Euangelium Christo genuissent. quo nomine ne multarentur, cavebant filiis suis esse oneri, victuique & indutui necessaria quenquam poscere non audebant, &c. Tanto Apostolis stetit nomen Patris. Quidnî ergo magni Thaumaturgi, & plusquam Apostolicorum miraculorum patratores Jesuitæ audiant, qui cum Regifico domiciliorum luxu, & insanis molium substructionibus orbem universum graviter à se offendi nequaquam ignorent, infirmos tamen paterna caritate suscipere, & offendicula eis de vita auferre nihil pensi habeant, auditoribus, civitatibus, populis & Regnis graves sint & onerosi, ac velut ignis, nunquam dicant, sufficit; & à filis thesaurizari sibi postulent; nec tamen ea causa minus Patrum nomen facile tutentur, & præ omnibus Religiosis καὶ ἐξοχὴν Patres appellari soleant? Taceo miracula illa Florentina, quibus Ignatii sanctitatem comprobare conati sunt, ab Alphonso de Vargas Relat. de Stratag. Jes. cap. 3. cum præscriptione versus
units.tr: CCXXXIV. Gregory, as we said above, had enrolled Ignatius Loyola, Xavier and others among the saints. But the canonization documents which he had not completed, whether prevented by death or for other reasons, Urban made it his first concern to complete. The Bullarium Romanum, vol. 4, p. 11, by Cherubini, contains the Canonization of St. Ignatius Loyola of this Urban, and p. 15 the canonization of Francis Xavier. In the Bull of canonization of Ignatius, Urban says that since Luther, that most foul monster, and other detestable plagues were trying to corrupt the old religion and every profession of a more perfect life in the regions of the North with their blasphemous tongues, and to detract from the authority of the Apostolic See, God had stirred up the spirit of Ignatius Loyola, who, called from the midst of his course of honours and from secular and earthly warfare by a certain wonderful design, so surrendered himself to be ruled and formed by the divine command that at last the new Society of Jesus, founded as a religious order which devoted itself entirely by its institute to other works of piety and charity, to converting the Gentiles, to recalling heretics to the truth of the faith, and to defending the power of the Roman Pontiff, brought its life to a most holy end, with admirable sanctity, and is illustrated by very many miracles. After praising the zeal of Clement VIII and Paul V, and the decree of his predecessor that he be entered among the saints altogether, that churches and altars be built in his honour, and that his feast be celebrated on 31 July, the Bull, recalling from the processes and acts of the cardinals a number of facts about Loyola's birth, life, sanctity and miracles, repeats them. The canonization of Xavier, whose miracles especially are proclaimed at length, was conceived in much the same way. Yet others, even Papists, have rightly called into doubt the miracles of both, so loudly celebrated by Urban. Indeed Pedro de Deza, in his oration on the Beatification of Ignatius, p. 52, ascribes to them only this miracle: that, unlike other religious orders, they not only beg, pray, flatter and fawn, but also most successfully get what they beg, pray for, coax, and wheedle. Since the Jesuit Fathers, I shall quote Deza's words, as cited also by the apostate Sciopius in Infamia Famiani, p. 159 etc., seek their own advantage and have the same plan as that which Joseph suggested to Pharaoh, to heap up a store of grain in their barns. This is a MIRACLE, and the finger of God is here, that in this present age, so perverse and greedy, while other religious orders find that they gain little by begging, the Jesuits know how and are able to extort abundantly whatever they need. It is not without a miracle that men, who are so sparing and tenacious, cannot bring themselves to deny the Jesuits anything or to reject any of their requests. This (Jesuit) MIRACLE can be compared with what God did among the Egyptians for the favour of His people, when they lent the Jews whatever they asked, which God wished them entirely to take away. The very same happens with the Jesuits, that they take away everything they ask for. This is a sign that they are cared for by God and loved by Him with the tenderest affection, since those who are so greedy nevertheless gladly and with joy of spirit supply these Fathers with whatever they need. I shall add the words of Sciopius, who, having at one time been a pupil of the Jesuits, reports among the Jesuit miracles the new gift of tongues and the title of Fathers claimed for themselves; and he at once adds: This, surely, is what Christ had promised to Ignatius and his companions: "At Rome I will be propitious to you." For He would not bring Himself to grant the grace of so great a miracle even to the Apostles. "These signs," he says, "shall follow: in my name they shall cast out devils, speak with new tongues, take up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover." That none of these signs happened to Ignatius and his companions, the propitious Jesus, is clear even from the life of Ignatius, carefully written by his son and disciple Ribadeneira, book 5, ch. 13, where he admits that Ignatius was by no means distinguished by such miracles. But neither, if it pleases the heavenly powers, was Francis Xavier, the Apostle of India, granted the gift of speaking in new tongues; this is clear from his own confession, or rather complaint, which is read in book 3, Indian letter 5: If we knew the Japanese language, I do not doubt that very many would become Christians. May God grant that we learn it soon; then at last we shall do some work for the Christian cause. For now we are among them as dumb statues. So far was he from being able to boast, as a minister of the New Testament made fit by Christ the propitious, and endowed with the gift of tongues for that purpose, after the example of Paul: I thank God, who speaks with all of you in tongues [1 Cor. 14:18]. Yet the Jesuits do not seem altogether without a share in the gift of tongues, since they are accustomed to speak with a double tongue, like serpents, when they use their ambiguities or equivocations and mental reservations, etc. And a little further down: The Apostles were regarded as Fathers of those whom they had begotten to Christ through the Gospel. To avoid being burdened with this name, they took care not to be a weight to their sons, and did not dare to ask anyone for what was necessary for food, clothing, etc. So great was the name of Father for the Apostles. Why then should the Jesuits, who by no means ignore that they are a grave offence to the whole world with their royal luxury of houses and their insane piles of buildings, yet take no care to receive the sick with fatherly love or to take away the stumbling-blocks of life from them, who are a burden and a weight to hearers, cities, peoples and kingdoms, and who, like fire, never say "enough," and demand to be stored up with treasures by their sons, not be heard as great wonder-workers and performers of miracles beyond the Apostles? And yet for this reason they do not give up the name of Fathers easily, and are commonly called καὶ ἐξοχὴν [pre-eminently] Fathers above all religious orders? I pass over those Florentine miracles, by which they tried to prove Ignatius's sanctity, reported by Alphonso de Vargas in Relat. de Stratag. Jes. cap. 3, with the superscription of a verse,

units.la: Nunc immēnsa cavi spirant mendacia folles; memorata, dignissimáque lectu.
units.tr: Now the hollow bellows breathe out immense lies; worth recording, and very much worth reading.

units.la: CCXXXV. Ignatii festum anniversarium die xxxi. Julii celebrari idem Urbanus jusserat. Eò igitur impudentiæ Ignatiani mox provecti sunt, ut ex fastis & Calendario ipso Romano, eraso nomine S. Germani, qui eum sibi diem hactenus vendicaverat, Ignatium suum substituerint. Ea res in Gallia, quæ Germanum præcipuè colit, turbis occasionem præbuit. Et Condeus quidem Princeps, Jesuitarum facinori patrocinatus finxit, sibi Romæ Jesuitarum festum eo die institutum præsentia sua cohonestanti, Ignatium vivum apparuisse. Displicuit nihilominus temeratorum fastorum nefas plerisque in Gallia, Germanum suum tanta contumelia affici quiritantibus. Lis ad Pontificem delata ridiculè ita decisa est, ut eodem die simul Germanus & Ignatius celebretur: quòd si simul stare nolle viderentur, expectaret Ignatius, ceu recentior, annum bissextilem, & diem, qui tum intercalatur, sibi eximium haberet. Laudi etiam merito datum eidem Pontifici, quòd edita Id. Jan. A. M. D. C. xxx. Bulla, in contemptum, uti putabatur, Jesuitarum, abolevit sectam Jesuitissarum, seu mulierum Jesuitici ordinis ac nominis, qui in Italia & Belgio caput exerens jam radices agere cœperat. In nonnullis Italiæ, ita Bulla loquitur, & Vltramontanis partibus certa mulieres, Jesuitissarum nomine assumpto, citra ullam Sedis Apostolicæ approbationem,
units.tr: CCXXXV. Urban had also ordered that Ignatius's anniversary feast be celebrated on 31 July. The Ignatians then advanced so far in shamelessness that, from the calendars and the Roman calendar itself, they erased the name of St Germanus, who had until then claimed that day for himself, and put their Ignatius in his place. This matter gave occasion for disturbances in France, which honours Germanus above all. Prince Condé, defending the Jesuits' deed, invented the story that Ignatius had appeared alive at Rome, while he himself was present, to lend credence to the feast the Jesuits had instituted on that day. Nevertheless, the outrage of violating the calendar displeased most people in France, who cried out that their Germanus was being treated with such insult. The dispute, carried to the Pontiff, was ridiculously settled thus: that Germanus and Ignatius be celebrated on the same day; but if they seemed unwilling to stand together, Ignatius, as the newer saint, should wait for the leap year, and have as his own the day that is then intercalated. Praise was also rightly given to the same Pontiff because, by the bull issued on the Ides of January 1630, he abolished, as was thought in contempt of the Jesuits, the sect of Jesuitesses, that is, women of the Jesuit order and name, which had already begun to raise its head and take root in Italy and Belgium. In some parts of Italy and the Ultramontane regions, the bull says, certain women, assuming the name of Jesuitesses, without any approval of the Apostolic See,

units.la: Jesuitæ expuncto Germano, & intruso Lojola, temerantes fastos, repressi.
units.tr: The Jesuits, having struck out Germanus and thrust in Loyola, profaning the calendar, were checked.

units.la: Jesuitissarum S. Ɵa ab Urbano abolita. ab aliquot annis in unum convenire solita, vita religiosa praetextu, peculiarem & distinctum à caeteris habitum usurpârunt, aedificia in Collegiorum formam redegerunt, domos probationum erexerunt, in eisque Superiorem, ac praetensa Congregationis sua Generalem, indito Praepositae titulo, & attributis facultatibus bene visis constituerunt, in illiusque manibus paupertatis, castitatis & obedientiae vota ad instar solennium emittere, clausuraque legibus non adstrictae pro libitu divagari, ac specie salutis animarum promovendae, aliaque permulta sexus & ingenii imbecillitati, & modestiae muliebri, ac virginali praesertim pudori minimè convenientia, & quae viri sacrarum literarum scientia, rerum usu, vitaeque innocentia spectatissimi, difficile admodum, & non nisi magna circumspectione adhibita aggrediuntur, attentare & exercere consueverunt. Sectam igitur illam, ceu arrogantem, contumacem, sanae doctrinae adversam, zizanium denique in agro Dominico pullulantem, ac proinde radicitus extirpandam, de consilio Cardinalium ac haereticae pravitatis, Inquisitorum, se penitus suppressisse, redegisse in nihilum, aeternae abolitioni subjecisse, ac à corpore sanctissimae ecclesiae amputâsse, sub excommunicationis poena, declarat. An verò penitus orcum subiverit novella illa mulierum religio, Jesuitae saltem non ignorant.
units.tr: The Jesuitesses, abolished by Urban, for some years had been accustomed to gather together under the pretext of religious life, had assumed a distinctive habit different from others, had reduced their dwellings to the form of colleges, had erected houses of probation, and in them had set up a Superior, and a so-called General of their Congregation under the title of Provost, with powers as seemed good; in his hands they had been accustomed to make vows of poverty, chastity and obedience in the manner of solemn vows, and, not bound by the rules of enclosure, to wander at will; and under the pretence of promoting the salvation of souls, to attempt and carry out many other things quite unsuited to the weakness of the female sex and its modesty, and especially to virginal modesty, which men of the most notable knowledge of sacred letters, experience in affairs and innocence of life approach with great difficulty and only with great circumspection. Therefore the bull declares that, on the counsel of the Cardinals and of the Inquisitors of heretical depravity, it has utterly suppressed that sect, as arrogant, obstinate, hostile to sound doctrine, a tare at last sprouting in the Lord's field and therefore to be uprooted; reduced it to nothing, subjected it to eternal abolition, and cut it off from the body of the most holy Church, under penalty of excommunication. Whether that novel religion of women has indeed gone utterly to hell, the Jesuits at least do not know.

units.la: CCXXXVI. Fervebat ob Vallem Telinam ab His- pano occupatam gravissima contentio Principum.
units.tr: CCXXXVI. The serious dispute among the princes over the Valtelline, occupied by the Spaniard, was boiling.

units.la: Galliarum Rex, unà cum Sabaudo ad recuperandam eam in Italiam expeditionem parabat. Ei Papa Urbanus obstitit, & per Barbarinum Legatum belli molem in Reformatos Galliae avertere molitus est. Cùm non succederet intercessio, eodem Barbarino in Hispaniam legato, Clero, qui Hispano in Italia paret, imponi tributum petiit, suámque adversus Gallum tota Italia pellendum operam, ipso Galliae Legato coram, obtulit. Arce proin S. Angeli, aliisque Romae locis munitis, ad occupandam vallem Telinam se accingit, & Bullam etiam edidit, qua omnibus Basilicam cam S. Petri, & Ecclesiam B. Mariæ trans Tiberim devotè visitantibus, & ibi Deum pro suæ Ecclesiæ exaltatione ab hostium conatibus in Italia cum primis, quæ, inquit, illibatæ religionis studio jure optimo gloriatur, defensione, hæresium extirpatione, Principum Christianorum vera pace ac imminentium in Europa necessitatum aversione oraverint, plenariam peccatorum indulgentiam elargitur. Neque segniter Papæ moliminibus Pallus restitit.
units.tr: The King of France, together with the Savoyard, was preparing an expedition into Italy to recover it. Pope Urban opposed him and, through the legate Barberini, sought to turn the weight of the war against the Reformed in France. When this intercession did not succeed, he asked the same Barberini, as legate in Spain, to impose a tax on the clergy who serve the Spaniard in Italy, and offered, in the presence of the French legate himself, his own efforts to drive the French out of all Italy. Accordingly, with the castle of St Angelo and other places in Rome fortified, he prepared to seize the Valtelline, and also issued a bull granting plenary indulgence of sins to all who devoutly visit the Basilica of St Peter and the church of St Mary beyond the Tiber, and there pray God for the exaltation of his Church, from the attempts of its enemies in Italy above all, which, he says, rightly glories in its zeal for undefiled religion, for its defence, the extirpation of heresies, the true peace of Christian princes, and the averting of the necessities impending in Europe. Nor did Pallus resist the Pope's efforts sluggishly.

units.la: CCXXXVII. Durante eo dissidio A. M. D. C. XXV. vulgati sunt adversus Regem Galliæ & Cardinalem Richelium incertis authoribus libelli duo, sub his titulis: Admonitio ad Regem; & Mysteria Politica. Summa librorum est, Regem in Gallia hæreticis, extra Galliam Catholicis bellum movere. Batavis enim Ordinibus contra Regem Catholicum eum opitulari: Palatinum in feuda sua restituere tentare: Reipublicæ Venetorum & Duci Sabaudiæ contra Genuenses & Valtelinos opem ferre. Impia hæc esse bella, juri Divino & naturali contraria, quocunque colore obumbrentur: Castigandos proin virga ferrea Reges Galliæ, non secus ac olim Josaphatus castigatus est. Senatum Venetum & Sabaudum hypocritas esse, & procul fide catholica rei duntaxat sua studere per ambitionem, quæ una ipsis loco religionis sit. Debere Philippum mutuas vices Ludovico, & si tuebitur adversus ipsum subditos rebelles, par pari relaturum. Richelium authorem esse matrimonii Anglicani, fœderis cum Batavis innovati, Valtelinæ in excidium Catholicæ fidei occupatæ. Tum quæstiunculæ proponuntur & solvuntur. quas inter hæ etiam: Vtrum ipso facto Rex Galliæ excommunicatus sit introductione hæreticos in Provincias externas, ubi Catholica religio una viguit ab antiquo? Vtrum pessimi consultores eadem censura teneantur? Vtrum fas sit subdito in tyrannum sævire? Num expediat posita in extremis Gallorum Republica, eligi virum probitate & authoritate illustrem, qui religionis Protectorem se ferat? Solvuntur quæstiones in hanc sententiam: Regem Galliæ ipso facto excommu- Occasione dissidii illius adversus Regem Galliæ & Richelium libellus seditionis vulgatus, in jugulum Regis denuo cultér acuitur. nicatum esse, quia Deo bellum movet, dum movet Catholicis; si perseveraverit, ipsius portionem infernum fore. Deinceps tum Pontificem Summum graviter hortatur, ut gladio ceu in membrum putidum utatur: tum Pontificios etiam Principes adversus eundem concitat. proposito etiam exemplo Henrici IV. non aliam ob causam, à Deo caede multati, quàm quòd Principibus haereticis, Brandenburgico & Neoburgico opitulari constituit. Concludit: eandem esse gentis Austriacae & Dei causam. qui Austriacae genti obstiterit, Deo ipsi obsistere. Constabat jam, denuo cultros & gladios in jugulum Ludovici mox adigendos, acui. Clerus proin Gallicanus in Comitiis libellos ad incudem revocatos damnavit, simúlque Stampesio Carnatensium Episcopo censurae in Anonymum stringendae negotium dedit. Composuit is Gallicè, & Clero exhibuit. Summam censurae ejus capitum Grammondus Histor. Galliae lib. xv. recitat. Probatane verò in Comitiis Episcoporum, an improbata Stampesii censura fuerit, gravis altercatio suborta est. Diversa scilicet Episcoporum, quorum Regi alii, alii Pontifici favebant, studia emicuerant. Atque id satis constat, indice eodem Grammondo, Censuram vehementer Pontifici displicuisse, eò quòd Regum & Principum Majestati quàm Pontificiae addictior videretur. Qui proin etiam Clero Gallicano, perinde ac si eam improbâssset, solennes gratias egit. Hinc patet, ita Grammondus ἀπολογ, quanto fervore Roma iurisdictionem in Reges suam tueatur, si quam habet. Certè summus Pontifex Reges docet suo exemplo, uti jura ipsi sua tueri in quoscunque debeant. Parlamentum contra censurae Stampesii favens graviter in Episcopos pronuntiavit, & approbationem Censurae inficiantes urbe absistere jubet; multùm refragante Clero, eò quòd Parlamento nihil adversus se authoritatis competat. Unde Curiae ausum vocat irritum, intolerabilem, contra Dei cultum, authoritatem Regis gis, & jura Ecclesiæ. Vicissim Curia Episcoporum Responsionem injuriæ & calumniæ manifestam, in eversionem legum Regni fundamentalium factam, lacerandam & cremandam declarat. Demum Rex summo jure litem ad se traxit, & quæ Anonymus adversus illum congesserat, in Regem Hispaniæ, cui cum veteribus Mauris amicitias, nupera cum Muhammedanis fœdera, Lutheranorum Principum & Cosacorum auxilia; Christianis Principibus amicis & affinibus adempta vano Religionis colore Regna & Principatus; fœdera cum Persis, Indis, Calecutis, aut Muthammedanis aut paganis, &c. objecit, masculè retorsit.
units.tr: CCXXXVII. During that dispute, in 1625, two pamphlets were published against the King of France and Cardinal Richelieu by unknown authors, under these titles: Admonitio ad Regem; and Mysteria Politica. The gist of the books is that the King of France makes war on the heretics outside France and on the Catholics within it. For he aids the Dutch States against the Catholic King; he tries to restore the Palatine to his lands; he brings help to the Venetian Republic and the Duke of Savoy against the Genoese and the Valtellines. These wars are impious and contrary to divine and natural law, whatever colour they are shaded with. The Kings of France must therefore be chastised with an iron rod, as Jehoshaphat once was chastised. The Venetian Senate and Savoy are hypocrites, and far from the Catholic faith, they care only for their own affairs out of ambition, which alone takes the place of religion for them. Philip ought to repay Louis in kind, and if he defends against him rebellious subjects, to return like for like. Richelieu is the author of the English marriage, of the renewed alliance with the Dutch, and of the occupation of the Valtelline to the ruin of the Catholic faith. Then little questions are proposed and solved, among which are these: Whether the King of France is excommunicated by the very fact of introducing heretics into foreign provinces where the Catholic religion has long flourished alone? Whether the worst advisers are bound by the same censure? Whether it is lawful for a subject to rage against a tyrant? Whether, with the Republic of the French in extremity, it is expedient to choose a man illustrious for probity and authority, who will profess himself Protector of religion? The questions are solved to this effect: that the King of France is excommunicated by the very fact, because he makes war on God while he makes war on Catholics; if he persists, his portion will be hell. On the occasion of that dispute against the King of France and Richelieu, the seditious pamphlet that was published sharpens the knife again at the King's throat. Next it earnestly urges the Supreme Pontiff to use the sword as against a rotten limb, and it also stirs up the Papist princes against the same king, citing the example of Henry IV, who was struck down by God for no other cause than that he resolved to aid the heretic princes of Brandenburg and Neuburg. It concludes: the cause of the Austrian nation and of God is the same; whoever resists the Austrian nation resists God himself. It was now plain that knives and swords would soon be whetted again at Louis' throat. The Gallican clergy therefore, in the Assembly, condemned the pamphlets, which had been hammered back into shape, and at the same time gave Stampesio, Bishop of Carnatensis, the task of drawing up a censure of the Anonymous author. He composed it in French and presented it to the clergy. Grammondus, Histor. Galliae lib. xv., recites the substance of its heads. But whether Stampesio's censure was approved or disapproved in the Assembly of bishops, a grave dispute arose. Clearly the zeal of the bishops diverged, some favouring the King, others the Pope. And it is quite certain, according to the same Grammondus, that the censure displeased the Pope greatly, because it seemed more favourable to the majesty of kings and princes than to the papal. So he also thanked the Gallican clergy with solemn thanks, just as if he had disapproved it. Hence it is plain, says Grammondus, with what fervour Rome defends its jurisdiction over kings, if it has any. Certainly the Supreme Pontiff teaches kings by his example to defend their rights against whoever they ought. The Parliament, favouring Stampesio's censure, pronounced severely against the bishops, and ordered those who denied its approval to leave the city; the clergy strongly objected, because the Parliament had no authority over them. Hence the Court calls the act void, intolerable, against the worship of God, the authority of the King, and the rights of the Church. In turn the Court declares the bishops' response manifest injury and calumny, made to overthrow the fundamental laws of the realm, to be torn up and burned. At last the King, by supreme right, drew the dispute to himself, and what the Anonymous author had heaped against him he manfully hurled back at the King of Spain, to whom he objected friendships with the old Moors, recent alliances with the Muhammadans, and the aid of the Lutheran princes and the Cossacks; kingdoms and principalities taken from Christian princes who were friends and kin, under the empty colour of religion; alliances with the Persians, Indians, and Calicut, whether with Muhammadans or pagans, etc.

units.la: CCXXXVIII. Prodiit eodem anno in publicum Santarelli è Societate Jesu Presbyteri de summi Pontificis potestate liber, quo variis capitibus plura contra Regum authoritatem & jura continebantur. Titulus libro erat: Tractatus de hæresi, schismate, apostasia, solicitatione Summi Pontificis; & de potestate Summi Pontificis in delictis his puniendis. Romæ apud hæredem Bartholomæi Lanoti M. D. C. XXV. Superiorum permissu. Cùm & solicitatione & permissu Pontificis libet hic editus sit, ejusdem interiora de sua & Regum potestate sensa eo contineri, dubium non est. Vin verò χυεῖας δόξας, & decreta illius libri? Ejusmodi scilicet sunt: Papa habet in Principes potestatem directivam; ergo & correctivam. Summus ergo Pontifex potest hæreticos Principes punire etiam pœnis temporalibus; proin non solum eos excommunicare, sed & Regno privare, eorumque subditos ab obedientia liberare. Papa deponit Imperatorem propter ipsius iniquitates, & dat Principibus curatores, quando ad regendos subditos inutiles fuerint. idque etiam sine Concilio, quia Papæ & Christi unum est tribunal. Papa potest deponere Reges non solum propter hæresin, aut schisma, aut aliud crimen tolerabile in populo, sed etiam propter insufficientiam; vel si non defendat ecclesiam. Potest etiam Reges negligentes, vel ob dictas causas pœna mortis ad aliorum correctionem & exemplum punire. Ea puniendi Reges morte etiam temporali potestas continetur in munere pascendi oves Petro commisso. Pertinet enim ad pastores punire oves suas ea poena, qua ratio indicat, illas esse puniendas. Si igitur propter bonum commune aliquando prudentia & recta ratio exigat, ut poenis temporalibus Principes inobedientes afficiantur, potest summus Ecclesiæ pastor eas poenas iis imponere. Nec enim Principes sunt extra ovile Ecclesiæ. Ausus insuper est verba Apostoli 2 Cor. x. 8. Deus nobis dedit potestatem ad ædificationem non ad destructionem; deleta vocula non contrarium in sensum torquere. Has scilicet ferientes sententias adversus Principes liber ille loquitur. Vix prodiit liber, cum in Gallia Collegium Sorbonæ acri censura authorem perstringit, & supremæ Curiæ decreto carnificis manu liber comburitur. Dicta quin etiam die, Collegii Claromontani Rector, præcipuique ex societate Jesu in Collegio eo Theologi, ad judicium citati, respondere ad interrogata Senatus, & judicii sui de Santarelli dogmatibus copiam facere coguntur. Omnium nomine P. Cotonus interrogantibus respondit, & metu gravi, ne denuo solum vertere Societas cogeretur, tum Santarelli doctrinam verbis saltem improbavit; tum fassus etiam est, doctrinam eam Romæ à Generali Societatis suæ, cæterisque sociis probari. quod negare, cum Generalis Jesuitarum, Mutii Vitellesci approbationem præscriptam liber habuerit, integrum non fuit. Sed quare, subjecit Cotonus, imputabitur nobis error Transalpinus, cui nemo nostrum subscripsit in Gallia? Interroganti Senatui, anne Summo Pontifici jus sit in Reges, adeò ut excommunicare, & ab eorum obsequio liberare subditos possit? idem Cotonus in hæc verba respondit: Absit verba invidia! Excommunicari Christianissimum Regem? Absit omen. Quis credat primogenitum Ecclesiæ futurum aliquando matris hostem, quam protexit semper & protegit? Quis excommunicandum, qui continuò pugnat hæresi in Regno suo extirpanda? Quæsitus, an diversam ergo à Generali Societatis sententiam Galli Jesuitæ teneant, respondit: Qui Romæ degit Præpositus noster Generalis vix est ut improbare possit, quod Roma probat. Interrogante Senatu: Quid si essetis Romæ? respondit Cotonus idem: Mutaretur nobis cum Cælo animus, sentiremus ut Romæ. Anquisiti, ut sine ambagibus & subterfugio omni suam de Romanæ Sedis in Reges potestate sententiam proferant, exigui temporis ad deliberandum moram cum petiissent, triduo elapso præcipui è Societate ad Regem misli palam Santarelli doctrinam abdicârunt, exhibito instrumento publico in hæc verba concepto: Nos subsignati declaramus, Santarellum perperam de Regibus & eorum authoritate scripsisse, quam diffitemur doctrinam, agnoscimus & profitemur, Regum immediatam esse à Deo potestatem, independensque ipsis jus esse in subditos; cui sententiæ ut veræ nostro omnium sanguine subscribitur, si opus, non secus ac censuris, si quæ à Clero Gallicano aut Sorbona in ejusmodi libros edentur. Promittimus insuper futuram nobis posthac unam & eandem super ea quæstione cum Sorbona, clero, & Regni Gallici Academiis sententiam. Actum Lutetiam XVI. Martii M.D.C.XXVI. Suscripserunt primore loco Cotonus, & quindecim alii, omnium nomine. Et hic quidem Jesuitis fuit δῆμος ἐν σιθεσι Lutetiæ; aliter longè, uti Cotonus ipse fassus est, arbitraturis, si Romæ vixissent. Neque enim eadem confessoribus illis conscientia Lutetiæ & Romæ fuit. Quanquam beneficio novi linguarum doni, quod iis obtigisse supra Scioppius dixerat, byssina verba sua interpretari pro lubitu, juxta ea etiam, quæ ss. ccxiv. diximus, in proclivi erat. Hæc tamen fide ipsius Grammondi, Tholosani Parlamenti Præsidis, Pontificiisque adeò partibus addictissimi, relata, Jesuitarum versutiæ, diversis fidibus eandem fidem ludentium, certissimam fidem faciunt.
units.tr: CCXXXVIII. In the same year there appeared in public a book on the power of the supreme Pontiff by Santarelli, a priest of the Society of Jesus, which in various chapters contained much against the authority and rights of kings. The title of the book was: Tractatus de hæresi, schismate, apostasia, solicitatione Summi Pontificis; & de potestate Summi Pontificis in delictis his puniendis. Romæ apud hæredem Bartholomæi Lanoti M. D. C. XXV. Superiorum permissu. That the author's inner feelings about the power of the Pontiff and of kings are contained in it, when the book was published with the Pontiff's solicitation and permission, is beyond doubt. But what of the false opinions [χυεῖας δόξας] and decrees of that book? They are of this sort: The Pope has a directive power over princes; therefore also a corrective power. The supreme Pontiff can therefore punish heretical princes even with temporal penalties; hence he may not only excommunicate them but also deprive them of their kingdom, and free their subjects from obedience. The Pope deposes an emperor for his iniquities, and gives curators to princes when they have proved useless for governing their subjects; and he does this even without a Council, because the Pope and Christ have one tribunal. The Pope can depose kings not only for heresy, or schism, or another crime tolerable in the people, but also for insufficiency, or if they do not defend the Church. He can also punish negligent kings, or kings guilty of the aforesaid causes, with the penalty of death, for the correction and example of others. This power to punish kings even with temporal death is contained in the charge to feed the sheep committed to Peter. For it belongs to shepherds to punish their sheep with that penalty which reason indicates they ought to be punished with. If, therefore, for the common good, prudence and right reason sometimes require that disobedient princes be visited with temporal penalties, the supreme Shepherd of the Church can impose those penalties on them. For princes are not outside the fold of the Church. He further dared to twist the words of the Apostle, 2 Cor. x. 8, God has given us power for building up, not for destruction, into the opposite sense by deleting the little word non. This book, of course, speaks these sentences striking against princes. Hardly had the book appeared when the Sorbonne in France censured the author with sharp condemnation, and by decree of the supreme Court the book was burnt by the hand of the executioner. On the same day, the Rector of the Clermont College and the principal theologians of the Society of Jesus in that College were summoned before the court and compelled to answer the questions of the Senate and to give a copy of their judgment on Santarelli's doctrines. Father Cotton answered on behalf of all, and in heavy fear lest the Society should again be forced to leave the country, he disapproved of Santarelli's teaching, at least in words; then he also admitted that this doctrine was approved at Rome by the General of his Society and the other associates. To deny this was not wholly possible, since the book bore the prescribed approval of the General of the Jesuits, Muzio Vitelleschi. But why, Cotton added, will the Transalpine error be imputed to us, when none of us in France has subscribed to it? To the Senate asking whether the Supreme Pontiff had a right over kings, so that he could excommunicate them and free their subjects from their allegiance, the same Cotton replied in these words: Far be it from us to speak with malice! Excommunicate the Most Christian King? God forbid. Who would believe that the firstborn of the Church will someday be an enemy of the mother whom he has always protected and still protects? Who should be excommunicated when he is constantly fighting to root out heresy in his kingdom? Asked whether the French Jesuits therefore held an opinion different from that of the General of the Society, he replied: Our Father General, who lives at Rome, is scarcely in a position to disapprove what Rome approves. When the Senate asked: What if you were at Rome? Cotton again replied: Our minds would change along with the sky; we would feel as they feel at Rome. When they were questioned, so that they might state without ambiguity or any evasion their opinion on the power of the Roman See over kings, and had asked for a short delay to deliberate, after three days had passed the leading men of the Society sent to the King and openly renounced Santarelli's doctrine, presenting a public instrument drawn up in these words: We the undersigned declare that Santarelli has written wrongly about kings and their authority; we deny that doctrine, we acknowledge and profess that the power of kings is immediately from God, and that they have a right independent of others over their subjects. To this opinion, as true, we subscribe with all our blood, if need be, no less than to whatever censures are issued by the French clergy or the Sorbonne against books of this kind. We further promise that henceforth we shall hold one and the same opinion on this question as the Sorbonne, the clergy and the Academies of the kingdom of France. Done at Paris, 16 March 1626. Cotton and fifteen others signed first, on behalf of all. And so this was for the Jesuits a people [δῆμος ἐν σιθεσι] in Paris; they would have judged quite otherwise, as Cotton himself admitted, if they had lived at Rome. For those confessors did not have the same conscience at Paris and at Rome. Yet by the benefit of the new gift of tongues, which Scioppius said above had come to them, they could interpret their fine-spun words as they pleased, and according to what we said at ss. CCXIV, this was easy. Nevertheless, this account, as reported on the authority of Grammond himself, President of the Parliament of Toulouse, and most devoted to the Papist cause, makes the trickery of the Jesuits, playing the same faith on different strings, most certainly credible.

units.la: CCXXXIX. Cæterùm Cotonus tœdio interroga- toriæ illius actionis, qua cum præcipuis ex societate ex-
units.tr: CCXXXIX. Cotonus, worn down by the tedium of that interrogation in which he had been expelled from the Society together with its leading men, was at once seized by illness and paid the debt of nature.

units.la: Cotonus tædio inquisitionis illius moritur. tra ordinem pulsatus fuerat, statim morbo correptus, satti legem implevit. Atque hic ille Cotonus est, qui Henrici IV. apud quem nunquam non flagranti in gratia erat, conscientiæ admotus, digna scilicet Theologo curiositate, non Dodonæam quercum, sed atrum Ditis tripodem excutiens, ex puellæ Pythonissæ, Hadrianæ Fraxineæ, Gerbiniaco pago in Ambianis natæ, impuro, quo misera corripiebatur, spiritu scissitari ausus est multa, quæ aliunde cognoscere spes non erat. Inter alias has etiam dæmoni quæstiones movebat: quid se spiritus scire velit circa Regem? quid de tempore, quo Calvini hæresis extinguetur? quid circa Geneve plagiarium? quid circa Geneve conservationem? qua ratione converti Rex Angliæ, Regina & Regnum maximè & facilè queant? Turcus, qua supplantari ratione, qua converti infideles? quid circa bellum Regis cum Hispanis & hereticis? an linguæ sint à Deo? quis evidentissimus Scripturæ locus ad probandum purgatorium & invocationem Sanctorum? quomodo animalia in arca Noæ capi potuerint? qui filii Dei filias hominum dilexerint? pedibusne incesserit Serpens ante Adæ lapsum? qui sint septem spiritus ante thronum Dei? quomodo insulæ animalia acceperint, & eò homines post Adamum pervenerint? ubi paradisus terrestris? quota pars conciderit Angelorum? aliásque plures, quas ordine Thuanus Histor. lib. CXXXII. recensét. Quærendorum horum aliorúmque indicem, manu propria & Latina lingua exaratum, in libro exorcismorum, ab amico commodato accepto, cùm per incuriam Cotonus reliquisset, atque is per multorum manus volitâsset, tandem Ronius Marchio manu agnita, Regi ipsi exhibuit. qui re in occulto minimè probata, Romio, ut autographum retineret, neque alii daret, enixè imperaverat. Evulgatum tamen post Rex indoluit, quòd provideret futurum ut apud bonos prudentésque multùm Cotoni, cujus ipse opera & industria, ut sibi videbatur, in multis rebus usus esset, exi-stimationi ex ea occasione detraheretur. CCXL. Edi-
units.tr: Cotonus dies from the tedium of that inquiry. This is the same Cotonus who, admitted to the confidence of Henry IV, always in flaming favour with him, and with the curiosity fitting a theologian, dared to consult not the Dodonean oak but the dark tripod of Dis. Through the foul spirit of the girl Pythoness, Hadriana Fraxinea, born in the village of Gerbiniacum in Amiens, by whom the wretched girl was seized, he presumed to ask many things that there was no hope of learning elsewhere. Among the other questions he put to the demon were these: what does the spirit wish to know concerning the King? What about the time when Calvin's heresy will be extinguished? What about the plot against Geneva? What about the preservation of Geneva? By what means can the King of England, the Queen and the kingdom be most easily converted? How are the Turk, and the infidels, to be overthrown and converted? What about the King's war with the Spaniards and the heretics? Are tongues from God? What is the most evident passage of Scripture for proving purgatory and the invocation of the saints? How could the animals be taken into Noah's ark? Who were the sons of God who loved the daughters of men? Did the serpent go on foot before the fall of Adam? Who are the seven spirits before the throne of God? How did animals reach the islands, and how did men arrive there after Adam? Where is the earthly paradise? How many of the angels fell? and many others, which Thuanus lists in order in his History, book CXXXII. The index of these and other questions, written in his own hand and in Latin, was in a book of exorcisms that he had received on loan from a friend. Cotonus left it behind through carelessness, and it passed through many hands until Ronius Marchio, recognising the handwriting, showed it to the King himself. The King, wishing the matter kept quiet, strictly ordered Romio to keep the autograph and give it to no one. Nevertheless, it was later made public, and the King grieved, because he foresaw that on this occasion the reputation of Cotonus would suffer among good and prudent men, though it seemed to him that he had made much use of Cotonus's work and diligence in many matters.

units.la: Ejusdem quæstiones curiosa dæmoni Hadriana Fraxinea propositæ.
units.tr: The curious questions of the same man, put to the demon by Hadriana Fraxinea.

units.la: CCXL. Edidit Urbanus duobus post annis Kal. April. M. D. C. XXVII. repetitam Bullam Coenae Domini, totidem verbis, quibus etiam Paulus V. sexto Id. April. A. M. D. C. X. eandem vulgavit.
units.tr: CCXL. Two years later, on the Kalends of April 1627, Urban published the Bull of the Lord's Supper, repeated word for word, in the same form in which Paul V had published it on 8 April 1610.

units.la: Titulus bullae est: Excommunicatio & anathematizatio haereticorum cujuscunque sectae, eisque faventium, auxilium aut consilium quoquo modo praestantium, ac schismaticorum, vel libertatem ecclesiasticam perturbantium, aut his, quae in ista Bulla die Coenae Domini legi solita continentur, contravenientium. Conflata est ex diversorum Pontificum constitutionibus & bullis die Coenae Domini recitari & progressu temporis mutari, augeri solitis. quas Cherubinus Bullar. tom. 3. pag. 248. nota bullae Pauli V. praefixa indigetat. Consuetudinem antiquam Julius II. bulla tali Kal. Martii A. M. D. XI. edita allegat. Consueverunt, inquit, Romani Pontifices praedecessores nostri, ad retinendam puritatem religionis Christianae, & ipsius unitatem, quae in conjunctione membrorum ad unum caput, Christum videlicet, ejusque Vicarium, principaliter consistit, & sanctam fidelium societatem ab offensione servandam, arma justitiae per ministerium Apostolatus in praesenti celebritate exercere. Tum ex parte Omnipotentis Dei, Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. authoritate Beatorum, Petri & Pauli, ac sua, anathemati subjicit omnes haereticos, Gazaros, Patarenos, Pauperes de Lugduno, Arnaldistas, Speronistas, Passagenos, Viclesistas seu Vsfitas, Fratricellos de opinione nuncupatos, & quoscunque alios haeretieos, &c. Primus Paulus III. Bulla Coenae Id. April. A. M. D. XXXVI. edita, post Fratricellos nominavit impiam & abominabilem Marthini Lutheri haeresin, per Leonem P. P. X. superioribus annis damnatam, sequentes, ipsique Martino, quo minus puniri posset, quomodo libet faventes. Gregorius XIII. simili bulla, septem articulis auctiore, prid. Non. April. A. M. D. LXXXIII. edita, omissis aliis exprimit Vsfitas, Viclevitas, Lutheranos, Zwinglianos, Calvinistas, Vgonottos, Anabaptistas, Trinitarios ac omnes & singulos haereticos &c. Neque que aliter Paulus V. & Urbanus VIII. Excommunicantur eadem bulla omnes ab ordinationibus seu mandatis Romanorum Pontificum ad universale futurum Concilium appellantes; nec non appellantes à gravamine, seu futura executione literarum Apostolicarum, etiam in forma Brevis, ad Curias Seculares; impedientes executionem literarum Apostolicarum, vel aliarum expeditionum, & alias causas à judicibus ecclesiasticis avocantes, seu cursum earum impedientes, aut se in illis ut judices interponentes; etiamsi Imperiali, Regali, Ducali &c. dignitate praefulgeant: judices Seculares trahentes personas Ecclesiasticas ad sua tribunalia; nec non qui statuta, ordinationes, constitutiones pragmaticas, seu quaevis alia decreta in genere, vel in specie, ex quavis causa, & quovis quaesito colore ac etiam praetextu cujusvis consuetudinis aut privilegii, vel quomodo libet fecerint, & publicaverint, vel factis & ordinatis usi fuerint. unde libertas ecclesiastica tollitur, seu in aliquo laeditur vel deprimitur, aut quovis modo restringitur, &c. Quibus, aliisque etiam sequentibus Reges ipsos & Ecclesias Galliae, libertates ejusmodi sibi vindicantes, stringi, & diro anathematì quotannis à Pontifice subjici, adeò manifestum est, ut non aliam ob causam Bullam illam in Gallia prohibitam rejectámque & Capucinos Archangelum Puteanum, nec non Alphonsum praetextu Bullae ejus se coram Magistratu Seculari sistere renuentes, & patrocinantes iisdem Brularum Curatorem Provincialam & Benedictum Angelum à Senatu supremo graviter increpitos, declarationem eorum laceratam, & decretum ipsum in coenobio Capucinorum vocatis universis fratribus recitatum, Thuanus Histor. lib. c. XXIII. testetur. Tametsi verò Petrus de Marca de Concordia Sacerdot. & Imper. lib. III. 10. omem lapidem moveat, ut anathema isthoc à capite Regum Franciæ amoliatur, praetexens, Reges suos in iis, quae jure Regio agunt, perstringi non posse; in caeteris Bullam esse tantum comminationem & protestationem; Bullam illam non esse receptam in
units.tr: The title of the bull is: Excommunication and anathematization of heretics of any sect, and of those who favour them, who give them aid or counsel in any way, and of schismatics, or those who disturb ecclesiastical liberty, or who act against those things contained in this Bull, which is customarily read on the day of the Lord's Supper. It was put together from the constitutions and bulls of various Popes, which were customarily read on the day of the Lord's Supper and, as time went on, changed and enlarged. Cherubinus, Bullarium, vol. 3, p. 248, cites them in a note attached to the bull of Paul V. Julius II, in a bull issued on the Kalends of March 1511, cites the ancient custom: Our predecessors the Roman Popes have been accustomed, to keep the purity of the Christian religion and its unity, which consists principally in the joining of the members to one head, namely Christ and his Vicar, and to keep the holy society of the faithful from offence, to exercise in the present solemnity the arms of justice through the ministry of the Apostolate. Then by the authority of Almighty God, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and of the blessed Peter and Paul, and of his own, he subjects to anathema all heretics, Gazari, Patarini, the Poor of Lyons, Arnaldists, Speronists, Passagians, Wiclefites or Hussites, the so-called Fraticelli, and any other heretics, etc. Paul III, in the bull of the Ides of April 1536, was the first to name, after the Fraticelli, the impious and abominable heresy of Martin Luther, condemned in former years by Leo X, and those who follow it, and those who in any way favour Martin himself so that he cannot be punished.
