Gregory XIII, in a similar bull, enlarged with seven articles, issued on 4 April 1583, omitting the others, names the Hussites, Wiclefites, Lutherans, Zwinglians, Calvinists, Huguenots, Anabaptists, Trinitarians, and all and each of the heretics, etc. Paul V and Urban VIII likewise excommunicate by the same bull all who appeal from the ordinances or mandates of the Roman Pontiffs to a future universal Council; and also those who appeal from a grievance, or from the future execution of apostolic letters, even in the form of a Brief, to secular courts; those who hinder the execution of apostolic letters or other dispatches, and who call other cases away from ecclesiastical judges, or hinder their course, or interpose themselves as judges in them; even if they shine with imperial, royal, ducal or other dignity; secular judges who drag ecclesiastical persons to their tribunals; and also those who make, publish, or use statutes, ordinances, pragmatic constitutions, or any other decrees, in general or in particular, for any cause and under any pretext, including the pretext of any custom or privilege, or in any way whatever, by which ecclesiastical liberty is removed, or harmed or depressed, or restricted in any way, etc. That by these and other following clauses the kings themselves and the Churches of France, claiming such liberties for themselves, are bound and every year subjected by the Pope to dire anathema, is so manifest that, for no other reason, Thuanus, History, book c. XXIII, testifies that this bull was prohibited and rejected in France; that the Capuchins Archangelus Puteanus and Alphonsus, who refused to appear before the secular magistrate under the pretext of this bull, and the provincial curator of the Brulars and Benedict Angelus, who defended them, were severely rebuked by the Supreme Senate; that their declaration was torn up; and that the decree itself was read in the Capuchin convent, with all the brothers summoned. Yet Peter de Marca, On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire, book III, c. 10, moves every stone to remove this anathema from the head of the Kings of France, pretending that their kings cannot be struck in those things which they do by royal right; that in other matters the bull is only a threat and a protest; that the bull was not received in France.

units.la: Reges & Ecclesias Gallia in ea excommunicari, adversus P. de Marca asseritur. in Gallia; Reges Gallia ex privilegio, non comprehendi excommunicatione generali; consuetudines privilegiarias meritis Regum innixas, per Bullam non censeri revocatas; eximia quaedam jura in rebus ecclesiasticis esse penes Reges Franciae &c. efficere tamen sane non poterit, quin, si quisquam alius, Rex Galliae in Bulla ex Pontificis Romani intentione perstringi intelligatur. quo jure, Divino, an Papali, non disputo. Diserte enim praetextus Marcae diluuntur f. 24. ubi Bulla quibuscunque contrariis derogans, negat obstare privilegia, indulgentias, indulta, & literas Apostolicas generales, vel speciales, aliquibus cujuscunque ordinis, status, conditionis & praeeminentiae fuerint, etiamsi Pontificali, Imperiali, Regali seu quavis ecclesiastica & mundana dignitate praefulgeant, etiam per viam contractus aut remunerationis &c. concessa.
units.tr: The Kings and Churches of France are excommunicated by it: this is asserted against de Marca. in France; that the Kings of France are not included in the general excommunication by privilege; that privileged customs resting on the merits of the Kings are not considered revoked by the Bull; that certain distinguished rights in ecclesiastical matters are in the hands of the Kings of France, etc. Yet he will certainly be unable to bring it about that, if anyone, the King of France is understood to be struck by the Bull according to the intention of the Roman Pontiff. I do not dispute by what right, divine or papal. For the pretexts of Marca are clearly refuted at f. 24, where the Bull, derogating from all contrary things, denies that privileges, indulgences, indults, and general or special apostolic letters, granted to anyone of any order, status, condition or pre-eminence, stand in the way, even if they shine with pontifical, imperial, royal, or any ecclesiastical or worldly dignity, even if granted by way of contract or remuneration, etc.

units.la: CCXLI. Sub finem Octobris A. M. D. C. XXVIII. Rupella, Galliae emporium & propugnaculum fortissimum, Euangelicorum asylum, ultra annum a Rege Ludovico XIII. administrante Armando Plesseo Richelio Cardinale, obsessa, fusis Anglorum auxiliariis copiis, a sociis etiam maligne destituta, tantaque jam fame pressa, ut pane carnibusque deficientibus, cute, corio, radicibus, cadaverum carnibus obsessi vescerentur, & mater filiam, soror fratris digitos derosos esurialem dapem absumeret; denique fame invalescente sola quindecim hominum millia extinguerentur; sese Regis arbitrio dedere coacta, victoris jugum subivit; magnoque, cui hactenus in mundo quidem, innitebantur, praesidio Euangelicos, precaria deinceps libertate fruentes, destituit.
units.tr: CCXLI. Towards the end of October 1628, La Rochelle, the emporium and very strong bulwark of France and refuge of the Evangelicals, besieged for more than a year by King Louis XIII under the direction of Cardinal Armand Richelieu, was abandoned by the English auxiliary forces, which had been routed, and was also left by its allies in a bad way. It was so hard pressed by famine that, with bread and meat gone, the besieged ate skin, leather and roots, and the flesh of corpses; a mother devoured her daughter, a sister gnawed her brother's fingers, and when the famine grew worse, fifteen thousand people perished. Forced to surrender to the King's will, it submitted to the yoke of the victor, and it deprived the Evangelicals of the great protection on which they had until then relied in the world, so that they now enjoy a precarious liberty.

units.la: In Templo D. Margarethae, Rege & Richelio praesentibus, S. Ambrosii & Augustini hymno decantato, Sufrenius Jesuita concionem habuit, explicans textum Davidis: Persequar inimicos meos & comprehendam illos, & non revertar, donec deficiant. Incredibilem laetitiam ea victoria attulit Urbano Pontifici, qui gratu-
units.tr: In the Church of St Margaret, with the King and Richelieu present, a hymn of St Ambrose and St Augustine was sung, and then the Jesuit Sufrenius preached a sermon explaining the text of David: "I will pursue mine enemies, and overtake them; neither will I turn again till they be consumed." That victory brought unbounded joy to Pope Urban, who, congratulating the King among other things, wrote: "A voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tabernacles. Let the sinner see it and be angry, and let the synagogue of Satan waste away."

units.la: Rupella a Ludovico XIII. Euangelicis erepta. tulatus Regi inter alia scripsit: Vox exultationis & salutis in tabernaculis. Videat peccator & irrascatur, & Synagoga Sathanæ contabescat. Cui insolenti triumpho & βλασφημίας crimini Josephus Hallus, Episcopus Exoniensis Anglus, publico scripto respondit, sic inter alia Urbanum graviter affatus: Audi, Pontifex Urbane, quod brevi pro tremendo Christi tribunali exaudies pallidus. Pastorem Christiani gregis parum decent hæ sanguinea literæ! tune ad arma tristis præco conclames? tune, ut Christianos Principes, nimio quàm plenos cruoris, ad profligationem suorum clademque horrendam acriter instiges? ideone tibi credita claves, ut ferratas belli portas, eburneasque Ditis inferni aperires? Euge Petri umbra, numquid hi tibi Malchi videntur, quibus dum aures præcidere voluisti, levi errore in guttura incididisti? aut numquid de quadrupedibus hisce in Gallia stabulantibus, dictum tibi pridem cælitus, occide & manduca? Similem ejusdem Urbani gratulationem Bredâ occupatâ Isabellæ & Spinolæ factam paulò ante A. M. D. C. XXV. apud Johannem Jonstonum Rer. Britan. lib. 21. p. 663. legere est. Neque tamen vel sic Pontifex Regem ad excidium omnium in Regno Euangelicorum inflammans, destinata apud ipsum perfecit. Sic enim DEUS cor Regis flexit, ut eos edicti Nannetensis beneficio frui ulterius permiserit.
units.tr: Rochelle was taken from the Protestants by Louis XIII. To this arrogant triumph, and to this crime of blasphemy, Joseph Hall, the English Bishop of Exeter, replied in a published writing, addressing Urban severely among other things: "Hear, Pope Urban, what you will hear soon, pale, before the dread tribunal of Christ. These bloody letters ill become a minister of the Christian flock! Will you, a gloomy herald, call the nations to arms? Will you sharply goad the Christian princes, already too full of blood, to their own destruction and dreadful ruin? Was the keys entrusted to you so that you might open the iron gates of war and the ivory gates of infernal Dis? Well done, shade of Peter! Do these men seem to you to be Malchus, whose ear you tried to cut off, and in a slight error you struck the throat instead? Or has it not been said to you long ago from heaven, concerning these four-footed beasts stabled in France: kill and eat?" A similar congratulation from the same Urban, made when Breda was taken by Isabella and Spinola, a little before 1625, may be read in John Johnston, Rerum Britannicarum, book 21, p. 663. Yet even so the Pope, who was inflaming the King to the destruction of all the Protestants in the kingdom, did not accomplish what he had intended. For God so turned the King's heart that he allowed them to continue to enjoy the benefit of the Edict of Nantes.

units.la: CCXLII. Non eadem Pontifici in Habessinorum, seu Æthiopum Christianorum, quæ in Galliæ Regno, fortuna risit.
units.tr: CCXLII. The Papists' fortune in Abyssinia, or among the Christian Ethiopians, did not smile on them as it did in the kingdom of France.

units.la: Jam pridem Regnum illud, olim florentissimum, at superiore Seculo Adelensium bellis, post etiam Gallanorum vi atque feritate ita debilitatum, ut vix hodie Habessiniam in ipsa Habessinia invenias, Sedi Romanæ subjicere Pontifices tentaverant. Et sub finem quidem Concilii Florentini, A. M. CCCC. XXXIX. Rex Habessiniæ Zera-Jacobus ad Eugenium IV. legationem miserat, nulla re memorabili gesta, quanquam de ea nescio quid Romani gloriantur. Superiore iterum Seculo Franciscus Al-va-
units.tr: Long ago the Popes had tried to bring under the Roman See that kingdom, once most flourishing, but in the last century so weakened by the wars of the Adal and afterwards by the violence and savagery of the Galla that today you can hardly find a Christian in Abyssinia itself. Near the end of the Council of Florence, in 1439, King Zera-Jacob of Abyssinia had sent an embassy to Eugenius IV, though nothing memorable was done, although the Romans boast about it somehow. units.la: Pontificum & Jesuitarum in Æthiopia seu Habessinia Sedi suæ subjicienda conatus, varezius, Lusitanicæ legationis in Æthiopia Sacerdos, literas à Rege Æthiopum Davide Clementi VII. A. M. D. XXXIII. obtulit, simúlque reverentiam & obedientiam Regis nomine ei obtulit. In spem sic erectus Papa est, fore ut damna, quæ jam in Occidente passus est, brevi Oriens & Meridies resarcirent. Mansit species quædam amicitiæ diu. Nam & Paulus III. Johannis Bermudis Romam missi, ut auxilia pro Davide aliquoties victo peteret, ordinationem à Metropolita Marco adeóque schismatico Præsule factam, confirmare non dubitavit. Spes sic affulsit, Regnum ecclesiæ Romanæ subjici posse, annitentibus inprimis Ignatio Lojala, & Nonio Berreto, cui à Julio III. Patriarchalis in Æthiopia dignitas conserebatur, quamvis eodem titulo jam ante à Pontifice Bermudes ornatus fuerit. adjuncto eidem Andrea Oviedo Episcopo, qui rem tum colloquiis sacris, tum asperis etiam remediis tantârunt frustra. Initio hujus Seculi nova tentata missione P. Petrus Pays Jesuita eò rem provexit, ut Zedengelus Rex scriptis ad Clementem VIII. & Philippum III. Hispaniæ atque Lusitaniæ Regem, amicitiam suam obtulerit, nec non milites, opifices & Patres è Societate Jesu, qui subjectos suos erudirent, petierit. quam ob causam à suis nova hæc molimina iniquo animo ferentibus occisus est. Ei post Jacobum succedaneus Rex Susneus, Romanis favens, colloquiis cum Jesuitis publicè institutis, eousque processit, ut edicto in Romanorum favorem condito, post turbas graves tum in Regno, tum ab Alexandrinis motas, publicè Alexandrini Patriarchæ excusso jugo, Romanam religionem amplexus, declaraverit, se Papæ Romano, Petri successori, utpote qui nec in fide, nec in moribus errare posset, obedire velle; subditos, ut idem facerent, adhortatus. Rebus ita ex voto fluentibus, Urbano Pontifice, & nominante Philippo IV. ex Jesuitarum ordine creatus est Æthiopiæ Patriarcha, Alphonsus Mendez, natione Lusitanus, Vir celebris, qui suetis ceremoniis Ulyssiponæ consecratus, mense Majo A. M. D. C. X X. I V. Goam Indiæ appulit, ac inde in Habeissiniam ad Regem penetravit. qui mox in genua procumbens in verba Summi Pontificis Urbani hoc modo juravit: Nos SultanSaghedus, (Sufnei hoc nomen) Rex Regum Æthiopiæ, credimus & confitemur, quod S. Petrus, Princeps Apostolorum à Christo Domino nostro caput totius Ecclesiæ Christianæ constitutus fuerit: & quod Principatus atque potestas in totum mundum ipsi data fuerit, dum illi dixit: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram ædificabo ecclesiam meam: & dabo tibi claves Cælorum; & alia vice, cum illi dixit: Pasce oves meas. Similiter credimus, Papam Romanum legitimè electum, verum successorem S. Petri Apostoli in regimine esse: eúmque eandem potestatem, dignitatem & primatum totius ecclesiæ Christianæ tenere. Igitur S. Petri Successori Urbano VIII. hujus nominis per Dei gratiam Papæ & Domino nostro, & successoribus ejus in administratione Ecclesiæ promittimus, offerimus & juramus veram obedientiam, & humiliter personam atque imperium nostrum pedibus ejus subjicimus. Sic Deus nos juvet, & sancta hæc Euangelia. Idem post Regem Basilides, futurus successor, fratres Reges, Pro-Reges atque Proceres omnes, nec non Clerici & Monachi præsentes jurarunt. Pronuntiatum simul est anathema in omnes juramenti hujus futuros immemores, & secuta sunt edicta, ne quis imposterum Missam diceret, aut ullo officio ecclesiastico fungeretur, sine licentia Patriarchæ; utque omnes sacra Romana sequerentur; nec quisquam rebellibus (Romano Pontifici obsequium negantibus) receptum daret; qui secus faxit, supplicio afficeretur. Post ædificata in Debson Sedes Patriarchalis, & diversis in Regni locis pro Jesuitis, quos secum Patriarcha adduxerat, Residentiæ extructæ sunt; introductum quin etiam computum Romanum, baptizati ordinatique denuo, qui jam ante baptigati & ordinati Alexandrino ritu erant; institutum seminarium sexaginta puerorum Habessinorum & Lusitanorum, comœdiæ agitatæ Europæo more, in quibus etiam producti Diaboli Habessinos graviter terruerunt. Jámque etiam Romanus ille Patriarcha excommunicare leves ob causas; sepulti, qui Alexandrinam religionem tenebant, in locis Romano ritu dedicatis, refodi & foras projici; malefici inscio Rege in carceres compingi; & nonnulli etiam, ministro sævitiæ Ras-Seelaxo, occidi cœperunt. Unde turbis in Regno atrocibus subortis, & Rege ab iis, qui Romanis infensi erant, impetito, Rex ipse tandem, suspicatus, quod res erat, peregrino se imperio subjici, à Patriarcha & Jesuitis alienior redditus, primùm invito Patriarcha veteres ceremonias indulsit; tum religionem Alexandrinam restituere, Romanam abolere certus, prospera cum rebellibus pugna (dolens tantum sanguinis jam ob Romana sacra profusum) Alexandrinorum persuasione, Reginæ & filii precibus inductus, frequente Procerum Concilio de restituenda religione Alexandrina decretum condidit; atque illud nequicquam Patriarcha ringente, minante, & rebus deploratis ad preces supplices converso, temperamentúmque suadente, promulgári, magno cum populi, cleri inprimis, applausu curavit. Mox templa Romanis adempta, & post mortem Sufnei, victo Ras-Seelaxo, Romanorum partium duce; Jesuitæ bonis armisque quæ inter bombardas plures habebant, exuti, Fremonam ablegati, tandémque una cum Patriarcha, mense Majo A. M. D. C. XXXIV. toto Regno, frustra ab Indis aliisque auxilia solicitantes, expulsi sunt. Et qui residui erant in Regno, Episcopus puta Apollinaris Almegdas, & Patres nonnulli, Hyacinthus Franciscus, Ludovicus Cordeyra, alii, variis casibus jactati, plerique etiam suspendio sublati; & ipsi Jesuitarum fautores Habessini occisi sunt. Accepto rei prorsus improvisæ nuntio Papa perculsus, ratúsque, odio mero adversus Jesuitas & nationem Lusitanicam, mutationem contigisse, aliam quercum excutere properus, sex Capucinos Gallos, quos mitiores & devotiores facilius receptum iri considebat, in Habessiniam legavit; ex quibus duo à Cafris occisi; duo in Habessinia lapidati; duo metuentes sibi domum reversi sunt. Demum tres alii Capucini spe melioris fortunæ secuti, cùm in Suoquenam venissent, petente Negucso (hoc Regibus Habessinis nomen) à Bassa Suaquenæ Turcico capite plexi sunt; tandémque etiam ultimus Jesuitarum, Bernhardus Nogueyra suspendio vitam finivit. Hunc exitum habuit Pontificia in Habessinia Romanæ Sedi & dominationi subjuganda præpostera contentio & negotiatio omnis, cujus seriem ex Balthasaris Tellezii & Gregorii Habessini scriptis dictisque Nobilissimus & Celeberr. Jobus Ludolfus, Linguæ & rerum Habessinarum ad stuporem usque doctus, Fautor noster Summus, in Historia Æthiopica, quam amplo etiam commentario locupletatam anxiè eruditus orbis expectat, magno judicio parique fide collegit.
units.tr: varez, a priest of the Portuguese embassy in Ethiopia, brought to Pope Clement VII in 1533 letters from the Ethiopian king David, and at the same time offered him reverence and obedience in the king's name. Thus encouraged, the Pope hoped that the losses he had suffered in the West would soon be made good by the East and the South. A certain appearance of friendship lasted for a long time. For Paul III did not hesitate to confirm the ordination made by the metropolitan Mark, and so by a schismatic prelate, when John of Bermudes was sent to Rome to seek help, several times, for David, who had been defeated. Hope thus dawned that the kingdom could be subjected to the Roman Church, chiefly through the efforts of Ignatius Loyola and Nonius Berreto, to whom Julius III granted the patriarchal dignity in Ethiopia, although Bermudes had already been honoured with the same title by the Pope earlier, with Andrew Oviedo, a bishop, added to him, who tried the matter with sacred conferences and with harsh remedies, but in vain. At the beginning of this century a new mission was undertaken, and Father Peter Paez, a Jesuit, advanced the matter so far that King Zadenghel offered his friendship to Clement VIII and Philip III, King of Spain and Portugal, by letters, and asked for soldiers, craftsmen and Fathers of the Society of Jesus to instruct his subjects. For this reason he was killed by his own people, who resented these new undertakings with ill will. After him came Jacob's successor, King Susneus, who favoured the Romans. After public conferences with the Jesuits he went so far that, by an edict in favour of the Romans, after serious disturbances both in the kingdom and stirred up by the Alexandrians, he publicly threw off the yoke of the Patriarch of Alexandria, embraced the Roman religion, and declared that he wished to obey the Roman Pope, the successor of Peter, who could err neither in faith nor in morals, urging his subjects to do the same. With affairs thus flowing as they wished, under Pope Urban and at the nomination of Philip IV, Alphonsus Mendez, a Portuguese by birth and a famous man, was created Patriarch of Ethiopia from the order of the Jesuits. Consecrated at Lisbon with the usual ceremonies, he landed at Goa in India in May 1624, and from there made his way into Abyssinia to the King. The King at once knelt down and swore in these words, as dictated by the Supreme Pontiff Urban: "We, Sultan Saghedus (Susneus is this name), King of Kings of Ethiopia, believe and confess that St Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, was established by Christ our Lord as head of the whole Christian Church, and that the principate and power over the whole world was given to him when he said: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and I will give you the keys of heaven; and at another time, when he said to him: Feed my sheep. Likewise we believe that the Roman Pope, lawfully elected, is the true successor of St Peter the Apostle in government, and holds the same power, dignity and primacy over the whole Christian Church. Therefore to Urban VIII, by the grace of God the Pope of this name, our Lord, and to his successors in the administration of the Church, we promise, offer and swear true obedience, and humbly submit our person and our empire at his feet. So may God help us, and these holy Gospels." Afterwards the same oath was sworn by the future successor Basilides, the brother kings, all the pro-kings and nobles, and also by the clergy and monks present. At the same time it was proclaimed as an anathema against all who forgot this oath, and edicts followed: "that no one from now on should say Mass or perform any ecclesiastical office without the Patriarch's permission; that all should follow Roman rites; that no one should give shelter to rebels (who refused obedience to the Roman Pope); whoever acted otherwise would be punished." After a patriarchal see had been built at Debson, and residences were erected in various parts of the kingdom for the Jesuits whom the Patriarch had brought with him, they even introduced the Roman calendar, and those who had already been baptized and ordained according to the Alexandrian rite were baptized and ordained again; a seminary of sixty Abyssinian and Portuguese boys was founded, and comedies were performed in the European manner, in which even Devils brought on stage terrified the Abyssinians greatly. And now that Roman Patriarch began to excommunicate people for slight reasons; those who held to the Alexandrian religion were buried in places consecrated by the Roman rite, and their bodies were dug up and thrown out; malefactors were thrown into prisons without the King's knowledge; and some were even put to death by Ras Seelaxo, the minister of cruelty. Then, when atrocious disturbances arose in the kingdom and the King was attacked by those who were hostile to the Romans, the King himself at last suspected what was happening, that he was being subjected to a foreign rule, and, becoming more alienated from the Patriarch and the Jesuits, first granted the old ceremonies against the Patriarch's wishes; then, resolved to restore the Alexandrian religion and abolish the Roman, and after a successful battle with the rebels (though grieving at the amount of blood already shed for the Roman rites), induced by the persuasion of the Alexandrians and by the prayers of the Queen and his son, he drew up a decree at a crowded council of nobles on restoring the Alexandrian religion, and took care that it was promulgated, to great applause from the people, and especially from the clergy. Soon the churches were taken from the Romans, and after the death of Susneus, when Ras Seelaxo, the leader of the Roman party, was defeated, the Jesuits, stripped of their goods and their weapons, of which they had several cannon, were sent away to Fremona, and at last, together with the Patriarch, in May 1634, they were expelled from the whole kingdom, after asking in vain for help from the Indians and others. Those who remained in the kingdom, namely the bishop Apollinaris Almegdas and some Fathers, Hyacinth Francis, Louis Cordeyra and others, were tossed about by various misfortunes, and most of them were hanged; and even Abyssinian supporters of the Jesuits were killed. When the Pope was struck by news of this completely unexpected event, and believed that a change had occurred out of pure hatred towards the Jesuits and the Portuguese nation, he hastened to shake out another oak, and sent six French Capuchins to Abyssinia, whom he thought would be more easily received because they were milder and more devout. Of these, two were killed by the Galla, two were stoned in Abyssinia, and two, fearing for themselves, returned home. At last three other Capuchins, following the hope of a better fortune, when they came to Massawa, were beheaded by the Turkish pasha of Massawa at the request of Negus (this is the name the Abyssinian kings bear); and finally the last of the Jesuits, Bernhard Nogueira, ended his life by hanging. Such was the outcome of the Papists' preposterous contention and all their dealings in Abyssinia, aimed at subjecting it to the Roman See and rule. Its whole course was gathered, with great judgment and equal fidelity, from the writings and sayings of Balthasar Tellez and Gregory the Abyssinian by the most noble and celebrated Job Ludolf, our very great patron, who is learned in the Abyssinian language and affairs to the point of astonishment, in his Ethiopian History, which the eager learned world awaits, enriched by a full commentary.

units.la: CCXLIII. Neque dissimilem circa eadem fere tempora catastrophen Pontificia in Japonia etiam, & paulò ante in Sina non tam Christiana salutari fide imbuenda, quàm Pontificis libidini subigenda, machinatio omnis sortita est.
units.tr: CCXLIII. Not dissimilar, at about the same time, was the catastrophe that befell all the Papists' schemes in Japan, and a little earlier in China, countries to be steeped not so much in the saving Christian faith as brought under the lust of the Pontiff.

units.la: In nullum quidem vel Orientis vel Occidentis Regnum Christiana religio feliciori successu introducta, in nullo crudeliori denique persecutione profligata est. A. M. D. XLII. primi ex Europa Lusitani in Japoniam delati sunt. Franciscus Xaverius cum duobus sociis Cosmo Turriano, & Johanne Fernando, opitulante Angero Japonio, Linguæ Lusitanicæ non ignaro, & discendæ religionis Christianæ desiderio ardente, quique jam tum baptizatus Pauli à Sancta fide nomen habuit; Euangelium (purum, an interpolatum heic non disputo, primi in eo Regno praedicarunt. Statim Rex edicta promulgavit, testatus, placere sibi Christianam religionem, & in ditiones suas induci cupere. Quatuor jam civitates, Congoxima, Firandum, Amongucium & Bungum Christianam fidem amplexae erant. Post Xaverii A. M. D. LII. in indiam reversi discessum successerunt ex eadem Societate plures, qui progressu temporis magnam Japoniae partem ad Christiana sacra traduxerunt, passim templa & Collegia extruxerunt. Conversi etiam sunt tres Reges, Bungi, Arrymae & Omurae, qui A. M. D. LXXXII. procurante Alexandro Walignano, Jesuitarum Visitatore generali, Romam missis legatis, ubique magnifice exceptis, & splendidis muneribus mactatis, Gregorio XIII. obedientiam promiserunt. Scilicet Jesuitae legatione isthac, ex magnificentia Ecclesiae Romanae religioni, quae splendori & magnificentiae externae plurimum debet, Pontifici inprimis apud Japones authoritatem fidémque se conciliaturos, eximium ordini suo decus & famam inde comparaturos, denique ingens inde lucrum reportaturos sperárunt? Maximam enim partem munerum, quae tum Pontifex, tum Hispaniae Rex per Legatos Japoniae Regibus illis transmiserunt, Jesuitas sibi vindicasse, Varenius de Relig. Japon. cap. 6. testatur. Idquoque à Papa Gregorio & Rege Hispaniae iidem impetrárunt, ut sine ipsorum consensu nemini vel Lusitano, vel alii etiam Christiano in Japonia sedem domiciliumque figere liceret. Neque Gregorius aliis quàm Jesuitis potestatem in Japonia praedicandi concessit. Sed extendit eandem mox Clemens VIII. ad Ordines mendicantes, siquidem ita necessitas postulaverit; ita tamen, ne fas sit nisi per Lusitaniam, atque inde Indiam & civitatem Goam, Japoniam, Chinam & finitima Regna intrare. Demum Paulus V. etiam per aliam viam, quàm per Lusitaniam in Japonicas, aliásque proximè adjacentes infulas aditum concessit. Itaque frequente Religiosorum Jesuitarum cumprimis, cæteris palmam facilè præripientium, in Japoniam accursu Christiana ibidem fides incrementa indies major a cepit. Et jucunda quidem fuit protasis; grata epitasis; sed miserabilis & ingratissima catastrophe. Vix enim profundiores radices religio Christiana egerat, cùm radicitus extirparetur, & innumerorum Christianorum sævissimè profuso sanguine suffocaretur. Exardescens enim adversus Christianos omnes primùm A. M. D. C. XXXII. persecutio, aliquot annos continuata est apud eundem Varenium, Rejero Gysberto Belga ad A. M. D. C. XXXIX. usque, at Caronio etiam ultra ejus historiam lugubrem planè producente. Et primo quidem capite plecti & cruci affigi coeperunt. Cúmque hilari animo supplicia isthæc à Christianis tolerari persecutores cernerent, ad truculentiora & sæviora in dies progressi, alios palis alligatos lento exiguóque igne cremárunt; alios cratibus impositos assárunt; teneras virgines & uxores toto corpore nudas per compita tractas, impurorúmque libidine palam corruptas, demum prægrandibus ligneis cupis plenis serpentibus imposuerunt, serpentibus in pudendas partes irrepentibus incredibili cum earum dolore, donec veneni vis vel cruciatus intolerabiles mortem attulerunt; alios ferventibus aquis ad necem usque ustulárunt; alios suspenderunt pedibus sursum elevatis, & patibulo alligatis, capite ita deorsum pendulo, ut umbilico tenus in foveam quandam corpus immitteretur; quorum etiam ne sanguine suffocarentur, cutem capitis decussatim discciderunt, quò per scissuras sanguis exstillando exitum inveniret; alios (quod novissimum & deinceps usitatissimum Christianorum supplicium fuit) dissecto tantùm ventre ita suspenderunt, ut post ineffabilem cruciatum nono demum vel decimo etiam die, ad extremum usque cum ratione verba facientes, spiritum Deo redderent. Quibus supplicLorum horrendorum generibus multa Christianorum tum advenarum, tum Japonum ad Christum conversorum, millia, non multos intra annos, miserè extincta sunt; hanc, si à Bonziorum Sacerdotum adversus Christianos æmulatione perpetua discesseris; præcipuè, uti putatur, ob causam, quòd Hispani ferociùs insolentiúsque se gerentes dominationem affectare, & Jesuitæ concionibus tribunitiis subditos ad seditionem & rebellionem adversus Superiores minùs sibi addictos concitare, Regnúmque amplissimum alienæ libidini subjecturi visi sunt. quod posterius etiam ex Almeidæ epistola Varenius probat. Nam quòd de Belgarum mala fide Jesuitæ mussitare ausi sunt, Jesuitico more id fecerunt, neque fide digno testimonio ullo id comprobârunt. Neque tamen Urbanus Papa de re Christiana apud Japones in integrum restituenda prorsus spem abjecit. Is quippe Bulla die xxi. Febr. A. M. D. C. XXXIII. edita, ultra superiorum Pontificum decreta, missionem ad Japonicas & aliarum Indiarum Orientalium Regiones, ad Religiosos cujuscunque demum ordinis extendit, & impedientes missionem excommunicationis latæ sententiæ vinculo innodavit. Sed frustra ille Romæ decreta cudit, & adversus imparentes fulmina conflavit, dum interea Saguntus periit, & funditus pessum ivit. Ita enim persecutio ingravescens indies deinceps quoque arsit, ut jam A. M. D. C. XL. sanguinis Christiani in universa Japonia ne reliquiæ quidem ullæ repertæ sint; & Belgæ commerciorum duntaxat gratia, nullâque stabili sede gaudentes, insulam eam non sine periculo, rigidísque adeò legibus & interdictis constricti, frequentent, argumenta gravissimi judicii Divini adversus tum impiam cœcamque gentem, tum eorum etiam consilia, qui speciosō religionis, forte non bona etiam ubique fide,saltem prævia vocatione legitima nulla,traditæ, obtentu suis duntaxat commodis inhiantes, non tam oves, quàm ovium lanam quæsiverunt. Nec in Sina feliciorem res Jesuitarum successum habuere, ubi in aula Pekingensi, apud Imperatorem Vanlieum potentes, sua temeritate, & improvida Profelythismi, seu potiùs Pharisæismi propagatione, horribilem A. M. D. C. XV. persecutionem Christianis suis conciverunt. Bonzii enim videntes, lucrum suum à nova religione imminui, & ad peregrinos Sacerdotes transfire, sacra quin etiam sua universa vilescere, non ante quieverunt, quàm eos, tanquam priscæ religionis eversores, & Astrologiæ Sinensis destructores, in Nankingensi Metropoli in carceres conjicerent. quos inter etiam fuit P. Alvaro Semedo, qui totam hanc tragœdiam descripsit.
units.tr: Christian religion was introduced into no kingdom of East or West with more fortunate success, and was crushed by no more cruel persecution. In 1542 the first Portuguese were carried from Europe to Japan. Francis Xavier, with two companions, Cosmas Turrianus and John Fernandez, preached the Gospel (whether pure or adulterated I do not discuss here) in that kingdom first, helped by Anjiro the Japanese, who knew Portuguese and burned with desire to learn the Christian religion, and who had already been baptized and had the name Paul of the Holy Faith. At once the king issued edicts, declaring that he was pleased with the Christian religion and wished to bring it into his territories. Four cities, Congoxima, Firandum, Amonguchium and Bungum, had already embraced the Christian faith. After Xavier left for India in 1552, several members of the same Society followed, who in course of time brought a large part of Japan over to Christian rites and built temples and colleges everywhere. Three kings were also converted, of Bungo, Arima and Omura, who in 1582, through the efforts of Alessandro Valignano, the general Visitor of the Jesuits, sent envoys to Rome, who were received everywhere with great honour, and offered splendid gifts, and promised obedience to Gregory XIII. Clearly the Jesuits hoped by this embassy that, through the magnificence of the Roman Church, a religion which owes very much to outward splendour and pomp, they would win for the Pontiff, above all among the Japanese, authority and trust, would gain for their order a notable honour and fame, and finally would derive from it an immense profit. For Varenius, in his work on the Japanese religion, chapter 6, testifies that the Jesuits claimed for themselves most of the gifts which the Pontiff and the King of Spain then sent through envoys to those Japanese kings. They also obtained from Pope Gregory and the King of Spain that no one, neither a Portuguese nor any other Christian, might fix a residence or home in Japan without their consent. Nor did Gregory grant the power of preaching in Japan to anyone but the Jesuits. But Clement VIII soon extended the same power to the mendicant orders, provided that necessity should so require; yet on condition that no one might enter Japan, China and the neighbouring kingdoms except through Portugal, and from there through India and the city of Goa. Finally Paul V granted access to the Japanese and other nearby islands also by a route other than through Portugal. So, with the frequent influx into Japan of religious men, above all the Jesuits, who easily snatched the palm from the rest, the Christian faith there began to grow greater day by day. The beginning was pleasing, the middle appealing, but the end was wretched and most ungrateful. For the Christian religion had scarcely struck deeper roots when it was torn up by the root, and was choked by the most savage shedding of the blood of countless Christians. For a persecution against all Christians blazed up first in 1632, and continued for some years, as Varenius records, down to 1639 (Reijer Gijsbertsz the Belgian), and Caron carries it even beyond his mournful history. And at first they began to put them to death by beheading and crucifixion. And when the persecutors saw that these punishments were borne by the Christians with a cheerful spirit, they advanced day by day to more savage and cruel forms: some they tied to stakes and burned with a slow, small fire; some they placed on gridirons and roasted; tender virgins and wives they dragged naked over their whole bodies through the crossroads, and openly corrupted them for the lust of impure men; finally they placed them in very large wooden tubs full of serpents, the serpents creeping into their private parts with incredible pain, until the force of the poison or the intolerable torment brought death; others they burned to death in boiling water; others they hung up with their feet raised and bound to a gibbet, with the head hanging down so that the body was lowered into a pit up to the navel; and lest these should be choked by their blood, they cut the skin of the head crosswise, so that the blood might find an exit by dripping through the cuts; others (which was the last and thereafter the most common punishment of the Christians) they hung up with only the belly cut open, so that after unspeakable torment, on the ninth or even the tenth day, still speaking with reason to the very end, they gave up the spirit to God. By these kinds of horrible punishments, many thousands of Christians, both foreign-born and Japanese converted to Christ, were miserably put to death within a few years. This, if you set aside the constant rivalry of the Bonze priests against the Christians, was chiefly, as is thought, for the following reason: the Spaniards, behaving more fiercely and insolently, seemed to aim at domination, and the Jesuits, by tribune-like sermons, seemed to stir up their subjects to sedition and rebellion against superiors less devoted to them, and were about to subject that most extensive kingdom to foreign lust. Varenius proves this latter point also from the letter of Almeida. For as to the Jesuits' daring to murmur about the bad faith of the Dutch, they did so in the Jesuit manner, and proved it by no testimony worthy of belief. Nor did Pope Urban nevertheless utterly despair of restoring the Christian cause in Japan to its former state. Indeed, by his bull issued on 21 February 1633, he extended, beyond the decrees of earlier Pontiffs, the mission to the Japanese and other regions of the East Indies to religious men of whatever order, and bound those who hindered the mission with the chain of excommunication latae sententiae. But in vain did he forge decrees at Rome and blow thunderbolts against the disobedient, while meanwhile Saguntum perished and was utterly ruined. For the persecution, growing hotter day by day, then blazed on so that by 1640 no remnants of Christian blood could be found in all Japan; and the Dutch, enjoying only the benefit of trade and no stable seat, frequent that island not without danger, and bound by very rigid laws and prohibitions. These are proofs of the most grave judgement of God against both the impious and blind nation, and against the counsels of those who, aiming at their own advantage under the pretext of religion (perhaps not everywhere in good faith, and with no lawful prior calling), sought not so much the sheep as the wool of the sheep. Nor did the Jesuits' affairs have a happier outcome in China, where, powerful at the court of Peking with the Emperor Wanli, by their rashness and ill-considered propagation of proselytism, or rather Pharisaism, they brought upon their Christians a horrible persecution in 1615. For the Bonzes, seeing their profit diminished by the new religion, and passing over to the foreign priests, and even their own rites growing worthless, did not rest until they cast them, as overturners of the ancient religion, and destroyers of Chinese astrology, into prison in the metropolis of Nanking. Among these was Father Alvaro Semedo, who described this whole tragedy.

units.la: CCXLIV. Mirè deinceps Deus Ecclesiæ Romanæ labium confudit, excitatis in ea dissidiis, & tantùm non dextris ejus in se invicem armatis.
units.tr: CCXLIV. Then God further confounded the tongue of the Roman Church, stirring up dissensions within it, so that its right hands were all but armed against one another.

units.la: Et primò quidem potentia Hispani & Cæsaris, prosperis in Germania successibus increscens, ita jam Pontifici Urbano suspecta esse coepit, ut Regi Galliæ non obscurè favens, eundem admonuerit, ne statum Germaniæ proculcari sinat. Qua admonitione sponte currentem Gallum, adversus Cæsarem & Hispanos excitavit magis. Duravitque Urbani adversus Hispanos malivolentia, etiam post inclinatam eorundem per stupendos Suecorum Regis, Gustavi Adolphi, Herois incomparabilis, qui nixus præpotenti Dei manu, exiguis primùm copiis, auxiliis pene nullis, Germaniam jugo Austriaco-Hispanico, orbem universum metu liberavit; progressus, fortunam. Tum enim infensum erga Hispanos animum prodens, Legato Hispanico in pleno Cardinalium consessu dicere in os non dubitavit: Hispanum sua tyrannide & regnandi libidine effecisse, ut boni Catholici debeant exultare in victoriis haereticorum. In Hispania contra Jesuita quidam Duci Olivario à secretis confessionibus, abdicato genio Jesuitico, librum edidit de potestate Pontificis, quo eum Romae suae affixurus, palam docuit: Omnem potestatem, quam capitis ecclesiae titulo in Christianum orbem sibi Papa vendicet, meram usurpationem, intrusionem, violentiam esse: non existente Papa in alio (& forte etiam in isto) nulla est praerogativa supra alios Episcopos, nisi quantum ad dignitatem accidentalem, non ad superioritatem jurisdictionis: Non habet in sua quaque dioecesi, minorem quoad hoc jurisdictionem episcopi, quam habeat Papa in suo Episcopatu S. Johannis Lateranensis. Papa non est supra Concilium, sed contra: Proinde excommunicatio Bullae in Coena Domini adversus eum, qui à Papa appellaverit ad Concilium, est injusta, invalida, intoleranda. Hispanis ita à Pontifice dissidentibus, in eo consilia stetisse ferebantur, ut à Pontificibus auferrent collationem beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum in illo Regno, ac erecta ibidem, quam vocant, dataria, eos argento, quod inde hactenus perceperant, multarent.
units.tr: First, the power of the Spaniards and of the Emperor, growing with their successes in Germany, began to be so suspect to Pope Urban that, while openly favouring the King of France, he warned him not to allow the condition of Germany to be trampled underfoot. This warning only spurred the Frenchman, who was already running eagerly, against the Emperor and the Spaniards. Urban's ill will towards the Spaniards lasted even after their power had been broken by the wonderful victories of King Gustavus Adolphus, that incomparable hero, who, relying on the all-powerful hand of God, first with small forces and almost no allies, freed Germany from the Austro-Spanish yoke and, advancing, freed the whole world from fear and gained good fortune. Then, showing his hostility towards the Spaniards, he did not hesitate to say to the face of a Spanish envoy, in a full assembly of the Cardinals, that the Spaniard, by his tyranny and lust for power, had brought it about that good Catholics ought to rejoice in the victories of heretics. In Spain, on the other hand, a certain Jesuit, confessor to the Duke of Olivares, abandoned the Jesuit spirit and published a book on the power of the Pope, which he openly taught, intending to fix it up at Rome: Whatever power the Pope claims over the Christian world under the title of head of the Church is a mere usurpation, intrusion and violence. While the Pope exists in another (and perhaps also in this one), he has no prerogative over other bishops except in accidental dignity, not in superiority of jurisdiction. In his own diocese a bishop does not have less jurisdiction in this respect than the Pope has in his bishopric of St John Lateran. The Pope is not above the Council, but below it. Therefore the excommunication in the Bull In Coena Domini against anyone who has appealed from the Pope to a Council is unjust, invalid and intolerable. While the Spaniards were thus at odds with the Pope, it was reported that their plan was to deprive the Popes of the conferring of ecclesiastical benefices in that kingdom, and, by setting up there what they call the dataria, to fine them with the money they had hitherto drawn from it.

units.la: CCXLV. Graves etiam paulò post intestini motus Papatum concusserunt, occasione quaestionum de oeconomia gratia Divinae, Molinistas inter & Jansenium, ejusque assectas, quorum utrique Papam Romanum agnoscebant, vehementer agitatarum. Cornelius Jansenius, Episcopus Iprensis in Flandria, Vir doctissimus, & S. Augustini cumprimis scriptis, quae in universum omnia decies, seorsim vero libros de Gratia & Libero arbitrio, tricies, Liberto Fromondo teste, legit; innutritus, librum scripserat, titulo: Augustinus; seu Doctrina S. Augustini de humanae naturae sanitate, aegritudine, medicina adversus Pelagianos & Massilienses; tribus tomis comprehensa. Prodiit liber, verè demorsos sapiens ungues, biennio post mortem Authoris, A. M. D. C. XL. procurantibus Fromondo, Caleno, & Reginaldo Lamaeo executoribus testamenti ejus. In universum eo damnatur Theologia Scholastica, quòd in ea Epicuræa, Platonica & Pelagiana dogmata contineantur. Acri inprimis censura perstringitur. Molino-Suarezii, Fonsecæ, Lessii &c. de Scientia media opinio periculosissima omnium, utpote quæ hominem ἀὐλεξούσιον, adeóque Deum facit. Præterea ex Augustini sententia asseritur, gratiam Dei operari irresistibiliter; esse eam particularem, etiam ex intentione Dei antecedente; nullam esse sufficientem, nisi quæ actu secundo beatitudinem consummat; Christum pro solis electis mortuum esse. Qua in doctrina ita Reformatis suffragari visus est, ut nomen ejus, Cornelius Jansenius, nonnulli invidiam authori conflaturi, per anagramma reddiderint: Calvini sensus in ore. Primùm atque lucem liber aspexit, in Belgio & Gallia, apud Sorbonam inprimis, ingentem applausum meruit, habuitque. Lœtati doctissimi quique sunt, Augustini doctrinam, per Helenam illam Jesuitarum, aliorúmque Theologiam Scholasticam sepultam revivisce-re. Sed quò magis lœtabantur illi, hoc infestiores se doctrinæ ei tristioréfque gerebant illi, qui sodales suos, Molinam, Suarezium &c. eo opere aperto Marte oppugnari, & Pelagianismi etiam nota aspergi, dolebant non parùm. Unde statim Augustinus ille Jansenii non tantùm à privatis scriptoribus, Jesuitis, Dionysio Petavio, Isaco Hoberto, Antonio Richardo, Francisco Annato, Petro de S. Joseph, Philippo de Sancta Trinitate, Ripaldo, Brisacerio, aliis oppugnatus acerimè est; sed etiam, connitentibus iisdem, favore inprimis Francisci Barbarini Cardinalis usis, ab Urbano Pontifice, Bulla prid. Non. Mart. A. M. D. C. XLI. edita, damnatus proscriptúsque est, hoc videlicet prætextu, quòd in eo propositiones nonnullæ Michaëlis Baii, à Pio V. A. M. D. LXVII. damnatæ & prohibitæ, contineantur; quódque sic contra edictum Gregorii XIII. controversiæ de auxiliis gratiæ resuscitentur. cautúmtúmque simul, sub gravissimis censuris ecclesiasticis & poenis secularibus, ne quis impositerum de materia auxiliorum Divinorum, sine expressa & speciali licentia tractaret, donec aliud in hac materia à sede Apostolica fuerit ordinatum. Prohibiti quinetiam eadem bulla sunt omnes libri, qui vel pro Jansenio, vel contra eum de hac materia scripti essent, vel impositerum scribentur. Cúmque censurae huic Papali Belgae se non submisissent, neque ejus publicationem admittere se velle, priùs quàm Regis Hispaniae authoritas & consensus accesserit, declarâssent; Urbanus denuo Bullam suam A. M. D. C. XLIV. repetiit confirmavitque, perpetuúmque contradicentibus silentium impositit. Neque tamen sic ad ἐχεμυθίαν sese redigi Jansenitae passi sunt. Enimverò Jansenium defenderunt strenuè iidem, qui supra, Fromondus, ejus in cathedra Lovaniensi successor, Cario Parisiensis Theologus, Sorbonistae plerique, nec non Archiepiscopus Mechliniensis, Belgii Primas, unà cum reliquis Episcopis & Generalibus Provinciae, qui Bullam Papalem per dolum sub- & obreptionis extortam pertenderunt. qui proin æquè ac ipse Belgii Gubernator, Francifcus de Mello, induci non potuerunt, ut, quod à Papa severè jussi erant, bullam ejus executioni mandarent. Sed & Innocentius X. Urbani successor, cùm bullam Urbani eludi putaret, sedecim Brevia misit, nempe ad Marchionem Castri Rodrigi, Gubernatorem Belgii. Archiepiscopos Mechlinienfem & Cameracensem, Episcopos Belgii septem, Universitatis Sorbonae Theologos, Magistrum Guilhelmum ab Angelis S. T. D. Lovaniensem, Leopoldum Guilhelmum, Archiducem Austriae, & Episcopum Argentinensem; quibus confirmata Urbani Bulla, injunctum serió, ut illam tandem promulgarent & exequerentur. Et alicubi quidem, puta Antuerpiae, Duaci Namurci, aliisque locis nonnullis promulgari, adeóque Janseni assectae nonnihil premi coeperunt, interdictis adeò severis, ut imposterum ad animarum curam nemo admitteretur, quin post solennem fidei Concilii Tridentini confessionem, solenni formula praescripta, Janseni Augustinum damnassent prius. Verùm cum reputassent illi, eadem artes revocari, quibus quondam Ariani apud Imperatorem Constantinum usi fuerunt, Appellationem ediderunt ad Pontificem Romanum, titulo Planctus veritatis Augustinianæ in Belgio patientis; rogantes, ut priusquam adversus Jansenium subscribere cogantur, de fide suscipiatur disceptatio, nec tum demum de re cognoscatur, cùm persona judicata & damnata jam fuerit. Annexi sunt Planctui huic tres libelli, quorum primus fidem, secundus justitiam, tertius charitatem commendat. Sed surdo fabulam narrârunt, Jesuitis apud Innocentium impetrantibus facilè, ne aures Janseniistis arrigeret. Cùm igitur Bullæ & edicta Papalia acrioribus odiis hactenus partes inter se accendissent; & alii quidem Janseno falsa dogmata affingi; alii, sententiam ejus hæresis damnari non potuisse, quòd nec scripturis, nec Conciliis adversetur; alii denique non tam Janseni, quàm Augustini causam hic agi, & Janseno damnato Augustinum ipsum damnari, palam editis in publicum libris asseruissent; denique Jacobus Archiepiscopus Mechliniensis, Belgii Primas; Antonius Trieft, Episcopus Gandavensis, & Vicarii Generales Sedis Episcopalis Iprensis rationes, ob quas Bullam Pontificis promulgare non possent, luci publicæ exposuissent; induci se Innocentius à Jesuitis, & Episcopis nonnullis Galliæ, Jesuitarum instinctu in partes venientibus, (quanquam ἐπιλαῖον hoc πάθος Innocentii fuit) passus est, ut Propositiones quinque ex Janseni Augustino, uti putabatur, excerptæ, Romæ præsentibus & auscultantibus Cardinalibus nonnullis Johanne de Lugo, Carafla, Spada, &c. à Theologis tredecim, quos ininter Sforza Pallavicinus Jesuita primum locum obtinebat, ventilarentur. Justi autem sunt Theologi illi vota seu suffragia sua scripto consignata (quæ ab Episcopo Montispessuli Roma in Galliam allata, totidem verbis Montaltius post finem Epistolarum Provincialium edidit) Pontifici offerre. Ex quibus scripto & voce Theologorum oblatis, Innocentius palam in hac ipsa causa professus, se non esse Theologum; (testatur enim Theologus Pontificius Ludovicus de S. Amour, Romam ab Episcopis Galliæ ad orandam Jansenitarum causam missus, editi Diurnalis par. 3. cap. 12. rogatum Innocentium, ut ipse cognosceret, ne quidem scripta sibi oblata legere voluisse, & respondisse insuper: Non est mea professio; Præterquam quod senex sum. Ego nunquam studui Theologiæ. Dixisse alii ajunt: Io non sono Theologo: Ego non sum Theologus) post indictas, uti Bulla prid. Kal. Jun. A. M. D. C. LIII. ab ipso edita habet, ad Divinum implorandum auxilium, multorum Christianorum preces, tum publice tum privatim; & easdem postmodum ferventius iteratas; quin & solicitè implorata S. Spiritus assistentia; ad Declarationem & definitionem procedens, Propositionum quinque, pro lubitu hostium Jansenii formatarum, damnationem conflavit.
units.tr: CCXLV. Soon after, serious internal disturbances also shook the Papacy, arising from the questions about the economy of divine grace, which were vehemently debated between the Molinists and Jansenius and his followers, both of whom acknowledged the Roman Pope. Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres in Flanders, a most learned man, and steeped above all in the writings of St Augustine, which, according to Liberatus Fromondus, he read ten times in their entirety and the books On Grace and Free Will thirty times, wrote a book entitled Augustinus; or, the Doctrine of St Augustine on the health, sickness and cure of human nature, against the Pelagians and the Massilians; comprised in three volumes. The book appeared, a wise work that had truly bitten the nails of its opponents, two years after the author's death, in 1640, with Fromondus, Calenus and Reginald Lamaeus, executors of his will, arranging its publication. In general, it condemns scholastic theology, on the ground that it contains Epicurean, Platonic and Pelagian doctrines. It attacks with particular sharpness the opinion of Molina, Suárez, Fonseca, Lessius and others about scientia media, the most dangerous of all, since it makes man autexousios [ἀὐλεξούσιον], and therefore God. Moreover, following Augustine's view, it asserts that the grace of God operates irresistibly; that it is particular, even by God's antecedent intention; that no grace is sufficient except that which brings blessedness to completion in the second act; and that Christ died only for the elect. In this doctrine he seemed to lend such support to the Reformed that some, wishing to stir up hatred against the author, rendered his name, Cornelius Jansenius, by an anagram: Calvini sensus in ore [the sense of Calvin in the mouth]. When the book first saw the light, in the Netherlands and France, and especially at the Sorbonne, it won and enjoyed great applause. All the most learned rejoiced that the doctrine of Augustine, buried by that Helen of the Jesuits and by the scholastic theology of others, was being revived. But the more they rejoiced, the more hostile and bitter were those who were greatly grieved that their colleagues Molina, Suárez and others were openly attacked in this work and tainted even with the mark of Pelagianism. Hence that Augustine of Jansenius was at once fiercely assailed not only by private writers, Jesuits such as Denis Petavius, Isaac Hubert, Antoine Richard, François Annat, Pierre de Saint-Joseph, Philippe de la Sainte-Trinité, Ripalda, Brisacier and others, but also, with the same persons working hard and using above all the favour of Cardinal Francesco Barberini, he was condemned and proscribed by Pope Urban in a Bull issued on 4 March 1641, on the pretext, namely, that it contained several propositions of Michael Baius, condemned and prohibited by Pius V in 1567; and that thus, contrary to the edict of Gregory XIII, the controversies about the auxiliary grace were revived. At the same time it was enjoined, under the most serious ecclesiastical censures and secular penalties, that no one should henceforth treat of the matter of divine aids without express and special licence, until something else on this matter should be ordained by the Apostolic See. Moreover, by the same Bull all books which had been written either for Jansenius or against him on this subject, or which should be written in future, were prohibited. When the Belgians had declared that they would not submit to this Papal censure, nor admit its publication until the authority and consent of the King of Spain had been given, Urban again repeated and confirmed his Bull in 1644, and imposed perpetual silence on those who contradicted it. Yet the Jansenists did not allow themselves to be reduced to silence in this way. Indeed, those mentioned above defended Jansenius vigorously: Fromondus, his successor in the chair at Louvain; Carion, a theologian of Paris; most of the Sorbonists; and also the Archbishop of Mechlin, primate of Belgium, together with the other bishops and provincial superiors, who claimed that the Papal Bull had been extorted by deceit of subreption and obreption. Therefore, like the Governor of Belgium himself, Francisco de Mello, they could not be induced to carry out the Bull, though they had been strictly ordered to do so by the Pope. But Innocent X, Urban's successor, thinking that Urban's Bull was being evaded, sent sixteen Briefs: namely, to the Marquis of Castel Rodrigo, Governor of Belgium; to the Archbishops of Mechlin and Cambrai; to seven bishops of Belgium; to the theologians of the University of the Sorbonne; to Master Guilhelmus ab Angelis, S.T.D. of Louvain; to Leopold William, Archduke of Austria and Bishop of Strasbourg. In these, Urban's Bull being confirmed, they were earnestly ordered at last to publish and enforce it. And in some places, such as Antwerp, Douai, Namur and a few others, it began to be published, and the followers of Jansenius began to be pressed; the prohibitions were so severe that henceforth no one would be admitted to the cure of souls unless, after the solemn profession of faith of the Council of Trent in the prescribed formula, he had first condemned the Augustine of Jansenius. But when they considered that the same arts were being revived which the Arians had once used before the Emperor Constantine, they issued an Appeal to the Roman Pope, entitled Lament of Augustinian truth suffering in Belgium; asking that before they were forced to subscribe against Jansenius, the matter of faith should be debated, and that the matter should not be decided only when the person had already been judged and condemned. Appended to this Lament were three little books, of which the first commends faith, the second justice, the third charity. But they told their tale to a deaf man, since the Jesuits easily obtained from Innocent that he should not prick up his ears for the Jansenists. Therefore, when Papal Bulls and edicts had hitherto kindled the parties against each other with fiercer hatreds, some asserting that false doctrines were being attributed to Jansenius; others that his opinion could not be condemned as heresy, since it opposes neither Scripture nor the Councils; and others finally that the cause at issue here was not so much Jansenius's as Augustine's, and that by condemning Jansenius Augustine himself was being condemned, asserting this in books published openly; and finally when Jacob, Archbishop of Mechlin, primate of Belgium, Antonius Triest, Bishop of Ghent, and the Vicars General of the episcopal see of Ypres had set forth to the public the reasons why they could not publish the Papal Bull, Innocent allowed himself to be persuaded by the Jesuits and by some bishops of France, who came over to their side at the instigation of the Jesuits (though this passion of Innocent's was an ἐπιλαῖον [epilaion], that is, a fickle one), that five propositions, supposedly extracted from the Augustine of Jansenius, should be debated at Rome, in the presence and hearing of some Cardinals, John de Lugo, Carafa, Spada and others, by thirteen theologians, of whom the Jesuit Sforza Pallavicino held the first place. Those theologians were right to offer to the Pope their opinions and votes, signed in writing (which the Bishop of Montpellier brought from Rome into France, and which Montalte published word for word after the end of the Provincial Letters). From the written and spoken opinions of the theologians thus offered, Innocent, openly professing in this very matter that he was not a theologian (for the Papal theologian Louis de Saint-Amour, sent to Rome by the bishops of France to plead the Jansenists' cause, testifies in the third part, chapter 12, of the published Diurnal that when Innocent was asked to examine the matter himself, he not only did not wish to read the writings put before him, but also replied: It is not my profession, apart from the fact that I am old. I never studied theology. Others say he said: I am not a theologian), after calling for, as his Bull of 31 May 1653 states, divine help, the prayers of many Christians, both public and private; and after these had afterwards been repeated more fervently; indeed, after the assistance of the Holy Spirit had been anxiously sought, proceeded to a declaration and definition, and framed the condemnation of five propositions, formulated at the will of Jansenius's enemies.

units.la: CCXLVI. Operæ pretium fuerit, ex ipsa illa Innocentii Bulla fulminante quinque propositiones illas famosas, & obnuntiatas iisdem Innocentii diras repræsentari. Sic autem bulla Capitolini hujus Jovis sonat & tonat: Primam Propositionum: Aliqua Dei præcepta hominibus juste volentibus & conantibus, secundum præsentes, quas habent vires, sunt impossibilia: deest quoque illis gratia, qua possibilia fiant: temerariam, impiam, blasphemam, anathemate damnatam, & hæreticam declaramus, & uti talem, damnamus. Secundam: Interiori gratiæ in statu naturæ lapsæ nunquam resistitur; hæreticam declaramus, & uti talem, damnamus. mus. Tertiam: Ad merendum & demerendum in statu Naturæ lapsæ non requiritur in homine libertas à necessitate, sed sufficit libertas à coactione; hæreticam declaramus, &, uti talem, damnamus. Quartam: Semipelagiani admittebant prævenientis gratiæ interioris necessitatem ad singulos actus, etiam ad initium fidei; & in hoc erant hæretici, quòd vellent eam gratiam talem esse, cui posset humana voluntas resistere vel obtemperare; falsam & hæreticam declaramus, &, uti talem damnamus. Quintam: Semipelagianum est, dicere Christum pro omnibus omnino hominibus mortuum esse, aut sanguinem fudisse; falsam, temerariam, scandalosam, & intellectam eo sensu, ut Christus pro salute duntaxat prædestinatorum mortuus sit; impiam, blasphemam, contumeliosam, divinæ pietati derogantem & hæreticam declaramus, &, uti talem damnamus. Neve de prædictis propositionibus aliter quisquam sentiat, doceat, prædicet, quàm in declaratione & definitione illa continetur, sub censuris & pœnis contra hæreticos & eorum fautores in jure expressis, mandans, insuper omnibus Patriarchis, Archiepiscopis, Episcopis, aliisque locorum ordinariis, nec non hæreticæ pravitatis Inquisitoribus præcipit, ut contradictores & rebelles quoscunque per censuras & pœnas prædictas, cæteraque juris & facti remedia opportuna, invocato etiam ad hoc (si opus fuerit) auxilio brachii Secularis, omnino coerceant & compescant. Denique protestatur Papa, non intendere se per hanc declarationem & definitionem super prædictis quinque propositionibus factam, approbare ullatenus alias opiniones, quæ continentur in prædicto libro Cornelii Jansenii.
units.tr: CCXLVI. It will be worth the effort to set out from that very thundering Bull of Innocent the five famous propositions and the dire curses Innocent pronounced against them. The Bull of this Capitoline Jupiter thunders and roars as follows. The first of the propositions: Some of God's commandments are impossible for men who justly wish and strive to keep them, according to the powers they now have; the grace by which they might become possible is also lacking to them. We declare it rash, impious, blasphemous, condemned by anathema, and heretical, and as such we condemn it. The second: Interior grace is never resisted in the state of fallen nature. We declare it heretical, and as such we condemn it. The third: For merit and demerit in the state of fallen nature, freedom from necessity is not required in man; freedom from coercion suffices. We declare it heretical, and as such we condemn it. The fourth: The Semipelagians admitted the necessity of prevenient interior grace for each act, even for the beginning of faith; and they were heretics in this, that they wished that grace to be of such a kind that the human will could resist it or obey it. We declare it false and heretical, and as such we condemn it. The fifth: It is Semipelagian to say that Christ died or shed his blood for absolutely all men. False, rash, scandalous, and understood in the sense that Christ died only for the salvation of the predestined; impious, blasphemous, contumelious, derogating from divine goodness, and heretical, we declare it, and as such we condemn it. And lest anyone think, teach, or preach otherwise about the aforesaid propositions than is contained in that declaration and definition, under the censures and penalties against heretics and their supporters expressed in law, he commands, moreover, and charges all patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and other local ordinaries, as well as the inquisitors of heretical depravity, that they utterly restrain and check all contradictors and rebels by the aforesaid censures and penalties, and by other suitable remedies of law and fact, invoking also, if need be, the help of the secular arm. Finally the Pope protests that he does not intend, by this declaration and definition made concerning the aforesaid five propositions, to approve in any way those other opinions which are contained in the aforesaid book of Cornelius Jansenius.

units.la: CCXLVII. Quamprimum Bulla illa κεφαλαῖα in Galliam missa est, Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Episcopi Lutetiæ congregati plures prompti eam acceptârunt, probarúntque. Scripsit enim eorum nomine Petrus de Marca, nominatus tum Archiepiscopus Tholosanus, ad Innocentium Epistolam eucharisticam, qua inter alia eum cum Innocentio I. contendens; sicut, inquit, ille Pelagianam haeresin damnavit olim ad Episcoporum Africae relationem: sic ad Gallorum Episcoporum consultationem haeresin ex adverso Pelagianae oppositam, Innocentius X. sua authoritate proscripsit. Belle scilicet! Pelagianae haeresi ex adverso opposita fuit doctrina S. Augustini, S. Scripturae authoritate firmata. S. Augustini igitur doctrinam Scripturae authoritate firmatam, ceu haereticam Innocentius damnavit, proscripsitque. Digna planè proscriptio Innocentio, professo, se Theologum non esse. Qui doctrinam Pelagio ex adverso oppositam damnavit, Pelagianus certè fuerit oportet; Addit Marca, vetustae aetatis Ecclesiam Catholicam, sola Cathedrae Petri authoritate & communione fultam, Pelagianae haeresis damnationi absque cunctatione subscripsisse. Ea nos quoque, inquit, sententia ac fide imbuti, Romanae Ecclesiae praesentem, quae in Summo Pontifice Innocentio X. viget, authoritatem debita observantia colentes, Constitutionem Divini Numinis instinctu a Beatitudine vestra conditam, nobisque traditam ab Ill. Athenarum Archiepiscopo, Nuntio Apostolico, & promulgandam curabimus in Ecclesiis ac Diœcesibus nostris, atque illius executionem apud fideles populos urgebimus. Macte animo Viri! Non Divina ulla, non Prophetica, non Apostolica authoritas ad subscribendum Bullae vos subegit. Exolevit enim illa apud Romanos novissimis hisce temporibus penitus. Eique succedanea authoritas Pontificia Innocentii, non Theologi, nedum Prophetae, Apostoli, ita oculos vobis praestrinxit, ut ei ex quercu sua oracula fundenti, etiam cum nulla ratione illa roboravit, fidem coeco assensu habueritis! Et tamen Epistolae huic praeter Marcam, Virum caetera doctissimum, subscripserunt Julius, Cardinalis Mazarinus, Archiepiscopi quinque, & Episcopi viginti quatuor, suo quisque nomine; ita claudentes Epistolam assentationibus plenam: Porro nos Innocentio X. cujus ore Petrus locutus est, ut Leoni I. acclamavit quarta Synodus, hanc Divinam lauream gratulati, sacros inter Ecclesiæ fastos, quod olim de Synodis Oecumenicis fieri solitum, Constitutionem istam ab eo editam lubentes ex animo reponemus. Neque tamen in universum omnes Galliæ Episcopi subscripserunt. Inter subscriptos enim non comparent Archiepiscopus Senonensis, qui jam ante scripto, & Luthetiæ Regio prælo exscripto Augustino suo per se ipsum docente Catholicos, & vincente Pelagianos, Janseniii partibus se adjunxerat: non Episcopus Ambianensis, aliique.
units.tr: CCXLVII. As soon as that Bull, its chapters [κεφαλαῖα], was sent into France, many of the bishops of the Gallican Church, gathered at Paris, promptly received it and approved it. For Peter de Marca, then named Archbishop of Toulouse, wrote a letter of thanks to Innocent in their name, in which, comparing him with Innocent I among other things, he says: just as that one long ago condemned the Pelagian heresy on the report of the African bishops, so Innocent X, by his authority, proscribed the heresy set against the Pelagian, on the consultation of the Gallican bishops. Fine indeed! The doctrine of St Augustine, confirmed by the authority of Scripture, was set against the Pelagian heresy. So Innocent condemned and proscribed the doctrine of St Augustine, confirmed by the authority of Scripture, as if it were heretical. A proscription truly worthy of Innocent, who professed that he was not a theologian! Whoever condemned a doctrine opposed to Pelagius must surely be a Pelagian. Marca adds that the Catholic Church of ancient times, supported by the authority and communion of the Chair of Peter alone, subscribed without hesitation to the condemnation of the Pelagian heresy. We too, he says, imbued with that same opinion and faith, honouring with due observance the present authority of the Roman Church, which flourishes in the Supreme Pontiff Innocent X, will take care to publish in our churches and dioceses the Constitution enacted by your Beatitude at the impulse of the divine Majesty and handed to us by the Most Illustrious Archbishop of Athens, the Apostolic Nuncio, and we will urge its execution upon the faithful peoples. Well done, sir! No divine, prophetic, or apostolic authority compelled you to subscribe to the Bull. For that has entirely fallen into disuse among the Romans in these latest times. In its place a substitute, papal authority of Innocent, not of a theologian, let alone a prophet or apostle, has so dazzled your eyes that, although he poured out oracles from his oak, and confirmed them by no reason at all, you believed them with blind assent! And yet, besides Marca, a man otherwise most learned, there subscribed to this letter Julius Cardinal Mazarin, five archbishops, and twenty-four bishops, each in his own name. They closed the letter thus, full of flattery: Moreover, congratulating Innocent X, by whose mouth Peter spoke, as the Fourth Synod acclaimed Leo I, we will gladly and sincerely place this divine laurel among the sacred annals of the Church, namely that Constitution issued by him, as was customary long ago concerning the Ecumenical Synods. Yet not all the bishops of Gaul subscribed. Among the signatories do not appear the Archbishop of Sens, who earlier had already joined the party of Jansenius, in a work copied at the royal press in Paris, entitled Augustine, teaching the Catholics by himself and conquering the Pelagians; nor the Bishop of Amiens, and others.

units.la: CCXLVIII. Non idem Belgis animus, non eadem erga Bullam Pontificis devotio testata.
units.tr: CCXLVIII. The Belgians did not share the same spirit, nor was the same devotion to the Pope's Bull shown.

units.la: Testis est Franciscus Annatus, Jesuita, qui post Bullam Innocentii vulgatam, questus est, percussum esse errorem Jansenii nupera Sedis Apostolicæ constitutione, sed non extinctum: Jansenianos dissimulare malle vulnera, quam sanari: & utut commutata sententia facilè possint innocentem reddere censuram, eligere incolumes videri potius quam fieri. Cùm animadvertissent illi, nihil protestationibus adversus bullam se proficere, aliam viam ingressi, damnatas propositiones negârunt vel inveniri in Augustino Jansenii vel damnatas esse in sensu à Janseniο intento; accepturi etiam bullam, sed cum exceptione illibatæ authoritatis S. Augustini & Thomæ, cùm ipsimet à Pontifice in privato colloquio audiverint, non esse sibi animum damnare ullo modo doctrinam S. Augustini, vel controversiam de gratia per se ipsam efficaci Jesuitas inter & Thomistas agitatam attingere. Quod ipsum etiam testantem Jesuitam Annatum, induxerant. Sed fefellit illos opinio & spes concepta omnis. Statim enim post mortem Innocentii Alexander VII. Successor edita xvii. Kal. Nov. A.M.D.C.LVII. bulla, non tantùm Innocentii anathemata repetiit, confirmavitque; sed insuper etiam contra nonnullos iniquitatis filios, ad quamcunque dubitationem auferendam, declaravit & definivit, quinque illas propositiones ex libro Cornelii Jansenii Episcopi Iprensis, cui titulus est, Augustinus, excerptas, ac in sensu ab eodem Cornelio Jansenio intento damnatas suisse. Ita ostensurus digitum suum minimum grosliorem esse dorso patris & praedecessoris sui, rigorem Innocentii plurimùm auxit. Cùmque ne sic quidem moti fluctus componi se sivissent, & in Gallia maximè Jansenii partes crevissent, idem Alexander nova bulla xv. Kal. Mart. A. M. D. C. LXIV. vulgata, praefatus, Cornelii Jansenii haeresin, in Gallis praesertim serpentem, ab Innocentio X. fere oppressam, ad instar colubri tortuosi, cujus caput attritum est, in varios gyros & cavillationum deflexus euntem, altero assumptionis anno extinguere se conatum esse; queritur, nondum plenè consequi se potuisse, ut omnes errantes in viam salutis redirent; licet Archiepiscopi & Episcopi Galliae operam & industriam ad executionem constitutionum egregio studio contulerint, & Rex Christianissimus singulari pietate auxiliarem dextram strenuo ac constantissimo animo porrexerit. Deinceps, rogatu, uti Bulla praefert, Christianissimi Regis, certam formulam, cui Ecclesiastici omnes subscriberent, praeit, his verbis ab ipso conceptam: Ego N. Constitutioni Apostolicae Innocentii X. die XXXI. Maii M. D. C. LIII. & constitutioni Alexandri VII. datae XVI. Octobr. M. D. C. LVI. Summorum Pontificum me subjicio, & quinque propositiones ex Cornelii Jansenii libro, cui nomen Augustinus, excerptas, & in sensu ab eodem Authore intento, prout illas per dictas Constitutiones Sedes Apostolica damnavit, sincero animo rejicio ac damno, & ita juro. Sic me Deus adjuvet & sancta Dei Euangelia. CCXLIX. Tantae scilicet molis erat, bullatis & plumbeis illis declarationibus & definitionibus, rejicere, damnare, proscribere, non Cornelium Jansenium utique, sed S. Augustinum, celeberrimum Hipponae Praesulem, Pelagianorum illum malleum fulmenque, ad cujus tamen doctrinam, ceu normam, omnem illam de gratiae auxiliis disputationem, jam ante Clemens VIII. parùm certè hic Jesuitis propitius, adstrinxit; rationibus adductus pluribus, quas ejus verbis P. Giboeuf libro de libertate, & Archiepiscopus Senonensis, Octavius de Bellegarde, Augustin. doc. pag. 4. 5. recensent. Nunc verò prout Romæ obtinent annuæ & menstruæ de Deo fides, fides potius temporum, quàm Euangeliorum, ut B. Hilarii lib. 2. ad Const. verbis utar, ab Innocentio in Augustini potissimum caput coactas esse hasce diras, abundè Jansenii asseclæ demonstrârunt. Sanè famosus ille Jesuita Annatus Janseniatas, cùm profiterentur, paratos se demonstrare, quinque Propositiones ad sensum Jansenii, easdem esse ad sensum etiam Augustini, libello, qui inscribitur, Jansenianorum cavilli, cap. 3. falsè ridet, asseritque, deserendam potius Augustini sententiam, quàm sententiam Summi Pontificis, cùm id, quod definitum est, authoritatem petat non tam à S. Augustini consensu, quàm à præsidio speciali Spiritus S. Christi vicario, in Scripturis S. promisso. hoc est, à Pythagorico αὐτὸς ἔφα. Sed & Ludovicus de Marche, itidem Jesuita, in Apologia pro Innocentii constitutione, parte posteriore, totus est in elevanda authoritate S. Augustini, dum varios ejus errores recensèt, eum in Ecclesia esse irrefragabilis authoritatis pernegat, denique pertendit, non omnem Augustini de gratia Dei doctrinam ab Ecclesia Catholica admissam & approbatam esse. Denique in universa hac disputatione Jesuitarum hic Achilles fuit, omni exceptione majorem esse Romani Pontificis è cathedra loquentis authoritatem fallere & falli nesciam, non modò in Concilio Generali, verùm etiam extra illud. Christum non Augustino, non Conciliis, sed Petro ejúsque Successoribus denuntiâsse: Oravi pro te, ne deficeret fides tua. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Pasce oves meas &c. Atque ita tota illa Janseniistas seu Augustinianos (hoc potiùs nomine se insigniunt illi) inter & Jesuitas controversia tandem in infallibilem Papæ etiam exextra Universale Concilium, sive in fide sive in facto quidpiam decernentis, authoritatem resolvebatur. Atque in eo impudentiae numeros omnes Alexander implevit, quod definire ausus est, Jansenium eum sensum intendisse, in quo Innocentius Propositiones illas damnavit: & Innocentium intendisse propositiones eas damnare non alio in sensu, quàm qui Jansenii fuit. Ita καταδιογνώσης uterque, & Innocentius Jansenii asserentis, & Alexander Innocentii assertionem damnantis, intentionem, seu interiorem animi sensum compertum habuit; atque adeò τὰ τῆς ἀνθρώπης, ea quae in homine sunt, intentionem proin hominis animo abstrusam, non tantùm τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀνθρώπης τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ, Spiritus hominis, qui in ipso est, (uti quidem S. Paulus 1 Cor. 11. 11. asserit) sed etiam Spiritus Papae, qui extra hominem est, novit. Neque tantùm Papa, quod olim ipsi gnathones vendicârunt, omne jus Divinum; sed jam etiam omne dictum, factum, cogitatum humanum in scrinio pectoris sui clausum habet.
units.tr: Francis Annat, a Jesuit, is a witness. After Innocent's Bull was published, he complained that the error of Jansenius had been struck down by the recent constitution of the Apostolic See, but not extinguished: the Jansenists preferred to conceal their wounds rather than be healed; and although by changing their opinion they could easily make the censure harmless, they chose to appear unharmed rather than to be so. When they saw that protests achieved nothing against the Bull, they took another course. They denied that the condemned propositions could be found in Augustine's work by Jansenius, or that they had been condemned in the sense Jansenius intended. They would accept the Bull too, but with the proviso that the unimpaired authority of St Augustine and Thomas stood. They had heard from the Pontiff himself in private conversation that he had no intention of condemning the doctrine of St Augustine in any way, or of touching the controversy about grace, which is efficacious in itself, debated between the Jesuits and the Thomists. Annat the Jesuit, who also testified to this, had led them to it. But every opinion and hope they had conceived deceived them. For immediately after Innocent's death, his successor Alexander VII issued a Bull on 17 Kal. Nov. 1657. It not only repeated and confirmed Innocent's anathemas but also, against some sons of iniquity, to remove any doubt whatever, declared and defined that the five propositions excerpted from the book of Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres, entitled Augustinus, were condemned in the sense intended by Cornelius Jansenius himself. Thus, intending to show that his little finger was thicker than the back of his father and predecessor, he greatly increased Innocent's severity. When even this did not calm the waves, and the Jansenist party had grown especially in France, the same Alexander, by a new Bull published on 15 Kal. Mart. 1664, declared in its preface that he had tried, in the second year of his pontificate, to extinguish the heresy of Cornelius Jansenius, creeping especially in France and almost crushed by Innocent X, which, like a twisting serpent whose head has been bruised, goes off into various coils and turns of quibbling; he complained that he had not yet fully succeeded in bringing all who erred back to the way of salvation, although the archbishops and bishops of France had devoted their effort and industry with outstanding zeal to carrying out the constitutions, and the Most Christian King had extended his helping right hand with singular piety and a vigorous and most steadfast spirit. Next, at the request of the Most Christian King, as the Bull states, he laid down a fixed formula to which all churchmen were to subscribe, composed by himself in these words: I, N., submit to the Apostolic Constitution of Innocent X of 31 May 1653 and to the constitution of Alexander VII given on 16 October 1656, of the Supreme Pontiffs, and with a sincere mind I reject and condemn the five propositions excerpted from the book of Cornelius Jansenius, called Augustinus, and in the sense intended by the same author, as the Apostolic See condemned them by the said constitutions; and so I swear. So may God help me, and the holy Gospels of God. CCXLIX.
