Clearly it was a task of such great weight, by those sealed and leaden declarations and definitions, to reject, condemn and proscribe not Cornelius Jansenius, certainly, but St Augustine, the most famous Bishop of Hippo, that hammer and thunderbolt of the Pelagians, to whose doctrine, as to a rule, Clement VIII had already bound the whole disputation about the auxiliary graces, though he was hardly favourable to the Jesuits here. He was moved by many reasons, which Father Giboeuf lists in his words in his book de libertate, and the Archbishop of Sens, Octavius de Bellegarde, in Augustin. doc. pag. 4, 5. But now, as the yearly and monthly faiths about God prevail at Rome, faiths of the times rather than of the Gospels, to use the words of St Hilary, lib. 2 ad Const., the followers of Jansenius have amply shown that these dire measures were forced by Innocent chiefly against the chief point of Augustine. Indeed, when the Jansenists professed that they were ready to show that the five propositions in the sense of Jansenius are the same in the sense of Augustine too, the notorious Jesuit Annat scoffs at them falsely in the little book entitled Jansenianorum cavilli, cap. 3, and asserts that Augustine's opinion should rather be abandoned than the opinion of the Supreme Pontiff, since what has been defined draws its authority not so much from the consent of St Augustine as from the special protection of the Spirit of Christ's vicar, promised in Holy Scripture. That is to say, from the Pythagorean αὐτὸς ἔφα [he himself said it]. Ludovicus de Marche, likewise a Jesuit, in the Apology for Innocent's constitution, in its latter part, is wholly bent on lessening the authority of St Augustine. While listing his various errors, he denies that he has irrefragable authority in the Church, and finally contends that not every doctrine of Augustine on the grace of God has been admitted and approved by the Catholic Church. Finally, in this whole dispute, the Jesuits' Achilles was this: that the authority of the Roman Pontiff, speaking from the chair, is greater than any exception, able neither to err nor to be deceived, not only in a General Council but also outside one. Christ, they say, addressed this not to Augustine, nor to the Councils, but to Peter and his successors: I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. Feed my sheep, etc. And so that whole controversy between the Jansenists or Augustinians (they prefer to call themselves by this name) and the Jesuits was at last reduced to the authority of the infallible Pope, even outside a universal Council, decreeing something either in faith or in fact. In this, Alexander filled up every measure of impudence: he dared to define that Jansenius intended the sense in which Innocent condemned those propositions, and that Innocent intended to condemn them in no other sense than the one Jansenius held. Thus both of them, [καταδιογνώσης] Innocent in judging the assertion of Jansenius and Alexander in condemning the assertion of Innocent, claimed to have discovered the intention, or inner sense of the mind. And so he knows not only the things that are in man [τὰ τῆς ἀνθρώπης], the intention hidden in a man's mind, but also the spirit of man which is in him [τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀνθρώπης τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ] (as St Paul indeed asserts, 1 Cor. 11. 11.), and also the spirit of the Pope, which is outside man. Nor does the Pope merely hold, as those flatterers once claimed for him, all divine right; he now keeps shut up in the casket of his breast every word, deed and thought of man.

units.la: CCL. Tertia igitur haec, supra illas scilicet, quas Tridentinum Concilium stabilivit, post duas supra memoratas de licentia parricidali & aequivocationibus, Jesuitarum novella, seu mavis, recocta, & ex orco revocata Pelagianorum & Semipelagianorum veterum haeresis, ex pluribus aequè haereticis assertionibus conflata, quam illi approbante & definiente Pontifice Romano, adeóque Ecclesia Romana omni, qua Pontifici paret, Jesuitarum fraudibus miserè circumscriptâ adversus S. Augustinum, saniorésque antehac in Ecclesia Romana Theologos, Thomistas inprimis, perruptis pudoris, Divinae veritatis, canae antiquitatis repagulis omnibus, audacter & impunè sustinent, ὅτι πλεῖον προκόπτοντες ἀσεβείας, majorem ad impietatem proficientes in dies, dum sermo, doctrina eorum, ὡς γάγγραινα νομὴν ἔχει, gangraena instar serpit 2 Tim. 11. 17.
units.tr: CCL. This third error, then, beyond those which the Council of Trent established, follows the two mentioned above concerning parricidal licence and equivocations. It is the novel, or rather revived and called back from hell, heresy of the ancient Pelagians and Semipelagians, compounded from several equally heretical assertions. The Jesuits' frauds have miserably deceived the Roman Pontiff, who approves and defines it, and so the Roman Church, and all who obey the Pontiff. Boldly and with impunity they maintain it against St Augustine and the saner theologians of the Roman Church in former times, above all the Thomists, having burst through every barrier of shame, of divine truth and of venerable antiquity. They are advancing further into impiety [ὅτι πλεῖον προκόπτοντες ἀσεβείας] day by day, while their speech and doctrine spreads like gangrene [ὡς γάγγραινα νομὴν ἔχει], 2 Tim. 11. 17.

units.la: CCLI. Ad Urbanum, ut revertamur, eo adhuc Pontifice inde à d. XXIII. Octobr. A.M.D.C.XLI. Hiberni Papistæ horribili laniena in Protestantes tota insula sævierunt. Paucorum mensium intervallo plusquam ducenta hominum millia, & in sola Ultonia, quarta & minùs culta Hiberniæ parte, centum quinquaginta quatuor millia sex intra menses rabies illa absumpsit, ut nihil tormentorum & mortium reperiri potuerit, quod non furiales illæ bestiæ commiserint, solo religionis odio, & quòd Papæ gratum se officium internecione Protestantium præstituros, vitamque æternam absque purgatorii flammis consecuturos, Monachorum sanguinolentorum persuasione inducti crederent. rudibus omnis & fidei & humanitatis facile ad omne nefas propulsis. Ipsi certè Monachi & Sacerdotes accuratum catalogum lanienæ, Phelimo Oneal, Ecclesiæ Catholicæ archistratego, patratæ, authenticámque adeò publicorum actorum consignationem ediderunt. Ibi videbis innumerabilem miserorum Christianorum multitudinem, postquam omnibus ad cutim usque exuti & spoliati fuissent bonis, trucidatam; plerosque ferro, multos suspendio, submersione, vivicomburio, in Templis, ædibus, aliisque locis; plurimos spirantes adhuc terra defossos: aliquos à canibus dilaniatos ac discerptos, lapidibus obrutos: alios ferventibus ahenis mersos, nonnullos carbonibus tostos, intestina per posticum extracta, dissectos ventres, evoluta viscera, confracta funibus intortis crania, dorsum, brachia, crura, femora comminuta vel abscissa: alios toto corpore cruentatos, cùm nil nisi vulnus essent, in suo sanguine & frigore enectos: suspensos capillitio: impuberes secus parentum immolata cadavera, fletu, fame, inopia extinctos, multis ex innocuo illo sexu jam intermortua matrum ubera, morsu potiùs quàm lactendo, appetentibus. Nulla in Tigribus illis, non Hircanis, sed Hibernis, erga miserimos commiseratio; sed immissi porci, canes, aliáque Canibalibus Hibernis mitiora animalia, tandem deglutientes, quod restabat, carnium, finem tantis miseriis imposuerunt. Ita occisi, ita sepulti sunt. Multi ita ruptis omnibus artubus, ut loco sese movere non possent, cùm herbarum circumcirca pastu, bruto cibo vitam in triduum miserimè traxissent, ab Hibernis spectatum & insultatum venientibus, cùm mortem beneficii loco precarentur, nec impetrârunt omnes, in locum herbidum alium, ut diutiùs inter acerrima tormenta precarium spiritum traherent, ac oculos immanium belluarum gratissimo spectaculo, aures horrendis clamoribus satiarent, delati sunt. Mancipia in Dominos omni telorum & contumeliarum genere saevierunt. Misellæ mulieres, dependentibus de cervice aut cingulo liberis, &, ad majorem ignominiam, canibus simul ac felibus appensis, laqueo suffocatæ sunt. Multi, puteis subtus glaciem actis, submersi: alii mucronibus in mare & flumina protrusi; ac si qui ad littus aut ripam enatarent, elisो cerebro, aut contis affixi, denuo aquis immersi sunt. Ædium, castellorum, templorum ruinæ, cæsorum insepultis cadaveribus stipatæ; cùm paucos terra tegeret, multi sub stillicidiis, in fossis; hinc inde & plateis computrescerent. Innoxia ætas, dissectis carnibus, unco, velut in macello agnina, suspensi sunt. Miser nonnemo nudo corpore, asseri impositus, ab Hibernis ad singulos haustus, singulis vulneribus, sed non penitus in mortem adactis, ita passim diffissus, ut continuum vulnus videretur. Quem deinde in fimetum projectum, dolor, fames & injuria aëris extinxit, prohibitis omnibus, ne miserias tantas ullo modo levare aussint. Alius adacto per posteriora palo, ut altiùs infigeretur, velut per ludibrium circumscarificatus, donec inter atroces convulsiones, plaudentibus hostibus, animam Redemptori ri suo, sancta victima redderet. Pueri, parentum Catholicorum charitatem æmulati, denso agmine in agros egressi, ubi in cœsum Protestantem (quales passim totis sparsi sunt campis) inciderunt, ejus pudenda virgis lorisque tandiu flagellárunt, donec ruptis nervis, & carne dispersa, membrum à reliquo corpore dissolveretur, quod ipsi arreptum, festo clamore, parentibus gratissimum munus obtulerunt. Si fœmina cœsa, prono in terram ventre jacuissēt, eam in dorsum resupinatam, omnibus membris, iis maximè, quæ natura occulta esse voluit, taxárunt. Conclusi arctissima intra ædes & templa custodia, illis repente succensis, lamentabiliter conflagrárunt. In ipso templo pater filiúsque in partes sectí, eorúmque segmina matris extremùm sauciæ capiti impacta sunt. Nobiles virgines totam noctem capillitio de arbore suspensæ, cùm orta luce aliquid in illis vitæ residuum deprehenderetur, protinus obtruncatæ sunt. Tres orphani, quorum parentes à latronibus illis cœsi erant, cùm nudi, & frigore pœne enecti, in fornacem se abdidissent, ignibus immissis, immiseri-corditer combusti sunt. Uxor gravida cum liberis vitæ consultura, cùm terror fœtum ante tempus excussisset, illo à latronum canibus devorato, ipsa cum cæteris obtruncata fuit. Multæ nobiles dissectæ, fœtus utero excusi, & ipsæ viscéribus apertis, horrendum suspensæ. Infantes hastis præfixi rebellium, proeda ea gloriantium. Duæ filiæ toto corpore nudæ, metu mortis, decrepitum parentem lacertis suis in paludem trahere adactæ, ubi & ipsæ submersæ perierunt. Uxor jugulare maritum, filius matrem coacti: ipsos, velut ultimam victimam, latrones mactârunt. Equorum caudis alii alligati, tractati, excarnificati, fame enecti, mille tormentis excruciati sunt. Quibus corpus hebetius & obesum, evisceráti sunt, ut ex eorum pinguedine lychni efficerentur. Vir pius, & zelo Dei flagrans, terra, solo capite prominente, defossus, atque ita relictus, donec corvi & vultures oculos vivo eruerent, ferae bestiae reliquum abligurirent. Plurimi spirantes subtus terram defossi, quos inter unus cratibus & saxis depressus, cum diu lamentabiliter frustra inclamaret, nec uxor pedibus capta eum eruere posset, faciem aegre nudavit, & ut finem immensis doloribus imponeret, strophiolo spiritum ei interclusit. Multorum plantae ad lentum ignem tostae: alii securibus dissecti, funibus sursum deorsum per aquas raptati, nonnulli semineces relicti, vel ferro clausi, donec membris putrescentibus, animam exhalarent: & infinita tormina ad pecuniam prodendam, quam, omnibus jam ante spoliati, nullam habebant, excogitata. Ossa & cadavera dudum in Domino defunctorum, tumulis eruta, projecta vilisimis locis, per fimeta, aggeres, fruticeta, campos sparsa & dissecta sunt. Haec omnia, plurāque etiam, uti certis documentis ab ipsis etiam hostibus infandorum facinorum authoribus, supeditatis, constat, à Catholicis videlicet patrata, tam profecto dira sunt, ut ab Orci emissariis, extremae nequitiae daemonibus, diriora patrari non potuisse, ambiguum neutiquam habeatur.
units.tr: CCLI. To return to Urban: while he was still pope, from 23 October 1641, the Irish Papists raged with horrible butchery against the Protestants across the whole island. Within a few months more than two hundred thousand people were killed, and in Ulster alone, a quarter of Ireland and less cultivated than the rest, that frenzy destroyed one hundred and fifty-four thousand six hundred people in six months. There was no torment or form of death that those savage beasts did not inflict, moved by hatred of religion alone, and by the persuasion of bloodthirsty monks that they would do the Pope a welcome service by destroying the Protestants and would gain eternal life without the flames of purgatory. The ignorant, having no true faith or humanity, were easily driven to every crime. The monks and priests themselves published an exact catalogue of the slaughter, carried out under Phelim O'Neill, archstrategist of the Catholic Church, and an authentic record of the public proceedings. There you will see an countless multitude of wretched Christians slaughtered after they had been stripped of all their goods down to the skin: most killed by the sword, many by hanging, drowning or burning alive, in churches, houses and other places; very many buried in the earth while still breathing; some torn apart and mangled by dogs, some crushed under stones; others plunged into boiling cauldrons, some roasted over coals, their intestines drawn out through the back, their bellies cut open, their entrails pulled out, their skulls broken by twisted ropes, their backs, arms, legs and thighs smashed or cut off; others, bloodied over the whole body, since they were nothing but wounds, died of loss of blood and cold; others hanged by the hair; children killed beside their parents' corpses, dying of weeping, hunger and want; many mothers, already half dead, had their breasts gnawed by their infants, who bit rather than suckled. There was no pity at all for the wretched victims from those tigers, not Hyrcanian but Irish; instead, pigs and dogs and other animals, gentler than the Irish cannibals, were let loose, and at last devoured what remained of the flesh, and so brought such miseries to an end. Thus they were killed, and thus they were buried. Many, with all their limbs so broken that they could not move from the spot, after wretchedly prolonging their lives for three days on the grass around them as their only food, were carried off to another grassy place when the Irish came to watch and mock them. They begged for death as a kindness, and not all of them obtained it, but were carried away to be tormented longer, so that they might drag out their fading breath amid the sharpest torments, and so satisfy the eyes of those monstrous beasts with a most pleasing spectacle and their ears with dreadful cries. Servants raged against their masters with every kind of weapon and insult. Poor women, with their children hanging from their necks or belts, and, for greater shame, cats and dogs hung beside them, were strangled with a noose. Many were drowned by being thrown into wells beneath the ice; others were driven into the sea and rivers with swords, and if any swam to the shore or bank, their brains were dashed out, or they were impaled on poles and pushed back under the water. The ruins of houses, castles and churches were crowded with unburied corpses; while the earth covered only a few, many rotted under the dripping eaves, in ditches, and in the streets here and there. Innocent young people, their flesh cut open, were hung on hooks as lambs are hung in a butcher's shop. One wretched man, laid naked on a plank, was cut open by the Irish at every mouthful, each wound not being fatal, so that he was slashed in so many places that it seemed one continuous wound. Then, thrown onto a dunghill, pain, hunger and the foulness of the air finished him, since everyone was forbidden to dare to ease such miseries in any way. Another was impaled from behind on a stake, driven in deeper, and was cut around like a joke, until, amid terrible convulsions, while the enemies applauded, he gave up his soul, a holy victim, to his Redeemer. Boys, copying the charity of their Catholic parents, went out into the fields in a dense crowd, where they came upon a Protestant corpse (such lay scattered across the whole countryside) and beat its private parts with rods and whips for so long that, the sinews broken and the flesh torn, the member came away from the rest of the body; they seized it and, with a festive shout, offered it as a most welcome gift to their parents. If a woman, killed, had lain face down on the ground, they turned her over onto her back and mutilated all her limbs, above all those parts which nature wished to be hidden. Shut up within the tightest guard in houses and churches, they were suddenly set on fire and wretchedly burned. In the church itself a father and son were cut into pieces, and the pieces of them were thrown at the head of their mother, who was already mortally wounded. Noble virgins were hanged by the hair from a tree all night, and when at daybreak some remnant of life was found in them, they were at once beheaded. Three orphans, whose parents had been slain by those robbers, having hidden themselves naked and nearly frozen to death in a furnace, were burned alive without mercy when fire was set to it. A pregnant wife, who was seeking to save her children, was beheaded with the rest, after terror had brought on a premature birth, and the unborn child was devoured by the robbers' dogs. Many noble women were cut open, their unborn children torn from the womb, and themselves hanged horribly with their bellies laid open. Infants were impaled on the spears of the rebels, who boasted of their booty. Two daughters, stripped naked over their whole bodies, were forced by fear of death to drag their decrepit father by his arms into a marsh, where they themselves drowned and perished. A wife was compelled to cut her husband's throat, and a son his mother's; then the robbers slaughtered them, as the last victims. Others were tied by their feet to horses' tails, dragged, flayed, starved to death, and tortured with a thousand torments. From those whose bodies were dull and fat, they took out the entrails so that lamps might be made from their fat. A pious man, burning with zeal for God, was buried in the earth up to his head, which alone stuck out, and left so until the crows and vultures pecked out his living eyes, and the wild beasts licked up what remained. Very many were buried alive in the earth; among them one man, pressed down under hurdles and stones, cried out pitifully for a long time in vain. His wife, who had been seized by the feet, could not dig him out; with difficulty she bared his face, and, to put an end to his immense sufferings, she choked the breath out of him with a cloth. The soles of many were roasted over a slow fire; others were hacked with axes, dragged up and down through the water by ropes, some left half dead or shut up in iron, until their decaying limbs let out their souls; and countless torments were devised to extract money which they no longer had, since they had already been stripped of everything. The bones and corpses of those who had long since died in the Lord were dug out of their tombs, thrown into the vilest places, and scattered and cut to pieces across dunghills, embankments, thickets and fields. That all these things, and more besides, were done by Catholics, is plain from certain documents, which were even submitted by the enemies themselves, the authors of these unspeakable crimes; they are so dreadful that there can be no doubt they could not have been done more dreadfully by the emissaries of Orcus, the demons of extreme wickedness.

units.la: CCLII. In Romani scilicet Molochi honorem gratiamque immolatae hae victimae, adeo non ingratum ei nidorem attulerunt, ut delectatus etiam magnopere iis visus fuerit. assuetus pridem sanguineis & ignitis ex rationalium hominum corporibus, hostiis.
units.tr: CCLII. Indeed, these victims were sacrificed to the honour and favour of the Roman Moloch, and they brought him a smell so agreeable that he seemed greatly delighted by them, being long accustomed to bloody and fiery offerings from the bodies of rational men.

units.la: Constatque etiam, Urbanum eadem occasione in turbido piscaturum, per Nuntium suum Rinuccinum variis artibus Regnum ipsum Hiberniae, à Protestantium sanguine sic presse purgatum defoecatúmque affectâsse, usum praetextu juris in totum orbem, & omnia Regna hujus mundi, ipsismet ringentibus Papistis, & artes illas in detrimentum coronae vergentes detestantibus. prout haec aliáque prolixè in vindiciis Catholicorum Hiberniae exposita legere est. CCLIII. Ar-
units.tr: It is also established that Urban, fishing in troubled waters on the same occasion, through his nuncio Rinuccini, by various arts sought to purge and cleanse the kingdom of Ireland itself, so pressed with Protestant blood, and to use it under the pretext of right against the whole world and all the kingdoms of this world, while the Papists themselves gnashed their teeth and detested those arts, which tended to the detriment of the crown. This and more is set out at length in the Vindications of the Catholics of Ireland, as one may read. CCLIII. Ar-

units.la: In Pontificis gratiam tot in Hibernia caesa victimae sunt.
units.tr: Many victims were slaughtered in Ireland for the Pope's favour.

units.la: CCLIII. Arsit interea adhuc intestino bello Germa-
units.tr: CCLIII. Meanwhile Germany still burned with civil war

units.la: nia, tot jam exteris etiam in ea infesta arma sua circumferentibus, ut farciendæ denique inter Christianos pacis spes ferè nulla affulserit. Atque hic Urbanus Legatis in Hispaniam, Galliam, Germaniam missis, urbanis equidem lacteisque verbis pacem suasit, animo interea, ne degenerâsse à genio Paparum putes, nil nisi bella volutans. Cæsari enim ad continuandum illud ducenta millia coronatorum præsentanea numeravit, & post unius anni decursum, siquidem ita necessitas postulaverit, denuo centum millia se soluturum recepit. Instititpræterea vehementer, ne Pontificii de pace transacturi quidquam de religione & bonis ecclesiæ pacisc antur. quæ pacis remora haud postrema fuit. Cum igitur Deputati Francofurti d. XXII. Aug. A. M. D. C. LIII. de bonis Ecclesiæ Protestantibus tradendis nonnihil statuissent, consiliumque suum Cæsari probandum obtulissent, statim ille Breve Apostolicum d. XVII. Octobr. exaratum, ad Episcopum Augustanum misit, in hæc verba consignatum: Urbanus P. P. VIII. Propositam Francofurti de ecclesiasticis bonis hæreticorum potestati committendis sententiam ex Fraternitatis tuæ literis, tum etiam ex supplici libello ad nos transmisso, non sine ingenti molestia audivimus. Nempe facile est conjicere, quænam inde animarum pernicies, & sacri cultus imminutio expectanda esset. Et tamen Imperator electus pietate pollet, eam erga ecclesiasticos gerit propensionem, ut minime verendum arbitremur, ne improbum illud consilium constanter simul & religiose rejiciat. Nos quidem, ut Pontificii muneris partes impleamus, cuncta, quæ è re fore significasti, officia accurate adhibuimus, Deúmque precamur, ut optatus exitus gravissimo negotio nequaquam desit.
units.tr: Germany, with foreign powers also turning their hostile arms against it, was so far from peace that there was almost no hope of a peace being made among the Christians. Here Urban, sending legates to Spain, France and Germany, urged peace with smooth and honeyed words, while in his heart, lest you think he had degenerated from the spirit of the Popes, he was turning over nothing but wars. To Caesar he paid down at once two hundred thousand crowns to continue the war, and he undertook that, if necessity should require it, after one year had passed he would pay another hundred thousand. He also strongly insisted that the Papists should not agree to anything concerning religion and the goods of the Church in making the peace, and this was no small obstacle to peace. When the deputies at Frankfurt, on 22 August 1653, had decided something about handing over the Church's goods to the Protestants and had submitted their plan to Caesar for approval, he at once sent to the Bishop of Augsburg an Apostolic Brief, drawn up on 17 October, couched in these words: Urban, Pope, eighth of that name. We have heard, from your Brotherhood's letter and also from the humble petition sent to us, with no small distress, the proposal made at Frankfurt that the goods of the Church be entrusted to the power of heretics. Indeed, it is easy to guess what destruction of souls and what diminution of sacred worship would follow from it. And yet the elected Emperor is distinguished for piety and shows such goodwill toward churchmen that we do not think it need be feared that he will steadfastly and religiously reject that wicked plan. We, for our part, so that we may fulfil the duties of the Papal office, have carefully applied all the offices that you indicated would be to the purpose, and we pray God that the desired outcome not fail in this most serious business.

units.la: CCLIV. Sequentis anni M. D. C. XLIV. d. XXIX. Jul. Urbanus, capularis ferè octoginta annorum senex, im- plevit mortalitatis suæ legem. De novo Pontifice creando
units.tr: CCLIV. In the following year, 1644, on 29 July, Urban, an old man of nearly eighty who wore the cap of a cardinal, fulfilled the law of his mortality. On the creation of a new Pontiff

units.la: certatum miris studiis, factionibus Hispanica, Gallicana, Romana, Barbarina diu collisis. Sex jam hebdomadæ in Conclavi exactæ erant, cum Johannis Baptistæ Pamphilii ne mentio quidem creandi Pontificis ulla incidisset. Obstabant ingenium ejus à literarum, sacrarum inprimis studiis alienum, nonnili causis dicendis assuetum, quodque mancipium eum esse libidinis alienæ, Olympiæ Maldachini glotis, constaret omnibus. Alii alia caussabantur. Tandem inter Hispanicorum Gallicorum Cardinalium, æquis viribus certantium, acerima studia, Olympiæ inprimis artibus effectum est, ut præter opinionem Pamphilius, Romanus natione, Neapoli Nuntius, qui post Innocentii X. nomen sumpsit, Papa proclamaretur. quem mox Cardinalis Medicæus, corona capiti ejus imposita, sic affatus est: Scias, te esse Patrem Principum & Regum, Rectorem orbis.
units.tr: The contest was waged with remarkable zeal, the Spanish, French, Roman and Barberini factions having long clashed. Six weeks had already passed in the Conclave when no mention at all had been made of creating Giovanni Battista Pamphili as Pontiff. He was held back by his character, which was foreign to literary and especially sacred studies and accustomed only to pleading cases, and by the fact that everyone knew he was the tool of another's lust, the gluttony of Olympia Maldachini. Others gave other reasons. At last, amid the keen rivalry of the Spanish and French cardinals, who fought with equal strength, it was brought about, chiefly by Olympia's arts, that Pamphili, a Roman by birth and nuncio at Naples, was proclaimed Pope, contrary to general expectation. He took the name Innocent X. Soon afterwards Cardinal Medici placed the crown on his head and addressed him thus: "Know that you are the father of princes and kings, the ruler of the world."

units.la: CCLV. Statim atque Papatum aggressus est Innocentius, admisit is elogium insolentissimum omnium, quod in honorem ejus Cardinalis adhuc, sed jam jam creandi Pontificis, à nescio quo Italo-Græco, Joh. Baptista Calumsyrito, concinnatum, & à Melchiore Inchofer, fama notissimo, qui orbi Christiano epistolam B. Virginis nomine ad Messanenses scriptam obtrudere ante ausus fuerat, Pontifici recens creato oblatum, sic sonat: Eminentissime & Reverendissime D. Cardinalis Pamphili. 1. PHILIVS Dei (superlativus amor Patris, quia φίλιος, ideo Philius dictus) ex æterna ejus charitate, qua se Deo Patri obtulit, in amantissimum Intercessorem ac Mediatorem Dei ac hominum, ab instanti conceptionis in utero B. Mariæ Virginis, factus fuit Sacerdos in æternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, ac primus Pontifex Optimus Maximus. 2. Sed Filius fuit Philius, non PAMPHILIVS. 3. Fuit intercessor Dei & hominum. 4. Non fuit universalis Mediator Angelorum & hominum, seu Pamphilius. 5. Si ex nominis analogico Admittitis elogium blasphemiis referstum, ab Italo-Graeco cultum, quae Pamphilius Filio Dei praefertur. gico æternóque anagrammate præsagire licet, mysterium aliquod in tempore: Tu ab æterno prædestinatus es, esse Pamphilius in terris, ac dici Pamphilius, æmulus filii Dei in Cælis. 6. Pamphilius ergo eris. Universalis nimirum reconciliator Angelorum & hominum, in terris hostiliter pugnantium Regum & populorum. 7. Quod præstabis nonnisi electus in Pontificem Optimum Maximum. 8. In cujus faustissimum augurium Euangelus ego, felixque Nuntius ter Sanctos pedes Eminentiæ vestræ ex nunc deosculor. 9. Quod etiam Græcè scripsi decem abhinc annis in Græca nostra Academia Basiliana in Columbæ vestræ stemmata, τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης σύμβολα. Rex pacificus eris & clementissimus. Blasphema illa themata, apud inferos quandoque, cúm in terra iis impunè fuerit, arsura, vel à quoquam cusa, vel à Pontifice Summo pronis auribus, lætóque animo excepta esse, ut crederem, induci nunquam potuissem, nisi fide dignis testibus ita constare, Amplissimus & Celeberrimus Conringius Conclav. Alex. VII. pag. 55. &c. asseverâssset.
units.tr: CCLV. As soon as Innocent took up the papacy, he accepted the most insolent of all the eulogies that had been composed in his honour, while he was still a cardinal but about to be created Pope, by some Italo-Greek named Giovanni Battista Calumsyrito, and offered to the newly created Pontiff by Melchior Inchofer, a man notorious for his reputation, who had earlier dared to foist upon the Christian world a letter written in the name of the Blessed Virgin to the Messenians. It reads as follows: Most Eminent and Most Reverend Lord Cardinal Pamphili. 1. PHILIUS of God (the superlative love of the Father, because φίλιος, therefore called Philius), from his eternal charity, by which he offered himself to God the Father, was made, as the most loving Intercessor and Mediator of God and men, from the instant of conception in the womb of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a Priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedec, and the first Supreme and Greatest Pontiff. 2. But the Son was Philius, not PAMPHILIUS. 3. He was the Intercessor of God and men. 4. He was not the universal Mediator of angels and men, or Pamphilius. 5. If from the analogical and eternal anagram of the name one may foresee some mystery in time: you were predestined from eternity to be Pamphilius on earth, and to be called Pamphilius, a rival of the Son of God in heaven. 6. Pamphilius, therefore, you will be: the universal reconciler, forsooth, of angels and men, and of kings and peoples who fight hostilely on earth. 7. This you will accomplish only when elected Supreme and Greatest Pontiff. 8. As a most auspicious omen of this, I, the evangelist and happy messenger, kiss the thrice-holy feet of your Eminence from now on. 9. I have also written in Greek, ten years ago, in our Greek Academy at Basle, on the crests of your Dove, τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης σύμβολα. You will be a peaceful and most merciful king. I could never have been induced to believe that those blasphemous theses, which will one day burn in hell, could have been either printed by anyone or received with willing ears and a glad heart by the Supreme Pontiff, since they were allowed to circulate with impunity on earth, unless it were established by trustworthy witnesses that this is so. The most distinguished and celebrated Conring has asserted it, Conclav. Alex. VII. p. 55 etc.

units.la: CCLVI.
units.tr: CCLVI.

units.la: Toto ferè tempore, quo Innocentius Pontificiam Sedem occupavit (occupavit autem ultra decennium integrum) non tam Innocentium, quàm fœminam glotem ejus, Donnam, seu Dominam Olympiam Maldachinam, Fratris ejus defuncti uxorem, Papatum rexisse, constans fama erat, ab iis etiam, qui Romæ exquisitam omnium notitiam habuerant, tradita. Credideramúsque, ἡεχμοῖς ψεύδεσι, calidis mendaciis Innocentii innocentiam à Marphoreis aut Pasquinis aspergi oneraríque, nisi Abbas Gualdus testis, uti quidem de se profitetur, αὐτόπτης & αὐτήκοος, scripto Romæ de vita & rebus gestis Donnæ Olympiæ Maldachinæ, libello (qui mortuo ipso inter Manuscripta ejus repertus, publicíque juris in Italia factus est) plenam ampliorémque etiam ejus rei fidem fecisset. Narrat autem Gualdus ille, (liceat multa paucis constringere) ut Olympia illa à teneris unguiculis imperiosa, dominationem nem ubique affectaverit: ut nupserit Innocentii fratri Pamphilio, eumque anno conjugii circiter decimo, aversata, tota in amorem affinis Baptistæ Pamphilii (post Innocentii) rapta, ejusdemque in conclavi alibique, lateri individua comes hæserit, gravi suspicione incestorum amorum apud omnes: ut se totum ejus consiliis flectendum, regendum affinis commiserit: ut ex Hispania ad Olympiam scripserit, absente & inconsulta ea minus prosperè, quæ ibi gerebat, negotia, sibi ceu navi sine remo, succedere: ut Olympia affini Cardinali recens creato se solertius applicuerit, eumque iis dotibus, quæ Pontificem ornant, simulandi & dissimulandi artificio cumprimis, quod januam ad Papatum esse crebrò ei inculcaverat, imbuere conata sit: ut profecerit Cardinalis in artificio simulandi & dissimulandi omnia, excepto amore erga Olympiam, quem ut tegeret, induci nunquam potuerit: ut insinuaverit affinem Cardinalibus Hispanis æquè ac Gallis, mira versutia: ut post mortem Urbani in commendando Affine vigilantia & industria incredibili usa, id denique artibus suis consecuta sit, ut nequicquam repugnante Cardinale Antonio Barbarino, præter omnium expectationem ad Papatum evectus fuerit: ut post electionem Affinis ad Olympiam concurrerint frequentes, quotquot fortunis suis consultum cupiverunt: ut Antonio Barbarini, quicum privatæ ei simultates intercesserant, exitium mox acceleraverit: ut domicilium in Vaticano, proximè Pontificis conclave appetiverit, at dissuadente Panzirolo, Pontificis ædes proprias incolens, singularum dierum approximante vespera ad illum inviserit, & ad feram usque noctem cum eo subinde moram traxerit: ut filium Camillum Pamphilium, rerum omnium ignarissimum, ad Cardinalis Patroni dignitatem provexerit, & eundem infirmitatis conscientia dignitate ea se abdicantem, unà cum nova nupta de Roffano, devotum Pontificiis diris, ne dominationi suæ intercederet, aliásque ob causas, Roma relegaverit: ut negotia Pontificia cuncta ad se traxerit, supplices Pontifici subductos sola audiverit, reis poenas supra meritum irrogaverit, munera & dignitates pro libitu distribuerit, atque iis aliisque modis inexhaustam pecuniarum voraginem brevi tempore coegerit: ut leges novas fixerit, veteres Pontificum praecedentium refixerit: ut Nepotem Maldachinum omnium stolidissimum, animo & corpore deformem, adolescentem adhuc Cardinalitia purpura, invito Pontifice, donaverit: ut procurante Cardinale Panzirolo, Camillus Astalli, juvenili aetate Nepos ab Innocentio Pamphilii nomine adoptatus, & indignus licet, cum admiratione omnium ab eodem Cardinalis Patroni titulo & praecipua dignitate auctus, fortunæ Olympiæ imminutionem nonnullam attulerit, Pontifice altius ad animum, uti videbatur, revocante sequiora de sua cum Olympia familiaritate, & ejusdem plusquam virili dominatione, judicia tum Italorum, tum exterorum, à quibus nummus aureus recens cusus, una parte Olympiam corona Papali redimitam, & claves Petri manu prensantem; altera verò Pontificem cum implexa, mulieri more coma, & manu colum tractantem repræsentabat; (taceo tum ludum Scenicum, quem in contumeliam ejus rei in Innocentii & Olympiæ nuptias, Londini Cromwello coram lusum ipsimet Itali finxerant: tum Imperatoris Ferdinandi acre dicterium, quo Innocentii Nuntium Melzi contra Pacem cum Sueco initam murmurantem, excepit, his ferè verbis: Papæ verò non desunt otium & delicia, cui Olympia caput demulcet, ut suaviter dormire possit) ut delinificis verbis Olympiæ suæ persuaserit, quo interdiu saltem, ob sinistras omnium interpretationes, domi se contineret, & ab aditu Vaticani sibi temperaret, concessa interim licentia noctu, quoquoties luberet, Pontificem adeundi, & quidlibet cum eo transfigendi: ut mox Pontificis Nepos Camillus Romam cum conjuge revocatus in gratiam cum patruo redierit: ut post mortem Panziroli, Olympia pristinæ libertati restituta, interdiu iterum adeundi Pontificem facultatem nacta, ingravescente jam senesta & attrita valetudine Papæ, licentius quàm unquam aliàs, imperitans, summam rerum ad se denuo contraxerit, & colligendis undique pecuniis vigilantissimè sordidissimeéque incubuerit: ut prohibuerit Pontificem, ne pacem Gallum inter & Hispanum, cui universa Europæ pax innitebatur, ullo modo promoveret, certus scilicet, futurum, ut belli denique pertœsi ultro pacem ipsi ferirent; neve ullis Principum negotiis, ex quibus pecuniæ redigi non possent, se immisceret, metu scilicet, ne offensus quispiam quietam proficuámque dominationem suam turbaret: ut, Pontifice ad mortem propinquante, contracta cum Barbarinis, quos Pontificis hactenus odio flagrantes, & ab eodem seu Olympia potiùs, ad incitas feré redactos, eidem reconciliavit, & in pristinas possessiones restituit, affinitate, munimenta quæsiverit, quibus post mortem Pontificis adversus hostium insidias tutò insisteret: ut Barbarinis ita reconciliatis, Astallium seu Pamphilium adoptivum, Cardinalem Patronum, omni dignitate, fortunis omnibus provolutum, ad perniciem extremam præcipitaverit; non aliam ob causam, quàm quòd secreta Olympiæ & Barbarinorum de Regno Neapolitano Pontifici subjiciendo, ejusque ditione inter se distribuenda, Hispanis prodidisse, indice Azzolino, purpuram indicio tali promerito, compertus fuisset: ut Pontificis valetudine conclamata, Olympia in aulam accita, ægrotanti indivulsa adstiterit, & circa lectum obductis velis abstrusa, legatorum propositiones audiverit, & & prorumpens subinde ad easdem responderit, pro Pontifice cuncta gesserit, fœdissimum quæstum intra decem dierum intervallum media auri millione corrosa, exercuerit: ut die VII. Jan. A.M.D.C.LV. Pontifici oculos clauserit & relictos trium ferè millionum thesauros expilaverit: ut post in Cardinalium conclavi, institGuta etiam factione volante, ex Innocentii ferè creaturis conflata, extremis viribus, ut Papa sibi & Pamphiliis propitius prodiret, nequicquam laboraverit: ut denique ab Alexandro VII. Roma Orvietum relegata, ibique rationem administrationis & pecuniarum immensarum nefariè coactarum reddere jussa, pestilentia interim Italiam universam corripiente, epidemia lue extincta, hæredesque ejus Alexandro placando millionem auri ejusdem Nepotibus erogare compulsi fuerint, eaque ratione, juxta Cardinalis Sforzæ παῤῥησίαν, pars facultatum per simoniam inauditam ab Olympia collectarum à latrone ad latronem transiverit. Hæc non è Protestantis cujuspiam, sed Itali, Romani, Abbatis, testis oculati, auriti fide relata, si vera sunt (falsa autem esse, nemo, quantum sciam, contra Gualdum asserere, nedum probare sustinuit; præter famam passivam, veritatem historiæ inter alios etiam confirmante Francisco Carriere, Minorita Monacho, qui in Chronologia Pontificum narrat, populum Romanum, cum Innocentium audivisset per novendium agonizantem, cum acerbissimis mortis doloribus conflictari, Divino judicio mortem adeo diram ei infligi judicasse, eo quod in administratione Papatus nimium Olympiæ indulserit, & indulgentia ea deteriorem fœminam eam reddiderit) habuit seu passa potius hoc etiam Seculo est Roma redivivas Maroziam, Theodoram, Mathildem, Vannociam, Juliam Farnesiam, & quicquid olim Dominarum & Meretricum Principalium, Romæ fuit. Et Innocentium tamen hunc γυναικοκρατούμενον Sixtus Guardinus Ferrariensis amplissimis elogiis efferre, Innocentium Magnum, Oraculum Seculi, Miraculum totius mundi, Mortalium portentum, coram Deo, coram mundo Innocentem, referente Banckio Roma Triumph. pag. 298. insignire non dubitavit.
units.tr: For almost the whole time that Innocent occupied the Papal See (and he occupied it for more than a full decade), it was a constant report, handed down even by those who had the closest knowledge of everything in Rome, that the Papacy was governed not so much by Innocent as by a woman, his glutton, Donna, or Lady, Olympia Maldachini, the widow of his deceased brother. We had believed that Innocent's innocence was being smeared and burdened by Marforio and Pasquino with warm lies (ἡεχμοῖς ψεύδεσι), had not the Abbot Gualdo, a witness who, as he himself professes, was an eyewitness and earwitness (αὐτόπτης & αὐτήκοος), made the fact fuller and more certain by his written account at Rome, de vita & rebus gestis Donnae Olympiae Maldachinae. That little book, found among his manuscripts after his death and published in Italy, does this. Gualdo relates (let me sum up much in few words) that Olympia, domineering from her earliest years, sought dominion everywhere. She married Innocent's brother Pamphili, but after about ten years of marriage she turned away from him and gave herself wholly to love for her brother-in-law Giovanni Battista Pamphili (later Innocent), and was seized by it, and remained his inseparable companion in the conclave and elsewhere, under a grave suspicion of incestuous love in the eyes of all. She committed herself entirely to his counsels, to be guided and governed by him. She wrote from Spain to Olympia that the affairs she was conducting there, without her husband's knowledge or advice, were going less well, like a ship without oars. Olympia then attached herself more shrewdly to her newly created cardinal brother-in-law and tried to imbue him with those qualities that befit a Pontiff, above all the art of pretending and dissembling, since she had often urged him that this was the gate to the Papacy. The cardinal made progress in the art of pretending and dissembling in everything except his love for Olympia, which he could never be induced to conceal. She ingratiated her brother-in-law with the Spanish cardinals as well as the French, with wonderful cunning. After the death of Urban she used incredible vigilance and diligence in recommending her brother-in-law, and at last by her arts she brought it about that, although Cardinal Antonio Barberini resisted in vain, he was raised to the Papacy beyond everyone's expectation. After his election, many people flocked to Olympia, all who wished to secure their fortunes. She quickly hastened the ruin of Antonio Barberini, with whom she had private quarrels. She sought a dwelling in the Vatican, close to the Pope's conclave, but, Panzirolo dissuading her, she lived in her own house and every evening, as the day drew to a close, she visited him and often lingered with him until late at night. She advanced her son Camillo Pamphili, utterly ignorant of all affairs, to the dignity of Cardinal Patron. When he, aware of his own infirmity, renounced that dignity, she banished him from Rome, together with his new wife, a de Roffano, devoted to the Papists, so that he should not interfere with her rule, and for other reasons as well. She drew all papal business to herself; she heard the petitions that were submitted to the Pope alone; she imposed punishments on the accused beyond their deserts; she distributed offices and dignities at her pleasure; and by these and other means she soon forced the papal treasury into a bottomless pit of money. She set down new laws and revived the old decrees of earlier Pontiffs. Against the Pope's wishes she gave the cardinal's purple to her nephew Maldachini, the most foolish of men, deformed in mind and body, while he was still a young man. Through the influence of Cardinal Panzirolo, Camillo Astalli, a nephew of tender age whom Innocent had adopted in the name of Pamphili, was raised, though unworthy, by Innocent to the title and chief dignity of Cardinal Patron, to the admiration of all. This brought some diminution to Olympia's fortune, since the Pope, as it seemed, recalled to his mind more deeply the less favourable judgements, both Italian and foreign, about his familiarity with Olympia and her more than masculine rule. A newly struck gold coin bore on one side Olympia crowned with the Papal tiara and grasping the keys of Peter in her hand, and on the other the Pope with a woman's hair plaited, turning a spindle in his hand. (I pass over the stage play, which the Italians themselves had devised at London in Cromwell's presence, in mockery of this affair, on the marriage of Innocent and Olympia; and the sharp jibe of Emperor Ferdinand, who answered the murmuring of Innocent's nuncio Melzi against the peace concluded with Sweden, in roughly these words: "But the Pope lacks neither leisure nor pleasures, on which Olympia lays her head, so that he may sleep sweetly.") She persuaded him with soothing words to remain at home by day, at least, because of the unfavourable interpretations of everyone, and to abstain from the Vatican entrance; meanwhile she granted him leave to visit the Pope by night, as often as he pleased, and to transact anything with him. Soon the Pope's nephew Camillo was recalled to Rome with his wife and was reconciled to his uncle. After Panzirolo's death, Olympia was restored to her former freedom and, having again the opportunity to visit the Pope by day, while the Pope's old age and worn-out health were advancing, she ruled more licentiously than ever before and gathered the whole management of affairs into her own hands again. She applied herself with the closest and most sordid vigilance to collecting money from every side. She forbade the Pope to promote in any way the peace between France and Spain, on which the whole peace of Europe rested, being certain that men weary of war would eventually offer peace of their own accord. And she forbade him to mix himself into any affairs of princes from which money could not be extracted, for fear, of course, that some offended party might disturb her quiet and profitable rule. When the Pope was nearing death, she came to terms with the Barberini, whom the Pope had hitherto hated fiercely and who had been almost reduced to ruin by him, or rather by Olympia. She reconciled them to him and restored them to their former possessions, and she sought, through a marriage alliance, defences on which she could securely stand after the Pope's death against the snares of enemies. With the Barberini thus reconciled, she hurled Astalli, or Pamphili the adopted son, the Cardinal Patron, who had been raised to every dignity and fortune, down to utter destruction. The only reason was that he was discovered, by the information of Azzolino, to have betrayed to the Spanish the secrets of Olympia and the Barberini concerning the subjection of the Kingdom of Naples to the Pope and its division among themselves, and so earned the purple by such an informing. When the Pope's illness was declared hopeless, Olympia was summoned to the court and stood unceasingly by the sick man, and, hidden behind veils drawn around the bed, she heard the proposals of the ambassadors, and, bursting out from time to time, answered them. She did everything on the Pope's behalf, and within a ten-day period she practised the most shameful gain, having gnawed away half a million gold pieces. On 7 January 1655 she closed the Pope's eyes and plundered the treasure of nearly three million that he left behind. Afterwards, in the conclave of the cardinals, with a faction now flying, drawn largely from Innocent's creatures, she laboured with all her might, but in vain, to make the Pope come forth favourable to herself and the Pamphili. Finally she was banished from Rome to Orvieto by Alexander VII, and ordered there to give an account of her administration and of the immense sums wickedly collected. Meanwhile a plague was seizing all Italy; the epidemic plague was extinguished, and her heirs, to appease Alexander, were compelled to pay a million gold pieces to his nephews. By this means, according to the frankness of Cardinal Sforza, part of the wealth gathered by Olympia through unheard-of simony passed from robber to robber. These things are reported on the testimony of an Italian Roman Abbot, an eyewitness and earwitness, and not of some Protestant. If they are true (and no one, as far as I know, has ventured to assert or prove the contrary against Gualdo), then, apart from common report, the truth of the story is also confirmed by others, including the Franciscan monk Francesco Carriere, who relates in his Chronology of the Popes that the Roman people, when they heard that Innocent had been in agony for nine days, struggling with the bitterest pangs of death, judged that such a dreadful death had been inflicted on him by divine judgement, because in the administration of the Papacy he had indulged Olympia too much, and by that indulgence had made her a worse woman. In this century, too, Rome had, or rather suffered, the return of Marozia, Theodora, Matilda, Vannozza, Giulia Farnese, and whatever Lady and Principal Courtesan there was in Rome in former times. Yet Sixtus Guardinus of Ferrara did not hesitate to extol this Innocent, ruled by a woman, with the highest praise, calling him "Innocent the Great, Oracle of the Age, Miracle of the whole world, Portent of mortals, Innocent before God and before the world", as Banck reports, Roma Triumph. p. 298.

units.la: CCLVII. Quâm se gravem & iniquum Innocentius J- anfenitis præbuerit, supra narravimus; causásque obiter etiam indigitavimus.
units.tr: CCLVII. How grave and unjust Innocent showed himself toward the Jansenists, we have related above, and we have also touched on the causes in passing.

units.la: Favor scilicet erga Jesuitas, qui immediatè à sacerrima Sede illa pendent, ei obedientiam coecam vovent, ejus Metaphysicam & transcendentalem illam potestatem, quo jure, quáve injuria, acerimè & quibusvis interdictis, propugnant: odium verò insitum Pontificum erga Episcopos meliores doctiorésque, qui authoritatem, quam sibi à Christo collatam putant, studiosissimè afferunt, quales in Gallia & Belgio non pauci à Janseniii qui & ipsemet Episcopus celebris fuerat, partibus steterant, Innocentio ad damnandas Janseníi Propositiones faces subdiderant. Accessit opportuna occasio, qua in definiendis etiam fidei articulis infallibilitatem suam, etiam extra Concilium à Gallis Episcopis, aliisque etiam aliàs oppugnatam, stabiliri posse speravit. Quod eventus maximè probavit, quando successor ejus occasione Janseníitici hujus certaminis in Gallia infallibilitatem suam definiri, & ab ipso Rege Christianissimo agnosci petiit. Hæ similésque causæ, quas inter rerum Divinarum ignorantia & contemptus supinus, fatalisque Romanæ Ecclesiæ, justo Dei judicio, spiritu vertiginis perculsæ, & in pejus in dies proficientis malignitas, haud postremum locum obtinent, apud Nocentium hunc effecerunt, ut Cœlum ipsum stultitia sua petere, Gratiæ Divinæ giganteo conatu bellum indicere, & Pelagianam hæresin, à tot prædecessoribus suis damnatam, in arce reponere verecundatus non fuerit.
units.tr: Clearly the causes were his favour toward the Jesuits, who depend directly on that most sacred See, pledge blind obedience to it, and defend with the utmost vehemence and against every prohibition its metaphysical and transcendent power, whether by right or by wrong. Added to this was the innate hatred of the Pontiffs toward the better and more learned bishops, who most zealously assert the authority they believe Christ conferred on them. Many such bishops in France and Belgium had taken the side of Jansenius, himself a famous bishop, and they had fanned the flames for Innocent to condemn the propositions of Jansenius. An opportune occasion also presented itself, by which he hoped his own infallibility, which had been attacked by French bishops and others even apart from a council, could be established even in defining articles of faith. The outcome especially proved this, when his successor, on the occasion of this Jansenist controversy in France, sought to have his infallibility defined and acknowledged by the Most Christian King himself. These and similar causes, among which ignorance of divine things, supine contempt, and the malice of the Roman Church, struck by a spirit of giddiness through the just judgment of God and growing worse by the day, hold no small place, led this Innocent to be not ashamed to seek heaven itself with his folly, to declare war on divine grace with a giant's effort, and to set up on the citadel the Pelagian heresy, which so many of his predecessors had condemned.

units.la: CCLVIII. Neque Gratiam Divinam impugnare sa-tis
units.tr: CCLVIII. Nor was it enough for him to attack divine grace

units.la: Ejusdem & Nuntii ejus, tis habuit. Etiam humanam in terris gratiam & pacem, præclarum illud Dei immortalis munus, turbare, impugnare modis omnibus annisus est, dolens non parum, quòd Jesuitarum suorum, in perniciem Germaniæ à tot annis instar telæ Arachnes subtiliter contexta consilia, infelicem successum haberent. Testis est insana & ferocissima ejus adversus Pacem Westphalicam, Monasterio-Osnabrugensem, tandiu Europæ totius votis ardentissimis desideratam, difficilíque, adeò negotio inter Principes diversos, Pacificorum prudentiúmque virorum opera d. vi. Aug. & xxiv. Octobr. A. M. D. C. XLVIII. conclusam, Protestatio. Et primò quidem Pontificis nomine Fabius Chisius, Episcopus Neritonensis, & eo tempore Apostolicus in Germania Nuntius, post Papa, Alexandri VII. nomine famosus, geminam Protestationem, utramque Monasterii Westphalorum, & alteram quidem d. xiv. alteram xxvi. Octobr. A. M. D. C. XLVIII. insolentissimis amarulentissimisque verbis editam obtulit, professus inter alia, sese omnem etiam pulvisculum de pedibus excutere, qui commune quidquam habere possit vel cum minimo præjudicio S. Sedis; & promptum se exhibere pro illa Sede ad vitam & sanguinem profundendum. Sicut nempe Apostoli prædicaturi pulverem pedum excutere adversus eos, qui Christo obedire detrectarent, & in testimonium de Christo etiam sanguinem fundere jussi sunt: ita pro Papa suo idem factitandum Fabius censuit; quasi tantundem esset Papæ Regnum & Regnum Dei, Christum & Papam prædicare. quales tamen Fabios prædicatores & Martyres omnis prisca Apostolica & verè Catholica Ecclesia ignoravit. Supervenit d. xxvi. Nov. ejusdem Anni ex ipsa Tarpeja arce in Pacem Fulmen planè horrendum, ac quale ab orbe condito nusquam terrarum auditum fuerat; Bulla scilicet ipsius Innocentii feralis & infausta, cui titulus est: Sanctissimi Domini N. D. Innocentii Divina Providentia Papæ X. Declaratio Nullitatis Articulorum nuperæ pacis Germaniæ: Religioni Catholicæ, Sedi Apostolicæ, Ecclesiis, aliisque Locis piis ac personis, & juribus Ecclesiasticis quomodolibet præjudicialium. Ibi Principibus Pontificiis, pacem justa concessione eorum, quæ nullo vel Divino, vel humano jure legitimo inhiberi poterant, redimentibus, crimini datum, quòd Pace ea inter alia bona ecclesiastica, aliáque ab hæreticis occupata, illis, eorúmque Successoribus in perpetuum addicuntur; Hæreticis Augustanæ, uti vocant, confessionis liberum suæ hæreseos exercitium in plerisque locis permittitur, & locorum pro ædificandis ad hunc effectum templis assignatio permittitur; ipsique cum Catholicis ad publica munia & officia, ac ad nonnullos Archiepiscopatus, aliásque dignitates & beneficia ecclesiastica, precúmque primariarum Ferdinando in Imperatorem electo à Sede Apostolica concessarum participationem admittuntur: Annatæ, jura Pallii, confirmationes, Menses Papales, & hujusmodi jura ac Reservationes, in bonis ecclesiasticis dictæ Confessionis Augustanæ excluduntur; Confirmationes electionum, seu postulationum prætensorum Archiepiscoporum, aut Prælatorum ejusdem Confessionis, potestati Seculari attribuuntur; plures Archiepiscopatus, Episcopatus, monasteria, ballivæ, commendæ, canonicatus, & alia beneficia, & bona ecclesiastica, Principibus hæreticis, eorúmque hæredibus, etiam sublata denominatione ecclesiastica, in feudum perpetuum sub dignitatis Secularis titulo conceduntur; contra Pacem hujusmodi, ullúmve ejus articulum, nulla jura Canonica vel civilia, communia, specialia, Conciliorum decreta, religiosorum ordinum regulas, juramenta aut Concordata cum Romanis Pontificibus, ullave alia statuta, sive ecclesiastica, sive politica, decreta, dispensationes, absolutiones, aut alias exceptiones, audiri vel admitti debere; disponitur; Numerus septem Electorum Imperii, olim Apostolica authoritate præfinitus, sine nostro & Sedis præfatæ beneplacito augetur, & Electoratus octavus in favorem Caroli Ludovici, Comitis Palatini, hæretici instituitur; aliáque multa, quæ pudet referre, orthodoxæ religioni, Sedíque díque præfata ac Romana, & inferioribus ecclesiis, cæterisque præmissis summopere præjudicialia & damnosa decernuntur. Quibus omnibus cum pupillam oculi sui feriri, & ventrem, cujus quæsitissimus in Romana curia sensus est, tangi Papa existimâsset, is de Apostolicæ potestatis plenitudine, decreta illa & similia etiam ipso jure nulla, invalida, irrita, injusta, damnata, reprobata, inania, viribus & effectu vana omnino fuisse, esse, & in perpetuo fore; neminemque ad illorum, & cujuslibet eorum, etiamsi juramento vallata sint, observantiam teneri: neque ex illis cuiquam aliquod ius, vel actionem, aut titulum coloratum, vel causam præscribendi, etiamsi longissimi & immemorabilis temporis possessio, etiam citra ullam interpellationem aut interruptionem, subsequatur, acquisitum fuisse, nec esse, minusve ullo tempore acquiri, & competere posse: neque illa ullum statum facere vel fecisse: atque perinde, ac si non emanassent, pro non extantibus & non factis perpetuò haberi debere, decernit ac declarat. Neque sibi lœsa Majestas Pontificia satisfacere ullo modo valens, subjicit: Et nihilominus ad abundantiorem cautelam, articulos præfatos, aliáque præjudicialia, motu, scientia & deliberatione, & potestatis plenitudine penitus damnamus, reprobamus, nullamus, cassamus, annullamus, viribúsque & effectu vacuamus; & contra illa, déque eorum nullitate coram Deo protestamur. Piget reliqua Bullæ illius plumbeæ, nil nisi plumbeas iras, ob Pacem scilicet culinæ Pontificiæ commodis præhabitam, spirantis, prosequi. Tantus dolor fuit subductorum ventri pinguium aliquot patrimoniorum: adeò altè aqualiculo suavissimæ saginæ impressa memoria hærebat!
units.tr: Of the same man and his nuncio, he had. He also strove by every means to disturb and attack the human grace and peace on earth, that splendid gift of the immortal God, and he grieved not a little that the schemes of his Jesuits, subtly woven for so many years like a spider's web to ruin Germany, had an unhappy outcome. Witness is his mad and most savage protest against the Peace of Westphalia, concluded at Osnabrück and Münster on 6 August and 24 October 1648 through the work of peacemakers and prudent men, a peace that all Europe had longed for with the warmest prayers and that was so hard to reach, given the divergent interests of the princes. First, in the Pope's name, Fabio Chigi, Bishop of Nardò and at that time the Apostolic Nuncio in Germany, later famous under the name of Alexander VII, presented two protests at Münster, one on 14 October and the other on 26 October 1648, couched in most insolent and bitter words. Among other things he declared that he would shake off every speck of dust from his feet that could have anything in common, even the slightest prejudice, with the Holy See; and that he stood ready for that See to shed his life and blood. Just as the Apostles, when preaching, were ordered to shake the dust from their feet against those who refused to obey Christ, and to shed their blood as testimony to Christ, so Fabio thought the same should be done for the sake of his Pope, as if preaching the Papacy and the Kingdom of God, or Christ and the Pope, were the same thing. Yet all the ancient, truly Apostolic and Catholic Church knew nothing of such Fabian preachers and martyrs. On 26 November of the same year there came from the Tarpeian rock itself a thunderbolt against the Peace, truly horrible, such as had never been heard anywhere in the world since its creation: namely, the baleful and ill-omened bull of Innocent himself, entitled: Declaration of the Nullity of the Articles of the recent Peace of Germany, prejudicial in any way to the Catholic Religion, the Apostolic See, the Churches, other pious places and persons, and ecclesiastical rights, issued by our most holy lord Innocent X, by Divine Providence Pope. In it, the Papist princes, who had bought peace by the just concession of things that could not be forbidden by any legitimate divine or human right, were charged with a crime, because by that Peace among other ecclesiastical goods and other things seized by heretics, these were adjudged in perpetuity to them and their successors; the free exercise of their heresy is permitted to the heretics of the so-called Augsburg Confession in most places, and assignment of places for building temples for this purpose is permitted; and they are admitted with Catholics to public duties and offices, and to some archbishoprics and other dignities and ecclesiastical benefices, and to a share in the chief prebends granted by the Apostolic See to Ferdinand, elected as Emperor; the annates, the rights of the pallium, confirmations, the papal months, and rights and reservations of this kind are excluded from the ecclesiastical goods of the said Augsburg Confession; confirmations of elections, or of the nominations of so-called archbishops or prelates of the same Confession, are assigned to secular power; many archbishoprics, bishoprics, monasteries, bailiwicks, commendams, canonries and other benefices and ecclesiastical goods are granted to heretical princes and their heirs in perpetual fief under the title of secular dignity, even with the ecclesiastical designation removed; it is ordained that no canonical or civil laws, general or special, decrees of Councils, rules of religious orders, oaths or concordats with the Roman Pontiffs, nor any other statutes, whether ecclesiastical or political, decrees, dispensations, absolutions, or other exceptions, ought to be heard or admitted against this Peace or any of its articles; the number of the seven Electors of the Empire, once fixed by Apostolic authority, is increased without our and the aforesaid See's consent, and an eighth Electorate is established in favour of Charles Louis, the heretical Count Palatine; and many other things, which it shames me to recount, are decreed as most damaging and prejudicial to the orthodox religion, to the aforesaid Roman See, to the lower churches, and to the other matters set out above. When the Pope thought that the pupil of his eye had been struck by all these things, and his belly, whose most refined sense is in the Roman court, had been touched, he decreed and declared, by the fullness of apostolic power, that those decrees and similar ones were altogether null by law itself, invalid, void, unjust, condemned, reprobated, empty, and vain in their force and effect, and so they have been, are, and shall remain forever; that no one is bound to observe them, even if they are backed by an oath; that no right, action, colourable title or ground for prescription has been or can be acquired from them by anyone, even if a very long and immemorial possession follows, even without any protest or interruption; that they make, or have made, no state of affairs; and that, as if they had never been issued, they must be held forever as non-existent and never made. Then, his Pontifical Majesty, unable to satisfy his wounded dignity in any way, adds: And nevertheless, for greater caution, we completely condemn, reprobate, nullify, quash, annul, and empty of force and effect the aforesaid articles and other prejudicial matters, by our own motion, knowledge, deliberation, and fullness of power; and we protest against them and against their nullity before God. It irks me to pursue the rest of that leaden bull, which breathes nothing but leaden wrath, on account of the Peace, which was preferred to the advantage of the Papal kitchen. So great was the grief of those who had lost some fat patrimonies for the belly! So deeply had the memory of the most delicious feasting been impressed on their paunches!

units.la: CCLIX. Ante quàm Pax confecta fuit, in ipso scilicet deliberationum æstu, Fabii ejusdem instinctu, exaratum Monasterii prodiit judicium Theologicum personati cujusdam Ernesti de Eusebiis, quo probare is aggressus est, Pacem, qualem Protestantes desiderant, secundùm se illicitam esse; eò quòd pax ejusmodi hæresi tum directè, tum in-
units.tr: CCLIX. Before the Peace was concluded, namely in the very heat of the deliberations, at the instigation of the same Fabio, there appeared at Münster a theological judgement by a certain masked man, Ernst von Eusebius, by which he set out to prove that the peace the Protestants desire is in itself unlawful, because such a peace cooperates with heresy both directly and in-

units.la: Ernesti de Eusebiis de Pace Protestantibus non danda, liber, Fabii Chisii jussu vulgatus. indirecte cooperetur: Creatori & verae Religioni injuriam inferat: causa sit perditionis animarum: usurpatio sit potestatis non competentis: repugnet officio & juramento Caesaris, Statuúmque Catholicorum, maximè Episcoporum: frustratoria, ipsoque bello periculosior sit: sit magis inordinata mendacio: Ecclesiae Dei, Summorum Pontificum, S. Patrum, & veterum Doctorum suffragio destituatur & damnetur: quae sigillatim demonstrare conatur. Successit mox Judicii illius Theologici vehiculum, & Instrumenti Pacis Ponderatio. Respondentur ad Judicium illud ex Pontificiis, Abbas Caramuel, Vir doctissimus, qui arcanis consultationibus multis magno bono in lucem productis, praeterea opinione variae doctrinae & authoritate cum primis fidem sibi idoneam fecit: ex Augustanis verò tum Doctifs. Joh. Georgius Darchaeus; tum solidissimè inprimis Celeb Conringius, qui sub nomine Irenaei Eubuli, Theologi Austriaci pro Pace perpetua Protestantibus danda Consultationem Catholicam edidit. quam per hypothesis irrefragabiles, & conclusiones inde deductas, solutis etiam Ernesti argumentis, adornatam, dignissimam, quae truci & saevo Eusebii tenebrionis judicio opponeretur, esse J. C. famigeratissimus Jacobus Lampadius, praefatione praefixa judicavit. Sed & pace jam rata firmáque, & non attentis Romanis sive fulguritionibus, sive tonitribus, sive fulminibus in publicas perpetuasque Imperii leges recepta, refractariam illam Innocentii bullam idem Doctissimus Conringius ad partes ita vocavit, ut apertae veritati dederit, Declarationem Innocentii non necessariam, inutilem, publicè privatimque noxiam ac perniciosam, denique ab omni aequitate & justitia alienam esse: In Batavis quoque duo rei indignitate moti, alter David Blondellus, omnis antiquitatis promus condus, ficto tamen Amandi Flaviani nomine; alter Vir Clarissimus, Johannes Hoornbeckius, perdoctis scriptis Romanae Bullae impiedisputitur.
units.tr: Ernst von Eusebius's book, On the Peace not to be granted to the Protestants, published by order of Fabio Chigi: it cooperates indirectly; it inflicts injury on the Creator and the true religion; it causes the perdition of souls; it is a usurpation of a power not belonging to them; it is contrary to the duty and oath of the Emperor and of the Catholic princes, especially the bishops; it is frustrating and more dangerous than war itself; it is more disorderly than a lie; and it is stripped of the support of the Church of God, of the Supreme Pontiffs, of the holy Fathers and of the ancient Doctors, and is condemned by them. He tries to demonstrate each of these point by point. Soon after that theological judgement came its vehicle, and the Weighing of the Instrument of Peace. Replying to that judgement on the Papist side was Abbot Caramuel, a most learned man, who had earlier won for himself, through many secret consultations brought to light for great benefit, and through his reputation for varied learning and authority, a credit above most others. On the Augsburg side there replied Dr Johann Georg Dorsch, and above all most solidly the renowned Conring, who under the name of Irenaeus Eubulus, a Austrian theologian, published a Catholic Consultation for a perpetual peace to be granted to the Protestants. Jacob Lampadius, the most famous jurist, judged in a preface prefixed to it that this work, built on irrefutable hypotheses and conclusions drawn from them, and with Ernst's arguments also refuted, was most worthy to be set against the grim and savage judgement of the dark Eusebius. And when the peace had now been ratified and confirmed, and, regardless of the Roman lightnings, thunderclaps or thunderbolts, had been received into the public and perpetual laws of the Empire, the same most learned Conring called that refractory bull of Innocent to account in such a way that, to the open truth, he gave the verdict that Innocent's Declaration was unnecessary, useless, publicly and privately harmful and pernicious, and finally alien to all equity and justice. In the Netherlands too, two men, moved by the unworthiness of the matter, did not hesitate to pierce that Papal fire, which they rightly judged did not lack deceitful ash beneath it: one was David Blondel, the storehouse of all antiquity, under the feigned name Amandus Flavianus; the other, a most distinguished man, Johannes Hoornbeek, disputed against the Roman bull with most learned writings.

units.la: Hoornbeckius disputitur. pietatem, quòd doloso cineri suppositam illam Papalem prunam non carere judicâffent merito, confodere non dubitârunt.
units.tr: Hoornbeckius was attacked in the same way. Because they judged that the Papal firebrand, placed under deceitful ashes, was rightly lacking in piety, they did not hesitate to stab it.

units.la: CCLX. Innocentio d. vii. Jan. A.M.D.C.LV. acerba morte, uti supra diximus, defuncto, Cardinales undecimo à morte ejus die in Conclave sexaginta & novem celebris (vacabant tamen quatuor ob absentiam Sandovallii, Cuevæ & Mazarini, & mortem Carafæ) distinctum se contulerunt. In Cardinalem Sacchettum plurium Gallicæ factioni addictorum, coryphæo eorum Barbarino, vota inclinabant. Medicæi, Hispanicæ factionis principes, & cum iis Hispani ei summopere resistere. Duabus his accessit tertia factio (Squadron volante) volans (scilicet, quam factionem Spiritus S. blasphemè appellare ausi sunt,) ex Pamphilii seu Innocentii creaturis, Olympia annitente; & Cardinale Imperiali ejusdem duce, collecta, præ se ferens, quòd Papam non vel Hispanum, vel Gallum, sed dignissimum eligere constitutum habeant. Constat tamen, volantes illos Olympiæ desideriis velificari unicè voluisse. Cùmque Cardinales Innocentio sanguine conjuncti nulli extiterint (Astallius enim adoptione exciderat) æquum visum, ut in factione tali habeat nomen aliquod factio Pamphilia, ne ab Innocentio electi Cardinales velut mercenarii milites huc atque illuc divagari, & alienis signis nomen dare necessum haberent. Has veras Factionis volantis causas scripta ab Italis vulgata prodiderunt. Et junxerat se primùm volans hæc factio Barbarino, Gallicæ antesignano. Sed Sacchetti, cui Galli studebant, promovendi post plures, quibus in eligendo eo lapidem omnem frustra moverant, hebdomadas, spes omnis mox evanuit, Medicæis, qui jam ante illum excluserant, vindictam metuentibus. Confpirârunt tamen vota ad Pontificem Coronæ Gallicæ & Mazarino gratissimum eligendum. Placuit statim Rapacciolus, Barbarinorum rebus insuper addictissimus. Restiterunt Medicæi, & cum iis Hispani, eò quòd dignissimus Papatu licet, occulto favore nimium in Galli partes inclinaret. Rejecto sic Rapacciolo proponitur Card. Florenzola, Ordinis Dominicani Monachus. Neque ille Medicæis displicuerat. Sed obstitit Olympiæ acris tergiversatio, quæ propter simultates privatas invicem exercitas, ante Cardinalium in Conclave ingressum Pamphilios omnes seriis precibus, ne in electionem ejus, futuri sibi inimicissimi, consentirent, obtestata fuerat. Neque cùm ex Conclavi ei significaretur, electum Florenzolam esse, si acquiesceret illa, & universæ Pamphiliorum domui benevolum affectum spondere; Trivultio Cardinale etiam, qui ob morbum extra conclave degerat, pro eo multùm intercedente, flecti ullo modo, inducíque, ut quiesceret, potuit. Proponuntur igitur alii, Cecchinus, Franciottus, Bragadinus, & tandem, annitente Sacchetto; Fabius Chisius, patria Senensis, agminis volitantis quasi ocellus, is ipse, quem nuper adversus Pacem Westphalicam Pontificis nomine supra protestatum diximus. Quia tamen ad ejus, utpote ab Hispana factione propositus, electionem Galli venturi languidiùs credebantur, Sacchetti opera nuntius perniciissimè in Galliam ablegatus est cum ejusdem ad Mazarinum literis efficacissimis, quibus ejus virtutem, dotes & erga coronam Gallicam incredibilem affectum graphicè is depinxit. Interea, dum responsum ex Gallia expectatur, tempus inutiliter & inter mutuas fraudes, cùm alii aliis gnaviter imponerent, consumptum extractúmque est. Eóque res devenit, ut multi non tam tœdio, quàm scandalo offenderentur, haud obscurè innuentes, non sic gloriam Dei, nec ecclesiæ anxiè electionem Pontificis desiderantis, quæri. Responderunt, qui protela illa consultò nexuerant, nondum illuxisse diem, quo Deus populo suo de rectore prospicere decrevit. Illuxit tamen mox candidus ille dies, quando ex Gallia allatæ literæ, placere Chisium, & ob Sacchetti intercessionem, unicè illum à Rege expeti, significârunt. Sic Medicæos inter & Barbarinum, Hispanos, Gallos & medios, inde à die XXVIII. Martii cùm transactum esset, tandem post scrutinium verspertinum diei Martis, VI. nimirum Aprilis, negotium à Cardinalibus apertius tractatum, & sibi invicem, tam fuastam electionem Chisii gratulati sunt; ingruentéque nocte in cella Chisii, qui jam se in lecto composuerat, convenerunt. Gratulationes excepit Chisius; profusis lachrymis subinde orans, ut digniorem alium eligerent. Solent nimirum nonnulli specie recusantium flagrantissimè cupere. Pro sequentis diei, VII. Aprilis scrutinio matutino jam vespera præcedente suffragia certa pro Chisio præparata erant; Medicæis ac Hispanis viginti duo, Barbarino triginta novem vota promittentibus. Posteri diei VIII. Aprilis primo manè omnes, qui aderant, Cardinales ad Chisii cellam coiverunt, tum sacro in privato quodam sacello facto interfuerunt, ac demum Chisium more solito ad delubrum Sixti deduxerunt, ut ibi in scrutinio jam factam ejus electionem communibus votis publicè comprobarent. In quo scrutinio Hispanorum vota ad numerum vigesimum & quintum crevere, licet Medicæi viginti duo duntaxat promisissent; & sua triginta novem Barbarinus contulit, atque ita concordibus suffragiis omnium, sexaginta quatuor scilicet, Fabius Chisius Pontifex Romanus electus est. Qui antequam publicè (nam privatas gratulationes jam admiserat) dignitatem capesseret, precum causa, ab Altissimo auxilium impetraturus, aliquantum secessit. Vestitus postmodum Pontificali habitu Romanus Pontifex, ac visibile caput ecclesiæ sub nomine ALEXANDRI VII. (hoc enim Fabio nonomen placuit, nescio quo Numine vel omine) ab omnibus Cardinalibus salutatus & adoratus est.
units.tr: CCLX. When Innocent died on 7 January 1655 after a bitter death, as we said above, the Cardinals entered the conclave on the eleventh day after his death, sixty-nine of them (four places were vacant, however, owing to the absence of Sandoval, Cueva and Mazarin and the death of Carafa). They were divided. Their votes leaned towards Cardinal Sacchetti, favoured by many of the French party, while Barberini, their leader, favoured him too. The Medici, leaders of the Spanish party, and the Spaniards with them, strongly opposed him. A third faction joined these two: (Squadron volante), the flying squadron. They were called, blasphemously, the faction of the Holy Spirit. It was made up of Pamphili's, or Innocent's, creatures, and it was gathered under Cardinal Imperiali, their leader, with Olimpia working behind the scenes. They gave out that they meant to elect a Pope who was neither Spanish nor French but most worthy. It is certain, however, that these flying men wanted only to serve Olimpia's wishes. Since none of the Cardinals were related to Innocent by blood (Astalli had been dropped by adoption), it seemed fair that the Pamphili faction should have some name within this faction, so that the Cardinals chosen by Innocent would not wander hither and thither like hired soldiers, forced to give their name to other men's banners. Writings published by Italians have revealed these true causes of the flying faction. At first this flying faction had joined Barberini, the leader of the French. But after several weeks, in which they had moved every stone in vain to elect him, all hope for Sacchetti, whom the French supported, soon vanished. The Medici, who had already excluded him earlier, feared revenge. Nevertheless the votes came together on electing a Pope most pleasing to the Crown of France and to Mazarin. Rapaccioli was at once favoured, a man also wholly devoted to the Barberini interests. The Medici and the Spaniards with them resisted, because although he was worthy of the papacy, he leaned too much towards the French side by a secret favour. Rapaccioli being rejected in this way, Cardinal Florenzola, a Dominican friar, was put forward. He had not displeased the Medici. But Olimpia's sharp shifting stood in the way. Because of private quarrels carried on between them, before the Cardinals entered the conclave she had earnestly begged all the Pamphili to refuse their consent to his election, since he would be their bitterest enemy. Even when she was told from inside the conclave that Florenzola had been elected, and was promised that she would be granted goodwill if she accepted it and extended it to the whole Pamphili family, she could not be brought in any way to give way, even though Cardinal Trivulzio, who was staying outside the conclave because of illness, interceded strongly for him. Others were therefore proposed: Cecchini, Franciotti, Bragadin, and at last, through Sacchetti's efforts, Fabio Chigi, a Sienese, the little eye, as it were, of the flying squadron, the very man whom, as we said, he had lately protested against the Peace of Westphalia in the name of the Pope. Yet because the French were thought likely to oppose his election, since he had been proposed by the Spanish faction, a messenger was sent off to France with all speed, carrying Sacchetti's most effective letters to Mazarin, in which he described Chigi's virtue, gifts and incredible affection towards the Crown of France. Meanwhile, while the answer from France was awaited, time was wasted and spent in mutual deceit, as each party skilfully imposed on the others. The matter reached such a point that many were offended not so much by boredom as by scandal, hinting plainly that the glory of God was not being sought in this way, nor was the Church anxiously desiring the election of a Pope. Those who had deliberately contrived these delays replied that the day on which God had decided to provide a ruler for his people had not yet dawned. Yet that bright day soon dawned, when letters from France arrived, announcing that Chigi was acceptable, and that the King was asked for him alone, through Sacchetti's intercession.
