So, after the time from 28 March had passed between the Medici and Barberini, the Spaniards, the French and the moderates, at last, after the evening scrutiny of Tuesday, namely 6 April, the business was discussed more openly by the Cardinals, who congratulated one another on Chigi's election, which seemed certain. As night came on they gathered in the cell of Chigi, who had already lain down in bed. Chigi received their congratulations, shedding many tears and repeatedly begging them to choose someone more worthy. Indeed some men, under the appearance of refusing, most eagerly desire the office. For the scrutiny on the morning of Wednesday 7 April, the votes for Chigi were already secured on the previous evening: twenty-two were promised by the Medici and the Spaniards, thirty-nine by Barberini. On the next day, 8 April, early in the morning, all the Cardinals present gathered in Chigi's cell, then were present at a Mass held in a private chapel, and at last they escorted Chigi, as usual, to the church of Sixtus, so that there, in a scrutiny, they might publicly confirm by common votes the election already made. In this scrutiny the votes of the Spaniards rose to twenty-five, although the Medici had promised only twenty-two; Barberini contributed his thirty-nine. And so by the united votes of all, sixty-four in number, Fabio Chigi was elected Roman Pontiff. Before he publicly took up the dignity (for he had already accepted private congratulations), he withdrew for a while to seek help from the Most High by prayer. Afterwards, clothed in the Pontifical habit, the Roman Pontiff, and the visible head of the Church, was saluted and adored by all the Cardinals under the name ALEXANDER VII (for this name pleased Fabio, I know not by what divine power or omen).

units.la: CCLXI. Hanc Conclavis Alexandri VII. historiam, Authore Italo minimè suspecto, saltem ob profusissimas, quas Alexandro in eadem historia admetitur, laudes, Romae Italicè, & à Johanne Schwarzkopfio, Serenissi. Augusti Brunsuicensium Ducis, Consiliario, Viro Summo, Latinè, fusius proditam, delibatis summis ejus capitibus, repraesentare haud inconsultum omnino duxi, ut electionis Pontificum paradigma aliquod lectorum oculis subjicerem. Quaerere hic libet: An ita eligentibus censeri possit Spiritus S. praesedisse? An verosimile sit, Spiritu S. afflari Cardinales in factiones, & in illa consilia carnalia de inveniendo commodo suis Secularibus desideriis Pontifice? Num ad illum modum DEUS O. M. Prophetas & Apostolos (Apostolus autem etiam Papa haberi vult) miserit in mundum? An non potius Deus singulos Prophetas & Apostolos suos ab ipso orbe condito immediatè elegerit & miserit? An, si Papa est vicarius Dei, ac proinde ratione illius muneris major omnibus Prophetis & Apostolis, uno excepto S. Petro, verisimile sit eum ritè constitui modo aliquo, qui longè inferior est illo, quo electi olim fuere Prophetae & Apostoli? An in ejusmodi Pontificum electionibus quicquam appareat, quo electionibus Principum Secularium praeferri mereantur? Imò an non electiones Principum Secularium praeferri electionibus Pontificum vel eo nomine mereantur, quòd in illis salutis omnium promiscuè subditorum haberi ratio soleat: in his contra non omnium aequè Principum, sed vel Regis Hispaniae, vel Regis Galliae (prout haec vel illa factio vincit) duntaxat, vel praecipue commoda spectantur? An non Pontifices ita electi vitio & per simoniam creati censeri debeant? An proinde tales electiones non sint illegitimae & ipso jure re nullæ ; ipsique adeò Pontifices Pseudo-Pontifices? Hæc similiáque extricent illi, qui Pontifices ejusmodi à Cardinalibus, Carnalibus scilicet, electos pro Vicariis Christi, adeóque Vice-Deis venerantur. Jam olim quidem Baldi, Jurisconsulti veteris, de sententia (in l. 2. C. sententiam rescindi non posse) Papa non legitime electus, est Diabolus in terris & apostata: & ideo non habet claves Cæli, sed inferni. Quis verò ab hujusmodi, quæso, (sibi & Baldo ignoscat Roma, non mihi) diabolis, apostatis, inferni clavigeris, sanam incorruptámque Religionis Christianæ doctrinam sibi polliceatur?
units.tr: CCLXI. I thought it altogether not ill-advised to set before the eyes of readers an example of papal elections, by presenting the history of this conclave of Alexander VII in outline, after its main points had been touched upon. The history was written by an Italian author who is least of all open to suspicion, at least because of the extravagant praises he heaps on Alexander in it. It was published at Rome in Italian, and more fully in Latin by Johann Schwarzkopf, a most distinguished man and councillor of the most serene Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. Here it is fitting to ask: Can it be thought that the Holy Spirit presided over such an election? Is it likely that Cardinals inspired by the Holy Spirit would split into factions and, in carnal counsels, choose a Pope for the sake of their secular desires and advantage? Did God the Best and Greatest send Prophets and Apostles into the world in that manner (though the Pope also wishes to be regarded as an Apostle)? Or rather, has God not immediately chosen and sent each of his Prophets and Apostles from the beginning of the world? And if the Pope is the vicar of God, and therefore, by reason of that office, greater than all the Prophets and Apostles except St Peter, is it likely that he is lawfully appointed by some method far inferior to that by which the Prophets and Apostles were once chosen? Does anything appear in such elections of Popes by which they deserve to be preferred to the elections of secular princes? Indeed, do not the elections of secular princes deserve to be preferred to those of Popes for this reason, that in them the welfare of all subjects alike is usually taken into account, whereas in papal elections it is not the interests of all princes alike that are regarded, but only, or chiefly, those of the King of Spain or the King of France, according as this or that faction prevails? Should not Popes chosen in this way be considered as created through vice and by simony? And therefore are not such elections unlawful and void by law itself, and are not the Popes themselves pseudo-Popes? Let those who venerate Popes chosen in this way by Cardinals, that is, by carnal men, as vicars of Christ and so as vice-gods, work out these and similar questions. Long ago Baldus, an old jurist, held (on the law in C. 2, that a sentence cannot be rescinded) that a Pope not lawfully elected is the Devil on earth and an apostate, and therefore has not the keys of heaven but of hell. But I ask: who, from such devils, apostates, and keyholders of hell (let Rome pardon Baldus and himself, not me), may promise himself a sound and uncorrupted doctrine of the Christian religion?

units.la: CCLXII. Enimverò quid vel Cardinales, vel Seculares etiam Principes in Pontificum electione potissimùm spectent, experientia liquidò testatur. Ex quo enim Pontificis eligendi jus ad solos Cardinales devolutum, eorúmque Collegium in duas præpotentes factiones, Gallicam & Hispanicam scissum est, non jam conjectu sortis, sed prægrandi annua pecunia in aliquot Cardinalium aridas avidásque fauces conjecta, emptisque suffragiis, hæc ad Principum nutum, partibus studentium, Comitia peraguntur. Tum quid utrique spectent, ipsi etiam Pontificii graves neutiquam dissimulant. Jam dudum enim Joh. Franciscus Lottinus, Episcopus Volaterranus, ille Marcelli II. amicus summus, in Consilio, quod de Conclavi scripsit, sic inter alia censuit: In Pontifice, inquit, eligendo aliis studiis Principes & Prælati Ecclesiastici, aliis Seculares ducuntur. Hi quidem quantumvis religionis Catholicæ sint studiosissimi, magis tamen propriæ utilitatis respectu moventur. Idcirco Pontificem plerique malunt, qui animo timido sit & sollicito, quàm prompto & vehementi; ut bonis ecclesiasticis, quæ in ipsorum sunt ditionibus, tanto liberius uti frui possint. Quod si vel Rex Franciæ, vel alius quis Princeps Pontificem desiderent, qui animo magno sit & elato, non equidem ideo faciunt, quòd Sedis Apostolicæ dignitatem auctam cucupiant, sed ut eorum consiliis ad res in Italia novandas utantur. Hispaniarum quidem Rex, aliique Principes, qui ditiones suas pacifice possident, Italiae quieti unice student; ac propterea iis, qui illustri prosapia magnisque opibus subnixi inquieto sunt animo, minus favent. quod idem sine dubio Rex Franciae, si tantum terrarum in Italia possideret, facturus esset. Quoniam vero quietis in Italia conservandae praecipuum momentum in tali Papa est positum, qui humilis sit conditionis, ac nullis factionibus addictus: solent iidem omnium hujus farinae Cardinalium favorem, quibus possunt officiis sibi conciliare, eosque obnoxios sibi facere. Quales vero in Pontifice virtutes sibi Cardinales expetant, statim idem explicat. Cum plures sint, inquit, probitatis sive virtutis partes, ea Pontifici futuro magis necessariae existimantur, quae aliorum serviunt utilitatibus & commodis. ut sunt Beneficentia, Comitas sive Assabilitas, justitia, & similes. Parsimonia enim, temperantia, continentia, & aliae, quibus homo se ipsum regit, laude quidem dignissimae sunt virtutes, at multo magis in Principe ea desiderantur, quibus magnitudo ejus aliis quasi communicatur. In eandem sententiam scribit Anonymus, qui electionem Sixti V. narravit. Quorum, inquit, a Cardinalibus ratio habetur, virtutes illae sunt, quae alteri prosunt, ut justitia, affabilitas, mansuetudo, beneficentia, facilitas in communicanda sua cum aliis dignitate, similesque aliae. Caeterae enim virtutes animique perfectiones, ut temperantia, continentia, & quae sunt hujus notae aliae, minus hic requiruntur. Ac proinde raro eligi videntur, quibus multi & magni cognati vel propinqui, ne scilicet illis locupletandis & evehendis beneficentiae fontes aliis claudantur. Et Cardinales Pontificem desiderant, non qui ipsos amet tantum, sed qui causas habeat ipsos amandi. Sanctitatem igitur in eligendo eo, qui electus Sanctissimus Pater clueat, pietatem, rerum sacrarum peritiam pensi non haberi, res ipsa loquitur, & silentio virtutibus illis involuto Authores hi prodiderunt. Satis sanctus, satis pius, satis doctus censetur, qui Pontificia sacra professus, aliis utilis commodúsque, & usurpatæ potestati Romanæ Sedis vel confervandæ vel provehendæ par haberi possit. Et verò jam pridem Pontificum plerique aut fuere indocti, aut causidici, aut Politici: Theologis ad honorem illum gradus omnis tantùm non præclusus fuit. Perinde atque Curiam ipsam Romanam in legendis Episcopis postremam, vel ut plurimùm nullam omnino peritiæ rerum sacrarum curam habere, jam olim Marsilius Patavinus part. 2. c. 24. Defensor. scripsit. Quibus, inquit, de plenitudine potestatis conceduntur majores Ecclesiæ dignitates, & qui ad has gubernandas sufficientes putantur, causidici sunt. Hos enim tanquam utiles dignificat Romanus Pontifex, ut Ecclesiæ defensores, qui pro temporalibus conservandis vel amplius usurpandis contendere nôrunt, sacræ verò Theologiæ doctoribus tanquam inutilibus rejectis. Neque pridem adeò in ipsa Italia Papista celebris & bonarum partium desertor, edita sub ficto nomine Alphonsi de Vargas Toletani, Relatione ad Reges & Principes Christianos, hac de re graviter questus, Palam est, inquit, majorem eorum partem, qui hodie vel maximis in Ecclesia dignitatibus præsunt, & unctissimis Episcopatibus atque sacerdotiis fruuntur, quantulacunque juris ac legum notitia tinctos ad eos honores opésque pervenisse; cæterùm Hebraicè, Græcè & Latinè indoctissimos, tum sacrarum literarum non magis, quàm Scythici aut Japonici sermonis intelligentes esse. Quamvis enim S. Paulus eum, qui velit esse Episcopus, Doctorem esse jubeat, qui scilicet aut ab infantia sacras literas didicerit, aut saltim in lege Dei dies ac noctes meditetur: tamen eò res hodie rediit, ut qui Theologiæ Doctor sit, vix nomen inter Episcopatuum candidatos profiteri audeat.
units.tr: CCLXII. Indeed, what both the cardinals and even the secular princes chiefly look to in the election of a Pope is clearly shown by experience. Ever since the right to elect a Pope passed to the cardinals alone, and their college split into two all-powerful factions, the French and the Spanish, the business of the conclave has been carried on not by the drawing of lots but by large sums of money annually poured into the dry and greedy throats of some cardinals, and by votes bought, so that these elections are conducted at the nod of princes who promote their own parties. What each side wants, the Papists themselves, serious men, by no means conceal. Long ago Giovanni Francesco Lottini, Bishop of Volterra, a close friend of Marcellus II, wrote in his memorandum on the conclave, among other things, as follows: In electing a Pope, princes and ecclesiastical prelates are led by one set of aims, and secular princes by another. The latter, however devoted they may be to the Catholic religion, are moved more by regard for their own advantage. So most of them prefer a Pope of a timid and anxious spirit rather than a prompt and vehement one, so that they may use and enjoy more freely the church revenues that lie within their dominions. But if the King of France or some other prince wants a Pope of a great and lofty spirit, they do not do so because they desire the dignity of the Apostolic See to be increased, but so that they may use his counsels for stirring up affairs in Italy. The King of Spain, and other princes who hold their dominions in peace, devote themselves solely to the quiet of Italy, and for that reason they favour less those who, supported by famous ancestry and great wealth, have restless minds. The King of France would undoubtedly do the same, if he held so much territory in Italy. Since the chief safeguard of keeping Italy quiet lies in a Pope of humble condition, attached to no faction, they are accustomed to win over, by whatever services they can, the favour of all cardinals of this sort, and to make them beholden to themselves. What virtues the cardinals in turn look for in a Pope, the same writer goes on to explain: Since there are many parts of goodness or virtue, those are thought most necessary in a future Pope which serve the advantages and conveniences of others, such as beneficence, courtesy or affability, justice, and the like. For thrift, temperance, continence, and the other qualities by which a man governs himself are most praiseworthy virtues, but much more is wanted in a prince those qualities by which his greatness is, as it were, shared with others. The anonymous author who related the election of Sixtus V writes to the same effect: The qualities that the cardinals take into account are those that benefit others, such as justice, affability, gentleness, beneficence, readiness to share one's dignity with others, and other similar ones. The remaining virtues and perfections of the soul, such as temperance, continence, and others of that kind, are less required here. And so those are seldom chosen who have many great kinsmen or relatives, lest, forsooth, the springs of beneficence be closed to others in enriching and advancing them. And cardinals desire a Pope not merely to love them, but to have grounds for loving them. That holiness, then, and piety and skill in sacred matters are not taken into account in choosing the man who is to be hailed as Most Holy Father, the thing itself makes plain, and these authors have revealed it while passing over those virtues in silence. He is judged holy enough, pious enough, learned enough, who has professed Papal rites, is useful and agreeable to others, and can be considered equal to preserving or advancing the power that the Roman See has usurped. Indeed, for a long time now most Popes have been either unlearned, or lawyers, or politicians; for theologians, almost every rung of that honour has been closed. Long ago Marsilius of Padua wrote, in the same vein, that the Roman Curia, in choosing bishops, pays no regard at all to skill in sacred matters, or only very little. Those, he says, who are judged fit to govern the greater dignities of the Church, by the plenitude of power, are lawyers. For the Roman Pontiff honours these as useful men, as defenders of the Church, who know how to strive for preserving or increasing temporal goods, while doctors of sacred theology are rejected as useless. Not long ago, too, a Papist of renown in Italy itself, and a deserter from the good cause, published under the false name of Alfonso de Vargas of Toledo, in a Report to the Kings and Christian Princes, complained seriously on this very point: It is plain, he says, that the greater part of those who now preside over the highest dignities in the Church, and enjoy the most anointed bishoprics and priesthoods, have risen to those honours and wealth steeped in some slight knowledge of law and statutes; but as for Hebrew, Greek and Latin, they are most ignorant, and understand the Holy Scriptures no more than the speech of the Scythians or the Japanese. For although St Paul bids that a man who wishes to be a bishop be a teacher, that is, one who has learned the sacred letters from infancy, or at least meditates on the law of God day and night, yet matters have come to such a pass today that one who is a Doctor of Theology scarcely dares to declare his name among the candidates for bishoprics.

units.la: CCLXIII. Miras tamen in Alexandro effulsisse animi dotes, ejus encomiastæ plenis buccis decantant. Is enim, qui Conclavis ejus historiam scripsit, occasionem scilicet ei supparasitandi captans, augurium futuri Pontificis optimi ut faceret, sic eum commendat. Si nostro,
units.tr: CCLXIII. Yet his admirers sing with full mouths that remarkable gifts of mind shone forth in Alexander. For the man who wrote the history of his conclave, plainly seeking an occasion to fawn upon him and to make an omen of him as an excellent future Pope, commends him thus: If, in our age,

units.la: Alexandri encomium ab authore Conclavis ejus contextum. inquit, hoc seculo Principem quis cerneret, qui nudum corpus rigidissimo vestivisset cilicio, nemo non eum tanquam vitae integerrimae, exemplaris & sanctae studiosum, suspiceret. At talis noster, cum habitu Pontificali induceretur, repertus est. Qui etiam alias animi ab affectibus terrenis, mundanisque divitiis alieni, significationes haud dubias saepe jecit. Lectus enim ejus, in quo, cum Cardinalis esset, dormire consueverat, non mollibus ac delicatis plumis stratus erat, cum semper durissime quietem coeperit. Singulis quoque septimanis bis jejunando abstinentiam suam ostendit, nec jam Pontifex ab isto more tantillum recedit. Unde manifestissime apparet, quam penitus abhorreat a terrenis deliciis, mens coelestibus tantum dedita. Res sane nostri aevi Principibus rarissime usitata, ac proinde in nostro tanto magis admiranda & extollenda, qui profligato dominio sensus, solum spiritum sibi imperare patitur. Narrat deinceps, eum Papam creatum, cum solenni pompa in aedem Petri portatus esset, ut ibi super altari magno, in medio Templi extructo, ab omnibus Cardinalibus adorationis cultum publice reciperet, noluisse praecedentium Paparum more in altaris medio collocari, sed vehementer institisse, ut in angulo quodam altaris relinqueretur, indignum se professus eo loco, quem caeteri Pontifices tenuissent. Illic tandiu prostratum, imaginemque crucifixi amplexum, maxima cum animi dejectione jacuisse, quandiu adorationis solennitas duravit. Quam submissionem & modestiam signum certissimum Pontificis singulari Dei misericordia ac providentia concessi, ille interpretatur. Ubi vero relicto S. Petri templo ad proprium cubiculum Palatii Vaticani delatus fuit, prius quam se fessum jam molestis functionibus quieti daret, arcam e cupresso, plumbo intus obductam, ut illic post mortem reconderetur, sibi condi, & sub lecto suo reponi, quo sic morte ob oculos statuta, ad pietatis opera accenderetur magis, justisse; idem & author & prodigus laudator est. Sed & proxima ab electione die eum Olympiam, quæ gratulatura ei novam dignitatem palatium intraverit, rejectam facessere jussisse, eò quòd palatium Papæ à fœminarum pedibus calcari decorum non sit, idem refert. Addunt alii, indignabundum Olympiæ eum objecisse, satis diu jam Pontifices illam vidisse. Alia quoque sanctitatis & virtutis Alexandri τεκμήρια idem memorat. cujusmodi sunt, quòd cognatos suos Romam venire injussu suo prohibuerit, docens sic (ita adulator Φιλιππος) se jam cognatos non habere, nec domi suæ evehendæ studere, potiorémque curam illam habere, quomodo Ecclesiæ reditus usibus necessariis applicarentur: quòd oblata postridie creationis à diversis Principibus aliisque munera, promptè magnóque animo respuerit; inprimis verò Olympiæ lectum, variè acu pictum, & unionibus contextum, quadraginta millium aureorum pretio æstimatum, actutum eidem remiserit; (scilicet opimiorem prœdam ex illius rapinis animo jam præceperat devoraverátque, integrum auri millionem, Gualdo teste) eámque ad reddendam rationem furtorum suorum, inprimis arcæ, in qua octoginta millia aureorum, ab Innocentio, successori tradenda, repositá ipsemet Alexander adhuc Cardinalis viderit, restitutionem compulerit: quòd inter Principes dissidentes concordiam farcire, & animas hæresi pereuntes ad gremium ecclesiæ reducere, in consilium missis ilico vitæ probatæ & expertæ prudentiæ Cardinalibus, studuerit: quòd Venetis adversus Turcas suppetias statim tulerit: quòd denique totus motibus spiritualibus, meditationibus sanctissimis, & cogitationibus ad totius Ecclesiæ bonum collineantibus, & quidem non perfunctorie, sed serió & acriter deditus sit. An familiæ suæ splendorem (ita sub finem loquitur) auctum, nepotibúsque suis Cardinalatus aliásve dignitates largitura sit sua Sanctitas, nondum liquet. Sed liquere mox cœpit. Amphora enim cœperat instituí, sed currenrente rota nonnisi urceus exivit. Neque sic tamen adulator aliquid dixit, quod humanam fortem superet, vel Christo Vicario & Vice-Deo eximium fit. Omisit etiam nonnulla, quæ jam tum constare poterant, quorum alterum cum paucis Pontificibus commune, alterum sibi proprium habuit. Ac prius quidem, quòd literis utcunque imbutus sub nomine Philomathi poemata edidit. Posterius vero, quòd Mahometem eo ipso tempore Imperatorem Turcicum quinto gradu consanguinitatis, ex Alanc Moruglio, communi stirpe & Atavo utriusque Parentis Pontificii & Turcici; pessimo utique omine contigit. uti quidem Pastorius in Henninge redivivo pag. 159. demonstravit.
units.tr: he said, one were to see a prince who had clothed his bare body in the harshest hair shirt, everyone would regard him with awe as one of most blameless life, a zealous imitator of holiness. Yet such was our man, when he was brought forward in the Pontifical habit, and he was found to be so. Indeed, he often gave clear signs of a soul estranged from earthly passions and worldly riches. For the bed on which he used to sleep when he was a cardinal was not spread with soft and delicate feathers, since he always began his rest on the hardest of beds. Each week, too, he showed his self-denial by fasting twice, and as Pope he has not departed a whit from this custom. Whence it is most clearly apparent how thoroughly a mind given wholly to heavenly things abhors earthly delights. This is indeed a thing very rarely practised by the princes of our age, and therefore all the more to be admired and extolled in ours, who, having overthrown the dominion of the senses, allows himself to rule only the spirit. He then relates that when he had been created Pope and was carried with solemn pomp into the church of St Peter, so that there, upon the high altar built in the middle of the temple, he might publicly receive the worship of adoration from all the cardinals, he refused to be placed in the middle of the altar as his predecessors had been, and insisted strongly that he be left in a certain corner of the altar, professing himself unworthy of the place that the other Popes had held. There, prostrate for as long as the solemnity of adoration lasted, embracing the image of the crucified Christ, he lay in the utmost dejection of spirit. This submissiveness and modesty, the same writer interprets as a sure sign of a Pope granted by the singular mercy and providence of God. But when, having left the church of St Peter, he was carried to his own chamber in the Vatican Palace, before he gave himself to rest, already weary from the troublesome duties, he ordered a chest of cypress wood, lined inside with lead, to be made for him, to be laid up there after his death, and placed under his bed, so that with death thus set before his eyes he might be the more kindled to works of piety; the same author is both witness and extravagant praiser of this. But he also reports that on the day after his election, when Olympia, who had come to congratulate him on his new dignity, entered the palace, he ordered her to be thrown out, because it is not fitting that the Pope's palace be trodden by women's feet. Others add that, in indignation, he told Olympia that the Popes had already seen her long enough. The same writer also records other proofs [τεκμήρια] of Alexander's holiness and virtue, such as that he forbade his kinsmen to come to Rome without his command, thus showing (so the flatterer Philippus [Φιλιππος]) that he now had no kinsmen and was not eager to advance his family, and that he had a greater concern in seeing how the revenues of the Church might be applied to necessary uses; that the gifts offered him the day after his creation by various princes and others he refused promptly and with a great spirit; above all, that he at once sent back a bed, embroidered with various needlework and set with pearls, valued at forty thousand gold pieces (clearly he had already in his mind devoured the richer booty from its plunder, and a whole million in gold, according to Gualdo's testimony); and that he compelled restitution, in order to make an account of his thefts, above all from the chest in which Alexander himself, while still a cardinal, had seen eighty thousand gold pieces laid up, to be handed over to his successor Innocent; that he took care to restore concord among princes at variance and to bring back to the bosom of the Church souls perishing through heresy, by immediately sending to the council cardinals of approved life and tested prudence; that he at once brought aid to the Venetians against the Turks; and, finally, that he was wholly given over to spiritual movements, most holy meditations, and thoughts aimed at the good of the whole Church, and indeed not in a perfunctory way but seriously and keenly. Whether Your Holiness, he says at the end, will increase the splendour of your family and bestow cardinalates or other dignities on your nephews, is not yet clear. But it soon became clear. For an amphora had been begun, but as the wheel turned, only a little pitcher came out. Nor, however, has this flatterer said anything that surpasses human lot, or that is distinguished for Christ's Vicar and Vice-God. He also left out several things that could already have been known, one of which he shared with a few Popes, and the other was peculiar to himself. The first is that, somewhat steeped in letters, he published poems under the name Philomathus. The second is that Mahomet, the Turkish Emperor, was at that very time his kinsman in the fifth degree of consanguinity, descended from Alanus Moruglius, the common stock and ancestor of both the Papal and the Turkish parent; a most ill omen, to be sure. As Pastorius has shown in his Henninge Redivivus, p. 159.

units.la: CCLXIV. Vix admotus gubernaculis est Alexander, cùm honori ejus in Pedemontio per immissos Emissarios, igneos illos turbarum incentores nigris hostiis, humanis coesorum lamentabiliter victimis litatum est. Priusquam autem tragicum sanè, luctuque & miseriis plenum drama prosequimur, paulò altius rem repetere juvabit.
units.tr: CCLXIV. Alexander had scarcely taken the helm when, at his honour, hellish agents were sent into Piedmont, and the fiery instigators of those disturbances offered sacrifices of black victims, sacrifices of people butchered in a pitiable way. Before we pursue this truly tragic drama, full of grief and misery, it will be helpful to go back a little further.

units.la: In tribus Pedemontii vallibus, Lucerna, Perosa & S. Martino inde à quingentis annis Euangelici, Waldensium nomine, Romana Ecclesia, ceu Antichristiana & Apostatica deserta, segreges coetus fecerant. De eorum origine, propagatione & persecutione supra fi. c. cIV. cv. plusc ula diximus. Cruentissimam omnium adversus illos persecutionem Innocentius VIII. A. M. cccc. lxxxvii. instituit, misso Legato suo, Alberto de Capitaneis, delere & exscindere eos omni tormentorum genere connixus. Sed Waldenses captis pro justa sui adversus latrones defensione armis, libertatem à Philippo VII. Duce Sabaudiæ, postquam salsas & ineptas Monachorum jactantium inter alia, liberos Waldensium monstrosa esse forma, uno in fronte oculo, & quaterna nigrorum dentium serie, aspectu formidabiles; calumnias abun-
units.tr: In the three valleys of Piedmont, Luserna, Perosa and San Martino, evangelicals known as Waldenses had formed separate congregations for some five hundred years, since the Roman Church had abandoned them as Antichristian and apostate. We have said more about their origin, spread and persecution above, in chapters 104 and 105 fi.. Innocent VIII, in 1487, set in motion the most savage persecution of all against them. He sent his legate, Alberto de Capitaneis, and strove to wipe them out and destroy them by every kind of torture. But the Waldenses took up arms in their own just defence against the brigands, and by winning over Philip VII, Duke of Savoy, they obtained their freedom, after they had thoroughly exposed the foolish and silly slanders of the monks, who claimed among other things that the children of the Waldenses are monstrous in form, with one eye in the forehead and a fourfold row of black teeth, terrifying to behold.

units.la: Papatus ejus initia Pedemontana laniena fœdantur. abundè is perspexit, impetrârunt. Mox A. m. d. xxxiv. denuo eorum πανολεθεῖαι Carolus & postea Philibertus Emmanuel moliti sunt. adversus quos natura locorum, & angustiis alpium, animo invicto fortissimè sese defendentes vim vi repulerunt. donec A. m. d. lxi. nova illis pax & libertas concessa est. Quæ cùm A. m. d. lxv. denuo infringi cœpisset, Protestantes Germaniæ Principes eorum causam suscipere cœperunt. Et Elector quidem Palatinus Fridericus III. Pius, misso ad Ducem Sabaudiæ Legato, insignem ad illum Epistolam scripsit, qua ostendit, crudelitatem Papæ Romani erga fideles & Reformatos, Principi Christiano & justo haud quaquam tolerandam, neque combustiones & martyria legitima esse propagandæ religionis media. Quin cogitet Dux, sibi aliquando coram terribili tribunali Dei comparendum, & effusi sanguinis rationem reddendam esse. Abusus & errores Ecclesiæ Romanæ tam tetros & abominabiles esse, ut justam causam omnes, qui salvari cupiunt, habeant eos fugiendi. & quicunque eos propterea occidunt & persequuntur, hostes esse ipsius Dei, æternæque damnationis reos. Sed surdo, adversariorum criminationibus plane circumvento fabulam. neque à Papistis quies ulla impetrari potuit, donec A. m d. lxxx. Carolus Emmanuel denuo iis pacem & tranquillitatem concessit. Neque tamen ita stabilis illa fuit, quin subinde atrocior persecutio recrudesceret; anno inprimis Seculi hujus vicesimo secundo, tricesimo secundo, quinquagesimo; & cruentissimè omnium quinquagesimo quinto, quando Andreas Gastaldus, qui se Catholicæ Religionis adversus Reformatos Conservatorem Generalem ferebat, nomine Ducis Sabaudiæ, medio hieme, cùm omnia gelu nivibúsque riguissent, Reformatos Lucerna, Lucernella, S. Giovanni, La Torre, Pubbiana & Fenile, Campiglione, Bricheras & S. Secondo (hæc enim loca diu jam illi insederant) peremptorio decreto intra triduum sub pœna mortis & confiscationis bonorum omnium, nisi intra viginti dies Papistæ fierent, migrare jussit. Migrârunt cum uxoribus & liberis, decrepitis & ægrotis, mancis mutilísque, per aspera rupium nivibus & glacie candidarum, ventis pluviisque insuper sævientibus; & mox, in migrantium deserta habitacula ingressi latrones furésque grassati, cuncta diripuerunt, diruerunt, arbores frugiferas succiderunt, & in horridam vastámque solitudinem omnia redegerunt. Expulsi contra Gastaldum apud Ducem supplices questi, nequicquam restitutionem in integrum precati sunt. Falsis enim criminibus per subornatos magis magisque oppressi, & mox consilia de propaganda fide & extirpandis hæreticis horribilia eventu ipso patefacta sunt.
units.tr: The beginnings of his papacy are defiled by slaughter in Piedmont. In 1634 Charles, and later Philibert Emmanuel, again set about their total destruction. Against them, the nature of the terrain and the narrowness of the Alpine passes helped the invincible courage of the defenders, who resisted force with force, until in 1561 a new peace and liberty were granted them. When this peace began to be broken again in 1565, the Protestant princes of Germany took up their cause. The Elector Palatine, Frederick III the Pious, sent a legate to the Duke of Savoy and wrote him a notable letter, in which he showed that the cruelty of the Roman Pope towards the faithful and the Reformed is by no means to be tolerated by a Christian and just prince, and that burnings and martyrdoms are not lawful means of propagating religion. Let the Duke consider that he himself will one day have to appear before the dread tribunal of God and give an account of the blood shed. The abuses and errors of the Roman Church are so foul and abominable that all who desire to be saved have just cause to flee from them; and whoever kills or persecutes them for this reason is an enemy of God himself and guilty of eternal damnation. But the letter fell on deaf ears, the Duke having been completely taken in by his adversaries' accusations, and no quiet could be obtained from the Papists until 1580, when Charles Emmanuel again granted them peace and tranquillity. Yet this peace was not so stable that a more savage persecution did not break out from time to time: especially in the years 1622, 1632 and 1650 of this century, and most cruelly of all in 1655, when Andrea Gastaldo, who called himself General Protector of the Catholic Religion against the Reformed, in the name of the Duke of Savoy, in the middle of winter, when everything was stiff with frost and snow, ordered the Reformed of Luserna, Lucernetta, San Giovanni, La Torre, Pubbiana and Fenile, Campiglione, Bricherasio and San Secondo (for these places had long been their homes) to leave within three days by peremptory decree, under penalty of death and confiscation of all their goods, unless within twenty days they became Papists. They left with their wives and children, the decrepit and the sick, the maimed and mutilated, over harsh cliffs white with snow and ice, with winds and rains raging besides. Soon after, brigands and thieves entered the abandoned dwellings of the emigrants and ran riot, plundering everything, tearing down buildings, felling fruit trees, and reducing everything to a dreadful and desolate wasteland. The expelled, complaining as suppliants before the Duke against Gastaldo, begged in vain for restoration to their former state. For they were overwhelmed more and more by false charges brought by hired witnesses, and soon the plans for propagating the faith and exterminating heretics, dreadful in their outcome, were laid bare by the events themselves.

units.la: CCLXV.
units.tr: CCLXV.

units.la: Quippe nono post electionem Alexandri, decimo septimo scilicet Aprilis die A. M. D. C. LV. exercitus ingens ex toto Pedemontio, junctis sex Legionibus Gallicis Hibernisque conflatus, in valles Angrogniom, Villaro, Boblio, aliâque à Reformatis habitata loca, diro impetu penetrans, flammis ferróque omnia miscuit, horribilémque lanienam, vanissimo rerum minùs civiliter gestarum prætextu, patravit, tanta crudelitate, ut Thesalonicensis illa à Theodosio patrata, si cum ea comparetur, ludus merus fuerit; quin à Diocletiani temporibus par, à Christianis in Christianos commissa (si Hibernicam forte illam exceperis) nulla fuerit. Ex Samuele Morlando, qui Angliæ Legatus aderat, paucis lanienam illam sic Celeberrimus Hornius describit: Nunquam par crudelitas à Christianis in Christianos patrata legitur. Nam ut pauca tantùm ex multis referam, capita Barbetis (ita Reformatos in Pedemontio vocant) præcisa, & ahenis excoêta devorârunt: Fœminis dissecti incurvis silicibus ventres umbilico tenus; aliis exsecta ubera, quæ igne frixa devorârunt. Naturalibus præcisis ardentem candelam admoverunt, ungues candentibus forcipibus evulserunt,
units.tr: Indeed, in the ninth year after Alexander's election, on the seventeenth day of April 1655, a huge army, drawn from all over Piedmont and joined by six French and Irish legions, burst with dreadful force into the valleys of Angrogna, Villar, Bobbio and other places inhabited by the Reformed, and mingled everything with fire and sword, carrying out a horrible slaughter under the most empty pretext of misdeeds committed less than civilly. It was done with such cruelty that the massacre at Thessalonica, carried out by Theodosius, would be mere child's play in comparison; indeed, since the time of Diocletian there has been no equal, committed by Christians against Christians (except perhaps that Irish one). Of this slaughter the most celebrated Horn describes the following, drawing on Samuel Morland, who was present there as the English envoy: Never is such cruelty to be read of as committed by Christians against Christians. To mention only a few of many: they cut off the heads of the Barbets (as they call the Reformed in Piedmont) and boiled them in cauldrons and devoured them. They split open the bellies of women, cutting them open to the navel with curved flints; they cut off the breasts of others, roasted them over fire and devoured them. They applied burning candles to the private parts and tore out the nails with red-hot pincers.

units.la: Horribilis eorundem laniena ex Morlando repetita. semimortua corpora caudis bestiarum alligata ad mortem per aspera raptârunt. Leve hoc videbatur, præcipitare ab altissimis rupibus, ubi sæpe corpora semiviva arboribus implicata hæserunt, nullo ob inaccessa locorum auxilio, donec lenta morte, fame, vulneribus, frigore animam inter mille tormenta exhalarent. Concisi in minutas particulas, & per campos, dispersa Absyrti instar membra. Multis caro ossetenus excisa, & pulmentorum instar contusa. Puellis adactæ per naturalia collo tenus longæ & acuminatæ perticæ, quas impius miles, ut vexilla solent, humeris sublata, spectaculo circumgestabat. Johannem Pelanchion Villariensem juvenem, crure funibus alligato, totum per plateas Lucernæ asperimis constratas silicibus circumraptârunt. &, si quando ingentibus doloribus victus manus capútque elevare conaretur, saxis contusus fuit: tandem exsectis virilibus, & in fauces intrusis spiritum ei intercluserunt, amputatóque capite insepultum truncum ad ripam fluminis abjecerunt. Infantes ex cunis raptos manibus dilacerârunt; puellas vivas hastis alligatas ad ignem assarunt, & excisis uberibus degustârunt. Alias manibus ad naturalia alligatis funibus suspenderunt pensiles, immani & incredibili cruciatu. Aures, nares & alia corporis abscindere, ora pyrio pulvere implere, & eo incenso capita confringere, pudenda oribus intrudere, & vivos excoriare, pellem quadripartitam fenestris Lucernæ prætendere, decollare, excerebrare, & cerebrum frixum devorare, corda pectoribus evellere, vivos comburere, concidere, suffocare aquis, faciem exscindere, id verò vulgare credebatur. Sed hoc dignum tantis Catholicis, quod Garciglianæ in furnum Nubucadnezaris instar igne flammantissimo candentem undecim Waldenses conjecerunt, adactis miseris, ut unus alterum in ignem præcipitaret, donec ipsi latrones ultimum adjicerent, &c. Jacuit per omnes illas convalles, per aspera montium rupiúmque anfractus immensa strages,
units.tr: The horrible slaughter of the same people, as related from Morland. They dragged half-dead bodies to death tied to the tails of beasts over rough ground. This seemed a light thing: to hurl people down from the highest cliffs, where often semi-living bodies caught in the trees hung on, with no help possible because of the inaccessible places, until they breathed out their lives amid a thousand torments by a slow death, by hunger, wounds and cold. They were cut into tiny pieces and the limbs were scattered over the fields like those of Absyrtus. In many, the flesh was cut away down to the bone and mashed like stew. Long, sharp poles were driven up through the private parts of girls to the neck, and the impious soldiers carried them about for show on their shoulders, as they usually carry standards. They tied the leg of Johannes Pelanchion, a young man from Villar, with ropes and dragged him all round the streets of Luserna, which were paved with the roughest stones; and when, overcome by great pain, he tried to raise his hands and head, he was battered with stones. At last, having cut off his genitals and thrust them into his throat, they choked off his breath, and after cutting off his head they threw the unburied trunk to the river bank. They tore infants from their cradles and tore them apart with their hands; they roasted living girls tied to spits over the fire and, after cutting off their breasts, ate them. Others they hung up suspended by ropes tied from their hands to their private parts, in monstrous and incredible torment. They cut off ears, noses and other parts of the body, filled mouths with gunpowder and, setting it alight, shattered heads, forced genitals into mouths, flayed people alive, stretched a skin cut into quarters across the windows of Luserna, beheaded, scooped out brains and ate the fried brain, tore hearts from breasts, burned alive, cut to pieces, drowned in water, mutilated faces; these things were commonly believed. But this was worthy of such Catholics: at Garcigliana they threw eleven Waldenses, blazing like the furnace of Nebuchadnezzar, into a fire, the wretches being forced so that one pushed another into the flames, until the brigands themselves added the last. A vast slaughter lay across all those valleys, over the rough windings of the mountains and cliffs.

units.la: Alpinæ rubuere nives.
units.tr: The Alpine snows turned red.

units.la: Plateæ oppidorum & viæ, cæsorum & insepultorum constratæ membris: hic resectum caput, illic crura, alibi sparsa exta, & semipu-tritridis cadaveribus infecta flumina, ipseque aer & Sol ad tantam immanitatem inhorruit, ac in authores iram Dei de Caelo pronuntiavit. Quae vero plusquam barbaricae & Cyclopicae crudelitatis adversus miseros exercitae, intima causa fuit? Rebellio, inquient Caini & Tubalcaini illi. Qua porro in re rebellio isthaec sita fuit? Hac scilicet, (neque aliam ipsimet crudelitatis architecti proferre possunt) quod antiquas sedes, quas jam ultra mille & centum annos coluerant, ob religionis Christianae ex verbo Dei scripto haustae adversus Pontificias corruptelas professionem liberam, a Gastaldo, vel Duce ipso a Romano Pontifice ejusque satellitibus seducto, deserere jussi, non promptè satis deseruerunt. Haec rebellio illa, haec irarum sontica causa fuit. Neve aliam quam religionis causam actam putet quisquam, rapti sunt ad supplicia non alii, quam qui constanter in religione avita perstiterunt. Caeteris vero, qui infirmitate carnis subacti Pontificia amplexi sacra sunt, immanis illa crudelitas pepercit.
units.tr: The squares of the towns and the streets were strewn with the limbs of the slain and unburied: here a severed head, there legs, elsewhere scattered entrails, and rivers fouled with half-rotted corpses. Even the air and the sun shuddered at such monstrosity and pronounced God's wrath from heaven upon the authors. But what was the root cause of the savagery, more than barbarian and Cyclopean, practised against these wretched people? Rebellion, say those Cains and Tubalcains. And in what did this rebellion consist? Assuredly in this (and the architects of the cruelty themselves can offer no other): that when they were ordered by the Duke's steward, or by the Duke himself, who had been led astray by the Roman Pontiff and his henchmen, to abandon the ancient homes they had inhabited for more than eleven hundred years, they did not abandon them promptly enough. For they held to the free profession of the Christian religion, drawn from the written Word of God, against Papal corruptions. This was that rebellion, this the guilty cause of their wrath. And lest anyone think that any cause other than religion was at stake, those dragged off to punishment were none other than those who had steadfastly persisted in their ancestral faith. But those who, overcome by the weakness of the flesh, embraced the Papist rites, were spared by that monstrous cruelty.

units.la: CCLXVI. Neque tamen inulta plane manserunt in- fernalium Furiarum isthaec scelera.
units.tr: CCLXVI. Nor, however, did these crimes of the infernal Furies remain wholly unavenged.

units.la: Waldenses enim, cum se omnes internecioni destinatos, bona, vitam, ipsam denique animarum salutem extremo exitio devotam cernerent, ne pecorum instar inulti perirent promiscue omnes, freti jure naturae ipsius, quo defensio adversus latrones, aliosque non salutem, uti decebat, sed perniciem duntaxat spirantes, in extremae & inevitabilis necessitatis casu innoxia censetur merito; liberos, uxores, seque ipsos, quantum conscientia gentiumque jura sinerent, adversus praesentissimum exitium correptis armis tueri, animo in mortem usque obfirmato, statuerunt. Cumque sine Duce nil plebs audeat, lectus Dux Josua Gianavel, priscis Heroibus & populi Divini judicibus comparandus, exigua manu contra integras acies a Marchione Pianezzio ductatas, tas, incredibili felicitate & successu, ut præsentissimam opem Divinam nemo non agnoverit, pugnavit. Habuitque magnorum moliminum socium Jahierum, cum quo ceu altero Juda Maccabeo terrorem undique hostibus cladémque intulit, ulciscens innocentissimum, Divinam vindictam inclamantem sanguinem. Undecim proeliis totidem diversis locis, (quæ fuerunt Piampra, Garcigliana, San-Secondo, Briqueras, Lucerna, La Torre, Crufol, Angrognia, Ofac, La Vafchere, La Torre) commissis, Reformati ut plurimum superiores victorésque nefarie occisorum propinquorum & fidei suæ consortum manibus parentârunt.
units.tr: For the Waldenses, seeing that all of them were destined for slaughter, and that their goods, their lives, and finally the very salvation of their souls were devoted to utter destruction, resolved, lest they all perish without resistance like sheep, to defend their wives, children and themselves, as far as conscience and the laws of nations allowed, against imminent death, with arms taken up and their minds fixed on death. Relying on the law of nature itself, by which defence against robbers and others who breathe not salvation, as is fitting, but destruction only, is rightly judged innocent in a case of extreme and unavoidable necessity, they took up arms. And since the common people dare nothing without a leader, they chose as their captain Josua Gianavel, to be compared with the heroes of old and the judges of God's people, who with a small band fought against whole armies led by the Marquis Pianezzio, with incredible good fortune and success, so that everyone acknowledged the present help of God. He had as partner in his great undertakings Jahierus, with whom, like another Judas Maccabeus, he spread terror and slaughter on the enemy on every side, avenging the innocent blood that cried out for divine vengeance. In eleven battles fought in as many different places (these were Piampra, Garigliana, San Secondo, Briqueras, Luserna, La Torre, Crufol, Angrogna, Ofac, La Vaschere, and La Torre again), the Reformed, for the most part victorious and superior, avenged with their hands the wicked slaughter of their kinsmen and fellow believers.

units.la: CCLXVII. Accurrerunt primùm ex Helvetia & Anglia Legati, pacem, si fieri posset, afflictis adeò re- bus, conciliaturi.
units.tr: CCLXVII. Envoys first hastened from Switzerland and England, to bring about peace, if it could be done, in such a grievous state of affairs.

units.la: Quos inter Samuel Morlandus ex Anglia Legatus, in publica audientia, Regina & Duce coram, hæc in verba libera satis, sed necessitate extorta, os resolvit: Misericordiam hisce pauperimis & ejectissimis subditis impertiri dignemini rogo. Illis nimirum, qui radices Alpium & valles quasdam in ditione vestra incolentes, Protestantium religioni sua nomina dederunt. Audivit enim (quod nemo Celsitudinis vestræ Regalis voluntate factum esse dixerit) Olvarius Protector, miserrimos illos partim à vestris copiis crudeliter esse occisos, partim vi expulsos, domóque patria exturbatos, adeóque sine lare, sine tecto, inopes, omníque ope destitutos, per asperima loca atque inhospita, montésque nivibus coopertos, cum suis conjugibus ac liberis vagari. Quid enim per hosce dies, quod genus crudelitatis inausum illis militibus, aut præteritum fuit? Fumantia passim tecta, & laceri artus, & cruenta humus! Virgines post stupra differto lapillis ac ruderibus utero, miserè efflârunt animas. Centenarii nonnulli senes effœta ætate ac morbo clinici, in lectulis combusti! Infantum alii saxis allisi, alii jugulati, quorum cerebrum ab interfectoribus, immanitate plusquam Cyclopica coctum ac devoratum! Quid plura? quanquam vel vel plurima huiusmodi commemorare possem, nisi horreret plane animus. Si revivisccant omnes omnium temporum Nerones (quod sine ulla Celsitudinis vestrae offensione dictum velim, quemadmodum & nulla ejus culpa quicquam factum esse credimus) puderet profecto eos; ut qui nihil non mite ac humanum (ad haec facinora si spectas) excogitasse se reperirent. Interim exhorrescunt Angeli! mortales obstupescunt! Ipsum Coelum morientium clamoribus attonitum esse videtur, ipsaque terra, diffuso tot hominum innocuorum cruore erubescere! Noli, summe Deus, noli vindictam sumere tantis scelerib&us & parricidiis debitam! Tuus, Christe, sanguis eluat hunc sanguinem! Quos aculeos oratio acris in animis Matris & Filii Ducis reliquerit, incertum. Una semper perpetuaque crudelitatis tantae excusatio erat: Paternam tantum & lenem castigationem de immorigeris & rebellibus subditis sumptam fuisse. Si paterna fuit castigatio isthaec, cujusmodi hostilis castigationis formam animo patres miteque illi conceperunt? Missi tandem ex Anglia, Belgio, Helvetia solenniter Legati, quibus se Regis Galliarum nomine Legatus Servient conjunxit, imaginem pacis, in qua inter alia sancitum est, ut emissarii furiae facesque turbarum illarum, Pedemontium purgent, procurarunt, in qua promissa licet multa sint, exitu tamen ipso praestita perpauca sunt. Quin paulo post novae iterum persecutiones emerserunt, quando novo Gubernatore Bagnote exercitium Religionis contra Pacis nuperae tenorem hinc inde sublatum. Ministri nonnulli aliique proscripti, & denuo immisso exercitu innocentes oppressi, aedes dirutae, ditiones misere vastatae, denuoque afflictissimorum patientia mire fatigata est, donec suscepta iterum defensione innocua, & exoticorum intercessione urgente, mense Aprili A. M. D. C. LXIII. amnestia postliminio lancita, & qualiscunque pax impetrata est. Quae tamen non ita pridem rursus infringi coepta est, cum Convallenses ab infensissimo sibi clero fictis criminibus onerati, gravem offensam Regnatricis incurrerunt, & Ministris propriis destituti, aliunde, quod pacta indulserant, eos accersere prohibiti sunt. Ita strenui illi confessores Jesu Christi & veri Callinici, perpetuum quasi miseriæ theatrum præbentes licet, lucernulæ tamen seu phari in altissimis montibus, quam Deus per tot Secula, in ipso cœcitatis Romanæ Pantheo, ringente tenebrarum Principe, accensam conservavit; instar lucere nondum desierunt; utque nunquam deficiente oleo gratiæ & fidei, luceant ad illustrem usque adventum Christi & bonis operibus suis Patrem cœlestem glorificent, malevolósque ei lucrentur; in votis unicè boni omnes habent.
units.tr: Among them Samuel Morland, envoy from England, in a public audience, with the Queen and the Duke present, opened his mouth in words fairly frank yet wrung from necessity: We beg you to deign to show mercy to these most poor and cast-out subjects, who, dwelling in the foothills of the Alps and certain valleys within your dominion, have given their names to the religion of the Protestants. For Oliver the Protector has heard (a thing no one would say was done by the will of Your Highness) that these most wretched people have partly been cruelly slain by your troops, partly driven out by force and expelled from their native homes, and so, without hearth or roof, destitute and bereft of all help, wander with their wives and children through the most rugged and inhospitable places, over mountains covered with snow. For what kind of cruelty, in these days, has been unattempted or left undone by those soldiers? Houses smoking everywhere, mangled limbs, and ground soaked with blood! Virgins, after violation, have breathed out their lives miserably, their wombs crammed with stones and rubble. Some aged centenarians, worn out by age and disease, have been burned in their beds! Others of the infants have been dashed against rocks, others slaughtered, whose brains were cooked and eaten by their killers in a savagery beyond the Cyclops! What more? Although I could recall very many such things, my mind simply shudders. If all the Neros of every age were to come back to life (which I wish to be said without any offence to Your Highness, just as we believe nothing was done through any fault of yours), they would surely be ashamed, finding that they had devised nothing gentle or humane compared with these deeds. Meanwhile the angels shudder! Mortals are stunned! Heaven itself seems astonished at the cries of the dying, and the very earth blushes at the blood of so many innocent people poured out! Do not, O highest God, do not take vengeance for such crimes and murders! Let your blood, Christ, wash away this blood! What stings this fierce speech left in the minds of the Mother and the Son, the Duke, is uncertain. One constant and unvarying excuse for such great cruelty was this: that it was only a fatherly and gentle chastisement inflicted on disobedient and rebellious subjects. If this chastisement was fatherly, what sort of hostile chastisement did those gentle fathers conceive in their minds? At length envoys were sent solemnly from England, Belgium and Switzerland, and the envoy of the King of France, Servien, joined them in the name of his king. They arranged a picture of peace, in which, among other things, it was sanctioned that the agents of fury and the firebrands of those troubles should be cleared out of Piedmont. In it, though many things were promised, very few were in fact performed. Indeed, shortly afterwards new persecutions broke out again, when under the new governor Bagnole the exercise of religion was removed here and there, contrary to the terms of the recent peace. Some ministers and others were proscribed, and innocent people were oppressed by a re-sent army; houses were razed, districts miserably laid waste, and the patience of the most afflicted was again wonderfully worn down, until, with defence once more taken up in blameless fashion, and with the urgent intercession of foreigners, an amnesty with restoration of rights was proclaimed in April 1663, and some kind of peace was obtained. Yet not long ago this was again beginning to be broken, when the people of the valleys, burdened with false charges by a clergy hostile to them, incurred the grave displeasure of the Queen Regent, and, deprived of their own ministers, were forbidden to send for them from elsewhere, since they had been granted this by treaty. So those valiant confessors of Jesus Christ and true Callinici, though they present a kind of perpetual theatre of misery, have nonetheless not ceased to shine like a little lamp or beacon on the highest mountains, which God has preserved through so many ages, kindled in the very Pantheon of Roman blindness, while the Prince of darkness snarls; so that, with the oil of grace and faith never failing, they may shine until the glorious coming of Christ and by their good works glorify their heavenly Father, and win over those who wish them ill. All the good have this as their unique prayer.

units.la: CCLXVIII.
units.tr: CCLXVIII.

units.la: Non contentus autem ejusmodi Papatus sui primordiis Alexander, eodem anno, Suecos inter & Polonos ardente bello, nòvas, ceu alter Cœcias, nubes conflare annixus est. Etenim Bulla seu circularibus literis die xx. Sept. M. D. C. LV. pacis inter Catholicos Principes procurandæ prætextu, sed revera uniendorum eorum adversus Euangelicos, Ecclesiam Dei, insatiabili studio, ad Patriarchas, Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, clerúmque universum scriptis missisque, irarum odiorúmque adversus Protestantes semina jacere denuo constituit. Bullam illam Babylonii fastus, hypocriseos, crudelitatis adversus Euangelicos, & blasphemiarum adversus Deum plenam, cùm in manibus omnium non sit, repræsentare totam, nec sine Glossæ ordinariæ, quo haud indigna forte est, auctario quopiam à nonnemine fusius paulò, heic verò contractiùs admetiendo, lubet. Ita autem Bulla tumet: Alexander Papa Septimus. Venerabiles Fratres, Dilecti Filii, Salutem & Apostolicam Benedictionem. (An qualem S. Petrus, an qualem Judas ipse quoque Apostolus, habens, sicut Alexander, marsupium plenum denariis?) E Summo Apostolatus fastigio, Orbem universum, nostras VIDELICET curas, circumspicientibus nobis, misera sane luctúque plena se offert Reip. Christianæ facies. (Novus scilicet ille orbis terrarum Phaeton, æmulum hic se Alexandri Magni gessit. Sicut enim illi à Philippo, cùm in Bucephali sui fastigio orbem universum solicitè circumspiceret, dictum boni ominis ergò fuit: Fili, Macedonia te non capit: sic Alexander hic, non jam Pontifex, sed haruspex, in Bucephalo suo, sive Monte Cavallo, infulis & lituo insignis, non jam angulum, vel partem quampiam orbis, sed orbem universum, suas VIDELICET curas, adeóque Cœlum, montes, terras, maria circumspexit. Sed forte ophthalmia laborabat; in Septentrione nives & nebulæ aciem oculorum ejus præstringebant; versus Orientem & Austrum fulgor Solis, & æstus, & arenarum maria eum excœcabant; & in Italia luminibus ejus Waldenses, non in Pedemontio duntaxat, verùm etiam Venetiis & in Calabria, atque ipsa urbe Roma, officiebant. licet ab ophthalmia hac se liberaturus, collyrio Christiani sanguinis subinde oculos suos inunxerit. Ita circumspicienti orbem universum, suas videlicet curas, se obtulit misera luctúque plena Reip. Christianæ facies. in Hibernia scilicet & Pedemontio, ubi verè contemplari potuit, quæ ejus
units.tr: Alexander, however, was not content with such beginnings of his papacy. In the same year, while a fierce war raged between the Swedes and the Poles, he strove to raise new clouds, like another Caecias. For by a bull, or circular letter, dated 20 September 1655, under the pretext of securing peace among Catholic princes but in truth of uniting them against the Evangelicals, the Church of God, he resolved with insatiable zeal to scatter again the seeds of anger and hatred against Protestants, sending writings to the patriarchs, archbishops, bishops and the whole clergy. Since that bull, full of Babylonian pride, hypocrisy, cruelty towards the Evangelicals and blasphemy against God, is not in everyone's hands, I think it right to set it out here in full, though somewhat more concisely, with a commentary, which perhaps it does not deserve, added by someone else. The bull swells thus: Pope Alexander VII. Venerable Brethren, beloved sons, greeting and apostolic blessing. (Was he such as St Peter was, or such as Judas, himself also an apostle, who, like Alexander, had a purse full of denarii?) From the summit of the apostolic height, as we look round upon the whole world, that is, our cares, there presents itself the miserable and sorrowful face of the Christian commonwealth. (That new Phaeton of the world, here, played the rival of Alexander the Great. For as Philip is said to have told the latter, when he was looking round anxiously upon the whole world from the height of his Bucephalus, as a good omen: "Son, Macedonia is not big enough for you," so this Alexander, no longer a pontiff but a soothsayer, mitred and bearing the crozier, upon his Bucephalus, or Monte Cavallo, did not look round upon some corner or part of the world, but upon the whole world, that is, his cares, and so upon heaven, mountains, lands and seas. But perhaps he suffered from an inflammation of the eyes: in the north, snows and mists dimmed the sight of his eyes; towards the east and south the glare of the sun, the heat and the seas of sand blinded him; and in Italy the Waldenses hindered his eyes, not only in Piedmont but also at Venice and in Calabria and in the city of Rome itself, although he would soon free himself from this inflammation by anointing his eyes from time to time with the salve of Christian blood.) Thus, as he looked round upon the whole world, that is, his cares, there presented itself the miserable and sorrowful face of the Christian commonwealth, in Ireland, that is, and Piedmont, where he could truly contemplate what his

units.la: Relligio peperit scelerosa atque impia facta) Sortem enim Domini, atque ipsius hæreditatem, veris ejectis filiis alieni sibi diripiunt. (Sueciam scilicet & Poloniam, sortem & hæreditatem Domini Papæ, qui pridem ex hominum, Regnorum piscator factus est, partim jam SIBI, Papa in societatem saltem præda non vocato, (hoc nefas!) diripuit, partim direpturus erat Carolus Gustavus, Alienus ille.) Gentes quas pro Pontificia (crocodolina, quæ devorat, quos amat) charitate, in nostrum, hoc est, veræ fidei sinum (nam sinus Papæ qualiscunque ille vera fides est) traducere, (per ignem Molocho sacratas) arctissiméque complecti voluissemus (perinde ut nuper in Pedemontio complecte-batur Sinuosus ille, simia amplexu necans simios) hunc ipsum sinum dilaniare conantur; & ruptis maris atque ultimis terrarum claustris in Christi Gregem (neque tamen Alexander Christus fuit) effunduntur. Male denique concordes Catholici Principes (Hispanus & Gallus, uterque jam, secus quàm Alexander VI. Ferdinando Aragonio Catholici titulum donans, definivit, Catholicus) in se ipsos feruntur, &, quae olim extrema minatus est Deus inimicis nostris, atque iis, qui insurgunt adversus nos (at Deus, Alexander, suis inimicis, non igitur tuis ita minatus est.) se ipsos depascuntur, & (ceu Antropophagi, & velut in Tragoedia Cyclopes, aut Thyestes) proprio sanguine, quasi musto inebriantur. (belli scilicet Alexandri filii, Canibales, quibus liberaliter pro Pontificia charitate, ex thesauro Ecclesiae, novus Eli, indulsit) Haec eadem cum pridem tacitè nobiscum doleremus (Monasterii nempe, ubi dolens sanguinis & humanarum carnium velut interstitium quoddam solenni juramento pangi, protestatus est contra Principes, eò quòd se invicem depasci, & proprio sanguine velut musto inebriari desinerent) visum est ei, qui facit magna & incomprehensibilia, quorum non est numerus, (nota tamen sunt mysteria, notae artes, Deo non probante, nedum authore, quibus in conclavi per factionum certamen ad summum illud, Apostolatus videlicet, fastigium surrexit) invitos trepidantesque (invitantes, non invitos scribere debuit; trepidantes tamen metu, ne alius in Campo Martio candidatus offam praeriperet, corvumque hiantem deluderet) vocare nos ad Ecclesiae gubernacula (Romae, patrimonii Petri, Comitatus Avinionensis. aliae enim Nationes pleraeque gubernacula illa abnuunt, etsi quae admittunt, propter rationes status non nihil indulgent) atque inclinare in nos onus immensum, humerisque quamvis firmissimis formidandum. (quin igitur clitellas depositi exemplo Cœlestini, Felicis Amedei?) Testes autem mæroris nostri sunt publicæ supplicationes, quas ubi primùm summo Pontificatui admoti sumus, universis indiximus; (gratias acturis non Deo, sed lanionibus illis, qui Convallenses eodem tempore jugulárunt. Roma etiam festis ignibus collucente, cùm Pedemontana jugulatio nuntiaretur.) testes literæ, quas ad charissimos filios, non solùm Ferdinandum, Hungariæ & Boemiæ Regem Illustrem, (non hic Imperatori debitus titulus est. quàm fremeres, Alexander, si Te Beatissimi, Sanctissimi, titulo, etsi nullo jure Tibi debito, vicissim Imperator defraudaret?) ac in Romanorum Imperatorem electum (electum cùm dicis, approbatum vel coronatum tacitè negas, Hildebrandine, Tibi, Servo Servorum, jus approbandi & coronandi Dominum tot in terris Dominorum, nefariè vendicans. Petrus scilicet, paulò antequam cruci affigeretur, ut jus hoc Apostolicum ad Te transmitteret, Neronem in crypta subterranea coronavit! Verum etiam ad utrumque Regem (titulo Serenissimi, Potentissimi, vel quocunque alio, & nominibus suis indignum utrumque, sive quia Papæ hactenus conjunctionem virium adversus Protestantium fortunas & vitam suadenti dicto audientes segniter fuerunt, sive quia ambiguus hæsit utrum præponeret; metuens scilicet, ne postpositus ei in barbam capillósque involaret) dedimus; & quas iterum, cum importunissimum Adversarium (non Dei, sed Alexandri at quis ille? Carolus Gustavus, Sueciæ Rex, propter quem Tyria maria Alexander commovit, veritus, ne Polonis acie superior, libertatem Protestantibus in eo Regno acquireret, & Papæ in eodem nundinationibus nonnihil intercederet. quæ enim importunitas est, si hæc non est?) per inclyta Reip. damna, toti Europæ funera ac vastitatem inferre meditantem viderimus (Tu verò Serpens Epidaurie, lyncea acie Tua Caroli Gustavi meditamenta, præfractè adeò rem asseverans videre re potuisti? At Paparum hæc meditamenta sunt, qui per Jesuitas, Franciscanos, ceu Junitzaros suos, Christianos à tot retrò annis, hanc solam ob causam, quòd credere non potuerunt, eos in summo Apostolatus fastigio constitutos, jus habere universum orbem, suas videlicet curas circumspiciendi; immaniter non per capita modò, verùm stirpes, nationes ac populos, occiderunt, decollárunt, suspenderunt, submerserunt, combusserunt, torruerunt, coxerunt, jugulárunt, devorárunt, defoderunt, discerpserunt, quadripartiti sunt. nega Alexander, si fecisti! si ante te fecerunt alii!) magno cum animi dolore scripsimus, ut eos à mutuis discordiis in nefarium hostem converteremus (scilicet, Alexandro pronubo, & monitore vel ad Sanctos Sanctásque suas supplice, inveteratas iras simultatésque promptè deponent illi. an Petri claves confractæ, Pauli gladius rubigine obductus fuit, quòd discordes Cyclopicos Reges ad concordiam fulminibus, & traditione Sathanæ, Alexander, degener Hildebrandi, Malifacii, Julii, Pii, Sixti, Pauli successor, redigere non es ausus?) & quas nunc mittimus, eos admonentes, ut dum hiemis interventu tantisper bellorum impetus resederit, ad pacem constituendam omni conatu atque opera incumbant; (tantarum scilicet virium admonitionem tuam fore sperásti, ut pax una nocte, fungi instar, nata, in atrocia statim adversus Protestantem sanguinem bella coalescat. fefellit, fallétque te, Ausonie Præsul, augurium!) testes super hæc omnia, unam dies noctésque obversari animo solicitudinem, quoniam ad tanta, ac tam acerba mala sedanda, nulla nisi in communi concordia reliqua spes est, hanc omnium cordibus ac voluntatibus inferendi. (mactare in Hibernia, Pedemontio, comedere; at diurna nocturnáque solicitudine tua cordibus & voluntatibus, licet in conscientias dominatum exercens, concordiam inferre non potuisti) verum quia non hoc humanæ vires, aut terrena consilia moliri liri possunt; (homo igitur, Alexander, terrestris fuisti, quem nec hominem, nec Deum, sed medium inter utrunque, Vice Deum, spiritualem, omnia judicantem, judicandum à nemine illi, qui in sinu Fidei tuæ dormivere, crediderunt?) sed illius donum esse debet, super quem est disciplina pacis nostræ (cur Dei nomen omittis. quod bis duntaxat in Bulla occurrit? an quia magnificè quàm clarè loqui potius habuisti? Si concordia Dei donum est, quidni etiam vires humanas plus quàm concordia superans, Fides? Si fides Dei donum est, cur post pro Pelagianis adversus Jansenitas, Augustinianos pronuntiásti? Cur hæreticos comburis, qui credere non possunt, Te in summo Apostolatus fastigio constitutum?) qui aufert spiritum Principum; atque increpat mare & obmutescit. Quantum in Vobis est, Venerabiles Fratres, (Te ne in terris venerari quenquam, efferentem Te super ea, quæ in Cœlis sunt?) ac dilecti filii, non modò opera, studio, consilio, officiis, authoritate vestra contendite (quasi scilicet talibus Romanus Jupiter indigeret, qui unus omnia potest pollétque) verùm etiam in oratione, in lachrymis, in jejuniis atque eleemosynis scindite corda vestra, arripite thuribulum, hoc est, preces Sanctorum, & medii inter ignem & arsurum populum consistite. (at non tam promptè Venerabiles Fratres & filii, aliis longè curis distracti districtíque, hæc omnia facere potuerunt, quàm promptè, uno scilicet spiritu, hæc effari & efflare Alexander potuit! Si hæretici Tuis, Alexander, Fratribus & filiis Patriarchatus, Archiepiscopatus, Episcopatus, Abbatias, Monasteria, Collegia, indulgentias, purgatorium, Missas, Thaides, Lucretias, Olympias, verbo, ficum, vitem, oleum, fruges, aurum, argentum: si Tibi summum Apostolatus fastigium, Pontificiam charitatem, universum orbem, tuas videlicet curas, relinquerent; nec illis, nec tibi orandi, lachrymandi, jejunandi, eleemosynas dandi, corda scindendi, preces Sanctorum & Sanctarum implorandi, vel animus, vel otium esset unquam; neque nos de cœtero credentes quidvis, toto die occideretis, & velut oves mactationis, exitio devoveretis! Mirum insuper est, non imperasse potius Alexandrum Fratribus & Filiis, ut lumbos suos cingant gladio, & hæreticos trucident. cum hactenus suetum iis fuerit, non orando, sed pugnando; non lachrymis, sed ensibus; non jejuniis, sed coedibus; non eleemosynis, sed incendiis; non cordium scissione, sed ventrium dissectione; non clamoribus, sed jugulationibus; non calice, sed secespita homines in sinum Papæ traducere.) Vos, qui statuti estis custodes super muros Jerusalem, noctu atque interdiu clamate, (ita enim etiam Baalis flamines clamârunt voce magna) atque estote cœlestis ira, ac Divinæ ultionis placamina. Eximamte calicem furoris & ruinæ, calicem, quo potati sumus, doloris & tribulationis meracissimæ.) nondum ita potati, quin immineat adhuc tempus illud, quo Babylon magna veniet in memoriam ante Deum, ut det illi calicem vini indignationis iræ suæ.) Nobis quippe, quibus non prius tuto creditas oves suas putavit Christus (imo parum tuto creditæ fuissent oves Alexandris, suetis non pascere, sed jugulare, cutim deglubere, carnes devorare, ossa dispergere) nisi postquam iterum ac tertio de amoris magnitudine admoniti fuimus in Petro (parum memores admonitionis. Si enim Christum Alexandri amarent, ejus membra non occiderent) quibus solis sanctuarium ingredi, & ante altare preces Deo repræsentare concessum est, (Vobis, Alexander, solis? Non igitur Christus, verus Pontifex noster, Sanctuarium ingredi potuit. Et si Vobis solis, cur ergo Fratres & Filios vestros ad orationes & thuribulum, hoc est, preces Sanctorum adhortamini? Blasphemi estis, Alexander, & Christo vero Pontifici, qui unus semel intravit Sanctuarium, honorem sacrilegè rapturitis!) sedulo elaborandum, ne irascatur Dominus, & dicat; quæquæsivi virum, qui interponeret maceriam, & staret oppositus contra me pro terra, ne dissiparem eam, & non inveni, & effudi super eos indignationem. (Hic ne Vir Alexander, Vir sanguinum? Scilicet oppositus contra Deum stetit, non ut Mediator, sed ut hostis; non ut placaret iratum, sed ut accenderet provocarétque iram, plenis phialis quandoque in ipsum, eósque, qui signaturam ejus habent, effundendam. quando destruet eos Deus, qui terram destruxerunt.) Hoc enim habet Divina ultio, ut tum maximè Altissimus sit exorabilis, & ad lenitatem, clementiamque, hoc est, ad ingenium suum redeat, (ô te, Alexander, hæreticum insignem! Itáne Deus puniens damnatos, puniens fideles in Christo, judicium & justitiam exercens, ab ingenio suo deflexit? An magis ipsi lenitas, clementia erga morigeros, quàm justitia erga refractarios, naturalis est? Id si verum est, cur unigenito filio suo non pepercit Pater? Non magis Theologus es, Alexander, quàm Innocentius prædecessor tuus. Fatere modò ingenuè, sicut ingenuè & assa voce pariter fassus est ille) cum in brachio forti, & manu valida gladium exertat, ut feriat. Sint pedes vestri pedes evangelizantium pacem (conciliantium pacem inter hostes Dei, ad feriendos, jugulandos, excruciandos dirissimè, unitis scilicet viribus, amicos Dei. hic interior animi vestri sensus est. quem prodidit etiam P. Ribaldus Jesuita, quando ita carnificem hæreticos mactantem instituit: Exilio portato, rogis imponito, Ponte Mergito, forcipibus cædito, ferto feris: Ense feri, necato fame, serráque secato, Compede stringe pedes, fune ligato senes: Offa revellito, crura refringito, rumpito membra, Lictor, & in plures scindito particulas. Hinc aditum ad crates reserato, notatóque fibras, Cerne ßnisterius, dexteriúsque latus.
units.tr: Religion has brought forth wicked and impious deeds) For they seize for themselves the lot and inheritance of the Lord, the true sons having been cast out. (Namely Sweden and Poland, the lot and inheritance of the Lord Pope, who long ago was made a fisherman of men and kingdoms. Some of it he has already seized for himself, the Pope not having been invited to share the plunder (what a crime!), and some Charles Gustavus, that stranger, was about to seize.) The nations which, out of Papal charity (the crocodile, which devours those it loves), we wished to bring over into our bosom, that is, of the true faith (for the bosom of the Pope is the true faith, of whatever sort it is) and to embrace most closely (just as that Sinuous one recently embraced Piedmont, strangling monkeys with a monkey's embrace) —these very nations are tearing apart that bosom; and, the barriers of the sea and the furthest limits of the earth having been broken, they pour out into the flock of Christ (though Alexander was not Christ). Finally, the Catholic princes, badly in agreement (the Spaniard and the Frenchman, both now, contrary to Alexander VI, who granted the title Catholic to Ferdinand of Aragon, are not Catholic) are turned against one another, and what God once threatened as the furthest punishment against our enemies and those who rise up against us (but God, Alexander, threatened this against his own enemies, not against yours) they devour one another, and (like cannibals, and like the Cyclopes or Thyestes in tragedy) they grow drunk on their own blood as on new wine. (Namely the wars of the sons of Alexander, cannibals, to whom he generously granted indulgence from the treasury of the Church, out of Papal charity, a new Eli.) When we were quietly grieving over these same things with you (namely at Münster, where, grieving over blood and human flesh, he solemnly swore, as it were, a kind of truce, and protested against the princes that they should stop devouring one another and growing drunk on their own blood like new wine) it seemed good to him who does great and unsearchable things, of whom there is no number, (yet the mysteries are known, the arts are known, with God not approving, let alone authoring them, by which in the conclave, through the contest of factions, he rose to that highest summit of the Apostolate) to call us, unwilling and trembling (he ought to have written "inviting," not "unwilling"; yet they trembled with fear lest another candidate on the Campus Martius snatch the morsel and cheat the gaping crow) to the helm of the Church (at Rome, the patrimony of Peter, the county of Avignon; for most other nations refuse that helm, though those they do admit, for reasons of state, grant it a little indulgence) and to lay upon us an immense burden, dreadful even to the strongest shoulders. (Why not then lay down the packsaddle, following the example of Celestine and Felix Amadeus?) The witnesses of our sorrow are the public supplications which we proclaimed to all as soon as we were raised to the supreme Pontificate (to be thanked not God but those butchers who at the same time slaughtered the Waldenses of the Valleys; Rome too was blazing with festal fires when the slaughter in Piedmont was announced) —witnesses are the letters which we sent to our dearest sons, not only to Ferdinand, the illustrious King of Hungary and Bohemia (this is not the title due to an Emperor. How you would rage, Alexander, if the Emperor in turn cheated you of the title Most Blessed, Most Holy, though it is due you by no right!) and the Emperor of the Romans elect (when you say "elect," you tacitly deny that he is approved or crowned, Hildebrand, usurping wickedly for yourself, the Servant of Servants, the right to approve and crown the Lord of so many lords on earth. Peter, shortly before he was nailed to the cross, in order to transmit this apostolic right to you, crowned Nero in an underground crypt!) but also to each King (both unworthy of the title Most Serene, Most Powerful, or any other, and of their own names, either because they have been slack in obeying the Pope's urging to join forces against the fortunes and lives of the Protestants, or because, hesitating, it was unclear to him which of the two to put first, fearing, namely, that the one set second might snatch at his beard and hair) we have sent; and which again, when we saw the most troublesome Adversary (not of God, but of Alexander; but who is he? Charles Gustavus, King of Sweden, on whose account Alexander stirred up the Tyrian seas, fearing that, superior in arms to the Poles, he might win liberty for the Protestants in that kingdom, and that the Pope's trading in that same kingdom might be somewhat hindered. For what troublesomeness is there, if not this?) plotting to bring to all Europe ruin, death and devastation, through the grievous losses of the Commonwealth (but you, serpent of Epidaurus, could you with your lynx's eye see Charles Gustavus's schemes, and assert it so stubbornly? These schemes, however, belong to the Popes, who through their Jesuits and Franciscans, as their Janissaries, have for so many years slaughtered Christians for this one reason only, that they could not believe that those set at the highest summit of the Apostolate had the right to look after the whole world, their cares, that is. Monstrously, they have killed, beheaded, hanged, drowned, burned, roasted, boiled, slaughtered, devoured, buried alive, torn apart and quartered not only individuals but whole families, nations and peoples. Deny it, Alexander, if you did it! If others did it before you!) we wrote with great grief of mind, so that we might turn them from mutual discord toward a wicked enemy (namely, Alexander being the go-between and urging them, even suppliantly, to his holy saints, male and female, those men would quickly lay aside their long-standing wrath and enmities.
