Or were Peter's keys broken, or Paul's sword covered with rust, that Alexander, the degenerate successor of Hildebrand, Malifacius, Julius, Pius, Sixtus and Paul, did not dare to bring the discordant Cyclopean kings back to concord with thunderbolts and by delivering them to Satan?) and which we now send, admonishing them that, while the onset of wars subsides a little with the coming of winter, they should apply every effort and labour to establishing peace (you surely hoped your admonition would have such force over such great powers that peace, born in a single night like a mushroom, would at once grow into savage wars against Protestant blood. Your augury has failed and will fail you, prelate of Ausonia!) We bear witness, in all these matters, that day and night one care is before our mind, since for quelling such great and bitter evils no hope remains except in common concord, which we wish to bring into the hearts and wills of all. (To slaughter in Ireland, to devour in Piedmont; yet by your day and night care, though exercising dominion over consciences, you have not been able to bring concord into hearts and wills) But since neither human strength nor earthly counsels can accomplish this (so you were a earthly man, Alexander, whom they believed to be neither man nor God but a mediator between the two, a Vicar of God, spiritual, judging all things, to be judged by no one, those who slept in the bosom of your Faith?) but it must be the gift of him over whom is the discipline of our peace (why do you leave out God's name, which occurs only twice in the Bull? Was it because you preferred to speak magnificently rather than clearly? If concord is God's gift, why not also faith, which surpasses human strength far more than concord does? If faith is God's gift, why afterwards did you pronounce for the Pelagians against the Jansenists and Augustinians? Why do you burn heretics, who cannot believe that you are set at the highest summit of the Apostolate?) who takes away the spirit of princes, and rebukes the sea and it becomes still. As far as lies in you, Venerable Brothers (you, who exalt yourself above what is in heaven, should be venerated by no one on earth?) and beloved sons, strive not only with your work, zeal, counsel, offices and authority (as if the Roman Jupiter, who alone can do and has power over all things, needed such helpers) but also in prayer, in tears, in fasting and almsgiving rend your hearts, take up the censer, that is, the prayers of the Saints, and stand between the fire and the people about to be burned. (But the Venerable Brothers and sons, distracted and pulled apart by many other cares, could not do all this as promptly as Alexander could utter and breathe out these things with one breath! If heretics left you, Alexander, your brothers and sons, the patriarchates, archbishoprics, bishoprics, abbeys, monasteries, colleges, indulgences, purgatory, masses, Thaïs, Lucretias, Olympias, in a word the fig, the vine, oil, grain, gold, silver; if they left you the supreme summit of the Apostolate, Papal charity, the whole world, your cares, that is, then neither they nor you would ever have the mind or leisure to pray, weep, fast, give alms, rend your hearts, implore the prayers of the Saints male and female; and we, believing anything else from now on, you would kill all day long and devote us to destruction like sheep for slaughter! It is also astonishing that Alexander did not rather command his Brothers and Sons to gird their loins with the sword and butcher the heretics, since hitherto it has been their custom to do this not by praying but by fighting, not with tears but with swords, not with fasting but with slaughter, not with almsgiving but with burnings, not by rending hearts but by cutting open bellies, not with outcries but with throat-cutting, and to bring men into the bosom of the Pope not with the chalice but with the knife.) You who have been set as watchmen on the walls of Jerusalem, cry out by night and by day, (for thus also the priests of Baal cried out with a loud voice) and be the placating of heavenly wrath and divine vengeance. Take away the cup of fury and ruin, the cup from which we have drunk the strongest wine of grief and tribulation. (not yet so drunk that the time has not yet come when great Babylon will come into remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of his wrath.) For to us, whom Christ did not first think it safe to entrust with his sheep (indeed the sheep would have been entrusted to Alexander's care rather unsafely, since he is used not to feed but to slaughter, to flay the skin, devour the flesh, scatter the bones) unless we had been admonished a second and third time, in Peter, of the greatness of love (rather forgetful of the admonition. For if they loved Alexander's Christ, they would not kill his members) —to us alone it is granted to enter the sanctuary and present prayers before the altar, (to you alone, Alexander? Then Christ, our true High Priest, could not enter the sanctuary. And if to you alone, why then do you exhort your Brothers and Sons to prayers and the censer, that is, the prayers of the Saints? You are blasphemers, Alexander, and you sacrilegiously usurp the honour due to Christ the true High Priest, who alone entered the sanctuary once for all!) and we must take care that the Lord not be angry and say: I sought a man who would build up a wall and stand in the gap before me for the land, so that I would not destroy it, and I found none; and I poured out my indignation upon them. (Is this the man, Alexander, the man of blood? Certainly he stood against God, not as a mediator but as an enemy; not to appease the angry one but to kindle and provoke wrath, which is sometimes to be poured out with full bowls upon him and those who bear his mark. When God destroys those who destroyed the earth.) For this is the nature of divine vengeance, that the Most High then becomes most placable, and returns to mildness and clemency, that is, to his own disposition, (O you, Alexander, notable heretic! Does God, punishing the damned and punishing the faithful in Christ, exercising judgement and justice, turn aside from his own nature? Or is mildness and clemency toward the compliant more natural to him than justice toward the refractory? If this is true, why did the Father not spare his only begotten Son? You are no more a theologian, Alexander, than your predecessor Innocent. Confess it now frankly, as he too frankly and openly confessed it together with you) when with a strong arm and a mighty hand he draws the sword to strike. Let your feet be the feet of those who preach peace (of those who bring about peace between the enemies of God, so that, with united strength, the friends of God may strike, slaughter and torment most dreadfully. This is your inner feeling of mind, which Father Ribadeneyra the Jesuit also revealed when he instructed the executioner slaughtering heretics in this way: Carry the exile, place him on the pyres, throw him from the bridge, beat him with pincers, hand him to the beasts. Strike him with the sword, kill him with hunger, saw him through; bind his feet with shackles, tie the old men with ropes. Tear out the bones, break the legs, wrench the limbs, lictor, and cut him into many pieces. Then open the way to the grate, and mark the fibres; see the left side and the right.) These are your feet when you preach peace, so that the bow and arrows may be broken, and God may command the winds and make calm; which we eagerly desire to obtain through you (and why not through you alone, Alexander, to whom alone it is granted to enter the sanctuary?), and to you the Apostolic blessing…

units.la: Hi pedes sunt Vestri, cùm pacem evangelizatis) ut conteratur arcus & sagittæ, atque imperet Deus ventis, & faciat tranquillitatem; quam per Vos assequi (& cur non per Vos, Alexander, solos, quibus solis concessum intrare Sanctuarium?) vehementer optamus, Vobisque Apostolicam benedictionem (minùs non poteras. nunquam dicturus tamen cum S. Petro ; Aurum & argentum non habeo: Surge & ambula.) peramanter impertimur. Datum Romæ apud Sanctam Mariam Majorem (quot Marias igitur, Alexander habuisti? Majorem, Minorem; Medioxumam? Nihil hæc ad B. Mariam, Matrem Christi!) sub Annulo Piscatoris (cur non hamo aureo Piscatoris, quo Regna & Opes, è Summo Apostolatus fastigio, per universum Orbem, Tuas videlicet curas, piscaris? Scilicet quia piscati jam pro Te alii, pridem ceperunt Romam, Latium, Æmiliam, Flamineam, Regnum Neapolitanum, Siciliam; ac præterea omnem potestatem in Spiritualibus & temporalibus, in Cœlo & in terra. quanquam nassa tua nonnihil confracta est, & dilapsi sunt scombri in Anglia, Scotia, Hibernia, Dania, Norwegia, Suecia, Germania, Gallia, Hungaria, Polonia, Belgio. ubi licet diu noctúque piscari pergas, nihil, vel parùm piscaris tamen. nisi forte pisces Tibi fuerunt homines illi, quos in Pedemontio hamo transfixos dirum miserandúmque in modum discerpsisti, assasti, torruisti, devorâsti.) die xx. Sept. m. d. c. lv. Pontificatus nostri Anno Primo. (Zelus enim teli instar femori meo defixus, diu latere non potuit. Adeste, Fratres Filiíque, cernite zelum meum, quem primo statim Pontificatus Anno profero, prolaturus in dies magis, dummodo, in Nepotum saltem meorum gratiam, multiplicabuntur Anni Pontificatus mei : Hæc meorum est, hæc vestrorum quoque sit votorum Summa!) Non puto interiorem Bullæ hujus sensum (amat quippe Apollo non Delphicus duntaxat, sed Romanus etiam, animi sui sensa in-volvolvere) Glossam acu non tetigisse. Sicubi tamen à lineis illa excidit, meliora, quæ optaffemus utique, alii divinent.
units.tr: These are your feet, since you proclaim peace: so that the bow and the arrow are broken, and God commands the winds and brings calm. We earnestly desire to attain this through you (and why not through you alone, Alexander, to whom alone it is granted to enter the Sanctuary?), and we lovingly give you our Apostolic blessing (you could not have said less, though you would never say with St Peter: Silver and gold I have not; rise and walk). Given at Rome, at St Mary Major (how many Marys, then, did Alexander have? Major, Minor, Middling? None of this has to do with the Blessed Mary, Mother of Christ!) under the Fisherman's Ring (why not under the golden hook of the Fisherman, with which you fish for kingdoms and wealth through the whole world from the summit of the Apostolate, that is, for your own cares? Of course, because others have already fished for you and long since taken Rome, Latium, Emilia, Flaminia, the Kingdom of Naples and Sicily, and in addition all power over spiritual and temporal things, in heaven and on earth. Yet your net has been somewhat broken, and the mackerel have slipped away in England, Scotland, Ireland, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Germany, France, Hungary, Poland and Belgium. Here you may go on fishing day and night, yet you catch nothing, or very little. Unless perhaps those men were your fish, whom you pierced on a hook in Piedmont, and tore apart, roasted, broiled and devoured in a dreadful and pitiable manner.) On the 20th of September 1655, in the first year of our Pontificate. (For zeal, like an arrow fixed in my thigh, could not long remain hidden. Stand by, brothers and sons, and see my zeal, which I display at once in the first year of my Pontificate, and which I shall bring forth more and more from day to day, provided that the years of my Pontificate are multiplied, at least for the favour of my nephews. This is the sum of my wishes, and may it be the sum of yours too!) I do not think that the inner meaning of this Bull has escaped a gloss (for Apollo, not only the Delphic but also the Roman, loves to wrap up the feelings of his mind). If, however, that meaning has fallen out somewhere between the lines, let others guess the better things we would surely have wished.

units.la: CCLXIX. Ampla nihilominus statim ex Suecia spolia Alexander retulit. Anxius nempe metu, ne Regna & Principatus perderet, Reginam saltem & Principem Suecorum inclytam Christinam lucratus, in suum, hoc est, veræ fideisinum traduxit. Illa enim M. D. C. LIV. Regnum simul atque religionem, pro qua Optimus Parens ad mortem usque pugnaverat, abdicavit, successorem nacta Carolum Gustavum, Gustavi Adolphi è Sorore Catharina Nepotem, Comitem Palatinum Rheni, Bavariæ, &c. illum ipsum, quem Bulla sua truculenter adeò Alexander impetiit. Profecta ex Regno Christina, aliáque omnia simulans, per Daniam Hamburgum, atque inde Bruxellas concessit, ibidémque die XXIV. Decembris anni dicti Pontificiam Religionem amplexa, ad autumnum usque anni sequentis M. D. C. LV. hæsit. Alexandro verò Papatum adepto, Romam proficisci statuit. Bruxellis proin defertis Oenipontem ad Ferdinandum Archiducem migravit. Eò missus ab Alexandro Lucas Holstenius, Hamburgensis, Protonotarius Apostolicus, & Vaticani Bibliothecarius, Pontificium Reginæ Breve obtulit. quo accepto die III. Nov. ibidem in principe Templo Pontificiam religionem solenniter professa est. Inde per Tridentum in Italiam promoto itinere, passim magnificè, institutis in ejus gratiam celebribus ludis, (cujusmodi Pesari fuit ludus Herculis, à Legato Pontificio, Cardinale Aloysio Homodei ei repræsentatus) excepta, Lauretum die VIII. Dec. venit, ubi in Domo B. Virginis duas horas agens, privatim peccata confessa, Mariæ imagini Coronam auream, liliatis floribus, pretiosis unionibus interstinctis, exornatam; nec non sceptrum aureum, cujus manubrium & lilium trecentis sexaginta octo pretiosissimis adamantibus, & centum ac sexaginta rubinis ejusdem magnitudinis consitum fuit, Regia scilicet Reginæ Cœli munera obtulit. Cùmque Regia illa munera sua in thesaurum illata B. Virginis, sequenti carmine,
units.tr: CCLXIX. Nevertheless Alexander at once brought back ample spoils from Sweden. Anxious indeed lest he should lose kingdoms and principalities, he gained at least the Queen and the famous Princess of the Swedes, Christina, and brought her over to his own side, that is, to the side of the true faith. For in 1654 she gave up the kingdom together with the religion for which her excellent father had fought even to death, and found a successor in Charles Gustavus, nephew through Catherine, sister of Gustavus Adolphus, Count Palatine of the Rhine, of Bavaria, etc., the very man whom Alexander attacked so savagely in his Bull. Leaving Sweden and pretending all other things, she went through Denmark to Hamburg, and from there to Brussels, and there on 24 December of that year embraced the Papist religion, and stayed until the autumn of the following year, 1655. But when Alexander had obtained the Papacy, she resolved to set out for Rome. Leaving Brussels therefore, she moved to Oenipontum to the Archduke Ferdinand. Sent there by Alexander, Lucas Holstenius of Hamburg, Apostolic Protonotary and librarian of the Vatican, presented her with a Papal Brief. Having received it, on 3 November she solemnly professed the Papist religion in the principal church there. Then, travelling on through Trent into Italy, she was received everywhere magnificently, with famous games being arranged in her honour (such as the Games of Hercules at Pesaro, presented to her by the Papal Legate, Cardinal Luigi Omodei). She came to Loreto on 8 December, where, spending two hours in the house of the Blessed Virgin, she privately confessed her sins, and offered to the image of Mary a golden crown, adorned with lily flowers and set with precious pearls, as well as a golden sceptre, whose handle and lily were studded with three hundred and sixty-eight most precious diamonds and one hundred and sixty rubies of the same size. These royal gifts, of course, were a Queen's offering to the Queen of Heaven. And when the royal gifts had been placed in the treasury of the Blessed Virgin, she saw them inscribed with the following verse,

units.la: Hanc tibi sacravit spretam Regina Coronam, In Cœlo tribuas ut meliore frui; inscripta vidisset, insulsum Poetam falsè risit, & à se spretam coronam Mariæ Virgini donatam negavit. Demum die XXIII. Decembris magnificentissimâ pompâ adductâ Romam intravit, & in S. Petri Templo peractis sacris, ad Palatium Pontificis perrexit. ubi ter incurvata, Alexandri throno insidentis pedes osculata, & post ab eodem Alexandro amplexu salutata, simul gaudium suum, quòd in gremium Ecclesiæ Romanæ recepta esset, declaravit, simul pro honore sibi habito gratias egit. Respondit Papa: Conversionem Reginæ tantum opus esse, ut propter eam grandius in Cœlo festum eo die agitetur, quàm ipsa in terra agitari videat. Postero die Papa Sacramentum confirmationis eidem impertitus, nomen ei Christinæ Mariæ Alexandræ indidit. Proximo Solis Regali Pontificis convivio excepta est, in quo Pontifex mensæ sublimiori sub medio Cœlo seu Baldachino suo; Regina humiliori, sub parte extrema Cœli (neque tota tamen Cœlo Pontificio tecta) accubuerunt. orationem habente Jesuita Oliva, quam liberè Regina, neque sine pudore Olivæ perstrinxit. Fertur Alexander admodum Christinæ in Literas & Literatos amorem laudâsse. Hoc forte amore stimulata Romam ad Regem Regum, Regibúsque æquiparatos Literatos venit, stabilémque eam sibi Literatorum scilicet sedem optavit. An amorem sincerum seriúmque Religionis Pontificiæ laudare merito Alexander potuerit, alii dijudicent. Admodum enim difficile, vel impossibile etiam ei fuit, tot intricatos sinus sui articulos de Apostolatu & Hildebrandina potentia ejus, Transfubstantiatione, Purgatorio, Indulgentiis, Reliquiis, Justificatione Papæ & Cardinalium per merita operum, aliáque ejusmodi, Sapientissimæ, & πεόπων ἐ ἐπίπων oculatæ Reginæ persuadere. Vel enim talia nunquam, vel difficulter admodum credidit, credétve unquam.
units.tr: To you the Queen has consecrated this crown, which she despised, so that you may grant her to enjoy a better one in Heaven; and she laughed falsely at the foolish poet, and denied that the crown she had despised had been given by herself to the Virgin Mary. At last, on 23 December, she entered Rome with the most magnificent pomp, and after the sacred rites in St Peter's Church she went to the Pope's Palace. There, bowing three times, she kissed the feet of Alexander, who was seated on his throne, and afterwards was greeted by an embrace from Alexander himself. At the same time she declared her joy that she had been received into the bosom of the Roman Church, and gave thanks for the honour shown her. The Pope replied: The conversion of the Queen was such a great work that, on account of it, a greater festival is celebrated in Heaven on that day than she sees celebrated on earth. On the following day the Pope administered the sacrament of confirmation to her and named her Christina Maria Alexandra. She was received at a royal banquet of the Pope on the following Sunday, at which the Pope reclined at a higher table under the canopy or baldachin, and the Queen at a lower table under the far end of the canopy (yet not wholly covered by the Papal canopy). A Jesuit, Oliva, gave the oration, which the Queen freely criticised, and not without shame for Oliva. It is said that Alexander greatly praised Christina's love of letters and learned men. Perhaps stirred by this love, she came to Rome to the King of Kings, and to the learned men, who are equal to kings, and she wished to make it her permanent home among the learned. Whether Alexander could rightly praise her sincere and serious love of the Papist religion, others may judge. For it was very difficult, or even impossible, for him to persuade that most wise and keen-sighted Queen of the many intricate folds of his doctrines: of the Apostolate and his Hildebrandine power, of Transubstantiation, Purgatory, Indulgences, Relics, and the justification of the Pope and the Cardinals by the merits of works, and others of that kind [πεόπων ἐ ἐπίπων]. For she either never believed such things, or believed them with great difficulty, and never will believe them.

units.la: CCLXX. Quàm pleni bonæ spei per initia Papatus Alexandri omnes fuerint, fore scilicet, ut temperet sibi ab Ecclesiæ bonis in Nepotes & consanguineos profundendis, supra assentatorum ejus non nemo prodidit. Faculam quinetiam bonæ spei nonnullam accendit ipse Alexander, quando electus Papa consanguineis, ne Romam venirent injussu suo, serió interdixit. Fertur etiam juramento apud Crucifixi imaginem deposito se obligâsse, quòd nunquam Nepotes suos Romæ excepturus sit. Jámque Cardinalis Pallavicinus in ejus laudes effusissimus, Historiæ Concilii Tridentini Galeatum Prologum præfixerat, quo Alexandri ceu Angeli ἀπροσωπολήπτης heroicum isthoc neglecti Nepotismi facinus tertium usque in Cœlum tulit. quem tamem, cùm res alium longè eventum sortita esset, non sine pudore & impensarum jactura (plurima enim folia, jam impressa, laudes has fictitias ebuccinantia, suprimi debuerunt) ceu abortivum fœtum, tollere, & cum nescio quo Epilogo Operis, (qui ipse tamen post mortem Alexandri, saltem in Latina editione Baptistæ Giattini omissus etiam fuit) commutare necesse habuit. Non diu enim Romanorum credulitati Alexander illusit; quinimò vix exacto Pontificatus anno Nepotibus suis paternæ charitatis sinum amplissimè pandit. similis naufrago, qui merces suas jactare se simulans, funi easdem alligavit, & manu funem trahendo servavit. Sic omnino Alexander, visus Nepotes & charitates suas Roma arcere, & à reti suo piscatorio procul amandare, non tantùm clanculum pri-
units.tr: CCLXX. That all were full of good hope at the beginning of Alexander's Papacy, that is, that he would refrain from pouring out the goods of the Church upon his nephews and kinsmen, one of his own flatterers has disclosed. Alexander himself even kindled a certain torch of good hope when, having been elected Pope, he seriously forbade his kinsmen to come to Rome without his command. It is also said that he bound himself by an oath, sworn before an image of the Crucified, that he would never receive his nephews at Rome. And Cardinal Pallavicini, who was most lavish in his praises of Alexander, had already prefixed a bombastic Prologue to his History of the Council of Trent, in which he carried this heroic deed of neglecting nephews, as of an angel of Alexander's [ἀπροσωπολήπτης, without respect of persons], up to the third heaven. But when events had turned out quite otherwise, he was obliged, not without shame and loss of expense (for very many pages, already printed and trumpeting these fictitious praises, had to be suppressed), to remove it like an abortive foetus, and to replace it with some Epilogue of the work (which Epilogue, however, after Alexander's death, was at least omitted in the Latin edition of Battista Giattini). For Alexander did not long mock the credulity of the Romans; indeed, scarcely a year of his Pontificate had passed before he opened wide the bosom of paternal love to his nephews. He was like a shipwrecked man who, pretending to throw his goods overboard, tied them to a rope and saved them by hauling in the rope with his hand. Thus Alexander, who seemed to keep his nephews and his affections away from Rome, and to drive them far from his fishing net, did not only at first secretly

units.la: primò continuis eos muneribus mactavit; sed paulatim etiam ad honores fortunasque summas provexit. Obstiterat quidem juramentum solenne. Cæterùm Confessorius ejus Cardinalis idem Pallavicinus, ex eo Sodalium ordine, qui novo linguarum dono præditi callidis interpretationibus juramentorum religionem laxare didicerunt, scrupulum ingeniosè, sed parùm piè, ei exemit. Cùm enim interrogatus ab eo Alexander, ob præstitum juramentum anxius nonnihil, de conceptis, quibus juravit, verbis, respondisset, jurasse se, quod Nepotes & proximos suos Romæ excipere nunquam velit; author ei fuit, ut non Romæ, sed tendentes Romam in media via exciperet. Ita Sena venientes bonis avibus proximos Nepotulosque suos in media via lætus ovansque excepit, & ex Pontificiæ potestatis suæ plenitudine Fratri quidem Mario in administratione summæ rerum, & pecuniarum exquisitissimo aucupio non minùs quàm vel Urbanus VIII. Barbarinis suis, vel Olympiæ Innocentius indulsit: Nepotes vero quinque, unum ex Mario Fratre Flavium, duos ex fratre ante Papatum defuncto, Augustinum & Sigismundum, & duos ex Sorore, quæ Senæ in matrimonio Nobilis Bichi vixerat, ita unctos delibutosque, & dignitatibus fortunisque amplissimis auctos reddidit, ut similis Nepotismi in Pontificia Sede exemplum perfectius hactenus nullum extiterit. Et Flavium quidem, hominem perditissimum Cardinalem Patronum; Sigismundum septendecim annos natum primo Abbatem, ac post etiam Cardinalem creavit: Augustinum, futurum Chisianæ familiæ columen, cui Principis Borgesii Neptim opulentissimam Conjugem, dote centum millium ducatorum & viginti insuper millibus duplionum loco margaritarum expensis, denique sexaginta millibus duplionum in manus ipsius Sponsi resignatis, impetravit, tantùm non Regalibus opibus ex thesauris Ecclesiæ liberaraliffimè depromptis, maƈtavit: denique ex Sorore Nepotes alterum Cardinalem Ofimum creavit, alterum Equitem Melitenfem, & navium Pontificiarum Generalem constituit. Præterea nec uxori Marii, D. Berenicæ, ejúfque filiabus defuit, quibus singulis eleemosynæ titulo ex Petri patrimonio tria millia duplionum contulit. Taceo consanguineos remotiores, ad quos non minùs hosce Paƈtoli fluvios derivandos, munificentiffimus ex alieno, eóque sacro peculio seu Pater, seu Quirinalis prædo, putavit. Et hic tamen rapaciffimus depeculator patrimonii S. Petri, & thesaurorum Ecclesiæ is ipse est, qui paulò ante Monasterii severè adeò contra Pacem Monafterienfem protestatus est, præcipuam ob causam, quòd in ea abalienationem bonorum Ecclesiæ indulgeri putaret. Quam ipsam indulgentiam necessitate extortam partes pacifcentes caussati sunt: cùm Alexander nulla necessitate, sed avaritiæ solius acri stimulo, contra juramenti etiam religionem, & cum offensione summa omnium Ecclesiæ bona dilapidârit.
units.tr: but at once overwhelmed them with constant gifts; and gradually he also raised them to the highest honours and fortunes. A solemn oath stood in the way, to be sure. But his confessor, the same Cardinal Pallavicini, of that company of men who, endowed with the new gift of tongues, have learned to loosen the sanctity of oaths by clever interpretations, cleverly, but not piously, removed the scruple for him. For when Alexander, somewhat anxious about the wording of the oath he had sworn, was asked by him, he replied that he had sworn that he never wished to receive his nephews and close relatives at Rome; and Pallavicini advised him not to receive them at Rome, but to receive them on the way, while they were travelling to Rome, in the middle of the road. So, when they came from Siena with good omens, he joyfully and exultantly received his kinsmen and little nephews in the middle of the road, and by the fullness of his Papal power he granted to his brother Mario, in the management of the highest affairs and of the most exquisite pursuit of money, no less than Urban VIII had to his Barberini, or Innocent to Olimpia. He made the five nephews, one of them Flavio, son of his brother Mario, two of them Agostino and Sigismondo, sons of a brother who died before his Papacy, and two sons of his sister, who had lived in marriage with the nobleman Bichi at Siena, so anointed and steeped in ointment, and raised to such very ample dignities and fortunes, that hitherto no more perfect example of nepotism has existed in the Papal See. Flavio, a most abandoned man, he made Cardinal Patron; Sigismondo, seventeen years old, he made first an Abbot and afterwards also a Cardinal; Agostino, who was to be the pillar of the Chigi family, he obtained as husband the very wealthy granddaughter of Prince Borghese, with a dowry of one hundred thousand ducats, and besides twenty thousand doubloons in place of pearls, and finally sixty thousand doubloons paid into the hands of the bridegroom himself; he enriched him, not far short of royal wealth, by drawing it very liberally from the treasures of the Church. Finally, from his sister he made one nephew a Cardinal of Osimo, another a Knight of Malta, and appointed him General of the Papal fleet. Besides, he did not neglect the wife of Mario, Lady Berenice, nor her daughters, to each of whom under the title of alms he gave three thousand doubloons from the patrimony of St Peter. I say nothing of the more distant kinsmen, to whom he, the most generous father, or rather the Quirinal robber, thought these Pactolus streams ought to be diverted, from another's and therefore sacred money. Yet this most rapacious plunderer of the patrimony of St Peter and of the treasures of the Church is the very man who, shortly before, protested so severely against the Peace of Münster, chiefly for this reason, that he thought it permitted the alienation of the goods of the Church in that peace. That same indulgence the peace-making parties alleged had been wrung from them by necessity; whereas Alexander, with no necessity but only the keen spur of avarice, and against the very sanctity of his oath, and to the great offence of all, squandered the goods of the Church.

units.la: CCLXXI. Sic ad summum haud dubiè gradum provectus ab Alexandro Nepotifmus, ad animum mihi, ad apicem hunc Simoniæ Pontificiæ obstupescenti, revocavit veterem querelam Alvari Pelagii Johannis XXII. Pœnitentiarii, quam de planctu Ecclesiæ lib. II. art. 15. consignatam, cùm Nepotifmi hujus χρυπτὰ & ἀισχύνης, Arcana verè pudenda in aprico collocet, heic totidem verbis repræfentari, è re maximè fuerit.
units.tr: Thus Nepotism, advanced by Alexander to the highest rank without doubt, recalled to my mind, as I stood astonished at this summit of papal simony, the old complaint of Alvarus Pelagius, penitentiary of John XXII. He recorded it in De planctu Ecclesiae, book 2, art. 15. Since he sets out the secret things and shame [κρυπτὰ, αἰσχύνης] of this nepotism, truly shameful secrets, in plain view, it will be most useful to have his words presented here exactly as he wrote them.

units.la: Romani multi Pontifices nostri hypocritalis temporis, inquit, & jam multa lustra transiverunt, licet Dei veri vicarii, Jesu Christi pauperis crucifixi, & successores Petri pauperis piscatoris, manu & arte victum quærentis reti & navicula; prædivites Nepotulos & alios consanguineos clericos nedum ad altas prælationes promovent ditissimas & altissimas: sed etiam ad statum Cardinalatus inscios totaliter & indignos: & comIii mitmittunt eis judicare & regere totum mundum, qui regere nesciunt semetipsos. Magistri fiunt, qui discipuli non fuerunt. Qui pendebant modo ad matrum ubera, sedent ad Dei Vicarii latera. Consanguineis autem Secularibus procurant aut emunt, nedum campos, terras & vineas, & simplicem militiam, sed etiam baronias & Comitatus, Marchionatus, & alios omnes mundi potentatus. Et tales Papæ consanguinei, qui ante ejus Papatum soli vagabantur per mundum peditando, nunc stipati militum agminibus incedunt. Qui ante cum mulieribus plebeiis, aut aliis suis partibus contraxissent; post cum Comitissis aut Marchionissis, aut Ducissis contrahunt. Qui ante forsan byrrho, aut alia veste humili induti fuissent, post sericis auratis pallio & aliis fucatis vestibus ornati incedunt. Et qui ante habitabant in domibus patrum suorum aut mercatorum, aut agricolarum, aut artificum, vel aliàs pauperum despectorum, post habitant in domibus Regum & Imperatorum. Et qui ante Papatum sui consanguinei, nati in paupere domo & tugurio rusticano, vix mille & cibario pane rugientem ventrem saturare poterant, post similam & mella fastidiunt. Cardinales quidam & alii Prælati multi, talia à Romanis Pontificibus multis exempla videntes, sequuntur eos sic gratanter in carnalibus hujusmodi, quocunque ierint, non Christum Agnum. O quot nepotes & consanguineos Prælati præmittunt & sequuntur ad inferos, ei beneficia impetrantes & conferentes, quorum amplissima stipendia recipient non militaturi in eis, nec debitum servitium in suis beneficiis Domino impensuri. De cura animarum non curantes, sed de bursa, proventus beneficiorum luxuriosè impendentes, aut in suis pompis, possessiones sibi vel suis ementes, & Ecclesias defraudantes.
units.tr: Many of our popes of this hypocritical age, he says, and many years have passed, although they are the vicars of the true God, of Jesus Christ the poor and crucified, and successors of Peter the poor fisherman, who sought his living by hand and craft, with net and little boat, promote their very rich nephews and other clerical relatives not only to high and most wealthy prelacies, but also to the rank of cardinal, though they are wholly ignorant and unworthy; and they entrust to them the judging and governing of the whole world, though they do not know how to govern themselves. They become masters who were never disciples. Those who only lately hung at their mothers' breasts now sit at the side of God's vicar. For their secular relatives they procure or buy not only fields, lands and vineyards, and simple military commissions, but also baronies, counties, marquisates and every other worldly power. And such relatives of the pope, who before his papacy wandered the world alone on foot, now walk about surrounded by crowds of soldiers. Those who before had married plebeian women, or women of other low station, now marry countesses, marchionesses or duchesses. Those who perhaps once wore coarse woollen cloth or other humble dress now walk about adorned with silk, gold cloth and other showy garments. And those who once lived in the houses of their fathers, who were merchants, farmers, craftsmen or otherwise poor and despised men, now live in the palaces of kings and emperors. And those relatives who, before the papacy, were born in a poor house or a rustic hut and could scarcely fill their growling bellies with a thousand [loaves of] barley bread, now scorn fine flour and honey. Certain cardinals and many other prelates, seeing so many examples of this kind from the Roman popes, follow them so eagerly in such carnal things, wherever they go, not following the Lamb Christ. O how many nephews and relatives do prelates send ahead and follow to hell, obtaining and conferring benefices for them, whose generous stipends they receive though they will not serve in them, nor render the due service to the Lord in their benefices! They do not care for the cure of souls, but spend the revenues of the benefices from their purses in luxury, on their own pomp, buying estates for themselves or their families, and defrauding the churches.

units.la: CCLXXII. Quæstus de eodem Nepotismi studio
units.tr: CCLXXII. A complaint about the same zeal for nepotism

units.la: jam olim etiam est Franciscus Rothomagensis, de Rebus Ecclesiæ lib. 1. cap. 9. ubi sic Pontifices Nepoturientes perstringit: Quæ carnis sunt, sapiunt, & secundùm carnem ambulant, ac ecclesiastica, ut temporalia, non meritis, sed personis committunt. Scilicet se suáque regere, ac quidvis ex negligentia agere, re, velut hæreditario jure, tanquam Heli filios, Nepotes sinunt, quod malum centum abhinc annis detestandum in modum, gravissime in Ecclesia, contra Ecclesiasticum canonem, antiquum Apostolicum repullulat. Digitum ille intendit ad Canonem Apostolicum LXXVI. qui sic sonat: Ὅτι ἃ χρὴ Ἐπίσκοπον τῷ ἀδελφῷ, ἢ τῷ υἱῷ, ἢ ἑτέρῳ συγγενεῖ χειροτονεῖν, ὃν βούλεται. Κληρονόμως γὰρ τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν ποιεῖν δίκαιον, τὰ τῆς θεοῦ χαριζόμενον παθῇ ἀνθρωπίνῳ. ...
units.tr: Long ago too, Franciscus of Rouen, in De rebus Ecclesiae, book 1, chapter 9, lashed out at popes who lust after nephews, where he speaks thus: They relish the things of the flesh, and walk according to the flesh, and they entrust ecclesiastical offices, like temporal ones, not to merit but to persons. Clearly they let their own affairs and their own selves be governed, and do whatever they like out of carelessness, and, as if by hereditary right, like the sons of Eli, they allow their nephews [to take over]. This evil, which ought to be detested in the manner of a hundred years ago, sprouts again most grievously in the Church, contrary to the ancient apostolic canon of the Church. He points his finger at the Apostolic Canon 76, which reads: [Οὐ χρὴ Ἐπίσκοπον τῷ ἀδελφῷ, ἢ τῷ υἱῷ, ἢ ἑτέρῳ συγγενεῖ χειροτονεῖν, ὃν βούλεται. Κληρονόμως γὰρ τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν ποιεῖν δίκαιον, τὰ τῆς θεοῦ χαριζόμενον παθῇ ἀνθρωπίνῳ. ...]

units.la: Quòd non oportet Episcopum fratri, vel filio, vel alii cognato gratificantem, ad Episcopatus dignitatem, quem vult, eligere. Episcopatus enim hæredem facere justum non est, ea, quæ Dei sunt, humano affectu largientem. Non enim licet ecclesiam Dei inhæredes conferre. Si quis autem hoc fecerit, irrita quidem electio maneat, ipse autem segregatione multetur. Concilium quoque Toletanum X. sic jam olim canone 3. sanxit: Quicunque Pontificum deinceps aut sanguine propinquis, aut favore personis quibuscunque sibi conjunctis talia loca commendare tentaverit ad suum nefandæ præsumptionis excidium, & quod jussum fuerit, revocetur in irritum, & qui ordinaverit, annuæ excommunicationi subjaceat. Sed & Tridentinum ac Basileense Concilia eandem Nepotismi Papalis licentiam coercentia, Julius Clemens Scotus Not. Saxag. quot. adversus Pallavicinum pag. 126. inducit, ubi tamen recentiores, Jesuitas inprimis, invenisse modos, quibus Beneficiarii, & multò magis Summi Pontifices, utpote Conciliorum legibus soluti, beneficia suis consanguineis elargiantur, observat.
units.tr: It is not right for a bishop, gratifying his brother, or son, or another relative, to elect to the dignity of the episcopate whomever he wishes. For it is not just to make the episcopate an heritage, by bestowing things that belong to God out of human affection. For it is not lawful to hand over the Church of God as an inheritance. If anyone does this, the election shall remain void, and he himself shall be punished by deposition. The Council of Toledo X also long ago decreed this in canon 3: Whoever among the bishops henceforth shall attempt to commend such places, whether to kinsmen by blood or to persons joined to him by favour, to his own destruction through a wicked presumption, let what has been ordered be revoked as void, and let the one who ordained them be subject to an annual excommunication. But Julius Clemens Scotus, in his Notae Saxagi, cited against Pallavicini, page 126, also brings forward the Councils of Trent and Basel, which restrained this same licence of papal nepotism; yet he observes that more recent writers, the Jesuits above all, have discovered methods by which beneficed clergy, and far more the supreme pontiffs, who as men free from the laws of the councils, bestow benefices on their relatives.

units.la: CCLXXIII. Deinceps Alexander Deificus etiam ad Apotheosin se convertens, primò quidem in gratiam Hispanorum, Thomam Villanovanum, Augustinianum Eremitam & Valentiæ quondam Archiepiscopum, ante centum annos defunctum, & à Paulo V. Beatis accensum, cucujus vitam & prodigiosa facta seu miracula Nicasius Baxius scripto prodidit; in album Divorum die I. Nov. A. M. D. C. LVIII. retulit. procuratore Rege Philippo IV. qui ex Regno Valentiæ ad impetranda & celebranda solenniter illa sacra grandem pecuniarum summam contulit. Philippus enim & Valentii, nisi prius Sancto suo propitii fuissent, latuisset ejus Sanctitas intra privatos lares, neque illi devotissimis cultoribus suis propitio esse licuisset. Scilicet ad eam solennitatem veniri non solet, priusquam de pecuniarum ingenti summa vel magni Principis, vel communitatis cujuspiam impensis probè cautum fuerit. Laterem verò planè lavarent, qui non numerata pecunia Sanctum suum in Divorum numerum referri ambirent.
units.tr: Next, Alexander Deificus, turning himself also to deification, first, to gratify the Spanish, enrolled Thomas of Villanova, an Augustinian hermit and formerly archbishop of Valencia, who had died a hundred years earlier and had been declared Blessed by Paul V., whose life and prodigious deeds or miracles Nicasius Baxius published in writing, in the roll of the Saints on 1 November 1658, at the request of King Philip IV, who from the kingdom of Valencia contributed a great sum of money to obtain and solemnly celebrate those rites. For unless Philip and the Valencians had first been favourable to their saint, his Holiness would have remained within private household gods, nor would it have been permitted for him to be favourable to his most devoted worshippers. Clearly, no one usually proceeds to that solemnity until a great sum of money has been carefully provided for from the expenses of a great prince or some community. Those who sought to have their saint numbered among the Saints without counting out the money would indeed be washing a brick.

units.la: CCLXXIV. Ne verò Hispanis gratificando æmu- los Gallos Alexander offenderet, in eorum etiam gratiam, commendatum ab iisdem Franciscum de Sales, Episco- pum Gebennensem, seu Anicien-sem, in eundem Divorum chorum cooptavit.
units.tr: CCLXXIV. Lest he should offend the Spaniards by favouring their rivals the French, Alexander also enrolled in that same company of saints, as a favour to the French, Francis de Sales, Bishop of Geneva or Annecy, who had been recommended by them.

units.la: Summos ille etiam Procuratores, Regem Galliarum, Reginam matrem, Clerum universum, Reginam Angliæ viduam, & Carolum Emmanuelem Ducem nactus fuerat. quibus quo pacto resisteret Papa? Lento nihilominus canonizatio gradu processerat. Primò enim Beatum eum Alexander nondum Beatus declaravit, & ceu Confessorum Pontificis (Christi enim confessor neutiquam fuit) à quibusdam religiosè coli permisit. Eam in rem Bullam apud S. Mariam Majorem sub Annulo Piscatoris die XXVIII. Dec. A. M. D. C. LXI. Cusam emisit. Urgente mox Rege Apotheosin ipsam, petiit Papa, ut Illustrem quempiam Legatum, Regis nomine negotium curaturum, Romam Rex ablegaret. Missus Dux Crequius Junio Anni M. D. C. LXII Romæ appulit, qui mox XX. Augusti à Corsis, Prætorianis Papæ militibus, gravem contumeliam passus, in Galliam re infecta rediit. Duravit eam ob causam Regem inter & Papam ardentissimum dissidium biennio integro. cujus culpam ita Salesius ille luit, ut Sanctificatio ejus interea procedere non potuerit. Demum A. M. D. C. LXIV. composito Pisæ dissidio, denuo Rege Galliæ Apotheosin urgente, & Crequio eodem Romam remisso, desiderata obtinuit. Námque die XIX. April. A. M. D. C. LXV. non sine pompæ singularis magnificentia per auream munerum Pontifici solenniter à tribus Cardinalibus oblatorum scalam Sanctorum chorum ingressus est. Vitam & res gestas novelli hujus Deastri Carolus Augustus Salesius, Ecclesiæ Gebennensis Præpositus, Francisci ex Fratre nepos, pompose descripsit. Librum eum quisquis ὑπερέογκα ματαιότητι prætumida vanitatis, & novas veluti novi hujus Francisci cum Christo Conformitates cognoscere gestit, evolvat licet. Inter alia Lib. X. pag. 457. patrui hujus sui ἀναμαγετησίαν & perfectionem omnibus numeris consummatam, postquam religiosæ cujusdam fœminæ visionem, affirmantis, se inter contemplandam Empyrei Cœli gloriam Sanctum Præsulem Salesium vidisse Divinæ Majestati intimè unitum, ostensumque sibi ab Angelo inter Seraphinos maximæ gloriæ thronum, cum significatione, eam esse Sedem, quam Episcopo Gebennensi Divina providentia præparaverit; narrásset, his verbis prædicat: Siquidem Seraphicus erat Vir ille magnus, qui nihil nisi per amorem, in amore, ex amore & ob amorem Dei agebat. Unde sæpe testatus est ejus Confessarius Michael Faber, nihil eum formidine pœnæ, vel spe salutis æternæ unquam patravisse, verum propter simplicem & purissimum amorem Dei, ab omni mercenaria consideratione expurgatum; ac denique sic vixit, ut in suis libris docuit, & ut ex Epistolarum suarum volumine videre est, nulli vitio obnoxius, in virtutibus omnibus plane compositus; quoque magis mirere, NE MINIMAM quidem IMPERFECTIONIS ATOMVM, totam licet ejus ejus vitam AB IPSA, si vis, CONCEPTIONE perscruteris, animadvertere possis; quod vix in reliquis mortalibus reperias. Adeò Cœlestibus PRÆVENTUS fuerat à Deo benedictionibus, & adeò ipse tractus à Deo currebat in odorem unguentorum ejus, & quasi lux splendens crevit usque in meridiem. Quæ Christo Salvatori, qui solus fuit κεχωρισμένος τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν separatus à peccatoribus, Patriarchis, Prophetis & Apostolis ita iniqua sunt, ut gravissimam blasphemiam spirent.
units.tr: He had secured as his chief advocates the King of France, the Queen Mother, the whole clergy, the widowed Queen of England, and Charles Emmanuel, Duke of Savoy. How could the Pope resist them? Still, the canonization advanced at a slow pace. At first Alexander did not declare him Blessed, but allowed certain religious men to honour him as a Confessor of the Pontiff (for he was not a confessor of Christ at all). To that end he issued a Bull, stamped with the Fisherman's Ring, at St Mary Major, on 28 December 1661. Soon the King pressed for his deification itself, and the Pope asked that the King send an illustrious envoy to Rome to see to the business on his behalf. The Duke of Créqui was sent, reached Rome in June 1662, and on 20 August, having suffered a grave insult from the Corsicans, the Pope's Praetorian soldiers, returned to France with nothing accomplished. For this reason a most bitter quarrel lasted between the King and the Pope for two full years. Salesius paid the penalty for this fault in that his sanctification could not proceed in the meantime. At last, in 1664, after the dispute was settled at Pisa, and the King of France again pressed for his deification, Créqui being sent back to Rome for the same purpose, the Pope obtained what was desired. For on 19 April 1665, not without a singular magnificence of display, he entered the company of the saints by a golden ladder solemnly offered to the Pontiff by three Cardinals. The life and deeds of this new little god were pompously described by Charles Augustus de Sales, Provost of the Church of Geneva, a nephew of Francis through his brother. Let whoever is eager to learn about this book, swollen with overblown vanity [ὑπερέογκα ματαιότητι], and about the new, as it were, conformities of this Francis with Christ, read it through. Among other things, in Book X, page 457, he praises his uncle's sinlessness [ἀναμαγετησίαν] and perfection, completed in every respect, after he had related the vision of a certain religious woman, who affirmed that while contemplating the glory of the heavenly Empyrean she had seen Saint Bishop Salesius, intimately united to the Divine Majesty, and that an angel had shown her, among the Seraphim, a throne of the greatest glory, with the explanation that this was the seat which Divine providence had prepared for the Bishop of Geneva. He speaks of it in these words: For that great man was indeed a Seraphic man, who did nothing except through love, in love, from love and for the love of God. Hence his confessor Michael Faber often testified that he never acted from fear of punishment or hope of eternal salvation, but purged of every mercenary consideration on account of the simple and purest love of God; and finally he lived as he taught in his books, and as can be seen from the volume of his letters, liable to no vice, perfectly composed in all the virtues; and the more you will marvel at this, if you search out his whole life from its very CONCEPTION, you may observe that there is NOT THE SMALLEST ATOM of IMPERFECTION, which you would hardly find in the rest of mortals. So greatly had he been ANTICIPATED by heavenly blessings from God, and so greatly was he himself drawn by God, that he ran after the fragrance of God's ointments, and grew like a shining light until midday. These claims are so impious toward Christ the Saviour, who alone was separated from sinners [κεχωρισμένος τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν], and toward the Patriarchs, Prophets and Apostles, that they breathe the most grievous blasphemy.

units.la: CCLXXV. Causam tamen non omnino nullam Pontifex habuit, ut Confessorum huncce suum in Pontificium Sanctulorum suorum Cœlum inferret. Adeò enim is Romanæ Sedi devotus militabat, ut hæreticos omnes ad Romani Pontificis obedientiam reducturus seducturusque putaretur. Et plures seduxisse, ejus encomiastes commemorat, ea scilicet, uti Lib. II. p. 66. scribit, in conversione Caballiana (unde Caballii Apostolus audit) methodo usus, ut, antequam hæreticos, Ministros maximè, disputatione aggrederetur, cacodæmones exorcismis fatigaret, submissa tamen pronuntiatione. Nam, hæreticos omnes ajebat Franciscus, eos maximè, qui docent & prædicant, à Diabolo vel possessos, vel obsessos esse, atque ita primum in eos exorcismorum fulmen contorquendum esse. Novæ Missionariorum Methodi insigne arcanum! Pulso enim cacodæmone exiguus in convertendis hæreticis labor relinquitur. Genevæ præcipuè ad caulam Pontificis reducendæ, & focis potiùs quàm aris suis ibi restituendis, Salesius incubuit; dicere, uti lib. II. pag. 98.99. habetur, solitus, hac civitate domita non dubium esse, quin Europæa hæresis vehementi deinceps concussione & debilitate laboraret: est enim sedes Sathanæ, & quæ hæresin per universum orbem dispergit. Idque mox sex capitibus diducit, ex quibus concludit, eversa Geneva hæresin dissipatum iri. Quo verò pacto everti posset, consilia quædam fraudulenta suggerit. Quomodo etiam lib. VIII. pag. 370. idem remedia ultilissima, quiquibus Helvetiorum Reformatorum, aliorumque etiam non religio duntaxat, sed status etiam labefactari & concuti posit, excogitavisse narratur. Si sic (his verbis ejus judicium describitur) relinquantur Helvetii, Tigurini, Basileenses, Bernenses, aliique fœderati, idémque de Anglia & aliis regionibus, nunquam convertentur, imò verò Religionem suam statui jungentes illam cum hoc stabilient, & quemadmodum ab assuetis non fit passio, ita cum antiquitate hæresis illa ultra quidem non proficiet, sed quod magni est momenti; ultra etiam non deficiet, & erit in nobilissimis illis Europæ partibus Paralysis incurabilis. At vero quodnam remedium? Sic secum perpendebat Salesius. Et quidem remedia utilissima excogitavit, sed quæ minime promulgRanda, Apostolicus apud Serenissimum Ducem Nuntius eorum conscius factus est. An Apostolicæ Sedi proposita fuerint, ignoratur. Caterùm Salesii manu propria scripta adhuc extant, & utinam ad ea vellet Apostolica Sedes attendere. Exhibebuntur autem, quotiescunque vel ᴀpus fuerit, vel ipsa jubebit; neque enim omnia vulgo tradenda sunt. Pereant licet hæc mysteria iniquitatis, quibus opponimus dulcissima illa Filii Dei, habentis clavim Davidis, quo aperiente nemo claudit, & claudente nemo aperit, ad Angelum Philadelphiensis Ecclesiæ Apoc. III. 8. Ecce dedi coram te ostium apertum, & nemo potest illud claudere.
units.tr: CCLXXV. Yet the Pontiff had not altogether no reason for bringing this Confessor of his into the Papal heaven of his little saints. For he had served the Roman See so devotedly that he was thought likely to bring back to obedience to the Roman Pontiff, and to lead astray, all heretics. His panegyrist records that he had led many astray, namely, as he writes in Book II, page 66, by a method of conversion at Chablais (whence he is called the Apostle of Chablais) which was this: that, before attacking heretics in disputation, especially the ministers, he wearied the evil spirits with exorcisms, though in a subdued tone. For Francis used to say that all heretics, especially those who teach and preach, were either possessed or obsessed by the Devil, and therefore the thunderbolt of exorcisms must first be hurled against them. A remarkable secret of the new method of the missionaries! For once the evil spirit is driven out, little labour is left in converting heretics. Salesius applied himself especially to bringing Geneva back under the Pontiff's care, and to restoring it to its hearths rather than to its altars there; he was accustomed to say, as is recorded in Book II, pages 98–99, that once this city was subdued there was no doubt that European heresy would thereafter labour under a violent shaking and weakening, for it is the seat of Satan, and it scatters heresy throughout the whole world. He divides this at once into six heads, from which he concludes that heresy will be scattered once Geneva is overthrown. As to how it could be overthrown, he suggests certain fraudulent plans. It is also related that in Book VIII, page 370, the same man devised most useful remedies by which not only the religion but also the states of the Reformed Swiss and others might be weakened and shaken. His judgment is described in these words: If the Swiss, the people of Zurich, Basel, Bern, and the other allied states are left alone, and the same is done with England and other regions, they will never be converted; rather, by joining their religion to the state, they will make it firm, and just as a habitual thing does not cause suffering, so that heresy, through its antiquity, will indeed make no further progress, but, what is of great importance, will not fail either, and there will be an incurable paralysis in those most noble parts of Europe. But what remedy was it? Salesius weighed this over with himself. And indeed he devised most useful remedies, but such as must by no means be published; the Apostolic Nuncio at the court of the Most Serene Duke was made aware of them. Whether they were laid before the Apostolic See is not known. Meanwhile the handwritten papers of Salesius still survive, and would that the Apostolic See were willing to attend to them. They will be displayed whenever it is either useful or the See itself commands; for not everything is to be handed over to the common people. Let these mysteries of iniquity perish, and let us set against them the most sweet words of the Son of God, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, and who shuts and no one opens, addressed to the Angel of the Church of Philadelphia, Rev. 3:8: Behold, I have set before you an open door, and no one can shut it.

units.la: CCLXXVI. Alexandro Pontifice nova Jesuitarum de Pontificis Romani infallibilitate, æquali cum infallibilitate Christi, etiam extra Concilium generale, in quæstionibus non juris duntaxat, sed etiam facti, hæresis, quæ quarta iis singularis est, in lucem emersit, æternis tenebris dignissima. Ab illis nempe die XII. Dec. A. M. D. C. LXI. Lutetiæ Collegio Claromontano affixæ & propugnatæ sunt thesis, quarum duas Seculi X sect. 19. 20. Conceptas heic repetere haud pigebit. Prior ita habet: Hoc tandem seculo (decimo) schisma Photii invalescens Græcos ab ecclesiæ capite disjunxit. Christum nos ita caput agnoscimus, ut ipsius regimen, dum in Cœlos abiit, primum Petro, deinde successoribus commiserit, & EANDEM, QVAM IPSE HABEBAT INFALLIBILITATEM concesserit, quoties ex cathedra loquerentur. Posterior vero ex priore deducta sic sonat: Datur ergo in Ecclesia Romana controversiarum fidei judex infallibilis, ETIAM EXTRA CONCILIVM GENERALE, tum in quæstionibus juris, tum FACTI. Unde post Innocentii X. & Alexandri VII. constitutiones fide Divina credi potest, librum, cui titulus est, Augustinus Jansenii, esse hæreticum, & quinque propositiones ex eo decerptas esse Jansenii, & in sensu Jansenii damnatas. Neque theses illas novitias Catholicarum titulo venditatas, Parisiis duntaxat defenderunt, sed per emissarios etiam suos easdem, similesque spargere, & aperte hinc inde propugnare religioni non duxerunt.
units.tr: CCLXXVI. Under Pope Alexander there emerged into the light a new heresy of the Jesuits concerning the infallibility of the Roman Pontiff, equal to the infallibility of Christ, even apart from a General Council, in questions not only of law but also of fact, a heresy which is peculiar to them and is most worthy of eternal darkness. For on 12 December 1661, at Paris, at the Clermont College, theses were posted and defended, two of which, Century X, sections 19 and 20, it will not be tedious to repeat here. The first reads thus: In this (tenth) century the schism of Photius, growing stronger, separated the Greeks from the head of the Church. We acknowledge Christ as head in such a way that, when he went up into heaven, he committed the government of himself first to Peter and then to his successors, and granted them THE VERY SAME INFALLIBILITY WHICH HE HIMSELF HAD, whenever they spoke ex cathedra. The second, deduced from the first, sounds thus: There is therefore in the Roman Church an infallible judge of controversies of faith, EVEN APART FROM A GENERAL COUNCIL, both in questions of law and of FACT. Hence, after the constitutions of Innocent X and Alexander VII, it can be believed with divine faith that the book entitled Augustinus by Jansenius is heretical, and that the five propositions extracted from it are Jansenius's, and condemned in the sense of Jansenius. Nor did they merely defend these novel theses, which were marketed under the title of Catholic, at Paris alone; they did not think it right to scatter these same and similar theses through their own agents as well, and openly to champion them on all sides for the sake of their religion.

units.la: CCLXXVII.
units.tr: CCLXXVII.

units.la: Non parum equidem castiores aures portentosæ illæ assertiones, occasione certaminis, quod cum Jansenitis circa Propositiones ab Innocentio X. & Alexandro VII. in sensu etiam Jansenii damnatas, an scilicet illæ in Jansenii Augustino occurrant, & cum sensu Jansenii conveniant, nec ne? iis intercessit, propalatæ offenderunt. Statim enim à sanioribus Theologis earum ad universos Episcopos Galliæ obnuntiatio facta est, libello in orbem emisso, cui titulus est: Nova hæresis Jesuitarum, defensa publice Parisiis in Collegio Claromontano die XII. Dec. M. D. C. LXI. quo his fere verbis universæ Ecclesiæ exortam novam hæresin denuntiant: Quod igitur notum sit universæ Ecclesiæ: dies est XII. Decembris Anni M. D. C. LXI. quæ primum in lucem produxit monstrosam Jesuitarum opinionem, quam tot jam annis foverunt; dies est, qua illi velut assertionem Catholicam publice statuerunt: Papam quoties ex cathedra loquitur, eandem habere infallibilitatem, quam habuerit Jesus Christus, non solum in quæstionibus JVRIS, sed etiam FACTI, & FIDEDIVINA credi posse, quinque Propositiones esse Jansenii. Assertionem illam vocant errorem non simplicem, nec vulgarem haeresin, sed errorum maximorum originem, & GENERALEM HAERESIN, quae totam religionem evertit; eámque quatuor argumentis gravissimis confutant, inde scilicet petitis, quòd novitia illa haeresis, statuens rem non revelatam à Deo, nec Divino testimonio comprobatam, qualis est: Num Propositiones quaedam sint recentioris horum temporum authoris? esse fidei Divinae objectum, quia Papa dicit; pro fidei fundamento substituat authoritatem humanam, adeoque fidem evertat: ex Papa Deum, ex verbo Papae verbum Divinum faciat: id quod non haeresin duntaxat, sed horrendam impietatem & idololatriae speciem sapiat: quòd plurimum Pontificum infelicia facta & consilia nota sint: quod plures Pontifices in facto notorie errârint: quòd denique periculum sit, ne Graeci, aliive haeretici Papae primatum negantes, nova hac assertione nimiùm irritati, Ecclesiam Romanam magis magísque ita fastidituri sint, ut conversionis illorum spes omnis deinceps evanescat.
units.tr: Those monstrous assertions, brought out into the open during the dispute with the Jansenists over whether the propositions condemned by Innocent X and Alexander VII, also in the sense of Jansen, occur in Jansen's Augustinus and agree with Jansen's meaning, certainly offended more delicate ears. Soon after, the saner theologians announced them to all the bishops of France in a pamphlet circulated widely, entitled A New Heresy of the Jesuits, publicly defended at Paris in the Collège de Clermont on 12 December 1661. In nearly these words it denounced to the whole Church the new heresy that had arisen: "Let it therefore be known to the whole Church that on 12 December 1661 the Jesuits first brought into the light their monstrous opinion, which they have cherished for so many years; on that day they publicly laid down, as if it were Catholic doctrine, that the Pope, whenever he speaks ex cathedra, has the same infallibility that Jesus Christ had, not only in questions of RIGHT but also of FACT, and that a matter of DIVINE FAITH can be believed on the ground that five propositions are Jansen's." They call that assertion not a simple error, nor an ordinary heresy, but the source of the greatest errors and a GENERAL HERESY that overturns the whole religion. They refute it with four very weighty arguments. The first is that this novel heresy makes something that God has not revealed, and that is not confirmed by divine testimony (such as the question, "Are certain propositions of a more recent author of our times?"), an object of divine faith merely because the Pope says so. The second is that it puts human authority in place of the foundation of faith and so destroys faith. The third is that it makes the Pope into God and the word of the Pope into the word of God, which tastes not merely of heresy but of horrible impiety and the appearance of idolatry. The fourth is that the unhappy deeds and counsels of very many Popes are well known, that several Popes have notoriously erred in fact, and finally that there is a danger that the Greeks and other heretics, who deny the primacy of the Pope, will be so provoked by this new assertion that they will despise the Roman Church more and more, so that all hope of their conversion will thereafter vanish.

units.la: CCLXXVIII.
units.tr: CCLXXVIII.

units.la: Neque tamen sic à coepto Jesuitae se dimoveri patiuntur. Quin Sorbonam ipsam in partes suas pertrahere moliti etiam sunt. Nam post unius anni, & quod excurrit, intervallum, nimirum die xix. Jan. A. M D. C. LXIII. disputatio in magna Sorbona, propugnante M. Gabriele Drueto, Villanovano Britone, Theologiae Baccalaureo, habenda, affixa est. Ejus secunda thesi dicebatur: Christum S. Petrum, ejúsque successores summa supra ecclesiam authoritate donâsse. Tertia: Romanos Antistites privilegia quibusdam ecclesiis, sicut Ecclesiae Gallicanae, impertivisse. Octava: Concilia generalia ad extirpandas haereses, schismata & alia incommoda tollenda admodum esse utilia, non tamen absolutè necessaria. Hanc disputationem Suprema Curia Parisiensis, citatis & auditis Syndico Facultatis Theologicae, M. Vincen-fi, centio Meursio, Doctore ejusdem Facultatis in Collegio Navarreno, Disputationis Præside destinato, nec non Drueto, Respondente designato, haberi vetuit, supprimendámque decrevit, simulque omnibus Baccalaureis, Licentiatis & Doctoribus, aliisque universis interdixit, ne quis, ita verba decreti die xx i i. Jan. ejusdem anni factí sonant, scribere, sustinere, disputare, docere vel explicare audeat, directè vel indirectè, in publicis scholis, vel ullo alio loco, similes Propositiones, aliasque doctrinæ antiquæ ecclesiæ, Sanctis Canonibus, decretis Conciliorum Generalium, Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Libertatibus, atque antiquis Facultatis Theologicæ Parisiensis decretis contrarias, cum interminatione debito modo in delinquentes animadvertendi; Syndico Facultatis, Præsidi, Doctoribus simul interdicens, ne permittant, ut ejusmodi propositiones ulli disputationi inserantur; denique decernens, ut præsens sententia in Generali Congregatione dictæ Facultatis Theologicæ legatur in præsentia duorum Senatorum dictæ Curiæ; inseratúrque decretum in Acta Facultatis Theologicæ, atque inde ad alias Vniversitates mittatur. Paulò post, annitentibus Regibus Advocatis, Talæo & Bignonio, Syndicus Facultatis Theologicæ, unà cum septem aliis Facultatis ejusdem Doctoribus Senioribus, ad edendam circa authoritatem Papæ declarationem Facultatis, in Curia comparere jussi, die xxx. Maii A. M. D. C. LXIII. declarationem suam, ex actis Facultatis extractam Curiæ obtulerunt.
units.tr: Yet the Jesuits do not allow themselves to be turned aside from their undertaking. Indeed, they even tried to draw the Sorbonne itself to their side. For after an interval of one year and a little more, namely on 19 January 1663, a disputation was posted for the great Sorbonne, to be held with M. Gabriel Druet, a Breton of Villeneuve, Bachelor of Theology, as defender. Its second thesis was: "Christ gave St Peter and his successors supreme authority over the Church." The third: "The Roman bishops have granted privileges to certain churches, as to the Gallican Church." The eighth: "General councils are very useful for uprooting heresies, schisms and other evils, but are not absolutely necessary." The Supreme Court of Paris, after summoning and hearing the Syndic of the Theological Faculty, M. Vincentius Meursius, a Doctor of the same Faculty in the Collège de Navarre, who had been designated president of the disputation, and also Druet, who had been designated respondent, forbade the disputation to be held, decreed that it be suppressed, and at the same time forbade all bachelors, licentiates, doctors and all others, so that no one, as the words of the decree of 21 January of that year have it, should dare to write, maintain, dispute, teach or explain, directly or indirectly, in public schools or in any other place, propositions like these, or other doctrines contrary to the ancient teaching of the Church, the holy canons, the decrees of the general councils, the liberties of the Gallican Church and the ancient decrees of the Theological Faculty of Paris, under threat of punishment to offenders in the proper manner. At the same time it forbade the Syndic, the President and the Doctors to permit such propositions to be inserted in any disputation. Finally it decreed that the present sentence be read at a general assembly of the said Theological Faculty in the presence of two senators of the said Court, that the decree be inserted in the Acts of the Theological Faculty, and that it then be sent to the other universities. Shortly afterwards, through the efforts of the royal advocates Talon and Bignon, the Syndic of the Theological Faculty, together with seven other senior Doctors of the same Faculty, were ordered to appear before the Court in order to issue a declaration of the Faculty concerning the authority of the Pope. On 30 May 1663 they presented to the Court their declaration, extracted from the Acts of the Faculty.

units.la: CCLXXIX. Sequentibus autem capitibus Sorbo- næ declaratio comprehensa fuit.
units.tr: CCLXXIX. In the following chapters the declaration of the Sorbonne was set out.

units.la: 1. Facultatis doctrinam non esse, quòd Summus Pontifex aliquam in temporalia Regis Christianissimi authoritatem habeat: imò obstitisse Facultatem etiam iis, qui indirectam saltem authoritatem illam esse statuerunt. II. Doctrinam Facultatis esse quòd Rex Christianissimus nullum omnino agnoscat nec habeat in temporalibus Superiorum præter Deum, eámque antiquam doctrinam esse, à qua nunquam recessura sit. III. DoctriEtrinam Facultatis esse, quòd subditi fidem & obedientiam Regi Christianissimo ita debeant, ut ab iis nullo prætextu dispensari possint. IV. Eandem Facultatem non probare, neque unquam probâsse propositiones ullas, Christianissimi Regis authoritati, aut germanis Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Libertatibus, & receptis in Regno Canonibus contrarias: verbi gratiâ, quòd Summus Pontifex deponere possit Episcopos adversus eosdem Canones. V. Doctrinam Facultatis non esse, quòd Summus Pontifex sit supra Concilium Oecumenicum. VI. Facultatis dogma non esse, quòd Summus Pontifex, nullo accedente Ecclesiæ consensu, sit infallibilis. Quæ declaratio Sorbonæ, Curiæ jussu, actis inserta statim, & exemplaria ejus ad omnes Diœceses & Universitates publicas transmissa sunt, ut illic comprehensi articuli prælegantur, publicentur & in acta referantur. Hæc aliáque ex ipso Parlamenti Parisiensis Protocollo excerpta, & è Gallico in Latinum idioma à Thoma Stegero conversa, in vulgus emanârunt.
units.tr: (1) The doctrine of the Faculty is not that the Supreme Pontife has any authority over the temporal affairs of the Most Christian King; rather, the Faculty has opposed even those who have held that such authority is at least indirect. (2) The doctrine of the Faculty is that the Most Christian King acknowledges and has no superior in temporal matters except God, and that this is the ancient doctrine, from which it will never depart. (3) The doctrine of the Faculty is that subjects owe faith and obedience to the Most Christian King in such a way that they cannot be released from them on any pretext. (4) The same Faculty does not approve, and never has approved, any propositions contrary to the authority of the Most Christian King, or to the genuine liberties of the Gallican Church, or to the canons received in the kingdom; for example, that the Supreme Pontiff can depart from those canons by deposing bishops. (5) The doctrine of the Faculty is not that the Supreme Pontiff is above an ecumenical council. (6) It is not the Faculty's dogma that the Supreme Pontiff is infallible without the consent of the Church. This declaration of the Sorbonne, by order of the Court, was at once inserted in the Acts, and copies of it were sent to all dioceses and public universities, so that the articles contained in it might be read out there, published and recorded in the acts. These and other things, excerpted from the official protocol of the Parliament of Paris and translated from French into Latin by Thomas Steger, were published abroad.

units.la: CCLXXX. Dissidium mox gravius Sorbonam inter ac Curiam Parisiensem, & Jesuitas, in nervum erupit; libris de eo adversam in partem conflictantibus, quorum prior authore Jacobo Vernantio A. M. D. C. LXIX. tertia vice Lovanii editus, Defensionem Papæ, Cardinalium &c. alter Monasterii A. M. D. C. LXXI. excusus, Collectionem variorum Scriptorum, concernentium censuras Facultatis Theologicæ Parisiensis, de Hierarchia Ecclesiæ & Theologia Morali complectitur, vulgatum. Occasio dissidii gemina est, à Monachis, Jesuitis maximè, eorumque assectis & complicibus suppeditata. Prior versabatur circa controversiam, quæ Pastoribus Curatis, seu Sacerdotibus Parochialibus cum Monachis à longo jam tempore intercesserat. Monachis enim olim in Ecclesia prædicare, aut ecclesias curare integrum non fuit. Ad Episcopos, Parochos & Pastores apud ecclesiam residentes omnis ea cura pertinuit. Paulatim Episcopis & Pastoribus ministerii sui curam negligentitibus, Monachi ecclesiis obrepere, & in iisdem prædicandi munus affectare cœperunt. Cumque de eo Pastorum querelæ ingeminarentur, Bonifacius VIII. condita Decretali, quæ inserta est Clementinæ Dudum, tit. de sepulturis, ut dirimeret lites inter Prælatos & Rectores, seu Sacerdotes & clericos Parochialium ecclesiarum per diversas mundi Provincias, ex una parte, & Prædicatorum & Minorum Ordinum fratres ex altera, suscitatas super prædicationibus fidelium populis faciendis, eorum confessionibus audiendis, pœnitentiis iisdem injungendis, & tumulandis defunctorum corporibus, duorum istorum Ordinum Monachis amplam satis dedit licentiam, & odiosum, uti glossa loquitur, privilegium, quo freti omnia illa in ecclesiis & locis eorum peragerent. Decretalem illam Benedictus XI. revocaverat. At Clemens V. successor in Concilio Viennensi innovavit, & Benedicti revocatoriam, Concilio urgente, antiquavit. Bonifacii & Clementis Decretales Johannes XXII. in Extravagante frequentes, tit. de judiciis non solum confirmavit, sed ad Augustinianos etiam & Carmelitas privilegium illud extendit. Tandem idem privilegium Paulus III. etiam Jesuitis indulsit. Per Concilium Tridentinum privilegium Monachis Sess. XXIV. cap. 4. de Reformat. ubi singuli ex populo ad parochiam suam amandantur, abrogatum, Curati pertenderant. Cumque Monachi decretum illud eluderent, ipsique Pontifices Curatis caput illud allegantibus contradicerent, evenit, ut curati nonnulli in Papæ ipsius, seu odiosi privilegii illius & conditoris & defensoris, authoritatem insurgerent. Etenim Curatus quidam in Gallia Gersonis sermonem Bullæ Allexandri V. oppositum, vernaculum in idioma Gallicum conversum edidit. Sed & Franciscus Bonichon, Presbyter Congregationis Oratorii Andegavensis, libro de authoritate Episcoporum edito, asserere visus erat, authoritatem Curatorum esse juris Divini, æque ac authoritatem Papæ & Episcoporum. Quæ res adeo Papæ gnathones offendit, ut Vernantius Papæ defensionem libro A. M. D. C. LVIII. Metis edito, aperte suscepit. Cumque in defensione illa Papæ Monarchiam supra modum extenderit, Conciliorum & Episcoporum authoritati palam detraxerit, factum est, ut Facultas Theologica Parisiensis, annitentibus Parochialibus Civitatis Pictonum, in Vernantium, ejusque Propositiones, ceu Pontificiæ authoritati nimium velificantes, censuram publicam d. XXIV. Mart. A. M. D. C. LXIV. stringeret, eamque paulo post solenniter confirmaret.
units.tr: CCLXXX. The dispute between the Sorbonne and the Parisian Court on one side and the Jesuits on the other soon broke out more seriously. Books contending on opposite sides were published about it. The first, by the author Jacques Vernant, was published at Louvain for the third time in 1669 under the title Defence of the Pope, the Cardinals, etc.; the other, printed at Munster in 1671, contains a Collection of various writings concerning the censures of the Theological Faculty of Paris on the hierarchy of the Church and moral theology. The occasion of the dispute was twofold, and was supplied chiefly by the monks, especially the Jesuits, and their adherents and accomplices. The first concerned the long-standing controversy that had arisen between the parish priests (the curates, that is, the parochial priests) and the monks. For in former times it was not at all permitted for monks to preach in the Church or to take charge of churches. All such care belonged to the bishops, parish priests and ministers who resided at the church. Gradually, as the bishops and ministers neglected the care of their ministry, the monks began to creep into the churches and to aspire to the office of preaching in them. When the complaints of the ministers about this were repeated, Boniface VIII, by a decretal which is inserted in the Clementine Dudum, title De sepulturis, in order to settle disputes between prelates and rectors, that is, priests and clergy of parish churches in various provinces of the world, on the one side, and the friars of the Preaching and Minor orders on the other, which had arisen over the preaching to the faithful people, hearing their confessions, imposing penances on them, and burying the bodies of the dead, gave the monks of those two orders ample licence and, as the gloss puts it, a hateful privilege, relying on which they might do all those things in the churches and places belonging to them. Benedict XI had revoked that decretal. But Clement V, his successor, renewed it at the Council of Vienne, and at the urging of the council he annulled Benedict's revocation. John XXII, in the Extravagant Frequentes, title De iudiciis, not only confirmed the decretals of Boniface and Clement but extended that privilege also to the Augustinians and Carmelites. Finally Paul III granted the same privilege to the Jesuits as well. The curates had sought that the privilege be abrogated by the Council of Trent, Session XXIV, chapter 4, On Reformation, where each individual of the people is sent back to his own parish. But since the monks evaded that decree, and the Popes themselves contradicted the curates who cited that chapter, it came about that some curates rose up against the authority of the Pope himself, or rather against that hateful privilege, and against its author and defender. Indeed, a certain curate in France published in the vernacular French translation a sermon of Gerson opposed to the Bull of Alexander V. And Francis Bonichon, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Angers, in a book On the Authority of Bishops which he published, seemed to assert that the authority of curates is of divine right, just as much as the authority of the Pope and bishops. This matter so offended the Pope's flatterers that Vernant openly took up the defence of the Pope in a book published at Metz in 1668. And since in that defence he extended the Pope's monarchy beyond measure and openly detracted from the authority of councils and bishops, it came about that the Theological Faculty of Paris, at the urging of the parish priests of the city of Poitiers, passed a public censure on Vernant and his propositions, as sailing too freely in the direction of papal authority, on 24 March 1664, and shortly afterwards solemnly confirmed it.

units.la: CCLXXXI. Inter Propositiones porro Vernantii à Sorbona obelo confixas sequentes erant:
units.tr: CCLXXXI. Among the propositions of Vernantius that the Sorbonne marked with an obelus were the following:

units.la: quod Papæ unius sit emergentia circa fidem dubia infallibilis veritatis oraculo tollere & explanare; nec continuo indictis ad hoc ipsum Conciliis, indicat. ad Alex. VII. quod Papa sit vera fidei regula, pag. 73. quod Papæ aliquid ad salutem pertinens mandanti parendum sit, ita ut non inquiratur in rationem ejus, quod facit, aut ejus, quod ordinat, pag. 68. quod Ecclesiæ Romanæ oracula terminent infallibiliter omnes controversias, quæ oriuntur in Ecclesia, quia Papa non potest errare in suis judiciis, quando proponit in qualitate vicarii Jesu Christi dogma fidei, ut recipiatur generaliter à tota ecclesia, quæ non possit falli in eo recipiendo; quia duplex sit species infallibilitatis, una activa, altera passiva, quarum illa ad Papam, quando dogma aliquod fidei in qualitate Vicarii Jesu Christi decidit; hæc vero ad Ecclesiam, quando illa recipit ejus decisiones, pertineat; utraque authoritatem habens à verbo Dei, qui non potest nos fallere. pag. 144. quod Pontifex Max. utpote authoritate certò Divina pollens, nec ex fidelium multitudine amplificetur, nec ex paucitate eorum minuatur. Dedic. ad Alex. quod D. N. Jesus Christus S. Petro & ejus Successoribus dederit omnem illam authoritatem, quam ipse recepit à suo Patre ad gubernandum suum gregem. pag. 82. & 138. quod Papa sit depositarius thesaurorum scientiæ &
units.tr: that the emergence of a doubtful question of faith belongs to the Pope alone, to settle and explain by the oracle of infallible truth, without the immediate summoning of councils for this purpose; to Alexander VII, that the Pope is the true rule of faith, p. 73. that whatever the Pope commands that pertains to salvation must be obeyed, so that no inquiry is made into the reason for what he does or for what he ordains, p. 68. that the oracles of the Roman Church infallibly end all controversies that arise in the Church, because the Pope cannot err in his judgements when, in the capacity of vicar of Jesus Christ, he proposes a dogma of faith to be received generally by the whole Church, which cannot be deceived in receiving it; because there are two kinds of infallibility, one active and the other passive, of which the former belongs to the Pope when, in the capacity of Vicar of Jesus Christ, he decides some dogma of faith, and the latter belongs to the Church when it receives his decisions; both having their authority from the word of God, who cannot deceive us, p. 144. that the Supreme Pontiff, as one endowed with authority certainly divine, is neither increased by the multitude of the faithful nor diminished by their paucity, Dedication to Alexander. that our Lord Jesus Christ gave to St Peter and his successors all that authority which he himself received from his Father to govern his flock, pp. 82 and 138. that the Pope is the depositary of the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge

units.la: Ubi Sorbona Vernantii de potestate Papæ propositiones varias obelo configit. Sapientiæ Jesu Christi, & (horresco referens) in ipso omnes thefauri sapientiæ & scientiæ sint absconditi. pag. 82.
