Harum fimiliumque blasphemiarum potiùs, quàm assertionum meritissima condemnatio à Sorbona facta Papam & Sorbonæ, & Curiæ Parisiensi, partes Sorbonæ suscipienti, insensum denuò reddidit.
units.tr: Here the Sorbonne marks with an obelus various propositions of Vernantius concerning the power of the Pope. of Jesus Christ, and (I shudder to say it) in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. p. 82. The Sorbonne's most deserved condemnation of these and similar blasphemies, rather than assertions, made the Pope and those of the Sorbonne, and the Parisian Curia that took up the Sorbonne's side, hostile once again.

units.la: CCLXXXII. Posterior dissidii occasio ex novitiæ Theologiæ Moralis Jesuitarum, ceu quintæ singularis eorundem hæresèos non simplicis, sed ex multis compositæ, portentosis dogmatibus nata est.
units.tr: CCLXXXII. The second occasion of the dispute arose from the portentous dogmas of the new Moral Theology of the Jesuits, which is, as it were, the fifth peculiar heresy of the same men, not simple but composed of many.

units.la: De qua, occasione sic se aptante, pauca hèic differenda fuerint, ut quo pacto non in fidei duntaxat, sed morum etiam vitæque doctrina Ecclesia Romana in pejus quotidie præcipitaverit, liquidò appareat. Quemadmodum Ecclesia Romana pietatis sanctitatisque morum in Decalogo præscriptæ speciem mentita, ejusdem vim abneget, & legem Divinam plumbeam regulam, nasúmqne cereum faciat, comparatione singulorum Decalogi præceptorum, & doctrinæ de Moribus Pontificiæ, alibi fusiùs ostensum est. Sed id magis etiam novitia illa Moralis & Casuistica Jesuitarum Theologia, à Navarro, Toleto, Emmanuele Sà, Azorio, Diana Panormitano, Lessio, Sanchez, Filliucio, Escobario, Mendoza, aliis prodita, demonstrat. Hoc unum satagunt, ut peccata populi elevare, sceleribus decumanam portam aperire, turpissima quæque quæsitis frivolis & Sophisticis prætextibus, velut fuco & cerussa quadam obducta & palliata, incautis mentibus propinare & instillare, denique scelera authoritate fidei docere queant. Adeò quidem id verum est, ut Papista quidam Hallerius, in Baunium laxum Casuistam, memorante Montaltio in Epistola Provinciali quarta, detorquere non dubitaverit verba illa Baptistæ de Christo: Ecce qui tollit peccata mundi? Caramuelis quoque in Epistola ad Dianam verba haud equidem cedro digna, sed carbone notanda sunt: Ego ingenium Dianæ veneror. Ejus industria multas opiniones evasisse probabiles, quæ ante non erant, invidus sit, qui non affirmet. Si jam sunt probabiles, quæ ante non erant, jam non peccant, qui eas sequuntur, licet antea peccaverint. Ergo si ejusmodi peccata ab orbe literario Diana sustulit, merito dicitur AGNVS DEI, QVI SVSTVLIT PECCATA MVNDI. Habento Navarrus & veteres Casuistæ gloriam suam. Sunto leones, & à rigore ac severitate laudantur. Esto AGNVS tu, laudandus à benignitate. Scilicet illi leones fuerunt, Diana & sequaces lenones dicuntur merito. Quis non lectis auditisque talibus stupescat totus!
units.tr: Since the occasion presents itself in this way, a few things should be discussed here, so that it becomes clear how the Roman Church has daily sunk lower, not only in matters of faith but also in the teaching of morals and of life. Just as the Roman Church, pretending to the appearance of piety and holiness of life prescribed in the Decalogue, denies its force and makes the divine law a leaden rule and a waxen nose, has been shown more fully elsewhere by comparing each precept of the Decalogue with the Papist doctrine of morals. But this is shown even more by that new Moral and Casuistic Theology of the Jesuits, put forward by Navarro, Toledo, Emmanuel Sá, Azor, Diana of Palermo, Lessius, Sánchez, Filliucius, Escobar, Mendoza, and others. They have this one aim: to lift up the sins of the people, to open the great gate to crimes, and to pour and instil the most shameful things into unwary minds, covered and cloaked with trivial and sophistical pretexts, as with some rouge and white lead, and so to teach crimes with the authority of faith. So true is this that the Papist Haller, against the lax casuist Bauny, as Montalte recalls in the fourth Provincial Letter, did not hesitate to twist the words of the Baptist about Christ: Behold him who takes away the sins of the world? Also in Caramuel's letter to Diana there are words not worthy indeed of cedar but to be marked with charcoal: I honour the genius of Diana. Let him who does not affirm that by her industry many opinions have become probable which before were not, be envious. If now those are probable which before were not, those who follow them now do not sin, even if they sinned before. Therefore if Diana has removed such sins from the literary world, she is rightly called THE LAMB OF GOD, WHO TAKES AWAY THE SINS OF THE WORLD. Let Navarrus and the old casuists keep their glory. Let them be lions, and be praised for rigour and severity. Be thou the LAMB, to be praised for kindness. Clearly those were lions, and Diana and her followers are rightly called pimps. Who, having read and heard such things, would not be utterly astounded!

units.la: CCLXXXIII. Lubet heic in scenam producere præcipua Theologiæ Moralis Jesuiticæ capita, quæ Je- suitis Viri docti in ipso Papatu, quibus nondum plane conclamatus pudor est, tanquam fœda ὑποθέσεις ob- jectârunt, & utramque in Theologia illorum Morali & Casuistica paginam faciunt.
units.tr: CCLXXXIII. It is worth bringing onto the stage here the principal heads of the Jesuit moral theology, which learned men within the Papacy itself, who have not yet entirely lost their shame, have thrown at the Jesuits as foul hypotheses [ὑποθέσεις], and which make up both pages of their moral and casuistic theology.

units.la: Principium ejus & fundamentum est Probabilitas, de qua axiomata illorum tria sunt, Probabilem scilicet opinionem omnem, etiam falsam & legi Divinæ contrariam à peccato coram Deo excusare: E duabus opinionibus probabilibus minùs probabilem, & minùs tutam amplecti licere: Probabilem opinionem esse, quæ certitudinem non habens, vel gravi authoritate, qualis est unius viri docti & probi; vel non modica ratione nitatur. Summa huc redit, opinionem unius viri docti authoritate, vel ratione modica nixam conscientiæ & actionum moralium regulam esse. Posito ejusmodi fundamento nihil excogitari potest, quod veri peccati rationem habeat. Nunquam enim deerit σοφὸν Φάρμακον, vel probabilis ratio, vel authoritas viri docti & scelerum amantis, qua certissimo peccato aliquis recti color inducatur. Sternitque adeo Probabilitas hæc, illa tantopere Jesuitis damnata Helena, expeditissimam ad Atheismum viam.
units.tr: Its beginning and foundation is Probability, of which their three axioms are: that any probable opinion whatever, even one that is false and contrary to the divine law, excuses from sin before God; that it is lawful to embrace the less probable and less safe of two probable opinions; that an opinion is probable which, not having certainty, rests either on the grave authority of one learned and upright man or on no small reason. The sum of it comes to this: an opinion resting on the authority of one learned man, or on a reason of no small weight, is a rule for conscience and for moral actions. Once such a foundation is laid, nothing can be devised that has the character of real sin. For there will never be lacking a clever remedy [σοφὸν φάρμακον], either a probable reason or the authority of a learned man who loves wickedness, by which some appearance of right may be brought over even the most certain sin. So this Probability, that Helen so greatly condemned by the Jesuits, lays the easiest road to atheism.

units.la: Cujus præcipuæ hypotheses,
units.tr: The chief of these hypotheses are

units.la: veluti de probabilitate, viam, ut merito jam olim Ludovicus Faber, Ludovici XIII. Galliarum Regis Præceptor, totam hanc Casuistarum scientiam nihil aliud esse, quàm artem cum Deo cavillandi dictitaverit. Dogma illud nefarium de Probabilitate excipit alterum de Intentione, seu Methodo dirigenda intentionis. Quam in eo Casuistæ illi collocant, ut in suis quisque actibus licitum aliquem finem intueatur. Actus ipsos ajunt ab hominibus expeti: intentionem à Deo. Qui igitur rectam intentionem habent, eos peccare pernegant. Doctrinam eam, scelerum fœtam matrem, Montaltius Epistola Provinciali Septima ex Jesuitarum plurium scriptis promit, & detestabundus explicat. Illud porro in ea doctrina pervertissimum est, quòd Casuistæ illi intentionem eam non ad Deum & gloriam ejus, sed ad commodum, honorem & concupiscentiam hominum dirigunt: quódque officia suapte natura mala, aut nullis circumstantiis emendata, sola intentione, solo animi flexu, qui in rebus ipsis immutet nihil, bona fieri contendunt. Merito hic cum S. Augustino contra Mendac. cap. 7. exclamamus: Quod sceleratissimum facinus, quod turpissimum flagitium, quod impurissimum sacrilegium non dicatur fieri posse recte atque juste, si semel concesserimus, in omnibus malis operibus hominum ideo non quid fiat, sed quare fiat, quærendum, ut quacunque propter bonas causas facta reperiuntur, nec ipsa mala esse judicentur? Tertium succedit Casuisticæ illius dogma, Ars nimirum mutandi definitiones virtutum & vitiorum. Qua arte subtili quælibet peccata purgantur facile. Ita simonia iis non est oblatio temporalis pro spirituali simpliciter, sed modò, si temporali tanti, vel pluris æstimetur quàm spirituale, & alterius cum altero pretium commutetur. Quartum dogma est de Cogitationibus bonis. Negant peccare hominem in quocunque opere, si Deus gratiam bonarum cogitationum, qua de Deo cogitare, peccatum agnoscere, ei resistere, & si libitum sit, illud evievitare possit, non suppeditet. Id vero belle Epicuræis, aliisque profligatis hominibus, à quorum mentibus semper Deus abest, patrocinatur. Quintum non minus profanum dogma est de (Attritione. quam definiunt illi imperfectam contritionem, seu dolorem ob peccatum, ortum ex pœnarum metu, qui quamvis destitutus charitate Dei, & conjunctus cum solo Sacramento absolutionis, peccatorem justificet. Unde corollarium isthoc, faventibus Jesuitis, Sirmondo, Annato, Pinterello, Moynio, aliis, Montaltius idem deducit: Per totam vitam sic peccata elici, adeoque contingere posse, ut salutem adipiscatur, qui nunquam Deum in tota vita dilexit. Pauca hæc Theologiæ hujus Moralis & Casuisticæ Jesuitarum dogmata, speciminis & veluti πεῷγύμαλῶ loco, in medium afferre libuit.
units.tr: such as that on probability, by which Ludovicus Faber, tutor of Louis XIII, King of France, rightly said long ago that this whole science of the casuists was nothing other than the art of trifling with God. Next to that impious dogma on probability comes the other, on intention, or the method of directing the intention. In this the casuists place the rule that in each of one's actions one should look to some lawful end. They say that men desire the actions themselves, but God looks to the intention. Therefore they deny that those who have a right intention sin. Montalte, in the seventh Provincial Letter, brings out this doctrine, the mother of crimes, from the writings of several Jesuits and explains it with detestation. Moreover, the most perverse thing in this doctrine is that these casuists direct the intention not to God and his glory, but to the convenience, honour and lust of men; and they maintain that deeds evil in their own nature, or not corrected by any circumstances, are made good by the intention alone, by a mere turn of mind that changes nothing in the things themselves. Here we rightly cry out with St Augustine, against Lies, chapter 7: What most wicked deed, what most shameful crime, what most impure sacrilege would not be said to be possibly done rightly and justly, if we once granted that in all the evil works of men one must ask not what is done but why it is done, so that whatever is found to have been done for good reasons is not judged to be evil in itself? A third dogma of that casuistry follows: the art, namely, of changing the definitions of virtues and vices. By this subtle art any sins are easily purged. Thus simony for them is not simply the offering of a temporal thing for a spiritual, but only if the temporal is esteemed as much as or more than the spiritual, and the price is exchanged for one thing against another. The fourth dogma is on good thoughts. They deny that a man sins in any work if God does not supply the grace of good thoughts, by which he may think of God, recognise sin, resist it, and, if he so wishes, avoid it. This indeed favours Epicureans and other profligate men, from whose minds God is always absent. The fifth, no less profane dogma is on attrition, which they define as imperfect contrition, or sorrow for sin, arising from fear of punishment, which, although lacking the love of God and joined with the sacrament of absolution alone, justifies the sinner. From this corollary, which is favoured by the Jesuits Sirmond, Annat, Pinterel, Moyen and others, Montalte draws the same conclusion: that sins may be so repeated throughout life, and so it may happen, that one attains salvation who never loved God in his whole life. I have chosen to bring forward these few dogmas of this Jesuit moral and casuistic theology as a specimen and, as it were, a sample.

units.la: CCLXXXIV. Hinc igitur posterior illa, quam dixi, occasio dissidii nata est.
units.tr: CCLXXXIV. Hence arose that later occasion of dispute which I mentioned.

units.la: Etenim Amadeus Guimenius, Lomarensis, personatus Jesuita, Opusculum Latino idiomate conscriptum edidit, quo probare sustinuit, Theologiam illam Moralem Jesuitarum, quæque illi de probabilitate, intentione, mutatione definitionum, &c. sciscunt, celeberrimorum, Ecclesiæ Doctorum authoritate neutiquam destitui, adeóque in numero falsorum, improbabilium, scandalosorum, erroneorum haberi non debere. Sorbona vero libri impietate commota d. 111. Febr. A.M. D. C. LXV. dogma Probabilitatis nominatim, aliásque consimiles Propositiones, in Opusculo Amedei comprehensas, tanquam falsas, temerarias, libertati ecclesiæ Gallicanæ, Facultatibus Theologiæ, & orthodoxis doctoribus contrarias, solenniter damnavit jugulavítque.
units.tr: For Amadeus Guimenius, Lomarensis, a Jesuit holding a benefice, published a little work written in Latin, in which he maintained that the Moral Theology of the Jesuits, and what they teach about probability, intention, the change of definitions, etc., is by no means destitute of the authority of the most celebrated teachers of the Church, and so ought not to be counted among false, improbable, scandalous, erroneous doctrines. The Sorbonne, however, moved by the impiety of the book, on 11 February 1665 solemnly condemned and crushed the doctrine of probability by name, along with other similar propositions contained in Amadeus's work, as false, rash, and contrary to the liberty of the Gallican Church, to the Faculties of Theology, and to orthodox teachers.

units.la: CCLXXXV. Videri equidem Alexander ipse voluit perniciocifsima illa in Theologiam moralem inducta dogmata penitus improbare. Author enim est Vir doctissimus, Pontificiæ Communionis, Julius Clemens Scotus, in Notis suis adversus Pallavicini Historiam Concilii Tridentini vulgatis, pag. 69. cum Patribus Dominicanis in eorum Generali Capitulo A. M. D. C. LVI. Romæ celebrato, à Magistro Ordinis illius Johanne Baptista Marino referri voluisse, tœdere Beatissimum Patrem tot novarum opinionum hoc Seculo in Theologiam Moralem inductarum, quibus disciplina Evangelica resolvitur, ac conscientiis cum gravi animarum periculo illuditur, & se maximè velle à Theologis in Ecclesia hoc morbo occulto laborantis remedium opus parari ex severiori & tuta Sanctissimi Præceptoris (Thomæ) doctrina, quo HÆC MORUM ET OPINIONUM LICENTIA, quæ in dies grassatur, quasi cauterio cohiberetur. Attamen impietatem illam, qua disciplina Euangelica resolvitur, & conscientiis cum gravi animarum periculo illuditur, ex Cathedra S. Petri damnare non ausus, toleravit utique, qui officii, quod sibi arrogavit, ratione habita proscribere severè debuit; adeóque impietatis ejusdem merito reus peragitur. Scilicet Nepotismo suo Theologiam illam lenocinari cùm animadvertisset, in sinu eam mox fovere cœpit. Monitus enim à Cardinali quopiam, ne adeò effusus esset in Nepotes suos divitiis ac Principatibus augendos, respondit: Domine mi Cardinalis, alios habemus Theologos (Casuistas Jesuitas) qui nobis id fas esse concedunt ac docent.
units.tr: CCLXXXV. Indeed Alexander himself wished to seem to disapprove utterly of those most pernicious doctrines introduced into moral theology. For the author is a very learned man of the Roman communion, Julius Clemens Scotus, who in his notes against Pallavicini's History of the Council of Trent, published, p. 69, reports that at the general chapter of the Dominicans held at Rome in 1656, the Master of that Order, Giovanni Battista Marino, said that the Most Blessed Father was weary of the many new opinions introduced into moral theology in this age, by which evangelical discipline is dissolved and consciences are mocked with grave danger to souls, and that he especially wished a remedy for this hidden disease in the Church to be prepared by the theologians from the stricter and safer doctrine of the most holy Teacher (Thomas), so that this LICENCE OF MORALS AND OPINIONS, which is spreading day by day, might be restrained as if by a cautery. Yet he did not dare to condemn from the Chair of St Peter that impiety by which evangelical discipline is dissolved and consciences are mocked with grave danger to souls. He at least tolerated it, though he ought to have proscribed it severely, given the office he had claimed for himself; and so he is rightly convicted of the same impiety. Indeed, when he noticed that his nephews were being favoured by that theology, he soon began to foster it in his bosom. For when a certain cardinal warned him not to be so lavish in enriching his nephews with wealth and princedoms, he replied: My lord Cardinal, we have other theologians (the Jesuit casuists) who grant and teach us that this is lawful.

units.la: CCLXXXVI. De eo quicquid sit, Alexander utraque illa, & priore & posteriore, unius anni intervallo di- sparata Sorbonæ Parisiensis censura mirum in modum exulceratus est.
units.tr: CCLXXXVI. Whatever the case, Alexander was greatly exasperated by the Sorbonne's censure of Paris, both the earlier and the later, which were separated by an interval of one year.

units.la: Nam Pace cum Rege Galliæ ob violatum à Corsis Legatum offenso, & armis jam insistente, ac extrema quæque interminante, interventu Principis Florentini A. M. D. C. LXIV. hac scilicet præcipua lege, ut Corsis ejectis Cardinalis Chisius Lutetiam Parisiorum deprecatum veniret, sancita, Brevi ad Regem Christianissimum Romæ apud S. Petrum sub annulo Piscatoris die VI. Aprilis A. M. D. C. LXV. da-
units.tr: For, being offended by the violation of the Legate by the Corsicans, and already taking up arms and threatening every extremity, he concluded a peace with the King of France in 1664 through the intervention of the Florentine Prince, on the chief condition that, the Corsicans being expelled, Cardinal Chigi should come to Paris to make his apology. A Brief was issued at Rome, at St Peter's, under the Fisherman's ring, on 6 April 1665, and was da-

units.la: Sorbonam apud Regem ob geminam censuram idem graviter accusat. dato, & per Nuntium ad eundem ablegatum, omni studio obnixéque petiit, uti authoritate Regia præsto esse vellet, quò Sorbona illa condemnatio utraque (qua scilicet & Vernantii Propositiones de infallibilitate Papæ, & Guimenii librum, ac cum eo tetra illa Theologiæ Moralis dogmata confixerat) revocaretur. Subjungit Apostolicum Breve: Quod profecto speramus de singulari pietate tua, quæ Propositiones Apostolicæ Sedi tam adversas & injuriosas in Regno & Academia tua tolerare non poterit. Hic nempe intimus & quæsitissimus dolor animum Pontificis ussit, quòd per Censuras Sorbonæ denuo prætensam infallibilitatem suam tentari evertique, & intra unius anni spatium duos libros ob assertam Papæ Monarchiam ad rigidam censuram vocari cerneret.
units.tr: [continued from above] given and sent by a nuncio to the same King. The Pope earnestly and insistently asked him, by royal authority, to be present so that the Sorbonne's condemnation, both parts of it (namely, the propositions of Vernantius on the infallibility of the Pope, and the book of Guimenius together with those foul doctrines of moral theology), might be revoked. The apostolic Brief adds: This we indeed hope from your singular piety, which will not be able to tolerate in your kingdom and academy propositions so hostile and injurious to the Apostolic See. Here indeed a deep and intimate sorrow pierced the Pontiff's mind, because he saw his supposed infallibility being again challenged and overthrown by the censures of the Sorbonne, and within the space of a single year two books, condemned for asserting the Papal monarchy, being called to rigorous censure.

units.la: CCLXXXVII. Cæterum dolor Papæ, Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ capitis, consentientem membrorum συμπαθείαν heic non invenit.
units.tr: CCLXXXVII. Moreover, the sorrow of the Pope, the head of the Papal Church, found no answering sympathy of the members here.

units.la: Neque enim Rex Christianissimus, gnarus utique, quantum ex Majestate peteretur, si Papæ authoritas infallibilis declarata foret, gratificandum Pontificiis desideriis censuit. Providit quippe, si infallibilis Papa pronuntietur, futurum, ut, ceu Infallibilis Judex, Reges pro lubitu excommunicare, regnis & vita spoliare, regna auferre, donare aliis, denique absolutum Monarcham totius Orbis Romano-Catholici inprimis, & in sacris & in Civilibus se iterum gerere, ita ut in Monarchia hac impleatur illud: Dixit, & factum est; Dominabitur à mari ad mare, & Regni ejus finis non erit; animum inducat: quandiu vero fallibilis haberetur, potestatem ejus tanquam fræno constrictam intra modestiæ cancellos coerceri, decreta ejus tanquam erronea rejici, fulmen excommunicationis contra Reges (Henricum III. & IV.) tanquam brutum sperni, ipsúmque Papam Concilio in doctrina, vita & moribus, manentibus saluberrimis decretis & antiquissimis regulis istis: Papa falli, errare potest, Concilio subjacet; corrigendum subjici posse. Statim igitur atque Rex Pontificium Breve Parlamento examinandum obtulit, illud prolixo, efficaci, multisque rationibus munito responso demonstravit, Regem sine laesione jurium Coronae, suaeque authoritatis non posse assentiri postulato Pontificis. Et cum Sententiae Facultatis Theologicae in censuris expressae eadem sint, quae Patrum & Conciliorum, S. Sedis, omnium Parlamentorum & Universitatum Regni, tantum abesse, ut condemnari illae debeant, ut potius Facultas debeat validè excitari ad perseverandum in illis. Extátque Consilium Parlamenti integrum in libro, quo Collectio variorum scriptorum in Censuras Facultatis Theologicae Parisiensis de Hierarchia Ecclesiae & Theologia Morali continetur.
units.tr: For the Most Christian King, fully aware of how much would be sought from his Majesty if the authority of the Pope were declared infallible, did not think fit to grant the Papists' desires. He foresaw that if the Pope were pronounced infallible, he would, as an infallible judge, excommunicate kings at will, strip them of kingdoms and life, take away realms and give them to others; and that, in short, he would once more act as an absolute monarch of the whole Roman Catholic world, especially in both sacred and civil affairs, so that in this monarchy there would be fulfilled the saying: He spoke, and it was done; he shall rule from sea to sea, and his kingdom shall have no end. But so long as he was held to be fallible, his power, as if bridled, would be restrained within the bounds of moderation; his decrees would be rejected as erroneous; the thunderbolt of excommunication against kings (Henry III and IV) would be scorned as harmless; and the Pope himself, in doctrine, life and morals, could be made subject to correction by a Council, the most wholesome decrees and most ancient rules remaining in force: The Pope can fall and err; he is subject to a Council. So, as soon as the King submitted the Pontifical Brief to Parliament for examination, Parliament showed by a lengthy, effective response, fortified with many arguments, that the King, without injury to the rights of the Crown and to his own authority, could not assent to the Pope's demand. And since the judgments of the Theological Faculty expressed in its censures are the same as those of the Fathers and Councils, of the Holy See, of all the Parliaments and Universities of the realm, so far is it from being right that these should be condemned, that rather the Faculty ought to be vigorously stirred up to persist in them. The full counsel of Parliament survives in a book containing a Collection of various writings on the censures of the Parisian Theological Faculty concerning the Hierarchy of the Church and Moral Theology.

units.la: CCLXXXVIII. In eo Consilio agnoscit Suprema Curia, Papam, utpote Episcopum primum, esse caput ecclesiae; idque per Galliam, & in omnibus Scholis Facultatis Theologicae semper receptum fuisse profitetur.
units.tr: CCLXXXVIII. In that judgment the Supreme Court acknowledges that the Pope, as first bishop, is the head of the Church, and it declares that this has always been received throughout France and in all the schools of the Theological Faculty.

units.la: Hanc ἀπροχλὼ & praerogativam diserte negat eo valere, ut Papa infallibilis, & Canonibus non subjectus statuatur. Galliam porro, non obstante concordia, quam semper cum Romana sede coluerit, à Curiae Romanae illegitimis usurpationibus sibi cavisse semper, omnémque Ecclesiae Gallicanae libertatem duobus his magnis principiis inniti, quòd Papa subjectus sit decretis Conciliorum; & quòd ejus authoritas non sit Monarchia, sed authoritate ecclesiae inferior. Post infallibilitatem Papae pluribus exemplis oppugnat & convellit; veluti Sixti V. cujus Biblia & Bullam editionem eorum approbantem Clemens VIII. suppresserit; Pauli IV. Praedecessorum suorum fallibilitatem in pleno Consistorio agnoscentis; Adriani VI. qui in IV. Sententiarum librum, etiam in secunda editione, ejus jam Pontificis jussu procurata, asša voce scripsit, plures Romanos Pontifices haereticos fuisse; Gregorii XI. in Testamento revocantis & detestantis ea, in quibus erravit; Johannis XXII. negantis, animas mortuorum ante unionem cum Corporibus Cœlo frui; Bonifacii VIII. in Extravagante Vnam Sanctam, ceu articulum fidei definientis, quòd Reges in temporalibus à Sede Romana dependeant; Innocentii III. qui Serm. 2. de consecrat. fatetur, se propter peccatum, quod in fide committit, ab Ecclesia judicari posse; Paschalis II. qui investiturae privilegium, primò concedens, post se errâsse fassus in Concilio Lateranense veniam petiit; Honorii I. Monotheletae; Vigilii condemnationem trium Capitulorum prohibentis; Gelasii I. Leonis I. & Siricii agnoscentium, quòd Concilio inferiores sint. Ex quibus Pontificum dictis factisque hoc ad extremum συμπεφωσμα Curiae Assessores formant: Quando sententiae sunt oppositae, oportet ut alterutra pars erret. Jam vero inter Pontifices veteres omnes fere agnoverunt se fallibiles & Conciliis inferiores. Recentiores contra praetendunt, quòd errare non possint, & quòd tota ecclesia summè ab illorum imperio dependeat. Oportet ergo ut alterutri errârint, ac proin ut infallibilitas non sit inseparabilis praerogativa suprema illorum dignitatis. Pontificum dictis factisque Constantiensis & Basileensis Conciliorum, quorum eam in rem decreta tuentur, definitiones subjiciunt; distinctionem Papae ut privati & publici Doctoris, nec non praejudicium ob receptas Innocentii X. Bullas Anti-Janseniticas, discutiunt; tandemque concludunt Papam haud dubie praeoccupatum & pessimè informatum Censurarum revocationem exegisse. Esse multa ex adverso, de quibus alii juste conquerantur, veluti quod singulis annis Romae publicetur Bulla, dicta in Caena Domini, Summis Potestatibus iniqua: quod nuper iterum typis impressum sit Decretum Inquisitionis, quo condemnetur Senatusconsultum factum contra Johannem Castellum.
units.tr: It flatly denies that this primacy [ἀπροχλὼ] implies that the Pope is infallible and not subject to the canons. It further states that France, despite the harmony she has always maintained with the Roman See, has always guarded herself against the illegitimate usurpations of the Roman Curia, and that all the liberty of the Gallican Church rests on two great principles: that the Pope is subject to the decrees of councils; and that his authority is not a monarchy, but is inferior to the authority of the Church. It then attacks and overthrows the infallibility of the Pope with many examples: for instance, Sixtus V, whose Bible and whose bull approving its edition were suppressed by Clement VIII; Paul IV, who in full consistory acknowledged the fallibility of his predecessors; Adrian VI, who in the fourth book of the Sentences, even in the second edition made by order of that same pope, wrote in plain words that several Roman pontiffs had been heretics; Gregory XI, who in his testament revoked and detested the things in which he had erred; John XXII, who denied that the souls of the dead enjoy heaven before their union with their bodies; Boniface VIII, who in the Extravagant Unam Sanctam defined, as an article of faith, that kings depend on the Roman See in temporal matters; Innocent III, who in Sermo 2 de consecratione confesses that he can be judged by the Church for a sin committed against the faith; Paschal II, who at first granted the privilege of investiture, and afterwards, having confessed his error in the Lateran Council, sought pardon; Honorius I, the Monothelite; Vigilius, who forbade the condemnation of the Three Chapters; and Gelasius I, Leo I and Siricius, who acknowledged that they are inferior to a council. From these sayings and deeds of the popes, the assessors of the Curia form this final conclusion: When opinions are opposed, one side must be in error. Now indeed nearly all the ancient popes acknowledged that they were fallible and inferior to councils. The more recent ones, on the contrary, claim that they cannot err, and that the whole Church depends wholly on their command. Therefore one of the two sides must have erred, and so infallibility is not an inseparable prerogative of the supreme dignity of those men. They then set against the sayings and deeds of the popes the definitions of the Councils of Constance and Basel, whose decrees on this matter they uphold; they examine the distinction between the Pope as a private and as a public teacher, and also the prejudice arising from the bulls of Innocent X against the Jansenists, which had been received; and at last they conclude that the Pope, doubtless preoccupied and very badly informed, demanded the revocation of the censures. There are many things on the other side about which others justly complain: for example, that every year at Rome the bull read on Maundy Thursday, unjust to supreme powers, is published; and that recently the decree of the Inquisition condemning the senatus-consultum passed against John Castel has been printed again.

units.la: CCLXXXIX. Alexandri jussu A. M. D. C. LXIV. pro- diit novus Index Librorum Prohibitorum, una cum ejus- dem eam in rem Bulla die v. Martii ejusdem anni edita. Vi-
units.tr: CCLXXXIX. By the order of Alexander, in the year 1664, a new Index of Prohibited Books came out, together with the bull issued for that purpose on 5 March of the same year.

units.la: dere ibi inter alia est Indicem Decretorum, quæ vel à Magistro sacri Palatii, vel ab ipsis Congregationibus Sacris Indicis & S. Officii emanárunt. Animadversionem meretur nonnullam, quòd in solo Decreto LXVII. d. x. Jun. A. M. D. C. LVIII. condito à Sacra Indicis Congregatione libri sequentes, Pontificii omnes, ne exceptis quidem ipsorum Pontificum summorum, Urbani VIII. & Innocentii X. Bullis, prohibiti proscriptíque sunt. I. Anonymi Opusculum; quod inscribitur A. S. C. Dissertatio pro Francisco Suarez de gratia ægro oppresso collata per absolutionem à Sacerdote præsente impensam, prævia peccatorum expositione Epistolari. II. Magni Bullarii Romani Tomus quartus SS. Pontificum Urbani VIII. & Innocentii X. Constitutiones complectens: Donec expurgetur ab adjectis. Expurgari autem debet, ut sequitur. Auferatur Constitutio 25. incipiens: Sacrosanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ. Auferantur præterea sex paginæ à pagina signata 289. usque ad paginam signatam 300. III. Domus Sapientiæ, quam septem suffulta per allegoriam columnis Fr. Lucas à Monteforti, Mariæ cultoribus novissimè ædificavit. IV. Libri omnes impressi, & qui inconsulta S. Congregatione imprimentur, tractantes controversiam de vera & non interrupta successione filiorum S. Francisci, & de vera forma capitii ejusdem. V. Elenchus librorum omnium prohibitorum ab A. 1636. usque ad A. 1655. ordine Alphabetico per F. Thomam de Augustinis digestus, &c. VI. Petri Picherelli Opusc. Theolog. Dissert. de Missa, item de imaginibus, habita ad fanum Germani coram Regina matre. Appendix ad Dissert. de Missa, & Maldonati Prælectio in Psal. 110. Denique VII. Vera & dilucida expositio præsentis status totius Seraphicæ F. F. Minorum Religionis à S. & magno Francisco Patriarcha inclito, Numine Divino inspirante fundata, per Franc. Bonitum Combassson. Unde de misera servitute eorum, qui Pontifici Romano subsunt, quin & lubrica forte Bullarum & Definitionum Papalium in ipso Papatu, judicium ferri potest.
units.tr: You will find there, among other things, an index of the decrees that were issued either by the Master of the Sacred Palace or by the Sacred Congregations of the Index and of the Holy Office. One point deserves some comment: in decree LXVII alone, issued by the Sacred Congregation of the Index on 10 June 1658, the following books, all of them Papist, were prohibited and proscribed, not even excepting the bulls of the supreme pontiffs Urban VIII and Innocent X themselves. (I) An anonymous little work, entitled A. S. C. Dissertation in favour of Francisco Suárez, on grace conferred on a sick man oppressed by absolution given by a priest present, with a prior epistolary exposition of sins. (II) The fourth volume of the great Roman Bullarium, containing the constitutions of the Supreme Pontiffs Urban VIII and Innocent X: until it is purged of the additions. It must be purged, as follows. Constitution 25, beginning Sacrosanctae Romanae Ecclesiae, is to be removed. Moreover, six pages are to be removed, from the page numbered 289 to the page numbered 300. (III) The House of Wisdom, which Fr. Lucas of Montfort, a lover of Mary, has most recently built, supported by seven columns in an allegory. (IV) All printed books, and those to be printed without the consent of the Sacred Congregation, treating of the controversy about the true and uninterrupted succession of the sons of St Francis, and about the true form of their tonsure. (V) A list of all books prohibited from 1636 to 1655, arranged in alphabetical order by Fr. Thomas de Augustinis, etc. (VI) Petri Picherelli's little theological work, a dissertation on the Mass, likewise on images, delivered at Saint-Germain before the Queen Mother; an appendix to the dissertation on the Mass; and Maldonatus' lecture on Psalm 110. Finally (VII) A true and clear exposition of the present state of the whole Seraphic Religion of the Friars Minor, founded by the illustrious St Francis, Patriarch, under the inspiration of the Divine Will, by Franc. Bonitus Combassson. From this one may pass judgment on the wretched servitude of those who are subject to the Roman Pontiff, and indeed on the slippery character of the bulls and papal definitions within Papacy itself.

units.la: CCXC. Sed & in alio decreto, quod numero LXXII. est, d. XII. Jan. A. M. D. C. LXI. edito gravissimè Alexander in quosdam in Regno Gallia perditionis filios, in perniciem animarum novitatibus studentes, & Ecclesiasticas sanctiones ac praxin contemnentes invehitur; questus scilicet, ad eam nuper vaefaniam eos pervenisse, ut Missale Romanum Latino idiomate tot Seculorum usu in Ecclesia probato conscriptum, ad Gallicam vulgarem linguam (proh scelus!) convertere, sicque conversum typis evulgare, & ad cujusvis ordinis & sexus personas transmittere ausi fuerint, & ita Sacro-sancti Ritus majestatem Latinis vocibus comprehensam (ut majestatem omnem rituum Romanorum & sacri mysterii dignitatem in ignota majori longè Ecclesiae parti Latinitate, adeóque in verbis, non in rebus consistere inde constet. quod magiam sapiat nec ne, judicet, qui volet) dejicere & proterere, ac sacrorum mysteriorum dignitatem vulgo exponere temerario conatu tentaverint. Eam novitatem ait Alexander se abhorrere & detestari, ceu perpetui ecclesiae decoris deformatricem, inobedientiae, temeritatis, audaciae, seditionis, schismatis, aliorumque plurium malorum facile productricem. Deinceps contra librum eum sententiam fert his verbis: Missale praedictum Gallico idiomate à quocunque conscriptum, vel imposterum aliàs quomodolibet conscribendum & evulgandum; Motu proprio, & ex certa scientia ac matura deliberatione nostris, perpetuo damnamus, reprobamus & interdicimus, ac pro damnato, reprobato & interdicto haberi volumus, ejusque impressionem, lectionem & retentionem universis & singulis utriusque sexus Christi fidelibus, cujuscunque gradus, ordinis, conditionis, dignitatis, honoris & praeeminentiae, licet de illis specialis & individua mentio foret, existat, sub poena excommunicationis latae sententiae, ipso jure incurrendae, perpetuo prohibemus. Mandantes, quòd statim, quicunque illud habuerint, vel in suturum quandoque habebunt, realiter & cum effectu exhibeant & tradunt locorum ordinariis vel Inquisitoribus, qui nulla interposita momora exemplaria igne comburant, & comburi faciant. En ferventem Alexandri pro Latinitate sua, zelum, qui eo ipso se λατινον Irenæi esse, manifeste prodit!
units.tr: CCXC. But also in another decree, number LXXII, issued on 12 January 1661, Alexander attacks very severely certain sons of perdition in the Kingdom of France, who, eager for novelties to the destruction of souls, despise ecclesiastical sanctions and practice; he complains, namely, that they have fallen into such a frenzy that they have dared to translate the Roman Missal, written in Latin and approved in the Church by the use of so many centuries, into the French vulgar tongue (what a crime!), and, having so translated it, to publish it in print and send it to persons of every rank and sex; and that they have attempted with rash effort to cast down and trample on the majesty of the sacred Rite, comprehended in Latin words (from which it is clear that all the majesty of the Roman rites and the dignity of the sacred mystery consist in Latinity, unknown to the far greater part of the Church, and so in words and not in things; whether this smacks of magic or not, let whoever wishes judge), and to expound publicly the dignity of the sacred mysteries. Alexander says that he abhors and detests this novelty, as a disfigurer of the perpetual glory of the Church, and an easy producer of disobedience, rashness, audacity, sedition, schism and many other evils. Next he pronounces sentence against that book in these words: We, of our own motion, from certain knowledge and mature deliberation, condemn, reprobate and forbid for ever the aforesaid Missal, written or in future to be written and published in the French language by anyone whatever; and we will that it be held as condemned, reprobated and forbidden; and we forbid for ever its printing, reading and keeping to all and each of the faithful of Christ of either sex, of whatever degree, order, condition, dignity, honour and pre-eminence, even if they are named specifically and individually, under the penalty of excommunication, latae sententiae, to be incurred by the law itself. We command that at once whoever has it, or shall at any time have it hereafter, shall really and effectively hand it over to the ordinaries of the places or to the Inquisitors, who without any delay shall burn the copies with fire and cause them to be burned. Behold Alexander's fervent zeal for his Latinity, which manifestly shows him to be himself a Latinist [λατινον] in the sense of Irenaeus!

units.la: CCXCI. An Ecclesia Romana quoad mores saltem, procedente tempore, & post Tridentinum inprimis Concilium melior, an deterior evaserit, hoc potissimum tempore, editis à Julio Clemente Scoto, Italo, Viro doctissimo, A. M. D. C. LXIV. in Pallavicini Historiam Tridentini Concilii Notis, disceptari in ipsa Ecclesia Romana coepit.
units.tr: CCXCI. Whether the Roman Church, at least as regards morals, has as time went on, and especially after the Council of Trent, become better or worse, is now being debated within the Roman Church itself, since the publication in 1664, by Julius Clement Scotus, an Italian and a most learned man, of his notes on Pallavicini's History of the Council of Trent.

units.la: Dixerat Suave Polanus, Mundum recentem vitiis deteriorem esse, quàm antiquum. Ei Pallavicinus regessit, Comœdorum hoc esse proverbium, & vulgi querelam. Suavi patrocinatus Julius Clemens artic. 42. pertendit, assertionem ifthanc repugnare tum Pelagio Papæ, c. Fratern. d. 43. dicenti: Quia defectus nostri temporis, quibus non solum merita, sed corpora ipsa hominum defecerunt, districtionis illius non patitur manere censuram: tum Innocentio c. 10. de hæret. cujus initium: Vergentis in senium Seculi corruptelam, &c. Addit invalescentis corruptionis argumentum, quòd antiquiores plurimi canones propter rigorem, quem fidelium posteriorum animi visi sint haud absque salutis dispendio ferre posse, mutati & aboliti sint. Neque aliam ob causam Adrianum VI. antiquum Canonum Pœnitentialium usum, à multis jam Seculis insuetum revocare conatum esse. Infirmitatem quinetiam horum temporum inde arguit, quód in locum pœnæ peccatis debitæ succesferint indulgentiæ, quas Pontifices Summi superiori & hoc Seculo amplissimas concesserunt. Quid indicant, quæso, inquit, tot leges multiplicatæ à posterioribus Pontificibus, quæ & in dies multiplicantur, ita ut Pontificiæ Bullæ hisce duobus Seculis conditæ amplissima duo volumina conficiant, cùm tamen vix unum conficiant parvum Bullæ quatuordecim Seculis conditæ? Annon tot Reformationis decreta à Concilii Tridentini Patribus promulgata summam in Ecclesia jam morum deformitatem indicant? Observaverat autem jam ante artic. 16. leges Concilii Tridentini ad Reformationem spectantes, arguisse deformatam vehementissimè Christianam Rempublicam fuisse ante Concilium Tridentinum, imò NUNQUAM MAGIS deformatam: in quo, inquit, accusantur Pontifices Summi anteriores cuncti post Martinum V. in Concilio Constantiensi electum A. 1417. Novembr. 11. qui morum hujusmodi deformitates è summa in proprio munere incuria permiserunt, negotiis aliis à Pastorali alienis cura imprimis distenti.
units.tr: Suave Polanus had said that the world has become worse in its vices than it was in antiquity. Pallavicini replied that this is a proverb of comic poets and a complaint of the common people. Julius Clemens, defending Suave in art. 42, maintained that this assertion is contrary both to Pope Pelagius in c. Fratern. d. 43, who says: Because the defects of our time, by which not only merits but the very bodies of men have failed, do not allow that severity of discipline to remain; and to Innocent in c. 10. de hæret., which begins: Of the corruption of an age that is growing old, and so on. He adds, as evidence of the growing corruption, that many of the older canons, because their rigour seemed to the minds of later believers hardly bearable without loss to salvation, have been changed and abolished. Nor was there any other reason why Adrian VI tried to revive the ancient use of the penitential canons, which had long been out of practice. He argues further from the weakness of these times that indulgences have taken the place of the punishment due to sins, indulgences which the supreme Pontiffs have granted most liberally in the last century and in this one. What, I ask, do so many laws, multiplied by later Pontiffs and still multiplying day by day, indicate? The Papal bulls issued in these two centuries fill two very large volumes, whereas the bulls issued in fourteen centuries hardly make one small volume. Do not the many decrees of reform promulgated by the Fathers of the Council of Trent indicate the great deformity of morals already present in the Church? He had observed earlier, in art. 16, that the laws of the Council of Trent concerning reform proved that the Christian commonwealth was most grievously deformed before the Council of Trent, indeed never more deformed: in which, he says, all the supreme Pontiffs before the Council are accused, all of them from Martin V, who was elected in the Council of Constance on 11 November 1417, who through their great carelessness in their own office allowed these deformities of morals, being absorbed in other business foreign to the pastoral care.

units.la: CCXCII. Post Concilium vero Tridentinum concedit equidem Author idem, in plurimis Tridentinas leges ecclesiam reformâsse, nec adeò manifesta conspici in Ecclesiasticis, ac potissimum in animarum Pastoribus, vitia, nominatim carnalia, sicut ante illud Concilium. Addit tamen, reprehensionem non magnopere meruisse Suavem, cùm dixit, post Concilium Tridentinum idem evenisse, quod ante. Nam ut omittatur, aliquot, & non exigui ponderis Tridentini Concilii decreta non servari, veluti de lectione S. Scripturæ, cujus loco alia, præcipuè apud Regulares, reposita sint; de admittendis ad sacros inprimis ordines, Ecclesiasticáisque dignitates, de munere suo explendo à constitutis in Minoribus, de Conciliis Provincialibus ac Diœcesanis, de Dispensationibus, &c. insuper observari à nonnullis monet, post Tridentinum Concilium defectus ingentes, veluti 1. Venerationis Ecclesiarum. in qua Catholicis pluribus præstent non tantùm Græci schismatici, verùm etiam Hebræi ac Turcæ ipsimet. Ut mirandum non sit, si Christus inde irritatus permittat potiùs in Templis jam Christianorum loco suo adorari Mahumetem, ac honorem potiùs Diaboli propagari in hæreticorum fanis. 2. Humilitatis Christianæ. Nam plurimos mercari etiam titulos, ut aliis sint pares vel superiores; vel eos Post Concilium Tridentinum Ecclesiam Pontificiam in melius mutatam non esse, idem Julius Clemens fuse efficaciterque demonstrat supra conditionem suam exigere; quærere nonnulla observantiæ ac venerationis suæ signa sibi exhiberi olim insueta, vel non debita, quæ nisi exhibeantur, acriter eos indignari, nec non indignationis argumenta præbere; in cunctis motibus corporis faštum quendam præ se ferre cæteris odiosum; præferre se aliis vel in nobilitate, vel in doctrina, vel in pietate, aut etiam in his omnibus. Idque etiam magis detestabile esse, si sentiant, esse potius humilitatis speciem, Communitatem suam cæteris omnibus anteferre, ac re ipsa præferre; nihil non sibi deberi arbitrentur; supra alios honores, prærogativas, privilegia sibi acquirere satagant; ferè toti sint in suis & communitatis suæ laudibus extollendis, ac interdum falsis; prædicent, aliqua à se præclarè gesta, quandoque mentientes, vel exaggerantes; humanam duntaxat gloriam in actionibus cæteroquin piis, ut in ædificandis ecclesiis, donanda supplectile sacra &c. propositam habeant, nedum in iis, quæ circa proximorum salutem agunt. 3. Dierum festorum observationis. Cùm enim illi sint indicti præsertim ad Dei cultum, plerosque dæmonem potiùs colere, indulgentes Veneri, gulæ & ludis. 4. Simplicitatis Christianæ à Christo commendatæ Matth. cap. 10. non solùm in vestitu & victu, verùm in verbis etiam & factis. Atque defectum eum ait à non paucis adscribi sententiæ hoc Seculo propagatæ de Restrictione Mentali, causisque ea utendi, addito etiam juramento de ea non adhibenda, juxta Sanchezium. Inde scilicet fieri, ut perraro ullus possit esse tutus de ullius promissione; aut certò credere possit, eum, qui nonnulla scribit aut edit, ita interius sentire. Apud aliquos inductam hinc esse opinionem, quòd liceat publicum & religiosum cultum exhibere idolo, eidem offerre incensum, flores &c. illi sacrificantibus ministrare, dummodo crucem vel in manu gestaret, vel inter flores, aut supra pectus repositam. tam quis haberet. Infelix hoc esse Seculum, quòd illa sententia tot, & quosdam præcipuè, sortita sit assertores. Similiter quot, inquit, simulationes in vultu, gestu, aliisque motibus corporis, ita ut sæpissimè, qui nonnullis arridcnt præsentibus, absentes postea irrideant. Simplicitati porro calliditatem, fallaciam; sinceritati adulationem successisse, ita ut complures instar Gnathonis in omnibus planè ad quorundam Magnatum voluntatem seu voluptatem loquantur & agant, quin etiam omnia eorum gesta, etiam minùs recta commendent. Affine huic esse hypocriseos vitium, Sicut enim sub specie pietatis hæreses fermè omnes in Ecclesiam inductæ sunt, ita quoque pravas multorum cupiditates eadem specie obtegi. 5. Prudentiæ Christianæ: quæ dictat, nunquam æternam salutem posthabendam commodis quibuslibet temporalibus. Ejus locum subiisse Politicam quandam falsam ac Ethnicam, dictantem, dummodo quis temporalem, vel status sui felicitatem assequatur, nullam juris Divini, imò nec naturalis rationem habendam, ita ut illa sit omnium prorsus suprema lex, quam amplectantur inprimis illi (horum, inquit, NB. hoc Seculo maximè censetur major numerus, quàm ut sic Lutheranorum, Calvinistarum &c.) qui à quibusdam Politici etiam post Concilium Tridentinum appellantur, Atheismo communiter infecti; sive hic sit ille, qui est insipientium, nullum planè Deum, seu nullam planè incorpoream agnoscens substantiam; sive sit ille, qui dicitur Aristotelicus à quibusdam, admittens primam causam saltem finalem rerum, omni materia carentem, curæ tamen rerum inferiorum, seu Providentiæ expertem. Cui sententiæ connexam ait illam de animæ rationalis mortalitate, qua hæresi nulla sit perniciosior vel animabus nostris, vel bonis moribus. Quod, inquit, Seculum protulit tot ex omni genere scriptores de Politicis, sicut nostrum? Quosdam ex Ecclesiasticis etiam majori sibi tribuere laudi ait, si dicantur vel existimentur Magni Politici, aut in Politicis versatissimi, quàm si egregiè probi & docti. Et utinam, inquit, non hoc nomine Ecclesiasticæ Dignitates, etiam primariæ compluribus deferantur! 6. Charitatis. cujus desectum varie arguens, consistere eum docet Tum in non erogandis pauperibus verè superfluis, & quæ à tineis & muribus sæpe comeduntur. quod in Ecclesiasticis beneficiis fruentibus maximè vituperandum monet, qui si erogarent liberalius, non tot pauperes ac mendicos fore in urbibus, tot honestas familias ad incitas redactas pudorem minorem passuras, nec tot meretricium quæstum facturas; quibus noxiam dicit opinionem à recentioribus Theologis & Canonistis probatam, quod ecclesiastici è sola charitate, non ex justitia ad superfluorum erogationem tenantur; reprehensa etiam eorum detestabili avaritia, qui in operibus piis in proximorum salutem non reapse quærunt animas Deo lucrari, vel Deo acceptiores reddere, sed marsupia sibi, ac domesticam suppellectilem auctiorem reddere; nec non opera quædam spiritualia excogitant potissimum, ut inde lucra sibi, vel suis reportent; atque in ipsamet Sacramentorum administratione, vel in Reliquiarum propositione, vel ejusmodi aliis pecuniæ exhibitionem intendunt, qui nunquam satis esse dicerent, quamvis copiosissimos reditus haberent, excusantes se, quò illis abundantiores forent, hoc ampliorem numerum Ecclesiasticorum seu Religiosorum alendum esse: Tum in bellis inter Principes injustis: Tum in inimicitiis perpetuis non raro inter præcipuas in civitatibus familias; nec non discordiis domesticis: Tum in odiis complurium immortalibus, etiam inter Ecclesiasticos & Regulares, controversias sæpe acerbissimas cum aliis quærentes, Pacis osores, scriptis librisque non raro se invicem lacerantes. Ejusmodi di autem dissensiones inter Regna, familias, Ecclesiasticos, Religiosos etiam Romanæ Curiæ vigere queritur, ut verendum sit, ne sicut Gentiles priscis Ecclesiæ Seculis mutuam Christianorum charitatem attendentes, & admirantes exclamabant, teste Tertulliano Apolog. cap. 29. O quantum se diligunt Christiani! merito nunc cum lachrymis exclamari queat à Catholicis piissimis, & harum dissensionum consciis: O quantum se oderunt Christiani! Deinceps invehitur in homicidia, quæ in aliqua Christiana regione plura, quàm in Imperio Turcico patrari innuit: in detractores famæ adeò frequentes, ut nullum vitium sit communius. Ubi Patres inprimis Societatis Jesu criminis ejus reos convincit testimonio P. Mutii Vitellesci, in libro ad Vniv. Societ. qui prolata querimonia B. Francisci Borgiæ, Societatis illius Generalis, quòd multi ad Societatem veniant, ut fiant ditiores, pauci, ut fiant meliores; subjungit: Ne quæso nobis, Patres, Fratresque blandiamur. Non pauci hoc in genere (detractionis vitio) valido fræno indigent. Nomini parcunt, nimia agunt libertate & licentia, non sine gravi charitatis justitiaque interdum injuria; dum aliena seu dicta, seu facta nunc amplificata augent, modo ultro citróque renuntiant, nunc in deteriorem partem accipiunt; ad motus animi, atque consilia Deo reservata dijudicanda progrediuntur; haud scio, an dicendum sit, res neque gestas unquam, neque per somnium quidem oblatas comminiscuntur & jactant. Equidem mihi persuadeo, consultò ac dedita opera non delinqui, qui sciam, quantus Dei timor ipso adjuvante, in Societate vigeat. Verùm affirmo inconsiderantiam, indiligentiam, lubricitatem hac in re malum esse longè gravissimum; atque utinam interdum Divina Majestas nihilo magis, quàm leviter lædatur, eóque periculosius, quò minùs inde conscientia onerari alicui fortasse videbitur. Ego verò, quoniam exonerare meam statui, mihíque persuadeo, innumera hinc bona nobis intercludi, atque ex hoc fonte inprimis, & universè derivari mala, quæ æquissimo Domini judicio toleramus, ex intimis cordis mei visceribus obtestor, Examen, quod vocamus, Particulare, accuratum per hosce dies in hoc vitium instituant; quandoquidem LATIVS quàm opus esset, illud SERPERE per Societatem DEPLORAMVS OMNES, fatemúrque, venenosæ hujus atque EXCRABILIS plantæ fibris evulsis, terrestrem quendam Paradisum illam futuram. Addit testimonium ejusdem Societatis Generalis Aquavivæ, cui cùm indicâssent Patres Congregationis Romanæ, detractionis isthoc vitium & loquendi libertatem ita in Societate ea crescere, ut non pauci videantur id sine scrupulo facere, & quidem in materiis & rebus non levibus, sic ille respondit: Magno nostro dolore videmus, propositionem hanc veram esse. Et ab hac Societate posthac manâsse isthoc detrahendi cacoethes ad alios, ac potissimùm Claustrales, Author idem mox graviter quiritatur. Quin & Pallavicinum, qui Suavis de corruptione crescente Ecclesiæ assertionem inter Comœdorum Proverbia retulit, testimonio etiam Urbani VIII. & Alexandri inprimis VII. affirmantis, per novas opiniones hoc Seculo in Theologiam moralem inductas disciplinam Euangelicam resolvi, & conscientiis cum gravi animarum periculo illudi; morúmque & opinionum licentiam in dies graßari convicit. Denique licet concedatur, minora vitia tum contra castitatem, tum contra temperantiam patrari nunc in Ecclesia, ab Ecclesiasticis inprimis, post Concilium Tridentinum quàm ante; non minùs tamen spiritualibus vitiis, superbiæ, avaritiæ, invidiæ, detractioni, susurrationi, dolosæ simulationi, fidei datæ violationi, malevolentiæ, hypocrisi, aliisque similibus deditos esse Catholicorum animos, mox fusè ibidem comprobat; totámque ea de re dissertationem claudit S. Bernhardi in verba illa Esajæ cap. XXXVIII. Ecce in pace amaritudo mea amarissima, commentatione, quæ serm. 33. in Cantic. ejusmodi extat: Amara prius in nece Martyrum: Amarior post in conflictu hæreticorum: Amarissima in moribus domesticorum. units.tr: CCXCII. After the Council of Trent, the same author does concede that in many respects the Church has been reformed by the Tridentine decrees, and that the vices of ecclesiastics, and especially of the ministers of souls, particularly carnal vices, are not as plainly seen as they were before that Council. He adds, however, that Suavis did not deserve much criticism when he said that after the Council of Trent the same thing has happened as before. For, to pass over the fact that several Tridentine decrees of no small weight are not observed, such as those on the reading of Holy Scripture, which in many places, especially among the regular clergy, has been replaced by other things; on the admission to sacred orders, above all, and to ecclesiastical dignities; on the performance of their duties by those appointed to the minor orders; on provincial and diocesan councils; on dispensations, and so on; he also warns that after the Council of Trent, enormous defects have been noticed by some, such as (1) the reverence due to churches, in which not only the schismatic Greeks but even the Jews and the Turks themselves surpass many Catholics. So it is no wonder that Christ, provoked by this, allows Mahomet to be worshipped in the temples of Christians in place of Himself, and that the honour of the Devil is spread rather in the shrines of heretics. (2) Christian humility. For many seek out titles, so that they may be equal or superior to others; or they seek certain signs of observance and reverence that were formerly unusual or not due to them, and if these are not given, they become angry and provide grounds for indignation; in all their bodily movements they display a certain pride that is hateful to others; they set themselves above others in nobility, in learning, in piety, or in all of these; and it is even more detestable, if they perceive it to be rather a semblance of humility, that they prefer their own community to all others and do so in fact; they think nothing is not owed to them; they strive to acquire for themselves honours, prerogatives and privileges above others; they are almost wholly occupied with extolling their own praises and those of their community, sometimes falsely; they proclaim certain things done by themselves as splendid, sometimes lying or exaggerating; they keep human glory in view even in otherwise pious actions, such as building churches, donating sacred furnishings, and so on, not to mention those actions that concern the salvation of their neighbours. (3) The observance of festival days. For since these have been appointed especially for the worship of God, most people rather worship the devil, indulging in lust, gluttony and games. (4) Christian simplicity, commended by Christ in Matth. cap. 10., not only in clothing and food but also in words and deeds. And he says this defect is ascribed by not a few to the opinion propagated in this century concerning mental restriction, and to the reasons for using it, with an added oath not to employ it, according to Sanchez. The result, namely, is that scarcely anyone can be sure of anyone's promise, or be certain that the man who writes or publishes certain things thinks so inwardly. He says that from this an opinion has been introduced among some that it is permissible to render public and religious worship to an idol, to offer incense or flowers to it, and to minister to those who sacrifice to it, provided one carries a cross either in the hand or hidden among the flowers or on the breast. Who would have thought it? This century is unhappy, he says, in that this opinion has found so many, and some especially, as its advocates. Similarly, he says, there are so many pretences in the face, the gesture and other movements of the body, so that very often those who laugh with some to their faces laugh at them afterwards in their absence. Moreover, cunning and deceit have taken the place of simplicity, and flattery that of sincerity, so that many, like Gnatho, speak and act in every way according to the will or pleasure of certain great men, and even commend all their deeds, even the less upright ones. Closely related to this, he says, is the vice of hypocrisy: for just as almost all heresies have been introduced into the Church under the appearance of piety, so too the wicked desires of many are covered by the same appearance. (5) Christian prudence, which dictates that eternal salvation must never be set aside for any temporal advantage. In its place there has come a certain false and heathen Politics, which dictates that, provided one attains temporal happiness or the well-being of one's state, no account at all should be taken of divine law, or even of natural reason; so that this becomes the supreme law of all, to be embraced above all by those (of these, he says, NB. in this century the greater number is thought to be of such a kind, as the Lutherans, the Calvinists, etc.) who are called by some Politicians, even after the Council of Trent, commonly infected with Atheism; whether this is that atheism of fools, recognising no God at all, or no incorporeal substance at all; or whether it is that which some call Aristotelian, admitting a first cause, at least a final cause, of things, lacking all matter, yet without care for or providence over inferior things. He says that connected with this opinion is the one about the mortality of the rational soul, a heresy than which none is more harmful either to our souls or to good morals. What century, he asks, has produced so many writers of every kind on Politics as ours? He says that some from among the ecclesiastics think it a greater honour to be called or considered great Politicians, or men most skilled in Politics, than to be outstandingly upright and learned. And would that, he says, ecclesiastical dignities, even the chief ones, were not conferred on many under this name! (6) Charity, whose defect he argues in various ways, and teaches that it consists (1) in not giving to the poor what is truly superfluous, and what is often eaten by moths and mice. This he rightly condemns above all in those who enjoy ecclesiastical benefices: if they gave more generously, there would not be so many poor and beggars in the cities, so many respectable families reduced to want would not suffer less shame, and so many would not make a trade of prostitution. He says that a harmful opinion, approved by more recent theologians and canonists, that ecclesiastics are bound to give away superfluities out of charity alone, not out of justice, is to blame for this. He also rebukes the detestable avarice of those who, in pious works for the salvation of their neighbours, do not really seek to gain souls for God or make them more acceptable to God, but to enlarge their own purses and household furnishings; and who devise certain spiritual works chiefly so that they may gain profit for themselves or their own people; and who, in the very administration of the sacraments, or in the display of relics, or in other such things, aim at extracting money, and who would never say that enough is enough, however abundant their revenues might be, excusing themselves on the ground that the more abundant their income, the greater the number of ecclesiastics or religious that must be supported. (2) in unjust wars between princes; (3) in the perpetual enmities, not infrequently among the chief families in cities, and also in domestic quarrels; (4) in the immortal hatreds of many, even between ecclesiastics and regular clergy, who often seek very bitter disputes with others, enemies of peace, and not infrequently tear one another apart in writings and books. He complains that dissensions of this kind flourish among kingdoms, families, ecclesiastics, and even religious of the Roman Curia, so that one must fear lest, as the Gentiles in the early centuries of the Church, observing and marvelling at the mutual charity of the Christians, used to cry out, as Tertullian witnesses (Apolog. cap. 29.), O how much the Christians love one another! so now the most pious Catholics, and those who are aware of these dissensions, may rightly cry out with tears: O how much the Christians hate one another! Next he attacks the homicides, which he suggests are more numerous in some Christian region than in the Turkish Empire; and the slanderers of reputation, so frequent that no vice is more common. Here he convicts the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, who are guilty of this crime, by the testimony of Father Mutius Vitelleschi, in his book to the whole Society, who, when the complaint of Blessed Francis Borgia, General of that Society, was put forward, that many come to the Society to become richer, few to become better, adds: Let us not, I beg you, Fathers and Brothers, flatter ourselves. Not a few in this respect (the vice of detraction) need a strong bridle. They spare the name, they act with too much freedom and licence, not without serious injury at times to charity and justice; while they now magnify and increase the words or deeds of others, now they report them back and forth, now they take them in a worse sense; they proceed to judge the motions of the mind and the counsels reserved to God; I do not know whether it should be said that they invent and boast of deeds never done and never even dreamed of. I, indeed, am persuaded that those who, as far as I know, do this, do not do so deliberately and with set purpose, since, with God's help, a great fear of God flourishes in the Society. But I affirm that thoughtlessness, carelessness and levity in this matter are a very grave evil; and would that the Divine Majesty were sometimes offended no more than lightly, and that much more dangerously, the less the conscience of anyone may perhaps seem burdened by it. But I, since I have resolved to unburden my own, and am persuaded that countless goods are cut off from us by this, and that from this source in particular, and generally, come the evils which we endure by the most just judgement of the Lord, I beseech from the inmost depths of my heart that they institute, in these days, a careful so-called Particular Examination against this vice; since we all DEPLORE that this has CREPT through the Society more WIDELY than was needful, and we confess that, with the roots of this poisonous and DETESTABLE plant torn out, that will become a kind of earthly Paradise. He adds the testimony of the same General of the Society, Aquaviva, to whom the Fathers of the Roman Congregation had reported that this vice of detraction and this freedom of speech grow so much in that Society that not a few seem to do it without scruple, and indeed in matters and affairs that are not trivial; to which he replied: To our great sorrow we see that this proposition is true. And the same author soon bitterly complains that this itch of detraction has since then spread from this Society to others, and especially to the cloistered religious. Indeed, he also convicts Pallavicino, who included Suavis's assertion about the growing corruption of the Church among the proverbs of the comedians, by the testimony of Urban VIII and especially of Alexander VII, who affirms that through new opinions introduced into moral theology in this century, the Evangelical discipline is dissolved, and consciences are mocked to the grave peril of souls; and he proves that licence of morals and opinions rages more each day. Finally, although it be conceded that lesser vices, both against chastity and against temperance, are now committed in the Church, especially by ecclesiastics, less than before the Council of Trent; yet he at once proves at length in the same place that the minds of Catholics are no less given over to spiritual vices, to pride, avarice, envy, detraction, whispering, deceitful pretence, violation of faith once given, ill will, hypocrisy, and other similar things; and he closes the whole discussion on this matter with the words of Saint Bernard on the verse of Isaiah ch. XXXVIII., Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter, in a comment which appears thus in Sermon 33 on the Canticles: Bitter at first in the slaughter of the Martyrs; more bitter afterwards in the conflict with heretics; most bitter in the morals of those of the household. units.la: CCXCIII. Silentio prætereundum non est hujus potissimum temporis σιδηρόξυλον, Episcopus scilicet Miles. Episcopi enim nonnulli, quorum munus fuerat attendere gregi suo, & pascere ecclesiam Dei sanguine ejus proprio redemptam, in Germania cum primis, strenuè Mavorti litantes, novo etiam & insolito armorum fœtore tantùm non obvias enecantium genere, ad ferrum & flammam omnia vocabant. Quorum in censu Christophorus Bernhardus à Galen, Monasteriensis Episcopus, verus Seculi nostri Cyclops, qui inter arma adolevit, & consenuit, nominari cumprimis meretur. Non tantùm enim urbem celebrem Monasteriensem Westphaliæ armis suis domitam sub jugum misit, & post in Bello HungaricoTurcico, Imperialis Militiæ Directorem se gessit: sed etiam auro promiscuè, modò Angliæ, modò Galliarum Regis, conduci se ad ferenda infesta signa passus, τὰς προφὰς ἐιωθὼς ἔχειν ἐκ τῆς μισθοφορίας, quæstum unum habens ex militia, uti Philippus Macedo apud Didorum Sicul. lib. xviii. mercenarios milites describit; bis Belgis Fœderatis atrocissimum bellum intulit, urbes florentissimas dirum in modum quassavit, cœdibus omnia miscuit, & à Turcico milite Janitzaro nihil admodum discrepans, vi & dolo grassatus ubique est; denique in electione Coadjutoris A. M. D. C. LXVII. victus suffragiis spretóque Electore Coloniense, cui plura vota favebant, armis placitum sibi obtrusit. Ut non huic minus, quàm cuiquam flamini alii illud Palingenii quadret: Pontifices nunc bella juvant, sunt cætera nugæ. Tantísque in deliciis pullum huncce suum Alexander habuit, ut Roma ipsi gladium sacratum, cœdis impunè patrandæ auctoramentum submiserit, virtutémque ejus militarem non semel impensè collaudaverit. CCXCIV. Postulat heic occasio, ut de Ecclesiæ Romanorum... Verbi Divini & vetustæ manæ Episcoporum Bellatorum iniquitate nonnihil differamus. ut vel inde constet, plus recentiores Episcopos à veris & veteribus differre, quàm simia purpura induta ab homine, mus farina aspersus à pistrini domino differt. Quàm severè Christus Regnum suum, cujus se Ministros profitentur Episcopi, à Regnis hujus mundi, quæ armis non raro parantur retinenturque, disparaverit, non jam dicam. Abundè id ex Matth. xx. 25. xxvi. 52. Joh. viii. 36. 1 Cor. iv. 9. &c. liquet. Canon certè Apostolicus Paulinus Episcopum πλήκτην percussorem esse disertè vetat. Sed & Canon Apostolicus alter, huic conformis, numero lxxxiii. jam olim Ecclesiasticis militiam his verbis interdixit: Ἐπίσκοπος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, στρατείαν ἀσκοῦν ... Episcopus, aut Presbyter, aut Diaconus, exercitui vacans, & utraque obtinere volens, Romanum Magistratum & Sacerdotalem administrationem, deponatur. Quæ sunt enim Cæsaris, Cæsari: & quæ sunt Dei, Deo. Ubi per στρατείαν χολάζοντα sive cum Balsamone, Zonara, Harmenopulo militantem, vel militarem rem administrantem; sive cum Doctiss. Beveregio civile quodvis officium administrantem intellexeris; Bellatores Episcopos feriri palam est. Proxima etiam ætas tantùm abest, ut Episcoporum militiam probaverit, ut quadam etiam ἀμελεία ἢ ἀνθολκῆς etiam quamvis militiam, saltem, qualis eo tempore in usu fuit, improbaverit. Primus Gregorius Cappadox Arianus militari manu, pulso Athanasio, Alexandrinam Sedem occupavit. Damasi & Ursicini tragœdiam supra narravimus. Sed isthæc per tumultum contigit. At quarto adhuc Seculo Ambrosius oratione contra Auxentium; Non pila, inquit, quærunt ferrea, non arma Christi milites. Coactus repugnare non novi: sed dolor, fletus, orationes, lachrymæ fuerunt mihi arma adversus milites. Talia enim sunt munimenta Sacerdotis. Aliter nec debeo, nec possum resistere. Sequente quinto Seculo Concilium Chalcedonense canone VII. decrevit, Eos, qui semel in clero taxati fuerint, sive in Monasterio deputati, μήτε ὅτι χρείαν, μήτε ὅτι ἀξίαν κοσμικὴν ἔχειν, neque ad militiam, neque ad honores Seculares venire debere. Eos vero, qui hoc ausi fuerint facere, & non ejus rei poenitere maluerint, ut ad hoc idem revertantur, quod ante obtentu Dei sibi proposuerint, anathematizari convenire. Seculo Septimo circumfertur vulgaris gnome Gregorii M. Episcopi Romani, quae lib. VII. Epist. 1. ad Sabinianum continetur. Si, inquiebat ille, in mortem Longobardorum me immiscere voluissem, hodie Longobardorum gens nec Regem nec Ducem haberet. Sed quia timeo Deum, in mortem cujusquam hominis me miscere formido. Vel igitur Gregorius ea in re non timebat Deum, vel recentiores Pontifices & Episcopi Bellatores Deum non timent. Invenitur equidem inter Epistolas Gregorii alia, cujus fragmentum in c. 2. X. de immunit. Eccl. extat, ex qua communiter Canonistae concludunt, tempore necessitatis ipsos etiam clericos non excusari à custodia civitatis. Sed quid custodire civitatem, stare in excubiis, necessitatis tempore, quod probi civis cujuslibet officium est, commune habet cum eo, quod Episcopi Bellatores ab aliquot inde Seculis fecerunt? Taceo, quòd, notante Augustino Barbosa ad d. c. 2. Modernus observavit, non loqui textum illum de Clericis, sed de hominibus Ecclesiae, qui immunitate Ecclesiae gaudebant. Sanè eodem Seculo in Concilio Toletano IV. can. 44. statutum est, ut Clerici in quacunque factione arma volentes sumere, amisso ordinis sui gradu in Monasterio poenitentia tradantur. Insigne etiam verae ἀπλομαχίας Sacerdotalis exemplum Beda Histor. Eccl. lib. II. 2. narrat; Monachos videlicet è Monasterio Mancor magno numero seorsim stantes, & adversus Regem Edilfridum non armis corporalibus, sed jejuniis & precibus pugnantes. Octavo adhuc Seculo Zacharias Papa Epistola ad Episcopum Moguntinum Bonifacium, de Sacerdotibus queritur, quòd Deum ad iram provocantes majora committant facinora, dum propriis manibus Christianos atque paganos necant, &c. Epist. 3. Qualis, inquit, victoria datur, ubi Sacerdotes una hora Dominica pertentant mysteria, & Christianis Dominicum porrigunt corpus pro suarum animarum redemptione, & propter Christianos, quibus hoc ministrare debuerant, aut paganos, quibus Christum prædicare, propriis sacrilegisque manibus necant. Militum porro & Sacerdotum officia hic idem Zacharias Epist. 7. ad Pipinum Regem distinguit: Principes & Seculares homines atque bellatores convenit curam habere & solicitudinem contra inimicorum astutiam, atque Provinciæ defensionem. Præsulibus verò, Sacerdotibus atque Dei servis pertinet salutaribus consiliis atque orationibus vacare, ut vobis orantibus & illis bellantibus, Deo præstante, Provincia salva persistat. Caroli M. ætate crevit equidem non parum ejusdem indulgentia & liberalitate potestas Episcoporum. Neque tamen Sacerdotibus bellare permissum est; quin potiùs non obscurè id in Concilio Meldensi A. D. CCC. XLV. habito canone 37. interdicitur his verbis: Quicunque ex clero videntur esse, arma militaria non sumant, nec armati incedant; sed professionis suæ vocabulum religiosis moribus, & religioso habitu præbeant. Quod si contempserint, tanquam sacrorum canonum contemptores, & Ecclesiasticæ authoritatis profanatores, proprii gradus amissione multentur, quia non possunt simul Deo & Seculo militare. Inter Capitula quoque Coroli & Ludovici Impp. Lib. VI. num. 61. ejusmodi habetur constitutio: Si quis Episcopus, Presbyter aut Diaconus vel subdiaconus ad bellum processerit, & arma bellica indutus fuerit ad belligerandum, ab omni officio deponatur, in tantum, ut nec laicam communionem habeat. Quin & Leo IV. Papa homil. de cura Pastorali Clericos sui temporis ita alloquitur: Nullus vestrum arma ferat in seditione, quia arma vestra spiritualia esse debent. Quanquam non temperavit sibi Leo, quò minus faceret id, quod aliis prohibuit; dimicans ipse fortiter adversus Saracenos, si vera sunt, quæ de ipso Platina scripsit. Nicolaus I. referente Gratiano c. Clericum 6. dist. 50. Cum discreti sint, inquit, milites seculi à militibus ecclesiæ, non convenit militibus Ecclesiæ militare sæculo, per quod ad effusionem sanguinis necesse sit pervenire. In Concilio quoque Triburiensi A. D. CCC. XCV. celebrato cap. 27. ejusmodi decretum extat: Semel in clero deputati nec ad militiam, nec ad aliquam veniant dignitatem mundanam, uti in Synodo Chalcedonensi statutum est; ne tales sint, sicut S. Isidorus loquitur, similes hippocentauris, qui nec equi nec homines, sed quasi bruta animalia libertate ac desiderio suo feruntur. Pro Clerico quinetiam in bello mortuo vetat Concilium idem vel in oblatione vel in oratione postulari. Seculo demum Decimo, quo temporalis potestatis incrementa Pontifices ceperunt, à veterum Pontificum pietate etiam hic degeneratum Sabellicus Ennead. IX. lib. 2. queritur his verbis: Illi (veteres Pontifices) suo sanguine Pontificum decus auxerunt; hi auctum cædibus & rapinis prophanârunt: donariis illi templa ditârunt, hi sacrilegiis exuerunt, &c. Jactáque alea bellandi libido ita processit, ut A. M. LIII. Leo IX. primus Romanorum Pontificum contra Normannos in Apulia & Calabria Siciliáque imperium auspicantes exercitum nebulonum potiùs quàm militum eduxerit; profligatum à Normannis occulto Dei judicio, uti Hermannus Contractus piè 'Θπιχείρης, quia tantum Sacerdotem spiritualis potiùs, quàm pro caducis rebus carnalis pugna decebat. Reprehensúmque inprimis est à Petro Damiani Cardinale Ostiensi lib. IV. Epist. 9. isthoc Leonis facinus, universáque cleri belligerantis audacia severis verbis perstricta. Vita, inquit, quam Servator noster gessit in carne, non minus quàm prædicatio Euangelica nobis est propositá tenendæ linea disciplinæ. Sicut ergo ipse cuncta mundi furentis obstacula non per [illegible, ~1 letters] districti examinis ultionem, sed per invictam superavit inconcussæ patientiæ Majestatem: ita docet mundi rabiem potius æquanimiter ferre, quàm vel arma corripere; vel lædenti læsionibus respondere, præsertim cum inter Regnum & Sacerdotium propria cujusque distinguantur officia, ut & Rex armis utatur Seculi, & Sacerdos accingatur gladio spiritus, qui est verbum Dei, &c. Deinceps factum Leonis cum peccato Davidis & Petri abnegatione comparat. Mox Gregorius VII. in Dictatibus suis retulit, ut Pontifici Romano Imperialia ornamenta, adeoque gladium etiam gestare liceat: & Bonifacius VIII. definivit, in Ecclesia esse duos gladios, unum pro ecclesia, alterum ab ecclesia exercendum; illumque huic subesse; quin & Petro temporalem gladium fuisse. Quod igitur antehac in vitio merito fuit, id deinceps postquam jurisdictione temporali, & feudorum dominio Principum superstitio & incuria Pontifices & Episcopos mactavit; in virtutem & pietatem vertere coepit. Sacra inprimis seu cruciata militia in Concilio Claromontano ab Urbano II. decreta, Episcopis Sacerdotibus & Monachis tractare arma assuetis. Eoque ventum dementiæ, ut teste Chopp. lib. II. S. Polit. tit. 1. num. 7. Episcopi nonnulli sacra facientes supra altare suspensum gladium, vitæ necisque indicem custodiant. Jucundum quin etiam spectaculum Ximenius, Archiepiscopus Toletanus, Gometio teste, Hispanis præbuit, cernentibus Goncaldum Fernandum, cui tot victoriæ Magni Ducis nomen pepererant, in abdito secessu sacris operantem, & orationibus vacantem; Ximenium contra inter milites, lorica indutum, ferocientem. Dignissimus inprimis ludibrio omnium habitus est Philippus Belluacensis Episcopus, qui Auth. Helinsh. in Chron. Rich. 1. nec non Guilhelmo Neubrigensi Rer. Anglic. lib. V. 22. contra Richardi Angliæ Regis exercitum A. M. D. XCVII. infestum militem ductans, acie captus est: Quemcum donari sibi tanquam Filium Pontifex expetiisset, Richardus Romam arma Episcopi misit, cum lepida denuntiatione: Vide, Beatissime Pater, num hæc sit tunica Filii tui! De Gallorum consuetudine sic Joh. Tilius Rerum Gallic. lib.
