II. refert: Quanquam Scripturæ Sacræ armis toti clero interdicant, tamen Antistites Pares Galliæ pro dignitate Parium temporaria tenentur Regibus ministrare, & eos sequi cum equitum ac militum suorum comitatu, si quando Reges ipsi in bellum processerint: quod officium à quibusdam aliis, qui Pares non sunt, Episcopis debebatur. Adeò Gallia in his conditionibus rem militarem æstimavit magni. Eam verò consuetudinem Baronius ad A. D. CCC. LXXXVIII. his verbis detestatur: Execrandum plane diu istiusmodi facinus (ut Episcopi armati ad bella procederent) innolevit in Galliis, &c. Sed eò deterius, quòd iidem etiam ab ejus temporis scriptoribus laudati reperiuntur nomine bellicæ fortitudinis: cum tanquam (NB.) sacrorum canonum violatores, & muneris Pastoralis ac nominis desertores detestandi fuissent. Tales igitur, Baronio ipso judice, Pontifices & Episcopi Polemarchi omnes fuerint. Saltem ex iis, quæ attulimus, ad liquidum perduci potest, Pontifices & Episcopos, qui post Hildebrandum bella gerere sibi fas piumque duxerunt, immane quantum à veris & veteribus Episcopis differre, neque grandis istius nominis mensuram ullatenus implere.
units.tr: CCXCIII. Nor should we pass over in silence the iron-wood [σιδηρόξυλον] of this present time, namely the soldier bishop. For some bishops, whose duty was to watch over their flock and to feed the Church of God, which was redeemed by his own blood, especially in Germany, offered vigorous sacrifices to Mars. With a new and unusual stench of arms, they nearly killed everyone in new ways, and they called all things to the sword and the flame. Among these, Christoph Bernhard von Galen, Bishop of Münster, a true Cyclops of our age who grew up and grew old among arms, deserves to be named first of all. For he not only subdued the famous city of Münster in Westphalia by his arms and brought it under the yoke, and afterwards acted as director of the imperial army in the Hungarian-Turkish war. He also let himself be hired indiscriminately for money, now by the King of England and now by the King of France, to bear hostile standards, accustomed to draw his income from mercenary service [τὰς προφὰς ἐιωθὼς ἔχειν ἐκ τῆς μισθοφορίας], having one source of gain from soldiering, just as Philip of Macedon, as Diodorus Siculus book 18 describes, dealt with mercenary soldiers. Twice he waged most savage war on the United Dutch, shattered their most flourishing cities in a dreadful manner, mixed everything with slaughter, and, differing little from the Turkish Janissary soldier, raged everywhere with force and fraud. Finally, in the election of a coadjutor in 1667, he was defeated in the votes, and, spurning the Elector of Cologne, who had more votes in his favour, he forced on himself the position he wanted by arms. So that line of Palingenius fits this man no less than any other priest: "Now bishops love wars; all else is trifles." And Alexander had this little colt of his in such delight that Rome sent him a consecrated sword, as a reward for murder to be carried out with impunity, and more than once praised his military valour lavishly. CCXCIV. The occasion here calls for us to say something about the iniquity of the Roman Church's bishops who were warriors, contrary to the Word of God and the ancient practice, so that it may be clear from this alone that recent bishops differ from the true and ancient ones more than a monkey dressed in purple differs from a man, or a mouse sprinkled with flour differs from the master of the mill. How strictly Christ separated his kingdom, whose ministers the bishops profess to be, from the kingdoms of this world, which are often acquired and held by arms, I need not say now. This is sufficiently clear from Matt. 20:25; 26:52; John 8:36; 1 Cor. 4:9, etc. Certainly the Apostolic Canon forbids a bishop to be a striker, a percussor [πλήκτην] in plain words. But another Apostolic Canon, conformable to this, long ago forbade ecclesiastics military service in these words: "A bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, who practises the military life [στρατείαν ἀσκοῦν] and wishes to hold both the Roman civil magistracy and the priestly administration, shall be deposed. For what belongs to Caesar is to Caesar, and what belongs to God is to God." Whether by στρατείαν one understands, with Balsamon, Zonaras and Harmenopulus, one who is engaged in soldiering, or one who administers a military matter, or, with the most learned Beveridge, one who administers any civil office, it is plain that bellicose bishops are struck. The next age was so far from approving the military service of bishops that, through some carelessness or sluggishness [ἀμελεία ἢ ἀνθολκῆς], it disapproved even any soldiering, at least of the kind then in use. Gregory the Cappadocian, an Arian, was the first to occupy the Alexandrian See by military force, after Athanasius had been driven out. We have related above the tragedy of Damasus and Ursinus; but those things happened in a tumult. Yet still in the fourth century, Ambrose, in his speech against Auxentius, says: "Iron spears are not sought, nor arms by the soldiers of Christ. I have not learned to resist when compelled; but grief, tears, prayers, and weeping were my arms against the soldiers. For such are the defences of a priest. Otherwise I neither ought nor am able to resist." In the following, the fifth century, the Council of Chalcedon, in canon 7, decreed: "Those who have once been enrolled in the clergy, or assigned to a monastery, shall not, whether from need or from any worldly dignity, go to military service or to secular honours. Those who have dared to do this, and have preferred not to repent of it, so that they return to that same thing which they had previously proposed to themselves for the sake of God, ought to be anathematized." In the seventh century the common saying of Gregory the Great, bishop of Rome, is in circulation, which is contained in book 7, letter 1, to Sabinian: "If," he said, "I had wished to mix myself in the death of the Lombards, today the Lombard people would have neither king nor duke. But because I fear God, I am afraid to mix myself in the death of any man." Either therefore Gregory did not fear God in this matter, or recent popes and bishop-warriors do not fear God. Indeed, another letter of Gregory's is found, a fragment of which stands in c. 2, X, de immunitate Ecclesiae, from which the canonists commonly conclude that even clerics are not excused from guarding the city in a time of necessity. But what does guarding the city, standing on watch in time of necessity, which is the duty of any upright citizen, have in common with what bishop-warriors have done for some centuries? I pass over the fact that, as Augustine Barbosa notes on the same c. 2, a modern writer observed that the text does not speak of clerics but of men of the Church who enjoyed the Church's immunity. Certainly in the same century, in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 44, it was enacted "that clerics who wish to take up arms in any faction, having lost the rank of their order, shall be handed over to penance in a monastery." Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 2, ch. 2, also relates a notable example of true priestly non-fighting: monks from the monastery of Bangor, in large number, standing apart and fighting against King Æthelfrith, not with bodily arms but with fasting and prayers. In the eighth century Pope Zachary, in a letter to Boniface, bishop of Mainz, complains of priests who, provoking God to anger, commit greater crimes "while with their own hands they kill Christians and pagans," etc. Letter 3: "What kind of victory is given," he says, "where priests on a single Lord's day handle the mysteries, and offer the Lord's body to Christians for the redemption of their souls, and with their own sacrilegious hands kill Christians, to whom they ought to have ministered this, or pagans, to whom they ought to have preached Christ?" The same Zachary, in letter 7 to King Pepin, distinguishes the duties of soldiers and priests: "It is fitting for princes, secular men and warriors to take care and be concerned against the cunning of enemies and for the defence of the province. But it belongs to prelates, priests and servants of God to be free for salutary counsels and prayers, so that, while you pray and those fight, by God's help the province may remain safe." In the time of Charlemagne the power of bishops indeed grew not a little through his indulgence and liberality. Yet priests were not permitted to make war; rather, this was not obscurely forbidden in canon 37 of the Council of Meaux, held in 845, in these words: "Whoever seem to be of the clergy shall not take up military arms, nor go about armed; but they shall show the name of their profession by religious morals and religious dress. But if they despise this, as despisers of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical authority, let them be punished by loss of their rank, because they cannot serve God and the world at the same time." Among the Capitularies of the emperors Charles and Louis, book 6, no. 61, there is such an enactment: "If any bishop, presbyter, deacon or subdeacon has gone to war, and has put on warlike arms to fight, let him be deposed from every office, to such an extent that he may not even have lay communion." Indeed Pope Leo IV, in his homily on pastoral care, addresses the clerics of his time thus: "None of you shall bear arms in sedition, because your arms ought to be spiritual." Yet Leo did not restrain himself from doing what he forbade to others, fighting bravely himself against the Saracens, if what Platina wrote about him is true. Nicholas I, as Gratian reports, c. Clericum, dist. 50, c. 6: "Since the soldiers of the world are distinct from the soldiers of the Church," he says, "it is not fitting for the soldiers of the Church to serve the world, by which it must necessarily come to the shedding of blood." Also in the Council of Trebur, held in 895, chapter 27, there is such a decree: "Those once assigned to the clergy shall come neither to military service nor to any worldly dignity, as has been established in the Council of Chalcedon; lest they be like hippocentaurs, as St Isidore says, who are carried, not as horses or men, but like brute beasts, by their own freedom and desire." The same Council also forbids that, for a cleric who has died in war, prayer be requested either in the offering or in the prayer. Finally, in the tenth century, when the popes began to increase their temporal power, Sabellicus, Ennead 9, book 2, complains that the piety of the ancient popes was degenerate here too, in these words: "Those ancient popes increased the dignity of the pontiffs with their own blood; these, by slaughters and plunder, have profaned what was increased. Those enriched temples with gifts; these stripped them by sacrileges," etc. And the die being cast, the lust for war advanced so far that in 1053 Leo IX, the first of the Roman pontiffs to undertake a campaign against the Normans in Apulia, Calabria and Sicily, led out an army of ruffians rather than soldiers; it was overthrown by the Normans by the hidden judgment of God, as Hermann the Lame piously [ἐπιχείρης] says, because a battle of the spirit rather than a fleshly battle for perishable things became a priest alone. And this deed of Leo, and the boldness of the whole warlike clergy, was sharply reproved by Peter Damian, Cardinal of Ostia, book 4, letter 9. "The life our Saviour lived in the flesh," he says, "is set before us as a line of discipline no less than his evangelical preaching. Just as he overcame all the obstacles of the raging world not by the vengeance of a strict judgment, but by the invincible majesty of unshaken patience, so he teaches us to bear the rage of the world calmly rather than to seize arms or to answer injuries with injuries, especially since the duties of kingdom and priesthood are distinct, so that the king may use the arms of the world, and the priest may gird himself with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, etc." Then he compares Leo's deed with the sin of David and the denial of Peter. Soon afterwards Gregory VII, in his Dictates, reported "that it is lawful for the Roman pontiff to bear imperial ornaments, and so even the sword." And Boniface VIII defined "that there are two swords in the Church, one to be wielded for the Church, the other by the Church; that the one is subject to the other; and indeed that Peter had a temporal sword." Therefore what formerly deserved to be counted a vice, afterwards, when superstition and carelessness of princes had enfeoffed the popes and bishops with temporal jurisdiction and the lordship of fiefs, began to be turned into virtue and piety. Above all the sacred or crusading warfare decreed by Urban II at the Council of Clermont, to which bishops, priests and monks accustomed to bearing arms were brought, took place. And to such madness it came that, as Choppin witnesses, book 2, Sacred Politics, title 1, no. 7, some bishops, while performing sacred rites, kept a sword hung above the altar, as a sign of life and death. Ximenes, Archbishop of Toledo, as Gomez testifies, also offered the Spanish a delightful spectacle, when they saw Gonzalo Fernández, to whom so many victories had earned the name "Great Captain," at work in a remote retreat, performing sacred rites and devoting himself to prayers, while Ximenes, clad in armour, raged among the soldiers. Above all, Philip, Bishop of Beauvais, was judged most worthy of everyone's ridicule, who, as Holinshed reports in his Chronicle of Richard I, and also William of Newburgh in History of English Affairs, book 5, ch. 22, leading soldiers hostile to the army of King Richard of England in 1197, was captured in battle. When the Pope sought that he be given to him as a son, Richard sent the bishop's arms to Rome with a witty message: "See, Most Blessed Father, whether this is your son's tunic!" Concerning the custom of the French, John Tillet thus reports in History of Gaul, book 2: "Although the Holy Scriptures forbid all the clergy arms, nevertheless the bishops who are Peers of France are bound, by the dignity of the Peers, to serve the kings temporarily and to follow them with the retinue of their horsemen and soldiers, whenever the kings themselves have gone to war; a duty owed by certain other bishops who are not Peers. So highly did France in these conditions value military affairs." But Baronius, at the year 388, detests that custom in these words: "Truly this execrable crime (that bishops went armed to war) had long grown up in Gaul, etc. But it was worse, because the same men are found praised by writers of that time for the name of warlike courage, when they ought to have been detested as (NB.) violators of the sacred canons and deserters of pastoral duty and of the name." Such, then, by Baronius' own judgment, were all the popes and bishops who were generals. From what we have brought forward, at least it can be made clear that the popes and bishops who after Hildebrand thought it lawful and pious to wage wars differ immensely from the true and ancient bishops, and in no way fill the measure of that great name.

units.la: CCXCV. Liceat autem turpitudinem istam Episcoporum πλήκτων Erasmi etiam & Wicelii verbis μάλα ἐμφατικοῖς prodere. Sic autem Erasmus Dedicatione ad Francicum Regem Paraphrasi in Marcum præfixa, scribit: Duplex est gladii genus, duplex est Regni genus. Habent & Sacerdotes suum gladium: habent suum Regnum. Pròque diadematibus & galeis habent mitras, pro sceptro pedum, habent loricam, baltheum: denique totam panopliam, quam illis non uno in loco strenuus ille bellator Paulus describit. Reges Euangelici Pastores dicuntur. Sed & profani Reges Homero dicuntur Pastores populi. Idem agunt utrique, tametsi diversa est functio, quemadmodum in fabulis iisdem alias alii partes agunt. Quòd si suum utrique gladium semper haberent expeditum, hoc est, potestate tradita, sicut oportet, uterentur: non toties, opinor, Christiani, qui vocamur potiùs, quàm sumus, in fratrum viscera gladium impium stringeremus. Porrò dum utrique suo munere neglecto, quod est alienum, affectant, neutri satis tuentur neque dignitatem suam, neque tranquillitatem. Quando Rex plus habet Regiæ Majestatis, quàm cùm in Judiciis sedens dictat jus, cohercet injurias, dirimit lites, sublevat oppressos: aut quum in consiliis sedens prospicit Reip. commodis? Cæterùm Episcopus quando plus habet dignitatis suæ, quàm cùm è suggesto docet Euangelicam Philosophiam? Tum enim verè in solio suo est Rex Euangelicus. Quàm verò Neroni fuit indecorum in theatro certare aut cum phonascis, & citharœdis, aut in circo cum aurigis: tam indecorum est Regi in humilibus ac sordidis negotiis versari, quæ pertinent ad privatos affectus ipsius, & officiunt incolumitati Reip. Rursum quàm indecorum esset, si philosophus cum pallio & barba fabulam saltaret in proscenio, aut in harena falcem teneret ac rete, gladiatoriam canens cantionem, non te peto, piscem peto, quid me fugis galle? tam indecorum est Euangelicum regem belligerari, aut nundinari, ne quid dicam inhonestius. Quur nunc invenitur Episcopus, qui sibi pulchrius ducit, trecentos equites balistis, lanceis ac bombardis instructos secum ducere, quàm piis & eruditis diaconis comitatum sacros libros secum circumferre? Quur earum rerum ostentatione sibi magni videntur, quarum contemptu magni fuerunt illi, in quorum locum successerunt? Quur illis dulcius sonant tubæ & cornua, quàm sacra lectio? Age, quid si Rex pro diademate & trabea sibi imponat mitram & infulam: contra pro mitra & infula sibi diadema & trabeam sumat Episcopus, nonne portenti simile videbitur? Adeò movent inversa insignia, cur non magis movet inversa functio? &c. Sed & Georgius Wicelius, Ferdinandi I. Imperatoris Consiliarius, in libello nomine via Regia scripto, sic inter alia loquitur: Magnopere probamus ist hoc discrimen, sicut discrimen ponimus inter Cælum & terram. Potestas ecclesiastica de CæCœlo est, at politica de terrâ. Vtramque vero in uno eodemque homine conjungi posse, disputent alii, qui solent objicere de gemino dispari:
units.tr: CCXCV. Let me also expose the shameful condition of these bishops, "strikers" [πλήκτων] as Erasmus calls them, in the words of Erasmus and Wicel, which are very emphatic [μάλα ἐμφατικοῖς]. In his dedication to the King of France, prefixed to his Paraphrase on Mark, Erasmus writes: There are two kinds of sword and two kinds of kingdom. Priests too have their sword and their kingdom. In place of diadems and helmets they have mitres, and in place of the royal sceptre they have the shepherd's staff; they have the breastplate and the belt, in short the whole armour which that valiant warrior Paul describes in more than one place. Evangelical kings are called shepherds, but profane kings too are called by Homer shepherds of the people. Both do the same work, although their function differs, just as in the same fables different actors play different parts. But if both always had their own sword ready, that is, used the power entrusted to them as they ought, I think we Christians, who are called rather than are Christians, would not so often thrust the impious sword into the bowels of our brothers. Moreover, while each neglects his own office and grasps at what belongs to the other, neither adequately guards either his dignity or his tranquillity. When does a king have more of royal majesty: when sitting in judgement he pronounces law, restrains wrongs, settles disputes and relieves the oppressed, or when sitting in council he looks to the interests of the commonwealth? And when does a bishop have more dignity: when he teaches Evangelical philosophy from the pulpit? For then the evangelical king is truly on his throne. As it was unbecoming for Nero to compete in the theatre with singers and lyre players, or in the circus with charioteers, so it is unbecoming for a king to be busied with low and sordid affairs, which concern his private desires and harm the safety of the commonwealth. Again, how unbecoming it would be if a philosopher, in cloak and beard, danced a farce on the stage, or in the arena carried a sickle and net, singing the gladiators' song, "I do not seek you, I seek the fish; why do you flee from me, cock?" So unbecoming is it for an evangelical king to make war or to trade, not to say anything more disgraceful. Why is there now a bishop who thinks it finer to lead three hundred horsemen armed with crossbows, lances and bombards than to have pious and learned deacons attend him while he carries the holy books? Why do they seem great to themselves in displaying those things, by despising which those whose place they took were great? Why do trumpets and horns sound sweeter to them than sacred reading? Come, if a king put on a mitre and fillet instead of a diadem and robe, and a bishop took the diadem and robe instead of the mitre and fillet, would it not seem a monstrous thing? So inverted insignia move us; why does an inverted function not move us more? And so on. But Georg Wicel, counsellor of the Emperor Ferdinand I, in a little book written under the title Via Regia, speaks thus among other things: We greatly approve this distinction, just as we draw a distinction between heaven and earth. Ecclesiastical power is of heaven, but political power is of the earth. Others, who are accustomed to object with the double disparity, may dispute whether both can be joined in one and the same man:

units.la: Non bene conveniunt, nec in una sede morantur.
units.tr: They do not agree well, nor do they dwell in one seat.

units.la: Verùm disputetur ad vivum investiganda veritatis ergo: Vtrum idem existere possit Pastor spiritualis, & miles plus quàm carnalis? Ac iurene gestet altera manu pedum Pontificale, seu Episcopale, & simul altera ensem cruentum, galeam thoracémque Martialem? Verùm hæc sacra non aliter constant! tanto difficilius est contra tractum fluminis niti, & cum suo depugnare Seculo. Alioqui enim provocari poterat ad Ecclesiæ principia, quando tam Pontifices quàm Episcopi uni vacabant potestati ecclesiasticæ, in timore & tremore Dominum suum audientes: VOS NON SIC. Quin & cum Bernhardo quæri poterat: Sícne fecit Petrus? Sícne Paulus? Talia gestavit arma Linus? Talem Zonam Clemens? & Episcopi, Dionysius, Ignatius, Augustinus, Ambrosius, & infiniti horum similes? Sed esto alius, & alii hominum mores, & tempora periculosa non instant jam, sed extant.
units.tr: But let it be disputed, in order to search out the truth to the quick: whether the same man can be a spiritual pastor and at the same time more than a carnal soldier? And whether he may rightly carry in one hand the pastoral or episcopal staff and at the same time in the other a bloody sword, the martial helmet and breastplate? But these things do not agree in any way! It is so much harder to struggle against the current of the river and to fight one's own age. For otherwise one could appeal to the principles of the Church, when both Popes and bishops devoted themselves to the one ecclesiastical power, hearing their Lord with fear and trembling: "It shall not be so among you." Indeed, with Bernard one could ask: Did Peter do so? Did Paul? Did Linus bear such arms? Did Clement wear such a belt? And the bishops Dionysius, Ignatius, Augustine, Ambrose, and countless others like them? But grant that other men, other manners and dangerous times no longer press, but still exist.

units.la: Hæc Bernhardus. Attamen nihilo segnius fatendum id, quod res est: Nimirum Pontifices, Episcopos, Cardinales, Patriarchas primam omnium curam ac operam impendere oportere in eo, quæ solius Dei sunt, memores mandati Pauli, quando inquit: Dicite Archippo: Vide ministerium, quod accepisti in Domino, ut illud impleas.
units.tr: These are Bernard's words. Nevertheless, we must no less admit what the matter is: namely, that Popes, bishops, cardinals and patriarchs ought to devote their first care and effort to the things that belong to God alone, mindful of Paul's command when he says: "Say to Archippus: See the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfil it."

units.la: Quod munus proprie suum si sincerè obicerint vel biennium sensim, crede mihi, nauseabunt ad seculària. Semel statuant, potestatem ecclesiasticam, qua Episcopi sunt, omnino excellere, & longè inferiorem esse potestatem, qua Principes sunt. Quod cùm sit irrefragabile atque immotum, tamen gaudent tantum adire Principes, & propemodum pudet Episcopos dici. Imò illorum aula non sustinet patienter audire, si quis roget, ubi Rev. Episcopus sit: præcisè dicendum est, ubi reperiam meum gloriosissimum Dominum & Principem. Sin secus, ad suspicionem malam protinus rapientur. Cujus rei forsan causa est, quòd malint esse reipsa Principes, quàm Episcopi ; pi; & propensiores sint ad Principatum quàm Episcopatum. Si qui tales existunt, ipsi constituunt semet Episcopi nomine ultra modum indignos. Sed hoc pacto non subterfugiunt iram venturam. Hactenus illi.
units.tr: If they sincerely undertook that office for only two years, believe me, they would gradually become sick of secular affairs. Once they had decided that the ecclesiastical power, by which bishops are what they are, altogether excels, and that the power by which princes are princes is far inferior, which is unshakable and immovable, they would still be glad to approach princes, and would almost be ashamed to be called bishops. Indeed their court cannot patiently bear to hear someone ask where the Reverend Bishop is: one must answer precisely, "Where shall I find my most glorious Lord and Prince?" Otherwise they are at once carried off into bad suspicion. The reason for this is perhaps that they prefer to be princes in fact rather than bishops, and are more inclined to principality than to episcopate. If such men exist, they themselves make themselves bishops in name, far too unworthy of it. But in this way they do not escape the wrath that is coming. So far those men.

units.la: CCXCVI. Certatum hoc tempore potissimum in Schola Pontificia inter Theologos acriter est: An illa attritio, quæ concipitur ex metu gehennæ, excludens voluntatem peccandi cum spe veniæ ad impetrandam gratiam in Sacramento pœnitentiæ, requirat insuper aliquem actum dilectionis Dei? Affirebant id Jansenii sequaces, negabant Jesuitæ potissimum Sirmondus, Annatus, Pinterellus, Moynius, alii; ex quorum sententia Montaltius Epistola Provinciali decima hoc porisma elicuit: Per totam vitam sic peccata elici, adeóque contingere posse, ut salutem adipiscatur, qui nunquam Deum in vita dilexerit. Et Sirmondus quidem in libello, quem virtutis defensionem inscripsit, Pontificiorum de necessitate amoris Divini opiniones ad calculos revocat his verbis: Diligendi Dei præcepto homines obligari affirmat S. Thomas statim ab usu rationis. Hui tam citò? Scotus singulis Dominicis. Unde petitum? Alii cum urget tentatio. Recte, si non alia esset via effugiendæ tentationis. Scotus post acceptum beneficium. Grati quidem animi istud indicium est. Quidam in mortis articulo. Nimis serum est. Ne quidem quoties recipitur Sacramentum aliquod, eam obligationem urgere existimem. Sufficit enim attritio cum confessione, si commodè fieri possit. Aliquo tempore teneri, censet Suarez. At quo? Tuo judicio remittit: ipse nescit. At quod ille nescivit, quis sciat, nescio. Quid verò in euripo hoc opinionum Sirmondus ipse? Concludit, eum qui nullo Deum affectu diligat, nec voluntatem suam ad ipsum convertat, dummodo eum non oderit, & coeteris mandatis obsequatur, legi Divinæ satisfacere. Itaque, verba ejus sunt, quæ miranda est in homines bonitas Dei, non tam amorem sui præcipit, quàm odium vetat. Alibi impudentissimum os effutit, hoc Euangelicæ legis susupra Judaicam praecipuum esse privilegium, quòd nunc ab amandi Dei praecepto Christiani immunes sint. Æquitati, inquit, consentaneum fuit, in lege gratiæ & Novi Testamenti illud durum & difficile exercenda ad obtinendam justificationem perfectæ contritionis, id est, charitatis actus praeceptum resolvi: æquum, inquam, fuit, instituì sacramenta, quæ charitatis defectum suppleant, nec tam arduam animi affectionem requirerent: alioqui Christiani, qui filii sunt, nihilo facilius Patris sui gratiam sibi reconciliarent, quàm Judæi, qui tantum servierunt, & Domini sui misericordiam impetrabant.
units.tr: CCXCVI. At this time especially there is a sharp dispute among the theologians of the Papist school: whether that attrition which arises from fear of hell, excluding the will to sin, joined with hope of pardon, in order to obtain grace in the sacrament of penance, further requires some act of love of God? The followers of Jansen affirmed it; the Jesuits denied it, chiefly Sirmond, Annat, Pinthereau, Moya and others. From their opinion Montalte, in the tenth Provincial Letter, drew this corollary: Thus sins may be removed throughout life, and it may happen that someone obtains salvation who never loved God in his life. Sirmond himself, in the little book he entitled The Defence of Virtue, calls the opinions of the Papists on the necessity of divine love to account in these words: St Thomas affirms that men are bound by the precept to love God from the beginning of the use of reason. So soon? Scotus, every Sunday. Whence is that taken? Others, when temptation presses. Rightly, if there were no other way of escaping temptation. Scotus, after receiving a benefit. That is indeed a sign of a grateful mind. Some at the point of death. That is too late. I do not think this obligation is urged even whenever some sacrament is received, for attrition with confession suffices, if it can conveniently be made. Suarez thinks one is bound at some time. But when? He leaves it to your judgement; he himself does not know. But what he did not know, who knows? I do not know. What, then, does Sirmond himself think in this whirlpool of opinions? He concludes that one who loves God with no affection and does not turn his will toward him, provided he does not hate him and obeys the other commands, satisfies the divine law. Thus, in his words, the wonderful goodness of God toward men does not so much command the love of himself as forbid hatred. Elsewhere he utters the most impudent thing, that it is a principal privilege of the Evangelical law over the Jewish that Christians are now exempt from the precept to love God. It was consistent with equity, he says, that in the law of grace and of the New Testament that hard and difficult duty, the act of perfect contrition, that is, of charity, required for obtaining justification, should be dissolved. It was fair, I say, to institute sacraments which make up for the lack of charity and do not require so arduous an affection of the mind; otherwise Christians, who are sons, would no more easily reconcile to themselves the favour of their Father than the Jews, who only served and obtained the mercy of their Lord.

units.la: CCXCVII. Hæc sexta singularis Jesuitarum de attritionis efficacia, & nulla diligendi Deum in hac vita ad salutem necessitate, hæresis est, quam Montaltii potiùs Doctoris Pontificii, quàm meis verbis detestabor. Vah, ita ille eadem Provinciali Epistola exclamat, in apertum totius Evangelicæ legis excidium profana quidvis audendi licentia grassatur. Violatur magnum illud mandatum, unde lex pendet & Prophetæ: cor ipsum pietatis attentatur: expulso inde spiritu vivificante inane pietatis simulachrum relinquitur: postremò negatur, ad salutem necessarium esse, Deum diligere. Quid restat amplius, nisi ut non amandi Dei privilegium à Christo hominibus allatum praedicetur. Hoc etiam vestri (Jesuitæ) praedicârunt. Crescere jam non potest impietas. Ad summum pervenit! Neque tamen Alexander Papa haereseos istius impietatem mussare, nedum fulmine Papali ferire ausus est. Quin potiùs eadem impietate se alligavit, edita & d. VII. Maii A. M. D. C. LXVII. ad valvas Basilicæ Petri, & in acie Campi Florae, aliisque locis affixa, publicatáque Bulla, qua ille (verba Bullæ referam) cupiens pacis vinculum inter fideles servari, omnémque scissuræ fomitem extingui, auditis votis Eminentissimorum & Reverendiss. D. D. Cardinalium adversus haereticam pravitatem Generalium Inquisitorum; nec non D. D. Consultorum & Qualificatorum Sac. Congregationis ejusdem Generalis Inquisitionis, in virtute Alexandri Bulla, quæ haeresin illam reprehendi impiè vetat. sancta obedientiæ, & sub pœna excommunicationis latæ sententiæ Sanctæ Sedi reservatæ, aliisque pœnis ejusdem Sanctæ Sedis arbitrio taxandis, præcipit cunctis & singulis fidelibus quocunque gradu ac dignitate etiam Episcopali, & majori, imò & Cardinalitia fulgentibus, ut si deinceps de materia Attritionis præfatæ scribent, vel libros aut scripturas edent, vel docebunt, vel prædicabunt, aut alio quovis modo pœnitentes aut scholares, cæterosve erudient, non audeant alicujus Theologicæ censuræ, alteriúsve injuriæ, aut contumeliæ nota taxare alterutram sententiam, sive negantem necessitatem aliqualis dilectionis Dei in præfata Attritione ex metu gehennæ concepta; quæ hodie inter Scholasticos communior videtur; sive afferentem dictæ dilectionis necessitatem; donec ab hac Sancta Sede fuerit aliquid hac in re definitum, &c. Sic Alexander iterum Therfitem se gerit, nescio annon Ethnico quovis deterior, qui non tantum impiam illam sententiam negantem, hodie scilicet inter Scholasticos communiorem (pessima enim quæque hodie in Papatu communiora sunt) diris configere ausus non est, sed in gratiam Jesuitarum suorum, Pallavicini inprimis, ocelli fui, negantem aliqualem necessitatem dilectionis Dei in attritione ex metu gehennæ concepta, censuræ, injuriæ, contumeliæ nota taxare vetuit, donec aliquid à Sancta illa Sede (quæ aliqualem necessitatem dilectionis Dei asserere & definire inpræsentiarum dubitavit) hac in re definitum fuerit. Quid si igitur vel nunquam Sancta illa Sedes hac in re aliquid definiverit (nam hactenus quidem definitione cessatum est) vel pro more sententiam deteriorem, negantem scilicet, definiverit, ansic perpetim nefas fuerit, censuræ, injuriæ, contumeliæ nota taxare eum, qui aliqualem dilectionis Dei necessitatem negaverit? Apage impietatem intolerandam! Certè impunè non tulerit is, qui aliqualem dilectionis Papæ necessitatem in dubium vocaverit. Et ausus est Papa censuræ, contumeliæ, injuriæ notam amovere ab eo, qui alialiqualem dilectionis Dei necessitatem non in dubium revocat, sed aperte negat: Crimine ab uno noscite omnes!
units.tr: CCXCVII. This sixth peculiar heresy of the Jesuits, that attrition is effective and that there is no necessity of loving God in this life for salvation, I shall denounce more in the words of Montalte, a Papist doctor, than in my own. Vah, so he exclaims in the same Provincial Letter, the profane licence to dare anything rages to the open ruin of the whole Gospel law. That great commandment, on which the law and the Prophets hang, is violated; the very heart of piety is assailed; the life-giving Spirit is cast out, and an empty image of piety is left behind; lastly, it is denied that it is necessary for salvation to love God. What remains, except that the privilege of not loving God, brought to men by Christ, should be proclaimed? Your Jesuits have preached this too. Impiety cannot grow any further. It has reached its height! Yet Pope Alexander did not dare to murmur against the impiety of this heresy, much less to strike it with a papal thunderbolt. Rather, he bound himself to the same impiety, when he published and posted on the 7th of May 1667 at the doors of the basilica of St Peter, and in the Campo di Fiore and other places, a bull, which (I shall give the words of the bull) desiring that the bond of peace be kept among the faithful and every spark of division be extinguished, having heard the votes of the most eminent and most reverend lords the cardinals, general inquisitors against heretical depravity, and likewise of the lords consultors and qualifiers of the same sacred general congregation of the Inquisition, by virtue of holy obedience, and under penalty of excommunication latae sententiae reserved to the Holy See, and other penalties to be fixed at the discretion of the same Holy See, commands all and each of the faithful, of whatever rank and dignity, even episcopal and higher, and even those shining with the cardinalate, that if henceforth they write about the aforesaid matter of attrition, or publish books or writings, or teach or preach, or in any other way instruct penitents or students or others, they shall not dare to brand with the mark of any theological censure or any insult or contumely either of the two opinions, whether one denying the necessity of some love of God in the aforesaid attrition conceived from fear of hell, which today seems more common among the Schoolmen; or one asserting the necessity of the said love; until something has been defined in this matter by this Holy See, etc. Thus Alexander again conducts himself as a Thersites, I know not whether worse than any heathen, who not only did not dare to strike with curses that impious opinion, today, that is, more common among the Schoolmen (for every most wicked thing is today more common in Papacy), but for the sake of his Jesuits, above all Pallavicini, the apple of his eye, forbade anyone denying some necessity of love of God in attrition conceived from fear of hell to be branded with the mark of censure, insult or contumely, until something has been defined in this matter by that Holy See (which for the present has hesitated to assert and define any necessity of love of God). What then, if that Holy See never defines anything in this matter (for hitherto indeed there has been no definition), or, as is its custom, defines the worse opinion, namely the denial? Would it then be forever a crime to brand with the mark of censure, insult or contumely the man who denies any necessity of love of God? Away with such intolerable impiety! Certainly he would not go unpunished who called into doubt any necessity of love of the Pope. And the Pope has dared to remove the mark of censure, contumely and insult from him who does not call into doubt but openly denies some necessity of love of God. From one crime, know them all!

units.la: CCXCVIII. Cygnea haec scilicet cantio fuit Alexandri, aliqualem dilectionis Dei necessitatem a censura, injuria, contumelia vindicantis. Nam quinto & decimo post editam bestialem illam Bullam die, nimirum xxii. Maii A. M. D. C. LXVII. spiritum exhalavit, & quam ipse in terra suspendit de necessitate dilectionis Dei definitivam, coram tremendo tribunali Dei tremebundus haud dubie percepit. Morte ejus propalata passim ingens gaudium obortum est, & quam furiosa plebs adversus Pontificem vivum exercere vindictam non potuit, exercuit adversus defuncti Consanguineos, fratrem Marium & Cardinalem Chisium, quorum palatia sine mora perfracta & collutulata turpiter violavit. Novi Pontificis electio agitata in conclavi est per octodecim dies, inde a xxiii. Maii ad x. usque Junii. Prodiitque tandem Julius Rospigliosus, patria Pistojensis Florentinus, Tituli S. Sixti Cardinalis, annum jam aetatis agens septuagesimum secundum, qui nomine Clementis IX. nomen sumpsit. Non alia re insignis, quam quod in numerum Divorum Beatos Beatasque quosdam, nimirum Ludovicum Beltrame Hispanum ex Dominicanorum ordine; Petrum de Alcantara Hispanum, ex Franciscanorum sella, & Magdalenam di Paley Florentinam, retulit: Judaeos, exceptis paucis, Roma exegit, per reliquas Pontificis ditiones dispersos: pro conservanda Candia pervigil excubavit: denique dissoluto Alphonsi Portugalliae Regis & Conjugis Mariae Franciscae Isabellae Sabaudae matrimonio, nuptias inter eandem Sabaudam & Alphonsi Fratrem Petrum Portugalliae Infantem & Regentem, ratas firmasque habuit.
units.tr: CCXCVIII. That, clearly, was the swan-song of Alexander, defending from censure, insult and contumely some necessity of love of God. For on the fifteenth day after that beastly bull was published, namely on the 22nd of May 1667, he breathed his last; and that definitive judgement on the necessity of love of God which he had pronounced on earth, he undoubtedly received, trembling, before the dread tribunal of God. When his death became known everywhere, great joy arose; and the raging populace, which could not take vengeance on the living Pontiff, took it on the kinsmen of the dead man, his brother Mario and Cardinal Chigi, whose palaces they broke into without delay and shamefully ravaged. The election of the new Pope was debated in the conclave for eighteen days, from the 23rd of May to the 10th of June. At last there emerged Giulio Rospigliosi, a Florentine from Pistoia, Cardinal of the title of St Sixtus, now in his seventy-second year, who took the name of Clement IX. He was distinguished by nothing else than that he enrolled among the saints certain blessed men and women, namely Luis Beltrán, a Spaniard of the Dominican order; Peter of Alcántara, a Spaniard, from the Franciscan seat; and Magdalena di Pazzi, a Florentine. He expelled the Jews from Rome, except for a few, who were scattered through the remaining provinces of the Pontiff; he kept watch day and night for the defence of Candia; and finally, when the marriage of Alfonso, King of Portugal, and his wife Maria Francisca Isabella of Savoy had been dissolved, he ratified and confirmed the nuptials between the same Savoyard and Alfonso's brother, Prince Peter of Portugal, who became regent.

units.la: CCXCIX. Sic Clemens duobus & dimidio annis in Papatu exactis d. xxix. Nov. A. M. D. C. LXIX. obiit. Die decima. ma Decembris ejusdem anni Cardinales Conclave ingressi in eo quatuor pœne mensses integros commorati, & factionibus quatuor, Barbarina, Chisia, Rospigliosa & volante, quibus se Hispanica & Gallica immiscuere, ad desperationem usque eligendi Pontificis novi, distracti, rejecto tandem Cardinale Vidone, pro quo, populo inviso licet, factio Chisia, Volans Gallica & Hispanica consentientes diu frustra nitebantur; & conspirantibus tribus factionibus Chisia, Barbarina & Rospigliosa, quinquaginta & octo suffragiis Æmilius Altieri, Romanus, decrepitus senex, octagesimum quippe ætatis annum jam agens, Papatum adeptus est. qui statim electus Clementis X. nomen sibi aptavit. Elephantinum huncce partum statim atque enixi Cardinales sunt, populo omnem de Papa novo spem jam abjicienti, his verbis Cardinalis Maldachinus electionem ex fenestra proclamavit: Annuntio vobis gaudium magnum; Papam habemus. Eminentissimus & Reverendissimus D. Æmilius, S. R. E. Presbyter. Cardinalis Alteierius electus est in Summum Pontificem, qui sibi nomen imposuit Clemens X.
units.tr: CCXCIX. So Clement, after two and a half years in the Papacy, died on the 29th of November 1669. On the tenth day of December of that year the cardinals entered the conclave, and remained in it almost four full months; split into four factions, the Barberini, Chigi, Rospigliosi and Volante, into which the Spanish and French also intruded, they were driven almost to despair of electing a new Pope. At last, Cardinal Vidoni was rejected, for whom the Chigi faction, the French and Spanish, though hateful to the people, had long and vainly striven. Then the three factions of Chigi, Barberini and Rospigliosi agreed, and with fifty-eight votes Emilio Altieri, a Roman, a decrepit old man, now in his eightieth year, obtained the Papacy. He was at once elected and took the name Clement X. As soon as the cardinals had brought forth this elephantine offspring, and the people had already given up all hope of a new Pope, Cardinal Maldachini proclaimed the election from the window in these words: I announce to you great joy: we have a Pope. The most eminent and most reverend lord Emilio, Cardinal Altieri, presbyter of the Holy Roman Church, has been elected Supreme Pontiff, and has taken the name Clement X.

units.la: CCC. Neque tamen Clemens ille λεγόμενος clementem admodum se erga Ecclesiam Dei gessit, quam per subornatos & satellites suos pervertere non minus, quam Inclementes omnes, laboravit. Testis inprimis est Ecclesia Hungarica, cujus immanis persecutio unà cum Clemente Pontifice facto, Jesuitis maximè annitentibus, æstuare cœpit. de qua nonnihil differere haud abs re fuerit, cùm si uspiam alibi, hic certè fallaciæ causæ regnent, & Hungaricos motus, periculáque à Turcis Hungariæ, Christiani orbis munimento validissimo, imminentia, perduellioni civium imputare Lojolitæ ausi fuerint, quæ inexpiabili Vatinianóque erga Religionem Euangelicam odio uni solíque, adeóque in solidum imputanda fuerant. Rem ab ovo, quatenus quidem ad notitiam nostram pervenit, ὡς συλλήβδην recensere conabimur. CCCI. Di-
units.tr: CCC. Yet this so-called [λεγόμενος] Clement did not conduct himself at all clemently towards the Church of God; he laboured no less than all the unclement men to pervert it through his hirelings and henchmen. The Hungarian Church bears witness above all, whose monstrous persecution, begun when Clement became Pope, with the Jesuits chiefly pressing it on, began to blaze up. It will not be out of place to say something about this, since if anywhere else, here certainly the causes of deceit reign, and the Jesuits have dared to impute the Hungarian disturbances, and the dangers from the Turks hanging over Hungary, the most powerful bulwark of the Christian world, to the treason of the citizens; whereas these things should have been imputed solely and wholly to that inexpiable and Vatinian hatred of the Evangelical religion. We shall try to recount the matter from the egg [ὡς συλλήβδην], as far as it has come to our knowledge. CCCI. The dire decrees against those who had first professed the Evangelical religion were drawn up under the counsel of the clergy by Ludovic, King of Hungary, by which all who had abandoned the Papist religion were adjudged to the fire, even unheard and undefended, as is clear from the decrees of Ludovic II, in the year 1523, article 54, and in the year 1525, article...

units.la: CCCI. Dira adversus Euangelicam religionem primitus professos decreta, suasu Cleri, Ludovicus Hungariae Rex condiderat, quibus igni adjudicati sunt, quotquot religionem Pontificiam deseruissent; etiam inauditi indefensique, uti ex Ludovici II. Decretis A.M. D. XXIII. art. 54. & A.M. D. XXV. art. ult. colligitur. Sequente statim anno M. D. XXVI. Ludovicus ab Episcopis ad bellum Turcicum, non expectatis Germanorum, quae in procinctu erant, auxiliaribus copiis, ineundum inductus, & Divinam ob sanguinarium decretum, attentatámque in conscientias tyrannidem, Nemesin expertus, in Mohacsiensibus campis a Turcis caesus, sine mascula prole occubuit. Mox Regni Proceres alii quidem Johannem de Zapolya, Stephani Scepusiensis Filium, Transylvaniae Vayoadam; alii Ferdinandum I. Regem Pannoniae elegerunt. Ferdinandus post mortem Johannis solus Regno potitus, tum quinque Hungariae Superioris Civitatibus Liberis, Cassoviensi, Bartphensi, Eperiesiensi, Leuchoviensi, & Cibinensi; oppidis item Sepusii tredecim; tum Hungariae inferioris, Civitatibus Pulsonensi, Sopronensi, &c. ut de caeteris Regni Proceribus nihil dicam, liberum religionis exercitium concessit. Cùm verò varii nihilominus ob religionis libertatem motus Hungariam diu satis exercerent, demum Seculi hujus anno sexto Pacificationi Viennensi Imperatorem Regemque Hungariae Rodolphum inter & Stephanum Bothskai Kis-Maria insertus articulus primus ita habet: Quantum ad negotium religionis attinet, non obstantibus, pro tempore, prioribus constitutionibus publicis, sed nec articulo postremo A.M. D. C. IV. deliberatum est, ut juxta Sacrae Caesareae Regiaeque Majestatis priorem Resolutionem, ad quam se Regnicolae in sua Replicatione referunt, nimirum quòd omnes & singuli status & Ordines intra ambitum solùm existentes, tam Magnates Nobiles, quàm Liberas Civitates & Oppida privilegiata im-meomediatè ad Coronam spectantia, item in Confiniis quoque Regni. Milites Hungaros in sua religione & confessione nusquam & nunquam turbabit, nec per alios turbari & impediri sinet; Verum omnibus prædictis Statibus & Ordinibus liber religionis ipsorum usus & exercitium permittetur, absque tamen præjudicio Catholicæ Romanæ religionis, & ut Clerus, Templa, & Ecclesiæ Catholicorum intacta & illibata permaneant, atque ea, quæ hoc disturbiorum tempore utrinque occupata fuere, rursum eisdem restituantur. Post Imperator & Rex Matthias ita articulum hunc publico diplomate interpretatus est, ut verba illa, absque tamen præjudicio Catholicæ Romanæ religionis, bona fide adjecta esse, hoc scilicet sensu, ut utraque pars in religione, eius exercitio & Templis non turbetur, declaraverit. A. M. D. C. VIII. eadem libertas non confirmata duntaxat, sed ad oppida etiam, villas rusticosque extensa est. Idem articulus tempore Coronationis Ferdinandi II. conditionibus Diplomatis Regii num. 6. art. 2. insertus, ac deinceps non semel, puta connitente Gabriele Bethlenio A. M. D. C. XVIII. art. 77. A. M. D. C. XXV. art. 22. A. M. D. C. XXX. art. 33. A. M. D. C. XXXV. art. 29. A. M. D. C. XXXVIII. art. 1. cond. 6. renovatus est. Sed & A. M. D. C. XLVII. art. 5. condit. 4. Imperator & Rex Ferdinandus III. occasione pacis cum Georgio Rackozio, Transylvaniæ Principe initæ, sic mentem suam declaravit: Quæstiones circa gravamina negotium religionis & occupationis Templorum concernentes, tam quæ in A. M. D. C. XXXVIII. suæ Majestati exhibita sunt, quàm post subsecuta, in futura primitus celebranda Diæta, propter Regni tranquilliorem permansionem, unionemque animorum, ut vel amicabili Dominorum Regnicolarum compositione sopiantur, vel authoritate suæ Majestatis complanentur cum satisfactione Euangelicorum. Ac pro quibus usus Templorum determinabitur, proventus Parochiarum quod ad eosdem pertineat, nec ultra occupationes Templorum fiant. Ea autem Templa, quæ disturbiorum tempore utrinque occupata fuerunt, statim post perpermutationem Diplomatum prædictis Euangelicis restituantur, prouti etiam Catholicis. Gravamina autem futuris quoque temporibus in eodem negotio Religionis emergentia, tam Catholicorum, quàm Evangelicæ religionis hominum: quàm etiam alia Gravamina Regnicolarum, tam Euangelicorum quàm Catholicorum, secundum 17. Conditiones sua Majestas singulis Diætis plenariè complanabit absque injuria Euangelicorum. Denique idem articulus per modernum quoque Imperatorem & Hungariæ Regem Leopoldum A. M. D. C. LV. tempore coronationis, & quidem in Pace non Hungariæ tantum, sed totius etiam Imperii art. 11. condit. 6. confirmatus est. Diplomatis Regii sexta conditio his verbis concepta est. Quod Religionis negotium inter universos status & Ordines Hungariæ, militibus Hungaris, propter Regni tranquilliorem permansionem, juxta Constitutionem Viennensem, & articulos ante coronationem editos, maneat liberum, illæsum & illibatum, ita videlicet, ut Religionis exercitium tam Baronibus, Magnatibus & Nobilibus, quàm liberis etiam civitatibus, universisque Statibus & Ordinibus Regni Hungariæ, nec non Oppidis & villis, illud sponte ac libere acceptare volentibus, ubique liberum relinquatur, nec quisquam cujuscunque status & conditionis existens, in libero ejusdem usu ac exercitio Religionis à Serenitate sua & aliis quibusvis Dominis terrestribus, QVOVIS MODO, aut QVOVIS PRÆTEXTV impediatur. Concluditur autem his verbis: Nos itaque prædicta universorum Statuum & Ordinum inclyti Regni Hungariæ & partium ei subjectarum instantia, benignè admissi, pro benigna animi nostri propensione, ipsisque benignè gratificandi voluntate, præinsertos VNIVERSOS articulos, ac omnia & singula in iis contenta, rata, grata & accepta habentes, eisdem nostrum consensum benevolum pariter & assensum præbuimus, ac illos, & quævis in iis contenta acceptavimus, promittentes & assecurantes Status & Ordines verbo nostro, quòd præmissa omnia, tam nos ipsi, quàm Regiminis nostri tempore observabimus, quàm per alios fideles subditos nostros, cujuscunque condi-tio tionis & status existant, observari faciemus, uti vigore hujus nostri diplomatis acceptamus, approbamus, ratificamus, confirmamus atque promittimus. In cujus fidem & testimonium literas has manu propria subscripsimus, & sigilli nostri impressione muniri fecimus. In arce Regia Posoniensi die xxv. Junii A. M. D. C. LV.
units.tr: CCCI. Ludovicus, King of Hungary, had enacted, at the urging of the clergy, harsh decrees against those who first professed the evangelical religion. Under them, everyone who abandoned the Papist religion was condemned to the fire, even if they were unheard and undefended. This appears from the decrees of Ludovicus II, A.D. 1523, art. 54, and A.D. 1525, last art. In the very next year, 1526, Ludovicus was persuaded by the bishops to join battle with the Turks without waiting for the German auxiliary troops, who were already ready for the field. Having experienced the vengeance of God for his bloody decree and for his attempted tyranny over men's consciences, he was cut down by the Turks on the plains of Mohács and died without male offspring. Soon afterwards some of the nobles of the kingdom chose John de Zápolya, son of Stephen of Szepes, as king, and others chose Ferdinand I, King of Pannonia. After John's death Ferdinand alone obtained the kingdom. He then granted the free exercise of religion to five free cities of Upper Hungary, namely Kassa, Bártfa, Eperjes, Lőcse and Kisszeben, to thirteen towns of Szepes, and to the free cities of Lower Hungary, Pozsony, Sopron and others. I say nothing of the other nobles of the kingdom. But since various disturbances over religious liberty kept Hungary in turmoil for a long time, in the sixth year of this century the first article of the Peace of Vienna, concluded between the Emperor and King of Hungary Rudolf and Stephen Bocskai of Kismarja, reads thus: As far as the matter of religion is concerned, notwithstanding the earlier public constitutions for the time being, and not even the last article of A.D. 1604, it has been decided that, according to His Sacred Caesarean and Royal Majesty's earlier resolution, to which the inhabitants of the kingdom refer in their Replication, namely that all and each of the estates and orders existing within the realm, both the magnates and nobles, and the free cities and privileged towns immediately subject to the Crown, and likewise those on the frontiers of the kingdom, the Hungarian soldiers in their religion and confession, will nowhere and never be disturbed, nor allow others to disturb or hinder them. But to all the aforesaid estates and orders the free use and exercise of their religion shall be granted, without prejudice to the Catholic Roman religion, and so that the clergy, temples and churches of the Catholics remain intact and unharmed, and that those things which were occupied on either side during these times of disturbance be restored again to them. Afterwards the Emperor and King Matthias interpreted this article by public diploma, declaring that the words without prejudice to the Catholic Roman religion were added in good faith, in this sense: that each party shall not be disturbed in religion, its exercise, or its temples. In A.D. 1608 the same liberty was not only confirmed but extended also to towns, villages and country folk. The same article was inserted among the conditions of the Royal Diploma at the coronation of Ferdinand II, no. 6, art. 2, and thereafter was renewed more than once, for example under the influence of Gabriel Bethlen in A.D. 1618, art. 77; A.D. 1625, art. 22; A.D. 1630, art. 33; A.D. 1635, art. 29; A.D. 1638, art. 1, cond. 6. Moreover, in A.D. 1647, art. 5, condit. 4, the Emperor and King Ferdinand III, on the occasion of the peace concluded with George Rákóczi, Prince of Transylvania, declared his intention thus: The questions concerning grievances touching the matter of religion and the occupation of temples, both those presented to His Majesty in A.D. 1638 and those arising afterwards, shall first be dealt with at the future Diet, for the more peaceful continuance of the kingdom and the union of minds, so that they may be settled either by the friendly agreement of the lords of the kingdom, or be smoothed over by the authority of His Majesty, with satisfaction to the Evangelicals. And for what purposes the temples are to be used will be determined, and the revenues of the parishes as far as they pertain to them, and no further occupation of temples shall take place. Those temples which were occupied on either side during the times of disturbance shall immediately after the exchange of the diplomas be restored to the aforesaid Evangelicals, just as to the Catholics. Moreover, grievances that arise in future times in this same matter of religion, both of Catholics and of Evangelicals, as well as other grievances of the inhabitants of the kingdom, both Evangelical and Catholic, according to the seventeen conditions, His Majesty will fully settle at each Diet, without injury to the Evangelicals. Finally, the same article was also confirmed by the present Emperor and King of Hungary Leopold in A.D. 1655 at his coronation, and indeed in the peace not only of Hungary but of the whole Empire, art. 11, condit. 6. The sixth condition of the Royal Diploma was worded in these words: That the matter of religion among all the estates and orders of Hungary, and the Hungarian soldiers, shall remain free, unharmed and unimpaired for the more peaceful continuance of the kingdom, according to the Constitution of Vienna and the articles issued before the coronation, so that the exercise of religion shall be left everywhere free, both to barons, magnates and nobles, and to free cities, and to all the estates and orders of the Kingdom of Hungary, and also to towns and villages, to those who are willing to accept it freely and of their own accord; and no one of whatever estate or condition, existing in the free use and exercise of that religion, shall be hindered by His Serenity or by any other lords of the land IN ANY WAY, or UNDER ANY PRETEXT. It concludes with these words: We, therefore, having graciously admitted the aforesaid petition of all the estates and orders of the illustrious Kingdom of Hungary and of the parts subject to it, and out of our gracious disposition and our willingness to grant them favour, holding all and singular the articles inserted above, and all and singular things contained in them, as ratified, pleasing and accepted, have given to them our benevolent consent and assent, and have accepted them and whatever is contained in them, promising and assuring the estates and orders by our word that we ourselves, and during our government, will observe all the aforesaid things, and will cause them to be observed by our other faithful subjects, of whatever condition and status they may be, as by virtue of this our diploma we accept, approve, ratify, confirm and promise. In witness and testimony of which we have subscribed these letters with our own hand and caused them to be strengthened with the impression of our seal. In the Royal Castle at Pozsony, on the 25th day of June, A.D. 1655.

units.la: CCCII. Expressissima hæc liberi in Hungaria Religionis exercitii decreta quò minùs ἀσυλα & Sacrosanêta manerent, efficere Clerus Pontificius, Episcopi & Jesuitæ inprimis, Regnorum evertendorum architecti, potuerunt. Neque id amplius dissimulare Clerus ipse potuit. Nam sub novissimæ persecutionis initia A. M D. C. LXXI. prodiit Viennæ Classico sacri belli Sciopiano haud dissimilis libellus, sic inscriptus: Veritas toti mundo declarata, argumento triplici ostendens, Sac. Cæs. Regiámque Majestatem non obligari tolerare in Hungaria Lutheranam & Calvinianam sectam. Quam Catholicæ Religionis zelo concinnavit G. B. E. V. P. S. S. C. R. M. C. C. seu, uti ænigma facilè rerum hominúmque gnari extricârunt, Georgius Barzon, Episcopus (titularis) Varadiensis, Presbyter Societatis, Sacræ Cæsareæ Regiæque Majestatis Consiliarius. Tractationi præmisit S. Augustini in illud Psal. 57. Ad nihilum devenient tanquam aqua decurrens; verba isthæc: Non nos terreant, Fratres, quidam fluvii, qui dicuntur torrentes. Decurrit aqua, ad tempus perstrepit, mox cessabit. Diu stare non possunt. Multæ hæreses jam emortuæ sunt; cucurrerunt in rivis suis, quantum potuerunt; decurrerunt, sicuti sunt rivi, vix eorum memoria reperitur. Ita non tam zelo pro Catholica religione, seu aris, quàm pro focis suis commotus, animum suum certa spe implevit, fore scilicet brevi, ut Jesuitarum artibus Euangelica religio ex toto Hungariæ Regno eliminata plorare cogatur. Quos verò ille tot Regiis ediȸtis promissisque omni exceptione majoribus, concutiendis, arietes admovit? Triplex scilicet argumentum ceu æs triplex circa pectus male munitum, quod ad incudem obiter vocatum Authoris perfidiam prodet. CCCIII. Pri-
units.tr: CCCII. The clergy of the Papists, and above all the bishops and the Jesuits, the architects of the overthrow of kingdoms, were able to ensure that these most explicit decrees of free exercise of religion in Hungary did not remain inviolable [ἄσυλα] and sacrosanct. Nor could the clergy themselves dissemble this any longer. For at the beginning of the latest persecution, in A.D. 1671, there appeared at Vienna a little book, not unlike the Sciopian Sacred War of the Classicum, entitled as follows: The truth declared to the whole world, showing by a threefold argument that His Sacred Caesarean and Royal Majesty is not obliged to tolerate the Lutheran and Calvinist sect in Hungary. Composed out of zeal for the Catholic religion by G. B. E. V. P. S. S. C. R. M. C. C., or, as those acquainted with affairs and men easily unravelled the enigma: Georgius Barzon, (titular) Bishop of Várad, Priest of the Society, Councillor of His Sacred Caesarean and Royal Majesty. He prefaced his treatment with these words of St. Augustine on Psalm 57, They shall come to nothing, like water that runs away: Let not certain rivers, which are called torrents, terrify us, brethren. The water runs away, roars for a time, and soon will cease. It cannot stand long. Many heresies are already dead; they have run in their channels as far as they could; they have run away, like streams, and their memory is scarcely found. Thus, moved not so much by zeal for the Catholic religion, or for the altars, as for his own hearth, he filled his mind with the certain hope that soon, by the arts of the Jesuits, the Evangelical religion would be eliminated from the whole Kingdom of Hungary and forced to lament. But against what did he bring up his battering rams, to shake so many royal edicts and promises, which exceed every exception? A threefold argument, indeed, like a threefold bronze plate around a chest poorly defended, which, when struck on the anvil in passing, will betray the author's treachery. First-

units.la: CCCIII. Primum igitur argumentum à tribus Pacificationis Viennensis conditionibus, sub quibus liberum religionis exercitium pactum est, Barzonius ille arcessit. Concessum scilicet, illud esse, primò absque prejudicio Catholicæ Romanæ; quæ cum sit impossibilis, pro non adjecta habenda sit: secundò, ut Clerus, Templa & Ecclesiæ Catholicorum Romanorum intacta & libera permaneant; quæ conditio violata ab iis sit, qui sub Bethlenio & Rakozio Templa hominesque Pontificios violârint: tertiò ut occupata disturbiorum illorum tempore restituantur; quod nunquam Euangelici præstiterint. Cujus argumenti vanitatem vel inde agnoscere licet, quòd, si conditio impossibilis pro non adjecta habetur, non iccirco pactum & promissio nutat, sed conditio ceu inutilis, salvo pacto, rescindi debet: quòd conditionem illam, ut libertas concedatur absque prejudicio Catholicæ Religionis, Imperator Matthias statim ita interpretatus est, ut aperte negaverit, ad evertendam libertatem religionis trahendam esse: quòd non obstantibus iis, quæ sub Bethlenio & Rackozio acta sunt, deinceps etiam Regiis Pacificationibus & diplomatis religionis libertas confirmata & obsignata est: quòd, si qui à clero Pontificio graviter irritati, defensionis & vindictæ modum antehac exccesserunt, innocentes id luere non debuerint, cùm noxa sequatur caput: quòd denique pacta restitutio eorum, quæ disturbiorum tempore occupata sunt, non ad restitutionem Templorum pridem possessorum, sed eorum, quæ ad Regem forsitan Hungariæ pertinentia à Stephano Botzkajo occupata sunt, obstrinxerit. Neque plus candoris vel soliditatis habet secundum argumentum, inde petitum, quòd articuli, quibus libertas religionis promittitur, non sint conditi consensu & unanimi voto Statuum quatuor Regni, puta Prælatorum, Baronum, Magnatum & Nobilium, utpote ad quos antiquo jure pertinuerit, Rege consentiente & confirmante, leges condere. Contradixisse enim Prælatos omnes, Barones, Magnates & Triplex ejusdem argumentum ad partes vocatum. & Nobiles Pontificios. Cum igitur violentum nullum durabile sit, articulos illos abolendos merito esse. Quod argumentum ad summam Regum Hungariæ, Imperatorum & Regum Rodolphi II. Matthiæ, Ferdinandi II. III. & Leopoldi, quorum consensu, authoritate & fide juramento obstricto, articuli confirmati receptique sunt, ignominiam pertinet. Quasi vel non æquè illis, ac Infulato huic Titulari, hoc est Scenico Episcopo, Hungariæ jura cognita fuerint; vel adversus eadem jura ea in re prævaricati fuerint. De cætero constat satis, quemadmodum negotium hoc in Pacificatione saltem Lintzensi A. M. D. C. XLV. conclusa, & Georgio Rakozio exhibita, gestum fuerit. Ex primo Ordinis Ecclesiastici statu contradixerat omnino Archiepiscopus Strigoniensis, Georgius Lippai, eique Seculares nonnulli, Ladislaus Csakus, Franciscus Revai, & Franciscus Balassus astipulati sunt. At contradicenti fortissimè Comes Paulus Palfy. Curiæ Regiæ Judex, cæterique non Euangelici duntaxat, sed Pontificii etiam Proceres reclamárunt. Deinceps post gravissimas cum Clero contentiones, Status Euangelici in eo esse cœperunt, ut per Georgium Barna ad Regem tota causa devolveretur. Tum igitur Archiepiscopus, eique adhærentes nonnulli alii, Euangelicorum Statuum supplicationem ad Regem impediverunt anteverterúntque ejusmodi responso: Ne fortissimum hoc antemurale Christiani orbis cum universali ruina in manus Turcarum perveniret, facileque universam Nationem deleri contingeret, ad ea evitanda primum in A. M. D. C. VI. Pacificationis Viennensis Articulo I. libertatem religionis concedi oportuit; quæ quidem concessio prius tantum Statibus & Ordinibus, oppidis item privilegiatis & militibus facta in A. M. D. C. VIII. ad villas quoque & oppida extensa fuit. Porro eadem concessiones in A. M. D. C. XVIII. ampliatæ, postmodum vero A. M. D. C. XXII. art. 6. Diplomati Regio inserta fuerunt, ac deinceps quibusvis ferè Comitiis addito artiticulo confirmata. Quibus non agnoscunt Catholici se contravenisse, aut occasionem turbandæ quietis pacisque publicæ exhibuisse, neque concessiones semel factas extinguere aut abolere conatos; quin potius Articulis præsertim Pacificationis Viennensis, quæ fundamentum est ac robur totius status admissæ religionis, prædictis articulis, atque adeo præsentis Diplomatis Regii art. I. se accomodare studuerunt. Sic Diploma tractatus Lintzensis à Statibus Regni universis, cum solenni hac clausula; Contradictionibus Cleri, aliorumque Secularium non obstantibus, imò iisdem in perpetuum nullum vigorem habentibus, consentiente Rege, ratihabitum, articulisque Anni M. D. C. XLVII. insertum est. Quòd si Titularis ille in manifesta luce adhuc dum cæcutit, Pacificationis Viennensis ab universis Statibus Ecclesiasticis & Politicis subscriptæ, clausulam, quæ sic sonat: Nos itaque subscripti nunc invicem concordati nomine omnium Statuum & Ordinum inclyti Regni Hungariæ & Partium sibi annexarum, liberè & spontanee, animóque bene deliberato spondemus, promittimus & recipimus, &c. expendat, & perfidiæ suæ tela amentata agnoscat. Tertium argumentum manifestam Authoris ejusdem fraudem propalat. Inde enim petitum est, quòd. si omnino tolerandi Euangelici in Hungaria essent, Calvinistæ tolerandi forent, quatenus Confessionem Helveticam; Lutherani verò, quatenus Augustanam profitentur. Atqui & Calvinistas ab Helvetica, & Lutheranos ab Augustana Confessione descivisse. Et Calvinistas quidem ab Helvetica, quia cum hac cap. XI. profiteatur, se comprehensa symbolis ac sententiis quatuor primarum & præstantissimarum Synodorum, celebratarum Nicæ, Constantinopoli, Ephesi & Chalcedone, corde sincero credere; illi contrà pertendant Primò, bigamum clericum esse posse, quod Nicænam Synodum vetuisse, Justinianus Novell. 123. c. 1. 12. 14. & Ambrosius Epist. 82. testentur; Secundò, Episcopum Romanum non esse Principem omnium Patriarcharum, quod ipsum tamen Concilium Nicæanum Canone 39. ex Arabico per Pisanum conversò, nec non Chalcedonensis Concilii Patres Act. 3. in relatione Concilii, definiverint: Tertiò negant Sacerdotem in Eucharistia offerre corpus Christi, quod ipsum quoque Canone 16. Concilii Nicæni difinitum sit: Quartò Orationes pro mortuis Canone 65. Arabico probatas, rejiciant: Quintò Episcopi Romani in Conciliis præsidentiam in Concilio Ephesino tamen exemplo confirmatam improbent: Sextò denique Monachatum Concilii Chalcedonensis Act. 14. Can. 16. stabilitum damnent. Sed & Lutheranos defecisse ab Augustana Confessione, inde comprobat, quòd ipsi in Præfatione libri Concordiæ eam variatam posteriorem rejiciant; contra invariatam autem profiteantur; Primò contra articulum 10. Christum in Cœna Domini non esse sub speciebus panis & vini: Secundò contra Art. 21. Missam abolendam esse; Tertiò contra art. 1. Episcopos controversiarum non esse judices. Longæ sunt ambages, injuriæ verò fraudésque longissimæ: Taceo, quòd Diplomata, quibus liberum religionis exercitium Euangelicis in Hungaria conceditur, Helveticæ & Augustanæ Confessionis ne uno quidem apice meminerint, nedum Euangelicos ad alterutram restrinxerint. Qua verò fide scripsit Barzonius, Helveticam Confessionem cap. xi. comprehensa symbolis ac sententiis quatuor primarum & præstantissimarum Synodorum, simpliciter scilicet & in universum recepisse, cùm tamen verba confessionis non de quibuslibet Synodorum illarum sententiis, sed de iis duntaxat, quæ de incarnationis Domini nostri Jesu Christi mysterio loquuntur, id pronuntiaverit. Quid verò ad mysterium illud sententiæ ex Conciliis à Barzonio citatæ? Ita notoriæ fraudis coram toto orbe ille reus est. Quid quòd simili etiam fraude non ex veris & γνησίοις, sed suppositiis, Arabicis inprimis Concilii Nicæni, nec à Gelasio, nec à Justello, nec à Petro de Marca, nec à quoquam Antiquitatum Ecclesiasticarum perito agnitis, sed à Melchitis & Nestorianis, uti Doctiss. Beveregius Annot. in Concil. Canones pag. 212. probat, confictis canonibus, sententiarum suarum quisquilias collegit: quòd insuper Novellam 123. citat, quæ Concilii Nicæni ne quidem meminit, Imperatori Justiniano affingens, quod ex glossa nescio qua arripuit: atque etiam Canonibus Concilii Ephesini supponit id, quod de Concilio Pontificius forte impostor aliquis scripsit? Par ratio eorum est, quæ Lutheranis objicit, utpote qui invariatæ Confessioni adhærentes, vel Art. 10. per species nuda accidentia designari: vel Missæ nomine sacrificium incruentum venire: vel Episcopis in Confessione infallibile & supremum controversiarum potius, quàm ministeriale judicium tribui, constanter meritóque haftenus negârunt. Annon igitur in re seria gravísque momenti publici impostoris notam personatus ille Episcopus meruerit, periti rerum judicent.
units.tr: The first argument, then, Barzonius takes from the three conditions of the Peace of Vienna under which the free exercise of religion was agreed: that it was granted, first, without prejudice to the Roman Catholic religion, which, since that is impossible, should be treated as if it had not been added; second, that the clergy, the temples and the churches of the Roman Catholics remain untouched and free, a condition that was violated by those who, under Bethlen and Rákóczi, damaged the Papist temples and people; third, that what was occupied during those disturbances be restored, which the Evangelicals never did. The emptiness of this argument can be recognised even from this: if an impossible condition is treated as not added, the pact and promise do not thereby totter, but the condition, as useless, should be cancelled while the pact stands. Emperor Matthias at once interpreted the condition, that liberty be granted without prejudice to the Catholic religion, in such a way that he plainly denied it was to be taken as a means of overturning the liberty of religion. Notwithstanding what was done under Bethlen and Rákóczi, the liberty of religion was afterwards confirmed and sealed by royal pacifications and diplomas. And if some who were gravely provoked by the Papist clergy previously exceeded the bounds of defence and revenge, the innocent ought not to pay for it, since the guilt follows the head. Finally, the pact to restore what was occupied during the disturbances bound them not to the restoration of temples formerly possessed by others, but to the restoration of what Stephen Bocskai had perhaps occupied and which belonged to the King of Hungary. The second argument, drawn from the fact that the articles by which liberty of religion is promised were not established by the consent and unanimous vote of the four estates of the kingdom, namely the prelates, barons, magnates and nobles, to whom by ancient right it belonged to make laws with the King's consent and confirmation, has no more candour or soundness. For all the prelates, barons, magnates and Papist nobles contradicted it. Since therefore nothing violent is lasting, those articles ought rightly to be abolished. This argument brings disgrace upon the highest authority of the Kings of Hungary, the Emperors and Kings Rudolf II, Matthias, Ferdinand II, III and Leopold, by whose consent, authority and faith, bound by oath, the articles were confirmed and received. As if the rights of Hungary were not as well known to them as to this titular bishop, that is, this stage bishop, or as if they had transgressed those rights in this matter. Moreover, it is sufficiently clear how this business was conducted in the Peace of Linz, at least, concluded in 1645 and presented to George Rákóczi. From the first estate of the ecclesiastical order the Archbishop of Esztergom, George Lippay, had entirely contradicted it, and some secular men, Ladislaus Csáky, Francis Révay and Francis Balassa, agreed with him. But Count Paul Pálffy, judge of the royal court, and other nobles, not only Evangelical but also Papist, cried out most strongly against it. Afterwards, after very serious disputes with the clergy, the Evangelical estates began to aim at having the whole matter referred to the King through George Barna. Then the Archbishop and some others who adhered to him prevented and anticipated the Evangelical estates' petition to the King, with this answer: In order that this most strong bulwark of the Christian world not come, together with universal ruin, into the hands of the Turks, and that the whole nation not easily be destroyed, it was necessary, to avoid these things, that liberty of religion first be granted in the first article of the Peace of Vienna in 1606. This concession, made at first only to the estates and orders, and to the privileged towns and soldiers, was in 1608 extended also to villages and towns. Moreover, the same concessions were enlarged in 1618, and afterwards in 1622 were inserted in art. 6 of the royal diploma, and thereafter confirmed by an added article at almost every diet. The Catholics do not acknowledge that they have contravened these, or given occasion to disturb the quiet and public peace, nor have they tried to extinguish or abolish the concessions once made. Rather, they have striven to conform themselves especially to the articles of the Peace of Vienna, which is the foundation and strength of the whole state of the admitted religion, and so to the aforesaid articles and to art. 1 of the present royal diploma. Thus the diploma of the Linz treaty was ratified by all the estates of the kingdom, with the king's consent, and inserted in the articles of 1647, with this solemn clause: Notwithstanding the objections of the clergy and of other laymen, indeed having no force in perpetuity against them. But if that titular bishop, who still gropes about in the plainest light, would weigh the clause of the Peace of Vienna subscribed by all the ecclesiastical and political estates, which runs thus: We, therefore, the undersigned, now mutually agreed in the name of all the estates and orders of the renowned Kingdom of Hungary and of the parts annexed to it, freely and spontaneously, and with a well-considered mind, pledge, promise and receive, etc., and recognise the weapons of his perfidy as ill-conceived. The third argument reveals the manifest fraud of the same author. For it is drawn from the claim that, if Evangelicals were to be tolerated in Hungary at all, Calvinists would be tolerated insofar as they profess the Helvetic Confession, and Lutherans insofar as they profess the Augsburg Confession. But Calvinists have departed from the Helvetic Confession, and Lutherans from the Augsburg Confession. Calvinists have departed from the Helvetic Confession, because in chapter 11 it professes that they sincerely believe in the creeds and opinions of the four first and most excellent synods, held at Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon; but they, on the contrary, maintain: First, that a cleric may be a bigamist, which the Nicene Synod forbade, as Justinian in Novel 123, chapters 1, 12 and 14, and Ambrose in Epistle 82 attest; second, that the Roman bishop is not the prince of all the patriarchs, which the Council of Nicaea itself in canon 39, in the Arabic text as translated by Pisanus, and the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon in Act 3, in the report of the council, have defined; third, they deny that the priest offers the body of Christ in the Eucharist, which was also defined in canon 16 of the Council of Nicaea; fourth, they reject prayers for the dead, which are approved in Arabic canon 65; fifth, they disapprove of the presidency of the Roman bishop in councils, although it was confirmed by the example of the Council of Ephesus; sixth, finally, they condemn monasticism, which was established in the Council of Chalcedon, Act 14, canon 16. But that the Lutherans have also departed from the Augsburg Confession he proves from this: that in the preface to the Book of Concord they reject the later, altered version and profess the unaltered one; first, against article 10, that Christ is not in the Lord's Supper under the species of bread and wine; second, against article 21, that the Mass is to be abolished; third, against article 1, that bishops are not judges of controversies. These are long detours, and the injuries and frauds are very long. I pass over the fact that the diplomas by which the free exercise of religion is granted to Evangelicals in Hungary do not mention the Helvetic or Augsburg Confession even by a jot, much less restrict Evangelicals to one or the other. But with what good faith Barzonius wrote that the Helvetic Confession, chapter 11, simply and in general received the creeds and opinions of the four first and most excellent synods, when the words of the confession pronounce this not about any opinions of those synods whatever, but only about those which speak of the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. What, moreover, do the opinions cited by Barzonius from the councils have to do with that mystery? Thus he is guilty before the whole world of notorious fraud.
