What of the fact that by a similar fraud he gathered the scraps of his opinions not from genuine [γνησίοις] canons but from spurious ones, especially Arabic canons of the Council of Nicaea, which were recognised neither by Gelasius, nor by Justellus, nor by Peter de Marca, nor by anyone skilled in ecclesiastical antiquities, but were fabricated by the Melchites and Nestorians, as the most learned Beveridge proves in Annotations on the Canons of the Council, page 212? And what of the fact that he further cites Novel 123, which does not even mention the Council of Nicaea, attributing it to the Emperor Justinian, something he snatched from some gloss or other; and also foists upon the canons of the Council of Ephesus what some Papist impostor perhaps wrote about the council? The case of the Lutherans is the same: he objects to them that, adhering to the unaltered confession, they either hold that in article 10 the bare accidents are designated by the species, or that by the name of Mass is meant an unbloody sacrifice, or that in the Confession infallible and supreme judgment of controversies, rather than ministerial judgment, is attributed to bishops, and that they have consistently and rightly denied this until now. Has that masked bishop not therefore deserved the mark of a public impostor in a matter of serious and weighty importance? Let people skilled in these matters judge.

units.la: CCCIV. Sicut verò Barzonius ille Hungaricarum Ecclesiarum privilegia testatissima in aperta luce, futilissimis ratiunculis, perfidiæ cleri horrendæ certissimis testibus, oppugnare non dubitavit: ita nunquam non Clerus in Hungaria Pontificius eò consilia sua apud Principes cætera optimos direxit, ut Transactiones universæ verbis speciosæ, re inanes, imò subdolæ deprehenderentur. Etenim nunquam ferè pactis potentiores fleterunt. Hinc adeò Pacis A. M. D. C. VI. conditiones, Botskajo urgente, initæ mox ita violatæ impunè fractæque sunt, ut A. M. D. C. XVIII. Bethlenius magno labore easdem redintegrare necessum habuerit. Redintegratas denuo ita Pontificius clerus lacessivit infinitis modis temeravitque, ut A. M. D. C. XLVII. Georgius Rakotzius, Transsylvaniæ Princeps, ingenti labore restituere, nonaginta Templis, quæ vi erepta fuerant, recuperatis, coactus fuerit. Quanto igitur sanguine Hungaris Euangelica libertas constiterit, judicabunt, quibus res gestæ obiter compertæ sunt. Verùm neque sic alma pax & libertas Ecclesiæ in tuto navigavit. Denuo quippe eversis, quæ Pacificatio reddiderat, Templis, apertæ persecutiones ubique per Terrestres Dominos, quos adversus publica pacta consurgentes coerceri par erat, grassari cœperunt. Comes Franciscus Nadasti, Divinæ mox vindictæ virgulam passus, in Comitatu Castriferrei, Sopronienfi, Nitrenfi, ferro flammáque cuncta miscere: alter Paulus Esterhazius, à Pontifice Romano nuptias cum germani filia incestas indulgente, ad persequendos Euangelicos voto obstrictus, in Comitatibus Vesprimiensi, Posoniensi, nec non districtu lacus Torto, adversus Evangelicos carceribus, proscriptionibus diris, suppliciis sævire. Testes hodieque sunt Ecclesiæ olim florentissimæ, Gapensis, Szenciensis, Cheitensis, Chepregiensis, (quæ multorum fidelium in ipsis Templi penetralibus internecionem, aliorum ex turri præcipitationem perpessa est) innumeraque aliæ. Secuti Archiepiscopi & Episcopi, in suis quique ditionibus, in insula præsertim Challökötz, in cæteris etiam locis Barones Nobilesque ad summam crudelitatem nil facere reliqui.
units.tr: CCCIV. Just as that Barzonius did not hesitate to attack the most well-attested privileges of the Hungarian Churches, which lie in plain light, with the flimsiest little arguments, despite the most certain witnesses to the clergy's horrible perfidy, so the Papist clergy in Hungary never ceased to direct its schemes through other Princes, mostly the best, so that every agreement, fine in its words but empty in substance, and even deceitful, was found out. For they hardly ever kept faith with agreements when they were the stronger party. Hence the conditions of the Peace of 1606, entered into at Bocskai's urging, were soon violated and broken with impunity, so that in 1618 Bethlen had to restore them again with great effort. Once restored, they were harassed and disturbed by the Papist clergy in countless ways, so that in 1647 George Rákóczi, Prince of Transylvania, was forced to restore them with enormous effort, recovering ninety churches that had been seized by force. Those who have learned the events in passing will judge how much blood Evangelical liberty cost the Hungarians. But even so, the blessed peace and liberty of the Church did not sail in safety. For once the churches restored by the Pacification were thrown down again, open persecutions began to rage everywhere through the landed lords, who ought to have been restrained, since they rose up against public pacts. Count Francis Nádasdy, soon suffering the rod of divine vengeance, threw everything into confusion with fire and sword in the counties of Vas, Sopron and Nyitra. Another, Paul Eszterházy, who had been granted by the Roman Pontiff a marriage with his brother's daughter, an incestuous union, and who had bound himself by vow to pursue the Evangelicals, raged against them with prisons, dire proscriptions and torments in the counties of Veszprém and Pozsony, and in the district of Lake Balaton. Witnesses to this today are the once most flourishing churches of Gyöngyös, Szentgyörgy, Kethely, Csepreg (which suffered the slaughter of many faithful within the very precincts of the church, and the throwing of others from the tower), and countless others. Following them, the archbishops and bishops, each in his own domain, and especially on the island of Csallóköz, and the barons and nobles in other places, left nothing undone in the way of the greatest cruelty.

units.la: CCCV. Immunes tamen hactenus Regiæ, liberaeque Civitates, à solo Rege dependentes, manserant. Inventa tamen eadem infestandi ratio est, quando occasione quorundam Procerum Pontificiorum, Nadasti, Serini, Frangipani, aliorum, Francisco Rackotzio adhærentium, quorum privata studia eò proterviæ delapsa sunt, ut armis Regiam Majestatem impetere non dubitaverint, A. M. D. C. LXXX. miles Austriacus in Hungariam introductus, victricia ubique ferè arma circumtulit. Tum enim Archiepiscopi, Episcopi & Jesuitæ, in turbido piscaturi, militis illius opera ubique ferè Templa occupare, verbi Divini Ministros alios expellere, alios in carceres compingere, alios trucidare: plebes vi & multis ad amplectendas Cerimonias Pontificias cogere, Nobilibus aliisque Euange-gegelicis milites obtrudere, tributa imponere, atque his pluribusque violentiae contra jus & fas attentatae modis, fractos partibus suis adjungere ausi, Euangelicae Religionis in Regno isthoc <bl>ποντοληθεία</bl>... moliti sunt. Militari brachio succincti, Georgius Betzeni, Archiepiscopus Colothensis, Jaurino, Comarino, Owarino, universaque regione circumjacente: Leopoldus à Colonitsch, Episcopus Neostadiensis, infernalis furia, Posonio: Johannes Pangratz, Episcopus Vaciensis, Tirnavia: alii Patakino, Rivalino, Tokajo, Berentzino, Modino, Tolyaino, Tarzalino, Lizkaino, Bopsino, Uniguarino, Berexazino, Chremnitio, Neofolio, Eperiesino, Regiomonto, &c. imò ex totius ferè Hungariae superioris & inferioris omnibus ferè oppidis & villis verbi Divini Ministros, aliis supplicio mortis affectis, aliis carcerum squalore maceratis, aliis in tristissimum exilium abactis, exegerunt. Adversus Benizenses, Pakovienses, & Juralukenses diris modis saevitum, & post occisos plurimos, nonnullos etiam ad Templi valvas suspensos, civitates ipsae igni incensae, tantum non solo adaequatae sunt. Ecclesiae Reformatae Ecclesiensis Pastor Johannes Baki, una cum vidua Laurentii Surii, Ecclesiae quondam Comariensis Ministri, ille vivicomburio, haec gladio Comarini vitam finierunt. Taceo innumeros hinc inde, Cassoviae inprimis & Posonii, ex omni hominum statu, aetate, sexu, indicta causa, diversisque fatis, ad novissima supplicia raptos, exilióve multatos, quos inter Comes etiam Stephanus Cotskai, inclytorum Hungariae vindicum nobilissima propago, & gente & mente inclytus, Claudiopoli in exilio mortem oppetiit.
units.tr: Yet the royal and free cities, which depended on the King alone, had remained exempt until then. But the same method of harassment was found when, on the occasion of certain Papist magnates (Nádasdy, Zrínyi, Frangepán, and others) who adhered to Francis Rákóczi, and whose private designs had gone so far in wantonness that they did not hesitate to attack His Royal Majesty with arms, an Austrian soldiery was brought into Hungary in 1680 and carried its victorious arms almost everywhere. For then the archbishops, bishops and Jesuits, fishing in troubled waters, with the help of that soldiery occupied almost every church, expelled some ministers of the Divine Word, thrust others into prison, and slew others. They forced the common people by violence and many threats to embrace Papist ceremonies, imposed soldiers on the nobles and others of the Evangelical faith, laid taxes upon them, and by these and many other forms of violence, contrary to law and right, they dared to win over the broken to their side, and they plotted the total ruin [ποντοληθεία] of the Evangelical religion in that kingdom. Girded with the military arm, George Bethlen, Archbishop of Kalocsa, at Győr, Komárom, Ógyalla and the whole surrounding region; Leopold von Kollonich, Bishop of Wiener Neustadt, that infernal fury, at Pozsony; John Pangrácz, Bishop of Vác, at Trnava; others at Patak, Rimavská Sobota, Tokaj, Berettyóújfalu, Modor, Tolcsva, Tarcal, Liszka, Bodrogköz, Ungvár, Beregszász, Körmöcbánya, Nagyszombat [Neufeld], Eperjes, Királyhida and elsewhere, in almost all the towns and villages of nearly the whole of Upper and Lower Hungary, drove out the ministers of the Divine Word: some they put to death, others they wore down with the squalor of prisons, and others they drove into the most wretched exile. Against the men of Benisze, Pakovicze and Jolsva they raged with dreadful cruelty, and after killing very many, hanging some even at the church doors, they set the towns themselves on fire and reduced them almost to the ground. John Baki, pastor of the Reformed church at Ecsed, along with the widow of Laurence Surius, once minister of the church at Komárom, ended their lives, he by being burned alive, she by the sword, at Komárom. I pass over the countless others here and there, especially at Kassa and Pozsony, drawn from every rank, age and sex, condemned without a hearing, and carried off to the final punishments by various deaths, or punished with exile; among them Count Stephen Cotskai, most noble offspring of the famous defenders of Hungary, famous in both birth and mind, met his death in exile at Kolozsvár [Claudiopolis].

units.la: CCCVI. Ne verò juris quodam praetextu crudelitas, & calidissima callidissimáque evertendae religionis consi- lia destituerentur, Posonii extraordinarium tribunal, judi-
units.tr: CCCVI. Lest cruelty, however, and the most fervent and cunning plans for overthrowing religion should be left without some pretext of law, they set up at Pressburg an extraordinary tribunal,

units.la: Tribunal Posoniense rebellionis praetextu Euangelicorum. dicibus constans Partim Ecclesiasticis, partim Politicis, Pontificiis & juratis Euangelii hostibus omnibus, erigere, atque eo ad dicendam objectæ miro æstu perduellionis causam, spectatissimos quosque citare placuit. Initium factum est ab ovibus, Politicis Magnatibus, aliisque, quos facilius perverti posse, persuasum hostes habuere. Qui innocentiæ suæ confisi vadimonium prompte obiverunt, illi plerique contra jura Regni, etiam non auditi, convicti, in carceres abrepti, arrestis detenti, impensis gravissimis exhausti, ad mutandam denique religionem, libertate promissa, invitati pellectique sunt. Quorum adversus apostasiam pectora satis munita deprehenderunt, iis prætextu fidelitatis obligandæ, oblati sunt libelli (reversionales dicti) quibus subsignatis protectionem Pastorum suorum ejurarent, promitterentque, non impedituros se, quo minus sacrificuli Templa occupare & Pontificia iis sacra inferre possent, donec scilicet accedente illuminatione Spiritus S. & ipsi à sacrificulis meliora edocti, abdicata hæresi sua, Pontificias cerimonias amplecterentur. Ita Magnates, Nobiles, plebeii coram Phalaridis tauro illo comparentes innumeri, pars in carceribus, aliisque modis vita orbati, pars horrendum in modum exagitati divexatique, pars denique carnis imbecillitate subacti, fidei in gravissima illa tempestate naufragium passi, quam Christo & Euangelio ejus fidem debuerunt, reclamante conscientia, fregerunt.
units.tr: The Pressburg tribunal, under the pretext of rebellion by the Evangelicals. It seemed good to set up, consisting of judges partly ecclesiastical and partly political, all of them Papists and sworn enemies of the Gospel, and with wonderful zeal to summon thither all the most distinguished persons to answer the charge of treason laid against them. The beginning was made with the flock: with the political magnates and others whom the enemies were persuaded could more easily be perverted. Those who, trusting in their innocence, promptly answered the summons were for the most part, against the laws of the kingdom, convicted even unheard, dragged into prisons, held under arrest, exhausted by very heavy expenses, and at last invited and enticed to change their religion with promises of liberty. Where they found hearts sufficiently fortified against apostasy, they were offered, under the pretext of binding them to loyalty, little documents (called reversals) by signing which they would renounce the protection of their pastors and promise that they would not hinder the priests from occupying the churches and bringing Papist rites to them, until, the illumination of the Holy Spirit coming and the priests teaching them better things, they should abjure their heresy and embrace Papist ceremonies. Thus countless magnates, nobles and commoners, appearing before that bull of Phalaris, some deprived of life in prisons and other ways, some horribly harassed and vexed, and some at last overcome by the weakness of the flesh, suffered shipwreck of the faith in that most grievous tempest, breaking, while conscience cried out, the faith they owed to Christ and his Gospel.

units.la: CCCVII. Sed gravior & flagrantior vis incubuit Ecclesiarum Pastoribus, in quorum, in irruptione stantium, salute cardinem verti incolumitatis tot Ecclesiarum, persecutores non ignoraverant. Qui proin rebellium, investigandorum prætextu, judiciorum extraordinariorum facultatem nullo negotio impetrârunt. Tria igitur ejusmodi judicia constituere placuit, unum Tirnaviæ, cui se Posonienses: duo Posonii, quibus se reliqui per Hungariam Ministri sisterent. Neque tamen primo statim coetu cunctos citare è re visum, sed paucos duntaxat, eósque Augustanæ Confessioni addictos; ut ex paucorum successu, quid de reliquis spei affulgeat, periculum facere integrum foret. Cúmque firmum ratúmque habuerint, rebellionis obiectæ calumnia religionem universam abolere, mortis metu libellos subsignandos obtrudere extremis viribus conati sunt. Summa libellorum capita erant: ut Ministri Evangelici utriusque Confessionis, Scholarum Rectores, cantores, studiosi & aeditui (I.) Aut ministerium omne sive ecclesiasticum, sive scholasticum, ad evitandum sententias judiciales, sibi propter obiectum rebellionis crimen imminentes, propria subscriptione sigillo munita penitus abdicent, neque partem ullam sive clam sive palam exercere amplius sustineant, ac de caetero ceu fideles Regis subditi vitam quietam pacificámque in Regno transigant, capitis supplicio turbantibus vel leviissime, indicto: (II.) Aut spontaneum exilium, ceu rei mortis, suscipiant, obligata libello propria manu subscripto, sigilloque munito, fide, quod nunquam in patriam reversuri neque etiam vel hæreditarias Regis Provincias, vel Imperiales, nedum hostiles ditiones adituri sint: (III.) Aut, quod prae caeteris gratum sibi acceptúmque futurum sit, Religionem Romanam Catholicam amplectantur. Et priora quidem duo palam in judiciis urgebantur. Tertium vero prora puppisque consiliorum omnium χυεἰως intentum fuit.
units.tr: CCCVII. But a heavier and fiercer force bore down upon the ministers of the churches, on whose safety, since they stood in the breach, the persecutors knew the hinge of the safety of so many churches turned. Therefore, under the pretext of investigating rebels, they obtained without difficulty the power of extraordinary judgments. They thought it right to set up three such courts: one at Trnava, to which the Pozsony men were to appear; two at Pozsony, to which the rest of the ministers throughout Hungary were to present themselves. Nor did they think it expedient to summon all at the first session, but only a few, and those committed to the Augsburg Confession, so that it would be safe to test, from the success with a few, what hope might shine for the rest. And when they were firmly convinced that the calumny of rebellion could be used to abolish the whole religion, they strove with all their might to force upon them, under fear of death, documents to be signed. The main heads of the documents were these: (I.) that the Evangelical ministers of either Confession, the rectors of schools, cantors, students and sextons, either should completely renounce, by their own signature sealed with a seal, all ministry, whether ecclesiastical or scholastic, to avoid the judicial sentences hanging over them on account of the charge of rebellion, and should no longer dare to exercise any part of it, secretly or openly, and henceforth, as faithful subjects of the King, should pass a quiet and peaceful life in the kingdom, with the penalty of death for anyone disturbing it even slightly; (II.) or should undertake voluntary exile, as men condemned to death, binding themselves by a document signed with their own hand and sealed, with a pledge that they would never return to their country, nor even enter the hereditary provinces of the King, or the Imperial, let alone the hostile territories; (III.) or, which would be more welcome and acceptable to them than the others, should embrace the Roman Catholic Religion. And the first two were indeed pressed openly in the courts. The third, however, was the prow and stern of all their plans, aimed at secretly.

units.la: CCCVIII. Ita prima dies paucis nonnullis xxv. Sept. A. M. D. LXXIII. dicta, qua se Posonii sisterent dele- gatis judicibus, impacti atrociissimi criminis causam dic- turi.
units.tr: CCCVIII. So the first day, called by a few people the 25th of September 1673, when they were to present themselves at Pressburg before the appointed judges and answer for a most atrocious crime.

units.la: Comparent Fratres triginta duo Augustanae, & unicus, Carponensis Ecclesiae Minister, Helveticae Confessioni addicti, haud postremi nominis plerique. His à Fisco Regio & Archiepiscopo Strigoniensi Georgio Szelepzeni, mira arte industriáque praemonitis, maturè consulitur, ne sententiam mortis contra se pronuntiandam operiri; quàm saluti suæ libellis exhibitis consulere malint. Ita mortis citatis, ast inauditis, indefensisque indictæ metu perculsi, neque satis libellorum virus cum animo expendentes, nimia certè in primo isthoc ferocissimoque impetu infirmitate carnis, pars Ecclesiastico Scholasticóque munere omni juxta præscriptam libelli formam sese abdicant: pars licet rebellionis rei nullo modo peracti, reatum tamen falsò confessi, exilium eligunt: unus etiam insigni levitate religionem, & cum ea bonam mentem ejerat.
units.tr: Thirty-two ministers of the Augsburg Confession and one minister of the church at Karpfen, adherents of the Helvetic Confession, most of them men of no small standing, appeared. The Royal Fisc and the Archbishop of Esztergom, George Szelepcsényi, with remarkable skill and diligence, had forewarned them and advised them in good time not to wait for a sentence of death to be pronounced against them, but to look to their safety by presenting written submissions. Thus, struck with fear by a summons to death that was issued without a hearing, without a defence, and without any inquiry, and not weighing the poison of the documents sufficiently in their minds, some, through an excessive weakness of the flesh in that first and most furious assault, renounced their ecclesiastical and teaching office entirely, in accordance with the prescribed form of the document. Some, although they were accused of a rebellion they had in no way committed, falsely confessed guilt and chose exile. One, with remarkable levity, even cast off his religion and, with it, his sound mind.

units.la: CCCIX. Cùm non malè se dedisse citationis initia hostes animadvertissent, & plures jam metu potiús, quàm criminis ullius conscientia victi libellos obtulissent, instante Fisco Regio, Nicolao Mailath, ad universalem omnium reliquorum per totam Hungariam, etiam tributariam, Ecclesiæ Scholæque Ministrorum, quorundam etiam ante ex Ecclesiis suis exturbatorum; nec non cantorum, studiosorum, ædituorum, in mensem Februarium Anni sequentis M. D. C. LXXIV. processum est. Citatoriæ literæ Georgii Szelepzeni, Archiepiscopi Strigoniensis, ceu vicariam Regis in Hungariæ Regno potestatem, defuncto pridem Regni Palatino, Ordinibus invitis obtinentis, manu subscriptæ, sigillóque munitæ fuerant. Citati alii quidem, in tributariis maximè Regni partibus, à Superioribus suis comparere diserté prohibiti sunt: alii adversariorum fraudes sæpius experti, atque etiamnum subodorati, nondum forte ita periclitantibus ecclesiis suis, suga occultationéque saluti suæ consuluerunt: alii Deo & causæ confisi, non obstante judicii forma plane suspecta, utpote quæ non tam convincendis puniendisque maligne intentati criminis reis, quàm evertendæ tot Ecclesiarum libertati, aucupandóque tot violentiis prætextui inservie-bat.
units.tr: When the enemies saw that the opening of the summons had gone well, and many, conquered more by fear than by any consciousness of crime, had already offered written submissions, the proceedings were extended, at the urging of the Royal Fisc (Nicholas Mailáth), to all the remaining ministers and teachers of the churches and schools throughout the whole of Hungary, including the tributary regions, as well as some who had earlier been driven from their churches, and also cantors, students and sextons. The proceedings were set for February of the following year, 1674. The summons letters were signed by hand and sealed by George Szelepcsényi, Archbishop of Esztergom, who held the royal power in the Kingdom of Hungary as its vicar, since the Palatine of the kingdom had died long before and the Estates were unwilling. Some of those summoned, especially in the tributary parts of the kingdom, were expressly forbidden by their superiors to appear. Others, who had often experienced the deceits of their adversaries and still suspected them, provided for their safety by flight and concealment, perhaps because their churches were not yet in such danger. Others, trusting in God and in their cause, did not allow themselves to be deterred by a form of trial that was plainly suspicious, since it served less to convict and punish those maliciously accused of crime than to overthrow the liberty of so many churches and to find a pretext for so many acts of violence.

units.la: cui alii obedire prohibentur; alii parent, gravibus rationibus inducti. bat, Posonii coram judice infensissimo, juratissimóque se sistere statuerunt, partim quòd sub fictitio prætextu causam Dei & Christi verti penitius cognovissent, quam ab universis deseri Deo contumeliosum rebantur merito; partim quòd instans à sacrificulis jamjam subrepere paratis, gravissimum Ecclesiarum periculum id efflagitasset; partim ut toti mundo constaret de innocentia Pastorum, qui capitali crimine arcessiti, si non comparuissent, gravem haud dubiè patrati suspicionem incurrissent; partim quòd obedientiam Magistratui testificandam censuissent; partim denique quòd consiliis, precibus, obtestationibus Ecclesiarum, prudentiorúmque judiciis se ad comparendum urgeri intellexissent. Memoratu haud indignum est, quòd procedente ea citatione Georgius Getseni, ab aulæ familiaribus interrogatus, quid sibi tot Pastorum, de quorum innocentia constet omnibus, citatio vellet? respondit: Funiculum Euangelicis Hungaris texuimus, quem si collo eorum implicare poterimus, nunquam se deinceps in pedes eorundem religio eriget. Si verò id non effecerimus, nobis, non vobis, inutilem molestiam facessiverimus.
units.tr: To this summons some were forbidden to obey, while others obeyed, led by weighty reasons. They resolved to present themselves at Pressburg before a most hostile and most sworn judge, partly because they had come to know more clearly that the cause of God and Christ was being subverted under a feigned pretext, and they rightly thought it an insult to God that it should be abandoned by everyone; partly because the imminent danger from the priests, who were already prepared to creep in, demanded this in the gravest peril to the churches; partly so that it might be clear to the whole world that the ministers were innocent, since, if they had not appeared when summoned on a capital charge, they would undoubtedly have incurred a grave suspicion of guilt; partly because they judged that obedience to the magistrate ought to be attested; and finally, partly because they understood that they were being urged to appear by the counsels, prayers and entreaties of the churches and by the judgment of the wiser men. It is worth recording that when this summons was being carried out, George Getseni, questioned by the courtiers as to what such a summons meant for so many ministers whose innocence was known to all, replied: We have woven a rope for the Evangelical Hungarians, and if we can entangle it around their necks, religion will never again raise itself to its feet. If we do not manage this, we shall have brought a useless trouble upon ourselves, not upon you.

units.la: CCCX. Comparuerunt igitur secunda citatione isthac non exiguo numero Pastores, aliíque Ecclesiarum & Scholarum Ministri, ultra ducentos quinquaginta, quorum plerique Augustanæ Confessioni, quinquaginta septem verò Reformatæ addicti fuerunt. Singulorum illorum actiones, diversa fata, exitúsque describere, instritutæ tractationis brevitas haud patitur. Summa tamen capita, quando res est omnis posteritatis memoria longè dignissima, obiter ut delibem; ante omnia ad tribunal seu Excelsam, uti vocabant, Sedem, provocatis ex tanto numero sex tantùm, (ex quorum ore reliquos omnes, atque eos etiam, quorum ipsi nomina ignoraverant, & plerosque etiam adeò locis dissitos, ut se invicem pauci noverint, judicare statuerant) per Regium fiscum actio ejusmodi intentatur, quòd scilicet postposito Dei hominúmque timore totum Hungariæ Statum Romano-Catholicum, ipsúmque adeò Regem idololatriæ insimulare, contra B. Virginem Mariam, Sanctos demortuos, eorúmque & Christi imagines pro concionibus ad populum habitis gravissimè debacchari, Venerabile Sacramentum conculcare sceleratis rebellibus, Suæ Maiestatis hostibus, consensu, ope & commeatu succurrere, eorum adventu gaudere, Turcis ad occupandum Hungariæ Regnum viam aperire non reformidassent, criminisque adeò læsæ Divinæ & humanæ Majestatis capitisque & bonorum omnium amittendorum reos se fecissent. Hic reorum quisque pro se pertendere, ut accusatio, quoad ea, quæ religioni Euangelicæ in reliquo orbe Christiano receptæ communia non sunt, homines notet, crimina argumento probet, testibus confirmet. Palam enim ex accusationis plerisque capitibus fieri, non tam rebellionem, cujus causa citati sint, spectari, quàm religionem peti. Longum verò esset Actoris & judicum adversus reos se defendentes masculè, in obtrudendis procuratoribus, ferendis præjudiciis, declinando legitimæ probationis onre, suadendo per subornatos Forgatium, aliósque ante latam sententiam, ad evitandum supplicium, quod effugituri nunquam sint, subscriptione libellorum, & spontanei exilii, traditionisque Basilicarum electione, strophas pertexere.
units.tr: At the second summons, therefore, a considerable number of ministers came, along with other ministers of churches and schools, more than two hundred and fifty in all, of whom most adhered to the Augsburg Confession and fifty-seven to the Reformed. The brevity of the treatise I am undertaking does not allow me to describe the actions, varied fates and outcomes of each one. Yet since the whole matter is most worthy of remembrance by posterity, I shall touch briefly on the main points. First, six only were summoned from so great a number to the tribunal, or what they called the Lofty Seat, and from their mouths they had resolved to judge all the rest, even those whose names they did not know, and many who lived so far apart that few of them knew one another. By the Royal Fisc an action of this kind was brought against them, namely that, having cast aside the fear of God and of men, they had accused the whole Roman Catholic state of Hungary, and the King himself, of idolatry; that in sermons delivered to the people they had raged grievously against the Blessed Virgin Mary, the departed saints, and the images of them and of Christ; that they had trampled upon the Venerable Sacrament; that they had not feared to aid the wicked rebels, enemies of His Majesty, with consent, help and supplies; that they had rejoiced at their arrival; and that they had opened the way for the Turks to seize the Kingdom of Hungary, and thereby had made themselves liable to the crime of injured divine and human majesty, and to the loss of life and of all their goods. Each of the accused argued for himself that the accusation, insofar as it concerned matters that are not common to the Evangelical religion as received in the rest of the Christian world, branded men, proved its charges by argument and confirmed them by witnesses. For it was plain from most of the heads of the accusation that it was not so much the rebellion, for which they had been summoned, that was aimed at, as religion itself that was attacked. It would be a long business to recount how the prosecutor and the judges, fighting vigorously against the accused who defended themselves, wove their snares: in foisting on them procurators, in bringing prejudices, in evading the burden of lawful proof, in persuading them, through the suborned Forgách and others before sentence was passed, to escape death, which they would never escape, by subscribing the documents, by voluntary exile, and by choosing to surrender the churches.

units.la: Certè ficto immanis criminis perduellionis adversus Regem, prætextu causam Christi & Euangelii ejus oppugnatam esse, argumenta plane <bl>φερόντα</bl>, arguunt; veluti quòd jam ante fine ullo rebellionis prætextu plures Ecclesiis suis moti sunt: quòd ne unius quidem Pastoris comparentis rebellio idoneo sive teste unico sive testimonio probari potuit: quòd Pastorum Euangelicorum, siquidem rebellionis complices fuissent, vitæ Judices Pontificii non magis utique quàm Magnatibus Pontificiis parciturí, neque rei sce-
units.tr: Certainly the fabricated charge of the monstrous crime of treason against the King, under the pretext that Christ's cause and His Gospel were being attacked, is plainly contradicted by the facts [φέροντα]. For example: many had already been driven from their churches before any pretext of rebellion existed; the rebellion of not even one minister who appeared could be proved, either by a single witness or by any testimony; and if the Evangelical ministers had been accomplices in the rebellion, the Papist judges, who would no more spare the Papist magnates, would not have spared those guilty of so horrible a crime, one most destructive to the King and the realm.

units.la: Perduellionis culpa accusati liberantur prægnantibus argumentis. scelus adeò horrendum Regi Regnóque perniciosissimum, exilio vel muneris abdicatione spontanea luituri fuerint: quòd Pontificii saniores in Hungaria, nominatim etiam Forgatsius Præses Judicii, & Zitzius ejusdem Assessor, innocentiæ eorum quoad rebellionem testimonium perhibuerunt, non aliud quàm contumaciam in subsignandis libellis iisdem exprobrantes, & solam hanc carcerum vexationumque causam allegantes: quòd Rex Hungariam universam ad unitatem fidei reducere, & hæresèos pestem extirpare statuerit: quòd jam ante Barzonius edito libello cleri Hungarici propositum aperuerit, priusquam in Ministris ullam rebellionis noxam, vel ejusdem speciem invenire hostes potuere: quòd Judices Delegati omnes Pontificii, partium studio ducti, Romanóque Pontifici singulariter obnoxii fuerunt. Qui enim aderant Politici, Pontificii erant omnes, cleri præsentis mancipia ὑβρόσταλγα, ne hiscere quidem adversus Purpuratos ausi. Forgathsius certè Rima-Szombathensibus, pro Pastoribus suis intercedentibus, sic respondit: Nolite, per Deum, me molestare, quia, sic me Deus adjuvet, ne ipse quidem securus sum. Si vel hiscam, rebellem me dicent, & in carcerem abripient. Igitur boni Pastores subscribant, & vias suas abeant. Ecclesiastici verò erant Archiepiscopus Szlepzenius, nec non Episcopi Hungariæ præcipui, qui Romano Pontifici, æquè ac alii Episcopi, juxta Pontificale Romanum Pii V. sic inter alia conceptis verbis jurarunt: Hæreticos etiam, omnesque rebelles Pontifici, extremè me persecuturum, ac infestaturum, juro. Denique non rebellionem, sed religionem crimini à Judicibus illis datam esse, clarissimo indicio est, quod consiliorum omnium principium & finis non fuit nisi subscriptio libellorum, quibus se tradituros ecclesias, vel exulaturos reciperent. Quibus aliisque etiam argumentis prægnantissimis fretus Illustris Præpotentium Unitarum in Belgio Provinciarum ad Aulam Cæsaream Legatus, Gerhardus Hammel Bruininx, libello Earundem Provinciarum nomine Cæsareæ Majestati A. M. D. C. LXXV. oblato, inter alia demonstravit, Posoniensis Judicii Processum non Rebellionis, sed Religionis Euangelicæ persequendæ causa institutum fuisse, atque sub-et obreptionibus optimum falli Principem; Non convictos, verum innocentes esse Prædicantes Euangelicos, quotquot A. M. D. C. LXXIV. ad purgandam tuendamque innocentium citationi parendo, in Posoniensi judicio comparuerunt; ac proinde iniquissime ad Reversalium subscriptionem Prædicantes urgeri. Neque aliam ob causam in Comitiis Soproniensibus à XXVIII. Maii ad XXIII. Dec. A. M. D. C. LXXXI. celebratis Judicia illa Extraordinaria adversus Euangelicarum Ecclesiarum Ministros inde ab A M. D. C. LXX. Tirnaviæ & Posonii celebrata, à Statibus Regni revocata, libellique etiam, quos Reversionales nuncupaverant, in iisdem judiciis extorti, in perpetuum aboliti sunt.
units.tr: The accused of treason are cleared by weighty arguments. Those who would have atoned for it by exile or by voluntary renunciation of their office were not guilty of such a crime. The more sensible Papists in Hungary, namely Forgách, president of the court, and Zitius, his assessor, bore witness to the innocence of the accused as far as rebellion was concerned, reproaching them only for their obstinacy in signing those documents, and alleging this alone as the cause of the imprisonments and vexations. The King had resolved to bring the whole of Hungary back to unity of faith and to root out the plague of heresy. Barzony had already, in a published book of the Hungarian clergy, declared this plan before the enemies could find any fault in the ministers or any trace of rebellion in them. All the delegated judges were Papists, driven by partisan zeal and wholly bound to the Roman Pontiff. For all the politicians present were Papists, mere tools of the clergy of the day, not daring even to open their mouths against the purple-clad. Forgách certainly, answering the men of Rimaszombat who interceded for their ministers, said: Do not, for God's sake, trouble me, for, so help me God, I am not even safe myself. If I so much as open my mouth, they will call me a rebel and drag me off to prison. So let the good ministers sign and go their ways. The ecclesiastics were Archbishop Szelepcsényi and the chief bishops of Hungary, who, like the other bishops, swore to the Roman Pontiff, according to the Roman Pontifical of Pius V, among other things in these words: I swear that I will persecute and harass to the utmost heretics and all rebels against the Pontiff. Finally, that the charge brought by those judges was one of religion and not of rebellion is the clearest indication, since the beginning and the end of all their deliberations was nothing but the signing of documents by which the ministers would hand over their churches or go into exile. Relying on these and other very weighty arguments, the illustrious legate of the most powerful united provinces in Belgium to the imperial court, Gerhard Hamel Bruininx, in a petition presented to His Imperial Majesty in 1675 in the name of those same provinces, demonstrated, among other things, that the proceedings of the Pressburg court had been instituted not to pursue rebellion but to pursue the Evangelical religion, and that the best of princes had been deceived by underhand and subreptive means; that the Evangelical preachers who appeared before the Pressburg court in 1674, obeying the summons in order to clear their innocence, were not convicted but innocent; and that therefore the preachers were most unjustly pressed to sign the reversal documents. Nor for any other reason did the Diet of Sopron, held from 28 May to 23 December 1681, revoke those extraordinary judgments against the ministers of the Evangelical churches, begun in 1670 at Trnava and at Pressburg, and abolish forever the reversal documents, called Reversionales, that had been extorted in those judgments.

units.la: CCCXI. Adversus innocentes Pastores & inauditos etiam plerosque post libellos diu satis, mira minarum promissionumque (nam subscripturis in exilium singulis à Colonitzio ex Hungarica Camera quinquaginta floreni, viatici loco promissi sunt,) mixtura, frustra obtrusos; feralis sententia mortis diro carmine d. IV. Aprilis A. M. D. C. LXXIV. & triduo post eadem adversus Rectores Scholarum lata, & à damnatis omnibus imperterrito lætóque animo, paratis hactenus propter Christum vita fortunisque omnibus exui, excepta est. Atque utinam, qui tanto animi præsentissimi robore sententiam mortis exceperunt, omnes temporis mora à Judicibus de industria eum in finem delecta, constantiam suam frangi, séque, metu mortis paulatim præcordia subeunte, ad Judicum nutum inflecti, passi non fuissent! Gloriosius certè de hostibus suis triumphassent omnes. Sed en Judicum consiliis suis de evertenda da religione uninè insistentium technas! Post sententiam mortis latam Regius Procurator ab Archiepiscopo Delegato Judice demum submonitus, ab Excelsa Sede impetrat, ut damnatos ad tempus executionis usque carceribus mancipare liceat. Cumque neque hoc terrore damnati moverentur quicquam, in liberam laxamque custodiam, ex qua non invitis Judicibus quisque, dummodo Christi causam prodere animus esset, fugam capessere poterat, traditi, in eadem omnes, (exceptis Papensi, Fileckiensi, Vesprimiensi, Levensique Pastoribus Praesidiariis Reformatis, ad terrendos caeteros die v. Maii, adeóque quinta demum à damnatione hebdomada, ferro apud domum Leopoldi Colonitzii vinctis, & in arcem Posoniensem abductis) octo hebdomadas integras exegerant. Quo temporis intervallo exquisitissimas quasque artes denuo Judices ipsi, inprimis Archiepiscopus Szeepzenius, & immanis illa Tigris Colonitschius, pervertendis & ad subscriptionem libellorum, quam solam redimendae vitae, & pretii etiam impetrandi conditionem praefigebant, subigendis explicuerant. Modò ex libera custodia excedere, fugam arripere jussi: modò verberibus ad sanguinem usque, ipsius etiam Colonitschii manu, caesi: modò novis inquisitionibus vexati: modò triremium propositio metu ad facienda desiderata invitati sunt. Forti animo tentationes omnes superarunt hactenus. Ad extremum die xxv. Maii Fratres Augustanos à Reformatis separari; & illos quidem ad aulam Archiepiscopalemevocari placuit. Hoc demum artificio nonnihil persecutores efficiunt. Nam separatis ita Augustanis ab Archiepiscopo, Colonitschio & Hoffkirchero, nullum non ad labefactandam eorum constantiam lapidem moventibus, optio tandem datur vel subscribendi, sive ad abdicationem muneris spontaneam, sive ad exilium, sive ad amplectenda Pontificia sacra,
units.tr: CCCXI. Against the innocent ministers, many of whom had not even been heard, the libelli were pressed on them in vain for a long time, with a strange mixture of threats and promises (Colonitz promised fifty florins from the Hungarian Chamber to each one who signed and went into exile, as travel money). The deadly sentence of death, in a dreadful form, was pronounced on 4 April 1674, and three days later the same sentence was passed on the rectors of the schools. All the condemned received it with an undaunted and cheerful spirit, ready until then to be stripped of life and fortune for Christ's sake. Would that those who received the sentence of death with such presence of mind had not allowed their constancy to be broken, once the judges, by design, had let time drag on, and had not let themselves, as fear of death gradually crept into their hearts, be bent to the nod of the judges! All of them would then have triumphed more gloriously over their enemies. But see the tricks of judges who alone set themselves to overthrow the religion! After the sentence of death had been passed, the royal Procurator, at last reminded by the archbishop acting as delegate judge, obtained from the Exalted See permission to keep the condemned in prison until the time of execution. When even this terror did not move the condemned at all, they were handed over to a free and loose custody, from which anyone could escape without the judges' objection, provided his mind was set on betraying Christ's cause. In this custody all of them, except the Reformed ministers of the garrisons at Papa, Fülek, Veszprém and Léva, who were bound in iron on 5 May to frighten the others, taken to the house of Leopold Colonitz and then led off to the citadel of Pozsony (that is, in the fifth week after the condemnation), spent eight full weeks. In this interval the judges themselves, above all Archbishop Szécsényi and that savage tigress Colonitschius, tried every most exquisite art to pervert them and to bring them to sign the libelli, which they laid down as the only condition for buying back their lives and obtaining a reward. Sometimes they were ordered to leave the free custody and take flight; sometimes they were beaten until they bled, even by Colonitschius's own hand; sometimes they were harassed by fresh investigations; sometimes the prospect of the galleys was held out to frighten them into doing what was wanted. Hitherto they had overcome all these temptations with a brave spirit. At last, on 25 May, it pleased the persecutors to have the Augustana brethren separated from the Reformed, and to summon the former to the archbishop's court. At last this trick achieved something for the persecutors. For with the Augustana men thus separated, and the archbishop, Colonitschius and Hoffkirchen moving every stone to shake their constancy, they were finally given the choice either of signing, that is, of voluntarily giving up their office, or of exile, or of embracing the Papist rites,

units.la: {y} variis artibus ad subscriptionem libellorum pellectis.
units.tr: variously enticed by different arts to sign the libelli.

units.la: Subscribentibus Augustanis fratribus non paucis, cra, libellis; vel carceres subeundi. Subscriptionem eligunt non pauci, carnis infirmitate victi: carceres reliqui numero quadraginta sex, unà cum duobus Reformatis, qui eventum speculaturi se Augustanis miscuerant. Illi singuli cum mercede quinquaginta florenorum dimissi: hi in carceres ablegati; inde post horas aliquot protracti, & circa tertiam ejus diei, alii navibus in Danubio, alii curribus impositi, ex urbe suburbiisque in diversa Regni fortalitia vecti, novendecim, quibus Reformatus unus accessit, Comarinum: octo Sarwarinum: octo Berenthschinum: octodecim, quibus itidem Reformatus unus accessit, Leopoldopolin deportati, ferro constricti omnes, & foedissimis carceribus inclusi sunt. Et postremis quidem octodecim additus lictor unà cum restibus, proximè patibulum in campo suspendium minatus, nihil terrore isthoc apud obstirmatos, & pro Christo mortem quamvis oppetere paratos, promovit. Qui Posonii supererant Reformati, duobus exceptis, omnes subscriptionem constanter abnuentes, separatorum à se Fratrum aliorum quidem inconstantiam summo cum dolore, aliorum vero constantiam pari cum laetitia spectantes, se Deo devovebant totos, eadem gratia praeclarum agonem ad ultimum spiritum usque certaturi.
units.tr: Not a few of the Augustana brethren signed the libelli, while the rest chose to go to prison. Not a few chose to sign, overcome by the weakness of the flesh; the rest, forty-six in number, together with two Reformed men who had mingled with the Augustana men to watch the outcome, chose prison. Each of the signers was released with a payment of fifty florins; the others were sent to prison, and after some hours were dragged out again, and about the third hour of that day, some were placed on ships on the Danube, others in carts, and were carried out of the city and its suburbs to various fortresses of the kingdom. Nineteen, to whom one Reformed man was added, were taken to Komárno; eight to Sárvár; eight to Berettyó; and eighteen, to whom again one Reformed man was added, were carried to Leopoldstadt. All were bound in iron and shut up in the most foul prisons. To the last eighteen an executioner was added, with ropes, threatening that a gallows would soon be set up for them in the field; but this terror did nothing to move men who were obstinate and ready to face death for Christ. The Reformed who remained at Pozsony, except two, all steadfastly refused to sign. They watched with the greatest grief the inconstancy of the brethren who had separated from them, and with equal joy the constancy of others, and they devoted themselves wholly to God, resolved to fight this noble contest with the same grace until their last breath.

units.la: Vocatis igitur ad eandem Archiepiscopi aulam Thomæ Palfy, Episcopi Nitriensis, Regiæ Aulæ Cancellarii, Epistola praelegitur, cujus summa erat, Majestatis Regiæ de Praedicantibus contumacibus, eò quod Posonii conventicula celebrent, & forte etiam sacramenta administrent, atque adversus tot Episcoporum monita praefractum obstinatúmque animum prodant, (en decreti causas!) ultimam sententiam esse, ut in varia fortalitia distributi mortificentur. Tum Archiepiscopus simulata de Colonitschii, quem rufi militis convitio aspergere solebat, crudelitate & sanguinariis, quae continuè adversus Pastores agitet, consiliis, querimonia eosdem demulcens, iterum iterúmque subscriptionem suadet, ceu reremedium unicum, quo non tam suo, quàm efferato Colonitschii animo satisfieri, ejúsque tyrannica libido reprimi posset. Sed obsurduerant pridem ad Sirenes hasce castissimæ servorum Christi aures. Denuo igitur iisdem, qui supra, in Archiepiscopi aula coactis, Colonitschius, Hoftkircherus, Lapsankius, unà cum Archiepiscopo dirissima quæque interminati, inter alia Regiæ Majestati stare sententiam immotam, atque à se nunc Ejus nomine promulgari, ne librum Religionis Euangelicæ exercitium in Regno Hungariæ amplius exerceatur, asserunt. Excipientibus Pastoribus, se non intelligere, quemadmodum Rex nondum à sacramento juramenti, quod Regni Statibus præstiterit, solutus, sententiam ejusmodi per Ministros suos promulgare voluerit, iracundi, non hic locum esse disputandi, regerunt. Sine mora Ministris quadraginta & uni, Reformatis omnibus (reliqui enim sedecim ex numero universo quinquaginta septem, Posonii comparentium, partim jam in carceres detrusi erant, partim se maturè ante latam sententiam, non subscriptis libellis ullis, se subducentes ad Ecclesias suas, defensi à terrestribus dominis, redierant, duobus duntaxat ex omni Reformatorum choro, Pastore uno, & Ludimagistro altero, à terrestri suo Domino, Judicii Assessore ad muneris sui abdicationem seductis;) in vincula raptis obnuntiatum, ad triremes illis eundum, ubi senes etiam addiscere linguam Italicam debeant, futurúmque sit, ut lac etiam maternum illis amarescat; Archiepiscopo ipso animam suam Diabolis discerpendam devovente, si ulli, etiam religionis mutationem posthac promissuro, unquam liberatio inde obtigerit. Ex eo tempore non amplius subscriptio libellorum, sed mutatio religionis unicè urgebatur. Et ex carcere producti eodem die viginti, curribus tectis impositi, prosequentibus furiosis militibus, alió deportati sunt; Sarwarinum septem; Kapuwarinum totidem, Eberhardinum castellum sex. ubi catenis onerosissimis constrictí, in carcerésque teterrimos conjecti, omne ludibriorum & calamitatum genus, inter efferatos in extremam rabiem hostes, Jesuitas cumprimis certatim affluentes, & ad apostasiam captivos solicitantes, forti animo inter' preces assiduas, hymnósque ceu laetum Pæana, toleràrunt. Reliqui viginti & unus elapsa hebdomade eodem carcere Posoniensi soluti, curribus, militum insolentissimorum catervis stipati, & vestimentis honestioribus, aliisque, quæ residua secum ferebant, Colonitschii jussu stipati, Leopoldopolin avecti, atque ibi in carceres iterum obscuros profundissimósque abjecti sunt.
units.tr: Then Thomas Pálffy, Bishop of Nyitra and Chancellor of the royal court, was summoned to the same archbishop's court, and a letter was read to the men who had been called there, the substance of which was this: Since the contumacious ministers hold conventicles at Pozsony, and perhaps even administer the sacraments, and show a stubborn and obstinate mind against the warnings of so many bishops (behold the causes of the decree!), it is the final sentence of His Royal Majesty that they be distributed among various fortresses and left to die. Then the archbishop, feigning sorrow at the cruelty and bloodthirsty plans which Colonitschius (whom he used to abuse with the insult "red soldier") was continually pursuing against the ministers, soothed them with complaints and again and again urged them to sign, as the only remedy by which the savage mind of Colonitschius, rather than his own, could be satisfied and his tyrannical lust restrained. But the most chaste ears of Christ's servants had long been deaf to these Sirens. So again, with the same men as before gathered in the archbishop's court, Colonitschius, Hoffkirch and Lapsanky, together with the archbishop, uttered every most dreadful threat, and among other things asserted that the royal majesty's sentence stood unchanged and was now being proclaimed by them in his name: that the exercise of the Evangelical religion in the kingdom of Hungary should no longer be practised. The ministers objected that they did not understand how the King, who had not yet been released from the oath he had sworn to the Estates of the kingdom, could wish such a sentence to be proclaimed through his ministers. In anger they replied, that there was no room here for dispute. Without delay, forty-one ministers and all the Reformed (for of the whole number of fifty-seven who had appeared at Pozsony, sixteen had already been thrust into prison in part, and the others, withdrawing before the sentence was passed without signing any libelli, had returned to their churches, defended by their lay lords, while of the whole Reformed company only two, one minister and one schoolmaster, had been seduced by their lay lord, an assessor of the court, into giving up their office) were seized in chains and told that they were to go to the galleys, where even the old men would have to learn the Italian language, and it would come to pass that even their mother's milk would turn bitter to them. The archbishop himself vowed that his soul should be torn to pieces by the devils if any of them, even one who promised a change of religion, were ever freed from there. From that time on, not the signing of the libelli but a change of religion alone was insisted upon. On the same day twenty of them were led out of prison and placed in covered carts, with raging soldiers escorting them, and were carried elsewhere: seven to Sárvár, the same number to Kaposvár, and six to Eberhardsburg castle. There they were bound with the heaviest chains and thrown into the most horrible prisons, and endured, with a brave spirit, amid constant prayers and hymns as a joyful paean, every kind of mockery and calamity, from enemies raging to the utmost fury, above all the Jesuits, who flocked in eagerly and tried to solicit them to apostasy. The remaining twenty-one were released a week later from the same Pozsony prison, surrounded by carts and by bands of the most insolent soldiers, and, by Colonitschius's order, were carried to Leopoldstadt with the more respectable clothes and whatever other belongings they had with them, and there were again thrown into dark and very deep prisons.

units.la: CCCXII. Ita in diversorum locorum dirissima captivitate infandum in modum vexati cruciatíque, documentum dederunt, quid expectari à Romanis illis Draconibus, (Pontificium clerum intelligo) sicubi iis suæ satis vires placent, debeat. Pauca recenseri haud abs re fuerit.
units.tr: CCCXII. Thus, through the most dreadful captivity in various places, they were tormented and afflicted in an unspeakable manner, and gave proof of what one ought to expect from those Roman dragons (I mean the Papist clergy), wherever they are pleased with their own strength. It will not be out of place to recount a few instances.

units.la: Qui Posonio Berenthschinum asportati, atque ibi bini atque bini sub jugo, boum instar, constricti, in arcem deducti, & carcere ejusdem abscondite fuerant; quatuor Reformati, (atque inter eos unus præcipuæ dignitatis & authoritatis) & Augustanus unus tam strictis compedibus, vectes ferreos & quadrangulos acuminatos, transversim utrosque pedes lancinantes, habentibus constricti sunt, ut neque incedere, neque ab attritu earum, ferro transversim inter utrosque pedes immisso, calceos omnémque vestem pedibus superinductam corrodente, pedes defendere possent. Carcer ipse, in quem abtrusi fuerant, tenebricosus, excrementis fœdissimè scatens, extrema supplicia passuris destinatus, qui per angustum foramen subiri nisi à genibus palmisque innixis non poterat, infectorum insuper tanta copia refertus erat, ut eorum morsibus, aliisque incommodis infestati, noctes plerasque insomnes captivi ducere coacti fuerint. Cúmque Præfectus ipse Arcis Colonitfchio significaret, captivos ob debilitatem corporum tolerandis malis istis impares esse, respondit ille: Parum referre, tumulúmque forte in agro toto repertum iri, in quo miseriis illis confecti sepeliantur. Prohibiti insuper sub poena centum & amplius baculorum, nec non Turcicorum verberum captivi sunt, ne de sua captivitate quicquam cuiquam communicent. Jesuita nescio quo urgente, rigidissima hyeme, captivi ligna in usum praesidii allata, in superioris arcis aream deportare, & aquam ex profundissimo puteo exhaurire coacti sunt. Comarinum adducti viginti, Reformatus unus & Augustani novendecim, postquam eodem cum Turcis carcere clausi, compertoque, à Reformato confessore magnanimo non parum reliquos confirmari, ita separati sunt, ut Reformatus Turcicis compedibus illigatus, à reliquorum consortio divulsus, in cacere peculiari, eoque foedissimo solus delitescere quinque menses integros coactus fuerit: reliqui vero exceptis duobus, omnes, Sclavonicae gentis, taedio squaloris carcerum vexationumque victi, subscriptionem de abdicandis sponte muneribus suis, frustra obtulerunt. Praefecto enim apud Colonitzium intercedente, ut ea conditione liberentur, responsum est, fero nimis, finito jam gratiae tempore, libellos offerri. Neque alia jam conditione liberari eos posse, quam si religione solenniter ejurata, Pontificia sacra amplecterentur. Sic male consulti, post quatuor fere mensium patientiam, horribili apostasia, jurantes in verba insolentissima novae fidei novissimis Hungariae Catholicis praescriptae, carcerum molestias, mortisque metum redemerunt, & impietatis suae plus quam Bileamicae mercedem, alii quinquaginta, alii pauciores florenos, prout dignitas vel meritum personae postulare visum est, retulerunt. Sed paulo post, visa Leopoldopoli reliquorum constantia, conscientiae furiis ita agitati sunt, ut eorum nonnulli diei nativitatis suae maledixerint. Qui ve-
units.tr: Those who were taken from Pozsony to Berettyó, and there, two by two, yoked like oxen, were led into the castle and hidden in its prison: four Reformed men (among them one of special dignity and authority) and one Augustana man were bound with such tight fetters, with four-sided iron bars sharpened at the ends, which cut into both their feet crosswise, that they could neither walk nor protect their feet from the friction, as the iron, laid crosswise between their feet, gnawed through their shoes and all the clothing drawn over their feet. The prison into which they had been thrust was dark and full of filth, intended for those about to suffer extreme punishment; it could be entered only through a narrow hole, on hands and knees, and it was moreover so crowded with vermin that, troubled by their bites and other discomforts, the prisoners were forced to pass most nights without sleep. When the commandant of the castle informed Colonitschius that the prisoners, because of the weakness of their bodies, were unable to bear these evils, he replied: It matters little; perhaps a grave will be found somewhere in the whole field, in which they may be buried, worn out by their miseries. The prisoners were also forbidden, under penalty of more than a hundred blows with the stick and Turkish beatings, to communicate anything of their captivity to anyone. At the urging of some Jesuit, in the hardest winter, the prisoners were forced to carry the wood brought in for the garrison into the courtyard of the upper castle, and to draw water from a very deep well. At Komárno twenty were taken, one Reformed man and nineteen Augustana men. After they had been shut up in the same prison with the Turks, and it was learned that the magnanimous Reformed confessor was no little strengthening the others, they were separated in such a way that the Reformed man, bound with Turkish fetters and torn from the company of the others, was forced to hide alone for five full months in a separate cell, and that the most foul one. The rest, except two, all of Slavonic race, overcome by the tedium of the filth of the prisons and their harassment, offered in vain a signed statement of giving up their offices of their own accord. For when the commandant interceded with Colonitz that they might be freed on that condition, the answer came: It is too late; the time of grace is now over, and libelli can no longer be offered. Nor can they be freed on any other condition than by solemnly abjuring their religion and embracing the Papist rites. So ill advised, after nearly four months of endurance, they bought off the discomforts of prison and the fear of death by a dreadful apostasy, swearing to the most insolent words of the new faith prescribed to the latest Hungarian Catholics, and they received the wage of their impiety, more than Balaam's, some fifty florins, others fewer, as the rank or merit of each person seemed to deserve. But soon afterwards, when the constancy of the rest was seen at Leopoldstadt, they were so tormented by the furies of conscience that some of them cursed the day of their birth. Those who...

units.la: Comarinum, vero Comarini supererant tres confessores constantissimi, ad sordidissimos quosque labores, quibus Turcas & Zigaros captivos ibi adstringi mos est, ab ortu Solis ad occasum usque, nullo æstus, frigoris, hiemis, æstatis discrimine, exantlandos coacti, Deo illibatam fidem constanter servarunt. In carcere Eberhardino Archiepiscopus jam octogenarius propriis manibus, malleorum subsidio, ita captivos contudit, ut membra etiam nonnullorum luxata officio defungi amplius nequiverint: eosdem convivis suis illudendos, exagitandos exposuit, tandemque in eorum conspectu ad labores sordidissimos relegavit, & se aliisque præsentibus, risu contumeliisque omne genus eos prosequentibus, ad sanguinem usque desudare subegit. Horrendum cum primis in modum divexati sunt ii, qui Leopoldo poldopoli in carceribus dirissimis attinebantur, numero triginta novem, Augustani septendecim, & Reformati viginti duo. ex quorum censu Augustani tres & Reformatus unus (resipiscens tamen illico) unius & alterius diei inedia, laboribus, compedibus fracti defecerunt. Reliquos Jesuita Nicolaus Kelio, quo homine monstrum crudelius vix Sol vidit, his verbis salutavit: Ego ratione tum officii, tum specialis mandati vos visito, simulque vobis denuntio, gravissima vobis, nisi jussa feceritis, imminere. Pane nigerimo militari & aqua, ferreis compedibus vincti, omnibusque miseriis subjecti, vitam morte tristiorem tolerabitis. Tali Euangelio convertere miseros primo impetu satagerat. Quos ubi ad obnuntiationem ejusmodi imperterritos videt, sine mora compedibus præsens senes juvenesque, firmos infirmosque juxta constringi Turcico more, curat. De innocentia sua protestantibus respondit: Equidem duplicis rebellionis ecclesiasticæ adversus Ecclesiam, & Politicæ adversus Regem, crimina laboratis. Quod si maxime politice rebelles non effectis, uti credo, plures vestros de rebellione ne cogitasse quidem: tamen ob rebellionem ecclesiasticam omne genus poenarum commeruistis. Labores plus quàm serviles & nunquam, subinde ne diebus quidem Dominicis interruptos, obscoenissima quaeque loca intensissimo æstu expurgandi, carceres aggeresque effodiendi, fortalitii aream, uligine madidam, lapidibus & arenis obducendi, aggeres circa muros congerendi, nives densas ventilabris avehendi, profligatissimorum denique mancipiorum occupationibus suetis defungendi, ita exactores furibundi milites, mercede ad saeviendum conducti, summo ἐγχειρίδιον Kellione, perpetuis verberibus, adhibitis etiam hastis, sclopetis, & restibus aqua madefactis, induratis, & in nodos colligatis; conculcatione perpedes, capillorum evulsione, aliisque dirissimis saevitiae modis exasperárunt, ut simile quid vix ulla historiarum monumenta adversus vilissima mundi καταγμάτων patratum commemorent. Cùm carcer effodiendus esset, his verbis haud postremus inter Pastores, Vir praecipua authoritate spectabilis, apud Jesuitas praesentes operis protestabatur: Coram Deo, Angelis & hominibus protestamur, quòd crudelius longè nobiscum agatis, quàm olim cum Apostolis crudelissimi persecutores egerunt. Apostoli enim fuerunt in carcere: sed carcerem sibi effodere nunquam coacti sunt. Nos Apostolorum discipuli non solùm in carcere sumus, sed etiam inaudito exemplo carcerem nobis effodere cogimur. Quamobrem ut vos, ceu authores crudelitatis tantae, inexcusabiles reddamus, en primus ego clavum infigam. Risu profuso haec Jesuitae excipientes, responderunt: Laborabitis ergò tantò alacriùs, quia causas impulsivas tam graves habetis. Labores istos durissimos & poene intolerabiles subeuntibus, panis nigri exiguum demensum, tertio quoque die, ubi optimè eum iis actum est, libum quatuor librarum praebitum est; noctu verò in carcere degentibus nunquam aquae tanta copia facta, ut sitim ex diurnis laboribus contractam levare possent. Interdictum insuper omnibus, ne iis ininterdiu extra carcerem occupatis, vel in carcere etiam agitantibus, sive clam, sive palam vel minimus cibus potúsque offerretur.Quod interdictum violantes ex συμπαθείας æstu quodam, tum vir coæpas misero offerens, unâ cum accipiente, inflictis verberibus pluribus gravissimísque, tum muliercula carnis & panis nonnihil ἐν παροδῷ porrigens, à Jesuitis deprehensa, collum manúsque numellis meretricum inclusa, & publicè per compita, intensissimo frigore circumducta, nefas expiárunt. Vestimenta & calceamenta semel attrita non reparabantur à quoquam, ita ut nudis pedes, seminudísque reliquum corpus, in conspectu omnium mandatis laboribus defungendum fuerit. In carceribus angustissimis, pluviis nivibúsque perviis, inter homines maleficos ob capitalia delicta captos, maledictis continuis sacro cultu defungentibus obstrepentes, non raro cum serpentibus & bufonibus confligendum fuerat: à reliquis vero infectis identidem, quies somnúsque turbati. Etiam in carceribus verbera horrenda ictúsque inflicti non raro, ob causas levissimas. Captivus enim, Vir egregius doctissimúsque, ex carcere ad amicum de calamitatibus suis nonnihil scripsisse compertus, hanc, præsente & dictante Jesuita Kellione, poenam subiit, ut in terram projectus, à novem militibus percutientibus, baculis spissis & nodosis ita cœsus, & Præfecti calcibus horribiliter ita impetitus conculcatúsque fuerit, ut pro mortuo sublatus, ac mox respirans in novum carcerem solus, & ense stricto custoditus, sine ulla corporis sanguine fœdati dilaniatique cura, conjectus fuerit.
units.tr: Of the Comarno prisoners, three most steadfast confessors remained at Comarno. They were forced to endure the filthiest labours, to which captive Turks and Zigari are customarily bound there, from sunrise to sunset, with no distinction made for heat, cold, winter or summer, and they kept their unblemished faith in God steadfastly. In the prison of Eberhard, the archbishop, already over eighty, beat the captives with his own hands, using mallets, so that the limbs of some were dislocated and could no longer do their work. He exposed them to be mocked and harassed by his guests, and at last, in their sight, he sent them back to the most degrading labours and forced them to sweat blood while he and others looked on and pursued them with laughter, insults and every kind of abuse. Those held in the most dreadful prisons at Leopoldopolis, thirty-nine in number, seventeen Augsburg Confession men and twenty-two Reformed, were treated with especial horror. From this group three of the Augsburg men and one of the Reformed (though he repented at once) collapsed, worn out by starvation for a day or two, by labour and by fetters. The Jesuit Nicolaus Kelio, a monster more cruel than the sun has ever seen, greeted the rest with these words: "In my capacity both as an officer and under a special commission, I visit you, and at the same time I warn you that the gravest penalties hang over you unless you do as you are ordered. Bound in iron fetters, and subjected to every misery, you will endure on black military bread and water a life sadder than death." He had tried to turn these wretched men with such a gospel at the first attack. When he saw that they were not dismayed by this threat, he at once arranged for the old and young, the strong and the weak alike, to be bound in fetters in the Turkish manner. To their protests of innocence he replied: "Indeed you labour under the charges of a double rebellion, ecclesiastical against the Church and political against the King. Even if most of you were not political rebels, as I believe, and had not even thought of rebellion, yet on account of ecclesiastical rebellion you have deserved every kind of punishment." They were worn down by labours more than servile, never interrupted, not even on the Lord's Days. They were made to clean the most filthy places in the most intense heat, to dig out prisons and ramparts, to cover the fortress yard, soaked with damp, with stones and sand, to heap up embankments around the walls, to carry away dense snow with shovels, and to perform the usual tasks of the most abandoned slaves. Their furious overseers, soldiers hired at a wage to rage, harassed them with Kelio's dagger [ἐγχειρίδιον] above all, with constant beatings, also with spears, muskets and ropes soaked in water, hardened and tied into knots, with trampling, with pulling out hair, and with other most dreadful forms of savagery, such that the histories hardly record anything like it inflicted on the most wretched fractures [καταγμάτων] of the world. When the prison was to be dug out, a man of no little standing among the ministers, distinguished by his great authority, protested to the Jesuits present at the work with these words: "Before God, the angels and men we declare that you treat us more cruelly than the most cruel persecutors ever treated the Apostles. The Apostles were in prison, but they were never forced to dig out a prison for themselves. We, the disciples of the Apostles, are not only in prison, but by an unheard-of example we are compelled to dig out our own prison. Therefore, so that we may make you, as the authors of such cruelty, inexcusable, here I, the first, will drive in the nail." The Jesuits received these words with a burst of laughter and replied: "Then you will labour all the more eagerly, since you have such weighty motives." To those who bore these very hard and nearly intolerable labours, a small ration of black bread was given every third day, and when they were treated at their best, a loaf of four pounds. At night, however, those who lived in prison were never given water in such quantity that they could quench the thirst gathered from the day's labours. Moreover, it was forbidden for anyone to offer, secretly or openly, even the smallest food or drink to those kept busy outside the prison during the day or who were confined in prison. Those who broke this prohibition, moved by some feeling of compassion [συμπαθείας], paid for their offence: a man who offered bread and meat to the wretched prisoner, together with the one who received it, was beaten many times and severely; and a little woman who handed on some bread and meat in passing [ἐν παροδῷ] was caught by the Jesuits, had her neck and hands enclosed in the harness of prostitutes, and was paraded publicly through the crossroads in the most intense cold. No one repaired clothing or shoes once they were worn through, so that the prisoners had to perform the assigned labours barefoot and half-naked, in view of everyone. In the narrowest prisons, open to rain and snow, among wicked men held for capital crimes, who shouted continually to disturb the sacred worship, they often had to fight off snakes and toads, and their rest and sleep were disturbed again and again by the vermin. Even inside the prisons, horrible beatings and blows were often inflicted for the slightest reasons. For when a prisoner, an eminent and very learned man, was discovered to have written something about his misfortunes from prison to a friend, he suffered this punishment, dictated in the presence of the Jesuit Kelio: he was thrown to the ground and beaten by nine soldiers with thick, knotted clubs, and was horribly kicked and trampled by the prefect, so that he was carried off as dead. Soon, breathing again, he was thrown alone into a new prison, guarded with a drawn sword, without any care for his body, which was stained and torn with blood.

units.la: CCCXIII. Innumeræ certè concatenatæque calamitates fuerunt, quas captivi, incredibili robore ex alto instructi, fortissimè sustinuerunt; quarúmque apud posteritatem fides propemodum laborabit. Singulas verò cùm prosequi, institutæ brevitatis ratione cohibitis non liliceat: omittere tamen id unum adhuc, quod impietatis, nisi fallor, & crudelitatis numeros omnes implet, non possumus. Cùm nec authoritate sua, nec suasionum illecebris ullis; nec promissorum melle, nec comminationum cruciatuúmque omnium felle id hostes impetrare à confessoribus constantissimis possent, ut vel sponte muneribus suis abirent, vel exilium deligerent, vel religionem mutarent; aliam quercum excutiendam rati, captivos ad Templa aliáve loca, quibus Panaceum Numen vel osserebatur à sacrificulis, vel adorandum ostentabatur, violenter pertraxerunt. Vidisses ibi contentionem furiosam impellentium cogentiúmque, & ex adverso certamina Confessorum μέχει ἁμαλῶ ad sanguinem usque reluctantium: Singulis ferè diebus Solis, festis, & jejuniorum temporibus, Kellio per armatos milites, veluti prœlium inituros, captivos seu extra carceres laborantes seu in carceribus delitescentes adoriri solitus, in Templi aream compellere conatus est. Restitantes omnibus viribus, ex carceribus raptatos bipennium & sclopetorum ictibus plagisque horrendis, tanto quandoque impetu, ut uno impulsu ad secundam usque, quæ atrii carceris erat, januam jactarentur, protrusos eò redegerunt, ut humum prostrati terræ se affigerent. Mox igitur capillis erectos stantesque sclopetorum stimulis lateri dorsoque infixis, compungebant, propellebant, raptabant iterum, ita ut totum isthoc Templum versus tragicum iter non aliud, quàm continua quædam cadentium, ægrè surgentium, ac denuò in terram propulsorum miserabilis jactatio & provolutio fuerit. Demum feralium istorum raptuum pertœsi, consilio inito captivi consentiunt, se deinceps jussos, non expectata amplius jactatione, Templum intraturos, conciones audituros, preces pias ad Deum fusuros, ea tamen lege, ut mortem potiùs præsentissimam subire, quàm vel miminimam partem cultus illiciti obire malint. Ita atrium Templi ingressi, blasphemas Jesuitarum conciones audiunt, & hostibus ad altare usque eos trahere, atque ad cultum Dei Maozim cogere molientibus, & tantum non ejus rei causa in atrio Templi bellum cum iis gerentibus, adeò fortiter, mortem etiam oppetere parati, resistunt, ut violenta hostium molimina universa irrita ceciderint. In festo Ignatii, ut casus tragicos plures, qui in numerato sunt, recensere omittam, summo mane captivi ad labores sordidos expulsi, instante Missa, interruptis laboribus Templum adire jubentur. Obfirmant illi animum eo potissimum die, quo se ad vetitum cultum adactum iri majori contentione, metuebant merito; Templumque se ingressuros simpliciter negant. Obloquitur Kellio: Itane boni Pastores, vim metuitis? Atqui cum daemonium habeatis, hoc, non alio modo, expelli illud debet. Accersuntur milites, qui propere alios baculis feriunt, alios sclopetis urgent, alios strictis ensibus, bipennibus alios propellunt, & instrumenta ejusmodi in dorsis obnitentium frangunt, tandemque fessi, & crudelitatis sub dio, inspectante hominum multitudine ingenti, patrati pertœsi, absistentes ulteriori ferocia, Jesuitas destituunt. Tum Kellio, in furorem conversus, duos venerandos senes corripi jubet, qui à sacrificulo subornato verberibus plagisque contusi, & semimortui, nullis ad resistendum viribus residuis, unus ad atrium Templi, alter vero ad altare usque rapti, pedibus baculisque promiscuæ multitudinis calcandi proterendíque objiciuntur. qui humi, dum Missa celebrabatur, jacentes, & pœne exanimes, finita Missa à reliquis captivis in carcerem deportati, nunquam posthac valetudinem recuperárunt, continuisque artuum doloribus fracti, pias animas, alter Neapoli, Curiæ Rhetorum alter, Deo Redemptori suo reddiderunt. Præterea, ne unquam ansa fæviendi deesset, sacrificuli cum Sacramento ad ægros pergentes, ea plerunque loca, quibus laboribus suis insudantes captivi deprehenderentur, transibant. Atque tum iterum adversus eos cultum Panaceo Numini negantes brutis verberibus, imò ardentibus quandoque etiam facibus sævitum, neque cessatum ante est, quàm bipennes, enses, sclopeti confracti, & captivi, ceu animalia mactationi destinata, in terram prostrati, cernuíque, in sanguine suo volutati misere sunt; sacrificio incruento, quod Kellioni unus sanguine madens nuntiari petiit, in cruentum converso; & Pilatis illis sacrificia sua innocentum sanguine permiscentibus, cruentantibúsque. Sic singulos, quibus ad laborandum protracti sunt, dies supremos sibi illuxisse rati, reditum in carceres pro beneficio ingenti deputabant; neque precarium inter tot mala spiritum traxerant, nisi in infirmitate illorum Divina potentia perfici, & velut triumphare coram toto mundo gestivisset.
units.tr: CCCXIII. Certainly there were countless and linked calamities, which the captives bore most bravely, endowed from on high with incredible strength; and belief in them will scarcely hold up with posterity. Since I am not permitted, given the limits of the brevity I have set myself, to pursue them one by one, I cannot, however, omit this one thing, which, unless I am mistaken, fills up every measure of impiety and cruelty. Since the enemies could obtain nothing from the most steadfast confessors, neither by their authority nor by any enticements of persuasion, neither by the honey of promises nor by the gall of threats and every torment, to make them either give up their offices of their own accord, choose exile or change their religion, they judged that another tack must be tried, and they forcibly dragged the captives to the temples or other places where the Panacean Deity was either offered by the little priests or displayed to be worshipped. There you might have seen the furious struggle of those who drove and compelled, and on the other side the fights of the Confessors, who resisted to the point of blood [μέχρι αἵματος], even unto blood. Nearly every day, on Sundays, feast days and fast days, Kelio, through armed soldiers, as if they were going into battle, used to attack the captives, whether they were working outside the prisons or hiding inside them, and he tried to drive them into the courtyard of the temple. They resisted with all their strength; they were dragged from the prisons by blows from axes and muskets and by horrible wounds, sometimes with such force that with one push they were thrown as far as the second door, which was the gate of the prison yard, and driven down there until they were stretched out on the ground and clung to the earth. Then, seizing them by the hair and making them stand upright, they goaded them, pricked them in the side and back with the muskets, pushed them, and dragged them on again, so that the whole of that tragic journey to the temple was nothing but a continual miserable tossing and rolling about of men falling, rising with difficulty and being driven again to the ground. At last, weary of these deadly dragging-ons, the captives agreed, after deliberating, that from then on, when ordered, they would enter the temple without waiting to be tossed about any more, would listen to the sermons, and would pour out pious prayers to God, on this condition, however, that they preferred to face immediate death than to take part in even the smallest portion of illicit worship. So they entered the courtyard of the temple and heard the blasphemous sermons of the Jesuits. When the enemies tried to drag them to the altar and force them to worship Maozim, and when they were ready even to meet death, fighting almost to the death in the courtyard of the temple for this very reason, they resisted so bravely that all the violent efforts of the enemy collapsed in vain. On the feast of Ignatius, to pass over the many tragic incidents that could be listed, early in the morning the captives were driven out to their filthy labours, and when Mass was about to begin they were ordered to interrupt their work and go to the temple. They steeled their minds especially on that day, which they rightly feared would be the day when they were most strongly compelled to the forbidden worship, and they flatly refused to enter the temple. Kelio objected: "Are you, good ministers, afraid of force? Yet since you have a demon, it must be expelled in this way and no other." Soldiers were summoned, who quickly struck some with clubs, pressed others with muskets, drove others on with drawn swords and axes, and broke such instruments on the backs of those who resisted.
