At last, weary and ashamed of the cruelty they had carried out in the open air, in the sight of a huge crowd of people, and no longer willing to go on with their fierceness, they gave up the Jesuits. Then Kelio, turned to fury, ordered two venerable old men to be seized. They were beaten and bruised by blows and clubs at the instigation of the little priest, and, half-dead and with no strength left to resist, one was dragged to the courtyard of the temple and the other as far as the altar, and they were thrown down to be trampled and crushed by the feet and clubs of the common crowd. Lying on the ground while the Mass was being celebrated, and nearly lifeless, they were carried back to prison by the other captives when Mass was over. They never recovered their health afterwards; broken by constant pains in their limbs, one at Naples and the other at Chur, they gave up their pious souls to God their Redeemer. Moreover, so that there should never be a lack of occasion to rage, the little priests, when they went to the sick with the Sacrament, would pass by those places where the captives were caught sweating at their labours. Then again they raged against them, because they refused worship to the Panacean Deity, with brutal beatings, and sometimes even with burning torches, and they did not stop until the axes, swords and muskets were broken and the captives were struck down to the ground, lying face-down and rolling in their own blood, like animals destined for slaughter. The bloodless sacrifice, which one of them, dripping with blood, asked to be announced to Kelio, was turned into a bloody one; and those Pilates mixed their sacrifices with the blood of the innocent and stained them with it. Thus each of them, thinking that the last day of their lives had dawned on them as they were dragged off to labour, counted their return to prison a great favour. Nor, amid so many evils, did they draw breath uncertainly, except that the divine power was made perfect in their weakness, and seemed to rejoice as if triumphing before the whole world.

units.la: CCCXIV. Quis verò talia fando audivit unquam?
units.tr: CCCXIV. But who ever heard such things told?

units.la: Caret exemplis diritatis immanitatisque tantæ omnis retrò antiquitas, in qua persecutores etiam sævissimos, veri etiam Dei prorsus expertes, flagitiosæ ejusmodi crudelitatis puduisset. Et puduit tandem sævitiæ ipsum etiam Kellionem, postquam ejus crudelitas calamitate innocentum utcunque satiata est, atque si non vindictam præsentem Dei, at infamiam certè apud homines, quibus paulatim facinora hæc innotuerant, extimescere cœpit. Tum enim ad strophAM Jesuitica dignam se convertens, tot malefactis simulata quædam beneficia miscuit. Nam & amicos quosdam captivorum aliquando admisit, & munera nonnulla illis consecrata administravit in speciem; at pessima revera fide, partem majorem militibus aliisque diripiendam relinquens, uti postea captivis compertum est. Ut igitur apud exteros fucum quendam crudelitati suæ obduceret, à captivis die xv. Febr. A. M. D. C. LXXV. confessionem beneficiorum illorum propria singulorum manu signatam petiit. Suboluit satis captivis, quò tentatio illa tenderet. Neque tamen post longam gravémque cum Jesuita disceptationem, re maturè deliberata, testimonium ejusmodi denegandum plerique saltem duxerunt, veriti scilicet, ne in re licita repulsam ferens sævire t atrociùs, cùm atrociter adeò sævierit hactenus adversus detrectantes obsequium in rebus illicitis. Apochas igitur manu propria signatas exhibent, quibus testantur, gratos se agnoscere, quòd R. P. Kellio pecuniolam à suis submissam admiserit ...
units.tr: No precedent for such savagery and monstrous cruelty can be found in all of antiquity. Even the most savage persecutors, who had no knowledge of the true God, would have been ashamed of so shameful a cruelty. Kellio himself at last felt shame at his savagery, once his cruelty had been somehow sated by the calamity of the innocent. He began to dread, if not God's present vengeance, at least infamy among men, to whom these deeds had gradually become known. Turning then to a stratagem worthy of the Jesuits, he mingled certain pretended kindnesses with so many wrongs. He at times admitted some friends of the captives and, in appearance, handed out some gifts set aside for them. But in truth he acted in the worst faith, leaving the greater part to be plundered by the soldiers and others, as the captives later discovered. So, to cast a kind of veil over his cruelty before outsiders, on 15 February 1675 he asked the captives for a written acknowledgement of those benefits, signed by each one's own hand. The captives understood well enough where this trap was aimed. Yet after a long and serious dispute with the Jesuit, having deliberated maturely, most of them at least thought such a testimony should not be refused. They feared that, meeting refusal in a lawful matter, he would rage more savagely, since he had so savagely raged hitherto against those who refused obedience in unlawful matters. They therefore present receipts signed with their own hands, by which they testify that they acknowledge themselves grateful that Reverend Father Kellio admitted the little sum sent by their people ...

units.la: admiserit. circumstantiis temporis personarúmque additis. Acceptis ejusmodi dinstinctis apochis in sinu gaudens impostor, non tantùm eas pro lubitu interpolavit, sed statim etiam divulgavit, simul fidem detracturus famæ, quæ ejus barbaram crudelitatem, & servorum Christi horrendas calamitates in mundo propalaverat: simul gratiæ & commiserationis apud Regem & bonos omnes fontem vaferima isthac techna obstructurus. Certè vix facta ipsi apocharum ejusmodi copia est, cùm ad pristinam crudelitatem reversus, atrociùs, quàm unquam antehac, miseros affligere perrexit.
units.tr: admitted, with the circumstances of time and persons added. Having received such specific receipts, the impostor, exulting in his bosom, not only altered them at will but also promptly published them. He intended at the same time to undermine the reputation that had spread abroad his barbarous cruelty and the horrible calamities of Christ's servants in the world, and by this crafty device to block the source of favour and pity with the King and all good men. Indeed, scarcely had he been given such a supply of receipts when, returning to his former cruelty, he went on afflicting the wretched more savagely than ever before.

units.la: CCCXV. Nec dum tamen persecutionis adversus tot Ecclesiarum Pastores, imò in eorum personis adversus universam Ecclesiam Hungariæ Euangelicam, æstus de- tumuit.
units.tr: CCCXV. Yet the storm of persecution against so many ministers of the Churches, indeed against the whole evangelical Church of Hungary through their persons, had not yet subsided.

units.la: quinimò efferbuit in dies magis. Cùm enim hostes parùm adhuc apud constantissimos Christi Confessores diversis cruciatuum calamitatúmque generibus se prosecisse sentirent, jam eos æternis triremium Hispanicarum, quarum toties terrore miseros perculerant, carceribus mancipare statuunt. Tantáque Clerum Hungaricum improbibitas & audacia transversum abripuit, ut horrendam illam ad triremes damnationem deportationémque non tantùm Rege inscio, sed contra mandatum etiam Regium fusceperint. Etenim captivorum Patroni jam à Clementissimo Rege mandatum ad Colonitzium obtinuerant, quo is captivos dimittere jussus est. Mandatum isthoc Thomas Palfy, Episcopus Nitriensis, Cancellarius Regni, Judicii Posoniensis Assessor, Colonitzio exhibere jussus, ita adulteravit, ut in tergo ejus adscriptis verbis, ut orare (scilicet in triremibus discant) insinuaverit, mentem Regis esse, ut ad triremes captivi ablegentur. cùm tamen omnia & singula mandati illius Regii verba nonnisi gratiam liberationémque spiraverint. Colonitzius qui non semel antehac Posonii Pastoribus in faciem dixerat: Vos multum Regis vestra clementia confiditis. sed nihil vobis ea proderit. Si enim vel decies clementissima de vobis mandata exhibuerit, ego centies eadem mutabo; accepto mandato Regio, non dimissionem, sed ablegationem ad triremes eo contineri pertendebat. Cúmque eo ipso tempore cohortes aliquot in Hungaria Austriáque conscriptæ, in subsidium Regis Hispaniæ adversus Messinenses mittendæ, in procinctu itineris stetissent, occasione ea usus, die XVIII. Martii A. M. D. C. LXXV. triginta sex (duo enim ob infirmitatem ex vexationibus contractam redditi inhabiles ad iter, relicti sunt) ex mediis laboribus sub vesperam abreptos, & per occultum foramen quoddam Arcis Leopoldopolitanæ eductos, militiæ Austriacæ ductori Neapolin deportandos, ibique certo pretio vendendos, atque in triremium servitutem redigendos tradidit. Ita stipati cohortibus equitum quadringentorum circiter, totidémque peditum, curribus impositi, per avia & ambages præter urbes & oppida Hungariæ, Moraviam versus, circumvecti, Sotviennæ tandem cum captivis quinque Berentschino allatis in amplexus mumutuos lamentabiliter ruentes, tot miserias patienter toleratas sibi gratulantes, & ad constantiam invictam invicem animantes; conjunguntur. Reliquum iter pedites, compedibus gravissimis utroque singuli pede onusti, inter furiosos milites, perpetuis verberibus, ensium & sclopetorum ictibus eos, sine ætatis, virium, viarum cultarum incultarúmque & asperarum discrimine ullo, ad promovendum iter impellentes, maledictisque continuis eos obruentes lancinantésque, & obviorum quorumque horrendis ludibriis exponentes, ad oram usque Maris Adriatici emetiuntur. Tanta fuit asperitas itineris, tanta miserabile isthoc agmen cingentium & abigentium crudelitas, ut captivi hiantia pedum nudatorum vulnera circumferentes, ubique vestigia sanguine suo cruentaverint. Ut pedes exulceratos & intumescentes Tergesti curare ipsi utcunque possent, coacti sunt ipsi saxorum & cultellorum adminiculo suos invicem compedes perfringere. quod sine cruentis vulneribus, & distractis carnium fructulis fieri non potuit. Depraedatio ibidem miserorum, qui nonnisi laceras vestes, & forte abscond/ conditas pecuniolas, ægrè hactenus à ruina defensas habebant, adeò exquisita fuit, ut truculentissimi milites scrutandis partibus, quas natura erubescit, non pepercerint. Demum naturæ & gentis illius ornamentis, capillis barbisque & mystacibus violenter privati, fœdissiméque tonsi, triste atque lachrymabile spectaculum præbuerunt, adeò deformatis illis, ut se invicem nisi ex lingua novaque velut consuetudine noscere amplius non possent. Accessit dira fames, ægrè impetrantibus miseris, quantum ad trahendum precarium spiritum, nedum ad iter adeò exercitum, totque militum plus quàm Scythica & barbarica ferocitate adversus juvenes senesve, firmos & infirmos grassantium, vexationibus infestum conficiendum, satis esset. Singulorum dierum rum stipendium tres teruncii erant. subinde etiam nihil omnino datum. Noctu pecorum instar in stabula aliáque loca sordida coactis, vix quietem ullam ob cruciantia pedum, totiusque corporis vulnera capessere licuit. Duo non postremi, pietate & doctrina insignes, tot vexationibus illis confecti in itinere mortui, & canum instar, feminudi insepultíque, abjecti sunt. Prior senex cum pergere amplius non posset, incudis instar, horrendis verberibus coefus & contusus, moribundus à captivis duobus iter cum eo continuantibus, & altera manu ferrum, altera ægrum sustinentibus, utrinque à latere suffultus, & à lapsu aliquandiu prohibitus, in præcipiti loco, neutro auxiliatorum sustinere valente, in terram prolapsus expiravit. Alter plaustro injectus, & mortuus ex eodem fine mora abjectus est. Accesserat pœne tertius, vir fpectatiffimus, & captivorum princeps, qui asello impositus, cum ob tardiorem ejus gressum subsequi reliquos non valeret, plagis adeo prægnantibus mactatus est, ut ex confractis naribus copiosissimo sanguine profuso, toto corpore madens, parum à mortuo abfuerit. Accessit ad crudelitatis cumulum, quòd captivi iidem jumentis ob defatigationem nimiam progredi non valentibus, impositi, jumentorum loco cœfi, & sic ad propellenda jumenta adacti sunt. Sex itidem fratres malis his prorsus enervati fractíque, in carcere Theatino relicti sunt; ex quorum numero quatuor pias animas in eodem exhalárunt; duo reliqui post diram famem, aliáque mala tolerata, sub ipsum liberationis tempus Neapolin deportati sunt. Quis verò talia, & plura etiam non minùs atrocia fando Myrmidonum, Pelopúmve, & duri miles Vlyffis Temperet à lachrymis?
units.tr: Rather, it grew hotter by the day. For when the enemies felt that they had not yet inflicted enough torments and calamities of various kinds on the most steadfast confessors of Christ, they resolved to consign them to the eternal galleys of Spain, with whose terror they had so often struck these wretched men. The Hungarian clergy were carried away by such shamelessness and recklessness that they undertook this dreadful condemnation and deportation to the galleys not only without the King's knowledge but even against the King's own mandate. For the patrons of the captives had already obtained from the most merciful King a mandate addressed to Colonitz, ordering him to release the captives. Thomas Palfy, Bishop of Nitra, Chancellor of the Kingdom and assessor of the court at Pozsony, was ordered to hand this mandate to Colonitz, but he falsified it, adding on its back the words to row (that is, that they were to learn it in the galleys), to suggest that the King's intention was that the captives be sent away to the galleys, although every single word of that royal mandate breathed nothing but grace and liberation. Colonitz, who had more than once said to the ministers of Pozsony to their faces: You put too much trust in your king's clemency, but it will do you no good. For even if his most merciful majesty issued ten mandates about you, I would change each of them a hundred times, now that he had received the royal mandate, insisted that it contained not a release but a dispatch to the galleys. At that very time some cohorts raised in Hungary and Austria, to be sent in aid of the King of Spain against the Messinese, were standing ready to march. Seizing the occasion, on 18 March 1675 he handed over thirty-six men (two had been left behind, unfit for the journey because of the injuries they had suffered from their ill-treatment) who were seized in the evening from the midst of their labours and led out through a secret opening of the fortress of Leopoldstadt, to be taken to Naples by the commander of the Austrian army and there sold for a fixed price and reduced to slavery in the galleys. Thus escorted by about four hundred horsemen and as many foot soldiers, loaded onto wagons, they were carried by unfrequented and winding roads past the cities and towns of Hungary toward Moravia, and at Znaim at last they were joined with five captives brought from Beroun. Weeping pitifully, they fell into one another's arms, congratulating each other on having patiently endured so many miseries and encouraging one another to unconquered constancy. For the rest of the journey the men on foot, each weighed down by very heavy fetters on both feet, were driven forward among furious soldiers by constant beatings and blows from swords and muskets, without any regard for age or strength, over roads cultivated and uncultivated, rough and smooth alike; they were overwhelmed with continual abuse and torn to pieces, and exposed to the dreadful mockery of whoever they met, and so they measured out the journey as far as the shore of the Adriatic Sea. So harsh was the journey, and so great the cruelty of those who surrounded and drove this wretched column, that the captives, displaying the gaping wounds of their bare feet, left bloody traces of their blood everywhere. Since they could not somehow treat their ulcerated and swollen feet at Trieste, they were forced to break each other's fetters with the aid of stones and knives, which could not be done without bloody wounds and torn pieces of flesh. The plundering of these wretches, who had nothing but torn clothes and a little money, perhaps hidden, and had until then barely saved it from destruction, was carried out so thoroughly there that the most savage soldiers spared no part of the body, when searching, that nature blushes to name. Finally, stripped by force of the adornments of their nature and their people, their hair, beards and moustaches, and shaved in the most hideous way, they presented a sad and tearful spectacle, their faces so disfigured that they could no longer recognise one another except by their language and their new, almost habitual, appearance. To this was added dire hunger; the wretches could scarcely obtain enough to keep their precarious breath, let alone enough to endure such a journey, and the many soldiers, with more than Scythian and barbarian ferocity, raged against young and old, strong and weak, harassing them with mistreatment. The daily pay was three farthings, and sometimes nothing at all was given. At night they were herded like cattle into stables and other filthy places, and scarcely any rest was allowed them because of the agonising wounds of their feet and their whole body. Two men of no small standing, notable for piety and learning, were worn out by these vexations and died on the road, and were cast aside like dogs, half-naked and unburied. The first was an old man who could no longer go on; battered and bruised by dreadful blows as if on an anvil, he was dying, supported on each side by two captives who continued the journey with him, one holding him up by the hand and the other the sick man, and he was kept from falling for some time; but on a steep place, when neither of his helpers could hold him, he fell to the ground and expired. The other was thrown into a wagon, and when he died he was at once cast out from the same wagon without delay. Almost a third had also been added, a man of the greatest distinction and a leader of the captives, who was placed on a little donkey; but since he could not keep up with the others because of his slow pace, he was beaten with such heavy blows that, with his nose broken and copious blood flowing out, drenched over his whole body, he was barely distinguishable from a dead man. To the climax of cruelty, these same captives, when the beasts of burden could no longer go on from exhaustion, were harnessed in place of the beasts and forced to drive the animals forward. Six brothers, utterly enervated and broken by these evils, were left behind in the prison at Theate; of these, four pious souls breathed their last there; the other two, after dire hunger and other evils endured, were carried to Naples just at the time of their liberation. Who, indeed, could refrain from tears at such things, and many others no less atrocious than can be told, not even if he were a Myrmidon, a Dolopian, or a hard soldier of Ulysses?

units.la: CCCXVI. Antea verò quàm triremium præfectis maneiparentur, tentationem novam, ad incitas jam ferè
units.tr: CCCXVI. Before they were handed over to the commanders of the galleys, they were subjected to a new temptation, which was now almost at its height.

units.la: Tentationes eorundem redacti, subeunt. Ductor copiarum, cui à Colonitzio commendati fuerant, significaverat, Regem Colonitzio de captivis statuendi quidlibet plenum arbitrium concessisse. Hunc verò copiarum colonello sub gravi omittendorum honorum fortunarumque omnium pœna injunxisse, ut in ea loca eos deducat, ex quibus nullus unquam liberari, nedum in Hungariam redire posset. Hæc autem mala uno modo evitari posse, si nomina sua militiæ Hispanicæ dare vellent. Hoc demum modo miseros, tot jam exantlatis calamitatibus, penitus extingui, & æterna oblivione sepeliri, vel certè majori vi ad Papatum cogi posse, Colonitzius, ex cujus præscripto cuncta gerebantur, arbitratus est. Sed captivi tot malis obruti licet, & majoribus mox obruendi, cordatè responderunt, in militiam ejusmodi, utpote à munere & vocatione, quin & virium suarum facultate prorsus alienam, nec ullo modo futuram Regi suo vel utilem vel honorificam, se consentire neutiquam posse. Captivi vestri, inquiebant, sumus. Statuendi de nobis quidvis plena vobis potestas est. Statuite pro lubitu. Militiæ vestræ nomen dabimus nulli. Sic repugnantes excipiunt verbera, correptúsque unus ex robustioribus militaribus vestibus invitus induitur. qui mox eadem exuens, ab ipso Capitaneo calcibus feritur, pedibus truditur, fustibus pulsatur, militibúsque exquisitissimis modis divexandus objicitur. In stabulum verò relegati omnes tridui integri spatio cibi potúsve usura omni privantur, & tantum non inedia enecantur.
units.tr: Brought back to their former trials, they underwent them again. The commander of the troops, to whom they had been committed by Colonitz, had made it known that the King had given Colonitz full discretion to decide whatever he liked about the captives. He had ordered the colonel of the troops, under severe penalty of forfeiting all his honours and property, to take them to places from which none of them could ever be freed, let alone return to Hungary. These evils, however, could be avoided in one way only, if they were willing to give their names to the Spanish army. Colonitz, by whose orders everything was being done, thought that in this way the wretched men, already worn down by so many calamities, could be utterly destroyed and buried in eternal oblivion, or at least forced by greater violence to embrace Papacy. But the captives, though overwhelmed by so many evils and soon to be overwhelmed by greater ones, answered sensibly that they could never consent to military service of that kind. Such service was entirely foreign to their calling and vocation, and indeed to their ability, and in no way would it be useful or honourable to their King. We are your captives, they said. You have full power to decide anything about us. Decide as you please. We will give our names to no one in your army. Resisting in this way, they received blows. One of the stronger soldiers was seized and forced, against his will, into military clothing. He at once took it off again, and was kicked by the captain himself, pushed along with feet, beaten with clubs, and handed over to the soldiers to be harassed in the most exquisite ways. Shut up in a stable, all of them were deprived of food and drink for three full days, and were almost starved to death.

units.la: Theatræ primùm colonellus in conspectum eorum prodiens interrogat: Vultis esse catholici? Dabitur sic optio vobis eligendi statum seu ecclesiasticum, seu seculârem, seu militarem. Tacentibus omnibus, verberum metu, pergit: Nondum meliores ergo estis? Propediem triremes vos, quid sit fides Catholica, docebunt. Tum juvenis, parcens senioribus, reliquorum loco respondit, & symbolo Athanasiano allegato, quæ sit fides Catholica, explicavit. Risu exceptus à Jesuita astante, denuo interrogatus est: Quid verò de Papa sentitis? Respondit idem: De eo sæpius mentem nostram explicavimus. nihil inpræsentiarum addituri, quia ferro pedibus constrictorum linguam etiam constrictam esse oportet. Propulsi igitur amplius, die VII. Maii Neapoli ex numero quadraginta & unius, residui triginta (nam duo in itinere mortui coelestem patriam cum imminentibus horribilibus triremibus commutárunt, sex ob infirmitatem Theatræ relicti fuerant, tres commoditate oblata, Caprocottam inter & Capuam aufugerant) semimortui, utpote quorum vix ossa cutis amplius sustinebat, appellunt, ubi sequenti die pretio quinquaginta scutatorum in singulorum capita erogato, ad triremes venduntur; mox denuo tonsi palatia Officialium Maritimorum, bini atque bini catenis constricti subeunt, & libro captivorum, seu Mortis potius certis in corpore, capite potissimum notis compuncti, neque expressa, uti aliàs fieri solet, captivitatis triremium causa, inscribuntur, in variásque triremes distribuuntur. Cúmque tardius venditionis pretium solveretur, Germanicæ militiæ Duces die xx. Julii sanguinolentum consilium iniverant captivorum simul omnium repetendorum, & isclopetis configendorum. Repetierántque & confixerant miserè, nisi à Pro-Rege Neapolitano, Petro Alvarezio prohibiti, ne meditatum scelus exequerentur, fuissent. Nihil hic de horrendis, quas in triremibus per novem menses integros, graviores etiam iis, quas Turcæ, Æthiopes, Mauri bello capti, nec non malefici notorii, legitimè convicti, & capite damnati in iisdem triremibus subire solent; fortissimo & constantissimo animo sustinuerunt, calamitatibus & miseriis, quibus fracti quatuor sub ipso triremium jugo expirárunt: nihil de Divinis, quibus se affici senserunt consolationibus: nihil de Evergetarum nonnullorum, quos inter unus, cujus nomen in Cœlo lo scriptum, chartis hisce illinere supersedemus, principem locum obtinebat, charitate erga captivos incredibili: nihil denique de Divina verè, & miraculo proxima eorundem ex fovea leonum, fornace Babylonica, & utero ceti per incomparabilem Heroem, Michaelem de Ruyter, alterum Belgii invictum Periclen, seu malumus dicere, Gedeonem, vindicatorum, liberatione dicam. Talia enim singula hæc sunt, ut paucis dici nequeant; dignissima etiam, quæ spissiori quondam volumine consignata, ad seram posteritatem, persecutionis inauditæ, & patientiæ plus quàm adamantinæ exempla cum sacro horrore quodam admiraturam, transmittantur.
units.tr: At the theatre, the colonel first came before them and asked: Do you want to be Catholics? An option will be given you to choose a state, either ecclesiastical, or secular, or military. When all were silent through fear of blows, he went on: Are you not yet better, then? Soon the galleys will teach you what the Catholic faith is. Then a young man, sparing the older men, answered in place of the rest, cited the Athanasian Creed, and explained what the Catholic faith is. He was met with laughter by a Jesuit standing by, and was questioned again: But what do you think of the Pope? The same man replied: We have often explained our mind about him. We will add nothing at present, because the tongue of men whose feet are bound with iron must also be bound. Then they were driven further on. On the 7th of May they reached Naples, forty-one in number, of whom thirty remained. Two had died on the way and exchanged their heavenly homeland for the dreadful galleys that loomed; six had been left at the theatre because of their weakness; three had escaped between Caprocotta and Capua when the chance offered. They were half dead, for their skin scarcely held their bones together. There, on the following day, a price of fifty crowns per head was paid, and they were sold to the galleys. Soon, shaved again, they went up to the palace of the naval officials, two by two bound with chains, and were marked in the book of captives, or rather of Death, with certain marks on the body, especially the head. They were not registered with the reason for their captivity given, as is usually done, namely the galleys, and they were distributed among various galleys. When the payment for the sale was delayed, the German military commanders, on the 20th of July, adopted a bloody plan to take back all the captives at once and to fix them to muskets. They had indeed taken them back and wretchedly fixed them, had not Pedro Alvarez, the Viceroy of Naples, forbidden them to carry out the crime they had planned. Here I shall not speak of the horrors which, for nine full months in the galleys, they endured with the most brave and steadfast spirit, horrors even greater than those which Turks, Ethiopians and Moors taken in war, and notorious criminals lawfully convicted and condemned to death, are usually made to undergo in the same galleys. By these calamities and miseries four of them, broken, expired under the very yoke of the galleys. I say nothing of the divine consolations by which they felt themselves strengthened, nor of the benefactors, among whom one, whose name is written in Heaven, held the chief place through his incredible charity towards the captives; I shall refrain from writing these things on these pages. Finally, I say nothing of the divine and almost miraculous deliverance of the same men from the lions' den, the Babylonian furnace and the belly of the whale, by the incomparable hero Michael de Ruyter, the other invincible Pericles of Belgium, or rather, as I prefer to call him, Gideon, the avenger. Each of these things is such that it cannot be told in a few words; they are most worthy to be recorded in some fuller volume, and handed down to later posterity, which will admire with a certain sacred awe the examples of unheard-of persecution and of patience more than adamantine.

units.la: CCCXVII. Atque hæc series est afflictionum, hic eventus confessorum sanctissimorum, Posonio Berentzinum, Comarinum, Eberhardinum, Leopoldin, ac tandem Neapolin ad infames triremes deportatorum.
units.tr: CCCXVII. This is the sequence of afflictions, this the outcome for the most holy confessors, who were carried from Pressburg through Berzenc, Komárno, Eberhard and Leopoldstadt, and at last to Naples, to the infamous galleys.

units.la: Neque verò mitioribus fatis reliqui viginti, tredecim scilicet Reformati, & Augustani septem, in carceribus Sarwar, Kapuwar, Tergesti Istriæ, & Buccaris Dalmatiæ nefanda & plusquam Scythica crudelitate pressi, & nonnulli etiam sive morte tragica corporali, sive spirituali etiam, per triste naufragium fidei, oppressi, urgebantur. Et Posoniensi quidem carcere extracti, postquam imperatam à Colonitzio subscriptionem abnuerunt, constringendi statim restibus, ipsomet Colonitzio numerata pecunia eas comparante, educti, & pars Sarwarinum, pars Kapuwarinum rapti, ibidémque Turcicis compedibus constricti, in carceres stercoreos, soricibus, ranis, bufonibus, serpentibus scatentes, detrusi, fame, siti, frigore, laboribus durissimis, indignissimis, sordidissimis, contumeliisque nefariis ita discruciati sunt, ut & superiorum & horum confessorum afflictiones ab uno eodemque Phalaride dictatas esse, liquidò cognosci potuerit. Inde d. 1. Julii A.M.D.C.LXXV. produćti triremiúmque, dummodo emptores inveniri potuissent, (nam & Veneti, & novus Pro-Rex Neapolitanus, cui prædecessoris emptio displicuit, compellati, diserte negârunt, se tot jam miseriis confectos & forte innocentes mercari velle) servituti destinati, postquam quatuor mille, adeóque pro singulis ducentos florenos, ea lege oblatos, ut libellis subscriberent, respuissent; ductore Gabriele Köver, Colonitziani furoris satellite, campanarum, quocunque venissent, pulsu, ceu Dæmoniaci, uti latrones illi proclamaverant, excepti, ludibrióque habiti, Tergestum, in litore Maris Adriatici situm, adducti, atque ibi primò haris & stabulis inclusi sunt. Ibi propter unius fugam, cœteris insciis arreptam, innumeris plagis excarnificantur, barbisque & mystacibus, quin & pilis omnibus violenter, non sine menti læsione, evulsis, privantur cuncti; & fugitivus ex fuga reductus, cùm exquisitis quæstionibus & tormentis subditus, ut reliquos fugæ conscios fuisse confiteretur, induci non potuissit, ipsorum fratrum captivorum verberibus ita objicitur, ut carnificum instar singulis diebus bis fratrem suum, passionum haetenus consortem, percutere, multarum atrociúmque plagarum renuentibus inflictarum metu, coacti fuerint.
units.tr: Nor did the remaining twenty, namely thirteen Reformed and seven Augsburg Confession men, meet with gentler fates. They were held down in the prisons of Sárvár, Kaposvár, Trieste in Istria, and Buccari in Dalmatia, oppressed with unspeakable and more than Scythian cruelty, and some were also threatened with a tragic death, whether of the body or, worse, of the soul, through the sad shipwreck of faith. They were taken from the Pressburg prison after refusing the subscription Colonitz ordered. Ropes were at once put round them, which Colonitz himself bought with money counted out. Some were dragged to Sárvár, some to Kaposvár, and there, bound with Turkish fetters, they were thrust into dungeons full of dung, swarming with mice, frogs, toads and serpents. They were tormented with hunger, thirst, cold, the hardest labours, the most unworthy and filthy treatment and wicked insults, so that it could clearly be recognised that the afflictions of these confessors and of the earlier ones were dictated by one and the same Phalaris. Then, on the 1st of July 1675, they were brought out, and destined for slavery in the galleys, provided buyers could be found. (The Venetians and the new Viceroy of Naples, who disliked his predecessor's purchase, were pressed, but plainly refused, saying they did not wish to buy men already worn down by so many miseries and perhaps innocent.) When they had rejected an offer of four thousand, that is two hundred florins apiece, on condition that they sign the documents, they were led by Gabriel Köver, a satellite of Colonitz's fury. Wherever they came they were received with the ringing of bells, as demoniacs, as those robbers had proclaimed them, and were treated as a laughing-stock. They were brought to Trieste, a town on the shore of the Adriatic Sea, and there were first shut up in sheds and stables. There, because of one man's escape, which the others did not know of, they were cruelly flogged with countless blows, and all of them were deprived of their beards and moustaches, and indeed of all their hair, torn out by force, not without injury to their minds. The fugitive, brought back from his flight, was subjected to exquisite questioning and torture, to make him confess that the others had known of the escape. When he could not be induced to do so, the captives were exposed to the blows of their own brothers, so that, like executioners, they were forced each day to strike twice their brother, a fellow sufferer until then, through fear of the many and atrocious blows that would be inflicted on them if they refused.

units.la: Non satis erat harpyis istis, miseros turpiter spoliare omnibus, & seminudos, unico longiori indusio é tela crassissima præparato tectos, relinquere. Etiam alios eorum-causa expilandi libido eos incessit. Pactum enim cum captivis iniverant, quo quinque illorum mille & centum; quindecim verò mille quingentorum Imperialium lytro soluto se liberaturos receperant. Mittitur captivorum unus Viennam, comitibus nonnullis, qui pro liberandis juxta pactum captivis quinque lytron, mille & centum Imperialium ab amicis impetrat, solvitque. Neque tamen nisi unus ille, qui missus, ab amicis ut non Tergestum, sed in Hungariam reverteretur, monitus est, non tam volentibus hostibus, quàm consulentibus amicis, liberatur. Reliqui etiam soluto pretio in carcere plorant. Missus etiam captivorum alius est Venetias, qui opera Viri Clarissimi, & de captivis meritissimi Nicolai Zaffii τῆς μαχαιέιτσ, didimidiam lytri partem acquirit, eámque spe certa residuæ partis mox ab amicis impetrandæ, Duci offert. Ipse quidem missus, at solus liberatur; reliqui verò in carcere, perinde ac si nihil omnino solutum esset, attinentur, diriúsque etiam exercentur. Tergesto mense Octobri anni ejusdem, militibus Croatis cincti, per prærupta saxa, nudis pedibus, diu noctúque inter continua à tergo & lateribus verbera & ictus, non tam erecti ambulantes, quàm humi prostrati, manibus pedibúsque reptantes, Buccarim, Dalmatiæ castellum, ad mare Adriaticum situm, inde jugo triremium Melitensium mox subjiciendi, avehuntur, ibíque Andreæ Godermanno, homini truculentissimo omnium, mancipati, in carcerem sordidissimum, utpote qui non tam carcer erat, quàm contigui carceris cloaca, stercoribus humanis inde à quinquaginta annis nunquam expurgatis, ex quibus etiam panem injectum, & fœtore eorum jam infectum tollere, & comedere coacti sunt, referta, compinguntur. Tam fœdæ custodiæ traditi, sine mora tredecim numellis ferreis, quibus ob latitudinem mentum sursum sublatum inclinare prohibebantur, per catenas durissimas, quibus vel onerati currus in præcipitio sustentari poterant, ordine constricti, & miseris modis colligati; reliqui verò cippis ligneis, & manicis ferreis supini coarctati, & per triginta novem dies integros in miserabili hoc statu detenti sunt. Atque ita concatenati, horribile spectaculum, nonnunquam extra carcerem educti, ludibrióque protervorum quorumque expositi sunt. occasionem sic captantibus nonnullis, Monachis inprimis, apoapostasiam, ob mala tum praesentia, tum imminentia suadendi. Neque omnino irritae suasiones ceciderant. Nam decem numero, septem Augustani & tres Reformati persuasi, totque inauditis calamitatibus fracti die xxii. Dec. nomina libellis dederunt, & liberatione nihilominus procraftinata, sequentis insuper anni, mensis Februarii die xix. tristissimum fidei naufragium passi, vinculis equidem corporis sese exsolverunt, at gravioribus longe animae intricârunt. Ex superstitum constantissimorum numero, duo, septimo decembris, hora octava eadem, consummato militiae & patientiae suae cursu, piè in Domino obdormiverunt, & à captivis reliquis, effosso propriis eorum manibus in litore maris sepulchro, & decantato ad tumulum Psalmi lxxxviii. threno humati sunt. Die xiii. Febr. A.M.D.C.LXXVI. superstites sex denuo in prius illud sordidissimum & obscurrisimum ergastulum, ex quo, ob praesentissimae mortis periculum (longioribus scilicet miseriis eos macerare placuit) aliquandiu relaxati fuerant, detrusi sunt, tanta cum saevitia, ut captivorum superstitum unus, morti proximus, solis suspiriis, cùm nec verbum quidem proloqui amplius posset, ex imo pectore gemebundam animam trahens, violentis lictorum manibus correptus, per distortos gradus saxa & ligna, angustúmque carceris foramen ita raptatus fuerit, ut ex nudo moriturientis corpore cutis & carnis frusta, copioso cum sanguine, detrita lapidibus haeserint. qui paulò post in carcere foetidissimo piè defunctus, omni sepultura caruit. Reliquis quinque in cloaca illa denuò uti priùs, compeditis, & cum intolerabili foetore, infectis, fame, siti certantibus, obnuntiatur rigidè, fore ut in sterquilinis istis miserè ita concatenati computrescant, nisi tandem apostatarum exemplo Euangelicam religionem ejurent. Respondentibus confessoribus, se pro Christo libenter subituros, quicquid impositum fuerit, panis hactenus usitatus commutatur in panem ex milio & furfure coctum, eúmque modicum, quem à puerulis per angustum carceris foramen injectum, pedibus manibúsque proreptantes, denuo ex stercoribus aliisque immunditiis tollere necessum habuerunt. Additum parumper aquæ, sed turbidæ; quandoque etiam nihil. ita ut panem durissimum, quò comedi posset, urina sua macerare coacti fuerint. In statu isthoc, continuísque tenebris, manserunt dies octoginta, ita interea toto corpore corrupti, ut jam vix loqui, vel loquentes invicem intelligere potuerint: sanguis & aqua continuò ex ore eorum, nihil etiam comedentium vel bibentium, quódque amplius claudere non poterant; copiosè profluxerit; gingivæ & fauces putredinem totæ contraxerint; dentes non sentientibus cum sputo exciderint, denique os maxillare & linguæ vitiosis humoribus tantùm non consumptæ fuerint. Protestantibus contra inauditam tyrannidem captivis, quantum fari poterant, de sua innocentia & Christi causa, Vice-Præfectus Stanko respondit: Jacetis equidem in umbra mortis, doleóque ego vicem vestram. Sed vel invitus hæc facio, quia sub pœna capitis, ut facerem, à Godermanno mihi injunctum est: huic verò sub eadem capitis pœna mandatum à Colonitzio est, ut his potissimum modis vos excruciet. Dum vero in medio omnis munditiei profundè demersi, miseréque concatenati, in sanguine suo, sputo & fimo volutabantur, non amplius se in hanc vel illam partem inclinare, vel capita extollere valentes; atque ita mortis hora non procul abesse visa est: nuntium liberationis, intercessione Ill. Legati Belgici impetratæ allatum est. quod tantùm non agonizantibus parùm profuturum credebatur. Ex carcere nihilominus, compedibus & numellis soluti, à sanguine inquinamentísque purgati, à militibus, cùm ob infirmitatem incedere non possent, in honestius domicilium
units.tr: It was not enough for those harpies to plunder the wretched men shamefully of everything and leave them half-naked, covered only by one long shirt of very coarse cloth. Some of them were also seized by a lust for plunder on account of their captives. They had made an agreement with the captives, by which five of them would be freed for 1,100 Imperial thalers and fifteen for 1,500 Imperial thalers, once the ransom was paid. One of the captives was sent to Vienna with some escorts, and obtained from friends 1,100 Imperial thalers for the ransom of the five, as the agreement required, and paid it. Yet only that one man who had been sent was freed, and he was advised by his friends to return not to Trieste but to Hungary. He was released less because the enemies wished it than because his friends counselled it. The rest remained in prison even after payment. Another captive was sent to Venice, who through the efforts of the most distinguished Nicolas Zaffius, a man most deserving of the captives, obtained half the ransom and offered it to the Doge, with a firm hope that the remaining part would soon be obtained from friends. He himself was sent and freed alone; the others, as if nothing at all had been paid, were kept in prison and treated even more harshly. In October of the same year they were carried from Trieste, surrounded by Croatian soldiers, over steep rocks, barefoot, day and night under continual blows to the back and sides, walking not upright but prostrate, creeping on hands and feet, to Buccari, a Dalmatian fortress on the Adriatic Sea. From there, to be soon put under the yoke of the Maltese galleys, they were handed over to Andreas Godermann, the most brutal of men, and thrust into a most squalid prison, which was less a prison than the sewer of the adjoining gaol, its human dung not cleaned out for fifty years. From it they were forced to take up the bread thrown in, already tainted with its stench, and eat it. Delivered to such foul custody, they were at once bound in a row by thirteen iron rings, by which they were prevented from raising their chins because of their width, and by very hard chains, such as could hold even loaded carts on a precipice, and were wretchedly bound. The rest were pressed supine into wooden stocks and iron manacles, and kept for thirty-nine whole days in this miserable state. So chained together, they were sometimes led out of the prison as a horrible spectacle and exposed to the mockery of any wanton people. Some, especially monks, seized this occasion to persuade them to apostasy, pointing to the evils both present and impending. Nor were these persuasions entirely in vain. For ten of them, seven Augsburg Confession men and three Reformed, were won over and broken by so many unheard-of calamities. On 22 December they signed written recantations, and although their liberation was nonetheless postponed, on 19 February of the following year they suffered the saddest shipwreck of faith. They freed themselves from the chains of the body, but entangled their souls far more grievously. Of the surviving most steadfast, two, on 7 December, at the eighth hour, having completed the course of their warfare and patience, fell asleep piously in the Lord. The other captives buried them in a grave dug with their own hands on the sea shore, and they were laid in the tomb with Psalm lxxxviii sung as a lament. On 13 February 1676 the six survivors were again thrust into that same most squalid and dark dungeon from which they had been released for a time because of the most imminent danger of death. (It pleased their tormentors, of course, to wear them down with longer miseries.) They were thrust in with such cruelty that one of the surviving captives, close to death, who could no longer utter even a word and could only draw groaning breaths from the depths of his chest, was seized by the violent hands of the jailers and dragged down twisted steps, over stones and wood, and through the narrow opening of the prison. So much of the naked body of the dying man was torn away, pieces of skin and flesh with copious blood, scraped off by the stones, that they stuck there. A little later he died piously in the most foul prison and lacked all burial. The remaining five were again placed in that sewer, as before, in fetters, infected by the intolerable stench, struggling with hunger and thirst. They were sternly told that they would rot wretchedly chained in those dunghills unless at last they abjured the evangelical religion, following the example of the apostates. The confessors replied that they would gladly undergo for Christ whatever was imposed. The bread used until then was changed into bread baked of millet and bran, and the small amount, which boys threw in through the narrow opening of the prison, they, creeping on hands and feet, were forced to pick up again from dung and other filth. A little water was added, but it was muddy, and sometimes there was nothing at all. So they were forced to soak the very hard bread in their own urine so that it could be eaten. In this state, in continual darkness, they remained eighty days, and meanwhile were so corrupted in their whole body that they could scarcely speak, or understand one another when they did. Blood and water flowed continually and copiously from their mouths, though they ate or drank nothing, and they could no longer close them. Their gums and throats had wholly contracted putrefaction. Teeth fell out with spittle without their feeling it. Finally the jaw bone and tongue were all but consumed by corrupt humours. While the captives, as far as they could speak, protested against this unheard-of tyranny, and affirmed their innocence and the cause of Christ, Vice-Prefect Stanko replied: You indeed lie in the shadow of death, and I grieve for your plight. But I do this against my will, because under penalty of death I was ordered to do it by Godermann; and to him, under the same penalty of death, Colonitz has commanded that he torment you in these very ways. While they wallowed in their own blood, spittle and dung, deeply sunk in every filth and miserably chained, no longer able to bend this way or that or lift their heads, the hour of death seemed not far off. Then news of their liberation was brought, obtained through the intercession of the Illustrious Belgian Envoy. It was believed that this would do little good to men who were almost dying. Nevertheless they were released from the prison, from their fetters and rings, cleansed of blood and filth, and since they could not walk because of their weakness, they were carried by soldiers to a more honourable dwelling.

units.la: {&} vicina jam morti liberatur. lium deportantur, lectisque puris linteaminibus stratis impositi, Sospitatori suo, cadavera potius quàm homines die II. Maii M. D. C. LXXVI. traduntur. Cùmque post quindecim dierum inediam, cibi offerrentur, ob exulceratas fauces vesci iis, nisi ingestis leniter, non poterant; jusculi vel vini guttis injectis ita fauces urentibus, ut ægerimè cibum potumque admiserint. Exquisitissimâ acerbissimáque medicinâ illis à Medicis Pontificiis Johanne Nonno Anconitano, & Francisco Rinaldi, qui propria etiam manu, jurejurando interposito, testati sunt, ita labefactatos, viribus destitutos, ob salsos acresque humores in fœtidissimo carcere ex capite descendentes, calorémque internum conficientes, in ore, palato, lingua, faucibus exulceratos liberatos se invenisse, ut morituros potius quàm convalituros crediderint; adhibitâ, quatuor per Dei gratiam, stigmata sua, etiam à me non sine horrore visa, in exilio circumferentes, convaluerant: quintus vero die XXIV. Maii Venetiis ob deploratam valetudinem, mortalitatis legem implevit.
units.tr: and, now close to death, were freed. They were carried there, laid on clean linen sheets, and on 2 May 1676 were handed over to their deliverer as corpses rather than men. And when food was offered after fifteen days without eating, they could not take it except when it was gently poured in, because their throats were ulcerated. Even drops of broth or wine, poured in, burned their throats so that they scarcely admitted food and drink. They were given the most exquisite and most bitter medicine by the Papist physicians Johannes Nonnus of Ancona and Franciscus Rinaldi, who also testified with their own hand, under oath, that they had found them so weakened and deprived of strength, with salty and sharp humours descending from the head in that most foul prison, burning up their internal heat, ulcerated in the mouth, palate, tongue and throat, and freed, so that they believed them more likely to die than to recover; yet with this remedy applied, the four, by the grace of God, recovered, carrying their stigmata about in exile, which I too saw not without horror. The fifth, on 24 May at Venice, fulfilled the law of mortality because his health was despaired of.

units.la: CCCXVIII.
units.tr: CCCXVIII.

units.la: Frustra vero inauditam, omníque diritate immaniorem tyrannidem suam coram mundo utcunque tegi posse, Colonitzius, & furoris ejusdem fuscep-tores pessimi Jesuitæ, sperárunt. Percrebuit maturè satis in universo orbe, & architectis suis non apud Evangelicos duntaxat, sed ipsos etiam melioris notæ Pontificios infamiam incredibilem conciliavit. Hanc vero infamiæ notam ut abstergerent, simúlque cornicum oculos configerent, ferocissimi omnium tyranni illi, Tyrnaviæ imprimi curarant libellum famosum, cum inscriptione ejusmodi: Succinctus & verax Judicialis Extractus, quo clarissimè demonstratur, Pastores Hungariæ Acatholicos non ob religionem, sed ob rebellionem depositos Regnóque ejectos, singulósque eos judiciali-ter convictos, justéque damnatos esse; Delegato Regio Judicio Posoniensi accensus, & per ejusdem Secretarium, qui ratione officii rebus omnibus interfuit, omniaque calamo fideliter tradidit, consignatus. Erat equidem in Judicio Posoniensi Secretarius Regiæ Tabulæ Johannes Labsantzky. Forte etiam fœtui huic edendo obstetricatus est. Sed Jesuitas, Kellionem inprimis, ejus authores suisse, verisimile prorsus est. Larvam mox scripto illi detraxit captivorum unus, qui ad triremes ductus fuga saluti suæ consuluit, edita funda Davidis contra Goliathum, qua triginta crassimorum mendaciorum reum personatum illum Labsantzky, solidissimè peregit. Excepit paulò post Apologia Ministrorum Euangelicorum Hungariæ, ad innocentiam suam orbi Christiano declarandam, opposita Judicio Tribunalis Posoniensis, à quo perduellionis crimine contra Regiam Majestatem iniquissimè accusati & condemnati, non modo toto Regno proscripti sunt, sed exemplo à pietate & mansuetudine Christiana prorsus alieno, magnam partem ad triremes Hispanicas damnati. Operæ pretium autem fuerit, personati illius Labzanky argumenta, quibus Pastores rebellionis legitimè convictos damnatósque esse, probare sustinuit, ad incudem revocare, eademque opera Pastorum innocentiam ad liquidum perducere. Et primò quidem occasionem rebellandi sumpsisse Pastores arguit inde, quòd stipendia à Rackozio in ejusdem ditione, Saros-Patakiensi maximè, sibi subtracta animo ægerrimo tulerint, imò Pastorum nonnemo, compositione à Zerinio Rakozii Socero tentata dixerit: Hodie Rakozius latus suum vicies mille acinacibus cinxit. Responderunt Pastores fusè ad isthoc ἐγκλημα. Summa huc redit: Cautum cùm fuerit Regio diplomate, ne proventus reales ad Scholas & Parochias Euangelicorum, ab antiqua fundatione per Patronos Euangelicos facta, pertinentes à quoquam occupari possit, Franciscum Rakozium apostatam, unâ cum matre violenter illos occupâsse; ea occasione Rakozianos inter & Proceres Euangelicos subortam controversiam esse; quam cùm Rex componere nec potuerit, nec voluerit, rit, Zerinius Rakozii Socer authoritate sua, juxta tenorem articulorum Posoniensium, interposita, sopiverit. Porro Pastores injuria affectos, jure suo controversiam movisse non Regi, contra quem fiat rebellio, sed Rakozio raptori: turbas eo nomine movisse nullas, Patronis Euangelicis jura eorum defendentibus: post transactionem nihil unquam cum Zerinio vel Nadastio, Euangelii persecutoribus acerimis, commercii iis fuisse: Pastorum illum nonnneminem fuisse neminem: si enim nonnemo fuisset, nomen ejus editurum fuisse personatum illum haud dubie, non parcentem aliās nominibus: denique id omne pertinuisse ad Pastores Hungariae non omnes, sed paucos, & quidem ad tales, qui pridem ante citationem violenter expulsi sint, nemine eorum Posonium citato, vel ibi comparente unquam. Sic desperatae causae indicium initio statim turpissime Extractum illum prodidisse, liquet. Secundo allegat personatus literas hieroglyphicas Stephani Wittnyedy, Nadastii Secretarii eo tempore defuncti, eäsque geminas, priores ad Ambrosium Közerum, posteriores ad Nicolaum Bethlen exaratas, & a ministro Rebellis cujusdam, Pastoris Hungarici filio, pretio mille Imperialium conducto, ex Transylvania allatas, quarum tenor fuerit, se Pastores in utraque Hungaria ad movendos auditorum ad conciendam rebellionem animos rite praeparasse. Atque in his literis Posonienses judices judicii sui proram puppimque collocaverant. Tametsi vero Judices illi literarum γνωσιότητα simpliciter credi (quod a judice justo alienissimum est) praeceperant: adulterinas tamen fuisse, non Pastores duntaxat Posonii coram tribunali comparentes, suspicati sunt merito, sed postea etiam plane plenéque compertum est, postquam Nicolaus Bethlen in Transylvania Sedis Siculicalis Uduarhelyensis supremus Capitaneus, ad quem posteriores scriptae ferebantur, su-perperstes adhuc, eas penitius excussit, & supposititias esse, irrefragibilibus argumentis, publico scripto asseruit. Sed fuerint etiam literæ illæ, verè à Witnyedio scriptæ. Itane verò ad unius, & quidem jam tum demortui testis testimonium, tot homines Posonii comparentes, quorum ne unus quidem in testimonio illo nomine suo expressus fuit, rebellionis crimine arcessi, nedum condemnari potuerunt? Atqui tum Divina lex unius testis testimonium Deut.xix. 15. diserte rejicit, duorumque vel trium testium os exigit: tum civilis etiam hominis mortui allegationem, adeóque testimonium adversus viventem ratum haberi, 2. Part. tit. 23. vetat. Tertio crimina horrenda Pastorum, velut quòd fuerint incendiarii, cœdium patratores, stercora sua Pontificiorum infantibus devoranda dederint, Sacerdotes Turcis vendiderint, iisdem munimenta præcipua tradere conati fuerint, aliáque nefanda, personatus allegat. Sed Diabolicis mendaciis innocentium famam ab eo proscissam esse, satis constat. Aliud enim certè, Cicerone sapienter observante, est maledicere, aliud accusare. nedum condemnare. Maledictio nihil habet propositi, præter contumeliam. Accusatio verò crimen desiderat, rem ut definiat, hominem ut notet, argumento probet, teste confirmet. Tu verò, personate, accusator fratrum, quos homines notâsti, quo argumento probâsti, quo teste confirmâsti? Quin potiùs centumcubitalia, à Diabolo in inferno cusa esse, quæ protulisti, mendacia, accusati pertendunt. Si accusâsse sufficit, quis innocens erit? Quarto fugisse Pastores, alios in Transsylvaniam, in Turciam alios, cùm Coppius in Superiore Hungaria acie cum rebellibus confligens, superior evasit, personatus ait, atque inde rebelles fuisse infert. Egregia, si qua alia, prolatio: Rebellis igitur David, qui furorem sanguinarii Saulis evitaturus ad Regem Achis aufugit: rebellis ipse Christus (absit dicto blasphemia) qui audiens captivitatem Johannis, ex Judæa in Galilæam fugit, fuerit. Tot Apostolos, Sanctosque Patres omitto. Si qui igitur Pastorum fugerunt, non id sceleris conscientia, sed persecutorum immanitate adacti fecerunt, ante omnem quippe citationem, & contra omnia jura, sedibus suis exturbati, bonis privati, solum vertere coacti majorem apud ethnicos, quàm apud professos Christianos catholicos humanitatem experti. An verò illi, adversus quos ferro flammáque sævitum est, expectare citationem, hoc est, oves fugatæ & dissipatæ, luporum citantium judicium ultro subire debuerunt? Alii etiam, ne citationi parerent, à potestate legitima prohibiti sunt: alios vestigia nimis proh dolor! sanguinolenta terruerunt. Sed fuerit levis causa sugientium: quid verò id omne faciet adversus eos, qui non fugerunt, sed comparuerunt, non aliam ob causam, quàm quia comparuerunt, crudeliter oppressi? Sed Achilles personati est, quòd tot Pastores libellis subscribentes ultro rebellionis crimen confessi fuerint. Atqui ut præjudicium nonnullum meticulosi illi, qui metu nimio subacti nomina sua libellis subsignárunt, bonæ causæ creaverint; at at reos fuisse eosdem rebellionis, neutiquam consequitur. Neque enim aliis argumentis vel testimoniis rebellionis rei peracti sunt, quàm quibus eos etiam, qui ad finem usque constantes permanserunt, ejusdem criminis convincere hostes tentaverant. Cùm verò invalida prorsus hæc fuisse, hactenus ostensum sit, invalida quoque illa fuisse, conficitur merito. Non igitur rebelles fuerunt Libellatici illi, seu, uti vocantur, Reversionaliste, sed meticulosi; externo hominum persecutorum, non interno conscientiæ ob crimen objectum accusantis, terrore perculsi; tam leves plerique, ut nec dum auditis contra se accusationibus ex præscripto cleri quidvis subscripserint; inprimis cùm subscribentibus etiam merces, præsentaneæ pecuniæ pa-ra-
units.tr: Colonitzius and his most wicked Jesuit accomplices, who undertook this outrage, hoped in vain that their unheard-of tyranny, more monstrous than any cruelty, could somehow be hidden from the world. Within a short time the news spread through the whole world, and it brought an incredible infamy not only upon its architects among the Evangelicals but also upon the Papists of better repute. To wipe away this mark of infamy and at the same time to blind the eyes of the crows, those most savage tyrants had a libel printed at Tyrnau, under this title: A brief and truthful Judicial Extract, by which it is most clearly shown that the non-Catholic ministers of Hungary were deposed and expelled from the kingdom not on account of religion but on account of rebellion, and that each of them was judicially convicted and justly condemned; sealed by the Royal Delegated Court of Pozsony, and by its secretary, who in the course of his office was present at everything and faithfully committed everything to writing. Indeed, the secretary of the Royal Table, Johannes Labsantzky, was in the Court of Pozsony. Perhaps he even served as midwife to this offspring. But that the Jesuits, and Kellio above all, were its authors is entirely probable. Soon one of the captives, who had been led to the galleys and had looked to his safety by flight, tore the mask from that writing, publishing David's sling against Goliath, by which he thoroughly convicted that masked Labsantzky of thirty very gross lies. Shortly afterwards there followed the Apology of the Evangelical Ministers of Hungary, opposed to the judgment of the Court of Pozsony, to declare their innocence to the Christian world; by which they were most unjustly accused and condemned of the crime of treason against His Royal Majesty, and not only proscribed throughout the whole kingdom, but, by an example utterly foreign to Christian piety and gentleness, for the most part condemned to the Spanish galleys. It will, however, be worth the effort to call back to the anvil the arguments of that masked Labzanky, by which he undertook to prove that the ministers had been lawfully convicted and condemned of rebellion, and at the same time to bring the innocence of the ministers to clear light. And first, he argues that the ministers took the occasion for rebelling from the fact that they had borne with very great distress the stipends withdrawn from them by Rakoczy in his domain, especially that of Sárospatak, and indeed that one of the ministers, when an agreement was attempted by Zrinyi, Rakoczy's father-in-law, said: Today Rakoczy has girded his side with twenty thousand scimitars. The ministers answered this accusation at length. The sum of it comes to this: although it had been provided by royal diploma that the royal revenues belonging to the schools and parishes of the Evangelicals, established from ancient foundation by Evangelical patrons, could not be seized by anyone, Franz Rakoczy, an apostate, together with his mother had seized them by force; on that occasion a dispute arose between the Rakoczians and the Evangelical nobles; and when the King could neither settle it nor was willing to, Zrinyi, Rakoczy's father-in-law, interposed his authority, according to the terms of the Articles of Pozsony, and quieted it. Further, the ministers, having been wronged, pursued the matter by their own right, not against the King, against whom rebellion is made, but against Rakoczy the plunderer; they stirred up no tumults on that account, while the Evangelical patrons defended their rights; after the settlement they never had any dealings with Zrinyi or Nádasdy, the fiercest persecutors of the Gospel; that "one minister" of the ministers was someone, that is, no one: for if someone had been there, the masked man would undoubtedly have published his name, since he does not otherwise spare names; finally, all of this pertained to not all the ministers of Hungary but to a few, and indeed to such as had been violently expelled long before the citation, none of them ever having been cited to Pozsony or appearing there. Thus it is clear that this most shameful Extract revealed from the very beginning a sign of a lost cause. Second, the masked man cites the hieroglyphic letters of Stephen Wittnyedy, secretary of Nádasdy, who had died at that time, two letters in all, the earlier written to Ambrosius Közer, the later to Nicholas Bethlen, and brought out of Transylvania by a servant of a certain rebel, a son of a Hungarian minister, hired for a thousand imperial coins; the tenor of which was that the ministers in both Hungaries had properly prepared the minds of their hearers for stirring up rebellion. And in these letters the judges of Pozsony had placed the prow and stern of their judgment. Although those judges had commanded that the genuineness [γνησιότητα] of the letters be believed without question (which is most alien to a just judge), it was deservedly suspected not only by the ministers who appeared before the tribunal at Pozsony that the letters were counterfeit, but afterwards this was also fully and plainly established, when Nicholas Bethlen, chief captain of the Székely seat of Udvarhely in Transylvania, to whom the later letters were said to have been written, still surviving, examined them more thoroughly and declared in a public writing, by irrefutable arguments, that they were spurious. But let us grant that those letters were truly written by Wittnyedy. Could so many men appearing at Pozsony, of whom not one was named in that testimony, be summoned on a charge of rebellion, much less condemned, on the testimony of one witness, and one who had already died? And yet the divine law expressly rejects the testimony of a single witness (Deut. xix. 15), and demands the mouth of two or three witnesses; and the civil law also forbids that the testimony of a dead man be allowed, and so testimony against a living man, 2. Part. tit. 23. Third, the masked man cites the horrible crimes of the ministers, such as that they were arsonists, perpetrators of murders, that they gave their own excrement to be devoured by the children of the Papists, that they sold priests to the Turks, that they tried to hand over the chief fortifications to the same, and other unspeakable things. But that the good name of the innocent was torn to shreds by his diabolical lies is quite clear. For, as Cicero wisely observes, it is one thing to slander, another to accuse, much less to condemn. Slander has no purpose except insult. But accusation requires a charge, so that it may define the matter, mark the man, prove by argument, and confirm by witness. But you, masked accuser of the brethren, which men did you mark, by what argument did you prove, by what witness did you confirm? Rather, the lies you have put forward are hundred-cubit lies, forged by the Devil in hell, as the accused maintain. If to accuse is enough, who will be innocent? Fourth, the masked man says that the ministers fled, some into Transylvania, others into Turkey, when Coppius, fighting with the rebels in Upper Hungary, came out the victor, and from this he infers that they were rebels. A splendid conclusion, if ever there was one! Then David was a rebel, who fled to King Achish to escape the fury of bloodthirsty Saul; Christ himself was a rebel (God forbid such blasphemy!), who, hearing of John's imprisonment, fled from Judea into Galilee. I pass over the many Apostles and holy Fathers. Therefore, if any of the ministers fled, they did so not from a consciousness of guilt but driven by the savagery of their persecutors; for they were thrown out of their seats, stripped of their goods, and forced to leave their country before any citation, and against all laws, and they experienced a humanity greater among the heathen than among those who professed to be Catholic Christians. But ought those against whom sword and flame were raged to wait for a citation, that is, sheep scattered and dispersed, to submit of their own accord to the judgment of wolves who cite them? Others too were forbidden by the lawful authority from obeying the citation; others were terrified by footprints, alas, too bloody. But let the flight of those who fled be a light matter: what will all this do against those who did not flee, but appeared, and were cruelly oppressed for no other reason than that they had appeared? But the masked man makes a great point of this, that so many ministers, subscribing to libels, freely confessed the crime of rebellion. Yet although those timid men, who, overcome by excessive fear, signed their names to the libels, may have created some prejudice against a good cause, it by no means follows that they were guilty of the same rebellion. For they were not convicted of rebellion by other arguments or testimonies than those by which the enemies had tried to convict of the same crime even those who remained steadfast to the end. Since it has been shown up to this point that these were altogether invalid, it is rightly concluded that those were invalid too. Therefore those libellatics, or, as they are called, the "Reversionalists," were not rebels but timid men, struck with fear of the external terror of their persecutors, not with an inner fear of conscience accusing them of a crime charged against them; most of them were so weak that, before the accusations against them had even been heard, they signed whatever the clergy prescribed, especially since merchandise and ready money were also given to those who signed [ . . . ]

units.la: {*} Ἡ Τοῦ meticulosi ratæ fuerint. Accedit, quòd venenatæ formulæ libelli, quam Extractus recitat, quenquam comparentium subscripsisse, sceleste personatus in aperta luce mentiri ausus est. Omnes equidem libellatici quodammodo adversariis criminandi ansam dederunt. Et formulæ libellorum in prima citatione oblatorum duriores sanè fuerunt. At in posteriori citatione formulæ inserta plerunque à subscribentibus sunt verba: quamvis non simus rebelliosæ complicitatis nobis conscii. Qua denique conscientia saltem Reformatis in Hungaria Pastoribus libellaticos ejusmodi personatus objecit? In tanto enim libellaticorum ducentorum triginta sex, quos ille allegat, numero, non ultra duos Reformatos reperire est, qui sive in priore, sive in posteriore termino citationis, munus suum se abdicaturos subscripserint. Constantioribus quinetiam Augustanis inconstantes jure præjudicare non potuerunt. Si qui enim inconstantium adversus constantes testimonium perhibuissent, in judicio haud dubiè allegatum, iisdémque objectum suisset. Cùm igitur jam supra idoneis argumentis Pastorum innocentiam comprobaverimus; atque etiamnum personatus ille adversus innocentiam eandem imbellibus calumniarum potius, ex puteo abyssi extractarum, quàm probationum telis pugnaverit: Pastores eosdem non perduellionis ullius merito, sed puro puto religionis odio, non aliam scilicet ob causam, quàm quia exemplo Divi Ambrosii, Mediolanensis Episcopi, sicut ille Basilicas furioso Auxentio, sic hi Ecclesias, Basilicas suas, ob solius Dei timorem, furiosissimo Colonitzio tradere recusârunt; atrocissimam tempestatem isthanc subiviisse, concludimus.
units.tr: ...were judged timid. Moreover, the poisonous formula of the libel that the Extract recites is one that a disguised man has shamelessly dared to misrepresent in plain sight, claiming that none of those who appeared subscribed to it. Admittedly, all the libellatici gave their adversaries some occasion for accusation, and the formulas of the libels offered at the first citation were indeed harsher. But at the later citation, the words most often inserted by those who subscribed were: although we are not conscious of any rebellious complicity. With what conscience, then, did he charge these libellatici with disguised pretence, at least against the Reformed pastors in Hungary? Among the two hundred and thirty-six libellatici he cites, no more than two Reformed can be found who subscribed, at either the first or the second term of citation, that they would give up their office. The inconstant could not rightly prejudice the more constant, even the Augsburg men. For if any of the inconstant had given testimony against the constant, it would undoubtedly have been cited at the trial and put to them. Since, therefore, we have already demonstrated the pastors' innocence above by sound arguments, and since that impostor has fought against the same innocence with feeble calumnies, drawn up from the pit of the abyss rather than with the weapons of proof, we conclude that these same pastors underwent this most savage storm not on account of any treason, but from pure hatred of religion, for no other reason than that, following the example of St Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who refused to hand over his basilicas to the furious Auxentius, they refused, out of fear of God alone, to hand over their churches and basilicas to the most furious Colonitz.

units.la: CCCXIX. Longius, fateor, Hungaricæ persecutionis historiæ, salutarium documentorum feracissimæ, & patientiæ constantiæque, si quando similis tempestas fideles Dei servos premet, (quid enim inveteratis odiis, & crescente in dies hostium Ecclesiæ sævitia, mitius nobis promittere ausimus?) acerimum stimulum infixuræ pertexendæ, æstus quidam calamum huncce provexit, quòd interesse posteritatis, ne tristes memorabilésque imprimis ejusmodi ecclesiæ casus ignoret, dubitaverim omnino nullus. In viam ut revertamur, eodem Clemente Pontifice, in ipso Papatu veritas circa B. Virginis Mariæ & imaginum cultum nonnihil erumpere visa, at mox in herba iterum suffocata est.
units.tr: CCCXIX. I admit that I have gone on at greater length than I intended about the history of the Hungarian persecution, which is so rich in salutary lessons of patience and constancy, should a similar storm ever press upon the faithful servants of God (for what milder thing can we dare to promise ourselves, given long-standing hatreds and the savagery of the Church's enemies growing day by day?). A certain zeal has driven my pen to add this sharp goad, and I doubt that anyone would deny that it concerns posterity not to be ignorant of such sad and especially memorable events of the Church. To return to our path: under the same Pope Clement, within the Papacy itself, the truth concerning the cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of images seemed to break out somewhat, but soon it was nipped in the bud again.

units.la: CCCXX. Etenim quoad B. Mariæ cultum, Lovanii quarta vice edita sunt Monita salutaria B. V. Mariæ ad cultores suos indiscretos. Juxta leges Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ primum A. M. D. C. LXXIII. prodierant munita facultate & approbatione Censoris Ordinarii, J. Gillemans, S. Theol. L. Ecclesiæ Cathedralis Gandavensis Canonici & Archipresbyteri. Cúmque in manus cecidissent quorundam, qui, verba Authoris referam, Monita illa vel non intelligentes, vel nolentes intelligere, in pravum sensum, imò & hæreticum, prorsus contra mentem Authoris & animum conati sunt torquere, atque ita vulgò suspecta & exosa reddere, pro illorum defensione subsidiariis copiis & approbationibus utendum ratus, quartæ editioni præfixit approbationem P. de Walenburg, Episcopi Mysiensis, & Suffraganei Coloniensis; Pauli Aussemii Vicarii in Spiritualibus, Generalis ejusdem Archidiaecesis; Francisci Francken, S. Theol. D. & ad SS. Apostolos Decani; Henrici Patricii, SS. Theol. D. & Prof. Coloniensis; & Johannis Polch, Pastoris ad S. Cunibertum. Tametsi vero in Monitis illis non omnem prorsus illegitimum sui cultum B. Virgo, quæ inducitur, Maria prohibet: improbat tamen, rejicitque S. Scripturæ testimoniis perpetuis unicè freta, plurimos colendæ Θεοτόκε modos, qui partim olim à Mariolatris præscripti, partim hodieque in praxi publica passim recepti sunt. ita ut tum veteres illos novósque Mariolatras, quos indiscretos sui cultores Maria vocat; partim praxin ipsam Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ obliquè feriri & perstringi, manifestum sit. Utque monitis nonnullis huc translatis fidem faciam, testatur monétque Maria, Se, quos amatores vult, imitatores cupere: Non omni spiritui credendum, nec facile recipiendas omnes & quasvis historiunculas, quæ de suis apparitionibus, aut revelationibus, aut beneficiis & privilegiis promiscuè circumferuntur: Nemini confidendum, se cultores suos ex inferno ad pœnitentiam revocare, aut propter aridas aliquas devotiunculas in judicio defendere: neminem cultum sibi exhibentem, si charitatem non habeat, prædestinatum esse: Non esse privilegium ullum peccatori impœnitenti concessum, ut æternum non patiatur incendium, quantumvis se colere præsumpserit, nec quicquam tales adjuturas formulas & precatiunculas, aut signa & instrumenta pietatis, quæ gestaverit, nec confraternitates & Sodalitates, quibus nomen dederit: Cavendum esse à laqueo Diaboli, qui sub prætextu facilis externæ pietatis securitatem peccatoribus suadet, ut pœnitentiam differant, præsumentes de Divina misericordia, & sua intercessione illis non defutura: Non compati vel collachrymari se illis, qui à Filio suo damnantur: Baculum esse arundinum, putantium, quod pietas externa sufficiat: Laudem, quæ sibi, ut sibi defertur, vanam esse: Se ante pedes Agni mittere coronam suam, & conservam nostram esse: Nolle se quidquam Deo subtrahere, vel cum illo dividere: Non se ita colendam, ac si non sufficeret Deus: Nullo alio, quàm Deo nos indigere, & in ipso habere omnia: Non desperandum ei, qui se non habeat, sed confidendum esse Christo: Non ita se colendam, ac si non daretur sine se aditus ad Deum per Christum: Non se colendam, quasi Deam subalternam: Non se Mediatricem vel Advocatam esse eo sensu, quo Filius est Mediator & Advocatus: Cavendum, ne per hyperbolen vel zelum immoderatum quidquam sibi tribuatur, quod soli Deo, vel Christo debetur: Non esse se omnipotentem, Salvatricem, Coredemptricem. A tribunali Divino ad suum appellari non posse: Nol
units.tr: CCCXX. As for the cult of the Blessed Mary, the Salutary Admonitions of the Blessed Virgin Mary to her indiscreet worshippers were published for the fourth time at Louvain. According to the rules of the Papal Church, they had first appeared in 1673, with the permission and approval of the ordinary censor, J. Gillemans, Licentiate in Sacred Theology, canon and archpriest of the cathedral church of Ghent. When they fell into the hands of certain people who, to quote the author's words, either did not understand those Admonitions or were unwilling to understand them, and tried to twist them into a wrong, even heretical, sense, quite contrary to the author's mind and intention, and so rendered them generally suspect and hateful, he thought that auxiliary forces and approvals should be used in their defence. So he prefixed to the fourth edition the approval of P. de Walenburg, bishop of Mysia and suffragan of Cologne; of Paul Aussem, vicar in spiritual matters and general of the same archdiocese; of Francis Francken, Doctor of Sacred Theology and dean of the Holy Apostles; of Henry Patricius, Doctor of Sacred Theology and professor at Cologne; and of John Polch, pastor at St Cunibert's. Yet although in those Admonitions the Blessed Virgin, who is introduced as speaking, does not forbid absolutely every illegitimate cult of herself, she does disapprove of and reject, relying solely on the constant testimonies of Holy Scripture, the many modes of honouring the Theotokos [Θεοτόκε] which were partly prescribed of old by Mariolaters and partly are still widely received in public practice today. It is thus manifest that she calls both those old and new Mariolaters indiscreet worshippers, and that the very practice of the Papal Church is obliquely struck at and censured. To give some proof of this, I will translate some of the admonitions here. Mary testifies and warns that she wishes those whom she loves to be imitators. One must not believe every spirit, nor readily accept all and any little stories that are circulated indiscriminately about her apparitions, revelations, benefits and privileges. No one should trust that she will call her worshippers back from hell to repentance, or defend them at judgment on account of some dry little devotions. No one who offers her worship is predestined if he has no charity. No privilege is granted to an impenitent sinner so that he does not suffer eternal fire, however much he presumes to honour her; nor will such formulas and little prayers, or signs and instruments of piety which he has carried, nor confraternities and sodalities to which he has given his name, help him. One must beware of the devil's snare, which under the pretext of easy external piety persuades sinners to put off repentance, presuming on divine mercy and on her intercession, which will not fail them. She does not suffer with or weep with those who are damned by her Son. A staff of reeds is for those who think external piety is enough. Praise which is given to her as to herself is vain. She casts her crown before the feet of the Lamb, and is our fellow servant. She is unwilling to take anything from God or to share it with him. She is not to be honoured as if God were not sufficient. We need no one but God, and in him we have all things. One should not despair who does not have her, but must trust in Christ. She is not to be honoured as if there were no access to God through Christ without her. She is not to be honoured as a subordinate goddess. She is not a Mediatrix or Advocate in the sense in which the Son is Mediator and Advocate. One must beware lest, through hyperbole or immoderate zeal, anything is attributed to her which is due to God alone, or to Christ. She is not omnipotent, Saviour, or Co-redemptrix. An appeal cannot be made from the divine tribunal to hers. She is unwilling
