units.la: Nolle se excessiva encomia, vel vanas adulationes: Dicendum non esse, quòd Christus sit Judex severus, Maria mater misericordiæ: Accedendum cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ, nec trepidandum; trepidantes tamen se ad illum ductūram: Non plus temporis aut precum sibi, quàm Deo impendendum: Sibi, ceu medio ad Deum, non fini, non nimium inhærendum: Cum homines sua mancipia non sint, abstinendum esse servilibus titulis & signis inanibus & auticis submissionibus: Se & sanctos cultu duliæ, sive dilectionis & societatis; solum Deum cultu latriæ colendum: Non rectè se diligi, si statuæ suæ pretiosis vestibus & monilibus fulgeant, Christus verò in pauperibus suis egeat: Non sibi placere, quòd splendeant luminaribus imagines suæ; dum juxta illas squalent receptacula corporis Christi: Nullam statuis vel imaginibus suis virtutem inesse: Non existimandum, se fuscam aut nigram, aut quicquam momenti in colore situm esse: Non aliam se esse hic, aliam ibi; aliam in Monte-ferrato, aliam in Monte-acuto: Non contendendum esse pro hac vel illa figura, hoc vel illo loco: Circa dotes & prærogativas suas contendendum non esse: Beatum esse, qui cum Apostolo se nihil judicat scire, quàm Jesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum. Quamvis verò simplices adeò stolidíque non sumus, quin fistulam dulce canentem agnoscamus ultro; Hypothesēs hásce & χνεῖας δὁξας, qui volet, conferat licet cum iis, quæ B. Virgini Mariæ attribuerunt Scriptores veteres & recentiores, inprimis Pelbarti de Temesware, Bernardini de Senis, & de Bustis, Jacobi de Voragine, Cæsarii, Antonini, Alani de Rupe, Salazares, Pozæ, Cosferi, Mendozæ, alii: cum praxi inprimis Papatus, in cultu B. Virginis Mariæ totius religionis Christianæ arcem collocantis. Nullo certè negotio, qui id tentaverit, Papatum ἑαυτῷ μωρᾷ μένον, adeóque αὐτοκαταδίκην deprehenderit. Oppugnatus equidem libellus est tum ab Episcopo Rhodensi, Ludovico Abelly; tum à Jesuita Johanne Crasseto. Neque tamen ei defensores & hyperaspistæ defuerunt, quos inter E-
units.tr: to receive excessive praises or empty flatteries. One should not say that Christ is a severe judge and Mary the mother of mercy. One should approach the throne of grace with confidence and not tremble; yet she will lead those who tremble to him. No more time or prayers should be spent on her than on God. One should not cling too much to her, as to a means to God, not as an end. Since men are not her chattels, one should abstain from servile titles, empty signs, and ancient submissions. She and the saints are to be honoured with dulia, that is, with love and fellowship; God alone is to be honoured with latria. She is not rightly loved if her statues shine with precious garments and necklaces while Christ is in want in his poor. She is not pleased that her images shine with lamps while beside them the receptacles of Christ's body are squalid. There is no virtue in her statues or images. One should not think that she is dark or black, or that anything of importance lies in colour. She is not one person here and another there, one on Monte Ferrato and another on Monte Acuto. One should not contend for this or that figure, or this or that place. One should not contend about her endowments and prerogatives. Blessed is he who, with the Apostle, judges that he knows nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. Although indeed we are not so simple and foolish as not to recognise readily the pipe that plays sweetly, whoever wishes may compare these hypotheses and opinions [δόξας] with those which ancient and more recent writers have attributed to the Blessed Virgin Mary, especially Pelbartus of Temesvár, Bernardine of Siena, and de Bustis, Jacob of Voragine, Caesarius, Antoninus, Alan de la Roche, Salazar, Poza, Cosfer, Mendoza, and others, together with the practice of the Papacy above all, which places the citadel of the whole Christian religion in the cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Anyone who attempts this will with no trouble find the Papacy remaining foolish to itself [ἑαυτῷ μωρᾷ μένον], and thus self-condemned [αὐτοκαταδίκην]. This little book was indeed attacked both by the bishop of Rhodes, Louis Abelly, and by the Jesuit John Crasset. Nor were defenders and hyperaspistes lacking to it, among whom E-

units.tr: These hypotheses ... the Bishop of Tournai stands out by his published pastoral letters.

units.la: CCCXXI. Sed & circa cultum imaginum doctorum in Papatu discordia gliscere coepit. Ex Jesuitarum officina prodierat liber Maimburgii, adversus Iconoclastas, quo imaginum cultum ab antiquitate ejusdem commendare operosè sustinuit, pro more gravissimè in detractatores cultus illius invectus. Ei se Pontificius Doctor haud incelebris oppositus, edito adversario scripto, in quo passim Maimburgium castigans, solidè efficacitérque probat, tribus primis Seculis in Ecclesiis & Proseuchis nullas omnino imagines expositas, nedum cultas esse; quarto Seculo à plurimis adhuc Ecclesiis imagines abfuisse; initio quinti non ad cultum, sed ad ornamentum & memoriam Martyrum erigi hinc inde eas coepisse; cultum verò earundem serius in Ecclesiam irrepsisse, ac demum in Concilio septimo stabilitum esse. De Caroli M. libris adversus Concilium Nicænum secundum, & Concilio Francofurtensi ita adversus Maimburgium eundem Author doctissimus disputat, ut libros illos jussu, authoritate, consensu, quin & opera collocata Caroli M. scriptos, & ad Pontificem Adrianum missos esse, clarissimè demonstret. Cœterum liber doctissimus cum rationibus refutari amplius non potuerit, authoritate, nisi fallor, proscriptus, paucis, quæ in manus nostras inciderunt, exemplaribus exceptis, tenebris damnatus est.
units.tr: CCCXXI. But discord also began to flare up among the Papist doctors over the cult of images. From the Jesuits' workshop had come a book by Maimbourg against the Iconoclasts, in which he laboured to defend the cult of images from antiquity and, in the usual solemn manner, attacked those who disparaged that cult. A fairly well-known Papist doctor opposed him by publishing a reply, in which, castigating Maimbourg at every turn, he solidly and effectively proves that in the first three centuries there were no images at all displayed or venerated in churches or places of prayer; that in the fourth century many churches still lacked images; that at the beginning of the fifth century images began to be set up here and there, not for worship but for decoration and as memorials of the martyrs; that the cult of images crept into the Church later; and that it was finally established at the Seventh Council. Concerning the books of Charlemagne against the Second Nicene Council and the Council of Frankfurt, the same most learned author argues against Maimbourg in such a way that he clearly demonstrates that those books were written by Charlemagne's command, authority, consent, and even labour, and sent to Pope Hadrian. Nevertheless, since the learned book could no longer be refuted with arguments, it was, unless I am mistaken, proscribed by authority and consigned to darkness, except for the few copies that have come into our hands.

units.la: CCCXXII. Clementi X. die xi. Jul. A. m. d. c. lxxvi. defuncto, Cardinalis Benedictus Odescalchi Comensis natus, & in Conclavi Cardinalium à celebri præcone Papæ, Recannati, Capucino, effusè laudatus, die x. Sept. ejusdem anni Gallis præ cæteris annitentibus successit; Benedicti nomen in Baptismo acceptum, in nomen Innocentii XI. in gratam Innocentii X. à quo in Cardinalium numerum allectus est, memoriam commutans. Hac—tenus quidem ita se gessit, ut laude Pontificis in posteriorum illorum numero optimi, cum Adriano forte & Marcello paria facientis, defraudandus non videatur; suturus etiam servus Dei revera bonus, si Asæ, Josaphati, Josiæ, Ezechiæ exemplo, excelsa abolere, quod tamen οὐχὶς μάλλον, ἤ ἐλπιδῳ έπι, conatus quandoque fuerit. Livio Odoschalchi Nepoti suo, ne in publico compareret, vel munera acciperet, neu spe ulla promotionis altioris animum suum lactaret, præcepit. Mox equidem Nobilis Venetus renuntiatus, & Dux Ceri creatus est. Ad altiora tamen ut promoveret Nepotem huncce, & vel Generalem Ecclesiæ, vel Nepotem, more hactenus recepto, declararet, nullis vel Nepotis ipsius, vel aliorum precibus induci hactenus se passus est, exemplo laude dignissimo Prædecessorum suorum nimia erga Nepotes studia damnans. Abolito Cardinalis Patroni nomine, Cardinalem Cibo Secretarium status & Superintendentem declaravit. Missis in Galliam, Hispaniam, Poloniam & Portugalliam nuntiis, pacem suasit. Judæorum Romæ commorantium numerum ad quinque mille contraxit, iisdemque urbem Romam à sordibus purgandam commisit, & fœnore iniquo interdixit. Episcopos Roma facessere jussos, ad Diœceses suas relegavit, & nonnisi idoneos, probéque exploratos, & examini rigido subjectos posthac eligere constituit, edita etiam lege, ne nisi literati Sacerdotes ad obeundas functiones promoveantur. Reformandorum ecclesiæ abusuum negotium quatuor Theologis, quos inter Recannati eminebat, dedit. Advocatis pauperibus eleemosynam dispertitus est liberalem, tanta confluentium, invicémque prementium multitudine, ut septem mulieres, duóve pueri oppressi extinctique fuerint. Cameram Apostolicam pecuniis mirè exhaustam cùm vidisset, ad familiares suos dixisse fertur, nunquam se credidisse, S. Petri vineam.
units.tr: CCCXXII. When Clement X died on 11 July 1676, Cardinal Benedetto Odescalchi, a native of Como, was eagerly praised in the conclave of the Cardinals by the famous herald of the Pope, Recanati, a Capuchin. On 10 September of the same year, with the French striving harder than anyone else, he succeeded, changing the name Benedict, which he had received at baptism, to Innocent XI, in grateful memory of Innocent X, by whom he had been admitted to the number of Cardinals. So far he has conducted himself in such a way that he does not seem to be cheated of praise as one of the best of the later Popes, who perhaps matched Hadrian and Marcellus. He will also be a truly good servant of God, if he abolishes the high places after the example of Asa, Jehoshaphat, Josiah, and Hezekiah; though he has at times attempted this not so much out of zeal as [οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἢ ἐλπίδι] out of hope. He ordered his nephew Livio Odescalchi not to appear in public or accept gifts, and not to cherish any hope of higher promotion. Soon, to be sure, he was made a Venetian noble and created Duke of Ceri. Yet he has so far allowed himself to be persuaded neither by the pleas of the nephew himself nor of others to raise this nephew to a higher rank, or to declare him General of the Church or Cardinal-nephew, as was customary hitherto; in this he has set a most praiseworthy example, condemning the excessive favours shown to nephews by his predecessors. Having abolished the title of Cardinal Protector, he declared Cardinal Cibo Secretary of State and Superintendent. He sent nuncios to France, Spain, Poland, and Portugal, and urged peace. He reduced the number of Jews living in Rome to five thousand, entrusted them with cleansing the city of Rome of its filth, and forbade them unfair usury. He ordered the bishops to leave Rome and sent them back to their dioceses, and decided that from now on only suitable men, carefully tested and subjected to a rigorous examination, should be chosen. He also issued a law that no priests be promoted to perform their functions unless they are learned. He gave the task of reforming the abuses of the Church to four theologians, among whom Recanati stood out. He distributed a generous alms to the poor who had been summoned, but with such a crowd of people pressing in on one another that seven women and two boys were crushed and killed. When he saw that the Apostolic Chamber had been wonderfully drained of money, he is reported to have said to his close associates: I never believed that the vineyard of St. Peter had been laid waste so greatly. [Here the Latin of the unit is garbled.]

units.la: cujus studium reformandi nonnulla, leviora licet, commendatur. neam tantopere vastatam esse. Ut igitur splendidissime eadem locupletetur, & S. Petrus Apostolus auri & argenti inops, in Cræsum Crassúmque quempiam convertatur, nullum non lapidem, artis chryso-poetices haud indoctus, movit, movetque. Altieriis Roma discessuris, ut subsisterent ulterius, mandavit, ne alibi locorum artes expilandi antehac Romæ ab illis exerceri solitas, liberius exercerent. Reginæ Christinæ reditus annuos duodecies mille coronatorum decrevit, ea tamen lege, ut Cardinalibus ampliorem posthac honorem haberet. Ita vero minora nonnulla reformare occœpit, ut saniorum judicio, magis necessaria, non tam sua forte, quàm aliorum, quibus reformatio Ecclesiæ sudes in oculis est, ardorem ejus sufflaminantium culpa, omiserit; luporum inprimis dentes, quibus innocuum gregem lacerare soleant, frangere & excutere neglexerit; Recannati inter alia pro suggestu pronuntiante, adeo tardas esse ejus conceptiones, ut metuendum sit, ne abortus sequantur. Quem alias etiam Papam pro suggestu eodem monentem, ut in sceleratos severius animadvertat, & Ministros deligat non juniores, sed adultiores, idem Papa lachrymabundus audivisse fertur. Bullam contra Nepotismum, quem inde à Clemente VIII. ad sua usque tempora septendecim auri millionibus Cameram Apostolicam emunxisse, rationibus initis, subductisque calculis, deprehendit; adornari curavit. quæ tamen, reclamantibus Cardinalibus pluribus, iis maximè, qui ad Papale solium quandoque se consurrecturos, spem animo conceptam tenebant, promulgata non est, frustra identidem monitoriis suis consensum eorum solicitante Pontifice. In Jansenitarum partes propensior, Arnaldo, nec non Episcopo Gratianopolitano, Jansenitæ utrique, literas humanissimas perscripsit. Bellarminum quoque in Divorum numerum relaturus fuerat, nisi proposito Cardinales non pauci ci intercessissent. Frustra quin etiam Monachos ad legem Κοινοβιωλιχὼ, seu vitam communem revocare magno nisu conatus est, adversantibus instituto ejus, præter Franciscanos, omnibus.
units.tr: Whose zeal for reform is commended, though in lesser matters. ... that the vineyard had been so greatly devastated. So that it may be enriched most splendidly, and that St. Peter the Apostol, lacking gold and silver, may be turned into some Croesus or Crassus, he has moved, and still moves, every stone, being no mean practitioner of the art of gold-making. When the Altieri were about to leave Rome, he ordered them to remain there longer, so that they might practise more freely elsewhere the arts of plunder that they had previously been accustomed to practise in Rome. He decreed for Queen Christina an annual income of twelve thousand crowns, on the condition, however, that he would henceforth show greater honour to the Cardinals. He began to reform some minor matters in such a way that, in the judgement of the saner men, he has neglected the more necessary ones, not so much through his own fault as through that of others, whose efforts to reform the Church are a thorn in their eyes, and who have hindered his zeal. Above all he has neglected to break and knock out the teeth of the wolves, with which they are accustomed to tear the innocent flock. Recanati, among other things, said from the pulpit that his conceptions were so slow that one should fear they would end in miscarriage. The same Pope, when Recanati from the same pulpit warned him to punish the wicked more severely and to choose ministers not younger but more mature, is reported to have heard him with tears. He had the reckoning made and the sums calculated, and found that from Clement VIII to his own time nepotism had drained the Apostolic Chamber of seventeen million gold pieces; he had a bull against nepotism prepared. Yet, since many Cardinals objected, especially those who held in their minds the hope of one day rising to the papal throne, it was not published, though the Pope repeatedly, by his edicts, sought their consent in vain. Being rather inclined to the party of the Jansenists, he wrote most courteous letters to both Arnauld and the Bishop of Grenoble, both Jansenists. He would also have enrolled Bellarmine among the saints, had not not a few Cardinals interceded against the proposal. He even strove with great effort, but in vain, to recall the monks to the communal life [Κοινοβιωτικὴν], or cenobitic rule, opposed by all except the Franciscans, since it ran against his own order.

units.la: CCCXXIII. Gestivit vero admodum Pontifici huic animus, officia nonnulla, indulgentiasque, quas superfluas rebatur, abolere. dicere verissimè solitus, brevem orationem penetrare Cœlum, & ex indulgentiarum multitudine confusionem in Ecclesia obortam esse. Die igitur XVII. Febr. A. M. D. C. LXXVIII. Raimundus Capisuccus, sacri Palatii Apostolici Magister, de mandato speciali Sanctissimi Domini Innocentii, Papæ XI. uti verba Decreti sonant, edito eodem decreto, libellum inscriptum: Officium immaculatæ conceptionis Sanctissimæ virginis nostræ Dominæ, approbatum à Summo Pontifice Paulo V. quo devote illud recitantibus centum dierum indulgentiæ promittuntur, sicut apparet ex Brevi ejus x. Jul. A. M. D. C. XV. Mediolani impresso; ita prohibuit, ut nemo cujuscunque ordinis, gradus & conditionis existat, Officium illud apud se retinere, legere, imprimere, vel imprimi curare audeat, sed statim à decreti illius notitia, quicunque illud habuerit, locorum ordinariis, aut inquisitoribus tradere, sub poenis in Indice librorum prohibitorum contentis teneatur. Paulò post, die nimirum VII. Martii A. M. D. C. LXXVIII. Congregatio Sacra indulgentiis, sacrisque reliquiis præposita, cuncta sua Sanctitate probante, & inviolate servari jubente, decretum prægnantius, cui Aloysius Cardinalis Homo-Deus, & Michaël Angelus Riccius Secretarius subscripserunt, die XII. Martii ejusdem anni ad valvas Curiæ, & in acie Campi Floræ, aliisque solitis urbis locis affixum publicatumque, edidit, quo indulgentiarum magnam farraginem suppressit. Delatæ, ita Decretum præfatur, sæpius fuere ad sacram Congregationem, indulgentiis, sacrisque reliquiis præpositam, Indulgentiæ quædam confi-ctæ
units.tr: CCCXXIII. This Pope was very eager to abolish certain offices and indulgences, which he thought superfluous; he was accustomed to say, most truly, that a short prayer penetrates heaven, and that confusion had arisen in the Church from the multitude of indulgences. So on 17 February 1678, Raimundo Capisucchi, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, by the special command of our Most Holy Lord Innocent, Pope XI, as the words of the decree sound, published a decree and prohibited a book entitled: The Office of the Immaculate Conception of the Most Holy Virgin our Lady, approved by the Supreme Pontiff Paul V, to those who recite it devoutly is promised an indulgence of one hundred days, as appears from its Brief of 10 July 1615, printed at Milan. He forbade that anyone, of whatever order, rank, or condition, should dare to keep, read, print, or have printed that Office; and that whoever possessed it, as soon as he learned of that decree, should be bound under the penalties contained in the Index of Prohibited Books to hand it over to the local ordinaries or inquisitors. A little later, namely on 7 March 1678, the Sacred Congregation charged with indulgences and holy relics, with the whole approval of His Holiness, and ordering it to be kept inviolate, issued a more weighty decree, signed by Cardinal Luigi Omodei and by the Secretary Michelangelo Ricci. It was posted and published on 12 March of the same year at the doors of the Curia, on the Campo de' Fiori, and at the other customary places of the city, and it suppressed a great heap of indulgences. Certain indulgences, the Decree begins, have often been brought to the Sacred Congregation charged with indulgences and holy relics, indulgences that have been devised

units.la: Indulgentias idem complectres abolet. ste & omnino falsæ, quæ per diversas orbis Christiani partes circumferuntur; aliæ vero examinandæ, quæ adhibito studio inventæ sunt vel Apocryphæ, vel à Romanis Pontificibus revocatæ, vel nullæ, quòd datum iis tempus præteriisset: quarum quidem plurimæ, cùm non facilem cognitionem habeant Christi fideles, harum rerum minùs peritos fallunt, qui spe indulgentiæ remissionisque peccatorum suorum consequendæ frustrantur. Quamobrem eadem sacra Congregatio vehementer cupiens huic malo magis in dies serpenti occurrere, animarum profectui, & indulgentiarum dignitati consulere, plures illarum singulari diligentia colligi, & in indicem referri curavit. Mox referuntur prolixa serie indulgentiæ variæ, concessæ à Pontificibus Johanne II. Sixto IV. Urbano II. Eugenio III. Innocentio III. Bonifacio IX. Johanne XXII. Alexandro VI. Leone X. Pio IV. Clemente VIII. Paulo V. Gregorio XV. Urbano VIII. Clemente X. Subjiciuntur etiam aliæ à nonnullis Romanis Pontificibus tributæ, ut ajunt, coronis mysteriorum passionis Christi; quæ magno numero recensentur: demum omnes indulgentiæ concessæ ante decretum Clementis VIII. rosariis, granis, seu calculis, crucibus & imaginibus sacris; vel ante Breve Pauli V. quod incipit: Romanus Pontifex &c. editum XXIIII. Maii A. M. D. C. VI. personis Regularibus quarumcunque religionum & Ordinum, etiam mendicantium; vel ante constitutionem CXV. Clementis VIII. & LXXVIII. Pauli V. habitas per aggregationem, vel aliam communicationem ab Archiconfraternitate ulla, Ordine, Congregatione, Societate etiam Jesu, Capitulo vel cœtu quocunque; vel ab eorum Officialibus, Superioribus, aliisque personis: tum Summaria indulgentiarum pro Congregationibus doctrinæ Christianæ, confraternitatibus S. Trinitatis & Redemptionis Captivorum nominis Dei, Rosarii B. Mariæ, &c. Tandem indulgentias stationum urbis, quæ à Romanis Pontificibus singulari quodam ibe-neneficio vel communicatæ sunt, vel communicabuntur interdum aliquibus locis, ordinibus, aut personis; diebus tantum stationum in Missali Romano descriptis, suffragari posse; Semel autem duntaxat in die plenariam indulgentiam in certos dies Ecclesiam visitantibus, concessam, vel aliud pium opus peragentibus lucrifieri. Utrique huic decreto variæ Conciliorum, Patrum & Theologorum gnomæ, quibus decreti illius æquitas defenditur, subjiciuntur. Memorabilis inter alias est illa Innocentii III. lib. 1. Epist. ad Cantuariensem & alios Episcopos, ubi sic ille: Sicut ea, quæ à Prædecessoribus nostris provida fuerunt deliberatione statuta, nullatenus irritari volumus vel infringi: sic ea, quæ ab eis sunt per obreptionem obtenta in honestatis Ecclesiasticæ detrimentum corrigi volumus, & in statum redigi meliorem. Sed & Bulla Sabbathina ibidem critico Theologorum Parisiensium Claudii Bloini, Natalis Vareti, & Natalis de Bretigneres, veru confodiuntur. Denique clauduntur decreta isthæc verbis Petri Damiani Præfat. vit. 1. Mauri Cæsen. Episcopi, quæ ejusmodi sunt: Contemnendus pincerna est, qui dum vini copiam jactat, fæcem quoque punienda temeritate propinat. Constat satis decreta isthæc, non malo certè animo condita, adeò diversis animorum motibus excepta esse, ut non defuerint hodierni Papatus magni Atlantes, qui, Jesuitarum, quibus moderni Pontificis candor displicere videtur, haud dubiè instinctu, assa voce asseverarent, plus illa Papatui nocere, quàm Euangelici quinquaginta annorum intervallo nocere integro Regno cuipiam potuerint.
units.tr: and are altogether false, and that are circulated through various parts of the Christian world; others, which on careful examination have been found to be either apocryphal, or revoked by the Roman Pontiffs, or null because the time granted for them had passed, are yet to be examined. Since most of these are not easily recognised by the faithful, they deceive those less skilled in such matters, who are disappointed in their hope of obtaining an indulgence and forgiveness of their sins. Therefore the same Sacred Congregation, earnestly wishing to meet this evil, which spreads more each day, and to provide for the spiritual progress of souls and the dignity of indulgences, has taken care that many of them be collected with special diligence and entered in an index. Next follow, in a long list, the various indulgences granted by the Popes John II, Sixtus IV, Urban II, Eugene III, Innocent III, Boniface IX, John XXII, Alexander VI, Leo X, Pius IV, Clement VIII, Paul V, Gregory XV, Urban VIII, and Clement X. Then are added others, said by some Roman Pontiffs to have been granted to the crowns of the mysteries of Christ's Passion, which are enumerated in great number. Finally come all the indulgences granted before the decree of Clement VIII on rosaries, beads or counters, crosses, and sacred images; or before the Brief of Paul V beginning Romanus Pontifex etc., issued on 24 May 1606, to regular persons of whatever religious orders, even the mendicant orders; or before the constitution 115 of Clement VIII and 78 of Paul V, obtained through affiliation or some other communication with any archconfraternity, order, congregation, society, even the Society of Jesus, chapter, or assembly whatever, or from their officials, superiors, or other persons. Then the summaries of indulgences for the Congregations of Christian Doctrine, the confraternities of the Holy Trinity and of the Redemption of Captives, of the Name of God, of the Rosary of the Blessed Mary, etc. Lastly, the indulgences of the stations of the city, which have been or will be granted by the Roman Pontiffs by a certain special favour to some places, orders, or persons, may be gained only on the days of the stations described in the Roman Missal; and a plenary indulgence granted for certain days to those visiting the church, or performing some other pious work, may be gained only once a day. Various maxims of Councils, Fathers, and Theologians, by which the fairness of that decree is defended, are appended to both decrees. Among others, memorable is that of Innocent III, Book 1, Letter to the Archbishop of Canterbury and other Bishops, where he speaks thus: Just as we do not wish those things that were established by our predecessors with prudent deliberation to be annulled or infringed in any way, so we wish those things that were obtained by them through misrepresentation to be corrected, to the detriment of ecclesiastical honesty, and restored to a better state. The Sabbatine Bull is also pierced through there with the critical spear of the Parisian theologians Claude Bloin, Noël Varet, and Natalis de Bretigneres. Finally these decrees are closed with the words of Peter Damian, Preface to the Life of Maurus, Bishop of Cesena, Book 1, which are of this kind: He is to be despised as a cupbearer who, while boasting of the abundance of wine, also serves the lees with punishable recklessness. It is clear enough that these decrees, composed certainly with no ill intent, were received with such different movements of minds that there were not lacking the great Atlases of today's Papacy, who, undoubtedly at the prompting of the Jesuits, to whom the candour of the present Pontiff seems displeasing, asserted loudly that those decrees harm the Papacy more than the Evangelicals could harm any entire kingdom in the whole fifty years' interval.

units.la: C- CCXXIV. Quantopere Pontificius Clerus Angliæ Regnum ad Romani Pontificis obedientiam postliminio reducere non semel conatus fuerit, supra non uno loco narravimus.
units.tr: CCCXXIV. How often the Popish clergy of England tried to bring the kingdom back under obedience to the Roman Pontiff, I have related in more than one place above.

units.la: Et magnis quidem ausis, quæ Dei, fidi Israëlis custodis, ineffabilis bonitas est, nunquam non excidit. Quiescere equidem pertinaces insidiæ post pulverariam contoconspirationem visæ sunt. quanquam in tristissima tragœdia illa, qua Carolus Jacobi Filius dirissimo & inaudito exemplo è medio sublatus est, haud postremas partes, accendendis intendendisque saltem partium exulceratarum odiis, tractasse Pontificios, non desunt, qui exquisitis rerum documentis comprobent. Cœterum insidiarum machinationumque perpetuarum ignem sub doloso cinere latuisse, quin & sæviisse sine intermissione ulla, fidem facit novissima conspiratio adversus moderni Angliæ Regis vitam, Regni statum, & Religionem in eo Euangelicam, quæ diu ante concepta, demum Octobri Anni M. D. C. LXXVIII. indicio accuratissimo Titi Oatis, Bedlovii & France juratorum testium; nec non Edmundi Berry Godfrey, ad cognoscendam conjurationis ab Oate primum detectæ causam delegati judicis primarii subitanea & clancularia cœde, nec non reorum non unius generis, Colemanni inprimis Secretarii, cui nomen Langshornii erat, & Jesuitarum aliquot convictione, consensuque Parlamenti totius, patefacta & comprobata est. Conspirationis architecti denuo Jesuitæ, parricidiorum doctores ductoresque fuerunt; Oliva inprimis, eorum Generalis, qui officia sua conjuratis, etiam exercitui ingenti conscribendo distribuit; nec non Jesuitæ Angli, Thomas Whitebrand & Richardus Strong, Provinciales, Ahsly, Harcourt, Jennison, Keines, Wright, aliique Hispani etiam complures; quibus alii quoque tum Monachi Angli, Benedictini, Carmelitæ, Franciscani & Dominicani; tum Sacerdotes, quorum singulorum, ut & aliorum complicum, nomina in Actis, Parlamenti Anglicani jussu vulgatis, edita videre est; suppetias tulerunt. Bullam equidem, qua nova Papalis, quam in Angliam introducere conjurati meditabantur, tum Hierarchia, tum regiminis Politici forma præscripta continebatur, conjurati iidem, ceu à Pontifice ipso profectam venditaverant. quam tamen à Jesuitis potius confictam fuisse, saniores judicarunt. De eo quicquid sit, id certum est, Londini in Concilio Jesuitarum, Sathanico œstro percitorum, Regem capitaliter accusatum damnatumque esse; & damnatione eadem etiam Regis fratrem, siquidem coronam Regni, ceu beneficium Papæ accipere, novam hierarchiam tueri, in Regis fratris, & subditorum Protestantium dirissimam necem, urbisque Londinensis & aliarum incendium consentire, denique universa Protestantium sacra abolere, & Papatum invehere recusaverit, nec non Principem Araufionensem, utpote Stuartorum propaginem, comprehensos fuisse. Steteratque sententia, Regem quidem per Monachos Benedictinos Anglos, Andertonum & Coniers, nec non allectos in societatem facinoris Hibernos quatuor, gladio seu cultro oblongo; atque si id non succederet, per Pickeringium & Graves, sclopeto; demum, si & hic conatus irritus caderet, opera Georgii Wakemanni, Reginæ Archiatri, quindecim mille librarum mercede, Doctore Forgathy & Colemanno cum eo contracturis, conducendi, veneno propinato: Fratrem Regis, siquidem spem de se conceptam fefellerit, aliis dirisque etiam modis: denique Principem Araufionensem, duodecim Jesuitis in Hollandiam ablegandis, sanguinaria adversus eum consilia machinaturis, è medio tollere, atque sic Regnatricem domum Stuartorum radicitus extirpare. Occupatio vero & subjugatio Regnorum Angliæ, Scotiæ & Hiberniæ ejusmodi decreta & conclusa est, ut Hibernia quidem tum intestinis motibus, post cædem Ducis Ormontii, per quatuor sicarios Hibernos designatos, patrandam, excitatis; tum peregrinorum armorum vi, suppetias Hibernis ab Episcopo & Clero Dublinensi à fidelitatis juramento Regi præstito relaxandis, latura, in potestatem redigatur: Anglia vero & Scotia, sparsparsis in utraque per Jesuitas Presbyterianorum personas mentientes, & sub hac larva populum adversus Episcopos, in Scotia cumprimis, concitantes, discordiæ seminibus, internis dissidiis collisæ, debilitatæ, & post violentam mortem Regis, consurgente exercitu triginta millium Pontificiorum, occultè, ducibus cum Provinciali Angliæ imperia distribuente, arcto fœdere colligatis, dispolito, & cum superveniente exotica potestate conjuncto, urbibusque etiam præcipuis incendio subito destinatis, occupatæ subversæque, sub jugum Romani Pontificis mittantur. Novi etiam illius, quod meditabantur, Regni administros in antecessum designari placuit. Nominatim autem Jesuitæ Provinciali Whitebrando dignitas & munus Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis; Calcari Episcopi Londinensis; Bellasi, Generalis; Comiti Arundelii, Cancellarii, Powes, Archithesaurarii; Wilhelmo Godolphin, Secreti Sigilli Custodis; Stafforto, Quæstoris; Colemanno, Secretarii Status; aliis alia munera dignitatesve destinatæ fuerant.
units.tr: Yet their great undertakings never failed, by the unspeakable goodness of God, the faithful guardian of Israel. The stubborn plots seemed to lie quiet after the gunpowder conspiracy. Still, there are those who prove by careful evidence that the Papists took no small part in that most grim tragedy, in which Charles, the son of James, was removed from the world by a most dreadful and unheard-of act, at least by stirring up and inflaming the hatreds of the embittered parties. That the fire of plots and continual machinations lay hidden under deceptive ashes, and raged without any pause, is shown by the latest conspiracy against the life of the present King of England, the state of the kingdom, and the Protestant religion in it. This was conceived long before and was finally brought to light in October 1678 by the most careful information of the sworn witnesses Titus Oates, Bedloe and Prance, and also by the sudden and secret murder of Edmund Berry Godfrey, the chief judge appointed to investigate the cause of the conspiracy first revealed by Oates. It was also exposed and confirmed by the conviction of the accused, not of one kind only, especially of the secretary Coleman, whose name was Langhorn, and of several Jesuits, and by the consent of the whole Parliament. The architects of the conspiracy were again the Jesuits, who were the teachers and leaders of the murders. Above all there was Oliva, their General, who assigned their duties to the conspirators, including the enlistment of a large army. Also the English Jesuits Thomas Whitebread and Richard Strong, provincials, with Ashby, Harcourt, Jennison, Keynes, Wright, and several other Spaniards, gave their aid, as did other English monks, Benedictines, Carmelites, Franciscans and Dominicans, and priests. The names of each of these and of the other accomplices are set out in the records published by order of the English Parliament. The conspirators, for their part, had put about a bull which they claimed came from the Pontiff himself, prescribing the new Papal hierarchy and the form of political government which they planned to introduce into England. More sensible men judged, however, that it had been fabricated by the Jesuits rather than issued by the Pontiff. Whatever the truth of that, it is certain that in London, in a council of Jesuits stung by Satanic frenzy, the King was accused of a capital crime and condemned. The same sentence was pronounced against the King's brother, since he refused to accept the crown as a gift from the Pope, to defend the new hierarchy, to consent to the most dreadful slaughter of the King's brother and of the Protestant subjects, and to the burning of London and other cities, and finally to abolish all Protestant worship and bring in Papacy. The Prince of Orange was also seized, as a scion of the Stuarts. The decision stood that the King was to be killed by the English Benedictine monks Anderton and Coniers, with four Irishmen enlisted in the crime, with a sword or a long knife; and if that failed, by Pickering and Graves with a musket; and finally, if this attempt too came to nothing, by the work of George Wakeman, the Queen's physician, who was to be hired for fifteen thousand pounds, with Dr. Forgathy and Coleman to take part with him, by poison administered. As for the King's brother, if the hope conceived of him failed, he was to be removed by other and dreadful means. Finally, the Prince of Orange was to be removed by twelve Jesuits, to be sent into Holland to plot bloody designs against him, and so the royal house of the Stuarts was to be uprooted completely. The occupation and subjugation of the kingdoms of England, Scotland and Ireland were so decided and settled by these decrees that Ireland, with internal disturbances stirred up first, after the murder of the Duke of Ormonde, which was to be carried out by four appointed Irish assassins, was to be brought under control by the force of foreign arms. Its bishop and clergy of Dublin were to release the Irish from the oath of loyalty sworn to the King. England and Scotland, however, were to be divided by Jesuits sent into each, pretending to be Presbyterians, who under this mask would stir up the people against the bishops, especially in Scotland. Weakened by the seeds of discord and internal dissensions, and after the violent death of the King, they were to be overwhelmed. An army of thirty thousand Papists was to rise secretly, with leaders who would distribute commands together with the Provincial of England, bound together by a close league. Then, joined with a foreign power that would arrive, and with the principal cities destined for sudden burning, they were to be seized and overthrown and sent under the yoke of the Roman Pontiff. They also decided that the administrators of the new kingdom they planned should be appointed in advance. Specifically, the Jesuits designated the office and dignity of Archbishop of Canterbury for Provincial Whitebread; of Bishop of London for Calcar; of General for Bellasis; of Chancellor for the Earl of Arundel; of Lord Treasurer for Powis; for William Godolphin, Keeper of the Privy Seal; for Stafford, Paymaster; for Coleman, Secretary of State. Other posts and dignities were assigned to others.

units.la: CCCXXV. Cùm eousque consilia conjuratorum promota fuissent, ut res propediem in nervum eruptura videretur, Deus Uncti & Ecclesiæ suæ pervigil custos; qui in Cœlo habitans hostium Regni sui consilia ridere & subsannare solet, quíque toties Anglicanam Ecclesiam è præsentissimo discrimine liberavit, eandem etiamnum sibi, pro ineffabili gratia & bonitate sua, curæ esse, testificatus est.
units.tr: CCCXXV. When the plans of the conspirators had advanced so far that the affair seemed about to break out at any moment, God, the watchful guardian of his Anointed and of his Church, who dwells in heaven and is accustomed to laugh at and mock the counsels of the enemies of his kingdom, and who has so often delivered the English Church from the most imminent peril, testified that, by his unspeakable grace and goodness, he still takes care of it.

units.la: Movit enim cor conjuratorum non postremi, Titi Oatis, qui nefariæ societatis illius Secretarius, minima quæque calamo consignaverat, ut meditati sceleris, jam jam patrandi, horrore perculsus, & pia pœnitudine ductus, impia consilia detegere animum suum induxerit. Et primò quidem illa in Tongii, Theologi Angli, quem Jesuitis ob privatas simultates & infensum & invisum esse cognove-rat,
units.tr: For it moved the heart of one of the conspirators, and no small one: Titus Oates, who was secretary of that wicked society and had written down every smallest detail with his pen. Struck with horror at the wicked deed, now about to be carried out, and led by a pious repentance, he resolved to reveal the impious plans. At first he chose to pour out those things in the bosom of Tongue, an English theologian, whom he knew to be both hostile to and hated by the Jesuits because of private quarrels,

units.la: Titum Oatem detecta per rat, sinum effundere placuit. Mox vero circa initium Octobris A. M. D. C. LXXVIII. tota conjurationis series ex Ephemeridibus ejusdem Oatis, Regiis prodita est. Absente Rege sine mora nonnulli in vincula rapti, judicésque iis, qui causam cognoscerent, dati sunt. Inter eos haud postremus Edmondus Berry Gothfrey die XII. Octobr. in secretum conclave, eo prætextu, quòd conjurationis arcana nonnulla detegenda ei sint, seductus, conscìis Jesuitis tribus, per Robertum Grien, Laurentium Hill, aliósque nefariè strangulatus, & cadaver ejus pugione consossum in foveam projectum est. Conjurati non pauci convicti, damnatíque legitimè, tragica morte conceptum animo nefas expiârunt. quos inter Colemannus ex propriis scriptis testibúsque pluribus convictus licet, pertinaciter crimen diffiteri non desiit. Eadem pertinacia Jesuitæ & sacerdotes Whitebrandus Provincialis, Harcourtus, Fenwikius, Gavanus & Turnerus d. xx. Junii M.D.C. LXXIX. ad supplicium ducti, crimina, quorum legitimè convicti sunt, morientium fide inficiari, Deóque sic & hominibus illudere non erubuerunt. quod juxta receptam æquivocationum doctrinam illos apud suos quidem excusatè facere potuisse, libro publica authoritate Londini eodem anno edito, clarissimè probatum est. Cœterùm universæ conspirationis illius sacerimæ, à novissimis Cyclopibus, Regni Pontificii propagandi fervore sideratis, institutæ historiam, Parlamenti Anglicani authoritate publici jurisfactam, prolixius repetere superseddemus, Deo T. O. M. quas debemus, maximas & immortales gratias persolventes merito, quòd à cervice Regis, Regni & Ecclesiæ, inprimis suæ iterum exquisitissimas hostium insidias, exitiúmque præsentissimum, clementer adeò potentérque averruncavit.
units.tr: Titus Oates, after the matter had been detected, chose to pour them out. Then, however, at the beginning of October 1678, the whole series of the conspiracy was made public from the diaries of this same Oates, by royal authority. The King being absent, some men were at once seized and put in chains, and judges were appointed for those who were to examine the case. Among them, not the least was Edmund Berry Godfrey, who on 12 October was lured into a secret room, on the pretext that some secrets of the conspiracy were to be revealed to him. With three Jesuits privy to the plot, Robert Green, Lawrence Hill and others, he was foully strangled, and his body, pierced with a dagger, was thrown into a ditch. Many of the conspirators were convicted and lawfully condemned, and they atoned for the crime they had conceived by a tragic death. Among them, Coleman, although convicted by his own writings and several witnesses, did not cease to deny the crime stubbornly. With the same obstinacy the Jesuits and priests Whitebread the Provincial, Harcourt, Fenwick, Gavan and Turner, led to execution on 20 June 1679, were not ashamed to deny with their dying breath the crimes of which they had been lawfully convicted, and so to mock both God and men. That, according to the accepted doctrine of equivocation, they could have done so with a clear conscience among their own people, was very clearly proved in a book published that same year at London by public authority. Meanwhile, we shall not go on at length to repeat the history of that whole accursed conspiracy, drawn up by the latest Cyclopes, inflamed with zeal for extending the Papal kingdom, a history made public by the authority of the English Parliament. We rightly pay to God, Best and Greatest, the very great and immortal thanks we owe, because he has again mercifully and mightily turned aside from the neck of the King, the kingdom and especially of his Church the most carefully laid plots of the enemies and their most imminent ruin.

units.la: CCCXXVI. Magnis conatibus in Anglia cùm sic
units.tr: CCCXXVI. Since the Roman clergy had thus failed in England despite great efforts

units.la: Clerus in Anglia magnis Ecclesiæ Romanæ clerus exciderit, impetum posthac omnem in Hugenotos Galliæ, seu Ecclesias Protestantes Gallicanas, majore hactenus tristioriqúe, Deo permittente, & suam inibi familiam longæ pacis usura corruptam, vel explorante, vel castigante; successu, convertit. Forte etiam Jesuita præcipuæ in Gallia authoritatis, qui in Anglicanæ conspirationis ulcere ungues suos nimiùm demersos habuisse ferebatur, sive attentati criminis reus fuit, sive nullo suo merito delatus est, vindictam spirans, insito præterea adversus Protestantes odio, novissimæ persecutionis æstum non parùm auxit, animósque exulceratos ad meditandam πολιτείαν amplius exasperavit. Invitus equidem, fateor, nec sine gravi dolore animi, ad memorandas novissimas Ecclesiæ illius afflictiones, attingendámque adeò nigerrimam illam nubem, qua Cœlum hodie Gallicanum asperatur & contristatur, accedo, cùm talibus malis, uti S. Augustinus Epist. 122. loquitur, non tam prolixi libri, quàm prolixi fletus & gemitus debeantur. Quia tamen res gravis momenti visa est, modúsque persecutionis non tam novus quàm renovatus ejusmodi est, ut simulationum involucris violentiam suam tegat, eíque vela quædam obtendens, dum vim differt, mille obliquarum & Sinoniarum artium dolorúmque vafritie incautos hominum animos premat & tantùm non opprimat; omittere non possum, quin rei totius seriem paucis pandam, eademque opera piorum συναγωνισμὸν ardentissimum provocem. Exquisitæ verò persecutionis illius culpam in doli machinatore Ecclesiæ Romanæ, cujus solius historiam prosequimur, clero simulata pietate in potentum animis regnante, unicè residere, res ipsa certè clamat.
units.tr: The clergy of the Roman Church, having failed in England with great efforts, afterwards turned all its attack against the Huguenots of France, that is, the Protestant Gallican Churches, with greater and more grievous success than before. God permitted this either to test or to chastise their own household there, which had been corrupted by a long period of peace and was about to enjoy it. Perhaps also a Jesuit of chief authority in France, who was said to have sunk his claws too deeply into the sore of the English conspiracy, whether he was guilty of the attempted crime or was denounced without any merit of his own, breathing vengeance and moved besides by his inborn hatred of Protestants, greatly increased the heat of the latest persecution and further inflamed their embittered spirits to plot against the commonwealth [πολιτείαν]. I approach the memory of that Church's latest afflictions, and the very black cloud by which the Gallican sky is now darkened and saddened, unwillingly, I confess, and not without deep grief of mind. As St Augustine says in Epist. 122., not so much long books as long tears and groans are owed to such evils. Yet since the matter seemed of serious importance, and since this manner of persecution is not so much new as renewed, hiding its violence under the wrappings of pretence, veiling it with certain screens, and while it defers open force, pressing down and almost crushing the unwary minds of men with a thousand oblique, Sinonian arts and the cunning of griefs, I cannot refrain from setting out the whole course of the affair briefly, and by the same work I call the pious to a most ardent co-striving [συναγωνισμόν]. That the blame for this exquisite persecution lies solely with the contriver of deceit, the Roman Church, whose history alone we are pursuing, and with its clergy, whose feigned piety reigns in the minds of the powerful, the thing itself surely cries out.

units.la: CCCXXVII. Quàm sævis cum tempestatibus Ecclesia Gallicana puriorem Dei cultum amplexa, superiore Seculo conflictata fuerit, in loco abundè expositimus. Pri- mus
units.tr: CCCXXVII. How fierce were the storms with which the Gallican Church, which embraced the purer worship of God, was struggled with in the previous century, we have set out fully in the proper place. The first

units.la: Edicti Nannetensis, quo Ecclesiarum Gallicarum mus Henricus IV. Magni nomen promeritus, post domitum in Regno toto Henoticæ factionis monstrum, non alia ratione Regno pacem & quietem solidam constare posse censuit, quàm si post varia edicta Prædecessorum, minus ad stabilem concordiam proficua, legem concordiæ inter partes hactenus distractas civilibus bellis perpetuam & irrefragabilem, solenniter modo, sanciret. Auditis itaque, uti ipse Rex loquitur, Catholico-Romanorum querelis de cultu suo non ubique per Regnum exercito; Reformatorum vero de violata edictorum præcedentium fide, deque iis, quæ ad exercitium religionis suæ addi petebant, libertate conscientiarum, personarum & fortunarum securitate, collatis & recognitis præcedentibus edictis; Edictum A. M. D. XC. VIII. condidit, quod à loco Nantes, quo conditum est, Nannetense dicitur. Componendi ejus negotium Viris ex utraque religione sapientia & moderatione maximè conspicuis, Schombergio, Thuano, Vico & Calignoni datum est. Scopus edicti erat, ut si nondum ea forma religionis permisisset se coli à subditis, eadem saltem intentione id fieret, & tali cum regula, ut nihil religionis causa tumultuum aut turbarum in Regno existeret, utque sic cultus Dei fieret ab omnibus subditis, interque eos firma & durabilis pax staturminaretur, ablata causa turbarum, quæ ob religionem accidere possent. Post Rex Deum precatur, omnibus is persuadeat firmiter, in legis hujus observantia, post officium erga Deum & Regem positum esse præcipuum unionis & concordiæ fundamentum, restitutionémque totius status in pristinum splendorem, robur atque opulentiam. Addit: Necessarium judicavimus omnibus subditis hac de causa ponere legem generalem, claram, disertam & absolutam, per quam regantur in omnibus controversiis religionis causa & natis & nascituris, in qua utrique consentiant. Item: Hoc edicto perpetuo & irrevocabili statuimus, &c. Plura ejusmodi in præfatione edicti legere est. Ex quibus liquet, conditoris decreti, quod à Rege jam Pontificio, eo tempore, quo bella per religionis causam antehac mota quiescebant, adeóque liberima sponte, nullo metu, vi nulla adacto, profectum est, eam mentem fuisse, ut Edictum isthoc Nannetense lex Regni fundamentalis, generalis, clara, diserta, absoluta, regula controversiarum ob diversitatem religionis oborientium, irrevocabilis, &c. habeatur ab omnibus. Eadem necessitatis, utilitatis ad salutem Regni, eandem ἀυθεντίαν & perpetuitatem Edicto illi Filius Ludovicus XIII. declaratione 1. Maii A. M. D. C. X. edita, qua declarat, licet edictum hoc sit perpetuum & irrefragabile, ut confirmatione per novam declarationem non indigeat; Se tamen ex sententia sua Principúmque Sanguinis, Parium & Officiariorum Coronæ, statuere, ut edictum illud in omnibus capitibus & articulis, una cum decretis & statutis super interpretatione & executione ejus factis, inviolatum servetur, & contraeuntes, ceu publicæ quietis perturbatores, severè puniantur; attribuit. Et ne Reformati ob motus, quibus Duce Rohanio nonnulli impliciti fuerant, libertate per edictum illud stabilita excidisse viderentur, idem Rex novo edicto, mense Julio A. M. D. C. XXIX. Nemausi promulgato eandem confirmavit his verbis: Volumus, ut Reformati per omnia fruantur Edicto Nannetensi, & aliis edictis, Articulis, Brevibus, Declarationibus in acta Parlamentorum relatis, & propterea habeant liberum exercitium dictæ religionis in omnibus locis, ubi pax illa conceditur. Nihil de moderni Regis Christianissimi benignissimis declarationibus, d. VIII. Julii A. M. D. C. XLIII. nec non XXI. Maii A. M. D. C. LIII. editis, quibus luculentissimè cum Edictum Nannetense, tum alia etiam in gratiam Reformatorum condita, confirmantur, dicam. Edicti porro illius Pontificiorum maximè respectu utilitatem Illustris Vir Petrus Bellojus, Consiliarius Regius, & Advocatus in Parlamento Tholosano Generalis, publico scripto; nec non Petrus Matthæus Histor. Henrici IV. lib. II. demonstrârunt. Præterquam enim quòd vi Edicti illius Reformatis in quibusdam duntaxat locis, at Pontificiis promiscuè in omnibus, liberum religionis exercitium concessum est; grande etiam emolumentum ex eo ad Clerum Pontificium redundavit, cùm per illud praeter alia bona ecclesiastica, quibus antea privati fuerant, etiam decimarum pensiones, quas Reformati iis, qui eorum Pastores non erant, ante Edictum illud non debuerant, ei redditae fuerint. Statuerat quidem solenni diplomate Henricus IV. ut Reformatis in compensationem decimarum, quas clero Romano pendere cogebantur, ex aerario Regio quotannis, in sumptus alendis Pastoribus necessarios, centum triginta quinque millia librarum erogentur. Diu tamen est, quòd summam eam sibi, legi obtemperantibus, decimásque pendentibus licet, non persolvi amplius iidem conqueruntur.
units.tr: Henry IV, who earned the name the Great, after he had subdued the monster of the Henotic faction throughout the whole kingdom, judged that peace and solid quiet could not stand for the kingdom in any other way than if, after the various edicts of his predecessors, which did less to secure a stable concord, he should now solemnly sanction a law of concord between the parties hitherto divided by civil wars, one that was perpetual and irrefutable. Hence, as the King himself says, having heard the complaints of the Catholic Romans that their worship was not everywhere practised throughout the kingdom, and of the Reformed concerning the violated faith of the earlier edicts, and concerning the liberty of conscience, the security of persons and property, and the additions they sought for the exercise of their religion, the earlier edicts having been collated and recognised; he issued the Edict of 1598, which is called the Edict of Nantes from the place where it was issued. The task of drafting it was entrusted to men most conspicuous for wisdom and moderation from both religions: Schomberg, de Thou, Vic and Calignon. The aim of the edict was that, if the form of religion had not yet been permitted to be worshipped by the subjects, it should be done at least with the same intention, and with such a rule that no tumults or disturbances arise in the kingdom on account of religion, and that thus the worship of God might be carried on by all subjects, and a firm and lasting peace be established among them, the cause of the disturbances that might arise on account of religion being removed. Afterwards the King prays to God, that he may firmly persuade all men that, after duty towards God and the King, the chief foundation of union and concord, and the restoration of the whole state to its former splendour, strength and wealth, lies in the observance of this law. He adds: We have judged it necessary for all subjects to lay down in this matter a general law, clear, explicit and absolute, by which they may be governed in all controversies of religion, both those already arisen and those yet to arise, and to which both parties may agree. Again: By this edict, perpetual and irrevocable, we decree, etc. Many such statements may be read in the preface of the edict. From these it is clear that the intention of the framer of this decree, which was issued by a King who was then already Papist, at a time when the wars previously stirred up over religion were at rest, and so of his own most free will, under no fear and under no compulsion, was that the Edict of Nantes should be held by all as the fundamental, general, clear, explicit, absolute, irrevocable rule for controversies arising from difference of religion, and so on. His son Louis XIII gave the same edict the same necessity, usefulness for the safety of the kingdom, the same authority [ἀυθεντίαν] and perpetuity in the declaration of 1 May 1610, in which he declares that although this edict is perpetual and irrefragable, so that it needs no confirmation by a new declaration, yet he, with the opinion of the princes of the blood, peers and officers of the Crown, decrees that the edict be kept inviolate in all its heads and articles, together with the decrees and statutes made concerning its interpretation and execution, and that transgressors be severely punished as disturbers of public peace; and so he ascribes it. And lest the Reformed should seem to have lost the liberty established by that edict because of the disturbances in which some of them were involved under the leadership of Duke Rohan, the same King confirmed it by a new edict promulgated at Nîmes in July 1629, in these words: We will that the Reformed enjoy the Edict of Nantes in all respects, and the other edicts, articles, brief declarations recorded in the acts of the parliaments, and that they therefore have the free exercise of their religion in all places where that peace is granted. I say nothing of the most benign declarations of the present Most Christian King, issued on 8 July 1643 and on 21 May 1653, by which both the Edict of Nantes and the other edicts made in favour of the Reformed are most splendidly confirmed. That the edict was useful, especially with respect to the Papists, the illustrious man Pierre de Bellejoy, royal counsellor and advocate general in the Parliament of Toulouse, demonstrated in a public writing, and Pierre Matthieu in Histor. Henrici IV. lib. II. For apart from the fact that by force of that edict the free exercise of religion was granted to the Reformed only in certain places, but to the Papists promiscuously in all, a great advantage also flowed from it to the Papist clergy, since by it, besides other ecclesiastical goods of which they had been deprived, the pensions of tithes, which the Reformed had not been bound to pay to those who were not their ministers before that edict, were restored to them. Henry IV had indeed decreed by solemn diploma that, in compensation for the tithes which they were forced to pay to the Roman clergy, a hundred and thirty-five thousand pounds should be paid out each year from the royal treasury for the support of the ministers needed by the Reformed. Yet it is long since the same people have complained that this sum is no longer paid to them, although they obey the law and pay their tithes.

units.la: CCCXXVIII. Non obstante salutari Edicto, quod ex conditorum mente irrefragabile & sacrosanctum esse debuerat, inde ab annis potissimùm viginti, & quod excurrit, Clerus Pontificius, continuis machinationibus, insidiis, interpretationibus subdolis, aliisque artibus vaferrimis eò fere rem deduxit, ut ejus cardines & fundamenta pleraque convulsa jam sint, & convellantur indies. Cùm enim ejus praecipua capita, Euangelicos concernentia, circa libertatem conscientiae, consolationem aegrotantium & afflictorum, educationem liberorum, loca exercitiorum & Scholarum publicarum, disciplinae Ecclesiasticae liberum exercitium, Camerarum Edictalium tribunalia, Justitiae ἀπροσωπολήπλως administrandae ergo institu ta, admissionem Reformatorum ad pares praerogativas, omnes artes, professiones & munera publica, versentur; singula isthaec labefactata esse nimium, & labefactari quotidie, experientia tristis nimium proh dolor! nimiúmque comprobat.
units.tr: CCCXXVIII. Notwithstanding the salutary Edict, which, according to the mind of its framers, ought to have been irrefragable and inviolable, the Papist clergy, since about twenty years ago especially and for some time since, by continual machinations, snares, crafty interpretations and other most subtle arts, has brought the matter to such a point that most of its hinges and foundations are already shaken, and are being shaken daily. For its principal chapters, concerning Evangelicals, touch freedom of conscience, the comfort of the sick and afflicted, the education of children, places of worship and public schools, the free exercise of ecclesiastical discipline, the tribunals of the Chambers of the Edict, instituted for administering justice without partiality, the admission of the Reformed to equal privileges, and all arts, professions and public offices. Experience, alas, too sadly and too plainly proves that each of these has been weakened too much, and is being weakened daily.

units.la: CCCXXIX. Etenim quoad libertatem conscientiae, cautum tum est Edicti articulo Generali sexto, ut Reformatis æqué ac Pontificiis liberum sit vivere & habitare in omnibus urbibus & locis Regni, ita ut non inquirantur, non vexentur, molestia nulla afficiantur, nec constringantur quicquam facere in religionis causa contra conscientiam suam, nec propter illam quæstionem ullam patiantur in domibus & locis, ubi habitare volunt. Articulo quin etiam decimo nono sancitur, ne Reformati ullo modo adstringantur, aut maneant obligati ratione abjurationum, promissionum, aut juramentorum antehac præstitorum, aut cautionum & fide jussionum per eos datarum, in causa religionis; neque ideo possint vexari aut molestia affici quocunque modo. Judicet porro, qui volet, an ejusmodi conscientiæ libertas amplius constet iis, qui inconsideratius ad Pontificios transeuntes, redire ad Reformatam, quam prius confessi fuerant, religionem, quantumvis angente & torquente conscientia, prohibentur; quos vel perpetuo conscientiæ tormento flagellari, si obediverint; vel perpetui exilii, si non obedierint, multam sustinere oportet: qui post subitos semel ordines sacros, imò hodie Pontificii sine discrimine omnes, Reformatam religionem amplecti quolibet prætextu vetantur, adeóque pœnarum metu eam religionem, quam pravam existimant, retinere coguntur: qui hostiam à sacrificulo circumgestari solitam ex improviso obviam, & indeclinabilem, reverentia & capitis apertione, alicubi etiam geniculatione, aliisque modis, quibus professi Pontificii Sacramentum sibi occurrens prosequuntur, honorare, sub gravi pœna, imperantur; adeóque ad idololatriam adstringuntur, etiam ex mente Pontificiorum, cùm ab ipsis exigatur adoratio Divina ejus rei, quam se pro Deo nec habere, nec habere posse, disertis verbis testantur: qui qualibet occasione, veluti cùm præsentibus Pontificiis, quos movere sermo potest, fidei suæ rationem reddunt, vel objectionibus motis respondent, vel quærentes de religione instituunt, vel potentibus libros orthodoxos mutuos concedunt, subornationis & inductionis, quam Edictum Nannetense ad infantes invitis parentibus solicitatos & impuberes restringit, accusantur, & non raro peracti rei poenam luunt: qui auditores suos de fidei Pontificiae falsitate ex Dei verbo instruentes, vel violati respectus, vel impietatis & blasphemiae ilico coram judice infenso insimulantur: qui laudum Divinarum celebratione, & hymnorum Davidis à Spiritu S. inspiratorum cantu intra privatos parietes interdicuntur: qui errores & superstitiones, qui in Romana Ecclesia invaluerunt, arguere ex Dei verbo, & scapham scapham appellare vetantur: qui libros religionem concernentes, superstitionémque Pontificiam paulò liberius perstringentes imprimere & vendere, citra permissionem Magistratuum & Procuratorum Regiorum prohibentur: qui Templis & exercitiis religionis publicis innumeris, celebribus quin etiam hactenus scholis & Academiis privati, verbum Dei vel plane non, vel non sine gravissimis sumptibus & difficultatibus audire possunt: qui ob solam religionis professionem tot vitae & fortunarum discrimina subire, tot taedia molestiásque devorare, tot ludibria & opprobria sacrificulorum, Zelotarum iniquissimorum, & eorundem tribunitiis concionibus inflammati, saevientis & lascivientis populi perferre coguntur: qui in deplorato ejusmodi statu positi, nec aliò sine ingenti vitae & fortunarum discrimine migrare, nec in Regno tutò vivere, vel spirituali verbi Divini cibo vesci possunt; adeóque Regnum pro carcere, ex quo pejora in dies metuenda sunt, habere coguntur. Atqui pleraque haec recentissimis edictis, quorum dies, anni & tenor vulgo notissimi sunt; confirmata, & quotidie impune patrata, conscientiae libertatem vel imminutam plurimùm, vel alicubi etiam sublatam penitus, manifestè arguunt.
units.tr: CCCXXIX. For as regards liberty of conscience, provision was made in the sixth general article of the Edict that the Reformed, just as much as the Papists, may freely live and dwell in all the cities and places of the Kingdom, so that they are not inquired after, not harassed, not subjected to any annoyance, nor compelled to do anything in matters of religion contrary to their conscience, nor suffer anything on account of that question in the houses and places where they wish to dwell. Moreover, in the nineteenth article it is also decreed that the Reformed are in no way constrained or kept bound by reason of abjurations, promises or oaths made before, or of cautions and sureties given by them in matters of religion; nor on that account may they be harassed or troubled in any manner whatsoever. Let anyone who wishes judge whether this liberty of conscience still holds for those who, having rashly passed over to the Papists, are forbidden to return to the Reformed religion which they had professed before, however much their conscience gnaws and torments them; who must bear either to be scourged with perpetual torment of conscience if they obey, or to suffer the penalty of perpetual exile if they do not obey. For those who, once they have received holy orders, and indeed today all Papists without exception, are forbidden on any pretext to embrace the Reformed religion, and so are compelled by fear of punishments to retain that religion which they think depraved. For those who, when the host usually carried about by the priest meets them unexpectedly and cannot be avoided, are ordered under heavy penalty to honour it with reverence, with uncovering of the head, in some places even with genuflection, and with other gestures by which professed Papists pay honour to the Sacrament they meet; and so they are bound to idolatry, even by the Papists' own judgment, since adoration is demanded from them of a thing which they expressly testify they neither hold nor can hold to be God. For those who, on any occasion, such as when Papists are present whom the discourse may move, give an account of their faith, or answer objections raised, or instruct inquirers about religion, or lend orthodox books to those who ask for them, are accused of subornation and enticement, which the Edict of Nantes restricts to children solicited against the wishes of their parents and under age, and not infrequently pay the penalty of a crime committed. For those who instruct their hearers from the Word of God about the falsity of the Papist faith are at once accused before a hostile judge of violating respect, or of impiety and blasphemy. For those who are forbidden to celebrate divine praises and to sing the hymns of David inspired by the Holy Spirit within their private walls. For those who are forbidden to refute from the Word of God the errors and superstitions which have prevailed in the Roman Church, and to call a spade a spade. For those who are forbidden to print and sell books concerning religion which touch somewhat more freely on Papist superstition, without permission of the magistrates and royal procurators. For those who, deprived of the innumerable public temples and exercises of religion, and even hitherto of schools and academies, can hear the Word of God either not at all, or not without the gravest expense and difficulties. For those who are compelled, inflamed by the sermons of the sacrificing priests, most unjust zealots, and their tribune-like harangues, to undergo for the sole profession of religion so many dangers to life and fortune, to swallow so many weariness and troubles, and to endure the mockery and insults of a raging and wanton populace. For those who, placed in such a desperate state, can neither migrate elsewhere without great danger to life and fortune, nor live safely in the Kingdom, nor feed on the spiritual food of the divine Word; and so are compelled to regard the Kingdom as a prison, from which worse things are to be feared day by day. And yet most of these things, confirmed by the most recent edicts, whose dates, years and tenor are commonly well known, and carried out daily with impunity, clearly show that liberty of conscience has either been very much diminished or in some places entirely abolished.

units.la: CCCXXXX. Ægrorum & afflictorum consolatio, si quid aliud, ad conscientiæ libertatem pertinet.
units.tr: CCCXXXX. The consolation of the sick and afflicted, and whatever else pertains to freedom of conscience.

units.la: De ea sic Edicti articulo quarto particulari cautum legimus: Non tenebuntur hortationes accipere, cum ægrotabunt, aut morti appropinquabunt, sive per Magistratum damnati, sive alii, ab aliis, quam religionis suæ consortibus; poterúntque frui consolationibus & visitationibus Ministrorum suorum sine ulla turbatione. Articulo huic conformes sint nec ne novissimæ circa ægrotantes & afflictos consolandos & visitandos declarationes, edicta & decreta, iterum pii & prudentes arbitrentur omnes. Eousque Ecclesiasticorum potentia & inhumanitas prævaluit, ut declaratio ejusmodi jam A. M. D. C. LXIV. promulgata fuerit, licere Parochis locorum (Pontificiis) comitibus judice, scabino aut consule, ægrotanti se sistere, & ex illo cognoscere, in Religione Pontificia, an Reformata, mori velit. Leve hoc videbitur, sacrificulum tale quid ex ægrotantibus percontari, dummodo ad mutationem religionis solicitare quenquam integrum ei non sit. Atqui & turbatio manifesta hæc est ægrotantium, & fidem omnem experientiámque superat, Parochum Curatum, super insitam licentiam adversus eos, qui omnium injuriis expositi sunt; nixum athoritate præsentis Magistratus Pontificii, compotémque ita & dominum conclavis, in quo æger decumbit, nihil prolaturum, illi ad partes suas solicitando, inprimis cum neglecta conditione apposita, Curati sive Parochi, imò alii etiam sacrificuli & Monachi non vocati, soli ad ægrotantes multis in locis ingrediantur; quin & (fit hoc plane præter tenorem edicti, ab iis, qui odiosa non restringunt, sed pro lubitu ampliant) ægrotantis consanguineis proximis, ei hactenus assistentibus, secedere jussis, scrutinium isthoc, ferè peragi soleat. Ita, dum æger, sive ob morbum parum mentis suæ compos annuens votis, sive ambiguo generalíque verbo bona rectáque intentione usus, sive civilibus bus verbis prolocutus id, quod præter mentem ejus ad religionis negotium rapi potest, sive nutu etiam & gestu, cujus interpretatio huc illuc torqueri potest, usus, statim Pontificius proclamatur; ilico uxor à marito, liberi à parente, propinquus à propinquo, amicus ab amico avellitur, solisque Pontificiis ingressus in conclave, cœteris charitatibus non sine contumelia, ceu hostibus ab arce obsessa procul amotis, conceditur: mortuus Romano ritu sepelitur, & liberi impuberésque in Pontificia confessione educantur: convalescens verò nequicquam protestatus de injuria, vel ad Pontificia sacra adigitur, vel Relapsi pœnam statutam subit. Testor fidem hominum, an dirius aliquid excogitari potuerit perturbatione tanta morientium, qui in decretorio isto certamine, quo pro æternitatis brabeo, si unquam aliàs, decertandum iis validè est, adeóque eo etiam temporis articulo, quo
units.tr: On this point we read the following particular provision in the fourth article of the Edict: They shall not be compelled to receive exhortations when they are sick or approaching death, whether they have been condemned by the magistrate or are with others who are not companions of their own religion; and they may enjoy the consolations and visits of their own ministers without any disturbance. Whether the most recent declarations, edicts and decrees concerning the consoling and visiting of the sick and afflicted conform to this article, all the pious and prudent may judge for themselves. So far has the power and inhumanity of the churchmen prevailed that a declaration of this kind was already published in the year 1664: that the parish priests of the places (of the Papists) may, together with the count, the judge, the alderman or the consul, present themselves to the sick person and learn from him whether he wishes to die in the Papist or in the Reformed religion. This will seem a trifling matter, that a little priest should ask the sick such a question, provided it is not permitted to him to urge anyone to change his religion. Yet this disturbance of the sick is plainly evident, and it surpasses all belief and experience: the parish priest, relying on the authority of the present Papist magistrate, and so on the strength of the lord of the room in which the sick man lies, presses his case on them, in particular when the condition attached is neglected, that the curate or parish priest, and even other little priests and monks who have not been called, enter alone to the sick in many places. Indeed (and this happens plainly beyond the wording of the edict, since those who do not restrict odious measures but extend them at their pleasure do so), when the nearest relatives of the sick man, who had been helping him until then, have been ordered to withdraw, this inquisition is usually carried out almost completely. Thus, if the sick man, either being somewhat out of his mind nodding assent to their wishes, or using an ambiguous and general phrase with a good and upright intention, or speaking words of civility that can be twisted into a matter of religion beyond his intention, or even by a nod or gesture whose meaning can be turned this way or that, he is at once proclaimed a Papist. Immediately the wife is torn from the husband, the children from the parent, the kinsman from the kinsman, the friend from the friend, and only the Papists are admitted into the room, while the others, removed far off like enemies from a besieged citadel, are denied any charitable office, not without insult. He is buried in the Roman manner, and the children, while still under age, are brought up in the Papist confession. If he recovers, he protests in vain against the wrong, and is either forced into Papist rites or undergoes the penalty established for relapsed persons. I call the faith of men to witness: could anything more cruel be devised than such disturbance of the dying, who in this decisive contest, in which, if ever at any other time, they must strive hard for the prize of eternity, and therefore at that very moment of time in which

units.la: Labuntur frigida letho
units.tr: They slip away, cold in death

units.la: Lumina, purpureus quondam color ora relinquit; à novis veluti furiis istis ita torquentur cruciantúrque, ut valentes adhuc de agone ejusmodi nunquam sine horrore cogitare possint. Taceo quòd ii, qui sive inquilini, sive advenæ, Xenodochia & nosocomia subire coguntur, si lethalem in morbum inciderint, passim consolatoribus Evangelicis privantur, substitutis sacrificulis & Monachis, qui ad perverterndos miseros nullum non lapidem movent: quodque captivos & damnatos nonnisi summissa voce, quod surdastris nihil prodest, & in conclavi separato, quod non ubique vel conceditur, vel præsto est, consolari licet. Forte etiam huc referri potest edictum inhumanissimum, quo puerperis ne obstetrices alias quàm Pontificias adhibeant, interdicitur, cùm nec semper tales in promptu sint; & horrorem id ipsum imbelli sexui incutiat haud dubiè, & Baptismo mulierum viam muniat. niat; & alia post fe non minùs tristia & funesta trahat.
units.tr: The eyes, the purple colour once in the face, leaves it; by such new frenzies they are so tormented and racked that even those still in health can never think of such a struggle without horror. I say nothing of the fact that those who, whether as lodgers or as strangers, are compelled to enter hospitals and infirmaries, if they fall into a deadly illness, are everywhere deprived of evangelical comforters, with priests and monks substituted who leave no stone unturned to pervert the wretched; and that captives and condemned persons may be consoled only in a lowered voice, which profits the deaf nothing, and in a separate room, which is not everywhere either allowed or at hand. Perhaps the most inhuman edict may also be referred here, by which women in childbirth are forbidden to employ midwives other than Papist ones, since such women are not always at hand; and this will doubtless strike horror into the weaker sex, and will pave the way for the baptism of women, and will drag behind it other consequences no less sad and deadly.

units.la: CCCXXXI. De educatione liberorum quid dicam? Edicti quidem articulo decimo octavo generali prohibetur quibusvis liberorum ablatio, sive per vim, sive per inductionem, contra parentum voluntatem. Non hic commemoro, quòd impuberes castigationis paternæ impatientes, seducti profugíque, & ad Pontificia sacra illecti ita detinentur, ut parentes etiam sumptus iis alendis suppeditare cogantur: quódque liberis utroque parente orbis tutores nonnisi Pontificii dantur. Hoc verò omnes inhumanitatis, ne quid aliud dicam, numeros implet, quòd juxta edictum die XVII. Junii A. M. D. C. LXXXI. promulgatum liberis septennibus, adeóque infantiæ adhuc proximis, sacrificulorum examini subjectis optio data est, quam velint, religionem amplectendi; ea lege, ut si sacrificulorum blanditiis persuasi professionem religionis contrariæ qualemcunque ediderint, hæc eorum professio adeò habeatur rata, ut nulla ratione revocari vel retractari queat; nec à Parentibus, in quorum potestate liberi hujus inprimis ætatis versantur: nec à liberis ipsis, cùm adultiores facti pœnitentia ducuntur eorum, quæ in pueritia imprudentes & seducti egerunt. Sic parentes sua in liberos potestate spoliantur: pueris verò, quibus intellectus nullus vel exiguus est judicandi de rebus & negotiis vitam hanc præsentem concernentibus, 1. Cor. XIII. 11. nedum de rebus fidei, utpote quibus comparantur expertes notitiæ religionis, nec non inconstantes, & in ea fluctuantes 1. Cor. XIV. 20. Ephes. IV. 14. ea judicii tribuitur maturitas, quæ ad rem maximi momenti, electionem scilicet religionis ad salutem æternam unicè ducentis; ad quam sensus exercitati in scriptura, nec non potestas probandi spiritus, & quod bonum est, retinendi 1. Joh. IV. 1. 4. 1. Thess. V. 20. Hebr. V. 14. requiruntur, sufficiat. Cujusmodi judicium qui in septenni nato quærit, næ fructum is maturum in surculo quærit. Tametsi verò edictum isthoc omnium funestissimum, cum Edicti Nannetensis articulis variis, declaratione ipsius Regis A. M. D. C. LXIX. edita; jure naturali, quod minorennes parentum potestati & educationi subjicit; nec non civili, ecclesiastico & gentium omnium, Christianarum inprimis, è diametro pugnare, supplice libello Subditi & misericordiam & justitiam implorantes humiliter, demonstrarunt, hactenus tamen operam perdiderunt omnem, & edicto mortis ipsius sententia ferali tristiori cervicem submittere miseri coguntur.
units.tr: CCCXXXI. What shall I say about the upbringing of children? Indeed, article eighteen of the general Edict forbids to anyone the taking away of children, whether by force, or by enticement, against the wish of the parents. I do not mention here that minors, impatient of their father's correction, seduced and fleeing, and enticed to Papist rites, are so detained that the parents are even compelled to supply the money to support them; and that orphans, whose both parents are dead, are given guardians only if they are Papists. But this fills up all the measures of inhumanity, not to say anything else: that according to the edict published on 17 June 1681, children of seven years, and therefore still close to infancy, subjected to the examination of the priests, are given the choice of embracing whichever religion they wish, on this condition: that if, persuaded by the flatteries of the priests, they have made any profession of the contrary religion, this profession is held so valid that it can in no way be revoked or retracted, neither by the parents, in whose power children of this age especially are, nor by the children themselves, when, having grown older, they repent of what they did in boyhood through thoughtlessness and seduction. Thus parents are stripped of their power over their children; yet to boys, who have little or no understanding for judging matters and affairs concerning this present life (1 Cor. 13:11), much less matters of faith, since they are inexperienced in the knowledge of religion and also unstable, and wavering in it (1 Cor. 14:20; Eph. 4:14), is attributed that maturity of judgment which is needed for a matter of the greatest moment, namely the choice of a religion which alone leads to eternal salvation; for this the senses trained in Scripture, and also the power to test the spirits and to hold fast to what is good, are required (1 John 4:1, 4; 1 Thess. 5:20; Heb. 5:14) — let it suffice. Whoever seeks such judgment in a seven-year-old seeks ripe fruit on a young shoot.
