Although the subjects, in a humble petition, have shown with sorrow and in supplication, imploring both mercy and justice, that this edict, the most destructive of all, is in direct conflict with the various articles of the Edict of Nantes, with the declaration of the King himself published in 1669, with natural law, which subjects minors to parental power and upbringing, and also with civil, ecclesiastical and the law of all nations, especially Christian nations, nevertheless up to now they have labored in vain, and the wretched are compelled to submit their necks to the sadder sentence of death of the edict itself.

units.la: CCCXXXII. Quantopere publicum religionis exercitium labefactetur infringatúrque in dies, experientia tri- stis nimiùm proh dolor testatur.
units.tr: CCCXXXII. How greatly the public exercise of religion is weakened and undermined day by day, sad experience, alas, attests all too well.

units.la: Etenim Edicti Nannetensis articulo trigesimo quinto particulari definitum est, licere populum congregare pulsatis campanis, & exercere omnes actus & functiones pertinentes ad exercitium dictæ religionis, & ad regimen disciplinæ, cujusmodi sunt Consistoria, Colloquia, Synodi Provinciales & Nationales, cum permissu Regis. Articulo decimo sexto generali etiam facultas construendi Templa conceditur. Jus illud Edictum evidenter attribuit locis distinctis harum classium; primò illis, quæ possidebant publicum, aut possidere debebant A. M. D. LXXVII. articulo Generali decimo; Secundò illis, quæ possidebant exercitium constitutum & publicè peractum sæpius A. M. D. XCVI. & M. D. XCVII. articulo Generali nono; tertiò binis locis in quolibet distinctu seu Ballivatu, quæ petituri erunt Euangelici præter superiora, articulo generali undecimo, & particularibus sexto, septimo & octavo; quartò illis, quæ ad Nobiles aut Dominos Reformatos pertinentia plenum habent feudum & altæ justitiæ, articulo generali septimo. Quibus addi possunt domus illæ, quæ feuda minora sine alta justitia possident, ubi cœtus non potest esse plus quàm triginta hominum, præter familiam Domini, articulo generali octavo. Post conditum jam Edictum A. M. D. XCIX. Henricus Magnus in Provincias misit Delegatos seu Commissarios, Edicti executores, qui rebus juxta tenorem edicti compositis maxime providerent, ut in dictis locis exercitia collocarentur, quod in plerisque effectum est. Ex eo tempore omnia exercitia sua, fundamentis illis innixa in locis illis habuerunt, exceptis iis, quæ ex jure feudi seu altæ justitiæ per edictum novis Dominis instituere licuerat, & paucis etiam aliis, quæ primùm indubitatè institui debuerant, & de quibus etiamnum jure constabat; aut quæ ob singulares causas, velut inopiam sumptuum, & Pontificiorum eo in loco obstaculo, interrupta fuerant. Si quæ nova Templa constructa sunt, factum id est secundum tenorem Edicti iis in locis, quæ jus exercitii, aut jam ante etiam Templa habuerant. Atque exercitia ejusmodi per Commissarios, Edicti executores rebus maturè expensis constituta & approbata, vi legis ipsius perpetuæ & irrefragabilis judicata merito ejusmodi sunt, ut nullo tempore revocari & aboleri possint.
units.tr: Indeed, article thirty-five of the Edict of Nantes specifically provides that the people may assemble with the bells rung, and carry on all the acts and functions pertaining to the exercise of that religion and to the governance of its discipline, such as consistories, colloquies, and provincial and national synods, with the King's permission. Article sixteen of the general articles also grants the right of building churches. The Edict clearly assigns that right to particular classes of places: first, to those which possessed, or ought to have possessed, public exercise in the year 1577, by general article ten; secondly, to those which had an established exercise, carried on publicly, in the years 1596 and 1597, by general article nine; thirdly, to two places in each district or bailiwick, which the Evangelicals may seek in addition to the above, by general article eleven and particular articles six, seven and eight; fourthly, to those which belong to nobles or lords of the Reformed faith and have full fief and high justice, by general article seven. To these may be added those houses which hold lesser fiefs without high justice, where the gathering may not be more than thirty persons, not counting the lord's household, by general article eight. After the Edict had been issued in 1599, Henry the Great sent into the provinces delegates or commissioners, executors of the Edict, whose task was chiefly to see, with matters arranged according to the terms of the Edict, that the exercises were established in the said places, which was largely accomplished. From that time all their exercises have rested on those foundations in those places, except those which the Edict had allowed new lords to establish by right of fief or high justice, and a few others which should undoubtedly have been established at first, and whose right is still certain, or which had been interrupted for particular reasons, such as lack of funds, or the obstruction of the Papists in that place. If any new churches have been built, this has been done, according to the terms of the Edict, in those places which already had the right of exercise or even earlier had churches. And such exercises, established and approved by the commissioners, executors of the Edict, after matters had been carefully weighed, have by the force of that law been judged, as is right, perpetual and irrefutable, so that they can at no time be revoked or abolished.

units.la: CCCXXXIII. Hic verò, si uspiam alibi, vires odiúmque suum erga Reformatos Pontificio Clero periclitari placuit. Postquam enim hinc inde varia exercitia & Templa aggressi sunt, & nonnulla etiam, infirmioribus ob magnitudinem impensarum infinitásque litium ambages succumbentibus, everterunt; nova etiam Edicta, religioni Reformatæ πανολεθεία minitantia, Regi extorserunt. Etenim non tantùm XXII. Febr. A. M. D. C. LXIV. edicta edita varia sunt, quibus Pastoribus, ne extra locum residentiæ & in annexis Ecclesiis, quarum tantus numerus erat, ut alicubi Ecclesiarum Principalium numerum superaverint, concionarentur amplius, prohibitum est; Nobilibúsque insuper, aut habentibus feuda altæ justitiæ exercitium publicum in locis de dominio Regis emptis sublatum est: verùm insuper etiam missis in Provincias Commissariis, in speciem Edicti Nannetensis, in gratiam etiam & favorem Reformatorum executoribus futuris, omniáque ad Edicti normam revocaturis, (unde Reformati certam malorum, quæ patiebantur, ob erepta hinc inde exercitia, medelam sperabant) ita delusi iidem & artificiosissimis technis circumscripti sunt, ut ingentem exercitiorum Templorumque plurimorum jacturam intra tempus brevissimum fecerint, faciántque adhuc. Munus isthoc Edictum Nannetense exequendi datum est, Intendenti cuipiam Provinciarum, Viro præcipuæ authoritatis, exploratæque in rebus gerendis dexteritatis, qui ascito in speciem comite homine Reformato vel obnoxio, vel nullatenus cum Intendente comparando; Provinciam obivit, Euangelicas Ecclesias sine discrimine omnes, adeóque eas etiam, quarum exercitia Edicti tempore per Regios, uti diximus, Commissarios dijudicata, ritéque constituta fuerant, jura exercitii sui idoneis documentis demonstrare jussit. Et probationes quidem olim facilimæ evaserunt difficiles, imo alicubi post tanti temporis lapsum impossibiles; præsertim quia prima illa exercitiorum per commissarios constitutio semel solenniter facta posthac sutura plane immota & inconcussa credita est; & documenta etiam plurima per incendia, nec non religionis mutationem in familiis, quæ illa asservabant, urbium expugnationes, fraudes varias, aliósque casus, perierant. Ibi igitur arbitrio Intendentis Templa clausa, exercitia abolita sunt. Si quæ probationes supererant, ex Seniorum, etiam Pontificiorum testimoniis de possessione A.M.D.XCVI. & M.D.XCVII. collectæ, per edictum Regium A.M.D.C.LXII. rejectæ simpliciter sunt. Reliquæ probationes ex Codicibus Notariorum, libris Baptismatum, Consistoriorum, aliisque scripturis depromptæ plerunque etiam, ceu minùs nùs validæ neglectæ; quin & ipsa priscorum commiflariorum acta, fi qua etiamnum in promptu erant, parvi habita, & quandoque etiam planè spreta sunt. Aderat Intendenti perpetuusferè consultor & instigator Jesuita recoctæ fraudis Meinerius, qui stipendio ejus rei causa accepto varias Provincias circumivit, judiciisque interfuit. Ita, procedentibus Commissariorum judiciis, factum est, ut intra breve tempus Exercitia irrefragabili jure nixa, abolita sint incredibili numero; templa destructa plurima pulcherimáque, operi instantibus, manúsque admoventibus etiam clericis Romanis, cum infinitis contumeliis & violentiis, & sumptus ingentes imponentibus iis, qui ipsimet Templa sua destruere abnuissent. Quamobrem etiam clerus Gallicanus Lutetiæ novissimæ congregatus Regi amplissimas gratias, quòd ejus auspiciis innumera multitudo Templorum Reformatorum cultui hactenus inservientium destructa solóque adæquata sint, professus fertur.
units.tr: CCCXXXIII. Here, if anywhere else, the Papist clergy have chosen to test their strength and their hatred against the Reformed. For after they had attacked various exercises and churches on every side, and had overthrown some, the weaker ones yielding to the size of the expenses and the endless windings of lawsuits, they also extorted from the King new edicts threatening total destruction [πανολεθεία] to the Reformed religion. For not only were various edicts issued on 22 February 1664, by which the ministers were forbidden to preach outside their place of residence and in the annexed churches, which were so numerous that in some places they exceeded the number of principal churches; and the public exercise was also removed from nobles or from those holding fiefs of high justice in places purchased from the King's domain. Moreover, the commissioners were sent into the provinces, in the guise of the Edict of Nantes and as a favour and kindness to the Reformed, with executors to come who would restore everything to the standard of the Edict (whereby the Reformed hoped for a sure remedy for the evils they were suffering, since their exercises had been snatched away on every side). Yet they were so deceived and entangled by the most artful tricks that in a very short time they have brought about, and are still bringing about, a huge loss of exercises and of very many churches. This office of executing the Edict of Nantes was given to a certain Intendant of the provinces, a man of outstanding authority and proven skill in managing affairs, who, taking with him in appearance a Reformed companion, either dependent on him or in no way equal to the Intendant, went through the province and ordered all the Evangelical churches, without distinction, and especially those whose exercises had been judged and duly established at the time of the Edict by the King's commissioners, as we have said, to demonstrate the rights of their exercise by suitable documents. And indeed the proofs, once very easy, became difficult, and in some places, after so long a lapse of time, impossible; especially because that first establishment of the exercises by the commissioners, once solemnly made, was believed thereafter to stand wholly unmoved and unshaken; and many documents had perished through fires, through the change of religion in the families which kept them, through the capture of towns, through various frauds, and other accidents. Therefore, at the Intendant's will, the churches were closed and the exercises abolished there. Whatever proofs remained, gathered from the testimony of elders, even Papists, concerning possession in 1596 and 1597, were simply rejected by the royal edict of 1662. The remaining proofs, drawn from the registers of notaries, the books of baptisms, of consistories, and other records, were for the most part neglected as less than valid; indeed the very acts of the earlier commissioners, where any were still at hand, were held of little account and sometimes even utterly scorned. The Intendant had almost constantly at his side as adviser and instigator a Jesuit, Meinier, a man of revived fraud, who, having received a salary for this purpose, went round the various provinces and took part in the judgements. Thus, as the commissioners' judgements proceeded, it came about that within a short time exercises resting on an irrefutable right were abolished in incredible numbers; very many fine churches were destroyed, with Roman clerics pressing the work on and laying hands to it too, with endless insults and violence, and imposing huge expenses on those who had refused to tear down their own churches. For this reason the Gallican clergy, assembled lately at Paris, is also reported to have professed the most ample thanks to the King, because under his auspices an innumerable multitude of Reformed churches serving worship until now has been destroyed and levelled to the ground.

units.la: CCCXXXIV. Taceo vexationes & pericula mille Pastorum in Ecclesiis adhuc superstitibus eorum inprimis, qui spiritu Dei fervent; qui tot recentibus edictis constricti, sicubi adversus illa vel revera prudentes imprudentésve, vel falsa delatione hostium impegerint; si à subornatis concionum auditoribus, plerunque rudibus & malitiosis, rectè piéque dicta maligné interpretantibus, & falsa etiam fingentibus, pro Reformata religione adversus Pontificiam aliquid dixisse liberius accusati fuerint, hinc inde in vincula rapti, grandibus multis pecuniariis afficiuntur, palinodiam probrosam canere judicibus coram coguntur, aliquando à carnificibus etiam raptantur, bonis fisco addictis universæ Galliæ finibus exterminantur.
units.tr: CCCXXXIV. I pass over the vexations and a thousand dangers that the ministers suffer in the churches still standing, especially those who burn with the Spirit of God; hemmed in by so many recent edicts, whenever they have stumbled against them, whether truly prudent or imprudent, or through false information from enemies, if they have been accused of having said something rather freely in favour of the Reformed religion against the Papist one, because hearers of their sermons, bribed, usually rough and malicious, have twisted what was rightly and piously said into evil meaning and have even invented falsehoods, they are seized and thrown into chains, are fined heavily, are compelled before the judges to sing a shameful palinode, are sometimes even dragged off by the executioners, and, with their goods surrendered to the treasury, are banished from all the borders of France.

units.la: CCCXXXV. Jam & Scholis, ex quibus viri pii, docti, periti, verbo & opere potentes; universi etiam gnari sermonis justitiæ prodire sueverunt, evertendis unicè clecleri studia infudárunt. Statutum equidem est Edicti articulo generali decimo tertio, & speciali trigesimo octavo, ut Reformatis iis locis, quibus exercitium publicum permittitur, fas sit habere Scholas publicas, & exercere actus instructionis publicæ puerorum in eo, quod religionem concernit. Contra novitiis edictis, cleri violentia extortis, non aliæ in locis exercitii publici Scholæ permittuntur, quàm eæ, in quibus doceantur tantùm legere, scribere & arithmeticam. quasi indigni essent, qui in Grammatica, humanioribus literis, aut ritè colendi Dei studiis exercerentur. Ne quod autem malo præsentissimo remedium privata institutione quæri possit, vix privatis præceptoribus familias frequentare licet: Scripturam & arithmeticam profitentibus per Edicta Parlamentorum, præsertim Rhotomagensis, magisterium artis denegatur; Pastoribus quinetiam, ne plures quàm duos commensales & discipulos alant, interdicitur. Denique novissimo edicto sancitum, ut in locis iis, quibus religionis adhuc exercitium viget, præceptor seu Ludimagister unicus toleretur; cùm pluribus locis juventus adeò frequens sit, ut ei instituendæ vix sex sufficiant. Edicti scopus haud dubiè est, ut Pontificias scholas reliqui frequentare, non sine manifesto seductionis ad Papatum, Monasticos inprimis ordines ætate nec dum matura subeundos, periculo subigantur. Nihil dicam de Scholis & Academiis celeberrimis, ex quibus ceu Trojano equo, γνήσιοι Apollines prodierunt hactenus, quæ vel clausæ planè, imò & hostibus Euangelici nominis traditæ, vel cum aliis etiam obscuris permutatæ sunt.
units.tr: CCCXXXV. Now too they have poured their efforts into the complete overthrow of the schools, from which pious, learned and skilled men have been accustomed to come forth, powerful in word and deed, and all men knowledgeable in the word of justice. It is indeed laid down in article thirteen of the general articles and article thirty-eight of the particular articles of the Edict that in those places where public exercise is permitted to the Reformed, it shall be lawful to have public schools and to carry on public instruction of children in what concerns religion. On the contrary, by edicts wrung out by clerical violence, in places of public exercise no schools are permitted other than those in which they teach only reading, writing and arithmetic, as if men were unworthy to be trained in grammar, the humane letters, or the studies of worshipping God rightly. Lest, moreover, a remedy for this most pressing evil might be sought in private instruction, it is scarcely permitted for households to attend private tutors: by the edicts of the Parlements, especially that of Rouen, the teaching of the art of writing and arithmetic is denied to those professing it; and it is even forbidden to ministers to maintain more than two boarders and pupils. Finally, a most recent edict has decreed that in those places where the exercise of religion still flourishes, only one teacher or schoolmaster is to be tolerated, although in many places the young are so numerous that barely six could suffice to teach them. The aim of the edict is undoubtedly that the rest, not without manifest danger of seduction to Papacy, should be compelled to attend the Papist schools, especially the monastic orders, which they are to enter before they are of mature age. I say nothing of the most celebrated schools and academies, from which, like the Trojan horse, genuine Apollos [γνήσιοι] have hitherto come forth; these have either been wholly closed, or even handed over to the enemies of the Evangelical name, or have been exchanged for other obscure ones.

units.la: CCCXXXVI. Sine disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ exercitio externus religionis cultus ferè frigere solet.
units.tr: CCCXXXVI. Without the exercise of ecclesiastical discipline, the external worship of religion tends to grow cold.

units.la: Cautum proin est Edicti articulo particulari tricesimo quinto, licere Reformatis facere omnes actus pertinentes ad regimen disciplinæ (cuius scilicet corpus pluribus ante edictum annis compositum, longáque praxi confirmatum Rex noverat) veluti, habere consistoria, colloquia, Synodos Provinciales & Nationales, Regis permissu; in locis, ubi exercitium permittitur. Recentioribus contra edictis exercitii disciplinæ nervus non parum equidem solutus atque incisus est. Non tantum enim colloquiorum sive classium, quæ quotannis celebrari, & in quibus urgentiora negotia per paucos expediri, continua septuaginta annorum praxi, fuerant, celebrationes interdictæ sunt, præterquam durantibus Synodis; quo tempore ne quidem institui possunt, cùm Delegatus Regius, qui unicus est, simul Synodo, simul Colloquiis septem vel octo interesse non potest; absente verò eodem nec Synodi, nec Colloquia celebrari valeant: sed etiam correspondentias cum aliis Provinciis habere, etiam occasione appellationum ab aliis Synodis; aut in Synodorum interstitio de ulla re deliberare per literas circulares, aliove modo; aut recipere Candidatos; aut delegationes curandis negotiis mandare, prohibitum est. Ita enim impeditur convocatio Synodorum, quæ nisi per literas circulares fieri nequit; & judicium de rebus ecclesiasticis, circa quas provocatio est; utpote quod differre jubentur ad Synodum usque Nationalem, hoc est, in duodecimum, vel decimum quintum etiam annum usque, cùm tamen tertio quoque anno ex disciplina celebrari debuerit. Non aliò hæc tendunt, quàm ut per scandala & ἀταξίας perpetuas Ecclesiæ destruantur. Denique libertas etiam Synodorum, Regiis Commissariis, juxta edictum novissimum, duobus in illis comparentibus, & arcanissima quæque rimantibus, exquisitáque indagine cingentibus, tantùm non pessumdata jacet.
units.tr: Accordingly, it was provided in the particular article thirty-five of the Edict that the Reformed may perform all acts pertaining to the government of discipline (the King was of course aware of the body of it, drawn up many years before the Edict and confirmed by long practice), such as to hold consistories, colloquies, and provincial and national synods, with the King's permission, in places where the exercise is permitted. By the more recent edicts, however, the sinews of the exercise of discipline have been not a little loosened and cut. For not only have the celebrations of colloquies or classes, which were held every year and in which more urgent business was settled by a few men, as in a continuous practice of seventy years, been forbidden, except while synods are in session; and at that time they cannot even be convened, since the Royal Delegate, who is the only one, cannot attend a synod and seven or eight colloquies at the same time; and if he is absent, neither synods nor colloquies can be held. Moreover, it is forbidden to keep correspondence with other provinces, even on the occasion of appeals from other synods; or to deliberate on any matter by circular letters or in any other way between synods; or to receive candidates; or to entrust business to delegations. Thus the convocation of synods is impeded, since it cannot be done except by circular letters; and judgment on ecclesiastical matters that are under appeal is hindered, since they are ordered to be deferred until the National Synod, that is, to the twelfth or even the fifteenth year, although by discipline a synod ought to be held at least every third year. These measures aim at nothing else than the destruction of the Church through scandals and perpetual disorder [ἀταξίας]. Finally, the freedom of the synods too, under the newest edict, lies all but ruined: two Royal Commissaries attend them, pry into all their most secret matters, and surround them with close and searching inquiry.

units.la: CCCXXXVII. Unicum innocentiæ afflictorum, post Deum & Regem, Reformatis in Gallia præsidium positum erat hactenus in Tribunalibus Camerarum edicti, in gratiam eorundem ad vitæ bonorúmque securitatem, ab Camerarum Edicti infus.
units.tr: CCCXXXVII. Hitherto the sole safeguard for the innocence of the afflicted Reformed in France, after God and the King, had been the tribunals of the Chambers of the Edict, established for their benefit, for the security of their lives and goods, by the Chambers of the Edict.

units.la: ab Henrico Principe Optimo & justissimo erecta. Providerat is, experiundo etiam & rebus ipsis hactenus edoctus, injustitiam ubique regnaturam, neque finem modumque futurum querelarum & contentionum in Regno, si pars debilior fortiori, religionis odio flagranti, justitiamque & leges pensi non habiturae, hoc est, Reformati judicum mere Pontificiorum tribunalibus subjicerentur. Summum igitur a Deo in Regno suo justitiae Sacerdotem cum se constitutum agnosceret merito, ut justitia tribuatur & administretur subditis sine ulla suspicione, odio & favore, cum hoc perspexerit esse ex praecipuis remediis ad eos in pace & concordia tuendos; constituit Cameras Edicti, seu, Edictales; tres quidem bipertitas Gratianopoli, Castris & Burdegalae, in quibus Pontificii & Reformati judices aequali numero judicarent; duas vero Parisiis & Rhotomagi, in quibus tamen unus duntaxat sedebat judex Reformatus, licet in istis etiam aequalis judicum numerus promissus, ast ecclesiasticorum astu praestitus non fuerit. De Rhotomagensi Camera Edicti articulo generali trigesimo; de caeteris trigesimo primo, secundo, tertio, &c. legere est. Articulo tricesimo quarto sic jurisdictio judicum illorum definitur: Cognoscent & judicabunt supremo judicio & ultimo per arresta, aliis omnibus exclusis, omnes lites & controversias motas & movendas, in quibus Pontificii & Reformati erunt partes principales, aut fideiussores, actores sive rei, in omnibus materiis sive civilibus sive criminalibus. paucis casibus, qui ibi exprimuntur, exceptis. Articulo quinquagesimo secundo jurisdictio illa extenditur ad ea omnia, quae pertinent ad executionem Edictorum, quando praedicti erunt partes. Articulo sexagesimo quarto: Inhibemus & interdicimus omnibus curiis nostris supremis, & aliis hujus Regni, ne cognoscant & judicent lites civiles & criminales illorum praedictae religionis, quarum cognitio attribuitur per nostrum edictum cameris.
units.tr: by Henry, the most good and most just Prince. He had foreseen, and had also learned from experience and from the facts themselves, that injustice would reign everywhere, and that there would be no end or limit to complaints and disputes in the kingdom, if the weaker party were subjected to the stronger, burning with hatred of religion and not regarding justice and the laws, that is, if the Reformed were subjected to the courts of judges who were purely Papists. Therefore, recognizing that he himself had been constituted by God in his kingdom as the highest priest of justice, and wishing justice to be rendered and administered to his subjects without any suspicion, hatred or favour, he judged this to be one of the principal remedies for keeping them in peace and concord; he established the Chambers of the Edict, or Edictal Chambers: three of them divided into two parts, at Grenoble, Castres and Bordeaux, in which Papist and Reformed judges would sit in equal numbers; and two at Paris and Rouen, in which, however, only one Reformed judge sat, although an equal number of judges had been promised in these too, a promise which the cunning of the churchmen did not fulfil. Concerning the Rouen Chamber of the Edict, see the general article thirty; concerning the others, read articles thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, and so on. By article thirty-four the jurisdiction of those judges is defined thus: They shall take cognizance of and judge, by final sentence and as the supreme judgment, to the exclusion of all others, all suits and controversies, past and future, in which Papists and Reformed are principal parties, whether as sureties, plaintiffs or defendants, in all matters, whether civil or criminal, with the few exceptions named there. By article fifty-two that jurisdiction is extended to all those things which pertain to the execution of the Edicts, when the aforesaid are parties. By article sixty-four: We forbid and prohibit all our supreme courts, and others of this kingdom, from taking cognizance of and judging civil and criminal suits of those of the aforesaid religion, the cognizance of which is assigned by our edict to the Chambers.

units.la: CCCXXXVIII. Tam potens verò Clerus Roma- nensis fuit, ut sacrum etiam isthoc justitiæ intemeratæ pal- ladium paulatim concuteret, tandémque etiam penitus subverteret.
units.tr: CCCXXXVIII. So powerful, moreover, was the Roman clergy that they gradually shook this sacred palladium of unspotted justice, and at last utterly overthrew it.

units.la: Et primùm quidem edicto 2. April. A. M. D. C. LXVI. lato statutum est, ut omnes, qui accusantur criminis Relapsus, apostasiæ (hoc est, transitus Ecclesiasticorum ad Evangelicos) aut blasphemiarum & impietatum in mysteria religionis Catholicæ prolatarum, per unumquodque Parlamentum in districtu suo judicentur. Ita relapsi, à Papatu ad Euangelicos conversi, & liberius de Pontificiæ Religionis mysteriis prolocuti, Cameris Edicti subtracti, & Parlamentorum, in quibus Pontificii Judices rerum potiuntur, judiciis obnoxii redditi, adeóque in præsentissimum vitæ ac fortunarum omnium discrimen adducti sunt. Prostant exempla horrendarum poenarum à Parlamentis ejusmodi, Reformatis innocentibus inflictarum. Sed fuerunt hæ ἀρχαὶ τῶν ὠδίνων. Mox enim A. M. D. C. LXVIII. Camerae Edictales Parisienses & Rhotomagenses; ac novissimè etiam Bipartitæ reliquæ in universum suppressæ, Reformatíque adeò omnes in controversiis qualibuscunque cum Pontificiis sibi intercedentibus, judicum infensissimorum tribunalibus, ceu libidinis & odii illorum piaculares victimæ, miserandum in modum subjecti sunt. Quæ mala inde innocentissimorum quorumque cervicibus impositerum etiam impendeant, non sine horrore cogitari potest.
units.tr: And first, by the edict of 2 April 1666, it was enacted "that all who are accused of the crime of relapse, of apostasy (that is, of the passage of ecclesiastics to the Evangelicals), or of blasphemies and impieties uttered against the mysteries of the Catholic religion, shall be tried by each Parlement within its own district." Thus relapsed persons, converted from Popery to the Evangelicals and speaking more freely about the mysteries of the Papist religion, were withdrawn from the Chambers of the Edict and made liable to the judgments of the Parlements, in which Papist judges hold power, and so were brought into the most immediate danger of their lives and all their fortunes. There are examples of the dreadful punishments inflicted by such Parlements on innocent Reformed people. But these were the beginnings of the birth pangs [ἀρχαὶ τῶν ὠδίνων]. For soon, in 1668, the Edict Chambers of Paris and Rouen, and most recently also the remaining mixed chambers, were entirely suppressed, and all the Reformed were thus subjected, in every dispute that arose between them and the Papists, to the tribunals of most hostile judges, like sacrificial victims of their lust and hatred, in a pitiable manner. What evils from this may yet hang over the necks of the most innocent people can hardly be thought of without horror.

units.la: CCCXXXIX. Denique Edicto eodem Reformati ad pares cum Pontificiis prærogativas admissi sunt.
units.tr: CCCXXXIX. Finally, by the same Edict, the Reformed were admitted to the same prerogatives as the Papists.

units.la: Articulo quippe vicesimo septimo declarantur capaces ad exercendum & tenendum omnes status, dignitates, officia & quævis munera publica, Regia, dominica, aut urbium Regni, &c. non obstantibus omnibus juramentis in contrarium, atque promiscuè ad illa admittuntur. Item vacantibus muneribus providebitur per nos de personis idoneis, sine distinctione & indifferenter. cùm id faciat ad unionem subditorum nostrorum. Item admittentur ad omnia consilia, functiones, &c. nec ob eorum religionem inde arcebuntur. Reformatos vero muneribus publicis defunctos hodie passim exauthorari, & eo aspirantes removeri, perinde ac si honoribus & procurationibus publicis nunc demum indigni esse coepissent; satis constat. Sed majus est, quod recentioribus declarationibus & edictis vis illa antiqui, quod perpetuum, irrevocabile esse debuerat, etiam heic resolvitur. utpote quarum vi Senioribus Magistratibus Reformatis praesidentia, ingressus ordinum Provinciae & coetuum, qui ad tributorum impositionem fiunt, quo sic prae reliquis impositionibus obrui possint; munera municipalia unica, veluti graphiariorum, Curatorum, horologii, imo & Janitorum; nec non Procuratorum, Notariorum, apparitorum, advocatorum, &c. sublata sunt. Induistriis porro media rem familiarem augendi eripiuntur, divites exhauriuntur, opificia artesque aliae seu liberales seu illiberales iis vel abrogantur, vel affliguntur, pauperes ad desperationem adiguntur, litigantes in foro judicem minus faventem & aequum experiuntur. Eo denique perventum, ut recentiori seu edicto seu declaratione constitutum sit, ut conversi ad religionem Pontificiam immunes sint a solvendis debitis Reformatorum, e quorum scilicet numero erant eo tempore, quo debita contracta sunt.
units.tr: In Article 27 they are declared capable of exercising and holding all estates, dignities, offices and any public functions, royal, seigniorial, or of the cities of the Kingdom, etc., notwithstanding all oaths to the contrary, and they are admitted to them indiscriminately. Likewise, when offices fall vacant, provision will be made by us for suitable persons, without distinction and without partiality, since this serves the union of our subjects. They shall also be admitted to all councils, functions, etc., and shall not be excluded from them on account of their religion. It is well established, however, that the Reformed who have held public office are now everywhere being dismissed, and those aspiring to it are being removed, just as if they had only now begun to be unworthy of public honours and offices. But what is worse is that by the more recent declarations and edicts that force of the earlier law, which ought to have been perpetual and irrevocable, is also here annulled. By their power the Reformed senior magistrates have been deprived of the presidency, of entry into the provincial assemblies and of the gatherings that meet to impose taxes, so that they may be overwhelmed by these impositions beyond the others. The single municipal offices, such as those of registrars, curators, clock-keepers, and even the janitors, as well as those of attorneys, notaries, officers, advocates, etc., have been abolished. Moreover, the means of increasing their household wealth by trade are being taken from them; the wealthy are drained; their manufactures and other arts, whether liberal or mechanical, are either abolished or harassed; the poor are driven to despair; and litigants find in court a judge less favourable and less fair. At last it has come to this, that by a recent edict or declaration it has been decreed that those converted to the Papist religion are exempt from paying the debts of the Reformed, to whose number they belonged at the time when the debts were contracted.

units.la: CCCXL.
units.tr: CCCXL.

units.la: Neque vero recentiorum sive edictorum, sive declarationum afflictionumque finis vel modus ullus est. Quin potius unda undam trudit, & abyssus abyssum invocat. Laborantque quotidie exquisitissima ingenia in comminiscendis novis artibus, quibus miseri καταςοφιζεσθε, circumveniri, irretiri, & edictorum declarationumque talium numero (intra triennium enim proxime exactum plusquam triginta emanarunt) atque mole ita confusi & & distracti, ut parere junctim omnibus & singulis, vel ob solius memoriæ infirmitatem & defectum, pœnè impossibile sit; in exitii nassam pertrahi valeant. Atque dum ita male habentur, nefas iis est, quiritari, quòd persecutionem ullam patiantur. Expresso enim edicto cautum est, ut persecutionis nomine abstineant. Quin & recentiora illa edicta nonnisi declarationum edicti ad casus singulares decidendos nomine venditantur. Salvóque Nannetensi edicto cuncta isthæc adversus Protestantes in Gallia attentari, publicis etiam scriptis authores nonnulli, Bernardus cumprimis & Filleau, Nannetensis Edicti famosi interpretes, persuadere conati sunt. Quanquam non desunt, qui assa voce profiteantur, edictis recentioribus Nannetense & violari, & jure violari. Constat tamen, sceleris, maleficii vel perfidiæ erga Regem, cujus merito pacta, Edicta perpetua, irrevocabilia rescindi jure, atque illi gratia Regis sui excidere debuerint, nullius compertos unquam esse, adeóque pati illos non ut latrones, fures, maleficos, sed ut Christianos, ob solam religionem, quam ex Dei verbo adversus Ecclesiæ Romanæ corruptelas Sole meridiano clariùs probatas, ὡς ἐξ εἰλικρινείας tanquam ex Deo, coram Deo, & in Christo (2. Cor. 11.17.) constanter profitentur. In fidelitate certè & obedientia Regi debita adeò non subditis Pontificiis cedunt, ut eos etiam superaverint hactenus, superéntque, saltem secundùm sanctæ religionis suæ placita, quibus post Deum ad unius soliúsque Regis, ceu legitimi Magistratus sui unici obedientiam, Imperium qualecunque aliud in Imperio illo agnoscentes nullum, obstringuntur. Quinimò de intemerata illorum erga Regem fide, ipsius etiam Regis Christianissimi testimonio omni exceptione majori, sœpiúsque, puta d. xxi. Maii A. m. d. c. liii. nec non i. Jun. A. m. d. c. lv. Epistola ad Ducem Dignierium, & xxx. Nov. A. m. d. c. lx. literis ad Synodum Nationalem Julioduni sedentem exaratis, repetito abundè li-
units.tr: Yet there is neither end nor limit to these recent edicts, declarations, and afflictions. Indeed, wave follows wave, and deep calls to deep. Every day the most ingenious minds labour to devise new arts by which the wretched people may be deceived [καταςοφιζεσθε], entangled and ensnared; and so confused and distracted by the number of such edicts and declarations (for within the last three years more than thirty have been issued) and by their sheer mass, that it is almost impossible to obey them all, both individually and collectively, even apart from the weakness and failing of memory, they may be dragged into the net of destruction. And while they are treated so badly, it is wrong for them to complain that they suffer any persecution. For the express edict provides that they must refrain from the name of persecution. Indeed, those more recent edicts are advertised only under the name of declarations of the edict, for deciding individual cases. While the Edict of Nantes is left intact, some authors have tried by public writings to persuade us that all these measures are being attempted against the Protestants in France; Bernard above all, and Filleau, the notorious interpreters of the Edict of Nantes. Yet there are not wanting those who openly profess that the Edict of Nantes is violated by the more recent edicts, and that it is rightly violated. It is nonetheless established that no crime, wrongdoing or treachery against the King has ever been found in them, by which their perpetual and irrevocable agreements, deservedly, might have been rightly rescinded and they might have fallen from the favour of their King. Therefore they suffer not as robbers, thieves or criminals, but as Christians, solely for the religion which they constantly profess [ὡς ἐξ εἰλικρινείας], as from God, before God, and in Christ (2 Cor. 11.17), a religion proved from the Word of God against the corruptions of the Roman Church more clearly than the midday sun. In loyalty and obedience due to the King, they are so far from yielding to the Papist subjects that they have hitherto surpassed them, and still do, at least according to the precepts of their holy religion, by which, after God, they are bound to obey the one and only King as their lawful magistrate, acknowledging no other sovereignty whatever in that realm. Moreover, the innocence of the afflicted and the oppressed is made plain by the testimony of the Most Christian King himself, beyond all exception, and especially by his letter to Duke Dignierius dated 21 May 1653, and by his letter of 1 June 1655, and by his letter of 30 November 1660, written to the National Synod sitting at Jouy, which repeated these things abundantly and in full;

units.la: & pressorum oppressorumque innocentia, liquet. In mediis etiam afflictionum procellis hactenus, quæ singularis Dei erga illos gratia est, contra stimulum non calcitrárunt; quin potius in obedientia, erga Regem continuè perstantes, atque in silentio & spe unicè robur suum collocantes, animum suum fiducia erga Deum, humilitate & patientia corroborant, cum populo Dei ingeminantes Mich. VII. 7. I. &c. Ego ad Jehovam respiciam, Expectabo Deum salutis meæ. Audiet me Deus meus. Ne lætteris, inimica mea, propter me, quòd ceciderim. Surgam. Cùm sedero in tenebris, Jehova lux mea erit. Indignationem Jehovæ feram, quoniam peccavi, donec judicet causam meam, & faciat judicium meum. Educet me in lucem meam, videbo justitiam ejus.
units.tr: and the innocence of the oppressed and of those who are oppressed is clear. Even in the midst of the storms of affliction up to now, which is the singular grace of God towards them, they have not kicked against the goad; rather, remaining steadfast in obedience to the King, and placing their strength solely in silence and hope, they strengthen their spirit by trust in God, humility and patience, repeating with the people of God (Micah 7:7–9): As for me, I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me. Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me. I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned, until he plead my cause, and execute judgment for me: he will bring me forth to the light, and I shall behold his righteousness.

units.la: CCCXLI. Raró Protestantibus in Gallia contentiones Regem inter & Pontificem obortas profuisse, & experientia dubitare non sinit, & diserté Historicus Gallus percelebris Mezerayus in vita Henrici II. observavit. Id ipsum hic quoque accidit. Vetus intercessit Regibus Galliæ cum Romanis Pontificibus controversia de Investituris, quæ, prout cum consensu Regum definitæ fuerunt in Conciliis Claromontano & Rhemensi, & à Callisto II. Papa A. M. C. XXII. ipsóque etiam usu post tempora ejusdem Pontificis explicatæ sunt, Regaliæ nuncupatæ sunt, quòd earum jus merè Regium, inter nobiliores Regiæ dignitatis partes ita recensetur, ut cùm soli Regi competat, cum nemine alio communicari possit, exclusis etiam ab eo jure iis, penes quos sub Rege puero administrandæ Reip. cura est. qui Regentes Regni nominari solent. In eo autem jus illud consistit, quòd vacante Episcopatu, ad investituram usque novi Episcopi, Regi & usus fructus Episcopalium reddituum, & collatio præbendarum cedit. quod jus demum A. M. CC. LXXIV. in Concilio Generali Lugdunensi à Gregorio X. convocato confirmatum est in iis scilicet Galliæ Ecclesiis, quibus consuetudo illa hactenus recepta erat. Tametsi vero Regum illorum, qui primi leges in hac Regalium materia condiderunt ad fori usum accommodatas, Constitutiones jus illud coercuerunt ad Ecclesias, in quibus usu veteri receptum erat Regem eo uti; & in Camera etiam Computorum Pasquierio Disquisit.Franc. lib.III. 37. citante, extat vetus Regestum, in quo enumerantur Ecclesiæ juri huic Regaliæ subjectæ, itémque Ecclesiæ, in quibus Reges eo jure non utebantur: ante trecentos tamen annos Johannes Butillerius in sua Summa Rurali, jus Regalium esse jus merè Regium, & ad Coronam pertinere, atque adeò ad universas Regni Ecclesias absque discrimine porrigendum esse, pertendit. Quin & Arresto Parlamenti Parisiensis A. M. D. C. VIII. edictum est, ne Advocati in dubium revocent, an Rex jure Regaliæ uti possit in universis Regni Ecclesiis. adversus arrestum illud querelam mox Clero Gallicano apud Regiam Majestatem instituente.
units.tr: CCCXLI. Experience does not allow us to doubt that conflicts arising between the King of France and the Roman Pontiff have rarely benefited the Protestants in France, and the very famous French historian Mézeray has observed this plainly in his life of Henry II. The same thing happens here too. There was an old controversy between the Kings of France and the Roman Pontiffs concerning Investitures; as it was settled with the consent of the Kings in the Councils of Clermont and Reims, and was explained by Pope Callixtus II in the year 1122, and also by usage after the times of that Pontiff, the Regalia were so called because their right is purely royal. Among the more noble parts of the royal dignity it is reckoned so that, since it belongs to the King alone and cannot be shared with anyone else, those are also excluded from that right to whom under a boy-king the care of administering the realm is entrusted, who are usually called Regents of the Kingdom. This right consists in this: when a bishopric is vacant, the revenues of the bishopric, and the conferral of prebends, pass to the King until the investiture of the new bishop. This right was finally confirmed in the year 1274 by Gregory X in the General Council of Lyons which he convened, namely for those churches of France in which that custom had hitherto been received. Although the Constitutions of those Kings who first drew up laws on the Regalia, adapted to the use of the court, restricted that right to the churches in which by ancient usage it had been received that the King should use it; and although, as Pasquier cites from the Chamber of Accounts in his Disquisitiones Francicae, book 3, chapter 37, there exists an old register listing the churches subject to this right of the Regalia, and also the churches in which the Kings did not use that right; yet three hundred years ago John Buttiller, in his Summa Rurali, maintained that the right of the Regalia is purely a royal right, belonging to the Crown, and that it must therefore extend without distinction to all the churches of the realm. Moreover, by an arrest of the Parisian Parlement in the year 1608 it was decreed that the advocates should not call into doubt whether the King could exercise the right of the Regalia in all the churches of the realm; against that arrest the French clergy soon lodged a complaint with His Royal Majesty.

units.la: CCCXLII. Argumentum isthoc præter alia fusè admodum prosecutus cùm fuisset Petrus de Marca Archiepiscopus Parisiensis, scriptis de Concordia Sacerdotii & Imperii seu libertatibus Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ libris octo, non parùm iis lectis Innocentius XI. commotus est; qui etiam refellendorum eorundem provinciam Celebri Canonistæ Lupo, Augustiniano Monacho, Aprili Anni M. D. C. LXXIX. impositit. Accessit indulgentia Clementis IX. qui Brevi expresso Regi gratiam fecerat investiendi Episcopos, quorum, flagrante tum bello, dioeceses vel occupaverat jam, vel occupaturus fuerat. quæ indulgentia Successoris Innocentii ejusdem animum anxium non parùm habuit. Præterea Rex à Clero Gallicano seu tributa seu donaria exegerat, intercedente exactioni in Occitania Apamiensi Episcopo, qui etiam Sanctimoniales Urbani antiquo more Abbatissam liberè eligentes, adversus Parisiensem Curiam Recentissima circa illud dissidii historia. jus ifthoc Regi vindicantem, apud Pontificem acriter tutatus est: Qua in controversia Pontificis Bulla in Sanctimonialium gratiam vulgata, ab eadem Curia suppressa, aliáque à Jesuitis etiam, Chaifio & Maimburgio, parùm Pontifici Romano faventibus, altè fatis in pectus Pontificis exulceratum penetrantia, commissa sunt; adeò ut non semel ad diras Pontifex fe converterit, & libros etiam nonnullos ceu potestati & authoritati suæ derogantes, devoverit. Quorum in numero inprimis liber de Causis majoribus, à Sorbonico Doctore in Episcoporum gratiam scritus, & acri Pontificis Bulla proscriptus, nec non Maimburgii libelli varii, etiam Lutheranismi famosa historia, fuerunt. Ex adverso Curia Suprema Parisiensis librum Episcopi Apamiensis pro Pontificiis partibus scriptum, nigro carbone notatum suppressit. quem mox Pontifex Italicum in idioma transferri vulgarique jussit. Apamiensis quondam, uti s. cxx. narravimus, Episcopus erat, ob quem in simili causa carceri inclusum Bonifacius VIII. Philippum Pulchrum Galliæ Regem excommunicare ausus est. Apamiensis Episcopus denuo in causa investiturarum se Pontifici Innocentio XI. mancipare, & Regi suo opponere sustinuit. Eo A. M. D. C. LXXX. defuncto, Vicarius Capitularis Pontificis causam suscepit, Curiæque Supremæ Regaliæ in Episcopatu eo vacante jus Regi asserenti, sese oppositu. Pontifice acriter tendente, & subinde etiam Apostolicarum censurarum metum incutiente, Lutetiæ coacti quindecim Episcopi Regium jus strenuè defenderunt, atque insuper Regi, ut Nationale Concilium, causam eandem disceptaturum, properè conciret, persuaserunt.
units.tr: CCCXLII. Peter de Marca, Archbishop of Paris, having treated this subject at great length, among other matters, in his eight books on The Concord of Priesthood and Empire, or the Liberties of the Gallican Church, Innocent XI was much disturbed on reading them; and in April 1679 he assigned the task of refuting them to the celebrated canonist Lupus, an Augustinian monk. There was also the indulgence of Clement IX, who by an express Brief had granted the King the favour of investing bishops whose dioceses, while the war was then raging, he had either already occupied or was about to occupy; and this indulgence caused no little anxiety to the mind of Innocent's successor. Besides, the King had exacted taxes or gifts from the French clergy, and the Bishop of Apamea in Occitania, who also vigorously defended the Ursuline nuns' ancient custom of freely electing their Abbess, intervened against this exaction, opposing the Parisian Court's claim to this right for the King before the Pontiff. In this controversy a Bull of the Pontiff in favour of the nuns was published, but suppressed by the same Court; and other writings, also by the Jesuits Chaiffius and Maimbourg, who were little favourable to the Roman Pontiff, were issued, reaching deep enough and inflaming the Pontiff's heart. So it was that more than once the Pontiff turned to curses, and also cursed several books as derogating from his power and authority. Among these, above all, were the book On the Greater Causes, written by a Sorbonne doctor in favour of the bishops and condemned by a sharp Bull of the Pontiff, and various pamphlets of Maimbourg, including his notorious History of Lutheranism. On the other side, the Supreme Court of Paris suppressed the book written by the Bishop of Apamea in favour of the Papist party, marking it with black charcoal; the Pontiff soon ordered it translated into Italian and published. The Bishop of Apamea was once, as we related in section 120, the one for whose sake, when he was imprisoned in a similar case, Boniface VIII dared to excommunicate Philip the Fair, King of France. The Bishop of Apamea again, in the question of investitures, undertook to surrender himself to Pope Innocent XI and to oppose his own King. When he died in 1680, the Pontiff's Vicar Capitular took up the cause, opposing the Supreme Court, which asserted the King's right of regalia in that vacant bishopric, while the Pontiff pressed hard and from time to time also instilled fear of apostolic censures. Fifteen bishops gathered at Paris vigorously defended the royal right, and moreover persuaded the King to summon quickly a National Council to decide the same cause.

units.la: CCCXLIII. Convenerunt igitur Lutetiæ Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ Archiepiscopi octo unà cum Episcopis viginti quatuor, aliisque pluribus, nomine Congregationis Generalis Cleri Franciæ insigniti, qui Regaliæ jus unanimi consen-
units.tr: CCCXLIII. Therefore the eight Archbishops of the Gallican Church, together with twenty-four Bishops and several others, distinguished as the General Assembly of the Clergy of France, met at Paris and, by unanimous consent, recognised the regalian right.

units.la: Congregatio Cleri Gallicani jus Regaliæ Regi vindicat, & literis ad Ponsu in Regem, hoc scilicet ei reddituri hostimentum pro Edictis adversus hæreticos, uti in Instrumento cessionis Regaliæ d. iii. Febr. Regi oblato, disertis verbis profitentur; conferentes, d. iii. Febr. A. M. D. C. LXXXII. literis ad Pontificem exaratis, seu rationem ei reddituri, seu excusationem allaturi rerum in Comitiis suis actarum significârunt, se appellâsse Secularem Magistratum, sed ab eo victos discessisse; magnopere insuper periculum metúmque suum exaggerantes, ne ob exortam controversiam illam Sacerdotium & Imperium inter se collidantur, & mala, quæ in Ecclesiam & Rempublicam consequi possent; proinde existimâsse se ad officium suum pertinere, aliquam inire rationem tollendi de medio nascentis dissidii; nullam verò commodiorem apparuisse remedio ab Ecclesiæ Patribus indicato, utili condescensione canonis temperandi pro temporum necessitate, ubi neque veritas fidei, neque morum honestas periclitantur. Deberi ab Ordine suo, deberi à Gallicana, imò ab universa Ecclesia plurimùm Regi, tam præclarè de Religione Catholica merito, & in dies magis mereri cupienti. Propterea se de jure suo decedentes jus illud Regaliæ in Regem contulisse.
units.tr: The Assembly of the Gallican Clergy vindicates the regalian right for the King, and by letter to the King it professes in express words, in the Instrument of cession of the regalia presented to the King on 3 February, that it renders him this as a return for the Edicts against heretics. Writing to the Pope by letter dated 3 February 1682, it explained or excused what had been done at its Assembly, declaring that it had appealed to the Secular Magistrate, but had departed defeated by him. It further magnified its own danger and fear, lest from the controversy that had arisen the Priesthood and the Empire should collide with one another, and the evils that could follow for the Church and the Commonwealth. Therefore it had judged that it belonged to its office to adopt some plan of removing the dissension as it arose. No more convenient remedy had appeared than the one pointed out by the Fathers of the Church, namely the useful relaxation of a canon, to be tempered according to the need of the times, where neither the truth of the faith nor the honesty of morals is endangered. Much is owed to the King, by its Order, by the Gallican Church, indeed by the whole Church, for having deserved so well of the Catholic Religion, and for desiring to deserve more and more every day. Therefore, yielding up its own right, it had conferred that regalian right upon the King.

units.la: CCCXLIII. Cùm diu satis responsum ad literas
units.tr: CCCXLIII. When the Pope had for a long time delayed a sufficient reply to the letters of the Clergy

units.la: Cleri Pontifex distulisset, ulterius progressa Congregatio certis definitionibus Romani Pontificis potestatem, in temporalibus quidem prorsus abolevit; in spiritualibus verò non parùm coarctavit, atque infra potestatem Concilii dejecit. Postquam enim die xvii. Martii solenni in Congregatione auditi sunt, quibus paulò ante injunctum fuerat, ut sex Propositiones, A. M. D. C. LXIII. à Sorbona Regi exhibitas, & supra thesi cc. LXXIX. expressas, accurato Examini subjicerent; die xix. ejusdem mensis unanimi Cleri totius consensu edita declaratio est, quatuor sequentibus definitionibus comprehensa: I. Quòd Papa, imò Ecclesia ipsa in Regum temporalia, nec directè, nec indirectè, potestatem ullam habeat: quódque Rex deponi, vel subditi ejus à juramen-
units.tr: the Assembly, proceeding further, by certain definitions entirely abolished the power of the Roman Pontiff in temporal matters, and in spiritual matters greatly restricted it and reduced it below the authority of a Council. For after the members who had shortly before been ordered to examine carefully the six Propositions exhibited to the King by the Sorbonne in 1663, and expressed above in thesis 279, had been heard in a solemn Assembly on 17 March, on 19 March of the same month a declaration was issued with the unanimous consent of the whole Clergy, comprehended in four following definitions: I. That the Pope, indeed the Church itself, has no power at all over the temporal affairs of kings, neither directly nor indirectly; and that kings cannot be deposed, nor their subjects absolved from

units.la: tu. to fidelitatis, quamcunque demum ob causam, absolvi nequeant. II. Quòd Concilium Generale sit supra Papam, idque vi doctrinæ, quam Constantiense Concilium quarta & quinta Sessione confirmavit; sicut Congregatio præsens declaret, quòd doctrina isthæc ab Ecclesia plenam efficaciam, approbationémque nacta sit; ex adverso autem opinionem eorum, qui pertendunt, id, quod in citatis Sessionibus conclusum est, eo duntaxat tempore, quo schismata invalescunt, obtineat; plane improbet. III. Quòd exercitium potestatis Pontificiæ limitandum & restringendum sit juxta Canones; quódque Papa nihil facere in præjudicium antiquarum consuetudinum, nec non libertatum Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ valeat. IV. Quòd in rebus quidem fidei Papa præcipuam authoritatem habeat; nihilominus ejus decisiones sine consensu Ecclesiæ certæ & infallibiles non sint. Decretum insimul est, ut, literis ad singulos Galliæ Episcopos exaratis, Propositiones hæ communicentur, commendentúrque, unà cum Declaratione, ut omnes Professores Theologiæ & Juris Canonici doctrinam articulis illis contentam, ceu veterem receptámque doctrinam Regni, profiteantur publicè, neque fas sit cuiquam seu Seculari seu Regulari contrarium docere. Postero die Archiepiscopus Parisiensis, comitibus Commissariis, Regi tum instrumentum, quatuor propositiones illas complexum; tum literas eam in rem ad Episcopos Galliæ destinatas, obtulit, simúlque Regem, ut peculiari Edicto id omne sanciret, rogavit. Impetratum id à Rege Edictum edente, quod d. XXIIII. Martii etiam à Suprema ejusdem Curia confirmatum. Edicti sententia est, ut declaratio illa Cleri Gallicani Protocollis omnium Curiarum, Communitatum, Academiarum, Facultatum Theologiæ & Juris Canonici inseratur: contrarium ei doctrinæ à quoquam subditorum vel advenarum, sive Secularium, sive Regularium ne asseratur: electi Prfessores Theologiæ Declarationi isti subscribant, & ad docendam eandem sese obstringant: in omnibus Collegiis ex pluribus Professoribus seu Regularibus seu Secularibus constantibus, uni injungatur tur quotannis, ut declarationem illam doceat; ubi vero Professor unicus est, teneatur per tres annos continuos docere. Syndici Theologicarum Facultatum quotannis Professorum talium nomina Episcopis edant; Professoresque iisdem, vel Procuratoribus eorum Generalibus postulantibus, scripta sua exhibere parati sint; neque Baccalaureus quisquam, sive Secularis, sive Regularis, Licentiatus, vel Doctor Theologiæ, iurisve Canonici creari possit, quin prius doctrinam illam publicis thesibus propugnaverit: Prælati omnes eandem in universa Diœcesi sua doceri curent: Decani denique & Syndici Facultatum Executionem Edicti, sub pœna fontis, urgeant. Pontifex Romanus Propositiones illas tanto cum mœrore excepisse fertur, ut lectis iis amare fleverit. Erectus tamen mox recreatúsque nonnihil est, quòd easdem in Galliæ Regno acribus adeò studiis propugnatas, non minori zelo in Hispaniæ Academiis oppugnari intellexisseт.
units.tr: the oath of fidelity, for whatever cause at all. II. That a General Council is above the Pope, and this by virtue of the doctrine which the Council of Constance confirmed in its fourth and fifth Sessions; as this present Assembly declares, that this doctrine has obtained full efficacy and approval from the Church; but on the contrary it plainly disapproves the opinion of those who maintain that what was concluded in the cited Sessions holds good only at the time when schisms prevail. III. That the exercise of papal power is to be limited and restrained according to the Canons; and that the Pope can do nothing to the prejudice of ancient customs, nor of the liberties of the Gallican Church. IV. That in matters of faith the Pope indeed holds the chief authority; nevertheless his decisions are not certain and infallible without the consent of the Church. At the same time it was decreed that, by letters written to each of the Bishops of France, these Propositions should be communicated and commended, together with the Declaration, so that all Professors of Theology and of Canon Law publicly profess the doctrine contained in those articles, as the old and received doctrine of the Kingdom, and that it be lawful for no one, whether secular or regular, to teach anything contrary to it. On the following day the Archbishop of Paris presented to the King, with the Commissioners attending, the instrument embracing those four propositions, and also the letters addressed to the Bishops of France for that purpose, and at the same time asked the King to sanction all of this by a special Edict. The King issued the Edict as requested, and it was confirmed by his Supreme Court on 24 March. The substance of the Edict is that this Declaration of the Gallican Clergy be inserted in the registers of all the Courts, Communities, Academies and Faculties of Theology and Canon Law; that no one among the subjects or foreigners, whether secular or regular, assert anything contrary to this doctrine; that the chosen Professors of Theology subscribe to this Declaration and bind themselves to teach it; that in all Colleges consisting of several Professors, whether regular or secular, one be enjoined each year to teach that declaration; and where there is only one Professor, he be obliged to teach it for three continuous years. The Syndics of the Theological Faculties shall each year give the names of such Professors to the Bishops; and the Professors shall be ready to present their writings to the same, or to their General Procurators, when requested; and no Bachelor, whether secular or regular, may be created Licentiate or Doctor of Theology or Canon Law unless he has first defended that doctrine in public theses; all Prelates shall take care that it is taught throughout their whole Diocese; and finally the Deans and Syndics of the Faculties shall press the execution of the Edict under penalty of loss of office. The Roman Pontiff is said to have received those Propositions with such grief that, having read them, he wept bitterly. Yet he was soon somewhat raised up and comforted, because he learned that the same propositions, so eagerly defended in the Kingdom of France, were being attacked with no less zeal in the Academies of Spain.

units.la: CCCXLIV. Demum 11. Aprilis A. M. D. C. LXXXII.
units.tr: CCCXLIV. Finally, 11 April 1682.

units.la: Pontifex Congregationi responsum misit ςηλῶβλυκόν, & si quod aliud, aculeatum virulentumque maximè, tantùm non catapultis suis Cleri Gallicani latera transfigens. Quæritur ante omnia, cogi se multis cum lachrymis usurpare Propheticum illud: Filii matris mea pugnârunt adversus me. Epistolæ Cleri initium quo metum suum in Pontificis sinum se effundere testatur, his verbis perstringit: Nihil sanè lætum, & vestris nominibus dignum eas literas continere, in ipso earum limine intelleximus. Nam præter ea, quæ de norma in Comitiis convocandis peragendisque servata afferebantur, animadvertimus vos oriri à metu vestro, quo suasore nunquam Sacerdotes Dei esse solent in re ardua & excelsa pro Religione & Ecclesiastica libertate vel aggrediendo fortes, vel perficiendo constantes. Quem quidem metum falsò judicavistis posse vos in sinum nostrum effundere. In sinu enim nostro hospitari perpetuò debet charitas Christi, quæ foras mittit & longè arcet à se timorem, &c. Timuistis ergò, ubi non erat timor. Id unum vobis timendum erat, ne apud Deum hominesque redarguí gui jure possetis, loco atque honori vestro, & Pastoralis officii debito defuisse. Tum Ivonis Carnutensis in turbulenta contentione Urbanum Pontificem inter & Philippum Regem, contra Regiam indignationem stantis, bonis spoliati, carceres & exilia perferentis, deserentibus aliis causam meliorem, facta imitanda fuisse monet. Officii vestri, erat, inquit, Sedis Apostolicae authoritati studia vestra adjungere, & Pastorali pectore, humilitate Sacerdotali causam Ecclesiarum vestrarum apud Regem agere, ejus conscientiam de Ista re instruendo, etiam cum periculo Regium in vos animum irritandi, ut possetis in posterum sine rubore in quotidiana Psalmodia Deum colloquentes Davidis verba proferre: Loquebar de testimoniis tuis in aspectu Regum, & non confundebar. Idque magis etiam faciendum fuisse, tam perspecta atque explorata Optimi Regis justitia & pietate, quem singulari benignitate Episcopos audire, Ecclesiis favere, & Episcopalem potestatem intemeratam velle, ipsimet scripserint, asserit. Scribentibus porro, quod in controversia victi sint, quod causa ceciderint, respondet: Quomodo cecidit, qui non stetit? quomodo victus est, qui non pugnavit? Et quis vestrum tam gravem, tam justam causam, tam sacrosanctam oravit apud Regem? cum tamen Praedecessores vestri eam in simili periculo constitutam non semel apud superiorem Galliae Regem, imo apud hunc ipsum libera voce defenderint, victoresque a Regio conspectu discesserint, relatis etiam ab aequissimo Rege praemiis officii Pastoralis strenuè impleti. Quis vestrum in arenam descendit, ut opponeret murum pro domo Israël? Quis ausus est invidiae se offerre? Quis vel vocem unam emisit memorem pristinae libertatis? Clamaverunt interim, sic enim scribitis, & quidem in mala causa, pro Regio jure clamaverunt Regis administri, cum vos in optima pro honore Christi silueritis. Omittimus hic commemorare, quae significatis de appellato à Vobis Seculari Magistratu, à quo victi discesseritis. Cupimus enim enim ejus facti memoriam aboleri, & volumus ea vos verba & literis vestris expungere, ne in actis Cleri Gallicani resideant ad dedecus nominis vestri sempiternum. Remedium porro Sacerdotii & Imperii per condescensionem utilem Canonis temperandi pro necessitate temporis, ubi neque veritas fidei, neque horum honestas periclitantur, conciliandi à Clero propositum, his verbis Pontifex disputungit: Cæterum ultro admittimus & laudamus consilium relaxandi Canonum disciplinam pro temporum necessitate, ubi id fieri possit sine fidei & morum dispendio; imò addimus cum Augustino, toleranda aliquando pro bono unitatis, quæ pro bono æquitatis odio habenda sunt, neque eradicanda esse zizania, ubi periculum sit, ne simul etiam triticum eradicetur: Sed ita tamen accipi oportet, ut in aliquo tantùm peculiari casu & ad tempus, ubi necessitas urget, licitum sit; sicuti factum est ab Ecclesia, cùm Arianos & Donatistas Episcopos ejurato errore suis Ecclesiis restituit, ut populos, qui secuti eos fuerant, in officio contineret. Aliud est, ubi disciplina Ecclesiæ per universum amplissimi Regni ambitum sine temporis termino, & cum manifesto periculo, ne exemplum latius repat, labefactatur, imò evertitur ipsius disciplinæ & Hierarchiæ Ecclesiæ fundamentum, sicuti evenire necesse esset, si quæ à Rege Christianissimo in negotio Regalia nuper acta sunt, conniventibus, imò etiam consentientibus, vobis contra Sacrorum Canonum, & præsertim Concilii Ludunensis authoritatem, contra notam jam pridem vobis ea in re mentem nostram, & contra ipsam jurisjurandi religionem, quo vos Deo, Romanæ, vestrisque Ecclesiis obligâstis, cùm Episcopali charactere imbuerimini; hæc Sancta Sedes executioni mandari, & malum invalescere deferendo permitteret, ac non ea nos, pro tradita Divinitus humilitati nostræ Summa in universam Ecclesiam potestate, solemni more, prædecessorum nostrorum vestigiis inhærentes improbaremus, cùm præsertim per abusum Regalia non solùm everti disciplíplinam Ecclesiæ, res ipsa doceat, sed etiam fidei ipsius integritatem in discrimen vocari facilè intelligatur ex ipsis Regiorum decretorum verbis, quæ jus conferendi beneficia Regi vendicant, non tanquam profluens ex aliqua Ecclesiæ concessione, sed tanquam ingenitum & coævum Regiæ Coronæ. Acri præ cæteris censura declarationem illam Cleri, quòd jus Regalia in Regem contulerit, Pontifex ferit. Illam verò partem literarum, inquit, vestrarum non sine animi horrore legere potuimus, in qua dicitis, Vos jure vestro decedentes, illud in Regem contulisse. Quasi Ecclesiarum, quæ curæ vestræ creditæ sunt, essetis arbitri, non custodes, & quasi Ecclesiæ ipsæ, & spiritualia earum jura possint sub Secularis potestatis jugum mitti ab Episcopis, qui se pro earum libertate in servitutem dare deberent. Vos sanè ipsi hanc veritatem agnovistis & confessi estis, dum alibi pronuntiastis, jus Regalia servitutem quandam esse, quæ in eo præsertim quod spectat beneficiorum collationem, imponi non potest, nisi Ecclesia concedente, vel saltem consentiente. Quo jure Vos ergo jus illud in Regem contulistis? Cúmque SS. Canones distrahi vetent jura Ecclesiæ, quomodo ea Vos distrahere in animum induxistis, quasi eorundem Canonum authoritati derogare Vobis liceat? Revocate in memoriam, quæ inclytus ille conterraneus vester, Claræval-lensis Abbas, non Gallicanæ modò, sed etiam universalis Ecclesiæ lumen à vobis merito nuncupatus, Eugenium Pontificem officii sui admonens, reliquit scripta præclarè: Meminisset, se esse, cui claves traditæ, cui oves creditæ sunt. esse quidem alios Cœli janitores & gregum pastores; sed cùm habeant illi assignatos greges, singulis singulos, ipsi universos creditos, non unum; non modò ovium, sed & Pastorum Eugenium esse Pastorem, adeóque juxta Canonum statuta, alios Episcopos vocatos fuisse in partem solicitudinis, ipsum in plenitudinem potestatis. Ex quibus verbis quantum nos admonere par est de obsequio & obedientia, quam debetis huic sanctæ Sedi, cui nos, Deo authore, quanquam im-memeriti præsidemus ; tantundem nostra Pastoralis solicitudo excitatur ad inchoandam tandem aliquando in hoc negotio, quam nimia forte longanimitas nostra, dum pœnitentiæ spatium damus, hactenus distulit, Apostolici muneris executionem. Tandem Cleri in Regaliæ negotio acta universa severè sic Pontifex abolet atque rescindit: Quamobrem per præsentes literas, tradita nobis ab Omnipotente Deo authoritate, improbamus, rescindimus & cassamus, quæ in istis vestris Comitiis acta sunt, in negotio Regalia, cum omnibus inde secutis, & quæ in posterum attentari continget, eáque perpetuò irrita declaramus; quamvis cùm sint ipsa per se manifestè nulla, cassatione atque declaratione hujusmodi non egerent. Speramus tamen, Vos quoque ipsos, re melius considerata, celeri retractatione consultoros conscientiæ vestræ, & Cleri Gallicani existimationi, ex quo Clero sicuti non defuere hucusque, ita in posterum non defuturos confidimus, qui boni Pastoris exemplo libenter animas ponere parati sint pro ovibus suis, & pro testamento Patrum suorum. Propositum denique suum etiam in posterum his verbis declarat & concludit: Nos quidem pro officii nostri debito parati sumus Dei adjutrice gratia sacrificare sacrificium justitiæ, & Ecclesiæ Dei jura ac libertatem, & hujus S. Sedis authoritatem dignitatémque defendere, nihil de nobis, sed omnia de Deo præsumentes, qui nos confortat, & omnia operatur in nobis, & qui jussit Petrum super aquas ad se venire. Præterit enim figura hujus mundi, & Dies Domini appropinquat. Sic ergo agamus, Venerabiles fratres ac dilecti filii, ut cum Summus Pastor & Paterfamiliâs & Princeps Pastorum rationem poscere voluerit à servis suis, sanguinem pessumdatæ & lacerataë Ecclesiæ, quam suo acquisivit, de nostris manibus non requirat. Vobis interim omnibus Apostolicam benedictionem, cui cœlestem accedere optamus, intimo amoris paterni affectu impertimur. Romæ apud S. Petrum, sub Annulo Piscatoris. Die II. April. A. M.D.C.LXXXII. Pontificatus nostri anno sexto. Verba totidem Bullæ, seu Monitorii hujus referre non piguit, ut Pontificis hujus tum typhum insolentem, quo Prædecessoribus suis parum concedit; tum zelum violentum (hunc enim etiam Archiepiscopus Tholosanus literis ad Pontificem exaratis ei exprobrasse fertur) non tam pro aris, quàm pro focis suis; tum denique artificium insigne, quo etiam sub sanctioris disciplinæ, fidei, periculi evertendi Hierarchiæ fundamenti & Testamenti Patrum suorum (non utique à Deo Patre, sed ab Hildebrandis & Bonifaciis pro se & Patribus suis conditi) velamine insatiabiles cupiditates suas, ob quas etiam in Prophetia Malachiæ, Archiepiscopi Armachani, jam duodecimo Seculo edita, Insatiabilis Bestia nomine venit; abscondit texítque, propius omnes contueri valeant. An verò impostorum Clerus Galliæ mentem sententiámque suam mutaturus, & studia sua Sedis Apostolicæ authoritati adjuncturus sit, nec ne, dies volvenda docebit.
units.tr: The Pontiff sent the Congregation a reply that was honey-sweet and yet, if anything, most barbed and venomous, nearly running the sides of the Gallican clergy through with his catapults. First of all he complains that he is compelled, with many tears, to take up that prophetic line: The sons of my mother fought against me. At the opening of the clergy's letter, where it declares that its fear is poured into the Pontiff's bosom, he rebukes them in these words: We perceived at the very threshold of that letter that it contained nothing at all cheerful and worthy of your names. For, apart from what was put forward about the rule observed in convoking and conducting the Assembly, we noticed that you spring from your fear, a counsellor under whose influence the priests of God are never bold in attacking, or steadfast in carrying through, a difficult and lofty matter for religion and ecclesiastical liberty. Yet you judged wrongly that you could pour this fear into our bosom. For the charity of Christ ought to dwell perpetually in our bosom, and it drives fear out and keeps it far away, etc. So you were afraid where there was no fear. The only thing you had to fear was that you might justly be reproved before God and men for having failed in your place and honour and in the duty of the pastoral office. Then he advises that, in the turbulent dispute between Pope Urban and King Philip, Ivo of Chartres, who stood against the King's indignation and endured spoliation, prisons and exile while others deserted the better cause, should have been imitated. It was your duty, he says, to join your efforts to the authority of the Apostolic See, and with a pastoral heart and priestly humility to plead the cause of your churches before the King, instructing his conscience about this matter, even at the risk of arousing the King's anger against you, so that you might be able henceforth, without blushing, to speak in your daily psalmody to God the words of David: I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and was not confounded. And this ought to have been done all the more, he asserts, given the well-tested and clearly understood justice and piety of the most excellent King, whom they themselves have written hears bishops with singular kindness, favours the churches, and wishes episcopal power to remain inviolate. To those who write that they were defeated in the dispute, that they fell in their cause, he replies: How did he fall who did not stand? How was he defeated who did not fight? And which of you has pleaded so grave, so just, so sacred a cause before the King? Yet your predecessors, when their cause was placed in similar danger, more than once defended it with a free voice before the earlier King of France, indeed before this very King, and departed from the royal presence as victors, with rewards from the most equitable King for having strenuously fulfilled the pastoral office. Which of you has gone down into the arena to set up a wall for the house of Israel? Who has dared to expose himself to hatred? Who has uttered even one word recalling former liberty? Meanwhile, as you write, and indeed in a bad cause, the King's officials cried out for the royal right, while you kept silence in the best of causes for the honour of Christ. We omit here to recall what you say about the appeal you made to the secular magistrate, by whom you were defeated. For we wish the memory of that deed to be abolished, and we want those words expunged from your letters, lest they remain in the records of the Gallican clergy to the eternal dishonour of your name. Next the Pontiff dismisses in these words the clergy's proposal to find a remedy for the conflict between priesthood and empire by a useful condescension, moderating the canons according to the needs of the times where neither the truth of the faith nor their honour is endangered: Moreover, we readily admit and praise the plan of relaxing the discipline of the canons according to the necessity of the times, where this can be done without loss to faith and morals; indeed we add with Augustine that things which must be regarded with hatred for the sake of equity are sometimes to be tolerated for the good of unity, and that tares are not to be uprooted where there is a danger that the wheat would be uprooted at the same time. But it must be understood in this way: that it is lawful only in some particular case and for a time, where necessity presses, as was done by the Church when it restored Arian and Donatist bishops to their churches after they abjured their error, in order to keep in obedience the peoples who had followed them. It is different where the discipline of the Church is weakened throughout the whole extent of the most extensive kingdom, without limit of time and with manifest danger that the example spreads wider, indeed where the foundation of the discipline and hierarchy of the Church is overthrown. This would necessarily happen if the things recently done in the matter of the Regalia by the Most Christian King were to be carried into effect by this Holy See, with your connivance or even consent, against the authority of the sacred canons and especially of the Council of Lyons, against our mind on this matter, long since made known to you, and against the very religion of the oath by which you bound yourselves to God, to the Roman Church and to your churches when you were imbued with the episcopal character. And if we did not disapprove, by the solemn custom and following the footsteps of our predecessors, of permitting the evil to grow strong by deferring it, since by the power divinely entrusted to our humility over the universal Church, the thing itself teaches that the discipline of the Church is overturned by abuse of the Regalia, and it is easily understood that the integrity of the faith itself is put in peril from the very words of the royal decrees, which claim for the King the right of conferring benefices, not as flowing from any concession of the Church, but as innate and coeval with the royal crown. With more severe censure than the rest, the Pontiff strikes that declaration of the clergy that they had conferred the right of the Regalia upon the King. Yet that part of your letter, he says, we could not read without a shudder of mind, where you say that you, by surrendering your right, conferred it upon the King. As if you were the arbiters, not the guardians, of the churches entrusted to you; and as if the churches themselves and their spiritual rights could be sent under the yoke of secular power by bishops who ought to give themselves into servitude for their liberty. You yourselves surely recognised and confessed this truth when elsewhere you pronounced that the right of the Regalia is a certain servitude which, especially as regards the conferring of benefices, cannot be imposed except with the consent, or at least the assent, of the Church. By what right, then, did you confer that right upon the King? And since the sacred canons forbid the rights of the Church to be divided, how have you resolved to divide them, as if it were permitted to you to derogate from the authority of those same canons? Call to mind what that famous fellow countryman of yours, the Abbot of Clairvaux, whom you have rightly named the light not only of the Gallican but of the universal Church, left written so finely in admonishing Pope Eugenius of his office: He should remember that he is the one to whom the keys were handed over, to whom the sheep were entrusted. There are indeed other gatekeepers of heaven and shepherds of flocks; but while they have flocks assigned to them, each his own, he has all of them entrusted to him, not one. Eugenius is shepherd not only of the sheep but also of the shepherds, and so, according to the statutes of the canons, other bishops have been called to share in the care, while he himself holds the fullness of power. From these words, how much we ought to remind you of the obsequiousness and obedience you owe to this Holy See, over which we preside, though unworthy, by God's authority; and so much does our pastoral solicitude stir us to begin at last, in this matter, the execution of the apostolic office, which perhaps our excessive forbearance, while we give room for repentance, has hitherto deferred.
