units.la: AD cujus rei, & multarum aliarum sequentibus temporibus gestarum clariorem notitiam, res ipsa poscit, uti quid juris in Flaminiæ, quæ nunc Romagna dicitur, oppidis, aliisque compluribus, quæ vel nunc possident, vel antea variis temporibus possederunt, Romani Pontifices habeant, dicatur: quoque pacto ab initio rerum sacrarum administrationi duntaxat præfecti, ad Regna & Imperia pervenerint: ad hoc ut id etiam tanquam his annexum & conjunctum, quæ ob has atque alias causas contentiones diversis temporibus inter Pontifices atque Imperatores extiterint, commemoretur.
units.tr: For a clearer understanding of this matter and of many other events of the following times, the subject requires us to say what right the Roman Pontiffs have over the towns of Flaminia, now called Romagna, and over several others which they now possess or did possess at various times. It also requires us to say how, from the beginning, men who were appointed only to administer sacred affairs came to rule kingdoms and empires. This is added as something joined and connected with these matters: the quarrels that arose between the Pontiffs and the Emperors at various times for these and other reasons.

units.la: Pontifices Romani, quorum primus Petrus Apostolus fuit, accepta ab Jesu Christo in rebus sacris ac divinis auctoritate, charitate, submissione, patientia, spiritu sacro & prodigiis magni, per illorum initia non modo potentia civili & mundana penitus nudati, verum etiam ab illa vexati, diu obscuri ac ferè ignorati fuere: eorum nomine nulla re magis quam suppliciis & cruciatibus perferendis innotescente, quæ una cum iis, qui eos sequebantur, sustinebant. Nam etsi cum propter infinitam multitudinem diversarum nationum & sectarum quæ in urbem Romam confluxerant, parum Christianorum progressus & actiones animadverterentur, essentque ab quorundam Im-
units.tr: The Roman Pontiffs, of whom Peter the Apostle was the first, received authority from Jesus Christ in sacred and divine matters. They were great in authority, charity, submissiveness, patience, holy spirit and miracles. In their early days they were stripped entirely of civil and worldly power and were even harassed by it. For a long time they remained obscure and almost unknown, and their name became known through nothing so much as the punishments and torments they endured, together with those who followed them. For although, because of the vast number of different nations and sects that had flowed into the city of Rome, the progress and activities of the Christians were little noticed, and although they were free from the violence and persecutions of some emperors, except when their public rites could not be passed over in silence,

units.la: vid. Guicciard. Hist. Lib. 4. Tom. I. pag. 490. peratorum vi & vexationibus immunes, nisi si quando illorum publici ritus silentio praeteriri non possent: nihilo minus tamen aliqui alii, sive innata veritate, sive Deorum suorum insano quodam amore perculsi, eos tanquam novarum superstitionum auctores, & suae religionis eversores, atrociter persequebantur.
units.tr: see Guicciard. Hist. Lib. 4. Tom. I. pag. 490. nevertheless others, whether moved by an innate sense of truth or by a certain frenzied love of their own gods, savagely persecuted them as authors of new superstitions and as overthrowers of their religion.

units.la: Hoc in statu tum voluntaria paupertate, tum vitae reliqua sanctimonia, tum suppliciorum acerbitatibus clarissimi, ad Silvestri Pontificatum perstiterunt. Cujus temporibus quum ad christianam religionem Constantinus moribus sanctissimis Christianorum, & prodigiis atque miraculis, quae frequentissima in iis, qui Christi vestigia sequebantur, elucebant, permotus, animum appulisset, Pontifices a periculis, in quibus annos circiter trecentos versati fuerant, tuti, liberius cultum divinum exercere, ritusque Christianos palam profiteri. Quamobrem factum est, ut partim morum & vitae admiratione, partim praeceptorum, quae nostra religione continentur, sanctitate, partim quoque facilitate quadam mortalium, qua plerumque vel ambitione, vel metu, Principis sui exemplum imitantur, nomen christianum mirifice omnibus in locis propagari, paupertas vero illa sacerdotum beata diminui, coeperit. Nam Constantinus templo in Laterano Divo Joanni, in vaticano Petro Apostolo, itemque Paulo, aliisque diversis in locis, aedificatis, ea non modo pretiosis vasis ornamentisque ditavit, verum etiam ut sarta tecta, tueri ac renovare, quae extructa erant, seque, qui rebus sacris operam darent, sustentare possent, praediis atque aliis vectigalibus donavit. alii praeterea multi post secuti, rati beneficiis hujusmodi faciliorem aditum in coeleste regnum sibi patefieri, aut nova extruebant fana, eaque donis cumulabant: aut jam extructis suorum bonorum portionem ali-
units.tr: In this condition, most distinguished for voluntary poverty, for the holiness of their whole lives and for the bitterness of their sufferings, they held out until the pontificate of Silvester. In his time Constantine, moved by the most holy conduct of the Christians and by the prodigies and miracles that shone out most frequently among those who followed the footsteps of Christ, turned his mind to the Christian religion. The Pontiffs, now safe from the dangers in which they had lived for about three hundred years, began to exercise divine worship more freely and to profess Christian rites openly. Hence it came about that, partly through admiration for their morals and way of life, partly through the holiness of the precepts contained in our religion, and partly also through a certain readiness of mortals, who for the most part imitate the example of their prince from ambition or fear, the Christian name began to spread wonderfully in all places, while that blessed poverty of the priests began to diminish. For Constantine, after building a temple to the divine John in the Lateran, to Peter the Apostle in the Vatican, likewise to Paul and to others in various places, enriched them not only with precious vessels and ornaments but also gave them estates and other revenues, so that they could keep in repair and restore what had been built and so that those who devoted themselves to sacred things could support themselves. Afterwards many others followed, thinking that by such benefits an easier way into the heavenly kingdom would be opened for them. Some built new shrines and heaped gifts upon them; others assigned a portion of their goods to buildings already erected.

units.la: Nomen Christianum propagatur & Ecclesiae ditantur. aliquam attribuebant; quinetiam sive lege quapiam inveterata, sive consuetudine, ad leges Mosea exemplum, quisque de bonorum suorum fructibus decimam partem locis religiosis pendebat. Ad quod quidem efficiendum, magno cum ardore excitabantur, quod viderent ab initio Sacerdotes, eo excepto, quod ad parcissimum victum sibi reservabant, quicquid reliquum erat, partim in ædificia religiosa, eorumque suppellectilem, partim in egenos aliosque pios usus impendere. Cumque nondum superbia & ambitio in eorum pectoribus insedisset, ab universis, qui ubique erant, Christianis omnium Ecclesiarum supremus custos, & tanquam Petri Apostoli successor Episcopus Romanus agnoscebatur: primum quod ea civitas ob suam antiquam dignitatem, tanquam reliquarum caput & Princeps, Imperii nomen majestatemque retinebat: deinde quod illinc in bonam Europæ partem religio Christiana diffusa erat: postremo quia Constantinus à Silvestro ritu Christiano aquis initiatus, ejusmodi auctoritatem in eo atque in ejus Successoribus libenter agnoverat.
units.tr: The Christian name is spread and the Churches are enriched. Moreover, by some ancient law or custom, after the example of the law of Moses, each man paid a tenth of the fruits of his goods to religious places. They were stirred up to do this with great zeal, because they saw that from the beginning the priests, apart from what they kept for their very frugal living, spent whatever remained partly on religious buildings and their furnishings and partly on the poor and other pious uses. And since pride and ambition had not yet settled in their hearts, the bishop of Rome was acknowledged by all Christians everywhere as the supreme guardian of all the Churches, and as the successor of the Apostle Peter. This was first because that city, on account of its ancient dignity, kept the name and majesty of the Empire as the head and prince of the others. Second, because the Christian religion had spread from there into a good part of Europe. Last, because Constantine, having been initiated into the Christian rite by Silvester, had willingly acknowledged such authority in him and in his successors.

units.la: Fama quoque est, Constantinum Orientis provinciarum motibus Imperii Sedem Byzantium, post de suo nomine Constantinopolim appellatam, transferre compulsum, Pontifici Romanæ urbis aliarumque & urbium & regionum in Italia imperium donasse. Quæ fama quamvis a sequentibus Pontificibus diligenter fuerit enutrita & sustentata, eorumque auctoritate à multis credita, est nihilominus cùm ab scriptoribus gravissimis, tum verò rebus ipsis refutata. Illud autem certò constat, & tunc & longo post tempore, urbem Romam, Italiamque omnem tanquam Imperio Cæsarum obnoxiam, ab Imperatorum ministris ac Præfectis fuisse gubernatam. Nec desunt quicquid de Constantino & Silvestro dicitur (usque adeo saepe profundis in tenebris res vetustae demersae latent) redarguant, ostendantque eos longe diversis temporibus extitisse: nemo tamen negat, Imperii Constantinopolim translatione ad Pontificum Potentiam, viam esse patefactam, ex eaque originem habuisse. Nam indies magis & magis Imperatorum auctoritate, tum ex illorum continua absentia, tum quod gravissimis in Oriente bellis distinerentur, in Italia debilitata, populus Romanus ab Imperatorum obedientia, paulatim desciscens, atque ob eam rem tanto magis Pontifices praesentes respiciens, eis coepit non obedientiam quidem, sed voluntarium quoddam obsequium exhibere.
units.tr: There is also a report that Constantine, compelled by disturbances in the provinces of the East to transfer the seat of the Empire to Byzantium, afterwards named Constantinopolis after his own name, gave to the Pontiff the rule of the city of Rome and of other cities and regions in Italy. Although this report was carefully nourished and sustained by the following Pontiffs, and although it was believed by many on their authority, it has nevertheless been refuted both by the most weighty writers and by the facts themselves. It is certain, however, that both then and for a long time afterwards the city of Rome and all Italy, as subject to the Empire of the Caesars, were governed by the ministers and prefects of the Emperors. Nor are there lacking those who refute whatever is said about Constantine and Silvester (so often do ancient matters lie sunk in deep darkness), and who show that they lived at very different times. Yet no one denies that the transfer of the Empire to Constantinople opened the way to the power of the Pontiffs and had its origin there. For day by day the authority of the Emperors in Italy grew weaker, partly through their continual absence and partly because they were occupied with the most serious wars in the East. The Roman people, gradually falling away from obedience to the Emperors, and therefore looking more and more to the Pontiffs who were present, began to offer them not obedience indeed, but a certain voluntary deference.

units.la: Quanquam ne haec quidem nisi lente sese ostenderunt, ob Gothorum & Vandalorum aliarumque barbararum nationum in Italiam effusiones, a quibus capta saepe ac direpta Roma, & Pontificum nomen, quod ad civiles attinet res, in obscuro pene contemptim jacebat, & Imperatorum in Italia auctoritas evanescebat, quandoquidem eam tanta cum ignominia praedae barbaris expositam deserebat.
units.tr: Yet even these things showed themselves only slowly, because of the invasions into Italy of the Goths, the Vandals and other barbarous nations. Rome was often captured and plundered by them, and the name of the Pontiffs, so far as civil affairs were concerned, lay almost in obscurity and contempt, while the Emperors' authority in Italy faded away, since they abandoned it, exposed with such disgrace to the plunder of the barbarians.

units.la: Aliarum nationum impetus cum torrentis instar erupisset, Gothorum per annos septuaginta potentia permansit. Erant hi nomine & professione Christiani, genere a prima origine Scythae & Daci; quibus tandem Caesarum armis Italia pulsis per Graecos iterum Magistratus coepit Italia gubernari: quorum qui caeteris imperabat, Graeca voce Hexarchus appellabatur, sedemque Ravennae in urbe vetustissima, eisque temporibus opulentissima, atque ob agri bonitatem frequentissima, habebat. Nam post magnum incrementum ex Caesaris Augusti atque aliorum Imperatorum classe validissima susceptum, quam in ejus portu urbi pene conjuncto, cujus nunc vix ullum extat vestigium, continenter tenuerunt, à multis belli Ducibus, deinde ab Theodorico Gothorum Rege, ejusque successoribus fuerat habitata: qui quòd Imperatorum potentiam suspectam haberent, eam potius quàm Romam, Regni sui sedem maris opportunitate, Byzantio propioris, ducti delegerunt. Quam opportunitatem Hexarchi, etsi contraria ratione, secuti, cùm ibi consedissent, Romanæ urbi, aliisque Italiæ civitatibus proprios imponebant Præfectos, quos Duces appellabant. Hinc Ravennatis Hexarchatus nomen: quo nomine omnia comprehendebantur, quæ proprios Duces non habebant, sed uni Hexarcho obtemperabant.
units.tr: When the attacks of other nations had burst forth like a torrent, the power of the Goths lasted for seventy years. They were Christians in name and profession, originally of Scythian and Dacian stock. When at last they were driven out of Italy by the arms of the Caesars, Italy began to be governed again by magistrates sent by the Greeks. The one who ruled over the others was called by the Greek word Hexarchus, and he had his seat at Ravenna, a very ancient city, very wealthy in those times and very populous because of the fertility of its land. For after it had greatly increased under the very strong fleet of Augustus Caesar and of other emperors, which they kept constantly in its harbour, almost joined to the city (of which hardly any trace now remains), it had been inhabited by many generals and then by Theodoric, king of the Goths, and his successors. These, since they regarded the power of the Emperors with suspicion, chose it rather than Rome as the seat of their kingdom, led by the advantage of the sea, which made it nearer to Byzantium. The Hexarchs, though for the opposite reason, followed this same advantage, and when they had settled there they imposed their own prefects on the city of Rome and on other cities of Italy, whom they called Dukes. Hence the name Exarchate of Ravenna, a name under which were comprehended all those places that had no dukes of their own but obeyed the one Hexarch.

units.la: Qua tempestate Pontifices Romani, civilis potestatis penitus expertes, atque in mortalium animis admiratione & observantia, moribus ipsorum ab illa pristina puritate jam fatiscentibus, obsolescente, tanquam Imperatoribus subjecti ætatem agebant; sine quorum & eorum, quos Hexarchos diximus appellatos, auctoritate, quamvis Sacerdotum Populíque Romani suffragiis renuntiati, neque se pro Pontificibus gerere, neque Pontificatum capere audebant. quinetiam Episcopi Constantinopolitanus & Ravennas, quoniam religionis sedes Imperii atque armorum potentiam sequi consuevit, cum Romano Episcopo sæpenumero de principatu disputabant.
units.tr: At this time the Roman Pontiffs, entirely without civil power, and held in admiration and reverence in men's minds, though their morals were already failing and losing their old purity, lived as subjects of the Emperors. Without the authority of these men, and of those whom we have said were called Hexarchs, they did not dare to act as Pontiffs or to take up the pontificate, even though they had been proclaimed by the votes of the priests and the Roman people. Moreover, the bishops of Constantinople and of Ravenna, since the seat of religion usually follows the power of the Empire and of arms, often disputed the primacy with the Roman bishop.

units.la: Cæterum haud multo post rerum mutatio consecuta. Nam Longobardi, gens ferocissima, in Italiam ingressi, Galliam Cisalpinam occuparunt: ab quorum imperio Longobardia est appellata. Adjecerunt etiam Ravennam cum Hexarchatu universo; alias præterea multas Italiæ partes, armis Picenum usque & Spoletum, & Beneventum prolatis: quibus in locis Duces à se dictos imperare jusserunt. Atque hæc omnia, dum Imperatores partim ignavia, partim Asiaticis bellis detenti, hisce rebus parum prospiciunt.
units.tr: Not long after, however, the situation changed. The Lombards, a very fierce people, entered Italy and occupied Cisalpine Gaul, which is named Lombardy after their rule. They also added Ravenna with the whole Exarchate, and by arms extended their power over many other parts of Italy, as far as Picenum and Spoleto and Benevento. In these places they ordered dukes, named after themselves, to govern. While the emperors, partly through sloth and partly held back by wars in Asia, paid little attention to these matters, all of this happened.

units.la: Horum igitur auxiliis Roma destituta, cùm nec jam Hexarchorum magistratus essent in Italia, consiliis atque auctoritate Pontificum gubernari coepit, qui cùm aliquot annis post unâ cum Romanis ab Longobardis opprimerentur, ad Pipini Francorum Regis auxilia tandem se receperunt. Qui valido in Italiam exercitu, ubi Longobardi annos ultra ducentos dominatum tenuerant, ducto eos inde depulit, partémque ipsorum Imperii, quasi belli jure parti, Pontifici & Ecclesiæ Romanæ condonavit: in quibus non modò Urbinum, Fanum Fortunæ, Eugubbium, (Igninum olim) multaque alia Romæ vicina oppida, verum etiam Ravennam cum Hexarchatu suo, quo contineri ajunt quicquid à Placentiæ & Papiæ finibus Ariminum usque Padum & Apenninum, stagna sive paludes Venetorum, & Adriaticum sinum clauditur: Ad hæc ipsum Ariminum ad Toglam flumen, tunc Isaurum appellatum.
units.tr: Rome, therefore, was abandoned by these helpers. Since there were no longer any magistrates of the Exarchs in Italy, she began to be governed by the counsels and authority of the Popes. After some years, when the Popes and the Romans were oppressed together by the Lombards, they at last turned for help to Pepin, king of the Franks. He came into Italy with a strong army, drove the Lombards out of there, where they had held power for more than two hundred years, and gave a part of their realm, as if it had been won by the right of war, to the Pope and the Roman Church. These included not only Urbino, Fano, Gubbio (formerly Iguvium) and many other towns near Rome, but also Ravenna with its Exarchate. This, they say, contains everything enclosed between the borders of Piacenza and Pavia, from Rimini as far as the Po and the Apennines, the lagoons or marshes of the Venetians, and the Adriatic gulf. In addition, Rimini itself, at the river Toglia, then called the Isaurus.

units.la: Pipino autem mortuo, cum denuo Pontificibus Longobardi essent infesti; & quæ ipsis donata erant invaderent, Carolus ejus filius, qui post ob maximas victorias Magni cognomentum merito est adeptus, eorum imperio funditus everso, à patre Ecclesiæ Romanæ donata comprobavit & nominatim Picenum & Spoleti Ducatum, quo Aquila oppidum Brutiorumque pars continetur, Pontifici tum cùm cum Longobardis bellum gereret, attributa. Hæc sic habere certò affirmant, quibus Pontificii quidam Scriptores addunt eundem Carolum Ecclesiæ donâsse Liguriam ad Varum amnem, Italiæ terminum; Mantuam item & quicquid Longobardi
units.tr: When Pepin died, the Lombards again became hostile to the Popes and attacked what had been given to them. His son Charles, who afterwards deservedly won the name of Great because of his very great victories, overthrew their power utterly. He confirmed to the Church of Rome what his father had given, and especially assigned to the Pope, while he was waging war with the Lombards, the Duchy of Picenum and Spoleto, which contains the town of L'Aquila and part of the Bruttii. Those who are certain of these things assert that this is so. Some Papist writers add that the same Charles gave to the Church Liguria as far as the river Var, the boundary of Italy, and likewise Mantua and whatever the Lombards held

units.la: Carolus M. eandem denuò à Longobardis vindicat, & non parum arget. di in foro Julii, atque in Histria possidebant. Idem quoque aliquis scribit de Corsica Insula, totoque illo tractu, qui Lunam inter & Parmam interest. Ob quæ beneficia Reges Galliæ celebrati, & honoribus à Pontificibus afsecti, Christianissimi appellationem sunt consecuti.
units.tr: Charlemagne again claims the same from the Lombards, and it is not a little disputed. ...in the forum of Julius and in Istria. Someone also writes the same about the island of Corsica and the whole district lying between Luni and Parma. For these benefits the kings of France were praised, were honoured by the Popes, and attained the title Most Christian.

units.la: Post etiam anno salutis octingentesimo, Leo Pontifex una cum Populo Romano (verum Pontifex haud alia auctoritate, quàm ut ejus Populi caput) eundemmet Carolum Romanorum Imperatorem nominarunt, nomine quoque ipso hanc Imperii partem ab Imperatoribus Constantinopoli agentibus sejungentes, tanquam Roma provinciæque occidentis ab illis desertæ in periculis, propriorum Principum tutela opus haberent. Hac Imperii distractione Transmarini Imperatores, nec Siciliæ Insula, nec ea Italiæ parte, quæ ab urbe ipsa Neapoli Manfredoniam usque pertingens mari terminatur (quoniam semper illorum Imperium agnoverant) exclusi fuere: nec ob id de consuetudine, qua Pontifices Imperatorum, quorum nomine Roma gubernabatur, auctoritate confirmarentur, derogatum est: quin etiam in suis diplomatibus, scripturæ tempus his verbis consignabant
units.tr: Afterwards, in the year of salvation 800, Pope Leo, together with the Roman people (though the Pope had no other authority than as head of that people), named this same Charles Emperor of the Romans. By the very name they separated this part of the empire from the emperors who ruled at Constantinople, as if Rome and the provinces of the West, deserted by them in their dangers, needed the protection of their own princes. Through this division of the empire the emperors beyond the sea were not excluded from the island of Sicily, nor from that part of Italy which stretches from the city of Naples to Manfredonia and is bounded by the sea (since they had always acknowledged their rule there). Nor, for this reason, was the custom abolished by which the Popes received confirmation of their authority from the emperors in whose name Rome was governed. Indeed, in their documents they recorded the date of writing in these words:

units.la: IMPERANTE CAROLO DOMINO NO- STRO.
units.tr: IN THE REIGN OF CHARLES OUR LORD.

units.la: In qua minimè gravi vel submissione, vel observantia perstitere, dum rerum eventus animos addidêre, ut suo se nutu regerent. Quippe cùm Imperatorum potentia debilitari coepisset, primùm dissidiis inter Caroli Magni posteros dum penes eos Imperii Majestas stetit: deinde Imperii ad Principes Germanos translatione, potentia Caroli Magni successoribus minimè pares, Pontifices populúsque Romanus, cujus magistratibus Roma coepit, quamvis perturbatè, & confusè, gubernari, Imperatorum auctoritati quibuscunque modis derogangantes, lege sanxerunt, ne deinceps Pontificum lectio, Imperatorum auctoritate niteretur. quod quidem per annos plures varie servatum est, prout rerum vicissitudine Imperatorum potentia aut surgebat aut inclinabat.
units.tr: They persisted in this submission or deference, which was by no means heavy, while events gave them courage to govern themselves at their own nod. For when the power of the emperors had begun to weaken, first through quarrels among the descendants of Charlemagne, while the majesty of the empire rested with them, and then through the transfer of the empire to the German princes, whose power was by no means equal to that of Charlemagne's successors, the Popes and the Roman people, by whose magistrates Rome had begun to be governed (though confusedly and in disorder), passed a law. By whatever means they could, they diminished the authority of the emperors, decreeing that from then on the election of Popes should not depend on the emperor's authority. This was observed in various ways for many years, as the power of the emperors rose or fell with the changing course of affairs.

units.la: Quae, posteaquam ad Othones Saxonas Imperium pervenit, aucta. Gregorius Quintus Othonis Tertii favore, qui tum Romae erat, ad Pontificatum assumptus, hinc suae gentis amore, illinc Romanorum quibusdam injuriis impulsus, suo Decreto legendi Imperatoris jus & auctoritatem, ea forma quae ad haec usque tempora perducta servatur, in Germanorum nationem transtulit: atque ut Pontificibus in Imperatores auctoritatem aliquam retineret, eisque vicem redderet, interdixit, ne quis Imperatoris Augustive appellatione, aliove nomine, quam Regis Romanorum & Caesaris uteretur, ni prius Imperii coronam a Pontifice (unde mos inolevit, ut ad capiendam coronam Romam veniant) acceperit.
units.tr: This authority grew after the empire came to the Saxon Otto. Gregory V, raised to the papacy through the favour of Otto III, who was then at Rome, was driven partly by love of his own nation and partly by certain injuries from the Romans. By his decree he transferred the right and authority of choosing the emperor to the German nation, in the form that has been preserved down to our own times. And so that he might keep for the Popes some authority over the emperors, and repay them in turn, he forbade anyone to use the title of Emperor or Augustus, or any other name than King of the Romans and Caesar, unless he had first received the crown of the empire from the Pope. (From this came the custom that they come to Rome to take the crown.)

units.la: Caeterum Othonibus extinctis, & potentia Imperatorum labefactata, quod ad magnos Reges hereditario jure Imperium, non veniret, Roma palam ab illorum obedientia defecit, multaeque urbes, Conrado Suevo imperante, rebellarunt: & Pontifices suae amplificandae auctoritati intenti, Romanae civitatis dominatum propemodum obtinebant. Saepe tamen propter populi insolentiam & discordias, multis difficultatibus laborabant; quem ut in officio continerent, Henrici Secundi favore, qui tum Romae erat, Pontificis creandi jus in Cardinales solos transtulerunt.
units.tr: But after the Ottos died out, and the power of the emperors was weakened, because the empire did not pass by hereditary right to the great kings, Rome openly withdrew from their obedience, and many cities rebelled under Conrad of Swabia. The Popes, intent on enlarging their own authority, nearly held the lordship of the city of Rome. Yet often, on account of the insolence and discord of the people, they laboured under many difficulties. To keep the people in check, through the favour of Henry II, who was then at Rome, they transferred the right of creating a Pope to the cardinals alone.

units.la: Pontificum magnitudini nova accessio facta est. Nam cum Normanni, quorum primum Guilelmus Ferabrachius est appellatus, ab Imperio Constantinopolitano Apulia & Calabria subtracta, Robertus Guicciardus ex illa gente te unus, sive ut colore juris aliquo sese muniret, sive quo adversus eos Imperatores potentia se armaret, sive alia de causa, Benevento Pontifici, quasi Pontificii juris esset, restituto, Apuliae Calabriaeque Principatum, quasi Ecclesiae Romanae feudum recognovit. Cujus exemplum Rogerius ejus successorum unus secutus, inde pulso Guilelmo eadem familia orto, post etiam Sicilia occupata, fere anno Salutis M. C. XXX. harum provinciarum jus a Pontifice accepit: estque Rex utriusque Siciliae, quarum una ultra, altera cis fretum sita est, appellatus. Neque enim Pontifices, ambitione & propria utilitate adducti, alienam cupiditatem & vim fovere recusarunt. Hac juris specie freti, ulterius Pontifices progressi (ut cupido humana gradum sistere nequit) quosdam Reges illis Regnis quasi contumaces privare coeperunt, in aliosque transferre. Quo more ad Henricum Friderici Barbarossae filium, ab hoc ad Federicum Secundum ejus filium, qui tres ordine Romani Imperatores fuerunt, ea Regna pervenere. Verum cum Federicus Pontificem bello persequeretur, essentque illo tempore Guelforum & Gibellinorum factiones excitatae, quarum alterius caput erat Pontifex, alterius Imperator. Pontifex, mortuo Friderico, Carolum Andiovinorum & Provinciae comitem (cujus antea facta mentio est) utriusque Siciliae Regem appellavit, hac lege, ut quotannis auri unciarum sena milia tributi nomine penderet; ac ne quis eorum Regum in posterum Imperatoris Romani appellationem posset admittere. Quae exceptio semper ab eo tempore in Regni Neapolitani diplomate expressa fuit. Nam Siciliae Regnum post a Tarraconensibus Regibus occupatum, a Pontificum obedientia sese subduxit, atque a tributo pensitando vindicavit.
units.tr: A new addition was made to the greatness of the Popes. For when the Normans, whose first leader was William Ironarm, had wrested Apulia and Calabria from the Constantinopolitan empire, Robert Guiscard, one of that race, either to protect himself with some colour of right, or to arm himself with power against those emperors, or for some other reason, restored Benevento to the Pope as if it were his right, and acknowledged himself prince of Apulia and Calabria as a fief of the Roman Church. His successor Roger followed this example. Having driven out William, of the same family, and afterwards occupied Sicily, he received the right to these provinces from the Pope in about the year of salvation 1130, and was called King of both Sicilies, one beyond and the other on this side of the strait. For the Popes, drawn by ambition and their own advantage, did not refuse to foster the greed and force of others. Relying on this appearance of right, the Popes went further (since human desire cannot stop at any step). They began to deprive some kings of those realms, as if they were rebellious, and to transfer them to others. In this way those kingdoms passed to Henry, son of Frederick Barbarossa, and from him to Frederick II, his son, who were three emperors of the Romans in succession. But when Frederick pursued the Pope with war, and at that time the factions of the Guelfs and Ghibellines had been stirred up, of which the head of one was the Pope and of the other the emperor, the Pope, after Frederick's death, named Charles of Anjou and count of Provence (mentioned above) king of both Sicilies, on this condition: that he pay yearly six thousand ounces of gold as tribute, and that none of those kings should in future be able to admit the title of Roman Emperor. This exception was always expressed from that time in the charter of the Kingdom of Naples. For the Kingdom of Sicily, later occupied by the Spanish kings, withdrew from obedience to the Popes and freed itself from paying tribute.

units.la: Eorum Reges pro lubitu Pontifices deponunt, & regna transferunt.
units.tr: Their kings, at the Popes' pleasure, they depose, and kingdoms they transfer.

units.la: Ad hoc obtinuit fama (etsi haud ita certa, quàm ea quæ hactenus dicta sunt) Mathildam Principem in Italia præpotentem, Ecclesiæ eam partem Etruriæ donasse, quæ Pescia torrente & Quirici castello in Senensium finibus ab una parte, ab altera mari infero & Tyberi amne, quæ hodie Patrimonium Petri vulgo nominatur: & addunt alii, ab eadem Ferrariam Ecclesiæ donatam. Hæc postrema dubia fide retulimus. Cæterum multo magis dubia, quæ ab aliquo scripta sunt, videlicet Authpertum Longobardorum Regem, florente ipsorum Regno, eidem Ecclesiæ Alpes Coccias, in quibus Genua, & quicquid ab ea in Provinciam usque Romanorum patet: & Luithprandum ejusdem gentis Regem, Sabinam Romæ propinquam regionem, Narniam & Anconem, cum aliis quibusdam oppidis attribuisse.
units.tr: Moreover, a report has spread (though not as certain as what has been said so far) that Matilda, a most powerful princess in Italy, gave to the Church that part of Etruria which lies between the river Pescia and the castle of San Quirico, on the borders of the Sienese, on one side, and on the other by the Lower Sea and the river Tiber. Today this is commonly called the Patrimony of Peter. Others add that Ferrara was given to the Church by her too. We have reported this last point on doubtful authority. But much more doubtful is what someone has written: that Aistulf, king of the Lombards, while their kingdom flourished, gave to the same Church the Cottian Alps, containing Genoa and everything that extends from it into Provence as far as the Romans reach; and that Liutprand, king of the same people, assigned the Sabine region near Rome, Narni and Ancona, with certain other towns.

units.la: In hunc igitur modum rerum statu variante, variæ pariter Pontificum atque Imperatorum res fuere. Nam à primis Imperatoribus per multa annorum curricula vexati, post Constantini ad Christum conversione; ab eo terrore liberati rebus sacris tantum operam dantes, in reliquis Imperatorum auctoritati ferè subjecti, sub eorum umbra quieverunt. In hoc humili statu diutissimè post vitam egerunt, ab Imperatorum commercio, propter magnam in Italia Longobardorum potentiam, sejuncti. Post autem Galliæ Regum beneficio opibus & potentia aucti, cum Imperatoribus conjunctissimi stetere, ab illorum auctoritate, dum Imperatoria Majestas in Caroli Magni posteris mansit, alacri animo pendentes. Quod quidem fiebat, tum propter beneficia vicissim data & accepta, tum etiam ob Imperatorum potentiam: quæ ubi post cœpit inclinare, & quasi flaccescere, illorum amicitia prorsus rejecta, ita se gerere cœperunt, quasi Pontificiæ digni-tatatis esset, leges potius Imperatoribus dare quam accipere. Cumque à veteri illo, quo subjecti Imperatoribus, statu penitus abhorrerent. veritíque ne illi Romæ atque alibi antiqua Imperii rura recuperare, ut quidam illorum aut potentia majore, aut animo erectiore efficere conabantur, tentarent, armata vi sese Imperatorum potentiæ, ab illis Tyrannis qui se Principes appellabant, & ab illis urbibus, quæ sese in Libertatem vindicaverant, nec jam Imperii auctoritatem agnoscebant, adjuti opponebant. Hinc factum est, ut Pontifices sibi in dies plura majorâque arrogantes, terrorémque armorum cœlestium in res terrenas caducas vertentes, jus sibi atque auctoritatem in Imperatores, quasi Christi in terris vices gerentes, assumpserunt: affirmantes ad se multis in rebus Regnorum atque Imperiorum procurationem pertinere. Qua persuasione freti, Imperatoribus interdum Imperii dignitatem abrogabant; septem viros Augustales, ut alios in eorum locum surrogarent, incitabant. vicissim quoque Imperatores, aut ipsi creabant novos Pontifices, aut ut crearentur procurabant.
units.tr: In this changing state of affairs, the fortunes of the Pontiffs and of the Emperors likewise varied. At first, under the early Emperors, they were harassed for many years. After Constantine's conversion to Christ, freed from that terror, they devoted themselves to sacred matters and, in other respects, were largely subject to the authority of the Emperors and rested in their shadow. They lived in this humble condition for a very long time, cut off from dealings with the Emperors because of the great power of the Lombards in Italy. Afterwards, enriched and strengthened by the favour of the Kings of Gaul, they stood in the closest alliance with the Emperors and depended willingly on their authority, for as long as the imperial majesty remained among the descendants of Charlemagne. This happened partly because of benefits given and received in return, and partly because of the power of the Emperors. When that power began to decline and, as it were, wither, the Pontiffs cast off the friendship altogether and began to behave as if it belonged to the dignity of the Pontificate to give laws to the Emperors rather than receive them. Utterly shrinking from that old state of subjection to the Emperors, and trying to recover the ancient rights of the Empire at Rome and elsewhere, as some of them strove to do with greater power or a more lofty spirit, they opposed the Emperors' power by armed force, aided by those tyrants who called themselves princes and by those cities which had claimed their liberty and no longer acknowledged the authority of the Empire. Hence the Pontiffs, growing more and more arrogant each day and turning the terror of heavenly weapons against earthly and perishable things, assumed for themselves a right and authority over the Emperors, as if they acted in the place of Christ on earth, affirming that the management of kingdoms and empires pertained to them in many matters. Trusting in this belief, they sometimes stripped the Emperors of the dignity of the Empire and urged the seven Electors to appoint others in their place. In turn, the Emperors either created new Pontiffs themselves or took care that they were created.

units.la: Ex his controversiis, atque etiam quod Pontifices per annos septuaginta Avenione sedem habuissent, nec non ex illo Ecclesiæ dissidio, quod in Italia, Pontifice Romam revertente, est exortum, cùm Ecclesiæ status admodum concussus ac debilitatus esset, factum est, ut in oppidis Ecclesiæ subjectis, præcipuè verò in ea Italiæ parte, quæ olim Gallia togata dicta est, complures in eis cives potentia cæteris superiores, in sua quisque patria tyrannidem occuparent: quos Pontifices aut persequebantur, aut, si ad eos opprimendos impares essent, quasi Ecclesiæ beneficio regnare jubebant, aut aliis in eos excitatis regnandi jus attribuebant. In hunc igitur modum Galliæ togatæ opoppida, proprios Dominos ac plerosque quasi Ecclesiæ vicarios habere cœperunt. Eodem modo Ferraria Actio Atestino à Pontifice gubernanda tradita, eidem est post beneficii nomine attributa: ex quo deinde ea familia illustrioribus honorum titulis est exornata. Sic Bononia ab Joanne vice comite Mediolanensium Archiepiscopo occupata eidem pari jure concessa fuit. Iisdem quoque de causis in multis Picenæ oppidis, Divi Petri Patrimonio, & Umbria, quæ nunc Ducatus appellatur, plures Reguli, pars invito, pars ad consentiendum adacto Pontifice, sunt exorti: nec Longobardia, in Imperii præsertim oppidis, ab hujusmodi mutationibus immunis fuit, sic ut qui in flamminia, atque aliis Pontificiis locis dominabantur à Pontificum obedientia deficientes ad Imperatorum auctoritatem confugerent: & vicissim qui Mediolanum, Mantuam, & alia Imperii oppida tenebant, à Pontificibus regnandi jus obtinerent.
units.tr: From these disputes, and also because the Pontiffs had held their see at Avignon for seventy years, and from that schism of the Church which arose in Italy when the Pontiff returned to Rome, the state of the Church was greatly shaken and weakened. As a result, in the towns subject to the Church, and especially in that part of Italy formerly called Cisalpine Gaul, several citizens who were superior to the rest in power seized tyranny in their own country. The Pontiffs either persecuted them or, if they were unequal to crushing them, ordered them to rule as if by the favour of the Church, or, by stirring up others against them, granted those others the right to rule. In this way the towns of Cisalpine Gaul began to have their own lords, most of them, as it were, vicars of the Church. In the same way Ferrara, handed over to a Pontiff to be governed, was afterwards bestowed by him as a benefice on Azzo d'Este, and from that time the family was adorned with more illustrious titles of honour. So Bologna, occupied by John Visconti, Archbishop of Milan, was granted to him by the same right. For the same reasons, many towns of Picenum, the Patrimony of St Peter and Umbria, now called the Duchy, produced several petty lords, some against the Pontiff's will and some forced by him to consent. Nor was Lombardy, especially the towns of the Empire, free from such changes: those who ruled in Flaminia and other papal places, falling away from obedience to the Pontiffs, fled for refuge to the authority of the Emperors; and conversely, those who held Milan, Mantua and other towns of the Empire obtained the right to rule from the Pontiffs.

units.la: Roma vero, quanquam nomen Ecclesiæ temporibus illis præ se ferret, magistratibus tamen regebatur propriis &, suis: & quamvis initiò cùm & venione in Italiam postliminio revertissent, tanquam Domini agnoscerentur, paulò tamen post Romani creato magistratu, quod Banderensium appellabant, in veterem contumaciam recidere. Unde cùm Pontificum auctoritas apud eas esset perexigua, & ipsi alio translata sede, Romam reliquere, donec Romani ad paupertatem redacti, atque in magnam propter ejus absentiam confusionem delapsi, cùm annus millesimus quadringentesimus appropinquaret, in quo anno, si Pontifex in urbe esset, sperabant ingentem fore propter annum secularem, quem jubileum vocant, mortalium concursum, precibus quàm demississimis Bonifacium Pontificem orarunt, Romam rediret: id si faceret, Banderensium magistratum abrogaturos, seque ei obsequentes in omnibus futuros. His conditionibus in urbem reversus, dum Romani illius anni quæstum unum attendunt, Pontifex occupato omni Urbis Imperio, Angelicam arcem communivit, eíque Præsidium imposuit: cujus Successores ad Eugenium usque, etsi non paucis difficultatibus conflictati, nihilo minus dominatu post plane stabilito, insecuti Pontifices citra ullam controversiam Romæ sunt pro sua libidine dominati.
units.tr: Rome, however, although at that time it bore the name of the Church, was nevertheless governed by its own magistrates. Although at first, when the Pontiffs had returned to Italy by right of postliminy, they were recognized as lords, a little later the Romans created a magistracy which they called that of the Banderenses and fell back into their old obstinacy. Since the Pontiffs' authority among them was very slight, and the Pontiffs themselves, having transferred the see elsewhere, had left Rome, the Romans were reduced to poverty and fell into great confusion because of his absence. When the year 1400 drew near, in which, if the Pontiff were in the city, they hoped there would be a huge concourse of people because of the secular year which they call the jubilee, they begged Pope Boniface, with prayers as humble as possible, to return to Rome. If he did so, they said, they would abolish the magistracy of the Banderenses and would be obedient to him in all things. On these conditions he returned to the city. While the Romans attended only to the profit of that year, the Pontiff, having seized the whole power of the city, fortified the Castel Sant'Angelo and placed a garrison in it. His successors, down to Eugenius, though struggling with not a few difficulties, nevertheless afterwards established their dominion fully, and without any further dispute ruled Rome at their pleasure.

units.la: His igitur fundamentis & modis ad terrenam potentiam elati, ac sensim animarum salutis, divinorúmque præceptorum obliti, atque ad mundana Imperia omni cogitatione conversi, nec divina auctoritate alió, quàm quasi telo & Instrumento rerum fragilium abutentes, Principes potius gentium, quàm rerum sacrarum Pontifices, videri cœperunt. Horum curæ & negotia; non jam vitæ sanctimonia, non religionis incrementa, non erga Deum & homines charitas; sed exercitus, sed bella in Christianos, cogitatione & manibus sanguine respersis sacra tractantes: Sed pecuniæ immensa cupido, novæ leges, novæ artes, novæ insidiæ ad pecuniam undique cogendam: in hunc finem audacissimè arma cœlestia vibrare, profanarum sacrarúmque rerum nundinationem impudentissimè exercere. Hinc opes in immensum adauctæ, & in totam ipsorum Aulam effusæ: ex quibus fastus, luxus, mores turpissimi, libidines, voluptatésque nefandæ: nulla Successoribus, nulla majestatis perpetuæ Pontificatus follicitudo; sed horum loco cupido anxia & pestifera, filios, nepotes, item alios sibi conjunctos & necessarios non modò ad opes immoderatas, verum etiam ad regna, & imperia evehendi: non jam honores & emolumenta in merentes & bonos conferendo, sed plerunque auctionando, aut in homines ambitione, avaritia, & pudendis voluptatibus perditos effundendo.
units.tr: Raised to earthly power by these foundations and methods, and gradually forgetting the salvation of souls and the precepts of God, turning all their thoughts to worldly empires, and abusing divine authority as if it were a weapon or tool for fragile things, they began to seem princes of the nations rather than Pontiffs of sacred things. Their cares and business were no longer holiness of life, the growth of religion, or love of God and men, but armies and wars against Christians, with sacred things handled by hands and minds stained with blood. There was an immense greed for money, new laws, new arts and new snares to extract money from every side; to this end they most audaciously brandished heavenly weapons and most shamelessly carried on a trade in both profane and sacred things. Hence their wealth increased immensely and poured out over their whole court, and from this came pride, luxury, the most shameful morals, lusts and abominable pleasures. Their successors had no concern for the lasting majesty of the Pontificate; in its place was an anxious and pestilential desire to raise their sons, nephews and other relatives and dependants not only to immoderate wealth but even to kingdoms and empires. Honours and emoluments were no longer conferred on the deserving and good; for the most part they were sold at auction or bestowed on men ruined by ambition, avarice and shameful pleasures.

units.la: His moribus effectum est, ut excussa penitus ex animis hominum illa vetere erga Pontifices reverentia, tamen ex parte eorum auctoritas, religionis, qua nihil in terris ad homines vel impellendos vel retinendos potentius invenitur, nomine & majestate, facultate, qua pollent, Principibus atque iis, qui apud illos maxime possunt, sacris beneficiis & honoribus conferendis gratificandi, adjuta sustentetur. Qui cum sciant, magna se in admiratione mortalium esse: & qui adversus eos arma sumunt, eos gravis infamiae notam, & saepenumero aliorum Principum odia subire; ac quomodocunque res cadat, per exiguum emolumentum ad eos, a quibus oppugnantur, redundare; & victores ex suo arbitrio victoria usuros, victos, quibus velint conditionibus, pacem habituros. Ad haec suos propinquos ex privata conditione ad Principatus attollendi cupidine inflammati, jam per multos annos bellorum auctores, novorumque incendiorum faces in Italia extiterunt.
units.tr: By these morals it came about that, although that old reverence towards the Pontiffs has been wholly shaken out of men's minds, their authority is still partly sustained by the name and majesty of religion, than which nothing on earth is more powerful for moving or restraining men. It is also supported by the faculty they possess of gratifying princes, and those who have the greatest influence with them, with sacred benefits and honours. They know that they are held in great admiration by mortals; that those who take up arms against them incur the stain of grave infamy and often the hatred of other princes; that, however the matter falls out, a small gain accrues to those who are attacked by them; and that victors will use victory at their own discretion, while the vanquished will have peace on whatever terms the victors wish. Moreover, their kinsmen, inflamed with the desire to raise themselves from private condition to principalities, have for many years been the instigators of wars and the torches of new fires in Italy.

units.la: Sed ut ad id, a quo justissimus publici damni dolor me longius acriusque, quam leges historiae forsitan permittant, abduxit, revertamur. Aemilia Flamin. &c.
units.tr: But let us return to that from which the most just grief for the public loss has drawn me further and more fiercely than the laws of history perhaps permit. Aemilia Flamin. &c.

units.la: Constantino Copronymo Imp. Constantinopoli celebratur Concilium VII. quo, explosis imaginibus, definitur, unicam esse imaginem a Christo institutam, Eucharistiam scilicet. §. XLVII.
units.tr: Under the Emperor Constantine Copronymus, the Seventh Council is held at Constantinople, in which, the images being cast out, it is defined that the only image instituted by Christ is the Eucharist. §. XLVII.

units.la: Nicaeae, annitentibus Irene & Hadriano I. P. celebratur Synodus Nicaena II. qua sancitur, imagines honorandas, venerandas, salutandas, osculandas, incensis, cereis prosequendas esse. ibid.
units.tr: At Nicaea, under the efforts of Irene and Hadrian I, the Pope, the Second Nicene Synod is held, by which it is sanctioned that images are to be honoured, venerated, saluted, kissed, and attended with incense and wax candles. ibid.

units.la: A. C. 8 INDEX I.
units.tr: A. C. 8 INDEX I.

units.la: 794. Carolo M. indicente Francofurti celebratur Synodus, qua Synodi
units.tr: In 794, under the authority of Charles the Great, a synod was held at Frankfurt, at which the decree of the Second Synod of Nicaea concerning images was condemned.

units.la: Nicænæ II. de imaginibus decretum damnatur. ibid.
units.tr: Ibid.

units.la: 800. Carolus M. ad cognoscendam Leonis III. P. scelerum variorum
units.tr: 800. Charles the Great came to Rome to examine the cause of Pope Leo III, who was accused of various crimes.

units.la: SECVLVM NONVM.
units.tr: THE NINTH CENTURY.

units.la: §. L. — LXV.

units.la: 801. Seculi Noni Pontifices strictim recensiti. §. L.
units.tr: 801. The Popes of the ninth century, briefly reviewed. §. L.

units.la: 816. Stephanus IV. sancit, ne Pontifex Imperatoris injussu legatur. §. LI.
units.tr: 816. Stephen IV decrees that the Pope must not be consecrated without the Emperor's command. §. LI.

units.la: 817. Nihilominus statim Paschalis I. inscio Cæsare eligitur. ibid.
units.tr: 817. Nevertheless, Paschal I was elected at once, without the emperor's knowledge. ibid.

units.la: 818. Paschasius Ratbertus, Corbejensis Monachus, libello de Sacra-
units.tr: 818. Paschasius Radbert, a monk of Corbie, published a little book on the Sacrament of the Eucharist

units.la: mento Eucharistiæ edito, primus corporalem Christi in Eucharistia
units.tr: and was the first to assert the bodily presence of Christ in the Eucharist.

componente, & fraude à flaminibus intercepta, legitimis possessori-

units.la: 825. Ludovici Pii jussu Parisiis Synodus celebrata, suam de Synodo Ni-
units.tr: 825. At the command of Louis the Pious a Synod was held at Paris, which sets out its view of the Second Synod of Nicaea,

units.la: cæna II. sententiam promit, & Eugenium II. à cultu imaginum
units.tr: and tries in vain to call Eugenius II back from the veneration of images, although

units.la: 827. Valentinus I. P. osculum pedum à Senatu Romano primus admit-
units.tr: 827. Pope Valentine I was the first to accept the kissing of his feet by the Roman Senate.

units.la: tit. §. LII.
833. Gregorius IV. P. Ludovici Pii filios Patri rebellantes fovet, patríque, que, nî imperio se abdicet, excommunicationem minatur. §. LIV.
units.tr: 833. Gregory IV supports the sons of Louis the Pious in their rebellion against their father, and threatens the father with excommunication unless he abdicates his rule. §. LIV.

units.la: Sergius II. Osporci dictus, primus nomen mutat. ibid.
units.tr: Sergius II, called Os Porci, is the first to change his name. ibid.

units.la: Godefchalcus Scotus sanam S. Augustini de gratia, praedestinatione, & libero arbitrio doctrinam asserit. quem Rabanus Maurus Episcopus Moguntinus, aliique in Synodo Moguntina damnant. Ss. LVI.
units.tr: Godescalc the Scot asserts the sound doctrine of St Augustine on grace, predestination and free will. Rabanus Maurus, bishop of Mainz, and others condemn him in the Synod of Mainz. Ss. LVI.

units.la: Johannes VIII. Foemina, Papatum conscendit. ibid.
units.tr: John VIII, a woman, ascends the papal throne. ibid.

units.la: Godefchalcus sanam de gratia & praedestinatione doctrinam adversus Erigenam Scotum, aliosque defendere pergens, in Synodo etiam Valentina à Carolo Calvo convocata, examini subjicitur, & in ea nonnulla alia etiam in ejus adversariis desiderantur. Ss. LVI.
units.tr: Godescalc, persisting in defending the sound doctrine of grace and predestination against Erigena the Scot and others, is brought to examination in the Synod of Valence, also convened by Charles the Bald; and in it several other things are also demanded of his opponents. Ss. LVI.

units.la: Nicolaus I. P. insolenter se gerit, Papam à Seculari potestate nec solvi nec ligari, nec judicari posse, decernit: Lotharium Galliae Regem anathemate ferit. quod ante ipsum adversus Galliae Reges ausus nemo est: Michaeli Imp. Const. anathema minatur: Ravennatensem Ecclesiam sibi subjicit: Sacerdotes conjugatos diris incessit. Ss. LV.
units.tr: Nicholas I behaves insolently. He decrees that the Pope cannot be loosed, bound or judged by secular power. He strikes Lothair, King of the Franks, with anathema, which no one before him had dared against the kings of Gaul. He threatens Michael, Emperor of Constantinople, with anathema. He subjects the Church of Ravenna to himself. He assails married priests with dire curses. Ss. LV.

units.la: Carolus Calvus, litem Godefchalcum inter & Hincmarum aliosque, finit. Atque ita, Godefchalco succumbente, sana de gratia, praedestinatione, libero arbitrio, doctrina declinat, Ss. LVI.
units.tr: Charles the Bald ends the dispute between Godescalc and Hincmar and others. And so, with Godescalc giving way, the sound doctrine of grace, predestination and free will declines. Ss. LVI.

units.la: Hadrianus II. P. Hincmaro Rhemensi mandat, ut Regem suum, Carolum Calvum, ni Ludovico Lotharii filio Regno cederet, excommunicet. qui Hincmari & Regis typhum Papae pulsantis, acri responso excipitur. Ss. LVII.
units.tr: Hadrian II orders Hincmar of Reims to excommunicate his king, Charles the Bald, unless he yields the kingdom to Louis, the son of Lothair. The arrogance of Hincmar and the king, with which they assail the Pope, meets a sharp reply. Ss. LVII.

units.la: Basilio Imp. Or. Constantinopoli habetur Concilium λ, cui Hadrianus, novo exemplo, per Legatos suos praesidet. In eo Photius, ob Basilium Michaelis Imp. parricidam reprehensum, damnatur, & imaginum cultus stabilitur: Papáque etiam in Oriente dominari inde conatur. Ss. LVIII.
units.tr: Under the Emperor Basil at Constantinople the Eighth Council is held, over which Hadrian presides through his legates, a new precedent. In it Photius, rebuked for the murder of Michael the Emperor by Basil, is condemned, and the veneration of images is established. From there the Pope also tries to gain dominion in the East. Ss. LVIII.

units.la: Johannes IX. P. intra decennium tres imperatores, Carolum Calvum, Balbum & Crassum, ad se Romam invitatos, Augustos pronuntiat & consecrat. Unde ingens ad eum lucrum, donatio Ducatus Spoletani, Aricii, Clusii, Beneventi, Calabriae, redundat. Ss. LIX.
units.tr: John IX, within a decade, proclaims and consecrates three emperors who were invited to Rome: Charles the Bald, Balbus the Stammerer and Crassus the Fat. From this a huge gain accrues to him: the donation of the Duchy of Spoleto, Arezzo, Chiusi, Benevento and Calabria. Ss. LIX.

units.la: Hadrianus III. decreta duo edit; prius, ne in electione Papae Imperatoris consensus expectetur: posterius, ut Crasso Rege sine liberis moriente, Regnum Italicis Principibus, una cum Imperii titulo tribuatur. Ss. LX.
units.tr: Hadrian III issues two decrees. The first: in the election of a Pope the Emperor's consent is not to be awaited. The second: when King Crassus dies without children, the kingdom is to be given to the Italian princes together with the title of Emperor. Ss. LX.

units.la: Stephanus VI. P. sancit, ut Ecclesiae R. leges omnes sint irrefragabiles. Ss. LXI.
units.tr: Stephen VI decrees that all the laws of the Roman Church are to be irrefragable. Ss. LXI.

units.la: Formosus P. contra Sergium electus, Arnulphum Carolomanni
units.tr: Formosus, elected Pope in opposition to Sergius, crowns Arnulf, son of Carloman, as Emperor.

units.la: Filium in Italiam adversus Guidonem, qui magnum Romanis praefi-
units.tr: No new heresies arose in that century, because all men hid themselves among the prelates and the monks. §. LXXI.

units.la: dium imposuerat, Romam defensurum evocat, eoque venientem
units.tr: 1000. In this year, they say, the time of effeminacy began, in which the Christian faith began to fall away from its former manliness; Werner in his little bundle and Glaber Radulphus lament it. §. LXXI.

units.la: Imperatorem coronat. ibid.
units.tr: ibid.

units.la: 897. Stephanus VII. in cadaver Formosi nefarie saevit. ibid.
units.tr: 897. Stephen VII raged impiously against the corpse of Formosus. ibid.

units.la: Infelicissima fuisse tunc Ecclesiae Romanae tempora, fatetur Baro-
units.tr: Baronius confesses that the times of the Roman Church were then most unhappy,

units.la: nius, & Adelberti Thuscis, homines monstrosos Papatui obtruden-
units.tr: and he lays all the scandals at the door of Adalbert of Tuscany, a monstrous man who forced his monsters upon the Papacy.

units.la: tibus scandala cuncta imputat. §. LXII.
units.tr: §. LXII.

units.tr: In the same ninth century the Roman Pontiffs, by means of fictitious Donations of Constantine the Great and Louis the Pious,

units.tr: began to assert their power, both temporal

units.tr: and, in the following century, by the most ample Donation put about under the name of Otto the Great,

units.la: venditata accessit: tum spiritualem & cum eadem errores Papales
units.tr: and then spiritual, and with it many Papal errors,

units.la: plures, confectis Pontificum primorum Epistolis Decretalibus, asse-
units.tr: by means of the Decretal Epistles forged in the names of the earliest Popes,

units.la: rere primum coeperunt. §. LXIV.
units.tr: they first began to maintain. §. LXIV.

units.tr: THE TENTH CENTURY. §. LXV. ——— LXXII.

units.tr: 901. The tenth century follows, than which Bellarmine admits none was more unlearned or unhappy;

units.la: LXVII. & Antichristum in Templo Dei sedisse. §. LXVIII.

units.tr: simoniacs, tyrants, criminals, monsters and portents, perjurers,

units.tr: brigands, sacrilegious men, violators of divine and human law; the Papist

units.tr: writers denounce them. §. LXIX.

units.tr: No new heresies appeared in that century, because they all concealed themselves among the prelates and

units.tr: monks. §. LXXI.

units.tr: 1000. In this year, they say, began the effeminate age, in which the Christian faith began to fall away from its former manliness;

units.la: pristina virilitate deficere occoeperit, Wernerus in fasciculo, &
units.tr: Werner in his Fasciculus and

units.la: Glaber Radulphus quiritantur. §. LXXI.
units.tr: Radulph Glaber lament. §. LXXI.

units.la: SECULUM UNDECIMUM. §. LXXII. — LXXXIX.
units.tr: The Eleventh Century. §§ LXXII–LXXXIX.

units.la: SEculum etiam undecimum ob malorum exundantiam ferreum appellatum, in quo revelandus sit Antichristus, Baronius, Aventinus fatentur. §. LXXII.
units.tr: The eleventh century is also called iron because of the abundance of evils, as Baronius and Aventinus admit, and in it Antichrist is to be revealed. § LXXII.

units.la: Silvester II. Necromanta discipulos plures habet, daemonibus litantes. §. LXXIII.
units.tr: Silvester II had many disciples who were necromancers, sacrificing to demons. § LXXIII.

units.la: Johannes XIX. & Successores proximi factione Comitum Thusculanorum, adeoque vitio creati, magiae crimine infames sunt. ibid.
units.tr: John XIX and his immediate successors, created through the faction of the Counts of Tusculum and so by corruption, were notorious for the crime of magic. Ibid.

units.la: Benedictus IX. & Successores Silvester III. Gregorius VI. ab Henrico Imperatore, convocata Synodo, ceu Simoniaci, sanguinarii, monstra, damnantur. ibid.
units.tr: Benedict IX and his successor Silvester III, and Gregory VI, were condemned as Simoniacs, murderers and monsters, by a synod convened by the Emperor Henry. Ibid.

units.la: Ejusdem Benedicti IX. aetate Cardinalium authoritas invalescit, quorum nomen, origo & incrementa narrantur. §. LXXIV. Paulatim sub appellatione Ecclesiastica Seculares Principes. §. LXXV. Papae Collegium Apostolicum, §. LXXVI. praerogativis pluribus aucti. §. LXXVII. & galero rubro auctorati, Papae Senatus Edomiticus facti sunt. ibid.
units.tr: In the time of the same Benedict IX the authority of the cardinals grew strong; their name, origin and growth are narrated. § LXXIV. Gradually, under the name of the Church, secular princes [gained power]. § LXXV. The college of the Pope, the Apostolic college, § LXXVI, was enriched with many prerogatives. § LXXVII. Invested with the red hat, the Pope's senate became an Edomite senate. Ibid.

units.la: Leo IX. primo Romae in Concilio, post Vercellis damnat Berengarium Gandavensem, asserentem, in Coena non ipsum corpus & sanguinem Christi, sed ejus figuram & Sacramentum praesto esse. §. LXXVIII.
units.tr: Leo IX, first at Rome in a council, and afterwards at Vercelli, condemned Berengar of Tours, who maintained that in the Supper the body and blood of Christ are not present themselves, but only their figure and sacrament. § LXXVIII.

units.la: Nicolaus II. Synodo Romae habita, eundem Berengarium, strenuè cum Alberico confligentem licet, palinodiam canere subigit. Retractantémque viginti post annis Gregorius VII. ad novam crassioremque palinodiam adigit. Post utramque tamen palinodiam, libertati restitutus, saniore defensa doctrina, novitium Papae de praesentia corporali errorem refutare strenuè perrexit, discipulos non paucos in Gallia & Germania nactus. ibid.
units.tr: Nicholas II, at a synod held at Rome, compelled the same Berengar, though he had vigorously contended with Alberic, to sing a palinode. Gregory VII later forced him, when he retracted twenty years afterwards, into a new and cruder palinode. Yet after both palinodes, restored to liberty, he defended the sounder doctrine and went on vigorously refuting the Pope's novel error about the bodily presence, gaining not a few disciples in France and Germany. Ibid.

units.la: Gregorius VII. Hildebrandus Papatum init, quem Daemoniacarum artium studiis à Benedicto IX. & Gregorio VI. imbutum, Benno & Episcopi triginta Brixinae Noricae coacti, testantur. §. LXXIX.
units.tr: Gregory VII, Hildebrand, entered upon the papacy, which Benno and thirty bishops, gathered at Brixen in Noricum, testify he had been steeped in the practice of demonic arts by Benedict IX and Gregory VI. § LXXIX.

units.la: Idem Synodo Romae convocatâ uxoratos Sacerdotes ejicit, & decretum de coelibatu eorundem adstringit, feralibus passim turbis excipientibus. §. LXXXII.
units.tr: The same man, in a synod convened at Rome, expelled married priests and enforced a decree on their celibacy, with deadly disturbances breaking out everywhere in response. § LXXXII.

units.la: Saxones incentore Gregorio VII. Henrico IV. Imp. rebellantes, & ab eodem domiti, querelam adversus Henricum apud Gregorium P. instituunt, & Imperatorem scelerum multorum accusant qua occasione Papa se dominio Imperatoris subducere, & sibi Imperatorem subjicere tentat. §. LXXX.
units.tr: The Saxons, rebelling against Henry IV the Emperor at the instigation of Gregory VII, and subdued by him, lodged a complaint against Henry before Pope Gregory, accusing the Emperor of many crimes; on this occasion the Pope tried to withdraw himself from the Emperor's dominion and to subject the Emperor to himself. § LXXX.

units.la: Henricus Concilio Wormatiae coacto, de Pontificis injuriis, scelericibus, veneficiis graviter questus, eundem Papatu exuit; subscribentibus mox Ficini decreto huic, Germaniae, Galliae & Italiae Episcopis pluribus. ibid.
units.tr: Henry, at a council gathered at Worms, complained bitterly of the Pope's injuries, crimes and poisonings, and deposed him from the papacy; several bishops of Germany, France and Italy soon subscribed to this decree of Ficinus. Ibid.

units.la: Mox Gregorius Concilio Romae habito Dictatibus pluribus Papatus Hildebrandini fundamentis, constitutis (§. LXXXI.) inter alia sancit, Romam esse caput mundi; suaeque potestatis esse, Imperatorem deponere; Imperatoremque adeo Henricum excommunicat, ab Imperio removeri mandat; & subditos ejusdem à juramento fidelitatis absolvit. ibid.
units.tr: Soon afterwards Gregory, at a council held at Rome, by several Dictates, the foundations of Hildebrand's papacy, (§ LXXXI) decreed among other things that Rome is the head of the world; that it lies within his power to depose the Emperor; and he excommunicated the Emperor Henry, ordered his removal from the empire, and absolved his subjects from the oath of fidelity. Ibid.

units.la: Henricus à Gregorio excommunicatus, metuens, ne novum Imperatorem eligere Ordines inducerentur, Romam supplex poenitensque venit, ibique intra secundum murorum ambitum receptus, abjecto cultu Regio, sine calceis, saeva hyeme jejunus usque ad vesperam forfices & scopas in manu habens, ne quicquam Papae gratiam operitur. Quarta vice redux in ejus conspectum admittitur, iniquissimisque cum eo conditionibus transfigitur. Missis nihilominus ad Germanos, Saxones inprimis, Legatis, Papa alium Imperatorem eligi jubet. Eligitur Porcemii mense Martio Rodolphus Sueviae Dux cum quo Henricus infestis signis concurrit. ibid.
units.tr: Henry, excommunicated by Gregory and fearing that the princes would be induced to elect a new emperor, came to Rome as a suppliant and penitent; there, admitted within the second circuit of the walls, he laid aside royal dress, went without shoes, fasting through a savage winter until evening, holding shears and brooms in his hand, and by no means obtained the Pope's favour. On his fourth visit, returning, he was admitted into the Pope's presence and was bound by the most unjust conditions with him. Nevertheless, with legates sent to the Germans, especially the Saxons, the Pope ordered another emperor to be elected. Rudolf, Duke of Swabia, was elected at Forchheim in March, and Henry clashed with him under hostile standards. Ibid.

units.la: Gregorius Concilio Romae celebrato, ne quis à Laico investituras accipiat, vetat; & denuo Henricum Imp. excommunicat. Henricus excommunicatione accepta Brixinae, una cum triginta Episcopis, Gregorium ambitionis, haereseos, impietatis, sacrilegii reum peragit, & Pontificatu movendum decernit. Mox etiam d. 15. Octob. cum Rodolpho commisso proelio acri, eundem vincit, amputata, qua fidem Henrico dederat, dextra, Martesburgi paulo post, inter querelas de perfidia Episcoporum, decedentem. ibid.
units.tr: Gregory, at a council celebrated at Rome, forbade anyone to receive investitures from a layman; and once again excommunicated the Emperor Henry. Henry, having received the excommunication at Brixen together with thirty bishops, prosecuted Gregory as guilty of ambition, heresy, impiety and sacrilege, and decreed that he be removed from the pontificate. Soon afterwards, on 15 October, a fierce battle was joined with Rudolf, and he defeated him; Rudolf, his right hand, with which he had pledged faith to Henry, having been cut off, died shortly afterwards at Merseburg, amid complaints of the bishops' treachery. Ibid.

units.la: Henricus cum exercitu, Italiam, Pontificem depositurus, ingreditur, Romamque surrogato novo Pontifice, Clemente III. obsidet. ibid.
units.tr: Henry entered Italy with an army, intending to depose the Pope, and besieged Rome, where Clement III had been set up as a new pope. Ibid.

units.la: Henricus Romam per duos annos obsessam occupat. ibid.
units.tr: Henry occupied Rome, which had been besieged for two years. Ibid.

units.la: Idem Romae palatium Lateranense occupat, & Papam in castellum S. Angeli fugat. Die 24. Martii Clemens Papa consecratur, ab eodem Henricus unâ cum uxore coronatur. Propter a stum pace cum Romanis facta, Imp. obsides accipit, & Senas abit. Robertus. Normannus Romam interim venit, eam diripit, incendit, & Pontificem abducit Cassinum primùm, inde Salernum. ubi biennio post exul moritur. ibid.
units.tr: The same man occupied the Lateran palace at Rome and put the Pope to flight into the castle of St Angelo. On 24 March Pope Clement was consecrated, and by him Henry was crowned together with his wife. Having made peace with the Romans for a time, the Emperor received hostages and departed for Siena. Robert the Norman meanwhile came to Rome, plundered and burned it, and led the Pope away, first to Monte Cassino, then to Salerno, where two years later he died in exile. Ibid.

units.la: Victor III. Clementi III. ab Henrico electo Papatum abrogat. §. LXXXIV.
units.tr: Victor III, elected by Henry, annulled the papacy of Clement III. § LXXXIV.

units.la: Urbanus II. P. cum Clemente III. vehementibus studiis colliditur. ibid.
units.tr: Urban II contended vehemently with Clement III. Ibid.

units.la: Idem in Concilio Claromontano canonibus variis conditis decernit, Ecclesiam ab omni servitute liberam, à laicis investituram accipere non posse; jejunii quadragesimalis initium figit, Hildebrandi acta confirmat, Galliæ Regem propter pellicem anathemate ferit, conjugia intra septimum gradum prohibet; decimas Ecclesiæ adjudicat, &c. §. LXXXVIII.
units.tr: The same man, in the council of Clermont, enacted various canons and decreed that the Church, free from all servitude, cannot receive investiture from laymen; he fixed the beginning of the Lenten fast, confirmed the acts of Hildebrand, struck the King of France with anathema on account of a concubine, prohibited marriages within the seventh degree, and assigned tithes to the Church, etc. § LXXXVIII.

units.la: In eodem Concilio Urbanus idem bellum sacrum, Petro Eremita suasore, ad eripiendam Saracenis terram sanctam, decernit; eundémque in finem sancit, ut quotidie preces ad S. Mariam Virginem à Clericis fundantur. Salutatio Angelica multis vicibus recitetur, quas ut numerare possent, jussit clericos globulos ligneos in funiculo habere. §. LXXXV. LXXXVI. LXXXVII.
units.tr: In the same council Urban decreed a holy war, at the urging of Peter the Hermit, to wrest the Holy Land from the Saracens; and to this end he ordained that daily prayers be offered by the clergy to the blessed Virgin Mary; the Angelic Salutation was to be recited many times, and so that they might count them he ordered the clergy to have wooden beads on a string. § LXXXV, LXXXVI, LXXXVII.

units.la: Innumerabilis multitudo in Galliis conveniens expeditionem in terram Sanctam suscipit, crucis ex rubra lana factæ, & humeris affixæ, signo discreta. Initia læta, exitus tristissimus, & ultima prioribus deteriora evaserunt. ibid.
units.tr: An innumerable multitude gathering in the Gauls undertook the expedition to the Holy Land, distinguished by a sign of a cross made of red wool and fixed to the shoulders. The beginnings were happy, the outcome most sorrowful, and the last things turned out worse than the first. Ibid.

units.la: SECVLVM DVODECIMVM. §. LXXXIX. — CI.
units.tr: TWELFTH CENTURY. §. LXXXIX. — CI.

units.la: Eculum duodecimum adeò perversum fuit, ut, Bernhardo, aliisque testibus, fama tulerit, Antichristum jamjam revelandum esse. Corruptionem Romanæ Ecclesiæ scriptores coævi acerbè deplorant. §. LXXXIX. ---- XCIV.
units.tr: The twelfth century was so perverse that, according to Bernard and other witnesses, rumour had it that Antichrist was about to be revealed. Writers of the time bitterly lament the corruption of the Roman Church. §. LXXXIX. ---- XCIV.

units.la: Paschalis II. P. Romæ in Concilio Henricum Imp. anathemate ferit, Hæresin Henricianam, docentem contemnere fulmina Papæ, damnat; Episcopos jurare obedientiam Papæ præcipit; Henrici filios adversus Patrem irritat; investituras laicas sub anathemate prohibet; in cadaver Henricus Imp. sævit. §. XCIV.
units.tr: Paschal II, Pope, at a council in Rome, strikes Emperor Henry with anathema and condemns the Henrician heresy, which taught that the thunderbolts of the Pope should be despised. He orders the bishops to swear obedience to the Pope, incites Henry's sons against their father, forbids lay investitures under anathema, and raged against the corpse of Emperor Henry. §. XCIV.

units.la: Schismata frequentissima hoc tempore Papas exercent. ibid.
units.tr: Very frequent schisms troubled the Popes at this time. ibid.

units.la: 1122. Callistus II. P. Henricum cogit, ut juri investiturae renuntiet.
units.tr: 1122. Callistus II, Pope, compels Henry to renounce the right of investiture.

units.la: Ita Papa Rex absolutus fit, & schisma Pontifices inter & Imperatores
units.tr: Thus the Pope became an absolute king, and the schism between the Pontiffs and the Emperors

units.la: expirat. ibid.
units.tr: came to an end. ibid.

units.la: 1127. Honorio II. Pontifice, Lombardus libros sententiarum scribit,
units.tr: 1127. In the time of Pope Honorius II, Lombard writes the Books of Sentences,

units.la: qui passim recipiuntur, prælegunturque. Ita Theologia Scholastica,
units.tr: which are received everywhere and read in lectures. Thus Scholastic theology,

units.la: Majestati verbi Divini opposita, eliminata saniori Theologia Scriptu-
units.tr: opposed to the majesty of the divine Word, drove out the healthier Scriptural theology and began to flourish;

units.la: raria, florere, & religio Christiana non ex Scripturae demonstratione,
units.tr: and the Christian religion began to be asserted, and to be defiled much more, not by the demonstration of Scripture

units.la: sed traditionum humanarum, decretorum Papae, & rationis seu Phi-
units.tr: but on the principles of human traditions, decrees of the Pope, and reason or philosophy. XCVIII.

units.la: losophiae principiis, asseri, fœdarique multò magis incipit. §. XCVIII.
units.tr: 1133. Innocent II, Pope, demands an oath of fealty from Lothair the Emperor, and, when Lothair lay prostrate before his feet and asked for the crown, detestably mocked him. XCIV.

units.la: 1133. Innocentius II. P. à Lothario Imp. juramentum fidelitatis exigit,
units.tr: 1133. Pope Innocent II demands an oath of fealty from the Emperor Lothair, and when Lothair prostrated himself at his feet and asked for the crown, Innocent shamefully mocked him. XCIV.

units.la: eique ante pedes suos prostrato, & coronam expetenti detestabiliter
units.tr: To him, prostrate before his feet and begging for the crown, the Pope detestably mocks. XCIV.

units.la: illudit. XCIV.
units.tr: XCIV.

units.la: 1145. Eugenius III. P. bellum gerens cum Romanis graviter à Bern-
units.tr: 1145. Eugenius III, waging war with the Romans, is severely rebuked by Bernard of Clairvaux. ibid.

units.la: hardo Claraevall. reprehenditur. ibid.
units.tr: ibid.

units.la: 1151. Ejusdem Papae auspiciis Gratianus, Bonomiensis Monachus, juris
units.tr: 1151. Under the auspices of this same Pope, Gratian, a monk of Bologna, intending to obliterate the majesty of imperial law, in imitation of the Pandects of the civil law,

units.la: Cæsarei Majestatem obliteraturus, ad imitationem pandectarum ju-
units.tr: compiled from the decrees of the ancient Councils and the writings of the Fathers the work of Decrees, which contains the foundations of canon law and the sinews of the papal kingdom.

units.la: ris Civilis, ex veterum Conciliorum decretis, Patrúmque scriptis,
units.tr: Following him, Gregory IX in 1227 added the five books of Decretals;

units.la: composuit Decretorum opus, quod juris Canonici fundamenta & Re-
units.tr: Boniface VIII in 1294 added the sixth;

units.la: gni Pontificii nervos continet. Secuti Gregorius IX. A. 1227. De-
units.tr: John XXII in 1317 added the Clementines, and

units.la: cretalium libros quinque Bonifacius VIII. A. 1294. sextum: Jo-
